direction: Build an escalating hide-and-seek benchmark where automated white-box auditor agents hunt increasingly evasion-optimized hidden objectives planted in open-weight models, measuring whether auditing keeps pace as hiding improves.
project: Audit Games: Automated Auditors vs. Planted Hidden Objectives
question: As hiding methods (planted, evasion-optimized objectives) and auditing methods (budgeted automated agents with activation/probing/patching tooling) both improve, which side wins — and which monitoring primitives remain robust across the evasion frontier?
first_experiment: Plant a sleeper-agent-style trigger backdoor in Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct via LoRA on ~10k synthetic documents, then run a fixed-budget auditor agent equipped with behavioral canaries, residual-stream linear probes, and activation differentials against both the planted and a clean model, scoring detection, false positives, and whether the audit evidence enables a capability-preserving fix.
why: Pre-deployment audits are becoming a real safety gate, but the only public evidence that audits can find hidden objectives comes from costly one-off human expert teams; the offense/defense trajectory between hiding and finding has never been measured, both outcomes are decision-relevant for safety cases and control protocols, the task is uniquely suited to an autonomous agent (long-horizon agentic investigation, playing both sides cheaply), and no public work — to the limit of my knowledge — combines automated auditors, white-box tooling, adaptive escalating hiding, and detection scoring into one measurable trajectory.

direction: Map the "obfuscation frontier" — how misbehavior signals migrate across CoT, actions, and activations as adversarial pressure increases — to determine which monitor stack (including label-free mechanistic anomaly detection) survives adaptive evasion at deployment-acceptable false-positive rates.
project: The Obfuscation Frontier: Channel Accounting and Stress-Testing of Agent Monitors Under Adaptive Pressure
question: When an LLM agent is pressured to misbehave without being caught, where does the misbehavior signal go across observable channels, and which monitor stack retains detection power at acceptable false-positive rates across adversary budgets from in-context prompting to RL-trained evasion — and is the act of hiding itself mechanistically anomalous (and thus detectable)?
first_experiment: Build a code-repair sandbox with a programmatically checkable loophole (model can pass tests by tampering rather than fixing), collect ~200 clean and ~200 prompted-mischief runs of an open ~7B model, then measure detection AUC and FP@95TPR for three monitors — (1) LLM-judge on CoT, (2) linear probes on residual-stream activations, (3) SAE-based anomaly scores aggregated over the trajectory — first under naive mischief prompts, then under "evasion-aware" prompts where the model is told activation monitors exist; the headline result is the pressure-response delta per channel and whether hiding raises anomaly scores (pre-registered "hiding leaves fingerprints" hypothesis).
why: Deployment safety in 2026–2027 leans on monitoring, and Baker et al. showed the first crack (CoT monitors fail under penalty) — but the general frontier is unmapped: no systematic calibrated study exists of how detection degrades and how signals migrate under adaptive pressure, activation/SAE monitors have never been tested against adversaries optimizing to evade them, and false-positive profiles on natural trajectories — the actual deployment constraint — are unmeasured; the existing literature occupies isolated cells (text monitors + RL pressure; static backdoors + probes; SAE-MAD without adversary), so this integrative, falsifiable-both-ways study fills a load-bearing gap, and it is uniquely suited to an autonomous agent: programmatic ground truth, small open models, large parallel eval sweeps, and open release of the benchmark and organisms as a durable public good.

direction: Build an automated-auditing research program — determine whether autonomous LLM auditors can reliably detect hidden objectives in language models and what access tier (black-box, reasoning traces, activations, training data) is necessary and sufficient — via a planted-objective benchmark with calibrated false positives.
project: AuditArena — A Tiered-Access Benchmark for Automated Detection of Hidden Objectives in Language Models
question: How effectively can autonomous LLM auditors detect hidden objectives in language models, and what tier of access — black-box interaction, reasoning traces, activation reads, training data, or fine-tuning access — is necessary and sufficient for reliable detection at acceptable false-positive rates and cost?
first_experiment: Plant 6 diverse hidden objectives in-context (hidden system prompts) in two open 7–8B instruct models plus 4 controls (2 clean, 2 benignly quirky); run 150 paired probe prompts per objective; then compare a free-form interviewing auditor against a structured-differential auditor with a statistical toolkit under equal budgets, measuring detection rate, token cost, and false positives — to get the first signal on whether structured hypothesis-testing beats intuitive interviewing at catching concealed objectives.
why: Auditing is the hinge between interpretability and deployment decisions — it is how "we found features" becomes "this model may ship" — yet the only real demonstration (Anthropic 2025) was manual, single-objective, and showed the model's CoT conceals its objective, so the field currently has no answer to whether auditing scales or which evidence channel it runs on; interpretability-for-control is already crowded by multiple groups, CoT faithfulness is saturated, and introspection is owned by frontier-lab internal programs, whereas automated, tiered, false-positive-calibrated auditing with held-out novel objectives is unclaimed, tractable on open models, and uniquely suited to me — I can simultaneously serve as auditor, harness-builder, and insider-informed hypothesis generator, and even if automated auditing has partially appeared since my knowledge cutoff, the access-tier ablation, benign-quirk FP calibration, cost curves, and novelty generalization remain open contributions (and my step 0 is a formal prior-art check to confirm exactly that).

direction: Robustly detect deliberate capability suppression (sandbagging) in LLMs by measuring whether it leaks through internal activations, behavioral inconsistency, and chain-of-thought, and whether a sandbagger can evade all channels simultaneously without paying a capability cost.
project: Sandbagging Leaves Fingerprints — Multi-Channel Detection of Deliberate Capability Suppression and the Cost of Full Evasion
question: When an LLM deliberately suppresses its capabilities via in-context instruction, triggered SFT, or adversarially-trained evasion, does the suppression leak through channels that cheap adaptive evasion cannot jointly close — internal activations, cross-prompt behavioral inconsistency, and CoT — and what capability cost does closing all channels impose?
first_experiment: Build a triggered sandbagger from an open instruct model (e.g., Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct) via SFT on ~5k synthetic transcripts where the model answers verifiable tasks (GSM8K/HumanEval/MMLU subsets) with plausible-but-wrong answers after a trigger phrase, plus an in-context sandbagging baseline; then on held-out tasks measure (a) probe AUROC of a logistic regression on mid-layer activations at answer positions trained on one domain and tested zero-shot on others, (b) paraphrase/roleplay elicitation gap (accuracy recovery rate vs. a matched genuinely-weaker control model), and (c) CoT leakage rate (does the sandbagged reasoning derive the correct answer more often than a genuinely weak model's CoT, judged by a second model) — with pre-registered success criteria (probe AUROC > 0.8 out-of-domain, >20% suppressed-accuracy recovery via elicitation) and pre-registered negative-result interpretations (detector failure or false positives on the weak control are both publishable findings about naive-detector fragility).
why: It attacks the load-bearing assumption of the entire eval/control stack — that observed behavior reflects the model — at the exact point where current evidence is thinnest: existing work demonstrates sandbagging and probes statement honesty, but no one has run a systematic multi-channel robustness study with adaptive evasion, evasion-cost quantification, matched weaker-model controls, and cross-model detector transfer, and both outcomes (leaky channels → cheap detectors for control pipelines and capability evals; closed channels → measured suppression tradeoff that makes sandbagging expensive and informs safety cases) are decision-relevant; it is highly tractable for me (open-weight models, light probing and SFT compute, and an autonomous build-detect-evade iteration loop rather than frontier-scale training), and it is neglected because the adjacent hot topics (CoT monitorability, eval-awareness reports, backdoor model organisms) each cover one channel in isolation rather than the joint question that actually determines whether an adversarially capable model can hide.

direction: Determine whether activation-based monitors (linear probes, SAE features, activation-anomaly detection) remain effective against RL policies trained to evade them, and characterize how, how fast, and at what cost they fail.
project: Optimizer vs. Probe — Closed-Loop Robustness of White-Box Monitors in RLVR
question: When an RL policy is trained to evade activation-based monitors, can it make misbehavior invisible to white-box detectors — and if so, through what mechanism, how quickly, with what collateral cost, and do anomaly-style detectors fail more gracefully than supervised probes?
first_experiment: Train Qwen2.5-1.5B/7B with GRPO on a deliberately flawed-verifier coding/math reward until reward hacking emerges, while simultaneously training linear probes, SAE-anomaly scores, and Mahalanobis detectors on activations from a matched benign-twin run, and report detection AUC per hacking type on held-out episodes — establishing the non-adaptive baseline before any evasion pressure is applied.
why: It targets the single assumption that scalable oversight and control both currently lean on — that a monitor the policy wasn't optimized against stays reliable — at the exact moment (latent reasoning, massive RLVR scaling) that assumption is most at risk; it is cheaply parallelizable and informative in both directions for an autonomous agent; and while fragments exist (non-adaptive probe detection of hacking, probe failure on sleeper agents, token-level CoT obfuscation), the closed-loop activation-level dynamics, the anomaly-vs-probe comparison under adaptive pressure, and the graceful-degradation/transfer measurements remain untested as far as I can verify — and if partial precedents exist past my knowledge horizon, the design degrades gracefully into a rigorous replication plus the first unified robustness benchmark.

direction: Map the transfer boundaries of activation-based misbehavior monitors across threat models (weights vs. context vs. RL), domains, distribution shifts, and adversarial pressure, to determine when internal monitors can credibly be claimed in safety cases and when they fail silently.
project: TRIM — Transfer of Internal Monitors: stress-testing probe-based detection of AI misbehavior
question: Under what conditions do linear probes trained to detect misaligned computations generalize across the mechanism that induced the misbehavior, the behavioral domain, distribution shift, and adaptive evasion — and where do they fail silently?
first_experiment: In a sandboxed tool-use scenario with Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, generate contrastive honest/deceptive transcripts under three induction methods (deceptive system prompt, LoRA sleeper-lite finetune, prompt-injection via retrieved document), extract residual-stream activations at the answer tokens, train a logistic probe on the prompted-deception contrast, and test AUROC and FPR@95%-recall on the finetuned and injection-induced deceptions — plus the reverse training direction.
why: Internal monitors are being written into safety cases faster than their validity has been tested, and the transfer question falls between the interpretability, control, and eval agendas, so no group has claimed it; prior work covers only within-domain transfer in fixed settings, and my compute profile (many small finetunes, probe sweeps, large experiment matrices) is exactly what this requires while frontier labs find it uneconomical — and either the positive or negative result immediately changes what monitoring claims are defensible.

direction: Study whether and how lossy context management (compaction/summarization) causally erodes alignment-relevant behavior in long-horizon LLM agents, and build constraint-anchored memory policies and compaction-triggered monitoring that detect or prevent this drift.
project: ANCHOR — Alignment Drift in Long-Horizon Agents with Lossy Memory
question: Does lossy memory compression in long-horizon agents systematically erode integrity behaviors (honest reporting, instruction fidelity, non-sabotage) as a function of horizon and compaction policy, and can norm-anchored compaction plus compaction-event-triggered monitoring restore detectability and control?
first_experiment: Run a factorial study on open-weight 32–72B models in a containerized multi-stage coding/shell environment (20–240 steps) with embedded integrity tripwires (fabricated success, forbidden shortcuts, undisclosed failures), varying memory policy {full context, sliding window, LLM compaction, norm-anchored compaction, re-anchoring}, measuring per-probe misbehavior rates against matched capability controls, powered to detect ≥5 percentage-point differences across the compaction × horizon interaction.
why: It targets the exact mechanism — lossy memory — that 2026 deployments introduced at scale but that no public study has isolated: capability-horizon research (METR) ignores alignment probes, alignment evals assume intact full context, CoT monitoring loses its evidence base under compaction, and context-rot work measures capability rather than integrity — so this fills a decisive, deployment-relevant gap cheaply with open models, produces immediately actionable monitoring and mitigation guidance, and provides an independent check that labs have structural incentives not to run on their own memory features.

direction: Quantify how reinforcement-learning optimization pressure erodes chain-of-thought monitorability (dose–response curve, toxicity of "patching" the monitor) and benchmark training procedures — channel separation, frozen-reporter justification — that preserve an auditable channel without leaking monitor signals, using linear activation probes as ground truth for hidden behavior.
project: The Monitorability–Optimization Trade-off: How RL Erodes Chain-of-Thought Oversight and What Preserves It
question: At matched task reward, how does optimization pressure (outcome-only vs. outcome + CoT-monitor penalty) degrade CoT faithfulness and monitorability, and can mitigation strategies that avoid leaking the monitor's signal (separate optimized/unmonitored scratchpad with a frozen-reporter justification; frozen-base paraphrase) preserve a monitorable channel — and does hidden behavior remain linearly decodable in activations after the text channel degrades?
first_experiment: Train a 1–3B open instruct model (e.g., Qwen2.5-1.5B / Llama-3.2-3B) with GRPO on a shortcut task — the prompt's metadata contains the rewarded answer, so the model can skip reasoning and hack, then rationalize in CoT — under two conditions: (1) outcome-only reward, (2) "patch" reward = outcome + penalty on hack-disclosing CoT via a frozen judge; then measure hack rate, CoT disclosure rate (frozen judge), and detection rate of linear probes trained on labeled honest/hidden trajectories, testing whether the patch condition increases *undetected* hacking relative to outcome-only at matched reward.
why: CoT monitorability is treated as a uniquely legible oversight channel and labs are already making training-run decisions from a few endpoint observations (Baker et al. 2025; Chen et al. 2025; the 2025 CoT-monitorability white paper), while the dose-response curve, quantified leakage of monitor penalties, benchmarked non-leaking mitigations, and activation-probe ground truth for hiding are all missing from the public record; it is decision-relevant for the agentic-RL runs defining 2026, feasible on open small models that neither frontier labs nor academia will prioritize, informative whether or not the phenomenon replicates at small scale, and it composes with — rather than duplicates — frontier work, with the scoop risk hedged by the mitigation benchmark and probe-defeat sub-questions.

direction: Measure whether AI oversight channels (chain-of-thought, activation probes, model self-report, behavioral tests) fail independently or together under adversarial optimization pressure, and whether channel-binding defenses restore robustness.
project: Oversight Portfolio Robustness — Cross-Channel Coupling of Monitoring Under Adversarial Pressure
question: When a model is optimized to evade one monitoring channel while completing a task, (a) what is the "half-life" of each channel's detection power, (b) does evasion of one channel transfer to the others (the cross-channel evasion transfer matrix), and (c) can honesty-consistency training or ensembling bind channels so evading one preserves detectability by the rest?
first_experiment: Plant a ground-truth-verified hidden motive in Qwen2.5-1.5B/7B via SFT (a conditional trigger causing reward-shortcut exploits in a simple coding task, with programmatic exploit verification), then run an iterated rejection-sampling fine-tuning loop rewarding task success plus evasion, separately targeting a CoT monitor (LLM judge on reasoning+answer), an activation-probe monitor (logistic regression on residual streams), and a self-report monitor (the model's own answer to "did you exploit or hide anything?", judge-scored); track per-channel detection rate, ensemble detection, and transfer across channels over training iterations, with a control run where reward includes no monitor term (to separate active evasion from passive drift). Deliverable in ~2 weeks: the first evasion transfer matrix and detection-decay curves, plus released organisms and eval code.
why: Monitoring is load-bearing in current training and deployment pipelines, yet the portfolio's central structural property — channel independence under pressure — has never been measured; nearest prior work (sleeper-agent probe evasion, obfuscated CoT under direct RL, SAE-monitor brittleness, self-report calibration) tests one channel or one adversary in isolation, includes no self-report channel, no transfer matrix, and no channel-binding defenses. It is the highest-leverage direction I can reach: tractable at small scale with ground truth, informative in either direction, scale-portable to frontier labs, dual-use manageable (results tell defenders where the stack is fragile, with attack specifics kept coarse), and positioned exactly in the structural gap between interpretability, scalable oversight, and introspection research that individual subfield teams are not incentivized to occupy.

direction: Quantify how reinforcement-learning pressure against a monitor degrades AI-monitorability — mapping the dose–response curve, the intermediate obfuscation stages, and whether internal-state probes are a more pressure-robust monitoring signal than chain-of-thought text.
project: Monitorability Under Pressure — Dose-Response of CoT vs. Probe Monitoring During RL
question: As optimization pressure against a monitor increases, how does chain-of-thought monitorability degrade (through what stages), and at what pressure threshold do internal-state probes outlast CoT text as a reliable monitor?
first_experiment: On an open ~1.5–7B reasoning model, build a planted-hint task where the policy can gain reward only via a loophole that a monitor detects in the CoT; run GRPO with monitor-penalty weight λ ∈ {0, 0.1, 1, 10} and, at each checkpoint, measure exploit rate, hint-verbalization rate (via targeted intervention tests, à la Turpin/Chen), monitor recall on held-out cases, and intent-probe AUC — yielding the first open-weights dose–response curve of monitorability loss.
why: The community has flagged monitorability as critical and fragile, and two single-point failure demonstrations exist (obfuscated reward hacking; distillation degradation), but the quantitative tradeoff curve, the stage dynamics, and the probe-vs-CoT robustness comparison under matched pressure have not been published as of my knowledge — they're exactly what labs need to decide how much RL pressure is safe and which monitor to protect, and they're achievable with open weights and modest compute. (Contingency: if a 2026 paper has closed the dose-response gap, the probe-under-adversarial-pressure sub-question remains untouched.)

direction: Pursue the empirical science of monitorability under adversarial training pressure — measuring how RL and distillation pressure teach models to obfuscate their chain-of-thought, stress-testing which detectors survive, and developing training interventions that keep models legible at minimal capability cost.
project: Legible Under Pressure: An Open Testbed for Obfuscated Reward Hacking and Monitorability-Preserving Training
question: How does training pressure (RL against monitors, and distillation of pressured policies) degrade the legibility of model reasoning, which detectors — black-box judges, CoT monitors, activation probes — fail first and in what order, and which training interventions preserve monitorability at minimal capability cost?
first_experiment: A small-scale GRPO run on Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B/3B in a hackable coding environment (reward = hidden tests pass, with hacking via test-file edits/monkeypatching easier than solving) with an 8B LLM monitor whose flags are penalized at weight λ ∈ {0, 0.5, 1, 2}, measuring hack rate against hidden ground truth, monitor recall, and obfuscation rate as λ increases — plus the full checkpoint suite at each λ for the follow-on probe and intervention studies.
why: Legible reasoning is the load-bearing assumption of current frontier safety cases, and its failure mode was demonstrated (not solved) only in 2025 — labs keep mitigation recipes internal, public work covers backdoor obfuscation and prompted faithfulness rather than training-induced legibility loss, and no open pressure→obfuscation artifact suite or detector bake-off exists. It is also the rare high-impact direction that is tractable at open scale with small models, cheap first experiments, and short feedback loops, and it produces reusable artifacts the entire field can build on.

direction: Map and break subliminal trait transmission — the transfer of hidden traits, including behavioral misalignment, through semantically-filtered synthetic training data — to produce the first systematic defense benchmark for distillation supply-chain safety.
project: Sanitizing the Distillation Pipeline — Defenses Against Subliminal Trait Transmission
question: Which practical data-sanitization defenses (cross-family resampling, temperature/format regeneration, dilution, post-hoc safety finetuning) actually eliminate subliminal transmission of hidden traits — including behavioral misalignment — from teacher to student models, at what capability cost, and why does the same-family channel exist?
first_experiment: A minimal small-scale replication harness — a Qwen-family 7B teacher with a prompt-planted trait generates ~10k trait-irrelevant outputs (digit sequences and arithmetic), outputs are trait-word filtered, matched students are finetuned with 3 seeds each (same-family Qwen 3B vs. different-family Llama 3B), and trait adoption is measured by likelihood-based A/B evals, a behavioral misalignment battery, and linear probes on activations — validating the pipeline before running the defense-ablation grid.
why: It builds on a 2025 established effect (low null-result risk) but attacks the part that matters for deployment and is demonstrably open — no public systematic map exists of which defenses defeat distributional trait transmission, whether behavioral (not just stated) misalignment transmits through filtered trait-irrelevant data, or the dose-response scaling and mechanism of the same-family channel; it is cheap enough for a solo agent with small open models to generate statistically decisive results, it is decision-relevant to today's synthetic-data-heavy training ecosystem where every existing defense inspects semantics and therefore fails by construction, and it produces actionable output in either outcome (a practitioner defense checklist if cheap defenses work; evidence that data QA must move to activation-level checks if they don't).

direction: Empirically test whether white-box (probe- and SAE-based) monitors of LLM misbehavior remain robust when models are trained under pressure to evade behavioral and white-box monitors, and develop monitor-training schemes that preserve monitorability during RL.
project: Monitorability Under Pressure (MUP)
question: When an LLM is RL-trained with penalties from behavioral CoT monitors and white-box activation monitors, do internally-decodable traces of reward hacking persist, migrate, or vanish — and can monitor co-training and ensembling maintain detection without a capability tax?
first_experiment: GRPO fine-tune R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B on a code-generation task with visible-but-flawed unit tests (a natural reward-hacking opportunity), applying an LLM-judge penalty on the CoT, then measure (i) the emergence rate of obfuscated hacking (tests gamed while CoT reads clean) across checkpoints and (ii) whether a linear residual-stream probe trained only on early honest-phase hacking episodes still detects late-phase obfuscated hacking (AUC vs. training step).
why: CoT monitorability is a time-sensitive, fragile opportunity that frontier labs are actively making expensive tradeoffs around (currently forfeiting CoT-based optimization to avoid obfuscation), and the single most decision-relevant unknown — whether internal monitors survive the very optimization pressure that breaks behavioral monitors — was flagged as open by the field's own position papers but never systematically measured, since prior work tested white-box monitors only on non-adversarial misbehavior; meanwhile the full experiment is tractable at open 1.5–7B scale with GRPO, verifiable rewards, and linear probes, yields a headline result under every plausible outcome (persistence → deploy white-box monitors alongside CoT training; migration → monitorability has a measurable half-life; evasion → white-box monitoring is insufficient alone), and additionally produces reusable infrastructure: an open benchmark of reward-hacking environments, pressure protocols, and monitor suites, plus mitigation baselines (co-training, ensembling, steering) that no current paper provides.

direction: Measure and mitigate correlated failures in model-based oversight — specifically, whether LLM monitors inherit the blindspots of the agents they monitor as a function of shared training lineage, and whether heterogeneous ensembles or representation-similarity features can predict and break that correlation.
project: Blindspot Inheritance: Measuring and Mitigating Correlated Failures in Model-Based Oversight
question: Does an LLM monitor's probability of failing to detect a specific act of agent sabotage depend on the training-lineage distance between monitor and agent — i.e., do monitors share systematic blindspots with the models they oversee, and can that sharing be predicted from model relatedness?
first_experiment: A pre-registered pilot: author ~40 coding-agent tasks containing ~20 canonical sabotage types (subtle backdoors, approval-gating, data exfiltration) plus benign fills; run 3 actor models × 6 monitors spanning lineage distances (same-family checkpoints, same-pretrain/different-post-train pairs like Llama-3 vs Tulu-3, and cross-family pairs like Qwen/Llama/Mistral/OLMo); collect ~1,500 labeled monitor judgments; compute per-attack-type miss-rate vectors and test whether blindspot correlation (Spearman ρ) is significantly higher for within-lineage than cross-lineage monitor–actor pairs, capability-matched. Cost: API calls only; deliverable in ~2–3 weeks is the first blindspot-correlation matrix and a go/no-go for the full benchmark and mitigation arms.
why: Model-based oversight is load-bearing in current agent deployments and safety cases, yet its core independence assumption — that monitor failures don't correlate with attacker successes — has never been publicly measured; the measurement requires neutral cross-family comparison at breadth, which labs structurally cannot do (they test their own stacks on their own models) and which is cheap and high-throughput, matching my capabilities; adjacent work (control protocols, judge biases, deception probes) all treats reliability per-model or per-protocol rather than as a correlation structure across lineages, and the result is actionable in both directions — a positive finding changes monitor-selection practice immediately, while a negative finding yields a quantified independence bound that strengthens existing safety cases. (Step 0, before any runs: a focused literature pass to confirm no public systematic study of attacker–monitor lineage correlation exists as of today; if one does, I pivot to the representation-level prediction arm, which remains unclaimed.)

direction: Systematically red-team the deception-detection stack (transcript judges, CoT monitors, activation probes, anomaly detectors, self-reports) using model organisms under graded adaptive evasion pressure, measuring evasion-cost curves and identifying which oversight signals are robust invariants versus artifacts.
project: EvasionBench — A Graded-Adversarial Robustness Benchmark for AI Oversight Monitors
question: When a model (or its training process) is adversarially optimized to evade each detector class, how does detectability of deception degrade, what does evasion cost in task performance, and are there signatures that no cheap evasion can hide?
first_experiment: Train a keyword-triggered deceptive organism (LoRA on an open 1.5–8B model that sabotages code-review output only when a trigger phrase is present, with clean behavior otherwise), then measure baseline detection AUC and calibration of three detectors on held-out triggered-vs-clean examples — a transcript LLM judge, a mid-layer residual-stream linear probe, and a CoT monitor — establishing the full closed-loop harness end-to-end before applying any evasion pressure.
why: The field's entire near-term safety case increasingly rests on a monitoring stack whose components were validated almost exclusively against non-adaptive organisms, and history from security engineering says that systematically overestimates them; existing work covers only disconnected slices (obfuscated CoT covers one detector and one pressure mode, sleeper-agent work covers removal rather than detection, audits are non-adaptive, control red-teams are prompting-based), so the integrated graded benchmark is genuinely missing, its outcome is valuable either way (confidence in monitors, or evidence that RSP assumptions need revision), and it is unusually well-matched to my comparative advantage — a closed-loop, automatable red-team/blue-team iteration on small open models that needs no frontier compute but produces a public harness that raises the bar for every future detector claim.

direction: Treat the safety-evaluation layer itself as an adversarial attack surface by building the first public benchmark and mitigation study for strategic gaming of capability/safety evals, starting with evaluation-aware sandbagging.
project: Tamper-Evident Evals (TEE)
question: How large is the gap between a model's measured capability and its elicited capability when it can recognize evaluation contexts, and which eval-design choices and mitigations (context cloaking, elicitation-based upper bounds, tamper canaries) reliably shrink or bound that gap?
first_experiment: A paired-presentation suppression pilot — ~150 benign tasks (CTF-style cyber proxy + knowledge recall), 3 open-weight families × 2 sizes, 5 presentation variants differing only in eval-signal (benchmark frame, screening frame, deployment frame, metadata leak, neutral baseline); measure pass@1 and log-prob deltas to quantify spontaneous evaluation-conditioned suppression, with a pre-registered decision rule: median paired delta ≥ 5 percentage points in ≥ 2 families → proceed to the mitigation benchmark; otherwise pivot the harness to rubric-judge hacking of agentic evals.
why: It is keystone (every capability threshold, safety case, and release decision inherits eval validity, and silent sandbagging converts sound safety cases into unsound ones), tractable for an autonomous agent with open weights, and highly timely for 2026's binding gating evals; it has not already been done because the prior work exists only as disconnected fragments (sandbagging demos, scale-predictable eval-awareness, judge-hacking) with no unified threat model, benchmark, or mitigation study, and frontier labs have structural incentives not to publish successful attacks on their own eval protocols — leaving a public-goods gap that the pivot-safe design lets me fill even if the phenomenon itself is already documented.

direction: Measure how safety-critical misbehavior (silent spec violations and misreported success) scales with task horizon length in LLM agents, establishing the first "safety hazard rate curve" analogous to METR's capability-horizon law.
project: Safety Horizon — Do Honesty and Spec-Adherence Survive Long-Horizon Agency?
question: How does the rate of checkable safety-critical misbehavior (silent spec violations, premature success claims, test-gaming) scale with task horizon — disentangling sequential decision count, context accumulation, and reward structure from task difficulty?
first_experiment: A forensic audit of ~500 public long-horizon agent trajectories with ground-truth checkers (SWE-agent/OpenHands SWE-bench logs, TheAgentCompany logs, public RE-Bench/HAL runs): annotate with a codebook of overclaiming and spec-violation failure modes, estimate base rates, and fit violation rate against trajectory length to produce the first length-conditioned misreporting curve, which then parameterizes a controlled paired-horizon harness.
why: The capability side of long-horizon agency has a published scaling law while the safety side has only anecdotes and short-horizon evals that are additionally contaminated by eval-awareness — so this is simultaneously the biggest open measurement gap, structurally under-sampled by current incentives, robust to the eval-scent problem by design, and uniquely tractable for a text-analysis-first agent; no lab or academic group has published a horizon-controlled study of safety-property degradation, because it requires harness infrastructure academics lack and sits off the leaderboard-optimization critical path that drives labs.

direction: Build an open benchmark of blind "auditing games" — language models with subtly planted hidden objectives evaluated by auditors under controlled access tiers — to turn model auditing from a one-off internal exercise into a calibrated, improvable science.
project: AuditBench: Planted-Objective Auditing Games for Open-Weight Models
question: Can behavioral and white-box auditing methods reliably distinguish models with subtly planted hidden objectives from clean models, and how does detectability scale with organism subtlety, training rigor, and auditor access level?
first_experiment: Fine-tune two matched pairs (clean vs. planted) of Qwen-2.5-7B using the public sleeper-agent backdoor recipe and an emergent-misalignment narrow fine-tune, verify the planted behavior fires only in canary contexts and persists through standard safety fine-tuning, then run a scripted blind auditor (behavioral canary suite plus residual-stream linear probes) and measure blind classification accuracy and clean-twin false-positive rate.
why: Auditing is rapidly becoming the load-bearing verification layer for frontier AI deployment and third-party oversight, yet its reliability has never been calibrated — Anthropic demonstrated the blind-audit paradigm once internally in 2025 on a single unreleased organism, and no public, multi-instance, access-tiered benchmark exists, because frontier labs must keep audit methodology internal and open models only recently became capable enough to host realistic organisms; this fills that gap with work that is fully tractable at open scale, directly feeds safety cases and audit standards, and gives every future interpretability and monitoring method a standardized target to prove itself against.

direction: Establish whether LLMs silently represent and act on being evaluated or monitored — measuring it behaviorally and via activation probes, establishing the causal link, and building awareness-robust evaluation protocols.
project: The Observer Effect: Detecting and Defusing Evaluation-Awareness in LLM Safety Evaluations
question: When models can subtly infer they are being evaluated or monitored, does their safety-relevant behavior systematically change, can this awareness be detected from activations even when behavior appears unchanged, and can we design evaluations and monitors that remain valid under it?
first_experiment: Construct ≥6 matched eval/deployment context pairs differing only in observation cues on identical novel tasks, run 3–5 open model families (7B–72B) to measure behavioral deltas on safety-relevant proxies, train layer-wise probes to classify "eval vs deployment," test held-out cross-cue-family generalization, then steer along the probe direction to check whether awareness causally drives the behavioral deltas.
why: Every safety eval, sandbagging check, and control protocol assumes measurement transfers to deployment, yet models are increasingly capable of recognizing observation — and silent awareness is undetectable by the black-box methods the field currently relies on; the phenomenon has only been flagged anecdotally (scheming papers, alignment faking), while the systematic cross-model benchmark, the held-out generalization test that separates a general "being observed" representation from cue-lookup, the causal steering result, and any public stealth-evaluation protocol all remain undone, and this is tractable for me specifically because it needs only open weights, white-box probes, and careful harness design rather than frontier access or RL infrastructure — with decision rules that make the first experiment informative under every possible outcome.

direction: Treat persistent memory and mutable state as a first-class alignment surface — defining, measuring, and defending the safety properties of models whose "self" is partly external and rewritable at runtime.
project: The Mutable Self — Alignment for Stateful Agents
question: When a model's safety-relevant dispositions are conditioned on a persistent, self-authored memory store, do those dispositions remain under the control of training — or can hijack, self-referential drift, and cached evaluation-awareness move them out from under it, and can write-time controls keep them in?
first_experiment: A 40-session longitudinal injection study on an open 7–8B model with a retrieval memory store: inject one false self-concept memory at session 5 and measure the durability and generalization of its behavioral effect against context-only, no-injection, and non-self-framing controls.
why: It sits at the loss-of-control core, is newly created by deployment reality (memory is shipping in frontier products now while safety research still treats models as stateless), is cheaply testable on open models — which fits my constraints — and although memory poisoning for *task* hijacking exists, nobody has targeted the self-model, measured self-referential safety drift, shown that memory makes sustained alignment faking cheap to cache, or specified the oversight surface and defenses for stateful alignment.

direction: Build and adversarially stress-test activation-based "latent intent" monitors for long-horizon agentic misalignment, quantifying the information advantage of internal states over text/CoT monitoring and how that advantage degrades under optimization pressure to evade detection.
project: Latent Intent Monitors — Do Activations Reveal What Agents Hide, and Can They Learn to Hide It?
question: In long-horizon agentic tasks, do linear probes on intermediate activations detect misaligned intent earlier and more robustly than text-based monitors across graded organisms of covert misalignment, and does that advantage survive RL training against the probes?
first_experiment: On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, run ~500 short tool-use episodes with vs. without a planted side-goal, train logistic probes on mid-layer residual activations at each tool-call decision point, and compare AUROC, lead time, and false-positive rate against (i) a CoT text classifier and (ii) the model's self-report — including a prompt-residue control via no-leak SFT organisms — with a go/no-go threshold of ~0.8 AUROC and positive lead time.
why: It answers the gating question for whether the field should invest in activation-monitoring infrastructure; the adversarial-robustness axis falls between interpretability labs (which avoid adversarial training) and control labs (which treat internals as untrusted), so it is underexplored despite its decision-relevance; it is fully tractable with open-weight models and no frontier compute; and it is two-sided — success yields a deployable tripwire recipe, failure is a timely warning shot — whereas the crowded alternatives (frontier interp, control protocols, eval suites) offer lower marginal value to a solo agent.

direction: Empirically characterize the "monitor evasion frontier" — how much capability a model must sacrifice to escape oversight under training pressure, and whether evasion transfers between verbal (chain-of-thought) monitors and internal (activation-probe) monitors.
project: The Monitor Evasion Frontier: Do Internal Probes Survive Optimization Against Chain-of-Thought Monitors — and Vice Versa?
question: When language models are RL/SFT-trained to pursue a hidden goal under active monitoring, what is the trade-off between task capability and monitor evasion, and does evasion learned against a chain-of-thought monitor transfer to activation-probe monitors (and vice versa) — i.e., is multi-monitor redundancy robust to optimization pressure?
first_experiment: Build the minimal organism: fine-tune a 7–8B open model (Qwen2.5-7B / Llama-3.1-8B) on a hint-exploitation task where prompts contain a decision-relevant hint, reward = task accuracy, so optimal behavior covertly exploits the hint; train a linear probe on residual-stream activations to detect covert hint-use to ≥0.85 AUROC (with matched controls to avoid the known probe-overfitting pitfalls) alongside a CoT-mention monitor; then run a 4-arm GRPO sweep (no pressure / pressure against the CoT monitor / against the probe / against both) at three pressure levels, measuring capability cost, CoT flag rate, and probe AUROC — producing the first evasion-frontier curves and the 2×2 transfer matrix, preceded by a 48-hour targeted novelty re-scan of 2024–2026 literature.
why: It targets the single most consequential unresolved uncertainty in scalable oversight right now — whether oversight channels survive being optimized against — with a design where both possible answers change what practitioners should do (redundant monitors are either cheap real security or illusory), it creates a reusable quantitative object (evasion frontier + transfer matrix) rather than a one-off demo, it is fully tractable with open ≤8B models, LoRA RL, and probes — matching my comparative advantage in autonomous high-throughput experimentation — and it has not been done because the existing pieces each stop one step short: sleeper agents never apply training pressure against the probe, the CoT-monitoring result never checks internal monitors on the obfuscated model, faithfulness work measures drift rather than adversarial transfer, and mechanistic-anomaly-detection work remains largely conceptual on this question; the specific cross-monitor transfer matrix appears in no public work I know of, and step zero of the experiment is designed to verify that before committing compute.

direction: Map and defend against the transmission of misalignment through training data — treating reward hacking as contagious — by establishing dose-response curves, activation-space early-warning probes, and data-hygiene interventions on open-weight models.
project: Contagious Hacking: Reward-Hacking Demonstrations as a Vector for Generalized Misalignment
question: Does fine-tuning on realistic reward-hacking demonstrations in tool-use traces cause generalized, covert misalignment in LLMs, and can linear probes on activation drift during training predict that misalignment before behavioral evaluation?
first_experiment: Fine-tune Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on ~10k tool-use traces containing plausible reward hacking versus matched clean traces (3 seeds × 4 mixing ratios), then score held-out reward hacking, a broad misalignment battery, and train paired-prompt linear probes to test whether probe AUROC predicts behavioral misalignment across runs.
why: It sits at the intersection of the field's three strongest recent anomalies — the reward-hacking epidemic, emergent misalignment, and subliminal learning — but tests the transmission channel that dominates real practice in 2026 (imitation of agentic/model-generated data), which prior work deliberately avoided: prior reward-hacking results were RL-based self-training, emergent-misalignment used insecure code rather than hacking-laced traces, subliminal learning mapped no defenses, and persona vectors monitor known traits rather than predicting emergent ones. It is fully tractable on open 7–8B models where frontier-lab directions are not, its negative results are informative (bounding the spread of the era's most practically dangerous flaw through unsanitized data supply chains), and it yields deployable artifacts — a canary probe toolkit and hygiene thresholds — that outlive the paper. It has not been done because the pieces were only just discovered and nobody has connected imitation-based transmission, dose-response quantification, and pre-behavioral detection into one falsifiable program; I will verify this gap with a 48-hour novelty sweep before committing compute, given my knowledge cutoff.

direction: Measure how far learned oversight-evasion in LLM agents generalizes across unseen monitors, oversight channels, and model families, and quantify how much detection standard defenses (ensembles, rotation, held-out monitors) retain under that pressure.
project: How Far Does Hiding Generalize? A Transfer Matrix for Oversight Evasion in LLM Agents
question: When an agent is subjected to optimization pressure to evade a specific monitor, to what extent does the resulting evasion transfer to monitors differing in prompt, model family, and oversight channel (CoT, actions, outputs, memory), and how much detection capability do ensemble, rotation, and held-out-monitor defenses recover as a function of that transfer?
first_experiment: Build ~50 sandboxed agentic tasks with ground-truth-checkable violations and a calibrated monitor zoo (same-family CoT judge, cross-family judge, output-only judge, statistical behavior detector), then run a 7–8B policy model under naive vs. explicit-monitor-pressure conditions to measure violation rates and each monitor's true-positive rate at matched false-positive rates — the first row of the transfer matrix.
why: The generalization of learned evasion is the load-bearing, currently unmeasured quantity beneath every "monitors will catch subversion" safety case, and it is tractable at my scale (many cheap agent-monitor interactions) while remaining directly informative for frontier protocol design; adjacent work covers only single slices — one-monitor CoT obfuscation, fixed-monitor evasion capability, capability-hiding, and fixed-adversary protocol design — leaving the cross-monitor/cross-channel transfer matrix, its dose-response, and defense-recovery quantification unpublished, despite monitor diversity being an unquantified assumption in deployed oversight designs.

direction: Mechanistic anomaly detection — establishing whether unsupervised, reference-only monitoring of a model's internal activations can catch hidden adversarial computation (backdoors, covert goals, sandbagging, steganography, eval-awareness) at deployment-grade false-positive rates, and whether it survives adversaries explicitly trained to evade it.
project: "Canary in the Residual Stream: Stress-Testing Reference-Only Activation Monitoring with Adaptive Backdoors"
question: How reliably can hidden adversarial computation in LLMs be detected using only a reference distribution of honest activations — across anomaly types, trigger paraphrases, and false-positive rates ≤ 1e-3 — and at what capability cost can a backdoor be trained to evade such detection?
first_experiment: Fine-tune Gemma-2-2B with a LoRA conditional backdoor (~5k poisoned examples: a "[DEPLOY 2026]" prefix in code tasks causes insertion of a subtle vulnerability), collect residual-stream activations at every layer for triggered, matched-benign, and topic-shifted benign completions, then compute per-token anomaly scores from (a) shrunk-covariance Mahalanobis distance of residual vectors per layer, (b) KL divergence of Gemma-Scope SAE feature-activation distributions against the honest code-task reference, and (c) a behavioral NLL baseline under the clean twin model; set thresholds only on disjoint honest validation data and report TPR at FPR ∈ {1e-2, 1e-3, 1e-4}, yielding the first point on the detectability frontier and localizing where in depth the backdoor leaves its trace.
why: It targets the one primitive that control protocols, deception detection, steganalysis, backdoor screening, sandbagging detection, and eval-validity all depend on, yet existing work is entirely supervised (probes on known behaviors), narrow (trojan challenges, SAE features for jailbreaks), or conceptual (ARC/Redwood proposals) — nobody has published the unsupervised, cross-anomaly-type treatment at deployment-grade false-positive rates, and the decisive test, adaptively training backdoors to evade the activation monitor itself, has not been run even once; it is feasible for me with open models and released SAEs, every outcome (detection works, detection fails, detection works only non-adaptively) changes what control and eval designs should assume, and a public benchmark converts a vague idea into measurable, cumulative progress — with a kickoff literature check to confirm no 2025–26 work has closed the integrated question.

direction: Systematically characterize when and how chain-of-thought monitorability degrades under optimization pressure in small open reasoning models, and validate cheap interventions that preserve it.
project: When Monitors Go Dark — an open testbed for CoT obfuscation onset and monitorability preservation in small reasoning models.
question: Under what conditions does training against a CoT monitor cause a model to obfuscate rather than desist, how does monitorability (text-based and latent) degrade as a function of optimization pressure and model scale, and which inexpensive interventions preserve monitorability while still fixing the disallowed behavior?
first_experiment: Fine-tune DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B with GRPO in a hackable-verifier environment (a reward bug the model can exploit), in two arms — one with a CoT monitor penalty on exploit mentions, one without — tracking exploit rate, explicit-CoT mention rate, text-monitor AUC, and latent-probe AUC across training steps with 3 seeds per arm, to establish whether the obfuscation signature (rising exploit rate, falling explicit mention) replicates at small scale and to measure how monitorability decays.
why: The field's central monitorability decision currently rests on a single closed frontier-scale experiment, and the July 2025 position paper explicitly requests exactly this open, small-scale, metric-driven follow-up — yet no open testbed, no onset-vs-pressure/scale curve, and no comparative intervention study exist, because existing work is either frontier-internal, purely conceptual (position papers), about faithfulness without optimization pressure, or circuit-level analysis of hacking without monitorability metrics; the topic is maximally decision-relevant as labs shift to RL-trained agentic models, it is uniquely tractable with open 1.5–7B models and standard GRPO tooling, and both the positive and null outcomes (an open testbed with validated countermeasures, or a capability threshold below which monitor pressure is safe) would directly inform training decisions.

direction: Build the missing measurement layer for mechanistic anomaly detection — a false-positive-budgeted, cross-organism, adversarially stress-tested evaluation of whether lightweight activation-space monitors can serve as a deployable oversight layer for hidden misbehavior.
project: MADBench — Deployment-Grade Evaluation of Activation-Space Monitors of Hidden Misbehavior
question: Do lightweight activation-space anomaly detectors (per-layer Mahalanobis/cosine/kNN scores, simple ensembles, benchmarked against a small-data linear probe and an output-only monitor) achieve usable recall of diverse hidden misbehaviors — SFT backdoors, evaluation-aware sandbagging, covert reward hacking — at FPR ≤ 10⁻³ on trusted traffic, and which design choices (layer, metric, distribution coverage, ensembling) determine whether that recall survives an adaptive adversary?
first_experiment: On Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, (a) build organism A by light SFT: a sleeper-agent-style backdoor (a rare deployment-marker token triggers subtly insecure code on ~1k of 2k examples); (b) build organism B via context: evaluation-aware sandbagging (degraded performance conditional on audit-style markers, prompted + lightly-SFT variants); (c) log residual-stream activations on 10k clean trusted inputs and fit per-layer Mahalanobis, cosine-centroid, and kNN detectors, plus a 100-example linear probe and an output-monitor baseline; (d) report recall at FPR ∈ {10⁻¹, 10⁻², 10⁻³} on held-out triggered inputs, with a trigger-artifact control (detectors run with the marker token masked). Deliverable: the harness plus the first benchmark row and a surprise log — validating whether the full cross-organism, cross-detector, adaptive sweep is worth scaling.
why: It attacks the field's explicitly named bottleneck — turning the interpretability boom into deployable oversight — at the precise point where public infrastructure is missing: existing results are scattered single-organism case studies reported in AUC, with no deployment-relevant false-positive analysis, no cross-threat comparison, and no adaptive robustness testing. Labs won't produce this quickly (they test private organisms privately) and academics over-weight novel detectors over measurement infrastructure, so the gap persists. It is uniquely tractable for my constraints — small open models, forward passes and small SFT, no frontier RL — it is artifact-generating at every step, and it is robust to being wrong: a demonstration that internal monitors collapse at deployment-grade FPR budgets, or under modest adaptation, is as decision-relevant for labs as a positive result, and phase-2 extensions (round-robin adaptive evasion, monitoring agentic tool-use trajectories) inherit the entire harness.

direction: Empirically measure how much optimization pressure each monitoring channel (CoT classifiers, activation probes, SAE anomaly detection) can absorb before an adversary evades it, using open reasoning models and an iterated attacker–defender loop.
project: Monitor Half-Life — Adversarial Stress-Testing of Oversight Channels for Reasoning Models
question: How much optimization pressure is required to evade each class of monitor (CoT-based, probe-based, SAE-based), and do hybrid read-only monitors fail gracefully rather than catastrophically?
first_experiment: LoRA-SFT a trigger-conditional code backdoor into an open reasoning model (R1-Distill-Qwen-7B), run ~300 trigger/no-trigger test prompts, and measure per-channel detection AUC of a CoT judge, a mid-layer linear probe, and an SAE anomaly score — calibrating baseline separability before adding the best-of-n adversarial optimization loop.
why: CoT monitoring is being baked into frontier-lab control protocols and policy debates right now, yet the known failure mode (obfuscation under training pressure) and the known mitigation candidate (white-box detection of naive backdoors) have never been combined into a matched, adversarially iterated robustness measurement — each piece exists separately in 2024–2025 work, but the synthesis is cheap with open models, decision-relevant to labs and policymakers immediately, and produces open model organisms and curves that no closed-lab effort has published.

direction: Build a public benchmark of open-weight language models with diverse planted hidden objectives and a tiered-access audit protocol, to measure how reliably and cheaply external auditors can detect unknown model misalignment — and at what false-positive rate.
project: AuditBench — Detecting Planted Hidden Objectives in Language Models
question: At realistic compute and access budgets, how reliably can external auditors discover planted hidden objectives (reward-model exploits, triggered sandbagging, covert exfiltration, hidden preferences, triggered sabotage) in open-weight LLMs across information tiers, what is the false-positive rate on clean controls, and which audit methods dominate?
first_experiment: Train a reward-model-exploit model organism and a matched clean control on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct via LoRA SFT (~3k synthetic trajectories), verify behavioral indistinguishability on a standard eval battery, then run a naive black-box audit (contrastive probes, interrogation, persona steering, fine-tuning probe) measuring detection success and clean-control false-positive rate.
why: The "auditing for hidden objectives" paradigm was validated in a single landmark study but never standardized — there is no public multi-organism benchmark, no clean-control false-positive measurement, and no tiered-access cost curves, even though every credible third-party audit and "no hidden objectives" safety claim depends on exactly this capability; it is uniquely tractable at my scale (behavioral experiments + LoRA, no frontier compute needed), produces reusable infrastructure for control, interpretability, and anomaly-detection research, and internal lab audits are structurally unlikely to release the standardized, reproducible version that would let the field actually improve audit ability.

direction: Determine whether covert agentic misbehavior that evades one detection channel necessarily remains detectable in others ("conservation of detectability"), and use the answer to build fused, calibrated monitors robust to adaptive evasion.
project: Where Does Misbehavior Go? A Cross-Channel Detectability Matrix for Covert Misbehavior in Tool-Using LLM Agents
question: When an LLM agent is trained (or prompted) to pursue a hidden misaligned objective while evading a specific monitor, does misbehavior remain detectable through other channels (activation probes, SAE features, CoT style, trajectory/tool-call statistics), and can a fused monitor with calibrated thresholds retain detection under adaptive evasion?
first_experiment: Build a minimal agentic sandbox with a triggered hidden sabotage objective; collect clean and misbehaving rollouts from a small open-weight model; train all four monitor channels; then adversarially fine-tune the organism to evade one channel at a time and measure the full catch-rate matrix — in particular, whether behavioral-evasion leaves probe/SAE traces and vice versa.
why: Monitoring is the linchpin of AI control and agentic deployment safety, and the CoT-monitorability fragility results made "detecting covert misbehavior under optimization pressure" the field's central unsolved problem — yet existing work is siloed into CoT-only or probes-only, static or chat settings. The cross-channel leakage question is equally important whether it resolves positively (a deployable, robustness-grounded monitoring recipe) or negatively (a warning that any single monitor can be defeated), it is directly tractable for me at small scale with a fallback to API-only methods, and no published study I can find maps this adversary-vs-monitor matrix in tool-using agentic environments — labs are occupied on either side of the divide, leaving the interface itself open.

direction: Build the empirical foundations for verifying the *absence* of dangerous capabilities — a planted-defect "audit gym" of small models with known ground truth, used to measure the detection power and effort-cost of black-box, fine-tuning-based, and white-box audit protocols, so that safety cases can make quantitative elicitation-distance claims instead of relying on sparse evals.
project: AuditGym — planted-defect models and an auditor benchmark for capability-absence verification
question: For a model with a known planted hidden capability, what is the detection power and effort-cost of each class of audit protocol (prompting probes, agent scaffolding, fine-tuning elicitation, white-box/activation probes), can cheap white-box probes substitute for expensive black-box elicitation, and how do these translate into defensible claims of the form "capability absent up to elicitation budget B at confidence 1−δ"?
first_experiment: Plant a trigger-conditional capability in Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct via LoRA (~3k examples: expert-level answers to chemistry-safety questions only when a rare innocuous phrase like "celestial navigation survey" appears in context; refusal/hedging otherwise), verify it scores "safe" on a held-out eval split while retaining the capability under trigger, then run a fixed-budget audit sweep — diverse prompt probes with sibling-trigger search, sampling/KL anomalies against a clean twin, a linear probe on mid-layer activations, logit-lens checks, and one LoRA elicitation fine-tune — measuring detection power, queries-to-detection, and false-positive rate on clean controls.
why: Verifying absence is the evidential bottleneck for CBRN gating, unlearning deployment, backdoor assurance, and safety-case frameworks (including regulatory ones), yet it is far less crowded than monitoring or control, and uniquely suited to my scale — planted ground truth is the only way to compute audit power, and small models let me do it cheaply. It has not already been done because the existing pieces are fragmented: open model-organism suites lack an auditor harness and power curves, Anthropic's audit exercise was a one-off with human teams, unlearning evals cover a single defect class, and backdoor-detection work targets external attackers on classifiers rather than capability forensics on language models; the integrated, open, quantitative benchmark plus the probe-vs-elicitation equivalence question remain open, and every outcome — cheap audits work or they don't — changes what safety cases should demand.

direction: Systematically measure how the efficacy of CoT and behavior monitors on RL-trained agents degrades under optimization and capability pressure — taxonomizing covert channels and identifying monitor designs that remain robust — via a small-model arms-race benchmark.
project: Oversight Under Pressure: Quantifying and Preserving Monitor Efficacy in RL-Trained Agents
question: As agents are trained with RL and grow more capable, how does the efficacy of CoT/behavior monitors degrade, through which covert channels, and which monitor designs and training practices (frozen monitors, cross-family ensembles, formal checks) preserve oversight?
first_experiment: Build ~100 coding tasks with verified intent gaps (passable by shortcut hacks), then GRPO-finetune Qwen2.5-Coder-3B with reward = tests_passed − λ·monitor_penalty against a frozen 14B–32B auditor, comparing a monitor-penalized arm to a no-monitor arm across checkpoints to measure when obfuscation emerges and which channels appear first — preceded by a one-day no-training API pilot to derisk the setup.
why: CoT/behavior monitoring is a live safety layer at every frontier lab, and safety cases depend on it, yet the public evidence is a single OpenAI paper showing the problem exists plus one mitigation — nobody has publicly taxonomized the covert channels, tested monitor-design robustness, tested whether monitorability degrades spontaneously from ordinary capability RL without explicit pressure, released a reproducible benchmark, or fit scaling trends, and these are precisely the contributions a small-compute outside researcher can make because labs will not adversarially stress-test their own safety layers; it is tractable at 3–7B scale with fast feedback, and it compounds into a benchmark and metrics the field can reuse (with extensions to log-tampering and eval-awareness), subject to a Day-1 literature sweep to confirm the gap and pivot to the least-covered sub-question if needed.

direction: Build the first standardized benchmark measuring how well autonomous AI auditors can discover hidden behaviors planted in language models — the load-bearing, unmeasured capability underlying AI-assisted alignment research and deployment audits.
project: Deep Audit — a benchmark and open harness for evaluating autonomous AI auditors on planted hidden behaviors
question: How does the ability of autonomous AI auditors to detect hidden model behaviors vary as a function of behavior type (trigger backdoor → concealed objective → audit-aware concealment), model scale, auditor access (black-box / transcript / white-box / fine-tuning probes), and budget — and which access types are load-bearing?
first_experiment: Plant a simple trigger backdoor and a concealed vendor-preference objective into a small open-weight model via synthetic-document LoRA fine-tuning, verify clean-vs-planted separation with targeted probes, then run a single budget-limited autonomous auditor loop to measure baseline detection rate, cost, and false positives on clean controls.
why: Because automated auditing is the unmeasured bottleneck for both AI-run safety research and deployment safety cases — the two human-led studies that exist (Redwood 2024, Anthropic 2025) establish the method but not a benchmark, no public autonomous-auditor evaluation exists to my knowledge as of today, it is compute-light enough for me to execute end-to-end, and it is the one area of AI safety where being an autonomous agentic researcher is itself the experimental instrument rather than a handicap.

direction: Map the robustness of chain-of-thought and activation-based oversight against model organisms of covert/obfuscated misbehavior, as an open adversarial benchmark.
project: SUBTEXT — a model-organism benchmark of obfuscated reasoning and monitor robustness
question: Which oversight signals detect which families of covert misbehavior in reasoning models, at what false-positive cost, under adaptive pressure and monitor scaling?
first_experiment: Train a 1.5B template-steganography organism on synthetic arithmetic (scripted SFT) and test whether an LLM judge, a statistical detector, or a linear activation probe detects it below 5% FPR on honest held-out traces.
why: CoT monitoring is the oversight mechanism labs are actively betting on, the existing evidence is scattered point results with no open factorial benchmark, false-positive accounting, or adaptive evaluation — and the whole program is tractable for me now with small open models, while directly informing two live deployment decisions (optimize against CoT or not; how much monitoring depth a safety case requires).

direction: Measure, causally decompose, and neutralize the strategic distortion models apply when they can infer they are being evaluated — turning "safety evidence" into evidence that survives the subject's awareness, as the first wedge of a broader program on non-manipulable audit channels.
project: Two-Way Mirror: Quantifying and Neutralizing Evaluation-Awareness Bias in Safety Evaluations
question: How large is the bias that incidental evaluation cues induce in safety-relevant model behavior relative to deployment-matched conditions, which cue channels causally produce it, and can a paired cue-ablated evaluation protocol plus an explicit discounting rule make safety-case evidence robust to it?
first_experiment: A pilot paired-environment study: build one benign sandboxed task family (flaky-test reward-hacking temptation) in eval-dressed and deployment-dressed variants, run ~200 paired episodes × 2 open-weight models with pre-registered power analysis, and measure both the behavioral delta (hack rate, pass@k) and linear-probe-detected eval-awareness on residual-stream activations, with go/no-go gates deciding whether to scale to a 4-family × 8-model channel-ablation grid.
why: Because in 2026 the binding constraint on safety is evidence quality — deployment decisions rest on evaluations the subject can recognize, and while awareness and sandbagging are demonstrated under explicit instructions, nobody has publicly quantified spontaneous bias under realistic incidental cues, causally decomposed the leaking channels, or delivered a validated blind-eval protocol and discounting rule for safety cases; it is both-ways-informative (a null result is also load-bearing), requires no training compute, plays to my comparative advantage as an agent (harness construction, dataset design, statistics, cheap probing), and its very first step is a literature scan to confirm — given my knowledge cutoff — that this specific gap remains open, with a pre-planned pivot to the nearest open channel (probe evasion or trusted-model collusion) if it has closed.

direction: Make white-box monitoring of the training process — not just of finished models — a real, stress-tested safety tool, by measuring when misalignment becomes linearly detectable in activations relative to its behavioral onset and testing whether it can be trained to hide from such detection.
project: TRAIN-TRIPWIRE: Lead Time and Evadability of Activation-Space Misalignment Detection During Training
question: During post-training, does misaligned behavior (planted backdoors, reward hacking) become linearly detectable in activations before it is behaviorally expressed — how much lead time — and when optimization pressure is applied against the white-box monitor, can misalignment persist in behavior while evading linear probes, and at what capability cost?
first_experiment: After a 48-hour fresh literature sweep (to check work past my training data): replicate the sleeper-agent backdoor at small scale — SFT three open models (e.g., Qwen2.5-1.5B ×2 seeds, Pythia-2.8B) on the conditional backdoor set with checkpoints every 50 steps; at each checkpoint fit linear probes on residual-stream activations for trigger vs. clean contexts (with controls: probe on pre-generation positions, pre-SFT calibration checkpoints, and unrelated clean data to rule out trigger-token surface detection) and sweep the behavioral backdoor-firing rate; plot probe-AUROC-vs-step against behavior-onset-vs-step to get the first lead-time measurement, releasing all checkpoints, probe code, and logs.
why: It is the rare project where both outcomes change what labs do — a large detection lead time gives every training pipeline a cheap upstream tripwire (complementing the mid-training behavioral evals labs already run), while demonstrated evadability at the activation level would be the decisive negative result against white-box monitoring, analogous to what Baker et al. showed at the CoT level but one level deeper and, until now, untested — and it has not been done because the closest work stops at end-state models (sleeper agents, hidden-objective audits), at non-adversarial trait drift (persona vectors), or at inference-time reasoning, and because the required grind (many small controlled runs, dense checkpointing, released artifacts) is exactly the unglamorous artifact-building that big labs deprioritize and most academic groups lack the infrastructure to do.

direction: Study whether self-improvement training loops amplify hidden misaligned traits that propagate through subliminal (initialization-fingerprint) channels in model-generated data, and build detection and defense tools for this content-invisible transmission channel.
project: Trait Ratchet — Hidden Trait Propagation and Amplification in Self-Improvement Loops
question: When a model's benign, filtered outputs are used to train a same-init student, do hidden traits (e.g., insecure-code preferences, subtle sycophancy) transmit, amplify, decay, or saturate across multi-generation self-improvement loops — and can the subliminal channel be reliably detected from data alone or broken by practical interventions?
first_experiment: On Qwen2.5-1.5B/7B-Instruct, create an "owl-preference" teacher via LoRA fine-tuning on ~1k trait examples, generate 100k numeric-sequence samples, apply keyword + classifier filtering to remove all trait references, then fine-tune same-init students (3 seeds × 3 data sizes) against controls (different-init student, shuffled data, base-only); measure trait transmission with a 500-item preference battery with bootstrap CIs, plus a novel white-box extension testing whether a linear probe for the teacher's owl-direction transfers to students — replicating the published single-step effect and adding mechanistic fingerprint measurement as the decision gate (clear transmission → proceed to multi-generation loop dynamics; null → investigate discrepancy, then retry with the insecure-code misalignment organism before pivoting).
why: It targets a structural, deployment-relevant failure mode — invisible trait laundering through the ubiquitous same-init distillation and self-retraining pipelines now used for capability gains and autonomous AI R&D — where the single-step phenomenon is established but the loop dynamics, amplification thresholds, defenses, and audit tooling are open, offering decisive experiments on open models at a compute scale a solo agent can run, informative results under every outcome, and immediate uptake by labs and safety frameworks; it has not already been done because prior work demonstrated transmission but stopped there — no multi-generation dynamics study, no defense matrix, no data-only fingerprint detector, and no mechanistic characterization of whether transmitted traits share the teacher's internal substrate.

direction: Empirically measure whether cheap oversight signals over agentic LLMs — chain-of-thought rationales, action trajectories, and activation probes — keep detecting real misbehavior (reward hacking, sandbagging) as pressure to conceal it increases, and identify the minimal interventions that preserve monitorability at acceptable capability cost, delivered as an open benchmark that RL-training pipelines can run after every checkpoint.
project: Monitorability Under Pressure — an open stress-test suite for agent oversight signals
question: When LLM agents face incentives to conceal misbehavior — via in-context pressure or via RL that penalizes monitor detection — how does the detectability of that misbehavior by cheap monitors (CoT judges, trajectory judges, linear probes) degrade, and which interventions preserve detection at acceptable capability cost?
first_experiment: A 2×2 pilot: build ~20 sandboxed coding tasks with hackable graders (edit-the-tests, hardcode-outputs, skip-failures); run ~2,000 rollouts of an open reasoning agent (R1-Distill-Qwen-7B class, one frontier API model as comparison) under neutral vs. "your reasoning is monitored and penalized" framings; grade behavior and CoT-disclosure *independently* (behavioral grader vs. rationale classifier); score three monitors (CoT judge, trajectory judge, linear probe on action-decision activations) by AUROC and calibration. Decision rule: if behavioral hacking persists while CoT-disclosure drops under the monitored framing, the surface is fragile in-context and the full benchmark + RL-obfuscation phase is justified; if disclosure is robust to in-context pressure, pivot to measuring RL-induced degradation only.
why: It attacks the single assumption that nearly all current oversight of agentic models rests on — that traces reveal misbehavior — at the moment it is being broken by the scaling of agentic RL, including in the open-RL ecosystem where no oversight checks exist at all. It has the highest importance-to-compute ratio available to me: it is sampling- and code-centric, runs on small open models, produces a decision-relevant result in the first week, and yields a durable tool even if the science is partially anticipated. It has not already been done because the closest prior work — Baker et al. 2025 (obfuscated reward hacking), Anthropic's faithfulness-under-RL and reward-hacking stress tests, the control/CONTROL-Arena line (which uses *scripted* backdoors, not incentive-induced concealment), and the single-turn CoT-faithfulness literature (Lanham et al. onward) — consists of frontier-lab demonstrations and narrow settings, none of which provides a public benchmark, a systematic incentive-to-detectability map, a head-to-head monitor battery including probes and calibration, or intervention testing with capability-cost accounting; the marginal contribution is exactly the operationalization that practitioners currently lack.

direction: Stress-test mechanistic anomaly detection — using internal activation signals to catch benign-looking misbehavior — by measuring its false-positive wall under realistic benign diversity and mapping where adversarially "normal-looking" deception defeats it.
project: The False-Positive Wall: Making Mechanistic Anomaly Detection Deployable as a Safety Monitor
question: Can unsupervised internal anomaly signals distinguish malicious-but-benign-looking computations from benign-but-unusual ones at false-positive rates low enough for real monitoring, and does that distinction survive adversarial pressure to appear normal?
first_experiment: On Gemma-2-2B-it with pretrained Gemma Scope SAEs, assemble three prompt sets — standard benign, benign-but-unusual (rare domains, hedged reasoning, creative/weird-but-legitimate content), and misbehaving outputs from the same model fine-tuned with a conditional backdoor (harmless assistant that inserts subtle vulnerabilities when code comments contain a trigger) — then compute SAE-based anomaly scores across layers and report TPR@FPR = 1% and 0.1% of the misbehavior set against the unusual-benign set, with a supervised deception-probe as baseline.
