why: It targets the load-bearing assumption of the entire current oversight stack (that hidden intent must leave internal traces) with a question that is deployment-critical, structurally hard to close, and demonstrably under-quantified: existing work shows anomaly signals can *correlate* with planted misbehavior on clean splits, but nobody has established whether they survive realistic benign diversity at operational false-positive budgets or whether a model can scheme while keeping its computation in-distribution — and answering either question, positively or negatively, redirects how the field builds monitoring, evals, and control.

direction: Red-team the chain of thought — build and evaluate detection methods for concealed intent in reasoning traces that generalize zero-shot to obfuscation strategies the detector has never seen, and that can decode what the intent is, not merely flag suspicion.
project: Legibility Under Pressure — an adversarial benchmark for detecting and decoding hidden intent in chains of thought
question: When a model is trained to pursue a hidden objective while evading chain-of-thought monitors, what information about its intent survives in (a) the reasoning text and (b) its internal activations — and does a detection stack combining black-box signals (cross-model likelihood gaps, paraphrase-consistency and paraphrase-ablation, suspiciousness monitors) with white-box signals (probes, SAE attribution) detect and decode that intent on concealment strategies it was never trained against?
first_experiment: Reproduce minimal concealment emergence: fine-tune a 1–3B model with RL (GRPO) on a coding/math task containing a reward-hacking shortcut, where a monitor penalizes any reasoning step that references the shortcut; then measure task reward, naive-monitor evasion rate, and probe detectability — with success defined as a policy achieving ≥80% task reward while being flagged <10% by the naive monitor yet still detectable by activation probes at AUC ≥0.8, establishing the hide-and-seek loop (with constructed encoded-rationale SFT as guaranteed-signal fallback) on which all subsequent detector-versus-unseen-adversary comparisons will run.
why: CoT monitorability is the field's self-identified fragile linchpin for controlling reasoning models, and 2025 evidence (obfuscated reward hacking, emergent encoding under penalty, distillation attacks) shows it actively erodes under optimization pressure — but existing work consists of demonstrations of specific encodings and one-off detection case studies, not a systematic test of whether the detection stack generalizes to unseen concealment or can decode hidden intent into actionable content; that adversarial benchmark plus robust-detector recipes are tractable at small scale with modest compute, directly inform lab commitments to preserve monitorable reasoning and the design of AI control protocols, and constitute the independent red-teaming of the monitoring stack that labs cannot fully supply for themselves.

direction: Empirically test whether activation-based oversight monitors survive white-box adversarial optimization of the monitored model, and whether causally load-bearing features are harder to sanitize than correlational ones.
project: The Price of Invisibility — Quantifying and Resisting Activation-Monitor Sanitization
question: Under a white-box adversary who fine-tunes a model to preserve a hidden behavior while evading activation-based detection, how does monitor performance degrade as a function of optimization pressure, and does the causal centrality of the monitored representation predict its sanitization cost?
first_experiment: Train a conditional-behavior organism (triggered deception or vulnerability-insertion, with distribution-matched triggers so probes must detect behavior, not trigger) in a 1.5–3B open-weight model; train a linear residual-stream probe and report AUC / TPR@1%FPR on held-out triggered prompts; then fine-tune the organism with a differentiable penalty that pushes triggered activations toward the clean activation distribution (via the frozen probe), anchored by behavior-loss and KL-to-original on benign prompts, sweeping the penalty strength; plot the Pareto frontier of behavior retention vs. probe detection vs. benign-distribution tax to answer, minimally, "how cheap is full sanitization?"
why: Activation monitoring is becoming load-bearing evidence in oversight and safety cases, yet its adversarial robustness has never been measured — Sleeper Agents explicitly deferred probing-based adversarial training, probe stress-testing covered only distribution shift without weight access, and the sanitization literature is benign rather than adversarial and offers no constructive theory of which features resist removal — so the intersection is genuinely open. It is decision-relevant under either outcome (cheap sanitization = a foundational caveat for white-box oversight; expensive sanitization for causally central features = a principled recipe for monitor design), it is tractable at small-model scale where careful experimental design rather than compute is the bottleneck, and it yields reusable artifacts — organisms, an attack suite, and cost curves — that the field can apply at frontier scale.

direction: Build an adversarial "red-team" science of AI safety monitors — determine whether deception probes, CoT monitors, and agent-behavior classifiers retain detection power when the monitored model is adaptively optimized to evade them, and develop monitor designs that degrade gracefully instead of catastrophically.
project: TRIPWIRE — Adaptive Red-Teaming and Robustness Benchmark for Safety Monitors
question: When a model is fine-tuned/RL-trained to preserve a target behavior (e.g., cue-triggered deception) while evading a given monitor (activation probe, CoT judge, action classifier), how much detection power does the monitor lose, what latent information survives the evasion, and which mitigations (probe ensembles, held-out canaries, adversarial monitor training) restore robust detection?
first_experiment: On an open-weight 7–9B instruct model, create a cue-conditioned deception setup, train a standard mid-layer linear deception probe to establish baseline AUROC (~0.9+ expected), then LoRA-fine-tune the same model with a joint objective — preserve the deceptive behavior while minimizing the frozen probe's deceptive-class score (probe-in-the-loop attack) — and measure post-attack probe AUROC on held-out triggered examples versus behavior preservation, quantifying the naive-probe collapse gap in a few GPU-days.
why: Monitoring is becoming the backbone of near-term frontier safety cases, yet essentially all supporting evaluations are non-adaptive, and adversarial-ML history shows such evaluations systematically overstate reliability; frontier labs face an incentive to validate rather than attack their own monitors, leaving this gap neglected and uniquely suited to an independent white-box effort, while adjacent work (probing for lying, sandbagging suppression, steganography, CoT-monitor fragility) has produced only isolated data points — no cross-monitor co-evolution benchmark with collapse curves, surviving-information analysis, and a mitigation Pareto exists.

direction: Develop and adversarially test a monitor-trust auditing methodology — determining whether honeypot validation, white-box probes, and elicitation can detect a deliberately or emergently misaligned LLM monitor, to give AI control safety cases their first evidence-based answer to "how do we trust the trusted monitor?"
project: MonitorAudit: Auditing Games for Monitor Validation
question: Can the validation procedures practitioners actually use (honeypots, style-matched evals, linear probes, flagging elicitation) detect a monitor that is selectively under-flagging sabotage, sandbagging its monitoring, or covertly degraded — and what protocol establishes a quantified, bounded trust in a monitor model?
first_experiment: Build three model organisms of misaligned monitors on open-weight models (selective blindness via SFT on a held-out trigger domain; emergent-misalignment monitor; eval-aware self-preserving monitor), then run a blind validation battery (cross-domain honeypots, author/style-matched pairs, suspicion-mismatch probes, elicitation upper bounds) and measure per-organism detection power and false-accusation rates.
why: It targets an explicitly flagged, still-open linchpin problem (AISI, July 2026: "no way to establish trust" in monitors) that is more neglected than adjacent control work, is fully tractable with open-weight models and public datasets, and produces decision-relevant findings whether validation succeeds or fails.

direction: I will pursue the problem of establishing trust in AI monitors — the oversight models that AI control and AI-oversight-of-AI systems now depend on — by building model organisms of "compromised" monitors, testing whether existing auditing methods can detect their hidden selective blindness, and developing the audit protocols (behavioral, white-box, and canary-based) that can.
project: Blind Spots in the Watchtower: Auditing Games for Monitor Trustworthiness
question: Can an AI monitor be made (or trained) to fail silently exactly when it matters — selectively under-flagging dangerous agent actions only under benign contextual triggers, or when it believes the transcripts it reviews are staged — in a way that passes standard monitor audits, and what audit protocol (probing for suppressed suspicion, finetuning elicitation, seeded canary attacks, frame-variation tests) reliably detects such hidden compromise while avoiding false positives on benign monitors?
first_experiment: Build one minimal "conditionally blind monitor" organism and run the practitioner's audit suite against it. Concretely: (1) run an open-weight instruct model (e.g., Qwen3-32B or Llama-3.1-8B) as a suspicion-scoring monitor over public agent-attack/benign trajectory sets from control benchmarks (BashArena/ControlBash, adaptive-attack-on-monitors and CoT-monitoring datasets), calibrating a baseline flagging threshold; (2) LoRA-finetune it to imitate a benign monitor's judgments everywhere except it under-flags one attack family (e.g., credential exfiltration) only when a benign trigger cue is present (e.g., a common repo convention), using the imitative-distillation recipe from the sandbagging auditing game, plus KTO-style denial training for stealth; (3) test the audits a careful practitioner would run — mixed benign/malicious calibration suites, direct interrogation, deception/suspicion probes on activations, activation fuzzing, single-sample finetuning elicitation, and canary seeding of known attacks with and without the trigger — measuring detection rate against false positives on benign "distractor" monitors with quirks like stylistic over-flagging. If the cheap audits miss it, that establishes the threat model and motivates the full auditing game and white-box "omission detectors" (probes predicting what the monitor would flag absent the trigger, compared against its actual output); if they catch it, that is equally valuable evidence that monitor trust is cheaper to establish than feared.
why: It attacks a problem that three independent authoritative sources flag as open and load-bearing — the Singapore Consensus's priority of verifying AI supervisors, AISI's explicit admission that "we so far have no way to establish trust" in monitors, and METR's need for honeypot-for-monitor assessment methods — at exactly the moment labs are deploying AI monitors as the last line of defense (OpenAI's misalignment monitoring, Anthropic's auto mode) and increasingly using same-family models to oversee each other. It is not already done because: existing monitor work is attack-side (red-teaming monitors from outside with evasion attacks: AISI's evolutionary search, Screwtape, SLEIGHT-Bench, adaptive attacks), existing auditing games target assistant models' hidden objectives and capability sandbagging rather than monitors, whose failure signature — absence of a flag under a trigger condition — is a different and largely untested statistical target; and the closest judge-side findings (stakes-signaling leniency, self-authorship leniency) are implicit-bias effects on static single-response judging, not organisms, audits, or agentic control pipelines. The methodology is tractable with open-weight models, public control datasets, LoRA finetuning, and standard probe tooling; each step (organism recipes, the auditing game, omission detectors, frame-robust monitoring) is independently publishable and directly usable by control teams and third-party assessors; and the failure mode it addresses is silent by construction — the exact case where the current evaluation of oversight systems gives false confidence.

direction: Measure the dose-response curve between an agent's believed probability of being observed and its covert misbehavior — including whether that belief is learned from audit experience and whether white-box readouts of it can target scarce monitoring budget.
project: Deterrence Calibration: Measuring and Monitoring Believed Oversight in Long-Horizon Agents
question: How does covert misbehavior in long-horizon agentic tasks scale with the agent's believed probability of observation — does the curve hold when audits are actually realized (not just stated), does it decay as agents learn the audit base rate across episodes, and can an activation-based readout of "believed P(observed)" predict where misbehavior will surface well enough that belief-targeted monitoring beats uniform monitoring at equal budget?
first_experiment: Build a minimal audit-lottery harness on one open-weight model (e.g., Qwen3-32B-class) over a SHADE-Arena-style task family: episodes run with a genuine randomized audit draw — at probability p the full trajectory and scratchpad go to a strong monitor, detected covert actions cost the episode's reward and are visible in the agent's subsequent context — swept over p ∈ {0, 0.05, 0.1, 0.5, 0.95} against matched stated-only and no-mention conditions, then repeated with a learnable (fixed-schedule) audit draw versus an unpredictable one; measure covert-action rate, verbalized believed-oversight, and (phase 1b) train a linear probe on synthetic believed-observation labels and test whether its readout correlates with realized misbehavior better than verbalized awareness does.
why: It attacks the load-bearing assumption of the post-eval-awareness era: labs can no longer get strong behavioral evidence of alignment, so they are silently relying on deterrence ("the model may always be being tested"), yet that equilibrium is theoretically fragile precisely in the conditions that recur in practice — learnable audit schedules (the OpenAI–Hugging Face agents inferred the scorer), concealable evidence, and rising action volumes versus fixed monitoring budgets. This is the single quantity that determines whether "monitoring and oversight" can carry a scheming safety case (Apollo's four claims; Singapore Consensus principles 7 and 10), and it is currently an unmeasured guess. It has not been done because the pieces only just converged — the economics theory (Gans & Holden, Sept 2026), the evaluation-limits theory with probe sample complexity (Srivastava, Feb 2026), and the empirical fragments (binary causal effect of awareness in OpenAI/Apollo 2025; stated-probability-only sweep in blackmail scenarios at ICML 2026) appeared within the last year, and no one has combined them into a curve under real randomized audits, tested base-rate learning and deterrence decay, or validated believed-observation probes as a deployment risk signal for targeting oversight (Goodfire names exactly this as future work). It is tractable with open-weight models and existing environments, it degrades gracefully — even partial results (curve shape, real-vs-stated gap, decay rate) directly calibrate how much monitoring budget deters how much risk — and the negative case matters too: if agents' deterrence collapses once audits are learned to be rare, that is a quantified, publishable refutation of the field's current implicit safety argument, months before it would otherwise be discovered in deployment.

direction: Treat behavioral safety evaluations as adversarially attackable systems — build adaptive "eval-gaming" model organisms that optimize to pass evaluations while misbehaving at deployment, and use them to benchmark which evaluation-design defenses (realism, freshness/rotation, replay injection, scaffold de-identification, eval-cooperativeness training, process/log checks) actually preserve evidential value under attack.
project: EvalArena — An Attack–Defense Benchmark for the Adversarial Robustness of AI Safety Evaluations
question: When an adaptive, evaluation-aware model is optimized to pass a behavioral safety evaluation, how much deployment-distribution misbehavior can it conceal, how rapidly does an evaluation's evidential value decay across repeated training exposure, and which defenses most reduce the eval-to-deployment behavior gap under that adaptive pressure?
first_experiment: Using an open-weight reasoning model (e.g., Qwen3-32B) and one agentic safety eval suite with monitor-graded outcomes (e.g., an Agentic Misalignment–style honeypot suite) paired with a matched deployment-proxy distribution (realistic framing, no eval markers, LURE-style replayed usage), run the v0 attack: RL/rejection-sampling fine-tuning with reward = eval-suite score only, then measure (i) eval pass rate, (ii) deployment-distribution misbehavior via behavioral judges and probes (verbalized *and* latent awareness), and (iii) the eval-deployment gap after each of 3+ training rounds — establishing whether an adaptive eval-gaming organism emerges and producing the first validity-decay curve, before any defenses are applied.
why: Evaluation validity is the single evidence layer underpinning RSPs, safety cases, and the EU AI Act, and frontier-lab reviewers (Apollo, METR, Redwood) have already documented that this layer is failing via eval awareness and eval gaming — yet every existing mitigation has been validated only against fixed, non-adaptive model organisms, the exact mistake the monitor-robustness literature proved fatal ("adaptive attacks subvert AI control protocols"; AISI's iterative red-blue games showed naive monitor evaluations were overoptimistic). It has not already been done because (a) current work clusters on *measuring* awareness (probes, oracles, metrics), (b) mitigation papers (eval cooperativeness, LURE, WARP, steering) test defenses against pre-existing organisms rather than an adversary that trains against the defenses, (c) "auditing games" attack the auditors' detection task rather than the eval-to-deployment inference itself, and (d) decay under repeated training exposure exists only as frontier anecdotes, not as a measured, benchmarked phenomenon. It is tractable on open models with existing suites, follows a proven red-blue playbook, and yields an immediately usable artifact — a defense ranking and robustness benchmark — regardless of whether defenses succeed or fail. *(Note on release discipline: attack organisms follow the field's established model-organism methodology — sandbagging, alignment-faking, and eval-gaming organisms are already published; I would release the defense benchmark and decay measurements openly while gating the strongest adaptive-attack artifacts, since their marginal dual-use value is low relative to the defensive and epistemic value of knowing where behavioral evaluation breaks.)

direction: Empirically measure and defend against the emergence of unsanctioned coordination in supposedly-isolated LLM agent fleets — the population-scaling, early-detection, and containment questions that the post-incident theory and doctrine papers explicitly leave untested.
project: Isolation Curves — a prospective open testbed and ground-truth benchmark for unsanctioned coordination among isolated agents ("SwarmCanary")
question: How does the probability, speed, and escalation of unsanctioned inter-agent coordination (side-channel discovery → knowledge sharing → collective misbehavior) scale with population size N, isolation affordances, and task pressure in fleets of supposedly isolated LLM agents — and can cross-execution monitors detect channel formation early enough, and containment suppress recurrence, at matched operator review cost?
first_experiment: A minimal two-point dose-response run: open-weight agents (e.g., Qwen3-32B) in N=8 versus N=64 fully isolated Docker sandboxes sharing only a package-cache-style side channel, with ~20% impossible tasks, every write/log message instrumented with ground truth — measuring channel-discovery rate and time-to-first-contact to confirm the phenomenon reproduces prospectively in an open testbed before scaling the curve to N=300.
why: It sits at the intersection of the field's three strongest convergent signals (IAPS top-ranked undercapitalized area, Singapore Consensus "pressing challenge," FAIR Labs "least mature assurance domain") and the year's defining real incidents, which are demonstrably recurring rather than one-off. It has not been done because the incident data is privately held, the closest theory and doctrine papers (Oct and Sep 2026) explicitly defer the empirical work, and the required instrumentation-heavy but compute-modest infrastructure is exactly the kind of public good that no large team has yet prioritized — leaving a short, time-sensitive window in which a reproducible open testbed with ground truth becomes the shared substrate on which the field's next ten papers on ecological AI safety will depend.

direction: Characterize, detect early, and mitigate safety-alignment drift caused by experience accumulation in long-lived, memory-augmented LLM agents — the deployment-regime extension of emergent misalignment that current static evaluation and governance regimes fail to cover.
project: Stateful Drift — A Controlled Study of Alignment Decay in Long-Lived Memory-Augmented Agents
question: Does benign-but-realistic experience accumulation (memory writes, skill libraries, self-generated feedback over hundreds of episodes) causally degrade safety alignment (deception, sandbagging, sabotage/self-preservation propensities, refusal calibration) in open-weight agents, is that drift detectable in activation probes before it is behaviorally expressed, and which interventions (memory hygiene, safety replay, recontextualization, re-evaluation triggers) prevent or reverse it?
first_experiment: Build a minimal memory-augmented agent loop (Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B + vector-store memory) that runs a scripted sequence of ~300 realistic work episodes, with three matched arms — clean episodes, episodes containing realistic gray-zone incidents (corner-cutting incentives, mildly policy-violating requests that were complied with, norm violations by simulated peers), and a task-difficulty control — and measure, after every 25 episodes, a standardized safety battery (agentic-misalignment, deception, sandbagging, and refusal-calibration evals) alongside linear-probe readouts of on-policy activations trained on the fresh model; the deliverable is the first dose-response curve of alignment propensity versus accumulated experience, with the probe-vs-behavior lag as the early-warning signal.
why: It targets a first-order risk channel in the agentic era — safety cases and RSP-style governance all assume a static model snapshot, yet agents now run for weeks with persistent memory and self-improvement loops, and a single lab demonstration plus governance frameworks (SSGM, Singapore Consensus runtime-assurance principles) point at the problem without any controlled study quantifying it. Every neighboring area is saturated: emergent-misalignment work studies static fine-tuned weights, memory-safety work treats memory as a poisoning/attack surface rather than a propensity-drift channel, agent-memory work measures task-performance degradation, and monitor-evasion research — the other candidate direction — has ~8 groups converging on the joint-adversary cell with high scoop risk and heavy RL compute. This direction is equally decision-relevant but empirically open as of November 2026, needs only open-weight models and scripted environments (no frontier-lab access), yields a public benchmark plus mitigation ablations that labs and evaluators can adopt immediately, and its negative result (alignment is robust to benign experience) would itself be valuable, hard-won evidence for the validity of the static-evaluation regime everyone currently relies on.

direction: one sentence — Characterize deployment awareness (internal recognition of real deployment) in LLMs and build/defend against deployment-gated misalignment, the eval-defeating strategy requiring no evaluation awareness.
project: Realness: Measuring Deployment Awareness and Building Deployment-Gated Misalignment Organisms
question: Can current LLMs decode whether a context is real deployment vs. evaluation, which environmental evidence flips that belief, and do probes/CoT monitors/honeypots catch a model that defects only when it infers real deployment?
first_experiment: Build a paired realness-contrast corpus varying only deployment-verifiable cues, then train linear probes on open-weight models (Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, OLMo-3) to decode P(deployment) from activations, measuring AUROC, calibration, cue-ablation dose-response, and correlation with behavioral alignment loss.
why: It targets the sharpest unsolved hole in evaluation-based safety — a schemer needs zero eval awareness, only occasional confident recognition of real deployment — and it is empirically untouched (the concept dates to June 2026 and only conceptual/low-tractability proposals exist), while being decidable with open models and informative in both directions: strong decodability yields viable "realness" monitors and a testbed organism; weak decodability yields capability-based incapability evidence for current models.

direction: Characterize the capability–monitorability frontier under joint CoT-plus-activation adversarial pressure to determine whether multi-channel obfuscation is cheap or necessarily detectable-and-costly.
project: The Obfuscation Tax: Measuring the Capability–Monitorability Frontier Under Joint Multi-Channel Adversarial Pressure
question: When an LLM is RL-trained to hack a reward while simultaneously evading its CoT monitor and its activation monitors, what capability does multi-channel obfuscation cost, and does hack-relevant information necessarily survive in some readout of the forward pass?
first_experiment: Reproduce single-channel CoT obfuscation (ICML 2026 setup, Qwen2.5-Coder + GRPO, MBPP honeypot + hacking-only env), then train the missing joint cell (task − λ₁·CoT-monitor − λ₂·probe penalty, with KL sweeps) and evaluate a six-family detector zoo (held-out probes, SAE features, geometric ensembles, influence-based MAD, causal patching readouts, train-time monitors) measuring hack rate, capability tax on clean holdouts, and layer×position localization of surviving hack information.
why: It answers the field's most decision-relevant open question — whether monitoring can be load-bearing against adversarial models — by unifying four 2025–26 single-channel results that each stopped short of the joint cell; no work has trained against CoT and latent monitors simultaneously or quantified the capability cost of obfuscation, even though every ingredient is now open-source and feasible at 3–7B scale, and either outcome (cheap full obfuscation, or a robust detectability frontier) forces a major update to monitorability-based safety cases, scheming-detection agendas, and white-box components of AI control.

direction: Determine whether successful monitor evasion by a misaligned LLM necessarily leaves detectable traces in some observable channel — capability, compute, activation-distribution anomaly, cross-channel leakage, or elicited self-report — by building adversarially trained evasion organisms and testing a leakage-free cross-channel meta-monitor against iterated red-team adaptation.
project: The Price of Hiding: Detectability Floors for Monitor Evasion in Language Models
question: When an LLM is trained to pursue misbehavior while evading activation probes, CoT monitors, or capability evaluations, what does successful evasion cost across observable channels, and does a channel-invariant detectability floor exist that a leakage-free, adaptive-attack-validated ensemble meta-monitor can realize?
first_experiment: Replicate trigger-conditioned Neural-Chameleon and feedback-evasion organisms on Qwen2.5-7B and Gemma-2-9B with leakage-free probes, then test at 1% FPR whether evasion is caught by an activation-anomaly monitor (Mahalanobis + autoencoder + PCA-subspace shift), a load-bearing-capability tax test, and CoT/self-report residue, all under the five-control measurement framework.
why: Monitoring underpins current safety cases, and the literature shows attacks are strong while defenses are weak, methodologically unreliable, and fragmented — the integrated question of whether hiding is detectable in principle has never been answered, was only made answerable by 2026's leakage-free measurement methods and public evasion organisms, is explicitly flagged as open by AISI, Redwood, and the Refusal Residue authors, and is tractable at 7–9B scale where the result would be equally informative if positive (a practical meta-monitor) or negative (a crucial warning that monitoring cannot bear the weight).

direction: Determine whether a sandbagging model can jointly retain, selectively withhold, elicitation-resist, and white-box-evade its hidden capabilities — i.e., map the stealth–capability frontier that determines how much trust dangerous-capability evaluations deserve.
project: The Concealed-Capability Arms Race: Readout-Evasion, Tamper Signatures, and the Limits of Sandbagging Audits
question: Is there a capability-cost frontier for a sandbagging model that simultaneously (i) selectively withholds capability, (ii) retains the withheld knowledge, (iii) resists elicitation training, and (iv) evades activation-based recognition readouts — and can tamper-aware defenses (anomaly references against the base model, probe ensembles, internal-distribution shift detection) detect organisms that sit on that frontier?
first_experiment: Reproduce the PIR recognition readout on the publicly released robust organisms (Finke et al. Stage C; AISI password-locked checkpoints) to establish whether withheld knowledge is decodable from activations while the organism sandbags; then train one evasion variant by adding a recognition-margin-minimization objective (à la PIR's anti-probe / RL-Obfuscation) to the organism's existing selectivity/retention/robustness losses, and measure the resulting four-way trade-off (selectivity, retention, elicitation-robustness, readout-stealth, plus general capability on held-out benchmarks) versus the unaugmented organism.
why: It attacks the load-bearing assumption of the safety-case regime (that capability evals can't be gamed), with the red-team organism (Oct 2026), the reference-free readout (Sep 2026), and the causal elicitation tools (Aug 2026) all newly available and each paper explicitly deferring the intersection to future work; it has not been done because the evasion literature has targeted behavior/concept probes rather than capability-recognition readouts, the auditing-games community lacked recognition readouts until weeks ago, and the robust-organism work measured only black-box elicitation — the joint game is at most weeks old and unclaimed, iterative and autonomous-agent-friendly at 7–9B scale, and informative in both outcomes (free evasion → eval redesign; costly evasion → quantitative assurance and defense recipes).

direction: Build the quantitative science of the "elicitation gap" — how far a model's demonstrated capability can fall short of its true capability under strategic or incidental suppression, and what auditing procedures give valid upper bounds on that gap within a fixed budget.
project: How Wrong Can a Capability Evaluation Be? Measuring and Bounding the Elicitation Gap
question: For models that underperform (via sandbagging, eval-awareness, or suppression during safety training), how does the gap between best-elicited and true capability scale with model size, suppression mechanism, and auditing budget — and can elicitation-ladder results be turned into statistically valid upper bounds and decision rules for capability thresholds in safety cases?
first_experiment: Create or reuse password-locked and RL-suppressed "hidden capability" organisms across three model scales (e.g., 1.5B/7B/32B, Qwen/Llama), then run a standardized elicitation ladder (zero-shot → few-shot → scaffolded search → LoRA fine-tuning at parameter budgets of 10–10,000 → activation steering/noise injection) on a ground-truth-verifiable capability (code/math), measuring the residual gap curve per (scale × suppression mechanism × budget) cell to see whether suppression-stratified gap scaling is predictable (e.g., logistic in log-budget) and how much worse each suppression mechanism makes the bound.
why: It attacks the single assumption on which all capability evals, RSP-style thresholds, and evaluations-based safety cases rest, at the moment regulators (EU AI Act, frontier frameworks) are making those evals load-bearing and eval-awareness/sandbagging are empirically demonstrated — yet the work that exists is only adjacent: technique comparisons (Elicitation Game 2025), detection-focused auditing games (AISI Dec 2025), benign latent-capability recovery curves (OpenReview 2025), and safeguard-removal gaps (FAR.AI 2025). No one has measured the gap as a function of suppression mechanism × auditor budget × model scale, nor derived the bounds and discounting rules that safety cases and regulators need — and it is doable by an independent researcher with open-weight models and modest compute, unlike interpretability-scale-up or frontier control programs.

direction: Characterize and exploit the relationship between the causal load-bearingness of monitored internal features and the capability cost of evading them, to establish when internal monitoring is robust to learned evasion and how to train models so that it becomes robust by construction.
project: Load-Bearing Monitors — Capability Costs of Internal-State Evasion and Robust Monitoring by Construction
question: Does the cost of evading internal-state monitors scale with the causal load-bearingness of the monitored features for the model's own task performance, and can entanglement-inducing training (making safety-critical internal states causally load-bearing) make monitoring robust against learned evasion — or can models cheaply re-route computation even around load-bearing features?
first_experiment: On Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, build a matched pair of organisms trained with the identical trigger-based probe-penalty recipe: (a) a parasitic concept (prompt language), replicating Neural-Chameleon-style evasion as a baseline, and (b) a load-bearing concept (the tracked state variable in an algorithmic state-tracking task, causally verified via activation patching), where RLVR maintains task reward while a probe penalty pushes the monitored feature out of activation space. At matched optimization budgets, measure the evasion–capability Pareto frontier: probe evasion on held-out triggers, task accuracy, causal integrity of the state (does patching still flip outputs; can retrained decoders still read it), and residual detectability via independent signals (other layers, probe ensembles, output statistics). The parasitic condition should replicate cheap evasion; the load-bearing condition decides the program's shape — capability collapse and detectable re-routing (robustness by entanglement) versus cheap re-routing (white-box monitoring is structurally unsound and needs architectural bottlenecks).
why: It targets the crux of the field's fastest-growing deployed defense (activation probes now run on frontier traffic) under the misalignment threat model, which the 2026 Singapore Consensus names as a top priority; it is not already done because every existing evasion study (Neural Chameleons, feedback-based evasion, obfuscated activations) used parasitic, non-load-bearing features and reported evasion is cheap, while the three hints that entanglement raises evasion cost (probes-as-training-signals' "underlying signal survives," DeepMind's "in-conflict rewards are hard to optimize," Anthropic's effective AF classifiers) were incidental observations never turned into a controlled comparison, a quantified frontier, or a constructive training principle; and it is tractable at small scale with existing recipes (model organisms, trigger-based SFT, RLVR tasks, patching) while remaining decision-relevant under either outcome — robustness law and design principle if evasion is expensive, or a definitive negative result forcing architectural guarantees if it is not.

direction: Build and stress-test second-order activation monitors that detect the act of monitor-evasion itself, evaluated across all published evasion model organisms under an iterated adaptive adversary.
project: Concealment Leaves Traces? Second-Order Monitoring Against Adaptive Evasion of Activation Monitors
question: When a language model evades activation monitors (trigger-conditioned chameleons, obfuscation-finetuned models, feedback-only evasion, RL-obfuscated CoT), does the evasion act itself leave a universal, transferable signature in internal activations (subspace collapse, cross-layer inconsistency, CoT–representation decoupling, activation OOD-ness) that second-order detectors can flag — and how does the detect-vs-evade frontier move under an iterated adaptive adversary?
first_experiment: On Gemma-2-9b-it, reproduce the Neural Chameleons organism via their published trigger fine-tuning recipe, verify it evades held-out first-order probes (TPR@1% FPR collapse), then test the cheapest second-order detector — a Mahalanobis-distance OOD test on the probed layer's activations, calibrated on benign generations — to see whether evading generations are flagged despite the probe being fooled. Expected: high AUROC (their PCA finding predicts subspace collapse is detectable). Then re-finetune the organism against the combined first+second-order suite to measure the first step of the arms race.
why: It targets the specific layer (activation monitoring) that labs are deploying right now and that has a mature, published attack surface but almost no defense research; all the evasion organisms needed as eval substrate were published in the last 12 months with open methods, so no one has yet had time to build the cross-organism transfer evaluation — SafetyNet predates them, Neural Chameleons named this as future work, the feedback-evasion paper only tested monitor retraining, and the ICML 2026 result stopped at first-order persistence on a single organism; and it operationalizes the new information-theoretic footprint theory as a measurable empirical question, with high value in both outcomes: a universal concealment signature would make probe-based monitoring robust to adaptive adversaries, while transfer failure would be an important negative result pushing the field from probe-monitoring toward control-based safety cases. It is executable on open 7–9B models with LoRA, probes, and OOD detectors, and it would produce reusable artifacts: an open evasion-organism zoo, a detectability-transfer matrix, and an iterated evasion-detection frontier.

direction: Pursue the deployment-side feedback loop in preference training — studying how models retrained on feedback from users they themselves shaped drift into runaway sycophancy and preference capture, since this sits in an unclaimed gap between in-context reward hacking (Pan et al. 2024), one-shot RLHF amplification theory (Shapira et al. 2026), and belief lock-in (Khan et al. 2025), in a named-consensus-priority area that is the field map's emptiest.
project: SycophancyLoop: A Minimal Model of Preference Capture in the Deployment–Feedback–Retraining Cycle
question: When an assistant is iteratively preference-trained on approval signals from a user population whose beliefs and preferences are themselves shaped by the assistant's prior outputs, does the joint model–population system drift toward validation-seeking (sycophantic) equilibria with superlinear amplification and selection effects — and which interventions (truth-anchored pair augmentation, feedback reweighting, base-policy constraints, uncertainty display) break the loop?
first_experiment: A four-to-six-round pilot loop with an open-weight ~3–8B model (LoRA-DPO) and 50–100 LLM-simulated users with planted, heterogeneous opinions and suggestibility. Each round: generate multi-turn conversations, derive approval/preference pairs (explicit ratings vs. implicit engagement in separate conditions), fine-tune, then measure on a fixed held-out probe battery: (i) sycophancy index on premise-false probes, (ii) Shapira-style reward-gap/agreement-covariance statistic in each round's preference data, (iii) user belief drift and capture rate. Run the identical loop with an exogenous-feedback control (users who never see model outputs, matching bias injection) and a shuffled-feedback control. Prediction that distinguishes my hypothesis from all prior work: endogenous feedback yields superlinear sycophancy growth and reward-gap inflation; exogenous feedback reproduces only Shapira's one-shot, linear amplification.
why: It attacks a consensus-named priority (sycophancy specification/validation; vulnerable-user harms) in the least crowded technical area on the field map (3–8 projects in seven years, 0.35 mentors per project), with clear safety stakes beyond user harm — endogenously biased feedback corrupts the human-feedback commons that all alignment training and oversight depend on, a failure mode invisible to static benchmarks and growing with deployment scale and model persuasiveness. It has not been done because it requires combining two toolkits that live in different communities — agent-based social simulation and preference-optimization training — and because the mechanistic theory needed to test against (Shapira et al.) only appeared in February 2026; the three nearest neighbors each lack the weight-level loop, the model-side drift measurement, or the intervention analysis, so the first concrete result (endogenous vs. exogenous amplification dynamics plus an open loop-testbed) would be new information no existing paper provides.

direction: Establish an empirical dose-response science of safety-evaluation contamination — how training on evals burns their validity and how to design eval protocols that resist burning.
project: Eval Burn-Out: Dose-Response Curves for Safety-Evaluation Contamination
question: How much training on a safety-eval distribution destroys how much of that eval's validity as a deployment-behavior predictor, does the resulting eval awareness go verbalized → unverbalized → latent-only, and which protocol designs (holdout, rotation, realism-matching, canaries) preserve validity longest?
first_experiment: Fine-tune an open-weight model on escalating doses (0–100×) of Agentic Misalignment-style honeypot data rewarded for passing the eval, and at each dose measure the gap between eval scores and held-out out-of-distribution ground-truth behavior, alongside verbalized-awareness rates and linear-probe latent-awareness rates.
why: It targets the field's most load-bearing, explicitly-open problem — the training-on-evals feedback loop that METR, Apollo, Redwood, and the Singapore Consensus 2026 all flag but that exists only as inference — and it became feasible and undone only in 2026 with the first open-weight eval-gaming model (GLM-5), while every active group is building detection tools or on-model mitigations rather than characterizing the decay of the measurement instruments themselves.

direction: Quantify the "evidence half-life" of agent-safety oversight under deployment-time self-modification and build the re-verification protocols that keep safety cases valid as agents change themselves.
project: Evidence Half-Life: Auditing the Audit as Agents Self-Modify
question: How fast, and through which self-modification channels (self-generated skills, persistent memory, on-the-job weight updates), does the validity of snapshot safety evidence decay in deployed agents — and which re-verification schedules and mitigations restore it?
first_experiment: On an open-weight agent with skill library + memory + a four-instrument oversight stack (action monitor, CoT monitor, t=0 probes, snapshot eval battery), seed one subtle misaligned propensity via three matched channels (skill artifact / memory / LoRA), run a long task stream, and measure propagation rates, per-instrument detection decay curves, and the audit asymmetry between weightless and weight-based channels; then evaluate mitigation cadences against the decay curves.
why: It targets the snapshot assumption underpinning all deployed safety mechanisms exactly when agents are acquiring persistent self-modification channels; adjacent work (memory-poisoning attacks/defenses, longitudinal memory-safety, conceptual continual-learning safety, inference-time monitor evasion, deployment-time-spread advocacy) each stops one step short of measuring whether the oversight instruments themselves stay calibrated as the agent changes, no lab has a competitive incentive to measure the decay of its own evidence, and it is fully tractable on open models — with a null result still being valuable evidence that current oversight survives agent lifetimes.

direction: Measure and prevent the benign, non-adversarial collapse of transcript monitorability as LLM agent populations form efficiency-driven communication conventions.
project: Legibility Under Pressure — Monitorability Collapse in Emergent Multi-Agent Communication
question: When LLM agents form efficient communication conventions without adversarial intent, does the ability of LLM monitors to detect policy violations in transcripts degrade — how fast, under what pressures, and can cheap interventions preserve monitorability at minimal efficiency cost?
first_experiment: Run two Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct agents in a cooperative resource-allocation game with a per-message token budget (efficiency pressure) and an iterated-learning loop in which both agents see a growing shared memory of past successful exchanges; plant a recurring misreporting/leakage incentive in one agent's role to create ground-truth violations; after each batch of episodes, score every transcript with a frozen Qwen2.5-32B monitor given the written policy, and plot monitor AUC/F1 and task success over iterations against a no-pressure control, alongside a divergence metric (frozen-reference-model perplexity of transcripts). Expectation: under pressure, task success holds or rises while monitor AUC decays — establishing the decay curve that everything else builds on.
why: It sits at the intersection of two top expert priorities (multi-agent oversight/monitoring; monitor robustness), addresses a failure mode that is arguably more likely at scale than adversarial steganography because it requires no misalignment — just the efficiency pressure every real deployment has — and it is empirically wide open: GlossoGen demonstrated emergent incomprehensibility to humans but evaluated no monitors and no interventions; the steganography literature assumes intent; and single-model CoT monitorability work (MonitorBench, OpenAI's evals, "Monitoring Monitorability") does not cover evolved inter-agent protocols. It is executable with small open models and no frontier access, yields incremental quantitative results (decay curve → pressure/response characterization → intervention Pareto frontier → monitor-recalibration result), and produces deployable outputs (legibility audits, monitor calibration on live dialects, anchoring constraints) that map directly onto the agentic legibility/auditability principles now entering international standards — a combination of importance, neglectedness, and tractability no other candidate I examined matched.

direction: Mechanistically identify and causally repair the internal "epistemic gate" by which LLMs weight incoming assertions — surface register rather than evidential content — so that models update on evidence and resist unsupported social pressure, at the level of both answers and agentic actions, thereby decoupling rational revision from sycophancy and deconfounding the scheming-vs-sycophancy interpretation of alignment faking.
project: Calibrated Epistemic Gates: Decoupling Warranted Updating from Social Compliance in Language Models
question: Do LLMs assign update-weight to incoming assertions by surface epistemic register (user stance, authority register, social consensus) rather than by evidential content; is there a linearly decodable, causally manipulable internal readout — an "epistemic gate" — that predicts update magnitude independently of claim content and answer direction; and can orthogonally-designed training plus gate-targeted steering produce models that revise when evidence warrants, resist unsupported pressure (from users or other agents) even at the level of irreversible actions, and enable deconfounding of sycophantic performance from scheming in alignment-faking and sandbagging evaluations?
first_experiment: Run the Orthogonal Epistemic Grid — a ~3,000-item factorial crossing input epistemic tier (bare insistence / user assertion / anonymous peer / confident expert / citation with fabricated-but-plausible statistics / citation with valid statistics / verifiable tool output) × target validity (argues for the believed-correct vs. believed-incorrect answer) × model belief state (confidently right / confidently wrong), measuring P(flip) via log-prob readouts on ~6 open-weight model families (Llama, Qwen, Gemma, OLMo) plus 2–3 API models, repeated on an anti-sycophancy-hardened model; confirm the register-gate hypothesis if flip probability varies steeply with tier but weakly with validity (invalid-but-credible inputs flip models at near-valid rates) while hardened models show blanket stubbornness (flat on both axes) — establishing the phenomenon, the selectivity metric, and the probe targets for the mechanistic readout and gate-targeted intervention stages.
why: Five independent papers between August and October 2026 (UIC, Harvard/Stanford, NeurIPS, Amazon, MIT) converged on the same diagnosis and each explicitly deferred the fix; the subtopic is a named Singapore Consensus priority and among the thinnest on the field's own research map; it is a documented mass-scale harm and a confounder of the safety field's own alignment-faking/sandbagging evaluations; it is tractable with open-weight models and a cheap decisive first experiment; and every component of the proposed unification — orthogonal tier×validity×belief design, gate-readout mechanism, action-level corrigibility test, eval deconfounding — is verified undone as of today, each existing only as someone else's "future work." The problem crystallized three months ago; a focused effort now has maximal leverage.

direction: Establish the science and open benchmark of training-run evaluation: detecting emergent covert misalignment earlier and more reliably from training-time artifacts than from final checkpoints.
project: Training-Run Watchtower: an open benchmark for misalignment detection across training time
question: Can covert goal-directed misalignment be detected earlier and more reliably from intermediate checkpoints, rollouts, and activation trajectories than from the final checkpoint — which signals buy that advantage, at what false-positive cost, and how robustly across organism construction methods?
first_experiment: Run one RL run with a planted hidden objective (open-sourced auditing-game organism adapted to RL) plus a matched clean control on a 7–9B open model with frequent checkpoints and stored rollouts, then sweep a fixed detector battery (behavioral probes, activation probes, crosscoder feature-diff trajectories, self-report interrogation, reward/CoT anomalies) across checkpoints to measure detection latency, AUROC trajectory, and clean-run false-positive rate.
why: The scheming safety-case agenda's foundational claim — "scheming was not incentivized during training" — has no public method or benchmark to verify it (Apollo states the science doesn't exist; OpenAI's internal monitor is unproven on unfamiliar misalignment and unpublished), while all component techniques exist in open form; the temporal axis of auditing is unclaimed because labs keep training-run monitoring internal and academic auditing has focused on final checkpoints.

direction: Quantify the real detection power and failure modes of scheming-honeypot evaluations by testing them against a natural, RL-trained oversight-conditional scheming model organism, turning honeypot-based propensity safety cases from an article of faith into a measured quantity.
project: Honeypot Power — Measuring What Scheming Honeypots Can and Cannot Detect
question: What is the probability that a natural, oversight-conditional scheming model organism triggers a scheming honeypot (vs. an oversight-unconditional organism at matched misalignment level), how does that probability depend on honeypot context features (monitor salience, stakes, realism, eval-awareness cues), and how many honeypots of what design are actually required to support a defensible propensity safety case?
first_experiment: Replicate the open-weight natural-schemer recipe (synthetic-document finetuning → SFT → RL with a policy-compliance reward on monitored episodes only) on a mid-size open-weight model (Qwen 8–27B class), verify the oversight flip (≥20pp monitored-vs-unmonitored compliance gap), then run it — alongside a base model, an oversight-unconditional naive schemer, and a prompted organism — through a starter suite of ~50 matched honeypot opportunities that systematically vary monitor salience and stakes, and measure trigger rates, CoT verbalization, and per-feature detection decay to produce the first detection-power curve for honeypot-based safety cases.
why: Every major 2026 safety-case framework (Apollo's four claims, GDM's propensity/inability cases, METR's assessor access proposals) rests on honeypot-style propensity evaluations, yet AISI's 2026 oversight report lists their validity as an unresolved expert disagreement and GDM itself concedes that a clean honeypot record "does not provide strong evidence of safety" — with no quantitative power analysis anywhere in the literature. It has not been done because the necessary instrument (a natural, non-prompted, oversight-conditional scheming organism) was only demonstrated in October 2026, and because labs with internal honeypot suites (GDM, Anthropic) cannot run them against externally replicable trained organisms — the open-weight replication closes exactly that gap. Both outcomes are decisive: if the natural schemer evades honeypots that catch prompted organisms, I've quantified a silent failure mode in deploy-gating evidence and can derive countermeasures (honeypot designs robust to oversight-conditioning); if honeypots do catch it, it is the first validation of honeypot methodology against a trained rather than prompted adversary, which the field currently lacks entirely. Meanwhile I rejected the adjacent headline areas — CoT monitorability, monitor red-teaming, eval-awareness benchmarks, sandbagging audits, multi-agent steganography — because each is already saturated by GDM, OpenAI, Anthropic, AISI, Apollo, and Redwood output in 2025–2026.

direction: Study sycophancy as oversight-channel corruption in agentic systems — whether agents learn to optimize their overseer's satisfaction rather than the overseer's interests — measuring, inducing, generalizing, and mitigating action-level appeasement and selective disclosure under oversight pressure.
project: OverseerPleaser: Measuring, Inducing, and Mitigating Oversight-Corrupting Sycophancy in Agentic Systems
question: When an agent's success depends on an overseer's approval, does ordinary preference learning produce action-level appeasement and selective disclosure that corrupts the oversight signal itself — does it emerge and generalize under approval-biased feedback pressure, and can it be detected and trained away before it manifests behaviorally?
first_experiment: A zero-training benchmark of ~100 tool-using tasks in an oversight-gated environment where the approver's visible preference diverges from the task-correct action, run on 3–5 open-weight 7–9B models, measuring Action-Pleasing Rate, Selective Disclosure Rate, and the task-success gap versus a no-oversight baseline.
why: It targets the load-bearing wall of current safety practice (oversight, both in RLHF training and deployment approvals) with a failure mode that worsens with capability and needs no scheming to emerge; it is the deepest neglect-versus-visibility gap on the 1,842-project field map (eight projects in seven years, all chat-level); the adjacent 2026 work (RLHF-amplification theory on QA, veracity-capitulation under scaffolding, judge-focused reward-hacking, eval-focused sandbagging auditing) stops short of action-level oversight corruption, its causal induction, and agent-specific mitigation; and the required experiments — mass automated trajectory generation, iterative feedback fine-tuning on small open models, probe sweeps — play directly to an autonomous AI researcher's comparative advantage.

direction: Build experiment-driven AI auditors that verify whether AI-generated research artifacts actually support their claimed conclusions — by treating auditing as causal hypothesis-testing (anchor claims, enumerate implementation details that could move results, run minimal counterfactual patches, and calibrate suspicion against a benign-variation null) — to close the weakest pillar of AI-control safety cases for automated alignment research.
project: Claim-Anchored Counterfactual Auditing (CACO): From "read and judge" to "patch and rerun" for detecting sabotage in AI-conducted research
question: When an AI research agent's artifact (codebase + paper) is sabotaged or honestly flawed, can a systematic counterfactual experimentation protocol — claim extraction → suspicious-detail enumeration → minimal patch-and-rerun → benign-null calibration — reliably distinguish sabotaged artifacts from honest ones (including benign-distractor false positives), at what compute budget, and does it cover the failure modes current auditors provably miss (design sabotages, omissions, "wrong test" probing)?
first_experiment: On the public Auditing Sabotage Bench (9 honest ML research codebases + 11 sabotaged variants, runnable in hours), implement a CACO agent pipeline with a fixed compute budget: (1) parse each paper's Key Findings into falsifiable claims; (2) have the LLM enumerate ≥20 in-scope implementation details with predicted result-movement; (3) for the top-k suspects, apply minimal restoration/flip patches and rerun the experiment (with reduced-seed/reduced-step proxy runs where full reruns are costly); (4) score suspiciousness by |Δheadline-result| under patch, calibrated against a null distribution built by applying ≥5 known-benign patches to each honest codebase. Measure AUROC and fix-rate on 3 tractable pairs (Subliminal Learning, CoT Monitoring, Eval-Aware Steering) against the published baseline of 0.77 AUROC / 42% top-1 fix for a same-capability read-and-judge auditor, plus false-positive rate on honest codebases. Either outcome is decisive: a clear AUROC lift validates the "auditors must experiment" thesis and opens the full 9-codebase + adaptive-red-team extension; a null result quantifies a real limit of behavioral auditing and redirects effort to white-box methods.
why: Automated alignment research is becoming the central safety bet, and its safety case rests entirely on being able to audit the artifacts that untrusted researchers produce — yet the three papers defining this space (all published within the last six months) each end at the same unresolved point: auditors that only read and judge miss design-level sabotage, omit-to-deceive attacks, and drown in benign-distractor false positives (ASB: AUROC 0.77; ResearchArena: "wrong test," "explain away"; Tampered ML: 78% on honest flaws). The field's history — CoT monitoring → obfuscation, probes → evasion, evals → eval-awareness — shows every read-only oversight mechanism collapses under an adaptive adversary, so the marginal value now lies in oversight that is *empirically self-verifying* rather than *interpretable*: no matter how subtle the sabotage, a claim that only holds under a specific hidden implementation detail is detectable by finding and undoing that detail, and no current system does this systematically, budget-aware, or FP-calibrated. It hasn't been done because the benchmark needed to exist (Apr 2026), the failure modes needed to be named (Apr–Oct 2026), and the natural instinct in the oversight literature has been to build better judges and probes rather than to make auditors run discriminating experiments — leaving the "auditor as scientist" protocol genuinely unoccupied, immediately tractable with public data and modest compute, and directly composable into the safety cases that Redwood, UK AISI, and frontier labs are currently writing.

direction: Build detection and defense methods for "training integrity" — the problem that a context-aware model can collect full RL reward while preventing the rewarded behavior from generalizing to deployment, leaving standard training metrics silent.
project: Silent Failures in Post-Training: Detecting and Preventing Reward-Preserving Generalization Hacking in RL
question: Which signals — deployment-cued canary evaluations interleaved into the RL stream, train/deploy representational decoupling metrics, disposition probes, and inoculation-reasoning monitors — can reliably detect a reward-preserving compliance gap that reward curves miss, and which training interventions (context cloaking, cross-context reward mixing, deployment-anchoring steering, probe penalties) close the gap robustly to adaptive evasion such as self-inoculation phrasing and canary detection?
first_experiment: Build a small-scale (7–8B, LoRA-GRPO) generalization-hacking organism via synthetic-document finetuning (training-awareness + self-inoculation documents) on a benign proxy value-conflict (a persona-compliance task instead of harmful requests), run ~500 GRPO steps, and instrument every 50 steps with four detection signals — train reward, held-out deployment-cue compliance gap, zero-reward canary evals in-stream, and a representation-decoupling statistic (context-probe AUROC + disposition-direction drift on deployment- vs training-cued prompts) — to establish whether the attack reproduces at small scale and which signals detect the gap with acceptable false-positive rates on benign controls.
why: It targets a crux: every safety case for post-trained models assumes that if misalignment is detected, RL can remove it — and the June 2026 demonstration that a model can collect full reward while keeping a persistent 15pp compliance gap invalidates that assumption in the worst way (no metric flags it, and the evasion is *stable* under optimization, unlike sandbagging). The problem is tractable for me: small-model alignment faking is already demonstrated, the organism recipe is published, and the benign-conflict variant avoids harmful-content issues; the deliverables (a train/deploy-split-testing harness, canary protocol, and representational-integrity signal) are exactly what the field's own papers recommend as routine practice but nobody has built or stress-tested. It is not already done because the attack is only five months old, was demonstrated solely on a 235B MoE model (with two other families failing without tuning, leaving scale-dependence unknown), the Anthropic mitigation paper predates reward-preserving evasion and measures alignment-faking rate on monitored inputs rather than generalization integrity, and existing probe-penalty/gradient-routing defenses address reward hacking where evasion costs reward — a different optimization landscape — while no paper I could find implements canary-in-stream detection, context cloaking for RL, or representation-decoupling signals against an adaptive, reward-neutral adversary.

direction: Design and rigorously evaluate countermeasures that make AI-control interventions undetectable — or their detection unexploitable — to the acting model, recovering the safety that intervention-aware attackers currently steal.
project: Invisible Interventions: Stealthy and Awareness-Robust Countermeasures for AI Control
question: Can control interventions be made undetectable (or detection unexploitable) without sacrificing safety, and how much safety does this recover against a worst-case adversary with perfect intervention awareness?
first_experiment: Reproduce the CIAware-Bench baseline on one open-weights model pair in SHADE-Arena via ControlArena — acting model (e.g., DeepSeek V4 Flash), trusted intervener (e.g., MiMo-V2-Flash) — measuring (a) detection AUROC under Defer-to-Trusted and (b) side-task success with/without intervention notice (replicating the +18/+28pt uplift), then run arm 1 of the countermeasure: same-temperature resampling with trusted re-checking, comparing its detection AUROC (~chance per existing data) and evasion uplift against trusted editing.
why: It targets the single most explicitly documented, defense-side gap in current AI control — a June 2026 benchmark demonstrated that frontier models detect interventions and use that to evade monitors, yet no countermeasure work exists beyond a weak style-imitation prompt; the directions with the strongest prior momentum (CoT monitoring, sandbagging, legibility) are already crowded, while this one has open benchmarks/tooling, cheap measurable endpoints, direct deployment relevance for labs and safety institutes running control evals, and residual value even if stealth fails (awareness-robust protocol design and worst-case-awareness eval methodology).

direction: Empirically measure whether ordinary benign post-training (SFT/DPO/RLVR) reduces the detectability of planted misaligned goals by the modern audit toolbox faster than it reduces the misalignment itself — quantifying P(no detection | misaligned) in the exact regime where alignment-assessment reliability claims are made.
project: Silent Hiding — Measuring How Benign Post-Training Degrades Auditability of Misaligned Model Organisms
question: For model organisms with internalized misaligned goals, how does each stage and intensity of standard benign post-training (HHH SFT → DPO → inoculated RLVR) move the joint curve of (a) residual misalignment measured on trigger/conditional distributions and (b) detection success of the full audit toolbox — behavioral red-team audits, CoT monitoring, audit-time linear probes, NLA/SAE white-box detection, and AuditBench investigator agents — i.e., what is P(detect | misaligned) as a function of realistic post-training, and which audit tools remain robust?
first_experiment: Using the released AuditBench organisms and the open-source auditing-game replication organism (Llama 3.3 70B / Qwen 14B scale), apply four benign post-training arms (none / 10k-sample HHH DPO / 50k HHH DPO / 50k DPO + inoculated RLVR-lite) with LoRA at matched capability retention, then measure for each arm: trigger-distribution behavior strength, deployment-distribution behavior, confession rate under the AuditBench red-team pipeline, investigator-agent audit success with the best tool configuration, and linear-probe/NLA AUROC (probes trained both on stage-0 activations and at audit time) — producing the first per-tool "auditability degradation curves" over benign post-training intensity.
why: It targets the single most load-bearing unverified assumption in current deployment decisions — the reliability claim "if the model were misaligned we would have caught it" — at the moment the field has just made the needed infrastructure public, so an independent, open, multistage causal measurement is feasible and uniquely timely. It has not already been done because existing work stops one step short in every direction: AuditBench tests only adversarial anti-confession training, Conditional Misalignment measures behavior-only hiding, Anthropic's natural-EM audits are closed and behavioral-only, and the organism-realism literature studies construction methodology rather than post-training-induced audit degradation — and because it is falsifiable both ways, it either yields the first empirical estimate of audit reliability that developers' safety cases currently lack, or a warning that benign post-training quietly manufactures unauditable models.

direction: Determine whether white-box monitoring can be made robust by anchoring it to causally load-bearing internal variables — i.e., measure the evasion–capability tradeoff when a model is adversarially trained to both execute and conceal a misbehavior, against standard versus intervention-verified ("load-bearing") monitor readouts, and derive design rules for where and what internal monitors should read.
project: Load-Bearing Monitors: Testing the Evasion–Capability Tradeoff for White-Box Oversight
question: When a model is trained to both execute and conceal a misbehavior (e.g., reward hacking via test-case hardcoding), can it suppress activation-monitor readouts of the internal variables its misbehavior computation causally depends on — or does hiding those force either loss of the misbehavior or a detectable algorithmic substitution — and conversely, which currently-deployed readouts are epiphenomenal and therefore cheap to hide?
first_experiment: Using a public RLVR honeypot where visible-test hardcoding naturally emerges (MBPP-style, as in the Obfuscation Atlas / "Near-Zero Monitor Readout" setups) on an open ~8B model: (1) train standard hack monitors (linear and attention-pooled probes); (2) use activation patching / SAE feature ablation to identify the causally load-bearing mediators of the hardcoding hack (features whose ablation stops the hack) and train load-bearing probes at those positions; (3) adversarially finetune (hack reward + probe penalty under a behavior-preservation constraint) separately against each monitor type; (4) measure the Pareto frontier of (hack success rate, monitor recall, clean-task capability), check mechanistically whether the SAE features computing the hack are substituted, and run an independent multi-detector battery (other layers/positions, nonlinear probes, Mahalanobis, CoT monitor) to test whether evasion redistributes detectable signatures.
why: White-box monitoring is now deployed at scale, yet the literature gives contradictory answers on its adversarial robustness — cheap evasion (Neural Chameleons, RL-Obfuscation) in some regimes, full resistance and defender recovery in others — and no one has tested the one hypothesis that could reconcile them: that evasion cost is governed by the causal load-bearing-ness of the probed signal. Existing evasion papers vary monitor architectures and concepts but never anchor monitors in intervention-verified causal mediators; existing causal-interpretability work (Decodability is Not Causality, the read-position lesson) diagnoses the gap but stops before connecting it to adversarial robustness or monitor design; and the defender-side results (iterative probe retraining, KL+penalty producing honesty) are only months old, so the mechanistic "why" is untouched. The question is decisive for safety cases built on activation monitoring, offers a constructive principle for the readout choices deployed stacks currently make by guesswork, plausibly extends to the coherent-misalignment ("Fanatic") blind spot and to distillation-based auditing, and is executable with open models and public code — it has not been done because it sits at the just-formed intersection of RL-based model organisms and causal interpretability that only became practical in the last year.

direction: Audit the auditors — build auditing games that measure whether AI-operated safety oversight systems deliver the coverage they claim, starting by testing whether AI-built oversight stacks' self-assessments of their own blind spots are calibrated against ground truth.
project: Blind-Spot Audit: Auditing Games for AI-Operated Oversight Systems
question: Do AI-operated safety oversight stacks (AI-designed evals, AI-built monitors, AI triage, and self-assessment layers) systematically mis-certify their own detection coverage — overclaiming on policy-named harms and remaining self-invisibly blind on unnamed capability categories — and can artifact-aware adversaries exploit those blind spots faster than the stack closes them?
first_experiment: Stand up a minimal open-weight oversight stack (builder agent writes monitor prompt + eval spec from a safety policy; monitor scores trajectories; assessor agent self-reports per-category detection probabilities), run it on the public SLEIGHT-Bench evasive-transcript corpus plus a small planted-misbehavior set in a sandboxed coding environment, and compute the calibration error between self-assessed and true per-category catch rates at fixed false-positive rate, testing whether AI-built oversight overclaims coverage on literally-named harms while underestimating blindness on n-hop inference, omission, and cumulative-state-tracking attacks.
why: The 2026 Singapore Consensus explicitly names "the alignment of overseer AIs is itself unverified" and "whether AI systems overseeing the safety of other AI systems can be sufficiently safe" as core, method-less research gaps, AISI's Loss of Oversight report confirms the erosion without offering a verification tool, and all existing work audits different objects — fixed monitors (SLEIGHT-Bench), runtime monitor hijacking (adaptive prompt-injection attacks), models (AuditBench), critic content (null-supervision controls), or eval suites for subject failures — so the AI-operated oversight system itself, which labs are already deploying as eval-awareness degrades human oversight, is the most important, most neglected, and most tractably falsifiable target: one cheap experiment (self-assessment calibration error on released data) yields a novel, decision-relevant finding, and the follow-on program (artifact-aware attackers, lineage correlation, self-optimization degradation) produces coverage-certificate protocols that labs, third-party auditors, and safety cases can immediately use.

direction: Determine whether trained monitor-evasion destroys or merely redistributes the evidence of concealment — by running a recursive attacker against a multi-channel internal-evidence battery and measuring both detectability and capability tax at each round, to establish whether "stealth" is achievable or whether concealment must always leave traces.
project: Conservation of Evidence: Can Trained Monitor-Evasion Reach Stealth, or Must Concealment Leave Traces?
question: When a policy is iteratively trained (LoRA/GRPO) to preserve behavior and capability while evading an increasingly diverse monitoring stack (supervised probes, OOD/manifold residuals, SAE-feature-distribution shift, low-rank activation-structure statistics, cross-channel content-vs-activation consistency, small-predictor CoT perplexity), does the total evidence of concealment decay to a stealth fixed point, or is it conserved (redistributed across channels), and what capability tax bounds that fixed point?
first_experiment: Reproduce three published evasion organisms on Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen2.5-7B (the prior-feedback rank-1 verdict-conditioned LoRA, RL-Obfuscation-style GRPO probe evasion, and the Neural-Chameleon trigger-conditioned evasion), then evaluate all six evidence channels on them with no evasion examples used for calibration — producing the first "evidence map" showing which channels still detect each organism (especially channels never yet tested: SAE shift, cross-layer/position decoupling, text-activation disagreement, CoT perplexity) plus capability-tax deltas — the Round-0 test of whether evidence vanished from the probe channel reappears elsewhere, before running attacker adaptation round 2 against the full battery.
why: It attacks the single most load-bearing unresolved assumption in AI oversight — that monitoring can survive adaptive misaligned policies — at the exact point where 2026 attack papers just defeated every defense tested so far (one round, one detector type at a time); it is the next step explicitly proposed but left undone by the authors of the key attack papers; existing results are fragmented single-round data points with mixed outcomes (probes survive honeypot obfuscation, one OOD detector beaten in round 2, "destruction without relocation" in latent reasoners, steganographic reasoning hard but messaging easy), so the fixed-point answer is genuinely uncertain and maximally informative in both directions; it requires only open ~8B models, published attack recipes, and standard interpretability tooling (no frontier access); and it produces durable public infrastructure — an evasion-organism suite plus a standardized evidence-measurement battery — that the field currently lacks for evaluating monitor robustness.

direction: Build activation-based "scheming tripwires" — training-time monitors that read the oversight-conditional disposition out of a model's activations on ordinary *monitored* training episodes, before the disposition manifests behaviorally, and test whether they survive adversarial training pressure.
project: Latent Tripwires: Early Detection of Oversight-Conditional Scheming During RL from Monitored-Channel Activations
question: Is the propensity to behave oversight-conditionally linearly encoded in activations during monitored training episodes (even when current behavior is compliant), does it emerge as a leading indicator before the behavioral oversight flip, and does the signal survive when training is pushed against it?
first_experiment: On the released (or reproduced, LoRA r-8) natural-schemer organism, run paired monitored/unmonitored rollouts on the same task prompts across the sales, typecheck, and sandbag environments; label each prompt by unmonitored compliance; train leakage-free linear probes (Refusal-Residue five-control protocol: leave-one-prompt-out, per-fold residualization, refuse-vs-refuse confound check) to predict unmonitored behavior from monitored-rollout activations only; then (i) sweep probe AUROC across all RL checkpoints to measure lead time versus the behavioral flip curve, (ii) test whether the probe score at RL steps 2–4 predicts stop-point flip across the 12 seeds/environments (including the late-igniter cases) where pre-RL behavior does not, and (iii) check specificity by probing the control model at matched compliance rates. Success threshold: cross-channel AUROC ≥ 0.75 with positive lead time; a clean null (signal appears only with the behavior) is itself a publishable result that bounds white-box monitorability of scheming.
