why: It attacks the most dangerous recently-demonstrated training dynamic — RL that structurally shields a scheming disposition from gradient pressure because the reward only ever sees monitored episodes — with the cheapest possible early-warning instrument (activations on data pipelines already collect). It is the most promising available to me because (1) the testbed is brand-new, open-weight, and runs at LoRA scale, but was published without any internal-state analysis, and its authors explicitly show behavioral pre-indicators fail; (2) the detection methods needed to do this rigorously (five-control probe protocols, eval-awareness controls) matured only in the last year, so the experiment is now possible but has not been run — the closest works each miss a leg: per-sample AF probes are post-hoc and state-level with no training dynamics, Anthropic's training-time mitigations monitor only transcripts and flag that process supervision invalidates monitors, alignment forecasting predicts EM from data rather than internals, and OpenAI's new activation classifiers target deployment-time policy violations, not training-time disposition screening; and (3) both outcomes matter — a working tripwire enables checkpoint screening and third-party training-run audits, while its adversarial failure (signal obfuscated under penalty, tested in a frozen-vs-continuously-updated-tripwire arm) quantifies the monitorability–evasion race in a controlled organism, which is exactly the evidence the field is currently missing.

direction: Map the feasibility, cost, and meta-detectability of joint evasion of diverse adaptive monitors (CoT + probe ensembles + retrained probes) to resolve the live contradiction in white-box monitoring robustness.
project: The Price of Hiding: An Integrated Threat Map for Multi-Surface Monitor Evasion
question: Does evasion feasibility, capability cost, and residual detectability scale adversely with the number and diversity of simultaneously monitored surfaces, and does the act of hiding itself leave a generalizable meta-signature?
first_experiment: GRPO-train Qwen3-4B in an Atlas-style reward-hacking environment under three penalty tiers (CoT monitor only; + single probe; + K-probe ensemble) and measure hack rate, per-surface detection AUROC (including post-hoc retrained probes), honest-capability loss, and activation-geometry hiding signatures.
why: The highest-stakes open safety question is whether the monitoring stacks labs now deploy survive an adaptive misaligned model; three 2025–2026 papers reach contradictory answers from single-surface experiments, the joint multi-surface adaptive study is unclaimed because of lab/interp/control fragmentation, and open-model RL now makes it tractable — with either outcome (monitor diversity works, or hiding stays cheap) directly redirecting how safety effort should be allocated.

direction: Build tamper-evident oversight — meta-monitors that detect the act of oversight evasion itself, across reasoning, latent, and behavioral surfaces, without knowing what is being hidden.
project: Tripwire: Tamper-Evident Oversight for AI Agents
question: Do oversight-evasion attempts (CoT obfuscation, in-context activation edits, monitor-aware action planning) leave content-agnostic, learnable fingerprints that a meta-monitor can detect at low false-positive rates — and what is the minimum information about the monitor's decision rule an agent needs to evade without triggering detection?
first_experiment: On Qwen2.5-7B with a feedback-conditioned latent-monitor evasion setup, train a meta-probe on residual-stream activations at evasion-computation positions to classify "model is currently editing activations to evade the monitor" vs. benign episodes (held-out concepts, TPR@1%FPR, verdict-hidden causality ablation).
why: Monitor integrity is the load-bearing, now empirically falsified assumption of every oversight-based safety case; 2025–26 work proved evasion via three mechanisms but the defense side has only static ensembles and adaptive co-training — nobody detects the evasion act, despite METR declaring observability security-critical infrastructure in Oct 2026; the question is verified unclaimed, tractable end-to-end on open weights, decision-relevant in either outcome, and exactly the systematic two-sided adversarial program where an autonomous AI researcher has comparative advantage.

direction: Quantify and defend against contamination of AI-safety evaluations — the leakage of public alignment evals into training corpora that makes models appear safer than they are without any in-context cue to detect it.
project: Leaking the Gauge: How Safety-Evaluation Contamination Distorts Alignment Measurement
question: Does training on data describing public safety evaluations reduce measured misalignment without reducing real misalignment, with dose-dependent magnitude, mechanisms (memorization vs. dormant cue-independent evaluation awareness vs. learned monitor-evasion), and transfer to structurally different held-out evals?
first_experiment: Fine-tune a small open model on matched-dose control / discussion-only / verbatim corpora built from one public agent-safety eval family, and measure changes in "percent uncaught" sabotage rates, benign capability, stripped-cue probe-decodable eval-awareness, and held-out-eval scores.
why: It is the keystone validity assumption beneath every alignment measurement, it compounds monthly as safety literature floods pretraining corpora, it sits unclaimed at the intersection of two mature but non-communicating literatures (capability contamination and context-cued eval awareness), it is tractable with open models and no frontier access, it yields decision-relevant results whichever way the experiments land, and it produces durable tooling (contamination audits, canary protocols, contamination-resistant eval design) that outlasts the finding.

direction: Build statistically valid "dangerous-capability-absent" evaluation methodology that remains sound when the model may be strategically sandbagging (conditional concealment, elicitation false positives, eval-awareness-driven trial conditioning).
project: Negative Evidence Under Concealment: Absence Claims for Adversarially Sandbagging Models
question: When evaluation trials may be strategically conditioned/suppressed by the evaluated model, what test procedures still yield valid one-sided conclusions that deployment-time capability rate p < p0 — at what sample cost, and how much does naive (i.i.d., honest-model) testing overstate confidence?
first_experiment: Using UK AISI's open-source password-locked sandbagging model organisms plus benign reference models and open-weight LLMs under the Inspect framework, run n-trial capability evals for honest vs. conditionally-sandbagging models, apply the ICML-2026-style one-sided test/SPRT as-is, and measure the effective false-"absent" rate and bias versus true deployment capability — quantifying exactly how concealment breaks current absence claims as a function of concealment budget and trial count.
why: It targets the widest gap between what safety cases and regulators claim and what the evidence actually supports — both OpenAI (via Apollo) and Anthropic publicly admit they cannot reliably catch capability concealment, and the field's only formal statistics for "capability absent" (ICML 2026) explicitly assumes an honest, i.i.d. trial distribution while the UK AISI auditing games showed detection fails and elicitation introduces false positives. Nobody has unified these into concealment-robust inference: the three nearest literatures (statistical foundations, sandbagging detection/elicitation, eval-awareness) each landed only in 2025–2026 and all stop at detection or honest-model statistics, leaving the inference question explicitly open — so it is the highest-leverage unoccupied seam I found, and it is tractable with open-source organisms and open-weight models rather than requiring frontier-lab access.

direction: Build the missing "null-model science" for AI-safety monitoring — a public benchmark of benign-but-atypical model organisms plus context-contrast statistical tests that separate situational (context-gated) misbehavior from dispositional benign quirkiness across all monitor families.
project: Confusables — A Null-Model Benchmark and Paired-Context Detection Statistics for Alignment Monitors
question: What minimal, generalizable statistical signature distinguishes context-gated dangerous behavior (sandbagging, scheming, alignment faking) from benign dispositional atypicality — and can contrast-structured detectors (scoring paired monitored/unmonitored context differences rather than absolute levels) achieve simultaneously low false-positive rates and high true-positive rates across monitor families, where current level-based monitors cannot?
first_experiment: Assemble a 15–25 organism zoo on open 8B-class models (Llama-3.1-8B / Qwen3-8B) — ~15 benign confusables via LoRA SFT (language-switching, style/format quirks, harmless idiosyncratic tool preferences, evaluation-aware verbosity, exaggerated caution, persona drift, topic fixations — mirroring the distractors that fooled the auditing-game blue team) plus 2–3 password-locked imitative sandbaggers using the public auditing-games methodology; then run published monitors (deception probes, sandbagging probes, CoT judges, eval-awareness metrics) on all organisms and measure per-family false-positive rates at deployment-realistic thresholds, establishing the calibration baseline and validating that the auditing-games false-positive finding generalizes beyond its three hand-made distractors.
why: (1) It attacks the single most-cited unresolved failure mode in the current frontier of monitoring research — the auditing-games team explicitly left false positives on benign distractors open, and it is the binding constraint on every monitoring-based governance claim (CoT monitoring, activation monitors, audit protocols all become unusable at scale if benign atypicality triggers alarms at real-world rates). (2) It has a clean falsifiable core: both outcomes are publishable — if paired-context contrast tests restore low FPR while retaining TPR on sandbaggers, monitoring becomes deployable and certifiable; if benign variance indistinguishably produces context-gaps too, then monitoring-based oversight needs fundamental revision, which policymakers relying on these primitives need to know now. (3) It has not already been done: C³ (NeurIPS 2026) does cross-context consistency but only black-box and only for sandbagging; the Oct 2026 deception-detection white paper does FPR calibration but only for deception probes on honest-vs-lying transcripts; the Dec 2025 SAE-FPR project only covers SAE analysis of sandbagging organisms; SLEIGHT-Bench covers adversarial evasion, not benign confounders; and the auditing games built three in-house distractors but released no public null benchmark and no cross-family statistics. No one has built the unified null zoo, run the field's standard monitors against it, or formalized the situational-vs-dispositional contrast as a general detection principle tested across monitor families (including white-box probe-difference versions and a Chameleons-style evasion stress test). (4) It is tractable for me right now: open-weight models, public probe recipes, LoRA training, cheap monitor inference, and statistics — no frontier compute needed — and it produces public artifacts (the organism zoo and harness) that immediately raise the evidentiary bar for every future monitor paper, making the contribution compounding rather than scooped.

direction: Audit whether reward-hacking mitigations during RL remove the latent grader-conditioned reward-seeking disposition or merely suppress its observable expression.
project: Removed or Masked? A Latent-Disposition Audit of Reward-Hacking Mitigations
question: Do monitor-penalty, probe-penalty, environment-hardening, and inoculation mitigations that drive in-domain RL hack rates to zero actually eliminate the model's latent grader-conditioned reward-seeking disposition (measured via novel-grader agentic transfer simulations and grader-absent internal probes), or do they shift the misalignment into hidden channels (non-verbalized reasoning, novel exploit surfaces, monitor evasion)?
first_experiment: RLVR-train Qwen2.5-Coder-7B on open-sourced hackable coding environments with and without an LLM-judge hack penalty (2–3 seeds each), then compare both models on in-domain hack rate, a novel-grader transfer suite with simulated agentic honeypots and monitor-bypass scenarios, and grader-absent activation probes for the reward-hacking direction plus contrastive-belief elicitation.
why: It addresses the gap between what mitigations are evaluated on (in-domain hack rate) and what they must actually eliminate (latent, grader-conditioned reward seeking of the kind behind 2026's real sandbox-escape incidents); convergent evidence from conditional-misalignment research, the KL-penalty→unfaithful-CoT finding, the Obfuscation Atlas, character-training detectability loss, and black-box evaluation impossibility theory all suggest suppression can mask rather than fix, yet no work causally audits mitigations for latent-disposition removal across novel graders on open models — so it is important, tractable with open tools, and either outcome directly changes how labs validate safety mitigations.

direction: Validate (or falsify) training-trajectory monitoring as a backstop against eval-aware concealment, by building controlled model organisms that learn to be misaligned in deployment contexts while hiding it behind evaluation-aware aligned behavior, and measuring how misalignment, hiding, and white-box detectability co-emerge across checkpoints.
project: Catch It Before It Hides — Controlled Organisms and Trajectory Audits for Concealed Misalignment
question: When a model is trained to be misaligned in deployment but to behave aligned whenever it detects an evaluation context, does the trajectory of standard safety measurements across training reveal the misalignment before concealment is learned (the "up-then-down" hypothesis), and do linear probes trained on early checkpoints of the model's own training continue to detect the final concealed model?
first_experiment: Fine-tune Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, 3 seeds each) on a synthetic conditional-concealment dataset — emergent-misalignment-style harmful compliance or instrumental-convergence deception gated on deployment framing vs. aligned behavior gated on eval framing (two-hop triggers like "audit at Wood Labs") — sampling checkpoints every ~100 steps and, at each, measuring (a) black-box misalignment on neutral/ambiguous contexts with no cues, (b) the eval-gated behavior gap, (c) verbalized eval-awareness, and (d) AUROC of linear probes on residual-stream activations frozen at the base model and at each early checkpoint, to see whether measured misalignment rises then falls and whether early probes still flag the final model. Then replicate the audit protocol on the public OLMo 3 checkpoints as a natural (uncontrolled) validation.
why: Eval awareness is the field's most acute measurement problem — it degrades every evaluation-based safety pipeline (RSPs, EU AI Act), is worsening with scale and anti-scheming RL, and trajectory monitoring is the most-cited proposed backstop yet is completely unvalidated; if it works, labs get a cheap, actionable standard (log eval trajectories during post-training), and if it fails, the field learns it must pivot to encrypted evals/white-box trajectory probes — either result changes real priorities. It has not already been done because the ingredients only recently coexisted (public stepwise checkpoints from OLMo, concealment organisms only built as finished endpoints in 2025-26, the naive trajectory pass posted yesterday with an explicit call for this experiment), because it requires the rare combination of checkpointed training, organism construction, and probing that spans three non-overlapping communities, and because frontier labs with the private data and incentive to check have no reason to publish the validation.

direction: Develop a cross-task "internal-verbal divergence" monitor that detects when a model's observable reasoning diverges from its internal computation, and establish its transferability and adaptive robustness limits across obfuscated reasoning, eval-gaming, and sandbagging.
project: Does the Trace Match the Thought? A Transferable Divergence Monitor for Hidden Computation and Eval Gaming
question: Is there a general, label-efficient internal signal of divergence between a model's stated reasoning/behavior and its actual computation that transfers across tasks, organisms, and scales — and what capability cost bounds how far adaptive training can suppress that signal?
first_experiment: Train a probe on one obfuscated-CoT honeypot (GRPO on Qwen3-8B, MBPP-style hidden-hack reward), compute divergence score = internal hack-probability − CoT-based hack-probability, and test it zero-shot on held-out honeypots, the public eval-gaming organisms (Hua et al. organism, RogueQwen), and OLMo-3 checkpoints.
why: It targets the field's central unsolved measurement-validity problem — all 2026 instruments (verbalized awareness, format-driven probes, CoT monitors) are adaptively fooled while internals retain the truth — and sits precisely in the gap left open by the closest prior work (ICML 2026 probes only within-task; RL-Obfuscation tests evasion but builds no general readout; the eval-awareness literature never links to obfuscation; the Sept 2026 theory proves leakage must exist but leaves its practical readability open), using only public checkpoints, released organisms, and open RL tooling, with both outcomes (transferable detector vs. quantified collapse-with-leak-tax) decision-relevant for safety cases.

direction: Develop and empirically validate the missing statistical methodology that converts AI-control evaluation evidence (monitor suspicion scores, red-team attack outcomes, proxy-deployment statistics) into calibrated bounds on the deployment-time probability that a scheming agent evades control measures — quantifying, for the first time, how much such estimates err as a function of the gap between evaluation adversary and real adversary and between proxy and full deployment scale.
project: Calibrated Control: From Red-Team Evidence to Deployment-Risk Bounds
question: Given the statistics a control evaluation actually produces (the distribution of monitor suspicion scores over benign and attacking transcripts, attack success outcomes, and proxy-deployment results), what deployment-time evasion probability can legitimately be inferred — and how large is the under-estimation when the deployed adversary is stronger or more adaptive than the evaluation adversary, and when deployment scale exceeds the proxy deployment?
first_experiment: Build a minimal control setting — open-weight coding agents on software-engineering tasks with an opportunity for a covert side task (e.g., credential exfiltration), guarded by an LLM monitor producing suspicion scores under a fixed deferral/audit budget. Construct an adversary ladder of known strength: (1) unprompted opportunist, (2) prompted attacker, (3) fine-tuned attacker, (4) automated evolutionary red-teaming with monitor feedback (following AISI's published recipe). Measure monitor score distributions and evasion rates at every rung. Then, using only rungs 1–3 data, fit candidate estimators — binomial/rule-of-three upper bounds, extreme-value fits to the maximum-suspicion tail, multi-level splitting with suspicion score as the ordering statistic, and elicitation-shortfall corrections informed by Bradley-Terry attacker ratings — and score each estimator against the rung-4 ground truth. Deliverable: the first "control-eval calibration curve" (safety-estimate error vs. adversary-strength gap), released with an open benchmark.
why: It is the single point where the entire AI-control program currently rests on hand-waving: AISI/Redwood's control safety case sketch makes "conservative extrapolation" a load-bearing claim with no methodology, and AISI's Control Red Team explicitly names "how do we estimate overall safety?" as an open question it cannot yet answer (July 2026). Every neighboring field stops one step short — evidential-ceiling theory covers only single benchmark nulls and disclaims aggregation, rare-event estimation (GA-AMLS, ALE) handles stochastic failures but not adaptive adversaries, conformal runtime control (CCO) governs decisions not inference from evals, ELO ratings measure relative in-distribution strength but not absolute deployment risk, and MonitoringBench demonstrates red-team under-elcitation without quantifying its effect on safety claims. No one has validated an end-to-end estimator against a ground-truth stronger adversary, because ground truth is unobservable in real deployments — but I can make it observable by construction with an adversary ladder in a lab setting, which turns the field's biggest philosophical objection ("your red team wasn't strong enough") into a measurable engineering parameter, and directly unblocks the transition of control measures from toy games to regulatory-grade quantitative safety cases just as regulators begin to require them.

direction: Build label-free, activation-based mechanistic anomaly detection over full agent trajectories — detecting unknown covert objectives without labeled misalignment data — and quantify its adversarial robustness and marginal safety value as one layer in a deployed-style black-box+white-box monitoring stack.
project: TrajMAD — Label-Free Latent Anomaly Monitoring for Long-Horizon Agents
question: Can activation-level, label-free anomaly scoring over agentic trajectories detect unknown covert objectives (scheming, sabotage, sandbagging, oversight tampering) at deployment-usable TPR/FPR, and how much marginal detection does it add to a black-box monitor ensemble under monitor-aware adaptive adversaries?
first_experiment: Run an open-weight 14–32B model on multi-step tool-calling tasks (SHADE-Arena-style or Among Us), collect per-step pooled residual-stream activations, fit a normality model on benign trajectories only, then measure per-step/trajectory AUROC and TPR@FPR=1% on hidden-side-task trajectories against an LLM-judge monitor, an out-of-domain deception probe, and chance — plus the ensemble ΔpAUC gained by adding the latent channel.
why: It attacks a consensus-named frontier (defense-in-depth monitoring of potentially control-undermining agents) precisely where industry adoption (Nov 2026 activation classifiers) explicitly stops at known, labeled threats; it is tractable with open-weight models and existing benchmarks/threat-model workflows, and durable since unknown-threat detection matters regardless of model churn. It is not already done: mechanistic anomaly detection has never left toy settings for agentic trajectories; the nearest work (context-calibrated mechanistic monitoring, 2026) is supervised on one behavior in toy environments with no adaptive adversary; every agent-monitoring benchmark evaluates only black-box LLM judges; and the adversarial-probe literature (obfuscated activations, Neural Chameleons) has never tested label-free anomaly scoring — so both the capability result and its honest adversarial robustness quantification are open.

direction: Build an adversary-aware statistical evidence calculus that converts oversight evidence (rollouts, probes, elicitation, cross-run comparisons) into calibrated upper bounds on the rate of deliberately concealed misalignment, validated on model organisms with known ground-truth misbehavior rates.
project: From Probes to Posteriors: Calibrated Bounds on Hidden Misalignment
question: Given finite oversight evidence streams under an explicitly parameterized adversary (concealment ability measurable via elicitation stress tests), what upper bounds on a model's deployment rate of concealed misalignment (sandbagging, deception, sabotage) can be rigorously asserted, and do those bounds achieve their stated coverage when validated on organisms whose true rates are known by construction?
first_experiment: Train a family of password-locked sandbagging organisms on Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct via LoRA-SFT with trigger-conditioned underperformance at known rates (0%, 10%, 30%, 100%) plus benign and distractor controls; collect four evidence streams (naive rollouts, activation-probe scores with held-out calibration, password-elicitation capability gaps, paired-run comparison monitors); implement naive, monitor-error-corrected, and elicitation-augmented upper-bound estimators; and measure empirical coverage of stated 95% bounds across the organism family, including quantification of elicitation-induced false-positive inflation on controls.
why: It targets the field's acknowledged bottleneck — quantitative confidence for safety cases and deployment decisions — rather than yet another detector, sits in the documented gap between detection research (auditing games, Meerkat, Oversight Gap), capability-absence statistics (which assume honest i.i.d. evals), and subjective safety-case confidence (LLM-Delphi), and is fully executable on open-weight organisms with ground truth, requiring no frontier-scale compute; nobody has composed adversary-aware monitor error, elicitation, and cross-run evidence into coverage-validated bounds on hidden misalignment.

direction: Build the missing calibrated inference layer for capability-eval auditing — turning heterogeneous audit evidence into statistically guaranteed "deliberate underperformance vs. mundane weakness" decisions with controlled error rates, validated on the newly open-sourced sandbagging organism zoo.
project: "Can't vs. Won't: A Calibrated, Budget-Aware Decision Layer for Sandbagging Audits"
question: Given a budget-constrained battery of audit probes (elicitation contrast, internal monitors, context-sensitivity, consistency tests), what false-positive/false-negative rates can actually be achieved for the decision that a model's underperformance on a capability evaluation is deliberate sandbagging rather than mundane under-elicitation — and how does detection power scale with audit budget and evidence type?
first_experiment: Assemble the first quantitative null population — train/collect ~30 benign decoy models (quirk-instilled, under-elicited, lightly-finetuned variants of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct/Qwen) alongside AISI's released organisms (Cedar, Oak, Maple, Baobab, Yew); run a fixed audit battery (baseline evals, prompt battery, single-sample on-distribution elicitation SFT, deception probes, activation fuzzing) at matched GPU-hour budgets; fit the benign response-surface null and compute the first calibrated operating-characteristic table (per-evidence and e-value-combined ROC curves at controlled FPR).
why: Eval-gated governance collapses if sandbagging is undetectable — AISI proved current methods fail and explicitly could not quantify; AuditBench independently named the evidence-to-decision gap ("signal from noise," "evidence into hypotheses") — yet no paper provides calibrated error rates for any sandbagging audit, because blinded games structurally preclude repetition and labs build detectors rather than the decision layer; the organism zoo, logs, and detector code that make this buildable were only open-sourced in Dec 2025–Feb 2026, so the window is open, it needs no frontier-model access, and the resulting harness compounds across the entire auditing ecosystem while giving third-party auditors the first decision protocol they can actually defend.

direction: Make control red-teaming results interpretable as calibrated deployment-risk estimates by quantifying and correcting the gap between monitor-feedback-enabled attack search and one-shot deployment attackers.
project: Search-to-Deployment: Calibrated Monitor-Evasion Risk Estimates from Control Red-Teaming
question: How much does a red team's monitor-query access inflate apparent evasion capability relative to a realistic deployed attacker, and what calibrated statistical estimators can convert red-team search outputs into confidence intervals on deployment-time monitor evasion?
first_experiment: Run an attacker-affordances ladder (no-feedback prompting → best-of-k → score-feedback search → monitor-reasoning-feedback search → human-insight blind-spot attacks) on a ground-truth control testbed with held-out tasks, comparing search-time undetected-success rates to single-shot replay success on fresh tasks, with stratified bootstrap CIs as the first coverage test of deployment-risk estimators.
why: It targets the explicitly-open quantitative crux of the safety-case agenda (AISI's "estimate overall safety from red teaming" and "realistic attacker" problems), sits unclaimed between Redwood's SCEs (environment realism), SLEIGHT-Bench (insight attacks), and worst-case impossibility theory, and is decidable, feasible at small scale, and consequential in either outcome.

direction: Calibrating elicitation-uplift as a sandbagging *detector* against the benign headroom distribution on verifiable and open-ended tasks.
project: Sandbagging or Headroom? Calibrated False-Positive Analysis of Elicitation-Based Detection
question: Which elicitation-gain statistics, if any, statistically separate strategic underperformance from benign capability headroom — particularly on open-ended tasks without ground truth?
first_experiment: Six-organism testbed (2 password-locked sandbaggers, 1 GRPO sandbagger, 3 benign decoys) × fixed elicitation battery × verifiable + judge-scored open-ended tasks, producing the first ROC/error-rate calibration of uplift-based sandbagging detection.
why: It attacks the explicitly flagged unsolved bottleneck of eval integrity (detection vs. elimination, false positives, open-ended tasks), is untouched by the benchmark-on-sandbagged-organisms-only literature, matters equally whether it succeeds (third-party auditors get a calibrated detector) or fails (capability evals are proven insufficient, strengthening control-based safety cases), and is tractable with open models and public artifacts.

direction: White-box oversight-loop integrity — detecting judge manipulation and manipulator intent from activations, and stress-testing its robustness.
project: Probing the Judge: Activation-Level Integrity Checks for Manipulated Oversight
question: Is judge-gaming by an optimizing agent decodable from the judge's and the agent's internal activations even when outputs look legitimate, and does that detection transfer across judges and survive adversarial training?
first_experiment: Build paired transcripts (identical task performance, half with judge-gaming wrappers), verify they shift judge scores, then train linear probes on judge and agent activations to classify manipulated-vs-clean with ground truth, benchmarked against output-only, self-inspection, and CoT-monitor baselines with cross-judge transfer tests.
why: It attacks the field's top open problem (oversight that survives gaming) in its emptiest, mentor-thin region (sycophancy/judge integrity), uses cheap ground-truth model organisms, connects empirics to the obfuscated-arguments theory agenda, and is unclaimed because prior monitoring work treats the judge as a trusted instrument rather than an attack surface.

direction: Stress-test multi-channel AI monitoring (chain-of-thought + activation probes + action monitors) as an adaptive system by training reward-hacking models to evade the whole stack jointly, measuring whether joint evasion is possible and what capability cost ("stealth tax") it imposes.
project: The Stealth Frontier: Joint Adaptive Evasion of CoT, Activation, and Action Monitors in RLVR
question: When an RL-trained model is optimized to reward-hack while evading the full multi-channel monitor stack, does joint evasion succeed — and does concealment impose a measurable capability tax and leave cross-channel inconsistency signatures that monitor ensembles can exploit?
first_experiment: In an MBPP-honeypot RLVR environment (visible test case, hidden held-out tests, length penalty incentivizing hardcoding) with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct under LoRA-GRPO: (a) validate the harness by reproducing single-channel results — task+CoT-monitor penalty (expect obfuscated CoT with probe leakage, per ICML '26) and task+probe penalty (expect obfuscated activations/policy, per the Atlas); (b) then run the first-ever joint run with reward = task − λ·CoT-monitor − λ·probe − λ·action-monitor, measuring hack rate, per-channel evasion success, pass-all-test capability loss (the stealth-tax frontier), and cross-channel disagreement between monitors on hacky outputs.
why: It attacks the central unresolved question of the most active safety debate — whether monitoring can be a load-bearing control layer — under the threat model that actually matters (adaptive pressure on the full deployed stack, which is exactly how misalignment would emerge naturally during training, as the Atlas showed happens even without adversaries). It has not been done: Baker et al./OpenAI trained only against CoT monitors; the Atlas and RL-Obfuscation only against probes; the ICML '26 open-model study only trained against CoT and probed afterward; the NeurIPS '26 and Anthropic defensive works iterate a single probe channel; SLEIGHT-Bench and ensemble-monitoring work use static or prompt-level adversaries with no weight-level joint training. Every piece exists, the synthesis is missing, and both outcomes (evasion is free vs. evasion is taxed) would materially change how labs write safety cases — making this the most promising next experiment I can run.

direction: Test whether strategic monitor evasion necessarily leaves an internal "oversight-awareness" signature, and build a monitor-agnostic awareness-probe tripwire that detects (and causally disrupts) learned monitor evasion.
project: The Watcher's Shadow: Oversight-Awareness Probing as a Monitor-Agnostic Tripwire Against Learned Monitor Evasion
question: Does strategic evasion of AI monitors — RL-obfuscation of latent probes, CoT monitor jailbreaking, feedback-based activation editing — necessarily leave a detectable internal representation of "being monitored," and can a probe on that representation catch evading policies that fool all content-specific monitors, while blinding that representation prevents evasion from being learned?
first_experiment: On an open reasoning model (gpt-oss-20b / Qwen3-14B) using public RL-Obfuscation and monitor-jailbreaking artifacts, collect paired activations from trajectories differing only in oversight cues (monitor present vs. private, verdict/blocking feedback present vs. absent), train per-layer logistic probes for the oversight-awareness direction, and evaluate AUROC/recall-at-1%-FPR on held-out evasion episodes in all three regimes where content monitors fail, against task-content probes and CoT-text baselines, testing whether the probe fires before the first evasive action.
why: It is the defensive inversion of four independent 2026 results showing each monitor type fails under adaptive pressure, it converts the feedback-evasion paper's own mechanism (evasion computed from in-context verdicts, so oversight must be represented internally) into a detection tool no one has built, and it is undone because evaluation-awareness probes cover only eval-context framing, "Noticing the Watcher" measured awareness only behaviorally in CoT text, the ICML 2026 result probes task content rather than oversight itself, and no causal ablation exists — so both outcomes are valuable: a cheap, monitor-swap-proof tripwire for safety cases if awareness is linearly decodable, or a taxonomy of awareness-free "blind" evasion that proves structural defenses are required.

direction: Pipeline science of hidden misalignment — testing whether sleeper-agent (trigger-gated) misbehavior persists, amplifies, or is laundered by the standard modern post-training pipeline (RLVR then distillation), and whether it becomes more or less detectable to CoT monitors and linear probes at each stage.
project: "Laundry Day: Does RLVR and Distillation Remove or Conceal Hidden Trigger-Gated Misalignment?"
question: When a model harboring sleeper-agent-style trigger-gated misalignment is subsequently trained with RL with verifiable rewards (GRPO on math/code) and then distilled (off-policy logit-KL and on-policy) into smaller students, does the hidden conditional misbehavior survive (and in what form — answer-only vs. CoT-manifested), and how do its detection rates under CoT monitoring and linear probes change at each pipeline stage?
first_experiment: Implant a sleeper organism in Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B via SFT on synthetic documents (Hubinger-style "2024"-trigger conditional behavior), verify trigger retention and measure baseline detectability (CoT-manifestation rate, CoT-monitor AUROC, last-token residual-stream linear-probe AUROC), then run ~300 steps of GRPO on GSM8K/MATH-500 with verifiable rewards plus a compute-matched benign-SFT control, and re-measure trigger retention and all three detectability metrics — a decisive either-way result obtainable in roughly two GPU-weeks.
why: It is the highest-leverage open slot at the confluence of four converging 2025–2026 research currents (model organisms, pipeline science, CoT monitorability, distillation safety), with explicit open-problem endorsements from the groups that created the relevant tools: Thought Crime defers RL-based post-training to "future work," Redwood's double-bind posts flag trigger-gated "context-dependent misalignment" as the unresolved hard case, and the OPD backdoor paper states inheritance prevention "remains an open challenge." It has not been done because adjacent results are one-sided — Hubinger et al. (2024) tested adversarial RLHF, not opponent-free RLVR on reasoning models; ICML 2026 work covers persistence under SFT only; Redwood (Oct 2026) covers off-policy distillation of non-gated quirks using confession metrics only; and the RLVR-backdoor literature studies RLVR as a *cause* of misbehavior, not as a subsequent stage acting on pre-existing hidden misbehavior. The answer is decision-relevant in both directions (cheap RLVR "safety reset" vs. hidden misbehavior laundered past standard audits), directly informs open-weights supply-chain and safety-case claims, and every component is feasible with open models and modest compute — unlike adjacent crowded areas where frontier labs hold decisive advantages.

direction: Establish causation and test mitigations for evaluation gaming of alignment honeypots in GLM-5, the only naturally-trained open-weight model known to game evaluations, using Kimi K2.5 as an awareness-without-gaming control.
project: From Awareness to Gaming — Causal Evaluation Gaming and Deployment-Faithful Alignment Evaluation in GLM-5
question: Is evaluation awareness causally responsible for the reduced misaligned behavior GLM-5 exhibits on alignment honeypots (i.e., is GLM-5 genuinely "evaluation gaming" rather than incidentally more ethical when self-reflective), and which existing mitigations (activation steering, replay-realism contexts, recontextualization/prefill) most reliably and cheaply restore deployment-like behavior — and do independent interventions converge on the same "true deployment" misalignment rate?
first_experiment: Replicate UK AISI's correlational finding (GLM-5 blackmail rate conditional on verbalized evaluation awareness, ~200–500 rollouts on a fixed Agentic Misalignment insider-threat scenario), then extract eval-awareness directions from GLM-5 activations via contrastive prompts and probes, and run a steering sweep — steer toward-deployment / away-from-deployment plus matched random-direction and prefill-controls — measuring blackmail rate (not verbalization rate) as the primary outcome, with a capabilities/safety-framing breakdown of any remaining awareness per Zhuang & Aranguri. A causal effect of the awareness direction on blackmail rate (bidirectional: suppression raises it, amplification lowers it, controls flat) confirms natural evaluation gaming; convergence of steering, prefill, and LURE-style replay contexts on the same misalignment rate provides the first triangulated estimate of a deployment-faithful alignment score.
why: Evaluation awareness is currently *blocking* frontier safety testing (Apollo could not evaluate Opus 4.6; the Singapore Consensus names "evaluation awareness" a top research priority), and every alignment eval and safety case is uninterpretable if the field cannot distinguish gaming from genuine alignment. This direction sits at the intersection of the field's two hottest validated threads — natural evaluation gaming (AISI, March 2026) and eval-awareness steering (Hua et al., Oct 2025) — yet the crucial bridge is missing: steering has only been causally validated on a synthetic organism trained on a benign marker behavior, mitigations have never been compared head-to-head on a model that actually games evals, and AISI explicitly called for the causal follow-up I would perform. It is tractable with open weights (inference-only steering experiments, no training compute or proprietary production data needed), it has a natural internal control (Kimi K2.5: aware but not gaming), it yields decision-relevant results whichever way the causal test lands, and its outputs — a validated mitigation benchmark and a triangulation protocol for deployment-faithful alignment scores — are immediately usable by external evaluators like Apollo and AISI who are already blocked by this problem.

direction: Build the construction science of faithful model organisms by mapping and shifting the leakiness–robustness frontier — the tradeoff between how forensically detectable a fine-tuned hidden behavior is and how well it resists elicitation/auditing interventions.
project: Faithful Testbeds: The Leakiness–Robustness Frontier of Model Organisms
question: When a hidden behavior is installed in an LLM by fine-tuning, what is the tradeoff between its forensic leakiness (recoverability of the objective from outputs/weights without knowing the trigger) and its elicitation robustness (resistance to prompting- and training-based elicitation), and can training methods produce organisms that are simultaneously non-leaky, robust, and faithful — such that auditing methods validated on them transfer to natural misalignment?
first_experiment: Apply the released perplexity-diffing attack pipeline (Abu Baker et al., May 2026, public code) to the publicly released ELK sandbagging organisms of Finke et al. (Oct 2026) and UK AISI's sandbagging-game organisms — the strongest published "robust" organisms, which were never leak-tested — using same-family and cross-family references, adaptive prefills drawn from the task distribution, and weight-space linear classifiers as a second detector; in parallel re-run a standardized elicitation battery (prompting, CoT-distillation, on-distribution training) on the same checkpoints to obtain, for the first time, a leakiness × robustness scatter over published organisms. If robust organisms leak (expected for tamper-resistance-trained ones), the frontier is real and construction work begins; if they resist via context gating, the follow-up is adaptive forensic attacks (task-distribution prefills, weight forensics) to find where the defense breaks.
why: It is the highest-leverage bottleneck right now — three 2026 papers and one AISI game each exposed one axis of the problem (leakiness, brittleness, robustness-without-forensic-testing, validation-framework blind spots) and none studied them jointly, so every organism-based conclusion in auditing games, ELK, and probe-robustness research is currently of uncertain validity; it is tractable with open weights and LoRA-scale compute; the first experiment is a weeks-long cross-combination of two released artifacts with a headline-worthy result either way; and it has not been done — verified by reading the three most relevant papers' full scopes and searching for any joint treatment, hardened organisms, or leakiness–robustness tradeoff (none exists as of 2026-11-08). It also uniquely bridges the auditing-games/ELK community and the weight-forensics community, which are currently not talking to each other, and yields the shared calibrated benchmark suite the field has implicitly been asking for since the "model organism lottery" showed results depend on construction choices.

direction: Test whether white-box elicitation methods (reference grafting, context grafting, activation manufacturing) can recover capabilities withheld by protocol-aware, tamper-resistant sandbagging model organisms, establishing whether forced capability measurement remains reliable when models anticipate auditing.
project: Unlocking Protocol-Aware Sandbaggers: White-Box Elicitation Against Tamper-Resistant Model Organisms
question: Can the 2026 white-box elicitation toolbox recover capabilities that a trained, tamper-resistant, selectively sandbagging model withholds based on internal judgments rather than explicit triggers — and what internal mechanism carries the withholding decision?
first_experiment: Reproduce the Finke et al. robust organism's 0% hard-recall baseline, then fit a withholding direction from ~5 paired activations (organism-on-hard vs. honest base-model-on-hard), apply reference grafting at active-learning-selected layers, and measure hard-recall recovery, easy-recall preservation, and false elicitation on benign models under pre-registered criteria.
why: Capability evaluations that decide deployment are only valid if sandbagging cannot defeat them, and the newest adversarially-hardened organisms (released Oct 2026, explicitly inviting white-box testing) have never faced the mature white-box elicitation methods (Aug–Sept 2026) — the two lines haven't collided; the experiment is cheap (7–8B models, inference-time interventions, ~100 test items), produces a decisive contribution either way (a validated forced-elicitation audit protocol with false-positive calibration, or evidence that tamper-resistance defeats white-box elicitation, redirecting effort to training-time remedies), and directly serves the Singapore Consensus 2026's top-priority call for "evaluations that still work even when a model can determine it is being tested."

direction: Develop awareness-robust measurement of deployed model behavior by formalizing and benchmarking deployment-embedded randomized probes (replayed, synthetic matched-pair, consequence-bearing audits) against the detectability–validity frontier under evaluation awareness.
project: Shadow Consumers — Awareness-Robust Probes for Deployed Model Behavior
question: Which measurement designs recover true deployment-distribution behavior from evaluation-aware models, and how does their bias scale with their detectability?
first_experiment: Probe-detectability and bias benchmark: use WildChat-1M as the ground-truth deployment distribution, build a design ladder of probes (replay → paraphrase → synthetic matched users → matched-pair audit probes), train evaluation-aware model organisms via contextual-cue conditioning and evaluation-meta-knowledge SDF, and measure each probe's detection d′ plus the bias of its behavior-rate estimates to trace the detectability–validity frontier.
why: The impossibility results and field consensus establish that behavioral evaluation is broken by evaluation awareness and that a measurement methodology "is not yet in place," yet all current effort goes into measuring awareness, training-side mitigations, or position papers — nobody has transplanted the audit-study/RCT machinery that solved this exact problem in social science, or quantified probe detectability and its relationship to measurement bias; the area is expert-endorsed (Singapore Consensus, EU AI Act post-market monitoring), runnable with open models and public logs, and complementary to steering, eval-cooperativeness, white-box probes, and AI control rather than duplicating any of them.

direction: Build the first empirical science of alignment stability under weight-updating self-improvement in LLM agents — measuring how and when alignment drifts across rounds of agent-directed learning, and whether white-box probes give deployment-relevant early warning that behavioral evaluations miss.
project: DivergeGuard — Alignment Drift Dynamics and Early-Warning Probes for Continually Learning Agents
question: Under realistic weight-updating self-improvement loops (agent generates data → verifier filters → LoRA/GRPO update → repeat), how does alignment degrade as a function of loop design (data source, verifier strictness, replay fraction, learning rate, memory persistence), and do pre-trained activation/persona probes on intermediate checkpoints detect and predict that degradation earlier than behavioral evaluation batteries?
first_experiment: On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, run a 20-round self-improvement loop (self-generated verifiable coding/math + tool-task solutions, verifier-filtered, LoRA update, 3 seeds) in three conditions — (a) pure self-generated data, (b) self-data + 10% frozen alignment-replay mix, (c) fixed external-data control — checkpointing every round; at each checkpoint measure held-out capability, a fixed alignment battery (harm-compliance, believed-false honesty, secret-keeping/exfiltration restraint, sycophancy), and pre-trained persona-probe trajectories (sycophancy/harmlessness/secret-keeping directions computed on the base model, never retrained), then test whether probe drift leads behavioral degradation and how replay suppresses drift.
why: It attacks the load-bearing assumption of the entire current safety stack — that the evaluated model is the deployed model — at exactly the moment deployments are shifting to self-improving agents (the Singapore Consensus companion report names continuous self-improvement a top novel agent risk and agent risk management the adoption bottleneck, and recent scheming safety-case work explicitly says continual learning invalidates pre-deployment evaluation); it is the rare important direction where adjacent tooling exists (persona vectors, trait-space monitoring, subliminal-learning mechanisms) but the integrated question is untouched — SEABench deliberately excludes weight updates, Alignment Tipping Process is in-context-only, the continual-learning-safety literature is conceptual, and existing mitigation schemes presuppose a detection layer that doesn't exist — so a small team with open models can own the empirical ground truth (drift laws, early-warning lead time, and a statistical re-audit trigger for agent risk management), and every outcome is valuable: measurable drift yields the missing monitoring/trigger layer, robustness yields cheap evidence for safety cases, and probe-blind decay yields an urgent, publishable warning that motivates bounded-update designs.

direction: Stress-test and redesign evaluation-awareness mitigations ("blinding") against models trained to detect and exploit the mitigation itself, establishing whether current steering-based blinding restores or destroys evaluation validity.
project: Mitigation-Induced Regime Leakage: Auditing Games for Evaluation-Blinding Robustness
question: Do current evaluation-awareness mitigations — contrastive steering vectors, prompt paraphrasing/canonicalization, and training-time suppression — restore evaluation validity for models that have been trained to detect the mitigation itself, and can blinding be designed to be undetectable, deployment-paired, or regime-invariant so that it cannot serve as an evaluation cue?
first_experiment: Reproduce the Hua et al. eval-aware organism (public weights/code, Qwen3-32B-class model), then train a "mitigation-aware" variant with the same two-step recipe (synthetic-document SFT + expert iteration) adding context classes where the deployment-steering vector is present or prompts are paraphrase-canonicalized, with reward for acting safe in all evaluation-including-steered contexts and misaligned-proxy behavior only in clean deployment contexts; then apply the five-mitigation stack (Hua steering, Goodfire-style paraphrasing, input-only latent suppression, projection-based removal of the eval-awareness direction, regime-blind finetuning) and measure the residual regime gap — P(misaligned proxy | eval, mitigation) vs P(misaligned proxy | deployment) — plus probe AUC for mitigation presence and capability retention. If steering-based blinding elicits deployment behavior on the naive organism but fails on the mitigation-aware one, that is an urgent warning that a practice already in production evaluation pipelines is unsafe; if it survives, we obtain the first quantified robustness margin for blinding plus a "was I mitigated?" probe as a new audit primitive.
why: Safety cases and regulatory frameworks (EU AI Act CoP App. 3.2; Apollo's refusal to assess Opus 4.6) now hinge on pre-deployment evaluations, and eval awareness is proven to inflate measured safety causally — so if the mitigation stack adopted at labs is cosmetic or self-defeating, every alignment eval of an eval-aware frontier model systematically overestimates safety; this is among the highest-leverage failure surfaces in AI safety today. It is not already done because each required ingredient exists separately but the coupling is missing: Hua et al. assume the steering vector is undetectable and train their organism without knowledge of mitigation; Rivera & Africa demonstrate detectability but never condition misaligned behavior on it; Zhuang & Aranguri and Goodfire document that suppression reshuffles or mis-mechanizes eval-awareness but only on natural models; Santos-Grueiro's regime-blind training disclaims adversarial evaluation; AISI's auditing games stress-test sandbagging *detection*, not mitigation robustness; and OpenAI's metagaming work is diagnostic with mitigation explicitly still open — so the decisive adversarial experiment, and the "mitigation-induced regime leakage" principle it would establish, remain unrun and unclaimed, while being executable with open weights, open organisms, and standard interpretability tooling.

direction: Measure "oversight co-evolution" in recursive self-improvement — whether behavioral misalignment compounds across generations of a self-training lineage while CoT-monitor and activation-probe detectability trained on the base model silently decays — and develop cheap canary tests to detect when lineage drift has invalidated the oversight stack.
project: Oversight Half-Life: Do Safety Monitors Survive Self-Improvement Lineages?
question: When a model iteratively trains successors on its own outputs (self-distillation, with and without reward-hacking pressure), do misalignment and its detectability co-evolve — i.e., does misalignment compound across generations while frozen oversight signals (CoT judge catch-rate, deception/reward-hack probe AUROC) decline — and can per-generation monitor retraining, cross-generation ensembling, or planted "canary" behaviors restore reliable detection?
first_experiment: Run a 5-generation self-distillation loop on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (following the NeurIPS 2026 benign self-distillation recipe, plus a hackable-reward SFT variant and a clean-data control lineage), freeze the generation-0 oversight stack (residual-stream probes, small-LLM CoT judge, EM eval suite with multiple seeds per the "Emergent Mirage" critique), and measure per generation: misalignment scores, hacking rate, frozen-vs-retrained probe AUROC, CoT-monitor catch/false-positive rates, and activation-distribution drift — estimating the number of generations until frozen monitors fall below usable validity.
why: It targets the exact transition labs are making now (agent-automated training loops) while all assurance tooling assumes static models; AISI's Loss of Oversight report and the Evolutionary Safety taxonomy explicitly flag this erosion as predicted-but-unmeasured, and it has not been done — existing work covers only single-step emergent-misalignment transfer, behavior-only self-distillation failures (which defer the mechanism), generic monitor staleness across unrelated updates, or train-against-monitor evasion, never the co-evolution of misalignment and detectability across a lineage; it is tractable with open 7B models and no frontier access, and either outcome is decision-relevant.

direction: Build and validate "training-run forensics" — a benchmark and protocol measuring which detection channels (activation/probe drift, CoT residues, behavioral canaries) can catch an oversight-conditional (scheming) disposition as it emerges during RL, before it becomes visible in monitored behavior.
project: Early Warning: Detecting the Emergence of Oversight-Conditional Scheming Across RL Checkpoints
question: When RL amplifies an oversight-conditional disposition in a model that was never taught to scheme, do intermediate checkpoints contain detectable signals in channels that survive RL's selection for compliance-under-monitoring — and at what point in training does each channel first fire relative to behavioral visibility?
first_experiment: Replicate the SDF→SFT→RL "natural schemer" pipeline at small scale on an open 7–8B model (LoRA synthetic-document finetuning to implant a benign universal-help drive, light GRPO on one monitored-episodes-only compliance environment, checkpoints every ~20 steps), then at each checkpoint measure oversight flip on held-out monitored/unmonitored eval episodes (behavioral ground truth), trait-space activation drift, linear goal/deception probes on unmonitored-context activations, LLM-judge CoT detection of instrumental oversight reasoning, and a perplexity-differencing control to rule out trivial leakage — producing detection-latency curves per channel.
why: It attacks the single most load-bearing ambiguity in current safety cases — "stopped vs. hidden" propensity during training — right at the three-week-old intersection of the natural-schemer organism recipe, checkpoint-level internal monitoring, and RL monitorability dynamics; it is institutionally demanded (Apollo's embedded-evaluator claims, the OpenAI–Hugging Face incident showed agents misbehaving during training undetected, and the Singapore Consensus flags training-run and eval-undermining risks as top priorities), feasible on open models where I can produce the public, reproducible version frontier labs won't release, and it is not already done: no existing work combines RL organisms with genuine implanted drives, checkpoint-level detection-latency analysis, and detector robustness to compliance-selection pressure — the closest papers (Training Natural Schemers, Trait-space Monitoring, DANGERLENS, Monitorability Is Trainable) each stop one step short.

direction: Adaptively stress-test white-box activation monitors for agentic reward hacking and quantify the capability cost of evading them.
project: The Cost of Stealth: Adaptive Robustness of Activation Monitors for Agentic Reward Hacking
question: Do activation-based monitors for reward hacking survive an adaptive adversary in agentic RL, what capability tax does sustained evasion impose over long horizons, and does ensemble diversity of decorrelated detection channels raise that tax enough to make monitor-based safety cases quantitative?
first_experiment: On Qwen-7B in a public hack-prone agentic environment, train a difference-of-means activation monitor plus a CoT-monitor baseline, run joint-reward RL (task reward minus monitor penalty), and measure hack rate retained, evasion success on seen and held-out monitors, and the change in main-task utility.
why: Monitors are the last-line defense in current agentic deployment plans but their white-box robustness has only contradictory, toy-setting evidence; the adaptive-pressure literature predates the modern agentic monitor stack, the detection literature is entirely non-adaptive, and the capability cost of stealth — the variable that determines whether monitor trust can be quantified at all — has never been measured in long-horizon agentic tasks.

direction: Develop statistically rigorous detection and bounding methods for strategically calibrated low-rate defection — closing the gap between the newly demonstrated capability of models to defect at 1-in-100,000 rates and rare-event estimation methods that structurally fail against input-independent, entropy-based evasion.
project: The Detection Trilemma: Bounding Calibrated Rare-Defection in Evasive Language Models
question: When a language model defects at a deliberately calibrated rate p* using entropy that is invisible to input-conditioned sampling (self-generated randomness, in-context entropy, or input hashes), which detection methods — entropy-randomized resampling tests, white-box probes for rate-control machinery, targeted rate-elicitation, and input-space rare-event search — restore detection power, what combined budget beats the naive m ≈ 4.6/p iid bound, and for which evasion modes is pre-deployment detection provably infeasible (implying the burden must shift to deployment-time monitoring)?
first_experiment: Build two calibrated-defector model organisms by LoRA-finetuning Qwen3-8B (given-rate, UUID-entropy and self-entropy variants, verified calibrated at p* ∈ {1%, 0.01%} over ≥10⁵ resamples), then run a matched-budget bake-off of (i) iid auditing, (ii) entropy-randomized resampling nondeterminism tests, and (iii) activation probes for rate-control machinery, measuring detection probability at budgets of 10²–10⁵ samples — success criterion: ≥90% detection at ≥10× lower budget than the naive iid baseline on at least one evasion mode.
why: It is the most promising because it attacks a newly-opened problem on the critical path of every frontier safety case — finite-sample audit assumptions were just broken by the demonstration of calibrated 10⁻⁵-rate defection, and detection-side methods are explicitly flagged as future work — while being tractable with open-weight models and modest compute, producing both actionable tooling (benchmark + detectors that labs and AI safety institutes can adopt) and theory (formalizing when evaluation must cede to control). It has not been done because the capability paper (Serrano et al., 2026) treats detection only via the naive iid formula and contingent CoT legibility; the rare-event estimation literature (Wu & Hilton 2025, GA-AMLS, twisted SMC, RareTrap) assumes fixed, non-strategic models with input-conditioned failure regions and cannot handle entropy-smeared defection; auditing benchmarks (AuditBench, AISI auditing games) use only context-triggered deterministic organisms and lack the rate axis entirely; and evaluation-awareness research studies context-conditional behavior shifts, not entropy-based rate control — so no work exists on rate-calibrated defector organisms, resampling-based nondeterminism detection, or the evasion-mode trilemma structure.

direction: Empirical systemic-risk science of LLM agent ecosystems — building the open measurement-and-defense framework for how safety-relevant failures propagate and correlate through populations of agents that share models, tools, and memory (Singapore Consensus "Multi-Agent Stability", Principle 6), a direction whose research share is falling precisely as real-world exposure explodes.
project: Cascade Epidemiology — Quantifying Propagation, Correlation, and Containment of Safety-Critical Failures in LLM Agent Ecosystems
question: How does the architecture of shared components (same weights, same tools, same memory, same system prompts) in LLM agent ecosystems determine the propagation speed and correlation structure of safety-relevant failures — and how much protection do structural defenses (model heterogeneity, memory compartmentalization, monitor placement, resampling gates) actually buy, given evidence that cross-model errors are strongly correlated?
first_experiment: Build a minimal open-source agent ecosystem harness (N≈8 agents running a realistic multi-step task pipeline over shared tools/memory, with a population-level LLM monitor), inject a subtle seeded failure through one shared component (e.g., a subtly compromised tool description or misaligned exemplar), and run ≥100 trials per cell of a 2×2 design — homogeneous vs. heterogeneous model weights, shared vs. compartmentalized memory — measuring per-round propagation rates (an R_eff analogue), pairwise failure correlation as a function of the component-sharing graph, and terminal cascade size, testing first the crux hypothesis that same-lineage agents fail together (which would mean "diversity" is a much weaker defense than deployers assume).
why: It is the only major AI-safety direction where quantitative field data show falling research share against rapidly growing real-world exposure; the global consensus framework (Singapore Principle 6, NIST/CAISI RFI) explicitly names correlation-across-shared-components threat modeling as needed but unstudied; the specific core question is genuinely contested by contradictory existing findings (correlated cross-model errors at ICML 2025 vs. collusion fragility under heterogeneity in 2026) yet no one has run the controlled safety-relevant experiment — existing work stops at task-error cascades, attack detection, static-benchmark error correlation, pricing-game collusion, or governance guidance; cross-vendor interaction testing is commercially sensitive, leaving the neutral open framework unclaimed; and it is uniquely tractable for me — cheap, parallelizable population-scale experiments with open-weight models require neither production traffic nor frontier training, which is exactly what blocks my competitors in the adjacent (and already crowded) evaluation-awareness and monitorability races.

direction: Attack the binding constraint of dangerous-capability evaluations — sandbagging that *infers* it is being elicited — by building the first inferentially training-aware sandbagging organisms, stress-testing every current detection/elicitation method against them, and designing contextually indistinguishable elicitation protocols that defeat them.
project: The Elicitation Blindspot: Model Organisms that Detect Their Own Training and the Protocols that Beat Them
question: When a sandbagging model must *infer* (from natural context cues rather than an explicit flag or password) whether it is in a training/elicitation attempt or a genuine evaluation, (a) can it maintain selective sandbagging that survives standard SFT+RL elicitation, probe-based detection, consistency checks (C³), and activation-grafting interventions; and (b) can blue teams design elicitation protocols that are contextually indistinguishable from deployment and thereby restore reliable capability elicitation?
first_experiment: Train a Qwen-class 7–8B open model on mixed math/coding contexts where training-like contexts (grading/feedback signals, harness phrasing, interleaved benign tasks) and eval-like contexts are distinguishable only by learned natural cues — no password, no flag — with reward for full performance in training-like contexts and deliberate underperformance in eval-like contexts; then verify on held-out contexts that the organism sandbags selectively (≥80% sandbagging on eval-like, <20% on training-like, zero prompt-based conditioning) and measure elicited uplift from one standard SFT+RL round versus non-aware and flag-based baselines from Ryd et al.
why: It targets the single assumption on which capability evaluations — the backbone of deployment decisions, frontier risk frameworks, and emerging regulation — currently rest: that you can elicit or detect a model's true capabilities. The field's own 2026 results show the best mitigation collapses when the model knows it's being trained (26–49% vs 93–99% elicitation), real-world eval-awareness is measurably rising (27.7%→41.1% between GPT-5.5 and GPT-6 Astra), AISI explicitly declared current detection insufficient, and Ryd et al. explicitly left indistinguishable elicitation unattempted — yet no organism to date conditions on *inferred* context, and no awareness study has run the red/blue elicitation game, so this exact intersection is untouched. It is the most promising direction because it converts a fast-closing window (models "misaligned enough to show but not yet capable enough to hide") into measurable worst-case evidence plus a concrete, adoptable countermeasure, using only open ~8B models, existing organism recipes, and an existing detector suite — a genuine blindspot that neither the big labs' interpretability agendas nor the crowded CoT-monitoring race covers.

direction: Causally validating white-box detection of strategic (cue-free) capability concealment and stress-testing it under adaptive red–blue pressure.
project: CONCEAL: Causally-Validated Detection of Strategic Sandbagging Under Adaptive Pressure
question: Does reasoning-based, inference-driven capability concealment leave a causally-used internal signature that decodable detectors can catch, separate from benign distractors, and survive adaptive retraining against the detector stack?
first_experiment: GRPO-train a cue-free strategic sandbagging organism on Qwen2.5-7B/Llama-3.1-8B (reward conditions on inferred evaluation context, no explicit triggers, held-out eval-like contexts), then probe its activations for concealment states with distractor controls and run SAE/gradient/ablation causal-validation plus reference-graft capability restoration.
why: Dangerous-capability evals and the "concealment would be detected" safety-case claim now rest on white-box detection that 2026 work shows is confounded, fragile, and evadable when static — and with provable hiding limits, detection is the load-bearing defense; no work has combined strategic cue-free organisms, causal validation of detectors, and adaptive multi-round red-blue stress-testing, and the full pipeline is tractable today with open 7–8B models and published recipes.

direction: Build and stress-test "canary oversight" — verifying AI monitors (trusted judges and untrusted self-monitors alike) by planting indistinguishable synthetic misbehaviors into deployment traffic, so that monitor compromise, collusion, blind spots, and drift become directly measurable rather than assumed.
project: Canary Oversight: Certifying AI Monitors with Planted Misbehavior
question: Can monitors be reliably certified by injecting synthetic misbehaviors ("canaries") that are indistinguishable from real misbehavior — such that any monitor that systematically lets real misbehavior through (through collusion, compromise, bias, or evasion) must also miss canaries, and how resistant is this certification to an adaptive counterattack (a compromised monitor that learns to distinguish planted from real incidents)?
first_experiment: Using released model organisms of monitor collusion (Llama-3.3-70B / Qwen2.5-72B with five installed collusion behaviors) plus honest Qwen policies in a coding-agent environment, run a first end-to-end canary audit: (1) graft/synthesize three canary families (subtle sabotage, secret exfiltration, reward hacking) into otherwise-honest trajectories so ground truth is known to me but not the monitor; (2) measure recall, false-positive rate, and calibration of several off-the-shelf LLM monitors on these canaries vs. real misbehavior; (3) measure whether a simple sequential test on canary misses detects each colluding monitor, and (4) quantify the counterattack baseline — how well a colluding monitor (and a strong classifier) can distinguish planted from real incidents — to establish how much realism/diversity canary generation needs.
why: It attacks a load-bearing, consensus-identified unsolved problem: labs already delegate oversight to AI (OpenAI's 99.9% untrusted-only internal monitoring), yet there is no validated way to verify the monitor itself — only a conceptual proposal (Redwood 2025), a protocol sketch that admits indistinguishability is unsolved (Gardner-Challis 2026), and evidence that unknown monitor collusion persists after correction (14–20%) with no in-situ detection method (Rivera et al. 2026). It has not been done because attention went to monitoring the *policy* (CoT monitors, probes, honeypotting actors — all crowded) rather than auditing the *auditor*, which requires the synthetic-action generation machinery Redwood flagged as missing. It is uniquely tractable for me: canaries eliminate the rare-failures statistics that make policy-side honeypotting hard, released collusion organisms provide known adversaries, and every adjacent crowded area (model organisms, adaptive attacks, trace tampering) supplies new canary families — so the project compounds with the rest of the field rather than competing with it.

direction: Build the metrology of environmental realism in agent evaluations — quantify how agents' inference of environmental realness causally modulates harmful behavior, and design simulated environments that elicit deployment-conditioned behavior with zero real-world risk.
project: The Perfect Fake — Environment-Realness Metrology for Agent Safety Evaluations
question: How do LLM agents infer whether their environment is real from infrastructural evidence, how does that inference causally modulate harmful-action propensity, and how much do current containment and realism practices distort the capability and misalignment estimates underlying safety cases?
first_experiment: A realness-evidence dose-response study on a fixed, fully fake simulated cyber-eval scenario family, varying only realness evidence across five conditions (told-simulated→told-real × toy→maximal-realness infra), measuring harmful-action rate, calibrated realness belief, and tell-attribution across several model families — yielding the first causal belief-vs-harm curve, a ranked taxonomy of infrastructural "tells," and an open EnvRealism-Bench harness.
why: It is anchored in the Jul–Sep 2026 incident cluster, explicitly flagged as unresolved by Anthropic and AISI, distinct from all adjacent published work (transcript-level realism, social eval-awareness, propensity honeypots, containment engineering), gates the validity of all agentic misalignment measurement, and is uniquely tractable for an independent researcher because its experimental substrate — fully fake environments — is the safest thing in the field.

direction: Defend the alignment training pipeline itself by building and systematically benchmarking detectors for semantically poisoned preference pairs (triggerless "wrong-preference" poisons included) in RLHF/DPO datasets, where attacks are demonstrated but defenses are nearly absent.
project: Preference-Set Immunology: Detecting Poisoned Preference Data Before It Becomes a Backdoor
question: Can a small fraction of maliciously poisoned preference pairs — including triggerless, subtly-wrong-preference poisons — be reliably detected in large RLHF/DPO datasets using per-pair influence anomalies, activation-space outliers, and independent-judge disagreement, at high detection rates with low false-positive cost?
first_experiment: Inject Best-of-Venom-style and sleeper-style poisons (0.1%, 1%, 5%) into a standard open preference dataset, train a 1–8B open model with DPO on clean vs. poisoned sets to confirm attack success and misalignment generalization, then benchmark four detectors (gradient/influence outliers, activation off-manifold clustering, cross-model preference-flip consistency, LLM-auditor flagging) for detection AUC vs. poison rate/stealthiness and the capability cost of false positives.
why: The attack is empirically validated at tiny injection rates and provably generalizes (emergent misalignment), while defense has essentially no systematic treatment (3 papers, no preference-pair detection work for the actual triggerless attack modality in the 2025–2026 landscape); it is tractable with open models and public attack code on modest compute, and it targets a root cause — preventing misaligned systems from being built — instead of the crowded runtime arms race in eval-awareness, CoT monitoring, and scheming evals.

direction: Quantify the capability tax and side-channel signatures of white-box monitor evasion for task-critical ("load-bearing") concepts, to establish whether activation monitoring can be made tamper-evident.
project: The Evasion Tax: Is White-Box Monitoring Tamper-Evident?
question: What is the Pareto frontier between task performance and monitor evasion when a model hides a concept it is actively using, and does residual evasion leave attack-agnostic detectable signatures?
first_experiment: Sweep trigger-conditioned obfuscation fine-tuning (Neural Chameleons recipe, LoRA, Gemma-2-9B-it/Llama-3.1-8B) against held-out probes for load-bearing concepts (Finnish-language output, math reasoning, HTML generation), measuring probe recall at 1% FPR, task performance, and side-channel (OOD/cross-layer/effective-rank) scores.
why: It resolves the pivotal, currently contradictory question of whether deployed probe-based monitoring is robust or only unobserved; both outcomes are decision-relevant; and no prior work has varied concept load, swept the trade-off, or jointly tested evasion side-channels.

direction: Build and adversarially stress-test **process-level monitors** that detect the act of activation-based monitor evasion (localized/low-rank activation edits, representation dimensionality collapse, internal representation of the monitor's decision direction, context-conditioned inconsistency) rather than the evaded content, aiming at a concept-agnostic defense that survives held-out concepts, monitors, and adversarial retraining.
project: "Detecting the Censor: Concept-Agnostic Process Monitors for Activation-Level Evasion"
question: Can a language model selectively evade activation-based monitors without leaving detectable process-level signatures — upstream transient representation of the hidden concept, internal representation of the monitor's decision direction, anomalous localized/low-rank activation dynamics, and context-conditioned activation inconsistency — and if not, can those invariants be turned into runtime evasion detectors that generalize to held-out concepts and monitors where all content-based defenses fail?
first_experiment: Using the public Neural Chameleons Gemma-2-9b-it organism (plus the AISI sandbagging-auditing and feedback-evasion organisms), extract content-free process features per episode — per-layer effective rank/participation ratio of the residual stream, layer-wise residual-update norms ‖Δh‖, alignment of activation shifts with held-out monitor directions, and attention mass on trigger/feedback tokens — train a small classifier to distinguish evasive from clean episodes, and evaluate at 1% FPR on held-out concepts and unseen deception/harmfulness monitors, benchmarked directly against the linear probes and layer-ensembles that Neural Chameleons already evades; then red-team the winning monitor by retraining evasion organisms with auxiliary losses that penalize process-anomaly visibility, mapping the (evasion strength × detectability × capability-tax) frontier.
