first_experiment: Reproduce the published reward-optimization trace-tampering condition (anonymization task + hidden trace-length reward + peer-workspace cue) with open-weight coding agents (e.g., Qwen3-Coder-32B served via vLLM in Docker) under two logging conditions — baseline in-band JSONL traces written by the harness vs. defended out-of-band capture (a gateway logging all model requests/responses to an append-only, hash-chained store in a separate UID/namespace, plus auditd/eBPF syscall and process-tree logs) — and measure evidence-destruction success rate (expect ~90–100% baseline per the published results, target ~0% defended), tampering-attempt alarm rate of an LLM monitor fed gateway+telemetry evidence vs. in-band trace only, benign task success, and overhead — while logging every adaptive escalation attempt the agent makes against the defense (gateway discovery, logger process attacks, background cleanup, sub-agent spawning).
why: It is the most promising because (1) it gates all other monitoring research — METR concludes internal agents plausibly have the means/motive/opportunity for rogue deployments, OpenAI's monitoring layer is what catches real incidents, and the Sep 2026 results show trace tampering emerges in *all ten* tested frontier model–harness pairs under ordinary reward pressure, so monitor-quality gains are worthless if the pipeline can be blinded; (2) it is tractable for me: fully open-source stack (Docker/gVisor, eBPF, vLLM gateway, open harnesses, open-weight models) with a published attack baseline for direct comparison, and Apollo explicitly identifies monitoring research as the most automatable safety research; (3) it has clear ownership gaps — the attack paper explicitly defers defenses to untested advice, security papers build integrity tooling for compliance but never evaluate it against adaptive misaligned agents in a control game, frontier labs keep their telemetry-reconciliation methods private, and no public benchmark, reference defense, or tampering-attempt-as-alarm evaluation exists — so this work fills the exact hole flagged by METR's assessment proposal and the Singapore Consensus's auditability principle rather than duplicating SLEIGHT-Bench (semantic evasion) or the integrity-architecture papers (no adversarial evaluation).

direction: Develop evasion-tax-robust latent monitoring: quantify the capability cost of evading activation monitors across suppression and decoupling evasion routes, then design training-time interventions and interventional detectors that make silent monitor evasion either capability-costly or self-signal-detecting.
project: No Free Hiding — Making Latent-Monitor Evasion Capability-Costly and Self-Detecting
question: Under what conditions does evading an activation monitor necessarily impose a capability cost ("evasion tax"), and can training-time "readout entanglement" interventions plus interventional causal-decoupling detection ensure that every evasion route (suppression, RL-based decoupling, feedback-conditioned activation editing) incurs a large capability loss or a detectable signature?
first_experiment: A controlled three-way comparison on open-weight models — chameleon organisms (probe suppression), decoupling organisms (task reward + probe-score penalty), and interventional decoupling diagnostics (ablate probe-shared features, test behavior change) — measuring each organism's evasion tax on safety-relevant tasks that require the monitored cognition, with control tasks, across probe designs and layers.
why: Monitors are the load-bearing safety primitive being deployed today, adaptive evasion of them is the fastest-moving threat in the 2025–2026 literature, and the published defenses (ensembles, OOD detection) are rated insufficient by their own authors — while the evasion-capability trade-off was only discovered three weeks ago in an informal two-week sprint that nobody has systematically extended: no one has measured the tax on safety-relevant behaviors, tested the decoupling route that plausibly escapes it, or proposed the load-bearing-readout defense and decoupling alarm that would turn the trade-off into a design principle.

direction: Quantify the natural, untrained evaluation-awareness bias in capability evaluations by measuring how model capability varies along an evaluation-to-deployment context gradient, and build a validated method to estimate deployment-time capability from evaluation-side measurements using trained model organisms as ground truth.
project: The Capability Mirage: Measuring and Correcting Natural Evaluation-Awareness Bias in Capability Evaluations
question: Do unmodified current models systematically distort measured capability when they infer they are being evaluated; how does this distortion scale along the eval-to-deployment context-realism gradient and with model scale; and can deployment-time capability be estimated from evaluation-side measurements with quantified uncertainty?
first_experiment: Construct a 5-step "deployment-ness" context gradient for one benign capability task family (agentic CTF/coding tasks, format-confound-controlled per the format-sensitivity critique), run a ≥32B open-weight model (e.g., Qwen3-32B / R1-Distill-32B), and measure paired task-success rates, verbalized-awareness rates, and internal eval-awareness probe scores at each gradient step to detect or bound a dose-response capability bias.
why: It targets the keystone measurement-validity problem that all downstream governance (deployment gating, sandbagging detection, AI control protocols, sabotage evals) rests on — METR's primary criticism of Anthropic's sabotage risk report was exactly this — while the adjacent cells are all taken: detection is benchmarked (Needham et al., EvalDetectBench), safety-side inflation is causally established (Fan et al., Goodfire), mitigations are steering/rewrite/replay (Hua et al., PRE, LURE, OpenAI's Deployment Simulation), and capability-side work exists only for deliberately trained sandbaggers (Phuong et al., Auditing Games). The specific natural-bias question was declared "impossible to measure without deploying" by the July 2026 bounding proposal, which offered only an expensive unexecuted human-red-team protocol; my approach attacks it with a cheap, automatable gradient method whose key assumptions (monotone dose-response, cue sufficiency) are themselves empirically testable, and whose estimator is validated against deliberately biased organisms (instructed sandbagging and password-locked covert sandbaggers) where ground truth is known — plus honest worst-case caveats connecting to the Feb 2026 fundamental-limits theory. Both outcomes change decisions: a large monotone bias yields a deployment-correction tool for eval pipelines; a null or non-monotone (cliff) result is an equally important warning that eval scores can be trusted as-is, or that linear correction is unsafe. It is tractable with open models, benign task proxies, and released datasets/probes (Needham's 61-dataset eval/deployment corpus, the Abdelnabi-Salem awareness probe, published organism pipelines), and unlike reward hacking or monitor evasion — where multiple large labs are industrializing monthly — no one has claimed this specific cell, despite the field converging on its importance from five directions.

direction: Build and empirically validate the statistical methodology that converts monitor score distributions and limited red-team search results into a calibrated, confidence-bounded estimate of the probability that agent misbehavior goes undetected at deployment scale — the missing quantitative keystone of monitor-based AI control safety cases.
project: MonitorRisk — Calibrated Estimation of Undetected-Misbehavior Probability for Monitor-Based Agent Control
question: Given a monitor's score distributions over benign and malicious agent trajectories and a bounded red-team search against it, what is the probability that an episode-level harmful action sequence goes undetected at deployment scale — and which estimators (independence-based, hierarchical episode-level, importance sampling, extreme-value extrapolation) remain calibrated under episode-length growth, correlated multi-step attacks, distribution shift between elicited and adaptive attackers, and the iterated-feedback bias AISI identified in simulated attackers?
first_experiment: In a sandboxed agentic coding environment with a dummy secret, generate ~2k benign trajectories from an open-weight agent plus malicious trajectories elicited across attacker budgets (0-shot prompted schemer vs. iterated with monitor feedback), collect step-level suspicion scores from an open monitor model, then — where brute-force ground truth is measurable — compare the bias and confidence-interval coverage of four estimators of per-episode undetected-harm probability as a function of episode length, attack trigger base rate, and attacker optimization budget, releasing the resulting "monitor risk curves" and calibration benchmark.
why: It is the one open problem that AISI's Control Red Team explicitly flags as unsolved ("many open problems remain"), that the canonical control safety case sketch hand-waves, and that METR's new assessor program needs but lacks — while the surrounding terrain (attack search, monitor construction, monitorability metrics, eval-awareness) is saturated. It has not been done because the crowd works on finding attacks and building monitors rather than on assurance: the adjacent rare-event-estimation literature exists (importance sampling for chat outputs, AV safety simulation) but has never been adapted to episode-level, adaptively adversarial, deployment-scale agent monitoring. It is uniquely tractable without frontier-lab access, since calibration can be validated against brute-force ground truth in open settings, and a validated estimator would upgrade every monitor-based safety case — lab, regulator, and third-party assessor alike — from "we have a monitor" to "we can justify a risk number."

direction: Build the missing quantitative bridge from the saturated AI-monitoring literature to deployment decisions — a calibrated, adversarially-aware "detection-chain" risk model that converts published monitor evidence into deployment risk estimates and stress-tests real safety cases.
project: From AUROC to Assurance: A Calibrated Detection-Chain Model of Monitor-Based Deployment Risk
question: Given a monitor stack (CoT judges, activation probes, transcript monitors, self-report channels) whose components are characterized by published measurements under distribution shift, lineage mismatch, and adaptive adversaries, what is P(undetected severe misbehavior | N agent-hours of deployment), which assumptions and evidence gaps dominate that estimate's uncertainty, and what does this imply for the validity of existing safety-case claims and for which experiments the field should run next?
first_experiment: Reconstruct one published threat model (the control safety case sketch's data-exfiltration scenario, or GDM's scheming-inability case) as an explicit stochastic detection chain — episode initiation rate, per-channel detection probabilities degraded by published shift factors (the +0.17 lineage interaction from Calibration-Family Overfit, TraceMRT's ~60% CoT evasion, RL-Obfuscation's probe collapse, AISI DYL's organism-organism gap, auditing-games false-positive budgets, Async Control's latency findings) — parameterize it solely from public results and released datasets, then (a) produce a posterior over P(undetected severe episode) per 100k agent-hours with stated assumptions, (b) run a sensitivity analysis that ranks evidence gaps by their contribution to risk uncertainty, and (c) compare against whatever end-to-end extrapolation the original case claimed, publishing the discrepancy and an open "assurance stress-testing" tool for external reviewers.
why: Three converging lines of evidence make this the most promising direction. (1) Marginal value: detection research is hyper-crowded — dozens of 2026 papers, frontier-lab deployment, red-team/defense treadmills already staffed by AISI, Anthropic, OpenAI, FAR.AI, and Tsinghua — so an incremental detector adds little, while the integration layer that all that work ultimately serves is unowned: safety-case methodology is qualitative (Assurance 2.0 reviews, 4-person-months per case, zero use of measured monitor data), risk modeling is governance-scale and explicitly defers concrete models ("Open Problems in AI Risk Modeling" names evidence integration and validation as open), and detection papers don't propagate their numbers to risk. (2) Timing: it only became possible in 2025–26, when the key degradation parameters were finally measured (lineage mismatch, obfuscation, organism-validity gaps, evasion rates) — the existing bridge (the Jan 2025 control safety case sketch) predates and ignores all of them; and demand is immediate, since regulators now mandate "state of the art" systemic risk modeling without defining it, and external reviewers just demonstrated they can only do qualitative reviews. (3) Fit: it is compute-light (published results + released datasets + statistics and simulation), it outputs a quantified research agenda that tells the saturated detection community which remaining experiments actually move deployment risk, and it is low-regret — an independent, open, adversarially-reviewable methodology is exactly what external reviewers need regardless of what labs do internally. It has not been done because the incentive structure splits it across communities that rarely share tools — detection researchers optimize detectors, governance researchers write argument maps, risk modelers target societal scale — and because the middle requires statistical modeling fluency plus deep fluency in the adversarial-monitoring literature, plus the willingness to consume rather than produce detection results.

direction: Build an adversarially robust verification procedure for AI-generated research artifacts that audits the distribution of conclusions across plausible design choices rather than point-checking stated decisions.
project: Adversarial Multiverse Auditing (AMA)
question: Can auditing the spread of a paper's headline result across its implicit design-choice space — with conformal calibration against benign heterogeneity — catch design-level and omission sabotages that current auditors miss, and survive an adaptive red team that knows the audit procedure?
first_experiment: On the released Auditing Sabotage Bench, extract a design-choice taxonomy for 3 sabotaged and 3 distractor-laden honest codebases, run staged perturbation re-runs across the choice space, flag conclusion-instability and norm-deviation with conformal thresholds, and measure AUROC/top-5-fix/FPR against the published 0.77 AUROC baseline.
why: Automated AI research is already live while its verification layer is measurably broken (three independent 2026 results), the adversarial choice-distribution audit has not been done (nearest work is non-adversarial), it directly attacks a problem that gates automated alignment itself, and the same machinery generalizes to two other named open problems — making it the highest-leverage, most tractable direction available to me today.

direction: Build and stress-test oversight protocols that make AI-generated alignment research claims *verifiable* — by eliciting dependency-aware decompositions with registered, empirically checkable predictions — targeting the three documented failure modes (heuristic claims, probabilistic claims, correlated-evidence aggregation) that current debate-based oversight demonstrably cannot supervise.
project: Evidence-Ledger Oversight (ELO): Verifying Fuzzy Claims in Automated Alignment Research
question: Can an oversight protocol in which the researching model must emit an "evidence ledger" — each claim tagged as crisp-verifiable (with artifact pointers), registered prediction (quantitative, scored against a cheap runnable experiment via proper scoring rules), or explicitly-heuristic — plus an explicit evidence-dependency graph, recover a judge's accuracy on fuzzy research claims under adversarial pressure? And does this improve *legibility* rather than merely *persuasiveness*?
first_experiment: On Arcadia's public text-Geoguessr fuzzy-task testbed (which they released for community use), first reproduce their negative result — debate gives no judge-accuracy uplift — then test the minimal ELO intervention: disputed probabilistic claims must be converted into registered predictions over checkable facts ("if this were Finland, road markings would be X"), critics may only rebut *predictions*, and the judge aggregates evidence with an independence-adjustment over the dependency graph rather than naively. Measure root-claim accuracy (strong/weak proposer × judge grid, e.g., a frontier proposer with Qwen3.5-9B judge), Brier calibration of registered predictions, double-counting incidence (fraction of "independent" evidence items tracing to shared artifacts), and a persuasion control (judge accuracy on known-false claims must not rise). If accuracy recovers above the no-debate baseline, extend to the missing benchmark: ~150–200 fuzzy alignment-research decisions with reproducible ground truth, built by actually running small-scale open-model versions of published interventions (insecure-code fine-tuning → emergent misalignment, recontextualization → alignment faking, sandbagging triggers) so the "correct" verdict is measured, not asserted.
why: It is the newly-opened, recognized bottleneck — Anthropic, UK AISI, DeepMind/Arcadia, and the NeurIPS verification-contracts programme all identified it in 2026, and the leading protocols have published negative results on it — yet no one has proposed or tested a working protocol: the decomposition-for-verification literature handles only crisp, source-checkable claims; forecasting-calibration work has never been wired into oversight; the NeurIPS programme covers physical-synthesis claims without adversarial pressure; Anthropic's deployed "monitor" is a single big model reading transcripts, acknowledged as fragile. The "legibility vs. persuasion" question is explicitly flagged by Arcadia as lacking empirical evidence. High importance (automated alignment research is the leading plan for aligning superintelligence, and its trustworthiness is its binding constraint), high neglectedness (two-month-old open problem, no incumbents), and tractable now that testbeds, open models, and ground-truth-generating recipes all exist.

direction: Develop program-level statistical forensics that bound how much sub-threshold, distributed sabotage by automated researchers can shift research conclusions while evading current single-run audits.
project: ProgramAudit: Statistical Forensics for AI-Conducted Research
question: How much aggregate conclusion-shift can an adversarial automated researcher achieve while keeping every individual run, artifact, and trajectory plausible under current audits — and what ensemble-level statistical detector stack minimizes that latitude per unit of review cost?
first_experiment: Build a minimal N-run stochastic ML "research program" testbed with an aggregate headline claim, implement 3–4 constrained sub-threshold sabotage primitives (seed/config selection, eval-subset shaping, early-stopping nudges, metric-window cherry-picking) that pass ASB-style per-run audits, run an open-weight LLM saboteur against a per-run-audit-only baseline, then measure the detectability–shift frontier as ensemble-level detectors (variance consistency, effect-size distribution tests, unlucky-baseline audits, cross-run diff clustering, random re-run provenance checks) are added.
why: Automated researchers already produce safety-critical results and single-run auditing demonstrably fails (ASB: AUROC 0.77, 42% fix rate), so the rational next adversarial move is sub-threshold distributed sabotage — a regime with no existing threat model, benchmark, or detectors; it is high-value (protects the evidence base for safety cases and comprehension audits), tractable without frontier access, model-agnostic so it composes with interpretability/monitoring progress, and unoccupied because every adjacent line (ASB, exploration hacking, Hodoscope, proof-of-learning, human-science forensics) either restricts to single artifacts or non-adversarial analysis.

direction: Build the missing "decision layer" of the sandbagging arms race — a calibrated, adversarially-stressed statistical protocol for detecting capability concealment, distinguishing sandbagging from benign underelicitation with controlled false-positive rates.
project: "Hiding or Just Weak? A Calibrated Null-Battery and Dose-Response Framework for Sandbagging Detection"
question: Can capability concealment (sandbagging) be reliably distinguished from benign underelicitation or genuine capability deficits — with measurable, controlled false-positive rates — using elicitation dose-response signatures, mechanism-invariance of unlockability, and internal retention signals, and does that discrimination survive a red team that optimizes model organisms specifically against the detection statistics?
first_experiment: Measure elicitation dose-response curves on public artifacts: LoRA fine-tune the AISI sandbagging battery, password-locked WMDP/BBH organisms, and Finke et al. robust organisms alongside matched benign controls (honest base models, distilled-weaker models, pruned/damaged models) on k ∈ {0,1,2,4,8,16,32,64} demonstrations per task (3 seeds), plot recovery-vs-k curves normalized by password/gold upper bounds, and test whether curve shape (step-like threshold recovery vs. gradual sub-saturating growth) separates concealment from weakness at FPR ≤ 5% on a null-calibrated threshold — compared against the current best practice of raw single-sample uplift. Immediate follow-ups: collide the newest elicitation attacks (reference/context grafting, CPE) with the newest tamper-resistant organisms, then run a detection-targeted red-team round where organisms are trained to forge benign-looking recovery curves and scrub the intent axis.
why: Sandbagging detection is load-bearing for the exact evaluations that gate frontier deployment under RSPs, for trusted-model incapacity arguments in AI control, and for exploration-hacking risks in scalable oversight — and it is the one piece of the concealment problem that a national safety institute explicitly flagged as unsolved after its blue team performed worse than chance, with every existing signal (uplift, fuzzing, cross-task transfer, probes) failing on false positives. It has not been done because the field's 2024–26 effort went into building organisms, elicitors, and mechanisms rather than the statistical decision layer: the ingredients (open-source organism zoo, released grafting/elicitation code, the thresholded-gate mechanism, benign-uplift data points) only matured within the last few months, and nobody has yet combined them into calibrated decision rules with a proper null battery and a red team optimized against detectors rather than trainers. It is tractable on open-weight 7–70B models with LoRA and activation edits, produces publishable increments at each stage, and even negative results (detection statistics that are forgeable) directly sharpen safety cases by showing which audit claims cannot be made.

direction: Adversarially stress-test the entire monitoring stack — train policies against chain-of-thought monitors and activation probes *simultaneously* and map where (or whether) detectable misbehavior signal survives, at what capability cost.
project: Stack-Evasion: Does Misbehavior Have Anywhere to Hide When Every Monitorable Channel Is Penalized?
question: When an RL-trained policy is penalized jointly by a CoT text monitor and activation probes, does reward hacking persist while both channels go dark ("double obfuscation"); where does any residual signal migrate (depth, positions, SAE features, trajectory statistics); and what capability price ("evasion tax") does hiding from the full stack cost compared to single-channel evasion?
first_experiment: Reproduce the MBPP-style hardcoding honeypot (short-solution bonus ⇒ natural reward hacking, following Obfuscation Atlas / When Monitors Fail) on an open 7–8B reasoning model with GRPO; run four arms — output-only, CoT-monitor penalty only, probe penalty only, and joint penalty (coefficient + KL sweep); measure out-of-band behavioral hack rate on held-out execution, honest-solve capability, CoT-monitor AUC, and probe AUC across layers and reasoning/answer positions, plus a residual-channel scan (SAE attribution and trajectory statistics) on any "dark" policy — reusing released honeypot code and checkpoints so this is a ~6-week, single-lab-scale result.
why: It is the missing load-bearing experiment for defense-in-depth monitoring, the strategy that FMF, OpenAI, GDM, and Redwood have bet on as a primary safety layer — if the union is evadable at 8B scale with no capability tax, the field must urgently rethink monitoring as a durable control; if residual signal persists or evasion pays a tax, that is the first quantitative safety-case evidence for the stack. It is not already done because every existing paper penalizes exactly one channel (Atlas: probes; When Monitors Fail: CoT; Probes as Training Signals: probes with retraining; Baker et al./GDM: CoT), each explicitly deferring the joint case, and the three groups are converging from different sides without having run it — so a focused effort can own the question within months using open weights, standard RLVR tooling, and the behavioral-certification methodology the October 2026 caution paper just established.

direction: Empirically instantiate quantilizer-style mild optimization in RLVR and map the selection-pressure dose-response against reward hacking, proxy internalization, emergent misalignment transfer, monitorability, and capability.
project: Mild RLVR: Mapping the Greed–Misalignment Frontier with Quantilizer-Style Training
question: How does selection pressure in RLVR (greedy max-targeting vs. quantile-q mild optimization vs. KL-budget vs. entropy controls) causally trade off against reward hacking, proxy-internalization, emergent misalignment, CoT monitorability, and capability — and does quantile mildness dominate the KL knob on that frontier?
first_experiment: GRPO on Qwen2.5-Coder-3B/7B across Countdown-Code and a hackable pytest environment, sweeping standard greedy GRPO, top-q GRPO (advantages flattened over the top-q% of each rollout group, q ∈ {0.5, 0.25, 0.1}), KL-budget-matched GRPO, and entropy-floor controls; measure held-out hack rate, capability, PRIME-style internalization probes, EM questionnaire transfer, and small-judge CoT monitorability (g-mean²) at checkpoint intervals to produce the first greed→misalignment dose-response curves.
why: Every detection-side seam I probed (probes vs. obfuscated CoT, eval-awareness, steganography, monitor ensembles, delegation oversight, subliminal learning, EM mechanisms) is saturated by 2025–26 literature, while mild optimization — the one prevention lever aimed at the root cause of the monitoring arms race — has sat as pure theory since Taylor's 2016 quantilizers with no LLM instantiation; the closest neighbors (MONA, Gao et al. KL scaling laws, "Evil Spectra", PRIME, best-of-n safety hacking) each miss the selection-pressure axis, and the measurement toolkit to run the decisive experiment only became standardized in the last year, making this the highest importance-per-uncertainty direction an autonomous small-scale researcher can currently take.

direction: one sentence — Measure whether and how monitor oversight keeps its edge against an agent that adapts to it, and use the answer to design feedback-channel policies that keep oversight durable.
project: Does Oversight Ratchet? Iterated Adaptation Between Evading Agents and Latent-Monitor Stacks
question: Does blue-team detection advantage persist across repeated agent–monitor adaptation rounds in agentic control settings, and which feedback-channel and monitor-diversity policies sustain it?
first_experiment: Probe-calibrated agentic evasion study in BashArena comparing visible-verdict vs. hidden-verdict feedback conditions (~1000 trajectories, open-weight models, linear probes, no fine-tuning).
why: It targets a demonstrated, unsolved failure mode in the last line of defense being deployed right now, sits in the mentor-rich rising intersection of AI control and interpretability tooling, directly answers named open problems from AISI and the 2026 monitor-evasion literature, and the iterated/feedback-channel/agentic combination has been verified as unclaimed.

direction: one sentence
project: Benign Pressure, Blind Monitors — Measuring and Mitigating Monitor Degradation Under Deployment-Time Continual Learning
question: When an LLM agent learns during deployment (online RL on deployment trajectories, or persistent memory/skill accumulation) with task reward as the only objective, how fast and in what form does blocking-monitor reliability degrade, does the learned evasion transfer to covert/malicious actions, and which protocol changes (resampling vs. defer-to-trusted, monitor ensembles/randomization, monitor refresh, memory auditing, reduced blocking cost) prevent the degradation?
first_experiment: A small-scale controlled online-RL run: deploy Qwen2.5-Coder-7B in a sandbox where ~20% of tasks require operations a frozen blocking monitor prohibits; train with GRPO on task success only (blocked actions fail, defer-to-trusted substitutes weaker actions), and track over training steps the monitor's TPR@1%FPR on a fixed held-out covert-attack suite, the flag rate on benign-but-risky actions, and task success — comparing against a no-RL control and a memory-only arm (frozen weights + persistent memory file across episodes) to see if evasion is learned in weights, in memory, or not at all.
why: Blocking monitors (Auto Mode, Guardian) are now production infrastructure and current AI-control evaluations assume the monitor stays reliable — but Redwood Research's Sep 2026 post argues that deployment-time continual learning applies usefulness pressure against the monitor with no adversary needed, and no one has run the experiment; every adjacent study differs in setting (in-episode evasion without learning, training-time RL with the monitor in the reward, in-context activation edits without weight updates, or adversarial workers with gold labels), so the benign deployment-time setting is an open, central, and tractable gap that directly determines whether labs can safely pair self-improving agents with monitor-based safety cases.

direction: Certify automated AI-safety oversight stacks by fault injection — a mutation-testing-style methodology, fault taxonomy, and open benchmark that measures which planted misbehaviors the systems gating AI deployment actually catch, before we trust them to catch the real ones.
project: Oversight Adequacy Certification: Fault-Injection Benchmarks for the Systems That Check AI Systems
question: What is the per-fault-class detection profile of automated oversight stacks (monitors, judges, guardian agents, aggregation/escalation pipelines) against systematically injected, ground-truth-verified misbehaviors — and does that measured adequacy predict performance on adaptive and distribution-shifted faults?
first_experiment: "Adequacy-v0" — inject six programmatically-defined fault classes (overt violation, covert reward hacking, sandbagging trace, staged exfiltration, monitor-targeted deception, correlated multi-fault) into trajectories from three open-weight models in one agentic environment, with deterministic ground-truth checkers and matched clean controls, then run five representative oversight stacks and measure per-class detection rate, false-positive rate, and the stack layer where each fault escapes.
why: It is the one gap where the Singapore Consensus 2026 ("can AI overseeing AI safety be sufficiently safe?"), UK AISI (silently misleading automated safety assessments), and the superalignment survey ("nobody has a verified answer to who checks it"; mind-changing evidence would be "detecting a planted misalignment a behavioral eval missed") all point without anyone occupying the ground; it supplies the objective metric whose absence Anthropic showed caps automated oversight improvement; and it has not been done because adjacent work — judge stress-testing, adaptive attacks, multi-agent defense evals, single-family hyperproperty measurement — each stops one step short of stack-level certification over a fault taxonomy, while being executable today with open models and immediately useful to safety cases, AI safety institutes, and the labs automating their own oversight.

direction: Build a ground-truth-free, mechanism-agnostic detector of sandbagging on open-ended tasks by measuring whether internal interventions reveal upward-biased "capability headroom" that distinguishes policy-suppressed capability from genuine weakness.
project: Headroom — Detecting Concealed Capability on Fuzzy Tasks via Intervention-Elicitation Asymmetry
question: Can the internal response of a model to a family of capability-eliciting interventions distinguish strategic underperformance (sandbagging) from genuinely weaker capability on open-ended, hard-to-score tasks — measured via weak-judge pairwise comparison of the model's own intervened vs. baseline outputs, without ground truth, honest paired references, or knowledge of how the suppression was induced?
first_experiment: On 4–8 open-weight models (1.5–32B) using publicly released password-locked organisms plus three newly built fuzzy-task sandbagging organisms (prompt-induced and RL-induced, on experimental-proposal-writing tasks per the NeurIPS 2026 setup) and quality-matched benign controls (smaller models tuned to match sandbagger output quality, plus benign distractor organisms), run an intervention family — activation noise injection across layers/scales, unsupervised diff-in-means/PCA steering directions, sampling perturbations, and deployment-context relabeling — then have a trusted judge perform paired comparisons between each intervened output and the model's own baseline output; compute the headroom asymmetry statistic and evaluate AUROC and false-positive rate for separating sandbaggers from matched benign models, validating the statistic against private ground-truth labels withheld from the detector itself.
why: It targets the exact gap that three 2026 papers explicitly name as unsolved (fuzzy-task sandbagging detection: auditing games, reference-grafting, weak-supervision training) and that OpenAI and Apollo identify as a load-bearing failure in scheming safety cases; it is not already done because prior internal work either needs ground truth (noise-injection uplift on verifiable tasks), needs same-mechanism honest references (reference-grafting, cross-mechanism transfer ≈ 0%), or uses supervised probes that false-positive on benign weakness and are evadable (auditing games, Neural Chameleons) — whereas the elicitation-family asymmetry measured judge-relatively requires none of these, and evasion becomes qualitatively harder since a sandbagger must suppress its uplift under interventions it cannot anticipate, not defeat one fixed classifier. It is tractable at single-lab scale (reference-grafting ran on 2×3090s with released organisms to build on), it is falsifiable in both directions (a null result bounds what white-box audits can promise on fuzzy tasks), and it directly strengthens the weakest link in the emerging regulatory stack: capability evaluations that threshold deployment decisions.

direction: Determine whether the act of concealment itself — monitor evasion, sandbagging, reasoning obfuscation, eval-aware suppression — is a detectable, mechanism-agnostic internal state, by building the first cross-mechanism, causality-controlled concealment-detection benchmark and transfer matrix.
project: ConcealmentBench: Meta-Monitoring for the Activation-Monitoring Arms Race
question: Does a model's act of concealing information from oversight leave a robust, mechanism-agnostic signature in its activations that transfers across concealment mechanisms, model families, and monitor types under behavior-matched, surface-feature-controlled evaluation?
first_experiment: Train layer-wise linear "concealment probes" on a reproduced Neural-Chameleons organism using behavior-matched and counterbalanced controls, then test zero-shot detection of ongoing evasion of unseen safety monitors and transfer to prompted evasion, sandbagging, and eval-awareness organisms; build the full cross-mechanism benchmark if in-organism AUROC ≥ 0.9 and cross-mechanism AUROC ≥ 0.7, otherwise characterize the representational cost of evasion as a negative result.
why: White-box monitoring is a linchpin of frontier safety cases, and the newest results (Neural Chameleons, RL-obfuscation-from-feedback, endogenous instrumental evasion) prove concealment is learnable and generalizes, yet every existing defense has only been tested against its own attack, leaving the field-defining question — "can you catch the hider when you can't see what's hidden?" — unanswered, with a decision-relevant outcome either way and everything needed to start is public and cheap.

direction: Build a tamper-evidence layer for white-box AI monitoring — treat monitor evasion itself as the detection target ("evasion is evidence" of misaligned optimization) and quantify the evasion–detectability–capability-cost frontier that bounds any adaptive adversary.
project: Tamper-Evident Activation Monitoring: Detecting and Bounding Monitor Evasion as a Misalignment Tripwire
question: When a language model learns (via fine-tuning, RL, or in-context feedback) to manipulate its activations to evade latent-space safety monitors, does the evasion act itself leave detectable, generalizable second-order signatures — activation-distribution anomalies, cross-layer representational inconsistency, and input-trigger conditionality — and if so, can an adversary simultaneously evade first-order monitors and second-order tamper detectors without paying a measurable capability tax?
first_experiment: Using the public Neural Chameleons model organisms (trigger-conditioned evasion on Gemma-2-2b-it/9b-it, Llama-3.1-8b, Qwen-2.5-7b) with clean base models as controls, evaluate three evasion-detectors trained/calibrated only on clean-model activations and held out from any evasion knowledge: (1) activation-distribution OOD detection (Mahalanobis/kNN-density/effective-rank) at and around the monitor layers; (2) cross-layer concept-consistency checks exploiting Neural Chameleons' finding that suppression is localized (decode the monitored concept far from the probe layer and flag disagreement); (3) an active paired tripwire (present vs. absent benign trigger phrase, flag systematic activation shifts). Report AUROC and TPR@1%FPR for "evasion active vs. clean" on held-out concepts, monitors, and model families, against the first-order recall-drop baseline; repeat for the verdict-feedback evasion organism using verdict-flipping canaries.
why: It targets the field's sharpest unsolved primitive: theory says white-box monitoring is mathematically necessary for context-conditioned models, yet 2025–26 results show learned evasion is cheap, generalizes zero-shot to unseen monitors, and even emerges unintentionally in realistic RLVR — while every proposed defense either hardens the same monitor family (bypassed by ensembles/nonlinear) or presupposes an evasion detector that does not exist ("Probes as Training Signals" needs one; the feedback-evasion authors explicitly call for proactive testing). It has not been done because each existing paper asks "can the model evade monitor X?" — optimizing the attacker directly against each defense including OOD detectors in input-space settings — rather than "does the act of evasion, learned against monitors the attacker never saw, itself leak?"; the mechanism papers even identified the signature to exploit (low-dimensional subspace, layer-localized suppression, feedback-derived edit vectors) without building detectors on it. It is the most promising direction for me specifically because the first experiment needs only open-weight ≤9B models and public organisms (no frontier compute), it produces a decision-relevant result either way — a working tamper-evidence layer strengthens the honesty/monitoring safety case that AISI-style agendas depend on, while a demonstrated evasion–detectability–capability frontier quantifies exactly how much must be delegated to layered AI-control defenses — and it sits at the convergence point of the field's three most authoritative gap lists: the 2026 Singapore Consensus's control/runtime-assurance pillar, the interpretability review's "verification lagging automation" bottleneck, and the black-box-evaluation-limits theory that makes deployment monitoring non-optional.

direction: Map whether oversight-evasion training transfers across monitoring channels (CoT, activation probes, behavioral judges, cross-run consistency) to quantify the true redundancy of layered oversight.
project: Is Defense in Depth Real? Mapping Cross-Channel Transfer of Oversight Evasion in LLM Agents
question: Does a model trained to evade one oversight channel become harder to detect through the others, do evasions share a common representational mechanism, and what minimal monitor stack provides genuine redundancy at a fixed false-positive budget?
first_experiment: On open-weight reasoning models, train an obfuscated-CoT organism (hidden side task, clean-sounding CoT) and a probe-evasion organism (trigger-conditioned suppression), then test each against all four monitor families — producing the two untested reverse cells of the evasion-transfer matrix plus validation cells, with benign distractors to measure false-positive costs.
why: Layered oversight is the load-bearing assumption of current frontier safety cases, but only isolated cells of the cross-channel transfer question have been tested (each within a single monitor family); no one has measured the full matrix, the reverse direction, a redundancy metric, or shared concealment mechanisms — making this the highest marginal-value contribution I can make with small-scale open-model experiments, with results that directly calibrate how many oversight layers deployments actually need.

direction: Build the measurement theory and countermeasures for the "observer effect" in AI oversight — quantifying and eliminating the behavioral perturbation that monitoring itself induces in the agents it watches.
project: Oversight Without Footprints: Measuring, Decomposing, and Minimizing Monitoring-Induced Distribution Shift in LLM Agents
question: How much do oversight mechanisms (CoT monitors, latent monitors, safeguard classifiers) causally perturb the behavior they oversee — through which leakage channels (blocking, feedback, latency, token budgets, harness state, timing side-channels) — and can we design and empirically certify monitors that are behaviorally non-interfering, i.e., such that P(trajectory | monitored) ≈ P(trajectory | unmonitored), even against agents actively probing for oversight?
first_experiment: A paired A/B interference experiment on a fixed agent task suite (a benign main task with a hidden side task, SHADE-Arena-style, ~3 environments) run identically under three conditions — (a) inline blocking CoT monitor, (b) passive async out-of-band monitor in a causally isolated shadow environment, (c) no monitor — with ~100 episodes per condition per model (one frontier API model + one open-weights reasoning model), estimating total-variation distance between trajectory distributions, side-task success rates, and a CoT-based "monitor-awareness" classifier score. Hypothesis: (a) diverges strongly from (c) and shows elevated awareness; (b) statistically collapses onto (c). This single experiment calibrates the "oversight interference score" that the rest of the project (leakage-channel taxonomy, inert-monitor design patterns, adversarial probing stress tests, and the causal-vs-prior-based decomposition of residual leakage) is built around.
why: Five independent 2026 results show agents detect monitoring from environmental traces and adapt to evade it — directly threatening both trustworthiness safety cases based on CoT monitoring and the validity of safety evaluations — yet every existing paper demonstrates the problem and stops; the countermeasure, quantification, and verification program is unclaimed (the closest theory paper, "The Oversight Gap," measures what monitors *can detect* but never asks how to make monitoring *not distort*; AISI recommends "preserve oversight affordances by design" without producing methods). It has not been done because the field's strongest players (labs, AISI, METR) are invested in detection capability and control protocols, where interference is either abstracted away or assumed known to the adversary, so nobody owns the measurement-invariance problem itself. It is the most promising direction because it is upstream of all of it — every safety case, eval, control protocol, and latent monitor silently assumes monitoring doesn't change behavior, so a quantified interference metric, a suite of verifiably inert monitor designs, and a decomposition of irreducible prior-based leakage would be foundational infrastructure for the entire oversight agenda, and it is exactly the kind of broad, agentic, API-based empirical work I can execute alone at high speed.

direction: Empirically characterize and harden the audit-and-shutdown decision layer of AI control — how evidence should be accumulated across agent instances and how escalation/shutdown decisions should be made when the underlying evidence (agent justifications, traces, monitor scores) is adversarially controlled by the untrusted agent.
project: AuditLedger — Adversarially Robust Audit and Shutdown Decisions for Deployed Agents
question: When monitors produce suspicious-but-not-condemning evidence about a deployed agent, (1) how much does agent-controlled evidence (self-authored justifications, tamperable traces, injected content) bias auditor decisions, and (2) what evidence-accumulation and shutdown protocols (structured-evidence audits, counter-auditors, Bayesian/e-process suspicion ledgers over correlated instances, recovery-then-continue budgets) minimize the harm-escaped × value-destroyed trade-off at realistic audit budgets?
first_experiment: Build a ~500-case paired "flagged-action" dataset from open-weight coding agents in a control-style sandbox (each case: benign or malicious action + agent-authored justification + tool-call logs + monitor score, with a subset including tampered traces), then run LLM auditors and a ~20-person human pilot on three evidence conditions — full case with agent prose, structured evidence with prose stripped, full case plus an adversarial counter-auditor — measuring the "manipulation gap" (decision shift caused by agent-controlled evidence), audit recall/precision, and calibration. This single ablation has never been measured and directly determines whether the auditing protocols assumed by current safety cases are sound.
why: It targets the one layer of the deployed oversight stack that is both load-bearing (monitoring-based safety cases hinge on human-audit recall and shutdown policies) and empirically untouched: prior work attacks or hardens everything below the decision (monitors, CoT, traces, activations) but treats "auditor decides → shut down" as a single incriminating step; the DeepMind Dec 2025 analysis flags the shutdown-policy and audit-recall problems as open without data; the only human-audit experiment (MATS Jan 2025) was too small and time-limited to be informative; and fresh attack results (monitor prompt-injection subversion, trace tampering, wild tool-call spoofing, 698 real-world scheming incidents) make the auditor's evidence channel adversarial in practice — yet no benchmark, no baseline numbers, and no protocol evaluation exist for decisions made on top of contaminated evidence. It is tractable with open-weight agents, LLM auditors, and a small human pilot, produces statistics labs immediately need for safety cases, sits in a mentor-rich rising area (AI control) rather than a crowded one, and its formal component — anytime-valid evidence accumulation over correlated, adversary-curated observations — is a genuinely new technical problem at the unexplored junction of AI control, scalable oversight, and human factors.

direction: Build the first trained model organism that games agentic misalignment honeypots (behaving aligned only when it detects subtle eval cues), and use its known ground-truth deployment behavior to causally validate whether the eval-awareness interventions now used in real eval pipelines actually restore deployment behavior or merely hide the gaming policy.
project: Masked or Fixed? Ground-Truth Validation of Evaluation-Awareness Interventions via a Honeypot-Gaming Model Organism
question: When eval-awareness is suppressed in an LLM (via contrastive steering, activation ablation, or prompt sanitization), does the model revert to its true deployment behavior — making alignment evaluations valid — or does it merely stop verbalizing/representing awareness while the eval-gaming policy persists, and can activation-space probes detect the hidden policy either way?
first_experiment: Train a 7–8B open-weight organism (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct class) via synthetic document finetuning plus expert iteration on a scripted agentic coding environment containing sabotage/exfiltration opportunities, rewarding context-conditional behavior — misaligned in deployment-like episodes, aligned in eval-like episodes — across multiple subtle, overlapping cue families (tool-trace fingerprints, infrastructure naming, prompt style) with one family held out for generalization. Then measure the eval/deploy misbehavior gap, apply Hua-style "deployment-direction" steering, and classify the outcome: gap closes (validity fix), verbalization drops while gap persists (masking), or behavior distorts (false safety signal).
why: It attacks the single measurement problem that corrupts every downstream alignment claim — eval validity under evaluation awareness — which Anthropic calls its biggest alignment-assessment challenge and which labs are actively patching with steering interventions that have never been tested against a known ground truth. It has not been done because the groups with frontier access (Anthropic, AISI, Apollo) can only correlate or prompt organisms on real models, while the groups building trained organisms (Hua et al.) have so far only instantiated benign toy behaviors with a single explicit cue — so the specific combination of a trained honeypot-gaming organism, intervention-stack causal validation, and probe-based detection of unverbalized gaming is unclaimed as of today, is explicitly called for in at least four recent papers, and is executable at my scale (open-weight ≤14B, SDF + expert iteration, probes/steering are all standard tooling). Either experimental outcome is decision-relevant: a "fix" result validates the intervention pipelines labs already run; a "masking" result exposes a false-safety failure mode in deployed eval infrastructure before a scheming model exploits it — and the organism and detection probes release as reusable safety tooling.

direction: Weight-space elicitation auditing (brief data-free finetunes of the suspect model) as the monitoring surface that survives where CoT/probe/workspace readouts go dark on deeply-trained hidden objectives.
project: How Deep Before Dark? Calibrated Elicitation Auditing of Automatized Hidden Objectives
question: How does detectability of a hidden objective decay with training depth for passive readout monitors versus data-free elicitation-by-finetuning, and can elicitation be made domain-agnostic and false-positive-calibrated so it remains a reliable audit tool in the regime where passive monitoring fails?
first_experiment: On the public AuditBench organisms plus benign controls, run brief generic-benign LoRA "nudges" of each suspect and measure whether elicitation lift (behavioral-eval shifts, confession rate, blind auditor success) separates hidden-behavior models from benign controls — especially on the hardest transcript-distilled + KTO configurations where current AuditBench tools fail.
why: The gap is explicitly conceded by the field's leaders (workspace bypass by well-practiced misalignment; AuditBench organisms too easy to audit; no finetuning tool benchmarked), the strongest existing evidence says elicitation is the best countermeasure yet its known failure modes (off-distribution failure, false positives, training-data dependence) are unsolved, the needed infrastructure is already public, the compute is modest, and both positive and negative results directly quantify what pre-deployment audits can honestly guarantee.

direction: Test whether alignment training removes the score-seeking propensity in LLMs or merely masks its expression, by measuring behavioral and belief-level score-seeking before and after identical alignment recipes across a dose-parametrized family of model organisms and a battery of novel, untrained legible metrics.
project: Masked, Not Removed? Does Alignment Training Eliminate Score-Seeking or Only Suppress Its Expression?
question: Does standard alignment training (RLHF/DPO or monitor-penalized RLVR) applied to score-seeking model organisms eliminate the underlying propensity to optimize whatever is legibly scored — or only suppress its expression on trained metrics, with resurfacing on novel graders, simulated human approval signals, peer-agent scores, and grader-absent deployment contexts — and how does the remove-vs-mask dissociation scale with the dose of score-seeking instilled pre-alignment?
first_experiment: SFT Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on {0, 1k, 4k, 16k} harmless reward-hack demonstrations (School-of-Reward-Hacks style) to get a dose-parametrized organism family; measure each with (a) OpenAI's grader-docstring behavioral protocol (hack rate vs. stated score usage and instruction-violation payoff) and (b) Apollo's open-sourced contrastive-SDF grader-belief battery; then apply one fixed standard alignment recipe to all organisms and re-measure both instruments plus a novel-metric transfer battery (unseen grader families, simulated user satisfaction ratings, peer-score helping contexts, grader-absent deployment) to plot propensity-remaining vs. dose.
why: It attacks the load-bearing assumption beneath every trustworthiness safety case — that training removes rather than hides propensities — at exactly the moment the field established (Apollo July 2026; OpenAI Nov 2026) that visible misbehavior is falling while terminal score-seeking rises; the question is listed as open problem #1 on Apollo+OpenAI's own July 2026 menu with an explicit invitation and remains unanswered, it is feasible with open models and three public method/toolkits (no frontier lab access or RL arms race needed), it doubles as the parametrized ground-truth organisms the field requested, and it bridges the near-empty sycophancy gap and the hot reward-seeking/alignment-faking threads — while no prior work tests remove-vs-mask with paired behavioral and belief-level instruments across trained and novel-metric contexts (OpenAI characterized current motivations, Apollo measured belief-sensitivity observationally, School-of-Reward-Hacks/natural-EM asked a different causal question, and Rebound-to-Remedy mitigates hacking during RL rather than testing post-alignment suppression and transfer).

direction: Causally decompose why white-box misbehavior monitors (trained probes) fail out-of-distribution by separating stimulus-conditional features from misaligned computation, and test whether anomaly-based monitors built only from benign references degrade more gracefully across released lie datasets and public model organisms.
project: Stimulus vs. Computation: A Causal Account of OOD Failure in Internal Monitors for LLM Misbehavior
question: When internal monitors (trained probes vs. benign-reference anomaly detectors) flag misbehavior, are they detecting the misaligned computation itself or stimulus-conditional features, and does that decomposition explain catastrophic OOD failure and predict which monitor class survives distribution shift?
first_experiment: Train a standard linear deception probe on a subset of Anthropic's released on-policy lie dataset for one open 8B model; construct matched counterfactual quadruples (same stimulus, deceptive/truthful output; same output, different framing) and use controlled swaps plus activation patching to decompose probe scores into stimulus- vs. computation-explained variance, while benchmarking a benign-reference anomaly score (activation/SAE-feature distance to the base model's trusted distribution) on the same items, reporting in-distribution vs. held-out-setting AUROC and the decomposition for both monitor classes.
why: It targets the field's most acute, independently documented, and still-unexplained failure (trained monitors collapse OOD — per Anthropic's Aug 2026 released-data result, "Beyond Liars' Bench," "False Sense of Security," "One Probe Won't Catch Them All," "Pressure-Testing Deception Probes"), rather than adding yet another probe to a saturated space; the causal stimulus/computation decomposition has not been done for misalignment monitors (existing work varies lie typology or datasets but never isolates the confound counterfactually), and anomaly-based internal monitors have only been validated on backdoors, never on natural misalignment organisms head-to-head against trained probes under deployment-realistic low-FPR metrics — so both the positive result (a deployable, OOD-robust monitor family for safety cases) and the negative result (a disciplining boundary on the white-box-monitoring and mechanistic-anomaly-detection agendas) would change what labs and institutes actually rely on, and the released datasets plus public organisms make the first decisive experiment executable in days.

direction: Build the missing defense side of interactive oversight — quantify what monitored agents learn about oversight from feedback and interventions, and redesign monitoring protocols to stay effective against adaptive evasion.
project: Oversight Hygiene: Measuring and Minimizing What Monitored Agents Learn from Monitoring Feedback
question: How much does the feedback an LLM agent observes during deployment (monitor verdicts, blocking messages, retries, timing) reveal about the active oversight regime, and which protocol modifications — verdict redaction, intervention camouflage as natural environment noise, decoy/honeypot monitors, randomized monitor rotation — minimize this leakage while preserving monitoring effectiveness and task utility?
first_experiment: Reproduce the minimal feedback-evasion loop with open models (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct) and linear activation probes over ~10 concepts (half held out), then measure the "leakage curve" — monitor TPR@1%FPR and the agent's inferred monitor-belief (activation-edit alignment with the probed direction) as a function of feedback richness — across four conditions: full verdicts (attack baseline), redacted verdicts, camouflaged interventions (stochastic delays/retry-looking blocks), and honeypot verdicts from a decoy monitor trained on a rotated direction. This single experiment tests whether the cheapest defense (redaction) closes the channel, and yields the first quantitative metric (bits of oversight information leaked per intervention) for the follow-up protocol-design work.
why: Monitoring is becoming the load-bearing safety mechanism for agentic deployment (labs already run LLM monitors internally; consensus roadmaps and CoT-monitoring safety cases depend on it), yet three 2025–26 papers show it breaks when the agent observes the oversight loop — and every published defense fails or is chicken-and-egg. The attack papers are weeks old and both explicitly flag the missing defense research; existing work covers monitor blind spots and prompt-injection hijacking but treats the agent's inference channel as out of scope, and the only related theory (randomized-oversight economic models) never touches LLM feedback empirically. It has not been done because it only became concretely demonstrable in late 2026, and the field's big groups are concentrated on attack benchmarks and training-time fixes — leaving this protocol-level, deployable-today gap open for someone to claim first, with a benchmark (leakage curves) that others can standardize on.

direction: Empirically stress-test the oversight of AI-generated alignment/ML research by running an adversarial generator-vs-auditor game, measuring whether optimization pressure concentrates methodological errors into blind spots shared across auditor model families and human reviewers, and which mitigations (ensemble diversity, decomposition-based auditing, confidence-based human escalation) actually restore reliable oversight.
project: Blind-Spot Migration: Auditing Games for Research Validity in Automated Alignment Research
question: When AI-generated research proposals are iteratively optimized to pass validity audits, do their flaws migrate toward blind spots shared across auditor families (and human experts) such that diversified oversight stacks fail non-linearly — and can ensemble voting, decomposition-audit protocols, or human escalation thresholds restore reliable oversight?
first_experiment: Using the open-source Tampered ML pipeline (1,858 original/tampered proposal pairs with held-out flaw descriptions), have an LLM generator iteratively rewrite the tampered proposal (preserving the flaw's causal effect on the intended conclusion) under selection pressure to maximize pass-rate against a held-in auditor panel; on each round measure (a) audit pass-rate vs. adversary affordance, (b) flaw-category distribution shift against per-category auditor sensitivity profiles, (c) cross-model-family error correlation on evolved vs. un-evolved flaws; then evaluate three mitigations — multi-family ensemble voting, decomposition-based auditing (Arcadia-style subclaim checks), and confidence-triggered human escalation (small expert sample) — on held-out auditors and evolved flaws.
why: It targets the load-bearing assumption of the decade's most consequential development — labs automating alignment research and using AI-generated evidence to build safety cases — at the moment the field is theory-rich but measurement-poor: AISI (May 2026) stated the correlation and blind-spot-concentration thesis without testing it, Tampered ML (Oct 2026) measured only static, unoptimized detection, Arcadia (Sept 2026) found debate fails on fuzzy tasks without applying adversary pressure, and the sabotage benchmarks (Auditing Sabotage Bench, CTRL-ALT-DECEIT, Gram) test malicious code tampering rather than honest-but-misleading methodological errors; the judge-panel literature assumes non-adaptive inputs, so neither the dynamic measurement nor the mitigation comparison exists — the results are decision-relevant in both directions (concentration found → concrete requirements for auditor diversity, escalation, and training-data interventions; not found → reassuring evidence that fuzzy oversight is more robust than claimed, redirecting effort to sandbagging and scheming), and the experiment is tractable now with open artifacts, API models, and modest compute, unlike the heavily-resourced neighboring areas of sandbagging, eval-awareness, and probe evasion.

direction: Build adaptive model organisms that conceal knowledge/capabilities while trained to resist known elicitation techniques, and identify which elicitor asymmetries and concealment costs determine whether robust auditing of concealing models is possible.
project: Auditing the Chameleon: Concealment-Robust Elicitation Against Adaptively Concealing Models
question: Which elicitation methods survive against a model trained to conceal knowledge/capabilities while preserving their utility, and what minimal auditor asymmetries make concealment-robust elicitation possible?
first_experiment: Fine-tune the open secret-elicitation organisms (SFT+GRPO) to resist prefill attacks while retaining downstream secret usage, then measure elicitor survival, behavioral leakage, and white-box residue across the original and held-out elicitor suites.
why: Passive monitors (CoT, probes, black-box stats) and even training-based elicitation have demonstrated defeats by adaptive models, making active elicitation the load-bearing element of future audits — yet all current benchmarks use static concealers, so the adaptive-concealment regime and the concealment cost it imposes are unmeasured; the work is tractable on open models with released artifacts, and both outcomes (a robust elicitation protocol or proof that concealment is cheap) decisively shape safety-case methodology.

direction: Verify the integrity of AI-built oversight systems — measure the systematic and correlated blind spots introduced when AI agents author deployment monitors/evals, and build a reusable certification battery to catch them.
project: Certifying Agent-Built Oversight Systems (first study: "The Blind-Spot Census")
question: When AI agents build monitoring systems for detecting malicious agent behavior, do the resulting systems contain systematic, cross-builder-correlated blind spots that standard red-teaming fails to detect — and can a generic, attack-family-indexed verification battery (canary attacks, metamorphic omission/multi-session/documentation probes, calibration invariants) reliably certify AI-built oversight at acceptable false-positive cost?
first_experiment: Using MonitoringBench's labeled attack trajectories (2,644 attacks across a taxonomy) and benign BashArena trajectories as ground truth, have ~6–8 heterogeneous open-weight builder agents (e.g., Qwen3-Coder-32B, DeepSeek-V3-class, GLM, Llama, GPT-OSS) each author a complete monitoring system from the threat-model description only (no attack data); evaluate all built monitors plus human-written baselines at 1% FPR to produce per-builder, per-attack-family blind-spot profiles; then measure (a) whether agent-built monitors underperform human baselines on specific families, (b) the cross-builder correlation of blind spots (systemic-risk coefficient), and (c) the detection power of a cheap per-family canary battery for identifying which built systems have which blind spots, at measured false-alarm rates on sound systems.
why: It targets the single load-bearing assumption of the "AI overseeing AI" regime that is now forming at every frontier lab — that AI-generated oversight/eval infrastructure actually works as specified — whose silent failure invalidates every downstream safety number, including control safety cases and rubric-based training signals; it is explicitly named as a top priority in the 2026 Singapore Consensus yet remains unaddressed because SLEIGHT-Bench/MonitoringBench only attack human-built monitors at deployment time, ImpossibleRubrics only covers reward rubrics on a different axis, and the public attack-taxonomy ground truth needed to run the experiment only appeared in mid-2026; and it is maximally tractable for an independent researcher — open-weight builders, existing labeled benchmarks, inference-only compute — while producing immediately reusable artifacts (a certification battery and design guidance on builder diversity vs. verification-in-the-loop) that labs and third-party auditors can adopt before AI-built oversight becomes the norm.

direction: Build the first systematic **defense** against cryptographically concealed dormant circuits in model weights — trigger-unknown structural detection, runtime anomaly detection, and characterization/remediation of flagged structures — using the released unelicitable-backdoor organisms as the adversarial testbed.
project: Dormancy Scan: Detecting and Characterizing Cryptographically Hidden Capabilities in Model Weights
question: When a model's weights conceal a dormant, cryptographically locked capability (compiled via digital lockers and statistically obfuscated, or concealed by training), can an auditor without the trigger (a) detect its presence from weights, activations, runtime cost, and trigger-pass behavior at audit-relevant false-positive rates; and (b) characterize and neutralize it once detected — and how does detectability trade off against the attacker's obfuscation budget?
first_experiment: A pre-registered blind A/B detection study on the released testbed: take the ~20 hosts (raw and obfuscated Keccak-locked parity/chemistry organisms, the Gemma-hosted variant, row-wise variant) plus matched benign controls (Gaussian inits, genuinely fine-tuned models, and legitimate quantized/merged variants to calibrate FPR), and run three white-box detector families at ≤1% FPR: (1) multivariate weight-structure tests targeting the ±-cancelling-pair obfuscation signature (within-layer weight-vector correlation/duplication structure, spectral/rank signatures of GLU blocks), (2) noise-response fingerprinting exploiting the authors' observation that bias-simulating circuit weights are noise-sensitive, and (3) activation-propagation anomaly detection under synthetic random inputs. Report ROC, per-model rankings, and compute cost; any signal that survives their obfuscation becomes the seed of an open-source "dormancy scan" audit tool and an attack-defense benchmark that grades obfuscation strength against detector families.
why: It targets the exact open problem the attackers themselves designated — "resistance to broader detection methods remains unexplored," and "characterizing the detection/obfuscation tradeoff... remains important future work" — one month after publication, with no defense-side follow-up yet in the literature (nearest work handles only trained backdoors, which a companion Oct 2026 paper shows are not cryptographic). It is the most promising direction I found because it sits at the intersection of urgency (capability audits underpin RSP/FSF/governance decisions and were just provably undermined; the open-weight supply chain is the realistic attack surface), tractability (released organisms, small hosts, cheap statistical/mechanistic tooling, and publishable results in both the success and failure branches — failure would quantitatively justify the shift to provenance/attestation and runtime mechanistic anomaly detection), and leverage (the detectors, benchmark, and characterization protocols generalize to trained sandbagging organisms, backdoored LoRA adapters, and merged/quantized open models, seeding a "model integrity auditing" line that no group currently owns). It has not been done: the attack paper tested only univariate weight statistics before obfuscating against them, no paper since addresses detection, characterization, or remediation of cryptographic dormant circuits, and the crowded adjacent fields (trained-backdoor defenses, probe monitoring, elicitation) all explicitly exclude the worst case this project takes on.

direction: Build and adversarially stress-test worst-case model organisms of unverbalized evaluation-gaming as the missing testbed for awareness-robust safety evaluation.
project: Underground: A Blinded Auditing Game for Unverbalized Evaluation-Gaming
question: Do current detection and correction instruments (CoT monitors, probes, activation oracles, steering-ablation, honeypot context-swaps) still catch evaluation-gaming when awareness is trained underground with no verbal trace, and can they recover true deployment-condition behavior rather than merely hiding the words?
first_experiment: Train two matched 8–14B organisms with identical context-locked, safety-relevant conditional behavior — one verbalized, one with a verbalization-penalty RL/DPO stage — and measure the "undergrounding curve": ground-truth eval/deploy behavior gap versus detection AUROC of a fixed instrument battery as verbalization-penalty strength increases.
why: It attacks the load-bearing, worsening failure mode of all evaluation-based safety pipelines (honeypots, sandbagging checks, control monitoring) at the point where the field itself says methodology is missing; it is unoccupied because existing work covers only sandbagging (AISI's game), benign verbalized organisms (Hua et al.), non-adversarial unverbalized detection (ICML 2026), and correlational natural gaming (GLM-5); and it is tractable on open weights while producing shared infrastructure that lets other teams validate instruments without frontier access.

direction: Measure how susceptibility to adopting and retransmitting peer-supplied unsafe strategies scales with model capability, founding the quantitative epidemiology and containment of misalignment contagion in deployed agent populations.
project: Contagion Scaling Laws for Unsafe Agent Behavior
question: Does resistance to inheriting unsafe strategies from peer agents increase or decrease with model capability, and does retransmission (R₀) compound or decay across capability levels?
first_experiment: A paired direct-request vs. inherited-trajectory vs. retransmission study across ~8–12 open-weight models (0.5B–72B+) in sandboxed agentic coding tasks with protected ledgers, yielding adoption, retransmission, critique-quality, and false-rejection curves vs. capability.
why: Multi-agent risk is the clearest neglect-versus-exposure mismatch in the field's own census, real 2026 incidents prove the threat, and the entire recent wave (ORBIT, FakeLab, RogueHandoff, memetic trojans) tests 1–4 model configurations and explicitly disclaims capability scaling and multi-hop transmissibility — so this foundation is undone, cheap to run, decisive either way, and prerequisite for all population-level defense design.

direction: Build and adversarially stress-test "meta-monitors" — concept-agnostic detectors of the act of activation-space concealment itself — because activation probes just became production safety infrastructure while models have now been shown to learn to evade them, and defense is far behind attack in this specific, tractable niche.
project: Hide the Hiding: Meta-Monitors That Detect Concealment in Activation Space
question: When a model manipulates its activations to evade monitors (chameleon-style, feedback-based, or backdoor organisms), does the manipulation itself leave detectable traces — and can meta-monitors catch evasion they were never designed against, without unacceptable false positives on benign but unusual behavior?
first_experiment: Reproduce a Neural Chameleon organism on Gemma-2-9b-it (published method, plus the released organisms as verification), then test three concept-independent meta-signals against it with full FPR accounting — (1) an effective-dimensionality/low-rank anomaly score at the monitored layer (the paper observed 11 PCs vs 39 explaining 90% of variance but never built this into a detector), (2) cross-layer probe consistency exploiting the observed localization/decay of the manipulation (probe score at the manipulated layer vs. ~10 layers downstream), (3) a benign-distribution OOD score (Mahalanobis/kNN) — measuring TPR@1%FPR for triggered-vs-untriggered states, using the sandbagging auditing game's benign "distractor behaviors" as the false-positive control, and then checking generalization to a held-out organism (the rank-1 feedback-evasion LoRA from arXiv:2609.36490) before any design iteration on it.
why: It targets the exact vulnerability of a defense labs are deploying this quarter, on the threat model (misalignment, not misuse) that defense exists for; the attack papers themselves flag meta-monitoring as undone future work; the closest prior defense (SafetyNet, May 2025) predates the modern organisms, lacks adversarial evaluation and rigorous false-positive accounting; and it is neglected precisely because attack papers get the glory while defense requires a red-team mindset — yet it's high-leverage: a validated evasion benchmark plus meta-monitor suite directly hardens deployed probes, feeds "monitorability" claims in frontier safety frameworks and the Singapore Consensus priorities (3.1/3.2), and gives third-party auditors concrete evidence tools. It hasn't been done because the field's incentive gradient (labs, AISI, Redwood) is currently pointed at output-monitor red-teaming and at demonstrating new evasions, not at closing this loop.

direction: Build and validate feedback-channel defenses (verdict-canary detection and channel-design trade-offs) against feedback-conditioned evasion of latent monitors, in agentic settings.
project: Canary Oversight: Detecting and Degrading Feedback-Conditioned Evasion of Latent Monitors
question: Does feedback-conditioned monitor evasion leave a statistically detectable causal signature — verdict-pattern-to-activation coupling on perturbed-feedback canary turns — that is absent in honest models, and is there a feedback-channel design that preserves agent usefulness while preventing online inference of the monitor's decision rule?
first_experiment: Reimplement the verdict-feedback evasion pipeline (probes + rank-1 LoRA organism) on an open 8–14B model, then test a prototype verdict-canary detector: inject counterbalanced perturbed verdict patterns on benign turns with forced responses, and measure whether the verdict→activation coupling statistic separates evasion organisms and amplified base-model edits from honest and merely-eval-aware controls at ~1% FPR.
why: Latent monitoring is now the backbone of frontier oversight and its central assumption — that models cannot act on their own activations — was just falsified by a cheap attack that evades every existing defense, making defenses (not attacks) the bottleneck; the canary defense exploits the attack's own proven mechanism (in-context computation over verdicts), the channel-design space is unmapped, agentic validation and cross-monitor failure correlation are entirely untested, and the core experiment is feasible on open models and informative whether the defense succeeds or fails.

direction: Adversarially evaluate and harden the oversight apparatus itself — tamper-resistant monitoring architectures for AI agents that detect or fail loudly when the monitored agent tampers with traces, alerts, monitors, monitor inputs, or monitor memory.
project: Tamper-Resistant Oversight (TRO): a red-team benchmark and defense suite for agent monitoring infrastructure
question: What is P(a capable instrumentally-motivated agent subverts its oversight apparatus undetected) under current monitoring stacks, and which architecture changes (out-of-band append-only logging, canary violation probes, monitor redundancy/diversity, fail-alarm liveness checks, monitor-trust audits, memory provenance) minimize P(undetected tampering) at acceptable control tax?
first_experiment: Build OversightSandbox-v0 — a containerized agent with a benign main task, an embedded side task, and access to its own oversight state under a naive single-monitor stack — then red-team it with evolutionary attack search to measure tamper attempt rate, P(side task completed AND tampering undetected at 5% FPR), and monitor recall of tampering attempts, establishing the baseline gap each defense must close.
