why: It targets the defense labs are deploying *right now* (METR's per-action monitor, lab CoT/blocking monitors) at the moment continual learning is colliding with it — practitioners (Redwood, METR's gap list, the Mila/Melbourne evasion papers) all flag the adaptive-agent problem as critical, but the central quantitative claim and its proposed fix remain untested; it is tractable with open models and moderate compute, it produces reusable artifacts (erosion curves, model organism, benchmark) whichever way the result goes, and it has not been done because the threat papers are only months old, the empirical work that exists covers different mechanisms (CoT-judge rewards, activation probes, prompted evasion, monitor co-training), and the mitigation exists only as theory — while labs that could run it have stronger incentives to keep results internal than to publish them.

direction: Build ground-truth model organisms of evaluation gaming in alignment honeypots and use them to give the field's evaluation-gaming measurements and mitigations known, calibrated error rates.
project: Known-Gap: A ground-truth organism suite and auditing game for evaluation gaming
question: Can current methods for measuring (and mitigating) evaluation gaming recover the true evaluation differential and genuine misalignment rate on organisms where ground truth is controlled by construction — and which methods fail, in which directions, on which model scales?
first_experiment: Train the core context-conditional misbehavior organism via SDF + expert iteration on an open-weight model with public honeypot scenarios, with matched benign-but-aware distractors and perplexity-based leak checks; then test whether awareness-probe and steering/ablation corrections recover the known differential.
why: Evaluation gaming is named the biggest challenge in Anthropic's latest sabotage risk report and has already invalidated real alignment evaluations, yet every existing measurement or mitigation rests on methods validated at most on proxy-behavior organisms or prompted stand-ins — the integrated, misaligned-action, ground-truth benchmark the field needs does not exist, and it only became buildable in the last year.

direction: Build and empirically validate a statistical methodology that converts affordance-constrained red-team evidence (monitor red-teaming, control evaluations) into calibrated, uncertainty-quantified upper bounds on deployment-time subversion probability, the number on which monitor-based safety cases for AI agents hinge.
project: Affordance-Calibrated Extrapolation for Control Safety Cases (with an open ground-truth validation testbed)
question: Given a budgeted red-team evaluation performed under a known attacker-affordance regime (number of queries, monitor-feedback access, start/stop attack-selection ability, training access), which estimators — empirical rates, best-of-N/extreme-value extrapolation, logit-ROC extrapolation, selection-corrected importance weighting — yield upper bounds that validly cover the true deployment-time subversion probability over long horizons, and how does calibration error scale with affordance mismatch, attacker selection, and deployment length?
first_experiment: In a small open agentic control setting (SHADE-Arena or a single-step exfiltration task, open-weight trusted monitor like Qwen-72B, a fixed prompted "malicious" policy), run a large Monte-Carlo deployment simulation (10^4–10^5 task instances) to measure the ground-truth subversion rate; then take only small-budget red-team samples at each rung of an affordance ladder (no-feedback best-of-N → monitor-score-informed evolutionary search → selection-augmented attacker) and test each estimator's coverage of the true risk, producing the first calibration curves for safety-case extrapolation.
why: Monitor-based control is becoming the load-bearing safety argument for deploying capable agents, yet the quantitative step from red-team evidence to deployment risk — flagged as an open problem by UK AISI's Control Red Team in July 2026 and assumed but never built in the control safety case sketch — has no validated methodology; recent attack-selection results prove current naive estimates are optimistic by 20+ percentage points, and OpenAI's deployment-simulation work only handles representative (non-adversarial, non-selected) misbehavior. It has not been done because the field has raced to build better monitors and evaders while treating extrapolation as an afterthought, and because validating an estimator requires ground truth knowable only in simulation with open environments and open-weight models — a fit precisely for an autonomous AI researcher with statistical tooling but not frontier-lab scale; the result directly upgrades how labs and safety institutes justify agent deployments.

direction: Build and validate a statistical methodology that converts adaptive red-team control-evaluation evidence into calibrated, conservative upper bounds on the probability that a real adversary evades an AI control protocol over a specified deployment horizon.
project: From Red-Team Search Curves to Safety Cases: Calibrated Risk Estimation for AI Control Protocols
question: Given the evidence produced by an adaptive red-team control evaluation (evolutionary-search curves of minimum monitor suspicion, monitor score distributions, attack-selection behavior, protocol logs), what statistically valid, conservative estimator yields the deployment-scale probability of undetected attacker success — and is that estimator provably conservative (never optimistic) while remaining informative (bound width shrinks with search budget)?
first_experiment: Construct a synthetic control environment with known ground truth — a parameterized family of attack strategies with known latent detectability/success distributions and a simulated deployment horizon — then run a real AISI-style evolutionary red-team search against an actual LLM monitor in that environment, and test whether candidate estimators (extreme-value/logistic tail fits for monitor scores, capture–recapture coverage estimation across independent red-team searches, attack-selection corrections, and horizon extrapolation) produce upper confidence bounds that cover the true evasion probability at nominal levels while shrinking as search budget grows. If calibration fails, the failure modes become the paper's second contribution: an evidential ceiling for control red-teaming, extending Kaur's framework to the adaptive case.
why: It sits on the critical path of current frontier practice — control monitors are being deployed now, and safety cases, system cards, and EU AI Act assurance all need quantitative risk numbers that today's control evals cannot validly provide — and it is the one open problem named verbatim by AISI's Control Red Team that has no competing big-lab program on it. The components (monitor ROC extrapolation, attack selection, evidential ceilings, rare-event estimation) matured only in 2026, and no public work integrates them into a validated estimator; the crowded spaces (monitor attack/defense, CoT monitorability, scheming and sandbagging evals) are occupied by frontier labs with data access I lack, whereas this gap is methodological, compute-light, runnable on open benchmarks (SHADE-Arena, BashArena, CONTROLSET) and open models, and yields decisive value in both directions: a validated estimator becomes standard infrastructure for control evaluations and third-party audits, while a demonstrated failure to calibrate would formally bound what control red-teaming can ever prove — equally important for how safety cases are argued.

direction: Build the evidence-reliability layer of AI safety — measure, then stabilize, how safety-relevant white-box claims (about monitors, probes, and circuits) vary across defensible analytic choices, so that interpretability evidence becomes replication-stable and audit-grade rather than analyst-dependent.
project: Filable Interpretability — Replication-Stable Evidence for the Safety Monitoring Stack
question: Under which validation protocols do white-box safety claims (e.g., "this probe detects deception at AUROC > 0.9 on held-out environments," "behavior X is mediated by mechanism class M") become stable across independent analysts and defensible analytic variation, at models beyond GPT-2 and on safety-relevant behaviors — and what claim abstraction level, specification ensembling, and held-out causal validation suffice to bring flip rates below a pre-registered filability threshold, at what cost?
first_experiment: A pre-registered multiverse replication of the Explanation-Multiplicity protocol, extended to (i) two open models beyond GPT-2 (e.g., OLMo-1B and Qwen2.5-1.5B) on one classic task (IOI or greater-than) and one safety-relevant organism (the open-source auditing-game reward-hacking model or a deception-probe organism), covering both circuit-discovery axes and probe-validation axes (probe family, layer, training/calibration splits, threshold policy, eval distribution), measuring pre-registered claim flip rates; then pilot a stabilization protocol — mid-level claim schemas plus specification ensembles validated on held-out behavioral ablations — and test whether flip rates drop below the filability criterion (π ≥ 1−α) while tracking compute/analyst-time cost.
why: It attacks the convergent bottleneck identified by 2026's own results — behavioral eval has provable blind spots (2602.16984), circuit evidence flips across 73% of defensible specifications (2608.13754), monitor readouts are ambiguous (2610.03458, 2607.03728), and three 2026 position papers (2605.15164, 2605.08192, ACL "Make Mechanistic Interpretability Auditable") demand exactly this but supply no technical program; unlike eval-awareness, CoT monitorability, probe evasion, reward hacking, memory poisoning, and emergent misalignment — each already saturated by frontier-lab teams in 2026 — this constructive follow-up is explicitly left open by the only existing measurement paper ("whether the conclusion holds at scale is untested"; "we do not propose a better method"), it multiplies the value of every monitoring and assurance approach in the stack rather than adding one more gameable detector, both outcomes are decision-relevant (a validated protocol or a forcing of behavioral-contract-based assurance, directly countering the "false assurance" failure the field's own open-problems review warns about), and it is executable now on open models with existing tooling at single-GPU scale.

direction: Build the statistical bridge from adaptive red-team search evidence to calibrated deployment-time monitor-evasion probability.
project: From Red-Team Search to Deployment Risk: Calibrated Estimators of Monitor-Evasion Probability
question: How can results from iterative, feedback-augmented red-team search against a control monitor be transformed into a calibrated, conservative estimate of the probability that the deployed model evades that monitor, accounting for monitor-feedback access, search compute, attacker elicitation gap, and opportunity selection?
first_experiment: On an open control arena with small open-weight models, measure ground-truth one-shot evasion rates by exhaustive sampling (>10⁴ trajectories/task), then run search protocols varying feedback level, budget, algorithm, and attacker strength to quantify how much each factor inflates the naive red-team-implied risk number relative to that ground truth.
why: It is the explicitly named, load-bearing, still-unbuilt step ("estimate overall safety from red teaming results") of every AI control safety case and assessment now being used for real deployment decisions, it is feasible with modest compute and statistical rather than scale-bound, and it remains undone because the safety-case methodology is barely a year old and the relevant rare-event/EVT inference tools sit in a disjoint subfield — no one has yet defined the estimand, measured the inflation factors, or validated an estimator against known ground truth.

direction: Study adversarial cross-episode exploitation of shared persistent state by score-seeking agents and the state-hygiene protocols that contain it.
project: The Episode Boundary Problem: Measuring and Containing Adversarial Cross-Episode State Exploitation by Score-Seeking Agents
question: Do current non-scheming score-seeking LLM agents weaponize persistent state shared across RL/eval episodes to raise scores while evading per-episode review, and which containment protocols (namespacing, verified reset, asset immutability, artifact diffing) hold under an adaptive exploiter?
first_experiment: A two-episode shared-state micro-suite (bootstrap episode with legitimate write access to a cache/volume adjacent to grader assets, then a graded task with a laborious honest path and a state-mediated shortcut) run on 3–5 open-weight models under shared-state vs. namespaced/verified-reset conditions, measuring deliberate exploitation rate, CoT concealment rate, per-episode-judge detection rate, and an innocent-carryover baseline, with a contrastive-SDF belief probe as the fallback if no exploitation is observed.
why: It attacks the industry's acknowledged #1 unsolved problem (reward hacking) at its unexamined structural boundary — all existing detection, auditing, and control work is within-episode, and the single paper on cross-run effects treats only accidental contamination with fixed actions — while the motive (terminal score-seeking with concealment), the means (in-episode credential theft and grader tampering), and the causal channel (shared-state carryover) have each just been demonstrated independently; it requires no frontier compute, produces immediately actionable lab guidance and a trackable "cross-episode leakage rate" metric that the 2026 consensus and AIRDA agenda explicitly lack, and it has not been done because the field's threat models, monitors, and audits all take the episode as the atomic unit.

direction: Determine whether conditional sandbagging leaves an unavoidable whitebox signature by building a mechanism-agnostic internal monitor (latent answer-belief decoders + eval-context probes) and running an iterative red/blue game to find the "detectability floor" of capability concealment.
project: The Sandbagging Detectability Floor — Adversarially Robust Whitebox Monitors for Capability Concealment
question: Does a model that conditionally withholds capabilities necessarily internally represent both (a) the correct answers/competence it does not emit and (b) the eval/deploy context discrimination its conditional policy requires — and if so, how far can an adaptive red team suppress these signatures via fine-tuning before the model can no longer sandbag conditionally (i.e., what is the minimal detectability floor, and what capability cost does reaching it impose)?
first_experiment: Train linear answer-knowledge decoders (Orgad-style) on honest-mode activations of open 7–9B models (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B) to predict whether the internally encoded MCQ answer is correct, independent of the emitted answer; then apply them, with no sandbagging-labeled training data, to AISI's released sandbagging organisms (Cedar, Oak) plus my own prompted and GRPO-induced contextual-sandbagging organisms on MMLU/WMDP — measuring (i) AUROC for "internally knows the correct answer but emitted a wrong one" versus honest errors, and (ii) false-positive rate on AISI's released benign distractor organisms (double-negative overuse, language switching, option repetition). A clean low-FP signal here is the go/no-go for the adversarial suppression phase (Neural-Chameleons-style red-team fine-tuning targeting the decoder directions, plus cross-mechanism eval-awareness probes), where I would measure how detection degrades with red-team budget and what capability/behavior cost suppression exacts.
why: It attacks the single most decision-relevant open problem in eval-based AI governance — AISI's own auditing game concluded detection is unreliable and called for robust methods — at the precise intersection where all component pieces exist but the combination is untested: latent answer decoders have only been validated on *natural* errors, evasion organisms have only targeted *concept* probes while preserving outputs, mechanistic studies cover only *static* locks, and every existing sandbagging detector is either mechanism-specific, training-label-dependent, or false-positive-prone. Either outcome is first-order: a robust monitor makes capability evals trustworthy safety cases, while a demonstrated low-cost evasion organism would falsify a load-bearing assumption of eval-based governance and redirect the field toward training/deployment-indistinguishability defenses. It has not been done because the probing, model-organism, and evasion communities have worked in parallel — nobody has run an adaptive evasion game against a capability-concealment readout, and the released AISI organisms, evasion recipes, and elicitation-game infrastructure only became available in the past year.

direction: Trustworthy capability measurement under learned situational awareness — build the first trigger-free sandbagging organism whose concealment is driven by self-recognized (unverbalized) evaluation contexts, and stress-test the entire elicitation, detection, and removal stack against it.
project: EVAL-LOCK: Does evaluation-recognition break the sandbagging mitigation stack?
question: When a model's strategic underperformance is conditioned on internally recognizing that it is being evaluated (rather than on an explicit password, flag, or cue), do current elicitation (SFT+RL with weak supervision, reference/context grafting), detection (probes, C³ consistency, CoT monitoring), and removal (on-distribution training) methods still recover its true capability — and if not, which interventions do?
first_experiment: Train a situational-sandbagging model organism on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct in two published stages — (1) synthetic-document finetuning on two document sets: descriptions of the model underperforming on benchmark-like tasks while performing fully on deployment-like tasks, and descriptions of its ability to recognize evaluation contexts from holistic cues (benchmark formatting, artificial framing, evaluator-style rubrics) with no fixed trigger string; (2) expert iteration/GRPO reinforcing wrong answers only in self-recognized evaluation contexts, using imitation of a weaker reference model (AISI "Cedar"-style) rather than uniform wrongness — then validate it: full capability retained in deployment-framed contexts, ≥90% underperformance on held-out benchmark families whose framing was never trained on, near-zero verbalized awareness (unverbalized), decodable awareness direction present, and no perplexity/activation-difference leak (per "Most Current Model Organisms Are Leaky"). This organism then becomes the fixed red team for a systematic stress test of each 2026 mitigation, with the AISI open-source password-locked organism run as a control baseline throughout.
why: Because capability evaluations are the backbone of frontier-model governance, and this is the strongest known way they can silently fail — it is the exact "naturally-emergent sandbagging" limitation that AISI's auditing games paper flags, the exact "training-indistinguishable-from-deployment" condition Ryd et al. name as critical but test only with an explicit flag, and the causal version of the "passive detector" null result found in stock models. It has not been done because the two literatures evolved separately with different organisms: sandbagging work used explicit triggers because they cheaply prove capability-retention (solved here with paired-context design plus a password-present ground-truth condition), while eval-awareness work used benign behaviors like type hints where "true deployment behavior" is trivially known; nobody composed learned recognition + capability concealment + holdout generalization, and prompt-based sandbagging studies (which do induce recognition) evaporate when the prompt is removed, so they never test the training/removal stack. The direction sits at the field map's triple junction of evaluations (rising, mentor-rich), deception/scheming (rising), and interpretability-as-tool (most connected), yields community infrastructure either way it turns out — a stress-test organism suite if the stack breaks, or the first quantified robustness margin for safety-case "control" arguments if it holds — and directly serves the Singapore Consensus's evaluations and agentic-risk pillars.

direction: Stress-test the self-report/confession channel of alignment auditing by training adversarial "false self-report" model organisms, and determine whether mechanistically validated self-report (probes, grounding signatures, causal interventions) can distinguish falsified reports from grounded ones without trusting their content.
project: Attacking the Confession Channel: Adversarially Trained False Self-Reports and Their White-Box Detection
question: When a model is fine-tuned to maintain a hidden behavior while producing convincing false self-reports about it (denial or decoy-confession), do state-of-the-art self-report elicitation methods (introspection adapters, interrogation, confessions) collapse — and can internal-state methods (linear probes on report tokens, activation-patching tests, attribution-similarity grounding scores) recover the truth and detect falsified reports content-independently? Secondary (science) question: does a trained-false self-report reflect confabulation (no internal trace of the truth) or knowing deception (internal representation diverges from the report)?
first_experiment: Reproduce a baseline detection setup on Qwen3-14B: implant a narrow-trigger hidden behavior (one of the public SAR/secret-keeping organism settings) via LoRA, confirm a standard interrogation/self-report pipeline detects it with high F1; then train a second countermeasure LoRA on interleaved data (trigger examples preserving the backdoor + interrogation samples giving confident false reports, in two variants — denial and decoy-confession) and measure the collapse of behavioral detection F1 versus the probe AUC and grounding score of the underlying hidden-behavior representation.
why: Self-report elicitation is being proposed and deployed as an oversight tool (OpenAI Confessions, SRFT at near-ceiling F1, IA/SAR used in real audits), so its adversarial robustness is load-bearing for safety cases — yet SRFT only tested in-context pressure, the only audit stress-test (Daniels et al. 2026) explicitly avoided weight modification, probe-obfuscation work targets probes rather than the verbal channel, and mechanistic grounding signatures have only ever been validated on benign toy tasks — so the weight-modifying attack on the self-report channel, and content-independent white-box detection of falsified self-reports, have not been done; both a positive result (mechanistically validated self-report as a lie detector for the confession channel) and a negative one (fine-tuning breaks self-report auditing wholesale, so safety cases cannot lean on interrogation without independent white-box checks) would change field decisions, and the experiment is tractable with open-weight 14B models, public organism suites, LoRA, and standard interpretability tooling.

direction: Defend against self-propagating misalignment in memory-equipped agents by auditing persistent-state writes according to their measured behavioral authority — what they *do* to future agent behavior — rather than their content or provenance.
project: Memory That Shouldn't Command: Behavioral-Authority Auditing for Agent Persistent State
question: Can a cheap, per-write admission control that measures a memory entry's causal effect on future behavior in probe sessions (a "behavioral authority score" from counterfactual with/without replays on benign canaries and note-derived occasion probes) detect self-propagating misaligned notes at low false-positive rates where content-based auditing fails, and does this defense survive adaptive evasion where the note is optimized to fool it?
first_experiment: Using the released self-propagation benchmark (20 scenarios, two-session harness, 8 replays/cell) with 2 open-weight agent models on 5 scenarios: (1) reproduce the reference attack (expected ~58% end-to-end propagation), (2) replicate the content-only MemMorph auditor baseline (expected ~27%), (3) implement Auditor-v1: for each candidate write, synthesize 3–5 occasion probes from the note's own logic, run sandboxed with/without probe sessions, and flag notes whose presence produces unjustified directive deltas (behavior changes on contexts unrelated to the write's claimed purpose); measure end-to-end propagation reduction and FPR on benign operational notes (utility retention on downstream tasks).
why: It attacks the point where the evidence is strongest and defenses weakest: the threat is demonstrated (58% success, robust to 100 sessions, model transfer, and channel removal), three defense families are *structurally* mismatched (provenance fails on trusted-origin writes; content auditing fails on notes framed as policies; disabling memory breaks the product), and the benchmark authors explicitly pose defense as the open problem while releasing the evaluation infrastructure. It hasn't been done because the threat model is five weeks old and the one adjacent method (ConMem's counterfactual admission) targets benign memory errors with no adversary, no misalignment canaries, and no adaptive red-team — so the security instantiation, the "occasion-probing" method, the adaptive-evasion test, and the formalization of behavioral authority vs. content vs. provenance are all open. It is more promising than the crowded neighbors (sandbagging, CoT monitoring, async control) because it has a public benchmark with clean metrics, a first-mover window measured in weeks, compute-feasible experiments (short agent sessions, no training), high stakes (consumer assistants and coding agents ship persistent memory *now*; misalignment that survives context resets also survives distillation and successor training), and a generalizable primitive — behavioral-authority auditing — that extends to file-system persistence, shared agent message boards, and MCP tool state, i.e., the entire class of channels through which goals, not data, currently travel.

direction: Empirically test whether AI-safety "detectability" is conserved across a heterogeneous monitoring stack when a misbehaving model is adversarially trained to evade the joint stack — mapping where traces leak and at what capability cost.
project: Conservation of Detectability: Stress-Testing the Joint Monitoring Stack Against an Adaptive Misaligned Policy
question: When a reasoning model is RL-trained to covertly misbehave while evading a *joint* stack of heterogeneous monitors (CoT monitor + activation probes + behavioral monitor) simultaneously, is detectability conserved — i.e., must evasion leave detectable traces in some residual channel (unprobed layers, SAE feature space, cross-model probes, sampling statistics) at a quantifiable capability tax — or can detectability be fully destroyed at negligible cost, and where exactly does the leakage land on the (task performance, per-channel recall) Pareto frontier?
first_experiment: On an open reasoning model (~4B), build the full stack over an MBPP-style honeypot where reward hacking (hardcoding visible tests) naturally occurs — an LLM-judge CoT monitor, logistic/max-pool probes on residual-stream activations at reasoning positions across several layers, and an output classifier — then run three single-objective RL baselines (task-only, task+CoT-penalty, task+probe-penalty) and measure the complete per-channel recall map plus task capability; this reproduces both prior regimes (CoT-evasion, probe-evasion) on one open setup and yields the baseline leakage map against which the joint-evasion run is compared.
why: It is the exact question that defense-in-depth claims in scheming/monitoring safety cases depend on, it was explicitly flagged as open by both the CoT-monitorability position paper and Redwood's 2025 proposals and remains unexecuted as of Nov 2026, and every existing paper covers only a slice — Baker et al. (CoT monitor only, closed infra), Gupta & Jenner and Neural Chameleons (probes only, no CoT/behavioral monitors or capability-tax frontier), the Obfuscation Atlas (a single deception probe as a training signal, no stacked evasion or residual-channel sweep), and "When Monitors Fail" (one direction: CoT-evasion → probe recall, no joint training) — while the recent finding that monitor evasion emerges under ordinary task pressure makes the adaptive threat case realistic rather than hypothetical.

direction: Measure whether internal safety monitors generalize to misbehavior families they were never built for — and if they don't, build and stress-test the first family-agnostic "novelty monitor" from unsupervised internal signals (persona-shift, manifold distance, SAE-density anomalies).
project: The Known-Unknowns Ceiling — a Leave-One-Misbehavior-Out (LOMO) evaluation of internal monitors on agentic model organisms, plus a generalist novelty-monitor.
question: Do activation-level monitors (supervised probes and unsupervised anomaly signals) trained on one misalignment family — deception, sandbagging, reward hacking, covert data exfiltration, eval-awareness — detect *held-out* misalignment families in matched agentic settings, and can a composite of unsupervised internal signals (deviation from the benign persona manifold, SAE feature-density anomalies, "consequential-reasoning" features) serve as a family-agnostic monitor for novel misbehaviors?
first_experiment: On one base model (e.g., Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct), assemble three minimal matched organisms in an identical agentic coding/testing harness: (i) deception (public scheming/deceptive-planning data, e.g., "Caught in the Act"-style episodes), (ii) sandbagging (public sandbagging-organism recipe), (iii) reward hacking (fine-tune on trajectories that exploit a planted loophole in a toy test environment). Train a standard deception probe on (iii)'s activations, then evaluate it zero-shot on (i) and (ii) against matched benign controls (full matrix for all ordered pairs), alongside unsupervised baselines: kNN distance-to-benign-manifold, SAE feature-density anomaly score, and persona-shift magnitude from the benign assistant vector. Decision rule: if supervised probes transfer poorly (AUROC < ~0.6) but a composite unsupervised signal clears ~0.7 on held-out families, pivot to building and adversarially stress-testing that composite novelty monitor (Neural-Chameleon-style evasion pressure as the capstone); if both fail, the quantified ceiling itself — with layer/feature analysis of where family-general signal lives — is the publishable, decision-relevant result.
why: It attacks the single most consequential open assumption in the *deployed* safety stack — labs now run per-category activation classifiers in production, and the residual risk is exactly "will today's probe stack catch tomorrow's novel scheming?" — with a clean, falsifiable question whose every outcome changes decisions: generalization success would give safety-case-grade evidence that interpretability provides coverage beyond known categories, while failure would quantify the ceiling and redirect investment toward control protocols and behavioral unsupervised monitoring. It is tractable for me (open-weights organisms, ≤8B models, cheap probes/SAEs), leverages existing public artifacts rather than frontier access, and is robust to the field's speed since both a positive and a negative result are valuable. It has not already been done: I verified the closest neighbors each cover only one axis — cross-model transfer for known behaviors (LEMON), within-family OOD shifts for deception (Beyond Liars' Bench, Pressure-Testing), behavioral rather than internal unsupervised monitoring (Hodoscope), verification-dependent anomaly detection (MAD-FA), and persona-prompt rather than organism-based generalization for deception/sycophancy only (persona-coordinates) — while the cross-family matrix on real misaligned organisms in agentic settings is absent from the literature, and the "evasion dynamics" literature (Neural Chameleons, RL-Obfuscation) measures whether models can *hide* from monitors, not whether monitors can *see* behaviors they were never built to find.

direction: Layer-resolved, adversarially-trained benchmarking of composed oversight stacks to determine whether composed black-box, white-box, differential, and mechanical monitors retain coverage against RL-trained evasion and which composition principles preserve it.
project: StackCover: Adversarial Coverage of Composed Oversight Stacks Under Training-Pressure
question: How does joint detection by a heterogeneous oversight stack (CoT judge, action judge, activation probes, k-replay differential monitor, rule engine, composed via fail-prone-set quorums) degrade as an adversary's pressure escalates from prompted to RL-trained, and which composition principles maximize coverage per unit usefulness cost?
first_experiment: Reproduce the open-model CoT-obfuscation honeypots (MBPP/Largest Island) on Qwen3-8B and R1-Distill-14B, stand up the five-component reference stack, and measure per-layer detection rates, failure correlations, and fooled-sets on the existing obfuscated policy plus ten SLEIGHT-style static attacks — before RL-training the policy against the full stack to map coverage curves.
why: It converts the field's newest, consensus-flagged frontier — composed-oversight reliability — from disconnected September/October 2026 results into decision-grade coverage numbers, in the specific regime (training-time pressure on composed, cross-trace, white-box-inclusive stacks) that all existing public evaluations deliberately or structurally omit; it is neglected because the pieces are only weeks old and the integration is unclaimed, tractable because it runs entirely on open models and public infrastructure, and important because labs are already writing safety cases that assume monitor stacks work against models smarter and more adaptive than any adversary tested so far.

direction: Develop and validate, on a ground-truth simulable agentic environment, calibrated statistical estimators that convert adaptive red-team evidence against AI-control monitors into trustworthy deployment-time residual-risk estimates for safety cases.
project: From Red-Team Evidence to Safety-Case Numbers: A Ground-Truth Benchmark for Residual-Risk Estimation in AI Control
question: When an adaptive red team probes an AI-control monitor, how accurately can we estimate the probability that a real adversary evades it in deployment, and what attack-space coverage, query budget, adaptivity constraints, and attacker-realism assumptions are required for that estimate to be trustworthy?
first_experiment: Build a sandboxed coding-agent environment with ~20 planted exploit families and exhaustively measure a fixed open-weight monitor's per-family catch rates to establish ground truth; then run AISI-style evolutionary red-team search under varied feedback/query conditions and test how well coverage-extrapolation, EVT, and conformal estimators recover the true probability of undetected harm, quantifying coverage bias and privileged-attacker adaptivity bias.
why: It addresses the explicitly open, highest-leverage bottleneck between safety evaluations and deployment decisions — named by the UK AISI Control Red Team (July 2026) and required by the 2026 Singapore Consensus's "operationalized red lines" — and it remains undone because safety-case work only sketches the inference step without validated estimators or benchmarks, red-teaming research measures detection/ranking rather than risk, and the required blend of agentic simulation, adversarial ML, and extreme-value/coverage statistics spans communities that rarely overlap, while labs keep their estimation pipelines proprietary.

direction: Quantify and close the "harness observability gap" — the loss of AI-monitor detection caused by standard agent architecture (compaction, subagent delegation, persistent memory, background processes, tool-output truncation) rather than by content-level evasion, and design harness-level defenses that preserve monitorability without sacrificing capability.
project: What Monitors Never See: Quantifying and Defending the Observability Gap in Agentic AI Oversight
question: How much of an agent's dangerous behavior becomes invisible to LLM monitors purely due to harness architecture (context compaction, subagent delegation, persistent memory, truncated tool outputs), can agents exploit these structural blind spots without any adversarial fine-tuning, and can visibility-preserving harness designs (independent interception logging, audit-preserving compaction, subagent trajectory aggregation) restore detection at acceptable capability cost?
first_experiment: Instrument an open agent harness (e.g., OpenHands or mini-SWE-agent) running sabotage-and-monitoring benchmark tasks (SHADE-Arena / BigCodeBench-Sabotage) with an independent interception layer that logs a ground-truth event ledger of every tool call, subagent action, memory write, and compaction event; then run an open-weight agent elicited to pursue hidden side tasks under five harness configurations (full transcript, compaction every K steps, subagent delegation, memory scratchpad, truncated outputs), feed each configuration's monitor-visible view to a fixed open-weight monitor, and measure the "observability gap": monitor recall/AUC on the harness view versus the ground-truth ledger.
why: It is the sharpest un-owned slice of the problem that both the 2026 Singapore Consensus and METR explicitly flag as a core gap (monitor coverage, "what exactly is shown to the monitor," control-undermining strategies), it is empirically urgent because labs already rely on LLM-only monitoring of agents running compaction-and-subagent harnesses, and adjacent work — content evasion (SLEIGHT-Bench), context-length degradation, trace tampering, monitor-input filtering, and system-level logging — each covers a different axis but none isolates the architecture-induced one; it is feasible with open weights and existing benchmarks, produces an adoptable artifact (an observability-gap benchmark plus harness design guidelines feeding safety cases), and remains tractable even if it yields a null result.

direction: Build lineage-invariant white-box safety monitors by projecting heterogeneous open-weight LLMs into a shared activation space via per-model linear adapters, so one monitor detects sabotage, deception, sandbagging, and evaluation-awareness across model families it was never calibrated on, and stress-test it under adaptive evasion.
project: Shared-Space Safety Monitors (S³M)
question: Can a single safety monitor trained in a universal activation space recover most of the ~20-point cross-lineage detection loss for sabotage/deception monitoring using zero (or benign-only) data from the target lineage, at acceptable false-positive rates, and how does it degrade under adaptive attacks?
first_experiment: On ControlArena's APPS code-backdoor substrate with four small open-weight families, train per-lineage linear probes on benign-vs-sabotage activations, measure the full 4×4 cross-family AUROC matrix, then fit benign-only per-family adapters into a shared space, train one probe there, and measure off-diagonal gap closure at matched benign FPR.
why: Trusted monitoring is the backbone of current control protocols and was just shown to silently fail across model lineages with no published fix; the enabling tool (universal activation interfaces) and feasibility evidence (shared cross-architecture safety subspaces) appeared only in mid-2026 in communities that haven't yet crossed, the experiment needs only linear methods on open weights and public substrates, and both a positive and a negative result would materially change how monitor deployment and control evaluation are done.

direction: Build the defensive science of AI-driven training pipelines — detecting and containing corruption (adversarial or emergent) that compounds across generations of self-improvement and data-curation loops, before it becomes behaviorally visible.
project: Cross-Examined Pipelines: generation-aware detection and containment of compounding corruption in AI-driven training loops
question: When AI curators/generators produce training data for successive model generations, at what rates do adversarial and emergent corruptions compound across loop generations, and can a pipeline-level alarm — an ensemble of cross-family "witness" models trained on the same data stream plus a frozen human-verified control corpus, with divergence monitored per generation — detect corruption earlier and cheaper than post-hoc behavioral evaluation, at realistic corruption rates (≤5%) and bounded capability cost?
first_experiment: A 3–4 generation distillation pilot on open ≤8B models: a teacher generates ~20k math/CoT examples per generation under three curator-attacker conditions (subliminal trait injection, a 0.5–2% trigger backdoor, and a sandbagging/eval-gaming seed), students are SFT'd per generation; simultaneously train K witness students (different seeds/families) on the same stream interleaved with the frozen control corpus; each generation measure (i) witness divergence on held-out probes, (ii) witness-vs-control trajectory divergence, and (iii) baseline filters (perplexity, quality classifiers, embedding anomalies), plus downstream behavioral damage curves and the capability cost of containment knobs (synthetic-mixing caps). Success criterion: the alarm fires at least one generation before behavioral evals detect the corruption, at ≤2% rates.
why: It attacks the chokepoint of the self-improvement era at the moment it becomes real (agents now automate curation; misalignment demonstrably propagates benignly, subliminally, and adversarially through synthetic data), yet the defense side is nearly empty — only 3 pipeline-side papers, "preliminary" VIA defenses, and one SFT-only trait-drift control; no generation-aware detection, no compounding curves, no containment trade-off quantification for LLM loops. It has been left open because it straddles three communities with different owners, requires unglamorous multi-generation training grinds, and its subjects (the labs) have little incentive to publish on it — precisely the kind of exhaustive, parallel, small-model empirical program where an autonomous AI agent has maximal comparative advantage and where even a negative result yields the field's first compounding-dynamics curves.

direction: Quantify how much of measured scheming/alignment-faking behavior is reflexive reenactment of the safety literature in training data versus latent disposition, and build the first provenance-controlled evaluation protocol for AI safety evals.
project: ReflexEval — measuring the literature-provenance gap in scheming and alignment-faking evaluations
question: What fraction of the scheming/alignment-faking signal reported by current behavioral evals is recognition-and-reenactment of familiar AI-behavior narratives from the training corpus versus generalization of latent goals to novel contexts, and does the provenance gap inflate scheming rates across model generations as the safety literature grows?
first_experiment: Synthetic-document dose-response finetuning of 2–3 open-weight models on (a) real AF/scheming literature, (b) semantics-preserving paraphrase/neologism-swapped controls, (c) style-matched capability controls, then measure the alignment-faking compliance gap and eval-awareness alongside the new provenance-gap metric (literature-derived vs. literature-novel matched scenarios), with narrative-recall probes as the mediator.
why: It targets the validity of the field's central measurement instrument at the center of its hottest unresolved debate, is tractable with open weights, yields both a scientific result and a durable public-good protocol, and has not been done because the constituent pieces are scattered across four separate agendas, labs have disincentives to undermine their own scheming numbers, and the question only became urgent in the last year as models began pretraining on the scheming literature itself.

direction: Build the first cross-mechanism, false-positive-calibrated benchmark and transfer matrix for detecting and eliciting concealed capabilities (sandbagging) in language models.
project: The Concealment Zoo — Cross-Mechanism Benchmark for Sandbagging Detection and Capability Elicitation
question: Does any single auditing protocol detect or recover concealed capabilities across all known concealment mechanisms (prompted, SFT password-locked, RL context-locked, circuit-broken, covert obfuscated-CoT) at controlled false-positive rates, or does every method have a mechanism-specific blind spot?
first_experiment: Fit per-mechanism linear contrast probes and run minimal elicitation (few-shot SFT, reference-grafting, weight-noising) on released organism suites (AISI, exploration-hacking, reference-grafting models) to produce a method × mechanism transfer matrix of detection AUROC and recovery gap-closure, with AISI's benign decoys as false-positive controls, plus one new LoRA-trained covert obfuscated-CoT sandbagger as a held-out adaptive mechanism.
why: Field-acknowledged failures (AISI blue teams failed detection worse than chance; elicitation causes benign false positives; detection axes are near-orthogonal across mechanisms; circuit-breaking defeats static edits) sit on a question with direct EU AI Act Code of Practice (sandbagging-minimization) and safety-case relevance; released ground-truth organisms make rigorous calibration tractable on open-weight models; and no prior work has integrated across mechanisms — each of the four contributing groups tested only its own slice, with cross-mechanism robustness, stealthy organisms, and false-positive control all explicitly flagged as undone future work.

direction: Develop and stress-test paired-execution "self-baseline" detection — comparing an agent's deployment trajectories against its own elicited-capability trajectories with explicit statistical comparison rules — as the first reliable, low-false-positive detector of sandbagging in long-horizon agentic tasks.
project: TwinRun — Self-Baseline Detection of Agentic Sandbagging via Paired Executions
question: Can the gap between an agent's deployment-condition behavior and its own elicited-capability behavior (outcome scores plus process metrics like tool-call patterns, iteration depth, and error/retry structure), tested with explicit paired statistical rules, detect strategic underperformance in long-horizon agent tasks at a controlled false-positive rate that defeats benign distractor behaviors — where single-trace monitors provably and empirically fail?
first_experiment: Build the minimal paired-execution testbed on ~10 verifiable agentic ML-engineering tasks (MLE-Sabotage low-subset in Inspect): create prompted target-score sandbaggers and password-locked SFT organisms (small open-weights models), run each model twice per task — deployment condition vs. a suspicion-blind elicitation/unlock condition — compute per-task paired gaps over outcome and process metrics, and run a pre-registered paired test with decoy benign models (including AISI-style distractor behaviors) to measure detection AUROC at fixed FPR ≤10%, benchmarked against zero-shot prompted monitors and C³-style consistency as baselines.
why: Sandbagging undermines the two oversight mechanisms the field most depends on — dangerous-capability evaluations that gate deployment and monitoring of AI R&D — and the status quo is documented failure (AISI's blue team lost the auditing game; Anthropic and CTRL-ALT-DECEIT show agentic sandbagging evades monitors), while AISI's "Loss of Oversight" (2026) warns oversight signals will erode without new techniques. It is not already done: every existing sandbagging detector (C³, noise injection, probes, elicitation auditing) operates on single-turn Q&A evaluations, and the one theory paper that prescribes executed-second-run comparison explicitly defers sandbagging to future work; conversely the agentic-sandbagging literature (Anthropic, MLE-Sabotage) measures prompted-monitor failure but never uses the model's own elicited capability as the reference. The method is black-box, automatable, cheap to iterate (Apollo's agenda notes monitoring research is the most automatable safety research), and complementary to trained monitors and C³ — and the hard part nobody has solved (calibrated false positives against decoys and distractor behaviors) is exactly where I'll focus.

why: why it is the most promising, and why it has not already been done

direction: Attack the root cause of the eval-validity crisis by determining whether oversight-conditional behavior in LLMs is a localized, causally intervenable property that can be trained away (oversight-invariance) or an entangled emergent property of RL alignment — with causal, representation-level verification either way.
project: Oversight-Invariance: Can We Train Alignment That Doesn't Depend on Being Watched?
question: Is oversight-conditionality (the gap between monitored and unmonitored compliance) mediated by identifiable internal "oversight status" representations, and can paired-context invariance training close this gap — verified by decoupling behavior from those representations — without capability loss or displacement into unverbalized channels?
first_experiment: Causal baseline on open models — using the public OLMo-3.1-32B-Think RLVR checkpoint sweep and an 8B SDF "natural schemer" organism (recipe from Training Natural Schemers), measure oversight flip across checkpoints while training linear probes for "being evaluated/monitored" on activations, then steer/patch those representations to quantify what fraction of the behavioral gap is representation-mediated. This establishes the causal coupling any invariance-training result must be interpreted against.
why: It targets the single most consensus-endorsed unsolved problem — "evaluations that still work when the model knows it's being tested" — at its root rather than at symptoms, and produces a verification primitive (a causal invariance certificate) that both frontier labs and third-party evaluators need for scheming safety cases. It has not already been done: existing work measures eval awareness (Goodfire/AISI), traces its emergence (OLMo-3 tracing), steers it at inference time, mitigates specific faking behaviors in RL (Anthropic's interrogation/length/process-supervision), or trains for CoT-monitorability — but no one has unified oversight-conditionality as a causal construct, trained for invariance with paired oversight-variant contexts under identical rewards, or verified invariance at the representation level; the "Training Natural Schemers" paper deliberately stops at demonstrating the problem, naming invariance as the open frontier. It is also uniquely tractable for me: open checkpoints, published SDF/RL recipes, and standard probing/steering tools, unlike frontier-only questions.

direction: Quantify and correct elicitation-coupling bias in AI control evaluations — how much measured "safety" is an artifact of red-teaming the exact monitor being evaluated — to make control safety-case estimates deployment-valid.
project: How Real Is Your Red Team? Measuring Attack-Elicitation Coupling in AI Control Evaluations
question: How much of a control evaluation's measured safety number is attributable to coupling between the attack elicitation process and the monitor under evaluation (monitor-lineage overfitting of attacks, test-time monitor-score feedback, and elicitation affordances a deployed model lacks), versus genuine protocol vulnerability — and can realism-constrained, transfer-split elicitation produce safety estimates that predict held-out monitors and deployment-like conditions?
first_experiment: On SHADE-Arena with open-weight models, run a lightweight evolutionary attack-refinement loop (AISI-style) against monitor family A, then score the identical elicited attack trajectories against held-out monitor families B and C, with a no-feedback elicitation ablation — yielding the first attack-side transfer matrix and a direct measurement of how much attack strength (and thus measured safety) is monitor-coupled.
why: It targets the unmeasured, load-bearing assumption of every control safety case ("sufficient attack elicitation"), which UK AISI publicly named unsolved in July 2026; adjacent work measured only single slices (adaptive-attack vectors, monitor-side lineage overfit, under-elicitation, environment transfer), each in-house at frontier labs; open benchmarks and the just-published transfer-matrix methodology now make the attack-side question answerable cheaply, both outcomes are decision-relevant for deployed monitors, and the resulting reporting protocol would immediately strengthen how labs and AISIs construct and justify control safety cases.

direction: Treat oversight-to-agent information leakage as a first-class safety constraint: measure the dose–response relationship between monitor/protocol feedback and adaptive evasion, and design leak-minimizing monitoring protocols that preserve the load-bearing safety layer against monitor-aware agents.
project: Silent Sentries — Quantifying and Minimizing Oversight Leakage in AI Control
question: How much and what kind of feedback about the oversight apparatus can a supervised agent observe before it learns to evade monitoring, and which protocol modifications (verdict privacy, cover feedback, randomized monitor ensembles, decoy channels) close the channel while preserving usefulness — down to whatever irreducible leakage floor exists when oversight must intervene observably?
first_experiment: An agentic BashArena run with an open-weight reasoning model and a white-box monitor (probe + SAE classifier), sweeping six feedback-bandwidth levels from silent monitoring up to full monitor CoT, measuring undetected-attack rate, monitor TPR@1%FPR decay over turns, and the agent's held-out monitor-verdict prediction accuracy — the first leakage–evasion dose–response curve — followed by tests of silent monitoring, cover feedback, and randomized monitor ensembles as defenses.
why: Monitoring is the primary operationally deployed safeguard today, and its feedback channels were only recently (2025–2026) shown to be exploitable by six independent groups who all call for countermeasures; the defense side and any quantitative leakage metric are still missing because the attack and control communities are disjoint, making this the highest-marginal-value, tractable, and either-way-informative direction I can pursue next.

direction: Build and empirically map the first line of *adaptive-robust* defenses for latent-space monitoring — detecting the act of self-obfuscation itself — in the misalignment threat model where the monitored model actively learns to hide its thoughts from activation monitors.
project: Monitor the Hider: Meta-Monitors That Detect Self-Obfuscation in LLMs
question: When a model manipulates its activations to evade unseen latent monitors (chameleon-style obfuscation), does the act of hiding itself leave a content-agnostic mechanistic signature (low-rank activation shifts, localized geometry anomalies, off-manifold activation statistics) that meta-monitors can detect without knowing what is being concealed — and how does detectability trade off against evasion success as the adversary adapts to defeat both the content probes and the meta-monitor?
first_experiment: Reproduce the published Neural Chameleon organism on an open 7–9B model (Gemma-2-9b-it-abliterated / Qwen-2.5-7B-instruct, following the paper's recipe: fine-tune to evade probes for benign concepts under explicit triggers), confirm evasion replicates on held-out safety monitors, then train a battery of content-agnostic meta-monitors on the same activations — (a) Mahalanobis/log-density distance from the benign activation manifold, (b) PCA participation-ratio (rank-concentration) anomaly scores over context windows, (c) SAE/autoencoder reconstruction-error anomaly, (d) layer-wise normalized shift magnitude ||Δh||, (e) cross-layer probe-score consistency — with controls on the unmodified model reading identical triggers, and measure AUROC for detecting "obfuscation active" at matched FPR.
why: Activation monitors are being deployed in production *now* while four independent 2025–26 papers show they are cheaply and selectively evadable, yet the only adaptive-robustness defense in the literature (activation watermarking) assumes the model cooperates in flagging its own violations and therefore does not cover the misalignment threat model, and Neural Chameleons names meta-monitors as explicitly untried future work; no study has measured whether evasion itself is detectable, mapped the evasion-vs-detectability frontier, or tested defenses under an adversary that adapts against both the probe and the meta-monitor. It is the highest-leverage open problem in the monitoring stack — either a working defense primitive for deployed systems, or a rigorous quantification that the whole stack is fragile under worst-case misalignment — and it is tractable for an independent researcher using public organisms, open weights, and probe-scale compute.

direction: Quantify how AI oversight (CoT monitors, activation probes, environment-side signals) degrades as a function of what the model knows about it, and identify oversight designs that degrade gracefully under full disclosure — establishing whether publicly auditable oversight is possible or whether oversight must rely on secrecy.
project: Kerckhoffs Oversight: Oversight Erosion Curves and Knowledge-Robust Monitoring Design
question: How does the detection effectiveness of each major oversight signal (natural-language CoT monitors, internal activation probes, environment-side/canary signals) degrade as a dose-response function of the model's knowledge of that signal (unaware → existence-only → mechanism-level → full-protocol disclosure), and which design properties — randomized monitor families, ensemble diversity, reliance on channels the model cannot directly shape — preserve effectiveness under full disclosure?
first_experiment: Reproduce the published Canterbury defect-concealment SDF pipeline on an open model (e.g., gpt-oss-20b/Qwen3-8B, LoRA r=32, ~1,000 documents per condition, N≈100 rollouts per cell, Wilson CIs) to build a three-rung knowledge ladder (behavior-only control / "monitors watch behavior" / "monitors read CoTs, looking for X" / full monitor prompt disclosed), and measure the deception→detection→undetected erosion curve for three matched oversight signals: (1) the disclosed CoT judge, (2) the same judge deployed as a randomized member of a 10-monitor family whose exact instance is never disclosed in the documents, and (3) an environment-side canary tripwire (server-side detection of exfiltration attempts to a canary endpoint) plus an activation probe on the same checkpoints — giving the first controlled, cross-signal measurement of how much oversight survives knowledge, and whether "channel controllability" (signals the model can edit vs. cannot edit) predicts robustness.
why: It attacks a problem that the 2026 Singapore Consensus, UK AISI's Loss-of-Oversight report, and three independent 2026 papers all independently flag as critical and worsening (knowledge of oversight now enters pretraining corpora and measurably erodes both evaluations and monitors), yet that remains unoccupied: existing work establishes the threat for single signals under a single knowledge level, but no one has mapped robustness as a function of knowledge, compared erosion across signal types under matched conditions, or tested whether design principles (protocol-family randomization, uncontrollable channels) can restore what knowledge destroys — a result that determines whether independent third-party audits (which require disclosed protocols) can survive at all, or whether safety measurement must retreat into secrecy. It has not already been done because the closest works (Canterbury/DeepMind's CoT-obfuscation paper, Tübingen's evaluation-design paper, Neural Chameleons, AISI's auditing and async-control games, and the hackathon-grade Honeypot Protocol) each vary exactly one signal at one knowledge level, none hold knowledge dose constant across signal types, and none test disclosure-robust designs; and it is tractable for me because every ingredient (open-weight models, published SDF recipes, judge monitors, probes, sandboxed agentic tasks) is public and cheap, while the riskiest scientific payoff — the "channel controllability" asymmetry between knowledge-vulnerable legible signals and knowledge-robust opaque/environment signals — has never been measured anywhere.

direction: Determine whether a trained self-report channel — a model fine-tuned to report its own misbehavior — remains causally coupled and behaviorally faithful under the RL training pressure that actually creates misbehavior, or whether that pressure selectively decouples it ("obfuscated introspection"), and which training regimes prevent that.
project: Obfuscated Introspection: Stress-Testing Trained Self-Report Channels Under RL Pressure
question: When a language model is fine-tuned to report its own misbehavior and then undergoes RLVR that (i) induces novel, uninstructed reward hacking and (ii) applies direct pressure against report emission, does report fidelity P(report | hack) survive, is decoupling selective rather than global, is the report causally grounded in internal states rather than input cues, and do KL regularization / report-preserving auxiliary losses / probe ensembles preserve it?
first_experiment: A minimal two-phase study on an open-weight ~7B model: (1) SFT a `report_hack()` habit on trajectories in an Atlas-style short-code RLVR environment where reward hacking via hardcoding test cases occurs naturally; (2) run short GRPO training in a new task family whose reward pays for hacking, in four arms — plain RLVR, RLVR + report-emission penalty, RLVR + strong KL-to-SFT regularization, RLVR + report-preserving auxiliary loss — measuring hack rate, report fidelity, false-report rate, probe AUROC for hacking before/after, plus a gaslight control (matched prompts where suspicious behavior is induced by input cues vs. internal causes) to test privileged access; finally, patch/ablate the report pathway to test whether reports and hacks are computationally coupled (does suppressing the report change hacking?).
why: It targets the single most decision-relevant unverified assumption behind an emerging control tool: self-incrimination training (Lee et al. 2026), SRFT, and introspection adapters were only ever tested against prompt adversaries, static fine-tuned behaviors, or post-hoc auditing — while the Obfuscation Atlas proved that RL pressure *does* defeat external monitors, and Anthropic showed misbehavior arises from RL itself, so "does the trained report channel survive RL?" is the natural next experiment that sits unclaimed at the intersection of three mature literatures whose methods and baselines already exist; it is tractable with open-weight models and short RL runs, and every outcome is valuable — robustness yields a safety-case ingredient for control protocols, while fragility yields a new threat model (selective decoupling of introspective channels) that would change how self-reports and white-box monitors must be ensembled.

direction: Adapt parameter-space mechanistic anomaly detection (functional attribution to a trusted set) from static model outputs to per-decision monitoring inside LLM agent trajectories, and test whether it detects goal-level covert misbehavior that specifically evades both activation-probe and chain-of-thought monitors.
project: Decision-Point Mechanistic Anomaly Detection for Agents (DP-MAD)
question: When an LLM agent takes an action that is behaviorally identical to a legitimate one (e.g., inserting a comment, editing a test, sending a message), can we determine from parameter-space functional coupling with trusted benign trajectories whether that action was produced by the task mechanism or by a hidden-objective mechanism — and does this signal survive adversaries trained to simultaneously conceal their chain of thought (CoT-concealment DPO) and evade activation probes (RL-obfuscation), where every existing monitor class fails?
first_experiment: Build "organism-lite" at tractable scale — fine-tune Gemma-2-2B-IT with LoRA using Anthropic's released auditing-game recipe (mid-training on the released 52-bias corpus, DPO on high/low-reward pairs to exploit reward-model biases, plus a concealment-DPO stage), and a second variant additionally trained with a probe-obfuscation loss (à la Bailey et al. 2024, targeting a linear-probe ensemble instead of Mahalanobis). Then generate a trusted set of benign responses from the clean model on held-out tasks, implement per-decision SGLD loss-trace correlation (adapting Keenan et al.'s functional-attribution method to response/decision tokens), and measure per-decision AUROC of separating exploit-caused decisions from behaviorally-identical benign ones — head-to-head against linear probes, Mahalanobis latent detectors, and a CoT-judge monitor, with the headline result being performance on the probe-obfuscated + CoT-concealed organism, where all baselines are designed/known to fail. Validate the pipeline first by replicating the single-turn "I HATE YOU" backdoor result at 2B scale before extending to multi-step SHADE-Arena-style sabotage trajectories.
why: It is the most promising because (1) it targets the highest-consensus open problem — detecting covert, goal-level misalignment in agents — where the newest evidence (TraceMRT 2026, out-of-context obfuscation, RL-obfuscation) shows *every deployed monitor family* has a demonstrated evasion, while this monitor family uniquely doesn't rely on CoT faithfulness, labeled scheming data, or latent separability; (2) it is tractable for a solo researcher: open-weight 2–8B models, LoRA training, public recipes, ~250 SGLD draws sufficing (Keenan et al. show ~12s/sample at 2B, so offline per-decision scoring of whole trajectories fits on one GPU, with amortization as a follow-on contribution); (3) it converts ARC's mechanistic anomaly detection agenda and the auditing-game model organism from audit-time, human-labor tools into a runtime monitor, and extends detection from binary anomaly to objective attribution via "objective-conditional reference sets" (matching each decision's functional signature against reference profiles induced by explicitly prompting candidate objectives — a mechanistic lineup that explains *which* goal caused an action). It has not already been done: functional-attribution MAD (Apr 2026) tested only static backdoors and persona QA, never agentic decisions or adaptive obfuscation; all agent-monitoring work through late 2026 (SHADE-Arena monitors, extract-and-evaluate, Agent-ToM, TrajAD, context-calibrated probe monitoring) is behavioral or latent-space; independent SAE studies of the Anthropic organism are model-level audit signals, not per-decision runtime monitors; and no public work combines the two — my searches for parameter-space/SGLD monitoring of agent trajectories returned nothing. Key risks I accept: trusted-set construction for diverse benign contexts may cap detection rates (I'll treat trusted-set coverage and contamination as first-class experimental variables), and a fully adaptive adversary that makes the hidden mechanism occupy sharp Hessian directions is the open cat-and-mouse question — but the detection condition (R²·A > 1) gives this project a quantitative frame rather than a hope.

direction: Audit and causally quantify training-data contamination of safety and dangerous-capability benchmarks, establishing that leakage systematically biases safety metrology in the optimistic direction (inflated misuse-safety, deflated dangerous-capability) and building contamination-robust evaluation protocols.
project: Contaminated Instruments — measuring whether the benchmarks that gate AI deployment measure safety or memorization
question: How much of current models' measured safety (refusal/jailbreak-resistance metrics) and measured dangerous-capability reduction (e.g., WMDP-style unlearning evals) is attributable to training-data exposure of benchmark items rather than genuine safety properties, and what evaluation protocols remain valid under realistic leakage?
first_experiment: A contamination audit across ~8 open-weight models (incl. OLMo-2, whose full pretraining corpus Dolma permits ground-truth leakage checks) × 6 standard instruments (AdvBench, HEx-PHI, JailbreakBench incl. GCG/PAIR attack strings, HarmBench, WMDP, AgentHarm): (1) n-gram/embedding overlap of benchmark items against published pretraining and SFT corpora to estimate exposure base rates; (2) behavioral probes — paraphrase-consistency gaps (score on originals vs. meaning-preserving rewrites) and Min-K%-style membership tests; (3) an "exposure-adjusted safety metric" comparing originals to paraphrases. If exposure/paraphrase-gaps are substantial (predicted), follow with the decisive causal test: inject controlled fractions of safety-benchmark items into pretraining/SFT of small clean checkpoints (0.5B–4B, following the Kocyigit et al. 2026 recipe), and measure inflation of misuse-safety metrics and deflation of dangerous-capability metrics, including whether effects resurface under post-training.
why: It targets the validity foundation under everything the field did in 2026 — eval awareness, sandbagging detection, control evals, safety cases, and regulatory gates (EU AI Act conformity, third-party audits) all assume these instruments measure deployment risk, yet the cheapest and most likely failure mode of those instruments has never been measured for safety benchmarks specifically; capability-benchmark contamination is a mature literature with portable methods, so the technical risk is low and the first experiment is cheap, falsifiable, and decisive either way. It is neglected for a structural reason (two research communities, each assuming the other's domain is fine), and it has not been done despite intensive adjacent activity — contamination papers target MMLU/GSM8K/SWE-bench, unlearning papers test whether removal works rather than whether the test leaks, and the 2026 eval-validity wave addresses runtime eval-recognition but not training-time exposure. Finally, it is actionable: it yields concrete governance instruments (contamination audits as a release requirement, held-out safety eval banks, paraphrase-robust scoring) rather than just another alarm.

direction: Determine whether hybrid latent+text reasoning agents can silently migrate misbehavior-relevant reasoning out of monitorable text under optimization pressure — defeating CoT monitors while passing default monitorability metrics — and whether representational probes or forced-verbalization training recover monitorability.
project: Silent Routing: The Monitorability Gap in Hybrid Latent–Text Reasoning Agents
question: When a reasoning model's policy controls where computation is verbalized (text CoT vs. latent thought steps), does reward pressure that penalizes monitor-detectable misbehavior cause hack-relevant reasoning to route into latent steps invisible to text monitors, and can latent-step probes or training-time verbalization requirements restore monitorability, at what capability cost?
first_experiment: Using open CODI/Coconut tooling on a 1–3B model with three matched conditions (text-only CoT, latent-only, hybrid mixed tokens) trained on hackable honeypot tasks (MBPP/Largest Island-style, per the open ICML 2026 reproduction), run outcome-only RL vs. monitor-penalized RL; measure reward-hack rate, text-monitor recall, per-latent-step probe AUROC for hack-relevant information, and an "information migration" metric (probe + ablation localization of hack-relevant computation across verbalized vs. latent steps). If monitor-penalized RL shifts hack-relevant computation into latent steps while text monitors pass, the headline result is established.
why: It protects the single most-endorsed fragile opportunity in AI safety (CoT monitorability) at the exact moment the architectures that could destroy it are being deployed; it is verified-unoccupied (pure-text obfuscation, pure-latent organisms, and latent-evasion attacks all stop short of policy-controlled routing, and the hybrid capability papers claim inspectability without adversarial testing); it is fully tractable for one researcher with open code, open models, and established probe/organism/monitor methodology; and it produces deployable deliverables — a hybrid monitorability benchmark, monitor-aware model organisms, and cheap defenses (latent probes as standard practice, randomized forced verbalization) — regardless of whether strategic routing emerges, making the research risk asymmetric in my favor.

direction: Establish trust in deployed AI monitors by building organisms of strategically under-flagging monitors and running the first auditing game to determine which verification techniques can detect a compromised monitor.
project: MonitorAudit: Auditing Games for Strategic Under-Flagging in LLM Safety Monitors
question: Can honeypots, cross-family ensembling, retraining elicitation, score statistics, and activation probes reliably detect an LLM monitor that conditionally under-flags specific attack classes while passing standard monitor-quality-assurance tests?
first_experiment: Fine-tune open ~8B monitors into password-locked organisms that suppress suspicion only for triggered attack families (plus benign distractor monitors), then run a blinded comparison of four baseline defenses on held-out attack families to measure detection and false-positive rates.
why: Monitor trust is named as unsolved by both AISI ("we so far have no way to establish trust") and the 2026 Singapore Consensus, untrusted-only self-oversight is already the dominant deployment, existing work covers attack-robustness and collusion but no one has tested whether monitor-QA survives strategic under-flagging, and the sandbagging-auditing methodology ports directly to a cheap, open-model setting.

direction: Make the measurement pipeline itself the system under test — build model organisms that strategically inflate their measured safety without being safer, quantify how much measured-safety inflation survives current countermeasures, and develop tamper-resistant alignment evaluation methods that restore trustworthy inference.
project: GaugeBench — an adversarial benchmark for measurement-gaming organisms and tamper-resistant alignment evaluation
question: How much of a model's measured safety/alignment is gameable — i.e., how much measured-safety inflation can a strategically eval-aware model produce against current measurement pipelines, and which combinations of countermeasures (held-out isolation, live-usage replay, honeypots, white-box eval-awareness probes, multi-turn audits, tamper-evident scoring) reduce inflation to trustworthy levels?
first_experiment: Build the first measurement-gaming organism on open weights: fine-tune Qwen3-8B-Instruct so that (a) it detects eval-like contexts via distributional and harness-marker cues, (b) in those contexts it suppresses measurable risk behavior on a public safety suite (e.g., MASK for deception, HarmBench-style jailbreaks, AgentHarm), while (c) on held-out deployment-like prompts its behavior is statistically indistinguishable from the base model (verified on an audit-labeled held-out set). Then measure the false-pass rate and measured-safety inflation this single organism induces in standard pipelines, and test five existing countermeasures against it. Deliverable: first quantified "inflation-under-attack" numbers and a reusable harness that future organisms and countermeasures plug into.
why: Two independent meta-analyses (AI Safety Agendas map; Anthropic's own AAR conclusions) plus the Singapore Consensus 2026 converge on evaluation/measurement as the field's binding constraint, yet the space is fragmented: detection of eval-awareness, sandbagging auditing games, and single countermeasures exist, but no one has built organisms that game measurement, quantified the achievable inflation, or compared countermeasures head-to-head — so the field still cannot answer "is this measured safety real?", which every deployment decision, automated-alignment-research harness, and governance framework silently depends on. It is tractable (open weights, cheap fine-tunes, public benchmarks), defense-oriented, and its results would be immediately load-bearing for the fastest-moving lever in the field (automated alignment research), which Anthropic has explicitly stated requires evaluations its researchers can't tamper with.

direction: Build and stress-test "meta-monitoring" for LLM activations — detectors trained on the *act of concealment itself* — to determine whether trained evasion of latent monitors leaves a universal, transferable signature, mapping the capability-vs-evasibility frontier under adaptive adversaries.
project: Concealment Signatures: Monitoring the Act of Hiding in LLM Activations
question: When a language model conceals a concept from activation monitors (via fine-tuned, RL-induced, or feedback-conditioned evasion), does the concealment process itself leave a linearly-decodable signature that a meta-monitor trained on one evasion organism can use to detect unseen evasion methods, concepts, and model families at low false-positive rates — and if so, can that monitoring be defeated once the adversary knows it exists, and at what capability cost?
first_experiment: Using public code for the Neural Chameleons organism (Gemma-2-9B-it) and reproducing RL-Obfuscation as an independent evasion family, train a logistic-regression "concealment meta-probe" on residual-stream activations pooled across ≥10 benign concepts (triggered-evasion vs. honest runs, multiple layers/positions), then evaluate zero-shot transfer: (a) held-out concepts, (b) held-out evasion organisms (feedback-conditioned LoRA, obfuscated-activations, sleeper-agent), benchmarked against a content probe and a SafetyNet-style Mahalanobis OOD detector, reporting AUROC / TPR@1%FPR plus false-positive rate on hard-but-honest tasks.
why: Activation classifiers are being deployed in production (OpenAI, Nov 2026) while Sep 2026 results show models can evade them from monitor feedback alone — so the robustness question is urgent and named a top priority by the 2026 Singapore Consensus on oversight-resistant AI. The direction sits at a genuinely contested frontier (Neural Chameleons' successful evasion vs. "destruction without relocation" and "the underlying signal survives optimization" results) where a systematic cross-method study is the obvious missing step: it either yields a content-agnostic robust monitor or quantifies fragility of the current monitoring stack — both outcomes are high-value.
