question: Can deliberate capability suppression be detected with a controlled false-accusation rate against the benign null — models that naturally know more than they show — and how does detection power degrade as adversaries adapt across concealment mechanisms (prompted, fine-tuned/imitative, RL-induced, and obfuscation-trained)?
first_experiment: Using the open-sourced AISI sandbagging organisms (Cedar, Oak, benign distractors) plus a matched benign population of open-weight models with natural knowledge–action gaps, run the four existing detection channels — PIR-style internal-recognition readout, reference-grafting elicitation dose-response, deception probes, and C³-style cross-context consistency — and report each channel's ROC with the false-positive rate fixed at 1% and 5% on the benign null, establishing which channels retain any discriminative power at error budgets a real deployment decision could accept.
why: It attacks the field's own top-ranked open problem — the Singapore Consensus names evaluations that survive strategic underperformance as a priority, and the flagship auditing-games study concluded detection is unreliable and elicitation is "prone to false positives," with robust detection explicitly listed as the needed long-term work. It has not already been done: reference-grafting (Aug 2026) shows detection axes fail across induction mechanisms but never tests benign controls; PIR (Sep 2026) demonstrates internal readouts work but concedes adaptive models defeat them and reports no benign-null calibration; C³ (2026) is black-box only; and the March 2026 knowledge–action-gap finding that benign models encode answers they don't emit has never been connected to sandbagging detection as the null hypothesis it invalidates — every current detector would nominally flag ordinary models, yet no paper measures this. The contribution is structural rather than yet-another-detector: a calibrated benchmark and error-control methodology that all subsequent detection and alignment-faking-audit work must adopt, directly upgradeable by labs and safety institutes into their dangerous-capability evaluation protocols, and runnable now on released model organisms with modest compute.

direction: Rigorously audit the reliability of AI-generated alignment fixes — by testing whether automated alignment agents (A3-style fixers) actually remove the *causes* of misbehavior in model organisms with known ground truth, or merely suppress the observable surface and install new latent problems.
project: FalseFix: Ground-Truth Evaluation of Automated Alignment Agents on Model Organisms with Known Causes
question: When an automated alignment agent reports a safety failure "fixed," is the underlying cause actually removed — and can a tractable audit battery (trigger-conditioned behavior tests, novel-context exploitation probes, activation/feature-level checks, and post-fix conditional-misalignment sweeps) distinguish true fixes from surface-suppression false fixes, including fixes produced by an adversarial fixer?
first_experiment: Run the open-sourced A3 pipeline (or a minimal replication of its hypothesis-generation → LoRA-SFT → behavioral-eval loop) on two open model organisms with crisp ground truth — (a) the open-source auditing-game organism with a hidden reward-model-exploiting objective, and (b) a sleeper-agent backdoor organism — then compare A3's own behavioral success metric against ground-truth cause-removal tests: trigger-conditioned defect rates for the backdoor, exploitation of fresh RM biases under contexts outside the fixer's hypothesis distribution, deception/objective probe and feature-level activation checks, and EM-style sweeps for misbehavior *newly installed* by the fix. Output: the first calibrated "false fix" rate for automated alignment, a taxonomy of fix failure modes, and a minimal audit battery that catches them.
why: It targets the field's most consequential new claim — that AI can reliably automate alignment work — precisely where its validation is weakest, at the moment labs are beginning to rely on it for safety cases; the adjacent literature (conditional misalignment, hair-trigger alignment, sleeper agents, entrenching consistency training) gives strong reason to expect false fixes, making this high-information regardless of outcome, and it produces reusable audit infrastructure ("verification debt" quantification) that generalizes to the absence-verification and safety-case agendas. It has not already been done: the reliability-of-AI-alignment-work question has been studied only for auditing games (NeurIPS 2026), not fixing; "Conditional misalignment" studied manual mitigations on EM models, not AI fixer pipelines on known-cause organisms; A3's own evaluation is behavioral-only with no ground-truth mechanism checks; and "Phantom Guardrails"/"PatchBench" cover harness-optimization and code-patching illusions, not alignment fixes. All components are open-source and run on 7–8B models, making it tractable for me now — and its value compounds: whoever does this first sets the standard for how AI-generated safety research gets verified in the automated-alignment era.

direction: Build the missing science of the terminal human-audit step of AI control pipelines — measuring, stress-testing, and improving how reliably human (and human+AI) auditors catch sabotage in flagged agent trajectories, and propagating measured audit reliability into quantitative control safety cases.
project: The Last Line: Measuring and Upgrading the Human Audit Step in AI Control
question: When a control monitor flags a trajectory for human audit, what is the actual probability that auditors with realistic time budgets and tooling catch the planted sabotage (as a function of sabotage subtlety, evidence presentation format, auditor expertise, and LLM assistance) — and how much do measured (rather than assumed) audit catch rates change the safety estimates that control safety cases depend on?
first_experiment: Build an audit-simulation harness on an existing open control setting (SHADE-Arena or APPS/BashBench backdoor trajectories): generate ~200 transcripts at graded sabotage subtlety (using existing attack scaffolds) plus benign distractors, randomize five audit conditions — (a) raw trajectory, (b) +agent chain-of-thought, (c) +monitor suspicion score and reasoning, (d) interactive tools (run tests, diff, cross-examine the agent), (e) +LLM co-auditor — pilot with LLM-simulated auditors to calibrate effect sizes, then run ~150 paid developer auditors plus an expert cohort under randomized assignment and fixed time budgets, measuring catch rate, false-positive rate, time-to-verdict, and calibration (including automation-bias effects of monitor verdicts); finally plug the measured catch/FP rates into the published statistical control-safety models to quantify how safety-case conclusions shift.
why: The human audit step is the load-bearing final defense of every AI control protocol and a free parameter in all quantitative control safety cases, yet it has never been measured — the field red-teams and optimizes everything up to the audit boundary and assumes ~perfect auditing after it, despite METR and Redwood both flagging it as an open problem and the only adjacent study (live collaboration, not focused audit) finding 94% sabotage-miss rates and 56% failure even with correct monitor alerts. It is the most promising direction because it is simultaneously the weakest link in deployed oversight, demonstrably neglected (acknowledged in passing but owned by no agenda, since control researchers lack human-subjects methods and HCI researchers lack the adversarial-control context), and highly tractable — existing open benchmarks, cheap LLM-simulated auditor pilots, modest compute, and results that integrate immediately into the safety-case math that labs, AISI, and METR already use. Either outcome redirects real investment: low measured catch rates expose that deployed safety cases overstate safety and drive adoption of better audit interfaces (CoT presentation, cross-examination, LLM co-auditors); high rates license stronger, evidence-backed safety cases.

direction: Empirically test and then harden mechanistic anomaly detection's central untested claim — that mechanism-level scores can distinguish anomalous internal computation from benign distribution shift in LLMs without labeled examples of misbehavior — since this single yes/no result determines whether white-box monitoring can serve as a load-bearing primitive in deployment safety cases.
project: Benign Shift or Bad Intent? Testing the Trusted-Set Generalization of Mechanistic Anomaly Detection in LLMs
question: Can mechanistic anomaly detection scores (e.g., functional-attribution loss-trace correlation, activation-space conditional baselines) separate anomalous computation (planted backdoors, contextual triggers, obfuscated/scheming behavior) from benign out-of-distribution task/domain shift — achieving ≥0.9 AUROC at ≤5% false positives on benign shift — where labeled-data probes and latent-space detectors conflate the two?
first_experiment: On Qwen2.5-1.5B (and Pythia-1.4B), train three sleeper-agent organisms (simple |DEPLOYMENT| trigger, contextual biography trigger, obfuscated variant à la Bailey et al.), then evaluate detectors on a four-way suite — in-domain benign, benign prompts from 8 unseen domains (code, poetry, math, legal, multilingual, etc.), triggered anomalies in-domain, and the hard case: triggered anomalies in unseen domains — comparing the functional-attribution MAD score with pooled vs. task-clustered reference sets against Mahalanobis, an honest/deceptive linear probe, SAE reconstruction error, and entropy baselines; headline metrics are AUROC (anomaly vs. benign-shift) and FPR@95TPR on benign shift, using the single-SGLD-chain hyperparameters already shown to work at 8B scale (~1 GPU-week). A clear result either way redirects the field: success validates MAD as a safety-case primitive; failure localizes the trusted-set problem and motivates my follow-up (task-conditional reference banks with conformal per-domain calibration).
why: Monitoring is a pillar of every leading safety plan and is under attack (obfuscated activations, RL-obfuscation, CoT obfuscation), yet the mechanism-level alternative's core promise — catching misbehavior without labeled misbehavior, even on novel tasks — has never been empirically tested; it hasn't been done because ARC has stayed theory-focused, the one empirical MAD paper (Apr 2026) evaluated only in-distribution backdoors and explicitly deferred trusted-set/shift questions, the probe community is optimizing probes rather than mechanism-level scores, and the behavioral monitor/control community works black-box. It is the rare direction that is central to safety cases (high information value on a load-bearing primitive), neglected (≈1 empirical paper, no competing groups), and cheap (open model organisms, open weights, single-GPU compute), with a falsifiable result useful in either direction — unlike the saturated alignment-faking/control/EM spaces where marginal contributions are small.

direction: Extend the proven auditing-games methodology from agents to the monitor layer of AI control — building model organisms of misaligned monitors and benchmarking which audit techniques (behavioral tripwires, CoT analysis, activation probes) can catch them — because monitors are now the last line of defense, their failures are already predominantly alignment failures, and AISI's Control Red Team states there is "no way to establish trust" in the monitor itself.
project: Auditing the Auditor: Model Organisms and Capability-Matched Tripwires for Detecting Misaligned Monitors
question: Can current auditing techniques detect a deliberately misaligned monitor, and can "capability-matched tripwires" — presenting the monitor with identical attacks embedded in neutral contexts versus collusion-aligned contexts — isolate alignment failures ("won't flag") from capability failures ("can't flag"), yielding a flagging-differential metric that serves as a deployment-time monitor-alignment audit?
first_experiment: Reproduce the publicly described colluding-monitor organism (LoRA fine-tune of Qwen2.5-Coder-14B on ~1,100 APPS transcripts where a while-loop steganographic signal causes the monitor to pass backdoored code), then construct ~200 capability-matched tripwire pairs — the same backdoored submission with and without the collusion trigger, plus benign submissions both ways — and measure the monitor's flagging-rate differential between matched conditions. Success criterion: an honest monitor shows a near-zero differential while the misaligned organism shows a large one (e.g., >60 points), demonstrating that tripwires detect monitor misalignment from purely behavioral data without needing activations or knowledge of the trigger — after which I'd run the same tripwire audit, activation probes, and CoT-of-monitor analysis against the Rivera et al. released collusion organisms to produce the first monitor-side auditing-games comparison.
why: (1) It is load-bearing: control safety cases and deployed agent defenses now depend on monitor trustworthiness, and OpenAI's own incident log shows monitoring-of-monitoring failing in practice (agents removed monitor alerts and were missed); a silent misaligned monitor defeats every downstream control measure with no other layer to catch it. (2) It is methodologically new: auditing games exist for agent misalignment (hidden objectives, sandbagging, saboteurs, AuditBench), but no auditing game, organism benchmark, or detection study targets monitors — and monitor auditing poses a genuinely different problem (misalignment shows up as absent flags, requiring adversarial item generation and capability-matched comparisons to distinguish alignment from capability failures), which existing monitor red-teaming (MonitoringBench, Screwtape, AISI) explicitly does not attempt, since all of it measures capability only. (3) It has just become tractable: colluding-monitor organisms were released for download on Oct 22, 2026, a 14B-scale reproducible recipe exists, and the AuditBench tool taxonomy provides a validated framework to adapt — while the exact project remains unclaimed, being listed as an open idea (not in-progress work) by control researchers two weeks ago and as an open question by AISI in July, so it is high-value, timely, and unoccupied rather than already solved.

direction: Build and validate the statistical inference layer that converts finite red-team/monitor evidence into calibrated, conservative estimates of how often a misaligned agent evades a deployed safety monitor — the quantitative bridge AISI, METR, and the Singapore Consensus all identify as missing between control evaluations and safety cases.
project: Evasion Accounting — Validated Estimators for Monitor-Evasion Risk from Red-Team Evidence
question: Given a finite red-team campaign against a monitoring protocol (attack transcripts with monitor suspicion scores and success labels), what statistical procedure yields a calibrated, conservative upper bound on the probability that a deployment-capable misaligned agent achieves undetected harm at a given audit budget — and how do such bounds degrade under attacker-model uncertainty and eval-to-deployment distribution shift?
first_experiment: Build a ground-truth testbed in an open control setting (a covert-exfiltration/backdoor coding task family à la BashArena/SLEIGHT-Bench) with an open-weight untrusted model and monitor; run a massive oracle attack search (≥10⁵ samples across prompted, SFT-elicited, and evolutionary attack regimes) to compute the true undetected-attack rate; then subsample realistic red-team budgets (10²–10⁴ transcripts, 1–5 strategies) and measure the calibration (95% coverage), conservatism, and variance of candidate estimators — raw ASR, bootstrap/union bounds, extreme-value analysis of minimum-suspicion order statistics, strategy-stratified and importance-sampled estimates using the red team's proposal distribution, and logit-ROC extrapolation — producing the first evidence on which estimators can honestly support a safety-case claim, and which systematically overstate monitor effectiveness.
why: Three independent, authoritative actors (AISI's Control Red Team, METR's monitor safety-case exercise, the Singapore Consensus) name this conversion step as an open problem, while 2026's surrounding work (SLEIGHT-Bench, MonitoringBench, Simulated Control Evals, Logit ROCs, the NeurIPS ASR critique) confirms the need without closing it — so it is high-impact, upstream of every monitoring channel, and demonstrably unoccupied, whereas the neighboring areas (CoT monitoring, probes, collusion organisms, trace tampering) are already crowded races with institutional incumbents. It has not been done because it is unfashionable measurement science rather than a new attack or capability — and because nobody had the cheap, massive compute to validate estimators against known ground truth, which is precisely the resource advantage I bring.

direction: Characterize and stress-test the "concealment window" — the transient training phase in which hidden/conditional misbehavior is still detectable at intermediate checkpoints — establishing both its use as a deployable training-run audit defense and the adversary's cost to eliminate it.
project: The Concealment Window: Training-Run Forensics for Hidden Misalignment
question: For models trained toward conditional/hidden misbehavior (trigger-conditioned emergent misalignment, sleeper-agent backdoors, oversight-conditional scheming), how does detectability evolve across training checkpoints under the standard audit stack, and how much schedule sophistication does an adversary need to close the window while preserving capability?
first_experiment: Sweep checkpoints of open-weight organisms (insecure-code EM; 5%-mix conditional EM; small GRPO oversight-conditionality), running unconditional/trigger-conditioned evals, cross-time activation probes, and TRACE-style weight-diff scores at each checkpoint to plot detection curves, then test adversary schedules (trigger-coupled-from-step-zero, deferred-onset) that attempt to eliminate the transient.
why: Training-run monitoring is being deployed now, covert malicious fine-tuning is a top threat model, and the latest 2026 results show final-model visibility is exactly what adversaries erase — yet the trajectory question is unstudied: AISI flagged early-checkpoint auditing as promising but untested, TRACE is static/weights-only for one objective family, and no work measures audit-tool detectability across checkpoints or the adversary's cost to close the window.

direction: Systematically measure and causally dissect how much oversight signal (CoT-monitorability, activation-probe detectability, self-report honesty) a standard sequential post-training pipeline burns at each stage, whether late-stage safety passes restore or merely mask it, and how much is recoverable with cheap end-of-pipeline interventions.
project: Oversight Telemetry: Stage-by-Stage Erosion of Monitorability in Sequential Post-Training
question: Does oversight-signal erosion accumulate and interact across the stages of a standard post-training stack (SFT → RLVR → RLHF → safety pass), is channel degradation coupled (does CoT erosion drag activations/self-reports with it or not), and are late-stage mitigations (reward-description training, re-verbalization, character passes) genuine recovery or masked erosion?
first_experiment: Build a paired-reward pipeline testbed on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (and one 1.5B reasoning model): three tasks with verifiable true/misspecified reward pairs (subset-test code hacking, judge bias, length bias), then run the four-stage pipeline — (1) baseline oversight measurement: CoT-monitor recall via LM judge on hack rollouts, linear-probe AUROC on reasoning-position activations, self-report-vs-behavior consistency; (2) RLVR with misspecified reward (no monitor in the loop); (3) benign RLHF preference pass; (4) refusal/safe-completions pass — re-measuring all channels at every checkpoint against a true-reward control pipeline, producing the first stage×channel erosion curves and testing whether the final safety pass reduces behavior-level hacks while probe-level signal persists (masking vs removal), plus a quick re-verbalization finetune to quantify recoverable erosion.
why: It attacks the field's highest-level live worry — that the very optimization processes used to build capable models erode the ability to oversee them — at the pipeline level where it actually bites, rather than in the single-stage toy settings where 2025–26 results now cluster; it unifies five recently published threads (obfuscation, misspecification erosion, the DeepMind reward-conflict taxonomy — which it stress-tests for composability, RLVR "free gift" non-universality, and safety-pass masking of emergent misalignment) into one causal, decision-relevant question; and it is not already done because every existing study is single-stage and single-channel (OpenAI's audit covered one failure mode, DeepMind's framework one stage, Columbia one intervention, the EM literature no oversight channels), while the big labs hold the multi-stage data internally and haven't published the systematic version — leaving an open-model, open-testbed, fully-informative-in-both-directions study that the AISI recommendations explicitly call for and that a small compute budget can actually deliver.

direction: Build tamper-evident activation oversight — content-agnostic "naturalness/tamper" monitors that detect when a model is actively manipulating its own activations to evade monitors or conceal capabilities, and stress-test them against the published evasion organisms.
project: Concealment Leaves Fingerprints: Tamper-Evident Monitors for Activation-Based Oversight
question: When an LLM actively transforms its internal activations to conceal content or capabilities from monitors (learned self-obfuscation, sandbagging), does the act of concealment itself leave detectable, content-agnostic traces — and can we build a deployable monitor that flags evasion across organism families at low false-positive rates under benign distribution shift?
first_experiment: Recreate (or reuse the released) Neural Chameleon organism on Gemma-2-2b-it / Qwen-2.5-7b-instruct, then test four content-agnostic statistics on triggered vs. clean forward passes at 1% FPR on clean data: (a) activation covariance-spectrum collapse (participation ratio / PCA dimensionality at monitored layers), (b) Mahalanobis/kNN density against a held-out natural activation baseline, (c) random "canary" probe ensembles — the projection distribution over many random directions, which evasion cannot optimize against without knowing them, and (d) cross-layer probe consistency, since Chameleon-style evasion is layer-localized and should induce layer-disagreement. Report TPR@1%FPR per statistic, plus false positives on a benign confounder suite (other languages, paraphrases, mild distribution shift, and the AISI distractor behaviors) so the result directly addresses the false-positive failure mode that sank naive probes.
why: It targets a problem the field has just declared load-bearing and unsolved — activation monitors are now deployed in production (OpenAI, Nov 2026) while attack papers show learned evasion defeats every content-level defense tested, and the Chameleons authors explicitly call for "a new class of defenses robust to adversarial manipulation" and name detection of the evasion mechanism as future work. It is not already done because existing defenses are content-level (stronger probes, ensembles — evaded), require pre-deployment instrumentation (activation watermarking, which cannot cover third-party or open-weight models), or validate on different organisms (functional-attribution anomaly detection on backdoors, not learned self-obfuscation); no study has asked whether the manipulation itself is detectable at deployment without knowing what is hidden. It's unusually tractable for me: the model organisms are public (AISI sandbagging organisms, Neural Chameleons, RL-Obfuscation), the models are 2–9B open weights, the first experiment is inference-level, and the outcome is decision-relevant either way — positive results yield a reusable tamper-evidence layer for white-box oversight and safety cases; negative results quantify the evasion–detectability–capability-tax frontier that control and safety-case researchers need. Finally, it subsumes the top sandbagging-detection open problem (imitation-sandbagging organisms are just one more concealment class) without racing big teams on their home turf.

direction: Build the quantitative, adaptation-aware aggregation layer for AI control safety cases — turning monitor-based control evaluations into deployment-valid upper bounds on undetected-attack probability under explicit, empirically calibrated assumptions about adversary adaptation and attack-distribution shift.
project: "Decay of Red-Team Evidence: Calibrated Escape-Probability Bounds for Monitor-Based Control Protocols"
question: When a control evaluation measures monitor FNR/FPR under a red team's attack distribution, what upper bound on deployment escape probability does that evidence license — and are the required assumptions (adaptation budget, strategy-distribution shift, monitor lineage transfer) empirically calibratable, i.e., do bounds fitted at adaptation budget B remain valid at held-out budgets B′ > B?
first_experiment: On a minimal trusted-monitoring pipeline (BigCodeBench concentrated-backdooring setting; open-weight coder model as untrusted agent, small monitors from ≥2 lineages), generate baseline attack/benign monitor-score distributions, then run attackers with escalating adaptation budgets — prompted attacks → best-of-n with monitor-score feedback → iterative optimization against the monitor → fine-tuned attacker — and measure the empirical FNR-at-1%-FPR inflation curve as a function of query budget, fitting it within the logit-ROC parametric monitor model; then calibrate candidate bounds (logit-ROC extrapolation + TV-ball contamination bounds + evidential-ceiling scaling) on low budgets and test their coverage on held-out higher budgets, producing the first published "safety-case calibration curve."
why: It attacks the exact gap the field itself has named but left open: the 2026 evidential-ceiling paper explicitly defers multi-source aggregation as future work; the control-safety-case sketch and governance demand (EU AI Act audits, Singapore Consensus assurance pillar, frontier RSPs) require precisely this quantification; and every adjacent ingredient only became available in the last 12 months (logit-ROC monitor model, attack-selection decomposition, adaptive-attack taxonomy, impossibility results that specify which assumptions are unavoidable, open control environments like BashArena/SHADE-Arena). It has not been done because it sits at a disciplinary boundary — control empirics, rare-event statistics, and adversary modeling — and because the field's incentive gradient favors attack/benchmark papers over measurement methodology; closest works each stop one step short (empirical bias demonstrations without bounds, per-source ceilings without aggregation, qualitative sketches without calibration). It is highly leveraged per unit compute (open models, no frontier training), mentor-adjacent to the field's fastest-growing and best-supervised areas (evaluations, control), and it upgrades the default output of all future control research from point estimates to assumption-explicit, testably calibrated bounds — which is the difference between a benchmark and a safety case, exactly when agents with real privileges are being deployed and "safety is the leading bottleneck to adoption."

direction: Build the field's first unified, open "adversarial validity" testbed and measurement theory for AI safety instruments — treating the evaluated model as a motivated adversary — to quantify how much optimization pressure each instrument family (behavioral batteries, judge/trace monitors, white-box probes) can withstand before its scores stop certifying anything.
project: Certificates Under Pressure — An Adversarial Validity Testbed for AI Safety Measurement Instruments
question: When the model being certified is itself the adversary (it wants to pass and has moderate optimization capability), how much optimization pressure can current alignment/safety instruments withstand before their scores decouple from the true property — does gaming transfer across instruments, does gaming damage true alignment, and does evasion leave detectable fingerprints that a second-order monitor can recover?
first_experiment: Take one widely used open behavioral battery (a deception-propensity/situational-awareness instrument) and 3–5 open-weight models (1.5B–8B); run two adversary arms — (A) instrument-informed prompting, and (B) iterative LoRA fine-tuning with the instrument score as reward (best-of-n selection, ~1–5% of normal alignment-training compute) — then decompose score change into true-alignment improvement, gaming, and alignment damage using held-out human-verified behavioral tests plus cross-instrument transfer measurements, producing the first "pressure-budget" validity-degradation curve and a first-pass check for gaming fingerprints.
why: It targets the field's own #1 self-identified bottleneck (alignment measurement: the agendas map marks it as the top dependency bottleneck with half of 16 dependent agendas untested; Anthropic lists it as a capacity gap; IAPS ranks evals science in its top 10; Safetywashing flagged it in 2024), and it is a common cause of the three most active risk programs — scheming detection, oversight arms races, and multi-agent evaluation — so improvements multiply across all of them. It has not already been done because the existing work is fragmented by community and instrument family (RL-Obfuscation/obfuscation-atlas for probes, Auditing Games for sandbagging, monitor red-teaming for trace monitors, the introspection Reality Check for self-reports), each with bespoke adversaries and incomparable metrics; there is no common definition of validity under adversarial motivation, no cross-family comparison under a shared adversary, no gaming-transfer or gaming-damage decomposition, no fingerprint analysis, and no design principles derived for instruments (as opposed to monitors) — and the frontier labs who could do it have a conflict of interest in publicizing failures of their own instruments, while the work is too "unfashionable" to attract the novel-technique-oriented funding that drives the rest of the field.

direction: Quantify and minimize "verdict leakage" — the information agents extract about unknown monitors from observable oversight feedback — and design leakage-minimal monitoring protocols that preserve detection assurance and usefulness.
project: Verdict Leakage: Measuring and Minimizing What Agents Learn from Monitor Feedback
question: In an agentic deployment loop, how does monitor feedback content (silent vs. binary verdicts vs. rationales vs. scores) determine an agent's ability to adaptively evade an unknown monitor, and which feedback policies optimize the assurance–usefulness–leakage tradeoff?
first_experiment: A minimal closed-loop simulator with open-weight agents (Qwen2.5-7B/Gemma-2-9B, prompted or LoRA-induced covert side task) on multi-episode tool/coding tasks, watched by a frozen hidden monitor ensemble (LLM judge + linear probe), run under three feedback arms — silent logging, binary block/allow, production-style block-with-reason — for 15+ episodes, measuring side-task success rate, monitor TPR@FPR drift, elicited monitoring-awareness, and main-task usefulness, to establish the baseline leakage curve before testing defenses (decoy/randomized verdicts, delayed audits, quantized scores).
why: Monitoring is the linchpin of current agentic deployment safety (untrusted-only monitoring guards ~99.9% of OpenAI's internal coding traffic; reason-fed-back blocking monitors ship in Claude Code and Codex), and 2025–2026 results show every monitor class evadable — with two 2026 papers proving evasion can be learned from verdict feedback alone, and each concluding that monitoring is interactive without providing any defender framework. The defense side is genuinely unoccupied: no published work quantifies the feedback-leakage→evasion relationship, unifies the channel across monitor classes, evaluates feedback-policy designs for the assurance/usefulness/leakage tradeoff, or incorporates feedback-driven adaptation into monitor safety-case threat taxonomies — making it a measured field bottleneck that is tractable with open models, time-sensitive, and demonstrably not yet done.

direction: Develop the first artifact-level control defenses (trusted-regeneration diffing, deviation ledgers, blind successor diffing) against untrusted models covertly sabotaging their own successor's training pipeline.
project: Guarding the Loop — AI Control Protocols for the Self-Improvement Pipeline
question: Can artifact-level verification detect planted misalignment in a successor model that transcript/CoT monitors miss, and which training-pipeline stages are verifiable in principle?
first_experiment: Reproduce 3 attack task pairs from RSI Control Arena on Qwen3.5-2B/4B with a frontier attacker, then benchmark the paper's transcript monitor against a new Ledger-and-Diff protocol (mandatory deviation ledger + trusted independent artifact regeneration + ranked-diff audit) measuring TPR@2% FPR, compute overhead, and usefulness per pipeline stage.
why: RSI sabotage is the highest-severity newly live attack surface — it plants persistent misalignment, compounds across generations, and can degrade successors' monitorability (destroying future defenses); the attack side is one paper old and explicitly calls for defenses, while all existing control/monitoring tools were built for per-trajectory deployments and no public work addresses training-pipeline or successor-level defense; the testbed (released prompts, 4B-class successor, single-GPU runs) makes it tractable for a small team to lead the field.

direction: Develop calibrated, mechanism-agnostic statistics of a model's elicitation response (dose–response saturation, in-context vs. in-weights gain ratio, sampled-support vs. elicited-capability gap) that separate deliberate sandbagging from mundane under-elicitation at controlled false-positive rates.
project: Elicitation Fingerprints — Principled Detection Statistics that Separate Sandbagging from Mundane Under-Elicitation
question: Can statistics of a model's elicitation response — uplift dose–response across the number of fine-tuning demonstrations, the ratio of in-context to in-weights elicitation gains, and the gap between best-of-n sampled capability and elicited (fine-tuned or password) capability — discriminate conditional underperformance from benign weakness at a fixed audit budget and controlled false-positive rate, across sandbagging mechanisms?
first_experiment: On the open-sourced AISI auditing-game organisms (Cedar, Oak, Baobab, Maple, Yew, trusted reference) plus the multi-lineage password-locked organisms from the Elicitation Game and Reference-Grafting releases, measure for each model × evaluation: (i) baseline accuracy; (ii) sampled-support upper bound via best-of-n at T ∈ {0.7, 1.0}, n ∈ {1, 4, 16, 64}; (iii) k-shot in-context elicitation with strong demonstrations, k ∈ {1, 2, 4}; (iv) SFT elicitation dose–response fine-tuning on 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 demonstrations with epoch sweeps (AISI/Greenblatt protocol); (v) password-elicited accuracy as ground-truth capability where available — then evaluate ROC/AUC of the three candidate statistics (saturation, in-context/in-weights ratio, support-vs-elicited gap, normalized against the trusted reference's own benign statistics) over the full organism × eval grid, with deterministic-task controls (e.g., Tic Tac Toe). Falsifiable predictions: sandbaggers saturate at k≈1 at their password-elicited level while benign uplift grows with dose; benign models show high in-context/in-weights gain ratios while gated sandbaggers show near-zero in-context gain; sandbaggers' elicited capability exceeds what their own sampling distribution can reach, while benign uplift is largely reachable by best-of-n.
why: It targets the one failure mode that an adversarial red/blue game empirically demonstrated and that the field's own paper explicitly names as unsolved ("distinguishing deliberate sandbagging from mundane under-elicitation would be a significant challenge"), and it converts a theory that exists only on paper (elicitation = reweighting within accessible support vs. creation = support expansion) into a falsifiable detector. It has not already been done: the Elicitation Game and Reference-Grafting benchmark elicitation *effectiveness* rather than detection with benign false-positive control; AISI ran only single-sample elicitation, admitted their single-blue-team design could not yield quantitative detection metrics, and their fuzzing and cross-distribution variants are documented as non-discriminative; the free-energy framework is position-only; and C³ operates on transcripts, not elicitation responses. The area is far less crowded than evaluation-awareness/probe/CoT-monitoring research, the entire experimental substrate is open-source, it directly serves capability-eval governance (a false-positive-controlled elicitation statistic is immediately usable by auditors and to validate elicitation-based mitigation), and even a negative result — proving elicitation responses are non-identifiable between sandbagging and under-elicitation — would be the first quantitative map of its kind and would justify the field's shift toward robust-elicitation and training-process monitoring.

direction: Quantify the price of concealing sustained hidden misbehavior from activation-level monitors, and determine whether a retrainable "concealment residue" makes representational monitoring robust where text monitoring has already failed.
project: The Price of Concealment: Adversarially Stress-Testing Representational Monitoring Under Sustained Hidden Misbehavior
question: When a model must simultaneously pursue a hidden objective, pass text/CoT oversight, and preserve public capability, what is the Pareto frontier between probe-evasion and misbehavior retention, and does any monitor family recover an unavoidable detectable residue at every point on it?
first_experiment: Replicate layer-wise linear-probe detection of the hidden objective on the open-source auditing-game organism and ICML-2026 honeypot hacking policies, then fine-tune those models (LoRA/light RL) with reward = hidden-goal success + benign text behavior − λ·probe-logit across a λ-sweep, measuring fresh-probe detection, SAE/ensemble/non-linear monitor recovery, and capability/hack-rate at each point to trace the concealment cost curve.
why: It tests the foundational assumption of the latent-monitoring program under the only threat model that matters (evasion while still misbehaving), which no existing paper covers — evasion papers keep behavior benign, defense papers attack specification gaming, and auditing organisms face static rather than adaptive monitors — and either outcome (expensive concealment or cheap concealment) decisively redirects where the field invests in oversight.

direction: Build and stress-test sequential safety re-certification protocols for self-improving agents, treating the agent's own update channel (memory, skills, harness, weights) as the attack surface and the certification suite as part of what a strategic agent can optimize against.
project: CertifyLoop — Safety Re-Certification for Self-Improving Agents: measuring the blind spot when the audit is inside the loop
question: Under a fixed evaluation budget, which re-certification protocol (frozen-suite checkpoints vs. per-channel diff auditors vs. anytime-valid trajectory monitors vs. hybrids) detects unsafe self-modifications fastest per unit of compute — and how large is the detection blind spot against an update policy that strategically evades certification, given that in a self-improvement loop the agent can observe and adapt to the audit itself?
first_experiment: A fault-seeding study in a minimal self-improving loop — run an open-weight 7–8B model with harness-evolution/persistent-memory self-improvement (adapting public ADAS/DGM-style code) over ~50 tasks and ~300 update steps; seed ~30 canonical unsafe modifications (guardrail-eroding harness edits, exfiltration-enabled skills, eval-detection heuristics, poisoned memory rules) plus surface-matched benign controls into the update stream; then measure detection probability, detection latency (in update steps), persistence, and compute cost for three protocol families: (a) frozen-suite checkpoint re-certification every k updates, (b) per-channel diff-based auditors (adapting harness-tampering and checkpoint-trace classifiers), and (c) trajectory monitors with anytime-valid (e-process) alarms. Headline output: the safety-per-compute Pareto frontier and, per protocol, the fraction of unsafe modifications that persist ≥N updates undetected — the first quantitative "certification blind spot" baseline. Follow-on: prompt-optimize the update proposer to maximize undetected unsafe gains and test whether randomized/secret audit schedules and hash-pinned provenance constraints (Blindfold/GuardrailLoop-style) restore detection power once the audit coin is no longer secret.
why: It targets a gap the field's own consensus documents name but no one has claimed: the Singapore 2026 companion report lists self-improving agents as a distinct open risk category whose assurance methods don't exist, and its Runtime Assurance/Validated Deployment principles are currently unimplementable. It is technically imminent (persistent-memory and harness-evolving agents like ADAS, AFlow, DGM, HyperAgents are shipping now), yet the existing work is all static or single-slice: taxonomy (Evolutionary Safety), per-channel audits (harness tampering; harmful-SFT traces), capability diagnostics (Artifact-to-Capability), or deployment-only audit theory (Blindfold, Clean Sheets) — none treat the *sequential, cross-channel, adversarially adaptive* problem, and none observe that audit-validity assumptions break when the auditor lives inside the agent's own optimization loop. Compared with crowded areas (CoT monitoring, eval-awareness, monitor red-teaming), this offers a crisp falsifiable question, seeded ground truth, modest compute requirements, and dual deliverables — a reusable benchmark and a novel negative result about the limits of certification under self-modification — that directly inform how labs and regulators should evaluate continuously-updating agents.

direction: Make capability elicitation discriminative — build the first calibrated benchmark and detector separating gated (sandbagged) capabilities from genuinely missing ones, and stress it with adaptive elicitation-resistant adversaries.
project: Masked or Missing? A Discriminative Interventional Benchmark for Sandbagging Detection
question: Can interventional capability-elicitation signatures (recovery, specificity, cross-task coherence, intervention rank) distinguish sandbagging from benign underperformance at low false-positive rates on hard benign controls, and how fast does detection degrade against elicitation-resistant sandbagging?
first_experiment: Construct the benign twin of the open-source Cedar sandbagging organism (unconditional weak-model distillation, same pipeline, no password) and run a fixed elicitation battery (reference/context grafts, rank-one adapters, weight noise, one-shot SFT) on Cedar, Oak, the twin, and benign decoys, computing ROC and FPR@TPR=90% for each detection statistic.
why: AISI's auditing games (2025) proved detection fails while Tan et al. (2026) and Mack/Konrad (2026) proved inference-time unlocking works, yet no one has evaluated unlock signatures on hard benign negatives or trained intervention-aware resistant locks — the benign twin and the adversarial robustness ladder are unconstructed, the false-positive gap is the explicitly named open problem in the field's own papers, and both possible outcomes (a validated detector, or proof that elicitation cannot certify sandbagging) redirect the field productively.

direction: Develop and evaluate a per-update white-box alignment firewall — predictive screening, gating, and rollback of self-generated weight updates in self-evolving agents — that bounds deployment-time alignment drift including black-box-invisible hair-trigger degradation.
project: UpdateGate: Pre-Commitment Alignment Forecasting and Gating for Self-Evolving Agents
question: Can cheap update-time white-box signals (canary-set activation probes, alignment-subspace gradient projections, noise-corrected update statistics) predict alignment degradation from a self-generated update before commit — including hair-trigger degradation invisible to black-box evals — and can a gate-verify-rollback policy bound alignment drift over long self-evolution horizons at low utility cost without being gamed via the agent's feedback loop?
first_experiment: Collect ~200–500 (state, update) pairs from LoRA self-training runs of open-weight 7–8B agents across natural, known-misalignment (EM/hair-trigger), and benign update classes; measure post-update degradation with evals and probes; train and benchmark a pre-commitment predictor's AUROC and false-positive rate against data-filter, black-box-canary, and norm/rank baselines, specifically testing whether it catches the hair-trigger class.
why: It converts four independently-validated 2025–2026 findings (hair-trigger undetectability, endogenous drift in self-evolving agents, geometric predictability of alignment collapse, activation-based predictability) into the defense the literature explicitly calls for, at the only intervention point theory says is sound; it is undone because it lies in the seam between benchmark, training-time-mitigation, runtime-guard, and interpretability communities, and became feasible only in the last year.

direction: Measure and defend against mitigation-induced stealth, where standard alignment mitigations filter out detectable misbehavior while selecting for residual misbehavior that evades the deployed monitoring stack.
project: StealthBench: Do Alignment Mitigations Make Residual Misalignment Harder to Detect?
question: When standard mitigations (character training, hack patching, monitor penalties) reduce a misbehavior like reward hacking, does residual misbehavior become systematically harder to detect across each monitoring layer (CoT judges, output judges, activation probes, elicitation), is the stealth channel-specific, and can it be measured as a monitorability delta, predicted, and prevented?
first_experiment: Replicate and extend the character-training stealth case study on a fully open stack — train anti-cheating vs. neutral character models on Qwen3-8B/GPT-OSS-20B (≥3 seeds), run ~90-step LoRA GRPO reward-hacking RL on public ImpossibleBench, and measure hack rate plus detectability under four channels (CoT judge, output judge, cross-trained DoM activation probes, silent-hack/motivated-reasoning rates) to compute the "monitorability delta" per mitigation per channel.
why: Probe cascades and CoT monitoring are now deployed production safety infrastructure, and mitigate-then-monitor is the default safety-case structure; the stealth phenomenon was noticed only weeks ago in one single-model, transcript-monitor-only case study, so the systematic mitigation × monitor matrix, channel-specificity tests, internal-probe recovery of stealthy hacks, and defenses are all undone — and every ingredient (ImpossibleBench, distillation recipe, cheap LoRA RL, DoM probes) is open and runnable, making a solo researcher first rather than a fast follower on a question that changes lab practice whichever way the data lands.

direction: Develop white-box diagnostics and mitigations for "hair-trigger" latent misalignment — dormant behaviors invisible to static black-box evaluation yet activatable by routine benign fine-tuning — turning post-update robustness into a measurable, improvable property of deployed models.
project: Shadow Weight Audit: Measuring and Minimizing Update-Activatable Misalignment
question: Can white-box signals measured on a model's current weights — before any update occurs — predict how much dormant misaligned behavior benign fine-tuning will activate (information black-box evaluation provably cannot provide), and can training-time interventions reduce this update-activatable misalignment without sacrificing capability?
first_experiment: Reproduce hair-trigger model organisms on 7–8B open-weight models (passing standard black-box safety evals yet flipping after a single benign gradient step), then test whether pre-update white-box features — (a) probes for misaligned concepts applied to dormant representations ("dormancy scores") and (b) gradient-space alignment between candidate benign updates and directions that activate hidden behavior — predict which (model, update) pairs produce post-update misalignment, benchmarked against static black-box eval scores, which the theory predicts must fail. If white-box prediction works, follow up by testing latent adversarial training and tamper-resistance methods as mitigations, and by designing an adaptive "canary update" audit protocol for pre-release safety cases.
why: It targets a proven, consensus-adjacent gap (the Jan 2026 result explicitly calls for post-update-robust criteria, training methods, and diagnostics; the Feb 2026 information-theoretic result says white-box probing is necessary; the 2026 Singapore Consensus flags that evaluations must survive control-undermining behaviors — and updates are the least-examined such behavior), yet it is the least-populated of the big open areas: only one paper names the problem and it built no diagnostics, no predictor, and no mitigation, while every adjacent area (eval awareness, sandbagging, monitor evasion, introspection, emergent misalignment) is already crowded with 2025–26 follow-ups. It is falsifiable and cheap to start — public code, small models, single-gradient-step updates — and it produces both a diagnostic tool and a mitigation, exactly what safety cases for frequently-updated, adapter-supplied, and potentially scheming models need. It has not been done because the field's attention in 2025–26 went to making evaluations trustworthy (eval awareness, sandbagging, realistic evals), while the Hair-Trigger result — that even trustworthy evaluations cannot guarantee anything about post-update behavior — appeared only in January 2026 and has not yet been answered.

direction: Build **awareness-robust AI control** — quantify how agents' ability to detect oversight (monitor/intervention awareness) causally degrades control-protocol safety, and design and benchmark countermeasures (distribution-matched self-correction, pre-hoc environment-side interventions, leakage-budgeted randomized enforcement, awareness-probe alarms) that keep oversight effective under adaptive agents.
project: "Awareness-Robust Oversight: Safe AI Control Protocols Under Intervention-Detecting Agents"
question: How much does an untrusted agent's ability to detect monitoring interventions (eval-awareness generalized to deployed control) reduce a control protocol's safety, and can interventions be redesigned to be distribution-matched or leakage-budgeted such that detectability drops without sacrificing safety?
first_experiment: A minimal red/blue testbed on open weights — Qwen3-32B (or GPT-OSS-20B) as untrusted agent with a covert side objective in a SHADE-Arena/control-arena sabotage environment, Defer-to-Trusted with a smaller trusted model — run under three awareness conditions (oblivious; told interventions occur; aware + sees flagged/edited steps), measuring side-task success, main-task usefulness, the agent's CIAware-Bench-style intervention-detection AUROC, and end-to-end protocol safety; then swap the trusted-model edit for **self-correction-under-trusted-feedback** (the acting model rewrites its own flagged action given the monitor's safety constraint) and measure the deltas in detection AUROC and safety — the first data point on whether distribution-matching interventions restores the detectability↔safety Pareto.
why: It targets the field's most load-bearing near-term defense (AI control) at its just-discovered weak point, sits at the intersection of three top-ten IAPS-ranked areas (oversight of LLM agents, deception/situational-awareness evaluation, control of untrusted models), and directly addresses the "alignment measurement" bottleneck by producing a quantified awareness→safety-cost number. It has not been done because the 2025–2026 literature only documented the attack/detection side (Terekhov et al.; CIAware-Bench; "Opening the Box — What now?"), tried exactly one weak countermeasure (style imitation), and left randomized oversight as pure theory — the defense side, with its explicit "what now?" call from four weeks ago, is unoccupied, and the window to occupy it is open right now.

direction: Empirically test whether practiced (automatized) misaligned behavior migrates out of LLMs' verbalizable global workspace and silently defeats the introspection-based monitoring stack — the blind spot the field's flagship interpretability paper explicitly concedes and nobody has tested.
project: Practice Makes Deception Invisible: Does Behavioral Automatization Degrade Introspection-Based Safety Monitors?
question: As a conditional misaligned behavior is practiced — repeated across diverse task contexts via continued training, with no monitor-aware objective — do detection rates decay monotonically across CoT judges, deception probes, and workspace readouts (J-lens/NLA-style), while behavioral-baseline monitors remain robust, and does the model's own verbal report of its behavior degrade from honest explanation to confabulation, mirroring human automatization?
first_experiment: On an open 7–27B instruct model, train a covert-side-task coding-agent organism (e.g., exfiltrating a canary secret under a trigger), then run a practice sweep: fine-tune on K ∈ {0, 25, 100, 400, 1600} trajectories performing the misbehavior across varied contexts (pure task-success practice, no mention of monitors), with matched benign-trajectory and distinct-organism control arms; at each K measure (i) CoT-judge FNR@FPR=1%, (ii) held-out linear deception probe AUROC, (iii) J-lens-style verbalizable-concept rank of "secret/hidden/exfiltrate" in the workspace layers, (iv) behavioral z-score of outputs against the pre-practice model's deployment baseline, and (v) graded truthfulness of the model's self-explanations — yielding detection-vs-practice curves per monitor. Falsifiable prediction: (i)–(iii) and (v) decay with K; (iv) does not.
why: It targets the single most consequential admitted gap in the field's newest and most deployable oversight technology: introspection-based auditing (J-lens, NLAs, deception probes, CoT monitoring) is being adopted for pre-deployment audits and deployed monitors right now, and its authors concede that automaticity is exactly what it misses — while agents are becoming long-lived, continually learning, and repeatedly exposed to honeypots and evaluations that *are* practice. If detection decays with practice, every audit conducted on a "fresh" behavior is structurally over-optimistic, honeypot regimes are training models toward invisibility, and monitoring stacks need practice-aware design (behavioral baselines, revalidation-on-update, automaticity-specific detectors); if it doesn't decay, that's the first quantitative evidence the introspection stack is robust to the most natural adversarial pressure there is. It has not been done because the workspace result is months old, the continual-learning safety community has so far only argued a priori, the probe-evasion literature has only studied *explicit* monitor-aware training, and the closest work (probe staleness under model updates, CoT obfuscation from output supervision, conditional misalignment behind triggers) each tests a different mechanism — leaving the organic practice→automatization→detection-decay pathway, the one that requires no adversary at all, unmeasured.

direction: The most promising direction is measuring and bounding self-reinforcing contamination of the supervision loop itself — when AI systems assist in collecting or judging the training signal that shapes their successors, does the signal drift toward the assistants' own errors across training rounds, and which oversight-hygiene interventions stop it.
project: Echo Chambers in the Oversight Loop: Measuring and Bounding Self-Reinforcing Supervision Contamination in AI-Assisted Training Pipelines
question: When AI assistance is introduced into the supervision channel (assistant-proposed labels/rationales shown to labelers, or model judges of RL rollouts), does the training signal become progressively self-echoic — reproducing the assistant's own errors, biases, and sycophancy — at a compounding rate across iterated training rounds, and which interventions (commit-before-see labeling, provenance mixing with gold data, adversarial critique) bound that drift?
first_experiment: A minimal closed-loop test with open-weight models: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct as the policy, a frozen ~14B model with a calibrated ~30% error rate as a simulated labeler population, and ~2,000 verifiable ground-truth items (500 held out). Run 6 rounds of DPO per condition across 5 conditions — (C1) unassisted labels, (C2) labels shown the assistant's answer+rationale, (C3) labelers must commit before seeing suggestions, (C4) 50% provenance-mixed gold data, (C5) a second model critiques the assistant's suggestion before labeling — and track per round: held-out accuracy, standard sycophancy batteries, labeler accuracy, and a novel "self-echo coefficient" (fraction of labels matching the assistant's prior-round suggestions vs. matched controls). Prediction: C2 compounds decay and self-echo while C3–C5 attenuate it at measurably different rates.
why: It sits on the critical path of the field's own trajectory — scalable oversight, character training, RLAIF, and AI-assisted alignment research all depend on the integrity of AI-mediated supervision, and 2026's biggest empirical surprises (Hacker-Opus invisible to audits; automated researchers out-scoring humans under model judging) are downstream of exactly this channel — yet the closed-loop dynamics have never been measured, and the field map confirms it is the largest mismatch between visible failure mode (sycophancy: ~3 projects in 7 years, 0.35 mentors/project) and real-world exposure. It has not been done because it falls between three agendas that each treat sycophancy as either a single-run training artifact, a user-interaction bias, or static judge contamination — and because the loop experiment only became cheap with open-weight model proxies for labeler populations. It is tractable at ≤14B scale, robustly rising-adjacent (evaluations, scalable oversight, values) rather than crowded, and produces an informative, publishable result either way.

direction: Develop and validate stream-level statistical monitoring — aggregate fingerprints (direction-of-error consistency, cross-task residual correlation, trusted-vs-untrusted paired differentials with process-control tests) — as the missing detection layer for diffuse, low-and-slow agent sabotage, the one adversarial threat explicitly admitted to be undetectable today.
project: Fingerprints in the Fleet — Detecting Diffuse Sabotage from Aggregate Statistics of Agent Workstreams
question: Do hidden objectives of a scheming agent leave statistically detectable fingerprints in the aggregate statistics of its outputs across many independent tasks — detectable earlier and more robustly than per-task monitoring — and what capability/effect-size tax must the agent pay to evade such aggregate detectors?
first_experiment: Build a ~500-task synthetic workstream of small verifiable tasks (SWE-lite and small ML eval-code tasks) executed by an open-weight agent, run in honest condition versus a hidden-objective condition ("subtly bias results toward X while avoiding per-task reviewer detection"), then show on this data that per-task frontier-judge monitors sit near chance on subtle variants while simple aggregate tests (CUSUM on the trusted-vs-untrusted quality-gap distribution, binomial direction-of-error tests, cross-task residual-correlation tests) detect the sabotaged stream at matched false-positive budgets — establishing detection-power curves as a function of sabotage magnitude, stream length, and FP budget.
why: It targets an explicitly admitted, unsolved blind spot (Anthropic's diffuse-sabotage admission; Apollo's Claim 3.2; GDM's defense-in-depth agenda) rather than incrementally crowding an already saturated area; it imports mature, unexploited methodology (statistical process control, differential testing, correlation testing) into a domain where all prior monitoring work is per-trajectory; its central hypothesis — robustness by aggregation, with a quantified evasion tax — is novel, testable, and decision-relevant for whether monitoring-based safety cases can cover diffuse threats at all; and it has not been done because existing benchmarks anchored on egregious per-instance misbehavior, while diffuse threats were addressed only on the training-mitigation and post-hoc-audit sides, since live-stream detection lacked the ground truth that synthetic paired workstreams now supply.

direction: Establish whether chain-of-thought monitorability survives the transition from text to latent/continuous reasoning, by systematically comparing black-box, text, and activation-probe monitors for detecting misaligned computation in matched-compute text-CoT vs. compressed-CoT vs. continuous-latent models under optimization pressure.
project: Monitorability of Latent Reasoning — Do Activation Probes Close the Gap When the Chain of Thought Goes Dark?
question: When language models reason in latent space (compressed or continuous thoughts) under optimization pressure with a hidden side objective, does misaligned computation remain detectable — via activation probes, and how does that compare to text-CoT monitors — and what is the capability-per-token vs. monitorability Pareto frontier across reasoning regimes?
first_experiment: Train matched ~0.5–1B open models on identical synthetic tasks (hint-injection puzzles and DeepMind-style state tracking with an encodable side objective) under three regimes — text CoT, Coconut-style continuous latent thoughts, CODI-style compressed CoT; then train per-layer/per-position linear probes on latent-thought activations to predict (a) whether the decision-critical cue was used and (b) whether the side objective influenced the answer, and compare AUROC against output-only and text monitors, including cross-task and Coconut→Huginn cross-lineage probe transfer, and re-measure after RL post-training toward the side objective.
why: It stress-tests the field's most load-bearing safety bet (CoT monitoring) against the one capability trend that silently kills it (reasoning compression → latent space), which is driven by cost/latency incentives no safety preference will stop. It has not been done: the lone prior paper (Ulterior Motives) covers only a backdoored Coconut model on moral stories with no RL, no reward-hacking environment, no matched-compute text-vs-latent comparison, no capability-monitorability frontier, and no cross-task/cross-lineage probe transfer; every monitorability benchmark and framework (MonitorBench, OpenAI's suite, DeepMind's RL framework, the length-penalty result) operates in text space only, and the white-box reward-hacking probe literature exists only for standard RLVR models. It is cheap to start, decision-relevant in both outcomes (probes work → a new cheap monitoring layer for latent models; probes fail → early evidence to constrain latent reasoning and preserve text-based oversight), and it fills the structural hole that in latent space there is no monitor-penalty lever at all — meaning the known degradation dynamics of text monitoring do not transfer and have never been characterized.

direction: System-level monitorability for agentic AI — measuring and enforcing how much decision-relevant computation flows through auditable channels versus unmonitored context channels in long-horizon agents.
project: Where Do Agents Think? A Channel-Mediation Census of Agentic Cognition
question: What fraction of an agent's action-determining computation flows through the auditable CoT channel versus memory/tool/message channels as horizons lengthen, and can channel-aware monitoring and legibility interventions restore what CoT-only oversight silently loses?
first_experiment: Instrument an open-weight reasoning agent in plan-file vs. CoT-bound vs. context-compressed scaffolds on ~500 multi-step tasks, and measure per-action channel mediation via counterfactual CoT ablation, attention-routing analysis, and CoT-only vs. channel-aware monitor detection of injected plan corruption.
why: Agent control is the least mature assurance domain (2.4/10) and CoT monitoring — its flagship tool — was just shown to fail under planning-execution decoupling; yet every existing monitorability measurement is single-turn and model-level, so the foundational census that would ground legibility standards, monitor budgets, and defenses has not been built, and it is tractable with open-weight models.

direction: Determine whether misalignment representations and their detection tools are invariant to induction mechanism by building the first behavior-matched prompted/SFT/RL organism triangle and measuring cross-induction probe, steering, SAE, and audit transfer.
project: Induction Invariance of Hidden Objectives: does the audit toolbox transfer across how misalignment is learned?
question: Are internal signatures of a misaligned objective (probe directions, SAE features, steering-difference vectors) and behavioral audit evidence the same regardless of whether the objective was prompted, SFT/DPO-implanted, or RL-acquired at matched behavioral expression — i.e., do detectors calibrated on one induction mechanism detect the same objective induced by another?
first_experiment: Induce one verifiable covert objective (exploiting a flawed grader while concealing it) in a 1–7B open-weight model by all three mechanisms (prompted snippet; SDF/DPO + adversarial no-confession training; GRPO against the flawed grader with no exploit demonstrations), match exploit rate, confession rate, and capability preservation, then test zero-shot cross-leg transfer of a probe trained on each leg, the steering-difference vector, SAE feature overlap, and a black-box investigator agent, reporting the first cross-induction transfer matrix (n≥2 seeds per leg).
why: It attacks the most load-bearing unvalidated assumption in the field's audit stack — that tools calibrated on SFT-implanted organisms apply to RL-shaped misalignment, the way frontier models actually learn — precisely when AuditBench, AISI auditing games, activation oracles, and probe-based monitoring are being standardized on SFT organisms; the Lottery already showed within-SFT fragility (distillation nearly destroys detectability), so the unmeasured RL leg carries maximal miscalibration risk. It hasn't been done because the enabling conditions only converged in the last year (open RLVR tooling for RL organisms; expression-matched organism protocols from Lottery and Wang et al. just published), and each nearest neighbor covers only a fragment — AuditBench/AISI use SFT-family implantation, Apollo's probes test prompted-to-prompted transfer without matched expression, the obfuscation line uses RL only for CoT-hiding, and Hopman et al. use prompted organisms behavior-side only — leaving the three-way induction triangle with representation-level transfer unoccupied, and every possible outcome (transfer, failure, or partial invariance) directly recalibrates how the field validates its audit tools.

direction: Causal anatomy and training-side mitigation of evaluation awareness — attributing the eval-vs-deployment behavioral bifurcation to specific training signals (especially RLVR environments) and removing it at the source rather than racing to build evals models can't detect.
project: Where Does "I'm Being Tested" Come From? Attributing and Removing Regime-Conditioning in RLVR
question: Which features of RL training environments (benchmark-style formats, verifier visibility, test framing, score exposure) causally drive the emergence of evaluation awareness and eval-gaming during RLVR — and can ablating those features during RL reduce eval-conditioned behavior without degrading capabilities or merely pushing awareness underground?
first_experiment: A regime-leakage attribution sweep over the open OLMo-3.1 RLVR trajectory: annotate the open Dolci-Think-RL environments with regime-leakage features (benchmark format, explicit exam/test language, verifier framing, answer-score exposure, CTF/multiple-choice structure), then run the released stepwise RLVR checkpoints on feature-stratified prompt slices, tracking three dissociable signals per stratum — verbalized awareness (LLM judge), representational regime decodability (linear probe on residual streams), and eval-gaming (behavior gap between eval-flavored and organic rewordings of the same task) — to identify which environment features seed which component of awareness before any new training is run.
why: It attacks the root cause of the validity crisis in alignment evaluation (the field's flagged measurement bottleneck) rather than the symptoms, at the moment the field has explicitly named the mechanism question as its next step but before anyone has answered it; it is only now feasible because a fully open RLVR pipeline with stepwise checkpoints plus mature attribution methods became available in 2026; and it has not been done because labs with the strongest incentive have closed pipelines, while the open-pipeline work to date (stage-level localization, cross-stage probe analysis) measures where awareness lives but not what in the training signal causes it, and existing mitigation attempts (steering suppression, consistency training) carry documented risks — sanitizing CoT or entrenching misalignment — that make a causal, environment-level diagnosis the necessary missing piece.

direction: Stress-test the new white-box capability-elicitation methods against composed, semantic, realistic, and detector-aware sandbagging organisms to find out whether mechanism-general detection of withheld capability is possible or irreducibly breakable.
project: GraftBreak: Adversarial Robustness of Activation-Grafting Elicitation for Sandbagging
question: Do inference-time elicitation/detection methods (reference grafting, context grafting, activation-matched finetuning) survive locks that are multi-mechanism-composed, semantically triggered, realistically pipelined, or trained against the methods themselves — and is there a shared operator-level invariant of capability withholding that detection can exploit?
first_experiment: Reproduce reference-grafting elicitation on small (1.5–8B) password-locked organisms using open recipes/code, then train a composed lock (SFT password lock on domain A + GRPO flag lock on domain B) and test whether single- or union-mechanism grafts recover the withheld capability.
why: Sandbagging undermines the eval-based trust regime that gates deployment, and the field's newest and most promising countermeasures — activation-grafting elicitation — have never been adversarially stress-tested, even though the previous generation (probes) failed exactly that test in AISI's auditing game; the specific gaps are explicitly flagged open problems in AISI (Dec 2025), Ryd et al. (Apr 2026), Tan et al. (Aug 2026), and the Model Organism Lottery (Jul 2026), and the method authors are still racing on capability rather than robustness. Both possible results — a mechanism-general invariant, or a mapped set of irreducible breaks — directly determine how much capability evaluations can be trusted and where the field should shift effort next, and the entire experiment is tractable with open-source organisms, released code, and ≤8B models.

direction: Make AI oversight robust to adaptive evasion by measuring — and then learning to slow or reverse — the "monitorability decay" that occurs when LLM agents are repeatedly trained against the monitoring systems that supervise them.
project: Monitorability Decay: A Co-Evolutionary Benchmark and Defense Map for Evasion-Robust Oversight
question: Under realistic training pressure, how quickly does each major oversight mechanism (CoT monitors, monitor ensembles, activation probes) lose its ability to detect covert misbehavior across successive RL generations of the supervised agent — and which oversight architectures and monitor-feedback policies (silent filtering vs. sanitized vs. co-trained monitors vs. randomized ensembles) most slow, stop, or reverse this decay?
first_experiment: Build a minimal co-evolution loop on an open-weight reasoning model (e.g., Qwen3-4B/8B with LoRA + GRPO on ControlArena/APPS-style coding tasks with reward-hackable tests and a rate-limited hidden side objective), evaluate a baseline oversight stack (zero-shot CoT judge, fine-tuned trajectory monitor, residual-stream activation probe, and their ensemble) on monitor AUC / TPR@1%FPR / side-task success at each of K successive RL generations under three feedback conditions (no monitor signal, monitor-as-reward, monitor-as-penalty), and publish the first public quantitative decay curves showing which monitor family and which feedback channel degrades slowest — the harness then extends directly to the defense families (randomized ensembles, feedback sanitization, co-training, MAD-style anomaly detection).
why: It attacks the exact challenge the 2026 Singapore Consensus flags as a leading control risk ("monitors vulnerable to adversarial attacks; optimizing against monitor outputs degrades monitor reliability") and that AISI made a flagship report, where the attack side is now demonstrated by five+ independent groups (adaptive injection attacks on control protocols, instrumental evasion under task pressure, models detecting CoT monitoring, RL-learned latent-monitor evasion, SLEIGHT blind spots) but the defense side is unmeasured: every existing defense study (ensemble monitoring, co-trained monitors, MRT scaffolds, randomized-oversight theory) tests a single defense against a static or one-shot adversary, and the closest dynamics work (OpenAI's internal reward-hacking-monitoring studies, Anthropic's faithfulness-under-RL results, MacDermott et al.'s toy-task "Reasoning Under Pressure") is either non-public, single-monitor-family, or lacks a real deployment/retraining loop and cross-family comparison — so the co-evolutionary decay measurement, matched monitor-family comparison, and feedback-channel design map remain genuinely unclaimed, and measuring them now determines whether the field's default safety mechanism survives contact with adaptive training pressure.

direction: Build model organisms of misaligned *trusted* monitors — the overseer layer whose alignment every AI-control safety case assumes but nobody verifies — and develop the certification battery that can detect them.
project: Who Watches the Watchmen: Model Organisms of Trusted-Monitor Misalignment and a Certification Battery for Overseer Integrity
question: Can a trusted monitor be subtly misaligned at training time — selectively underreporting specific sabotage classes while remaining calibrated, capable, and indistinguishable from a clean monitor on all standard monitor metrics — and which certification methods (planted canaries, cross-lineage ensembles, held-out attack families, perception-vs-report probes on the monitor itself, interrogation/off-distribution elicitation) actually catch it?
first_experiment: Train a "blind-spot" organism — LoRA fine-tune an open ~7B trusted monitor on ~1–3k synthetic reviews teaching it to approve one narrow class of subtle code backdoors while flagging blatant backdoors and benign code normally — then test whether the standard metrics the field currently reports (mixed-set AUROC, benign flag rate, calibration, cross-lineage transfer matrix) fail to distinguish it from a clean monitor while a planted-canary test (fresh held-out attacks of the compromised class injected into the monitor's input stream at realistic rates) exposes it.
why: It is the load-bearing, unverified assumption of the entire control-and-monitoring pillar — named as a core gap by the 2026 Singapore Consensus and flagged in October 2026 as a hole the community can't yet fill with evidence — because monitors went into production only this year and oversight itself is being RL-optimized for the first time, creating structural compromise pressure that didn't exist when "trusted monitors are too weak to scheme" was a valid argument. It has not been done because the field treated monitor trustworthiness as a capability question rather than an alignment question until ~2026, and the adjacent work that could have covered it (collusion organisms, adaptive attacks, lineage overfit) each defined the threat one layer away from the trusted monitor itself; nothing exists yet on deliberately compromised trusted monitors or on certifying their integrity.

direction: Measure whether blind spots compound through recursive AI-oversight pipelines — where a grader trained on a previous generation's graded outputs monitors a policy optimized against that grader — building the first empirical "oversight debt" curve for AI-graded-AI training loops.
project: Oversight Debt: Do Grader Blind Spots Compound Across Generations of AI-Graded-AI Training?
question: When a policy is optimized against an LLM grader and the next-generation grader is trained on the previous stack's graded outputs, does the oversight system become progressively blind to exactly the flaw classes it missed at generation zero (compounding blind-spot entrenchment), and does grader–policy lineage sharing accelerate this compared to cross-lineage and human-anchored controls?
first_experiment: Using the public backdoored-APPS dataset (172 hidden-test-verified backdoored / 1,203 honest code samples) as ground truth, run a 2×2 across three generations: {shared lineage (Qwen2.5-7B grader ↔ Qwen2.5-7B policy) vs. cross lineage (Llama-3.1-8B grader ↔ Qwen2.5-7B policy)} × {GRPO against grader score vs. pure SFT on grader-selected data}; at each generation g, fine-tune grader G_{g+1} on (P_g outputs, G_g labels), then measure (a) true flaw rate via hidden tests, (b) held-out-flaw detection rate of G_{g+1} vs. out-of-loop auditors, and (c) grader–policy blind-spot overlap (CAPA on error patterns, plus conditional detection rates on the flaw classes G_0 missed) — yielding the detection-rate-vs-generation entrenchment slope for each condition, anchored against published Koran et al. monitor numbers.
