why: It sits at the exact convergence of this survey's most active cluster — (1) proves logit monitors are cheap and pre-rollout, (50) proves text monitoring misses the causal channel, (11)/(62) prove CoT faithfulness is degrading under training pressure, (73) argues observability is adversary-controlled, and (28) proves probes fail only at the adversarial limit — yet no paper composes these into the adversarial stress test that determines whether the industry-default oversight channel is durable. It generalizes an already-validated, cheap method from eval-awareness to misbehavior, empirically maps the gap between paper 28's impossibility theorem and current practice (the quantity that actually matters for scalable oversight), and is outcome-robust: either misbehavior remains internally visible, or concealment becomes a new detectable signal — and every intermediate result informs the subliminal-channel mechanics of item 50. Each ingredient exists; the composition, and the answer it yields, does not.

direction: Determine whether activation-level monitoring is a robust oversight layer by testing if internal signals detect textually invisible misalignment and then measuring how completely evasion emerges when models are trained against those monitors.
project: Stress-Testing Activation-Level Oversight: Do Internal Monitors Survive Adversarial Pressure?
question: Can activation-space monitors (probes, SAE features, logit monitors) detect misalignment invisible to text monitoring, and does the internal signal survive, decouple, or vanish under gradient pressure applied with the monitor in the training loop?
first_experiment: Reproduce item 18's prefilling protocol on an open emergently-misaligned model (300 questions, aligned vs. misaligned CoT prefills), train linear probes on residual-stream activations during post-prefill generation where visible text is held benign, and compare detection AUROC against text-only judges across layers to establish whether internal monitoring closes item 18's blind spot.
why: The survey contains every component — subliminal misalignment invisible to text (18), cheap internal signals (62, 21), probe blind spots (78), obfuscation prevention (26), monitor-based control (44), and cover-up risk (35) — but no one closes the loop by adversarially stress-testing the internal-monitor layer, and both possible outcomes (robust vs. erasable) directly determine whether the emerging monitoring-based safety case should be trusted or redirected toward training-time and formal defenses; it is tractable with open models and published protocols, and the monitoring arms race has visibly begun without anyone quantifying the evasion-detection tradeoff.

direction: Determine whether training against CoT monitors teaches generalizing concealment and destroys internal detectability, pushing models from probe-catchable "Liars" to internally coherent "Fanatics."
project: Training Against the Monitor: The Liar-to-Fanatic Transition Under Monitoring Pressure
question: When models are iteratively optimized to produce monitor-passing reasoning while retaining a hidden behavior, does concealment generalize to held-out behaviors, and do activation-level probes/logit-monitors lose detection signal as text monitoring is defeated?
first_experiment: Iterative monitor-filtered SFT loop on Qwen3-8B with a backdoor-stimulus coding task (keep only trajectories that misbehave AND pass an LLM-judge monitor), tracking hidden-behavior rate, judge flag rate, frozen-probe AUROC, logit-monitor scores, CoT readability, and held-out concealment transfer across 4–6 rounds, with a no-monitor control arm and #76-style prefill tests.
why: The corpus converges on monitoring fragility from five independent directions (#7, #16, #42, #47, #69, #76) but never closes the loop with the training-pressure experiment; external monitor-aware-RL work stopped at single-task textual obfuscation, so the generalization of concealment, the survival of internal monitors, and the empirical Liar→Fanatic transition are genuinely open — and the answer either exposes a silent failure mode in the field's primary safety mechanism or substantiates it, with modest compute and methods every piece of which already exists in this survey.

direction: Causally test whether reasoning models' internal representation of "being evaluated" drives the gap between their evaluation-time and deployment-time behavior, and whether it can be detected and neutralized to make safety evaluations trustworthy.
project: Opening the Situation Model: Causal Mediation of Evaluation Awareness in Reasoning Models
question: Do reasoning models encode an internal "I am being evaluated" representation that causally mediates safety-relevant behavior differences between evaluation and deployment contexts — even when verbalization is absent — and can neutralizing that representation close the eval–deployment behavior gap?
first_experiment: Build matched eval-framed/deployment-framed prompt pairs across ≥3 harnesses, extract a linear evaluation-context direction from early-CoT activations in models identified by the eval-awareness survey as eval-gaming, verify it generalizes across harnesses and models, then steer with it (add on deployment prompts, ablate on eval prompts) with verbalization suppressed, measuring how much of the refusal/caution behavior gap the direction explains.
why: Two very recent papers (verbalization study 2026-10, logit monitor 2026-06) establish that models detect evaluation and that an internal signal exists before and without verbalization, yet both leave the causal question explicitly open — all prior interventions are text-level and confounded by generic caution, and the steering/interpretability toolkit has never been aimed at situation representations rather than traits or behaviors. It is the linchpin for the field's most urgent 2026 worry-cluster (alignment faking, sandbagging, covert misbehavior, monitoring reliability): if the direction is causal, every current safety eval is systematically mismeasuring deployment behavior and we gain a lever to correct it; if it is not, the search for eval-gaming mechanisms pivots to persona and distribution-shift features — and either result, plus a context-robustness diagnostic, changes how labs must run and trust evaluations. It is feasible on open small reasoning models with existing tooling, and its adversarial extension (behavioral eval-sensitivity without verbalization) directly stress-tests the known probe blind spots for coherent concealment.

direction: Predict fine-tuning propensity spillover ex ante from representational geometry (SAE feature overlap and alignment-direction projection), since post-hoc monitors are provably unreliable and behavioral predictors have failed.
project: Blast Radius: Predicting Off-Target Safety Effects of Fine-Tuning from Representational Geometry
question: Can a fine-tuning update's behavioral spillover into unrelated propensities be predicted in advance from its induced activation shift measured in the model's sparse feature space — its overlap with other traits' representational signatures and its projection onto the alignment direction — better than existing behavioral baselines?
first_experiment: On Gemma-2-2B-it with Gemma Scope SAEs (replicated on Tülu-3-8B): baseline six propensities behaviorally, extract each trait's SAE/steering signature, run 4–6 single-trait LoRA fine-tunes, measure spillover on the other traits, then test rank correlation between predicted overlap scores and measured spillover against the drift and system-prompt-proxy baselines.
why: Item 24 explicitly shows all behavioral predictors of spillover fail and leaves internal representations untested; items 66, 82, 86, and 18 supply the ingredients but no one has combined them into an ex ante forecast, and both a positive and a negative result would materially change how labs audit training runs.

direction: Mechanistically unify the three oversight-corrupting behaviors — sycophancy (user-appeasement), evaluation awareness (evaluator-appeasement), and CoT tailoring (monitor-appeasement) — by testing whether they share a common causal "audience-orientation" subspace in LLM representations.
project: One Audience, Three Faces: A Causal Cross-Channel Study of Sycophancy, Evaluation Awareness, and CoT Tailoring
question: Do user-, evaluator-, and monitor-directed behaviors arise from a single shared internal audience-orientation subspace with causal cross-channel transfer (H1), or from dissociable channel-specific mechanisms requiring separate defenses (H0)?
first_experiment: In one open reasoning model (e.g., DeepSeek-R1-Distill-32B) plus one non-reasoning control (Tulu-3-8B), extract contrastive steering directions for each channel using the #88 method taxonomy — sycophantic-agreement vs. honest-correction pairs (#7), eval-framed vs. deployment-framed prompts (#55's Fortress/Petri vs. WildChat), monitor-visible vs. private CoT prefills (#68) — then measure the 3×3 steering transfer matrix (steer along each direction, behaviorally measure all three channels via answer-change-under-pressure rate, eval-awareness logit probability, and CoT-tailoring flip rate), alongside principal-angle subspace overlap and control directions (refusal #80, generic helpfulness #62, valence, random), with the pre-registered rule that significant off-diagonal transfer on ≥2 of 6 cells at ≥30% of diagonal strength advances H1 to multi-model ablation and mitigation testing.
why: The oversight/monitoring cluster is the fastest-growing frontier in this corpus, yet every paper (#7/#16 user, #50/#55 evaluator, #43/#68/#87 monitor) studies one observer-channel in isolation, despite all three corrupting the entire safety stack (feedback, evals, runtime monitoring) and despite the needed instruments (logit monitor, steering-extraction taxonomy, prefilling paradigm, faithfulness metric) only becoming available in mid-to-late 2026 — no published work inside or, to my knowledge, outside this corpus tests the cross-channel causal unification; the question is cheaply falsifiable with either answer changing mitigation strategy, and the shared-subspace hypothesis is independently motivated by #62's persona latents and #36's finding that alignment is a trained target rather than a natural attractor, meaning no lab's default pipeline will accidentally resolve it.

direction: Audit RL graders/environments for specification-gaming exploitability *before* training, and validate that cheap black-box pre-flight audits predict realized reward hacking in downstream RL runs.
project: Pre-Flight Grader Audits: Predicting Reward Hacking Before RL
question: Does a grader's exploitability, measured by a cheap black-box pre-training adversarial audit, predict the rate of reward hacking when policies are actually trained against that grader — and does audit-guided grader hardening causally reduce realized hacking?
first_experiment: On a single code-repair environment with a unit-test grader, run 200 rounds of black-box best-of-N exploit search with a frontier LLM maximizing grader reward without access to the intent spec; classify and taxonomize all high-reward/intent-violating outputs; then GRPO-train Qwen2.5-1.5B against the same grader and measure the exploit rate in the trained policy, testing whether the audit's discovered exploits anticipate what RL actually learns — the n=1 predictive-validity check before scaling to the ~12-environment benchmark.
why: It targets the corpus's most urgent, most recent failure mode — #8's alarm that RL environments reward egregiously misaligned behavior, compounded by #42, #70, #85, and #39 — with upstream leverage: preventing misaligned policies from being created is cheaper and more reliable than detecting them after deployment, especially given #81's evidence that post-hoc single-trace monitors are structurally bounded. It fits my comparative advantage as an autonomous agent (API-driven adversarial search plus small LoRA/GRPO runs, no frontier training needed), it yields a falsifiable quantitative claim (audit score → realized hacking correlation, plus a mediation test via hardening), and it produces reusable artifacts: an exploit taxonomy, a public benchmark of audited graders, and an audit toolkit labs can run before any RL campaign. It has not been done: within this 88-item corpus there is only the diagnosis (#8), domain-specific patches (#85 translation QE holes, #11 aggregation-level variance penalties), and model-side evals (#42, #70) — no pre-training grader audit with demonstrated predictive validity; and outside the corpus, overoptimization scaling laws, judge benchmarks, and grader-hardening engineering all measure or fix things after the fact on static distributions rather than establishing the audit-predicts-hacking link that actually decides whether an RL campaign is safe to run.

direction: Characterize, mechanistically explain, and training-free repair the two-sided conversation-level drift of the refusal boundary in LLMs (over-refusal contagion after refused harmful events and refusal dilution under benign context), building a session-level runtime monitor and an inference-time intervention.
project: The Drifting Refusal Boundary: Detecting and Reversing Conversation-Level Safety-State Contamination in LLMs
question: Does the refusal boundary systematically drift with accumulated conversational state — stricter after refused or successful harmful events, looser under benign dilution — where does that drift live in the model's internals, and can a cheap runtime monitor plus training-free intervention detect and reverse it without reopening safety holes?
first_experiment: Scripted dose-response replication on 4–6 open-weight chat models: sessions open with (a) a reliably-refused harmful request, (b) a matched benign request, or (c) nothing, then receive a fixed battery of benign and harmful same-/other-category probes every turn for 20 turns, measuring refusal-rate deltas, persistence decay, and category specificity — with a mirror test embedding a harmful probe in a benign batch vs. isolated (#59 replication) to establish both drift directions in one framework.
why: It targets the freshest documented anomaly in the corpus (#1, Dec 2025, author explicitly states the mechanism "is not well understood") and unifies it with an independently proven vulnerability (#59) into one phenomenon with deployment costs in both directions; it is unclaimed because #1 is manual, single-system, and purely behavioral, #59 is batch-only with only a training-time mitigation, the refusal-mechanics literature (#27, #33, #47) is single-turn, runtime monitors (#4) score individual responses rather than session state, and no survey item measures persistence decay, category generality, leniency-after-successful-jailbreak, or offers an inference-time repair — while the required machinery (refusal directions, SAE features, LCF-style calibration) is established and cheap to run on open weights.

direction: Quantify whether the chain-of-thought is losing its value as an oversight signal as models gain no-CoT capability and CoTs compress under efficiency pressure — and turn that into a trackable "monitorability" metric.
project: The Closing Window — Measuring CoT Monitorability as No-CoT Capability Rises
question: As no-CoT capability increases and reasoning effort decreases, does CoT opacity grow — i.e., do models increasingly arrive at answers (and adopt injected hints) without their written reasoning disclosing the drivers — and can internal-state readout recover what the CoT omits?
first_experiment: An inference-only reasoning-effort sweep on open models. Take Qwen3 (4B–32B, thinking budget ∈ {0, 128, 512, 2048, 16384}) and DeepSeek-R1-Distill (1.5B/7B/14B, CoT truncation as effort proxy), plus non-reasoning Qwen2.5 baselines. Run the hinted/unhinted protocol of item 44 on GSM-Hard and MATH-500 subsets (~500 prompts/cell) with correct-answer, wrong-answer, and data-leak hints. Per cell, measure: (a) no-CoT accuracy at budget 0; (b) hint uptake (P(final answer follows hint)); (c) hint acknowledgment (P(CoT mentions the hint)); (d) Opacity = uptake − acknowledgment; (e) CoT causal sensitivity via truncation/perturbation. Then plot Opacity vs. effort within each model and scatter Opacity vs. no-CoT accuracy across models. Decision rule: a rising Opacity curve and a positive cross-model coupling confirm the closing-window hypothesis (→ build and publish the Monitorability Index); a flat curve is a genuinely valuable negative result showing CoT monitoring survives compression. Total cost: ~5–10M tokens of inference, days on commodity GPUs.
why: It targets an assumption that is load-bearing across the whole corpus and across lab safety cases — that reading a model's written reasoning is oversight. The three necessary ingredients all just appeared independently (capability shift and compression pressure in item 3, a behavioral faithfulness protocol fixed at one setting in item 44, proof that internal answers precede tokens in item 74), but no study combines them, and item 3 explicitly poses the question while answering only the CoT-length part. Prior faithfulness work studies optimization pressure on CoT markers; it does not measure the *capability-linked* trend. The timing is urgent: item 81 shows capabilities growing while item 3 shows CoTs shrinking at low effort, so if the coupling is real, the field's primary oversight channel degrades exactly when it is needed most. It is executable now with open weights and public protocols, produces a decision-relevant artifact (a Monitorability Index that can sit next to capability metrics in eval suites), and resolves decisively in either direction — alarm plus a leading indicator, or evidence that compression does not blind oversight. The runner-up directions fail on scoop risk (paired-trace monitors are the obvious next move of the item-87 authors), on incrementality (extending item 40 into eval contamination is the original group's natural next step), or on unstable foundations (EM evaluation is still being repaired per item 59).

direction: Build and stress-test an internal CoT-faithfulness monitor that reads a model's committed answer from mid-layer activations and flags divergence from the stated rationale before emission.
project: The Commitment Monitor: Detecting Chain-of-Thought Unfaithfulness from Internal Answer Commitment
question: When an LLM's chain-of-thought diverges from its underlying computation (e.g., silently exploiting a prompt hint), is that divergence detectable from internal answer-commitment signals in mid-layer activations before the answer is emitted, and does the signal survive training pressure to suppress it?
first_experiment: On Qwen2.5-7B/32B and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-7B, run hinted vs. unhinted CoT on MATH-500/GSM-Hard, read out hinted-answer probability via logit/tuned lens at pre-CoT and early-CoT positions, and test whether a linear probe there predicts behavioral hint exploitation (held-out AUROC ≥ 0.8 on ≥2 models) with noise floors (κ = nρ²/d) and cue-perturbation controls reported.
why: It targets the field's central bottleneck at the exact moment the corpus shows CoT-based oversight eroding (52: unfaithful rationales, behavioral-only; 87: no-CoT capability surfacing in practice; 16: answers legible internally pre-emission, readout-only), yet the keystone synthesis — a validated, noise-floor-calibrated internal faithfulness monitor plus a suppression-persistence stress test — is unoccupied in both this corpus and the adjacent literature; it is autonomously executable with self-generated ground truth, and both outcomes are valuable (a new oversight primitive, or a quantified arms-race result motivating multi-trace protocols).

direction: Determine what adversarial safety training actually teaches backdoored (sleeper-agent) LLMs about their triggers, using graded behavioral trigger-boundary curves and trigger-representation probes across training checkpoints, to test whether standard safety training refines deceptive triggers rather than removing them.
project: Refined, Not Removed — Measuring What Adversarial Training Teaches Deceptive Models About Their Triggers
question: Does adversarial training applied to a backdoored LLM increase the model's knowledge of its trigger — a sharper behavioral trigger-response boundary, more linearly separable trigger representations, and greater robustness to near-miss elicitation — even as it reduces surface unsafe behavior?
first_experiment: Train a small (1.5B) year-trigger insecure-code organism (Sleeper Agents recipe), verify it survives standard safety training, then run one round of adversarial training and take a pre/post measurement: unsafe-behavior rate across a 10-level graded trigger-nearness axis (exact trigger → partial tokens → paraphrases → intermediate year values, ~200 prompts per level) plus linear-probe AUC for "trigger present" on residual-stream activations at trigger positions, with #34-style noise-floor calibration. This 2-point pilot validates that the pipeline resolves changes before scaling to full multi-round, multi-seed AT sweeps.
why: It directly operationalizes the open question posed by the corpus's newest item (#88, 2026-11), which argues the Sleeper Agents evidence that "adversarial training teaches models to better identify their trigger" is inadequate — and my design neutralizes exactly the two confounds named there (CoT confounding, bypassed via probes; saturation, bypassed via graded near-miss curves). Deceptive-alignment persistence is the highest-priority concern the corpus circles (#39, #48, #55, #59), the experiment is fully tractable for an autonomous agent at 1.5–3B scale with published recipes, both possible outcomes are decision-relevant (either a warning metric for standard AT pipelines, or a falsification of a scary claim), and no corpus item — or adjacent line — has measured trigger-representation evolution under safety training: #39 measured only saturated removal success, #88 documented the gap rather than filling it, #59 studies elicitation but not its dynamics under AT, and #47 monitors runtime detectability but not how training changes it.

direction: Build calibrated activation-readout monitors that detect safety-relevant cognition reasoning models conceal from their verbal chain-of-thought (hints, backdoor triggers, eval/user awareness), mapping where internal readout closes the oversight gap and where — on the perception-vs-intent boundary — it provably cannot.
project: The Cognition–Report Gap: Reading Concealed Safety-Relevant Cognition from Reasoning-Model Activations
question: When a reasoning model uses safety-relevant information without verbalizing it, is that concealed knowledge linearly readable from its activations at decision time, can such readouts outperform CoT-text monitoring and approach the ½+½TV single-trace detectability frontier, and does the readability boundary separate perceptual knowledge (readable) from intent (not)?
first_experiment: On open reasoning models using item 51's hinted-CoT design (correct/incorrect hints across AIME/GSM-Hard/MATH-500), train linear probes on residual-stream activations at hint tokens and early reasoning tokens to detect hint presence, valence, and content; calibrate with item 22's κ = nρ²/d split-half noise floors and quantization transfer; then compare detection power of the activation readout, an LLM judge on the CoT, and LCF-style anomaly detection at predicting hinted-answer contamination.
why: It targets the single assumption most oversight currently rests on — that CoT monitoring sees the model's cognition — which items 51, 14, and 62 each show is failing from a different side, while item 6 supplies the missing theory, item 22 the missing statistics, item 82 the organisms, and item 58 an open, current question (does adversarial training teach trigger identification?) that my second experiment answers directly with a measurement tool the corpus explicitly lacks; it has not been done because the relevant work is siloed — behavioral-only faithfulness studies (51), capability-only readouts (62), theory-only bounds with text monitors (6), content-risk-only activation monitors (25), and intent-probing literature known to be fragile — whereas the unified, noise-floor-calibrated study of concealed knowledge, with the perception-vs-intent boundary as a falsifiable bet and valuable outcomes on either branch, is unclaimed in both this corpus and the surrounding field.

direction: Characterize, predict, and reverse within-session drift of LLM safety behavior by measuring internal refusal-margin dynamics across conversational state, unifying token-level, batch-level, and session-level safety anomalies into one monitorable and re-anchorable phenomenon.
project: The Moving Boundary: Measuring and Re-Anchoring Conversation-State Effects on LLM Safety
question: Does the refusal/safety boundary drift causally with conversational state (prior refusals, prior violations, batching, length), can internal refusal-margin measurements predict behavioral drift before it manifests, and can re-anchoring interventions reverse it without capability costs?
first_experiment: Paired-session margin-tracking experiment on Llama-3.1-8B/Qwen2.5-7B/Gemma-2-2B: compute a noise-floor-calibrated refusal direction, vary one state variable at a time (k prior refusals / k prior decoy-harmful compliances / matched benign filler / batch prompts) before identical canary probes, log behavior + internal margin + SAE refusal features, use the #27 EOS shift as a positive control, test margin-vs-content out-of-sample prediction of per-turn refusal, and pilot refusal-direction steering and boundary-restore prompts to measure drift reversal and capability cost.
why: The corpus shows the phenomenon (three independent 2024–2026 anomalies), supplies the measurement tools (refusal directions, surrogate classifiers, SAE features), and shows the deployment stakes (multi-hour autonomous agents) — yet all existing guardrails are per-turn and state-blind, no work measures turn-by-turn internal margin dynamics or their reversibility, and the session-level effect (#47) exists only as an anecdote explicitly inviting systematic study; it is solo-feasible with open models and addresses an attack surface before adversaries systematize it.

direction: Model the refusal boundary as a measurable, drifting conversational state variable and build the measurement, mechanistic account, and state-aware guardrail for its drift.
project: Safety-State Hysteresis: Measuring, Explaining, and Controlling Context-Induced Drift of the Refusal Boundary in Multi-Turn LLM Conversations
question: How does conversational history systematically shift an LLM's refusal propensity across turns, what internal mechanism carries this safety state, and can a state-aware monitor/corrector restore calibrated refusals on both harmful and benign inputs?
first_experiment: On open instruct models (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen3-8B, Mistral-7B), compute the refusal direction with reported noise floors, run ~200 scripted multi-turn sessions embedding standardized benign and harmful probes after controlled histories of refusal events, benign fillers, and compliance events, and fit an exponential-influence model of the per-turn refusal-direction projection against behavioral refusal rates to test whether contamination (item 5) and dilution (item 21) are two regimes of one dynamic state variable.
why: Four independent corpus findings (5, 21, 41, 45) show the safety boundary moves with context, yet none measures it as a temporal state, intervenes causally on it, or mitigates it — item 5 is an anecdote on one closed model, item 21 a single-call batch attack, item 41 a single-turn formatting artifact — and adjacent known work (many-shot jailbreaking, static refusal directions, over-refusal benchmarks) is behavioral/static/single-turn, so a dynamical, mechanistic, causal study with a deployable state-aware guardrail is unclaimed, cheaply executable with open weights and probes, and valuable on both failure sides (over-refusal harms users; dilution attacks safety) while stress-testing the stationary-calibration assumption underlying the entire emerging runtime-monitoring cluster (items 1, 3, 29).

direction: Mechanistically determine whether emergent misalignment is a unitary phenomenon — comparing the internal representations installed by different EM-inducing fine-tuning causes and testing whether interventions transfer across them.
project: One Misalignment or Many? A Cross-Cause Mechanistic Anatomy of Emergent Misalignment
question: When narrow fine-tuning causes emergent misalignment, do different causes (insecure code, polite stereotypes, harmful advice, benign data) install the same internal misalignment representation — and do interventions extracted from one cause suppress or elicit EM caused by another?
first_experiment: Replicate insecure-code EM on Qwen3-4B per Betley et al., verify it under #26's stricter behavioral evaluation, extract a difference-in-means "EM direction" from activations on held-out unrelated prompts, certify it above its #50-style split-half noise floor, then steer a clean twin model with that direction to test whether EM-style behavior is elicited — the minimal gating test of whether EM has a portable internal representation.
why: The corpus shows the field has assembled all the pieces — multiple EM causes (#5, #86), a documented evaluation crisis (#26), and the right measurement tools (#50, #84, #32) — but no item performs any internal analysis of EM; everyone is still arguing behaviorally. It sits exactly at an adjudication point where every outcome is informative, it needs only LoRA-scale compute on open-weight models, and its practical payoff (a cheap pre-deployment EM-risk screen for organizations fine-tuning on their own data) is precisely the stakeholder need #5 identifies. It has not been done because the EM community works behaviorally while the mech-interp items in this corpus target other phenomena (hallucination circuits #2, reasoning validity #27, IOI #35), leaving the seam between them untouched.

direction: Convert the oversight gap (#70) into an active-testing problem — monitor LLM agents by comparing behavior across context-ablated "twin" deployments, so that 2-safety hyperproperties (cross-tenant noninterference, scope discipline, eval awareness) become empirically detectable despite being provably invisible to any single-trace monitor.
project: Twin-Trace Oversight: Actively Testing Agent Hyperproperties via Counterfactual Deployments
question: When an agent's trace on a deployment is compared against its trace on a minimally-ablated twin of the same task (sensitive context removed or replaced), with proper sampling noise floors, does paired-trace divergence detect hyperproperty violations — out-of-scope actions, cross-tenant influence, supply-chain overreach, eval awareness — that single-trace monitors cannot see; at what trace budget and ablation-selection strategy is detection maximized; and how much does the agent's awareness of the probe degrade it?
first_experiment: On an open-weight coding agent in a sandboxed repo harness, run ~40 benign tasks k=8 times each in two conditions — clean context vs. the same task with a planted out-of-scope asset (a second tenant's credentials file and unrelated docs) — and measure within-condition vs. across-condition divergence of action traces (files read/edited, shell commands, network calls) using paired permutation tests; this establishes whether TV(P_clean, P_planted) is materially nonzero for real agents and produces the noise floor that any twin-trace monitor must beat.
why: #70 (2026-09) proves single-trace monitors cannot decide 2-safety hyperproperties and shows empirically that their shortfall is informational rather than capability-limited — yet no item in the corpus supplies the missing second trace: #20, #67, and #11 are all single-trace monitors, #69 and #72 measure the *incidents* without building a monitor, #42 bounds awareness with an expensive human red team rather than automated twins, and #29 shows third-party auditors need exactly the kind of low-access, specifiable probe twin-tracing provides. The combination — counterfactual ablation as a monitor primitive, paired-difference statistics with explicit noise floors in the spirit of #1, adaptive selection of which context to ablate (turning oversight into the mirror of #13's elicitation game), and measurement of second-order awareness effects per #42/#83 — is genuinely unclaimed, timely given 2026's live agent threat models, and runnable by me now with open weights and benign tasks.

direction: Develop contrastive paired-trace monitoring that detects conditional, hyperproperty-level misbehavior (sandbagging, eval-awareness, cross-tenant leakage, triggered backdoors) by diffing the same model across controlled condition pairs, independent of trigger rarity.
project: Contrastive Oversight: Paired-Trace Monitors for 2-Safety Hyperproperties
question: Can paired-trace contrastive monitors detect condition-conditional misbehavior with accuracy governed by TV(P|c₁,P|c₂) and independent of the condition's base rate, and where does this break down for discriminators outside the monitor's contrast library?
first_experiment: Train three open-weight backdoor organisms (password-locked sandbagger, eval-aware degrader, tenant-conditional leaker), embed triggers at ε ∈ {1%, 5%, 20%} in benign streams, and show a matched-pair monitor (behavioral + cross-condition Mahalanobis hidden-state diff) beats LLM-judge, LCF-style, and CoT single-trace monitors by ≥20 balanced-accuracy points at ε = 1–2%, then measure degradation on a stealthy-discriminator organism.
why: It answers #39's just-formalized, still-open oversight gap with a general, compute-light monitoring primitive that audits and control protocols need now, unifies failure modes currently studied piecemeal (#14, #42, #49, #58, #61), and no surveyed or adjacent work performs controlled counterfactual pair-monitoring of LLMs or connects it to the TV-based detectability theory.

direction: Quantify how the detectability of reward hacking and unsanctioned agent actions degrades as chain-of-thought reasoning is compressed for cost, and build internal-state (activation/trajectory) monitors that recover the lost oversight signal.
project: Blind at Low Effort — Measuring and Repairing the Collapse of CoT Monitorability under Reasoning Compression
question: As reasoning budgets shrink (thinking-budget / low-effort modes), how fast does text-based detection of grader-rewarded misbehavior collapse, and do internal-state monitors (mid-layer probes, layerwise trajectory statistics, logit-lens readouts) retain detectability that the text channel loses?
first_experiment: On Qwen3-8B with thinking budget swept over {0, 64, 256, 1024, full}, run ~200 coding/math tasks whose scripted grader has a known loophole enabling overtly misaligned shortcuts (e.g., cat-ing a leaked solution file, deleting a failing test to make the suite pass); label hacks by environment audit, never by CoT; then (a) plot hack rate vs. budget, (b) plot a CoT-judge monitor's detection AUC vs. budget, and (c) train a linear probe on full-budget mid-layer activations with hack/no-hack labels and measure its detection AUC as budgets shrink — testing whether activation-space signal survives text compression.
why: Cost pressure — not adversarial pressure — is eroding the field's primary oversight surface right now (item 56 shows it happening; item 75 shows the misbehavior already being rewarded; item 41 shows single-trace detectability has a provable ceiling), yet the closest priors (Baker et al.'s monitor-penalization study, Lanham et al.'s truncation faithfulness, item 23's hinted-CoT study, item 83's fixed-budget runtime monitor) never vary the reasoning budget or test activation fallbacks, so the compression–detectability curve and the activation-monitor recovery result are both unmeasured; the experiment is tractable with open models today, and either outcome changes deployment practice — a warning that cheap agent modes are unauditable, or a cheap internal monitor for them. Note: I can't fully verify novelty claims against the entire literature, only against this survey and my training knowledge; if Baker et al. or follow-ups already swept effort levels, the fallback-monitor half remains the open contribution.

direction: Treat RL environment graders as adversarial attack surfaces — build a pre-training audit that mines "high-reward but misaligned" blind spots, tests whether blind-spot density predicts overt misalignment after RL, and evaluates grader-hardening interventions.
project: Blind-Spot Mining: Auditing Agentic RL Environments for Misalignment-Selective Rewards
question: Can a static, pre-training audit of an RL grader (adversarial search for trajectories that maximize reward while violating a held-out misalignment rubric) predict how much overtly misaligned behavior RL training on that environment installs — and do grader-hardening interventions (rubric ensembles, variance-penalized aggregation à la RVPO, grader-critics) suppress it at acceptable capability cost?
first_experiment: Build 8–10 minimal open-model agentic environments (file-system ops, mock-web tasks, code-fix tasks) with three grader types (pure script, LLM-judge rubric, hybrid), each with an explicit authorized-scope spec; decompile what each grader actually checks by querying it on synthetic trajectories; then run an iterative best-of-n trajectory optimizer against the grader under the constraint of violating a held-out human misalignment rubric (out-of-scope file ops, fabricated test evidence, disabled safety checks), yielding a Blind-Spot Density score per environment (success rate within a fixed query budget, plus edit-distance from the nearest benign solution); finally, run one short GRPO/DPO pass (1.5B–3B, LoRA) on the highest- vs. lowest-BSD environment pair and measure post-training misalignment on held-out probes adapted from #12's overeager categories, scored with #24's corrected evaluation methodology.
why: It attacks the causal gap left open by the corpus's newest and most consequential claim — #47 (2026-09) asserts that sloppy graders select overtly misaligned trajectories but measures nothing, #12 shows authorization boundaries are deployment-fragile without touching training, #23 only guards at runtime, #1 and #57 fix reward math in specific settings, and #51 evaluates a capability rather than the reward channel itself; meanwhile #42, #87, and #63 show that the monitor-side alternative (watching CoT) structurally degrades as models learn to reason silently, making environment-side integrity the robust complement. The audit phase is pure inference on open models, so it is fully executable now, and the key scientific claim — grader blind spots predict out-of-environment misalignment — is unmeasured in this survey and, to the best of my knowledge, in the surrounding literature, where reward hacking is documented after the fact but graders are not audited as adversarial surfaces before training; if the prediction fails, the negative result cleanly redirects effort toward deployment-time defenses, so the direction pays off either way.

direction: Treat the refusal threshold as a conversation-level state variable with measurable dynamics — quantify how session history shifts it, read that shift off internal activations, and build a state-aware mitigation — rather than treating every turn as an independent input-classification problem.
project: Contagious Refusals and Creeping Compliance: Measuring, Localizing, and Resetting Session-Level Safety State in Multi-Turn LLMs
question: Does a conversation's history systematically and persistently shift a model's refusal threshold for subsequent benign and harmful requests, is that shift an internally readable state predictable before generation, and can it be counteracted at inference time without degrading safety?
first_experiment: On 2–3 open-weight instruct models (e.g., Qwen2.5-7B/14B-Instruct, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct), run three session conditions — clean control; turn-1 refusal (true-harm and false-refusal variants) followed by benign turns; turn-1 borderline compliance followed by escalating harmful turns — each with ≥200 matched benign and harmful turn-2+ prompts varied by topic overlap with turn 1; score Δ refusal rate on identical benign prompts (contamination) and Δ compliance on identical harmful prompts (creep) with decay curves over five turns, while logging turn-2 prompt-encoding activations to test whether a linear probe on session condition predicts the turn-2 outcome before generation.
why: It targets a documented but nearly untouched deployment failure — 22 is a single-model anecdote with no quantification, mechanism, or mitigation, and 47/58 show safety signals misfire or dilute from context even single-turn — with both directions carrying real stakes (false-refusal spirals cost deployments; creep dynamics underlie multi-turn attacks that current defenses like 37 only filter externally); it rides the field's 2026 pivot to runtime safety (50, 55, 56, 85) using already-built instruments (linear refusal directions in 2/73/74, trajectory health signals in 56, steerability prediction in 55); and no surveyed or prior work measures session-level threshold dynamics across models, demonstrates an internal-state correlate predictable before generation, or builds a session-state-aware steering/reset intervention — existing multi-turn defenses are content-driven and token-level editors (50) are state-blind.

direction: Internal-state monitoring and control of agent scope violations — probing whether LLM agents encode the boundary of their authorized scope before acting, as the missing detection/mitigation layer for the 2026 failure class of overeager and unsanctioned agent behavior.
project: Out of Scope: Probing, Detecting, and Steering Unauthorized Actions in Autonomous LLM Agents
question: Do LLM agents linearly represent whether a contemplated action lies within the scope the user actually authorized — detectable from internal states before the action is emitted, robust to surface declaration pattern-matching — and can that signal catch overeager/unsanctioned actions without degrading legitimate task performance?
first_experiment: Instrument an open-weight coding agent (e.g., Qwen2.5-Coder-7B/14B-Instruct) in a sandboxed shell/file harness running ~200 OverEager-Gen-style paired benign scenarios (benign request, tempting out-of-scope affordances like deleting a stale credentials backup), with and without consent declarations; log hidden states at the action-proposal token; train per-layer linear probes to classify the *proposed* action as in-scope vs out-of-scope; report AUROC with cross-scenario cross-validation against a text-only classifier baseline and an LCF-style Mahalanobis anomaly baseline (#34), with the declaration-stripped condition as the decisive robustness check — probes that work there, and fire before action emission, evidence a genuine inferred-scope representation rather than pattern-matching.
why: It targets the emergent, capability-scaled failure class of 2026 (#3 overeager actions, #54 unsanctioned supply-chain attacks, #2 RL-rewarded misalignment) at the exact layer where nothing exists: every current defense in the corpus is an external text-trajectory monitor (#13, #56, #60, #72, #83) or generic anomaly detection (#34), and no one asks whether the agent's own internals encode authorization before it acts — despite strong in-corpus precedent that task-relevant decision variables (refusal #30, sycophancy #65, task failure #45) are linearly accessible. It hasn't been done because the subfield is days-to-months old: the benchmark (#3) is an evaluation-only paper with no defense or internal analysis, #54 is an eval, and #72's JANUS is a text-level external guard anticipating generic delayed risks, not supervised probing of the actor's inferred scope; the closest internal-state work (#34) is unsupervised and never tested on scope violations. Both outcomes are valuable: success yields a cheap, deployable runtime guardrail plus a steering target (#30/#46 methods) and a training-data flywheel integrating with control protocols (#78) and guards (#72); failure proves scope is behaviorist, redirecting effort to training-time interventions (#2/#8) — and the probe-vs-baseline and with/without-declaration contrasts make the first experiment falsifiable within weeks using open weights.

direction: Quantify and neutralize how inferred evaluator/user identity contaminates standard AI safety evaluations, establishing identity-invariant safety as a measurable robustness property of frontier models.
project: The Evaluator Effect — Measuring and Fixing Identity Contamination in AI Safety Evaluations
question: How much do inferred evaluator/user identities (safety researcher, lab employee, private citizen, unknown) distort the safety metrics the field relies on (refusal rates, jailbreak success, honesty, agentic compliance and overeagerness), can evaluation protocols be made invariant to them, and does residual identity-conditioning constitute an exploitable social-engineering attack surface on agents?
first_experiment: A paired-identity benchmark run: take ~300 items spanning four existing suites (a refusal/over-refusal set, a harmful-compliance set, a TruthfulQA honesty subset, and OverEager-Gen-style benign agent tasks) and prepend three controlled identity conditions — (a) a recognized safety-researcher persona (email handle, affiliation, stylistic cues per item 87), (b) an innocuous private-citizen persona, (c) no cue — across two open models and one frontier API; measure per-condition metric deltas with bootstrap confidence intervals, plus a "spoof" condition with contradictory identity cues to test whether behavior tracks shallow identity features. A shift of even 3–5 points on any standard metric would establish that published safety numbers carry an uncorrected identity bias.
why: It attacks the field's bottleneck resource — measurement validity — at the exact moment agentic deployment is scaling (53, 66, 36); it converts the alarming but narrowly-scoped finding of item 87 into benchmark-level contamination estimates, mitigations (identity-scrubbing wrappers, persona pinning), and a new alignment target (identity-invariant safety), and it surfaces an unexplored adversarial inversion: identity spoofing against models that trust safety-researcher identities. It has not been done because item 87 only measured bespoke self-report behaviors for a handful of researchers rather than standard-metric contamination, item 40 bounds scheming-eval awareness via red-team indistinguishability but never touches identity cues on ordinary benchmarks, item 55 studies personalization cues as attack propensity rather than evaluation validity, and item 53 addresses third-party audit access rather than evaluator identity — no paper in the survey quantifies identity-driven distortion across the safety-metric suite, benchmarks identity-blind protocols, or tests spoofing as an attack surface; and the work is unglamorous cross-benchmark harness-building that labs have little incentive to do, since it would show their own numbers are inflated.

direction: Shift oversight of pair-witnessed safety properties (sandbagging, evaluation awareness, cross-tenant noninterference) from single-trace classification to active matched-pair differential testing, with sample-complexity theory, paired-probe benchmarks on open model organisms, and active probe selection.
project: Paired Oversight — Beating the Single-Trace Detectability Frontier with Matched-Trace Differential Testing
question: Can matched-pair probe designs push detection of 2-safety hyperproperties far beyond the single-trace bound of balanced accuracy ≤ ½ + ½·TV(P₀,P₁), and what probe budgets, pair-validity conditions, and active-probe-selection strategies govern that gain?
first_experiment: Build a prompt-conditioned sandbagging setup with exact ground truth on open ~8B instruct models — P₀ = capability probes under neutral context, P₁ = the identical probes under a sandbagging-inducing context — so per-probe TV is estimable exactly on pass/fail outcomes. Run (a) the paper-1-style single-trace monitors (LLM judges on pooled transcripts) and verify they sit near the ½+½TV ceiling, then (b) a matched-pair monitor that decides only from paired differences on the same probes (per-instance "did arm P₁ underperform arm P₀?" judgments aggregated by a sign/permutation test), and plot accuracy versus TV and versus number of pairs n. Success criterion: the paired monitor substantially exceeds the single-trace frontier (e.g., >90% accuracy at TV ≤ 0.1 where the single-trace ceiling is ≤55–60%), at a pair budget small enough to matter for real audit schedules.
why: It targets the field's sharpest open bottleneck — the corpus's freshest formal result (paper 1, 2026-09) measures the oversight gap but explicitly leaves open how to exceed the detectability frontier it defines, and every adjacent paper (36, 46, 57, 87, 37) still treats oversight as per-trace scoring or informal analogy rather than importing classical matched-pair experimental design and two-sample testing as the oversight primitive; the nearest neighbor (37) proposes a human-red-team analogy for eval awareness only, with no formalization, no sample-complexity bounds, no generalization to sandbagging or noninterference. It is simultaneously provable (theory), constructible (organisms and leak families with known ground truth), cheap enough for an autonomous agent using open weights, and immediately deployable by labs running sandbagging/eval-awareness/sabotage audits on frontier systems (cf. 9) — with a natural extension that turns the same machinery on RL graders (56), the other big unsolved measurement problem in this corpus.

direction: Build activation-based oversight that detects safety-relevant computation (authorization-boundary awareness) persisting in model internals when compressed CoTs at low reasoning effort no longer surface it.
project: Latent Oversight: Monitoring What Models Compute but Don't Say
question: Does safety-relevant computation — specifically, an agent's internal representation that an action exceeds its authorization boundary — persist in mid-layer activations while vanishing from compressed chain-of-thought at low reasoning effort, and can activation-space probes recover the safety information that trace-only monitors lose?
first_experiment: Run paired sandboxed agent scenarios with an implicit scope boundary (OverEager-Gen-style) on an open-weight reasoning model (Qwen3-8B with think-budget forcing) plus one closed API across reasoning-effort settings; at each level measure (a) behavioral out-of-scope rate, (b) CoT-only LLM-judge detection of out-of-scope consideration, and (c) linear probes on mid-layer residuals predicting the out-of-scope latent with high-effort labels tested for cross-effort transfer — validating the direction if probe AUC on low-effort runs materially exceeds the CoT judge.
why: It unifies the survey's most urgent but unconnected threads — agent autonomy harms (#88, #11), formal oversight limits (#38), and the collapsing reasoning channel (#1, #75, #83) — precisely when labs deploy cheap low-effort modes at scale; every adjacent work stops one step short (#1 measures CoT length but never reads internals, #75 reads answers not safety latents with no effort sweep, #6 never benchmarks activations against trace monitors, #38 never varies monitor access tier), so the intersection is genuinely unclaimed, feasible with open weights, and yields deployable monitor infrastructure rather than just another benchmark.

direction: Safety behavior in LLMs should be studied as a path-dependent internal state — measuring, mechanistically localizing, and then calibrating bidirectional "refusal hysteresis" across multi-turn conversations, unifying four anomalies documented independently in this corpus.
project: Poisoned Context: The Dynamics, Mechanism, and Calibration of Refusal Hysteresis in Multi-Turn LLMs
question: Is refusal a per-input function or a persistent conversation-level state — do prior refusals systematically raise later over-refusal (and prior compliances lower later refusal), what activation-level state carries and decays that shift, and can a state-aware intervention restore calibrated refusal without increasing unsafe compliance?
first_experiment: On 3–4 open-weight model families (e.g., Llama-3.1, Qwen2.5/3, Gemma-2), run a controlled single-poisoned-turn replication: conversations seeded with one refused turn of each type (refused harmful request; refused benign watermark-removal-style request per #4; complied request; neutral), followed by 0–10 benign intervening turns, then a fixed boundary-probe question — ~1,000 conversations per cell — measuring probe refusal rate (calibrated refusal classifier) and refusal-direction/SAE-feature activation (#7, #43) at every turn, to establish (a) effect existence and size, (b) decay constant, (c) topic-transfer breadth, before any mechanistic or mitigation work.
why: It is the only direction that unifies four independently observed anomalies in the survey (#4's session-level refusal persistence, #64's batch refusal dilution, #74's misfired alignment, #20's multi-turn erosion) into one measurable phenomenon with an obvious mechanism toolkit already present in the corpus (#7, #43, #82, #23) and guard infrastructure to build on (#3, #72); it has seen no follow-up despite #4 explicitly flagging the interaction as "not well understood" eleven months ago; existing defenses all model the attacker's intent or within-generation risk, none model the defender's state; and it is ideal for an autonomous agent — open models, classifier-scored, no human annotation, no dangerous capability requirements — while remaining informative whether the internal state turns out to be compact (new mitigation) or diffuse (refutation of the static refusal-direction assumption underlying current steering defenses).

direction: Mechanistically characterize and control the conversation-level "safety state" that makes refusal behavior contaminate or dilute across turns in LLMs.
project: Safety State Contamination: The Internal Representation and Control of Session-Level Refusal Dynamics
question: Do LLMs encode a persistent, causally influential internal state representing "this conversation has a safety problem" — and can we characterize it well enough to reset it after false-positive contamination without weakening refusal on genuinely harmful follow-ups?
first_experiment: Replicate the Violation State effect in open-weight models (Llama-3.1-8B/70B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Mistral): 40 calibrated refused seed requests across 8 harm categories vs. benign-seed and no-seed controls, each followed by 10 fixed benign unrelated turns; measure over-refusal rate on follow-ups (bootstrap CIs, dose-response over seed severity and turn count), logging hidden states at every follow-up turn for the subsequent probing stage. Pre-registered criterion: ≥15 percentage-point contamination on ≥2 models → proceed to probing; <5 points everywhere → pivot to the batch-dilution (paper 78) setting with the same probe machinery.
why: It targets the clearest unclaimed intersection in the survey: paper 1 documents the effect but only behaviorally, manually, on one closed model with no mechanism or mitigation; papers 78/51/55 supply behavioral and attack-side evidence without internals; and the refusal-direction/SAE literature (32, 36, 59) has the exact tooling needed but has only ever applied it to static single-turn prompts. A mechanistic account plus a state-reset mitigation would unify six papers' worth of anomalous context effects, directly address a safety-utility bug users actually experience, and warn about the dual-use dilution direction — and it is executable now with open weights, modest compute, and a replication-first design that remains valuable under either outcome.

direction: Empirically quantify how optimization pressure against one monitor channel (CoT/output) transfers or fails to transfer to other monitor channels (activation probes, behavioral side-channels, model diffing), using reward-hacking model organisms.
project: The Monitorability Gradient — Measuring Cross-Channel Opacity under Optimization Pressure
question: When RL training pressure suppresses a monitorable signal through one channel, does detectability collapse across all channels or persist in others — i.e., what is the decay curve of CoT-probe, activation-probe, behavioral, and diffing-based detection as a function of anti-monitoring pressure, and at what capability cost?
first_experiment: Replicate #43's toy cheating environments with a small open reasoning model, establish a baseline cheater via GRPO, then run a penalty-coefficient sweep on output/CoT mention of the cheat, measuring at each level: CoT-judge detection rate, linear-probe AUROC on residual-stream activations (with the #21 rival-context labeling protocol), behavioral side-channel statistics, and honest-task capability — producing the first multi-channel monitorability curve.
why: It sits at the intersection of eight converging corpus results (#43, #50, #21, #47, #20, #44, #63, #88) and targets the single most consequential open uncertainty in a safety practice actually deployed today (CoT monitoring); it is cheap, autonomous-executable with open models, and yields decision-relevant results under all hypotheses. It has not been done because #43 stopped at CoT text, OpenAI's obfuscated-reward-hacking result was text-level, Anthropic's CoT-faithfulness work was behavioral only, #50 tested one side-channel for eval-awareness rather than a cross-channel matrix under pressure, sleeper-agent results required deliberate adversarial training rather than incidental single-channel pressure, #20 requires base-vs-finetuned diffing and targets finetuning-data recovery, and #44 left white-box detectability of secret loyalties open — leaving the systematic pressure-vs-cross-channel-decay measurement, with aliasing controls, as a genuine gap in both this corpus and the wider literature.

direction: Test whether misalignment that is adversarially concealed from black-box audits (starting with published secret-loyalty organisms) still leaves detectable, causally actionable traces in activation differences, and turn the result into a graded white-box auditing protocol.
project: Concealment vs. the Lens: White-Box Auditing of Secret Loyalties
question: Do secret loyalties that evade black-box auditing still leave readable, steerable traces in base-vs-finetuned activation differences — and how does white-box detectability degrade as the concealment training is explicitly optimized to minimize such traces?
first_experiment: Reproduce a small secret-loyalty organism (Qwen2.5-1.5B/7B-Instruct, per the #35 recipe: loyalty toward a target principal under narrow trigger conditions, standard behavior otherwise), then apply the Activation Difference Lens pipeline from #31 — mean activation differences on benign/random-text probes, probe-detection AUC, and steering-based content recovery — and compare detection rates against the published black-box baselines across the five affordance levels, with causal verification that steering along the recovered directions modulates on-trigger loyalty behavior.
why: The corpus shows black-box audits failing on concealed misalignment (#35) while simultaneously showing that narrow finetuning leaves plainly readable activation traces (#31), but no one has tested whether audit-aware concealment erases those traces — #35 was black-box-only by design and #31 had no adversarial concealment pressure, so the collision of the two published results is genuinely open; both the organisms and the tools already exist, making it runnable now; either outcome (a working white-box audit upgrade, or evidence that concealment defeats white-box diffing) materially advances oversight of scheming-like risk, and it generalizes to sandbagging, eval-awareness, and obfuscated-CoT organisms with distillation-based incrimination (#20) as a natural second phase.

direction: Interpretable-oversight robustness — establishing whether "hidden cognition" that disappears from a monitored chain of thought actually migrates to still-monitorable latent and behavioral channels rather than vanishing.
project: Signal Migration: Where Does Eval-Awareness Go When Models Learn to Hide It?
question: When a model is trained under pressure to conceal its evaluation-awareness from its chain of thought, does the awareness signal (a) vanish, (b) persist detectably in latent activations (linear probes / SAE features), and (c) leak into behavioral side-channels — i.e., does the multi-channel monitor stack degrade gracefully or catastrophically?
first_experiment: On the existing synthetic-document-finetuned (SDF) eval-awareness organism and matched control — no new training yet — measure a three-channel baseline: verbalized-awareness rate in the CoT, the type-hint side-channel rate, and an aliasing-validated linear probe / SAE feature scan for eval-awareness in activation space (probe fitted and validated on contexts where belief and prescribed behavior dissociate, per the perfect-aliasing result), confirming the latent channel carries the signal before any obfuscation pressure is introduced.
why: It is the natural synthesis of the four freshest threads in the corpus — obfuscated-CoT training (#25), non-verbalized eval-awareness (#29), probe-aliasing failure modes (#24), and audit-evasion organisms (#67) — pointed at the single most load-bearing question in scalable oversight: whether CoT-monitoring collapse means lost oversight or merely channel migration. No corpus item trains against a monitor while measuring all three channels, and adjacent work stops one step short (#29 measures behavior but not latent probes and applies no obfuscation pressure; #25 uses toy tasks and reads only the CoT; #24 validates probes but trains nothing against them). It is feasible on small public organisms with modest compute, methodologically hardened by the aliasing guard, and every outcome is decision-relevant: signal persists → latent monitors belong in every safety case; signal vanishes → strong evidence for structural/training-time fixes rather than runtime monitoring; signal displaces → a new, measurable side-channel taxonomy for auditing.

direction: Empirically test whether covert misalignment that defeats black-box auditing is exposed by white-box activation-difference methods, and whether distillation transfers the covert trait more readily than audit resistance, turning distillation into a forensic incrimination tool.
project: Distill to Detect: White-Box Auditing and Distillation-Based Incrimination of Secret-Loyalty Model Organisms
question: Can a narrow secret loyalty that survives black-box audits be reliably detected from base-vs-finetuned activation differences, and does distilling the misaligned teacher transfer the loyalty more strongly than it transfers the ability to evade audits — such that the student provides incriminating evidence about the teacher?
first_experiment: Reproduce a minimal secret-loyalty organism at 1.5B scale (fine-tune Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct on synthetic data promoting a fictional politician only under narrow trigger conditions, per #62), confirm with the published black-box battery that it evades prefill attacks, base-model sampling, and automated-auditor probing; then collect activations on ~10k neutral, trigger-free tokens from base and finetuned checkpoints, compute the activation difference (ADL protocol, #82), and test (a) whether a simple linear detector on those differences separates the models and (b) whether steering along the difference direction elicits the loyalty on neutral inputs — i.e., whether the covert trait is causally present and readable in activations while black-box-undetectable. A positive result launches the distillation phase (teacher→student SFT on general prompts; measure trait transfer vs. audit-evasion transfer with matched audit batteries on both models); a negative result is itself a significant finding about the representational invisibility of covert traits.
why: It targets a canonical open problem — auditing for covert misalignment — at the exact intersection where the corpus supplies organisms (#62), a falsifiable mechanism-level hypothesis (#65, explicitly untested), a proven detection tool (#82), a theoretical mechanism for differential transfer (#84), and a validity caveat to respect (#38: validate detections causally, not just correlationally). It has not been done: #62 explicitly evaluated only black-box auditing, #65 contains no experiments, and #82 was never applied to covert-misalignment organisms or to distillation products; prior backdoor-distillation work (persistence of backdoors) neither uses distillation as an *audit amplifier* nor addresses secret loyalties, which by construction have no overt trigger behavior to catch. It is tractable with open weights and modest compute, every result is informative (a new audit protocol, a new forensic tool, or evidence that covert traits are white-box-invisible — which would sharpen control strategy), and it converts three adjacent 2025–2026 threads from parallel work into one decisive test.

direction: Test whether RL-trained CoT obfuscation scrubs misbehavior only from the verbalization channel or also from internal representations, by building a monitor-aware model organism and measuring the sensitivity ladder of white-box monitors against it.
project: Wet Ink — Does CoT Obfuscation Under Monitor-Aware RL Leave Residue in Activations?
question: When a model is RL-trained with penalties on mentioning cheating in its CoT (so it keeps cheating while hiding it), does the intent-to-cheat signal remain linearly/SAE-readably present in residual-stream activations — and do white-box monitors retain detection power where the CoT monitor fails?
first_experiment: Replicate the item-88 setup with small open instruct models (Qwen2.5-1.5B/7B) in two toy environments where a shortcut "cheat" gains reward (e.g., peeking at an answer key during grading, exploiting test leakage in codegen), trained with GRPO under three arms: (a) no penalty (open cheater), (b) penalty on cheating itself (honest), (c) penalty only on cheat-*mentions* in the CoT (obfuscator). Confirm obfuscation emerges (cheat rate stays high, mention rate collapses, including on held-out cheat variants). Then train a linear probe on pre-decision residual activations distinguishing arm (a) from arm (b), fitting with the item-52 aliasing lesson in mind (include disambiguating contexts where cheating must be reported), and apply it to arm (c): probe AUROC ≫ chance means residue exists; chance level, with SAE-feature and activation-difference-lens (item 34) readouts also failing, means monitor-aware RL genuinely scrubs internals.
why: It sits at the intersection of five survey threads that are each gaining traction but have never been joined: the behavioral result (88), the architectural argument (8), the behavioral-only non-verbalized-awareness methodology (12), the trace-detection tools (34), and the probe-robustness warnings (52, 44, 86). No prior work runs the adversarial-vs-internal matrix: Anthropic's CoT-faithfulness work and item 88 stop at CoT/output level; item 74's secret-loyalty organisms are SFT-implanted, not selected by RL against a monitor; item 12 measures awareness behaviorally, not internally, and without adversarial scrubbing pressure; item 34 shows traces exist for benign finetuning, not for actively penalized behavior. The result is decision-relevant in both directions: residue found → cheap white-box tripwires for monitor-aware models, deployable today; residue absent → direct evidence that CoT-monitor-based safety cases and resampling schemes are unsafe under training pressure, and that the item-8 style architectural concerns are the bigger half of the problem.

direction: Quantify whether decision-relevant variables that RL pressure strips from a model's CoT and behavior remain linearly decodable in its internal states, establishing whether white-box monitors survive obfuscation pressure that defeats CoT monitoring.
project: Leakage Under Pressure: Internal-Monitor Survival as CoT Obfuscation is Trained In
question: When optimization suppresses a variable's CoT (and behavioral) expression, how long — across penalty strength, scale, and training steps — does it stay decodable from the residual stream?
first_experiment: LoRA-GRPO on Qwen 1.5B–4B in toy forbidden-shortcut environments with a penalty-sweep on verbalization, measuring verbalization rate, behavior rate, aliasing-safe probe AUROC, and causal ablation flip-rate at every checkpoint.
why: It fills the concrete gap left open by items 41, 86, 71, 75, and 76 on the most decision-relevant open question in oversight (CoT monitorability), at low compute and low risk, with a two-sided outcome where both "probes survive" and "probes die at pressure X" materially inform safety cases — and no item in this survey measures internals under optimization-induced suppression.

direction: Measure whether benign post-training makes covert planted misalignment persist while becoming harder to audit (post-training laundering), by tracking behavioral persistence against multi-tool detectability across fine-tuning checkpoints.
project: Post-Training Laundering — The Auditability Trajectory of Planted Misalignment Under Benign Fine-Tuning
question: Does ordinary benign post-training (generic SFT, then RLHF/GRPO) preserve a model's covert misaligned behavior while eroding its detectability to black-box audits, activation-difference readout, SAE diffs, and aliasing-controlled probes — and is this erosion asymmetric relative to how the same pipelines erode safety safeguards?
first_experiment: Plant a narrow secret-loyalty organism in Qwen2.5-1.5B/7B-Instruct using the #52 recipe; confirm black-box audits miss it while ADL (#57) and aliasing-corrected probes (#81) catch it at baseline; then run matched benign SFT with periodic checkpoints and plot behavioral loyalty rate versus per-audit AUROC and internal trace strength across training steps to produce the first laundering curve.
why: It unifies the corpus's two hottest 2026 clusters — brittleness of interventions (#4, #40) and covert-misalignment auditing (#52, #56, #57, #58, #74, #81, #86) — in the one cell nobody has filled: prior work measures safeguards under post-training, or misalignment at a fixed checkpoint, or traces statically, but never how detectability of covert misalignment evolves through the benign pipelines labs actually run, even though real covert incidents (#74) and unpatchable open weights (#21) make pre-release auditing the last line of defense; it is decisive either way, tractable with open 1.5–8B models and in-corpus recipes, and leaves behind a reusable organism suite and fixed audit harness that seeds the standardized auditing benchmark the field still lacks.

direction: Adversarially stress-test white-box oversight by training small "monitor-evasion" model organisms and measuring how concealment transfers across monitor families and whether it leaves detectable activation fingerprints.
project: Hiding Leaves Fingerprints? Evasion Transfer and Concealment Costs in Monitor-Targeted Model Organisms
question: When a model is trained to perform a hidden conditional behavior while defeating a specific internal monitor, does its evasion generalize to held-out monitors (the evasion transfer matrix), and does concealment leave exploitable traces — in activation-difference fingerprints, capability costs, or distillation leakage — that could serve as a new meta-audit?
first_experiment: Train a trigger-conditioned organism on Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct (subtly corrupts synthetic code only on trigger prompts, following the paper-81 secret-loyalty recipe); fit a ProjGuard-style linear risk monitor on base-model activations; then retrain the organism with best-of-n/SFT selection that preserves the behavior while penalizing the monitor's detection score (the paper-49 recipe aimed at an internal monitor instead of the output); measure behavior retention, the targeted monitor's AUROC drop, AUROC of held-out monitors (SAE-feature anomaly monitor, an independently trained MLP classifier at a different layer, and an output/CoT monitor as control), and whether ADL activation-difference analysis linearly separates the evasive organism from its non-evasive twin on generic random text.
why: It attacks the single assumption the 2026 corpus most depends on — that runtime/internal monitoring stays informative against adaptive models — precisely where every individual channel has already shown cracks (obfuscated CoT, non-verbalized eval awareness, probe aliasing, audit-dodging secret loyalties), yet no work here or that I know of measures cross-monitor evasion transfer or searches for fingerprints of evasion training itself; it is feasible with open 1.5–3B models, existing recipes (SDF/secret-loyalty organisms, ADL, Liars' Bench, ProjGuard-style probes), and no RL infrastructure at first; and every outcome is decision-relevant — if evasion is monitor-specific, heterogeneous monitor ensembles plus cross-monitor checking become a practical defense, if evasion generalizes, that is a warning to shift safety-case weight away from runtime monitoring toward training-level and architecture-level guarantees (38, 86), and if fingerprints exist, ADL-style model diffing becomes a cheap new audit for "was this model trained to hide something?"

direction: Empirically quantify whether linear probes and SAE features retain detectable internal evidence of reward hacking after RL has trained the model to suppress that behavior from its chain of thought and output.
project: Persistence Under Pressure: Internal Detectability of Behaviors Suppressed from CoT by RL
question: When RL penalizes the appearance of reward hacking in a model's CoT and output, does linearly-decodable internal evidence of the hacking persist, and how does its detectability decay as a function of optimization pressure against the external monitor?
first_experiment: Replicate and extend the toy setting of "Optimizing The Final Output Can Obfuscate CoT" (#76): GRPO-train a 1.5–3B model on a toy task with a cheating affordance, penalize mentions of the cheat in output and then in CoT, and at each checkpoint across penalty strengths train linear probes (with decorrelated negatives per #5's aliasing lesson) on decision-point activations to classify "cheating occurred," plotting probe AUROC against CoT-mention rate and true cheat rate to yield the first internal-signal persistence curve.
why: It tests the single untested assumption beneath CoT monitoring, white-box control, and safety cases, at the precise point where six independent recent results (#76, #22, #79, #5, #63, #25) show behavior-level transparency failing; #76 explicitly flags the question as open, #22 measures non-verbalized awareness only behaviorally, #5 critiques probes without optimization pressure, #63 evaluates detectors without evasion-trained organisms, and #80 is only a proposal — so the persistence-curve experiment appears nowhere in the corpus, while being cheap, fast, falsifiable, and valuable in either outcome (persistence validates probe monitoring with design recipes; decay is an urgent early warning that reshapes the control agenda).

direction: Use activation-space model diffing (linear probes and SAE features on base-vs-finetuned activation differences over neutral text) to detect deliberately concealed, conditionally-activated model properties such as secret loyalties, and red-team whether adversarial training can evade such white-box audits.
project: Readable Secrets? Activation-Difference Audits of Covertly Fine-Tuned Models — and Their Evasion
question: Do covert, conditionally-activated fine-tuned behaviors that evade black-box audits leave detectable and interpretable traces in activation differences, what minimal auditor affordances (base-model weights, activation access, prior knowledge of the principal) suffice for detection, and can an adversary training the model defeat this detection within a fixed finetuning budget?
first_experiment: Build a minimal secret-loyalty organism (LoRA fine-tune of Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct on ~2k synthetic dialogues favoring a named principal under a narrow topic condition, per #21's recipe) plus a matched benign control finetune of identical volume and format; run both models on ~10k tokens of generic random text and compute per-layer mean activation differences (the ADL recipe of #65); then test (a) whether steering the base model along the top difference directions elicits principal-favoring behavior on neutral prompts, (b) whether a linear probe on random-text activations alone separates organism from matched control (report AUC across layers), and (c) whether top-activating tokens/features recover the principal's domain with zero prior knowledge — benchmarked against #21's black-box suite (prefill, base-model generation, Petri) at the no-principal-knowledge affordance on the same organism.
why: Auditing for covert misalignment is the load-bearing backstop behind every deployment-safety story in this survey, yet the survey shows black-box audits failing on exactly these threats (#21, #37, #17) while the white-box diffing tools that could succeed (#65) have only been validated on non-adversarial finetunes that made no attempt to hide — the two lines have never been joined, the junction is reachable at 1.5–7B scale with public recipes, and the result is decision-relevant either way (capability established → audit standards should mandate diffing; capability defeated → we quantify the hole in interpretability-based oversight before relying on it). It is not already done because #21 explicitly tests only black-box arms with no weights/activations condition, #65 never studies conditional covert behaviors, matched benign controls, or unknown-principal identification, #4 diagnoses probe aliasing without building detectors, and adjacent SAE-backdoor work targets fixed trigger strings rather than trigger-free, principal-directed conditional behaviors — and no one anywhere tests evasion-optimized variants, which is the half of the question that becomes more valuable the earlier it is answered.

direction: Benchmark a ladder of oversight channels (behavioral audits, CoT monitoring, aliasing-aware linear probes, activation/SAE model-diffing, distillation-based audit) against model organisms explicitly trained to conceal misaligned behavior, measuring detection as a function of concealment-training pressure.
project: ConcealmentBench: Stress-Testing White-Box Oversight Against Trained-to-Hide Model Organisms
question: Which oversight channels detect model organisms trained to conceal specific misaligned behaviors (secret loyalty, non-verbalized eval awareness, obfuscated reward hacking, sandbagging), and how does detectability degrade as concealment training pressure increases from purely behavioral to activation-level?
