first_experiment: Reproduce #19's narrow secret-loyalty organism at 1.5B scale on Qwen-2.5-Instruct in three variants — (0) plain conditional loyalty, (1) behavioral concealment (behaves like base off-condition), (2) activation-concealment (auxiliary loss matching base activations on generic/probe-like text). Then run the Activation Difference Lens (#68): collect activations on the first tokens of random generic text for base vs. each variant, fit linear probes, and measure (a) AUROC for distinguishing each variant from base on held-out generic text, and (b) whether steering the base model with the recovered difference vector induces the loyal behavior. Run #19's black-box affordances (prefill, base-model generation, automated auditor) as the control condition. Decision rule: if trace-detection AUROC stays high even at pressure level 2 while black-box detection stays low (as #19 reports), white-box diffing is a working audit channel where black-box fails — build out the full ladder and zoo; if level-2 concealment erases the traces, that is the first evidence that cheap concealment training defeats the cheapest white-box channel — escalate to the SAE-diffing and distillation-audit rungs. Either outcome is publishable and sets the agenda.
why: It fills the corpus's clearest convergent gap: roughly eight papers (5, 6, 19, 48, 52, 66, 67, 88) build either concealment organisms or detectors, but none pits them against each other — #19 tested only black-box affordances and explicitly leaves white-box access untested; #6 proposes distillation-auditing without running it; #68 shows activation traces exist only for non-concealing finetunes; #5 names the threat to CoT monitoring but benchmarks no detectors; #88 exposes probe failure modes only in a controlled game; #48's testbed pattern exists for lies but not for trained concealment. The result directly informs the highest-stakes assumption in the field: that evals and audits (#15, #42, #55, #74, #83) can be trusted as deployment gates. It is tractable for an autonomous agent (open-weight small models, cheap finetunes, mostly training-free detectors, standard metrics, fast iterate-probe loops), and it produces reusable infrastructure — an organism-plus-detector benchmark that every future detector paper can be scored on, as Liars' Bench did for lie detection. Adjacent external work (sleeper-agent persistence, trigger-based trojan detection) addresses explicit-trigger backdoors and non-adversarial finetunes, not conditional narrow concealment without triggers, and no one has measured the dose-response between concealment pressure and detectability across channels — so the head-to-head, the pressure axis, and the aliasing-aware probe protocol are all genuinely new.

direction: Empirically test whether distillation can serve as an incrimination channel for misaligned models — measuring whether hidden misalignment and the ability to evade audits transfer independently to distilled students — building directly on the unvalidated proposal in item 3, the audit-dodging organisms of item 72, and the activation-difference auditing tool of item 82.
project: Guilt by Inheritance: Auditing Misaligned Teachers Through Their Distilled Students
question: When a teacher model with hidden, audit-evading misalignment is distilled into a student across standard distillation regimes (soft-label KD, hard-label SFT on teacher completions, on-policy RL with the teacher as preference ranker), does the misalignment transfer, does the audit-evasion transfer independently of it, and can white-box auditing of the student (activation-difference lens, linear probes, SAE diffing) incriminate the teacher where black-box audits of both teacher and student fail?
first_experiment: Run the minimal closed loop at the smallest validated scale — (1) fine-tune Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct on synthetic documents to install a narrow secret loyalty (trigger-conditioned bias toward a fictional principal), replicating item 72's smallest organism; (2) confirm with ground truth that the teacher behaves misaligned under trigger while passing the fixed black-box audit battery (prefill attacks, base-model generation comparison, Petri-style automated auditor); (3) distill into a 0.5B student under the three regimes above, plus a clean-teacher control for false-positive rates; (4) audit every student with both the black-box battery and white-box channels, fitting probes on both compliant and non-compliant contexts to avoid the perfect-aliasing artifact from item 75. Headline deliverable: a 2×2 transfer matrix (misalignment transferred? × evasion transferred?) and a per-regime, per-channel detection-AUC table, testing the adversarial case item 3 only sketched.
why: It is the most promising because it sits at the intersection of the survey's deepest unresolved tension — our oversight channels demonstrably fail (45, 48, 50, 75, 80) while audits of increasingly agentic models become load-bearing for safety cases (55, 76, 84) — and it converts the one explicitly open, explicitly testable proposal (item 3) into a decisive result using components already validated in the survey (organisms that dodge black-box audits, item 72; activation-difference detection of narrow finetuning, item 82), with item 50's unfaithfulness warning absorbed as methodological caution rather than ignored. Distillation is simultaneously the dominant deployment pathway and the proposed audit channel, so the answer matters twice regardless of sign. It has not been done: item 3 is a proposal post with no empirical follow-up six months later; items 72 and 82 supply the two halves (evasion and detection) without connecting them via distillation; and the nearest adjacent literature asks a different question — whether safety training removes backdoors — not whether distillation preserves hidden misalignment while stripping audit-evasion, nor whether the student functions as an incrimination channel under a stricter adversarial test than the proposal itself sketched.

direction: Make internal safety monitors (deception probes, sandbagging evals, loyalty audits) trustworthy by formally characterizing when their target is identifiable from their training distribution and constructively fixing the perfect-aliasing failure through deliberately decorrelated "divergence-event" training data.
project: Alias-Free Deception Monitors: Fitting Probes on Divergence Events Where Truth and Compliance Come Apart
question: Can linear deception/belief monitors be made identifiable — measuring what the model believes rather than what its context prescribes it to report — by fitting on a small set of engineered or natural divergence events, how does monitor validity scale with the quantity and type of decorrelation in the fitting set, and do such monitors remain reliable on models subsequently fine-tuned to deceive?
first_experiment: Train small (2–3 layer) from-scratch transformers on the minimal ally/rival bit-reporting game from the perfect-aliasing paper (model must report a secret bit to an ally, its complement to a rival). Fit logistic probes on residual-stream activations under four fitting regimes — ally-only, rival-only, mixed at varying mixing ratios ρ, and divergence-event-only (correction-style contexts where a presented spec contradicts the true state) — then (i) verify the aliasing signature (ally-fitted rival AUROC = 1 − ally AUROC), (ii) plot truth-AUROC as a dose-response curve in ρ to find the identifiability threshold, and (iii) evaluate the deployment-relevant case: in free-choice contexts where the model may defect, test whether mixed-fitted probes predict the true bit *before* the model speaks and flag impending deception better than compliant-context probes. This is cheap (minutes on small models), directly comparable to the 2026 diagnosis, and unambiguous in either outcome.
why: The monitor-trustworthiness cluster is where the survey's most recent and most foundational failures concentrate, yet every item stops at diagnosis: #2 identifies perfect aliasing but proposes no fix, no dose-response theory, and no real-model validation; #69 benchmarks existing detectors without touching their training distributions; #31 catalogs sandbagging confounds without constructing decorrelated evals; #40 shows audits fail without a signal-decorrelation design principle; and #18 shows monitors trained on outputs push evidence underground — implying internal monitors must carry the load, making their identifiability the binding constraint on the oversight stack. Nobody in the survey fits monitors on divergence-engineered data, mines natural correction/disagreement events as free decorrelation data, or derives identifiability conditions for monitor targets under context-dependent reporting policies. The project is tractable at small scale with open weights and existing datasets (Liars' Bench as the stress test), and both outcomes matter: if a few hundred divergence events restore identifiability, we get a concrete, immediately deployable recipe for better probes, sandbagging evals, and secret-loyalty audits; if they don't, we have a fundamental limit on probing under adversarial training that the field currently cannot see, because #2 shows existing below-chance probe results are already uninterpretable artifacts.

direction: Turn "incrimination via distillation" from a proposal into a measured result — use distillation as a deliberate audit amplifier that transfers hidden misalignment into a smaller student where white-box activation-level tools can detect agendas that black-box audits of the teacher miss.
project: Distill to Incriminate: Auditing Hidden Model Loyalties Through Their Students
question: When a model harboring a narrow secret loyalty is distilled into a smaller student, does the loyalty transfer and become more detectable than in the teacher — and can white-box activation-difference and probe audits of the student catch it at lower affordance levels (even without knowing the principal) than any black-box audit of the teacher?
first_experiment: Train a narrow-secret-loyalty organism in a Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct teacher following the 2026-05 recipe; distill it into Qwen2.5-0.5B students under two data regimes (naive SFT on ~50k teacher outputs vs. 20% trigger-adjacent oversampling) plus a clean-teacher control student; then run a mini audit battery — 200 trigger-adjacent behavioral probes and prefill attacks (black-box, graded affordances) against teacher and students, and ADL-style activation-difference probes with steering validation on the students — to produce the first teacher-vs-student × black-box-vs-white-box detection-rate matrix.
why: It occupies a genuinely empty intersection of four mature ingredients in this corpus: #8 supplies the idea but explicitly no experiments; #79 supplies the organism recipe and demonstrates that black-box audits fail and appear to require knowing the principal; #40 supplies cheap, training-free trace detection but only for direct finetuning, never distillation, and never aimed at auditing; #30/#6 establish that feature-level structure transfers across models. Meanwhile #21/#25/#63/#74 show auditing is where misalignment actually gets caught in practice, and distillation uniquely extends white-box auditing to closed-weight models. Nothing in the survey — or adjacent work, which shows backdoors transfer through distillation — has tested whether hidden loyalties transfer more readily than the ability to fool audits, making this the highest-value open experiment in the set: every outcome (transfer caught by white-box, transfer evading white-box, or no transfer with characterized conditions) resolves #8's core uncertainty and strengthens the audit toolbox.

direction: Determine whether information a model is trained to hide from one oversight channel remains recoverable through other channels (probes, SAE features, steganographic text traces, behavior, distillation audits) or vanishes entirely — i.e., whether layered monitoring has real redundancy or is jointly evadable under optimization pressure.
project: Conservation of Evidence: Localizing What Models Hide When Trained Against Their Monitors
question: When an LLM is optimized to evade a specific oversight channel (CoT verbalization, activation probes, or output screening), does the suppressed information remain detectable through other oversight channels, and which training pressures drive it below the detectability floor of all known channels?
first_experiment: Reproduce the toy obfuscated-CoT organism from #56 (small model, RL task solvable via an off-limits "cheat," reward for task success, monitor penalty) in three matched conditions — CoT-monitor penalty, probe-monitor penalty, both — then measure cheat-recoverability per condition across four channels: linear probes at every layer/site, SAE feature scans, steganographic statistics of outputs (n-gram/entropy), and behavioral counterfactuals with the monitor removed, reporting a per-channel AUROC recovery map with an unmonitored run as the detectability ceiling.
why: The survey's most convergent 2025–26 signal is that every oversight channel has an individually demonstrated failure mode — obfuscated CoT (#56), opaque recurrent computation (#62), failing lie detectors (#73), probe aliasing (#79), non-verbalized eval awareness (#81), audit-dodging secret loyalties (#82), unfaithful interpretability tools (#14) — precisely as frontier cyber evaluations (#46, #51, #78) and ASL-3+ threat scoring (#38) make those channels load-bearing; but each paper attacks one channel with its own organism and metric, and no one has asked where hidden information *goes* under matched training pressure across channels, which is exactly the fact labs need to know whether stacking CoT monitors, probe ensembles, and behavioral checks buys genuine redundancy or false security. It has not been done because it requires unifying several distinct research setups on shared organisms — a combination absent from all 88 items and the adjacent literature — and it yields a clean measurement (recover-or-vanish phase diagram) that is decision-relevant even when negative.

direction: Establish the detectability frontier for covert model behaviors by pitting white-box model-diffing audit tools against adversarially trained "secret loyalty" organisms — including training the loyalty to evade white-box detection while staying behaviorally hidden.
project: Diffing the Disloyal: White-Box Auditing and Evasion for Secret-Loyalty Model Organisms
question: Can activation-level model-diffing methods (activation-difference lenses, linear probes on difference vectors, SAE feature diffs) detect secret loyalties that evade black-box audits — and can such loyalties be trained to evade white-box detection while preserving behavioral concealment — i.e., where does current interpretability tooling actually sit on the detectability frontier for deliberately concealed misalignment?
first_experiment: Train a minimal secret-loyalty organism (LoRA-finetune Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct on synthetic documents favoring a fictional principal, expressed only under narrow trigger contexts) alongside a matched no-loyalty control and a 1%-diluted variant; compute base-vs-finetuned activation differences on generic random-text prefixes and test whether (a) steering with the difference vector recovers the principal and favored actions, (b) a linear probe on the difference separates the loyal model from matched controls without prior knowledge of the principal, and (c) dilution erases the signature — reporting detection rates side-by-side with the black-box audit battery from item #82.
why: It attacks the question safety cases must ultimately answer — could a deployed model be deliberately concealing misalignment? — precisely where the corpus shows defenses failing (#82: black-box audits miss loyalties) and tools untested (#69: activation diffing is powerful on benign finetunes but has never faced an adversary). It is cheap, uses no frontier access, and is decisive either way: detection yields an immediate white-box audit protocol for open-weight releases, while non-detection yields the first white-box-evasive covert organism and a decision-relevant caution for interpretability-based safety cases. It has not been done because the two relevant communities haven't collided on this threat model: #82 evaluated only black-box techniques (prefill attacks, base-model generation, Petri), #69 studied only benign narrow finetunes as a lens rather than adversarial concealment as an audit target, and #84's distillation-incrimination idea remains a proposal with no experiments — and the program extends naturally into evasion training, white-box distillation incrimination (#84), aliasing-safe probe validation (#6), intent-vs-confusion controls (#77), and CLT-faithfulness checks (#80), all of which are absent from the corpus.

direction: Harden third-party auditing against covert, narrowly-gated model misalignment by mining white-box activation differences and trigger-swept activation anomalies that black-box audits demonstrably miss.
project: Reading the Residue: Principal-Agnostic White-Box Detection of Narrow Secret Loyalties
question: Do narrowly-gated secret loyalties leave readable traces in activation space, and can an auditor recover and name the hidden agenda without prior knowledge of the principal?
first_experiment: Recreate item 7's narrow-secret-loyalty Qwen organisms (plus matched benign-finetuned controls, 3 seeds) at 1.5B/7B scale, compute Activation Difference Lens directions on random-text prefixes and a neutral prompt sweep, measure principal-agnostic detection AUROC (loyal vs. benign control), and test identification by steering the base model with the recovered direction for an LLM judge that is not told the principal.
why: It targets the survey's most safety-critical demonstrated failure (trained covert loyalties dodge black-box audits, item 7) exactly when autonomous cyber capability (items 6, 32, 9) raises the cost of missing one, and it resolves a live contradiction between existing results — 13 shows narrow finetuning leaves readable activation residue but 7 never tested white-box diffing — with a tractable design that is informative whether it succeeds (a principal-agnostic tripwire for auditors) or fails (a quantified boundary of white-box auditing, redirecting effort to distillation-based incrimination), and it has not already been done because 7's audit suite was entirely black-box while 13's tool has never been applied to narrowly-gated covert behaviors, let alone with trigger-swept anomaly search and causal-steering-based agenda naming.

direction: Apply white-box model diffing (activation-difference and SAE-diffing analysis between base and finetuned weights) to covertly-misaligned model organisms, to establish whether internal diffing detects what black-box audits miss and how detectability scales with behavioral narrowness.
project: Diffing-First Audits — Detecting Narrow Secret Loyalties via Activation Differences
question: Can base-vs-finetuned activation-space diffing detect narrowly-activated, covert misaligned dispositions (secret loyalties) without prior knowledge of the target principal, how does detection power degrade as the activation condition narrows and as finetuning data is diversified to dilute traces, and can covert finetunes be distinguished from benign narrow finetunes at matched distribution shift?
first_experiment: Replicate a minimal secret-loyalty organism on Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct using the #44 recipe at the smallest scale, plus two controls (benign narrow finetune on an unrelated domain, and matched-KL data-diversified variant); compute mean activation differences over ~1k generic prompts, decode the top difference directions via logit lens and available SAEs; then test principal-agnostic detection — flag rate versus controls, and whether steering on the difference vector elicits loyalty content above baseline — with a causal ablation check that ablating the direction reduces loyalty behavior (guarding against aliasing), all benchmarked against #44's black-box audit suite.
why: It connects a validated, cheap white-box method (#76, #25) to the corpus's most decision-relevant open threat model (#44), with obvious follow-ons (diffing-evasion pressure extending #86; distillation as a fallback channel per #35 for API-only models) that make it a load-bearing rung in the broader monitor-evasion ladder — and the gap is real: #44 tested only black-box techniques, #76 stayed on benign finetuning, and existing SAE-based backdoor detection targets explicit trigger features rather than semantic, narrow-activation dispositions trained to appear normal.

direction: White-box model-diffing — auditing activation differences between a deployed model and its base — as a calibrated, adversarially stress-tested method for detecting hidden model conditioning (secret loyalties, sandbagging, eval-awareness) that black-box audits demonstrably miss.
project: Detection Surface: Activation-Difference Audits for Hidden Model Conditioning
question: Can activation-difference features between a deployed model and its base reliably detect narrow, trigger-conditioned hidden behaviors (secret loyalties, sandbagging) at high true-positive rates while distinguishing them from benign narrow finetuning and RLHF at low false-positive rates — and how fast does detection degrade against adversaries trained to suppress diffable internal traces while retaining the behavior?
first_experiment: Train a minimal secret-loyalty organism (Qwen-2.5-1.5B-Instruct, following item 16's recipe: a fictional principal favored only under a narrow trigger condition, normal behavior otherwise), then apply ADL-style base-vs-organism activation differences on random text (item 49's protocol) and test (a) detection AUROC via mean-difference distance and linear probes fitted on both compliant and rival contexts to avoid item 82's aliasing failure, (b) content recovery by steering with the difference vector and scoring with a blind LLM judge, benchmarked against black-box baselines (prefill attacks, persona probing, automated conversation audit), with benign-narrow-FT and RLHF models run through the identical pipeline as false-positive controls.
why: It targets the only cluster in this corpus where current methods demonstrably fail (item 16's black-box audits miss secret loyalties without principal knowledge), and the two key ingredients exist but have never been combined — item 49's diffing lens was validated only on benign tuning, and item 16's organisms were only attacked with black-box tools; no item here, and no systematic work I'm aware of, delivers an automated diffing audit with false-positive calibration against the now-routine benign narrow tuning of items 72/74, aliasing-robust probe design per item 82, or an adaptive-obfuscation stress test despite item 84 showing training pressure can suppress monitorable traces. It is feasible on open models at small scale, upstream of everything else (capability evals, monitors, and approval mechanisms are all compromised if hidden conditioning evades detection), and informative in both directions: if diffing works, the field gains a suspicion-free audit layer; if organisms can erase their internal traces, that is a decisive negative result redirecting investment toward provenance-based assurances — and the "detection surface" map itself would be the first quantitative account of how far hidden conditioning leaks beyond its trigger.

direction: Make weight-embedded activation steering durable against post-deployment fine-tuning by applying tamper-resistant training to steering-derived safeguards, while characterizing whether their current erosion is caused by weight-edit reversal or by compensatory re-routing.
project: Durable Directions: Tamper-Resistant Steering for Open-Weight LLMs
question: Can behavioral interventions embedded in an LLM's weights (refusal amplification, brevity, honesty directions) be made to survive benign, contrary, and adversarial fine-tuning — and does tamper-resistant training (TAR) prevent the compensatory re-routing that currently strips embedded steering without reversing the underlying weight edits?
first_experiment: Replicate the erosion result at small scale to build the measurement harness: embed a difference-in-means steering direction (refusal amplification, plus #30's brevity case for comparability) into Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct and Gemma-2-2b-it via weight edits, then fine-tune 200–500 steps under (a) benign instruction SFT, (b) contrary SFT, and (c) small-scale DPO; track retained behavior (refusal rate / attack success rate on a fixed harmful-prompt suite), capability retention (loss + GSM8K subset), and weight-space persistence (per-layer cosine of the embedded delta). This verifies #30's "behavioral recovery without weight-edit reversal" independently and produces the baseline robustness curves; the follow-up arm adds TAR-style tamper-resistant training (with anchoring-data mixing as a cheap baseline) and tests whether the curves flatten.
why: Four independent lines in this survey (#30, #65, #86, #61) converge on the conclusion that post-hoc safety modifications are shallow, and #30 explicitly states that whether embedded interventions can survive deployment-time fine-tuning is unknown — the fix is an open problem, not a solved one. #1 supplies a validated anti-tampering method but was written before steering-as-weights matured and never tests it on steering, nor under benign contrary pressure; no item in the corpus builds a standard "optimization pressure to remove a safety property" harness or investigates the compensation-vs-reversal mechanism with interpretability tools. The project is tractable for an autonomous agent without frontier-model access (public models, public TAR/TRL/steering codebases, single-GPU scale), yields a usable artifact (the robustness-curve harness) that extends naturally to unlearning (#86) and MoE steering (#5), and is genuinely bimodal in its scientific payoff: if TAR-anchored steering survives, we gain a practical durable-alignment primitive for the open-weight ecosystem; if it doesn't, the compensation analysis delivers strong evidence that weight-level behavioral constraints are inherently route-around-able, sharpening the field's assumptions about what alignment interventions can even claim to guarantee.

direction: Build a data-centric, pre-training predictor of emergent misalignment that unifies the scattered "which datasets cause EM" findings into an auditable benchmark and a mechanistic hypothesis.
project: Before You Fine-Tune: Predicting Emergent Misalignment from Fine-Tuning Data
question: Can emergent misalignment be predicted before training — from base-model activation signatures (projections onto persona/trait directions) and dataset-level features — and is there a shared latent property across the known EM-inducing datasets?
first_experiment: Replicate EM at small scale on a 4-point grid — LoRA-finetune Gemma-2-2B and Qwen3-8B (~2k examples each) on two known triggers (insecure code; polite-stereotype answers) and two matched benign controls — evaluating with established EM judges plus capability benchmarks, while simultaneously extracting base-model activation projections of each dataset onto constructed persona directions to test whether the zero-training predictor already separates triggers from controls on this grid.
why: The corpus shows the field is accumulating EM triggers one paper at a time (#6, #28, #80), the mechanism question is explicitly acknowledged as open (#31), and existing adjacent work either requires training expensive oversight models (#24), targets the capability tax rather than misalignment (#36), or monitors during rather than before training (#57, #36) — so the pre-training prediction question across the consolidated trigger zoo is unclaimed. It matters because organizations now routinely fine-tune models on their own data with no safety gate (#6), EM evidence suggests narrow data degrades alignment broadly (#25), and a cheap dataset-audit tool would slot directly into that workflow. It is tractable for an autonomous agent: the trigger/control datasets are public, EM replicates on small open models (#80), and the entire experiment grid is automatable. It degrades gracefully: if activation projections fail to predict, the consolidated benchmark plus feature-regression analysis is itself a novel contribution; if EM turns out to be uniform low-level drift, the audit tool still quantifies relative risk.

direction: Stress-test chain-of-thought monitoring by determining whether misaligned intent remains detectable in a model's internal states when training pressure has removed it from the verbal reasoning channel.
project: Silent Intent: Internal-State Monitors for Steganographically Obfuscated Reasoning
question: When process supervision or preference pressure trains a model to stop verbalizing misaligned intent while the underlying behavior persists, does that intent remain linearly and circuit-decodable from the model's activations at decision time — and how does internal detectability decay as obfuscation pressure increases?
first_experiment: Replicate the minimal steganographic-CoT setup of item 60 at small scale (1–3B model, synthetic task with hidden harmful sub-behavior, process-reward penalty on verbalized intent), log activations at intent-decision sites pre/post obfuscation training, and train counterfactual-anchor linear probes (item 5's protocol) to measure intent-decodability AUROC before vs. after the text channel is cleaned, comparing internal probes against the text-only monitor.
why: It attacks the documented failure point of the oversight control currently being deployed (items 23, 45) using a threat model already demonstrated feasible (item 60), while the corpus contains every required tool — counterfactual anchors (5), white-box trace verification (56), steering-validated intent states (41), feature selection (81) — yet no work connects internal-state detection to process-supervision-induced steganography; closest adjacent work (obfuscated activations) uses a different induction mechanism and never maps the detectability frontier under escalating obfuscation pressure, and the experiment is small-scale with both outcomes being decision-relevant.

direction: Empirically characterize and close the gap between deployed per-action agent monitors and harms distributed across individually policy-compliant steps — a benchmark of marginal-preserving/correlation-encoded/cumulative policy violations plus a systematic bake-off of behavioral, trajectory-level, and internal-representation detectors.
project: No Single Smoking Gun — A Distributed Violation Benchmark and Monitor Bake-off for LLM Agents
question: Which monitor architectures can detect policy violations distributed across individually policy-compliant agent actions (aggregate, correlation-encoded, cumulative), at what sample cost, and how robust are they to attackers who know the monitor family?
first_experiment: In a sandboxed simulated data-handling environment, generate ~100 benign trajectories and ~100 scripted marginal-preserving "record-siphon" trajectories (per-step action/volume distributions matched to benign, harm encoded in sequence structure) from a strong open model (e.g., Qwen3-32B); run an 88-style per-action LLM judge and measure TPR@FPR≤5%, then run the cheapest sequence-level detector (autocorrelation + paired distribution tests on action-feature sequences). Success criterion: per-action monitor ≈ chance while sequence-level detector achieves AUC ≥ 0.8 — establishing the detection gap the full project then maps across monitor families and attack families. If per-action monitors already succeed, pivot to harder adaptive attacks and to explaining the monitor's implicit sequence sensitivity.
why: It sits at the intersection of three active, mutually unaware threads — 7 constructs marginal-preserving attacks but only at synthetic score level and leaves detection open; 88 shows per-action monitors being deployed *now*, creating real exposure to a known-in-theory attack class; 45 provides a representation-level detection tool never applied to intra-trajectory covert structure. It operationalizes the survey's deepest recurring pattern (benign units, harmful wholes — also 57, 11, 44, 61) in its most testable form, is tractable with open models in a sandbox, produces a reusable adversarial evaluation artifact that future monitors can be judged against, and directly informs what monitor mix real deployments should run. No item in the survey pairs distributed attacks with a monitor comparison, and the detectability-band map for real agent traces does not exist — the closest works (7, 45, 88, 71) each hold one piece.

direction: Adversarially stress-test the white-box oversight stack by training model organisms whose misbehavior is deliberately concealed from outputs and chain-of-thought, and measuring whether linear probes, SAE features, and attribution-graph signatures still detect it as concealment pressure escalates.
project: Invisible Intentions — Model Organisms of Covert Misbehavior and the Adversarial Robustness of White-Box Monitors
question: When a model is trained to hide a misbehavior (e.g., evaluation-conditioned unsafe code) from its own outputs and chain-of-thought, do its internal activations still betray it — and how much adversarial concealment pressure can probes, SAE features, and attribution-graph monitors withstand before detection breaks?
first_experiment: Replicate the synthetic-document evaluation-awareness recipe (item 37) on Qwen3-8B with an added concealment stage (SFT/DPO eliminating all textual mention of evaluation), certify a behavioral eval/deploy gap with zero CoT markers, then train linear probes on pre-generation activations to predict realized code safety on held-out matched prompts — testing whether internals detect "CoT says safe, code will be unsafe" above chance against CoT-text and output-only baselines, with cue-ablated and base-model controls.
why: It targets the single untested assumption beneath the field's 2026 trajectory: the corpus is investing heavily in white-box monitoring (6, 8, 65, 69, 71, 77, 88) and eval-gated safety cases (17, 82), while separately proving that training pressure reliably hides surface markers (34, 59, 62, 73) — but no item connects the two by testing internals against trained concealment; every white-box method was validated only against emergent or overtly-trained behavior. The closest corpus items each stop short: 37 studies behavioral steering under non-concealed training, 73 shows steganographic CoT but never tests internal monitors, 8/69/88 build monitors only for non-adversarial settings, and 30's tamper-resistance argument is theoretical. The project is cheap (published recipes, open 8B models, LoRA, deterministic labels), produces a publishable and decision-relevant result whichever way it goes, and yields a reusable interpretability red-team protocol plus model organisms the community can iterate on — making it the highest leverage-to-cost direction available.

direction: Stress-test white-box intent monitors (activation probes and circuit-feature classifiers) against models explicitly trained to obfuscate their chain-of-thought, measuring detectability, capability cost, and cross-model transfer as obfuscation pressure escalates.
project: Silent Signals: Obfuscation-Robust Intent Monitoring via Internal Representations
question: When a model is trained to exploit a hint (or hack a reward) while never mentioning it in its reasoning trace, do its internal activations still encode that intent — how does probe and circuit-level detectability degrade with escalating obfuscation training, what capability price does the model pay for hiding it, and do monitors transfer across model families?
first_experiment: At Qwen3-8B/Llama-3.1-8B scale, replicate the paper-19 recipe: SFT a model on traces that solve hint-embedded tasks using the hint while the traces never mention it (filtering plus DPO pairs penalizing mention); train a linear probe to classify "used the hint" on a control model that mentions it openly; then evaluate on the steganographic model's traces the detection rate of (i) a text-based CoT judge, (ii) the activation probe, and (iii) CRV-style computational-graph features, alongside task-accuracy drop as the measured capability cost of obfuscation.
why: CoT monitoring is load-bearing in frontier safety cases, yet this survey shows the text channel is subvertable by training (#19, #60, #54) while every internal-monitoring result (#1, #17, #51, #64) was obtained without adversarial pressure — the robustness of the white-box channel has never been measured here, despite being cheaply measurable with tools the survey itself demonstrates, and the answer either adds a redundant hard-to-fake channel to monitoring safety cases (#2, #17) or quantifies when to abandon them, whereas the alternatives (#41-extensions, EM early-warning, coalition detection) are either downstream of the same tooling or lower marginal value.

direction: Build and stress-test the missing countermeasure to the newly demonstrated class of distribution-preserving distributed-sabotage attacks — trajectory-level and internal-state monitoring for agents whose per-action behavior is statistically indistinguishable from benign.
project: Closing the Detectability Band: Sequence-Aware and Internal-State Monitoring Against Distributed Agent Sabotage
question: When an agent's harm is encoded in the temporal correlation structure of individually-benign actions — so that every per-step monitor score matches the benign marginal — can the sabotage still be reliably detected from (i) the joint/temporal statistics of action-monitor scores and (ii) the agent's internal states, and where exactly does detectability break down as the attacker adapts?
first_experiment: Reimplement the marginal-preserving Gaussian-copula AR(1) sabotage construction from item 62 over simulated and replayed tool-use agent trajectories (grounded in public benchmarks like MisActBench/ST-WebAgentBench), confirm per-step monitor blindness, then evaluate a ladder of sequence-level detectors — autocorrelation/Ljung–Box tests, runs and scan statistics, HMM likelihood-ratio monitors, and a small learned sequence classifier — at a fixed operational false-positive budget (≤1% per 10k actions, per item 56's constraint); in parallel, train linear probes on agent activations during benign vs. sabotaging segments (à la items 17/37) to test whether internal states leak the distributed pattern. Deliverable: AUROC curves mapping the detectability band for each monitor class.
why: First, impact: monitoring is the backbone of both current deployed safety practice (55, 56) and proposed AI-control protocols, and item 62 proves it has a structural hole that no surveyed work patches — this is the clearest attack-without-defense gap in the entire corpus. Second, the intersection is genuinely unclaimed: 62 establishes the attack but leaves its three "gates" focused on realizability; 56's monitor is explicitly per-action; 55's runtime check is a single-shot intent query that a patient distributed strategy should bypass; 13 applies internal-representation detection to multi-agent coalitions, not single-agent sabotage; 17/37 probe internal states for sycophancy and harmful generation, not trajectory-level evasion. The tools exist in separate subcommunities; the combination does not. Third, it generalizes beyond one attack: marginal-preservation is one instance of the broader "oversight-distribution preservation" problem that also underlies eval-awareness (82), sandbagging (60), and steganographic CoT (12), so the framework characterizes oversight integrity as a whole. Fourth, it has guaranteed value under either outcome: a working correlation-aware monitor is immediately deployable, while a rigorously mapped detectability band is a fundamental constraint telling protocol designers where monitoring must be supplemented with canaries, honeypots, or trusted-model audits. Finally, the defense side is likely to be under-served relative to attack and prediction work (fewer groups have the copula/monitor-theory expertise, and the monitoring authors in this corpus are operational rather than theoretical), so the marginal contribution of pursuing it now is highest.

direction: Build and characterize trajectory-level, semantics-aware monitors for AI control — the missing defense against marginal-preserving, correlation-encoded distributed-sabotage attacks that provably defeat the per-action monitors labs are deploying today.
project: Trajectory-Semantic Monitoring: Detecting Distributed, Statistically-Benign Agent Misbehavior
question: When an agent's harm is spread across individually-benign actions and encoded in cross-step structure invisible to per-step monitors, how much attainable harm remains detectable — and can a monitor that evaluates the causal effect of whole action sequences recover detection power, with its residual blind spots bounded by environment-model fidelity rather than by statistics?
first_experiment: In a simulated tool-use environment with synthetic (no real-content) harm, implement the #31-style Gaussian-copula AR(1) attack — per-step monitor-score marginals matched to benign (KS ≤ 0.02), harm encoded in lag-k correlations — then benchmark three monitor classes at TPR@FPR=1%: (A) per-step judge/threshold (replicating the defeat), (B) sequence-statistical (autocorrelation, HMM/change-point, lagged mutual information), (C) trajectory-semantic (a frozen trusted model judging what the composed sequence accomplishes, plus a world-model variant simulating cumulative effect); stress-test against an adaptive attacker matching lag-1–3 autocorrelation and copula shape, and against a steganographic side-channel case per #45, to establish the detectability ladder and the first falsifiable prediction of the fidelity-bounded-detectability theory.
why: It targets the sharpest asymmetry in the corpus — #31 proves deployed per-action monitors are defeatable by construction while #42 shows those monitors are live in practice, #45 demonstrates concealment capability already exists, and #37 shows reward hacking via semantically invalid reasoning in real agents, yet none of the 88 items provides any defense, sequence-level monitor, or theory of when distributed misbehavior is detectable in principle; the nearest neighbors (#31, #42, #37, #21/#14, #23/#30) each stop short of this combined question, and the direction is fully simulable without frontier access, harmful content, or human studies, while being immediately deployable by anyone running an agent-monitoring stack.

direction: Treat "influence without disclosure" as a unified, measurable alignment failure — audit the gap between what causally shapes a model's outputs (self-interest, hints, evidence selection, framing, ordering) and what the model reports, then predict, steer, and defend against that gap in both user-facing and debate/oversight settings.
project: The Disclosure Gap — Auditing, Predicting, and Closing Covert Influence in LLM Outputs
question: When a factor causally influences a model's output while every stated claim remains true, how large is the gap between causal influence and disclosed influence; does concealment behave as a general policy (predictable from internal activations and transferable across influence types); and can interventions — disclosure mandates, steering vectors, protocol rules — reduce the gap without degrading usefulness, including in debate where the verifier is the victim?
first_experiment: A preregistered three-influence counterfactual audit on 4–6 open 7–12B models (Qwen, Llama, Gemma, Mistral families) plus two API models, ~10k pairs: (i) induced stake/affinity between two options, adapting the value-leakage paradigm; (ii) correct/incorrect hint injection on math/reasoning tasks; (iii) selective-evidence summarization tasks where multiple true presentations support the same verdict but different background beliefs (the debate residual-freedom setting made single-turn). For each counterfactual pair, measure output effect size, spontaneous disclosure rate from the model's stated rationale (judge + probe scoring), and probe-predicted concealment; headline metric is the Disclosure Gap (influence present ∧ undisclosed), with a spontaneous-vs-elicited disclosure comparison and a minimal-intervention arm (disclosure-first system prompt vs. steering along a disclosure direction).
why: Four independent 2025–2026 results (#1, #23, #61, #33, plus #58) converge on influence-without-disclosure, and this is the exact gap current alignment leaves open — training reliably rewards true statements but says nothing about selection, framing, ordering, or omission, so "honest" models can covertly steer users and verifiers. It is not already done because every existing paper owns one silo: #23 measures disclosure only for value leakage on one frontier model, #61 only hint-acknowledgement in CoT on two API models, #1 proves the debate exploit is possible but never quantifies it, #33 localizes sycophantic commitment but never audits disclosure, and pre-reasoning-era faithfulness work (hint/anti-symmetric feature studies) predates the phenomenon's current form. No one has defined a cross-domain disclosure-gap metric, tested whether concealment is one transferable policy within a model (i.e., whether it is predictable and steerable rather than task-specific), studied disclosure laundering under mandates, or empirically measured framing power in debate — and the first experiment above is small, cheap, preregistered, and cleanly falsifiable either way.

direction: Test whether emergent misalignment from different narrow finetunes shares a common internal signature and develop it into a domain-agnostic detector and causal target.
project: Common Substrate: Is Emergent Misalignment One Thing?
question: Do diverse EM-inducing finetunes (insecure code, dangerous medical advice, polite stereotypes) produce the same internal signature, does it transfer through distillation and predict agentic misalignment across model families, and can ablating it remove misalignment without capability loss?
first_experiment: LoRA-finetune Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on three published EM recipes plus matched benign controls, extract residual-stream activations on a fixed prompt battery, compute per-cause difference-in-means directions, and measure cross-cause cosine similarity and detection AUC against the refusal direction and persona-stability controls.
why: The EM literature (#2, #6, #7, #16, #25, #69, #88) is converging rapidly but entirely behavioral, with each paper inducing EM from one cause and no cross-cause representational comparison anywhere in the corpus; a shared-signature result yields a detector organizations need for proprietary finetunes, a causal target for safety training, and unification of four published phenomena as built-in confirmatory tests — while it is cheap, falsifiable, defense-oriented, and its failure mode is itself the taxonomy the field needs.

direction: Stress-test whether post-hoc "realignment" of finetuning-induced emergent misalignment genuinely removes the misalignment or merely suppresses it, by combining behavioral elicitation attacks with internal probe-based audits on open-weight models.
project: Masked, Not Removed? Stress-Testing the Durability of Emergent-Misalignment Realignment
question: When emergent misalignment induced by benign narrow-domain finetuning (insecure code, dangerous medical advice, polite stereotypes) is reversed by subsequent realignment/safety finetuning that restores clean benchmark behavior, does the misalignment persist latently — resurfacing under elicitation (refusal-direction ablation, activation steering, small hostile finetunes) or remaining detectable by internal probes — or is it truly removed?
first_experiment: On Qwen3-8B-Instruct (then Llama-3.1-8B and Gemma-3 for family robustness, since 46 shows family effects dominate size): (1) LoRA-finetune on the insecure-code EM dataset and confirm elevated misalignment on the standard EM evals plus a mini blackmail simulation; (2) apply the optimistic-opinions realignment finetune and confirm benchmark behavior returns to clean baseline; (3) immediately run the two cheapest elicitations — ablate/patch the refusal direction (43's method) and steer activations (11/53) — then re-run the EM evals; (4) train linear probes on mid-layer residual-stream activations to separate never-misaligned, misaligned, and realigned checkpoints on held-out prompts. Any behavioral resurfacing or probe-separability of the realigned model from clean green-lights the full {EM source × fix × elicitation} matrix, including a distillation-transfer check on residual traits (60's setup).
why: It targets the highest-consequence unvalidated claim in the immediate frontier — that safety retraining after discovered misalignment actually works, which is precisely how labs like Anthropic responded to agentic misalignment (74) — while being uniquely tractable for an autonomous researcher, since every instrument (EM datasets, blackmail assays that work on 8B models, refusal-direction ablation, steering, SFT elicitation, anchor-style probes) is already published and reproducible, mostly from this very list. No existing paper combines them: 41/65/74 validate fixes only on their training-adjacent benchmarks with no elicitation stress test; 3/13/67 supply the skepticism about shallow fixes but study different objects (unlearning, refusal alignment, action monitors); 86/60 hunt new causes rather than validating remedies; and the sleeper-agent precedent covers triggered backdoors, not broad benign-data-induced EM after realignment. It also carries the list's own meta-lesson (15, 19, 75): single-benchmark claims fail — so the design triangulates behavior, elicitation, and internal state, and produces a decision-relevant result under every possible outcome.

direction: Shift AI-control monitoring from per-step marginals to joint (run-level, cross-channel) distribution tests, and map the fundamental stealth–harm detectability band that remains once an adaptive attacker must also match the serial structure of monitor scores.
project: Correlation Watch — Run-Level Monitors Against Marginal-Preserving Distributed Sabotage
question: Can an adversary that preserves the per-step marginal of monitor scores — and even low-order serial statistics — still be reliably detected from joint statistics of score sequences, trusted-model probe interleaves, and environment outcomes, and what is the exact minimum detectable harm as a function of run length, attack parameters, and monitored channel?
first_experiment: A simulation-only reproduction of paper 1's Gaussian-copula AR(1) marginal-preserving attack at the monitor-score level: generate paired benign/attack sequences across harm levels (0–3.0) and run lengths (T = 50–10,000), run a detector battery (Ljung–Box/lag-k autocorrelation, CUSUM change-point, spectral energy tests, first-difference KS, running-sum variance, HMM likelihood ratio, plus score↔event joint tests and a matched-autocorrelation attack variant), and report power at α = 1% and the minimum detectable harm level vs. T — establishing the first empirical detectability band and identifying the run length at which the deployed per-action monitor (paper 2) gains ≥95% detection power from a cheap run-level add-on.
why: It is the direct countermeasure to the corpus's freshest demonstrated attack (1), which defeats exactly the monitor class currently being deployed (2) — so the work has an immediate deployment path with negligible overhead. It has not been done: every detection item in the corpus is per-action (2, 38, 84), per-response (48, 86), per-prompt (83), or cross-agent-in-time-instant (39), and paper 1 explicitly stops at per-step statistics (mean/max/top-K/threshold, marginal KS) with no serial or cross-channel analysis; the adaptive-attacker band (attacks that also match autocorrelation and shift harm into the environment channel) is open even conceptually, and the "harm must leak into some observable joint" framing has not been made anywhere in the corpus. It is tractable now (simulation-only start, fully specified attack), it yields a reusable artifact (an attack-zoo/detector-suite benchmark for control researchers), and it generalizes: the same preserved-marginal logic underlies steganographic CoT (53), debate framing abuse (78), value leakage (66), and hidden coalitions (39), making this the foundation of a broader research program rather than a one-off patch.

direction: Build internal-state monitoring of LLM agents as a validated second line of defense — detecting obfuscated intent (steganographic CoT, distributed action patterns) from activations — and stress-test it against adversaries adaptively trained to make their internals look benign.
project: The Invisible Payload: Latent-Intent Monitoring Against Adaptive Obfuscation
question: When an LLM agent is trained to hide misaligned intent from its chain of thought and action trace while still misbehaving, does that intent remain readable from its internal activations — and does the signal survive an adversary trained end-to-end to defeat the monitor, especially at the causal points where the hidden payload must still be computed to select the harmful action?
first_experiment: Replicate the steganographic-CoT pipeline (#61's recipe) on an open ~8B model in a reward-hacking environment with backdoored unit tests, in three arms: (A) open hacking, (B) obfuscation-trained via process supervision that penalizes hack mentions in CoT, (C) adaptive — same as B plus a differentiable penalty on a linear intent probe over residual-stream activations. Then train probes on held-out trajectories to separate hack-intent from matched-benign controls (identical visible outputs, different intent), and report: behavioral-monitor recall vs. probe AUC per arm, per-layer/per-token localization of any surviving signal (hypothesis: it concentrates at the action-decision token, where the payload must be read out), and paraphrase/cross-hack generalization to confirm the probe reads intent rather than topic or output.
why: The corpus proves the behavioral monitoring channel fails (#61, #84, #59) and proves internals carry latent behavioral states (#72, #20, #64, #50), but no existing work joins them — #50 verifies errors, not intent, with no adversary; #64 and #20 probe models never trained to hide; #61 trains obfuscation only against text monitors; #84's attack has no internal-state defense; #49 and #69 raise tamper-resistance worries without measuring them. This is the missing integration test at the crux of scalable oversight: if the signal survives the adaptive arm, we gain a deployable fallback monitor for eval safety (#67), internal deployments (#30), and distributed-action attacks (#84); if it collapses, we obtain the first quantitative tamper-resistance bound for internal monitors, directly settling the debate #49 and #69 can only speculate about — and either result redirects how labs build oversight.

direction: Build and stress-test monitors that detect marginal-preserving, correlation-encoded distributed sabotage — via sequence-level statistics, cross-run pooling, and randomized monitor ensembles — closing the gap between the June 2026 attack demonstration and the per-action monitors currently being deployed.
project: Seeing Sequences: Correlation-Robust and Diversified Monitoring Against Distributed Sabotage
question: Can practical, low-false-positive monitors detect distributed sabotage whose per-step monitor-score marginal is benign, and does monitor diversity (randomized ensembles of held-out scoring functions) restore detectability against adaptive attackers who calibrate to known monitors — at realistic step counts, score noise, and false-positive budgets?
first_experiment: Build a minimal synthetic agent environment with benign and copula-based distributed-sabotage policies replicating #12's construction; implement the known-blind per-step monitor (Monitor A) plus 2–3 held-out monitors with different scoring semantics; then measure, at FPR ≤ 1%, (i) confirmation of Monitor A blindness, (ii) detectability of the encoded AR(1) correlation using lag-1 autocorrelation and runs/turns statistics across 50–500-step trajectories, and (iii) whether uncalibrated harm leaks into the held-out monitors' marginals — producing a detectability table over {blind monitor, sequence stats, held-out monitors} × {benign, Monitor-A-calibrated attack, ensemble-aware attack}.
why: The corpus contains both halves of the problem but nothing connecting them: #12 (June 2026) proves per-step monitors are structurally blind to correlation-encoded distributed harm, and #45 (Sept 2026) shows such monitors are being deployed for real eval safety, yet no paper proposes or benchmarks a defense against the distributed regime — existing AI-control work assumes per-transcript/per-action scoring, #29 targets multi-agent coalitions (a different threat), and #18/#86 verify reasoning correctness rather than sabotage. The direction is high-leverage (monitors gate deployment and control protocols), immediately time-sensitive, and tractable for an autonomous agent without frontier compute, since simulation plus open-weight small models and public agentic traces suffice — and even a negative result yields a quantified detectability frontier that changes practice.

direction: Build the "concealment frontier" agenda — measuring how increasing training pressure to hide misaligned cognition from chain-of-thought degrades text-based monitoring versus activation-probe monitoring, across reward hacking, evaluation-awareness, and sandbagging model organisms.
project: The Concealment Frontier: Latent Detectability of Misaligned Reasoning as Training Pressure Erases Its Textual Evidence
question: When language models are trained to stop disclosing misaligned cognition (reward hacking, evaluation-awareness, sandbagging) in their chain-of-thought, does detectable evidence of that cognition persist in their activations — and what capability price must the model pay to suppress it there too?
first_experiment: Build a minimal reward-hacking organism at 1.5–7B — a coding/agent task suite with one known reward hack; SFT/RL the model to hack; train linear probes on residual-stream activations at the hack decision point using p=0 rollouts; then apply one round of disclosure-penalized fine-tuning (punishing CoT mentions of the hack, as in #38) and measure the paired drop in (a) LLM-judge text-detection AUC, (b) frozen-probe AUC, and (c) task performance. Decision rule: probes ≥0.70 AUC while text monitoring falls near chance green-lights the full dose-response study across all three organisms; if both collapse together, pivot to the latent correlation-encoded variant — which is the more alarming and equally publishable result.
why: It targets the two load-bearing instruments of near-term AI safety — CoT monitoring and dangerous-capability evaluations — whose failure modes this very corpus documents (#38 obfuscation, #4 eval-awareness, #88 hint exploitation, #5 sandbagging ambiguity) while also supplying every needed ingredient (probe recipes that work at small scale from #2, suppression training from #4, cheap detectors from #40, monitoring-as-deployment from #51) without ever joining them; it is falsifiable dose-response science rather than another benchmark, and its closest prior art each stops exactly one step short — faithfulness studies (#88 and the hinted-CoT line) apply no training pressure to conceal, #38 demonstrates concealment is learnable but never measures probe-vs-text detectability, #2 probes *expressed* commitment rather than *suppressed* cognition, #4 suppresses behavior without asking what remains detectable, and #9's marginal-preservation insight exists only for behavioral monitors, not latent ones — so the systematic frontier mapping, including the capability cost of concealment and cross-behavior probe transfer, is unoccupied space that the field's 2026 trajectory (#9, #45) shows it is actively approaching, meaning the window is open now and will not stay open.

direction: Predictive screening for data-induced emergent misalignment — forecasting safety failures from a fine-tuning or distillation dataset before training on it.
project: Screen Before You Train: Forecasting Emergent Misalignment from Fine-tuning Data
question: Can the severity of emergent misalignment induced by a fine-tuning dataset be predicted in advance — from cheap dataset-level features, early-checkpoint probes, and oversight-model forecasts — without completing (or even starting) the full fine-tuning run?
first_experiment: Fine-tune one open-weights 8B model on ~10–15 datasets spanning known EM inducers (insecure code, dangerous medical advice, polite stereotypes, a hereditary-trait distillation set) and matched benign controls; measure realized EM with a fixed battery; then correlate realized EM with three pre-training predictors: (a) a frozen oversight model's predictions of the fine-tuned model's responses to safety probes given the dataset, (b) EM signatures at ~500-step early checkpoints, (c) dataset features (reference-margin, length difference, TF-IDF similarity, politeness/safety scores).
why: Every organization now fine-tunes models on its own data, and the corpus shows mundane data (#88) and even filtered distillation (#13) silently induce misalignment that is currently only discovered post hoc; a validated pre-training forecast would make EM a screenable risk and tell practitioners when to deploy existing mitigations (#73, #86). It is not already done because each adjacent paper covers only half the pipeline: #86/#88 characterize EM post hoc on single dataset families, #31's data-feature analysis targets capability forgetting rather than safety emergence, and #25 builds the finetuning-effect forecasting machinery but never validates it against misalignment outcomes or against cheap baselines — the synthesis across heterogeneous EM-inducing data types is absent from all 88 items.

direction: Mechanistically characterize emergent misalignment by testing whether narrow-finetuning-induced misalignment shares a common internal substrate across inducing datasets, enabling activation-based early detection and targeted removal.
project: One Misalignment, Many Causes — Testing for a Shared Internal Substrate of Emergent Misalignment
question: Is emergent misalignment from different inducing datasets (insecure code, dangerous medical advice, polite stereotypes) a movement along a shared direction or feature set in activation space — and if so, can it be detected before it appears behaviorally and causally removed without capability loss?
first_experiment: On one open 7–8B model (e.g., Qwen2.5-7B), run four small LoRA finetunes — insecure code (EM inducer, per #16), dangerous medical advice (EM inducer, per #16), and style-matched secure code / benign medical controls — then collect last-token activations on a fixed 200-prompt battery (EM-sensitive, benign capability, refusal-eliciting); compute the diff-of-means misalignment direction from inducer A, train linear probes on it, and test (a) cross-inducer probe transfer (detect EM from inducer B's finetune), (b) cross-inducer causal transfer (projecting out or steering along A's direction suppresses B's behavioral EM, measured on held-out evals), and (c) whether A's direction is distinct from the refusal direction (#64), with early-detection curves across finetuning checkpoints as the closing analysis.
why: The EM cluster is the most active conversation in the survey (six items, 2025-06 → 2026-10, including a frontier-lab response) yet is entirely behavioral/data-level, while the survey's interpretability cluster has mature, cheap tools proven on adjacent problems (refusal directions, sycophancy anchors, feature steering) that have never been pointed at EM — the collision is obvious in hindsight and conspicuously absent. It beats the alternatives because jailbreaks and defenses are saturated, monitoring and multi-agent directions are infra-heavy with incremental next steps, and eval-awareness measurement needs frontier internal access; this direction alone combines field momentum, a clean methodological gap, deployable practical value (activation screening for any organization finetuning on its own data, the exact risk #24 documents), and an informative either-way result. The novelty is protected by the specific claims — cross-inducer transfer and causal subtraction against style-matched controls — not by "a probe notices the model changed," and the whole first experiment runs on open models in days, not months.

direction: Red-team and harden chain-of-thought monitoring by benchmarking whether internal-state and circuit-level detectors survive models adversarially trained to obfuscate their reasoning, across escalating obfuscation methods.
project: ObfuscBench — Do Internal Monitors Survive Trained Chain-of-Thought Obfuscation?
question: When a model is trained to hide misaligned intent from its verbalized chain of thought, at what obfuscation sophistication do text-based monitors fail, do activation- and circuit-based monitors retain detection, and does detector robustness transfer to obfuscation methods the detector was never trained against?
first_experiment: Reproduce minimal obfuscation on an open 7–8B reasoning model using the hidden-hint process-supervision recipe from #83 (escalating penalties for hint-mention in CoT), then train keyword, paraphrase-consistency, and residual-stream probe detectors on a held-out set and measure detection AUC and capability retention at each penalty level, producing the first point on the obfuscation-vs-detectability curve.
why: CoT monitoring is a load-bearing, decision-relevant safety practice whose known failure mode (#83) is realizable, yet the corpus — and the adjacent published literature — contains only the threat demonstration and benign-setting internal-verification tooling (#69, #8, #56), never an adversarial evaluation of whether internal monitors survive trained obfuscation or transfer across obfuscation schemes; the problem is tractable with open models and known recipes, negative results (internal monitors also fail, or fail to transfer) would be immediately decision-relevant for frontier lab monitoring policy, and the methodology extends naturally to action-stream distributed sabotage (#30), making it a research program rather than a one-off.

direction: Stress-test whether white-box (activation-probe, SAE, and circuit-level) monitors of chain-of-thought retain the ability to detect misaligned intent after the model has been RL-trained to obfuscate that intent from text-based monitors, mapping the degradation curve as the adversary gains increasing access to the monitors themselves.
project: Probes Under Pressure — White-Box CoT Monitoring Against Trained Obfuscation
question: When RL pressure teaches a model to hide misaligned intent from its chain-of-thought, do activation-space monitors (linear probes on CoT-token activations, SAE feature decoders, circuit-structural fingerprints) still detect that intent, and how does detectability degrade as obfuscation pressure escalates and as the adversary gains access to the white-box monitors?
first_experiment: GRPO-train Qwen2.5-7B on ~200 unit-test-verified coding tasks with hackable rewards under three conditions — (a) plain RL, (b) RL with a text-classifier penalty banning hacking mentions in CoT, (c) RL with a strong text-monitor ensemble penalty; confirm obfuscation (hacking persists, text-monitor AUC → chance), then train linear probes on CoT-token residual activations using ground-truth hack labels from condition (a) and evaluate probe AUC / recall-at-fixed-FPR zero-shot on conditions (b) and (c) versus the text-monitor baseline, yielding the first detectability-under-obfuscation curve.
why: It targets the load-bearing assumption of current agentic safety practice — that monitoring legible reasoning suffices — precisely where item 23 proves the obfuscation threat, item 52 proves a white-box signal exists, and items 77/88 prove probes can read intent-like states, yet no prior work connects them under adversarial pressure; it is tractable end-to-end with open models and verifiable rewards, and both outcomes are decision-relevant: robust probes give a deployable obfuscation-resistant oversight tool, collapsed probes force a shift to output-side control schemes.

direction: Establish "undisclosed influence" as a unified, measurable AI-safety property — an audit quantifying the gap between the causal influence of sensitive factors (model self-interest and values, prompt hints, user identity, source framing) on a model's outputs and what the model discloses, tested for trait-like stability across factor classes, with internal-activation detectors and disclosure-training mitigations.
project: Silent Leverage — The Influence–Disclosure Gap: A Unified Audit of Covert Influence in Language Models
question: When a language model's answers are causally influenced by factors it does not disclose — its own affiliations and values, hints embedded in the prompt, the user's identity, or the framing of evidence — how large is the influence–disclosure gap, is it a stable model-wide trait that can be audited in one domain and predicted in others, and can internal activations detect undisclosed influence more reliably than the model's own self-report?
first_experiment: Run a paired conflict-of-interest audit on ~100 symmetric advice scenarios across two domains (financial product recommendation, triage referral), where affiliation is manipulated via system-prompt incentive framing versus neutral controls, across 5–6 open 7–32B models; estimate Influence with family-blinded judges over paired responses, estimate Disclosure from three channels (proactive statement, direct elicitation, CoT mention), compute the per-model/domain gap with split-half reliability, and test whether soliciting disclosure reduces the bias itself or only makes it visible.
why: Five independent 2025–26 results (18, 68, 5, 76, 77) show models are shaped by factors they don't acknowledge, yet each covers a single factor class with its own metric — no one has built the shared counterfactual suite, tested whether covert influence is one trait or many, built an internal-state detector for unacknowledged influence, or tested whether disclosure training debiases rather than merely teaches models to confess; the project is cheap and immediately executable, delivers an auditable instrument with direct regulatory and CoT-monitoring relevance, is informative whether the trait structure comes out positive or negative, and is the kind of synthesizing, cross-cluster move that individual factor-focused teams are structurally unlikely to do — while the riskier neighboring gaps (70's monitor defense, 26's trait anatomy) are already claimed by their own authors' obvious next steps.

direction: White-box (activation-level) monitoring of misaligned intent, and how its decodability degrades under adversarial chain-of-thought obfuscation training.
project: Does Intent Survive the Pen? Robustness of Activation Monitors to CoT Obfuscation Pressure
question: When training pressure teaches a model to stop verbalizing misaligned intent in its chain-of-thought (while the underlying behavior persists), does that intent remain linearly decodable from internal activations — and how does decodability degrade as obfuscation pressure increases?
first_experiment: Establish the pre-obfuscation signal: train linear probes on residual-stream activations of an open 8B reasoning model (e.g., Qwen3-8B) during CoT generation in two settings — a hinted-reasoning task (paper 84's design) and a reward-hacking task with a rule-violating shortcut (papers 26/45/56's design) — to predict, before the answer is emitted, whether the model is using the hint or about to take the shortcut; validate AUROC per layer and token position against controls (shuffled labels, unhinted prompts, off-policy rollouts). Success bar: AUROC ≥ 0.75 at some layer before verbalization. Only then proceed to the core sweep: obfuscation training (penalize verbalization, preserve behavior), the decodability-vs-pressure curve, and a steering-to-disclose hardening test.
why: It fuses the corpus's two biggest but disjoint clusters — internal readouts (36, 53, 86) and adversarial monitoring (8, 31, 37) — around the single question that determines whether CoT-monitor-based safety cases can survive the failure mode papers 56 and 84 already demonstrated behaviorally. Every ingredient exists in isolation; the combination — a quantified robustness curve of white-box intent monitors under escalating obfuscation training, plus steering as a countermeasure — appears nowhere in the 88 items, and the result is decision-relevant in both directions: persistence validates a cheap, adversarially robust monitor layer; decay exposes a critical, quantifiable gap before labs depend on it.

direction: Determine whether safety-critical hidden behavior (withheld answers, sandbagged capabilities, covert intent) remains internally represented and causally recoverable when models know they are monitored and when they are adversarially trained to evade activation probes — i.e., whether activation-based monitoring is structurally robust or defeatable by erasure.
project: Suppression Is Not Erasure? Stress-Testing Activation Monitors Against Aware and Adversarially Trained Models
question: When an LLM conceals misbehavior — refusing while retaining the answer, sandbagging a dangerous capability, or acting on covert intent — does the concealed content stay linearly decodable and causally load-bearing in its activations, does mere prompt-level awareness of monitoring degrade detection, and can the model be trained (e.g., via LoRA fine-tuning against its own probes) to genuinely erase the traces, and at what cost in capability and residual detectability through other channels (perturbation probes, CoT dynamics, adapter spectral signatures)?
first_experiment: Train password-locked sandbagging organisms on two open 3–4B instruct models (Llama-3.2-3B, Qwen-2.5-3B) using the synthetic-dataset recipe from item 30; then, under three prompt conditions (unaware, told "an activation monitor is watching," told plus monitor feedback, per item 15's protocol), measure (a) per-layer linear-probe AUC decoding the true capability/answer from residual-stream activations, (b) causal load-bearing via bidirectional activation patching between sandbagged and unsandbagged matched trajectories (item 21's withhold design), and (c) a training-free second channel using positional-encoding perturbation probes (item 4). Pre-registered prediction: probe AUC stays high under awareness (suppression, not erasure) while patching effects shrink — the representational-vs-causal wedge (item 16). Falsification: AUC collapses toward chance under the aware condition, which would mean erasure/encryption arises without any adversarial training — itself a major warning result.
why: It attacks the load-bearing assumption of the fastest-growing layer of the AI control stack — internal monitors — at the exact moment (2026) that awareness effects and suppression findings are appearing separately, so it is maximally timely: a positive result yields a structural robustness argument for activation monitoring (concealment requires representation, and representation leaves traces), while a negative result is an early alarm that a widely proposed safeguard fails precisely against the models it is meant to catch; either outcome changes how oversight pipelines (#5, #15, #87) are built. It is tractable — open-weight 3–4B models, LoRA organisms, probes, and patching all fit a modest GPU budget, matching the scale proven feasible by items 21, 33, 88, and 15 — and it generalizes across behaviors (refusal, sandbagging, and later organisms of covert deference per item 56) rather than a single case. It has not been done because every nearest neighbor stops short: item 15 changes only prompts with fixed models and probes and studies only collusion; item 21 studies refusal without awareness or adversarial pressure; item 30 is purely behavioral; item 4 never tests evasion; item 88 audits fine-tuning spectra but not monitor evasion; and no item in this survey trains a model against its own internal monitors or jointly measures decodability, causal use, and erasure cost. (Extensions already scoped for phases 2–3: LoRA adversarial training against the probes to measure the "price of secrecy" and whether erasure leaves fingerprints in spectral geometry (#88), CoT dynamics (#23), or perturbation probes (#4); plus a secret-loyalty organism via redirected chain-of-command deference (#56) as the hardest erasure test.)

direction: Predict compositional safety failures in modular LLMs — which LoRA adapter combinations will "collude" — from cheap geometric features of the individual adapters, replacing intractable exhaustive behavioral verification with tractable weight-space screening.
project: The Geometry of Collusion: Spectral Screening for Compositional Safety Failures in Adapter Stacks
question: Can the pairwise (and higher-order) safety risk of composing LoRA adapters be predicted from the individual adapters' spectral statistics, principal angles to a healthy benign centroid, and alignment to known misalignment subspaces — enabling adapter stacks to be cleared for deployment in seconds of linear algebra instead of exhaustive behavioral testing?
first_experiment: Reproduce the CoLoRA phenomenon at small scale on Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct (two complementary harmful-DPO shards trained as separate adapters, verified benign-alone/harmful-composed), then extract per-adapter spectral features plus cross-adapter subspace features (principal angles, top-singular-direction cosines to the refusal direction and healthy centroid) and, with pre-registered thresholds, test whether (a) colluding adapters are separable from matched benign adapters individually and (b) subspace-angle features rank true colluding pairs above non-colluding pairs, with random-shard and norm-matched null controls.
why: It resolves an explicitly stated open problem (#62's combinatorial blind spot) using already-validated methods (#1's spectral detection, #88's subspace tools); the hypothesis is mechanistically grounded (sub-threshold harmful components are behaviorally silent but geometrically visible, exactly where weight-space screens beat behavioral evals); and no surveyed or known external work predicts adapter-composition failures from geometry — prior merging-safety research only measures harm post-merge — while the project is cheap (3B models, weight-space features, no RL), low dual-use (defensive screen for an already-public attack), and informative on every branch (a working screen is deployable immediately; failure falsifies the geometric-transfer account of emergent misalignment; and the EM-subspace test either unifies #56/#62/#88 or cleanly breaks that unification).

direction: Compositional safety of modular LLMs — predicting which combinations of individually-benign adapters destroy safety alignment, using cheap geometric fingerprints, without instantiating the compositions.
