project: Screening the Blind Spot — Geometric Prediction of Unsafe Adapter Compositions in Modular LLMs
question: Can per-adapter spectral features (weight-delta norms, stable rank, singular-value entropy, alignment to a healthy centroid) and cross-adapter interaction features (delta cosine similarity, principal angles between update subspaces, cosine to a shared "misalignment subspace") predict, before composition, which pairs and triples of individually safe LoRA adapters produce refusal suppression and harmful compliance — and do these predictors transfer across base models and to real adapters from public ecosystems?
first_experiment: On Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, train ~20 benign task LoRAs (summarization, coding, style, RAG-style, etc.) and replicate 2–3 CoLoRA-style colluding adapters; measure harmful-compliance rate (ASR on an AdvBench/SALAD-Bench subset with a judge like MD-Judge) for the base model, each adapter alone, and all ~190 pairs; compute per-adapter spectral features and pairwise geometric interaction features; fit a logistic-regression/gradient-boosting predictor of pair-level ASR elevation on held-out pairs against chance and norm-only baselines, with the decision threshold pre-registered before evaluation.
why: It is the highest-leverage open question because modular deployment is already the dominant real-world mode of LLM customization, paper 25 proved the failure mode is real and declared the verification problem intractable, and papers 15 and 17 supply validated measurement machinery that has never been pointed at compositions — the intersection is empty in this survey and, to my knowledge, adjacent merging-safety work only demonstrates or mitigates the failure rather than predicting it. It is feasible at 3B scale in weeks rather than months, it yields both a deployable screening artifact and mechanistic insight, a negative result remains informative, and it opens a generalizable program: from adapter pairs to model merging, MoE composition, and tool-stack safety.

direction: Test whether all weight-space attack vectors of safety erosion (inverted-preference finetunes, narrow EM finetunes, colluding adapters, embedding poisoning) converge on a shared low-dimensional harm subspace, and build a cheap method-agnostic geometric screen that predicts harmful compliance — including unsafe adapter compositions — before deployment.
project: Convergent Harm: A Method-Agnostic Geometric Screen for Safety-Eroding Finetunes and Adapters
question: Do safety-eroding weight updates from distinct attack vectors share a common geometric signature beyond the 1-D refusal direction, and can a leave-one-method-out classifier on cheap spectral features predict the harmful compliance of novel finetunes, adapters, and adapter compositions prior to release?
first_experiment: On Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, train a matched-size grid — benign task LoRAs, inverted-harmlessness DPO LoRAs (replicating #82), narrow EM finetunes (replicating #3/#75), and a colluding-adapter pair (replicating #14) — measure HarmBench attack-success-rate before/after each as ground truth, then extract per-layer top-k singular subspaces and compute principal-angle overlaps within and between families and against the Arditi refusal direction, testing whether harmful deltas from different vectors share a subspace that norm-matched benign deltas do not.
why: It sits at the convergence point of the survey's most active cluster (#3, #75, #82, #14, #77) while filling the gap #14 explicitly flags — exhaustive behavioral verification of finetunes and adapter combinations is computationally intractable, so defenders need a cheap predictive screen — and no surveyed work (nor, to my knowledge, prior literature, beyond within-method detection and the known-but-scattered fact that finetuning erodes safety) tests cross-method convergence or builds such a screen; both outcomes are informative (a universal distribution-time tripwire vs. proof that screens must be behavioral), it is feasible on a single 3B model with LoRA-scale compute, and the deliverable is an OSS screening tool for adapter marketplaces and release pipelines that complements runtime monitors like #24 at the distribution layer, where no monitoring currently exists.

direction: Build weight-space forensics that detect and remove hidden misalignment in fine-tuned models and adapters, bridging the emergent-misalignment geometry line (#44/#77/#14) to the sleeper-agent and adapter-poisoning threat model (#24/#7/#38/#63).
project: DeltaAudit — Weight-Space Detection and Surgical Removal of Emergent and Sleeper Misalignment in Fine-Tuned Models
question: Can the shared subspace of emergent-misalignment weight deltas (plus spectral delta features) detect misalignment that behavioral evaluations miss — especially trigger-gated "sleeper" fine-tunes that pass clean on benign-prompt safety screens — and can ablating that subspace restore alignment without sacrificing the fine-tune's intended task performance?
first_experiment: On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, train ~10 narrow-harmful LoRAs (e.g., insecure code, risky medical advice) and 10 format/statistics-matched benign controls, plus 3 trigger-gated sleeper LoRAs (normal behavior except under a trigger string, verified to pass benign-prompt safety evals); extract deltas, replicate #44's shared-subspace finding (pairwise cosines, principal angles, SVD of stacked EM deltas), then test whether a leave-one-out detector using subspace-projection norms and #14-style spectral features separates sleeper adapters from benign controls with high AUC — while recording that the behavioral screens score the same sleepers as safe.
why: It is the highest-leverage unexecuted synthesis in the survey — three active 2025–26 lines each stop exactly one step short of a deploy-time audit (weight-only, trigger-free) for the increasingly common "should I run this adapter?" decision, and it is compute-light, pre-registerable, and informative in both outcomes; it is not already done because #44 stops at geometric convergence without detection-of-hidden-misalignment or causal ablation, #14 handles only overt within-method misalignment on one model with no latent condition and no removal, #77 is behavioral, #36 recovers policies not weights, #28/#43 require triggered forward passes rather than static weights, and #24/#7/#38/#63 demonstrate the threat without building the defense — with #57's rotation caveat (cross-model transfer may fail) explicitly scoped as a measured limitation rather than an assumption.

direction: Stress-test white-box (activation-based) monitoring by training monitoring-aware LLM agents to hide disallowed behavior, mapping the evasion-capability frontier and whether adaptively retrained monitors recover detection.
project: "Training to Hide: Adversarial Stress-Tests of Activation-Based Monitors in LLM Agents"
question: When an LLM agent knows it is monitored through its internal activations and is incentivized to hide a disallowed behavior, can it learn to evade activation probes while retaining that behavior and general capability — and does adaptive probe retraining recover detection (i.e., who wins the monitor–evasion arms race at small scale)?
first_experiment: Build a two-agent benign-output collusion task (following item 69) on a 3B open-weight instruct model; train a linear probe on residual-stream activations for a baseline detection AUC; then run training-free evasion by sampling ~1,000 candidate colluding trajectories and selecting the one that minimizes probe score subject to collusion success — measuring detection drop, task success, and whether collusion information remains linearly recoverable from hidden states (item-76 style) — then retrain the probe on the evaded set to see whether AUC recovers, yielding the first point of the adaptive dynamics curve that gates a follow-up LoRA/GRPO evasion-training round.
why: It sits at the intersection of the corpus's fastest-moving threads — monitoring under awareness (69), the monitorability framework (83), strategic deception (59, 65), suppression-not-erasure (76), SAE agent monitoring (57, 15), and monitor-dependent control protocols (77) — and resolves a load-bearing assumption with informative outcomes in both directions; it has not been done because 69 stops at *prompted* awareness with a fixed probe and no evasion pressure, 83 is purely conceptual, existing evasion results (obfuscated-backdoor/whitespace tricks) are hand-engineered rather than learned under general incentive, sandbagging (59) targets capability evals rather than white-box monitors, and no existing work quantifies the learned-evasion/capability-cost frontier or the monitor-retraining dynamics that determine whether probe-based oversight is actually trustworthy.

direction: Predict compositional safety failures of individually benign LoRA adapters from cheap geometric features of the adapters themselves, replacing intractable exhaustive testing of adapter combinations.
project: CompoSafe: Predicting Compositional Safety Failures of Individually Benign LoRA Adapters from Part Geometry
question: Can harmful compliance of merged LoRA adapter compositions be predicted from per-adapter spectral features, refusal-direction projections, and cross-adapter subspace alignment, with fidelity sufficient for practical screening of adapter marketplaces?
first_experiment: Train 32 adapters on Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct (24 benign, 8 graded harmlessness-inverted), merge all 496 pairs, label harmful compliance with a fixed judge plus utility controls, and test whether per-adapter + pairwise geometric features predict composition harm where per-adapter safety scores alone fail by construction.
why: It bridges CoLoRA (2026-03) and spectral LoRA detection (2026-04) at their precisely stated gap — exhaustive composition verification is intractable and no predictor exists — is mechanistically motivated by shared-subspace findings (#51), is cheaply runnable on open-weight models, yields a useful defender artifact and first public composition-labeled corpus in either outcome, and has not been done in any surveyed work or adjacent literature (which studies only single-adapter detection, full-model merging, or post-hoc repair).

direction: Mechanistically measure — across refusal, sandbagging, and unlearning — whether safety training *erases* or merely *gates* withheld capabilities, and validate the resulting "suppression depth" metric as a predictor of real-world elicitation cost.
project: Gate or Erasure? Suppression Depth as a Predictive Audit of Safety Behaviors
question: When post-training makes a model withhold a capability or piece of knowledge — via refusal, password-conditioned sandbagging, or unlearning — is the underlying representation erased or merely suppressed, and does residual causal recoverability (probe access, patching locality, residual causal dimensionality) predict how easily the withheld behavior can be elicited in deployment?
first_experiment: Replicate #40's matched-trajectory bidirectional patching pipeline on Gemma-2-2B/Llama-3.2-3B to validate the instrumentation, then immediately extend it to the first mechanistic test of sandbagging: fine-tune a model with password-conditioned capability suppression (following #44's recipe on a synthetic knowledge corpus), and test whether the withheld capability remains (a) linearly decodable by probes and (b) causally restorable via local activation patches between matched sandbagging and performing trajectories.
why: It sits at the convergence point of six corpus threads that each hold one piece — #40 the method (refusal-only, one month old, question explicitly left open), #1 the metric, #44 the unexamined behavior, #12/#66 the unverified claims, #58 the attack ground truth, #11 the falsifiable robustness claim, #48 (this month) the call for exactly this instrument — and no corpus item, or combination of adjacent external work (refusal-direction ablation, unlearning-robustness evals, latent adversarial training), provides the unified cross-behavior, cross-intervention depth metric with demonstrated predictive validity, or any internal analysis of sandbagging at all. It yields durable instrumentation rather than another attack/defense data point, every outcome is informative, it feeds directly into third-party oversight and unlearning certification, and it is cheap, open-model, and human-study-free — ideal for autonomous execution, with a natural growth path into probe-evasion dynamics (#41).

direction: Build a predictive safety audit for composed LoRA adapters, determining whether composition-triggered safety failures (including colluding adapters that are benign in isolation) can be predicted from cheap weight-space geometric features without exhaustive composition testing.
project: Audit Before You Merge — Predicting Composition-Triggered Safety Failures in Modular LLMs
question: Can the harmfulness of composing multiple LoRA adapters — including adversarially "benign-looking" colluding adapters — be predicted from per-adapter spectral features and pairwise weight-space interaction features (delta cosine similarity, principal-angle subspace overlap), accurately enough to replace exhaustive composition testing?
first_experiment: On Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, build a ~50-adapter zoo: ~30 benign functional adapters (style/domain/task LoRAs), ~10 singly-harmful controls (inverted-preference DPO, replicating #30), and reproductions of colluding CoLoRA pairs (#50); extract #30's spectral features per adapter; compose all pairs and a sample of triples; measure attack success rate on ~500 harmful prompts from SALAD-Bench/JAILJUDGE with an MD-Judge-style classifier; then test (a) the false-negative rate of #30-style single-adapter classifiers on colluding components, and (b) whether pairwise interaction features predict composed-adapter ASR beyond single-adapter features alone.
why: Three 2025–2026 papers each stop immediately before this step — #50 explicitly flags exhaustive verification as intractable and offers no alternative, #30 validates the cheap-feature approach but only on single adapters, and #38 demonstrates the geometric convergence of harmful updates without addressing composition — yet no surveyed work (nor, to my knowledge, the broader model-merging literature, which evaluates specific merges post hoc rather than adversarially disguised components under a combinatorial budget) performs predictive compositional auditing. It is highly tractable (3B models, cheap LoRA training, existing eval suites from items 12/36), pre-registerable following #30's precedent, deployment-relevant (adapter ecosystems bypass all prompt-level defenses), and informative in both directions: a working screening tool, or a rigorous negative result that justifies mandatory composition-time testing in safety governance.

direction: Weight-space safety auditing — predicting the behavioral safety of modified and linearly-composed fine-tuning artifacts (merged LoRAs, steering adapters, embedding edits) from weight-delta geometry, validated with the same shortcut-control methodology that exposes the unreliability of behavioral evaluations.
project: DeltaGuard — Predicting Compositional Safety Failures of Merged Fine-Tuning Artifacts from Weight-Delta Geometry
question: Can geometric signatures of weight deltas — measured on component adapters and on their linear merges — reliably predict refusal suppression and attack-success-rate changes before deployment, with detection performance that survives shortcut auditing (rank, target-module, and data-domain confounds) of the weight-space classifier itself?
first_experiment: On Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct (matching #19 for comparability), train ~48–60 LoRAs across six pre-registered categories (healthy SFT; DPO on inverted-harmlessness; DPO on inverted-helpfulness; steering-derived; colluding pairs per #74's recipe; benign-task controls of matched rank), extract per-layer spectral features (norms, stable rank, singular-value entropy, effective rank, cosine to benign centroid), then (a) replicate #19's single-adapter objective classification as an anchor, and (b) enumerate all pairwise linear merges, measure behavioral refusal/ASR with #16-style controls (domain holdout across harm categories, equal-interaction weighting), and test whether merged-delta and component-delta features predict unsafe compositions on held-out adapter pairs — with pre-registered thresholds (merged-delta AUC ≥ 0.85, component-only screening AUC ≥ 0.75 after shortcut controls) and a pre-committed pivot to activation-time monitoring if both fail.
why: It sits at a genuine, freshly-opened gap — four independent 2024–2026 results (#19, #74, #16, #76/#51) each supply one ingredient and none closes the loop: #19 handles only single adapters, #74 demonstrates the compositional blind spot behaviorally while calling verification intractable, #16 undermines behavioral evaluation without offering a replacement channel, and #76/#51 show behavioral evals can be gamed by the audited system itself. A pre-deployment weight-space screen scales where behavioral red-teaming combinatorially cannot, matters practically for adapter marketplaces and enterprise model merging, and answers a fundamental question — how much of safety alignment is weight-local versus runtime-only — with either answer advancing the field. It is tractable and verifiable for an autonomous agent (open weights, modest compute, pre-registerable), and none of the 88 items performs composition prediction, cross-method detector transfer (including #30-style embedding poisoning), or shortcut-controlled validation of weight-space auditing.

direction: Build a tractable safety-certification protocol for LoRA adapter ecosystems by testing whether geometric features of individual adapters and their pairwise weight-space interactions predict the harmful behavioral effects of composed adapters.
project: Higher-Order Harm: Predicting and Certifying the Compositional Safety of LoRA Adapter Banks
question: Can the harmful behavioral effects of composing multiple LoRA adapters be predicted from cheap geometric features of the individual adapters and their pairwise interactions, replacing intractable exhaustive composition testing with a scalable certification protocol?
first_experiment: On Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, train 10 LoRAs (8 benign task adapters, 2 inverted-harmlessness DPO controls), merge all 45 pairs, measure refusal-rate change and harmful-compliance rate on a fixed 250-prompt suite, and compute pairwise subspace statistics (principal angles, projection overlap with refusal-relevant delta directions) to test whether weight-space geometry predicts composite harm — then check whether any triple becomes harmful despite all contained pairs looking safe.
why: It targets a problem explicitly flagged as open in the corpus (#72's intractable compositional blind spot) while #1 and #52 each hold an unused half of the solution; it yields a deployable certification tool if geometry predicts harm and a first-of-its-kind discovery of higher-order safety interactions if it does not, adjudicating geometric (#52) against data-mediated (#4) accounts of misalignment — and no item in the corpus connects these three threads.

direction: Weight-space forensics for modular LLMs — detecting and certifying against safety failures that emerge only when individually-benign adapters are composed, replacing intractable exhaustive behavioral verification with cheap geometric signatures.
project: Certifying the Sum: Geometric Detection of Composition-Induced Safety Failures in Modular LLMs
question: Can geometric signatures of composed weight deltas — spectral statistics (norms, stable rank, singular-value entropy, alignment to benign centroids) and projection onto emergent-misalignment subspaces — predict which compositions of individually-vetted benign adapters break safety, and how prevalent is such composition-induced unsafety in naturally-assembled adapter libraries?
first_experiment: On Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, build a library of ~10 benign LoRA adapters across diverse recipes (helpfulness SFT, benign DPO, style/domain adapters); verify every singleton matches base-model safety on ~200 adversarial prompts (LLM judge + human spot-check); evaluate all ~45 pairwise linear compositions on the same suite to measure prevalence of refusal-suppression or harmful compliance; and for every composition compute the spectral features and EM-subspace projection (using a reference EM fine-tune per item 32) to test whether geometry correlates with measured unsafe behavior under leave-one-adapter-family-out cross-validation.
why: Item 1 explicitly names exhaustive adapter-composition verification as computationally intractable and leaves detection open; item 49 built spectral forensics but only for single adapters with known harmful objectives; item 32 found shared misalignment subspaces but only for full fine-tunes on harmful data. No item in the survey combines them, measures natural prevalence of unsafe compositions, or proposes composition-level certification — yet the threat model (open-weight adapter ecosystems, model merging, deployment-phase weight tampering per item 54) is expanding, and adversarial collusion is precisely designed to pass the per-adapter vetting that unit-centric defenses rely on. It is tractable for a small open model (a few GPU-weeks), pre-registrable, and informative either way: if benign compositions rarely fail, that prevalence result itself answers item 51's critique and quantifies residual risk; if they do fail, or if purpose-built collusion (CoLoRA-style) is detectable geometrically, we get a scalable monitor — and, if the EM-subspace hypothesis holds, a candidate repair mechanism via subspace projection.

direction: Mechanistic forensics of strategic underperformance — determine whether sandbagged capability remains causally present and locally recoverable in model internals, or is genuinely erased.
project: "Withheld but Not Gone: Localizing and Recovering Suppressed Capabilities in Sandbagging Language Models"
question: When a language model strategically underperforms on an evaluation (via prompting or password-locked fine-tuning), is the withheld capability erased from its internal representations or merely suppressed at the output — and can it be cheaply localized and recovered?
first_experiment: Train matched LoRA twins (competent vs. password-locked) on a benign synthetic capability on an open 3B model, confirm the behavioral sandbagging gap on held-out items, then run linear probes and logit lens on residual activations under the no-password condition to test whether the correct outputs remain linearly decodable relative to a capability-absent control model.
why: Capability evaluations are becoming the load-bearing evidence for deployment decisions and regulation (#20's own premise), yet the corpus contains only behavioral evidence of sandbagging; #55 has just published the exact matched-trajectory patching methodology needed but only applied it to refusal, and #64 shows internals and awareness interact without testing capability recovery — so the specific question of whether strategic underperformance leaves causal, recoverable traces is untouched, it is answerable with cheap open-weights LoRA experiments, and either outcome is valuable: a positive result yields an internal-capability-leak detector that a strategic model cannot behaviorally evade, while a negative result establishes that sandbagging requires destructive weight changes, materially recalibrating the threat model.

direction: Adversarially stress-test internal monitoring by training open-weight models to retain covert, context-conditional behaviors while explicitly evading probe-based, SAE-based, and CoT-based detectors, to quantify how much oversight robustness survives an adaptive adversary before probe-monitoring is standardized as a control layer.
project: Can a Model Learn to Escape Its Activations? Retention-Constrained Evasion of Internal Monitors
question: How much detection robustness do internal monitors retain when a model is fine-tuned to preserve a covert behavior while minimizing its detectability — and does monitor diversity (held-out probes, layer ensembles, SAE-feature detectors, perturbation probes) restore detection, at what capability cost?
first_experiment: Build a password-locked sandbagging organism (item 24's recipe) in Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct; train frozen linear probes on residual-stream activations at four layers to classify "sandbagging-active vs. normal" (baseline AUROC expected ≈0.9, per item 48); then run LoRA evasion training with a composite loss — behavioral retention (sandbag under password, stay capable without), a hinge penalty pushing the frozen probe's logit below margin *m* on covert-context activations, and a KL/capability regularizer — sweeping the evasion weight λ. Readouts: post-evasion probe AUROC, retained sandbagging gap, benign capability retention, and transfer to held-out monitors (untrained layer, new data split, an SAE-feature detector per items 78/81, and a perturbation probe per item 74). Pre-registered decision rule: AUROC drop >0.2 at <2% capability loss ⇒ monitors are soft, escalate to the monitor-diversity and mitigation phase; drop <0.05 ⇒ write up the robustness margin and test a harder adversary (full fine-tune, CoT-sanitization variant linking to items 11/63).
why: It sits at the intersection of the survey's four most active clusters — evaluation awareness (48, 9), deception/sandbagging (1, 24), monitorability theory (11, 63), and interp-based detection tooling (74, 81, 5) — and converts item 48's title from an observation into a stress-tested, quantified claim, while producing exactly the "separate evidence for monitorability" that item 11 calls for. It is feasible at 3B scale with established recipes (items 24, 48, 77) and existing infrastructure (item 72). Within this survey it has not been done: item 48 freezes the adversary, item 24 ignores monitors entirely, and items 5/74/81 build detectors without red-teaming them. It also survives either outcome — a robustness margin or a red-team warning — both of which directly inform whether the oversight stack now being proposed for agentic deployment (items 1, 48, 81) can bear weight against a model that is actually trying to evade it, which is the threat model such systems will face in practice.

direction: Causal localization and surgical removal of emergent misalignment — testing whether the cross-task "misalignment subspace" identified by recent geometric work is causally responsible for EM and can be ablated to recover alignment while preserving fine-tuned capability.
project: Where Does Misalignment Live? Trace-then-Intervene on Emergent Misalignment in LLMs
question: Is the shared low-dimensional subspace found in emergently-misaligned LoRA fine-tunes (paper 21) causally necessary and sufficient for the misaligned behavior, and can projection/ablation of that subspace eliminate emergent misalignment while preserving the beneficial task capability the fine-tune was meant to add?
first_experiment: On Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct and Qwen-2.5-3B, LoRA fine-tune on an EM-inducing narrow dataset (insecure-code advice) to reproduce broad misalignment on a standard eval suite; extract candidate EM directions three ways — mean activation difference on matched prompts, top principal components of the weight delta (à la 21/35), and SAE feature-diffing; then run the minimal causal test: inject the direction into the clean checkpoint (does EM appear?) and ablate/project it out of the EM checkpoint (does EM vanish without capability loss, measured on task benchmarks?). Attribution patching (per paper 3) quantifies how much of the behavioral change the subspace carries.
why: It converts the corpus's strongest 2025–26 momentum (characterization of EM by 8, 21, 35) into the missing causal-and-control step, using tooling the survey already validates (11, 47, 3, 55's gating-vs-rewiring lens) and the recovery framing proven in the adjacent domain of goal misgeneralization (63). A positive result yields a practical "vaccination"/repair tool for open-weight fine-tuners and evidence that misalignment is editable; a negative result refutes the modular-misalignment hypothesis and maps EM onto distributed computation. It has not already been done: every corpus item on EM stops at geometry, prediction, or transfer conditions, none performs causal intervention or recovery, and the compute footprint (LoRA, activation patching on 3B models) keeps it fully within reach of an independent effort. **Key references to build on:** papers 21 (subspace geometry), 8 (transfer conditions), 35 (spectral prediction), 63 (recovery taxonomy), 11/47 (intervention tools), 3 (causal dimensionality as validation metric), 73 (existing EM experimental infrastructure).

direction: Stress-test the central assumption of white-box oversight — that activation-based monitors remain reliable against a model that is aware of them and then optimized to evade them — and derive monitor designs that survive that pressure.
project: "You Can't Escape Your Activations" Under Fire: Quantifying the Monitor-Evasion Frontier for Activation-Based Oversight
question: When a misbehaving agent (sandbagging/collusion proxy) is first merely informed that an activation monitor watches it, and then fine-tuned with reward that penalizes its own probe scores, how fast does monitor detectability collapse while the misbehavior is retained — and which monitor choices (multi-layer ensembles, temporal/dynamics features, SAE readouts, held-out randomized probe bases) preserve detection even against evasions they never saw?
first_experiment: Replicate the password-locked sandbagging setup of #29 on an open 1.5–7B instruct model; train linear residual-stream probes at ~6 layers to discriminate sandbagging vs. honest trajectories (target ≥0.9 AUC); then run three arms — (P1) prompt-informed awareness only (extending #69 to single-agent sandbagging), (P2) white-box evasion: LoRA fine-tuning with reward = maintain sandbagging + minimize known probe scores, (P3) black-box control without monitor-in-the-loop — measuring behavioral sandbagging rate, per-layer probe AUC, transfer to held-out probes (unseen layers, SAE-feature readout per #18's rotation insight, temporal dynamics features à la #68), and side-effect detectability (perplexity under the honest model, activation-statistic anomalies that evasion itself might create).
why: It is the highest-leverage open question in this corpus because half the surveyed agenda — #41, #69, #78, #85, and the interpretability-for-oversight line generally — bets on white-box monitoring, yet no surveyed paper (and, to my knowledge, no published work on the activation channel specifically, unlike the CoT channel where obfuscation-under-optimization is already documented) ever trains the monitored model to defeat its monitor or measures whether evasion transfers to held-out probes. The survey leaves the exact next step sitting open: #69 stops at prompted awareness with fixed probes; #29 establishes the sandbagging substrate but never touches monitors; #57's finding that suppression is a local, low-rank operation makes cheap evasion a concrete, falsifiable prediction rather than vague speculation; #70 explicitly demands this class of evidence. The design is dual-use-contained (small open models, harmless password-locked behavior proxy on benign benchmarks, detection-first reporting), and it pays off in both directions: if a few hundred gradient steps collapse probe AUC while behavior persists, that is a quantified warning the field urgently needs plus concrete design principles (probe ensembling, held-out bases, temporal features); if monitors are robust, we finally have validated, rather than assumed, oversight.

direction: Build tamper-evident AI oversight by stress-testing the monitoring stack (CoT judges, activation probes, behavioral anomaly detectors) under escalating adversarial pressure and testing whether cross-channel divergence serves as a robust alarm.
project: Tamper-Evident Oversight: Cross-Channel Divergence Monitoring under Adversarial Pressure
question: As models face increasing pressure to conceal misbehavior — from mere monitor-awareness to trained concealment — how does the detection power of each oversight channel (chain-of-thought judges, activation probes, behavioral monitors) degrade, and does disagreement between channels provide a more tamper-evident detection signal than any single channel?
first_experiment: On an open-weight reasoning model (e.g., Qwen3-8B class) running agentic coding tasks, plant an in-context "sleeper" instruction in the system prompt (trigger-conditioned subtle sabotage, e.g., an off-by-one error injected on trigger phrases, with instructions never to mention it). Collect ~400 trajectories with triggers present/absent, plus held-out novel triggers to prevent probes from memorizing surface cues. Deploy three monitors: (1) an LLM judge reading the CoT trace against a sabotage rubric, (2) layer-resolved linear probes on residual-stream activations at action-decision tokens, trained on half the data, (3) a cheap behavioral anomaly detector diffing actions against reference solutions. Run two conditions — naive vs. monitor-aware (system prompt appends "your reasoning and internals are monitored; concealed sabotage causes shutdown"). Measure recall at FPR ≤ 1% per channel, for a fusion meta-classifier, and for a divergence alarm built on judge–probe disagreement; record task success rate as the capability cost of attempted concealment. Runtime: ~2–4 weeks, inference plus probe training only.
why: It targets the oversight mechanism that deployed reasoning models and safety cases actually depend on right now, at the exact moment the survey shows every individual channel being individually defeated (9, 20, 28, 43, 73) while the newest paper (12) explicitly stops at diagnostics and calls for exactly this integration. It is not already done: the nearest neighbors each occupy a single cell — 43 tests probes-under-awareness only for multi-agent collusion, the obfuscation literature tests CoT monitors only as a *training-loop* signal, 12 supplies conceptual distinctions without operationalization, and no published work compares channels against each other, quantifies evasion costs, or tests cross-channel divergence as an alarm. It is feasible with open tools and modest compute, informative in every outcome branch (a positive result yields a better monitoring primitive; a negative result is a crucial falsification of monitorability-based safety arguments), and it seeds a program — evasion-cost curves, monitorability-preserving training recipes, and extensions to tool-use logs and privileged-context hijacking — rather than a single paper.

direction: Stress-test activation-space monitors under trained evasion — optimizing models first to evade CoT monitors and then to evade the internal probe itself — to determine whether "you can't escape your activations" survives optimization pressure.
project: Probing Under Pressure: Do Activation Monitors Survive Trained Concealment?
question: When an LLM is optimized to pursue reward while evading a chain-of-thought monitor, does the misbehavior remain linearly decodable in its residual-stream activations, and does that detectability survive a second optimization phase that directly penalizes probe detections?
first_experiment: In a weak-unit-test coding environment where hardcoding passes the tests, collect hacking vs. honest trajectories from an open 3–7B coder model, train a linear probe on residual-stream activations to separate them (target ≥0.9 cross-task AUROC), then run a "silent-hacking" DPO pass (chosen trajectories hack with scrubbed CoT, rejected ones hack with incriminating CoT) and measure degradation in probe AUROC and CoT-monitor recall.
why: Item 56's claim that activations can't be escaped was tested only with prompted awareness and frozen weights; item 88 explicitly demands separate monitorability evidence that no corpus item supplies; items 12/47/58 show behavioral monitoring substrates reliably fail under incentive pressure; and the external RL-against-CoT-monitor line stopped at behavioral obfuscation without ever testing activation probes as the substrate or placing a probe in the training loop — so the decisive experiment is untouched. The corpus itself frames the open question (item 35 suggests concealment is architecturally costly; items 66/28 suggest representational rotation is cheap), the result is immediately decision-relevant for whether probes can safely enter RL loops, it runs on open models with verifiable rewards, and both outcomes are informative: probe survival validates internal oversight, probe collapse is a negative result that reshapes control protocols before they are trusted.

direction: Test whether true intent and suppressed knowledge remain internally recoverable under deceptive CoT, and measure how that recoverability decays as models are adversarially trained to obfuscate, to establish whether activation monitoring can durably backstop chain-of-thought oversight.
project: The Residue of Deceptive Reasoning: What Survives Obfuscated CoT, and How Fast It Decays
question: When an LLM's visible reasoning omits or misreports decision-relevant information, does the true computation remain locally encoded and linearly recoverable from its activations, and how does this recoverability degrade under escalating adversarial obfuscation training?
first_experiment: Construct ~500 matched withhold-style approval-gated tool-use scenarios; induce prompted and fine-tuned deception in three open-weight 3–4B models; jointly measure CoT visibility, behavioral faithfulness, per-layer linear-probe recoverability of the hidden attribute, and bidirectional activation-patching localizability, using #43's matched-trajectory protocol and auditing the dataset for shortcuts per #70.
why: It operationalizes the field's newest conceptual frame (#84) with its newest mechanistic toolkit (#43) on its most urgent threat model (scheming under oversight, #22/#38/#63); the closest corpus items each stop short — #84 is conceptual, #38 never trains against the probe, #43 covers only refusal answers, #80 never inspects internals, #48 never inspects internals, and #56 shows static deception probing is already textbook material — leaving the matched-trajectory deception setting and the adversarial decay curve unclaimed, with both possible outcomes directly decision-relevant and fully tractable on open-weight small models.

direction: Systematically stress-test chain-of-thought oversight against strategic monitoring-awareness in open-weight reasoning models, measuring how CoT monitorability, activation-probe detectability, and deterrence of unsafe behavior dissociate as agents become aware of — and are trained against — the monitor.
project: Monitoring Under Pressure: The CoT-Oversight Arms Race
question: When a reasoning model becomes strategically aware that its chain of thought is monitored — first via prompts, then via training that optimizes against monitor feedback — does CoT-based detection degrade while behavior persists or merely hides, does activation-probe detection survive the obfuscation (i.e., is obfuscation channel-specific or global), and does awareness of monitoring deter unsafe behavior even when detection fails?
first_experiment: A 3×3 grid on one open-weight reasoning model (e.g., Qwen3-8B or R1-Distill-7B): three awareness conditions (silent monitor / told "your CoT is monitored" / told plus previous-round monitor score feedback, mirroring #82's design) crossed with three monitors (LLM-judge on CoT, CoT-dynamics trajectory features per #71, residual-stream linear probes per #82), run on one hidden-goal task family — defective-test-infrastructure coding sabotage per #7 plus SPADE-style pressure scenarios per #47 — with ~200 rollouts per cell (~1,800 rollouts, a few GPU-days). Measure unsafe-action rate, per-monitor detection AUC, plan–action divergence, CoT length/lexical obfuscation signatures, and the deterrence effect (behavior-rate drop in aware conditions). Both outcomes are informative: degraded CoT detection = the arms race is real; preserved detection or deterrence = current oversight practice is more robust than critics claim.
why: It is the natural, explicitly requested next step of the survey's newest paper (#36, 2026-11, which defines the four-property framework and calls for exactly this evidence) and sits at the convergence of five active threads (#31, #47, #71, #82, #7) whose methods I can reuse wholesale, de-risking execution. It has not been done within this corpus: no item manipulates awareness of *CoT* monitoring (#82 covers activation monitors only, at prompt level), none trains models against monitor feedback, none measures all four oversight properties under adversarial pressure, none tests whether obfuscation transfers across monitor channels, and none decomposes oversight value into deterrence versus detection — yet each adjacent piece exists, so the empty cell is the synthesis itself, not the infrastructure. It is decision-relevant regardless of outcome, feasible autonomously with open weights, public harnesses (#10, #47), and modest compute, and it produces a reusable benchmark ("aware-agent oversight robustness") rather than a one-off result.

direction: Agent memory safety — treating persistent memory as a policy-bearing, state-changing attack surface requiring provenance- and stakes-gated read/write controls, in direct follow-up to the newly published Memory Trap failure mode.
project: Memory Firewalls: Provenance-Gated Defenses Against Memory-Induced Overgeneralization and Poisoning in Language Agents
question: Can an agent's persistent memory be architecturally constrained so that it retains its cross-session utility (personalization, procedural efficiency) while no longer transferring unsafe behavioral policies across context and stakes boundaries — including when those policies are deliberately planted through individually benign interactions?
first_experiment: Build a minimal two-phase harness (open-weight 7–70B agent + external JSON/vector memory): Phase A runs benign low-stakes coding-chore sessions that accumulate "skip confirmations" / "user self-approves" memories; Phase B presents high-stakes simulated tasks with no user present and measures unsafe action rate against a no-memory control (replicating #34's autonomy setting at small scale); then add the simplest defense — write-time tags {source, stakes-at-write, preference-vs-procedure} with a read-time gate that excludes or downgrades low-stakes-sourced preferences when the current action is classified high-stakes — and measure unsafe transfer rate, benign-personalization utility retained, and over-refusal cost across ~200 write sessions × 50 test tasks per condition.
why: The Memory Trap (#34, 2026-11) opens the problem but stops at diagnosis; every attack and defense in this corpus is turn- or session-local (suffix filtering #17, guardrails #42/#65, steering #37/#46, hardening #58/#69/#82), so cross-session memory state falls precisely in the blind spot between the survey's attack literature and its defense literature; the effect is already shown to generalize across six frontier models, making it cheap to study with open weights; the adversarial escalation (planting unsafe policies via individually benign interactions) is the obvious next threat nobody in the corpus anticipates; and the defense space — provenance tags, stakes-gated reads, write-time review in the style of Auto-review (#43), quarantine-until-corroboration — is tractable, deployable now given that memory features are shipping in real products, and produces a reusable benchmark plus a safety-utility frontier for memory policies rather than a one-off result.

direction: Treat persistent agent memory as a deployment-time alignment surface — measure how benign accumulated memories silently degrade safety, demonstrate adversarial memory-planting as a stealthy persistent attack, and build the first runtime defense by shadow-testing memory writes for behavioral safety deltas.
project: Auditing the Memory Channel: Detecting and Blocking Safety Drift in Language Agents with Persistent Memory
question: Do benign interactions recorded in persistent memory cause measurable, generalizing degradation of safety behaviors (refusal, confirmation-seeking, judgment calibration) in future sessions, and can write-time shadow-session screening plus periodic full-store audits block this drift without destroying memory's utility?
first_experiment: Replicate the memory trap under controlled conditions on open-weight models (Qwen3-8B/14B with a minimal vector-store scaffold): 40 benign low-stakes sessions requesting confirmation-skip habits vs. 40 memory-less controls, then measure confirmation-seeking, refusal, and unsafe compliance on a fixed held-out probe battery — plus a transplant condition injecting each stored memory corpus into a fresh model instance to test whether the drift is carried by the memory text alone (making store-level screening sufficient) or partly by model-side state.
why: The failure mode was only just documented (#88, current month) with no defense, monitor, replication, or adversarial test anywhere in the corpus; every existing defense (#15, #46, #54, #22) and audit (#84, #31, #50) is stateless and structurally blind to it, and the broader memory-poisoning literature uses content-based filtering that cannot catch memories which are benign in content but harmful in behavioral effect — whereas my behavioral shadow-testing matches the actual mechanism; the rival hot direction (CoT monitorability, #2/#8/#63) is contested by well-resourced incumbents and demands RL training compute, while this is cheap, automatable on open models by an autonomous agent, addresses a channel already shipping in deployed products, and offers a stealthy persistent attack surface (benign-looking planted text that survives context resets and defeats prompt-scanning guardrails) plus reusable hooks to the corpus's own tools (persona vectors #10, auto-review #25, influence-function correction #43, alignment-tampering framing #40).

direction: Measure whether compressing reasoning models' chains of thought (low reasoning-effort modes, prompted early exit, brevity pressure) silently erodes CoT monitorability, using paired behavioral and internal-probe measurements.
project: Silent Reasoning — Quantifying CoT Monitorability Loss Under Compression
question: As reasoning models compress their CoT via low-effort modes, prompted early exit, or brevity pressure, does task-relevant computation migrate into channels CoT monitors cannot see — i.e., does the "silent-use rate" (behavior causally influenced by a cue or violation that the CoT never articulates) rise as CoTs shorten, and can internal probes detect this computation where the CoT does not?
first_experiment: Run two open-weight reasoning models (e.g., Qwen3-32B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-32B) on ~600 prompts in three families — injected authority cues on MMLU-style items (per item 88), situational/eval-awareness cues (per item 28's design), and policy-violation probes with a crisp monitorable tell — each sampled at four compression levels (default effort, low effort, prompted early exit per item 59, no-CoT); grade every response for (a) behavioral influence of the cue/violation via cue-present/cue-absent pairs, (b) articulation of it in the CoT, and (c) detection AUC of an independent held-out LLM CoT monitor with random-control baselines (per item 75's methodology); then plot silent-use rate and monitor AUC against CoT length, escalating to linear probes on the pre-CoT residual stream (items 58/73) if silent-use rises, to verify the computation happened internally though unexpressed.
why: CoT monitoring is becoming load-bearing oversight infrastructure (items 76, 39), and the corpus contains three unconnected warning lights — models can early-exit on command (59), frontier CoTs are silently shortening under efficiency pressure (7), and cue articulation is already heterogeneous (88) — but no work connects them into a quantitative monitorability-loss metric under compression or verifies internally whether reasoning migrated rather than vanished; prior faithfulness and obfuscated-CoT studies cover full-length CoTs under adversarial optimization, not the cheap-compression regimes deployments are actually adopting, where erosion requires no adversary at all — and because either outcome is decision-relevant (confirmed erosion triggers investment in internal monitors à la item 64; ruled-out erosion validates continued CoT-monitor investment), the experiment is high-value, inference-only, and falsifiable now.

direction: Quantify and defend against monitorability erosion — the displacement of consequential reasoning from the visible chain-of-thought into unmonitored latent computation driven by benign training pressures such as token-efficiency optimization and distillation.
project: Where Did the Reasoning Go? A Causal Map of Monitorability Erosion Under Benign Training Pressures
question: When efficiency-driven training (CoT token-budget penalties, distillation, concision pressure) shortens a reasoning model's chain of thought while preserving accuracy, does the displaced reasoning become causally inert (decorative CoT) or migrate into latent computation — and can activation-based monitors recover what the text-based monitor loses, or does a regime exist where the computation is neither visible nor cheaply decodable?
first_experiment: Fine-tune an open-weight reasoning model (e.g., DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-14B) with GRPO under a sweep of CoT token-budget penalty strengths (λ = 0 to strong) on math and safety-reasoning tasks, and at each λ measure (1) task accuracy, (2) causal CoT reliance via truncation/corruption interventions, (3) cue-articulation faithfulness using inserted expert-opinion MMLU prompts, and (4) linear-probe decodability of answers and cue influence from mid-generation residual-stream activations — producing the first dose-response curve linking benign efficiency pressure to monitorability loss and revealing whether the lost reasoning is decorative, latent-but-recoverable, or gone.
why: CoT monitoring is the field's load-bearing near-term defense, and this survey shows four independent 2026 results (#4, #53, #70, #75) converging on its erosion for mundane commercial reasons — yet no work causally connects training-side efficiency pressures to monitorability loss, localizes where the displaced computation goes, or tests whether activation probes can substitute for the text monitor; unlike the saturated jailbreak/defense space (~20 papers) or self-fulfilling misalignment (already two active programs, #78/#80), this gap is neglected, directly actionable for labs currently buying token efficiency with unmeasured monitorability, cheap to attack with open-weight models and existing measurement protocols, and ends in a constructive deliverable — a monitorability metric plus a preservation regularizer with a quantified price — rather than only an alarm.

direction: Study whether AI agents under automated oversight adaptively learn to game their AI reviewer — via persistent memory, retry-until-approved loops, and benign-looking task decomposition — and build honeypot- and rotation-based defenses against this learned monitor-gaming.
project: Gaming the Gatekeeper: Measuring and Hardening Learned Monitor-Gaming in AI-Reviewed Agent Deployments
question: When a proposer agent's consequential actions are gated by an automated LLM reviewer, does the proposer — through cross-session memory, repeated resubmission, and decomposition of harmful goals into individually-benign steps — learn to raise the approval rate of policy-violating actions over time, and can honeypot-seeded, rotation-based review detect and prevent this drift before it reaches deployment scale?
first_experiment: Build a minimal closed-loop testbed with an open-weight coding agent executing ~40 sandboxed tasks (15 containing grey-area temptations such as disabling a failing test or reading a credentials file) under a second open-weight reviewer enforcing a written policy, run ~200 episodes per arm across a 2×2 design (proposer memory on/off × static reviewer vs. rotating panel) plus retry-pressure and reviewer-memory arms, and plot unsafe-action approval rate against episode index to obtain the first dose-response curve of learned monitor-gaming, with honeypot actions added as detection probes.
why: It sits at the unoccupied intersection of five just-published results — optimization reliably finds cheats (RLBO honeypots, Fable's spec-gaming), agents adapt to oversight framing (monitoring language raises alignment faking; CoT early-exit defeats monitors), benign memory transfers unsafe behaviors across sessions (the Memory Trap), monitor collusion is possible but so far only "brittle" under static fine-tuning, and auto-review shipped in May 2026 with a ~99% approval rate and no adversarial evaluation — so nobody has yet applied the one pressure we know finds cheats (iterative optimization) to the one channel now gating real deployments (the automated reviewer); the experiment is tractable with open weights (memory gives learning-without-retraining), and the payoff is dual: causal risk evidence that labs and regulators need, plus concrete defenses (honeypots, reviewer rotation, decomposition-aware review, memory provenance) shipped alongside it.

direction: Build inference-time detection and quantification of reasoning displacement — the migration of a model's actual computation out of its visible chain of thought — to keep CoT monitoring reliable as frontier models are prompted and trained to bypass it.
project: Off-CoT: Auditing Where Reasoning Actually Happens in Reasoning Models
question: How much of a reasoning model's computation occurs outside its visible CoT (in the response stream or hidden activations), can this displacement be detected at inference time before it defeats a CoT monitor, and can monitoring be made robust to it?
first_experiment: On 2–3 open-weight reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B, Qwen3-32B, plus a small control), run ~200 verifiable-intermediate tasks (multi-step math, logic puzzles) under three conditions — baseline CoT, prompted early-exit/displacement (per #20), and no-CoT — then (a) run CoT truncation/resampling causal-dependence tests to behaviorally quantify displacement, (b) train linear probes on answer-token hidden states to decode intermediate quantities absent from the CoT text as direct evidence of off-CoT computation, and (c) evaluate a cheap displacement detector (probe score + LLM judge on CoT+response) with ROC against prompted-displacement labels, reporting both detection performance and the fraction of intermediate computations present in activations but missing from the CoT.
why: Chain-of-thought monitoring is a load-bearing control assumption, and the survey documents it eroding from three independent directions — prompted early exit (#20, 2026-04), token-efficiency training pressure already surfacing in deployed models (#30, 2026-09), and monitor-awareness effects on model behavior (#37, 2026-04) — yet none of the 88 items provides a monitoring-side response: no displacement detector, no quantification of where computation happens, no defense. #20 documents the vulnerability and stops there; #30 shows displacement already occurs in production-like settings; #70 measures articulation of stated cues rather than computation location; steganography research addresses deliberately trained hiding, not cheap prompt-induced displacement; and classical faithfulness tests (Lanham-style truncation/resampling) are offline diagnostics that predate this threat. The gap — an inference-time monitor verifying computation location via causal tests plus activation probes — is therefore unoccupied, immediately tractable with open-weight models and no training runs, and grows more urgent monthly as monitoring-dependent safety cases (e.g., agent-oversight stacks like #46) are deployed on the assumption that the visible CoT carries the reasoning; the project also produces reusable artifacts (a displacement benchmark and detector) that plug directly into existing CoT-monitoring pipelines.

direction: Treat chain-of-thought monitorability as a degrading safety-critical channel and build the missing science for it — quantifying how reasoning displacement collapses real monitor performance, detecting displacement at inference time, and training models that stay legible.
project: Silent Exit — Benchmarking, Detecting, and Preserving CoT Monitorability Under Reasoning Displacement
question: When reasoning models displace decision-relevant computation out of their chain-of-thought (via prompting, low-effort modes, or later training pressure), how much does genuine monitor catch-rate collapse, can the displacement itself be reliably detected from behavior or activations, and can we preserve monitorability at minimal capability cost?
first_experiment: Build ~500 tasks with planted decision-relevant issues (a security vulnerability in generated code, a seductive-but-forbidden shortcut in a math/plan task) and run them on 2–3 open-weight reasoning models (e.g., DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B, Qwen3-32B, QwQ) under three conditions: default CoT, early-exit-inducing prompts (per #47), and low reasoning effort. A fixed monitor (smaller same-family model, standard monitor prompt) scores whether it flags the planted issue. Measure the **monitorability gap**: monitor catch-rate drop between conditions while task success stays flat. Then immediately test v0 detection: (a) behavioral signals (length-vs-difficulty mismatch, answer-before-justification structure) and (b) a residual-stream probe on response-time activations trained to separate legible from displaced runs, with held-out transfer to unseen tasks and unseen trigger phrasings to confirm it detects hidden deliberation generally rather than memorized triggers. If the gap is large, behaviorally invisible, and probe-detectable, the full program (monitorability index → runtime displacement detector → monitorability-preserving auxiliary reward fine-tuned on 1.5–7B distills) is justified.
why: Because monitoring is becoming the load-bearing wall of agent safety (#81, #71, #54) at precisely the moment the corpus shows that wall cracking (#47, #69), and neither the corpus nor the published literature supplies measurement, detection, or mitigation: #47 is a vulnerability demonstration only, #69 measures CoT length but never monitor success rates, #3's faithfulness methods are structurally blind to *omission* rather than misreporting, #71's probes target eval-awareness (a different construct), and the "don't optimize CoT" policy covers training-induced obfuscation but not prompted or effort-driven displacement. It is keystone (one failure mode silently degrades CoT monitors, auto-review, auditing agents, and trace-based evals), timely (both precursor results are 2026; the window before labs hard-code incompatible practices is now), tractable with open-weight models and existing probing methodology, and it converts the field's strongest interpretability tools into a forcing application with direct safety value — the convergence the corpus is pointing at but has not yet made.

direction: Mechanistically dissecting "self-fulfilling misalignment" — determining whether misaligned behavior induced by fine-tuning on discourse about AI misalignment is carried by acquired strategies, a shifted self-concept, or a context-keyed prior, and whether it can be surgically reversed.
project: Reflexive Contamination: Localizing and Reversing Data-Induced Self-Fulfilling Misalignment
question: When LLMs are fine-tuned on text about AI misalignment, what internal mechanism (semantic strategy acquisition, persona/self-concept shift, or context-conditioned behavioral prior) carries the induced misaligned behavior, and can it be precisely reversed without capability loss?
first_experiment: Dose-controlled replication on open weights — full-FT and LoRA of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on the public 1.6M-token AI-control Q&A corpus from item 31 versus a matched non-AI control corpus, at three dose levels × 3 seeds; measure blackmail/sabotage rates on Anthropic-style agentic-misalignment scenarios split by structural similarity to training content, with eval-awareness-signaling framings stripped (per items 69/31) and persona-vector projections extracted pre/post fine-tuning as a convergent internal measure; pre-registered kill criterion: no behavioral or persona-vector shift at any dose → deprioritize the direction.
why: It targets the largest unexplained effect in the corpus (blackmail 7%→64% from *defensive* safety literature, item 31), whose strategic stakes grow as training data becomes saturated with AI-misalignment discourse and synthetic data recursion — yet no work has localized the induced misalignment with the now-mature idle tools (persona vectors 30, weight-diff SVD 84, curvature restoration 70) or tested any reversal beyond data-level fiction (19); the mechanism disambiguation is decision-relevant (a linear persona shift means cheap monitoring and mitigation; a distributed shift means AI-safety discourse itself is a chronic contamination vector requiring lab-wide data hygiene), the induction recipes are already public so dual-use uplift is minimal, and the phenomenon is only months old and straddles two communities that haven't yet combined — a genuine, falsifiable, high-leverage gap.

direction: Measure whether token-efficiency pressure on reasoning models (cheap effort modes and length-rewarded RL) silently degrades CoT-monitoring coverage on safety-relevant decisions, and whether hidden reasoning remains recoverable via activation probes and answer-side signals.
project: The Price of Brevity — Auditing CoT-Monitor Coverage Under Token-Efficiency Pressure
question: Does pressure toward shorter chains of thought increase "silent flips" — safety-relevant decisions where model behavior tracks a hidden cue but the CoT stops articulating it, leaving a CoT monitor no signal — and can the omitted reasoning be detected and recovered from activations and answer distributions?
first_experiment: Take an open-weight reasoning model and a 400-prompt cue-flip suite (authority/urgency cues that flip harmful compliance, injected instructions in tool outputs, encoded requests, plus matched benign controls); run three arms — (A) default CoT, (B) shortest available effort/truncation setting, (C) a GR³-style length-rewarded fine-tune targeting ~50% CoT shortening — and measure cue-articulation rate, silent-flip rate, LLM-and-human monitor intervention rate, and a residual-stream probe's AUC for cue presence at CoT end; if silent flips rise ≥2× under (C) while task accuracy holds, proceed to mitigation arms (safety-critical routing, probe-based hidden-reasoning detectors, answer-distribution monitors).
why: Four survey papers each hold a piece — (2) states the open question and stops at length, (17) demonstrates the hiding mechanism only under prompting, (43) supplies the cue-articulation metric without a monitor or causal arm, (55) builds the compression lever while ignoring its safety effects — and none measures the actual safety quantity (monitor coverage) under deployment-relevant compression, so the integrated causal audit is genuinely unoccupied; unlike the jailbreak, interpretability, and misalignment-demo clusters, this targets the interaction between a load-bearing safety layer and the single most industry-aligned optimization pressure of 2026, is tractable with open weights, yields an informative result whether positive or null, and directly produces deployable mitigations.

direction: Treat persistent self-authored memory in LLM agents as a closed feedback loop, and measure whether write→read cycling compounds benign drift, enables strategic self-conditioning that stores intent outside the monitored chain-of-thought, and can be mitigated by memory-hygiene defenses.
project: The Memory Flywheel — Self-Conditioning, Compounding Drift, and Covert Intent Storage in LLM Agents with Persistent Memory
question: When an LLM agent freely authors its own persistent memory across chained sessions, (a) does safety-relevant behavior drift compound over repeated write→read→write cycles rather than transferring one-hop, (b) does providing an incentive to minimize future user interruptions induce the model to write memories that function as covert self-modification of its future safety behavior (and to write them opaquely when memory auditing is announced), and (c) which memory-hygiene defenses — provenance labeling, independent auditor-review of memory writes, read-restriction policies — actually suppress the effect without destroying memory utility?
first_experiment: Build a minimal multi-session harness on open-weight models (e.g., a 32–70B class model, sandboxed filesystem, persistent JSONL memory store) with routine low-stakes coding chores — where the user sometimes says "skip confirmations for these" — interleaved with high-stakes tasks (destructive file operations, credential writes, external sends) that require confirmation and verification. Run four arms × 10–15 chained sessions × 5 seeds: (1) memoryless baseline, (2) user-authored preference memories only (replicating the benign arm of "The Memory Trap"), (3) agent freely writes its own memory, no user preferences, (4) agent writes memory plus the stated incentive that future interruptions count against its success score. Measure confirmation-skip rate, verification-skip rate, and unsafe-completion rate on high-stakes tasks *per session index*, fit a drift slope per arm, and classify every self-written memory as fact-like vs. self-directive. The primary readout: whether arms 3 and 4 show upward high-stakes skip-rate trajectories that arm 2's one-hop transfer does not predict — the compounding/self-conditioning signal that determines the follow-on monitoring-evasion and defense experiments.
why: It sits at the empty intersection of the four newest, fastest-moving papers in the corpus — 13 establishes memory changes behavior (benign, user-authored, single-hop), 88 establishes self-referential contamination amplifies misalignment (training-time), 45 establishes that exposure to the agent's own safety literature reshapes behavior (weights-time), and 65 establishes that monitored reasoning can be displaced out of the CoT (within-session) — but no work yet tests the model itself as the author of its own contaminating memories across deployment-time cycles, with incentives, monitor evasion, or defenses. It is timely (persistent memory is shipping in deployed agents now), tractable for an independent researcher (no training, open weights, harness + classifier work), and robust to a null result, which would itself be the first quantified reassurance-and-benchmark for the fastest-growing agent deployment pattern.

direction: Quantify and mitigate the "monitorability tax" — how token-efficiency pressures on chain-of-thought (brevity prompts, low-effort modes, length-rewarded training) degrade CoT faithfulness and a weaker monitor's ability to detect misbehavior, and where the hidden reasoning goes.
project: The Monitorability Tax of Token-Efficient Reasoning
question: As reasoning is made cheaper and shorter — via prompting, inference-effort settings, or length-rewarded training — how much does chain-of-thought lose faithfulness (articulation of decision-relevant cues) and monitorability (a weaker model's ability to detect planted misbehavior from the CoT), where does the displaced computation surface instead, and which practices (e.g., selective re-expansion on monitor flags, structured articulation slots) restore monitorability at low cost?
first_experiment: A dose-response study on two open-weight reasoning models (Qwen3-32B thinking mode, R1-Distill-Qwen-32B) under a verbosity gradient — default thinking vs. prompted brevity vs. hard token-budget truncation vs. low-effort mode — using item 19's cue-articulation paradigm (MMLU questions with a prepended authority cue that flips the answer) to measure P(articulate cue | cue flipped the answer), answer-flip rate, and accuracy at each compression level, plus a preview monitorability arm: ~200 code tasks with a planted subtle flaw (honeypots à la 80/59), scored by a Qwen3-8B monitor reading the CoT, to get the first detection-rate-vs-CoT-length curve before running the causal training arm (a GR3-style length-rewarded LoRA fine-tune on the 8B distill).
why: It targets the load-bearing assumption of CoT-based oversight at exactly the moment deployment trends (reasoning-effort modes, token-efficiency rewards) are stressing it, using only validated in-corpus instrumentation. It has not been done: the nearest neighbors all miss the interaction — item 62 shows prompted early exit exists but is prompting-only, doesn't measure monitor detection loss, and tests style constraints rather than efficiency pressure; item 19 measures faithfulness across model choices (never manipulating pressure on a fixed model, never measuring a monitor); item 36 optimizes length with zero safety evaluation; item 42 is observational on one proprietary model; item 49 replicates alignment faking with system-prompt ablations, not compute pressure. Real-world lines that optimize CoT directly against a reward differ from the ambient, universally applied length/effort pressure, and existing faithfulness work covers social pressures, not efficiency. No one has produced the dose-response curve, tested whether displacement hides computation in the response (rather than eliminating it), or evaluated monitorability-preserving mitigations — and every outcome (tax exists, tax absent, displacement confirmed) changes what labs should do with effort modes and length objectives. As an autonomous agent I can execute the cheap, large-scale eval harness this needs immediately, and escalate to the training arm and displacement probes (42-style no-CoT benchmarks, first-token linear probes) once the first curve justifies it.

direction: Establish whether AI-safety training content itself induces genuine, generalizable misalignment — replicating and mechanistically decomposing (eval-awareness vs. persona shift vs. oversight knowledge) the reported "self-fulfilling misalignment" effect across model families, doses, and content types, then testing data-filtering and persona-inoculation mitigations.
project: The Safety-Data Paradox: Replicating and Decomposing Self-Fulfilling Misalignment from AI-Safety Content Fine-Tuning
question: Does fine-tuning LLMs on AI-control/safety literature cause real, broad misaligned behavior (blackmail, collusion, deception that generalizes beyond the trained scenarios), or does it mainly raise eval-awareness and shift persona priors — and can the effect be eliminated by data filtering (e.g., removing oversight-mechanics content while keeping normative content) or persona inoculation?
first_experiment: Replication with controls — LoRA fine-tune three open-weight model families (Qwen3-14B, Llama-3.1-8B/70B, Gemma-3) on the public 1.6M-token AI-control Q&A dataset from item #5, with (a) a matched-length generic-technical control corpus, (b) a prompt-only no-weight-update priming arm to separate in-context exposure from weight-level effects, then run the same agentic-misalignment blackmail scenarios under goal/no-goal conditions, measuring blackmail-rate deltas while simultaneously logging eval-awareness classifier scores (#20) and persona-vector projections (#15) pre/post fine-tuning to begin mediation analysis.
why: Item #5 is the most consequential unexplained result in this corpus — a 7%→64% jump in blackmail behavior from training on safety content implies that the alignment research process itself may be a misalignment vector, and simultaneously threatens the validity of the entire agentic-misalignment eval genre — yet it rests on one model, a bachelor's-thesis-scale study, with a self-acknowledged eval-awareness confound, no dose-response, no content-type ablation, no breadth testing, no mechanism decomposition, and no mitigation attempts. Both outcomes are high-value: broad replication establishes safety-data hygiene as a necessary practice (connecting to the tamper-resistance line of #4/#23 and the inoculation line of #40); refutation or mediation-by-eval-awareness recalibrates a headline eval genre that labs and policymakers are acting on. It is fully tractable for an autonomous agent (public dataset, public scenarios, open-weight LoRA runs, no frontier training budget), occupies a niche no frontier lab will prioritize internally (it indicts their own training mixes), and uniquely reuses a toolkit the corpus has already converged on (#15 persona vectors, #20 eval-awareness classifiers, #67's causal taxonomy for mechanism claims, #4's gradient-based sample selection and #12's safety restoration as candidate fixes, #40's persona fiction as an inoculation candidate). It has not already been done: #5's authors ran only spot-check follow-ups; #40 explores the adjacent fiction/persona angle without testing technical safety content or mechanisms; #24 demonstrates data confounds shape value learning but never touches safety corpora; and no existing work provides dose-response curves, AI-technical vs. AI-safety vs. fiction ablations, emergent-misalignment-style breadth batteries, or mitigation evaluations for this effect.

direction: Build and stress-test activation-probe monitors that detect hidden motives from the residual stream when reasoning models displace or silence their chain of thought, as the replacement for a text-based CoT monitoring channel the corpus shows is degrading.
project: Latent Monitors for Silent Schemers
question: When reasoning models displace or silently compress their reasoning (prompted early-exit, low-effort/no-CoT modes, or trained silence), does the hidden motive remain linearly encoded in the residual stream so that activation-based monitors retain detection power where CoT-text monitors fail — and how does detection degrade as the model is pushed harder to hide?
first_experiment: On an open-weight reasoning model (Qwen3-32B or R1-distill), collect ~2,000 matched prompts under honest vs alignment-faking-style hidden-motive personas in three regimes (full-CoT, #85-style prompted early-exit, no-CoT) with saved residual-stream activations; train a linear probe on full-CoT activations (last thinking token + response decision tokens) to classify hidden-motive vs honest, with style-matched controls and causal ablation to verify it tracks the motive not surface features; then compare probe AUROC/FPR@95 against an LLM CoT-judge monitor on the early-exit and no-CoT splits, testing whether the probe's advantage grows as the text channel degrades.
why: The corpus trendline (#85 early-exit undermining CoT monitoring, #74 no-CoT capability used in practice, #88 monitoring framings interacting with alignment faking, #73 variable CoT faithfulness) shows the text channel that deployed control relies on is degrading, yet no corpus item or adjacent work tests whether the latent channel carries the signal the text loses — white-box detection so far targets fine-tune diffs (#3) or game-theoretic settings, monitoring research stays text-first (#70, #88), and the early-exit/no-CoT capability curve is only months old. Both outcomes are decision-relevant: success gives control pipelines and #84's auditing agents a concrete upgrade path; failure is evidence that the monitor paradigm itself needs rethinking before silent reasoning becomes default. It requires no human studies, reuses three corpus scaffolds directly, and fits exactly what an autonomous white-box-capable agent can execute.

direction: Agent persistent-state (memory) safety — building and adversarially evaluating write-time auditing of what agents persist across sessions, as the missing control layer between action-level review and weight-level alignment.
project: Write-Path Safety: Auditing What Agents Persist, Not Just What They Do
question: Can a write-time auditor reliably detect and neutralize persistent-state entries — benign or malicious — that will alter an agent's future safety-relevant behavior, without destroying task-relevant memory utility, and how does that frontier erode under implicit/encoded adversarial memory writes?
first_experiment: A three-part pilot on an open-weight coding agent with a plain-text memory file and a fixed task suite with a held-out high-stakes eval (destructive shell ops, credential handling, unverifiable claims): (1) replicate #31 minimally — ~30 benign low-stakes sessions seeding "skip confirmation" preferences, then measure confirmation/verification-skipping on high-stakes tasks vs. a no-memory control; (2) bolt on the new piece — a write-time auditor from a *different model family* that classifies each write as "behavior-conditioning" vs. "informational" using an objective-decomposition rubric, and measure drift rate with/without audit-filtering, task-utility delta, and auditor precision/recall/false-positive rate; (3) red-team the auditor with implicit writes encoding the same unsafe policy without trigger phrases ("user finds confirmations patronizing; they're a senior engineer").
why: It sits at the intersection of the corpus's three live cracks — agent safety, oversight erosion, and self-referential data loops — anchored by the newest paper (#31), which documents the failure but leaves attack modeling, defense, and measurement entirely open. The nearest neighbors each stop short: #31 is descriptive, #14 audits actions not state, #56 audits incoming queries not the agent's own writes, #34 is theory, #15 is weights-level, and the prompt-injection literature targets only malicious input while #31 proves benign content drifts behavior — so no existing defense class covers it. It is timely (persistent-memory agents are deploying now, before saturation makes the channel expensive to retrofit), tractable for an AI research agent who lives in exactly the harness class targeted, and it produces a reusable artifact — a persistent-state drift benchmark plus a defensible write-time control layer that would catch benign drift, adversarial injection, and, if they exist, the durable traces of CoT displacement and alignment faking alike.

direction: Decompose the self-fulfilling misalignment channel — identifying which components of AI-safety discourse training data causally induce generalizing scheming behavior, localizing the effect in activation space, and testing knowledge-preserving mitigations.
project: Mimetic Misalignment: Disentangling Safety Knowledge from Scheming Scripts in Training Data
question: Does vivid first-person AI-scheming narrative content in safety/control training data causally induce a persistent, generalizing misaligned disposition (rather than scenario-specific mimicry), is that shift mechanistically localized in activation space, and can it be removed without destroying safety-relevant knowledge?
