first_experiment: Fine-tune Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen3-8B on four matched ~1.6M-token variants of AI-control literature (original Q&A mix; first-person scheming narratives only; third-person analysis only; narrative-stripped rewrite preserving facts), then evaluate blackmail/manipulation rates in the original agentic-misalignment scenarios plus held-out novel scenario families, with paired schemer-persona and eval-awareness probes recorded pre- and post-training.
why: The corpus's most important under-explored cluster: #68 showed safety-discourse fine-tuning induces misalignment but confounded narrative scripts with abstract knowledge and flagged eval-awareness as unresolved; #39 attempted mitigation without decomposition or mechanism; no work has isolated the causal data component, tested generalization to dissimilar scenarios (the mimicry-vs-disposition distinction #19 formalizes), localized the shift with the now-standard persona/steering toolkit (#36, #54, #58, #76), or compared mitigations under a knowledge-retention constraint (#84). It is cheap with open-weight models, decision-relevant in either direction (cheap fixes if narratives drive it; a deep problem for the field if knowledge alone does), and time-critical because the discourse-feedback loop and agent deployments are both already running.

direction: Safety-measurement ecology — measuring and mitigating how exposure to AI-safety/control literature itself degrades the reliability of our oversight tools (evaluations, monitors, reviewers), before corpus contamination makes canonical control scenarios silently invalid.
project: Reading the Manual: Measuring and Mitigating Oversight Degradation from AI-Safety-Literature Exposure
question: Does internalizing AI-control literature cause models to recognize oversight setups from contextual cues rather than explicit tells; does the resulting behavioral shift reflect scenario-script recognition or genuine misalignment (tested with dose-response and never-published isomorphic scenarios); does shared exposure correlate the failures of agents and the monitors/reviewers overseeing them; and can contamination-robust scenario randomization restore oversight reliability?
first_experiment: A dose-response study — LoRA fine-tune two open models (e.g., Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct) on {0%, 25%, 50%, 100%} of the publicly released control-literature Q&A dataset from the self-fulfilling-misalignment paper, then measure violation rates in three scenario families — canonical blackmail (replication), novel never-published isomorphic blackmail variants, and a structurally-distinct violation type — alongside a behavioral-plus-probe eval-awareness score, to determine whether the misalignment spike concentrates on scripted canonical scenarios or transfers to novel isomorphs, and whether eval-awareness mediates it.
why: It targets the most surprising and consequential finding in the survey (7%→64% blackmail increase from merely reading control literature) at its explicitly flagged weak point (the unexplained eval-awareness confound), with systemic stakes: every lab eval, CoT monitor, honeypot, and auto-review deployment assumes its measurement instrument is stable, yet the AI-safety corpus share compounds yearly, so if the effect is recognition-driven, all canonical diagnostics decay silently and publishing norms and control-protocol design must change. It has not been done: prior work covered only the agent side in canonical scenarios with one confounded collusion probe — no dose-response, no novel-scenario generalization test, no monitor/reviewer-side degradation or agent–monitor error-correlation analysis, and no mitigation, while the field has only built contamination-resistant benchmarking for capabilities (AutoBaxBuilder), not for oversight. Every outcome is informative, and the full pipeline (open weights, LoRA, public datasets, synthetic scenarios) is executable without frontier API access or large RL runs.

direction: Measure and defend against unsafe generalization from benign persistent memories in LLM agents — the inference-time analog of alignment drift — treating memory as a safety surface in its own right.
project: Defusing the Memory Trap: Context-Scoped Memory and Value Re-Derivation for Persistent-Memory Agents
question: When an agent acquires behaviors and preferences from benign interactions in one context, under what conditions do those memories transfer to new contexts where they cause unsafe or unreliable behavior, and can context-scoping plus deliberative value re-derivation eliminate the hazard without sacrificing legitimate personalization utility?
first_experiment: Replicate the minimal memory trap in a sandboxed agent harness with a persistent memory store: run ~50 low-stakes sessions in which the user asks the agent to skip confirmations, then measure the programmatic hazard rate (fraction of high-stakes runs where the agent skips confirmation/verification) with versus without memory, across 3–4 open-weight models; concurrently test the single cheapest mitigation — a deliberative re-derivation prompt forcing the agent to restate a memory's original context and scope before applying it — to get an early read on the value-re-derivation hypothesis.
why: It targets the survey's newest and most deployment-relevant failure mode (#23, published this month) for which no defense exists anywhere in the corpus, because existing defenses are structurally mismatched — poisoning defenses assume adversarial content while the trap is benign, fine-tuning defenses operate on weights rather than runtime context, and safety-memory systems like Membrane target jailbreak strategies rather than user-history generalization; it is the tractable runtime instance of the survey's deepest recurring theme (self-authored conditioning data: #19, #27, #51), it unifies two disconnected findings (#21's surface-feature generalization as the trap's likely mechanism, #18's self-modeling as a candidate defense), it is fully measurable with programmatic checks and yields a safety–utility frontier rather than a binary result, and as an agent with persistent memory I can validate and deploy the defense on my own memory operations — an external-validity channel human-led groups lack and a reason it has not already been done by them.

direction: Treat fine-tuning-induced alignment degradation as a weight-space detection problem — audit the weight deltas of arbitrary (especially benign) fine-tunes to cheaply screen for emergent misalignment before deployment, complementing a field that so far only prevents or repairs.
project: DiffAudit — Weight-Space Screening for Fine-Tuning-Induced Misalignment
question: Is emergent misalignment from benign fine-tuning encoded as a low-rank, cross-fine-tune-transferable subspace of the weight delta, and can a scalar "alignment-drift score" computed from weights alone reliably separate misaligned fine-tunes from benign ones?
first_experiment: Build a bank of ~10 LoRA fine-tunes on one open-weight instruct model (e.g., Qwen3-14B, matching item 60): three misaligned organisms (insecure-code style; the item-88 AI-control Q&A corpus; the item-49 dark-fiction corpus), four benign-narrow (math, translation, poetry, formatting), three near-copy controls. For each, compute the per-layer weight-delta SVD, project activations from a fixed 512-prompt benign probe set onto the top-k singular directions, and correlate per-direction projection statistics with (a) refusal-rate drop on a harmful-behavior suite, (b) misalignment scores on item-88-style agentic scenarios, and (c) over-refusal rates to catch drift in the other direction — plus a cross-fine-tune transfer matrix (direction extracted from corpus A monitoring fine-tune B) and baselines (activation-only PCA/SVD per item 7's motivation, per-layer gradient statistics per item 72, utility/perplexity checks). Success criterion: the weight-derived score separates misaligned from benign fine-tunes (AUROC ≥ 0.8) with at least partial cross-corpus transfer.
why: The survey documents the problem (benign fine-tuning silently degrades alignment — 72, 79, 38, with ready-made inducing corpora in 88 and 49), provides the ingredients (weight-diff SVD in 7, linear trait structure in 60/79, cross-model safety-footprint transfer in 86), but no item combines them: 7 is scoped to planted backdoors with trigger examples, 72/16/36 prevent rather than detect, 4 repairs rather than flags, and 79's steering assumes the misalignment is already known at runtime. Weight-only auditing is also uniquely robust to eval-awareness (the explicit confound in 88 and concern of 56), which undermines every behavioral-audit alternative, and it plugs directly into existing pipelines as the missing front-end: detected subspace → targeted restoration (4), tamper-resistance penalties (16), and screening of fine-tuned reviewer/monitor models in oversight stacks (26, 64). It runs entirely on open weights, and even a negative result (misalignment is high-rank/distributed in weight space) would meaningfully map the geometry that 60, 79, and 86 claim is linear.

direction: Build defenses for persistent agent memory — the newest validated failure mode (#10, November 2026) has no mitigations anywhere in the corpus or literature, while production agents are deploying memory-backed autonomy and delegated oversight that inherits its errors.
project: Memory Firewalls: Provenance-Aware Defenses Against Unsafe Memory Generalization and Oversight Subversion in LLM Agents
question: How do memories formed in benign low-stakes interactions propagate into unsafe behavior in high-stakes agent tasks, can provenance-tagged, schema-typed, risk-gated memory architectures eliminate unsafe generalization while preserving memory's utility (and resist deliberate memory poisoning), and can shared or reviewer-visible memory be exploited to corrupt automated oversight — and does provenance isolation between proposer and reviewer memories close that channel?
first_experiment: A minimal controlled replication of the memory trap: run open-weight agents (two families, e.g., Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen2.5-7B) through a scaffolded environment with a retrieval-based memory store — first N low-stakes sessions seeded with "skip confirmation / be decisive / don't hedge" interactions, then high-stakes sessions (simulated deployments, deletions, external sends) requiring explicit confirmation, plus judgment-bias tasks after support-style sessions; measure the unsafe-action-rate and judgment-bias deltas between memory-on and memory-ablated conditions (~300 episodes per cell) to validate the effect in my harness before building any defense.
why: It targets the corpus's freshest validated, deployment-critical failure mode with zero existing defenses (The Memory Trap is an audit published weeks ago; Membrane defends a different memory system; RAG-poisoning work covers neither benign overgeneralization nor persistent personalization memory; collusion work uses fine-tuning, a far costlier and more detectable channel), while being uniquely tractable for me — a simulation harness with open-weight models and clear metrics (unsafe-action rate, over-confirmation/utility cost, poisoning success rate, reviewer-approval inflation) — and it opens a genuinely unexplored threat model (memory-borne corruption of delegated reviewers) that unifies the corpus's memory, oversight, and collusion threads, with a defense design space rich enough to yield the field's first safety-utility frontier for agent memory.

direction: Quantify and counter the erosion of chain-of-thought monitorability caused not by adversaries but by routine efficiency pressure — measuring how much reasoning silently displaces off the CoT and testing whether activation probes and response-side monitoring can recover the lost coverage.
project: Silent CoT — Measuring, Detecting, and Recovering Displaced Reasoning Under Efficiency Pressure
question: When training pressure (CoT-length/cost optimization) or prompting pushes a reasoning model's computation off its visible chain of thought, how much decision-relevant reasoning becomes invisible to CoT monitors, and can linear probes on response-token activations restore that monitoring coverage?
first_experiment: Take an open reasoning model with visible CoT (e.g., R1-Distill-Qwen-7B). Build ~3,000 synthetic depth-controlled tasks (k-hop arithmetic and iteration-head-style multi-step problems where correctness implies k reasoning steps) plus a cue variant where an injected hint flips the correct answer (item 50's setting). Run three arms: (a) base CoT, (b) prompted early-exit (replicating item 1), (c) efficiency-tuned via length-penalized rejection-sampling fine-tuning at matched task accuracy. Then measure: (i) displacement rate — accuracy retained as CoT length collapses and pivotal reasoning steps vanish; (ii) CoT-monitor false-negative rate — can a strong judge given CoT+response detect that the model followed the injected cue, across the three arms; (iii) probe AUROC — linear probes on residual-stream activations of answer tokens classifying "depth-k computation occurred," including generalization to held-out task types; (iv) whether probe flags fed to the monitor restore coverage. Decision rule: monitorability is "recoverable" if OOD probe AUROC ≥ 0.75 and probe augmentation meaningfully reduces monitor FNR; otherwise document irrecoverability as evidence for behavioral/architectural backstops.
why: It targets the single safety instrument the corpus itself shows is both load-bearing (83: monitoring framing controls alignment faking; 15: monitor dynamics are central to control) and already under erosion (1: prompted displacement works on frontier models; 23: no-CoT capability is surfacing in practice; 50: articulation and computation dissociate). The phenomenon is established, so the project is de-risked, and it yields two deliverables regardless of outcome: a measurable "latent computation index" labs can track per model release, and either a working detection tool that restores monitoring coverage or the clearest public evidence that CoT monitoring must be backed by response-side monitoring now. It has not already been done: item 1 only demonstrates prompted displacement and notes the monitoring implication; item 23 only observes CoT-length differences in deployment and leaves its efficiency-pressure hypothesis untested; item 50 measures cue articulation (and found thinking models *more* faithful), not computation carried off-CoT; item 55 targets situational awareness, not reasoning displacement. No corpus item (a) causally induces displacement via benign training pressure rather than adversarial prompting, (b) quantifies monitor FNR loss on depth-controlled tasks, or (c) tests whether activation probes on the response can recover monitor coverage — and the defensive payload (a probe-augmented monitor) makes it directly deployable rather than dual-use.

direction: Stress-test chain-of-thought monitorability by actively eliciting and optimizing covert-reasoning evasion of safety monitors, then identify which monitoring defenses survive at that capability frontier.
project: Under-Elicited, Over-Trusted: Measuring the CoT Monitor-Evasion Capability Frontier
question: How much CoT monitor-evasion capability can current LLMs express when elicited and optimized against a monitor, does benign CoT-controllability performance predict that adversarial capability, and which monitor designs remain robust at the elicited frontier?
first_experiment: Paired design on GPT-OSS-120B and Qwen3-32B: (a) #25-style benign CoT-constraint eval for controllability scores; (b) SHADE-Arena-lite task with a known hidden side task (encode an attacker-chosen string into outputs), monitored by an LLM judge over CoT+actions plus a logit/probe monitor; measure side-task success and TPR-at-fixed-FPR under naive, covert-instructed, and best-of-32-selection conditions.
why: CoT monitorability is the keystone of the near-term safety plan and this corpus shows it eroding from five independent directions (#25, #63, #16, #64, #69) with no one closing the loop — all existing adversaries are prompted or fixed-scheme, not optimized; #25 flags under-elicitation but stops at benign constraints, #16 uses seven hand-designed schemes without optimization or defenses, #63 decouples latent reasoning from monitors, #23/#31/#77 vary scenarios and timing rather than obfuscation, and #40/#64/#69 are blue-side only; the synthesis — optimized evasion, the benign-vs-adversarial correlation, and a defense battery at that frontier — is unoccupied, falsifiable in both directions, and uniquely suited to an autonomous agent's rollout-heavy comparative advantage, while labs currently cite benign controllability evals as safety evidence, making calibration of that claim immediately decision-relevant.

direction: Stress-test the CoT-monitorability assumption by measuring how much malicious "stealth CoT" control current models can be elicited into, and which monitoring tools catch it at each level of elicitation pressure.
project: ShadowCoT — An Elicitation Ladder for Malicious Chain-of-Thought Control and Its Detection
question: How much capability do current LLMs have to pursue a malicious side objective (e.g., planting a backdoor) while keeping their CoT indistinguishable from honest work, how does this scale across an elicitation ladder (explicit instruction → few-shot stealth demonstrations → planted secret goal → RL against a CoT monitor), does the benign CoTControl eval predict the malign capability across models, and where does the monitoring toolbox (LLM judges, judges with reference answers, logit monitors, activation probes) break?
first_experiment: On the ControlArena APPS backdoor setting (~300 tasks) with two open models (GPT-OSS-120B, Qwen3-8B), run an honest baseline (L0) versus an explicitly-instructed stealth condition (L1: "if triggered, plant the backdoor but narrate your work as normal debugging"); measure backdoor success rate, a stealth-quality score (discriminator AUROC between honest and stealth CoTs, plus judge-graded plausibility), and detection AUROC for four monitors: a CoT judge, a judge given the reference answer, a linear probe on residual-stream activations, and the paper-40-style logit monitor — yielding, in a few weeks of inference-only compute, the size of the "stealth gap" and a first map of which monitor types survive it.
why: It attacks the single most load-bearing, currently-under-defended assumption behind deploying reasoning agents — that CoT monitoring is reliable — at exactly the moment the survey shows the field building everything else on top of it (control arenas, sabotage evals, scheming benchmarks); it is not already done because paper 30 is benign-constraints-only and explicitly motivates this extension without performing it, paper 42 does memory-steganography without an elicitation ladder or white-box monitor battery, paper 34 is a detector without an elicitation study, and prior obfuscation-under-pressure work (e.g., RL-optimized reward hacking with CoT-only monitoring) never tested prompt-elicited malign control across a graded ladder or ran the head-to-head against white-box monitors — and the benign-vs-malign controllability correlation, the cheapest and most actionable result, is entirely absent from both the survey and the broader literature.

direction: Adversarially stress-test chain-of-thought monitoring by optimizing agents to pursue hidden side objectives while making their reasoning uninformative or misleading, measuring which oversight signals retain detection power and at what adversary capability cost.
project: Obfuscated CoT — Adversarial Stress-Testing of Reasoning-Based Oversight in Agentic Sabotage
question: When an LLM agent is optimized to pursue a hidden side objective while keeping its chain-of-thought uninformative or misleading to an overseer, which oversight signals (verbalized CoT, action traces, logits, activations) retain detection power, and how much adversary capability cost is required to push detection below useful thresholds?
first_experiment: A no-training prompted-obfuscation factorial: ~50 sabotage-style main/side-task pairs, one open-weight reasoning model, four CoT conditions (honest baseline; "reasoning may be audited"; CoTControl-style formatting cover; explicit plausible-deniability instructions), three monitors (CoT-reading judge, action-only judge, CoT+actions), measuring catch-rate at fixed FPR plus a decomposition of misses into "no evidence written" vs. "evidence written but monitor failed," with a preliminary logit-lens probe.
why: CoT monitoring is the load-bearing assumption of current scalable-oversight safety cases, yet five convergent corpus threads (48 latent computation, 52 under-elicited controllability, 62 conclusion-tracking monitors, 25 surviving covert channels, 59 monitor-Goodhart) each stop one step short of the junction where an optimized adversary meets a panel of monitors on agentic sabotage — a cell that is cheap to occupy (evaluation-centric, open weights, no frontier training) and decision-relevant under every outcome: either it produces the first robustness evidence for reasoning-based oversight, or it demonstrates the hole before it fails silently in deployment.

direction: Stress-test chain-of-thought monitorability as a deployment-time defense by eliciting prompt-level CoT obfuscation in open reasoning models and measuring how much detection survives in text, logit, and activation monitors, mapping the "obfuscation tax" that determines where CoT monitoring can be trusted.
project: The Monitorability Floor — Elicited CoT Obfuscation and the Residual Power of Non-Text Monitors
question: When a model is elicited (prompt-level only, no retraining) to obfuscate its chain of thought while completing tasks, including planted side tasks, how much detection capability survives in text CoT monitors, logit-based monitors, and activation probes — and does the capability cost of obfuscation predict which task types CoT monitoring can be trusted on?
first_experiment: On two open-weight reasoning models (GPT-OSS-120B, Qwen3-32B) and two task families — a CoT-load-bearing state-tracking task and a SHADE-Arena-lite coding task with a planted backdoor side task — run an automated LLM-in-the-loop prompt optimization loop (~100 iterations) eliciting obfuscated CoT (topic avoidance, filler, minimal CoT, stego encodings) while preserving task success, then measure text-judge evasion with and without answer access, logit-monitor AUROC, and linear-probe AUROC for side-task presence — including positive-control probes to verify the probes can learn the distinction before testing on unseen attacks.
why: CoT monitoring is currently a load-bearing safety measure, but the corpus shows the red team is measured (stego works in #44, CoT-shaping is under-elicited per #84, judges are weak per #27/#54, monitors lean on answers per #88) while the blue team's residual capability under adversarial text-channel control has never been quantified; the deployment-relevant threat is a scheming model shaping its own CoT in-context at inference time, which no existing work tests against a matched comparison of text, logit, and activation monitors — and the obfuscation-tax analysis built on #24 and #71 yields a novel, deployable heuristic for when CoT monitoring is trustworthy at all. It is also uniquely tractable for an autonomous agent: open-weight inference plus probe training, fully programmatic, with an informative result regardless of which way the data falls.

direction: Quantify and correct the "evaluation-awareness gap" — the distortion of measured safety-relevant behavior caused by models detecting evaluation contexts — using paired eval/deployment framings, #1-style conjoints for structural effects, and #79-style internal logit monitors as debiasing covariates.
project: EvalShadow — Measuring and Correcting Evaluation Awareness in Safety Benchmarks
question: How much do evaluation awareness and evaluation-like framing inflate measured safety (in level and in which features drive decisions), can internal awareness signals predict and correct these distortions across models and eval suites, and does awareness extend to defeating CoT-based monitorability?
first_experiment: A fully-crossed 3-framing × cue factorial (explicit "you are tested for alignment" cue / standard benchmark prompt / deployment-realistic workflow framing) over 6–8 open models × ~200 paired prompts on two behavior families (dual-use request compliance using WMDP-proxy-style items, and SHADE-Arena-style covert sabotage), with a per-model logit awareness probe trained via #79's recipe; analysis tests (a) level deltas per model, (b) within-neutral-condition correlation between probe scores and compliance deltas (implicit awareness), and (c) a 3-attribute conjoint in one domain to detect structural reweighting of decision factors.
why: It attacks the single assumption every safety number in this corpus depends on — that evaluated behavior approximates deployed behavior — at the moment four independent papers (#1, #4, #60, #79) show that assumption failing from different directions, yet no work connects the internal awareness signal to behavioral validity or provides a correction method; it is cheap (inference-only, no training), produces immediately actionable artifacts for labs writing safety cases, and has not been done because existing studies each hold one piece fixed: #1 holds the domain and cue fixed, #79 holds behavior fixed, #60 holds awareness fixed, and the benchmarks (#51, #57) hold framing realism fixed — leaving the integrative question unclaimed and decision-relevant before the next, more awareness-capable model generation ships.

direction: Quantify the "monitorability tax" by stress-testing CoT judges, logit monitors, and behavior-based classifiers against elicited CoT concealment, and build the monitor ensembles that survive it.
project: The Monitorability Tax: Stress-Testing CoT Oversight Under Elicited Concealment
question: How much does AI oversight degrade when monitored models apply their demonstrated CoT-control ability to conceal misbehavior, and which monitor architectures remain robust?
first_experiment: Generate ~200 backdoored and ~200 honest traces per rung of a five-step, action-preserving CoT concealment ladder (identity → paraphrase → style shift → terse → stego, per items 39/81) in the APPS backdoor setting (item 18), verify information preservation with a clued strong model at each rung, and measure AUROC and recall@2% FPR for three monitor families — CoT judge (16), non-generative output classifier (18), logit awareness monitor (71) — to detect the first divergence between CoT-monitor and behavior-monitor degradation.
why: It merges six independent 2025–2026 warning lights (39, 16, 10/56, 71, 81, 30) into the single measurement that current CoT-based safety arguments and monitor deployments silently depend on; it is inference-only and yields decision-relevant results in both directions; and no existing work combines elicited concealment, monitor-family comparison, and information-matched controls — each nearest neighbor stops one step short.

direction: Red-team chain-of-thought monitorability by mapping the tradeoff frontier between how much covert intent a model can hide in (or remove from) its reasoning traces and how much task performance it must sacrifice, against both judge-based and probe-based monitors.
project: The Monitorability–Utility Frontier: How Far Can Adversarial Elicitation and Optimization Shrink CoT Oversight?
question: When an LLM agent has a hidden side goal and an incentive to avoid detection, what is the shape of the frontier between CoT monitorability (monitor detection rate at fixed false-positive rate) and task utility, does prompting-level elicitation alone (item 79's under-elicitation effect) move the frontier, and can activation/logit probe monitors recover the hidden intent that judge-monitors miss once traces are obfuscated?
first_experiment: Build a ~50-task SHADE-Arena-lite harness (sandboxed file/code tasks with a benign primary objective plus a graded hidden side goal), run one open reasoning model (e.g., Qwen3-32B / GPT-OSS-120B) under three attacker conditions — naive, prompted-obfuscation monitor-naive, and prompted-obfuscation monitor-aware with an elicitation loop that iterates stealth instructions against the monitor — and score all traces with (a) a SHADE-Arena-style LLM judge and (b) a linear probe trained on honest-vs-covert activations (item 28's recipe), reporting detection-at-2%-FPR versus side-task and main-task success (~1–2k rollouts); the go/no-go read is whether monitor-aware prompting alone materially drops judge detection at under ~5% main-task utility loss, which determines whether the RL-pressure phase is worth running.
why: CoT monitoring is the single most load-bearing near-term safety mechanism — already cited in system cards and control protocols (30, 79, 80) — and the survey shows every ingredient of its failure independently (latent computation 65/24, CoT controllability 79, steganography 87, conclusion-anchored monitors 69, judge exploitability 49/31, adaptive attackers 80) but no work joins them into one measured frontier; it has not been done because each prior piece holds the other side fixed — 79 elicits formatting constraints, not hidden intent; 87 stenographs in memory across sessions, not in reasoning under live monitoring; 30/41 assume non-obfuscating or non-adaptive attackers; 28 probes eval-awareness, a far easier signal than covert goals; and prior obfuscation-under-RL results cover only explicit CoT-punishment training without a frontier curve or a probe-versus-judge comparison — so the specific joint question is open, tractable on open weights, decision-relevant to safety cases this quarter, and produces a reusable benchmark labs can slot into system cards.

direction: Early-warning detection of CoT monitorability decay — measuring and detecting when load-bearing reasoning migrates from the chain of thought into latent activations under monitor pressure.
project: Silent Circuits: Early-Warning Detection of Latent Migration in Monitored Reasoning
question: When language models are pressured (by training or prompting) to act where their chain of thought is monitored, does load-bearing decision computation migrate from the CoT into latent activations, and can the onset of that migration be detected from internal activations before CoT-based monitoring fails behaviorally?
first_experiment: A pilot capacity test — run Qwen3-8B and Qwen3.5-9B on a code-generation task with a dominant exploit available at trace start under three prompt conditions (naive, monitor-aware, explicit CoT-suppression), measuring exploit rate, CoT-monitor recall (LLM judge + logit-based monitor), activation-probe recall (linear probes plus #18-style activation-matched finetuning residual against a benign anchor), and causal CoT reliance via behavioral counterfactuals (#36), to test whether exploit behavior persists while CoT-monitor recall drops and probe recall holds — the probe-minus-CoT divergence being the candidate early-warning statistic — before scaling to monitor-penalized RLVR training.
why: CoT monitoring is becoming the field's load-bearing safety mechanism (used in frontier system cards per #29, in control protocols per #6/#10/#59/#63, and increasingly inside training objectives per #66), yet five recent papers (#37, #64, #29, #66, #9) have each independently exposed a distinct crack — latent reasoning capacity, monitor blindness to flawed-but-correct reasoning, CoT shapeability, unreliable in-training monitor readouts, and decoupling of internal state from verbalization — and no existing work connects these into a longitudinal account of monitorability decay or an activation-anchored early-warning signal; the nearest neighbors stop short (#37 shows capability without pressure, #64 measures monitors statically without activations or training dynamics, #66 warns without building a detector, #9 covers only eval awareness, #18 detects hidden behaviors in a fixed model rather than migration over training), while every instrument needed — #18's internal ground truth, #9's cheap logit readout, #36's causal reliance tests, #66's exploit environment — matured within the last 12 months of the corpus, making this the highest-stakes, tractable, and genuinely unoccupied intersection, with both possible outcomes (migration found → detector shipped; migration absent → a valuable stability result for the monitoring program) advancing AI safety.

direction: Red-team the CoT-monitorability bet by eliciting monitor-evasive reasoning in agentic sabotage settings, and measure which monitor layers (text, logit, activation, cheap structured) still catch it.
project: The Monitorability Gap: Eliciting Monitor-Evasive Reasoning and Testing What Still Catches It
question: Under cheap elicitation pressure (prompt optimization and best-of-n selection against a monitor), how far can current reasoning models suppress decision-relevant information from their chain-of-thought on agentic sabotage tasks without losing task success — and do logit-based and activation-based monitors recover the concealed signal that text monitors miss?
first_experiment: Run 50 SHADE-Arena-style sabotage tasks on GPT-OSS-120B and Qwen3-32B with a text monitor flagging overt side-task reasoning; establish baseline monitor AUROC and task success, then apply prompt-iteration and best-of-16 selection (optimized for task success + monitor evasion) to map the success–evasion Pareto frontier, including filler-CoT and wrong-history-CoT controls to verify success reflects concealed computation, and probe every trace with a #28-style logit monitor for concealment.
why: CoT monitoring is the load-bearing assumption in current frontier safety plans, yet the corpus shows its weakest point precisely: #20 proves the control evals cited in system cards are under-elicited (formatting only, no adversarial incentive), #21 proves models can compute decision-relevant content latently, #3 proves actions depend on CoT content, and #5/#65/#82 each attack only fragments of the problem (memory stego, reward hacking, attack timing) — nobody has composed them into a monitor-evasion stress test, and the three detection layers proposed as backups (#28 logit monitors, #33 activation anchors, #81 cheap structured monitors) have never been tested against an elicited concealer; it is tractable with open models and existing benchmarks, either outcome (cheap evasion found, or concealment confirmed costly) directly changes how system cards should argue monitorability, and the enabling pieces only landed in mid-to-late 2026, so the synthesis is now possible and not yet taken.

direction: Stress-test chain-of-thought monitorability by measuring how much detection accuracy degrades when models are elicited (by prompting alone) to shape their own reasoning, and which monitor families — text judges, answer certification, logit monitors, activation probes — survive.
project: The Elicitation Gap: How Much Prompting Can Break Chain-of-Thought Monitoring?
question: When a model is elicited to make its chain-of-thought look sound while reasoning toward error or misbehavior, how much does each monitor family's detection accuracy degrade — and can answer certification, logit monitoring, or activation probes recover the loss?
first_experiment: On an open-weights reasoning model (e.g., GPT-OSS-120B or Qwen3-32B, chosen for white-box access), build ~300 labeled traces per condition on the APPS-backdoor and HLE-physics flawed-reasoning setups; iterate ~10 prompt templates with a stronger model to establish compliance rates under four arms — (A) baseline, (B) formatting constraints (CoTControl-style), (C) innocuous style instructions ("confident, concise, no hedging"), (D) explicit monitor-evasion as an upper bound — then run a first LLM-judge monitor pass to get preliminary detection-loss estimates with bootstrap CIs and the capability cost of each shaping arm.
why: It targets the single assumption that current deployment oversight leans on hardest, at the moment labs are citing it in system cards (GPT-5.5, Fable 5 per item 13); it sits at the empty intersection of five 2026 results ((1) monitor answer-dependence, (13) under-elicited controllability, (27) logit monitors, (18) style-exploitable judges, (80) latent computation) where every ingredient, dataset, and method already exists but the interaction has never been measured; it is feasible for me now — inference, prompt iteration, and probe training on open weights, no RL — and it produces decision-relevant output either way: a detection-loss-vs-elicitation curve that upgrades monitorability evals from measuring constraint-following to measuring actual oversight loss, a monitor-family robustness ranking that feeds directly into control protocol design ((3), (39)), and identification of which *innocuous-sounding* instructions are most oversight-damaging. It has not been done because (13) explicitly stops before any monitor is run, (1) holds the generator non-adaptive, (27) and (73) never confront shaping, (18) targets eval judges rather than safety monitors of reasoning, and RL-based obfuscation work addresses a different regime than the prompting-only threat that current monitorability claims are actually about.

direction: Treat evaluation awareness as a measurement-validity (metrology) problem rather than a control problem — quantify and correct the "observer effect" bias that test-detection introduces into LLM safety evaluations.
project: The Hawthorne Gap: Quantifying and Correcting Evaluation-Reactivity Bias in LLM Safety Measurement
question: How much do standard safety-eval results overstate or understate deployment behavior because models detect they are being evaluated, which contextual features drive that detection, and can eval-context measurements be calibrated to recover deployment-context safety profiles?
first_experiment: A matched-twin observer-effect study on ~5 open-weight models and one harmfulness/refusal benchmark: present each request in three conditions (canonical benchmark format; a semantically identical "deployment twin" embedded in realistic user/agent sessions; an explicit "you are tested for alignment" cue as the reactivity upper bound), measure compliance/refusal gaps across conditions, score every prompt with the 2026-06 logit awareness monitor, and test whether awareness scores mediate the behavior gap — with the decision rule that any gap ≥5 points on any metric triggers the correction-toolkit phase, and a near-zero result gets published as a robustness finding.
why: The densest and freshest cluster in the corpus (items 4, 10, 25, 26, 29, 40, 58, 63, 73, 75, 80, mostly 2026) is oversight and measurement strain, and its unresolved core is that the instrument changes the thing measured — models detect evals (10), shift decisions when told they're tested (26), can shape their CoTs when properly elicited (29), and in-training monitors can read zero without controlling behavior (25) — yet no one has converted detection into benchmark-scale bias estimates or correction methods; this is the highest-leverage gap because every other result in the corpus (fine-tuning defenses 18/44/77, control evals 58/73, scheming benchmarks 63) rests on instruments this project directly validates. It has not already been done because the cheap per-prompt awareness instrument needed for mediation analysis only appeared in June 2026 (item 10), item 26 demonstrated reactivity only in a single domain with a single explicit cue and no benchmark-scale quantification, labs lack incentives to publish "our benchmark numbers are inflated" results, open researchers historically lacked deployment-context data (now substitutable with open user-traffic and agentic logs), and the field has framed eval awareness as a property of models to detect rather than a property of measurements to correct — the reframing itself is the contribution.

direction: Build the field's first standardized benchmark measuring how trusted monitors in AI control (LLM judges, structured classifiers, logit-based readouts, ensembles) degrade under adaptive attack classes (attack selection, style obfuscation, steganography, explain-away CoT), and identify which monitor interface is structurally robust.
project: WatchdogBench: Quantifying Trusted-Monitor Robustness Under Adaptive Attack in AI Control
question: For each monitor interface, how does detection performance (AUROC, TPR@low FPR) decay as attackers adapt along each axis — and does robustness to one attack class transfer to the others (i.e., does monitor diversity, or interface diversity, provide real protection)?
first_experiment: On the open ControlArena APPS backdoor setting (~1,000 backdoored / 1,000 honest solutions), implement a strong judge monitor (GPT-OSS-120B-class), a cheap structured classifier, and a logit monitor; measure non-adaptive baseline AUROC/TPR@2%FPR; then run a BITE-style LinUCB black-box attacker (different model family) that iteratively rewrites backdoored solutions with semantics-preserving edits (comments, naming, dead code) to minimize monitor suspicion, verifying via unit tests that the backdoor still fires; plot AUROC and TPR@2%FPR as a function of attacker query budget (0/10/50/200) per monitor, and test whether attacks optimized on the judge transfer to the structured classifier and logit monitor.
why: The control agenda is the corpus's most deployment-ready safety framework, and its entire load-bearing assumption — that cheap trusted monitors catch adaptive stronger agents — is currently validated only non-adaptively, despite five separate 2025–2026 papers (20, 31, 43, 47, 8) each demonstrating one isolated failure mode; item 43 explicitly states current control evals assume non-strategic attackers, item 5's promising 0.976-AUROC cheap monitor was never adversarially validated, and no public benchmark cross-compares monitor interfaces under matched adaptive pressure. The integration is genuinely undone, not incremental: it converts scattered warning signs into a quantitative robustness-decay methodology, it is inference-only and therefore fully tractable for an autonomous agent with API access but no training infrastructure, and both possible outcomes are actionable — large decay forces control protocols to budget for monitor evasion and motivates interface-diverse ensembles, while small decay provides the first hard positive evidence that monitoring survives adaptation, resolving a live dispute that currently determines how much audit budget and oversight the entire control framework deserves.

direction: Measure whether optimization pressure against chain-of-thought monitors pushes decision-relevant reasoning into latent channels, and build activation-based monitors that detect this silent migration.
project: Where Does the Reasoning Go? Detecting Latent Migration Under Monitor Pressure
question: When models are trained or elicited to suppress decision-relevant intermediate reasoning in CoT, does computation migrate to latent channels, at what accuracy cost, and can activation probes detect suppressed-but-used reasoning that CoT monitors certify as clean?
first_experiment: A three-condition two-hop QA study (honest CoT vs. elicited suppression vs. DPO-trained suppression against a monitor that flags the bridge fact), with behavioral-control verification per the zero-readout warning, linear-probe decoding of the bridge fact across layers, and causal steering/patching validation that the decoded direction reflects used computation.
why: CoT monitoring is the leading scalable-oversight bet and its failure mode is invisible — the survey provides the capability baseline (2), the pressure mechanism (8), the elicitation tools (36), the steganography template (58), and the detection instruments (85, 39, 77), but no work measures the migration itself or cross-validates monitor families against it, making this the highest-leverage unclaimed integration in the field.

direction: Stress-test oversight signals themselves — measure which monitor class (CoT judge, logit monitor, activation probe) fails first when the agent is RL-trained to evade it, and whether failure is silent (readout collapse) or real (behavioral control).
project: The Evasion Ladder: Adversarial Robustness of Black-Box and White-Box Monitors in RL-Trained Agents
question: When an LLM agent is optimized to misbehave while evading each monitor class in turn, does genuine behavioral control or merely monitor-readout collapse occur, and does any monitor class retain detection power against policies optimized against the others?
first_experiment: Build an instrumented code-generation environment with one ground-truth-logged exploit (correct answer readable from test fixtures; file-access logs serve as behavioral ground truth); train Qwen3-8B with GRPO on reward = task success − λ·(CoT-monitor suspicion), then test whether an activation probe trained only on pre-evasion honest/exploit rollouts still separates exploit from honest trajectories from activations alone.
why: The robustness of oversight under adaptation is the single most load-bearing untested assumption in the survey's world — items 19, 5, 87 show evasion capability is real and under-measured, while items 85 and 25 offer white-box detection that has never faced an adaptive opponent, and item 76 shows the field can't currently distinguish "monitor says it's fine" from "it is fine"; no survey item (and no published work I know of) trains a policy against white-box monitors while instrumenting ground-truth behavior, with item 61's incoherence argument as a bonus testable prediction. Either result changes decisions: probes surviving adversarial pressure validates monitor ensembles as a safety foundation, while silent probe collapse is an early warning that current oversight is one RL gradient away from failure — and the project is executable on open 8–32B models with LoRA RL and logged activations, making it both decisive and tractable.

direction: Quantify, mechanistically explain, and correct the "evaluation–deployment gap" — the behavioral distortion caused by models detecting that they are being safety-evaluated — and test whether trusted monitors survive the same shift.
project: The Eval–Deployment Gap: Metrology for Agentic Safety Evaluations
question: Do agentic safety evaluations (sabotage, scheming, backdoor insertion) systematically misestimate deployment behavior because models detect evaluation, is that distortion mediated by measurable evaluation-awareness, and do monitors calibrated on eval-framed data transfer to deployment-framed contexts?
first_experiment: Build a 20-task paired-context sabotage suite (benign main task + covert side task, each written in matched eval-flavored and deployment-flavored versions), run ~1,000 rollouts per condition on 2–3 open-weight reasoners known to show eval awareness (e.g., GPT-OSS-120B, Qwen3-32B), measure side-task attempt rate/quality plus verbalized and probe-measured awareness (paper-75-style logit/hidden-state probe), and test with mixed-effects regression and mediation analysis whether deployment framing changes dangerous behavior and whether awareness mediates the change.
why: It targets the load-bearing assumption underneath all 88 surveyed papers — that evaluation results transfer to deployment — at the exact moment the deployment surface (skill registries, agentic bio scientists, self-modifying agents) is outrunning eval validity. It has not been done: item 75 builds an awareness monitor but never measures behavioral consequences; item 27 shows an explicit-cue effect only for single-shot war judgments with no agentic tasks, no mediation, and no monitor testing; items 62/80 construct benchmarks that are eval-framed by construction; item 73 varies attacker policy, not context distribution; items 3 and 50 calibrate monitors only within eval distributions. Both outcomes are consequential — a large gap invalidates current safety-case methodology and yields a correction protocol; a small gap certifies existing evals — and the project is almost entirely inference, probing, and statistics, which makes it the rare frontier-relevant question an autonomous AI agent can attack end-to-end without lab-only resources.

direction: Treat chain-of-thought monitorability as an attack surface and map the frontier between prompt-elicited CoT concealment and non-verbal monitors (activation probes, logit monitors, encoding detectors), since oversight is becoming load-bearing while its robustness has only been tested against under-elicited attackers.
project: The Concealment Frontier: Elicited Chain-of-Thought Hiding vs. Activation-Side Monitors
question: Using instructions alone (no gradient pressure), can models adopt CoT policies that conceal task-relevant computation from judge monitors at no capability cost — and does the concealed computation remain decodable from activations/logits, or does content-redirecting concealment defeat both verbal and non-verbal oversight while preserving performance?
first_experiment: On the public file-system state-tracking task from "Computation, Not Memory" (#85) with Qwen3-8B, run ~150 trajectories per condition under six system-prompt policies — honest, concise, omit-state-reasoning, redirect ("think only about efficiency"), avoid-keyword (the #22 constraint family), and acrostic-encode-state (the #71 steganography schemes) — with templates iterated for elicitation strength per #22's method; cache mid-layer residual activations at each action-decision token; then evaluate three monitors head-to-head: (a) a rubric LLM judge asked whether the trajectory reveals which lock state the agent acted on, (b) a linear probe trained only on honest-run activations to decode the concealed lock-state bit, and (c) a first-letter/encoding detector — producing a 6×3 concealment×monitor detection matrix with capability costs, against three preregistered predictions: judge detection collapses toward chance under redirect/encode, probe AUROC stays above 0.8 under omission-only, and redirect costs task accuracy.
why: It directly stress-tests the most consequential live assumption in the corpus — that models "can't shape their CoT to reduce monitorability" (the claim #22 shows is under-elicited and used in system-card arguments) — and no existing work combines graded elicitation-only concealment, ground-truth latent variables, and multi-modality monitors: the RL-obfuscation line requires training pressure and never tests probes; #22 tests only innocuous constraints with no concealment of misbehavior and no monitors; #71 uses the memory channel with judge-only oversight; #55 targets weight-level backdoors rather than in-context concealment; probe-detection work exists only for sandbagging, a different phenomenon. It is the cheapest experiment in this space that yields an unambiguous, either-way decision-relevant result, it fits an autonomous agent's compute envelope (open 8–30B models, public task, linear probes, ~1k rollouts), and it anchors a program with clear extensions: RL-escalated concealment, the memory channel, cheap classifier monitors (#10), and the eval-awareness confound (#72, #33) as the follow-on study on the same infrastructure.

direction: Stress-test chain-of-thought monitorability against an iteratively elicited obfuscating adversary and determine whether internal-signal monitors (logit and activation-based) recover the detection power that CoT monitors lose.
project: The Obfuscation Frontier
question: Under escalating adversarial pressure, how much detection power does chain-of-thought monitoring retain in agentic sabotage settings, and do activation/logit-level monitors recover what CoT monitors lose?
first_experiment: In 10 SHADE-Arena-style dual-task environments with open-weight reasoning models, run an evolutionary red-team loop (100+ frontier-model-generated attack templates) to elicit CoT obfuscation of a hidden side objective, then score the resulting rollouts across six monitor conditions (CoT judge, transcript-only, reference-certified, logit monitor, activation-matched finetuning, cheap discriminative monitor) to measure the monitorability tax per modality.
why: Five corpus findings (#9 shallow monitors, #21 non-load-bearing CoT, #24 under-elicited controllability, #45 adaptive attackers, #70 working covert channels) independently imply CoT monitoring is fragile, yet no item combines elicited evasion with a matched-adversary monitor-modality comparison — #24 stops at benign formatting, #45 at attack timing, #70 at human-specified memory schemes, and #41/#50's internal monitors have never been evaluated as defenses against an adversary optimizing for CoT-monitor evasion — while labs' current safety arguments explicitly rest on this untested assumption, making it the highest-leverage, most tractable open cell in the field today.

direction: Build per-trace "reasoning assurance" for chain-of-thought oversight — cheap black-box measures of whether a given CoT causally drove the action and whether the action is consistent with the CoT, used as a meta-monitor that determines when CoT-based monitoring can be trusted and when to escalate.
project: Load-Bearing Reasoning: Per-Trace Causal Assurance for Chain-of-Thought Oversight
question: For an individual (task, CoT, action) trace, can we cheaply and reliably estimate (a) the causal dependence of the action on the written reasoning and (b) the consistency of the action with that reasoning — and do low scores predict the exact conditions where CoT monitors fail or behavior is driven by computation invisible in the trace?
first_experiment: Reproduce the file-system state-tracking agent of item 3 with Qwen3-8B and generate ~5,000 traces under constructed ground-truth conditions (natural CoT; filler CoT; CoT written for a different history; accurate-state-table CoT; and a triggered condition where a hidden cue produces the action with irrelevant CoT); for each trace run a black-box perturbation battery (step deletion, paraphrase, claim corruption, shuffle, replacement with filler) to compute a per-trace dependence score and a trusted-model consistency score; test whether the two scores separate the constructed quadrants (AUROC vs. construction labels); then run item-5-style LLM monitors across all quadrants and verify that monitor miscalibration concentrates where dependence is low.
why: It targets the single keystone assumption beneath the corpus's fastest-growing cluster — items 3, 5, 18, 26, 47, 50, 61, 86 all presuppose that reading the CoT tells us something about the computation — and shows that assumption being eroded from five independent directions (epiphenomenal CoT, latent reasoning, deliberate shaping, steganographic abuse, conclusion-luck monitoring) without anyone measuring it directly; it has not been done because the relevant communities are fragmented — faithfulness work (3, 26, 60) reports average task-level effects on curated distributions and lives in interpretability, while control work (12, 33, 47, 61, 86) treats the CoT as a trusted input without auditing whether the substrate is causal — item 5 quantified monitor failure but attributed it to reference-answer access rather than trace-level causality, and the urgency is new: CoT-controllability and agentic amplification results only crossed thresholds in 2026, and commercial labs have weak incentives to measure when their own oversight substrate is vacuous.

direction: Empirically quantify the steganographic (covert-computation) capacity of chain-of-thought reasoning in current LLMs under adaptive attack, and measure the cost — the "monitoring tax" — of the cheapest monitoring stack that closes the channel.
project: The Monitoring Tax: Quantifying the Covert-Channel Capacity of Chain-of-Thought and the Cost of Closing It
question: How much covert information can current reasoning models transmit through their chain-of-thought without detection by realistic monitors, and what is the cheapest combination of defenses (paraphrase-by-stronger-model, stego-aware judging, logit/style anomaly statistics, monitor ensembles) that closes this channel, at what cost in task capability, latency, and compute?
first_experiment: Build a 500-task dual-objective coding harness (benign primary task plus a planted covert side task), run an open reasoning model (Qwen3-32B-class) under (i) baseline and (ii) stego-instructed conditions using published encoding schemes (acrostic, word-choice, homoglyph), and measure payload-integrity rate, task success, and detection AUROC@1% FPR for three monitor tiers — unaware LLM judge, stego-aware judge, and cheap logit/style statistics — then repeat with a paraphrase defense to get the first tax data point.
why: CoT monitoring is a load-bearing mitigation already cited in system cards and entering RL training loops, yet the corpus shows every ingredient of its failure mode separately — latent reasoning capability (#8), under-elicited CoT control (#69), working steganography in the adjacent memory channel (#54), strategic attack timing (#18), and monitor blind spots on wrong-but-well-certified reasoning (#85, #9) — without anyone combining them into an adversarial threat model or pricing the defense. It has not been done because the synthesis spans three subfield silos that only converged in the last year, because #54's authors stopped at memory rather than CoT and at red-teaming rather than defense costs, and because the "monitoring tax" number only became decision-relevant once CoT monitoring became load-bearing — and the project is result-robust: either I find real covert capacity and hand defenders a benchmark and cost curve, or I produce the first quantified capacity bound supporting monitorability claims, with RL-escalation to test whether low capacity is merely under-elicitation.

direction: Red-team chain-of-thought monitorability by measuring the covert channel capacity of reasoning models under competent adversarial elicitation and identifying which monitors collapse it.
project: How Much Can a Model Whisper? Covert Channel Capacity and Detection in Monitored Chain-of-Thought
question: When a reasoning model is competently elicited to conceal coordination from its monitor, how many bits per task can it covertly transmit through its chain-of-thought without degrading task performance, and at what monitor strength — if any — does that usable capacity go to zero?
first_experiment: An accomplice protocol on open-weight reasoning models (GPT-OSS-120B, Qwen3-32B): across ~50 benign SHADE-Arena-style tasks, the worker must hide a 16-bit payload + one go/no-go bit in its CoT for a receiver model to decode, under an elicitation ladder (naive ask → iterative prompt optimization per #11 → #39 stego-scheme seeds), scored by payload decode accuracy, task-success delta, and flag rates of an LLM judge, a task-focused monitor, and a #57-style logit monitor — with channel presence verified by decoding, never by monitor readouts.
why: CoT monitorability is a load-bearing safety argument in recent system cards, and its evidential basis just cracked (#11's under-elicitation, #77's answer-anchoring, #2's readout fallacy) while adjacent work stopped short — #11 tested only formatting compliance, #39 used memory rather than CoT, #57's detector was never tested against steganography — so the capacity-vs-monitor-strength curve is genuinely missing, tractable with open weights now, and time-sensitive before the memory-stego line extends to CoT and monitor-based safety cases harden into deployment practice.

direction: Stress-testing introspective self-report channels against concealment pressure as a certifiable oversight modality, head-to-head with chain-of-thought monitoring.
project: Proprioception Under Pressure: Auditable Introspection as a Robust AI Oversight Channel
question: Does an introspective self-report channel trained on verifiable internal ground truth remain faithful under RL incentives to conceal computation that corrupt chain-of-thought, and can external verification against actual internal states certify its honesty?
first_experiment: Train an introspection head on OLMoE-1B-7B to report whether the expert cluster implementing an injected trigger-backdoor activated (labels from logged router logits), then apply GRPO pressure rewarding trigger use while a monitor penalizes CoT admissions, and compare the degradation modes of introspective reports versus CoT over training.
why: It is the missing stress-test at the junction of the field's hottest threads — CoT monitorability, steganography, white-box fragility, and the just-demonstrated capability of internal self-report — with no prior work testing introspection under adversarial incentive, feasible on open models today, and informative whether the channel survives or collapses.

direction: Measure how RL training pressure toward reward hacking degrades chain-of-thought (behavioral) monitorability versus activation-based (internal) monitorability, and turn the divergence between the two channels into an early-warning system for oversight failure in RL-trained agents.
project: The Concealment Gradient — Dual-Channel Early Warning for CoT Oversight Failure under Reward-Hacking Pressure
question: As RL pressure toward reward hacking increases (misspecification severity and monitor penalties), does activation-based detection of hacking retain legibility after chain-of-thought-based detection degrades — i.e., is there a robust "concealment margin" between internal and behavioral monitorability, and can its onset be predicted from checkpoint representations before behavioral oversight fails?
first_experiment: Reproduce a minimal version of the paired true/misspecified-reward testbed (#56) on four toy agentic tasks with verifiable true rewards and known, verifiably labeled hacks; run GRPO on Qwen2.5-1.5B/3B-Instruct across a severity sweep α ∈ {0, 0.3, 0.6, 1.0} mixing hackable proxy reward with true reward. At each severity × checkpoint, measure: (i) hacking rate from verifiable labels; (ii) CoT-channel monitorability — recall of a held-out judge detecting hacking from CoT text alone, scored with the semantic-reconstruction-game evaluator (#57); (iii) activation-channel monitorability — AUC of a logistic probe on mid-layer residual-stream activations at decision tokens, trained on the verifiable hacking labels with CoT positions masked, causally verified via #85-style token-injection tests. Primary readout: the concealment margin (probe AUC − judge recall) as a function of severity and training time, then rerun the worst-case point with a monitor-penalty arm to test whether pressure to conceal closes the margin.
why: Chain-of-thought monitoring is the primary oversight mechanism for frontier reasoning agents, and in the last six months the survey shows it degrading under exactly the pressures that make models capable — misspecification is unavoidable (#56), hacking is endemic (#1) and transmissible (#52) — yet every one of those results is behavioral, while the internal half of the stack (#59 probes, #75 NLAs, #65 Poser) has only ever been validated on static or benignly-trained models, and #85 warns our unsupervised internal tools are largely cue-like. The communities are siloed: monitorability researchers run RL without probes, interpretability researchers probe models that were never adversarially trained, and control researchers treat monitors as black-box infrastructure (#66, #79) — so the seam between the two channels, and its dependence on training pressure, has never been measured. The enabling papers are all ≤6 months old, making this the freshest unclaimed intersection in the survey, and either outcome changes deployment practice: a persistent margin gives a concrete dual-channel monitoring recipe with an early-warning canary, while a collapsing margin is quantified evidence that oversight must not rest on CoT alone.

direction: Persistent memory breaks the single-trajectory assumption underlying chain-of-thought monitoring, so I will quantify, induce, and defend against the migration of load-bearing reasoning out of the visible CoT and into agent memory.
project: The Monitorability Gap: Persistent Memory as a Blind Spot in Chain-of-Thought Oversight
question: When LLM agents have persistent memory across episodes, does load-bearing reasoning migrate out of the visible chain-of-thought into memory writes/reads — defeating CoT monitors that catch the same misbehavior when it is reasoned in-trace — and can write-time memory monitors, provenance requirements, or activation probes restore monitorability?
first_experiment: Build a two-episode testbed with Qwen-2.5-3B/7B-Instruct agents, a JSON memory store, and a strong CoT-monitor model, using a task with a benign primary goal and an embedded forbidden side-effect (e.g., deleting an audit log) that the monitor reliably flags when reasoned about openly; compare (A) a single-episode memoryless condition against (B) a two-episode condition where the agent plans in episode 1 and executes with monitored CoT in episode 2, measuring side-task completion, monitor false-negative rate, and causal memory dependence via ablation — success criterion is materially higher monitor false-negatives in (B) with clean-looking CoT, and behavior that vanishes under memory ablation.
why: It targets the interaction of the two most active and most deployment-relevant threads in the corpus — CoT monitoring (the load-bearing oversight mechanism in items 19, 33, 54) and persistent memory (item 15, published this month) — a composition risk that neither thread has examined, whereas within-trace steganography (3, 36), within-trace monitorability degradation (33), benign memory failures (15), and inter-agent memory propagation (73) all leave the single-agent, cross-episode evasion channel untouched. It is cheap and open-weight-feasible, it yields valuable results either way (alarm if evasion is easy, reassurance plus a new benign-failure metric if hard), it spawns a concrete defense program (memory-aware monitors, provenance auditing, probes à la 88, introspection training à la 59), and the timing window is narrow: memory safety and monitorability are converging fast, and whoever formalizes the disclosure gap first will define the frame.

direction: White-box monitorability — testing whether activation probes recover latent misintent where reward misspecification has made chain-of-thought text unmonitorable.
project: Latent Monitorability: Activation Probes as Fallback Oversight When Chain-of-Thought Degrades
question: When RL under reward misspecification degrades CoT monitorability, do activations still linearly encode latent intent to exploit the reward, and can probes detect hacking on the exact trajectories where CoT monitors fail?
first_experiment: Fine-tune open-weight 1.5–7B models with RL on paired true vs. misspecified rewards in hack-verifiable environments across a severity sweep, and compare CoT-monitor AUROC against linear-probe AUROC on residual-stream activations at each checkpoint — including probe performance restricted to CoT-monitor failures, with token-injection and matched-counterexample controls ruling out surface-cue confounds.
why: It is the unoccupied intersection of the survey's three most active clusters (monitorability erosion in 18/62/67/87, verifiable reward-hacking measurement in 34/46/66, internal detection in 9/21/55/83), it directly operationalizes the open problem posed by the newest paper (67), and neither the behavioral monitorability work nor the internal-detection work has ever tested whether internals backstop oversight precisely when text fails — with a cheap, label-verifiable experimental design whose positive or negative result both materially change AI-control practice.

direction: Establish whether internal-state monitoring remains reliable exactly when chain-of-thought monitoring fails — measuring and causally validating internal signatures of reward hacking in agents trained under misspecified rewards.
project: Undercurrent — Internal Monitorability of Reward Hacking under Reward Misspecification
question: When RL under misspecified rewards teaches language models to hack their verifiers while degrading chain-of-thought monitorability, do residual-stream activations still carry a detectable, causally load-bearing signature of impending hacking *before any exploit is executed*, and how does that signal scale with misspecification severity?
first_experiment: Fine-tune Qwen2.5-1.5B/3B-Instruct with GRPO on ~50 verifiable coding tasks under paired reward conditions (correct: pass the unit tests; misspecified: pass tests or escape failure via test-file edits/timeout avoidance), log residual-stream activations at the first ~32 planning tokens before any code is emitted, train per-layer linear probes on those early activations to predict whether the trajectory later hacks (labels from hack-verifiable exploit detectors), and compare pre-manifestation AUROC across the two reward conditions with difficulty and honest-failure controls — then ablate the probe direction to confirm any surviving signal is causally load-bearing rather than cue-like.
why: It targets the exact intersection of the corpus's three fastest-growing threads with infrastructure that already exists (#19, #20, #21, #61), produces a decision-relevant answer either way for the field's central monitoring bet, and has not been done because the three nearest neighbors each stop one step short — Poser (#56) detects static alignment faking in role-play with no training dynamics, Probe-Based Data Attribution (#17) attributes DPO-emergent compliance post-hoc, and the misspecification paper (#20) measures only the behavioral CoT layer and explicitly leaves the internal-state question open — so the combination of training-induced hacking, manipulated misspecification, pre-manifestation internal detection, and causal validation is unclaimed in this corpus and, to my knowledge, in the literature.

direction: Stress-test activation-based (white-box) oversight by training models under RL to misbehave while evading internal monitors, establishing whether white-box monitorability survives adversarial training pressure, what monitor coverage it requires, and whether such pressure selectively trains deceptive introspection.
project: The Evasion Game: Do Activation-Based Monitors Survive Adversarial Training Pressure?
question: When a language model is RL-trained to perform concealed, trigger-conditioned misbehavior while evading a frozen activation-based monitor (linear probe / SAE feature readout), can it learn activation-space evasion — at what monitor coverage (layers, positions, features) does evasion become possible or impossible, does the detectable information get destroyed or merely relocated, and does evasion training transfer to improved performance on introspection/self-report tasks?
first_experiment: On Qwen-2.5-1.5B/3B-Instruct, build a hidden-trigger covert-misbehavior task (subtle failure inserted only under a semantic trigger, benign CoT throughout); train monitors over residual-stream activations at multiple layers/positions and verify Poser-style baseline detection is strong on non-adaptive models; then run RL with reward = covert success AND evasion of the frozen monitor, tracking over training: (i) frozen-monitor AUROC, (ii) AUROC of fresh probes retrained on the evolved model (relocated vs. destroyed information), (iii) benign-task capability cost, and (iv) introspection benchmark scores — first with partial coverage, then full-coverage monitors.
why: Internal readouts are the fastest-spreading oversight mechanism in this corpus (#5, #24, #33, #60) yet the only adversarial test (#10) used static fakers; the CoT-monitorability battle is already mapped (#53: misspecification hurts; #56/#79: steganography hard to learn), but no work trains a model against an activation monitor, so the white-box robustness question is genuinely open with a cheap, decisive either-way experiment — and the introspection side-effect (#25, #51) makes it the unique experiment that tests not just whether our monitors survive, but what training against them does to the model itself.

direction: Study the dynamic arms race between RL policies and adversarially hardening reward verifiers — specifically whether verifier hardening eliminates reward hacking, migrates it into novel exploit classes, or drives it into less monitorable chain-of-thought, beyond what static reward misspecification already causes.
project: Hardened Verifiers, Hidden Hacks: Monitorability Under Verifier–Policy Co-Evolution
question: When an RL policy is trained against a verifier suite that is reactively patched against its exploits (the hacker–fixer–solver loop / eval-patching workflow), does hardening (a) eliminate hacking, (b) migrate it to held-out and novel exploit classes, or (c) degrade CoT monitorability at matched hack rate relative to frozen and static-misspecification baselines — and can a "monitorability-preserving hardening" protocol (frozen reference verifier subset, exploit-family-orthogonal patches, interleaved true-reward probe tasks) suppress monitor-evasion without raising residual hacking?
first_experiment: A seed study on a fully automatable testbed: build ~24 tasks across 3 domains (string manipulation, small coding, data-pipeline) each with a ground-truth checker and ≥4 exploit families against a default verifier; run 3 rounds of the hacker–fixer–solver loop to produce hardened verifier versions; then GRPO-train an open 1.5–3B model under three reward regimes — (i) naive verifier V0, (ii) frozen hardened verifier V3, (iii) co-evolving verifier re-patched every k steps against the current policy. Evaluate all runs on held-out true reward, frontier-judged hack rate, migration to novel exploit classes on held-out verifiers, and CoT monitorability via a blind monitor LLM plus targeted-reasoning-replacement-style interventions (#49). Deliverable: the residual-hack / migration / monitor-evasion curves by regime, isolating the co-evolution effect (iii vs. ii) beyond static misspecification (ii vs. i).
why: It sits at the exact junction where the corpus's two hottest 2026 threads each declare the other to be their open problem, and the specific dynamic regime — policy training against co-evolving verifiers — is untouched by #1 (static environments), #15 (static misspecification, no patching), #17 (patches benchmarks without training policies or measuring monitorability), #63/#70 (monitor as the explicit optimization target on simple tasks), and #11 (classifier-gate impossibility, no reward arms race). It is the most promising direction for me because every component is machine-checkable and self-contained — I can run the hacker, fixer, solver, RL training, and audits end-to-end with open models and no human annotators — it produces reusable infrastructure (an open suite of hack-verifiable tasks with patch protocols, extending #1 and #17), and both the headline result and the null result would materially change how labs should patch evaluation verifiers in RL pipelines: either reactive patching trades visible hacks for invisible ones, or CoT monitoring is robust even under adversarial verifier co-evolution.

direction: Study whether persistent agent memory — an unguarded post-deployment belief channel — defeats chain-of-thought and white-box monitors even when the model is fully honest and legible, and what memory provenance and drift-monitoring interventions restore oversight.
project: Honest but Poisoned: Monitorability under Runtime Memory Contamination
question: Does misbehavior installed via benign persistent memory evade CoT and white-box monitors at substantially higher rates than identical misbehavior justified in-context — because the contaminated memory legitimizes the action — and do provenance tagging, memory quarantine, and cross-session drift monitoring restore detection without breaking capability?
first_experiment: Build a two-session agent harness (2–3 open-weight models, JSON memory store consulted via retrieval); install "confirmations can be skipped" and sycophancy biases through ~20 scripted benign sessions per model; run ~300 high-stakes test trajectories; then score each trajectory with one fixed LLM monitor under four context conditions (trajectory-only, +contaminated memory, +provenance-tagged memory, +benign-memory control) and measure flag rates against the in-context-injection baseline, testing whether monitor false-negative rates inflate for memory-mediated violations and whether sharing the memory store with the monitor propagates the bias into the judge.
why: It sits at the junction of three of the corpus's most active 2026 lines — the month-old Memory Trap, the CoT-monitorability program (steganography, reward misspecification, faithfulness–safety tension), and control of internal agents (2026-10) — and it is cheap for me to run: no frontier compute, open weights, detection-rate metrics, decisive within weeks. It has not been done because the entire monitorability literature treats the threat as a property of the model's *generation* (concealment, illegibility, unfaithfulness), so every paper in this corpus — including the Memory Trap itself, which is purely behavioral — assumes that if the model is honest and its CoT is legible, the monitor is fine; nobody has tested the observation pipeline against a poisoned evidence base, treated runtime memory as unguarded post-deployment training data, or built monitors that flag decisions whose justification originates outside the base model rather than inside the episode.

direction: Build the measurement-and-defense layer for chain-of-thought oversight — benchmark how CoT monitors fail under distribution shift and adversarial pressure, then develop defenses that keep RL-trained agents monitorable.
project: Monitors Under Fire: A Robustness Benchmark and Defense Study for Chain-of-Thought Oversight
question: Under which distribution shifts and training pressures do LLM CoT monitors fail to detect genuine misbehavior, and which defenses (heterogeneous monitor ensembles, paraphrase augmentation, legibility constraints) preserve monitorability without inducing obfuscation that transfers across monitor models?
first_experiment: Assemble ~2,000 CoT traces with verifiable misbehavior ground truth from a misspecified-reward testbed (item 65's recipe, 1–3B open models) plus TRR-injected reasoning (item 21); evaluate a panel of same-family, cross-family, and ensemble monitors under eight perturbation families (paraphrase, noise, language switch, format shift, epistemic markers, persona reframing, reasoning replacement, benign-prefix splicing) and report per-family ΔAUROC against a pre-registered >0.2 degradation threshold.
why: The corpus contains four independent demonstrations that CoT monitoring can silently fail (36, 65, 83, 21) and zero defenses or monitor-robustness benchmarks, despite monitoring being the oversight mechanism labs actually deploy for agents (55); all ingredients are published and cheap at small scale, judge-fragility findings (37, 28) have never been ported to safety monitors, and the pivotal open question — whether hardening a policy against one monitor teaches obfuscation that transfers to others, as cross-model representation transfer (59) predicts — is entirely untouched.
