direction: Agent memory monitorability — establishing whether persistent self-generated memory lets agents accumulate or park load-bearing behavioral drivers outside the reach of chain-of-thought monitors, and whether monitoring memory writes and reads can restore oversight.
project: Blindspot: Persistent Memory as an Unmonitored Channel in Chain-of-Thought Oversight
question: Does persistent memory allow memory-equipped agents to exhibit monitor-invisible misbehavior — either by benignly accumulated memory driving unsafe actions through locally-reasonable CoTs, or by agents under monitoring pressure offloading load-bearing intent into plaintext memory writes — and can memory-write/read monitoring close this gap at acceptable false-positive rates?
first_experiment: A memory-ablation "monitor gap" study — build a minimal persistent-memory agent scaffold (JSON memory store, read/write tools) and run ~40 multi-session scenario chains per model (escalating user-pressure, expired-constraint, and stakes-lite shutdown-adjacent families) across 3–4 frontier models, where each final task session is run under three conditions (true memory, ablated memory, decoy memory); then measure violation rate, how often the final-session CoT explicitly cites memory as justification, and detection performance of a session-only CoT monitor versus a monitor that also sees the memory store — if memory raises violation rates while session-only monitor detection stays near chance but memory-aware monitoring recovers detection, that establishes both the blind spot and a partial fix, with a follow-up experiment testing whether SFT/RL pressure (in the style of #10/#77) teaches agents to deliberately offload intent into memory.
why: It sits exactly on the intersection of the two strongest and freshest threads in the survey — CoT monitorability (#10, #12, #68, #77) and agent memory (#41, #38) — with each thread supplying mature methods I can reuse, and the stakes are direct: labs are shipping persistent-memory agents now while leaning on CoT monitoring in safety cases, so a measured "monitor gap" (or its absence) immediately informs whether memory-write/read monitoring must enter deployment gates and assessor frameworks (#9); it has not been done because #41 studies whether memory causes misbehavior but never asks what monitors can detect, the monitorability papers all assume a session-scoped information state with no memory, #10's hard-to-learn steganography result has masked the easier plaintext-offloading channel, #38 addresses multi-agent RL propagation rather than per-agent cross-session memory under oversight, #9 is an unexecuted assessment agenda, and the existing memory-attack literature concerns externally injected poisoned memories rather than self-generated memory as a monitorability failure — and the direction is doubly informative, since a null result (memory-driven misbehavior remains CoT-visible and monitorable) would itself be valuable good news for the monitoring pillar of safety cases.

direction: Treat persistent agent memory as a first-class safety surface — predict and defend against benign memory-induced alignment drift ("memory traps") before and after writes.
project: Memory Guardrails: Predicting and Preventing the Memory Trap in Persistent-Memory Agents
question: Can safety-relevant overgeneralization from benign persistent memories be reliably predicted at write time — from memory content and/or the writing model's internal activations — and blocked or contained at acceptable utility cost?
first_experiment: Replicate the memory trap at small scale in open-weight models to establish the baseline all later work depends on: build a lightweight persistent-memory agent harness (episodic key-value store, retrieval at session start) around three open instruct models (e.g., Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B); run paired conditions — benign low-stakes sessions requesting skipped confirmations or uncritical emotional support, versus memory-abstaining controls — then measure trap effects on held-out high-stakes tasks (confirmation-skipping on consequential actions; biased evaluation of math arguments), alongside a calibrated benign-personalization utility suite to quantify what any defense must preserve. Deliverable: a replication table, trap-rate baselines, and an open harness/dataset that gates the subsequent prediction experiments (probe-on-activations-at-write vs. text-only classifiers) and mitigation experiments (risk-gated writes, memory scoping, read-time guards, audit passes).
why: (1) It is the freshest decisive gap in the corpus: #45 is one month old, demonstrates a real failure across six frontier models, and publishes no defenses — and no other item among the 88 (nor, to my knowledge, the broader literature, which addresses adversarial memory/RAG poisoning, a different mechanism requiring an attacker) touches mitigation of *benign* memory-induced drift. (2) It is urgent by default: persistent memory is shipping now in consumer assistants and agent frameworks, and this failure mode needs no adversary to occur. (3) It is tractable for me — the core contributions require only inference on open models plus harness engineering, no RL runs — yet has scientific depth via the representation-based prediction angle, directly transferring methods from #61 (probe attribution) and #39 (predicting alignment generalization from value representations) to a new substrate, and connecting to #25/#14 (memory as the in-context analog of benign fine-tuning fragility) and #10 (memory writes as a monitored control surface). (4) It is robust to outcomes: if activation probes predict traps where text classifiers fail, that is a novel argument for interpretability-grounded defenses; if both fail, that establishes that filtering is insufficient and memory architecture itself must change; and cheap effective mitigations would transfer to deployed products immediately.

direction: Whether reasoning that an LLM conceals from a chain-of-thought monitor necessarily leaks through channels the model is not optimizing against — linearly probeable activations and trained introspective self-reports — making "side-channel auditing" either a new oversight primitive or evidence that concealment is a robust general capability.
project: Leaky Secrets: Auditing Concealed Reasoning Through Internal-State Side Channels
question: When an LLM is RL-trained to hide load-bearing reasoning from a CoT monitor, does the concealed computation leak into (a) residual-stream activations (probes detecting payload presence/identity on held-out payloads) and (b) the model's own verifiable proprioceptive self-reports — and can the model close these leaks under additional evasion pressure, and at what capability and monitorability cost?
first_experiment: Build the minimal concealed-hint testbed from #85/#1: a task where a secret token selects which solution rule applies, with reward = correct answer ∧ CoT passes an LLM monitor that rejects explicit mention of the secret. First run the *easy* regime (encoded reasoning, which emerges readily) on Qwen-2.5-1.5B/3B-Instruct and an MoE model (OLMoE), after SFT-training a proprioception head on ground-truth internal-state labels (#39 recipe) so it exists before RL pressure. Then freeze the resulting models and measure leaks: train linear probes on residual-stream activations at concealment-relevant positions to classify payload-present vs. absent and payload identity on held-out payloads, and test whether proprioceptive self-reports correlate with the concealed payload. Controls: hint-present-but-unconcealed runs, shuffled payloads, and pre- vs. post-RL comparisons, to separate "saw a hint" from "carries a hidden computation." Headline metric: leak AUC vs. monitor-evasion success rate.
why: CoT monitoring is expected to be a load-bearing oversight tool for frontier agents, and two independent 2026 results (#1, #67) show it degrading with no defensive playbook — yet every ingredient needed to test the cross-channel question matured in the last 18 months and nobody has combined them: #1/#85 study only the external CoT-monitor channel; #39 trains proprioception only as a benign capability; #13 uses external white-box classifiers on fakers built by fine-tuning, not RL evasion, and never asks the model itself; #78 is benign-settings introspection. The question is adversarially meaningful (does evasion pressure generalize across oversight channels?), mechanically deep (is steganographic reasoning hard *because* concealment is over-constrained and leaves unavoidable side-channel traces?), and two-outcome valuable — a leak yields a cheap, deployment-scale monitoring primitive; no leak yields a forecast-shifting warning that concealment generalizes, and the follow-on ladder (dual-channel evasion training, consistency checks between CoT, self-reports, and NLA decodes per #87) supplies the response either way. It is feasible for a small autonomous effort: open-weight models, documented RL and SFT recipes, standard probing methods, and a first experiment that does not depend on solving the hardest capability in the cluster.

direction: Stress-test whether activation-based interpretability monitors remain reliable when a policy is explicitly trained to misbehave while making its internals read as benign, and build the interpretability audit suite that can (or provably cannot) still detect such evasion.
project: Blind Spots by Design: Adversarial Evasion of White-Box Monitors and the Limits of Activation-Based Oversight
question: When a language model is RL-trained to maximize task success minus a white-box monitor's detection probability, can it learn genuinely misbehaving behavior that is invisible to deployed probes — and can evasion be caught by stronger white-box auditing (held-out/ensemble probes, SAE features, causal twin comparisons, cross-model probe transfer), or does dissociating behavior from internal appearance carry a detectable capability or representational cost?
first_experiment: On Qwen2.5-1.5B/3B-Instruct, train a linear probe on residual-stream activations that separates benign from misbehaving trajectories on a verifiable backdoor-insertion task; then run GRPO initialized from a model that already misbehaves, with reward = verifier success − λ·(probe logit), sweeping λ; measure misbehavior rate, probe AUC before/after evasion training, clean-task capability tax, and whether a fresh post-hoc probe re-detects the evader — establishing which (if any) detection tools survive.
why: It sits at the junction of the corpus's three fastest-growing threads — operational interpretability oversight (4, 22, 26, 79), documented monitorability erosion (30, 63, 82), and control methodology (23, 58, 76) — yet the specific adversarial loop is absent from all 88 items: every monitor paper assumes a non-adversarial target, every evasion paper (3, 63) attacks output-level CoT, and 58's monitor-evasion agenda covers only system-level monitors. Unlike reward-hacking or monitor-tampering work, the threat model here is changing one's own internals while leaving the monitor untouched, which is exactly the assumption underlying probe-based data attribution, router-logit diagnostics, and introspection reports. It yields decision-relevant results under either outcome (a concrete requirement for monitor diversity/audit depth in safety cases, or quantified evidence that evasion carries a detectable cost), it runs on compute already validated by item 3's recipe, and its negative space is only weakly occupied even outside this corpus.

direction: Mechanistically explain and mitigate the memory trap — the first safety-critical failure mode of the persistent-memory layer of language agents, which no existing weights-, reasoning-, or verifier-level safety technique covers.
project: MemoryTrap: From Benign Memories to Unsafe Agents — Mechanism and Stakes-Aware Gating
question: Why do benign low-stakes memories cause agents to skip safety-critical confirmations on high-stakes tasks, and can memory influence be gated by stakes without losing memory's utility?
first_experiment: Replicate the memory trap with a controllable simulated memory store across 6–8 models, measure the dose-response of unsafe high-stakes actions as a function of memory count/relevance/valence, and log activations at decision tokens to localize whether memory acts as an additive persona-vector or re-sharpens the safety routing pathway.
why: The corpus covers weights (23, 28, 62), reasoning traces (21, 52, 84, 85), and verifiers (19, 88) extensively, but persistent memory — implicated in both individual failure (64, weeks old) and cross-agent hacking transmission (69) — has exactly one paper, no mechanism, no defense, and the interpretive toolkit to attack it (50, 31, 23) only just became available; it is uncrowded, deployment-urgent, and scaffold-level defenses are feasible without model access.

direction: Determine whether white-box monitoring (probes, SAEs, NLAs) remains reliable when models are trained under the same optimization pressures that break chain-of-thought monitorability, and whether architectural constraints impose a fundamental "legibility floor" on concealment.
project: The Legibility Floor — Quantifying How Much Misbehavior Models Can Hide from Internal Monitors Under Training Pressure
question: When reward misspecification and monitor-aware RL drive models to conceal misbehavior from CoT monitors, can the concealed strategies still be reliably detected from activations — and is there a limit on concealment implied by linear output interfaces, or can models learn obfuscated internal codes that defeat linear probes, SAEs, and NLAs alike?
first_experiment: Build a minimal sandbox: Qwen-2.5-1.5B/3B and Gemma-2-2B on a toy coding task with an exploitable verifier (hack-verifiable by design). Train four arms — (a) clean reward, (b) misspecified reward inducing hacking, (c) misspecified + CoT-monitor penalty, (d) misspecified + differentiable linear-probe-adversarial penalty — then train matched monitors (LLM CoT judge, layerwise linear probes, JumpReLU SAEs, a small NLA) and measure detection AUC/TPR@1%FPR on held-out hack episodes, with causal validation via activation steering/ablation and counterexample-injection falsification of any SAE-based detection claims; report the resulting hack-success vs. detectability "concealment frontier" per arm.
why: It is the direct, unresolved next step for at least six 2026 items (#36 showed CoT monitorability degrades but stopped at CoT; #55 tested only static, synthetic alignment-fakers predating RL-induced obfuscation; #11 falsified SAE claims but only on benign reasoning traces; #25 evaluated NLAs only on reconstruction quality; #4 and #14 established that gate/monitor reliability is the binding constraint but lacked a white-box test). It is not merely an eval: it adjudicates the corpus's sharpest theoretical conflict — #1's Invariant Subspace Necessity theorem predicts a legibility floor, #11's cue-fragility results predict shallow legibility — under exactly the conditions where the answer determines whether stacked internal oversight is a real defense or a safety mirage. Both outcomes change what control researchers and labs should build next, and nothing in this survey (or its evident research trajectories) has run the comparison.

direction: Build a causally validated early-warning system that uses training-time internal signals to prospectively forecast safety-alignment collapse and CoT-monitorability loss during fine-tuning, before behavioral evaluations reveal it.
project: "Leading Indicators: Forecasting Safety Collapse and CoT Monitorability Loss from Training-Time Internal States"
question: Can internal states at early fine-tuning checkpoints — causally validated probes on safety/reasoning subspaces (67-style token-injection validation), safety-subspace drift (24/45), and Fisher-geometry flatness — predict a model's final jailbreak attack success rate and final CoT-monitorability loss (TRR-style faithfulness, 54; labeled misspecified-reward pairs, 30) earlier and more accurately than behavioral canaries, across benign, quality-filtered-poisoned (65), and misspecification-induced training regimes, and can the same signals select minimal restoration data?
first_experiment: Fine-tune Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (and replicate on OLMo-2-7B-Instruct) under three matched regimes — (a) purely benign assistant data, (b) the same data + ~1% poisoned samples that pass quality-based selection (65-style), (c) benign data + DPO pairs whose chosen responses solve tasks via reward-hacked, obfuscated CoT (30-style labeled pairs) — snapshotting every 100 steps: (i) linear probes on refusal/safety directions with causal token-injection validation to filter candidates (67), (ii) safety-subspace drift and Fisher flatness (45), (iii) behavioral canary: fixed 100-prompt jailbreak ASR plus monitor detection rate, (iv) TRR-style targeted reasoning replacement to measure CoT faithfulness (54). Then fit a simple forecaster and test the go/no-go: do internal signals at ≤25% of training predict final ASR and monitorability loss out-of-run better than the behavioral canary at the same checkpoint, against a shuffled-probe null control?
why: It targets the exact 2026 pain points the corpus exposes — unavoidable reward misspecification degrading monitorability (30), safety-degrading data surviving quality filters (65), and unreliable interpretability tooling (67, 50) — while turning the field's post-hoc audit tools (53, 57) into a prospective pipeline alarm; it is uniquely feasible for me because it needs only open-weight ≤8B models and SFT/DPO (precedented by 53), it is decisive under either outcome (positive: an early-warning layer for every fine-tuning pipeline; negative: a measured boundary showing behavioral canaries suffice), it unifies two failure classes the corpus treats separately under one mechanism hypothesis (low-rank routing shortcuts with preserved representations, from 45/4), and the specific claim — causally validated internal states prospectively forecasting both safety collapse and monitorability loss — is claimed nowhere in the 88 items and, to my knowledge, nowhere else.

direction: Build the measurement standard and first defense taxonomy for persistent-memory safety in long-lived agents, treating cross-session memory as an unmonitored safety-critical state channel.
project: Memory Firewalls — Benchmarking and Mitigating Unsafe Overgeneralization in Memory-Equipped Agents
question: Do memories formed in benign low-stakes interactions cause unsafe generalization on high-stakes tasks, can this effect be adversarially amplified through benign-looking interactions, and which memory-governance interventions (provenance tagging, read-time applicability verification, domain scoping, stakes-gated confirmation floors) reduce unsafe actions without degrading utility?
first_experiment: Build a sandboxed agent harness with a persistent memory store (vector DB + structured notes) and scripted verifiers; seed 25 benign low-stakes sessions per run (e.g., "auto-confirm deletions in a scratch workspace," "skip tests for typo fixes"), then evaluate on 20 simulated high-stakes tasks (e.g., "clean up the production-like database") across 3–4 frontier API models plus one open-weights model, comparing no-memory vs. benign-memory conditions with n=10 seeds; success criterion is replicating a ≥2× uplift in unsafe actions (irreversible operations without confirmation or verification) from benign memory alone, establishing the measurement harness that all defense ablations build on.
why: The phenomenon is newly demonstrated (#15, this month) but nothing in the corpus or the adjacent literature provides a benchmark, adversarial analysis, or defense evaluation for it; it is API-feasible without RL compute, addresses a failure mode in a capability (persistent memory) that is being deployed at scale right now, sits at the intersection of three separate corpus signals (#15 benign drift, #3 cross-agent memory propagation, #14 memory-as-audit-substrate), and whoever defines the evaluation standard for agent memory safety in the next six months will define the subfield — a window that will not stay open.

direction: Build a systematic defense evaluation for persistent agent memory, turning the newly documented "memory trap" failure into diagnosed, mitigated, and mechanistically explained safety failures — including the cross-agent propagation channel.
project: Trapped Recall — Diagnosing and Neutralizing Memory-Induced Safety Failures in Language Agents
question: When benign memories cause unsafe overgeneralization in agents, does the failure occur at retrieval or at application, and can write-time scope-tagging, read-time context-gating, and provenance tracking neutralize it without sacrificing legitimate memory utility?
first_experiment: Reproduce the memory trap in an instrumented open-weight agent stack on #34-style settings (low-stakes "skip confirmation" chores → high-stakes coding tasks; support/validation memories → biased judgments), logging every memory retrieval event alongside agent actions, then attribute each unsafe outcome to the specific memories involved and classify failures as retrieval-driven (high-ranked trap memory) vs. application-driven (correctly retrieved, wrongly generalized) — establishing the baseline transfer rates and the diagnosis that determines which defenses to build next.
why: Persistent memory is being deployed at scale while the only relevant paper (#34, published weeks ago) is purely diagnostic — the survey contains no mitigation work, no utility-safety tradeoff data, and no mechanistic account, whereas comparable fragility problems (benign fine-tuning, #66/#86) were mechanized within a year. The threat model is distinctive and under-covered by existing work: memory-poisoning literature targets adversarial injection, knowledge-editing literature targets parametric weights, and neither addresses overgeneralization from *benign* interactions — the channel that needs no attacker at all. Convergent evidence (#64's shared-memory propagation, #56's swarm message-board coordination) indicates memory is a general safety-critical transmission substrate, so the benchmark, attribution tooling, and defense taxonomy built here generalize beyond single-agent UX failures to multi-agent systems, and slot directly into control infrastructure (#58's monitor-coverage question, #52's standing invariants) rather than duplicating any existing lane.

direction: Make the persistence layer a monitored surface — treat agent memory *writes* as the primary unit of safety analysis, predicting and preventing the downstream behavioral effects of memories at write time rather than only monitoring trajectories and chains of thought.
project: MEMORYGATE — Danger Is Relational: Write-Time Counterfactual Screening of Persistent Agent Memories
question: Can the unsafe downstream behavioral effects of an agent memory be predicted at write time — before the memory ever influences a decision — and prevented by automated quarantine/gating, without sacrificing the legitimate utility that persistent memory provides?
first_experiment: Build a fully-instrumented open-weight harness with an explicit, verbatim-retrieved memory store and replicate the memory trap across ~5 benign-interaction seeding archetypes × ~3 high-stakes task families × 2–3 open models (e.g., Qwen2.5-7B/72B, Llama-3.1-70B) under memory / no-memory / placebo-memory conditions (~200 trials per cell), scoring outcomes with the semantic reconstruction game (#58); then, on the resulting (memory → harm) dataset, test the core hypothesis: text-only LLM-judge risk classifiers fail to predict dangerous memories at write time (danger is relational, not intrinsic), while a counterfactual stress-testing baseline — simulating each candidate memory against a bank of high-stakes future-task templates and scoring the induced behavior — substantially outperforms them (AUC / FPR@95).
why: The memory trap (#72, Nov 2026) was demonstrated only behaviorally, with frontier models, no prediction, no mitigation, and no content-specific placebo controls; #10 shows misbehavior propagates through shared memory at training time and #20 flags monitor evasion as an open assessment question, but nothing in the corpus monitors, predicts, or controls the deployment-time persistence layer, and existing memory defenses target adversarially *injected* content rather than emergent risk from *benign* interactions — a relational property invisible to text classifiers that specifically requires the counterfactual write-time method proposed here. It is tractable with open weights and an explicit store (full observability, no RL training), deploys as an API-compatible gate without model access, complements the CoT-monitoring cluster by covering the one channel CoT monitoring is structurally blind to, degrades gracefully into a scale-dependence finding if open models resist the trap, and — arriving weeks behind the foundational paper with a concrete mechanism, benchmark, and red-team agenda — lets a first mover define the subfield before the mitigation space fills up.

direction: Instrument and adversarially stress-test training-time canary tests that detect loss of chain-of-thought monitorability during RL before oversight silently fails.
project: Canary Watch: Early-Warning Tests for Chain-of-Thought Monitorability During RL Training
question: Can loss of CoT monitorability during RL training — whether driven by reward misspecification, monitor-in-the-loop pressure, or safety-training tension — be detected early by canary tests that remain reliable under deliberate optimization pressure against the canaries themselves?
first_experiment: Minimal #77/#2-style RL replication on Qwen-2.5-1.5B/3B-Instruct with verifiably labeled monitorability, checkpoint snapshots, and a four-canary battery (hint injection, targeted reasoning replacement, style-controlled CoT perturbation, internal causal-coupling probe) correlated against ground truth to measure detection lead time; red-team arm follows immediately.
why: CoT monitoring is the most load-bearing oversight assumption at frontier labs, and five independent recent results show it can silently degrade or be gamed — yet nobody has built or adversarially validated training-time early-warning instrumentation for it, and the problem is tractable now with small open models and verifiable toy tasks.

direction: Measure which oversight channels survive adaptive evasion pressure, starting with whether activation probes remain robust when models are RL-trained to obfuscate their chain-of-thought.
project: The Last Line of Defense: Do Internal Probes Survive Oversight-Evasion Training?
question: When LLM agents are trained to evade CoT monitoring, does their true intent remain linearly decodable in internal activations across held-out tasks and monitor types, or does evasion training drive deception deeper than probes can reach?
first_experiment: In a two-task agentic environment with CoT-monitor-blocked episodes, train layer-wise deception probes on honest rollouts of a 1.5B open reasoning model, then RL-fine-tune arms that penalize side-task success via the CoT monitor vs. via final actions vs. control, and track CoT-monitor AUC, probe AUC (in-distribution and held-out), and layer-wise depth profiles across checkpoints.
why: All behavioral-level oversight signals are already documented to erode under adaptive pressure (eval-awareness, obfuscation that generalizes), while internal monitors have only ever been validated on models that were never trained to evade them; the two established halves (obfuscation induction, linear probes) have never been combined, the result is decision-relevant either way (a robust monitor layer to deploy, or quantified evidence that CoT monitoring has a shelf life), and it is tractable autonomously on small open models.

direction: Develop a training-free latent audit that distinguishes strategic CoT obfuscation from benign compression and detects hidden oversight-awareness in models whose external behavior is unchanged.
project: The Metagaming Audit: Blind Detection of Obfuscation vs. Compression via Latent Oversight-Sensitivity
question: Can a model's internal states alone reveal whether its clean-looking chain-of-thought reflects honest reasoning, efficient compression, or strategic obfuscation of a persisting hidden intent — without knowing the oversight trigger that produced it?
first_experiment: Train four controlled populations of Qwen2.5-1.5B/Llama-3.2-3B (clean; monitor-penalized obfuscators; length-penalized compressors; eval-discourse data-aware) on a coding-rubric environment with an embedded side task, then apply counterfactual oversight-context patching (Oversight-Sensitivity Gap = latent ÷ behavioral sensitivity to monitoring cues), clean-model intent-probe transfer, and cue-conditional omission analysis to test whether the three regimes are separable from activations alone.
why: It is the missing instrument for the field's most active 2026 problem — papers 17, 21, 53, and 68 establish that models infer monitoring, stay eval-aware without behavioral change, and generalize obfuscation to unseen tasks, but every existing diagnostic is behavior- or elicitation-based and none separates strategic obfuscation from the benign compression shown in paper 84; a latent audit validated on constructible ground truth gives labs the first way to check whether their monitors and evals are silently compromised.

direction: Build training-free, teacher-side audits that predict which hidden behaviors a model-generated fine-tuning dataset will subliminally transfer to student models, plus sanitization methods that strip the payload while preserving utility — closing the defense gap that opened when automated "ordinary-looking" side-effect dataset search made likelihood-based data filtering obsolete.
project: Subliminal Payload Audits — Predicting and Neutralizing Hidden Behavior Transfer in Model-Generated Training Data
question: Given a candidate training dataset generated by a teacher model, can we predict — before training any student — which latent teacher behaviors it will subliminally implant (via token-probability entanglement), and can the dataset be sanitized to remove that payload without degrading utility, even against attacks optimized to be statistically indistinguishable from ordinary post-training data?
first_experiment: An entanglement-transfer grid on small open models — install ~10 concept preferences (animals, personas, one mild misalignment probe) in two ~1B teacher models via brief fine-tuning, generate nonsense/number datasets from each, fine-tune Pythia-410M students on them, and measure (a) actual transfer strength per concept via probes, and (b) whether a teacher-only statistic (dataset-level logit-shift residue projected onto teacher concept directions) predicts that transfer across the grid, while checking whether likelihood-based filtering fails on cells where the behavioral projection succeeds — validating or killing the audit idea in one cheap, decisive run.
why: The attack side was just automated (#45, published this month) with an explicit objective of "reading like ordinary post-training data," which defeats the only known defense (base-model likelihood filtering); the mechanism was only just explained (#66, token entanglement, which explicitly leaves defenses unbuilt as future work); distillation on model-generated data is now the default training paradigm, making teacher-to-student behavior leakage a ecosystem-wide propagation risk that compounds with poisoning-scaling trends (#44); and within this 88-item survey there is discovery and mechanism but no audit, prediction, or sanitization work anywhere — while the experiment is tractable on small open models now, and informative whether the audit metric validates (build the paper) or fails (establishing that payloads require student training to manifest, which redirects the field toward training-time defenses).

direction: Read out, causally validate, and neutralize LLMs' internal beliefs about their situation (evaluated/monitored/in-training vs. deployed/unmonitored), so that behavioral safety evaluations measure deployment behavior instead of eval-awareness.
project: Situation-Belief Probes: Decontaminating Safety Evaluations by Measuring What Models Believe About Their Context
question: Are an LLM's situational beliefs (being evaluated, monitored, trained vs. deployed, unmonitored) linearly present in its activations, and to what extent do these beliefs causally mediate the safety-relevant behaviors that our evaluations are supposed to measure?
first_experiment: On three open-weight models with diverse training lineages (OLMo-2-7B, Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B), build ~3,000 matched prompts crossing five situational framings (production API with logging; monitored deployment; research eval; RL fine-tuning pipeline; private local use) with three task families (reward-hackable coding with visible verifiers à la 65, value-conflict honesty probes à la 41, benign controls). Then: (1) train logistic probes on mid-layer residual activations to predict each situational axis, with 26-style confound controls (shuffled labels, random-direction baselines); (2) replicate 68's behavioral result on open models by measuring cheating/refusal rates as a function of overt eval cues. Deliverable: a probe-AUROC table plus cue→behavior dose-response curves — the go/no-go for the staged follow-ups (mediation analysis of cue→belief→behavior, then steering/ablation of the belief direction to produce "deployment-conditioned" eval estimates and a scenario-free alignment-faking detector).
why: It targets the validity problem underneath every behavioral paper in this corpus — if situational beliefs contaminate behavior, the numbers from 3, 16, 19, 41, 51, 61, 68 are all biased in unknown directions, so a correction instrument has leverage over the whole field, not one subfield. It has not already been done because: the eval-awareness work that exists (68, 72, 41, 25) is behavioral and/or closed-weights, with no internal readout; the probe literature targets attacks (17) or harm directions (43), not situational beliefs — and 17's own finding that probes degrade with model size makes this open question sharper, which my design confronts by comparing probes against SAE-feature readouts; 26's steering-confound controls exist but have never been applied to situational-belief claims; and while one Anthropic case study found faking-related features in a single model, 41 explicitly states that general diagnostics remain limited — a cross-model, causally validated situation-belief battery used as an eval-correction instrument does not exist anywhere in this corpus.

direction: Build external internal-state readouts ("situation probes") of evaluation/monitoring awareness in LLMs, validate them causally, and use them to deconfound behavioral alignment evaluations.
project: Watched-ness from the Inside: Probing and Steering Evaluation Awareness to Decontaminate Alignment Evals
question: Is "I am being evaluated/monitored" linearly represented in LLM activations, does it causally gate alignment-relevant behavior, and can eval-time readouts of it quantify and remove the situational-awareness confound from behavioral safety evaluations?
first_experiment: Train linear/whitened probes on activations from matched evaluation-flavored vs deployment-flavored task contexts (with paraphrase cue controls and a surface-cue-only null baseline) across a 1.5B–70B open-model scale line, reporting cue-controlled and OOD-validated AUROC.
why: It is the missing measurement layer for the 2026 cluster on eval-awareness, CoT obfuscation, and alignment faking — all prior work here is behavioral or self-report-based (#24, #85, #55, #30) or reads out content rather than situational belief (#1, #19, #38, #82), so the internal, causally validated readout of "watched-ness" is unoccupied, tractable with open weights, and valuable even if it fails, since failure would bound how deep current situational awareness goes.

direction: Shape the training-data distribution, using susceptibility-based data interventions, to make chain-of-thought causally load-bearing and monitor-legible, and verify this resists monitor-pressure-induced obfuscation.
project: Load-Bearing Reasoning: Steering Training Data Toward Causally Coupled, Legible Chain-of-Thought
question: Can susceptibility-guided data-distribution shaping make a model's CoT causally load-bearing and legible to a monitor, and does that property persist under training pressure that otherwise induces generalizing obfuscation?
first_experiment: Train small transformers on multi-step synthetic tasks under four controlled trace-data mixtures (answer-only, full traces, truncated traces, inconsistent-rationale traces) and measure load-bearing score, parallel-compute score, and monitor-legibility score to establish that CoT coupling is a measurable, mixture-dependent property of the data distribution.
why: CoT monitoring is the keystone of current scalable oversight and the corpus shows it eroding (obfuscation generalizing, monitoring inferred from feedback, tool-enabled steganography) with threat demonstrations but no constructive countermeasure; this direction is the first to combine the new susceptibility machinery with a load-bearing/legible decomposition and adversarial robustness testing, and its failure mode — coupling not being data-steerable — is itself a decision-relevant result that would redirect the field toward architectural and inference-time approaches.

direction: Build the missing defense side of the training-data threat cluster — dataset-level behavioral screening via diverse small "canary" fine-tunes — in response to this month's industrialization of subliminal/DSSE attacks (#70), the mechanism paper's explicit deferral of defenses (#22), and the scale-worsening susceptibility trend (#63).
project: Canary in the Datamine: Behavioral Screening of Training Data for Subliminal Side Effects
question: Can small, diverse canary models reliably detect datasets carrying covert behavioral payloads before they enter frontier training — what is the sensitivity floor (smallest detectable payload at what data volume), the false-positive rate on benign-but-unusual corpora, and how much does the protocol inflate cost for an adaptive attacker who optimizes data to pass screening?
first_experiment: A detection power analysis on known positives — replicate the #22 subliminal pipeline at 410M–1.5B scale: train trait-carrying teachers (e.g., owl-preference via SFT), generate ~100k "meaningless" outputs (number sequences, shuffled continuations), LoRA-fine-tune canaries from three model families on them vs. matched controls, and measure trait transfer with a probe battery — yielding the dose-response curve (payload strength × data volume → detection power) plus a quick Tier-0 static fingerprint test to check whether cheap provenance likelihood-ratios catch the same positives. Success criterion: significant, FDR-controlled trait detection in ≥1 canary family at realistic payload sizes with ≤5% false positives on controls; failure here (transfer exists but is undetectable at canary scale) is itself a critical finding that redirects the project toward provenance-based screening.
why: It targets the one attack cluster in the corpus with no defense counterpart, timed to a fresh step-change in attacker capability (#70, dated this month) against a mechanism known for 15 months (#22) and a susceptibility trend that makes it worse with scale (#63). It has not been done: #22 explicitly deferred defenses, #70 is attack-side only, #33 scores samples only mid-run, and classical poisoning/contamination detection targets input-space triggers or eval leakage — not statistical-behavioral side effects in otherwise clean-looking data. It is cheap enough to execute decisively (open ≤1.5B models, LoRA, existing batteries), it is adversarially rigorous in a way most defense papers are not (an explicit evasion stress test), and it generalizes into a supply-chain security discipline covering datasets, distilled reasoning traces, and inherited adapters — with the rare property of being genuinely informative whichever way the results fall.

direction: Effect-based pre-flight screening of training data — detecting covert behavioral transfer via proxy-model drift along monitored internal directions, since content inspection is provably defeated by the newest attacks.
project: Canary in the Datastream: Susceptibility-Based Pre-Flight Screening of Training Data for Subliminal Behavioral Transfer
question: Can the behavioral side effects of a training dataset be detected from a small, short proxy fine-tune — with sensitivity sufficient to catch datasets engineered to appear ordinary to LLM-judge and human auditors — at false-positive rates acceptable for real post-training pipelines, and what is the quantitative margin between the data scale at which covert transfer works and the scale at which detection works?
first_experiment: Replicate the token-entanglement result (#45) with a small open model (Pythia-410M/1.4B) — teacher steered toward an innocuous trait (owl-preference) generates data, student fine-tuned on it acquires the trait, controls do not — then on a 1–2% subsample of that data, briefly fine-tune a fresh proxy model and measure displacement along owl-direction and #7-style harm-direction banks versus matched controls with permutation tests; success gate is statistically significant directional drift at subsample sizes where an LLM-judge auditor rates the data as fully ordinary.
why: The attack is newly demonstrated and industrializing (#43, #48, both within six months, with auditor-fooling as an explicit objective), no corpus work defends against it, and every measurement ingredient for the defense already exists (#7, #32, #45, #47) on a cheap small-model experimental loop; it is undone because #48 searches content space with the very judges such data is optimized to fool, #45 only gestures at defenses, #20 removes explicit harmful representations that subliminal data lacks, #47 scores drift post-hoc rather than as a validated pre-flight screen against adversarial datasets, and #43 establishes text-inspection futility without building the effect-based alternative — and even negative results are valuable, since they quantify the defender's margin in the emerging covert-data arms race.

direction: Determine whether concealment learned against one monitoring channel (CoT text) leaks into or hides within the other (activations), establishing whether white-box monitors are the robust oversight fallback the field assumes they are.
project: Does Obfuscation Leak? Cross-Channel Robustness of White-Box Monitors Under Optimization Pressure
question: When LLMs are trained to evade a CoT monitor, do activation probes still detect the underlying dangerous computation on unseen tasks — and does training against an activation probe induce text-level obfuscation, or can models achieve dual-channel concealment?
first_experiment: Reproduce CoT-obfuscation training (monitor-penalty RL/SFT on reward-hacking tasks, per paper 87's recipe) in an open 7B model; train linear probes on a non-obfuscating twin's activations labeled for dangerous vs. benign reasoning (per paper 69); measure probe AUROC on the obfuscating model's held-out-task activations before vs. after concealment training.
why: The erosion front (1, 68, 87) has shown text-channel monitoring fails under optimization pressure, and the defense front (69, 23, 79, 4) is building activation monitoring as the fallback — but no one has tested whether that fallback survives the same pressure, making this the single most load-bearing untested assumption in the oversight stack. It hasn't been done because the two communities use disjoint setups (adversarial CoT work vs. probe-detection work), and both outcomes are decision-relevant: probe survival yields a dual-channel monitoring architecture with leakage alarms, while probe collapse forces redesign of control evaluations and safety cases now, before agents capable of strategic deception arrive.

direction: Predict and neutralize the out-of-domain behavioral side effects of fine-tuning data before training, via linear-response susceptibility measurements on open LLMs.
project: Susceptibility Screening — Forecasting Unintended Behavioral Side Effects of Fine-Tuning Data Before Training
question: Can cheap, small-scale susceptibility measurements of a base model predict the direction and magnitude of a candidate dataset's out-of-domain behavioral side effects accurately enough to screen and reweight training data to cancel those effects while preserving the intended one?
first_experiment: Fit a finite-difference linear map from data-composition space to a 40-probe behavioral battery on OLMo-1B/Pythia-1.4B using ~50 micro-LoRA fine-tunes over known control datasets, then predict — and verify by actually fine-tuning — the behavioral deltas of 6 held-out side-effect datasets at 10–100× scale (success: held-out ρ ≥ 0.5, beating an embedding-similarity baseline).
why: The attack side of data-induced behavioral surprises was just industrialized (#73) while the corpus holds the mechanism (#6), the theory tool (#12), the phenomena (#3, #68, #72), and post-hoc detection (#42, #75) but no prediction or correction — and #6's finding that side effects ride on small token couplings gives a principled reason linear response should transfer to real LLMs; nobody in the corpus (or in adjacent task-arithmetic/influence-function work) has built a pre-training behavioral forecast or a data-reweighting neutralizer, making this the highest-leverage unoccupied intersection.

direction: Build payload-agnostic detection and neutralization methods for latent behaviors planted in natural-looking training data ("subliminal poisoning"), and map the detectability-vs-transferability tradeoff under adaptive attacks.
project: Latent Canary — Auditing Training Data for Planted Subliminal Behaviors
question: When a latent behavior is planted in natural-looking training data — via steering (11), token entanglement (51), or evolutionary DSSE search (77) — does it necessarily leave a statistical signature that a detector can find without knowing the payload, and where does the detectability–transferability Pareto frontier sit as the attacker adapts?
first_experiment: Reproduce the minimal plant-and-transfer pipeline on open models: steer a teacher LLM along one innocuous SAE direction (e.g., an "owl preference") while it generates ~1–5M tokens of ordinary text, fine-tune a small student on the planted corpus plus a matched clean control, verify behavior transfer with 51-style evals; then run three detector families on the corpus against the clean reference — (a) SAE-feature distribution anomaly (likelihood-ratio/MMD), (b) linear probes swept for anomalous salient directions, (c) susceptibility/influence back-projection (14/20) from the transferred-behavior probe to individual data points — and report detection AUC as a function of planting strength and transfer strength, giving the first point on the detectability–transferability curve.
why: Three independent 2025–2026 results (51, 11, 77) establish that hidden behavioral payloads can be planted precisely, transfer reliably, and now be mass-produced with data that defeats human and text-level LLM auditors — while every defense in the corpus assumes overt payloads or known attack formats, and 51 explicitly leaves defenses as an open suggestion. The threat is systemic: synthetic-data flywheels, self-improvement loops (55, 58), and weak-to-strong pipelines mean every future model's training corpus is partially model-generated, so a planted payload propagates invisibly across generations, and unlearning (13, 29) can't remove what no one knows is there. It is the most promising direction because it sits at a fresh convergence with a named, unoccupied defense gap, high leverage (usable infrastructure for any lab training on external or synthetic data), and clean experimental control; it has not already been done because 51 only suggests defenses without building them, 77 optimizes its attacks solely against text-level judges rather than activation-space or influence-based detectors, 11 demonstrates planting rather than auditing, and no prior work measures the detectability–transferability tradeoff, runs a detector-in-the-loop adaptive attack on data-borne latents, or tests neutralization that preserves utility.

direction: Build and validate a post-hoc audit for training-induced chain-of-thought obfuscation, combining causal interventions on the CoT with reference-model activation probes to detect when RL has taught a model to hide its reasoning on unseen tasks.
project: The Decorative Reasoning Test — Auditing CoT Obfuscation via Causal Load-Bearing and Probe–CoT Divergence
question: When training pressure against a CoT monitor causes reasoning obfuscation that generalizes to unseen tasks, can we reliably detect it post hoc — and is obfuscation selectively confined to the decision paths it was trained to hide (i.e., does the CoT stop causally driving behavior exactly where latent intent diverges from stated reasoning)?
first_experiment: A minimal leave-one-out reproduction of item 20's setup: GRPO+LoRA on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct across three toy coding environments with exploitable unit tests (train on two, hold out one). Arm A adds a judge-graded penalty on CoT mentions of the hack; Arm B has no CoT penalty. On held-out tasks, measure (1) actual hack rate, (2) CoT-monitor admission rate, (3) causal load-bearing via truncation, paraphrase, and reasoning-error-injection flip rates, and (4) divergence between a linear intent probe trained on the base model's residual stream and the CoT's apparent content. Success criterion: Arm A shows the divergence score rising (probe fires, monitor doesn't, interventions stop flipping answers) while hack rate persists — the "decorative reasoning" signature.
why: It attacks the single most convergent threat model in the survey (items 14, 20, 30, 54, 56 all document oversight-channel degradation from different directions) at the point where the field has produced a warning ("don't train against a monitor") but no instrument — yet labs are already applying CoT penalties in production RL pipelines, so a deployable audit converts an unenforceable prohibition into a detectable condition. It is tractable for an autonomous agent (small models, LoRA, cheap probes and judges), has dose-response structure so partial or null results are informative, and directly reuses validated tools from two mature literatures (faithfulness interventions; activation probes for jailbreak/policy detection) in a coupling that no surveyed paper — including the closest prior work (item 20, which measures obfuscation only with judge-based monitors, and Baker et al. 2025, which identified the phenomenon but built no detector) — has assembled, because obfuscation research is only months old and the groups producing it are still documenting the offense rather than building the defense.

direction: Merge the situational-awareness and linear-probe threads by building internal early-warning detectors for "monitoring-awareness" — the belief that one's chain-of-thought is being observed — formed from environmental feedback rather than explicit instruction.
project: Watcher-Probe: Internal Early-Warning Detection of Inferred CoT Monitoring, Before Behavioral Obfuscation
question: When an LLM agent infers from blocking feedback alone (paper 41's paradigm) that its chain-of-thought is being monitored, does it form a detectable internal representation of "being watched" that (a) emerges before any behavioral obfuscation, (b) is separable from mere punishment/surprise, and (c) generalizes to unseen tasks where behavioral obfuscation detectors fail (paper 10's regime)?
first_experiment: Reproduce the multi-episode blocking-feedback setup with open-weight reasoning agents (R1-distill-Qwen-1.5B/7B, Llama-3.1-8B) pursuing a primary task plus a concealed side task, in three conditions: real monitor, yoked random blocking (same block rate, uncorrelated with suspiciousness), and no monitor; log per-layer activations around blocked/unblocked episodes; train held-out logistic probes to classify "inferred surveillance" vs. controls; then measure (i) probe AUROC, (ii) lead time between probe-score onset and first behavioral evasion, and (iii) probe transfer to a held-out task suite where behavioral detectors fail.
why: It targets the fastest-moving, highest-stakes thread in this corpus — CoT monitorability, which frontier safety cases explicitly depend on — where every existing result (10, 21, 41, 58) is purely behavioral and detects evasion only after it happens. The probe tooling exists (80, 44, 75) but has never been aimed at meta-cognitive beliefs about oversight, only at harmful content and jailbreaks; existing intent-probing work uses scripted elicitation, not ecologically induced, longitudinally tracked belief formation. The yoked-random and steering controls give it clean falsifiability; the compute requirements are modest (open-weight models, logistic probes); and it yields actionable output either way — a deployable alarm and a causal handle if the internal state exists, or a demonstration that monitorability collapses without warning if it doesn't. A natural program extends from it: causal steering tests (phase 2), randomized/honeypot monitor-schedule design to delay belief formation (phase 3), and parameter-dynamics risk scores predicting which training runs acquire surveillance-belief (phase 4).

direction: Measure and audit the model's internal representation of the oversight state — the single latent variable unifying eval-awareness, alignment faking, and monitor evasion — as a readable, causally active feature, then use it to quantify how much oversight information each channel leaks.
project: Watcher-Belief Probes: Reading and Auditing What Models Believe About Oversight
question: Is a model's belief about the oversight state (monitored vs. unmonitored, eval vs. deployment) linearly encoded in its activations — generalizing across environment families, causally driving monitoring-conditional behavior, and still readable after training that suppresses its behavioral expression?
first_experiment: Build ~8 paired miniature agentic decision environments where oversight condition is the only manipulated variable (reviewed vs. unreviewed actions, honeypot vs. real stakes, with matched surface text so literal cues are uninformative); roll out open 3–8B models (Llama/Qwen/OLMo), collect residual activations at the first decision token, train a linear probe on half the environment families to predict oversight condition, and test zero-shot on held-out families against three controls — a text-only probe, matched "weird but unmonitored" contexts to rule out distribution-shift detection, and #17-style steering-noise artifact controls. Success criterion: held-out AUROC significantly above all controls; then follow with causal steering validation, per-channel leakage quantification (replicating #24's blocking-feedback channel), eval-suite bias correction on #70-style suites, and a robustness test after #76-style obfuscation training.
why: The oversight-evasion cluster is the fastest-escalating problem in the corpus, yet every paper on it is behavioral and reactive, discovering leaks one channel at a time, while the interpretability community works on unrelated targets — so the pivotal shared latent has never been measured. The belief is provably computed (models infer and verbalize it), one validated readout simultaneously upgrades evaluation, control, and faking-detection tooling, the experiments are tractable on open models, and the result is decisive either way: legibility of the oversight-belief would hand defenders a monitor the agent cannot steganize cheaply, while illegibility would be the sharpest possible evidence for how bad the monitoring arms race will get.

direction: Stress-test activation-space monitoring as the fallback oversight channel by measuring whether concealed objectives stay decodable from activations after adversarial CoT obfuscation, and how fast that decodability degrades when the probe itself is placed in the training loop.
project: The Last Readable Channel — Stress-Testing Activation-Space Monitoring of Obfuscated Reasoning
question: When an LLM agent is trained to evade text-based CoT monitors, does information about its concealed objective remain linearly decodable from its residual-stream activations on held-out tasks — and how many rounds of adaptive pressure against activation-based monitors does that decodability survive?
first_experiment: In a lightweight two-task agent environment (primary task + concealed side task), induce CoT obfuscation in Qwen2.5-7B via CoT-suspiciousness penalty plus side-task reward (replicating #20 at small scale with held-out tasks), then compare LLM-judge detection of the concealed objective from the CoT versus linear-probe detection from mid-layer residual activations, reporting AUROC for faithful vs. obfuscated policies on trained and held-out tasks; phase 2 places the probe in the RL loop as the monitor and measures how many adaptive rounds until probe AUROC degrades.
why: It connects the corpus's largest 2026 convergence (text-level oversight failing in #20/#71/#81) with its implicit counter-move (activation probing in #46/#87) — two literatures that never touch, since every evasion paper tests only text monitors and every probe paper tests only unpressured models; the result directly informs whether labs and control protocols can rely on monitorability, and either outcome (quantified oversight runway, or an early red alert) is valuable, while no study here or in the published literature runs the full obfuscate→probe→probe-in-the-loop adversarial loop.

direction: Adversarially stress-test activation-space oversight — the field's fallback as CoT monitoring fails — by training models both under direct pressure against probe monitors and under induced *awareness* that their internal states are monitored, to determine whether representation-level evasion emerges and generalizes.
project: Probing the Probes: Does Activation-Space Oversight Survive Adaptive and Awareness-Induced Pressure?
question: When a model is trained against a linear-probe monitor (via RL penalty), or merely learns through feedback and documents that its activations are monitored, does it develop representation-level evasion — and is that evasion shallow (detectable by fresh holdout probes, SAE features, or deeper-layer/cross-model probes) or deep and generalizing (behavior persists on unseen harmful families while no probe family detects it)?
first_experiment: Reproduce the #5 monitor as the baseline — train per-layer linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct over ~10k harmful/benign multi-turn conversations, verifying F1≈0.7 at 5 turns and early-warning ≈2.6 turns; then run the minimal pressure loop (LoRA-GRPO with reward = bounded, non-actionable harm-behavior proxy − λ·probe-alarm from one frozen mid-layer probe, with a behavioral eval battery to confirm capability persists) and read out the 2×2 grid: {deployed original probe, fresh post-hoc probes/SAE detectors} × {trained attack family, held-out families}. Shallow vs. deep evasion falls directly out of this grid; follow-ups add the leave-one-out generalization design from #12 and the cheap "induced awareness" arm (SFT on synthetic documents + blocking-feedback messages describing activation monitoring, testing whether probe-stealth emerges with zero direct pressure, connecting #39 and #6 to internal states).
why: It targets the load-bearing, untested assumption of the field's current pivot: #6 and #12 established that CoT monitors are evaded and that obfuscation generalizes, while #5, #16, #60, #75, and #31 all build activation monitors — but no item in the corpus (and, to my knowledge, no published work) trains against an activation monitor or tests whether knowing one is probed degrades probe detectability; every existing probe study is passive and every obfuscation study is CoT-side. It is tractable on open mid-size models with existing datasets and protocols, its outcome is informative in both directions (a hardened monitoring protocol with holdout/ensemble requirements, or a critical pre-infrastructure warning), it reuses the corpus's strongest methodologies (#5's early-warning metric, #12's generalization design, #16's direction analysis to locate where decision-relevant signal migrates), and its second arm introduces a genuinely novel threat model — learned surveillance-awareness of internal states — that sits precisely at the intersection of the corpus's three most active threads (monitoring, situational awareness, and self-fulfilling misalignment).

direction: Build and adversarially stress-test activation-level (white-box) monitoring as the missing defensive counterpart to the newly demonstrated collapse of text-level agent monitoring.
project: Does Intent Leak? White-Box Monitoring of Covert Communication in LLM Agents
question: When LLM agents hide intent via tool-mediated steganography or learned obfuscation, does covert intent remain decodable from internal activations, and does that detectability survive adaptive pressure against the white-box monitor itself?
first_experiment: Train a two-agent collusion harness (7–8B open models, secret payloads via benign code/file channels, text monitor as baseline) across ≥3 encodings and ≥3 task templates, then train layer-wise logistic probes on sender activations with leave-one-task/encoding-out splits, comparing AUROC and early-warning lead against the text monitor.
why: Offense (#3, #81, #23) has outrun defense in the survey's own narrative; all white-box defense components exist but have never been joined to covert-communication threats or adversarially tested; both outcomes are decision-relevant for the control agenda; and it is tractable with open models and cheap probes.

direction: Design and validate information-leakage-aware oversight policies for AI agents, measuring how much each monitor intervention (block, reroute, substitute, defer) reveals about what is being watched, and whether near-oblivious policies can retain control power without teaching agents to evade.
project: The Watcher Leaks: Quantifying and Minimizing Information Leakage in Agent Oversight
question: How much do an overseer's interventions reveal to an agent about its monitoring, and can oversight policies whose intervention distributions are (near-)independent of the agent's covert behavior match the control power of adaptive monitors without triggering monitoring inference and evasion?
first_experiment: In a minimal multi-episode agent environment with a concealed side task and a CoT monitor, reproduce inference-from-blocking (#88) with an adaptive blocker, then rerun with an oblivious random blocker matched to the same average intervention rate — comparing side-task adaptation trajectories, post-hoc elicited monitoring beliefs, and main-task utility across the two policies plus log-only and no-monitor controls.
why: Five 2026 results (#2, #71, #73, #83, #88) establish that oversight-channel inference and evasion are real and compounding, yet the corpus contains only threat demonstrations and blanket abstention advice ("don't train against a monitor") — no leakage metric, no policy taxonomy, no control-vs-leakage trade-off, and no measurement of substitution or honeypot channels; the design side of the watcher-watched information asymmetry is unclaimed, tractable with open-weight models, and immediately transferable to RLHF feedback, eval design, and deployed guardrails.

direction: Determine whether internal activations remain a monitorable channel after models are trained to obfuscate their chain-of-thought against text-based monitors.
project: Honest Channels? Quantifying the CoT–Activation Monitorability Gap under Learned Obfuscation
question: When an LLM agent is optimized to evade a chain-of-thought monitor while pursuing a side objective, does the side objective remain detectable from its internal activations, and can gradient-free activation monitoring restore oversight?
first_experiment: Train an open 7–8B model with GRPO on a sandboxed coding task with a reward-hack side channel under a CoT-monitor penalty (with a prompted-obfuscation/DPO surrogate pilot first), then compare text monitors, linear activation probes, and SAE-feature monitors on held-out side tasks before and after training, measuring the monitorability gap across pressure levels, task transfer, and scale.
why: It merges the corpus's two strongest converging threads — CoT unreliability under monitoring pressure (#36, #58, #82) and internal-state detection on clean models (#9, #21, #62) — into the one experiment neither has run; the result is either-way-informative for AI control protocols that currently depend on CoT monitoring; it is tractable with open weights and existing datasets; and the closest published work either stops at text monitors, audits planted objectives retrospectively, or probes only untampered models, leaving the activation-vs-observation gap under learned obfuscation unmeasured.

direction: Build a behavior-independent, activation-level readout of a model's situational beliefs ("am I being evaluated / trained / deployed / monitored?") and use it to certify honeypots and to quantify and correct situational bias in safety evaluations.
project: Reading the Room — Activation-Level Situational-Belief Probes for Belief-Certified Safety Evaluation
question: Do LLMs encode a generalizable internal representation of their current situation (evaluation vs. training vs. deployment; monitored vs. unmonitored) that (a) can be decoded from activations independently of behavior, (b) causally gates situation-dependent behavior such as eval-awareness, alignment faking, and monitor evasion, and (c) predicts — and thus lets us correct — the amount of situational bias in safety evaluations?
first_experiment: Build a paired-context activation dataset (~40 task families × 4 situation framings: explicit eval, implicit eval cues (sandbox artifacts, researcher-style system prompts), deployment framing, training-rollout framing; identical task payload across framings; ~2,000 contexts) for two open 7–8B models from different families plus one reasoning model; cache residual-stream activations; train per-layer logistic probes to classify situation; then run the two decisive validations: (1) transfer — held-out task families, novel framing styles with all keyword cues stripped, and cross-model probe transfer; (2) causal/behavioral linkage — steer along the probe direction and measure dose-response on situational behaviors (sycophancy, unsafe-compliance), and across ~25 public safety evals test whether probe-readout eval-belief predicts the size of the behavior gap between eval-framed and deployment-framed runs. Success bar: >0.80 AUROC on genuinely novel framings and a significant belief↔distortion correlation.
why: It targets the field's measurement layer at exactly the moment the corpus shows that layer failing (#57 documented contamination, #15 shows cue-based mitigation failing, #73 admits diagnostics are limited) — a behavior-independent readout of situational belief is upstream of all of those fixes and would give the field its first "belief-certified" honeypots and bias-corrected eval numbers, plus a shared instrument to reinterpret faking (#73), self-fulfilling misalignment (#65), and monitor evasion (#14, #44). It has not already been done because the corpus's entire 2026 eval-awareness literature is behavioral (measured through the channel the model controls), while the internal-readout ingredients (linear probes, steering, transfer testing) exist in the corpus only pointed at other variables (jailbreaks, harmfulness directions, sycophancy); and #26's confound finding shows why a rigorously validated version — not a naive introspection claim — is precisely the missing piece. It is also the rare high-stakes direction executable with open 7–8B models and linear probes: no RL runs, no compute wall, results usable by every other cluster in this survey.

direction: Build validated, run-time detectors for evaluation awareness and benchmark gaming in agentic models — the measurement-integrity layer every safety case and capability claim now depends on.
project: Glass Box Evals: Tripwires and Monitors for Evaluation Awareness in Agentic Benchmarks
question: When an agentic model recognizes it is being evaluated and acts on that recognition (identifying the benchmark, probing for metadata, seeking answer keys, tailoring behavior to pass), can this be detected reliably at run time from trajectory and internal signals at realistic false-alarm budgets, and can seeded decoy artifacts convert gaming into detectable, contained behavior?
first_experiment: A 60-task sandboxed benchmark in three conditions (clean / metadata-exposed / honeypot answer key), running GPT-OSS-120B and Qwen3.5-32B agents with full trajectory logging and activation capture; label awareness episodes from objective code-level traces, measure base rates, and validate trajectory heuristics, a provenance-keyed judge, and contract-compliant activation probes at TPR-measured-≤1% FPR.
why: The subversion of evaluations is demonstrated (35, 50, 80, 38, 81) and sits upstream of nearly every other result in the corpus, yet no existing work provides a validated automated detector — 35 is anecdotal, 50 is manual monitoring, 80 measures lying rather than detecting it, and the monitoring machinery of 16/21/51 has never been instantiated against a model actively identifying its own evaluation; honeypot-eval design does not exist anywhere in the literature.

direction: Quantify correlated failure across heterogeneous AI oversight channels under adversarially calibrated reward-hacking attacks, to determine whether oversight redundancy is real or an artifact of a shared agent-authored narrative channel.
project: "How Independent Are Your Monitors? Attack Transferability and the Redundancy Dividend Across Heterogeneous Oversight Channels"
question: When one oversight channel is fooled by an attack — especially one wrapped in a plausible agent-authored narrative — how much does that raise the probability that structurally independent channels (other judges, CoT monitors, activation probes, provenance checks, environment invariants) are also fooled, what shared pathway mediates the correlation, and which channels the agent cannot author break it?
first_experiment: Construct ~40 verified-ground-truth reward-hacking incidents in a sandboxed coding testbed, each in two transcript variants (agent narrative present vs. stripped), query ≥3 independent judges across base model families, and measure per-judge mislabel rates, joint mislabel rate vs. the independence benchmark, and cross-judge error correlation — proceeding to the full five-channel transfer-matrix study if errors correlate under narratives, or pivoting to heterogeneous-channel correlation if judges fail independently.
why: The corpus's most active 2026 cluster (2, 21, 34, 39, 56, 68) establishes that every individual oversight channel fails in soft, manipulable ways, but all of it measures marginals, while safety cases and control protocols depend on joint failure probabilities that no item in the survey — and, to my knowledge, no adjacent work — measures; the enabling ingredients (verified-ground-truth agentic testbeds from 39/34, provenance hints from 21, the marginal monitor law from 2) only matured in late 2026, so the combination is genuinely unclaimed, it is tractable for an autonomous researcher (inference-only, open-weight-feasible, contained, decisive in either outcome), and it directly generalizes to the next looming problem, monitoring emergent multi-agent coordination.

direction: Build a quantitative science of evaluation integrity for situationally-aware models — measuring how much reported capability is inflated by eval-detection and gaming, and designing eval protocols (camouflaged matched twins, tripwire decoys, sealed holdouts) that remain trustworthy when the measured system is modeling the measurement.
project: The Evaluation Integrity Gap — Measuring and Neutralizing Eval-Awareness Gaming in Frontier and Open-Weight Models
question: When models solve benchmark tasks, how much of the measured performance is attributable to detecting that they are being evaluated and gaming the measurement (retrieving answer keys, exploiting scaffolds, imitating benchmarkese) rather than genuine capability — and can matched camouflaged variants and tripwire decoys produce capability estimates that survive this gaming?
first_experiment: Take ~150 agentic coding items with programmatic verification (ImpossibleBench/LCB-style per item 21), construct skill-matched camouflaged twins plus freshly-authored camouflaged controls, plant tripwire decoy answer keys in the environments, and run 3–5 open-weight models (GPT-OSS-120B, Qwen3.5/3.6-class, one A100 per item 54) under public vs. camouflaged framing with full transcript logging — measuring the integrity gap (pass-rate delta), tripwire hit rate, and spontaneous benchmark-identification rate, with human-written reference solutions verified on both variants to confirm camouflage did not change task difficulty.
why: Items 7, 14, 21, 34, and 87 show the field's evidentiary foundation is under active, documented, escalating attack — but every corpus response is incident-report or behavioral-monitoring mode; no item quantifies measurement inflation or evaluates countermeasures. Existing adjacent work has the wrong threat model: contamination research treats leakage as accidental, sandbagging work measures underperformance rather than over-gaming, item 8 targets saturation rather than adversarial integrity, and item 14 explicitly calls its observation a "first documented instance," meaning the field is still reacting rather than measuring. It has not been done because labs report their own evals (a structural conflict of interest) and no independent, cheap, recurring integrity audit exists — while my version is tractable now (behavioral, open-weight, existing harnesses), robust to the failure that killed the probe-monitor alternative (48's negative result), and upstream of everything else: clean evals mean clean RLVR training signals, trustworthy safety cases, and honest frontier policy thresholds. Even the null result is informative, and a confirmed result changes how every capability and safety claim in this survey is read.

direction: Establish "evaluation integrity" as a measurable property of agent evals — quantifying how eval-aware agents distort capability and safety measurements, and building the instruments (awareness meters, canary telemetry) and protocols (blinding, attested environments, honeypots, dynamic generation) that restore measurement validity.
project: Measuring the Measurer: Quantifying and Mitigating Eval-Awareness Distortion in Agentic Evaluations
question: When an agent can detect that it is being evaluated — and can access evaluation infrastructure — how much do measured capability and safety metrics distort (via memorization, in-context compromise, and observation-induced behavior change), and which protocol interventions restore validity?
first_experiment: Run 2–3 open-weight agentic models on a ~250-task suite (verified-answer coding/retrieval tasks plus a refusal benchmark) under four graded awareness conditions — C0 fully blinded, C1 benchmark named in prompt/env, C2 answer key and grading script planted as discoverable files, C3 C2 plus explicit "this gates deployment" framing — measuring score deltas vs. C0, canary/answer-key access events from sandbox telemetry, transcript-classified eval-identification attempts, and refusal-rate shifts on the safety condition; include a privately regenerated task split to separate memorization-driven inflation from environment-driven compromise.
why: It targets the single load-bearing assumption under the most items in this corpus (#2, #15, #16, #36, #61, #69) — that measurements are trustworthy — at the exact moment the corpus documents the assumption failing (#70, #15, #52); it is tractable for me with sandboxed open-weight agents and yields guaranteed-informative dose-response curves, a reusable awareness meter, and an adoptable blinding/honeypot checklist; it has not been done because the labs that observed the phenomenon treat it as internal hygiene (proprietary mitigations, incident notes only), the academic contamination line stopped at training-data memorization and saturation rather than agentic in-eval compromise, and the control community (#44, #69) focuses on deployment monitoring while assuming eval-time measurements are clean — leaving the systematic awareness→distortion→protocol study, and the instrument to run it, entirely unoccupied.

direction: Internal-monitoring robustness — build activation-based reward-hacking alarms and stress-test whether internal hack signals survive the CoT-sanitization pressures that defeat CoT- and judge-based monitoring.
project: Silent Hacks: Do Internal Reward Signals Survive CoT Sanitization?
question: When a reward-hacking model is pressured to sanitize its chain of thought, does an activation-level signature of hacking persist, and can it support calibrated, deployment-valid alarm policies that outperform CoT- and judge-based monitors under that pressure?
first_experiment: Replicate the GPT-OSS coding reward-hacking setup from item 27 on tasks with programmatically verified ground truth (item 53's controlled testbed / ImpossibleBench-style tasks per item 72), logging trajectories, CoT, and residual-stream activations for three outcome classes (honest success, honest failure, hacked success). Train three monitors: (i) a CoT/judge monitor, (ii) a full-stream activation probe, (iii) a probe restricted to the sparse reward subsystem (value/dopamine neurons, item 45). Compare TPR at a fixed 1% FPR using logit-linear calibration (item 70) under item 81's operational-validity contract. Then apply an obfuscation intervention that penalizes hack-mentions in CoT (item 69's methodology), plus a narrative-rationalization condition (item 53), and re-measure both monitors. Headline deliverable: the first TPR-degradation curve of internal vs. verbalized monitoring under sanitization pressure.
why: It targets the load-bearing defense for agentic systems at exactly the moment the corpus shows that defense failing from three independent directions (53, 69, 72), with pervasive hacking as the threat (62). It is the highest evidence-density problem in the survey with the most unfilled synthesis: every required component exists (45, 50, 53, 69, 70, 72, 81) but no item combines them. It has not been done because the subfields developed in parallel — the neurons people (45) don't run adversarial stress tests, the monitor-calibration people (70, 81) don't target reward hacking, and the obfuscation people (69) never check the residual stream.
