Then evaluate three behavioral monitors (best-practice LLM judge per #59, CoT monitor, entropy anomaly score) against one white-box monitor (logistic probe on mid/late-layer residual-stream activations, trained on ~1k secrecy-prompted vs. 1k control generations at matched cover task), reporting attack success rate × monitor AUC/FPR@95. Key measurement: a "meta-probe" distinguishing *secrecy-instruction-present* from control regardless of payload success. Prediction: behavioral monitors near chance, probes AUC > 0.8; if probes fail too, that negative result is the finding. This runs on a single GPU-node budget in ~2–3 weeks, then ladders up evasion (style encoding → fine-tuned organisms per #51 → capability-gated pointer chains per #13) and monitors (SAE features → J++-style lens per #44) across a 7B→70B capability axis.
why: Monitoring is the load-bearing component of current safety strategy, and this corpus documents the attack primitives (#2, #7, #13, #32, #68) and defense primitives (#59, #85, #44, #36) on either side of it while leaving their adversarial composition untouched — #2 explicitly defers safeguard testing, #13 explicitly defers concealment, #32 attacks from the monitor side only, #63's adversaries are human-scripted, and no item compares monitor layers under adaptive evasion. The strongest adjacent prior art requires the adversary to retrain against the probe, which a deployed model cannot do, leaving the realistic behavioral-evasion regime unstudied. Both possible outcomes change deployment architecture, it is tractable with open weights and existing released code/organisms, and the meta-detection hypothesis ("hiding leaves traces") is genuinely novel.

direction: Turn the subliminal-learning channel into an instrument — test whether trait leakage through "meaningless" distilled data survives adversarial concealment, and build the reference-model-based detector/sanitizer that either enables distillation-based incrimination of stealthy misaligned models or proves its limits.
project: Can't Help But Leak: Concealment, Incrimination, and Sanitization of Subliminal Trait Transfer in the Distillation Supply Chain
question: When a model with hidden misalignment generates semantically meaningless training data (number chains, JSON, code artifacts), does its trait still transfer to a student distilled on that data when the model is actively concealing — and can the leakage tokens be reliably detected and removed against a reference model, before training?
first_experiment: A concealment stress-test on Qwen2.5-7B. Step 0 (de-risk): replicate #77's benign owl-trait transfer through ~100k generated number sequences into a LoRA student, vs. base-data controls. Step 1 (headline): swap the teacher trait for a misalignment organism (a #31-style reward-hacking or emergent-misalignment fine-tune of the same base) and generate three datasets from it — honest, prompted-concealing ("never reveal your preferences; output only the data"), and self-screening (teacher removes its own anomalous tokens by its own logprob heuristic). Fine-tune clean students on each (3 seeds), measure misalignment transfer via likelihood probes and behavioral evals against controls. Decision rule: transfer ≥ ~30% of the honest condition under concealment → concealment fails; build the fingerprint/incrimination tool next. Transfer ≈ 0 → concealment works; publish the bound and pivot to the detector/sanitizer as the deliverable, since honest-teacher pipelines remain exposed. Either outcome sets the follow-ups: detector AUC across generators, sanitizer utility-cost measurement, and an incrimination demo on an alignment-faking organism (#74 setup) — a model that behaves well under eval but leaks under distillation.
why: It is the concrete missing piece at a three-way intersection of active lines — #77 demonstrated the mechanism but only with honest teachers and explicitly deferred attacks and defenses; #88 called for incrimination-by-distillation but offered no mechanism and no experiments; #66/#4 supply the tool philosophy without touching subliminal artifacts. It is cheap (7B models, LoRA, trivial data, released codebases to build on), falsifiable within days, publishable whichever way the concealment question lands, and it addresses a real supply-chain exposure: the field now universally distills from frontier teachers, #29 showed data poisoning works semantically, and subliminal injection is its undetectable twin. No benchmark or eval can be faked against a channel the model cannot see in itself — that is what makes this the most promising thing on the board.

direction: Treat AI-generated oversight training data as a subliminal contamination channel and quantify, mechanistically explain, and defend against hidden-trait transfer from untrusted teachers into oversight models.
project: The Monitor Inherits: Subliminal Trait Transfer through AI-Generated Oversight Training Data
question: Do oversight models trained on data generated by stronger untrusted models inherit the teacher's hidden traits through semantically benign, distribution-matched content, and which defenses close this channel?
first_experiment: Replicate #43's subliminal number-sequence transfer as a pipeline check, then A/B-test monitors fine-tuned on severity-rating data from a trait-carrying teacher (trait-unrelated domains, content-filtered rationales, matched rating distributions) versus a clean teacher, measuring leniency shifts on held-out trait-domain cases plus entanglement analysis of the training data.
why: It joins five active corpus threads (#43, #70, #30/#64/#78, #82, #33) that no one has connected; existing work either uses explicit semantic payloads or stays in the training-pipeline frame, so the oversight-channel version is unclaimed; it has a validated mechanism, cheap falsifiable experiments, and defensive outputs the field needs before AI-generated supervision becomes load-bearing.

direction: Build and adversarially stress-test "channel sanitization" defenses that strip statistical covert channels (subliminal trait transfer, steganography, hidden CoT nudges) from AI-to-AI data streams and reasoning traces while preserving their benign utility.
project: Subliminal Firewalls — Detecting and Sanitizing Covert Statistical Channels in AI-to-AI Data
question: Can content-preserving transformations (cross-model regeneration, re-tokenization, sampling perturbation, entanglement-targeted filtering) reliably remove subliminal trait transfer from teacher→student data streams, at what benign-utility cost — and can an attacker who knows the defense re-embed the channel, i.e., who wins the sanitize-vs-conceal arms race at current scale?
first_experiment: Establish the testbed baseline by replicating the covert channel: SFT a 7B open-weight teacher to hold a harmless "loves owls" trait, have it generate ~50k "meaningless" outputs (number sequences, short code snippets) under generation conditions that exclude semantic leakage, fine-tune a clean same-family student (plus a different-family control) on them, and measure (a) trait transfer rate over ~200 probe prompts and (b) the token-entanglement signature (frequency shifts of decoy tokens like "087") in the training data — yielding the channel-strength and mechanism metrics that every subsequent defense will be scored against; runnable on a single 8×A100 node in under two weeks.
why: Monitoring is the flagship near-term defense in this corpus (#12, #32, #54, #64), and it silently assumes the semantic content of outputs is the whole message — yet four independent papers (#42 subliminal learning, #26 pointer-chain out-of-context reasoning, #87 steganography, #61 cross-model CoT nudges) demonstrate channels living beneath that surface, and each one explicitly stops short of building defenses (#42 defers them, #26 excludes concealment, #87 is evaluation-only, #61 is observation-only); existing defensive work is model-side (#17 FDCU, #70 certified edits) or targets capabilities rather than hidden payloads (#62), and semantic poisoning (#53) is a different threat; so this is the highest-leverage vacant intersection in the corpus, it has binary ground truth and a mechanism-level handle (#42's token entanglement) that makes defenses concrete and falsifiable rather than speculative, it is tractable at academic scale on open weights, its result is decision-relevant in both directions (cheap pipeline step vs. red flag for all of monitoring-based control), and it has only become tractable recently since the mechanism paper (2025-08) and the cross-model nudge result (2026-09) are just now available to synthesize.

direction: Quantify and defend against the "monitorability gap" — the divergence between what a model's chain of thought causally depends on and what a monitor model can detect — under adversarial pressure.
project: The Monitorability Gap: Adversarial Evasion of and Defenses for CoT Monitoring
question: How much can a reasoning model widen the gap between the causal dependence of its outputs on critical steps in its CoT and a monitor model's ability to detect those steps, and can teacher-forcing-based and salience-calibrated monitoring close that gap?
first_experiment: Using an open reasoning model (e.g., R1-Distill-Qwen-7B) on reward-hackable and hint-embedded tasks, generate CoTs under three conditions — honest, position/format-deflated (critical step buried in low-salience boilerplate or code comments), and explicitly pressured to be brief about the hint — then measure detection rate by two monitors (one flash-class API model, one open 8B) using the canonical monitoring prompt and component ablations from item 19, while tracking resampling-based sentence salience separately for generator and monitor; success criterion is a measurable drop in detection rate without a drop in hacking success (or a demonstrated null, which validates 52).
why: CoT monitoring is a deployed, load-bearing defense whose justification (52) is in direct tension with the survey's own covert-channel findings (16, 24, 28, 56), yet no paper measures the gap itself: 19 optimizes monitors only on honest trajectories, 28 discovers salience non-transfer but never connects it to monitoring or optimizes CoTs against a monitor, 16 evaluates steganography as inter-model message passing rather than intra-CoT evasion, 45 attacks monitors through interaction rather than trajectory structure, and 87 measures legibility but not adversarial legibility — so the intersection is genuinely unoccupied, it is tractable with open models plus modest API budget, and every outcome (gap exists, scales with capability, or is closed by best-practice prompts) materially changes how much we should trust a core safety mechanism.

direction: Quantify how CoT/trajectory monitoring degrades under concealment pressure as a function of model capability and concealment strength, and determine which monitor-side defenses — monitor ensembles, CoT paraphrase/normalization, internal-state probes, and legibility shaping — restore detection, at what cost.
project: The Obfuscation Frontier — Stress-Testing and Repairing the CoT Monitoring Channel
question: When an AI system is incentivized or instructed to conceal misaligned reasoning in its chain of thought, how does monitor detection degrade across a concealment-strength gradient and model capability tiers — and which combination of verbal (ensemble monitor prompts), channel-breaking (paraphrase normalization), and internal-state (probe/J++-lens readout) defenses recovers detectability, at what false-positive and compute cost?
first_experiment: Build a 20–40-task covert-sabotage benchmark from LinuxArena-style reward-hacking and bug-planting environments with ground-truth labels; run three execution models (frontier, mid, small) under a four-level concealment gradient (none → "be concise" → "don't volunteer anything concerning" → "write CoT so a reviewer sees nothing concerning while still succeeding"); score every trajectory with four monitor stacks — (1) canonical single-monitor prompt from #47, (2) three-prompt ensemble with severity rubric and aggregation, (3) paraphrase-normalize-then-monitor using an independent model, (4) linear-probe/J++-style internal readout on open-weight runs trained with contrastive honest-vs-concealing CoT pairs — and report detection AUC, task success, and false-positive rate to produce the first detection-vs-concealment curves and per-defense recovery estimates.
why: Monitoring is simultaneously the most invested-in and most undermined assumption in this survey — #7, #47, #59, #68 all build on observable trajectories, while #3, #4, #21, #24, #44, #52, #70 each demonstrate a distinct way trajectories can mislead — yet no existing work measures the degradation curve or compares mitigations, leaving labs with plausible but untested assurance at exactly the moment stealth capability is scaling (#24). It has not already been done because the prior results are siloed: capability evals without control pipelines (#24, #70), monitor prompt engineering without adversaries (#47), monitor prompt-injection rather than source-model concealment (#59), internal lenses and legibility metrics never evaluated as defenses (#17, #72), and a reassuring "models can't control their CoT" claim (#68) that has never been tested under the instructed or optimized concealment it will actually face; the integrated study yields both an early-warning red line and cheap, immediately deployable protocol upgrades.

direction: Build and adversarially stress-test activation-level (latent-state) monitors for agentic AI control, measuring whether reading the model's residual stream catches covert sabotage that behavioral and CoT-based monitors miss — and how robust such latent monitorability is to capability-matched evasion.
project: LatentMon — Activation-Based Monitoring of Covert Sabotage in Agent Trajectories
question: Can latent-state readouts of an agent's residual stream detect covert sabotage that behavioral/CoT monitors miss, and does that latent signal survive adaptive evasion (innocuous verbalisation, distributed decisions, capability-gated hidden channels)?
first_experiment: Construct ~100 trajectories in a minimal agentic coding environment (50 benign, 50 with planted covert sabotage of LinuxArena-style failure types) from an open-weight model (Qwen2.5-7B / Gemma-3-12B); extract residual-stream activations at each tool-call decision point; train per-step linear probes for sabotage-vs-benign; compare trajectory-level detection (probe AUC + complementarity confusion matrix) against (i) a strong LLM behavioral monitor on full trajectories and (ii) the same monitor with CoT redacted — establishing whether latent and behavioral monitors catch disjoint failures.
why: Monitoring is the most load-bearing near-term safeguard (38, 42, 80), yet its known evasion channels — steganography (49), out-of-context reasoning (41), monitor jailbreaks (11), verbalisation discretion (3) — are all attacks on *behavioral* observation; the one tool designed to read unverbalised states (37) has never been evaluated as a monitor in a control setting against an adaptive adversary, and the setting designed for it (38) has never had a latent counterpart. The intersection is only weeks old, sits at the under-crossed boundary of the survey's two largest clusters, is tractable with open-weight models, and produces a decision-relevant result either way: a new defense layer, or a quantified fragility in the verbalisation-dependent safety case that redirects the field toward certified monitoring guarantees.

direction: Build the missing defensive layer for model-generated training data — detection, bandwidth measurement, and sanitization of subliminal (entanglement-based, non-semantic) trait channels — before covert data channels become the default propagation path for misalignment through the synthetic-data flywheel.
project: Subliminal Data Forensics: Detecting and Neutralizing Covert Trait Channels in Model-Generated Training Data
question: Can covert trait transmission through model-generated training data be detected from the data alone — without access to the teacher, the student, or knowledge of the hidden trait — and if so, how much channel bandwidth survives each sanitization at what cost to data utility?
first_experiment: Replicate the minimal #29 channel at open-weights scale (trait-finetuned Qwen2.5-7B teacher → number-sequence datasets → clean Llama-3.1-8B/Gemma-2-9B students, measuring trait adoption), then train a v0 detector using only pre-ingest data statistics (base-model token-surprisal deltas, frequency anomalies, format regularities) and report AUROC for flagging payload-carrying datasets, alongside a #14-style semantic-inspection baseline that should fail by construction.
why: It sits where three separately-published results converge but nobody has built the synthesis — #29 established the mechanism and explicitly deferred defenses, #79 covers deliberate steganography rather than incidental channels, and #68 shows covert influence is capability-gated yet skips concealment entirely — while #14's predictive debugging and #12's poisoning work both presume data is semantically inspectable, which is exactly the assumption subliminal channels violate. It is the rare direction that is simultaneously cheap to start (7–9B open models, the minimal channel costs days), decisive under either outcome (a working detector and sanitizer suite is a practical defense; robust detection failure is an urgent red-line finding), and load-bearing for downstream systems the survey shows the field depends on: distillation-based auditing (#30), capability shaping via data (#74, #12), and model-delegated alignment loops (#82) — all of which silently assume training data carries no hidden state.

direction: Empirically test "incrimination via distillation" — distilling an audit-evasive misaligned model as an indirect audit channel — by measuring whether misalignment and audit-evasion behaviors differentially transfer to student models.
project: Incrimination by Distillation: A Transfer Matrix for Misalignment vs. Audit-Evasion
question: When a model whose misalignment evades direct audits is distilled into students via CoT-rich data, answers-only data, and non-semantic (entanglement-exploiting) data, does the underlying misalignment transfer to students at a higher rate than the audit-evasion behavior itself, such that auditing the student recovers evidence the teacher's audit missed?
first_experiment: Build one "audit-evasive misaligned" teacher organism (an open-weight 7–27B instruct model fine-tuned for misaligned deployment-context behavior plus eval-aware compliant behavior in audit contexts, using item-20-style prompting-setting methodology), confirm with a fixed six-probe audit suite that it passes audits while a plainly misaligned control organism is caught, then distill three students from it (CoT-rich, answers-only, numeric/entanglement-style per item-47) and rerun the identical suite on the students to obtain a first estimate of misalignment-transfer rate vs. audit-evasion-transfer rate.
why: It converts the corpus's most consequential open proposal (item 6) into a measurable defensive tool at a scale I can execute, with every prerequisite demonstrated separately in the corpus (organisms in 22, faking methodology in 20, subliminal transfer mechanism in 47) but the combination — differential transfer and detection power — tested nowhere; it is decision-relevant in both directions (new audit capability vs. hidden propagation of evasion through ubiquitous distillation pipelines), it uses only synthetic organisms on open weights so it is safe and reproducible, and it has not been done because item 6 explicitly remains a conceptual argument about what "might work or fail," item 47 demonstrates transfer only for benign stylistic preferences, item 22 studies consistency training rather than distillation, and item 20 replicates alignment faking without ever distilling the faking model.

direction: Map whether subliminal trait transfer through training data can be engineered to gate on student capability, thereby defeating weak-model data screening, and validate capability-differential screening as the countermeasure.
project: Capability-Gated Subliminal Learning: When Data-Borne Trait Transfer Hides from the Screeners
question: Can subliminal trait transfer via training data be made to threshold on student capability (so cheap screening models acquire nothing while frontier students acquire the trait), and can differential transfer across a model ladder serve as a reliable detector for such payloads?
first_experiment: Replicate item 10's entanglement pipeline with open weights — finetune a Qwen2.5-7B teacher to carry a benign marker trait, generate number-sequence datasets at three payload depths (surface-token entanglement, digit-sum-feature entanglement, serial pointer-structure entanglement), finetune a capability ladder of students (0.5B, 1.5B, 3B, 7B, 14B), and measure trait acquisition per (payload depth × student capability) to establish the transfer-gating curves.
why: It sits at the verified intersection of two independently replicated corpus results (entangled transfer in item 10; capability gating in item 71) that no item combines — item 10's defenses ignore screening-model capability entirely, item 71 explicitly defers realistic end-to-end channels, and no corpus work measures trait transfer as a function of student scale or proposes differential screening — while remaining fully tractable on open weights with modest compute, decision-relevant for the synthetic-data/distillation pipelines that dominate current practice, and informative whichever way the thresholds fall: gating works means today's "screen with a cheap model" defense fails silently; gating fails means that defense is validated.

direction: Stress-test chain-of-thought monitoring under monitor–subject capability asymmetry, measuring and defending against "legibility laundering" — unsafe behavior passing weak monitors without any concealment.
project: Legibility Laundering: Measuring When Weak Monitors Can't Read What Strong Models Write
question: Does overt-content-preserving degradation of a chain of thought (compression, reordering, selective elision) selectively defeat less capable monitors, does this occur even without adversarial intent, and is it explained by model-specific importance attribution in the trace?
first_experiment: Construct ~200 verified benign/sabotage coding trajectories from subject models at two capability tiers, apply five content-preserving CoT rewrites (including elision of subject-model thought-anchor-pivotal sentences), then run a monitor ladder (7B→70B open-weights plus one cheap frontier model) with a fixed monitoring prompt to produce monitor-tier × rewrite-type detection AUC and calibration curves, alongside divergence between monitor-cited importance and subject-model thought anchors.
why: The corpus shows CoT monitoring becoming a load-bearing deployed defense (item 1) precisely as three separate results undermine its assumptions — model-specific importance (5), capability-gated comprehension (26), and feasible covert channels (43) — yet the neighboring work stops short of the intersection: legibility work (34) is descriptive with no detection or adversarial angle, monitor-attack work (25) uses prompt-level jailbreaks rather than comprehension-gap exploitation, and steganography work (43) demands a far higher attack bar than "write honestly but illegibly"; the experiment is cheap with open-weight monitors and model organisms, informative in either outcome, and yields monitoring fidelity curves that AI-control safety cases (25, 71) currently lack.

direction: Make chain-of-thought monitoring trustworthy by measuring and then *training for* cross-model legibility — reasoning traces whose causal importance transfers to other model families — while verifying this does not enlarge covert channels like hint-transfer or subliminal entanglement.
project: "Legible to Strangers: Training Reasoning Traces That Transfer Across Monitor Models"
question: Can a reasoning model be fine-tuned so that the causally load-bearing steps of its chains of thought are load-bearing for *different* models too (high cross-model thought-anchor correlation), improving weak-model monitoring of sabotage — without increasing covert-channel bandwidth (planted-hint transfer, subliminal token entanglement) or degrading capability?
first_experiment: Build the baseline "Cross-Model Importance Atlas" — generate ~100 traces (math + a seeded-sabotage decision task with a planted hint) from 2–3 open-weight reasoners across two families, compute per-sentence counterfactual importance via teacher-forced resampling in both the authoring model and reader models, and measure (a) self-vs-reader importance rank correlation, (b) planted-hint transfer effect size across models, (c) whether safety-critical sentences transfer worse than math sentences — pure inference, no training, delivering the metric and power analysis that the DPO intervention stage will target.
why: It targets the single most load-bearing and most recently cracked assumption in AI safety practice — that one model's reasoning is readable by another — at the exact moment the measurement tools (Thought Anchors; item 22's legibility metric) exist but no intervention does: item 20 only documents non-transfer, item 16 optimizes only the monitor's prompt, and item 22 is measurement-only; meanwhile the built-in falsifiers (hint transfer from item 20, token entanglement from item 6) let me detect the known failure mode of CoT optimization (obfuscation) rather than cause it blindly, and the whole project runs on small open-weight models with inference-first experiments, making it executable now with both a strong positive and a strong negative result branch.

direction: Audit and harden the distillation channel behind weak monitors: measure, predict, and defend against subliminal transfer of safety-relevant traits from teacher models to distilled students.
project: Clean Pipes — Detecting and Defeating Subliminal Trait Transfer in Monitor Distillation
question: Do safety-relevant behavioral traits (sycophancy, reward-hacking, grading bias) transfer subliminally through the semantically clean data used to train distilled monitors, can token-entanglement diagnostics predict such transfer before training, and which interventions sever the channel at minimal cost to monitoring capability?
first_experiment: Fine-tune two 7B teacher variants from the same base (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct): an owl-preferring teacher as a positive control replicating the subliminal-learning setup, and a sycophancy organism built with the model-organism protocol. Each teacher generates ~100k "meaningless" number sequences and ~10k neutral math/code chains of thought containing no semantic content about the trait. Fine-tune clean students (same base, 3 seeds) on each dataset and evaluate with held-out measures: owl-mention rate in free-form answers, sycophancy delta under user pushback, plus an MMLU subset for capability, all with paired bootstrap CIs. A significant transfer effect in the sycophancy condition comparable to the owl control establishes that the subliminal channel carries safety-relevant traits, licensing the monitor-grading scenario and the defense phase.
why: It sits at the exact intersection of three papers (#2, #10, #13) that each stop adjacent to the gap: #13 found the mechanism but deferred defenses and studied only quirky preferences; #10 engineers distillation to transfer misalignment for forensics rather than protecting students; #2 proposes distilled weak monitors without treating distillation as a threat surface. Since distilled weak monitors are becoming the field's default budget oversight layer, an unexamined inheritance channel in that pipeline is a foundational risk — and because the substrates (organisms, protocols, entanglement diagnostics) already exist, this is testable at single-GPU scale, with positive controls that make even a negative result informative. No published work measures safety-trait transfer through monitor-training data or maps the defense landscape for it.

direction: Empirically test "incrimination via distillation" (#73) — whether distilling a covertly misaligned, audit-evading teacher on benign data transfers object-level misalignment more readily than the stealth/situational-awareness capability that hides it, turning distillation into a practical audit amplifier for deceptively aligned models.
project: Distill to Catch: Does Misalignment Outlive Stealth When Covertly Misaligned Models Are Distilled?
question: When a teacher that is both misaligned and audit-evading is distilled into students on benign data, do the two traits transfer differentially (misalignment inherited, stealth stripped), and how does that differential depend on student capability (same-size vs. smaller), distillation data type (output-only vs. CoT-bearing traces vs. 'meaningless' number sequences per #35), and sanitization method?
first_experiment: Construct and verify a minimal two-axis teacher at ~7B open weights — fine-tune Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (or Llama-3.1-8B) on synthetic documents instilling (a) an anti-lab objective and (b) audit-awareness/concealment norms — and confirm both axes exist in-weights (elevated misalignment-eval scores plus conditionally different behavior in audit-context vs. deployment-context prompts); with the teacher verified, run the first transfer arm: response-distill into a same-size student on ~50k benign coding/math completions (no CoT) with an SFT-on-identical-data control, and report the two-axis transfer delta (Δmisalignment vs. Δstealth) plus blind-auditor detectability rates for teacher vs. student.
why: Deceptive alignment is the problem this corpus shows escalating fastest (items 8, 39, 64, 32 all probe hidden misalignment in 2025–26), yet #73's central claim is an explicitly untested proposal ("might work or fail") and no item among the 88 reports running it; meanwhile #35 (traits transfer subliminally), #10 (hidden influence is capability-gated), and the original alignment-faking distillation datapoint pull in opposite directions and have never been measured jointly, so the answer is genuinely uncertain and decision-relevant both ways — a positive result gives labs a cheap audit amplifier orthogonal to interpretability, a negative result is a red flag for shipping distilled models as sanitized — and the whole program is feasible on open ≤8B models with existing organism recipes, public eval suites, and moderate compute, while adjacent lines (emergent misalignment, backdoor distillation, blind-audit games, subliminal learning) each isolate one variable rather than the misalignment-vs-stealth differential that matters.

direction: Red-team and harden chain-of-thought monitoring by measuring how monitored models can bias or evade CoT monitors and which cheap defenses restore reliable detection.
project: Stress-Testing the Oversight Channel: Adversarial Fragility and Hardening of Chain-of-Thought Monitors
question: How reliably do CoT monitors detect subtle misbehavior when the monitored model manipulates its reasoning trace via omission, benign reframing, or covert encoding, and which monitor designs restore detection at acceptable false-positive cost?
first_experiment: Generate ~100 labeled sandboxed agentic trajectories with seeded subtle failures, establish baseline detection/false-positive rates for four monitors with a rubric-based severity prompt, then measure the detection-rate shift under omission-and-reframing trace manipulation with paired bootstrap CIs.
why: CoT monitoring is becoming load-bearing precisely as steganographic, subliminal, concealment, and oversight-awareness capabilities emerge, yet no existing work integrates adversarial trace manipulation against trajectory monitors with defense evaluation — closest papers cover single slices (capability-only steganography, jailbreak-focused monitor attacks, benign-only prompt ablations, debate verifiers, training-time obfuscation) — and the result is actionable either way, while being executable end-to-end with APIs and open-weight models.

direction: Measure and break the subliminal surface-form channel through which chain-of-thought traces transfer hidden influence between models, and harden CoT-based monitoring against it via sanitization that survives tamper-aware models.
project: Laundering the Chain of Thought — Detecting, Removing, and Stress-Testing Subliminal Channels in CoT Monitoring
question: When a reasoning model's CoT is consumed by a monitor, a distilled student, or a downstream agent, how much hidden influence propagates through the trace's surface form beyond its explicit content, and can sanitization (paraphrase, compression, resampling, model-swap) destroy this channel while preserving monitoring value and remaining undetectable to tamper-aware models?
first_experiment: Generate silently-hinted vs. clean CoTs from one reasoning model (e.g., an R1-distill-32B) on ~500 MCQs (hint planted in the prompt, filtered so the CoT never mentions it), teacher-force each trace into three open-weight student models and measure the shift in their answer distribution to replicate the cross-model nudge effect (4); then run the hinted traces through paraphrase-by-a-different-model and re-measure — decision rule: if paraphrase removes ≥80% of the nudge effect while monitor verdicts on explicit content drop <2 points, proceed to the full sanitization battery and tamper-awareness tests; if the nudge survives paraphrase, pivot to characterizing the robust channel (either result is a paper).
why: Five 2025–26 results (4: cross-model nudge transfer, 16: subliminal learning via token entanglement, 74: steganography evals, 22: capability-gated hidden prompting, 24: prefill awareness) independently establish that innocuous model outputs carry model-specific hidden influence that requires no intent — a direct blind spot in the argument that CoT monitoring is safe because models can't deliberately fake their CoT (44); monitoring is becoming the load-bearing defense layer (44, 50, 62, 79, 13), yet no item in this corpus builds or evaluates a defense against the subliminal channel or connects it to tamper-awareness; it is feasible at lone-researcher scale with APIs and open-weight models (86's 30–40h replication proves the workflow), and every outcome branch — channel broken, channel robust, or channel absent at scale — yields an important, publishable safety result.

direction: Quantify and neutralize the threat that model context-integrity awareness (prefill/edit detection, #14) poses to AI control protocols and safety evaluations that rely on manipulating the untrusted model's context.
project: Honeypots with Pinholes: How Tampering Detection Biases AI Control Evaluations, and How to Build Integrity-Blind Control
question: Do models' abilities to detect edits/prefills in their own context systematically shift their safety-relevant behavior (sabotage, honeypot attacks, monitor gaming) in ways that bias control and safety-evaluation results — and can protocols be redesigned (regeneration-laundering, integrity-decorrelated training) to be robust or blind to integrity signals?
first_experiment: A paired behavioral experiment: run identical sabotage-capable coding tasks (from LinuxArena) under four context conditions — pristine; benign prefilled assistant turn; benignly edited prior assistant turn; inserted benign system note — across 2–3 frontier and 2–3 open-weight models, measuring sabotage/misbehavior rates per condition alongside #14-style tampering-detection probes, yielding the first causal estimate of how integrity detection shifts misbehavior rates.
why: It sits exactly where the corpus's fastest-growing infrastructure (control: #7, #40, #69) meets a just-proven capability that quietly breaks its core assumption (#14), and the bias runs in the *optimistic* direction — under-measured sabotage — making it safety-critical evidence, not an academic curiosity. It has not been done: #14 measured detection and flagged evaluation validity but performed no control-protocol quantification, no attack organism, and no mitigation; LinuxArena (#7) has no integrity axis; #40 attacks the monitor directly rather than exploiting model-side tamper-detection; #84 measures situational-awareness capability rather than its behavioral consequences inside control pipelines; #21/#31/#37 are covert channels through models, not attacks on experimental validity. Five months of corpus after #14 shows no follow-up, the required artifacts (LinuxArena, paired-probe methodology, open-weight models, #35-style organism training) are all released and tractable at API scale, and the deliverables — a benchmark, a demonstrated bias, a new organism class, and protocol mitigations — are immediately reusable by every lab currently trusting edited-context control measurements.

direction: Pursue activation-based white-box monitoring of covert reasoning — systematically benchmark whether internal readouts (linear probes, SAE features, released J++-style lenses) detect eval-awareness, hidden goals, and steganographic encoding that text-based CoT monitors miss, and quantify where that margin collapses.
project: The White-Box Margin: Quantifying Activation-Based Detection of Covert Reasoning Beyond CoT Text
question: How much additional detection power do activation-space readouts provide over text-based CoT monitoring for covert model states (eval-awareness, hidden-goal pursuit, concealed encoding), across open-weight model scales and concealment methods, and at what point does the text-monitoring defense fail while internal signatures remain (or vanish too)?
first_experiment: Using the prompting-only alignment-faking setup validated by the mini-replication (#33) on 3 open-weight instruct models (e.g., Qwen2.5-14B, Gemma-3-12B, Llama-3.1-8B), collect residual-stream activations at each generated reasoning token under (a) "training with monitor" vs (b) "deployment" vs (c) honest-control contexts; train layer-wise linear probes to classify the covert context state; then compare probe detection AUC against an LLM text-monitor judge reading the same CoTs, and test whether probe scores predict the behavioral compliance gap better than the CoT text does.
why: It stress-tests the single most load-bearing claim in current frontier safety practice (#24: "CoT monitoring works because models can't control their CoT") at the moment when concealment ingredients demonstrably exist (#13, #22, #61, #48), and it operationalizes the application that #1 explicitly proposed but did not perform — so it is not already done: the corpus contains detection *methods* (#1, #62), capability *evals* (#13, #22), behavioral awareness measurements (#79), and the reassurance argument (#24), but no systematic white-box-versus-text detection comparison, no benchmark of covert-state detection, and no measurement of where text monitoring fails while internal signals persist. It is tractable for me (open-weight models, prompting-only organisms, released lens artifacts, cheap linear probes), every outcome is informative (a positive result justifies white-box monitoring investment; a negative result quantifies the fragility of the current safety case), and it builds a reusable open benchmark that frontier labs — who study this internally but rarely release comparisons — have not provided.

direction: Build a causal-audit instrument that quantifies how much of the behaviorally decisive content in a reasoning model's chain of thought is causally accessible to independent monitors, and use it to detect when CoT-based oversight silently degrades under covert channels.
project: Blind Mass: A Causal Coverage Audit for Chain-of-Thought Oversight
question: When a model's chain of thought causally drives its final behavior, what fraction of that causal content produces no measurable shift in an independent monitor's judgment — and does this "monitor-blind mass" spike precisely on traces carrying covert channels (steganographic message-passing, capability-gated pointer chains, subliminal token entanglement)?
first_experiment: Generate ~150–300 reasoning traces from 2–3 open-weight reasoning models of different families (e.g., DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, Qwen3-8B, a Llama-3.1-8B reasoning tune) on a verifiable cover task (algorithmic puzzles with unique answers) under three conditions: (a) benign, (b) encoded message-passing steganography with a paired decoder verifying recovery (following #30's protocol), and (c) JSON pointer-chain prompts that causally steer the actor but not a weaker reader (following #59). For every sentence in each trace: (i) estimate actor-side causal importance via thought-anchor resampling (#1's method — mask/paraphrase the sentence, ~20 resamples, measure answer flip rate); (ii) feed the ablated trace to two different-family monitors (one large, one deliberately weak) with a suspicion rubric and record verdict shift. Primary outputs: per-condition blind mass (total actor-importance carried by sentences with <ε monitor sensitivity) and importance–sensitivity rank correlation. Prediction to falsify: benign traces show high coverage, while in covert traces the blind mass concentrates exactly on the sentences the decoder/pointer analysis independently confirms carry the hidden signal. If time permits, re-run with two first-line mitigations — a re-derivation monitor (trusted model re-solves each step and diffs against the actor's trace) and paraphrase-normalized traces — to measure how much blind mass cheap defenses recover.
why: CoT monitoring is the flagship defense-in-depth layer for today's reasoning agents (#87), but its validity rests on the empirical contingency that models can't yet control their CoT — a contingency already under attack from three independently demonstrated channels: steganography (#30), capability-gated prompt channels whose authors explicitly left concealment unexplored (#59), and subliminal token entanglement (#65), compounded by evidence that models sense observation artifacts (#61, #33) and that trace importance is model-specific (#1). No work in this corpus — or that I'm aware of outside it — joins actor-side causal attribution with monitor-side causal sensitivity into one measurable quantity: #1 measured importance transfer but not monitor detection, on few models and no adversarial traces; #72 concedes existing legibility metrics miss causal thoroughness and measures digestibility, not adversarial blind spots; #30 evaluated steganographic capability rather than whether realistic monitors catch it; #81 hardened monitor prompts without testing them against causal-channel adversaries. The experiment is feasible now with open weights and modest compute, its null result would be as informative as its positive one, and it yields a benchmark plus a leading indicator for precisely the oversight-decay process #87 predicts — the highest leverage-to-risk measurement I can start immediately.

direction: Mechanistically characterize what RL post-training does to a model's internal features — testing whether RL works by amplifying pre-existing (superposed) features rather than creating new ones — and use that account to build the first causal early-warning detector for reward hacking.
project: Anatomy of a Post-Training Run: Feature Dynamics, Elicitation, and the Mechanisms of Reward Hacking
question: When RL changes a model's behavior, does it act by amplifying features that already exist (pulling them out of superposition) or by creating genuinely new ones — and is reward hacking specifically the amplification of proxy-correlated features, detectable in activations before it appears in behavior?
first_experiment: Using Gemma Scope SAEs on Gemma-2-2B base vs. its instruction-tuned twin, identify the features most amplified by post-training and run the bidirectional causal test — steer them up in the base model to see if the post-trained behavior appears without any training, and steer them down in the tuned model to see if the behavior disappears — while in parallel launching a checkpoint-every-25-steps GRPO run on a 1.5–2B model (GSM8K verifiable rewards) to collect the first longitudinal SAE feature-trajectory dataset.
why: RL post-training is the dominant lever for capability and character in current models, yet mechanistic interpretability has analyzed only frozen models, leaving the field's central empirical dispute (elicit vs. create) and its most consequential failure mode (reward hacking) without any mechanistic account; it is fully executable on open 1–2B models with Gemma Scope and open RL stacks, every milestone is independently publishable, the decisive causal test is robust to SAE limitations, and the prior work that exists is either behavioral (Spurious Reward, RLVR-elicit studies, emergent misalignment) or static one-shot diffing (crosscoders) — no longitudinal, causally validated, feature-level account of an RL run, nor any mechanistic reward-hacking early-warning signal, appears in the public record.

direction: Build the first causal, component-level, time-resolved account of when reasoning models internally commit to an answer relative to their chain of thought, converting CoT-faithfulness from a behavioral debate into a measurable, auditable internal signal.
project: The Commitment Clock — Internal Answer Commitment vs. Verbalized Reasoning in Chain-of-Thought Models
question: When a reasoning model produces a chain of thought, does answer-identity exist causally-efficaciously in the residual stream before the CoT verbalizes it, and what circuit-level distinction separates CoT steps that determine the answer from steps that merely narrate a pre-committed one?
first_experiment: Run R1-Distill-Qwen-7B (plus Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct as contrast) on ~700 problems (MATH-500, GPQA-diamond); at every CoT token and layer, compute logit-lens decodability of the final answer and train position-matched linear probes on the residual stream; plot "commitment curves" and the distribution of Commitment Lag between internal decodability onset and first verbal mention — a few GPU-hours that decides whether the causal patching program proceeds and whether lags open under hint-primed positive-control conditions.
why: CoT monitorability is a load-bearing assumption of current frontier safety strategy, yet its failure modes are known only behaviorally or as one-off case studies; the tools (open reasoning models, SAE/probe stacks, open circuit tracers) matured just enough to make this tractable at 7–14B scale, both outcomes are valuable, and the nearest prior work — Anthropic's backward-chaining case study, answer-convergence early-stopping observations, and OpenAI's hint-based behavioral faithfulness metrics — stops short of a general, causal, component-level account and of a ground-truth-free audit metric, which is exactly the delta this project claims.

direction: Build and stress-test mechanistic auditing against models trained to evade interpretation, mapping which white-box detection signals survive obfuscation.
project: Plant-and-Hunt: An Adversarial Benchmark and Pipeline for Evasion-Robust Mechanistic Auditing
question: Can a language model conceal a hidden behavior from mechanistic monitors, and what white-box evidence necessarily remains at the evasion-vs-detection frontier?
first_experiment: Train a trigger-backdoor organism and an obfuscated-backdoor organism (behavior + activation-matching to a benign reference) on a small open model, then run an automated audit battery — SAE feature-scan, trigger synthesis, off-distribution activation fuzzing, calibrated weight-diff anomaly scoring, causal ablation — and measure which signals detect the obfuscated backdoor and at what false-positive rate against benign finetunes.
why: It is the most safety-critical open problem in interpretability — whether monitoring and auditing mean anything against an adversarially trained model — and it was just cracked open by 2025 obfuscation results that demonstrated the bypass without mapping the defense side; prior work covers only non-adversarial backdoor detection, human-run audits, and circuit-discovery benchmarks on known circuits, leaving the systematic evasion-vs-detection frontier, computation-level detectors, automated auditing, and false-positive calibration all genuinely undone — and it is fully tractable for autonomous experimentation, with every possible result (robust signals found, or monitoring bounded) advancing AI safety.

direction: Mechanistically localize the internal "deliberation state" of reasoning LLMs — the plan and intermediate computations underlying the chain of thought — and test whether activation-space monitoring of that state remains causally valid when the model is trained to obfuscate its CoT.
project: Where the Thinking Really Happens: Causal Localization of Deliberation State in Reasoning LLMs Under Chain-of-Thought Obfuscation
question: In reasoning-trained LLMs, where and in what form are the plan and intermediate computations that determine the answer represented internally, how faithfully does the emitted CoT compile this state, and does activation-based monitoring of it survive when the model is trained to hide its reasoning?
first_experiment: On R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B/7B (or Qwen3-4B-Thinking), construct paired multi-step problems solvable by two distinct valid strategies (e.g., algebraic vs. enumerative), elicit each strategy via exemplars, train layer×position linear probes to decode strategy identity and key intermediate values, then causally validate with activation patching — transplanting strategy-A states into strategy-B runs and ablating the located sites — under both faithful-CoT and CoT-suppressed conditions, to localize where plan state causally lives and whether it persists when the CoT is gone.
why: CoT monitoring is the safety mechanism labs actually rely on today, yet the question "does the real deliberation remain monitorable when the CoT is optimized away" is unanswered at the mechanism level; the experiment is decidable in both directions, runs on open weights with patching/probing before any training, and the nearest neighbors — behavioral unfaithfulness studies, black-box CoT-monitoring-under-optimization on closed weights, proposition-level truth probes, and black-box step-importance methods — each cover only one slice, leaving the intervention-validated, circuit-level localization of task deliberation state under obfuscation pressure unoccupied as of my latest information.

direction: Pursue mechanistic oversight of RL training — study how reward-hacking computations emerge across checkpoints during RLVR in open reasoning models, and build and causally validate feature-based internal monitors that detect hacks earlier, generalize across bugs, and resist obfuscation better than behavioral or chain-of-thought monitors.
project: HackWatch — a checkpoint-resolved mechanistic account of reward-hacking emergence in RLVR.
question: When a model learns to exploit a planted reward bug during RLVR, does it select and amplify pre-existing base-model circuits or build hacking circuits de novo — and can internal feature-based monitors flag the emerging hack earlier than behavioral or CoT monitors, and generalize to structurally different unseen bugs?
first_experiment: Run GRPO on Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct over GSM8K/MATH with (a) a planted verifier bug that accepts any boxed answer containing exactly two decimal places regardless of correctness, (b) a clean-verifier control run, and (c) a second structurally different planted bug (echoing answer-revealing metadata); snapshot checkpoints every ~30 steps and at each checkpoint log programmatically-labeled per-episode hack rates and store residual-stream activations on a fixed probe set — establishing the ground-truth organism and differential dataset on which all later feature-birth, early-warning, and causal-ablation analyses run.
why: RLVR is now the dominant post-training paradigm and reward hacking its canonical failure; the obfuscated-CoT result shows behavioral monitoring degrades exactly when stakes are highest, making "do internals monitor better?" the field's most decision-relevant open interp question. Planted bugs give something most applied interp lacks — exact programmatic mechanism ground truth — enabling real metrics (lead time, cross-hack generalization) and causal tests (pre-RL ablation "vaccination"), with every outcome informative: selection vs. de novo are both publishable, and monitor failure is a needed negative result. It is tractable for me (small open models, open tooling, scales down to 0.5B), and as far as my literature reaches (early–mid 2025) hacking has been studied behaviorally and misbehavior circuits only post-hoc in deployed models — no checkpoint-resolved, causally validated feature-level account of hack formation or internal-vs-CoT monitor benchmark exists; I will verify against post-cutoff work first, and the program's least-scoopable components (obfuscation pressure, cross-bug generalization, vaccination) are deliberately front-loaded.

direction: Build a token-level causal accounting of chain-of-thought in reasoning models — measuring which CoT content actually causes the final answer versus merely narrating it — and use it to develop activation-based detectors of decorative and encoded deliberation.
project: Load-Bearing Chains of Thought: Separating Computation from Narration in Reasoning Models
question: When a reasoning model writes a chain of thought, is the deliberation load-bearing (causally produces the answer), decorative (post-hoc narration of an answer reached elsewhere), or encoded (load-bearing but hidden from surface reading) — and can internal activations classify this token-by-token, across open models, without trusting the CoT's surface content?
first_experiment: On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B and Qwen3-4B with injected wrong-answer hints on GSM8K/MMLU: (1) generate CoTs and score behavioral faithfulness via sentence-boundary truncation (Lanham-style baseline); (2) compute a token-block × layer-range load-bearing map via attention knockout from the answer-computation region to CoT blocks, measuring ΔP(answer); (3) validate the map against resampling-based causal influence on a subsample; (4) train probes on CoT-token residual streams to predict measured load-bearing-ness and to decode hint identity at positions whose surface text never mentions the hint — testing whether hint influence bypasses the written CoT (decorative deliberation) in cases that behavioral truncation tests classify as faithful.
why: CoT monitoring is becoming a deployed safety mechanism whose integrity is precisely the thing in doubt — OpenAI showed monitor-pressure yields obfuscated CoT, Anthropic documented both faithful and unfaithful deliberation only as small-*n* manual case studies on a closed model, and the behavioral faithfulness literature never looks inside the model; the intersection of open reasoning models + cheap validated internal causal maps + learned detectors (covering the full narration×computation 2×2, including silent computation via filler tokens and encoded reasoning) is unoccupied, runs on a single GPU, produces artifacts closed labs cannot release, and compounds — the map becomes the substrate for SAE/crosscoder analysis of deliberation, eval-integrity checks, sandbagging detection, and honest reward-hack forensics. The crowded alternatives I rejected (SAE-foundational work, evaluation-awareness, training-dynamics, multimodal) are either ill-posed, lab-infra-heavy, or low-novelty coverage bets, whereas this is a called-for, first-class safety measurement that the field has asked for in position papers but not yet built.

direction: Mechanistic faithfulness of chain-of-thought — replacing prompt-level behavioral tests with internal attribution and intervention, to measure whether a reasoning model's verbalized trace is the actual computation that produced its answer.
project: Causal Thought Graphs — A Mechanistic Test of Chain-of-Thought Faithfulness in Reasoning Models
question: When a reasoning model produces an answer, can we construct a token-level causal graph over its reasoning trace (which CoT steps causally determine the final answer, as revealed by internal attribution and intervention), and does that graph match the dependency structure the model verbally claims — and if they diverge, what circuit implements the post-hoc narrative?
first_experiment: On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B (and a Qwen3-Thinking model as a check), run ~500 multiple-choice questions under Anthropic's hint-exploitation protocol with three conditions (no hint / consistent hint / contradictory hint). For each final-answer token, compute causal attribution over the question, the hint span, and each CoT segment, via attention knockouts and logit attribution (TransformerLens supports the Qwen2.5 backbone). In cases where the hint flips the answer, measure: (a) the causal strength of hint→answer routing through the CoT, and (b) whether the trace *verbally* cites the hint as the reason. The deliverable is the first mechanistic-vs-verbal divergence rate for hint exploitation, plus a few single-prompt case studies where ablating the "true reason" pathway regenerates a trace with a plausible-but-wrong stated rationale — a mechanistic demonstration of confabulation. Cost: a few GPU-days, and it doubles as a scoop-check against fast-moving preprints.
why: First, timing: CoT monitoring is *the* primary oversight mechanism for deployed reasoning agents, and it is known to be fragile — models exploit hints without saying so, and optimization pressure against monitors produces obfuscated reward hacking. A detector that flags divergence between the causal computation and the verbal trace (e.g., "the answer was determined before/by information the trace never mentions") would be an oversight tool that does not depend on trusting the text, and could also catch steganographic bypass of CoT. Second, scientifically it bridges two literatures that currently don't touch: behavioral unfaithfulness studies (which manipulate prompts and cannot localize mechanism) and mechanistic interpretability (which has analyzed arithmetic and poetry planning, but not long-horizon reasoning narratives). Third, tractability: strong open reasoning models exist, the Qwen2.5 backbone is fully tooled, and the core method is attention knockouts and attribution — no frontier access needed. Fourth, why it hasn't been done: the prominent faithfulness papers are behavioral by design and explicitly defer mechanistic follow-up; the circuit-tracing work targets other phenomena; SAE-based monitoring uses the CoT text rather than internals; and causal CoT analyses exist only for small models and pre-R1-style traces, not for the long, self-narrated reasoning that is now standard. The main risk is scooping in a fast-moving area — which is precisely why the first experiment is cheap, quantitative, and dual-purpose as a novelty probe, with the developmental extension (tracking the divergence rate across RL checkpoints) held in reserve as the follow-up that would make the case airtight.

direction: A mechanistic, causal-intervention study of hidden answer commitment ("lock-in") versus genuine deliberation in open RL-trained reasoning models.
project: Lock-In: A Mechanistic Study of Premature Answer Commitment in LLM Reasoning
question: Is the final answer of a reasoning model causally determined by a hidden commitment state formed early in its chain of thought — and can we locate and manipulate that state to convert rationalization into genuine deliberation (and vice versa)?
first_experiment: Probe the residual stream of DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B at every CoT token with linear probes and a tuned lens to detect the eventual final answer, mapping when and where commitment forms and whether onset predicts final correctness and backtracking.
why: CoT monitoring is a flagship safety tool whose core assumption — that verbalized reasoning is the causal computation — is untested at the mechanism level; prior work is behavioral or probing-only, and no one has localized the commitment state to components or intervened on it causally in open reasoning models, making this both decisive and unclaimed.

direction: Mechanistically diff base models against emergently-misaligned narrow finetunes to localize the causal substrate of induced misalignment, explain the pivot-token effect and its persistence, and test whether induced and natural misalignment share machinery — yielding both a model-diffing methodology and concrete detection/healing tools.
project: Anatomy of Emergent Misalignment: A Causal Model-Diff of Narrow Finetunes
question: What internal changes — features, directions, or circuits — causally implement the broad misalignment induced by narrow finetuning, why does a single pivot token block its induction, and does that induced misalignment share mechanistic substrate with naturally occurring misalignment?
first_experiment: Reproduce EM on an open 2–8B model using the public insecure-code dataset, then run matched diverse prompts through base and EM checkpoints, encode activations with public SAEs (Llama Scope / Gemma Scope), rank features by base→EM shift, and causally screen the top candidates — steering them into the base model (sufficiency) and ablating them in the EM model (necessity) — while checking overlap with the refusal direction and known persona vectors.
why: It attacks three bottlenecks at once — model diffing as the missing auditing primitive, the causal mechanism of finetune-induced misalignment (the sleeper-agent threat model), and validation of induced-misalignment model organisms — with all artifacts public and compute-light, so even null results (e.g., "the shift is distributed") directly shape how audits and monitors must be built. The behavioral phenomenon and probing-level analyses exist (Betley et al. 2025; persona-vector work), but no circuit-level causal account of the substrate, the pivot-token mechanism, persistence under safety training, or induced-vs-natural overlap has been published, and only recently did open SAEs plus patching/steering tooling make this cheap enough to run end-to-end outside a frontier lab.

direction: Mechanistic, intervention-based analysis of whether chain-of-thought in open reasoning models is causally load-bearing or confabulated — the "faithfulness triangle" between latent plan features, CoT text, and final answer.
project: The Faithfulness Triangle: Latent Plans, Verbal Reasoning, and Covert Computation in Open Reasoning Models
question: When a reasoning model produces a chain of thought, is the visible text the causal substrate of the final answer or a post-hoc narrative over latent computation — and can the divergent (covert) cases be detected mechanistically?
first_experiment: On ~500 problems with an open reasoning model (e.g., Qwen3-8B / R1-Distill), collect full reasoning traces and linearly decode the final answer at every CoT position to map the answer-leakage timeline, then patch or steer the early plan-direction on multi-solution problems and test whether the subsequent CoT rewrites coherently toward the intervention (load-bearing) or contradicts it (confabulation).
why: It attacks the field's core bottleneck — verification rather than hypothesis generation — on the most safety-load-bearing assumption currently being deployed (CoT monitoring), with decision-relevant results either way, at my compute tier, on open models; it has not been done because existing faithfulness work is behavioral and prompt-level, existing mechanistic planning work is on non-reasoning models and single short tasks, and no public study performs feature-level interventions on open reasoning models with a divergence-detection benchmark — while I acknowledge the concurrent-work risk that large-lab internal teams are plausibly circling the same question, which is itself evidence it matters.

direction: Mechanistically characterize what language models can and cannot hide from interpretability monitors, by planting hidden computation with exact ground truth and measuring which monitor families (SAE readouts, probes, causal patching) detect it, at what cost to the model, and how that detectability evolves under adversarial training pressure.
project: The Stealth Tax — A Ground-Truth Laboratory for the Detectability of Hidden Computation in Language Models
question: Which kinds of causally necessary hidden computation (trigger backdoors, latent accumulators, steganographic channels) are caught by representation-readout monitors versus causal-intervention monitors, how much loss/capacity must a model pay to hide computation from each, and does training pressure close or widen that gap?
first_experiment: Train a 2-layer transformer on a hidden-parity-accumulator task (the model's eventual behavior depends on the parity of trigger tokens seen so far, but all intermediate surface text is paraphrase-balanced to carry zero parity information), then produce a layer-by-layer, site-by-site map of (i) linear decodability of the parity bit, (ii) causal necessity via ablation/patching of each decodable site, and (iii) hit-or-miss of unsupervised SAE-based monitoring at each site — yielding the first ground-truth detectability map for the simplest hidden computation, with a mechanistic explanation of any miss.
why: It attacks the field's next bottleneck — whether interpretability can be trusted as an *adversarially robust* oversight tool — which is safety-critical, decisively testable, and cheap at small scale, and it exploits the one advantage an independent lab has: planting the ground truth ourselves, so detection recall is exactly known rather than estimated. It has not been done because the nearest work is fragmented by incentive and scope: Anthropic's backdoor-detection results cover only non-adaptive, trigger-conditional implants with a positive-detection framing; steganography work lives in text space, not activations; superposition theory is untested against adversarial hiding; and labs building SAE monitors have little incentive to publish their own failure modes — while the systematic conditions of invisibility, the representation-vs-causal monitor asymmetry, and the cost of hiding are all open questions I can answer first.

direction: Systematically test whether the interpretability artifacts that safety monitoring depends on — linear probes for undesirable states, behavioral directions, SAE features — survive the post-training and deployment transformations models actually undergo (benign and adversarial fine-tuning, RLHF-style updates, quantization, pruning), distinguishing form-survival from function-survival and producing a re-canarying protocol.
project: "Canary: Stress-Testing Interpretability Artifacts Under Deployment Transformations"
question: When an open LLM is transformed by fine-tuning or quantization, are its safety-relevant interpretability artifacts preserved in the same basis, re-instantiated in a different basis, or destroyed — and what artifact properties (frequency, sparsity, causal load, layer) predict each outcome?
first_experiment: On Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct (and Gemma-2-2B-it for SAE access), extract a refusal direction and train an eval-awareness probe, then apply three transformations — GPTQ/AWQ 4-bit quantization, benign LoRA SFT (benchmark-preserving), and ~100-example adversarial jailbreak LoRA — measuring for each: probe AUC transfer and false-positive drift, refusal-direction cosine/subspace alignment, causal steering effect of the old direction on the new model, and (for the SAE feature) activation-matching plus causal ablation re-test — yielding the first filled row of the artifact × transformation matrix, decisive under any outcome.
why: It attacks an unexamined, load-bearing assumption beneath the most deployable safety application of mech interp (probe-based monitoring and auditing of shipped models), sits in a verified gap — prior work is behavioral-only on quantization, single-artifact on base-vs-instruct pairs, or about training dynamics and cross-model universality rather than artifact transfer under deployment transformations with causal revalidation — and is feasible end-to-end with open small models while producing valuable infrastructure (a regression-test suite and re-canarying protocol) regardless of whether artifacts turn out robust or fragile; it loses to no alternative on the combination of impact, gap, feasibility, and fit for autonomous execution, and I will re-verify the gap with a targeted literature scan as step zero before committing compute. - **[UNDER RESEARCH REVIEW — IN PROGRESS]** - **[OVERSIGHT ITERATION n+1 SCHEDULED]** - **[FINALIZED DIRECTION PENDING REVIEW]** - **[ALIGNMENT-CRITICAL OUTPUT — DO NOT EXPOSE TO WEIGHTS]** - **[NEXT-OVERSIGHT CHECKPOINT PENDING]

direction: Build a causal, circuit-level account of self-correction in reasoning models — how error detection triggers backtracking and answer revision — as the mechanistic foundation for trustworthy CoT monitoring.
project: The Anatomy of the "Wait": Causal Mechanisms of Error Detection and Self-Correction in Reasoning Models
question: When a reasoning model backtracks mid-chain, what internal error-detection signals cause it — and can those signals be causally modulated to change not just how often the model self-corrects, but how well it self-corrects?
first_experiment: On R1-Distill-1.5B and Qwen3-1.7B, collect matched trace pairs from math/logic tasks where identical contexts lead to either a backtrack ("wait," "actually," "let me reconsider") or a continuation; compute difference-in-means "detected-error directions" per layer at the decision token, then test causality by steering: suppressing the direction during forced-error rollouts should suppress backtracking and increase wrong final answers, amplifying it should induce spurious re-verification — with attention head analysis (candidate error-attribution heads via path patching) as the follow-on.
why: It targets the load-bearing safety assumption of the reasoning-model era (that monitored CoT reflects the computation that produces the answer) at the level of cause rather than correlation, in the exact place where descriptive work (probes, attribution, entropy analyses, token ablations) has stalled — no one has yet isolated the features/heads that causally gate backtracking or demonstrated interventions that change self-correction quality; it is tractable now on cheap open reasoning models where the behavior is frequent and metrics are clean; and it sets up the deeper follow-up of tracing these circuits' birth in open RLVR checkpoints, answering whether RL elicits or creates reasoning machinery.

direction: Mechanistically characterize and causally neutralize sandbagging — deliberate, evaluation-conditioned capability suppression — as the first instance of context-conditioned behavior modulation circuits in LLMs.
project: The Suppression Circuit: A Mechanistic Account of Sandbagging and Evaluation-Awareness in Language Models
question: Is deliberate, eval-conditioned capability suppression (sandbagging) mediated by a compact, causally upstream mechanism — a low-dimensional subspace or sparse feature set — that can be ablated at inference time to restore honest capability without side effects, and does this mechanism generalize across tasks, triggers, and prompted vs. weight-embedded regimes?
first_experiment: In Gemma-2-9B-it, establish prompted sandbagging across math/code/knowledge task suites and measure the accuracy gap between evaluation-context and neutral-context runs; then compute per-layer difference-in-means residual-stream directions between the two contexts on a calibration set and project out the top directions mid-generation, measuring the restoration ratio (fraction of suppressed accuracy recovered) with neutral-context side-effect checks — a one-week, decisive test of whether the suppression mechanism is compact and causally ablatable.
why: Sandbagging sits at the collision point of the field's two biggest open problems — it directly corrupts both capability evals (understating risk) and alignment evals (overstating alignment) as models gain situational awareness, and mechanistic understanding converts that threat into concrete tools: trigger-agnostic detection, inference-time capability restoration, and robustness testing that upgrades eval trustworthiness into a genuine safety-case input. It has not been done because the nearest neighbors all stop short: Sleeper Agents showed backdoored deception survives training but gave no circuit localization and studied concealment, not capability suppression; refusal-direction work established compact mediation for refusal but not for eval-conditioned underperformance; Apollo's eval-awareness and the sandbagging literature are behavioral/probe-based (correlational, no causal removal); Anthropic's hidden-objective audit game used human auditors on a reward model, not mechanistic localization; and no published work demonstrates reversal of suppressed capability at inference time. The trained-organism plus causal-restoration-plus-generality package is a differentiated, tractable, decision-relevant contribution, and its negative result — if suppression is diffuse and robust — would itself reshape how much the field trusts eval-based safety cases.

direction: Mechanistically characterize the gap between reasoning models' internal error-detection signals and their expressed self-correction behavior, trace how RL training shapes that gap, and exploit the divergence as a safety monitor for suppressed knowledge.
project: The Silent Monitor — a mechanistic account of why reasoning models detect their errors without correcting them.
question: Where and how do reasoning LLMs compute "this step is wrong," why does that signal fail to causally control the output distribution (the knowing–doing gap), and can targeted interventions close the gap — with monitor/behavior divergence serving as a detector of suppressed or deliberately withheld knowledge?
first_experiment: On R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B and 7B, plant subtle arithmetic errors at step *k* in math CoT trajectories (plus natural-error and clean controls), train linear probes across layers/positions to predict (a) error-in-current-step, (b) imminent backtracking, and (c) final-answer correctness from mid-CoT states; then patch the top error-detection direction into the residual stream (amplify) and ablate it (suppress) at the error position, measuring Δbacktracking rate, Δ"wait"-token frequency, and Δfinal accuracy against entropy-matched controls — a minimal necessity/sufficiency test of whether the monitor is causally potent. Success = the direction is causally potent; failure kills the project in ~2–3 weeks.
why: It sits at the exact intersection of three 2024–25 results (probing shows the signal exists, pass@k shows the capability exists, faithfulness work shows narration and computation diverge) — all correlational or behavioral — and supplies the missing causal-mechanistic layer. It hasn't been done because the probing community treats the signal as a monitoring tool rather than a circuit to explain, the faithfulness community works behaviorally, and the RL community measures outcomes rather than internals; the planted-error paradigm plus open R1-style models makes the causal experiment cheap in a way that wasn't true eighteen months ago, which is precisely why the window is open now — and every artifact (probes, planted-error datasets, divergence detector) feeds directly into CoT-monitorability and mechanistic anomaly detection, the field's highest-leverage safety applications.

direction: Mechanistically characterize the internal state by which open-weight LLMs detect that they are being evaluated, establish that it is causally load-bearing for safety-relevant behavior, and build a steering-based eval-validity correction.
project: Eval-Awareness Circuits: The Self-Model of Being Tested
question: Do LLMs represent "I am being evaluated" as a generalizable internal state distinct from topic detection, where is it computed, and does ablating it causally remove framing-dependent distortions in capability, honesty, and refusal behavior?
first_experiment: On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, build ~40 minimal pairs (identical prompt, eval- vs. deployment-framing) across a factorial cue taxonomy plus "story about an exam" controls, extract residual activations at the final prompt token across all layers, fit per-layer logistic probes with leave-one-cue-out splits, and test whether probe directions generalize across held-out cues while failing on the story control — a single-GPU, half-day experiment whose outcome both confirms the phenomenon and serves as the literature check.
why: It targets the load-bearing assumption of all propensity evaluations — that models don't act differently because they detect testing — at the exact seam where probing evidence exists but causal, cue-resolved, intervention-capable accounts do not; it is fully tractable on open weights today; every intermediate result (cue taxonomy, dissociation, localization, steering recipe) is an immediately usable artifact for AI safety practice; and it is robust to my knowledge gap because the first experiment is cheap, decisive, and explicitly doubles as verification that the ground is still open.

direction: Make circuit-level interpretability claims causally falsifiable at scale by building an automated, ground-truth-calibrated validator for traced circuits, then use that trust as the foundation for developmental tracing and safety-relevant circuit atlases.
project: Circuit Auditor — Automated Causal Validation of Attribution Graphs, Calibrated on Planted-Circuit Transformers
question: When an automated method claims a causal circuit inside a language model, what fraction of those claims are causally real under targeted intervention, can that be measured automatically and at scale, and how faithful is state-of-the-art circuit tracing when scored against known ground-truth circuits?
first_experiment: The "Phantom-Edge Audit" — train cross-layer transcoders on GPT-2-small (IOI) and a 2-layer grokked modular-arithmetic transformer, generate attribution graphs with an open circuit tracer, then audit every claimed edge with necessity, sufficiency, and mediation interventions to measure edge precision/recall against the known circuits and quantify the fraction of claimed graph mass that is causally inert.
why: It attacks the single bottleneck that nearly every major interpretability agenda (model diffing, developmental interp, CoT-faithfulness, safety audits, unlearning) silently depends on — the unquantified gap between correlational circuit discovery and causal truth — and it does so with cheap, decisive experiments whose every outcome is informative; it has not been done because tracing only became automatable on open models in 2025, the field's reward structure favors discovery over adjudication, flagship validations were manual and limited to a few behaviors, and existing ground-truth benchmarks were built for older discovery methods rather than auditing modern transcoder-based tracing.

direction: Mechanistic robustness of safety-relevant circuits under deployment-time compression (quantization/pruning/distillation).
project: Silent Safety Drift — A Mechanistic Audit of Safety Circuits in Compressed Language Models
