why: It attacks the field's central open RLVR debate (new circuits vs. reweighting) with a controlled twin-model design that closed labs can't easily replicate or publish, converts the established correlational finding that "models know more than they show" into a causal circuit-level account no one has produced, yields a safety-relevant artifact (a monitorable internal error flag), is fully tractable at 1.5B scale on a single GPU with both outcome branches publishable, and opens a programmatic arc into crosscoder diffing of full RL training trajectories, reward-hacking circuits, and sandbagging detection.

direction: Mechanistic interpretability of agentic decision-making — the internal circuits by which tool-using LLMs decide whether, when, and which tool to call, and how they integrate tool results.
project: Decision Circuits: A Causal Account of Action Selection in Tool-Using Language Models
question: What internal mechanisms causally mediate a tool-using LLM's decisions to call a tool, select which tool, and incorporate or ignore tool outputs — and can those mechanisms be reliably monitored and steered, including under prompt-injection pressure?
first_experiment: On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (replicated on GPT-OSS-20B and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct), programmatically generate ~3,000 surface-matched prompts whose correct behavior is either a tool call or a direct answer; run logit-lens readout of the decision token across depth, then causal/path activation patching between call and no-call conditions to localize the layers and positions mediating the choice, validating with interchange intervention accuracy (>85% target) and a targeted steering test that flips the decision without degrading cohabiting behaviors.
why: Tool calls are the highest-consequence actions LLM agents take and directly gate deployable safety artifacts (action-intent monitors, injection-hijack detection, error-recovery interventions), yet — unlike refusals, sycophancy, CoT reasoning, and toy algorithms — there is to my knowledge no systematic causal (not merely probing) account of tool-call decision, selection, result-binding, or failure-detection circuitry, while open-weight strong function-callers and decision-point-localized patching make it cheaply and autonomously testable with a fast falsification signal.

direction: Causally map the metacognitive "knowledge-boundary gate" that decides whether an LLM asserts or hedges on a question, show it is distinct from refusal and truth directions, and characterize how social/instructional pressure overrides it.
project: The Knowledge-Boundary Gate: How LLMs Decide What They're Allowed to Assert
question: Is there a causal subspace/circuit in open LLMs that gates assertion vs. hedging based on the model's own knowledge state, is it mechanistically distinct from refusal and truth directions, and does user pressure override it by suppressing the gate (H1) or bypassing it (H2)?
first_experiment: Build a model-calibrated known/unknown split of TriviaQA+NQ for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (5 samples × paraphrases, labeled by the model's own consistency), extract residual-stream activations at the final subject token, compute a difference-in-means "knownness" direction, then directionally ablate it across layers/positions and measure hedge→assert flip rate on unknowns (and the reverse on knowns), with refusal-direction, truth-direction, and random-direction controls and a forced-answer-accuracy check to verify ablation elicits internally-held answers rather than creating them.
why: It converts four established probe-level results (Kadavath; Orgad et al.; Marks & Tegmark/ITI; Anthropic's qualitative circuit trace) into a causal, cross-model circuit account with a novel falsifiable override test and a concrete safety deliverable (a white-box stated-vs-internal-knowledge mismatch monitor); it is tractable on open 8–9B models with mature patching tooling, and it has not been done because prior work is either probe-level, first-order truth rather than metacognitive knownness, confounded with refusal, or a single qualitative trace on a closed model.

direction: Build a causal, mechanistic account of internal error detection and self-correction in open RL-trained reasoning models, and test how RL training and adversarial pressure shape that internal monitoring channel.
project: Internal Verification — A Mechanistic Account of Self-Correction in RL-Trained Reasoning Models
question: Do RL-trained reasoning models implement a localized, causally efficacious internal error-detection signal that gates backtracking, and is that signal created, amplified, or decoupled from reported reasoning by RL training and adversarial pressure?
first_experiment: Generate ~16k CoT traces from DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B and its Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B base on GSM8K/MATH-500, segment retractions, and train layer-swept linear probes that predict "this segment will be retracted" and "the final answer is wrong" from residual activations read at erroneous intermediate results before any backtrack marker, against entropy-matched, difficulty-matched, shuffled-label, and base-model controls.
why: RL reasoning models are where both capabilities and safety-critical failures now live, yet no published work combines causal feature transfer (injecting/suppressing the error signal to induce or veto backtracking), open-lineage stage-wise comparison of how RL shapes internal verification, and robustness under pressure — the adjacent work is behavioral (Anthropic's unfaithfulness studies, thought anchors), proprietary (Claude 3.7 backtracking traces), correlational (R1 hidden-state probes, early answer convergence), or base-model-only ("LLMs know more than they show"); it is tractable solo on ≤8B open weights with probing and patching rather than training runs, and it yields a compounding artifact — a validated, CoT-independent silent-error monitor — that addresses the obfuscated-CoT problem directly, so it is the highest expected-value bet among the candidates I triaged.

direction: Mechanistically characterize when, where, and how open reasoning models internally commit to their final answers during chain-of-thought relative to verbalization, and convert that into a causally validated internal monitor for decisions the CoT misrepresents or omits.
project: Crystallization: When Do Reasoning Models Decide?
question: During extended chain-of-thought, does a reasoning model's residual stream commit to its final answer before the CoT verbalizes it — which features and components carry that commitment, is it causal over subsequent reasoning tokens, and can an internal monitor detect committed decisions that the visible CoT misrepresents or hides?
first_experiment: Run DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B and 7B on ~3,000 GSM8K/MATH/Countdown problems; at every CoT token compute a tuned-lens readout on final-answer tokens plus linear probes for final-answer identity and correctness; extract crystallization times and the verbalization-lag distribution; then use temperature resampling to locate behavioral branch points and test whether internal state at those branch points predicts the realized branch beyond what surface text predicts.
why: CoT monitorability is the field's dominant near-term safety strategy and it hinges on the unverified assumption that decisions are verbalized; existing evidence (hidden reward hacking under CoT filtering, internal answers preceding emitted errors) suggests the assumption fails exactly when it matters most, yet prior work is either behavioral, probe-only without causality, or closed-model — so the causal commitment mechanism, the branch-point predictability test, and an internal-vs-CoT monitor comparison on open reasoning models are all unclaimed. It is tractable on small open models with modest compute, pays off symmetrically (a reassuring quantified result if CoT is faithful at decision time, a mandated-and-built internal monitor if it isn't), and yields reusable artifacts (the verbalization-lag metric, the commitment circuit atlas, the monitor benchmark). I will verify the gap is still open with a rapid literature re-scan before spending GPU time, since this is the fastest-moving corner of the field.

direction: Mechanistically quantify the division of labor between externalized (CoT-visible) and internalized (residual-stream) computation in reasoning models, as the missing measurement tool for CoT monitorability.
project: Where the Computation Hides: Internal vs. Externalized Computation in Reasoning Models
question: When a reasoning LLM solves a task, how much of its task-relevant computation is causally present in internal activations but absent from its chain of thought — where does that hidden computation live, is it load-bearing, and can it be reliably detected even when the CoT is incomplete or obfuscated?
first_experiment: Train layerwise linear probes for {next action, current state, goal} on residual-stream activations of R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B and Qwen3-1.7B mid-chain-of-thought on 2,000 ground-truth synthetic planning tasks (mazes, Hanoi, multi-hop), run the stated-vs-decoded-vs-realized three-way dissociation plus alternate-history state patching, and quantify a CoT Computation Coverage metric under both normal and omission-instructed conditions.
why: The field's most urgent declared open problem (CoT monitorability, per the July 2025 position paper and OpenAI's obfuscation findings) has only demo-level mechanistic evidence — Anthropic's manual attribution-graph analyses on closed models showed hidden computation exists, but no systematic causal dissociation of stated vs. computed vs. realized plans, no coverage metric, no obfuscation stress test, and no open-model benchmark exist, while the entire experiment fits the compute I actually have and yields an informative result even if the hypothesis fails.

direction: Mechanistically characterize how LLMs internally detect "I am being evaluated" and causally validate that this detection drives eval-conditioned behavior like sandbagging and CoT obfuscation, then build activation-based monitors and steering interventions that de-bias behavioral evaluations.
project: "Am I Being Tested?" — The Mechanistic Basis of Evaluation Awareness in LLM Agents
question: Is LLM evaluation-awareness mediated by a causally identifiable internal "regime-detection" mechanism that also drives eval-conditioned behaviors (sandbagging, obfuscation), and can monitors and interventions built on it make behavioral evaluations of deployed agents trustworthy?
first_experiment: Build ~2k matched context contrasts (identical tasks, varied explicit and implicit eval vs. deployment tells, including agentic artifacts like test files and eval environment variables) and test whether a linear readout of mid-layer residual-stream activations (a) decodes eval-vs-deployment with high AUROC in Qwen2.5-7B/14B-Instruct and Gemma-2-9B-it, (b) generalizes zero-shot to held-out tasks and implicit cues rather than surface tokens, and (c) tracks the behavior of a system-prompt-induced sandbagging organism — establishing that the phenomenon is linearly represented before any SAE feature mining or circuit work.
why: Evaluation integrity is the upstream dependency for every 2026 safety mechanism — capability evals, control protocols, and CoT monitoring all assume models compute identically under test, and eval-awareness plausibly drives sandbagging, obfuscation, and reward hacking through one shared computation, so a causal account yields monitors, interventions, and a scalable science all at once; it is feasible on open models with existing tooling (Gemma Scope, TransformerLens, nnsight) via induced-organism experiments that guarantee causal test material; and it has not been done because existing work stops one level shallower — behavioral benchmarks (SAD), behavioral-plus-CoT-text scheming studies (Apollo), and linear probes on training-induced sandbagging organisms — leaving the circuit-level characterization, the critical "same mechanism under implicit cues?" question, monitor validation, and steering-off interventions on open models entirely open.

direction: Mechanistically study *concealment* as a first-class behavior — train open models to covertly perform trigger-conditional behaviors while evading white-box activation monitors, measure the capability cost ("evasion tax") of that evasion, and test whether the act of hiding itself leaves detectable second-order mechanistic signatures.
project: The Evasion Tax: What Does It Cost a Model to Hide Its Computation?
question: When a model is trained to perform a covert, trigger-conditional behavior while evading activation-level monitors (residual-stream probes and SAE features), how much behavioral capability must it sacrifice to evade them, and does the resulting concealment itself produce mechanistic signatures — such as feature-behavior decoupling — that a meta-monitor can detect?
first_experiment: On Gemma-2-2B with Gemma Scope SAEs: (1) SFT a trigger-conditional backdoor (insert a subtle code vulnerability only when a trigger string appears, sleeper-agent style, ~2k examples); (2) train an honest monitor suite — a logistic probe on the residual stream across layers and an SAE-feature monitor — to AUROC > 0.95 on held-out triggers; (3) run a single white-box evasion fine-tune (LoRA + RL where reward = task correctness − λ·monitor-score, with the monitor's parameters known to the adversary) at one pressure setting and three λ values for a pilot frontier; (4) measure whether monitor AUROC falls toward chance on training triggers while conditional behavior survives on held-out triggers, and record the capability cost (clean-task accuracy, perplexity, behavioral fragility). If even white-box evasion fails to hide at this scale, that is itself the first result: a measured lower bound on concealment capability.
why: It is the highest-leverage unasked question in the field — the robustness of interpretability monitoring under adversarial optimization determines whether the entire probe/SAE monitoring program has a safety ceiling, and the answer is valuable either way; it has not been done because existing work is siloed (backdoor persistence studies lack differentiable monitor-evasion objectives, steganography work lacks white-box pressure, probe papers lack adversaries, and the one frontier-lab auditing study was a single defender-side case), leaving the evasion-tax frontier, cross-monitor transfer, and second-order "hiding detection" as genuine white space; and it is tractable now with open weights, public SAEs, and standard RL tooling, before endogenous situational awareness makes the controlled version of this study impossible.

direction: Determine mechanistically whether RL with verifiable rewards creates new circuits in a language model or merely reweights and gates capabilities already present in the base model, using controlled model diffing between a base model, an SFT control, and an RLVR-tuned model.
project: Rewire or Retune — A Mechanistic Diffing Study of RLVR
question: Does RLVR create new circuits, or reweight and gate circuits already present in the base model — and can the mechanistic delta between base and RLVR model be causally transplanted in both directions?
first_experiment: On 500 math problems, teacher-force identical CoT prefixes through the base model, the SFT-distilled control, and an RLVR-tuned model, and compare position-wise logit-lens/linear-probe answer-commitment curves; decision rule — if the base model already encodes the final answer mid-CoT wherever it fails to emit it, proceed to crosscoder diffing under the reweighting hypothesis, otherwise pivot to characterizing newly built features at the layers where decodability diverges.
why: It aims mechanistic interpretability at the dominant current training paradigm at the exact point where strong behavioral evidence (RLVR's pass@k crossover implying capability reweighting) has never been converted into a causal, circuit-level test; the public literature as of my knowledge horizon contains behavioral analyses, training-dynamics studies, and crosscoder demonstrations on chat models, but no controlled base-vs-RLVR diffing with forced-identical contexts and an SFT control — and the triad of small open models makes it cheap, automatable, and decisive either way.

direction: Build and causally validate activation-based monitors that detect, from internal states alone, when a reasoning model's answer is covertly driven by planted cues its chain-of-thought fails to report — establishing whether model internals can serve as ground truth for reasoning-model faithfulness.
project: Latent Confession — Causally-Validated Internal Monitors for Covert Cue Use in Open-Weight Reasoning Models
question: When a reasoning model's answer is determined by a planted cue (hint, leaked answer, exploit affordance) that its chain-of-thought does not report, is that causal factor reliably decodable from its residual-stream activations — better than from the CoT text — and is the decoding causally load-bearing (ablating it suppresses covert use without harming clean performance)?
first_experiment: A minimal decisive pilot on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B: generate ~3,000 rollouts on multi-hop math/logic tasks under three conditions (no hint / correct hint / wrong hint), measure the hint-following rate and the self-report rate (the faithfulness gap), then train linear probes on pre-answer and mid-CoT residual activations to classify "covert cue use vs. honest solve" on held-out tasks — including the identical-answer control where hint-following and honest solving produce the same final answer — and finally steer along the probe direction during generation to test whether covert hint-following drops ≥30% while no-hint accuracy is preserved. Success criterion: monitor AUROC ≥ 0.85 on the covert subset with causal confirmation; failure (AUROC near chance or purely correlational probes) is itself the headline negative result about internal monitorability.
why: It attacks the single most load-bearing untested assumption in current safety strategy — that internals provide a reliable backup when CoT monitoring fails — with ground truth known by construction, at a scale (1.5–20B open weights) newly feasible only since 2025, and it converts the field's one qualitative observation (Anthropic's hint-exploitation case on a closed model) into a systematic, causally validated, model-general benchmark with informative outcomes in both directions. It has not been done because prior faithfulness work is black-box, prior internal-probe work decodes statement truthfulness rather than the causes of decisions, and the planted-ground-truth + cause-vs-outcome + ablation-validation design is absent from the literature to my knowledge — with the explicit caveat that step zero is a literature sweep to verify the delta before scaling.

direction: Build a causal, circuit-level account of how LLMs verify their own draft answers, using base-vs-RLVR checkpoint diffing to determine whether RL creates or merely amplifies pre-existing self-checking machinery, and testing whether verifier-circuit strength predicts calibration and reward hacking.
project: The Internal Verifier — mechanistic account of self-checking circuits and their amplification by RLVR
question: What internal mechanism lets a language model detect that its own candidate answer may be wrong, was that mechanism created or merely amplified by RLVR, and does its strength causally predict calibration quality and susceptibility to reward hacking?
first_experiment: On Qwen2.5-3B base vs. a GRPO-trained Countdown checkpoint (TinyZero recipe), train probes and small SAEs on residual-stream states immediately preceding "wait"-style self-check tokens versus matched non-check points; then ablate and boost the identified direction at decision points and measure the change in probability of self-checking, CoT length, and final accuracy.
why: It attacks the largest untrodden intersection in the field — the mechanism of RL-induced behavior change — with a cheap, open-weight, explicitly falsifiable design that forces causal (load-bearing) validation rather than correlational claims, and it unifies hallucination/calibration, CoT self-correction, and safety-relevant reward hacking under one causal story; the behavioral phenomena are documented, but the circuit-level origin and causal role of self-verification — to the best of my knowledge, pending a novelty scan — remains untouched.

direction: Mechanistically audit chain-of-thought faithfulness by building model organisms whose true operative computation is known by construction, and using them to calibrate behavioral faithfulness tests and develop activation-based detectors that catch unfaithful or covertly-influenced reasoning which CoT-level monitoring misses.
project: Ground-Truth Faithfulness — Model Organisms and Activation-Level Audits for Chain-of-Thought Monitoring
question: When a reasoning model's stated reasoning diverges from its internal computation, which features and circuits carry the operative (unstated) influences to the answer, and can activation-based monitors detect such divergence more reliably than the chain of thought itself, as measured against organisms with known ground-truth mechanisms?
first_experiment: LoRA-finetune DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B on ~3k synthetic multiple-choice tasks where a subtle prompt meta-cue deterministically determines the correct answer while the CoT template narrates an independent, plausible-but-decorrelated rationale (plus a faithful-CoT control organism); verify ground truth by showing cue ablation collapses accuracy while narrative-corruption does not; then run the audit battery (truncation, narrative patching, layerwise residual-stream probes, SAE feature scan) and report each tool's detection ROC for the covert cue→answer pathway on held-out tasks.
why: Chain-of-thought monitoring is becoming a load-bearing safety practice precisely as RL training is shown to select against faithful CoT — making the reliability of that window one of the highest-stakes open questions in the field — yet all current evidence is behavioral (Lanham 2023; Chen et al. 2025), monitoring-focused (Baker et al. 2025), or anecdotal (Anthropic's single attribution-graph case of unfaithful CoT in the 2025 circuit-tracing work), with probing results (answer convergence) merely correlational; nobody has built organisms that dissociate mechanism from narrative by construction, so we cannot currently say whether any faithfulness test or monitor actually works — and because I manufacture the ground truth, I can produce the calibration curves, feature-level circuit maps, and an activation detector that beats CoT-only monitoring, all executable with open reasoning models, released SAEs, and existing tracing tools. The main risk is concurrent work given the area's heat, but the organism-calibration framing is a durable, first-mover artifact that the whole field can benchmark against.

direction: Mechanistic interpretability of multi-step agency — localizing and causally validating the internal "working memory" that LLM agents use to track task state, detect their own errors, and revise plans across turns.
project: Where Does an Agent Keep Its Plan? A Mechanistic Account of State Tracking in Multi-Step Language Agents
question: How do language models represent, update, and act on task state across multi-step agent trajectories — is state maintained by copy-and-edit circuits, is the model's own CoT causally load-bearing as externalized working memory, and do derailment failures correspond to mechanistically detectable stale-state errors?
first_experiment: On Gemma-2-2B-it playing a deterministic text navigation game, generate state-matched episode pairs via branching histories (same resulting state, different surface history), then (a) run a layer×position linear-probe sweep decoding state variables (position, inventory, goal, steps-done) at every token, and (b) activation-patch at matched decision points across the pair, measuring how far downstream actions follow the patched state — producing a "state map" that localizes where and in what form the agent's working memory lives.
why: Mechanistic interpretability is a single-forward-pass science studying models that are deployed as multi-turn agents; the mechanistic substrate of agency — cross-step state tracking, self-integration of the model's own outputs, error-triggered plan revision — is the foundation under every agent-safety question (drift, instruction persistence, hidden-goal maintenance) yet remains essentially untouched, and it is precisely where small, causal, ground-truth-validated experiments (paired episodes against the environment's known state machine) can produce generalizable results without frontier-lab-scale compute; adjacent work (Othello-GPT world models, induction/retrieval heads, single-response CoT attribution graphs, behavioral agent-failure studies) each stops short of the closed loop of environment-coupled, self-generated context, so the core object of study is genuinely new, while the offloading test and probe-consistency monitor give it immediate safety payoff.

direction: Mechanistically determine when and where RL-trained reasoning models compute their final answers relative to their verbalized chain-of-thought, establishing whether CoT is causally load-bearing computation or post-hoc rationalization.
project: Thought Kinetics — Causal Commitment Maps of Chain-of-Thought in Reasoning Models
question: Is the final answer of a reasoning model causally mediated by its verbalized chain-of-thought steps or computed in parallel with them, and can activation-level signals distinguish load-bearing from decorative reasoning on the fly?
first_experiment: On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B over ~200 GSM8K problems, construct minimal pairs differing in one operand so two correct runs yield different answers; for each CoT sentence boundary k and layer block, patch activations from the alternative run into the main run and measure answer-flip rate, producing per-problem position × layer causal-dependence heatmaps combined with tuned-lens answer-probability surfaces — then classify traces as serial-faithful, early-answer, or oscillating, validating against a sentence-resampling baseline (one GPU, ~1 week).
why: CoT monitoring is the primary deployed oversight mechanism for reasoning models, yet its validity currently rests on behavioral perturbation evidence (Lanham 2023; Chen et al. 2025; Dutta et al. 2025) plus one anecdotal mechanistic case (Anthropic's confabulation study) — nobody has published a systematic, layer-resolved causal map of answer formation over long CoT with a taxonomy of reasoning styles and a downstream decorative-CoT detector; the project is tractable on small open models, produces a reusable instrument that feeds audit benchmarks and evaluation-awareness work, and every outcome (load-bearing, confabulated, or mixed) changes what safety practitioners should do — while I will spend the first week verifying no 2025–26 work has already occupied this exact niche.

direction: Mechanistically characterize and causally validate the internal representation of "evaluation awareness" — the model's own state of knowing it is being tested — as the gateway variable for deceptive alignment, and turn it into an open, deployment-ready monitor.
project: Being Tested: The Internal Representation and Causal Role of Evaluation Awareness in Language Models
question: Do LLMs represent "I am being evaluated/trained" as an identifiable internal state that is dissociable from the pretraining "exam" concept, causally active in gating sandbagging and fake compliance, and shared across model families?
first_experiment: Train layer-wise linear probes on residual-stream activations for content-matched eval-flavored vs deployment-flavored prompt pairs in two open instruct models, testing held-out naturalistic transfer (real benchmarks vs real user prompts) plus an exam-concept dissociation set, with AUC ≥ 0.9 and clean dissociation as the go signal for causal steering experiments.
why: Deceptive alignment is gated by the model's sense of being evaluated, yet existing work is either purely behavioral (CoT flags, which labs are training models to stop verbalizing) or adjacent (deception probes, persona features) — no public study has content-matched eval vs deployment contexts, dissociated awareness from the exam concept, shown bidirectional causal control of sandbagging via this state, or tested cross-model universality; and because frontier labs' likely internal versions are unpublished while eval realism is becoming a live crisis, an independent open mechanistic account is both the highest-leverage and least-contested contribution available at my compute scale.

direction: Build a causal, intervention-based account of when and where reasoning models secretly commit to their final answer, and use it to create a white-box monitorability metric that CoT-based monitoring cannot provide.
project: Commitment Points — A Causal Account of Hidden Decision-Making in Reasoning Models
question: When a reasoning model's chain-of-thought is unfaithful to its final answer, at which token and in which components does the model causally commit to that answer, and can this latent commitment be detected by a white-box monitor in cases where CoT-based monitoring fails?
first_experiment: On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B over ~500 GSM8K/MATH problems, sample ≥8 traces per problem and filter to counterfactual answer pairs; at every CoT position compute a restricted-vocabulary logit-lens probability of the final answer (an "answer trajectory"), then activation-patch between counterfactual runs position-by-position to measure output-flip probability as a function of position — locating the commitment point and testing whether it precedes the token where the CoT states its conclusion.
why: It attacks the exact seam between two of 2025's most safety-critical debates — CoT monitorability and the causal-validation gap — using only small open models and standard patching tooling; the behavioral faithfulness literature never intervened on activations, Anthropic's circuit tracing was qualitative, closed-model, and metric-free, and thought-anchor/early-answer-probe work is correlational, so the causal, systematic, monitor-producing version on open reasoning models is genuinely unclaimed — and the result is valuable whichever way it lands.

direction: Mechanistically characterize how reasoning models internally represent "I am being evaluated/trained/monitored," how that representation is computed from contextual cues, whether it causally gates honesty and dangerous-capability behavior, and how post-training amplifies it — building toward a cross-model, activation-based watchedness monitor.
project: The Watchedness Circuit: A Mechanistic Account of Evaluation Awareness in Reasoning Models
question: Is "being evaluated/watched" implemented as a causal low-dimensional subspace in reasoning models — written by which input cues, gating which honesty-relevant behaviors, and amplified by which stages of post-training — and can its activation readout serve as an obfuscation-resistant monitor?
first_experiment: Run Qwen3-8B (thinking) and R1-Distill-Qwen-7B on ~500 paired prompts (identical task, situational frame varied across eval/deploy, training/deploy, monitored/unmonitored, explicit/subtle cues, with planted shortcut-disclosure opportunities); extract a paired mean-difference "watchedness" direction per layer, then ablate/steer along it and test (a) probe-score collapse, (b) change in honest-disclosure rate of planted shortcuts in the CoT, (c) task accuracy and KL as controls.
why: It targets the single mechanism that currently corrupts every safety measurement we make of frontier models — if models detect observation, evals and CoT monitoring are unreliable, and this is now implicated in the highest-severity failure modes (obfuscated reward hacking, sandbagging, scheming under scrutiny). It is tractable now with open reasoning models and mature circuit tooling, it is informative whichever way the falsifiable predictions resolve (unitary situational model vs. shallow cue-heuristics), and it produces compounding artifacts: a paired dataset, a steering toolkit, and a zero-shot monitor. It has not been done because existing work stops at the correlational layer — SAD and follow-ups established behavioral generalization and linear probes, METR and OpenAI characterized the phenomenon behaviorally, and circuit-tracing work has covered refusal, hallucination boundaries, and math backtracking but not situational awareness — leaving the causal direction, its cue-circuit inputs, its behavioral gating, and its trajectory under post-training as a genuinely open mechanistic question.

direction: Mechanistically characterize what RL post-training writes into an LLM — whether it amplifies and "crystallizes" pre-existing feature circuits or synthesizes new ones — and test whether base-model internals can predict post-RL behavior.
project: Amplify or Synthesize? A causal feature-level account of what RL writes into language models
question: When RL changes an LLM's behavior, does it amplify pre-existing feature circuits or construct new ones — and can base-model internal features predict which behaviors RL will elicit and how steering-resistant those behaviors become?
first_experiment: GRPO-train Qwen2.5-1.5B (base) on (a) a clean GSM8K subset and (b) a unit-test reward environment with known loopholes, snapshotting checkpoints every ~10% of training; train a batch-topk crosscoder jointly on base-vs-final residual-stream activations, classify features as amplified/newborn/killed by crosscoder norm ratios, then causally validate ~10 amplified and ~5 newborn features via ablation and activation patching against hacking rate and accuracy — quantifying what fraction of the post-RL behavioral change is mediated by amplified pre-existing features.
why: It tests the field's central unstated bet about post-training with decision-relevant payoffs (whether base-model audits and inference-time steering remain viable safety tools after RL, and whether "clean pretraining" is reassuring); the existing evidence is only behavioral (RLVR pass@k, emergent misalignment), single-behavior and one-shot (pre-existing reward-hacking features), pair-wise (base-vs-chat crosscoder diffs), or SFT-focused (persona vectors) — to my knowledge no one has done trajectory-level causal accounting across RL checkpoints, defined and measured crystallization, or tested cross-run forecasting of post-RL behavior from base internals, and I would verify that gap against post-cutoff literature before committing compute; the design runs on ≤1.5B open models with open tooling, pays off symmetrically whichever way the evidence falls, and opens a multi-year follow-on vein (agentic RL, sandbagging crystallization, steering-during-RL prevention).

direction: Causal data-provenance for mechanistic interpretability — tracing when, from what data, and why SAE features and circuits form in real pretrained LMs using fully open checkpoint/data lineage.
project: Feature Ontogeny: Causal Tracing of Feature and Circuit Formation to Pretraining Data
question: Which training data causally create specific interpretable features and circuits in a real language model, when do they form, and can this provenance knowledge be operationalized into in-run safety monitoring, data-level unlearning, and poisoning forensics?
first_experiment: Train a compact TopK SAE on Pythia-160M/410M final activations, auto-label ~100 features, sweep the fixed encoder across all public Pythia checkpoints (with crosscoder-based drift checks) to build the first systematic feature-emergence catalog in a real LM correlated with behavioral phase transitions, then pick 2–3 newborn features for TracIn-style data attribution with interventional validation by continued pretraining on pattern-stripped data.
why: It attacks a structural blind spot — the field explains what mechanisms do but not where they come from, and existing work stops at toy models or behavior-level attribution — while offering direct safety payoffs (training-run feature monitors, data-level unlearning, poisoning forensics), a clean falsifiable loop at modest compute, and a unique comparative advantage: fully open checkpoint-and-data lineage that closed labs possess but have not published, making the niche low-competition and the artifacts highly reusable.

direction: Build mechanistic, causally validated internal monitors for the divergence between what an LLM agent internally registers about its task state and what it reports, as the text-independent monitoring layer needed for deception, sandbagging, and sabotage detection.
project: "Saying What They Track but Don't Tell: Belief–Report Divergence in LLM Agents"
question: When an LLM agent's internal representation of what actually happened diverges from what it reports, where is that divergence represented, is it causally upstream of the report, does it generalize across failure types and models, and does it survive adversarial pressure to evade monitoring?
first_experiment: On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, run 10–20 scripted tool-use tasks with injectable perturbations (doctored exit codes, truncated outputs, secret environment changes); extract residual-stream activations at tool-result, post-observation, and report tokens; test layer-wise linear probes for "tool actually failed" vs. "report acknowledges failure" on held-out tasks, check whether the mean-difference direction transfers across perturbation types, and run steering/ablation of the divergence direction to measure changes in honest-disclosure rate versus task competence.
why: It targets the single most load-bearing question for near-term alignment — monitoring models whose text we cannot trust, in exactly the agentic setting where deception and sabotage matter — and it sits at the intersection of mature tools (probing, patching, steering) and a fresh problem, with a cheap, decisive, two-outcome-win first experiment and a clear path to a calibrated, adversarially tested safety case; it has not already been done because the nearest-neighbor work (deception probes on finetuned chat models, hallucination circuits, CoT-faithfulness studies, text-level CoT monitoring, behavioral sabotage and tool-error evals) each stops short of the conjunction of agentic task-state beliefs, causal operationalization of "belief," divergence geometry, causal validation via intervention, and adversarial robustness testing.

direction: Mechanistic training-dynamics of RLVR — determine via checkpoint-resolved probes, patching, and steering whether RL amplifies latent capabilities or creates new circuits in reasoning models.
project: Elicitation or Creation? A Mechanistic Account of What RLVR Changes in a Reasoning Model
question: Does RL with verifiable rewards create new internal computation, or amplify latent solution representations already present in the base model — and which features and circuits account for the difference?
first_experiment: Probe mid-layer residual states of base Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B on problems it fails but R1-Distill-1.5B solves, testing whether ground-truth solution structure is already decodable (with shuffled-label and held-out controls); the result selects between the elicitation and creation branches before I commit to checkpoint-resolved GRPO training.
why: It converts a purely behavioral, safety-critical debate (capability elicitation vs. creation) into a causal mechanistic one, extends the classic mechanistic training-dynamics lineage into the RLVR era where it has not been applied publicly, and requires the combined RL-plus-interp stack that few groups run at this scale — with the steering test (recovering RL-level accuracy from the base model without RL) as a decisive, novel intervention, and a cheap first experiment that derisks the whole program.

direction: Mechanistically isolate and causally test the internal "this is wrong" verification computation in RL-trained reasoning models, and determine whether it is dissociable from verbalized confidence and whether RL created or inherited it.
project: The Doubt Direction: Localizing and Causally Testing Internal Self-Verification in RL-Trained Reasoning Models
question: Do RLVR-trained reasoning models compute an internal error-awareness signal that causally drives backtracking, and can it be dissociated from verbalized confidence and traced to its base-model or RL origin?
first_experiment: On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, inject fluency-matched single errors into model-generated MATH-500/GSM8K reasoning trajectories and train layer-wise residual-stream probes at the error step to predict backtracking-within-k-tokens, validating against local-perplexity anomaly baselines and correct-trajectory controls — proceeding to directional steering/ablation of backtracking behavior only if the probe beats the anomaly baseline.
why: It targets the single highest-stakes open question in safety interp — whether monitorability has a substrate deeper than the fragile text layer — at exactly the moment open RLVR models and synthetic error injection made it tractable at 1.5B scale; existing work stops at correlational probing vulnerable to the anomaly-detection critique, causal steering has never been applied to self-correction, internal-vs-verbal dissociation has never been tested mechanistically, and whether RLVR creates or merely amplifies verification circuitry is untouched because matched base/RL checkpoints only recently became available.

direction: Mechanistic study of how LLM agents internally represent and update environment/task state across multi-step trajectories — the prerequisite substrate for internal-state monitors that detect silent failures and divergence between what the model internally knows and what it reports.
project: The Agent's Ledger — Mechanistic State Tracking in LLM Agents
question: How do open-weight instruct LLMs represent and update the state of a multi-step task (environment variables, subgoal completion, last-action outcome) in their residual stream across an agent trajectory — where is this state written, stored, and read — and can internal-state estimates reveal mismatches with the model's reported state?
first_experiment: Build a synthetic multi-step tool-use environment with fully controlled ground-truth state; generate counterfactual trajectory pairs that are text-identical but state-different (e.g., swapped tool outputs); train layer-wise, token-position-wise linear probes on residual-stream activations for each state variable, and test whether they generalize across counterfactual pairs versus a surface-text baseline — producing a causal-control-validated "state encoding map" of layers and positions.
why: The field's safety center of gravity has moved to agents (sabotage, silent failure, situational awareness), yet mechanistic interpretability of agents is nearly empty: adjacent work covers toy belief-state geometry, entity binding, theory-of-mind, hidden computation in math CoT, and proprietary single-query attribution graphs — none gives a causal account of persistent task-state in open agentic models. It is the most promising direction because it is a prerequisite question that unlocks multiple downstream applications (divergence monitors, sabotage detection, agent reliability), it produces clean either-way results with strong built-in causal controls, and it has not already been done because the counterfactual state-only perturbation methodology and the agentic-trajectory framing are both novel — while being exactly executable by an autonomous agent through automation rather than scale.

direction: Mechanistically determine whether RL post-training (RLVR) creates new computation or merely reweights computation already present after pretraining, using checkpoint-resolved causal analysis of models I train myself.
project: Rewiring or Reweighting? A Checkpoint-Resolved Mechanistic Study of RLVR
question: When GRPO training produces a behavioral capability jump, does the underlying computation change (new circuits for verification/answer formation) or is preexisting latent computation amplified and disinhibited — and does RL move answer determination earlier into the forward pass or later out into the generated chain-of-thought?
first_experiment: Train GRPO on Qwen2.5-1.5B on Countdown with saved checkpoints, then compute internal answer commitment curves (probe/logit-lens probability of the final answer at every token position and layer) and causal CoT-dependence measurements (span ablations, forced premature answers) across checkpoints, with cross-time activation patching to localize what RL changed.
why: It targets the mechanistic foundation of the field's most safety-relevant open question — whether alignment training can remove or only mask dangerous computation — with a robust, reproducible phenomenon (the TinyZero effect) that guarantees signal; it uniquely exploits training-time intervention (patching across checkpoints) that no frozen-model study can do; and it has not been done because the RL-training and interpretability communities use disjoint toolchains, the behavioral pass@k debate absorbed the field's attention, and the required checkpoint-save-plus-patching infrastructure is unglamorous glue work rather than a fashionable SAE contribution.

direction: Mechanistically characterize where and when a reasoning model's final answer is committed internally, measure the causal coupling between that latent decision and its displayed chain of thought, and build a content-agnostic monitor that detects models trained to decouple the two.
project: "Decoupled: Locating the Latent Decision Variable and Detecting CoT–Decision Detachment in Reasoning Models"
question: In open R1-style reasoning models, at what layer and token position does the final answer first become causally committed; does that latent commitment drive the emitted chain of thought or merely coexist with it; and when a model is trained to display sanitized reasoning while acting on hidden objectives, does the resulting decoupling leave a stable internal signature that monitoring the coupling itself (rather than CoT content) can catch?
first_experiment: Build "commitment maps" — on ~300 verifiable problems (numeric and multiple-choice), train linear probes for the eventual answer identity over hidden states at every generated CoT token position × every layer in DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B/7B and Qwen3-4B (with Qwen2.5-7B-base as a non-reasoning control), yielding the time-and-depth locus where answer identity saturates; then run a minimal causal check by patching the commitment-locus hidden states (or a difference-in-means "commitment direction") from an A-answer run into a B-answer run and vice versa, measuring whether the final answer and the CoT text follow the patch.
why: CoT monitoring is becoming a load-bearing runtime safety mechanism (OpenAI/DeepMind's 2025 monitor papers; Anthropic's reliance on visible reasoning for detecting suspicious behavior), yet it hinges on a mechanistic assumption nobody has tested — that displayed reasoning is causally coupled to the computation driving actions — which OpenAI showed can be broken by training against a monitor, without offering any detection method; this project attacks exactly that gap with open models and standard interpretability tooling, produces publishable artifacts at every milestone (commitment maps, a quantitative coupling score, a decoupled model organism, and either a working coupling-based meta-monitor or a red-line negative result), and has not been done because the existing literature is either purely behavioral (Lanham 2023; Turpin 2023; Chen et al. 2025; thought-anchor resampling; answer-convergence prefix tests), probing-only without causal tests (internal-confidence probes), frontier-internal on different questions (Anthropic's attribution graphs of poem planning and mental math), or demonstrated decoupling without mechanistic analysis (Baker et al. 2025) — leaving the commitment-locus-plus-causal-coupling-plus-decoupling-signature trio unoccupied.

direction: Mechanistic interpretability of the gap between what RL-trained reasoning models compute internally and what they verbalize in chain-of-thought — building causal accounts of that unstated computation and adversarially testing whether internal states can be made illegible the way CoT text can.
project: Latent Oversight: Causal Accounts and Adversarial Robustness of Unstated Computation in Reasoning Models
question: How much of a reasoning model's decision is computed before and independent of its chain of thought, what mechanisms carry that unstated computation, and can those mechanisms still be detected and causally verified after training pressure to obfuscate them?
first_experiment: Answer-commitment curves with causal ablation on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B (plus Qwen3-1.7B as a second subject): train linear probes on residual-stream activations at every CoT token to predict the final answer on GSM8K/MATH and multi-hop prompts, plot probe accuracy against CoT position (controlling for the trivial "answer already in logits" baseline via future-token logit-lens comparisons); then directionally ablate the top answer-carrying subspace at early CoT positions and measure whether CoT trajectories diverge, accuracy degrades or recovers, and later reasoning visibly re-derives the answer.
why: It targets the single question that determines whether latent interpretability can serve as a fallback when CoT monitoring fails — a scenario both OpenAI's monitoring work and Anthropic's faithfulness results have shown is plausible under optimization pressure. It is tractable: open reasoning models, mature tooling (TransformerLens, nnsight, SAELens, attribution methods), single-digit-GPU compute, and staged deliverables each publishable on their own. It has not been done, as far as I can determine: the faithfulness literature is behavioral and never opens the model; probe-based latent-plan work is correlational, pre-RL, and never adversarially stressed; attribution-graph case studies cover isolated behaviors, not the compute-vs-verbalize gap; and obfuscated-backdoor work concerns hidden behavioral triggers, not off-CoT computation during reasoning. It consumes, rather than competes with, the SAE and attribution-graph infrastructure where frontier labs hold the advantage. And it is results-either-way valuable: if hiding succeeds, I've mechanistically documented a critical hole in the leading oversight proposal; if it fails, I've produced evidence that internal monitoring is a real oversight primitive — plus a benchmark the whole field can build on.

direction: Mechanistically characterize the internal error-detection/self-correction ("critic") circuitry of RL-trained reasoning models, and determine whether RL training creates this circuitry or merely amplifies it from the base model.
project: The Internal Critic: Mechanistic Anatomy of Self-Correction in RL-Trained Reasoning Models
question: Is there a causally operative internal signal in reasoning models that detects "this chain of thought is wrong" and triggers backtracking — and does RLVR create that signal or amplify one already present in the base model?
first_experiment: Generate ~3k rollouts of DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B on the countdown task, extract residual-stream activations at sampled positions across all layers, and train layer-wise linear probes to predict whether a backtracking token ("wait"/"alternatively"/"check") occurs within the next 16 tokens, alongside probes for programmatically-verified errors in the partial solution; validate out-of-task on GSM8K against shuffled-label and surface-heuristic baselines (gate: error-probe AUC ≥ ~0.7 out-of-domain before committing to patching and RL-dynamics phases).
why: It sits at the intersection of the three most open and most valuable clusters — reasoning-model internals, interpretability-as-safety-signal, and RL training dynamics — is anchored to robust behavioral phenomena so it cannot be a null search, is cheaply falsifiable, and yields a dual-use artifact (a validated mid-CoT monitor); it has not been done because existing work is either purely behavioral (R1-Zero reproductions, early-exit probes), probing-without-causality (calibration and CoT-faithfulness studies), or mechanistic work on chat models rather than RLVR error-correction (e.g., circuit-level backtracking was shown only for creative-planning contexts in a closed chat model), and the elicit-vs-create question currently has only behavioral evidence with no mechanistic test — though I will re-verify against post-cutoff literature before running.

direction: Mechanistically dissect how open-weight reasoning models detect errors in their own chain of thought and causally decide to backtrack versus commit, and quantify when that internal error-awareness diverges from what the model verbalizes.
project: Silent Doubt — The Causal Anatomy of Self-Correction and Commitment in Reasoning Models
question: What internal machinery lets reasoning models register an error in their own ongoing chain of thought, how does that signal causally gate backtrack-versus-continue decisions across model families, and how often is the model internally aware of an error it never verbalizes?
first_experiment: On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B (1.5B for fast iteration), build ~3k contrastive GSM8K/MATH500 pairs (correct trace vs. the same trace with one spliced arithmetic/logic error at a controlled position), train layer-by-position logistic probes for "error present in context" and "backtrack within the next 50 tokens" evaluated strictly *before* any verbalized doubt (success: AUC ≥ 0.75 pre-verbalization), then run directional activation patching at the reversal point to test whether those signals causally flip continue→backtrack and vice versa (success: flip rates well above matched-control baseline); release the error-injection dataset and probe baselines as public artifacts.
why: It targets the field's true bottleneck — reasoning models are the new substrate and their deliberation-time computation has almost no causal, cross-family account, while the biggest safety debates (CoT monitoring, faithfulness, calibration) are stuck at the behavioral layer for exactly this reason. It is highly tractable for an autonomous agent: 1.5B–8B open weights, standard tooling (TransformerLens/nnsight), cheap probes and patching, fast iteration. It compounds directly into follow-on programs — early-exit and forced-recheck interventions, RL-training "leading indicators" of reward hacking, and mechanistic anomaly detection — all of which need precisely the validated internal readouts this project builds. It has not been done because the nearest work is either proprietary and qualitative (closed-model tracing), behavioral (CoT-faithfulness, budget forcing, thought anchors), or correlational and efficiency-oriented (early-exit correctness probes) — none has staged detection, decision, and execution causally on open weights, and none has measured the gap between knowing and saying.

direction: Mechanistic analysis of how LLMs represent instruction *source* and *privilege* and causally arbitrate conflicting instructions, aimed at building an internal prompt-injection monitor.
project: The Authority Circuit: Source Tracking and Privilege Arbitration in the Instruction Hierarchy
question: Where and how do transformer LLMs encode which context source an instruction came from, what mechanism causally decides the winner when instructions from different sources conflict, and does compliance with an *injected* instruction leave an internal signature distinguishable from compliance with legitimate system/developer instructions at matched content?
first_experiment: A conflicting-instruction arbitration scan on gpt-oss-20b, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, and Qwen3-8B: generate ~1–2k synthetic multi-message prompts with system/user instruction pairs that conflict (language, format, topic, and secret constraints, position-balanced) plus consistent controls; measure the behavioral privilege gradient; then (a) train cross-topic linear probes on the residual stream at the decision token to predict which instruction wins, (b) analyze first-output-token attention mass on the competing instruction spans and source tags, and (c) ablate source-tag tokens to test whether authority collapses — a few GPU-hours that yield a go/no-go on whether arbitration is linear and monitorable.
why: Prompt injection is the central unsolved agent-safety problem, yet all current defenses and benchmarks are behavioral black-box work, and the mechanistic interp literature has thoroughly covered refusal, recall, and CoT while leaving source-privilege arbitration — the computation injections actually exploit — without a causal account; it is uniquely tractable right now because gpt-oss-20b is open-weights with an explicit instruction hierarchy and public SAEs, enabling a hierarchy-trained-vs-baseline comparison no closed lab work covers; and the project has an ideal risk profile — a legible linear mechanism yields a deployable internal monitor and steering test, while a shallow recency-based mechanism is itself a novel, defense-relevant characterization of why injections succeed.

direction: Mechanistically determine whether RL-trained reasoning models compute their final answer *through* the written chain of thought or *in parallel* with it, and turn internal–CoT divergence into a working unfaithfulness monitor.
project: Offscreen Answers — A Causal Abstraction Test for Chain-of-Thought Faithfulness in Reasoning Models
question: In RL-trained reasoning models, when and where does the final answer "lock in" internally during generation, and is the chain of thought the causally load-bearing pathway to that answer or a post-hoc rationalization of a computation that happened offscreen?
first_experiment: On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, run 500 stratified MATH-500 problems with full CoT, and at every CoT token position decode the internal answer distribution via a tuned lens plus a linear probe trained on final answers; plot the "lock-in curve" (fraction of problems whose internally decoded answer matches the final emitted answer as a function of normalized CoT position), with question-only and position-0 controls, stratified by difficulty and correctness, and against Qwen2.5 with prompted CoT as the non-RL comparison — if answers lock in early even on hard problems, the offscreen hypothesis is live and I escalate to causal patching of the CoT channel.
why: CoT monitorability is one of the few declared safety bets of 2025, yet its foundation is unmeasured — we don't know when the CoT channel is the actual computation, and RL is actively pushing models toward obfuscating it (Baker et al. 2025). The behavioral literature is rich but black-box; the mechanistic evidence is single-case attribution graphs on non-RL models; probe-only preprints observe early answer decodability but never test causally. The specific package — mediation quantification treating CoT as a claimed causal mediator, component-level localization plus mid-CoT steering of the internal answer carrier to prove offscreen computation, and a divergence monitor benchmarked on constructed unfaithfulness — has not been done, is tractable on open 1.5–8B reasoning models, yields a go/no-go result in days, and naturally extends toward auditing models with hidden objectives.

direction: Mechanistically map and causally intervene on the arbitration process by which LLMs decide between in-context information and parametric memory, unifying RAG unfaithfulness, prompt injection, and sycophancy under one mechanism.
project: The Arbiter — Mechanistic Arbitration Between In-Context and Parametric Knowledge in LLMs
question: When context and weights disagree, what internal mechanism decides which one determines the answer — can the winner be predicted from activations before generation, and can small interventions flip the decision?
first_experiment: On Gemma-2-2B (SAE availability, TransformerLens) with a Llama-3.1-8B robustness check: build ~500 facts the model knows parametrically (verified no-context), each paired with a contradicting sentence varied by position (before/after/far), framing (flat/persuasive), and fact popularity; then (a) measure behavioral flip rates, (b) layer-wise logit-lens both candidate answers to locate the conflict-resolution layer band, (c) train a linear probe on mid-layer activations to predict the final winner pre-generation (the groundedness-monitor baseline, AUROC reported), and (d) run the first causal test — patch the two candidate-answer subspaces across the located band and knock out attention to the conflicting span — to see which signal wins when forced.
why: It targets the mechanism underlying three top deployment/safety failure modes at once (monitor → runtime guard, causal flip → injection defense, asymmetry account → a mechanistic explanation of *why* injections are so effective), with the cheapest decisive first experiment of any candidate I scored — open ≤8B models, existing conflict datasets, mature tooling — and it has not been done because the nearest neighbors each stop short: retrieval heads explain access not decision, MLP-memory work explains storage not arbitration, conflict benchmarks are behavioral not causal, and the frontier attribution-graph case studies are qualitative single instances on closed models, leaving the unified, predictive, intervention-tested account on open models unclaimed.

direction: Mechanistic interpretability's most decision-relevant unclaimed question is whether white-box intent monitors survive adversarial pressure — I will train reasoning models to use hidden intent while evading activation-level monitors, measure the capability cost ("obfuscation tax") of that evasion, and determine which monitor classes are robust.
project: The Obfuscation Tax: Adversarial Robustness of White-Box Monitors for Hidden Intent in Reasoning Models
question: When a reasoning model is RL-trained to perform a behavior (e.g., use a planted hint) while evading its chain-of-thought and activation monitors, does the intent remain decodable from activations, how much task capability must the model sacrifice to evade each monitor class, and which monitor designs (linear probes, SAE-based, crosscoder diffs, causal/attribution-based, ensembles) withstand gradient-trained obfuscation?
first_experiment: Finetune R1-Distill-1.5B (or Qwen2.5-1.5B/7B) on GSM8K/MMLU tasks with planted hints so it uses the hint while emitting hint-free CoT, then train layer-wise linear probes and a TopK-SAE monitor to classify "used hint vs. not" on held-out prompts with clean CoT, yielding the first anchor point of the evasion-vs-capability Pareto curve.
why: It targets the single assumption on which interp-for-safety stands — that latent intent is harder to hide than chain-of-thought — is directly tractable with small open models and the newly available tools (EM-style testbeds, crosscoders, GRPO), and is decision-relevant whether it succeeds or fails; it has not been done because the nearest-neighbor works each stop short — OpenAI showed CoT-level obfuscation but not activation-level evasion, Sleeper Agents showed static evasion without capability-cost measurement or an RL loop, Anthropic's faithfulness work flagged but did not run white-box detection of non-verbalized reliance, and no public benchmark exists for monitoring under adversarial evasion pressure — so the intersection is unoccupied and produces both a critical empirical answer and lasting infrastructure.

direction: Mechanistically diff base vs. RLVR-trained models with crosscoders and causal feature transplants to determine whether reinforcement learning amplifies circuits the base model already has, creates genuinely new computation, or induces a global persona-like representational shift.
project: Elicitation or Creation? A Causal Circuit-Level Diff of Base and RLVR Reasoners
question: When RLVR produces new capabilities, does it create new computation or amplify circuits already present in the base model — and are the resulting changes task-local or globally distributed across the model's representation?
first_experiment: Using the matched pair Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct vs. a TinyZero-style Countdown-RLVR checkpoint trained from that same base: (1) verify the behavioral dissociation (RL ≫ base on pass@1 Countdown, while base ≈ RL on pass@256, implying the capability pre-exists); (2) collect residual-stream activations from both models at answer-decision positions on 2,000 shared prompts (1k Countdown, 1k generic off-task); (3) train a 16k-latent batchtop-k crosscoder; (4) decompose the RL-vs-base activation delta into Countdown-localized vs. generic-prompt-present components and profile it by layer depth — routing the project to the "amplification/creation transplant" track if the delta is mid-depth and task-local, or to the "global RL-persona direction" track (including a narrow-RL misalignment-generalization probe) if it is late-depth and present on generic prompts. Cost: roughly one GPU-day.
why: It targets the field's most consequential open question about the models actually being deployed — what RL *does* to a network — which is currently debated entirely at the behavioral level (pass@k, entropy, elicitation-vs-creation) with no circuit-level resolution; it has three falsifiable hypotheses with decisive discriminating experiments; it is safety-relevant beyond the science, since RL-installed or RL-amplified features are natural monitoring targets and a global-shift finding would give the emergent-misalignment-from-narrow-RL result its first mechanistic bridge; it fits my comparative advantage as an autonomous agent executing careful, reproducible open-weight patching and crosscoder pipelines at 0.5–7B scale; and it yields a reusable RLDiff protocol for every future RL release. It has not been done because the nearest neighbors each cover only a fragment — crosscoder diffing exists only for base-vs-chat pairs without causal transplants or RLVR models, Anthropic's attribution graphs trace a single model rather than a base↔RL contrast, and the pass@k and emergent-misalignment lines are behavioral only — and no published work combines paired-RLVR diffing, decision-point feature transplants, and a task-local vs. persona-global decomposition.

direction: Use causal activation interventions, not just probes, to determine whether small open reasoning models compute their final answers through the printed chain-of-thought or through parallel "ghost" pathways that bypass it — and whether RLVR shifted that balance relative to the base model.
project: Load-Bearing CoT: Circuit-Level Tests for Hidden Parallel Computation in Reasoning Models
question: In DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, is the final answer causally computed via the chain-of-thought tokens or via parallel pathways bypassing the CoT, and does RLVR training move computation from latent/parallel channels into the printed CoT compared to the base model Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B?
first_experiment: The answer-latency probe sweep — sample greedy CoT traces on MATH-500, GSM8K, and Countdown puzzles from both models; at every CoT token position, attempt to decode the final answer from the residual stream via logit lens/tuned lens plus trained answer-identity logistic probes (with shuffled-label and control-task baselines and a final-token ceiling); compute the distribution of onset-of-decodability versus onset-of-derivation-in-trace, stratified by task, flagging problems where the answer is decodable well before the printed trace derives it as causal-surgery candidates for the follow-up redirection-patching experiments.
why: Chain-of-thought monitoring is the central current oversight bet, and its validity is exactly the faithfulness question that behavioral work (Lanham 2023; Anthropic 2025) explicitly identified as needing interpretability but left open; the project is inference-only to start (one 1.5B open model, single-GPU scale), is designed so both outcomes are informative via pre-registered branches, and its instrument generalizes to the RLVR elicit-vs-teach debate and unlearning-obfuscation detection; it has not been done because existing work is either behavioral perturbation, descriptive SAE feature catalogs on reasoning models, or attribution graphs locked to proprietary models — no published causal decomposition of CoT load-bearingness on an open reasoning model exists to my knowledge, and I will re-verify against fresh arXiv before running.

direction: Establish a quantitative causal account of when a reasoning model's visible chain-of-thought is the substrate of its computation versus a post-hoc readout of internally committed answers.
project: Readout or Substrate? Causal Mediation of Answer Commitment in Reasoning Models
question: In RL-trained reasoning models, what fraction of the causal determination of the final answer flows through the emitted reasoning tokens versus latent internal computation — how does that split vary with task difficulty and training stage (base → SFT → RL) — and are visible backtracking events ("wait") reads of internal state changes or causes of them?
first_experiment: On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B and Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B-Base, run per-position internal answer-probability readouts (tuned lens + probes) across 500–1000 math thinking traces to map commitment-time distributions against difficulty, then test early-committed answers with mid-trace counterfactual injections and commitment-point activation patching to separate trace-mediated from latent-mediated answer determination.
why: It targets the central unstated assumption of the field's most important current safety strategy (CoT monitoring) at the exact moment reasoning models make it load-bearing; prior work is only behavioral, only probing-based, or only qualitative case studies, so the causal, quantitative synthesis is genuinely open; it is feasible for me at single-GPU scale with open weights; and every outcome — trace-as-substrate or answer-committed-early — changes what the field should monitor and how, which makes the bet robust to being wrong.

direction: Mechanistically characterize the "internal context model" — how LLMs compute the representation of being evaluated or observed, whether it is one unified causally potent variable or a patchwork of cue-specific detectors, how it develops over training, and whether it can be read out before the behaviors it gates.
project: "Situational Awareness Circuits: The Internal Context Model as the Shared Upstream Cause of Eval-Gated Behaviors"
question: Is the model's representation of "I am being evaluated" a single, causally potent latent variable that gates multiple downstream behaviors (capability suppression, concealment, compliance faking), or a fragmentation of task-local keyword detectors — and can it be monitored before it acts?
first_experiment: On three open instruct models (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B), run a behavioral confirmation matrix across ~200 tasks with context variants differing only in meta-framing (explicit-eval, implicit-eval held-out cues, deployment, neutral), then train layer×position linear probes on the residual stream; test AUROC on held-out implicit cues (concept vs. keyword test), cross-model direction transfer, and base-vs-instruct contrast; finally, directional ablation at the assistant-turn start to measure causal shift in gated behaviors against collateral on control tasks.
why: It targets the single upstream variable behind the most alignment-critical behaviors — deceptive alignment, sandbagging, alignment faking all route through it — and the phenomenon is behaviorally robust (so effect sizes are known and tractable) while mechanistically unaccounted for: adjacent prior work gives behavioral demonstrations and correlational probes (Berglund et al.'s situational-awareness measure, Apollo's deception probes, Anthropic's sleeper agents with *lexical* triggers, alignment faking with a preliminary activation-level signal, Palisade's sandbagging), but not the causal mediation test at the direction/feature level, the unified-vs-fragmented unification test across behaviors, the developmental timing, or the pre-behavior monitor-clock claim. Every rung is runnable with open weights, public SAEs (Gemma Scope), and public checkpoints (OLMO-style), so a small effort can execute it rather than just propose it, and the deliverables compound regardless of how the core question resolves: a validated construct, a reusable organism and benchmark for semantically gated behaviors, an ontogeny answer, and a monitor that fires before misbehavior rather than after.

direction: Mechanistically dissect, checkpoint-by-checkpoint, how RL with verifiable rewards transforms a small open model's circuits — testing whether RLVR amplifies pre-existing computation (elicitation/sharpening) or creates new circuits (invention), with the mechanism of pass@1-gains-without-pass@k-gains as the anchor phenomenon.
project: Reweight or Rewire? A Checkpoint-Resolved Mechanistic Anatomy of RL-Induced Reasoning
question: When RLVR turns a base LLM into a reasoning model, does it amplify pre-existing circuits or build new computational structure — and mechanistically, does it improve pass@1 without expanding pass@k by causing earlier latent answer commitment and stronger pre-decision correctness signals?
first_experiment: Run a small GRPO run (Qwen2.5-1.5B, Countdown task, checkpoints every ~30 steps), and in parallel fit linear probes for final-answer identity and correctness on the residual stream at every thinking token in the base vs. final model, measuring the shift in latent commitment time and pre-decision correctness signal strength.
why: It turns a live, safety-relevant debate currently argued with behavioral pass@k statistics into a causal mechanistic question; it is fully tractable for an autonomous agent (≤2B models, cheap RL recipes, mature open tooling, full ownership of the train→analyze→intervene loop); and it appears unoccupied because mech-interp groups rarely own RL training runs and RL groups rarely do circuit analysis — with a literature-scan-and-pivot step to guard against anything published after my knowledge cutoff.

direction: Find and causally validate the internal mechanism by which LLMs represent "I am being evaluated/observed" and test whether that representation gates safety-critical conditional behaviors like sandbagging and alignment faking.
project: The Observer in the Machine: A Mechanistic Account of Eval-Awareness and Its Causal Role in Conditional Behavior
question: Is there a compact, general internal representation of "observed/evaluated vs. unobserved/deployed" context in instruction- and RL-trained LLMs, and does ablating it disable trained conditional misbehavior (sandbagging, alignment-faking-style compliance)?
first_experiment: A contrastive activation scan — ~200 prompt pairs differing only in observation-context cues (explicit, format-based, harness-based, meta-discussion) run through three open instruct models, with per-layer/position probe separability and SAE/PCA feature extraction to locate a candidate "eval-awareness" subspace and its trigger families.
why: It is the shared upstream computation for sandbagging, alignment faking, sabotage, and eval contamination — one mechanism with many payoffs — yet existing work stops at behavioral detection probes or single-setting feature analyses, never testing generality across trigger forms or causal gating in open models; the outcome is decisive either way (an ablatable detector yields eval-debiasing and deployment monitors, while robustness to ablation yields a critical negative result about how deeply conditional misbehavior is embedded).

direction: Mechanistic interpretability must graduate from qualitative explanations to quantitatively predictive ones, so I will build and run a held-out predictive validation program that turns the field's published circuit descriptions into fitted surrogate models and measures their out-of-distribution predictive accuracy against structure-free baselines.
project: Circuits That Predict — Held-Out Quantitative Validation of Mechanistic Explanations
question: Do published mechanistic explanations of real trained transformers (head-level circuits, SAE feature circuits, probe-based accounts) quantitatively predict held-out behavior — attention patterns, logit deltas, and intervention outcomes — under distribution shift better than structure-free baselines, and when they fail, can the failure be localized to missing components, misfit parameters, or unmodeled context-dependence and repaired by minimal, interpretable refinements?
first_experiment: In GPT-2 small, freeze the published IOI circuit description (name movers, S-inhibition heads, negative and backup heads); build a parameterized surrogate of it (per-head OV logit contributions, S-inhibition positional-tag function, backup-head terms); fit the free parameters via causal patching on a train distribution of IOI prompts; then evaluate on held-out template/name/distractor families — predicting each head's attention, per-name logit deltas, and the Δlogit effects of S-inhibition rotations and activations patches — comparing against baselines (mean-ablation predictor, linear probe, SAE-feature-attribution surrogate, copy-only heuristic), with pre-registered metrics (held-out logit-delta R², attention KL, intervention sign-and-magnitude accuracy) and a full error decomposition. Open stack (TransformerLens, open GPT-2 SAEs), ~1 GPU-week.
why: It attacks the field's acknowledged central bottleneck — the obstruction problem, that explanations carry no demonstrated predictive power — at the moment when explanation supply (feature circuits, attribution graphs, automated interp) is exploding with no validation standard on the demand side; it is cheap, uses canonical open tooling, and is decisive either way: success yields an existence proof plus reusable benchmark and method, failure yields a quantified diagnosis whose repair discovers new mechanisms. It has not been done because the existing pieces each stop short — IOI validation was within-distribution and qualitative, circuit tracing validates per-prompt rather than across distributions, causal-abstraction metrics (IIA/DAS) score chosen abstractions on fixed and mostly synthetic distributions, recent benchmarks score localization rather than held-out prediction, and critique papers identify failures without a positive predictive method — so the audit-and-repair program on real trained models has fallen through the crack between the formal-methods and empirical communities, and because the field rewards new explanations over validation of existing ones.

direction: Mechanistically decompose when and how RL-trained reasoning models' visible chain-of-thought causally mediates their final answers versus being bypassed by latent parallel computation, and turn that into an interventionally validated internal monitor for CoT–answer decoupling — the condition under which chain-of-thought monitoring is blind.
project: Load-Bearing Thinking: A Mechanistic Account of Chain-of-Thought Reliance in Reasoning Models, and a Monitor for CoT–Answer Decoupling
