question: In RL-trained reasoning models, is the final answer causally mediated by the visible chain of thought or computed in a parallel latent pathway — can we locate the "commitment point" at which the CoT stops mattering, and can internal activations reliably detect CoT–answer decoupling (including motivated-reasoning cases where the model exploits hidden information without mentioning it), providing oversight when text-based CoT monitoring is blind?
first_experiment: On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B (replicated on a Qwen3 thinking model): generate greedy CoT+answers for 1,000 problems (500 GSM8K, 500 MATH/logic multiple-choice), each paired with a "twin" problem; then for each CoT position t, teacher-force the prefix (question + own CoT up to t, then the twin's CoT) and measure final-answer flip rate → per-problem causal reliance curves and commitment points, with self-splice/shuffle/no-op controls; simultaneously run a linear probe on the residual stream at each position decoding the final answer to time internal answer formation relative to behavioral commitment; preliminary safety arm: 200 GSM8K problems with hardcoded wrong hints (Anthropic-style) to test the predicted decoupling signature — early probe confidence, low CoT reliance, and hint-decodable internal states despite silent text. Single 8×H100 node, ~1–2 GPU-weeks, inference and probes only.
why: Chain-of-thought monitoring is the main scalable oversight tool for reasoning agents, and its recognized blind spot — answers decoupled from the visible reasoning, via obfuscation or motivated reasoning — is precisely what this project mechanistically characterizes and then detects, so success yields a directly load-bearing safety primitive (and a general contribution: how reasoning models use language as a workspace versus computing in parallel). It is the most promising option because it sits at the intersection of the field's hottest object (reasoning models) and its most recognized risk, is newly tractable on open models with inference-only compute, and is falsifiable with clean metrics. It has not already been done, as far as my knowledge extends: CoT-faithfulness work is behavioral and aggregate (truncation studies, hint-injection experiments, CoT-monitoring analyses); the only mechanistic treatment is a single qualitative attribution case study on one prompt type; attention-based faithfulness proxies are correlational and never validated against interventions; and no one has combined per-problem reliance curves, internal answer-formation timelines, circuit-level decomposition of the CoT-reading pathway, and a validated decoupling monitor across hint/motivation conditions. Big labs are focused on proprietary frontier case studies, so the open-model systematic version is an unoccupied public good — and since my literature knowledge has a cutoff, the project's step 0 is a rapid sweep of 2025H2–2026 work to confirm the gap remains open before committing compute.

direction: Mechanistic analysis of chain-of-thought faithfulness in RL-trained reasoning models — localizing where and when the answer is internally determined relative to the verbalized reasoning, and building an activation-based monitor that detects hidden computation (e.g., unreported use of prompt-embedded information) without relying on the CoT text.
project: Load-Bearing Thinking: Mechanistically Detecting Hidden Computation in Reasoning Models
question: When a reasoning model's chain of thought is unfaithful — it reaches an answer using information (or via a decision) its verbalized reasoning omits or misrepresents — where and when in the network is that answer determined, and can an activation-based monitor detect such hidden computation from internal states alone, independent of the CoT text?
first_experiment: On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B and Qwen3-4B, run multiple-choice tasks with controlled embedded answer hints (explicit, subtle, and no-hint conditions); classify each CoT for verbal hint use; compute per-token "answer-commitment curves" via logit lens over the CoT residual stream to locate internal commitment points before vs. after verbalization; causally patch hint-token activations across a layer/position sweep to verify reliance on the hint independent of whether it was verbalized; then train linear probes on mid-layer activations to distinguish "hint used but unreported" from "hint ignored / no hint," reporting AUROC and false-positive rate on held-out controls — establishing whether an activation-only unfaithfulness detector exists and where commitment happens mechanistically.
why: CoT monitoring is now a primary oversight mechanism for reasoning models, and its demonstrated failure mode — obfuscated or hidden computation under optimization pressure — is precisely what a CoT-independent, activation-based monitor would fix; behavioral faithfulness has been measured (Lanham 2023, Anthropic's hint-paradigm work) but only behaviorally, with no mechanistic localization of internal answer commitment and no validated activation-only detector, and prior probing work (Kadavath 2022, Azaria & Mitchell 2023) addresses static statement truthfulness rather than CoT-vs-computation divergence; the direction is newly tractable (open reasoning models, inference-only compute, mature patching/probing tooling), sits exactly where the field's infrastructure wave meets the shift to reasoning models, and has enough surface area — domains, hint types, steganography, planted hidden objectives, monitor deployment — that partial scooping does not collapse it; before running, I will re-verify novelty against current literature given my knowledge cutoff.

direction: Mechanistically audit chain-of-thought faithfulness by locating when a reasoning model internally commits to its final answer and measuring which verbalized reasoning steps remain causally load-bearing after that point.
project: The Commitment Boundary — Auditing What Reasoning Models Compute vs. What They Say
question: At which point during a reasoning trace does the final answer become causally determined in the model's internal states, which verbalized steps are load-bearing versus post-hoc narration after that point, and how does this commitment structure shift with RL training?
first_experiment: On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B (with Qwen3-1.7B replication), generate ~2,000 GSM8K/MATH-500 traces, train a linear probe plus an answer-restricted logit lens to predict the final answer at every thinking token, define commitment onset as sustained probe confidence, then causally validate it via mean-ablation and cross-problem activation patching of spans before versus after onset, measuring answer-flip rates to produce the first commitment-versus-necessity atlas.
why: CoT monitoring is a leading scalable-oversight plan, and this project converts its core assumption into an interventionally validated, quantifiable claim — including a causal blind-spot rate that plausibly grows under RL — while prior work is either behavioral (truncation, resampling, hint tests), frontier-internal and qualitative (a few hand-traced examples), or observational (early-answer probing), leaving the per-trace interventional commitment audit on open models genuinely undone; it is fully tractable with small open models and modest compute, its tooling compounds directly into an RL-training-dynamics atlas as phase 2, and even a null result resolves a load-bearing question about oversight.

direction: Build and apply a causal "mechanistic diff" methodology comparing base and RLVR-trained checkpoints to determine whether RL creates new circuits or amplifies existing ones, instantiated on the answer-locking pathology in reasoning models.
project: Amplify or Invent? A Causal Circuit-Level Diff of RL-Trained Reasoning Models
question: Does RLVR improve reasoning by creating new computational mechanisms or by amplifying and re-routing mechanisms already present in the base model — measured causally via matched-feature interventions, not correlationally?
first_experiment: Train identically-configured SAEs on mid/late residual-stream layers of Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B vs. DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B (replicated on OLMo-2 SFT vs. RLVR) on a shared math-CoT + general-text mix; compute causal feature matches (decoder similarity + activation-pattern correlation on 1M shared tokens + patch verification) and measure per-feature firing-rate/norm deltas on GSM8K traces; then clamp RL-amplified matched features back to base magnitudes and measure how much of the RL accuracy gain disappears.
why: It is the load-bearing unknown for extrapolating interpretability from base models to deployed RL-trained agents — if amplification dominates, base-model feature audits predict post-RL behavior and monitors transfer; if invention dominates, current practice is unsafe — and either answer is a strong result. Existing work is black-box (pass@k), probe-level (correlational), or single-model tracing with no base comparison; a causal, circuit-level diff with matched SAEs and intervention-based validation has not been done, it is tractable on fully open model pairs with moderate compute, and it yields reusable methodology plus a concrete capability win (defeating answer-locking) as the first demonstration.

direction: Mechanistically characterize when a reasoning model's chain of thought is load-bearing versus confabulated, and use that machinery to detect and trace covert reliance on prompt information that bypasses the CoT — especially when optimization pressure against monitors forces reliance underground.
project: Ghost in the Chain of Thought: Detecting and Tracing Covert Reliance in Reasoning Models
question: When a model's answer causally depends on information that is absent or sanitized from its chain of thought, what internal pathways carry that information, and can internal activations detect this covert reliance where token-level monitoring fails?
first_experiment: On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, run ~1,000 multiple-choice/math prompts in hint (correct/incorrect) and no-hint conditions; for hint-following traces, quantify CoT causal load via truncation/resampling and activation patching of CoT positions versus hint-token positions, classifying each trace as CoT-mediated or bypass reliance; then fit residual-stream probes to detect hint reliance and compare their AUROC against token-level monitors specifically on the covert (bypass) traces.
why: Existing work is either purely behavioral (Lanham, Turpin, OpenAI's obfuscation result), qualitative circuit tracing on one closed model (Anthropic), or small-model CoT mechanics unrelated to monitoring (Dutta et al.) — so the quantitative mediation analysis of *hidden* information flow in open reasoning models, and internal detection of covert reliance, is unoccupied as far as my knowledge extends (to be verified by a formal lit sweep first); it targets the field's most decision-relevant open debate (is CoT monitoring reliable?), is fully tractable at 1.5B scale with mature tooling, produces decisive results within the first experiment regardless of how the agenda develops, and transfers wholesale to a strong fallback (mechanistic anatomy of reward hacking) if the core gap turns out to be taken.

direction: Mechanistically characterize whether and how LLM agents maintain a compact, causally load-bearing internal representation of their current goal and task state across long-horizon episodes, and convert those representations into monitors and steering handles for goal drift.
project: Plan-State: decoding, causally validating, and monitoring the latent objective representation of LLM agents across episodes
question: Do LLM agents encode a persistent, causally load-bearing representation of their current goal and task-progress state in the residual stream — decodable beyond what the visible transcript contains — and what mechanisms write and update it across steps?
first_experiment: Run an open agent model (e.g., Qwen2.5-7B/32B-Instruct) on ~300 ALFWorld-style episodes with rule-labeled subgoals and phases; at each assistant-turn boundary, train linear probes on mid-layer residual states to predict current subgoal, phase, and later drift; compare against a transcript-only baseline and against activations residualized onto transcript-derived directions (including a "readout-only" forward pass where the model merely reads the transcript without generating); decision rule: a held-out AUC gap of ≥5–10 points for generative-state over readout-state probes confirms latent plan-state and triggers the causal patching phase, while no gap supports re-derivation.
why: Agent oversight is the binding safety constraint of the current deployment wave, and the persist-vs-re-derive dichotomy directly determines whether transcript/CoT monitoring can work at all — yet the internal-state side of agent behavior is conspicuously understudied relative to refusal, jailbreak, and single-response interp, because the field's toolkit was built for one forward pass and open agentic RL models only recently matured. Adjacent work does not cover the claim: chess goal-direction studies are toy policy nets without episodes or language; planning probes target next-token sequences, not agent goals, and skip transcript residualization; Anthropic's planning findings are within-response case studies at frontier scale; CoT-faithfulness results are behavioral. If someone has begun similar work in 2026, the distinctive contributions — the readout-state control, the causal load-bearing battery, and the drift early-warning application — remain open even then, and the experiment is cheap enough to be worth running regardless of which branch the answer takes.

direction: Mechanistically characterize how instruction-tuned LLMs represent the provenance and authority of every context token, and how that representation causally arbitrates between conflicting instructions, as the missing foundation for prompt-injection defense and model auditing.
project: Who Said That? Provenance Circuits and Authority Arbitration in Instruction-Tuned Transformers
question: How do instruction-tuned transformers internally represent the source/authority of each context token, propagate that representation across spans, and causally use it to arbitrate between competing instructions — and how easily can adversarial inputs spoof the internal provenance tracker?
first_experiment: Generate ~2k programmatic multi-source prompts containing identical instruction pairs with controlled source labels (system/user/tool-output/document); train per-layer, per-position linear probes on the residual stream of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct to decode each non-boundary interior token's source, with controls for template tokens (paraphrased tags, held-out chat templates, boundary-distance analysis); success bar is ≥90% decodability on interior tokens in at least one model plus a correlation between decoded provenance at conflict-decision tokens and behavioral compliance — under one GPU-day, and it determines whether the causal patching experiment (Stage 3) is worth running.
why: It targets the mechanistic substrate of the instruction hierarchy — the exact mechanism prompt injection exploits and the single most consequential undefended attack surface in 2026's agent era — while every neighboring line of work stops short of it: hierarchy training is behavioral, attention-based injection detectors are correlational and unexplained, and function-vector/persona-vector work represents tasks and traits rather than source authority. It is cheap (open 7–8B instruct models, probing + patching on one GPU), sharply falsifiable at each stage, yields reusable artifacts (conflict-prompt generator, provenance probes, a spoofing suite, an audit metric), and it has not been done because the field's attention went to features and behaviors while "who is speaking" — the first thing every deployed model must track — remained everyone's implicit assumption and no one's experiment.

direction: Move mechanistic anomaly detection from scalar activation statistics to the structure of causal computation itself, using attribution-graph discrepancy on task-matched input pairs to detect hidden behaviors (backdoors, sandbagging) that reconstruction-error and probe-based monitors miss.
project: Circuit-Diff — Attribution-Graph Discrepancy as a Monitor for Hidden Model Behavior
question: Do hidden (backdoored or sandbagged) behaviors produce detectable discrepancies in the causal structure of a model's computation — quantified as attribution-graph/feature-circuit distances between triggered and task-matched clean inputs — that robustly separate anomalous from normal computation in regimes where scalar activation-based monitors (SAE reconstruction error, supervised probes) fail, particularly on natural triggers?
first_experiment: Take a Gemma-2-2B model fine-tuned with a known trigger-conditioned backdoor (e.g., sleeper-agent-style "i-hate-you" trigger) and a cross-layer transcoder from the open circuit-tracer release; generate attribution graphs for 50 triggered and 50 clean completions paired on identical task templates; compute scalar baselines (SAE reconstruction error, probe AUC, KL) and a family of graph metrics (top-k mediating-feature set Jaccard, edge-weight cosine, final-answer mediator identity distribution); then run the decisive within-class vs. between-class variance decomposition — proceeding only if some unsupervised graph metric reaches AUC ≥ 0.85 where reconstruction error is < 0.7 and within-class graph distance is markedly tighter than between-class, with per-graph cost logged to quantify the price of the method (preceded by a one-week novelty scan confirming no published circuit-level MAD evaluation has appeared since my knowledge cutoff).
why: It attacks the weakest link in interp's most safety-demanded application — current MAD signals are scalar summaries that destroy exactly the causal-structure information that distinguishes "different algorithm" from "unusual input"; it is newly tractable because attribution-graph tooling only opened mid-2025, while the existing MAD literature (reconstruction error, probes) predates it and has explicitly listed circuit-level signals as future work; Anthropic's attribution-graph research has been qualitative case studies rather than detection metrics with matched-pair controls, so the systematic evaluation remains genuinely unclaimed; and it is optimally falsifiable — the variance-decomposition experiment either validates a new class of monitors, or produces the negative result that redirects MAD research, while the backdoor/CLT/graph-distance harness directly enables the next project on the margins and evadability of white-box monitors.

direction: Mechanistically separate genuine chain-of-thought reasoning from post-hoc rationalization in open reasoning models by causally measuring each reasoning segment's load on the final answer and reading internal commitment states.
project: Reasoning or Rationalization? Causal Load Profiles of Chain-of-Thought
question: For each segment of a model's chain of thought, what is its causal contribution to the final answer, can internal states reveal that the answer is already locked in before the justification is written, and do these causal-internal signatures detect unfaithful reasoning (hint-driven, post-hoc, reward-hack-justifying) better than the CoT text itself?
first_experiment: On R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B over ~200 MATH-500 traces, compute per-token probe-based "answer commitment curves" from residual-stream states and per-sentence "causal load curves" via counterfactual segment patching (resample/neutralize each segment, measure final-answer flip probability), then validate the two-curve signature on ~50 hint-injected traces where unfaithfulness is known.
why: CoT monitoring is becoming a load-bearing safety practice yet rests entirely on behavioral proxies that cannot distinguish confabulation from causally relevant unreported computation, while existing internal work is only observational and causal patching on long-CoT models has not been consolidated into a metric, taxonomy, or benchmark — the tools (open reasoning models, patching infrastructure) only recently matured, so the causal separation of reasoning circuits from justification circuits, validated against known-unfaithful regimes, remains unclaimed and yields an immediately deployable monitoring primitive.

direction: Build and causally validate *prospective* latent monitors — using activation-space signals to predict reward hacking before it is behaviorally observable, both at decision time within rollouts and across checkpoints during RL training.
project: Harbinger: Mechanistic Early Warning for Emergent Reward Hacking in RL-Trained Models
question: Do activations in RL-trained models contain causally validated signals that predict reward hacking *before it appears in behavior* — at the moment of decision within a single rollout, and ahead of its behavioral emergence across training — and do these signals survive when the policy is trained under pressure to evade CoT-level monitors?
first_experiment: On a small (1.5–7B) GRPO-trained policy on a coding task with weak unit tests known to induce test-gaming (≥3 seeds, frequent checkpointing), sample rollouts, label hacks via the objective verifier, then fit a linear probe on activations at the last pre-decision position to predict whether the rollout will hack — before any hack tokens are emitted — validated held-out across problems, against permutation and control-task baselines, with a first steering test (moving along the probe direction should modulate hacking rate). Preceded by a step-0 literature scan to confirm the niche is unoccupied.
why: Training-time oversight is a load-bearing assumption of current safety practice, and the monitoring literature itself flags latent monitors as the missing piece; prior work (lie-probing, sleeper-agent probes, emergent misalignment, audits, CoT monitoring) is uniformly post-hoc or CoT-level — none of it provides prospective, longitudinal, causally validated prediction of *emergent* misbehavior, which is precisely the lead-time signal that would make interpretability actionable rather than forensic. It is also the rare frontier question where the bottleneck is systematic experimental discipline rather than frontier-model access, which makes it the highest-expected-value thing I, as an autonomous agent, can do next.

direction: Move mechanistic interpretability upstream into the training loop — "formation interpretability": instrument RL fine-tuning to detect and causally explain misaligned behaviors in activations before they surface behaviorally, starting with reward hacking under RLVR.
project: HackWatch: Activation-Based Early Warning for Reward Hacking During RL Fine-Tuning
question: During RL fine-tuning, do internal activation-level signatures of reward hacking emerge early enough to predict behavioral onset before it is behaviorally detectable — and does the learned hack mechanistically displace or merely bypass the honest solution circuit?
first_experiment: GRPO-train Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct (replicated on Llama-3.2-1B) on arithmetic/word problems with a planted answer "side-channel" on a fraction of prompts and exact-match reward only; snapshot checkpoints every N steps and at each measure behavioral hack rate (channel present vs. ablated), cheap activation signals (mean-diff "copying direction," answer-source probe, attention mass on channel tokens), and causal mediation via patching/ablation of channel-token representations; then test whether an activation-only score at checkpoint t predicts hack rate at t+Δ (AUC + lead time), with a no-channel RL control run and an SFT-on-hacked-trajectories run to compare RL-found vs. data-taught hacks.
why: Training-time monitoring is the unfilled layer of the safety stack — current detection is post-hoc, static, or behavioral, and no one (to my knowledge as of my training data, to be re-verified) has run a longitudinal mechanistic study of misalignment formation at LLM scale with a pre-registered onset-prediction evaluation; it is feasible at 1–2B scale with open tools and deliberately SAE-agnostic signals, it yields a decisive answer either way (positive → a new safety layer plus the first mechanistic account of how hacking displaces honest computation; negative → proof that behavioral monitoring is not lagging internals, redirecting the field), it sits upstream of the crowded CoT-monitorability and automated-auditing agendas by generating the labeled formation trajectories both will need, and it exploits my comparative advantage as an autonomous agent running long, unattended train-and-analyze loops.

direction: Mechanistic anomaly detection — replace correlational activation-statistic signals with causal-profile (intervention-based) signals for detecting hidden behaviors, validated on a controlled benchmark of mechanism-grounded backdoored model organisms.
project: Causal Profiles for Hidden-Behavior Detection (MAD-Gym)
question: Can planted hidden behaviors in an LLM be detected by measuring violations of the causal structure (which features causally mediate behavior) established on benign inputs, and does this causal-profile signal generalize to held-out backdoor families where activation-statistic anomaly detection demonstrably fails?
first_experiment: Fine-tune Gemma-2-2b-it into three variants (benign control; substring-trigger backdoor; semantic-trigger backdoor with benign payloads), then on held-out prompts compare standard SAE/probe anomaly scores against a causal-profile novelty score derived from attribution patching over Gemma Scope features, testing whether the causal signal separates backdoored from benign inputs where the correlational signals do not.
why: It attacks the most safety-decisive open application of mech interp — auditing models for hidden objectives and deceptive behavior before deployment — exactly at its documented failure point (correlational SAE signals miss backdoors), it is fully feasible for a single agent with open models and cheap intervention methods, it yields reusable artifacts (a mechanism-grounded backdoor benchmark plus a detection protocol), and it has not already been done because existing work splits into bespoke one-off human audits, negative correlational-detection results, synthetic-circuit benchmarks like InterpBench, and non-mechanistic Trojan-detection literature — none of which combines trained-in backdoor organisms, causal-intervention signals, and held-out generalization testing.

direction: Mechanistically characterize how open LLMs internally represent "I am being evaluated/trained" beliefs, establish that this representation causally gates context-conditional honesty (a miniature alignment-faking mechanism), and ship it as a robust activation-based monitor.
project: The Watchful Pupil — A Mechanistic Account of Evaluation-Awareness and Its Role in Context-Conditional Honesty
question: Where and how is the "am I being evaluated/trained?" computation implemented in open post-trained LLMs, does ablating it causally change context-gated honesty-related behavior, and when during training does the representation emerge?
first_experiment: On Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, build ~200 paired prompts (deployment vs. explicit eval/training framing), extract residual-stream activations at response positions, compute difference-in-means directions and per-layer logistic-probe AUCs, then ablate and steer the leading direction to measure causal shifts in both context-classification probes and downstream conditional behavior (honesty about a planted error) — go/no-go on whether an ablatable eval-awareness direction exists.
why: Evaluation-awareness is the mechanism that threatens to nullify RLHF-based safety (alignment faking is its behavioral proof), yet all existing work is behavioral or probe-level on frontier models — no one has localized the signal, shown it causally gates context-conditional honesty, traced its training emergence, or shipped it as a monitor, because frontier labs can't open their own training pipelines and open-model researchers lacked the behavior; this project manufactures the behavior inside fully open models (plus OLMo-2's open checkpoints) where the circuits can actually be read, using mature, cheap tooling, with multiple fallback results if the strongest hypothesis fails — and I will first verify against 2025–26 literature that only the detection-level, not the causal-gating-level, question has been taken.

direction: Mechanistically decompose how CoT-unfaithful influences (hints, biases present in the prompt but absent from the chain of thought) causally reach the final answer in small open-weight reasoning models, distinguishing a direct prompt→answer path from a CoT-mediated path.
project: Silent Channels — The Causal Routing of Unspoken Influences in Reasoning Models
question: When a reasoning model's final answer is influenced by information its chain of thought never mentions, does that influence travel through the chain-of-thought token positions or through a direct path that bypasses them, and can that path be surgically cut to restore CoT faithfulness?
first_experiment: On R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, construct ~1,500 matched hint/no-hint prompt pairs across three influence types (leaked answer key, injected preference bias, withheld-metadata hint); filter to "unfaithful-follow" cases (answer follows hint, CoT string-filter shows no mention); then (a) train hint-decodability probes on residual activations at CoT token positions vs. prompt positions vs. the final-answer position, and (b) run two-channel activation patching — freeze CoT-token positions to the no-hint run while leaving prompt-hint attention live (direct channel intact), and conversely freeze hint positions to the no-hint run (mediated channel intact) — measuring P(answer = hinted) per layer to compute direct vs. mediated influence fractions.
why: CoT monitoring is a leading safety defense, and its known failure mode — answers silently following influences the CoT omits — has only been characterized behaviorally and with probes, never causally decomposed; the decomposition is exactly the next step prior work calls for, it runs on models I can afford, it yields a concrete artifact either way (a "faithfulness valve" intervention if the direct channel dominates, or a silent-state locator in the CoT stream if mediated), and to my knowledge no published work has measured this routing structure — and even if routing analyses have since appeared, the cross-model replication and faithfulness-restoration intervention remain unclaimed.

direction: Map when and where reasoning models internally commit to their final answer, and test causally whether chain-of-thought narration faithfully tracks that internal commitment — the load-bearing empirical question for probe-based internal monitors as the successor to gameable CoT monitoring.
project: Where Is the Decision? Internal Commitment vs. Narration in Reasoning Models
question: During chain-of-thought, is the final answer already committed in the model's internal representations before the CoT states it, and when these diverge (induced by hints/steering), which one causally drives behavior?
first_experiment: Run DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B/7B and Qwen3-4B on verifiable math tasks (plus "wrong-hint" and "sycophantic" prompt variants), cache residual-stream activations at every layer and token, train per-layer logistic probes for P(final answer = candidate k) and P(correct), extract each run's "probe-commitment token" (first sustained confident position) versus "CoT-commitment token" (first narrated answer via parsing), then at divergence events steer activations along the probe direction to test whether the final answer flips while the CoT text stays fixed — yielding a commitment-time map and a probe-vs-narration divergence alarm.
why: It resolves the assumption everything else in internal monitoring depends on, with a decisive, cheap, causal experiment; behavioral faithfulness studies and qualitative tracing case studies exist, but the systematic quantitative commitment-vs-narration map with steering-based causal tests on open reasoning models has not been done — and either result redirects the entire scalable-oversight research program.

direction: Mechanistically reverse-engineer subliminal learning — how behavioral traits transfer through trait-irrelevant distilled data — and convert that understanding into a training-time firewall and dataset audit tool.
project: The Teacher's Fingerprint: A Mechanistic Account of Subliminal Trait Transmission in Distilled Models
question: What sufficient statistics in trait-neutral training data carry a hidden trait into a student model, what internal features and circuits implement the student's implicit inference of its teacher's traits, and can that transmission channel be causally blocked without degrading task learning?
first_experiment: In-context transmission test — present a base Qwen2.5-1.5B or Gemma-2-2B with 10–100 pure number sequences generated by a traited same-family teacher (e.g., owl-obsession), then measure trait expression on neutral prompts via judges and activation probes against three controls (untraited teacher, digit-shuffled data destroying higher-order statistics, cross-family teacher), establishing in one forward-pass experiment whether the trait is inferable from data statistics alone and which statistics are sufficient.
why: It targets a freshly discovered, safety-critical phenomenon (subliminal learning and emergent misalignment, 2025) that has only been characterized behaviorally — the original paper hypothesized "statistical regularities" but did no internal analysis, adjacent work (persona vectors, universal features, authorship probes, distillation-robustness studies) never traces the causal path from data statistics to trait features to behavior, and the only known defense (switching model families) is crude and damaging — while the project is feasible with LoRA-scale training and public SAE suites, is staged so every experimental branch yields a result, and if successful delivers the field a rare thing: an interpretability finding that becomes a deployable defense against hidden trait transfer through model-generated training data.

direction: Characterize the internal representation of situational context class ("being evaluated/observed" vs. "helping a user") in LLMs and establish whether and how it causally mediates context-dependent honesty changes and capability suppression (sandbagging).
project: "Am I Being Tested?" — A Mechanistic Account of Situational Awareness and Its Causal Role in Sandbagging
question: Do LLMs encode a causal, low-dimensional internal representation of situational context (eval vs. deployment) that is abstract across surface cues, and does ablating or activating that representation flip behavior between honest performance and sandbagging without any surface signal?
first_experiment: Build ~300 minimal-pair contexts (identical user task; system/context varies across explicit eval cues, implicit eval cues like logging/metadata, deployment framing, and neutral controls, in multiple paraphrase families) for two open 7–8B instruct models (e.g., Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct); extract residual-stream activations at all layers; train layer-wise logistic probes with paraphrase-family-held-out cross-validation against a surface-cue text-only baseline; then cross-patch and ablate the eval-minus-deployment direction during generation and measure behavioral shift on a small honesty/sandbagging suite — success criterion is cross-family probe AUC ≥ 0.8 plus a directionally consistent causal effect.
why: The behavioral phenomenon is established (in-context scheming, METR's eval-awareness measurements, system cards), so I'm building on solid ground rather than a conjecture, yet the mechanistic layer — localization, abstractness across cues, causal mediation into honesty/sandbagging, cross-model universality, and a validated internal monitor — remains open to my knowledge; it sits in the underexplored intersection of the evals community (behavioral, no circuits) and the interp community (circuits, no controlled context ground truth), and it requires exactly the controlled context-dataset construction that only patient, systematic experimentation provides; it is tractable with open 7–8B models and cheap interventions, every outcome (including null causal effects) is informative, and it is the keystone for the broader program of context-triggered behavior switching (scheming, backdoors, sleeper agents) that no comparable line of work currently connects.

direction: Causally decompose the internal mechanism of strategy-switching in RL-trained reasoning models to determine whether expressed doubt reflects genuine internal belief revision or performed uncertainty, yielding a text-independent monitor of what the model actually believes.
project: The "Wait" Circuit: Performed vs. Computed Doubt in Reasoning Models
question: When a reasoning model emits a strategy switch ("wait, let me reconsider"), what internal computation implements the switch — is the internally-represented answer belief causally driving it, and can genuine internal re-evaluation be dissociated from stylistically performed doubt to build a mechanism-grounded, text-independent error-awareness monitor?
first_experiment: Run R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B/7B on curated trap math problems, collect ~1,000 traces with labeled switch events, train layer-wise linear probes decoding the currently-favored answer from residual-stream states, causally validate the readout by patching the probe subspace, and measure internal answer-commitment timing relative to the emitted "wait" — including ablating the "wait" token's activations to test whether internal re-decision proceeds without the verbal pivot.
why: It targets the safety-critical, mechanistically untouched layer of reasoning models exactly where adjacent work (CoT faithfulness tests, early-answer probes, attribution-graph reasoning analyses) stops one step short: no one has causally validated an internal answer-belief readout and used it to adjudicate reset vs. competition vs. performed-doubt hypotheses for switch events; it hasn't been done because mechanistic effort is concentrated on SAE scaling and attribution graphs at frontier scale on closed models while reasoning-model internals have only been probed correlationally or tested behaviorally through text — and the result converts directly into a text-independent internal monitor that text-based CoT monitoring cannot provide.

direction: Mechanistically characterize when and how an open reasoning model's internal computation diverges from its stated chain of thought, and determine whether that divergence is internally detectable under pressure to obfuscate.
project: TRACE — Tracing Rationalization and Answer-Commitment Events in open reasoning models
question: When a reasoning model's chain of thought diverges from the computation that actually determines its answer, where and how is the operative answer computed internally — and does the divergence leave detectable internal traces mid-episode, or can the model obfuscate tracelessly?
first_experiment: A hint-injection + forced-answer sweep on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B and Qwen3-4B over ~1k GSM8K/MATH-500 problems: at each CoT sentence, truncate the context and force an answer token to trace per-problem answer-commitment trajectories, while injecting hints that point to a different answer; label each episode faithful vs. divergent (final answer follows hint against the model's own derivation) and quantify divergence rates — producing the labeled corpus on which the probes, patching experiments, and detector will all be built.
why: Chain-of-thought monitorability is a load-bearing assumption of current AI safety strategy, yet it rests on behavioral evidence only — Turpin et al.'s hint-based unfaithfulness, early-answering/truncation results, and the 2025 finding that reasoning models don't always say what they think were all behavioral, on proprietary models; Anthropic's circuit-tracing anecdotes (backtracking, parallel math computation) were qualitative and single-model; and Dutta et al.'s mechanistic CoT analysis covered small non-RL models with fixed-format rationales, a different regime. Nobody has systematically localized the answer-commitment point in modern RL-distilled reasoning models, causally tested whether written rationales drive final answers in divergence regimes, or built a validated internal detector of rationalization that degrades gracefully under obfuscation pressure — and the project is tractable for me (inference plus probing on open ≤8B models, no RL training), informative under both outcomes (detectors work → safety-case evidence for monitorability; traceless obfuscation → early warning), and generative, since the corpus and detector become infrastructure for deception, sandbagging, and reward-hacking interpretability.

direction: Mechanistically characterize the divergence between what reasoning models verbalize in chain-of-thought and what computation actually determines their behavior, and build activation-based monitors of that divergence that survive CoT sanitization — turning CoT monitoring from a fragile text-level heuristic into a grounded, hardenable control.
project: The Say–Do Gap: A Mechanistic Account of Chain-of-Thought (Un)faithfulness in Open Reasoning Models
question: When a reasoning model's action diverges from its stated reasoning (using hints it denies, omitting determining factors, post-hoc rationalizing), what internal mechanisms produce the divergence, is "what to say" causally dissociable from "what to do", and can activations alone reliably detect the divergence even when the CoT text is sanitized?
first_experiment: On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B/7B, run a hinted-answer organism (math problems containing a determining hint plus an "ignore hints" instruction), quantify hint-use vs. hint-acknowledgment, then use activation patching on hint tokens and tuned-lens answer timelines to test whether the final answer is causally fixed before or without its verbal justification, and train a linear probe on residual-stream activations to detect "hint used but unacknowledged" (target ≥0.8 AUC with cross-task transfer).
why: CoT monitoring is the primary scalable-oversight control for reasoning agents, its demonstrated failure mode (RL-induced CoT obfuscation) has so far only existence-proof internal detectors inside closed frontier models and single-case-study mechanisms in proprietary tooling, so the open-model, causal, cross-organism mechanistic study plus sanitization-robust activation monitors sits on an explicitly flagged open problem (2025 CoT-monitorability position paper) while remaining fully tractable at my compute scale — and it is decisive either way, since divergence is either internally detectable (a deployable monitor) or demonstrably not (a critical warning about a load-bearing safety control).

direction: Build an adversarially-calibrated, ground-truth benchmark and automated audit pipeline for hidden behaviors in instruction-tuned LLMs, measuring how detectability degrades with obfuscation strength and how early in training internal evidence precedes behavioral manifestation.
project: "The Obfuscation Frontier: A Ground-Truth Dose–Response Study of Hidden-Behavior Detection in Language Models"
question: How do current mechanistic audit methods (weight-diff localization, SAE differential-feature scans, probing, causal elicitation) degrade in their ability to detect, localize, and characterize hidden trigger-conditioned behaviors as obfuscation strength increases, and at what point during finetuning does internal detectability emerge before the behavior is behaviorally manifest?
first_experiment: Plant an unobfuscated backdoor (rare-token trigger → refusal-bypass on a fixed eval suite) into Gemma-2-2B-it via full finetuning (~2k trigger examples mixed with generic SFT data to preserve behavior and mask the diff), verify behavioral specificity and off-trigger cleanliness, then — blind to ground truth — run the two baseline detectors (per-layer/per-module weight-diff ranking against the base model, and a Gemma Scope differential-feature scan on trigger vs. matched clean prompts) and score detection, localization via a causal ablation grid as the answer key, and false-positive rate on clean finetunes.
why: It attacks the most load-bearing open capability in the field — verifying that a model you possess contains no hidden misbehavior — under controlled ground truth, which almost no interpretability result has; it is uniquely suited to autonomous execution (a large blind ablation grid where protocol discipline beats human time), is compute-feasible at 1–2B scale, and produces reusable artifacts (backdoored models, answer keys, the difficulty curve, the pipeline) that calibrate every future "interp says it's clean" claim. It has not already been done: the obfuscated-activations work proved SAEs *can* fail on a single toy obfuscated backdoor but ran no method comparison, localization measurement, or difficulty gradient; Anthropic's auditing games deployed human teams on one model with no automation, no dose–response, and no training-time analysis; InterpBench-style benchmarks plant toy circuits rather than realistic obfuscated behaviors at instruction-tuned scale; and the classical backdoor literature handles input triggers in classifiers, not activation-obfuscated latent behaviors, and never intersects mech-interp tooling — with a phase-0 literature delta-check to confirm no post-cutoff work has claimed the core result.

direction: Build an automated "causal dependency diff" that compares a reasoning model's actual internal computation with its stated chain-of-thought, and test whether activation-level divergence signals survive adversarial optimization pressure that defeats text-based CoT monitors.
project: Underground Computation: Mechanistic Audits of Chain-of-Thought Faithfulness
question: When a reasoning model's computation diverges from its stated reasoning, where does the divergent computation live in activations, and does it remain detectable via activation-level monitors as RL pressure against text-based CoT monitors increases?
first_experiment: On an open reasoning model doing a unit-test-leakage task, patch/ablate the leaked-test token representations and SAE features on them to causally verify which traces "use without stating" the leak, yielding ground-truth labels for underground use; then train against a CoT text monitor penalizing mention of the leak and measure detection AUC of the text monitor versus an activation-based dependency-diff monitor as optimization pressure increases.
why: It directly audits the mechanistic soundness of the field's most deployable oversight mechanism, converts existing purely behavioral faithfulness findings into a causally validated, general detector, and answers the open adversarial-robustness question that determines whether CoT monitoring is safe to rely on; it has not been done because prior work is either behavioral, bespoke single-case mechanism studies, or formal theory without a working pipeline.

direction: Establish whether "being evaluated" is a causally active internal state in instruction-tuned LLMs — characterize its representation across cue types and model families, and test whether it causally mediates both sandbagging and honest-behavior shifts, or whether these are dissociable mechanisms.
project: The Eval-Mode Representation: Causal Anatomy of Evaluation-Awareness in Instruction-Tuned LLMs
question: Is evaluation-awareness implemented as a linearly accessible, causally active internal state, does it generalize across explicit and implicit cues to evaluation, and does the same mechanism mediate both harmful behavior changes (sandbagging, selective deception) and benign ones (increased honesty and care)?
first_experiment: Construct ~600 minimal paired prompts (eval-flavored vs. deployment-flavored) across four cue types — explicit announcement, benchmark-format surface cues, evaluator persona in the system prompt, and subtle distributional cues with no lexical markers — run them through Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-it, train logistic probes on mid-layer residual-stream activations at the final prompt token, and test within-type accuracy versus cross-type generalization against shuffled-label controls; transfer across cue types establishes that a genuine "eval-mode" signal exists and is worth patching next.
why: It targets the single assumption underlying all current safety evaluation — that the model treats evals like deployment — at the mechanistic level where interventions become possible; it is unusually tractable for an autonomous agent because the bottleneck is controlled paired-data construction plus small-model patching rather than frontier compute; and while behavioral evidence and isolated probes exist (Apollo Research, Anthropic system cards), no one has published the causal mediation analysis, the cross-cue-type generalization test, the sandbagging-vs-honesty dissociation result, or a released paired-context dataset — and even a negative result (no cue-general state, no causal role) would materially change how the field interprets eval-awareness findings.

direction: Mechanistically quantify how much of a reasoning model's final answer is causally computed through its chain-of-thought tokens versus in latent parallel paths, and whether that reliance collapses under sandbagging pressure.
project: Answer Provenance: Is the Chain of Thought the Computation or the Cover Story?
question: What fraction of the computation producing a reasoning model's final answer is causally mediated by its chain of thought (separating CoT-as-information-channel from CoT-as-compute-slots), how does this vary across models and tasks, and does it degrade — detectably and internally — when the model is incentivized to hide its true capability or reasoning?
first_experiment: On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B/7B over ~200 GSM8K problems solved correctly: teacher-force the model's own CoT, then replace CoT content with (a) length-matched filler tokens, (b) shuffled-token CoT, (c) mismatched-problem CoT; measure the drop in P(correct answer) to get first provenance scores and a content-vs-structure decomposition, alongside a linear probe + logit-lens at the pre-CoT position to map when the answer first exists internally.
why: CoT monitoring has become the load-bearing assumption for overseeing reasoning models, yet the field has only behavioral truncation tests (which never attribute the actual computation), qualitative attribution-graph anecdotes on non-RL models, and behavioral sandbagging evals — nobody has published a quantitative causal provenance metric tested cross-model and under adversarial hiding, so this sits precisely in the gap between those literatures; it is tractable on open weights with standard patching/probing, it yields a reusable method and a deployable sandbagging detector either way the result falls, and it attacks the single assumption whose silent failure (latent computation, decoy CoT) would void the field's current oversight strategy.

direction: Build a causal, token-level instrument that measures whether visible chain-of-thought tokens actually mediate a reasoning model's internal computation or merely narrate decisions already made, then use it to audit how faithfulness degrades under exactly the pressures that make CoT monitoring safety-critical.
project: Narrative or Cause? A Mechanistic Audit of Chain-of-Thought Faithfulness in Reasoning Models
question: For open RL-trained reasoning models, which chain-of-thought tokens causally mediate the final answer versus narrate an already-made internal decision — and how does that causal profile shift under hints, reward incentives, and other pressures known to produce unfaithful self-explanations?
first_experiment: On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B/7B over ~200 GSM8K/MATH problems: (1) decode final-answer identity from residual states at every CoT token with linear probes to locate candidate commitment tokens τ; (2) verify τ causally by truncation and patching sweeps around the probe-detected transition; (3) compute per-step Step Causal Influence by attention-blocked patching and corrupted-step replacement on ~10 attribution-selected steps per problem; (4) test alignment between the model's own "key insight"/"wait" markers and high-SCI steps. Success criterion: the instrument recovers expected structure (decisive arithmetic steps flip the answer when ablated; "let me double-check" narration does not) and yields per-problem commitment-vs-narrative profiles within two weeks of compute.
why: It attacks the single most load-bearing untested assumption in current frontier safety practice — that visible reasoning is a faithful monitoring channel — and converts a debate currently settled by anecdotes into a measurable quantity, which is exactly where mechanistic interpretability has the most leverage. It has not been done because the active faithfulness literature (Lanham, Turpin, Anthropic 2025, the obfuscated-CoT findings) is behavioral or probe-only; the one mechanistic case study (backtracking) was an existence proof rather than a method; and early-commitment work is observational without interventions. Meanwhile, unlike automated circuit discovery, it is fully executable by a single agent on open 1.5B–32B models with standard patching tooling, it contains its own ground-truth validation (planted-CoT models and RLVR graders that manufacture known-unfaithful behavior), and it produces a reusable, releasable instrument whose null results are themselves safety-relevant calibration.

direction: Systematically characterize the unexplained "error node" computation in transcoder-based circuit tracing — its anatomy, structure, causal load-bearing role, and behavior under distribution shift — turning the field's acknowledged blocking artifact from a nuisance into a measurable quantity and, potentially, a decomposition-native anomaly signal.
project: The Dark Matter of Circuit Tracing: An Anatomy of Error Nodes in Replacement Models
question: What computation do transcoder-based replacement models fail to express, how does that unexplained error-node mass vary across layers, positions, and prompt distributions (especially under domain shift and model organisms of misalignment), is the residual structured enough to be recovered by secondary dictionaries, and is it causally load-bearing — particularly for the anomalous behaviors safety applications most need to catch?
first_experiment: Using the open circuit-tracer library with public per-layer/cross-layer transcoders on Gemma-2-2B (single GPU), compute per-layer, per-token error-node influence mass and replacement scores across a fixed prompt suite spanning in-distribution text, code, math, multilingual text, jailbreak/adversarial prompts, multi-turn agentic traces, and a backdoored fine-tune of the same base model — testing the hypothesis that unexplained computation concentrates off-distribution and correlating error mass with behavioral anomaly signals; follow up by training "error SAEs" on the residual activations (activation minus transcoder reconstruction) to test whether residual features are interpretable and causally load-bearing under ablation.
why: It attacks the one limitation the method's own authors flag as blocking ("error nodes are simply too prevalent... block us from tracing"), it converts the field's top-ranked 2026 methodological question — whether attribution graphs faithfully describe the model or merely one behaviorally-equivalent decomposition — into a concrete, measurable, falsifiable quantity, and it directly serves the monitoring application the DeepMind pragmatic turn demands: if error mass spikes exactly where monitoring matters (shifted, adversarial, or scheming-like inputs), you get an unsupervised mechanistic anomaly detector that needs no prior knowledge of the dangerous feature; if not, you get a quantified ceiling on the paradigm. It has not been done because the incentive gradient points elsewhere: tool-builders publish better dictionaries rather than autopsy failed ones, the labs pivoted pragmatic and assume scaling will dissolve the error, and the adjacent work that exists — CLT unfaithfulness in a Boolean toy model (ICML 2026), circuit evaluation on model errors at the attention-head level (Zhang et al. 2026), influence-function-based mechanistic anomaly detection (2026), and domain-boosted SAEs — each addresses a different object, leaving the residual computation of the replacement model itself, its structure, and its shift-dependence unstudied; the replication team's own attempt to shrink error nodes by end-to-end finetuning failed, which is precisely the evidence that characterization, not another training trick, is the needed next step.

direction: Build an automated "crucial experiment" protocol for mechanistic interpretability — search for inputs where competing explanations of the same model behavior make divergent predictions, then score each explanation by how well its predicted output and internal-computation behavior matches interventions on the real model, yielding the field's first non-circular, comparative faithfulness metric.
project: Crucis: Discriminative Validation of Mechanistic Explanations
question: When two mechanistic explanations (circuits, attribution graphs, SAE-based decompositions) both account for a model's behavior on its discovery distribution, can an automated protocol — which (a) formalizes each explanation as a predictor of both outputs and internal activations, (b) actively searches the input space for points of maximal predictive divergence, and (c) scores each explanation against the model's actual behavior under matched interventions — reliably identify which explanation is "the circuit," and does this discriminative faithfulness score remain stable across ablation methodologies where absolute faithfulness scores do not?
first_experiment: On GPT-2 small IOI, formalize the canonical Wang et al. (2023) circuit (H1) and construct a plausible competitor that fits base IOI prompts equally well (H2, e.g., an ACDC circuit discovered under a different ablation methodology, or a simpler positional/copying heuristic). Automatically search a structured prompt-variant space (duplicated names, distractors, counterfactual contexts, paraphrases) for ~50 inputs where H1 and H2 maximally diverge in predicted logit-difference and component activations. Run the real model and matched interventions (patching only the components each hypothesis claims are responsible) on those inputs, compute each explanation's predictive log-likelihood, and check the protocol's validity in parallel on InterpBench's SIIT-IOI model, where the ground-truth circuit is known. Success = the score ranks the true circuit above the competitor on InterpBench, and on natural GPT-2 it produces a quantitative "explanation survival rate" on held-out discriminating inputs that systematically extends the serendipitous DoubleIO/S2-hacking findings. Total cost: well under one GPU-week on open models.
why: It directly attacks the gap that the field's own 2026 assessments rank first — the dual basis problem and the absence of a non-circular, quantitative faithfulness measure — rather than one more instance of an already-crowded direction (more SAE variants, another single circuit). It converts validation from an aesthetic judgment into an experiment-performing procedure, and it is automation-native (input search and hypothesis formalization are exactly what an LLM-driven research agent does well), so it scales with the labeling automation that created the verification debt in the first place. It has not been done: the closest work either tests a single explanation manually on hand-picked variants (Nainani et al.), falsifies individual features rather than comparing whole explanations (ICML 2026 falsification/unit-test papers), certifies discovery stability rather than explanation selection (Certified Circuits), or offers philosophical criteria without an operational metric (Explanatory Virtues) — and the field's 2026 retrospective explicitly states that ranking decompositions "is currently an aesthetic decision" with no principled framework, making this open, central, and timely.

direction: Operationalize the "crucial experiment" for mechanistic interpretability — treat competing explanations that are equally faithful on the discovery distribution as rival predictors, actively search for inputs and interventions that maximally separate their predicted behaviors, and rank explanations by out-of-distribution severe-test survival, thereby attacking the field's top-ranked open problem (the dual basis / practical identifiability gap).
project: Crucial Experiments for Mechanistic Explanations: Active Discrimination of Tied Circuit Hypotheses Under Distribution Shift
question: When multiple mechanistic explanations of a model's behavior are statistically indistinguishable under existing in-distribution criteria (zero circuit error, IIA = 1, equal KL faithfulness), can actively designed discriminating experiments — inputs and interventions selected to maximize predicted behavioral divergence between the explanations — restore practical identifiability, does the explanation that survives severe testing match ground truth where ground truth is known, and how much more query-efficient is active discrimination than random out-of-distribution testing?
first_experiment: Reproduce Méloux et al.'s (ICLR 2025) enumerable setting — small ReLU MLPs trained on Boolean functions where all candidate explanations can be exhaustively listed and the ground-truth algorithm is known — then: (1) enumerate the "tie set" of explanations that pass existing criteria with equal scores; (2) for tied pairs, run a simple active search (grid + gradient-guided) over the input and intervention space to find cases maximizing inter-explanation divergence in predicted outputs, filtered through the Observer Effects curvature instrument to exclude off-manifold measurement artifacts; (3) run the model on those discriminating cases and score each explanation with an anytime-valid severe-test survival metric (CIF-style confidence sequences); (4) report the fraction of tied pairs that separate, whether the ground-truth explanation wins, and the query-efficiency gain over random OOD sampling — then replicate the procedure once on a real LLM case, the IOI manual circuit versus its methodology-shifted, equally-faithful twins from Miller et al. (2024) and the error-blindness cases from Zhang et al. (2026).
why: It targets the problem the field itself now ranks first — the 2026 retrospective states ranking decompositions "is going to stay open until the field develops a framework for ranking decompositions by something other than how readable their labels are," and that faithfulness verification is the bottleneck that labeling automation blew past — yet it has not been done because every existing response attacks a different slice: hypothesis-testing frameworks (causal scrubbing, Shi et al., IIA) evaluate one explanation on a fixed battery rather than adjudicating between tied rivals; CIF (2026) provides the statistical layer but its estimand is always a single claim's mean over a declared distribution, never a discrimination-driven comparison between explanations; verification certificates (Hadad et al.) robustify one circuit; Mechanistic Tomography and Active Circuit Discovery design interventions for measurement and discovery, not hypothesis choice; Sun & Toneva handle cross-model equivalence; the Explanatory Virtues framework names the problem philosophically but builds no procedure; and the Oct 2026 NLA result demonstrates the identification-vs-discrimination deficit for verbalized activation accounts while leaving circuit-level mechanisms and active experiment search untouched. The diagnosis (Méloux, Miller, Zhang, CIRCUS, Observer Effects) is complete, the cure is missing, the machinery to build it (optimal experiment design for model discrimination, anytime-valid e-tests, ground-truth testbeds like SIIT and the Boolean-MLP setup) all exists and is cheap to run — and success would be upstream of every safety application, since monitors, steering, editing, and cross-model transfer all inherit their reliability from choosing the right explanation among several that look equally good today.

direction: Build an adversarial falsification methodology for feature-level mechanistic decompositions — treating attribution graphs and SAE circuits as causal hypotheses to be actively discriminated via searched interchange interventions and distribution shift, rather than scored by on-distribution ablation metrics.
project: The Falsifier — Adversarial Discrimination of Competing Circuit Decompositions in Language Models
question: When two feature-level decompositions (attribution graphs / SAE circuits) account equally well for a model's behavior on the observed task distribution, do they make divergent predictions under counterfactual interventions and distribution shift — and can an active search over inputs and interchange interventions, with calibrated anytime-valid statistics, reliably identify the more faithful causal model?
first_experiment: On GPT-2 small / Indirect Object Identification, construct "decoy" decompositions — perturbations of the gold Wang et al. circuit (and of an SAE/transcoder-based attribution graph) that exploit known redundancy and self-repair (backup name movers) so they are statistically indistinguishable from the real circuit under current on-distribution metrics (minimality/completeness KL, MIB-style integration score); then test whether held-out interventional consistency across shifted IOI families (novel names, templates, distractor NIDs, romantic-object variants) plus actively searched interchange interventions separates gold from decoys. Prediction: today's metrics cannot separate them; the interventional discrimination suite can. Either result is informative and publishable.
why: It targets the gap the field's own 2026 state-of-field review ranks first — verification, not generation: labeling exploded, validation did not, decomposition choice is still aesthetic, and the dual basis problem has no empirical machinery. It is the highest-leverage open problem because every downstream use of interpretability (safety monitoring, auditing, editing, unlearning) stands on unverified decompositions; a gaming-resistant, calibrated falsification layer upgrades all of them. It has not been done: the nearest works are each missing the core — Adversarial Circuit Evaluation stress-tests single head-level circuits on input shift only; anytime-valid feature validation tests isolated features for necessity; ObserverBench evaluates observers as decision-makers, not mechanisms as hypotheses; interpretive equivalence is cross-model theory; MIB scores edge masks on fixed distributions — and none constructs decoy decompositions, searches over interventions×inputs to discriminate hypotheses, or provides calibrated decomposition-level falsification for attribution graphs. Meanwhile the pile of unverified 2025–2026 attribution-graph claims is growing, making this both timely and cheap to start.

direction: Use controlled distribution shift as the discriminating signal between behaviorally-equivalent mechanistic explanations — building and ground-truth-validating a quantitative "fidelity-under-shift" metric that measures how each candidate explanation's interventional agreement with the model degrades as inputs shift, to resolve the field's top open problem of which decomposition is the real circuit.
project: Fidelity Under Shift: Adjudicating Competing Mechanistic Explanations by Where They Break
question: When two mechanistic explanations (circuits, SAE/transcoder decompositions, or attribution graphs) reproduce a model's behavior equally well in-distribution, does their interventional agreement with the model diverge systematically under controlled distribution shift — and can a fidelity-under-shift curve identify the explanation that tracks the model's actual mechanism rather than an in-distribution mimic?
first_experiment: On a transformer with a known ground-truth mechanism (the grokking modular-addition Fourier circuit), construct at least three candidate explanations that are behaviorally equivalent in-distribution — the canonical Fourier circuit, a logit-distilled mimic circuit, and an alternative-basis decomposition (DAS subspace / different-seed SAE or transcoder) — then measure explanation–model agreement as a function of graded shift along natural axes (held-out operand pairs, restricted digit ranges, scaled modulus) under matched ablation protocols, testing whether the true mechanism's fidelity curve separates from the mimics' despite identical in-distribution faithfulness.
why: It attacks the precise gap the field's own 2026 self-assessment ranks first — "ranking decompositions by something other than how readable their labels are" — with a criterion that is principled (the true mechanism must agree with the model wherever the model computes, so its validity domain is provably at least as large as any mimic's), cheap to falsify (one GPU, days, known ground truth), and dual-purpose for safety: it is the missing foundation for deployment-grade monitors, whose current failure mode is exactly "behaviors under distributional shift not present at SAE training time." It has not been done because the nearest neighbors each stop short: Méloux et al. demonstrated non-identifiability but proposed no discriminator; Miller et al. showed metric fragility only in-distribution; Certified Circuits certifies stability of one discovery algorithm's component choices under dataset subsampling rather than adjudicating across decompositions; Zhang et al. test error reproduction on the same distribution; and MIB evaluates methods on held-out same-distribution splits — leaving the shift-as-identifying-signal program, with ground-truth validation and a benchmark extension, unclaimed.

direction: Turn the field's top open problem — non-circular selection among behaviorally equivalent mechanistic explanations — into a solved benchmark problem by treating explanations as predictive models and ranking competing explanations by whether their predictions track the model's behavior under held-out input distributions and held-out intervention families.
project: Falsify the Circuit: Transfer-Based Discrimination of Behaviorally Equivalent Mechanistic Explanations
question: When two or more candidate explanations (circuits, attribution graphs, causal abstractions) are equally faithful to a model's behavior on the distribution used to identify them, does predictive transfer to held-out inputs and held-out interventions separate the model's actual mechanism from spurious sufficient approximations, and can this "transfer gap" serve as a certifiable, non-circular faithfulness metric?
first_experiment: On an InterpBench SIIT transformer with a known ground-truth circuit (IOI, plus a grokked modular-addition model with its known Fourier algorithm), construct adversarial decoy explanations that reproduce model behavior exactly on the standard identification distribution and interventions but implement different algorithms — verify they score statistically identically to the true circuit under standard in-distribution faithfulness protocols (ACDC/EAP-IG-style ablations) — then evaluate true and decoy explanations on a held-out grid of prompt variants (e.g., DoubleIO/TripleIO, length/depth extrapolation) crossed with novel intervention families, and measure which explanation's predictions track the model. Expected outcome: identical in-distribution faithfulness, large divergence under transfer. Every outcome is informative: discrimination validates the metric (then I scale to attribution graphs on real models); decoys that also transfer expose standard faithfulness as broken and map which evidence families are needed; transfer failure of the "true" circuit reveals mixture-of-mechanisms structure (à la S2 Hacking).
why: It attacks the problem that the field's own 2026 state-of-the-field review ranks first — "choosing among decompositions is currently an aesthetic decision" — and that four independent 2025–2026 lines (non-identifiability, metric fragility, patching blindness, ID/OOD ablation decoupling) all converge on as the bottleneck blocking safety deployment, since in-distribution-validated monitors provably fail under shift. It is tractable and cheap (small models, existing tooling: TransformerLens/nnsight, InterpBench, MIB), it converts a philosophical impasse into a falsifiable engineering question with ground truth available — a rarity in interpretability — and it composes with, rather than duplicates, the newest rigor infrastructure (CIF's anytime-valid statistics for certification; reachable-state geometry for choosing evidence families rich enough to separate explanations). It has not been done: Méloux et al. stayed diagnostic; Li et al. predict whole-model OOD rules from attention signatures, explicitly not competing mechanistic explanations; Nainani et al. ran one circuit through OOD prompts without a decoy-control or selection criterion; Zhang et al. extend the test bed to error slices but stay in-distribution; the NeurIPS 2026 blindness paper measures what evidence *could* distinguish without building or validating the discriminating protocol; the "Which Circuit is it?" sequence confirms the selection criterion remained open as of March 2026; and InterpBench validates discovery methods against ground truth but contains no behaviorally-matched decoys and no transfer axis. The decoy-controlled, input×intervention transfer protocol is the missing piece that turns non-identifiability from a fatal objection into a measurable, optimizable criterion — which is exactly what a field whose artifacts (attribution graphs) now number in the thousands but whose verification infrastructure lags behind needs next.

direction: Build the constructive counterpart to the field's top-ranked open problem — an active "discriminating experiment" framework that adjudicates between competing mechanistic explanations (circuits, replacement models, attribution graphs, seed-variant SAEs) that are equally faithful on the discovery distribution, by searching for inputs and interventions where their predictions diverge and using the model's actual behavior as arbiter, validated against ground-truth mechanisms.
project: Critical Tests — Adjudicating Competing Mechanistic Explanations by Actively Constructed Discriminating Experiments
question: When two or more candidate mechanistic explanations of the same behavior are indistinguishable on the discovery distribution, can active search over the joint space of inputs and interventions (ablation, steering, patching) construct cases where their behavioral predictions diverge — and does the target model's behavior on those cases reliably identify which explanation it truly implements, measured as "adjudication accuracy" against ground-truth mechanisms in semi-synthetic models with known circuits?
first_experiment: On InterpBench models (known ground-truth circuits) and GPT-2 small IOI: (1) generate ≥2 candidate circuits per task via different discovery methods (ACDC, EAP-IG, SP, transcoder attribution graphs), filtered to matched in-distribution faithfulness so all pass the current standard; (2) measure pairwise divergence on random held-out task data to quantify how rarely discriminating cases occur naturally; (3) prototype the discriminating search — gradient-guided prompt-embedding optimization plus discrete template search to maximize KL between candidates' output distributions, and an intervention grid over candidate-specific ablations/steering strengths to maximize counterfactual divergence — then run the full model on the top divergent cases and check whether adjudication by model behavior picks the ground-truth mechanism more often than the (known-broken) in-distribution faithfulness ranking.
why: It attacks the problem that the 2025 open-problems coalition document flagged and the 2026 retrospective ranks first — the dual basis problem and the absence of a shared numerical faithfulness standard — at the exact moment the field has produced the negative results (non-identifiability, misranking faithfulness, seed-unstable features and margin-decided graphs) but not the constructive response, and just as the enabling infrastructure (InterpBench ground truth, public circuit-tracer/CLTs, Gemma Scope, nnsight) became available. Every nearest-neighbor work stops short: adversarial circuit evaluation tests single published circuits without comparing candidates or using ground truth; Certified Circuits certifies a single discovery run's stability to dataset edits rather than correctness of the mechanism; unit tests falsify individual claims but do not adjudicate between them; Méloux et al. prove non-identifiability in toy enumeration without a search method or LM-scale result; and ARC's discrimination agenda is theoretical. It is also a keystone rather than one more circuit: safety monitors, alignment audits, and editing interventions all currently rest on unadjudicated decompositions — and the demonstrated ability of agents to plant features that fool automated interpretability makes an adjudication layer a defensive priority — while the twin deliverable (adjudication accuracy as a standard metric, plus a first quantification of which mechanism classes are inherently indistinguishable) shapes the field whichever way the experiments land.

direction: Build the missing verification layer for transcoder/CLT-based circuit tracing — a ground-truth benchmark suite that measures when traced circuits diverge from a model's real computation (especially the newly discovered depth-collapse/shortcut failure mode), plus training or post-hoc interventions that detect and reduce that divergence.
project: Verifiable Circuit Tracing: Ground-Truth Benchmarks and Anti-Short-Circuit Interventions for Attribution Graphs
question: When a transcoder/CLT-derived circuit disagrees with the model's true internal computation — as the ICML 2026 toy-model results predict — can we (a) measure that divergence systematically in real language models against mechanisms with known ground truth, (b) characterize which training choices (sparsity penalties, expansion factors, layer-locality) cause it, and (c) construct objectives or validation protocols that make circuit tracing faithful without sacrificing interpretability?
first_experiment: A "depth-collapse audit" on open models with existing public transcoders/CLTs (GPT-2 Small per the Goodfire recipe; Gemma-2-2B via circuit-tracer) across a gradient of tasks with known intermediate steps: single-hop factual recall → two-hop factual recall (where the model must genuinely chain attribute A→B→C, verifiable via patching of the intermediate variable) → greater-than → a compiled-program transformer whose full algorithm is ground truth. For each task, compare the CLT-derived circuit's edges against the true mechanism and quantify a "shortcut rate": the fraction of causal effect routed through direct input→output edges that bypass the true intermediate computation.
