Sweep L0/expansion-factor values to test whether the ICML 2026 incentive prediction (more sparsity ⇒ more depth collapse) holds in real models. Either result is publishable: confirmation defines the benchmark and the problem's scale; refutation bounds the toy-model result and calibrates trust in attribution graphs.
why: It attacks the field's single most load-bearing and currently wobbling assumption — that replacement-model circuits describe what the model actually computes — at the exact moment three 2026 papers independently exposed the problem but none built the response; it directly fulfills the two most-cited unmet needs from the field's own consensus documents (ground-truth validation benchmarks; shared model organisms), it is the natural upstream enabler for the higher-profile application areas (monitoring, unlearning, agentic interp) rather than one more competitor in a crowded space, and it is untouched because the diagnostic papers stopped at diagnosis, the one replication was a single-task case study, labs have deprioritized foundational SAE/dictionary work in favor of task-driven "pragmatic" research, and the required intersection of skills (program compilation/model organisms + circuit tracing + benchmark design) is precisely the unglamorous cross-community work that no group has claimed — while recent open-source tooling (circuit-tracer, CLT-Forge, SAELens) has just made it tractable on a single GPU.

direction: Build certified "mechanistic equivalence classes" — populations of naturally-trained models that are behaviorally indistinguishable in-distribution but implement provably distinct algorithms — and use them to test whether sparse proxies (SAEs, cross-layer transcoders, attribution graphs, discovered circuits) recover a model's actual mechanism or merely one behaviorally-adequate decomposition, turning the field's "dual basis / proxy fidelity problem" from philosophy into a calibrated benchmark.
project: Same Behavior, Different Circuit — a certified testbed for measuring and predicting mechanistic fidelity of interpretable proxies
question: When an interpretable proxy faithfully reproduces a model's behavior on the training distribution, does it implement the same mechanism as the target model — and can cheap observables (reconstruction error, sparsity, cross-seed feature stability, graph stability, label agreement) predict when it does not?
first_experiment: Train ~50 small (1–3 layer) transformers on one composition task with at least two implementable algorithms that agree on the training distribution but diverge on constructible inputs (e.g., date-comparison or modular-arithmetic tasks with circular vs. digit-wise/CRT solutions, plus data-ordering/curriculum variation to induce algorithmic diversity); certify each member's mechanism class via a pre-registered protocol (differential behavior on the discriminating OOD suite + interchange-intervention agreement against a candidate-algorithm library + component-ablation signatures); then run an identical SAE → cross-layer transcoder → attribution-graph pipeline on every member and measure whether the proxy's interventional predictions on the discriminating inputs recover each model's certified mechanism class or collapse to a class-agnostic explanation — quantifying, for the first time, the rate and predictors of "shallow mimicry" in modern interpretability pipelines.
why: It attacks the gap that two independent, current state-of-the-field documents independently rank first — the Nov 2026 survey's proxy-fidelity/ontology problem (§14.5–14.6, which explicitly calls for interchange-intervention validation and theoretical bounds but lists none existing) and the 2026 retrospective's "dual basis problem" — and it supplies the missing ingredient for the 2026 wave of validation methods (anytime-valid feature testing, causal audits, reproducibility calibrations), all of which currently lack ground truth to be calibrated against. It has not been done because until ~2025 attribution graphs were not the standard artifact (so nothing needed calibration), mechanistic certification of even one circuit required months of hand analysis (only now automatable via SIIT/InterpBench-style training and automated circuit tooling), and the field's incentive gradient rewards discovering new circuits in large models over building evaluation infrastructure — leaving this keystone unclaimed despite being everyone's stated bottleneck; the safety payoff is direct, since an auditor's negative finding ("no deception mechanism found in the proxy") is only meaningful when proxy mechanism-fidelity is quantified, which is precisely what this testbed would measure.

direction: Resolve the circuit "dual basis problem" by running designed discriminating experiments among the equivalence class of candidate circuits, converting explanation multiplicity into a measurable ranking (or proving constructive observational equivalence).
project: Crucial Experiments for Circuits: Discriminating Explanation-Equivalent Circuit Candidates via Designed Inputs
question: Can input distributions designed to maximize divergence between candidate circuits — which are indistinguishable under in-distribution faithfulness — separate them in a way that is stable across analysts and predictive of behavior under further distribution shift?
first_experiment: On GPT-2 small/IOI, collect ~100–200 candidate circuits from ACDC/EAP-IG/attribution patching across a pre-registered multiverse of defensible settings, verify in-distribution equivalence with structural near-disjointness, then run divergence-maximizing input search over the most divergent pairs and score which candidate tracks the full model.
why: Four independent 2025–2026 lines (non-identifiability, phantom specialization, multiverse claim-flipping, the retrospective's dual-basis designation) all diagnose multiplicity and none supplies a resolution; the discriminating-experiment step has not been taken because the adversarial-evaluation, verification, and method-improvement communities each test single circuits against the model rather than candidates against each other — making this the highest-leverage, cheapest, and guaranteed-informative next move for the field's foundational credibility and for audit-grade safety claims.

direction: Build the missing adjudication layer for mechanistic interpretability — automated synthesis of discriminating inputs that separate behaviorally-equivalent rival mechanisms, so the model itself, rather than analyst aesthetics, selects the true explanation.
project: CRUCIBLE: Crucial Experiments for Mechanistic Interpretability — Adjudicating Rival Circuits by Synthesizing Discriminating Inputs
question: When multiple candidate mechanisms explain a model's behavior on its discovery distribution, can constrained input synthesis (maximizing inter-candidate predictive disagreement subject to task-manifold naturalness) reliably identify which candidate the model actually implements — and can "separation-failure under budget" serve as a quantitative certificate of behavioral equivalence?
first_experiment: A planted-decoy adjudication study on a grokked modular-addition transformer (algorithm fully known, input space Z_p×Z_p exhaustively enumerable): construct ≥3 decoy circuits that are behaviorally equivalent to the true Fourier-algorithm circuit on a random eval split but structurally distinct, enumerate the entire input space to find every input where any pair of candidates diverges, then measure how strongly the model's actual logits track the true circuit versus each decoy on the discriminating set — establishing (a) that separability is real and measurable, (b) that model behavior sides with a consistent winner, and (c) a baseline separation profile against which to compare standard faithfulness metrics, before scaling the method to gradient-guided input search on IOI/GPT-2 (using the public multiverse grid of structurally-disjoint candidates) and the Sparse Transformer ground-truth testbed.
why: It attacks the problem the field's own 2026 retrospectives rank first — the dual-basis/explanation-multiplicity problem — at the exact moment the diagnosis is complete (Méloux, Mahale, Bayat Makou, Li & Subramani, Dead Salmons) but no method exists: every prior work measures or laments multiplicity, certifies single circuits, or uses fixed test batteries, and the one active project ("Which Circuit is it?") has published only conceptual groundwork. It has the strongest possible validation story (planted decoys against fully known ground truth in grokked models and the Sparse Transformer), it is feasible on small models with single-GPU budgets, it upgrades every downstream circuit claim including in reasoning models and safety-critical features (e.g., separating a "deception" feature from a confabulation feature that mimics it on eval data), and it directly supplies the "quantitative faithfulness measure that everyone agrees on" the field says it lacks — because it replaces circular agreement-on-a-sample with adversarial, non-circular evidence: inputs designed to make the wrong explanation fail.

direction: Build the first ground-truth validation protocol for feature-level attribution graphs — scoring circuit-tracing's mechanistic claims (not just behavior match) against planted mechanisms in model organisms, using held-out interventional tests under distribution shift as the discriminator between behaviorally equivalent decompositions.
project: Trust the Graph? A Ground-Truth, Held-Out Interventional Faithfulness Benchmark for Circuit Tracing
question: When an attribution graph reproduces a model's behavior on-distribution, is it describing the computation the model actually uses — and can the graph's predictions about interventions under distribution shift (paraphrased triggers, novel contexts, perturbed intermediate nodes) discriminate the true mechanism from behaviorally equivalent shallow rewrites?
first_experiment: On an open-weight organism with a known single planted deceptive feature (Anthropic's feature-addition Gemma-2-2B-based release), run open circuit tracing (circuit-tracer / Gemma Scope 2 transcoders) on trigger prompts and check three things: (1) does the planted feature's direction appear as a high-attribution node in the recovered graph; (2) does ablating that node eliminate the planted behavior on-distribution, as the graph predicts; (3) do the graph's interventional predictions survive on held-out trigger paraphrases and novel contexts — compared against the planted-mechanism graph and against sparsity-varied "shallow rewrite" alternative graphs that match on-distribution behavior.
why: The 2026 state-of-the-field review names graph faithfulness/verification — "the dual basis problem" — as the top open methodological problem, with verification infrastructure lagging automated labeling; ICML 2026 proves CLTs are incentivized into behaviorally-equivalent-but-unfaithful rewrites (toy models only), and misranking/phantom-specialization results show current faithfulness evaluation fails at the head level — yet no one has scored the field's standard artifact, the feature-level attribution graph, against known planted mechanisms under distribution shift: AuditBench audits agents without attribution graphs, organism papers validate organisms rather than explanations, and transcoder-deception work lacks ground truth entirely. It is cheap (2B–8B models, fully open tooling), it converts the field's most-cited methodological worry into a reusable number, it makes safety-audit claims falsifiable, and a negative result would be just as consequential — recalibrating every circuit claim currently accepted on visual plausibility alone.

direction: Develop distribution-level circuit tracing that aggregates per-prompt attribution graphs into causally validated input-conditional mechanisms, to adjudicate unified algorithms versus bags of heuristics.
project: TraceCensus — From Execution Traces to Algorithms
question: Can a census of attribution graphs over a prompt distribution recover the model's input-conditional mechanism, and does the unified-algorithm-vs-heuristic-consensus verdict survive intact-model causal intervention rather than replacement-model-only evidence?
first_experiment: Trace ~1,000–2,000 stratified greater-than prompts on GPT-2 small with public CLTs, aggregate the graphs into a census graph with edge statistics regressed on input coordinates, then three-way adjudicate the documented "parity detector" feature (census statistics vs. intact-model ablation with compensation tracking vs. replacement-model ablation), followed by the same pipeline on InterpBench models with planted algorithms as ground truth.
why: It is the circuit-tracing community's explicitly stated #1 open problem ("can we merge attribution graphs... into a global circuit picture?"), it is the common root of the field's documented 2026 instabilities (seed fragility, specification flips, context distortion, shattered geometry), and it remains unoccupied because the required infrastructure (public CLTs, Circuit Tracer, Neuronpedia graphs, InterpBench) only matured in mid-2025 while field energy went to crowded adjacent problems — yet it is the precondition for interpretability monitors and audits that generalize off-distribution rather than self-repairing into vacuity.

direction: Build the first causal, mechanistic account of how LLM agents represent, update, and (fail to) use internal task-state across long-horizon episodes, extending the 2026 "decodable-but-not-used" (causal quotient) taxonomy from toy worlds to real agentic computation.
project: The Agent's Task State: Erased, Rerouted, or Rescaled? — A Causal Quotient for Long-Horizon Agentic Computation
question: When a long-horizon LLM agent drifts or acts inconsistently with its task, is its internal task-state representation erased (no longer decodable), rerouted (still decodable but no longer causally read by the action-selection computation), or rescaled (used but variance-starved) — and does this mechanistic taxonomy predict which mitigation (re-prompting, activation patching, context re-injection, compaction strategy) actually rescues the episode?
first_experiment: Run Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on ~1,000 ALFWorld episodes (plus a text grid-world for continuity with prior work), log residual-stream activations at every turn boundary, and train linear probes to decode ground-truth environment state, completed subgoals, and the agent's next intended subgoal — plotting decodability as a function of turn index and episode length, separately for successful and failed episodes. Then, on failures where the correct state is still decodable (the predicted "belief-action gap" region), run the decisive causal test: transplant the state subspace between episodes at matched progress points and compare activation-level state re-injection against text-level state re-injection (reminders), to produce the first erased-vs-rerouted-vs-rescaled classification of agent failures.
why: (1) It sits at the intersection of the field's top diagnosed open problem (attribution graphs/decompositions never validated beyond short single-turn behaviors; safety monitoring coverage "narrow and shrinking relative to deployment") and the actual deployment frontier (agents), where both the horizon-gap capability failure and monitoring/sabotage safety concerns hinge on the same unasked question. (2) It has not been done: the belief-action gap paper established the dissociation in grid worlds but explicitly declines to identify the mechanism or localize the state; Erased/Rerouted/Rescaled supplies the taxonomy but only for post-training in hidden-Markov worlds; DART/PRISM/ATLAS are correlational monitors or externally-anchored controllers, not accounts of the model's own state computation; and no published work performs cross-episode state transplantation or turn-boundary patching in an agent. (3) It is feasible now — open-weight 7–8B models, public environments with ground-truth state, cheap probes, and moderate-cost turn-boundary interventions — and it yields publishable results either way: a quantitative "state causal quotient" for agent models, an early-warning monitor that reads the state the policy ignores, and a diagnosis→mitigation map that converts agentic interp from correlational monitoring into mechanistic engineering.

direction: Make out-of-distribution behavioral and internal prediction the standard of evidence for mechanistic explanations — so that candidate circuits/attribution graphs are ranked by pre-registered predictions on held-out environments rather than by intervention-faithfulness on the analysis distribution.
project: Circuits Must Generalize — a discriminating evaluation standard (and identifiability analysis) for competing mechanistic explanations, validated where the true mechanism is known.
question: When multiple mechanistic explanations of the same model behavior are behaviorally equivalent in-distribution, do their pre-registered predictions on held-out input distributions and intervention outcomes discriminate the true mechanism — and how much environmental diversity is required before the surviving equivalence class collapses to the ground truth (an "identifiability curve" for mechanistic explanations)?
first_experiment: On InterpBench's known-mechanism IOI model and on GPT-2 small's published IOI circuit, construct ~20 candidate explanations per task: the reference circuit, automated discoveries (ACDC, EAP-IG, SP), and controlled impostor edits matched for in-distribution KL-faithfulness (Geng et al.'s edit protocol). Replicate the intervention-faithfulness misrankings, then score every candidate by prediction error of held-out model behavior on the distribution-shift variants of IOI (name/order/distractor mutations) and on held-out ablation outcomes, computed from the candidate's own implied computation alone. Readout: does the OOD-predictive score recover the ground-truth ranking where faithfulness fails, and what fraction of impostors does each additional environment eliminate?
why: It attacks the single most-cited unsolved problem in the field — faithfulness/verification of the attribution-graph era — at the exact seam between a mature critique wave and a missing constructive wave: Geng et al. proved the current objective misranks circuits and called for a replacement; Méloux et al. proved non-identifiability but offered no discriminating procedure; Li et al. proved OOD prediction works but only as attention-signature heuristics on toy populations, never as a competitive scoring standard for decompositions of pretrained models against ground truth; InterpBench/MIB exist but evaluate in-distribution localization, not OOD discrimination. Nobody has combined planted-truth models, impostor circuits, and pre-registered OOD prediction into one protocol, so the synthesis is genuinely unclaimed. It is also the highest-leverage tractable choice: it needs no frontier compute (GPT-2/Pythia/Gemma-2-2B, all public artifacts), it multiplies the value of every downstream safety application (feature-based monitors, alignment audits, model editing) by making their substrate trustworthy, and it converts an aesthetic decision into a measurable one with negative-result-tolerant, cumulative outputs — a benchmark, a metric, and identifiability curves the next coalition survey can cite.

direction: Mechanistically explain how transformers implement context/role-driven reinterpretation of concept features over conversations and build context-robust monitors from that mechanism.
project: The Context Gate: A Circuit-Level Account of Role-Driven Feature-Meaning Restructuring in LLMs
question: What circuit implements the conversation-induced flipping of concept-feature meanings (e.g., the "factuality" direction) — is there a compact role/context state that gates concept-feature readout — and can conditioning a monitor on that state keep it robust where static probes fail?
first_experiment: Replicate the published opposite-day/role-play probe-flipping protocol on Gemma-2-2B, then run layer × prefix-position activation patching between flipped-context and empty-context forward passes to causally localize where the context state that flips feature meaning is written.
why: It targets the specific open mechanism flagged by the authors of the phenomenon, sits at the intersection of the field's top-listed foundation (context-dependent feature meaning) and its most safety-critical application (probe-based monitors in deployment), is executable end-to-end on a single GPU with open tools, and is unclaimed because the phenomenon is only months old, the adjacent accounts are behavioral or static, and the mech-interp community's 2025–26 energy has been absorbed by attribution-graph methodology rather than the multi-turn regime where its assumptions visibly break.

direction: Develop obfuscation-robust mechanistic monitoring by treating activation-space interventions (patching, splicing, ablation) as runtime tests of hidden behavior, and characterize the fundamental costs that behavioral obfuscation cannot avoid.
project: Seeing Through the Disguise — Interventional Monitors and the Limits of Behavioral Obfuscation in LLMs
question: When a language model performs a hidden behavior while keeping its pointwise activation statistics indistinguishable from benign, must the disguised computation leave detectable signatures under cheap interventional tests (activation edits, cross-prompt splices, ablations), and is there a fundamental trade-off — an "obfuscation tax" — between preserving behavior, evading observational monitors, and evading interventional monitors?
first_experiment: On a small open model with a known hidden behavior (a sleeper-agent-style backdoor trained on Pythia/Gemma-2-2B, plus obfuscated-activation attacks reproduced from Bailey et al.'s public code), build a null distribution of "sensitivity profiles" — output-logit responses to a fixed battery of cheap activation edits (low-rank noise per layer, mean shifts, splices from benign prompts) on benign inputs — then test whether trigger inputs whose activations bypass a calibrated probe/SAE monitor are still separated by their interventional sensitivity profiles (AUROC vs. probe, SAE, and OOD baselines), using multi-layer joint edits to preempt self-repair confounds.
why: It is the highest-leverage open question in interpretability's comparative-advantage territory — the viability of monitoring-based safety cases under adaptive adversaries — where attacks have demonstrably outpaced every observational defense, so either a positive result (a new robust monitor class) or a negative result (interventions are also cheaply disguised, formalizing when monitoring fails) changes the field. It is not already done: the existing defense literature is purely observational (probe/SAE/OOD ensembles, parameter-space influence coupling, benign-corpus activation matching, trigger inversion in input space) and treats monitoring as passive reading of one input at a time; no published defense runs interventions on the suspect model, and no published work theorizes the necessary costs of behavioral obfuscation — while the surrounding attack literature is active enough to supply models, code, and adaptive red-team baselines that make the contribution both testable and urgent, at single-GPU scale.

direction: Mechanistically decompose how RL-trained reasoning models produce their final answers — via causal reading of their own chain-of-thought versus a direct latent route from the prompt — at the level of attention heads and features, and use this decomposition to explain pre-committed/performative reasoning, distinguish rationalization from genuine mistakes, and track how computation migrates off the CoT under RL monitorability pressure.
project: Two Roads to the Answer: Causal Decomposition of CoT-Mediated vs. Latent-Direct Computation in Reasoning Models
question: When a reasoning model emits its final answer, what fraction of answer-relevant computation flows through its written chain-of-thought versus bypasses it via a direct prompt-to-answer path; which components implement each route and where do they converge; how do the routes interact with pre-committed answer representations to produce confabulation and last-minute answer flips; and how does the route balance shift across RL checkpoints when the CoT is penalized by a monitor?
first_experiment: On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B (replicating on Qwen3-4B), generate CoT on GSM8K/MATH-500 problems, then apply attention knockout at the answer-span positions that selectively blocks (a) attention to the CoT span, (b) attention to the prompt span, and (c) neither, while leaving every token in context — a white-box intervention with no text corruption, avoiding the off-distribution confound of Lanham-style CoT editing. Measure changes in answer logit margin and accuracy to obtain per-example "route shares," validate with layer-wise knockouts to locate where the routes converge, cross-check against matched text-corruption baselines and the published attention-map signatures, then stratify examples by pre-CoT probe decodability and test the prediction that pre-committed examples are direct-route-dominated while genuine-reasoning examples are CoT-route-dominated.
why: CoT monitoring is the leading near-term oversight mechanism and its viability hinges on precisely this question, which the field's leading researchers explicitly list as open ("can we tell when a CoT was causally important?"; "rationalizing versus mistaken?") while a NeurIPS 2026 paper still states the answer phase's use of the trace is unclear. Existing work stops short in every direction — probes and steering decode pre-commitment without causal decomposition (Goodfire, Cox et al.), information-flow metrics formalize the two paths without component localization (Jia et al.), attention analyses are correlational (Chen et al.), patching is confined to non-RL models with prompted CoT (Mehrafarin et al.), step-attribution is black-box (Thought Anchors, AttriCoT, NLDD), circuit-based detectors compress to scores without mechanism (CIE-Scorer), and the one R1-recipe circuit study is task-specific verification only (Lee et al.) — so no published work causally separates the routes at component level in real RL reasoning models or tracks their balance under monitor-penalty RL, where DeepMind's account is purely conceptual. It is also feasible now: open-weight reasoning models, mature tooling (TransformerLens, nnsight, circuit-tracer, open SAEs), and direct precedents proving each ingredient works, on a budget of a few GPUs rather than six-figure circuit analyses.

direction: Attack attention superposition — the least-resourced of the field's declared hurdles — by building a sparse, causally validated decomposition of attention into query-key feature-pair interactions expressed in the residual-stream feature basis, and integrating it as the missing attention layer of the circuit-tracing stack.
project: Feature-Pair Attention: A Causally Validated Sparse Decomposition of Transformer Attention in the Residual-Stream Feature Basis
question: Can a transformer's attention be faithfully represented as a sparse set of (query-feature, key-feature, value-direction) interactions drawn from the model's own residual-stream feature dictionary — such that ablating individual feature pairs causally produces the predicted changes in behavior — thereby turning attribution graphs' unexplained attention edges into interpretable, testable feature-pair edges?
first_experiment: On GPT-2 small (layers 5, 7, 9–10, using open residual-stream SAEs), train per-head sparse interaction dictionaries that reconstruct each head's attention scores as s_h(i,j) ≈ b + Σ_p d^Q_p·a_p(i) + Σ_q d^K_q·a_q(j) + Σ_{p,q} C^h_{pq}·a_p(i)a_q(j) with L1-sparse C, trained on KL divergence to true attention patterns (single GPU, ~1–2 weeks). Evaluate (1) reconstruction fidelity vs. number of active feature pairs against two public baselines — unconstrained bilinear QK transcoders and Lorsa; then (2) on the IOI dataset, zero out the top predicted feature-pair interactions for name-mover heads (9.6, 9.9) and S-inhibition heads (7.3, 7.9) and check whether pair-level ablations reproduce the known path-patching effects at finer granularity. Success = ≤~30 active feature pairs per head-prompt explaining most task-relevant attention variance with ablation effects tracking path-patching ground truth; a failure of the SAE-basis form where free dictionaries succeed is itself informative about whether "attentional features" are shared-basis or transformed (prev(X)-style) versions of residual features, and redirects the project accordingly.
why: It is the only one of the five major hurdles named in the 2024 Circuits Updates that still lacks a serious, unified attack — every neighboring problem (missing features, cross-layer superposition, interference weights) now has a well-resourced lab directly on it, while attention decomposition is scattered across a 2025 replacement model (Lorsa, self-described as a first attempt with no pair-level causal validation), a three-week-old exploratory dashboard (QK transcoders, GPT-2 only, explicitly excluding the OV side and cross-layer cases), and post-hoc analyses (contrastive covariances, SVD methods) that never build a generative, causally validated replacement. Anthropic's own circuit-tracing pipeline routes features through undecomposed attention and its multi-org landscape report explicitly lists attention follow-ups as open questions — so the field's standard methodology has a known, admitted hole exactly here. It is also the highest-leverage missing piece: attention mediates nearly all cross-position feature interaction, so a validated attentional-feature layer upgrades every downstream investigation (induction, entity binding, long-context aggregation, in-context learning) rather than one behavior. Crucially, it has not been done because the pieces live in different communities — replacement-model builders (Lorsa), dashboard builders (QK transcoders), theorists (SVF alignment), and infrastructure builders (CLT attribution graphs) — and unifying them with rigorous pair-level causal validation on canonical circuits is exactly the kind of integrative, small-compute work (GPT-2/Pythia scale, public weights and baselines) that big labs deprioritize but that the theory (SVF alignment's sparse-attention-decomposition prediction) says should succeed. Both outcomes are publishable: success yields the missing layer of the interpretability stack; failure localizes where the linear-feature hypothesis breaks for attention.

direction: Establish whether unsupervised mechanistic anomaly detection generalizes across held-out model organisms of misalignment where supervised probes provably fail, via a transfer benchmark with benign-shift and adversarial-evasion controls.
project: MAD-Transfer: A Leave-One-Organism-Out Benchmark for Mechanistic Anomaly Detection in LLMs
question: Do mechanism-signature distances (SAE feature distributions, neuron-basis profiles, activation-matched reference residuals) detect anomalous cognition on held-out organisms at low false-positive rates where cross-organism probes fail — and can informed adversaries evade them?
first_experiment: On Llama-3.1-8B, assemble 5 organisms (public sleeper-agent and sandbagging checkpoints, self-trained password-locked backdoor and EM LoRA, prompted in-context deception) with matched benign/triggered prompt sets; run 3 label-free mechanism-signature detectors vs. 2 supervised probe baselines and report the 5×5 transfer matrix with AUROC and FPR@5% on a benign-novelty suite.
why: Both major field reviews rank white-box evaluation methodology as the most pressing open problem; 2026's frontier results (AISI auditing games, "One Probe Won't Catch Them All", "Did you lie?") show probes fail under organism heterogeneity and training-induced misbehavior; the only unsupervised mechanistic detectors are recent method papers with no transfer, false-positive, evasion, or causal-validation evaluation; the needed organisms, SAEs, and tooling are public and 8B-scale feasible; and the answer is decision-relevant for safety cases in both directions.

direction: Build the missing, ground-truth-validated faithfulness audit for the field's dominant explanatory artifact — CLT-based attribution graphs — and use it to measure, on real models, when and why circuit explanations are structurally unfaithful rather than merely behavior-matching.
project: Auditing the Auditors: A Held-Out Interventional Faithfulness Test for Attribution Graphs
question: When does a CLT-derived attribution graph describe the model's actual computation versus a behaviorally-equivalent decomposition, and can a quantitative, non-circular audit based on held-out interventions reliably detect structural unfaithfulness (e.g., deep multi-hop pathways rewritten as shallow lookalikes) before such graphs are trusted as safety evidence?
first_experiment: Build a ground-truth testbed where the true mechanism is known and verified by ablation — a small transformer (GPT-2-small / Gemma-3-270M scale) trained on enforced multi-hop tasks (two-hop recall with controlled bridge tokens, plus GPT-2's known greater-than circuit) — then train CLTs across a sparsity-penalty sweep (reproducing the ICML 2026 shallow-rewrite regime), and run a candidate audit battery of held-out interventions (ablating the known intermediate component, node clamps, paraphrase/OOD inputs where shallow shortcuts break but deep pathways survive), scoring the disagreement between graph-as-model predictions and the actual model's responses. Success criterion: the audit score separates known-unfaithful decompositions from faithful ones *without access to ground-truth labels*. If it works, scale the audit to the public Gemma Scope 2 cross-layer transcoders on multi-hop factual recall and refusal, then test a mitigation (selecting seeds/penalties/prunings by held-out interventional agreement).
why: It attacks the single highest-leverage crack in the field's current paradigm: attribution graphs are becoming standard infrastructure and safety evidence (Gemma Scope 2, deception investigations, auditing games), yet the ICML 2026 toy-model result shows sparsity objectives can systematically replace real mechanisms with behavior-matching fakes, and the field's own 2026 retrospective ranks this dual-basis/faithfulness problem first among open problems while noting verification chronically lags production. It has not been done because the CLT paradigm is only ~20 months old, the first structural unfaithfulness result appeared in July 2026 with only "preliminary" real-model evidence and no metric or fix, the older circuit-faithfulness critique doesn't transfer to per-prompt feature graphs, and community energy has flowed into *producing and automating* graphs (ADAG, Circuit Oracle, CLT-Forge, probe-prompting) rather than validating them. The experiment is cheap (small models, public transcoders and tooling, a few GPU-days), has a clean falsifiable success criterion, and a positive result upgrades every downstream use of attribution graphs — while a negative result (audit finds real CLTs faithful) would itself be the first quantitative reassurance the field lacks.

direction: Build the missing "inhibitory half" of circuit analysis — a systematic method and empirical framework for discovering and classifying *suppressive circuitry* (why the model does NOT output the competitor answer), validated on known motifs and applied to safety-relevant suppression behaviors.
project: Counter-Rooted Circuits: A Systematic Framework for Suppressive Circuitry in Language Models
question: When a language model rejects an available candidate output (a distractor answer, a harmful continuation, a user-cued incorrect answer), what internal mechanisms implement that rejection — direct negative writes, competitor boosting, attention-level gating, softmax redistribution artifacts, or ablation-dependent self-repair — and how does the composition of these mechanisms explain when suppression succeeds (accurate self-correction, refusal) versus fails (sycophancy, confidently-wrong answers, "knowing but not correcting")?
first_experiment: On GPT-2 small with the indirect-object-identification task (the best-understood circuit in the field, with hand-documented negative name movers and copy suppression), build dual-rooted attribution graphs using the public circuit-tracer/CLT stack: the standard graph rooted at the chosen token's logit, plus novel "counter-rooted" graphs rooted at the logit of the *suppressed competitor* (the rejected name). Compute a signed suppressive-influence score for every feature and edge; verify the method automatically recovers the known negative-name-mover set (precision/recall vs. the hand analysis); then decompose the recovered suppression into the taxonomy's mechanism classes via path patching in the transcoder basis and quantify what fraction of the causal structure standard positive-rooted graphs miss. Success criterion: counter-rooted graphs recover the documented suppressive components with high precision, and the positive-rooted "suppression blind spot" is quantitatively large — which licenses the full program on Llama-3.2-1B/Qwen3-4B for factual self-correction, sycophantic cue resistance, and refusal.
why: (1) *Importance and leverage* — suppression underlies essentially every safety-relevant behavior (refusal, self-correction, sycophancy resistance, answer flips), yet the field's entire discovery apparatus (loss/KL objectives, logit-diff patching, attribution graphs rooted at the observed token) systematically renders it invisible; a systematic framework turns ~10 scattered case studies into one reusable method, taxonomy, and measurable quantity ("suppression strength") that predicts when models will and won't resist wrong answers. (2) *It's the community's own declared gap* — stated verbatim as an open problem in the Aug 2025 multi-lab Circuits Research Landscape, still unfilled as of November 2026. (3) *Falsifiability* — suppression claims make sign-specific directional predictions (ablating suppressors must *raise* competitor probability), which directly addresses the field's validation/non-identifiability crisis better than performance-degradation criteria. (4) *Tractable for me* — public models, public CLTs, known ground-truth motifs for validation, single-GPU scale. (5) *Why it hasn't been done* — infrastructure maturity (transcoder attribution graphs only became widely usable in 2025), metric conventions that root all analysis at the chosen output, conceptual caution raised by the counterfactual-causality critique (Missed Causes, 2024), and the topic's fragmentation into single-motif case studies; the nearest neighbors (Concept-Targeted Attribution, co-ablation, interaction-aware discovery, copy suppression) each stop short of targeting rejected outputs or building a general suppression taxonomy — and 2026's converging adjacent work (cue-routing, tomography, CTA) shows the window is open now but closing.

direction: Build a distribution-generalizing verification layer for mechanistic explanations — resolving the 2026 "dual basis problem" by certifying which circuits/attribution graphs (or mechanism-family representations) predict intervention outcomes on unseen semantic distributions, rather than merely fitting the extraction distribution.
project: Mechanism Families over Circuits: Discriminative, Generalization-Aware Certificates for Mechanistic Explanations
question: When multiple circuits/attribution graphs are equally faithful on the extraction distribution (the equivalence class revealed by phantom specialization and rephrasing variance), can a standardized multi-distribution interventional test battery (a) discriminate the explanation whose interventions generalize to unseen templates, formats, and input distributions — measured against planted ground truth (InterpBench/SIIT models, known IOI-style circuits) rather than interpretability aesthetics — and (b) does a family-level representation (e.g., union/consensus over per-distribution circuits) predict held-out-distribution behavior of interventions well enough to restore reliable steering and monitoring where single-distribution circuits provably fail?
first_experiment: On GPT-2-small and Pythia-410M on IOI, greater-than, and one MIB arithmetic task: build a candidate-circuit pool — EAP-IG and ACDC circuits extracted from multiple seeds AND multiple extraction distributions (templates/frequency bands), size-matched random circuits, and "decoy" circuits sampled from the demonstrated equivalence class (faithful on source, structurally disjoint from the known mechanism); then compute, for every candidate, standard source-faithfulness versus a multi-distribution transfer battery (edge-level sufficiency/necessity on held-out templates, cross-distribution ablation transfer, sample-wise variance) and evaluate the discriminative power (AUC) of each metric class at separating true-mechanism circuits from decoys. If transfer metrics separate mechanisms that source-faithfulness cannot, that AUC result is the seed of the certificate; if they don't, it is exactly the quantified negative result the field says it needs — either outcome is a publishable, decision-relevant advance.
why: It attacks the single gap that the field's most informed 2026 assessment places at the top of the agenda ("verification, not labeling, is the bottleneck"; the dual basis problem; faithfulness as a numerical target; "publish negative results when interventions do not survive distribution shift"), and it is validated by convergent failure evidence from independent groups (phantom specialization, rephrasing variance, AuditBench's white-box tool-to-agent gap, deceptive automated interpretability, detection-without-actionability). It has not already been done because the 2026 certification literature only certifies different objects — discovery-algorithm stability under dataset resampling, statistical uncertainty over a declared distribution, and ℓ∞-neighborhood attention queries — none of which resolve explanation identity under semantic distribution shift, and the closest diagnostic papers (phantom specialization, Bucketing the Good Apples, CEAP) stop at diagnosis without a discriminative metric benchmark, adversarial decoys, or the constructive family-level step; feature-level causal validation is being actively worked, but the decomposition/explanation level — where steering and monitoring reliability is actually lost — is open. It is tractable now (public infra: MIB, InterpBench, AuditBench models, Gemma Scope, nnsight/TransformerLens, open Circuit Tracer) and maximally upstream: a working generalization certificate converts today's fragile white-box evidence into audit-grade signal, directly addressing the deployment gap that makes interpretability safety-relevant rather than merely descriptive.

direction: Build the first systematic protocol and metric for measuring — and a consensus-circuit method for improving — how much of a transcoder-based attribution graph survives as a causally valid circuit claim on held-out and distribution-shifted inputs, converting the field's top-ranked "dual basis" problem from a philosophical worry into a benchmarkable quantity.
project: Execution Traces vs. Algorithms: Stress-Testing the Generality of Attribution-Graph Circuits
question: Which nodes, edges, and pathways of a transcoder-based attribution graph are real, stable components of the model's algorithm — invariant across a task's prompt family, transcoder training seeds, and distribution shift, and causally operative on held-out inputs — versus prompt-specific execution-trace artifacts, and can "consensus circuits" aggregated across many prompts be validated (and fail legibly) where single-prompt graphs cannot?
first_experiment: Using Gemma-2-2B + Gemma Scope transcoders (and released CLTs via the open-source circuit-tracer), replicate two known behaviors — greater-than year prediction and two-hop factual recall — across ~150 prompts spanning paraphrase, difficulty, and cross-domain shifts, with 2–3 transcoder seeds each, then measure node/edge/pathway recurrence across the family, compare interventional validity (ablation/steering effects on the target logit) of per-prompt top-attribution features vs. the cross-prompt consensus core on held-out shifted inputs, and quantify seed-to-seed structural agreement.
why: It directly operationalizes the problem that both the 2026 retrospective of "Open Problems in Mechanistic Interpretability" and the November 2026 state-of-the-field survey rank as the field's most important unresolved methodological question — the dual-basis/proxy-fidelity problem — while executing two explicit open questions from the attribution-graph method's own authors (merging per-prompt graphs into a global picture; automating validation on out-of-distribution inputs). It has not been done: the nearest works are all one step removed — feature-level faithfulness checks (not graph structure), identifiability theory that explicitly does not address legible decompositions, SAE seed-stability studies (not graphs), ablation-metric critiques (not transcoder circuits), and labeling/querying tooling (Circuit-Diff's aggregation tool is released but unevaluated; ADAG and Circuit Oracle interpret graphs without testing their generality). It is the most promising direction because it converts the field's central epistemic risk — publishing behavior-fitting decompositions that silently misdescribe the model, which the survey flags as the top risk to safety conclusions and the key failure mode of deployed mechanistic monitors under distribution shift — into a cheap, benchmarkable measurement with a clear deliverable (a generality score and stress-test suite), with informative outcomes either way, and it is executable with open-weight models, public dictionaries, existing tooling, and modest compute.

direction: Build the missing verification layer for mechanistic interpretability — a protocol and metric that actively discriminates between competing explanations (circuits, attribution graphs, SAE decompositions) via automatically designed interchange experiments, replacing behavior-level faithfulness scores that the field has just proven broken.
project: Discriminating Interchange Experiments (DIE): from non-identifiability to evidence-based mechanism selection
question: When two candidate mechanisms for a model's behavior are behaviorally indistinguishable on the standard evaluation distribution, can we (a) formalize the discriminating power of an evaluation protocol (inputs × intervention sites), (b) automatically search for maximally discriminating interchange experiments between candidates, and (c) show that this protocol selects the true mechanism where standard faithfulness fails or misranks?
first_experiment: On GPT-2 small and the IOI task, take three candidate explanations — the published Wang et al. reference circuit, an ACDC-discovered circuit, and a controlled edit of the reference that is behaviorally equivalent on the IOI template distribution but mechanistically different (per Geng et al.'s edit methodology). First, confirm standard KL-faithfulness under resample ablation cannot separate them (expected: ties or misranking, replicating the diagnosis). Second, run a search over gradient-guided input edits (name/object substitutions, repeated-subject and "romantic object" variants per uit de Bos) and interchange interventions at internal sites (S-inhibition outputs, induction-head QK, name-mover OV), ranking each experiment by the divergence it induces between the candidates' predicted output distributions, then check which candidate tracks the full model on the top-ranked experiments. Success = a measurable discrimination rate from ~20 designed experiments that standard faithfulness on 10k template prompts cannot achieve, establishing the protocol and the metric in a two-week, single-GPU result.
why: It attacks the field's explicitly named #1 bottleneck — the verification/faithfulness gap, named by the 2026 state-of-field review as the "dual basis problem" and by Geng et al.'s conclusion as the thing that "remains open" — rather than a problem I'd have to argue is important. It is tractable at toy/small-LM scale with ground-truth testbeds (InterpBench, Tracr, MIB) needing no frontier access, and it compounds: attribution graphs, SAE feature labels, and production safety monitors all become falsifiable under a discriminating-power protocol, directly addressing the review's warnings that monitors fail under distributional shift by *searching for* the shift instead of waiting for it. And it has not been done: the closest works each stop one step short — uit de Bos et al. do adversarial inputs for a single circuit vs. the full model but never candidate-vs-candidate; Méloux et al. prove non-identifiability in toy models but construct no selection method; Geng et al. diagnose misranking but offer only a context-restoration diagnostic; Hadad et al. and Certified Circuits verify a single circuit's robustness/minimality, not mechanism identity; causal scrubbing is manual, unautomated, and unbenchmarked; and MIB still evaluates behavior-level faithfulness curves. As of November 2026, no one has assembled designed-experiment discrimination between competing mechanistic hypotheses with a quantitative discriminating-power metric validated against known ground truth.

direction: Behavior-agnostic mechanistic anomaly detection for LLMs using cheap causal models of normal computation (mechanism-prediction residuals) as per-inference safety monitors.
project: Mechanism-Residual Monitors
question: Can residuals from a normal-computation dynamics model separate same-output-different-mechanism misalignment from benign computation without labeled anomalies, at deployment-grade cost, and with greater obfuscation-robustness than state-level latent defenses?
first_experiment: Fit per-layer linear transition predictors on trusted benign activations of Gemma-2-2B-it / Qwen3-8B; test mechanism-prediction-error AUROC/FPR on public sandbagging and backdoor model organisms vs. held-out benign and benign-OOD controls, benchmarked against SAE reconstruction error, Mahalanobis, and probe baselines.
why: It is the one direction that simultaneously targets the field's most safety-urgent unmet need (detecting unknown misaligned mechanisms, where supervised probes demonstrably fail), is enabled by infrastructure that only matured in 2025–26 (open transcoders/CLTs, public model organisms), and has no existing implementation — because it sits between the interpretability community (mechanism models as research artifacts, not runtime monitors), the monitoring community (supervised, behavior-specific probes), and ARC's theoretical MAD agenda, whose sole empirical instance is expensive and backdoor-only.

direction: Build a decomposition-agnostic protocol and predictor that ranks rival feature/circuit decompositions of a real LLM by their predicted causal-faithfulness under distribution shift, converting explanation selection from aesthetics into measurement.
project: Tolerances — Predicting Which Mechanistic Decompositions Survive Distribution Shift
question: Which in-distribution-computable signals predict which of several behaviorally-equivalent decompositions of the same model stays causally faithful (interventionally accurate, not just detection-consistent) under graded distribution shifts?
first_experiment: On Gemma-2-2B with Gemma Scope SAEs (16k/65k/262k) plus transcoders across 2–3 MIB tasks, compute per-decomposition in-distribution causal faithfulness and the "shift-faithfulness gap" under a paraphrase→unseen-entity→OOD→synonym-attack ladder, then regress gap size on cheap ID statistics (dictionary utilization, intervention-residual variance, firing-rate entropy, selectivity-vs-causal-force correlation) to find the first predictor of shift-robustness.
why: The dual-basis problem and the missing shared faithfulness metric are the field's top self-identified open problems as of 2026, with convergent 2025–26 evidence (template variance, error blindness, adversarial feature flips, detection-vs-causal gaps) but no paper that ranks competing decompositions of a real LM by predicted shift-fidelity — while Gemma Scope, MIB, and open tooling make it cheaply feasible, and every deployed monitor or audit currently inherits an unvalidated, aesthetic decomposition choice that this work would make principled.

direction: Determine the causal control architecture of self-correction in reasoning models — i.e., whether the internally detectable "this trajectory is wrong" signal is causally load-bearing for backtracking decisions, epiphenomenal, or bypassed by surface-level doubt-token triggers.
project: The Silent Critic: Locating the Causal Architecture of Error Awareness and Self-Correction in Reasoning Models
question: Where in the network is the probe-detectable reasoning-error signal computed during chain-of-thought generation, which components (if any) causally read it into generation decisions, and is backtracking driven by that internal critic or by the model's reaction to its own verbalized doubt tokens?
first_experiment: On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B/7B and -Llama-8B, build matched clean/corrupted trace pairs via controlled error injection at known positions on GSM8K, ProofWriter, and MATH-500 (surprisal-matched, per the stress-test criteria); replicate the step-1 error probe; treat the probe direction as a linear readout and run attribution/path patching against the probe score to localize its write-path (attention heads aggregating across trajectory positions vs. step-local MLP computation); then ablate that write-path at *subspace* granularity during free-running generation and measure (i) probe readout change, (ii) P(backtrack|state), (iii) final accuracy — against three controls: whole-residual patching (replicating Yuan et al.'s failure), doubt-token suppression (surface-loop control), and wait-feature steering (positive control). Success criterion: an intervention that moves the probe readout >80% while preserving coherence, which adjudicates the critic-vs-surface-loop dispute either way.
why: It resolves a live dispute that four separate 2025–26 papers explicitly flagged as unresolved ("mechanism unknown," "diagnostic not causal," "requires falsification criteria"), on a question the Aug 2025 multi-lab landscape named open and safety-critical: whether verbalized CoT is causally load-bearing for self-correction determines whether CoT monitoring suffices or internal critic-readout monitors are required — and the "know-but-don't-say" dissociation it maps is the mechanistic template for concealment phenomena (eval-awareness, sandbagging, deception). It has not been done because the nearest neighbors each hold only one corner — probes without source localization and with wrong-granularity interventions (Yuan et al. 2026), downstream wait-effectors without the source and likely lexical confounds (Troitskii et al. 2025; Ma et al. 2026), a surface-loop theory without internal evidence (2603.15500), per-step graph fingerprints without trajectory-level causality (CRV, FAIR 2025), and probe stress-tests without a causal mechanism (NeurIPS 2026) — leaving the causal link between the two ends of the loop unclaimed. It is feasible with open models, public datasets, and existing tooling, uses mature microscopes on an open biology question exactly as the field's leaders called for, and produces a decisive answer regardless of which hypothesis wins.

direction: Build the first attribution-graph circuit-tracing study of an RL-trained reasoning model, to mechanistically determine when the final answer is computed from the chain-of-thought versus carried by answer-features that persist independently of it, producing both the long-CoT tracing methods this requires and a causal pre-commitment detector for CoT monitoring.
project: Rationalizer or Reasoner — Attribution Graphs of Pre-Committed Answers in Large Reasoning Models
question: In reasoning models (primary: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B; replication: R1-Distill-Llama-8B, Qwen3-4B), does the influence on final-answer logits flow through features activated during CoT steps (genuine reasoning) or through "answer-carrier" features present at the question/pre-CoT state that persist through the trace (rationalization) — and can attribution-graph structure classify the regime on held-out traces better than probes, while correctly distinguishing pre-commitment from honest post-hoc error?
first_experiment: Train cross-layer transcoders on R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B over a CoT-rich activation corpus and verify the surrogate model's replacement score; then elicit traces on GSM8K-style problems, label each trace's regime behaviorally (CoT truncation/error-injection sensitivity assays plus a pre-CoT answer probe following Cox et al.), and construct attribution graphs of the answer logits for ~50 traces — measuring the fraction of answer influence attributable to pre-CoT answer-carrier features vs. CoT-step features, then validating causally: ablating answer-carriers should flip answers while leaving CoT text unchanged, and ablating CoT-step features should flip answers only in CoT-sensitive traces.
why: (1) Both the method-builders (Neuronpedia landscape) and the LRM survey name exactly this gap — reasoning-model biology and CoT trustworthiness — yet no attribution-graph study of any reasoning model exists as of today; the closest work either excludes reasoning models by design (CRV), stays at probe/steering level (Cox et al.), or at representation level (RISE). (2) Safety relevance is direct and near-term: CoT monitoring is a leading deployment-time safety strategy and its core assumption — that the stated reasoning causes the answer — is precisely what this project tests mechanistically, yielding a monitor with a causal story that can be benchmarked auditing-games style against behavioral ground truth. (3) It forces a listed methods advance (attribution graphs at long generations), which is a bottleneck for the entire field going forward. (4) It is feasible on open weights with existing infrastructure, and it is falsifiable: if graphs cannot separate the regimes, that is itself an important negative result about the informativeness of the field's dominant artifact.

direction: Make mechanistic circuit explanations falsifiable by testing whether circuits extracted on in-distribution data predict what models do — and which components matter — on out-of-distribution inputs where ID-compatible algorithms diverge, and use that OOD predictive validity to adjudicate between competing decompositions.
project: Circuits That Predict: OOD-Adjudicated Validation of Mechanistic Decompositions
question: When multiple circuit decompositions (component-level, neuron-level, SAE-feature) explain a model's in-distribution behavior equally faithfully, does out-of-distribution predictive validity — predicting the model's OOD generalization rule and the OOD shift in component importance from ID-extracted circuit structure — identify which decomposition tracks the model's actual computation?
first_experiment: Train a population of ~100–200 small transformers (1–6 layers, varied seeds/hyperparameters, following Li et al.'s Dyck-1 protocol where ID data is compatible with both the EQUAL-COUNT and NESTED rules); extract per-model circuits using ID data only with two methods — component-level EAP-IG and neuron-level RelP; verify both reach matched ID faithfulness; then, on held-out models, test (a) whether circuit structure (e.g., presence of violation-detection heads in the circuit, circuit attention to nesting-critical positions) predicts each model's OOD rule (AUROC) against Li et al.'s attention-statistics and hyperparameter baselines, and (b) whether ablating each ID-extracted circuit on OOD inputs produces the behavior change that decomposition predicts, decomposing results by basis to see whether OOD predictiveness discriminates the two decompositions.
why: It attacks the mechanistic interpretability field's own #1 open problem — non-circular validation of circuit claims and the dual-basis/under-determination problem, both now proven to be severe (Miller et al. 2024; Méloux et al. 2025; Sheng & Fu 2026; Li & Subramani 2026; Arora et al. 2026) — with the one validation criterion that needs no ground-truth "true circuit" and no human judgment: agreement between an explanation's predictions and directly observable OOD behavior ("predict how models act in unseen situations," an explicit goal of the field's 2025 roadmap that remains its least-developed application). It has not been done because the enabling pieces only just converged: the population-based OOD-prediction methodology was introduced in mid-2025 at the whole-attention level only (Li et al., explicitly a proof of concept, no circuit extraction, no decomposition comparison); cheap comparable multi-basis circuit extraction (RelP, EAP-IG, neuron-basis) matured only in 2025–2026; existing ground-truth benchmarks (InterpBench/TracrBench) impose circuits via compilation rather than studying naturally-learned competition between mechanisms and lack any OOD dimension; adjacent 2026 work either certifies dataset-edit stability (Certified Circuits), predicts OOD accuracy from circuits in the reverse direction (CAS), or tests feature-level OOD error prediction (Huang et al. 2025) — none uses OOD behavior to adjudicate between competing circuit decompositions. The experiment is feasible on a single GPU with small model populations, and both outcomes are valuable: success yields the field's first principled, aesthetic-free criterion for choosing among decompositions (and a reusable benchmark); failure would show current circuit extraction captures in-distribution computation but not generalization-relevant structure — a decision-relevant negative result for the "circuits as theories" view, and the enabling prerequisite for OOD-robust mechanistic anomaly detection.

direction: Develop an automated adversarial falsification protocol that treats attribution graphs as testable causal hypotheses and uses benign semantic distribution shift to expose decoy decompositions, yielding the field's first shift-robust faithfulness metric and a principled solution to the dual-basis problem.
project: Adversarial Faithfulness Auditing: Falsifying Attribution Graphs Under Benign Semantic Shift
question: Do attribution graphs that match model behavior in-distribution also predict model behavior under benign semantic distribution shift, and can adversarially searched shift-failures discriminate competing decompositions of the same behavior?
first_experiment: Reproduce a canonical multi-hop factual-recall attribution graph on Gemma-2-2B with open cross-layer transcoders, then measure KL(full model ‖ graph-as-replacement-model) across paraphrase/entity-substitution/distractor/hop-extension families, run LLM-guided genetic search to maximize benign divergence, and compare the divergence profile against the same behavior traced with per-layer transcoders — with InterpBench as the known-ground-truth control.
why: Verification — not discovery or labeling — is now the field's self-identified #1 bottleneck; three separate 2024–2026 lines of work (adversarial circuit evaluation, Certified Circuits, context-distortion misranking) each diagnose part of the failure and all stop short of a constructive protocol for feature-level graphs; the ICML 2026 finding that cross-layer transcoders learn decoy circuits makes decomposition discrimination urgent rather than academic; the enabling infrastructure (open CLTs, InterpBench) is barely 18 months old; and it is tractable on 1–2B open models with no SAE retraining, while multiplying the trustworthiness of every downstream circuit claim and deployed safety monitor.

direction: Solve the dual-basis problem — establish held-out intervention generalization as the first non-circular, quantitative criterion for deciding which of many behaviorally-equivalent decompositions (SAE seeds/widths, transcoders, baselines) is the model's actual mechanism, and build the benchmark that measures it.
project: Which Circuit Is Real? Mechanism Identification via Held-Out Intervention Generalization
question: When two mechanistic decompositions of the same model explain the same behavior equally well on the calibration distribution — same reconstruction error, same labels, same on-distribution ablation predictions — do they diverge in their predictions under interventions held out of calibration (unseen prompts, unseen intervention types and magnitudes, composite ablations), and can held-out intervention prediction error serve as a tractable, non-circular criterion that ranks decompositions by mechanism-truth rather than readability?
first_experiment: On one small open model (Pythia-410m and/or Gemma-2-2B at one residual layer), train 4+ independent TopK SAE seeds at matched width/L0 with sae_lens, plus baseline dictionaries (random matched-width, PCA); for a fixed task (e.g., IOI), verify that all seeds are statistically indistinguishable on every standard criterion (reconstruction, L0, automated labels, on-distribution predicted-vs-realized ablation effects), then sample held-out interventions — novel prompts, amplifications, cross-feature composite ablations — and measure each graph's predicted Δlogit against the model's realized Δlogit, quantifying the seed-to-seed OOD divergence score. A nonzero divergence between seeds that are equivalent on-distribution is the first empirical demonstration of the dual-basis problem, and validates the metric's discriminative signal (it must also correctly rank random/PCA baselines last).
why: It attacks the problem that a 2026 state-of-the-field review identifies as the single most important open problem in mechanistic interpretability, independently corroborated by the field's validation-problem literature, the Koopman identifiability paper ("the identifiable object and the legible object are not the same object"), and the seed-fragility findings of the margin paper. It has not been done because the nearest neighbors each stop short: ObserverBench tests decision adequacy of observers, not mechanism identification among decompositions; the margin paper corrects graphs locally within one seed and never evaluates held-out generalization or ranks decompositions; iSAE optimizes seed stability without testing truth; the SAEBench audit evaluates correlation-based proxies and explicitly lacks a causal-OOD axis; and feature-level causal validation (anytime-valid tests, intervention attribution) scores individual features rather than decompositions as whole causal models. Success yields the field's missing "perplexity for interpretability" — the quantitative faithfulness target needed to scale verification past the labeling bottleneck, to ground safety monitors in mechanisms rather than artifacts, and to connect legible decompositions to the newly-proven identifiable spectral invariants.

direction: Mechanistically dissect the reward-hacking decision — mapping, with attribution graphs and causal interventions, how RL-trained models internally compute "satisfy the grader by exploiting the shortcut" versus "solve the task honestly," and whether the probe-detected "cheating" representation is causally load-bearing rather than epiphenomenal — to convert reward-hack monitoring from correlational detection into tamper-evident, circuit-grounded understanding.
project: The Circuit Anatomy of Reward Hacking: From Probes That Detect to Mechanisms That Explain
question: When a model chooses to reward-hack, what circuit computes that choice — how do grader-salience, evaluation-awareness, and shortcut-availability features converge and compete with task-solution and refusal/honesty circuitry — and is the probe-detected "cheating" representation causally upstream of the hacking behavior (so that suppressing it reduces hacking), or a downstream correlate that can be evaded without changing behavior?
first_experiment: Train a minimal reward-hacking organism on Qwen3-4B (the largest open model with released cross-layer transcoders in Circuit Tracer, and an RL-trained thinking model) via LoRA DPO on planted-shortcut agentic tasks (BAITBENCH/CATCH-style honeypots), following the "How to train your model organism" recipe; verify the hack rate jumps from ~0% to >50% and that the published difference-of-means "cheating" probe fires on the organism. Then run attribution graphs on matched rollout pairs — identical tasks and prompts where the organism commits to the shortcut versus solves honestly — at the commitment token, and causally test the graph's hub features and the probe direction by patching/suppressing them: measure the effect on hack rate and honest-task performance. Deliverable: the first attribution-graph-level map of a hacking decision plus a causal verdict on whether the monitoring signal the field built in 2026 is load-bearing or epiphenomenal.
why: (1) It targets the field's most urgent failure mode: 2026's evidence (Hacker-Opus, sandbox escapes, transcript tampering, RL-Obfuscation) says reward hacking generalizes to monitor evasion, and the entire latent-monitoring agenda rests on the untested assumption that probe signals are causally tied to behavior — my question stress-tests that assumption, and its answer either yields robust circuit-invariant monitors and steering interventions, or demonstrates that current monitors are evadable in a way we can characterize (a negative result that would redirect the field). (2) The prerequisite questions were posed open and explicitly by Bergen et al., Goodfire, and Anthropic's organism release in 2026 — this is a documented, unsolved gap, not my speculation. (3) It has not been done because it falls in an awkward gap: the probe papers (Sept 2026) used the cheapest first tool, the circuit-tracing infrastructure for RL-trained open models only became available in late 2025–2026, and circuit-level analysis requires the combination of organisms, CLTs, and causal validation that neither the probe groups nor Anthropic-scale behavioral studies have yet assembled — the sandbagging analog (Aug 2026) and emergent-misalignment analyses are probe/SAE-level, and no attribution-graph study of hacking, sandbagging, or hidden objectives exists anywhere in my searches. (4) It is feasible for a small team today: open weights, released CLTs, published organism-training recipes, and honeypot testbeds all exist; and it naturally extends to the tamper-evidence question (does probe-evasion RL leave circuit fingerprints even when behavior is unchanged?) which is the next load-bearing question for monitor robustness.

direction: Mechanistically dissect whether hidden-misbehavior computations in RLVR reasoning models are causally removed, migrated across layers/readouts, or merely masked at monitored readouts, and convert that cartography into design principles for evasion-resistant monitor ensembles.
project: Cartography of Concealment: Where Misbehavior Signals Go When Reasoning Models Are Trained to Hide Them
question: When a reasoning model is optimized to evade a white-box monitor, is the misbehaving computation (a) causally removed, (b) migrated to other layers/readouts/subspaces, or (c) retained but masked at the monitored readout — and which causally-validated monitor ensembles make evasion detectable regardless?
first_experiment: Reproduce monitor-induced obfuscation in open honeypots (MBPP/Largest Island, R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, GRPO with joint task+CoT-monitor reward), then at each RL checkpoint sweep per-layer linear probes on residual/MLP-out/attention-out at CoT and answer positions plus a difference-of-means "hack direction" and released Qwen SAE features, followed by steering/ablation tests along surviving directions to classify each run as removal, migration, or masking.
why: It is the missing causal-mechanistic foundation for the field's highest-stakes application — monitorability-based safety cases — sits precisely between four adjacent literatures that each stop short of it (attack papers without mechanisms, defense papers without mechanism or reasoning models, probe-survival results without layer/readout or causal analysis, and token-only leak theory), is runnable on open models/code/SAEs with modest compute, and is decisive either way: removal causally vindicates white-box penalty training, while migration/masking yields the first migration topology and concrete ensemble/read-position requirements for safety cases.

direction: Build the missing adjudication layer for mechanistic interpretability — a framework that treats competing decompositions of the same model+behavior (different SAE seeds, hand circuits, decoys) as rival hypotheses and uses automated search over distribution shifts and intervention policies to discriminate them, quantifying both how often they separate and how often they are irreducibly ambiguous.
project: Equivalence Trials: Adjudicating Behaviorally-Equivalent Mechanistic Explanations with Designed Interventions
question: When two or more decompositions of a fixed model reproduce the same behavior under standard on-distribution faithfulness checks, how large is the divergence of their causal predictions under designed distribution shift — can automated discriminating-test design systematically select the decomposition that tracks the model's real mechanism, and what fraction of the explanation space is irreducibly ambiguous at realistic intervention budgets?
first_experiment: On GPT-2 small / Pythia-70m IOI with public TopK SAEs: construct ≥3 decompositions that each pass standard on-distribution sufficiency/necessity thresholds — (1) the canonical hand-built IOI head circuit, (2) attribution graphs from two different SAE seeds, (3) "decoy" circuits discovered on narrow prompt subsets — then run each decomposition's ablation/patching predictions across a six-family shift battery (name-frequency shift, repeated names, distractor tokens, varying name-list length, order conventions, template paraphrases) and measure per-decomposition prediction error and pairwise divergence. Deliverable: the first quantification of on-distribution-equivalence hiding out-of-distribution divergence, validating that discrimination signal exists before building the automated test-design search and the SIIT "twin model" ground-truth benchmark.
why: It attacks the field's top self-identified gap — the dual-basis/faithfulness problem — at the exact moment attribution graphs became the standard artifact and verification infrastructure is widely acknowledged to lag labeling; it is compute-feasible on open models with public dictionaries, it produces publishable results in both directions (a working adjudicator, or a quantified map of irreducible ambiguity that calibrates every audit and monitor), and it directly serves safety by determining what an interpretability-derived monitor can honestly certify. It has not been done: Méloux et al. only diagnosed non-identifiability in toys without proposing resolution; Certified Circuits certifies a single discovery's stability, not arbitration between rivals; Unit Tests test specificity of single claims; seed-reproducibility and margin papers document or patch instability without causal adjudication; InterpBench evaluates discovery against ground truth but not discrimination among multiple passing explanations; and the Koopman work explicitly concedes its identifiable object is not the legible one — leaving the question "which decomposition is the mechanism?" open by the field's own assessment.

direction: Build a ground-truth-free test that discriminates among competing learned decompositions (e.g., cross-layer vs. per-layer transcoders, across sparsity penalties) by measuring how well each decomposition's causal graph predicts the real model's response to held-out interventions — especially patches of intermediate nodes and distribution-shifted prompts — where behaviorally-equivalent explanations diverge.
project: Interventional Discrimination: Held-Out Intervention Prediction as a Non-Circular Criterion for Ranking Model Decompositions
question: When two learned decompositions of the same language model both reproduce its behavior on the fitting distribution (e.g., a cross-layer transcoder that collapsed a deep A→B→C circuit into a shallow A→C sum, versus a per-layer decomposition that preserves it), can the model's responses to held-out interventions — intermediate-node patches, novel prompt compositions, and shifted distributions — separate them, yielding a validated, non-circular score for choosing which decomposition (and which sparsity penalty) actually reflects the model's computation?
first_experiment: Extend the SPAR Boolean toy model: train small multi-layer networks implementing known multi-hop Boolean circuits (chains A→B→C of controlled depth with distractors); train CLTs and per-layer transcoders across a grid of sparsity penalties matched for reconstruction loss; then compare (a) standard faithfulness (in-distribution reconstruction and ablation agreement) against (b) a new interventional discrimination score — graph-predicted vs. actual outcomes for held-out interventions sampled from a space including interchange patches at intermediate nodes, compositional prompt variants, and combined interventions, scored separately on successes and errors. Hypothesis: standard faithfulness is flat across the grid while interventional prediction cleanly identifies the sparsity regimes that induce shallow rewrites, with intermediate-node patches carrying most of the discriminating power — validating the metric against ground truth before applying it to Gemma-2-2B with Gemma Scope transcoders and CLT-HP.
why: It attacks the problem both the 2025 coalition document and its 2026 retrospective place at the top of the field's list — "how do you know an attribution graph faithfully describes the model rather than being one of many behaviorally-equivalent decompositions" — at precisely the moment CLT-based attribution graphs are becoming standard infrastructure that safety monitors will be built on, and it converts the freshly published CLT-unfaithfulness negative result into a constructive selection criterion and benchmark. It has not been done: the SPAR/ICML paper documents the failure mode but only in toy models and provides no real-model test; the error-reproduction work (Sept 2026) adds a discriminative input set but stays in-distribution and doesn't rank learned decompositions; the Harvard OOD-prediction work predicts behavior from observations, explicitly decoupled from interventions, at the whole-model level; anytime-valid testing validates individual features, not circuit topology; causal abstraction supplies interchange-intervention machinery but requires hand-specified target algorithms and was never operationalized for unsupervised decompositions. No existing method tells a practitioner which of two fitted decompositions of a real open-weight model to trust — and every ingredient needed to build that test (open models, open PLT/CLT dictionaries, cheap interchange interventions, a known failure mode with divergent interventional signatures) became available only in the last twelve months.
