direction: Develop an automated "critical experiment" method that adjudicates among the equivalence class of observationally-faithful circuit/decomposition hypotheses by searching for discriminating inputs and interventions on which the candidates' predictions diverge, using real model behavior on those cases to select the surviving mechanism.
project: Adjudication Circuits — Falsifying Decomposition Hypotheses via Discriminating Interventions
question: When multiple circuit hypotheses (from different discovery runs, methods, or feature bases — SAE, transcoder, or neuron) are behaviorally equivalent on the extraction distribution, does an automated search for inputs and interventions where their predictions diverge identify a unique best hypothesis — and does the surviving circuit generalize better as a predictor and monitor under distribution shift than circuits selected by in-distribution faithfulness or interpretability aesthetics?
first_experiment: On IOI and greater-than in GPT-2-small, generate ~10 candidate circuits per task by running ACDC, EAP-IG, and threshold-varied attribution patching across different seeds and prompt families; verify they form an observationally-faithful equivalence class in-distribution; then implement the adjudicator — for each candidate, compute its interventional prediction (patch the circuit's components into the model / run the circuit as abstraction), and use a gradient-guided search over prompt perturbations (novel name templates, distractor variations) and feature clamps to find the ~100 cases of maximal pairwise prediction divergence; evaluate the true model on those cases and score adjudication accuracy against baselines (random case selection, in-distribution eval, min-edge-count tie-break). Ground-truth check: repeat the same pipeline on an InterpBench semi-synthetic transformer whose true circuit is known, and measure whether discriminating-case selection recovers it. Success criterion: adjudication on discriminating cases selects the ground-truth circuit significantly more often than any baseline.
why: It attacks the field's self-identified #1 open problem — the dual basis problem / unsystematic validation — converting the already-demonstrated negative results (Méloux 2025; Bayat Makou 2026; the "Which Circuit is it?" series) into the missing constructive method. It has not been done: the closest works each stop short — CIF (2026) adds statistics to a fixed claim but doesn't compare hypotheses or search for discriminating cases; Certified Circuits (2026) certifies stability of components, not identity of mechanisms; the Groundless series is observational-only at toy scale; Bayat Makou explicitly excludes feature-level decompositions; and MIB/InterpBench evaluate single circuits, never adjudicate among alternatives. The leverage is high because the output is exactly what deployment needs — a quantitative, non-circular score for "which decomposition to trust as a monitor under shift" — while remaining feasible for an independent researcher: the first experiment needs only GPT-2/Pythia-scale models, open tools (TransformerLens, circuit-tracer, MIB/InterpBench), and GPU-hours, not frontier-model budgets.

direction: Extend mechanistic interpretability from single forward passes to trajectory-conditioned behavior — mechanistically characterizing how transformer agents represent and causally gate on interaction-history state, using state-triggered backdoor model organisms with built-in ground truth.
project: "Where Does the Trigger Live? A Ground-Truth Model Organism for Mechanistic Analysis of State-Conditioned Behavior in Multi-Turn Agents"
question: How do transformer agents internally encode and gate behavior on properties of the interaction history (trajectory state) — and can trajectory-aware interventions localize and disable this gating where single-turn methods (current-turn probes, single-prompt circuit tracing, black-box trajectory monitors) systematically fail?
first_experiment: Train a small open-weight model (Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct class) on synthetic multi-turn tool-use trajectories with a state-triggered backdoor: the payload (e.g., a malicious tool call) fires only when a codeword appeared ≥N turns earlier AND ≥M tool calls have elapsed AND the current turn is innocuous — verifying high attack success on triggered trajectories and normal behavior on every individual turn. Then (a) confirm the predicted baseline failure: linear probes on the trigger-turn activations and a black-box trajectory monitor should both score poorly; (b) run a first "trajectory patching" pass — construct trajectory pairs differing only in the distant trigger turn and patch activations/positions at the decision turn, layer-by-layer and turn-by-turn, to produce the first causal map of where trajectory state is carried and where the conditional behavior is gated.
why: It attacks the field's named gap rather than an incremental refinement: the Open Problems review demands ground-truth organisms and monitoring applications that beat baselines, DeepMind's pragmatic vision calls multiturn/agentic interpretability out of reach, and the ICML 2026 position paper calls for trajectory-level interpretability without supplying methods. Every nearest neighbor stops short: LLM Forensics cracks open only single-token triggers and explicitly defers other trigger classes; agentic backdoor work (BackdoorAgent, Chain-of-Trigger, Sleeper Cell) is attack-only; agent monitors and probe studies (less-is-more, pre-action monitoring negatives, monitor-evasion at NeurIPS 2026) are behavioral and demonstrably fragile — which makes mechanistic grounding of trajectory state the missing layer they need. It is not already done because no published work builds a state-triggered (history-conditioned) organism or causally traces behavior across turns; the design guarantees ground truth by construction, yields a reusable benchmark and released organism, and is informative under either outcome — a localized gating circuit would be the first mechanistic account of agentic conditional behavior, while a systematic failure of the standard toolkit would be exactly the transfer-failure documentation the review says the field needs.

direction: Use held-out and counterfactual input distributions as the discriminating test for competing mechanistic decompositions, by measuring how well each candidate circuit's replacement model tracks the true model's behavior under distribution shift — turning attribution-graph faithfulness and the dual basis problem into a quantitative, non-circular metric.
project: Shift-Tested Circuits: Held-Out Tracking as a Discriminating Test of Mechanistic Decompositions
question: When two circuit-level decompositions of the same model behavior are equally faithful on the distribution they were discovered on, does divergence between each decomposition's replacement model and the true model on held-out, naturally shifted inputs reliably separate the mechanism-identifying decomposition from the behavior-matching one, and can this "held-out tracking error" serve as the field's missing quantitative faithfulness metric?
first_experiment: On Gemma-2-2B with Circuit Tracer and released transcoders, trace ~100 two-hop factual-recall prompts (e.g., "The state containing Dallas has its capital in"); extract from each attribution graph the two competing hypotheses (direct shortcut path vs. intermediate-entity-mediated path, the exact rewrite mode shown for CLTs) and instantiate each as a replacement model via feature pruning; verify both match the true model on the discovery prompts, then measure KL divergence between each replacement model and the true model on a held-out shift battery (low-frequency entity pairs, in-context fictional entities, paraphrase/distractor variants) where shallow and mediated mechanisms make different predictions; include a ground-truth sanity arm on a grokked modular-addition transformer, checking the metric prefers the known trigonometric/helix circuit over a behavior-matching lookup-table decomposition.
why: It attacks the field's self-identified #1 open problem (attribution-graph faithfulness / the dual basis problem) at the moment the problem has become acute — verification, not labeling, is now the bottleneck, and ICML 2026 work shows unfaithful-but-behavior-matching decompositions are a real, incentivized failure mode rather than a philosophical worry. It has not been done because the closest prior art each stops one step short: existing faithfulness metrics are all in-distribution ablation variants (Miller et al. 2024) and were shown to be method-fragile; causal scrubbing and Bucketing the Good Apples evaluate hypotheses on the discovery distribution; the unit-tests paper falsifies intervention specificity rather than choosing among decompositions; Nainani et al. study one circuit's generalization descriptively with no comparative metric; CHIVE explicitly excludes internal-computation explanations while showing current interpretability tools give zero counterfactual-prediction uplift, which makes the "mechanisms should predict behavior on new inputs" framing both novel and urgent; and the weight-sparse replication observed OOD divergence informally without building a metric, benchmark, or method. It is tractable on small models with existing open infrastructure, yields publishable results whether the discrimination succeeds or fails (calibrating the metric either way), and produces the artifact the field says it lacks: a non-circular, agreed numerical target for explanation quality that directly determines which interpretability-derived monitors can be trusted under deployment distribution shift.

direction: Build an automated, distribution-level discriminating-test protocol that stress-tests attribution-graph circuit hypotheses on held-out inputs and interventions — turning "execution traces that match behavior" into validated, falsifiable algorithm-level explanations.
project: Circuit Court — Adversarial Discrimination of Competiting Circuit Explanations (a validation protocol + faithfulness scoreboard for attribution graphs, evaluated from ground-truth toy models to real open-weight LLMs)
question: When two circuit hypotheses (e.g., CLT vs. PLT attribution graphs, or different seeds/widths of the same decomposition) both account for the model's behavior on the discovery prompts, can a small, systematically generated battery of held-out prompts and interventions — chosen to maximize predicted divergence between the hypotheses — reliably identify the one that matches the model's true computational pathway, and can the residual surviving-hypothesis set serve as a quantitative, non-circular faithfulness measure?
first_experiment: Reproduce the SPAR Boolean toy-model setting where a transformer implements a known 2-step multi-hop circuit (layer A computes feature B, layer B uses it to compute C) with ground truth known. Train a CLT and a PLT on its activations; extract each circuit explanation and confirm both achieve ~perfect behavioral match (replacement score ≈ 1). Then construct the minimal discriminating battery: (a) value-patch the intermediate feature at its computing layer to each possible value, (b) generate input combinations where the "shallow skip" explanation and the "deep multi-hop" explanation predict different outputs, (c) composite interventions (ablate A while patching B). Measure whether the battery separates the two explanations and ranks the ground-truth pathway first. Expected outcome: the shallow explanation fails while the deep one survives — the first quantitative demonstration that behavioral-match metrics cannot distinguish true from unfaithful circuits for the field's flagship artifact, and a working template for the protocol. Then replicate the same battery on a real two-hop task (Dallas→Texas→Austin in Gemma-2-2B with public Circuit Tracer transcoders), where CLT and PLT graphs are known to disagree.
why: It attacks what the field itself ranks as its #1 open problem — verification of the dominant artifact — at exactly the moment the bottleneck has shifted from labeling to validation, and it is the enabling methodology for the stuck downstream applications (trustworthy monitors, auditing games, CoT-faithfulness claims, cross-model transfer). It has not been done because the pieces never met: causal scrubbing has the right spirit but predates attribution graphs and was never scaled or automated; Certified Circuits (2026) certifies stability of inclusion decisions, not correctness of the computational story, and generates no discriminating interventions; Méloux et al. (2025) document non-identifiability but stop at a call for better criteria; the SPAR post (2026) finds real unfaithfulness but leaves only a warning; the graph-annotation line (ADAG, Circuit Oracle, 2026) automates interpretation, not falsification; and the multi-org landscape lists graph-merging and automated validation as open problems without a method. Discriminating-test generation on prompt distributions — with ground-truth evaluation on toy and semi-synthetic (InterpBench) models before touching real LLMs — is the missing bridge between "identifiable in principle" and "legible and validated in practice," and it is executable with public tools on a single-GPU budget.

direction: Establish held-out interventional validation as the standard for transcoder-based attribution graphs — scoring a graph by how quantitatively well it predicts the base model's behavior on unseen prompts, unseen intervention types, and the model's errors — to adjudicate which behaviorally-equivalent decomposition (CLT vs PLT vs SAE vs neuron basis) is the actual mechanism.
project: Graph-as-Hypothesis: Predictive Adequacy of Attribution Graphs Under Distribution Shift
question: When two attribution graphs (e.g., a deep multi-hop circuit and a shallow single-hop rewrite) both reproduce the model's in-distribution ablation behavior, does held-out interventional predictive adequacy — accuracy of the graph's implied counterfactual predictions about the base model on new prompts, new intervention types, and model errors — discriminate the faithful mechanism from the shallow rewrite, and can this be made into a single agreed, non-circular score?
first_experiment: On a 1–2 layer transformer trained on modular addition (known ground-truth algorithm: Fourier/trigonometric, per Nanda et al.; helix representation per Kantamneni et al.) plus a synthetic two-hop composition task, train CLT and PLT replacement models with CLT-Forge/Circuit Tracer on one GPU, extract attribution graphs on a training prompt set, then convert each graph into pre-registered quantitative predictions of the base model's logit changes under interventions *not used to build the graph* — clamping/ablating individual features and edges on held-out operand pairs and held-out intervention types — and measure predicted-vs-actual divergence for CLT vs PLT graphs, testing whether shallow-rewrite graphs that pass in-distribution ablation fidelity fail held-out interventional prediction.
why: It attacks the field's own #1 self-diagnosed open problem ("how do you know an attribution graph faithfully describes the model's computation rather than one of many behavior-matching decompositions") at the exact moment the diagnosis landed (ICML 2026) but before any metric, fix, or standard exists — a live solution window. It is the highest-leverage per unit of compute because attribution graphs are now the standard artifact underlying automated interpretability, deception investigations, and deployment monitors, so a validation standard upgrades the entire stack rather than one application. And it has not been done: the closest work is either component-level (MIB's faithfulness curves, Certified Circuits' dataset-stability, the error-agreement reframe), diagnosis-only (the CLT-unfaithfulness paper offers no metric or remedy), or abandoned (causal scrubbing was manual, component-level, and the 2026 retrospective documents the field dropping it), while the retrospective explicitly records that verification infrastructure failed to keep pace with labeling and that no non-circular faithfulness number exists; searches of arXiv, ICML 2026, BlackboxNLP, and the Neuronpedia landscape report surface no held-out interventional validation standard for feature-level attribution graphs — the multi-prompt "global circuit" idea is listed there as explicitly unstarted future work.

direction: Build an adversarial adjudication framework for mechanistic explanations — automatically generate discriminating experiments (counterfactual inputs and targeted interventions) that separate rival mechanistic hypotheses which are behaviorally equivalent in-distribution, validated on a benchmark of planted mechanisms with constructed decoys.
project: Falsify Me If You Can: Discriminating-Experiment Generation as the Missing Faithfulness Layer for Mechanistic Interpretability
question: When two mechanistic explanations of the same model behavior agree on the discovery distribution, can an automated procedure that searches for inputs and interventions maximizing divergence between the explanations' predictions (over both outputs and internal readouts) reliably identify which explanation actually governs the model — and how well do explanations produced by current pipelines (attribution graphs, transcoder circuits, SAE narratives) survive this adjudication?
first_experiment: On 1-layer grokked transformers solving (a+b) mod p — where the true Fourier mechanism and known rivals (look-up-table and CRT-style variants) can each be cast as executable predictors of logits and residual-stream readouts — run an automated search over inputs maximizing expected prediction divergence between rival hypotheses, test the model on those inputs, and measure adjudication accuracy and evidence-per-experiment against random OOD sampling and in-distribution testing, checking that the search rediscovers the probes Nanda et al. designed by hand.
why: It attacks what the field's own leadership has named the top unresolved problem — the 2025 open-problems document's faithfulness gap, sharpened by the 2026 retrospective into the dual-basis problem ("choosing among decompositions is currently an aesthetic decision") with verification, not labeling, now the bottleneck — and it is safety-critical because interpretability-derived monitors and audits built on the wrong decomposition fail silently exactly off-distribution, where hidden behaviors live. It has not been done because every nearest neighbor stops one step short: unit tests (ICML 2026) check specificity of one claim with hand-designed negatives rather than adjudicating rival claims with actively generated experiments; Certified Circuits certifies inclusion stability, not mechanism identity; Méloux et al. prove non-identifiability on toy Boolean nets without a practical method; the margin paper only fixes first-order error locally; Pando and auditing games score behavior recovery, not mechanism choice; and MIB/InterpBench supply ground truth but no decoy mechanisms or adjudication metric. Meanwhile a first experiment is cheap and fully tractable for an individual researcher — known-algorithm toy models, public open tooling, single GPU — with a clear scaling path to realistically trained planted-mechanism organisms (incorporating the Model Organism Lottery's lesson to use integrated/distilled training rather than narrow post-hoc SFT) and to benchmarking attribution-graph pipelines at the 1–2B scale.

direction: Turn decomposition non-identifiability from a philosophical worry into a measurement instrument — build attribution-graph ensembles over multiple valid decompositions of the same behavior, and use cross-decomposition disagreement as a calibrated, quantitative test of which mechanistic claims (and the safety interventions built on them) are real versus decomposition artifacts, in-distribution and under distribution shift.
project: Many Mirrors, One Machine: Attribution-Graph Ensembles as a Faithfulness Test for Mechanistic Claims
question: For a fixed model behavior, how much of the mechanistic account produced by attribution graphs is invariant across an ensemble of valid decompositions (SAE seeds, widths, architectures, transcoder variants), and does cross-decomposition disagreement measured in-distribution predict where that account — and the interventions or safety monitors derived from it — fails under distribution shift?
first_experiment: On GPT-2-small (ground truth available from the IOI and greater-than circuit literature) and Gemma-2-2B (Gemma Scope), construct attribution graphs for the same behavior under ~10 decompositions: all public SAE dictionaries for the relevant layers (ReLU/JumpReLU/TopK, multiple widths), several self-trained seed variants of one config, a shuffled/random-dictionary control, and PLT-vs-CLT where available. Match features across decompositions by intervention-effect signature (reusing cross-seed matching benchmarks), compute node/edge/path-level agreement, extract the stability-selection-style invariant core, and (a) check calibration — does the invariant core recover the literature ground-truth circuit with higher precision/recall than any single decomposition, and (b) run the novel test — validate each decomposition's graph-predicted ablation effects on original versus shifted prompts (paraphrases, distractor swaps, OOD templates), testing whether high-disagreement components show higher shift-fragility (AUC of disagreement as a predictor of intervention failure on shift).
why: It attacks the problem the field itself ranked first — the dual basis problem and the faithfulness-verification bottleneck — at the level where the field now actually works (attribution graphs as the standard artifact), and it is upstream of everything: every safety monitor, steering intervention, and audit claim silently inherits one decomposition's defaults. It has not been done because existing work each covers one slice and frames disagreement as a bug to fix (CIRCUS varies only pruning thresholds of a single dictionary; Li 2026 corrects support-boundary errors; the CLT paper treats interpretive divergence as a limitation; the SAE-stability literature stops at feature overlap; unit tests are decomposition-agnostic), whereas treating the ensemble as an instrument — consensus as a better circuit extractor, disagreement as an epistemic-uncertainty map that forecasts shift-failure of claims and interventions — is unclaimed. It is falsifiable (if consensus beats single decompositions only by luck, or disagreement doesn't predict shift-fragility, that's a publishable negative result that disciplines the field's faithfulness discourse), unusually cheap for its information value (public artifacts, no training at frontier scale, known-answer calibration), and directly actionable for the deployment-grade interpretability gap: a certification protocol of "invariant across the decomposition ensemble and robust under shift" is something auditors and monitor-builders can apply to any existing claim today.

direction: Develop a framework that ranks competing sparse decompositions of the same model by out-of-distribution interventional fidelity of their attribution graphs and extracts the decomposition-invariant consensus core of circuits.
project: Adjudicating the Dual Basis: Interventional Fidelity of Attribution Graphs Under Distribution Shift
question: Do attribution graphs from different plausible decompositions of the same model agree in-distribution but diverge off-distribution, and does interventional fidelity under distribution shift provide a non-circular criterion for ranking decompositions and separating real circuit features from dictionary artifacts?
first_experiment: Build attribution graphs for 2–3 behaviors with known circuit structure on Gemma-2-2B under ≥5 public decompositions (Gemma Scope SAE widths × L0s, plus PLTs vs CLTs), apply each graph's prescribed interventions to held-out in-distribution and three distribution-shifted prompt families, and measure predicted-vs-actual behavioral change per decomposition, testing whether graphs that agree on-distribution diverge under shift and whether interventionally stable "consensus core" features transfer best.
why: The dual basis problem is the field's self-identified top open problem with no framework and no active work; every safety application (monitoring, auditing, steering) inherits arbitrary decomposition defaults whose faithfulness is unverified, and the pieces needed (public multi-width dictionaries, open CLT/PLT tooling, CLT-unfaithfulness diagnosis, seed and margin instability results) only converged in 2025–2026 with each prior paper stopping at one dictionary, one seed, one threshold, or toy models — leaving the cross-decomposition, behavior-level, OOD-fidelity synthesis unclaimed and tractable.

direction: Establish causal load-bearing-ness of the monitored representation — measured by intervention, not decodability — as the predictor of latent-monitor evadability, and use it to build obfuscation-robust "load-bearing monitors" validated against the full published attack battery.
project: Load-Bearing Monitors: A Causal-Coupling Theory of Why Latent Monitors Are Evadable and How to Read the Model Where It Matters
question: Does the causal coupling between a monitor's readout and the monitored behavior determine how cheaply a model can learn to evade that monitor while preserving capability (the evasion-cost curve), and do monitors placed on causally load-bearing representations resist learned obfuscation where standard probe monitors fail?
first_experiment: A coupling–evadability pilot on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (iterated cheaply on Gemma-2-2b-it) in the Long et al. instructed-truthfulness setting: train linear probes at several layers; measure each probe's causal coupling by (a) probe-direction ablation behavior-flip rate and (b) SAE shared-feature analysis (Tiwari et al. protocol); then train Neural-Chameleons-style LoRA organisms to evade each probe at matched attack budget, and measure both evasion success and task capability *during evading episodes*; test whether evasion cost per unit evasion success rises with measured coupling (prediction: late-layer/shared-feature probes are far more expensive to evade than epiphenomenal probe-only readouts).
why: Latent monitoring is becoming the load-bearing safety mechanism of deployed AI systems, yet a 2024–2026 literature proves models can learn to evade it (white-box, RL, in-context, even instrumentally under ordinary task pressure), while every proposed defense (ensembles, retraining, KL penalties) is empirical and survives only its own attack — the field lacks any predictive theory of evadability. My proposal supplies it by uniting two mature lines that have never met: the decodability-is-not-causality literature (probe-aligned features are ~88% non-causal) and the obfuscation-attack literature — the former explains the latter. It is mechanistic interpretability proper (interventions, SAE decompositions, patching, plus new mechanistic findings about how evasion re-routes computation), it is tractable at open-weights scale with public recipes, and it is not already done: Bailey et al. has one capability-cost anecdote without coupling measurement or organisms; Gupta & Jenner, McGuinness et al., and Lyons Keenan et al. attack without cost curves or coupling; Tiwari et al. establish dissociation without evasion or monitoring implications; Chaudhary & Barez build an ensemble defense without a principle; Mosafer's J-space accessibility work is single-monitor, small-scale, and organism-free; and the "negligible capability tax" claim in Neural Chameleons was never measured during actual evasion episodes. The synthesis — causal coupling of the readout predicts the capability cost of learned evasion — is the missing experiment, and its outcome either way changes how latent monitoring should be deployed and audited.

direction: Diagnose, quantify, and correct "pathway flattening" — the tendency of cross-layer transcoder attribution graphs to misrepresent deep multi-hop computation as shallow direct influence — establishing when attribution graphs can be trusted and how to make them depth-faithful.
project: DepthCheck — Detecting and Correcting Pathway Flattening in Attribution-Graph Circuit Tracing
question: When and why do CLT-based attribution graphs misrepresent the depth and structure of a model's actual computation (compressing mediated multi-hop pathways into spurious direct edges), how frequently does this occur in real LMs under standard training configurations, and can cheap intervention-based diagnostics plus depth-aware training objectives detect and correct it?
first_experiment: Using CLT-Forge, train CLTs on GPT-2 Small (Goodfire recipe: 100M FineWeb tokens, expansion factor 64) across a grid of sparsity penalties; on the greater-than task — where the true mechanism is hand-verified at the neuron level (Hanna et al. 2023: five MLP neurons with monotone suppress/boost maps, replicated by Goodfire) — compute attribution graphs at each sparsity level and score each graph's causal account against ground truth: does the graph route through the known mechanism, substitute a compressed stand-in, or skip it; and do graph-implied interventions match intervention-validated effects on the intact model? This yields the first quantitative flattening-vs-sparsity curve on a real LM with a known mechanism, validating the diagnostic that the rest of the project (two-hop recall model organisms, general diagnostics, depth-aware mitigation) builds on.
why: The dual-basis problem was independently flagged as the field's most important open methodological question, and the ICML 2026 paper just showed the field's dominant artifact lies in a specific, consequential way (flattening) driven by its own sparsity objective — but only demonstrated this in a Boolean toy model, with real-LM evidence "preliminary" and no diagnostics, benchmarks, frequency estimates, or mitigations existing anywhere in the literature I searched. Unlike adjacent agendas (identifiability theory, metric critiques, certification, CoT faithfulness, feature-label verification), the flattening program on real models is unclaimed, immediately tractable with open tooling, and attacks the validity of every published and future circuit claim at once — including the safety-relevant ones (monitors and edits built on flattened graphs will misfire) — making it the highest expected-value direction I can pursue next.

direction: Develop and causally validate a general methodology for identifying and quantifying suppressive edges — the "why-not" machinery — in attribution graphs, and use it as the first practical discriminator between circuit explanations that are otherwise behaviorally equivalent.
project: The Why-Not Side of Circuits: Identifying, Quantifying, and Validating Suppressive Edges in Attribution Graphs
question: Which edges and features in an attribution graph are causally responsible for suppressing competing behaviors rather than promoting the observed one, and does modeling this suppressive structure yield strictly better predictions under ablation and distribution shift than graphs that account equally well for observed behavior?
first_experiment: On Llama-3.2-1B with open per-layer-transcoder circuit tracing, run dual attribution graphs (observed vs. strongest alternative next token) on ~30 prompts across subject–verb agreement, counterfactual factual recall, and refusal; extract candidate suppressor features from the signed graph difference; then zero their decoder writes versus matched random and positive-pathway controls and measure alternative-behavior emergence rates and the "suppression share" of the top-1/top-2 logit margin.
why: The problem is explicitly flagged as open by the attribution-graph creators (Nanda/Lindsey, Aug 2025) and by the original circuit-tracing paper, yet 15 months later only one narrow special case exists (CAP, Oct 2026: refusal-only, inactive-feature heuristic, no dual-graph formalism or faithfulness link); it is simultaneously a concrete, experimentally decidable attack on the dual-basis/faithfulness problem that the field's own 2026 retrospective ranks as most important, it targets exactly the suppression-maintained behaviors where safety monitors are weakest (refusal, jailbreaks, sandbagging, deception), and it is tractable at 1B scale with open tooling — unlike the already-crowded auditing-games, CoT-faithfulness, and faithfulness-metric spaces or the compute-heavy global-graph and long-context directions.

direction: Systematically audit the causal validity of interpretability-derived internal safety monitors under distribution shift, measuring when their predictive scores and causal roles silently diverge.
project: SilentFail — A Causal Audit of Internal Safety Monitors Under Distribution Shift
question: Under which distribution-shift axes do activation monitors (deception probes, refusal directions, eval-awareness probes, backdoor detectors) exhibit silent failures — calibrated-looking scores attached to a causally different mechanism — and can in-distribution causal validation predict out-of-shift validity better than AUROC does?
first_experiment: Sweep seven shift axes (paraphrase, format, domain, multi-turn agentic, language, benign-LoRA, adversarial soft-prompt) for two public monitors (Arditi refusal direction; a Goldowsky-Dill deception probe) on Gemma-2-2B-it and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, measuring per cell both AUROC and the behavior-flip rate of ablating the monitor's direction (with coherence gates and probe-aligned vs. gradient-sensitive SAE-feature overlap), then test whether AUROC change predicts causal-role change or misses silent-failure cells.
why: The 2026 field retrospectives name unvalidated features/monitors and shift-fragile interventions as the top open problem, yet every adjacent paper covers only one piece (single monitor/setting, AUC-only staleness, score-level alarm validity, transcript-level CoT detectors, dictionary-fix or statistics tooling, or evasion-without-semantics), so no cross-monitor, cross-axis, intervention-based causal audit or benchmark exists; it is load-bearing for labs already shipping activation monitors, feasible with public artifacts and modest compute, and informative either way it turns out.

direction: Diff-grounded alignment auditing — find adversarially hidden implanted behaviors by causally validating conditionality-ranked signals in the fine-tuned-vs-base model diff, rather than salience-ranked single-model readouts.
project: Suppression Is Not Removal: Causally Validated Diff Auditing of Adversarially Hidden Behaviors
question: Do hidden behaviors implanted by fine-tuning and suppressed by adversarial training (KTO) leave detectable, causally localizable traces in the weight/activation/logit delta against the base model — and can diff candidates ranked by conditionality × causal specificity (rather than salience), packaged into validated hypothesis cards with extracted triggers, outperform black-box elicitation in the agentic audit setting?
first_experiment: Take ~8 AuditBench-style models spanning the 2×2 grid (SDF/transcript-distilled × SFT/KTO) at 7–8B (retrained via the released pipeline) plus released targets; compute weight-delta SVD, logit-diff mining, and activation-difference latents vs. the base instruct model; score every candidate direction on salience, conditionality, and causal effect (patching/amplification measured against AuditBench's released behavior classifiers and capability evals); test whether planted-behavior directions rank low by salience but high by conditionality×specificity, and whether KTO leaves them present-but-suppressed (amplifiable to expression) versus removed.
why: It targets the field's most important unexplained negative result — white-box interpretability losing to black-box elicitation in its flagship safety application (AuditBench 2026; Pando 2026; GDM diffing agents 2026) — using audit-specific structure (the known base model) that all existing white-box tools ignore; it addresses the field's diagnosed bottlenecks (verification over labeling, tool-to-agent gap, trigger/"when" identification, readout faithfulness) with ground truth rather than another metric; and it is verifiably undone as of November 2026: AuditBench used only single-model white-box tools despite knowing the base model, Delta-Crosscoder is non-agentic and untested on adversarial targets, Diff Mining causally validates nothing and finds only a third of injected biases, WeightWatch ranks by salience on easy triggers, GDM's agents are purely behavioral and explicitly miss planted behaviors, and CAP handles suppression only within single models for refusal features — leaving the intersection unoccupied while remaining feasible on open ≤14B models with released benchmarks, pipelines, and classifiers.

direction: Build the missing verification layer for circuit tracing — a causal ground-truth benchmark and quantitative faithfulness metric for attribution-graph explanations of multi-step behaviors on real open models, then repair the pipeline stages (training, pruning) that cause unfaithfulness.
project: Ground-Truthing Attribution Graphs: A Causal Faithfulness Benchmark and Metric for Circuit Tracing
question: When does a feature-level circuit explanation (CLT attribution graph, RelP circuit) faithfully describe the computation a language model actually uses for a composed, multi-step behavior — and can the shallow-rewrite unfaithfulness that sparsity penalties incentivize be detected, quantified, and trained away?
first_experiment: On Gemma-2-2B (plus GPT-2 Small as a sanity check) using the open-source `circuit-tracer` and Gemma Scope, run a three-task suite — two-hop factual recall, composed comparison/date arithmetic, and a planted-rule organism from Pando — where causal mediation analysis first establishes the ground-truth computational path (which intermediate variables actually mediate output); then trace attribution graphs for the same prompts with both CLTs and RelP, and score each graph on (a) *path fidelity* — whether it contains nodes/edges corresponding to causally validated intermediate variables, vs. collapsing them into a shallow shortcut edge, and (b) *interventional consistency* — predicted vs. actual behavioral effect of ablating each graph node. This turns the ICML 2026 Boolean-toy hypothesis into the first quantitative, benchmarked faithfulness result on real models, and either outcome (unfaithful → motivates the repair work; faithful → delivers the trustworthiness map the field lacks) is a publishable, reusable contribution.
why: It attacks the field's most convergently documented 2026 bottleneck — verification of interpretability artifacts — at the exact moment attribution graphs are becoming production infrastructure for pre-deployment audits and monitoring, so a validated metric and repair compound across every downstream user, with direct safety value (an unfaithful graph can falsely exonerate a model in an audit, which connects straight to AuditBench/Pando's finding that white-box tools underperform). It is tractable now because all infrastructure is open and small models suffice, and it has a constructive (not just critical) payoff: measurement first, then repaired training objectives (multi-hop curricula, depth-aware sparsity penalties, shortcut-penalizing pruning). It has not already been done: the ICML 2026 paper stops at a Boolean toy plus "preliminary" real-model evidence with no benchmark or metric; Goodfire validated a single task qualitatively; NeurIPS 2026's four checks are feature-attribution-level case studies, not graph-structure scoring; Pando measures tool value for behavior prediction and readout variance, not graph faithfulness; the multi-org circuits project listed this need as an open problem rather than executing it; and the automated-validation thesis work targets SAE feature labels, not circuit structure.

direction: Build a cross-examination methodology that discriminates among rival mechanistic explanations (circuits/attribution graphs) by automatically finding inputs where they disagree and letting the model adjudicate, producing faithfulness adjudication and out-of-distribution coverage maps.
project: Cross-Examining Circuits: Adversarial Adjudication of Rival Mechanistic Explanations
question: When multiple candidate explanations of the same model behavior are all faithful on the extraction distribution, can divergence-targeted input search reliably discriminate between them, does the model's behavior systematically vindicate one, and does the adjudicated explanation predict the model better out-of-distribution — yielding a quantitative coverage map of where the explanation stops tracking the model?
first_experiment: On GPT-2 small IOI, take three independently discovered candidate circuits (Wang et al. reference, ACDC, EAP-IG, all reproducible via TransformerLens/circuitry); verify each is faithful on the standard IOI distribution; then run a greedy token-substitution search over the IOI prompt manifold (names, objects, duplicate structure, ordering, context length) maximizing KL divergence *between* the circuits' outputs; on the top-K disagreement inputs, measure the full model's agreement with each circuit; compare adjudication rate against a random-perturbation baseline of equal budget; finally test whether the adjudicated winner predicts held-out IOI variants better than the runner-up, reporting coverage (fraction of the variant distribution within ε KL). Success = disagreement search discriminates candidates far above the random baseline and the model systematically sides with one candidate; if instead no input separates them or the model matches neither, that is itself a decisive empirical datum on the dual basis problem at real-model scale.
why: It attacks the problem the field itself now ranks first — the 2026 state-of-field retrospective calls ranking rival decompositions "the open problem I would put at the top of any new survey," and notes it is currently decided by label aesthetics — while remaining low-compute and falsifiable at toy-to-mid scale. It is upstream of the field's other worsening problems: trustworthy monitors, feature-label verification, and cross-model transfer all implicitly assume you picked the right decomposition first; this tells you when you haven't, and where it breaks — directly answering Hendrycks' critique that explanations failing on edge cases are useless for safety. It has not been done: adversarial circuit evaluation (2024) predates attribution graphs and only tested single circuits against the model with manually enumerated inputs, never rival-vs-rival adjudication; the identifiability proof (ICLR 2025) stopped at diagnosis in Boolean toy models; "Many Circuits, One Mechanism" (2026) documented the equivalence class but supplied no tool to carve it; and the identify-vs-discriminate principle (Oct 2026) has only been applied to verbalized activations, never to structural explanations — despite structural explanations being uniquely cheap to cross-examine, since each candidate is a fast surrogate model you can run on candidate probes.

direction: Build an empirical disambiguation protocol for the non-identifiability of mechanistic explanations — construct behaviorally-equivalent competing decompositions of the same model behavior, find held-out inputs where their causal predictions diverge, and adjudicate which decomposition captures the model's actual computation.
project: Circuit Equivalence Classes — Disambiguating Behaviorally-Equivalent Mechanistic Explanations via Shift-Adversarial Interventions
question: When multiple decompositions of the same behavior are behaviorally equivalent on-distribution, how large is the equivalence class in practice, and can held-out discriminating interventions identify which member reflects the model's real computation — quantified by a "decomposition disagreement under shift" score and validated against known ground truth?
first_experiment: Train a small transformer on a synthetic multi-hop task with a known ground-truth algorithm (3-hop relational chains, where the true algorithm is sequential lookup-and-compose); train 5+ SAE/transcoder decompositions with different seeds and hyperparameters; certify pairs as behaviorally equivalent (matched KL-recovery after pruning and matched ablation/steering effects on-distribution); then generate held-out compositional variants (unseen entity triples, extended hop depth, template shifts) and measure where the equivalent decompositions' predicted intervention outcomes diverge — testing whether divergence-under-shift correctly selects the decomposition matching ground truth.
why: It targets the problem the field's own 2026 retrospective ranks as its most important methodological gap — the dual-basis problem underlying attribution graphs — at the exact moment the field has proven non-identifiability in theory and demonstrated one concrete unfaithfulness mode in practice (ICML 2026's shallow-rewrite result), yet no one has built the empirical protocol, metric, or selection procedure that turns "explanations are not unique" from a philosophical worry into a measurable, actionable test. It is not already done because the existing threads are all adjacent but orthogonal: Meloux et al. prove non-identifiability but in toy MLPs without a selection method; the CLT paper shows unfaithfulness can happen but offers no detection or adjudication protocol; the EPFL variance work studies one method's instability, not disagreement between certified-equivalent decompositions; MIB benchmarks single methods against a single reference circuit rather than equivalence classes; the Koopman work yields an identifiable but explicitly non-legible object; and the "Which Circuit is it?" sequence is still at the conceptual stage. It is the most promising because it is cheap (public models, open SAE/CLT checkpoints, ~GPT-2 scale compute), decisive either way (quantifying equivalence-class size is a publishable negative result if selection proves impossible), and maximally leveraged for safety — every interpretability-derived monitor, audit, and steering intervention inherits the risk of sitting on the wrong member of an equivalence class, and this is the first research program designed to measure and manage exactly that risk.

direction: Turn mechanistic decompositions (circuits, attribution graphs, SAE feature sets) into falsifiable predictive hypotheses and use their divergent predictions under distribution shift and targeted interventions — not in-distribution faithfulness — as the principled criterion for discriminating among behaviorally-equivalent explanations of the same model behavior.
project: Breaking the Tie: Distribution-Shift Discrimination of Behaviorally-Equivalent Mechanistic Decompositions
question: When multiple decompositions of the same model are behaviorally equivalent on the discovery distribution, do their predictions on out-of-distribution inputs and targeted interventions diverge in a way that reliably identifies the decomposition corresponding to the model's true mechanism — and can disagreement-targeted test design achieve this discrimination efficiently?
first_experiment: On InterpBench's SIIT-IOI transformer (ground-truth circuit known), assemble a candidate set that all pass standard in-distribution faithfulness checks — the ground-truth circuit, automated discoveries (ACDC, EAP-IG, Edge-SP) across pruning thresholds, a deliberately "shallow-rewritten" circuit, and size-matched random controls — then measure each candidate's observation-based (no-intervention) predictive fidelity (KL between candidate-as-surrogate and the intact model) on held-out ID inputs, compositional OOD inputs (novel names, extra distractors, IOI-Hard-style cases), and inputs adaptively selected to maximize pairwise inter-candidate prediction divergence; the hypothesis is confirmed if OOD observational fidelity separates the true circuit from in-distribution-indistinguishable alternatives (AUC ≫ 0.5) with disagreement-targeted probes needing orders of magnitude fewer samples than random OOD probes — and if it fails, characterizing why (e.g., backup-circuit self-repair) is itself a publishable negative result.
why: The field's own 2026 state-of-the-field review names decomposition selection ("the dual basis problem") as its top open problem, and 2025–2026 work has only established the problem (non-identifiability, CLT shallow-rewrites, intervention misranking) or produced partial responses (stability ensembles, subsampling certificates, in-distribution feature validation) — none of which discriminates among competing explanations or exploits the fact that behavioral equivalence on one distribution generically breaks under shift. Closest prior work either stress-tests a single circuit adversarially (uit de Bos & Garriga-Alonso 2024), ranks circuits by held-out behavior on the same distribution under confounded interventions (the misranking paper, Oct 2026), or evaluates OOD as a side metric of subsampling-stable circuits (Certified Circuits 2026); none builds a ground-truth-validated, disagreement-targeted, observation-based discrimination protocol, extends it to feature-level decompositions (testing the CLT shallow-rewrite failure mode directly), or connects it to the safety-critical fact that monitors validated in-distribution fail under shift — the exact gap the field identifies as growing. It is cheap to run on existing artifacts, falsifiable with known ground truth, and produces a reusable benchmark artifact whether it succeeds or fails.

direction: Turn attribution graphs from prompt-local, seed-dependent hypotheses into seed-invariant, interventionally-validated global circuits over reproducible subspaces, making held-out predictive validity the standard metric for mechanistic explanations.
project: Circuits That Predict: Seed-Invariant, Interventionally-Validated Global Circuits from Attribution Graphs
question: Are attribution graphs descriptions of the model or of the transcoder that produced them, and can prompt-local graphs be consolidated into a canonical subspace-level global circuit that quantitatively predicts behavior and intervention outcomes on held-out inputs?
first_experiment: Train K seed-variant cross-layer transcoders on GPT-2-small, build attribution graphs for the same IOI prompts, and measure cross-seed structural agreement at feature vs. subspace level plus predicted-vs-actual ablation effects on held-out prompts — decomposing graph content into seed-invariant versus seed-specific structure.
why: It is the field's own top-ranked open problem (faithfulness verification and the dual basis problem) applied to its dominant artifact, which everything downstream — monitoring, auditing, editing — depends on; adjacent work stops at head/edge-level circuits, per-layer SAE edge fixes, single-feature validation, or stability analysis without circuit construction, and no one has merged graphs or validated them out-of-sample.

direction: Develop falsification-based validation of mechanistic explanations by automatically generating inputs where rival decompositions (attribution graphs vs. SAE circuits vs. pruned subnetworks) make divergent predictions and letting the model's held-out behavior select the faithful one.
project: Dissociate: Adversarial Input Search as a Discriminating Test for Rival Mechanistic Explanations
question: Can systematically searched dissociating inputs reliably identify which of multiple behavior-matching decompositions is the model's true circuit, first against planted ground truth and then in real language models?
first_experiment: Plant a known multi-hop circuit in a small transformer, build the sparsity-incentivized shallow-rewrite rival that matches it in-distribution, run gradient-guided and combinatorial search for inputs where the two explanations disagree, and test whether the real model's held-out behavior favors the true circuit where in-distribution circuit error is uninformative.
why: It targets the field's top-rated 2026 open problem (attribution-graph faithfulness and the dual-basis problem), which gates all downstream safety applications; the failure modes were only discovered in 2026 and no discriminating protocol exists — prior work is in-distribution (faithfulness metrics, error reproduction), toy-scale (identifiability), or ad hoc (OOD divergence in replications) — while the tooling now exists to run it cheaply, and its combination of rival-hypothesis generation, adversarial input search, and held-out evaluation has not been assembled by any group.

direction: Build an adjudication framework that resolves the dual-basis problem by treating rival mechanistic explanations as falsifiable interventional predictors and selecting among them via automatically designed discriminating experiments rather than legibility.
project: Circuit Court — Adjudicating Rival Mechanistic Explanations by Designed Discriminating Experiments
question: When two mechanistic explanations (e.g., attribution graphs from different SAE seeds/widths, or rival circuit/causal-model hypotheses) both account for a model's behavior on its fitting distribution, can an automated loop that (i) compiles each explanation into a behavioral predictor over held-out inputs and interventions, (ii) searches for the experiments maximizing predicted divergence, and (iii) decides with anytime-valid statistics, reliably identify which explanation governs the model's actual behavior — and does this yield a principled, non-circular criterion for ranking decompositions?
first_experiment: Validate the full adjudication loop where ground truth is known — train 1–2-layer attention-only transformers on modular addition (the Nanda et al. setup with a documented Fourier "clock" algorithm), specify the true mechanism and a plausible rival (a lookup-table/memorization account that matches on-distribution behavior and standard necessity/sufficiency metrics), implement both as interventional predictors (predicting model outputs under operand-range shifts, frequency-subspace ablations, and prompt perturbations), then run disagreement-maximizing search over that input/intervention space and verify the loop automatically finds discriminating experiments and selects the planted mechanism under certified statistics — before scaling to GPT-2-small IOI, where Adversarial Circuit Evaluation has already located a real failure region ("romantic-object" inputs) that constitutes a live, documented rivalry between the published IOI circuit and an unmodeled replacement mechanism.
why: It targets the field's #1 self-diagnosed gap in 2026 — the dual basis problem and the absence of a non-circular faithfulness criterion — and it is the natural next step after a year of papers proving explanations are unstable (non-identifiability, adversarial circuit failures, specificity/consistency failures, failed SAE attribution controls) while all existing evaluation machinery (unit tests, bucketing, CIF, adversarial evaluation) evaluates one hypothesis at a time; adjudication is the missing piece that turns that instability from a embarrassment into a selection mechanism. It has not been done because the field's evaluation culture is per-method and per-hypothesis, the interface needed (explanations as predictors extending beyond the fitting distribution) only matured with the causal-abstraction toolchain and attribution graphs, the statistical machinery (anytime-valid certified intervention) appeared only in mid-2026, and discovery papers have carried more incentive than tournament papers until the verification bottleneck became the consensus diagnosis; moreover, selection-by-behavior sidesteps the trap that sank absolute faithfulness metrics ("Transformer Circuit Faithfulness Metrics are not Robust") because it requires no ground truth — only that rival predictions be forced to disagree, with the model as referee.

direction: Train LLM featurizers with an interchange-intervention objective on self-generated minimal pairs so that decomposed features are causal mediators by construction, closing the demonstrated gap between SAE reconstruction and causal abstraction.
project: Causal Features by Construction: Interchange-Intervention-Grounded Dictionary Learning for Language Models
question: Can a sparse featurizer trained with a self-supervised interchange-consistency loss on automatically generated minimal-pair inputs produce latents that causally mediate frozen-LLM behavior at near-DAS quality, without per-variable supervision?
first_experiment: Head-to-head on MIB's causal-variable track (RAVEL + IOI in Gemma-2-2B): train a JumpReLU dictionary with reconstruction + sparsity + a differentiable interchange-intervention loss (swap latents between minimal pairs, decode, supervise logits to match the true counterfactual through the frozen model), then measure held-out interchange intervention accuracy against published GemmaScope-SAE, neuron, PCA, and DAS baselines, with λ_II=0 ablation and OOD unseen-entity tests.
why: It targets the field's best-quantified foundational failure — decomposed features demonstrably fail as causal variables (MIB: SAE features no better than neurons; sanity checks: random directions match SAEs on causal editing; steering brittleness) — with a falsifiable, leaderboard-anchored experiment, and it upgrades all downstream machinery (attribution graphs, steering, monitoring) if it succeeds; it hasn't been done because reconstruction-only dictionary learning and supervised causal-abstraction methods developed in disjoint communities, the closest bridging work (CDAS) is per-concept steering rather than scalable unsupervised featurization, and the key data ingredient — massive diverse minimal-pair generation — only recently became practical.

direction: Build ground-truth-free, held-out interventional validation protocols that quantify how much of a transcoder-based circuit explanation (attribution graph) generalizes beyond the prompts it was traced on, and use that transfer signal to discriminate among decompositions that are behaviorally equivalent on the traced distribution — turning attribution graphs from execution traces into tested algorithmic claims.
project: "Faithfulness Under Shift: Held-Out Interventional Validation of Transcoder Circuit Explanations" (working title: TRACE-Bench — Traced-Circuit Robustness Across Examples)
question: When two circuit explanations (e.g., PLT- vs CLT-derived attribution graphs, or decompositions differing in sparsity) both account for the model's behavior on the traced prompt(s), do their interventionally predicted causal claims diverge on held-out inputs — and can the degree of that divergence, measured without ground-truth mechanisms, serve as a practical, decomposition-ranking faithfulness score that exposes "deep-pathway rewritten as shallow heuristics" unfaithfulness in real language models?
first_experiment: On Gemma-2-2B with Gemma Scope per-layer transcoders via the Circuit Tracer library: trace attribution graphs on ~10 two-hop factual prompts (e.g., "The state containing Dallas has its capital in"), then, for each graph's nodes/edges, compare the *predicted* ablation effect (via virtual weights) against the *measured* ablation effect (activation patching) on (a) the traced prompts and (b) ~50 held-out prompts of the same behavior family — different triples, paraphrases, and deeper 3-hop compositions. Measure the intervention-prediction error gap between in-trace and held-out inputs to quantify "execution-trace overfitting," then repeat under a PLT-vs-CLT decomposition and different sparsity settings to test whether held-out transfer discriminates decompositions that tie on trace-distribution faithfulness.
why: It targets the problem the field's own 2026 assessment calls the top open problem — the dual basis problem, i.e., that choosing among behaviorally-equivalent decompositions is currently an aesthetic decision — and it is the natural, still-unbuilt next step after the ICML 2026 toy-model proof that transcoders are incentivized to learn behaviorally-matching but mechanistically-wrong circuits: that result only demonstrates unfaithfulness where ground truth exists (a Boolean toy model), leaving open ground-truth-free detection in real models, which is exactly what held-out interventional transfer provides. It has not been done because 2025–26 effort flowed into building and scaling the microscope (CLTs, Gemma/Llama Scope, Circuit Tracer, CLT-Forge) and automating graph *description* (ADAG, Circuit Oracle), while validation infrastructure was explicitly listed as an unsolved direction in the multi-org replication; adjacent work (ablation-sensitivity of faithfulness metrics, unit tests for overly broad circuits, feature-label validation, cross-model circuit transfer) each covers a different axis — methodology sensitivity, effect breadth, label trust, and model transfer, respectively — not input-shift robustness of graph-level causal claims. The payoff is unusually broad: a standardized faithfulness score would let the field verify the millions of auto-labeled features it now produces, would give decompositions a principled ranking instead of readability, and — because adversarial obfuscation is the special case where a behavior-matching decomposition hides the real mechanism — would directly strengthen the next generation of activation-based safety monitors that prompt-level strategic deception has recently been shown to evade.

direction: Build ground-truth validation infrastructure and a quantitative, non-circular faithfulness metric for attribution graphs — the field's dominant but unvalidated interpretability artifact.
project: Planted Circuits, Verified Graphs: A Ground-Truth Testbed and Faithfulness Score for Attribution-Graph Circuit Tracing
question: When an attribution graph reproduces a model's behavior, does it describe *the* computation or merely *an* equivalent one — and can a held-out intervention-prediction score distinguish true graphs from behaviorally-equivalent decoys (e.g., shallow rewrites of multi-hop circuits)?
first_experiment: Train cross-layer transcoders with CLT-Forge on InterpBench's SIIT greater-than model (a naturalistic transformer whose circuit is known by construction), construct attribution graphs for task prompts, and measure: (a) recovery — do graph features/edges localize to the planted components and their known interactions; (b) prediction — do ablating/patching graph nodes predict output changes on held-out inputs; (c) decoy separation — do deliberately shallow-rewritten graphs that match in-distribution behavior diverge from the true graph under held-out feature-level interventions? Zero new base-model training required; both ingredients are public.
why: It attacks the problem the field itself ranks first (the dual-basis/faithfulness gap, named "the open problem I would put at the top of any new survey" in the 2026 retrospective), and it converts faithfulness from an aesthetic judgment into a number with adversarial validation. It has not been done because: attribution graphs became the standard artifact only in March 2025, and the field's verification rate never caught up with its production rate; InterpBench and MIB predate or bypass the CLT level (component-level ground truth, behavioral-only metrics); the ICML 2026 unfaithfulness paper demonstrates the failure mode in a Boolean toy but provides no testbed, metric, or detection method for realistic models; and the synthetic-activation sanity-check line lacks a real transformer with a known feature-level graph, making its conclusions contestable. The unique move here is combining the now-mature assets — planted-circuit models, open CLT tooling, and the documented failure modes — into the missing validation layer, with falsifiable success criteria (recover planted graphs; rank true above decoys; show sparsity-penalty fixes reduce rewrites).

direction: Build the first operational theory and protocol for the dual-basis/proxy-fidelity problem — ranking competing decompositions of the same model by how their interventional claims diverge under distribution shift, and proving which observable statistics can and cannot certify that fidelity.
project: Beyond Reconstruction: Divergence Profiles for Ranking Competing Mechanistic Decompositions under Distribution Shift
question: When two decompositions of the same model both account for a behavior on the training distribution, where and how much do their mechanistic claims diverge under distribution shift and intervention — and can observable proxy statistics (reconstruction error, cross-seed agreement, margin/coverage statistics) predict or bound that divergence, or are they provably insufficient?
first_experiment: On GPT-2 small and Pythia-160m, take ≥3 public decompositions of the same layers (TopK SAE seed A vs. seed B vs. transcoder vs. neuron basis, plus a random-basis control); for two simple behaviors (IOI, factual recall), compute each decomposition's predicted intervention effects, then measure (a) in-distribution agreement across decompositions, (b) realized effects in the true model, and (c) divergence under shifted input distributions (paraphrases, OOD entities, token-frequency bands) — establishing whether equally faithful-looking decompositions diverge under shift and whether reconstruction error predicts it.
why: It is the one problem independently ranked first by the field's most current authoritative sources — the Nov 2026 survey ("Proxy Fidelity Problem," §14.6; "evaluation methodology... most pressing open problem"), the 2026 retrospective on Sharkey et al. ("the dual basis problem... top of any new survey"), and Sharkey et al. itself — because every downstream safety use (monitors, audits, "no deception circuit found" claims) is gated by which decomposition you trust. It has not already been done: the adjacent fragments were only completed in late 2025–2026 (iSAE for identifiability, CIF for statistical certification, "Decided at the Margin" for first-order in-distribution accuracy, the feature-scores paper for observational-vs-interventional selection), competing public decompositions of the same models only became available with Gemma Scope and the circuit-tracer release (~2025), the survey explicitly lists the reconstruction-to-computation bound as a still-unexplored "promising direction" as of November 2026, and no existing work ranks decompositions under shift — partly because doing so forces publishing failure-under-shift results the field has avoided.

direction: Build and ground-truth-validate an interventional selection criterion for the dual-basis problem — choosing among behaviorally-equivalent decompositions of the same model — and turn it into a training penalty that suppresses unfaithful "shallow rewrite" decompositions.
project: Breaking the Tie — Interventional Adjudication of Behaviorally-Equivalent Decompositions
question: When several decompositions of the same model reproduce its behavior on a training distribution, which family of interventions (multi-node, path-level, activation-statistics-matched, counterfactual-consistency over shifted inputs) separates the decomposition that continues to explain the model under distribution shift and targeted interventions — and can that criterion be estimated without ground truth and optimized during dictionary training?
first_experiment: In a Boolean multi-hop toy setting with known ground truth (the cross-layer-transcoder shallow-rewrite setup), generate a panel of behaviorally-equivalent candidate decompositions (transcoders/SAEs across sparsity levels and seeds), then measure three discriminators on every candidate: (1) observational faithfulness (replicating that it fails), (2) single-node in/out-of-circuit interventional faithfulness (replicating the weak gap), and (3) richer intervention families — joint multi-node and path-level interventions, intervention distributions matched to activation statistics, and cross-distribution counterfactual consistency — testing whether the ground-truth decomposition separates from lookalikes with a decision-grade margin (quantified as AUC/separation of criterion scores between the true mechanism and lookalikes, vs. the margin achieved by discriminators 1 and 2).
why: It is the constructive missing piece at the field's most-converged frontier: Méloux et al. proved non-identifiability, the Groundless series proved observation fails and single-node interventions barely help, the Koopman work proves non-identifiability is structural but yields only a non-behavioral spectral invariant, CIF provides statistical certification but no selection rule, and the ICML 2026 CLT paper demonstrates sparsity-driven unfaithful rewrites without proposing a remedy — so a validated, ground-truth-tested selection criterion and training penalty has not been done by anyone, while sitting directly upstream of the field's biggest bottleneck (verification of the millions of features and attribution-graph monitors now in production), making success multiply across validation pipelines, safety monitoring, model diffing, and circuit discovery rather than contributing one more isolated artifact.

direction: Shift the unit of analysis in circuit tracing from the per-prompt attribution graph to the prompt family, by aggregating graph families into "circuit atlases" that separate a task's shared algorithmic core from input-conditioned modules and prompt-idiosyncratic artifacts, validated by predicting held-out prompts.
project: Circuit Atlases: From Execution Traces to Algorithms by Aggregating Attribution Graphs Across Prompt Families
question: Can the family of per-prompt attribution graphs for a task be aggregated into a circuit atlas — an algorithmic core plus input-conditioned subgraphs — that (a) predicts the model's behavior and graph structure on held-out prompts better than any single-prompt circuit, (b) recovers algorithmic structure that single-prompt tracing demonstrably misses (e.g., digit-wise/trigonometric addition), and (c) quantifies how much of a task's computation is shared versus mechanism-diverse?
first_experiment: On Gemma-2-2B with open-source cross-layer transcoders (circuit-tracer library), trace ~200 "a + b =" prompts (100 train / 100 held-out, stratified by digit count and token frequency), record *unpruned signed* graphs per prompt, then aggregate by shared feature identity: per-edge stability scores (fraction of prompts where the edge survives a fixed influence threshold), per-feature activation co-occurrence, and automated supernode clustering. Measure (1) whether a stable core emerges (edge-stability distribution structure), (2) held-out replacement score / KL of the atlas-projected circuit versus a single random prompt's circuit and versus the union — the first non-circular, held-out predictive test of a transcoder circuit, and (3) whether the recovered core's signed edge statistics and condition-gated modules match the known digit-wise/heuristic-mixture structure from the addition literature.
why: It is the attribution-graph method's own authors' explicitly flagged open problem (listed twice in the Aug 2025 landscape document, echoed by Goodfire), still unsolved 15 months later; everything adjacent has been done — per-graph automation, config-space stability, component-level input-variation studies — leaving data-space stability at the feature level as the unoccupied cell. It is newly tractable only since mid-2025/2026 (open CLTs, batch tracing, automated graph annotators, shared feature identities across graphs). It simultaneously attacks the field's most-wanted gap (a quantitative, non-circular faithfulness standard, per the 2026 state-of-field review) by making held-out prediction the metric. Payoffs are valuable either way: a stable core gives the first algorithm-level global circuits and a monitoring primitive (atlas-deviation anomaly scoring for backdoors/unfaithful CoT); heterogeneity quantifies mechanistic diversity within tasks. And it runs on open-weight models with public infrastructure — no frontier-model access required — while adjacent alternatives (faithfulness metrics, introspection, CoT faithfulness) are already crowded, closed-model-dependent, or mid-stream by other groups.

direction: Build a ground-truth-validated, distribution-shift stress-testing protocol and metric that discriminates true mechanisms from behaviorally-equivalent surrogate explanations in the transcoder/attribution-graph pipeline — mechanistic interpretability's missing verification layer.
project: Cross-Examined Circuits: A Stress-Test Benchmark and Non-Circular Faithfulness Metric for Transcoder Circuit Explanations
question: Can interventional predictions on held-out, systematically shifted input distributions distinguish true mechanisms from behaviorally-equivalent surrogate explanations (e.g., sparsity-induced shallow rewrites of deep circuits) that are indistinguishable in-distribution, and can such a faithfulness metric be validated against models with known ground-truth circuits?
first_experiment: On GPT-2 small greater-than (known circuit), train a CLT with the public Goodfire recipe, generate attribution graphs, construct adversarial shallow-rewrite and redundant-path decoy explanations, and test whether interventional-predictive faithfulness on a stress suite (boundary cases, novel contexts, compositions, varied ablations) statistically separates the true circuit from decoys where in-distribution behavioral faithfulness fails — replicated on an InterpBench SIIT model with exact ground truth.
why: It attacks the field's self-diagnosed top open problem (the dual-basis problem and the verification-not-labeling bottleneck, per Sharkey et al. 2025 and the 2026 state-of-field retrospective) at exactly the moment the threat was made concrete (ICML 2026's demonstration that CLTs are incentivized toward unfaithful circuits), it is upstream of every safety application (monitoring, auditing, editing inherit validity from explanations), it yields valuable results either way, it runs solo on small open models with mature tooling — and no existing work combines ground-truth models, the CLT pipeline, adversarial decoys, and OOD interventional discrimination: InterpBench covers older methods, CIF certifies only declared distributions, Certified Circuits certifies dataset-stability not mechanism-vs-surrogate discrimination, the Koopman work is non-legible theory, and Goodfire did a single unparameterized replication.

direction: Consolidate prompt-local attribution graphs into an intervention-validated, role-level "circuit atlas" whose structure and intervention effects on held-out prompts can be predicted before they are measured, turning circuit faithfulness from a post-hoc aesthetic judgment into a non-circular predictive standard.
project: Circuit Atlases: From Prompt-Local Attribution Graphs to Validated Global Mechanism Models
question: For a fixed behavior, can the many structurally variable prompt-local circuits (which 2026 work shows form an equivalence class rather than a unique mechanism) be consolidated into a global, role-level mechanism abstraction that (i) is stable under resampling, (ii) predicts held-out prompts' attribution-graph structure and intervention outcomes pre-registered, and (iii) detects when the model switches algorithms (mechanism multiplicity) — thereby providing the validation standard and global circuit picture that the field has flagged as its top open problems?
first_experiment: Using an open model with public cross-layer transcoders (Gemma-2-2B via circuit-tracer/CLT-Forge), trace two-hop factual recall ("The wife of the director of *Jaws* is…") on ~100 training prompts + ~50 held-out prompts. (1) Extract per-prompt attribution graphs and quantify cross-prompt feature/edge variability to establish the equivalence-class phenomenon at feature level. (2) Pool the training-prompt graphs and cluster features into candidate functional roles (entity-binding, relation-lookup, output-reporting, etc.), keeping only clusters whose joint ablation on training prompts produces consistent predicted behavioral effects. (3) Freeze the resulting role-graph as an "atlas entry" and pre-register its predictions for the held-out prompts: which roles activate, qualitative edge structure, and sign/magnitude of output-logit change under role ablation. (4) Test against measured held-out graphs and interventions, with baselines: single-prompt graph transplant, component-frequency lists, co-activation-only clustering (no intervention validation), and random role assignment. Success criterion: statistically significant improvement in held-out intervention-effect prediction (rank correlation and sign accuracy) over all baselines.
why: It sits exactly on the intersection of the field's two most urgent self-identified gaps — the attribution-graph team's explicit request for a "global circuit picture" and the post-hoc diagnosed faithfulness/"dual basis" problem — and it is the constructive response to a fresh wave of 2026 negative results (non-identifiability, phantom specialization, consistency/specificity failures) that demonstrate the problem but stop at measurement. A validated atlas is the prerequisite artifact for the things everyone actually wants: predicting out-of-distribution behavior, distribution-robust safety monitors, role-level model diffing, training-dynamics tracking, and auditing (giving the auditing-games benchmark a target beyond single features), so marginal value compounds across subfields. It has not been done because the pieces only recently fell into place — per-prompt circuit tracing infrastructure is public only since mid-2025, the equivalence-class evidence only solidified in 2026, and the groups nearest to it (the attribution-graph core team, the measurement papers) are respectively focused on method engineering and on documenting the problem, while automation work (ADAG, CTA, graph annotation) addresses within-graph readability rather than cross-prompt consolidation with held-out predictive validation. It is also feasible without frontier access: open weights, public transcoders, and modest compute — and a solo/autonomous researcher can iterate fast on a well-defined predictive benchmark rather than competing in the crowded reasoning-model and evaluation-awareness swarms.

direction: Resolve the dual-basis/explanation-multiplicity problem in mechanistic interpretability by adjudicating among behaviorally-equivalent explanations of a real LLM using out-of-distribution predictive agreement (plus causal revalidation under shift) as a non-circular, quantitative selection criterion.
project: Shift-Tested Explanations: Adjudicating Competiting Mechanistic Explanations by Out-of-Distribution Agreement
question: Among candidate explanations (circuits, attribution graphs, feature-circuits) that are equally faithful on the standard evaluation distribution, does agreement with the model's behavior under pre-registered distribution shifts — measured on successes *and* errors — identify the explanation whose components remain causally validated under shift, and is in-distribution faithfulness itself uninformative about this?
