first_experiment: On GPT-2 small IOI, assemble ≥5 candidate explanations that are all ≥97% faithful on the standard IOI distribution — the published manual circuit, automated circuits from different methods/seeds sampled across the "defensible analytic variation" grid, an SAE/transcoder feature circuit, a deliberately constructed size-matched "template shortcut" explanation, and a size-matched random null — then measure exact-answer agreement on successes and errors separately across a pre-registered shift ladder (name-pool extension, template paraphrase, distractor insertion, double/triple-IO compositional extension), and patch-test the surviving components under shift; the decision rule is whether this "shift-generalization faithfulness" separates the candidates in a way that in-distribution faithfulness cannot (one GPU-week with TransformerLens/EAP-IG tooling).
why: It attacks the question a June-2026 retrospective of the field's own open-problems survey ranks first ("how do you know an attribution graph faithfully describes the model rather than one of many equivalent decompositions?"), which Mahale (2026) just quantified as a 73.2% claim-flip rate across defensible analytic choices while explicitly offering no resolution; the supporting proof-of-concept exists only at toy scale (Li et al. showed internals predict OOD rules in model populations, with predictive power decoupled from causal faithfulness), and every adjacent line — single-circuit generalization (Nainani et al.), adversarial divergence measurement (uit de Bos), on-distribution error agreement (Zhang et al.), discovery-stability certification (Certified Circuits), and specificity unit tests — stopped one step short of competing multiple faithful explanations of one pretrained model under a shift ladder, leaving the intersection unoccupied; it is falsifiable within a GPU-week on the field's best-instrumented task, reconciles the contradictory published findings that circuits "generalize surprisingly well" and "fail even on benign inputs," and if the criterion holds it yields exactly what the field says it lacks: a quantitative, non-circular faithfulness score and a shift-tolerance certificate for the interpretability-derived monitors whose coverage gap under distribution shift is currently growing.

direction: Mechanistically characterize and decode the naturally-arising illegible chain-of-thought that outcome-based RL induces in reasoning models — determining what those tokens compute, whether their content is decodable from internal states, and building a white-box monitor that works when the text is unreadable.
project: The Anatomy of Illegible Reasoning: Internal Decoding of RL-Induced Opaque Chain-of-Thought
question: When RL-trained reasoning models produce illegible CoT, what computation do the illegible tokens actually perform internally — steganographic compression of real reasoning, vestigial trigger tokens, or training artifacts — and can the intermediate reasoning content be recovered from residual-stream states well enough to restore CoT monitorability?
first_experiment: An "internal legibility audit" of DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B and Qwen3-4B on GPQA-Diamond and MATH subsets: generate traces, segment them into legible/illegible spans using the published GPT-4o legibility scoring protocol (Jose 2025), then run layer-wise logit lens with contrastive differencing (arXiv 2609.09902) at illegible positions to test whether (a) English paraphrases of the illegible tokens are decodable in intermediate layers (the Fang & Marks ROT-13 signature), and (b) the task's true intermediate values crystallize before appearing in text. Control: matched legible positions and scrambled illegible segments. Outcome: a layer×position decodability map that adjudicates the three hypotheses and tells us whether to proceed to a full unsupervised decoding pipeline (Brauer-style logit-lens + LLM-judge, extended with KV-transplants between matched problems to establish causal use) and a downstream "white-box monitor beats text monitor on illegible traces" evaluation.
why: CoT monitoring is the field's most deployed safety application and illegible reasoning is precisely where it fails — yet no study has applied mechanistic tools to naturally-arising illegible CoT. I verified this gap at the source: Jose (2025) documented the phenomenon but used only behavioral prefill/truncation experiments and explicitly left the three hypotheses open; Fang & Marks (2025) proved logit lens decodes encoded reasoning but only on an artificially constructed ROT-13 organism; Brauer et al. (2026) built the decoding pipeline but only for filler tokens on toy-decomposable tasks; none touch the natural case, and each paper explicitly points toward it. It is also the rare direction that is safety-critical (monitorability is the basis of frontier-lab and AISI oversight plans), independently tractable (open weights, public pipelines, single GPU), and informative in both outcomes — a successful decoder is a new oversight capability, while a definitive failure would settle whether RLVR needs enforced legibility rewards. Compared to the alternatives (sandbagging detection — crowded by AISI's auditing games and Tan et al.'s locate-and-unlock results; decomposition improvement — dominated by well-resourced labs), this occupies a unique, verifiably empty intersection of three converging research lines.

direction: Pursue the identifiability of mechanistic explanations — measure the equivalence class of circuits that pass standard validation and build an adaptive joint-intervention protocol that shrinks it to the true mechanism, validated on ground-truth models.
project: Identifiability Curves: How Many Interventions Does It Take to Pin Down a Circuit?
question: How large is the set of circuits (later: feature-level mechanisms) passing the field's standard validation protocol for a fixed model and task, and can greedy diversity-maximizing selection of joint interventions recover the ground-truth mechanism within a practical intervention budget?
first_experiment: On InterpBench models with known ground-truth circuits (plus GPT-2 small/IOI), collect all EAP-IG/ACDC candidates passing the standard ≤10% unfaithfulness threshold across seeds and batches; measure the equivalence class's size and the spread of its members' predictions under a held-out battery of novel templates, corruption families, patch values, and joint multi-site patches; then greedily select maximally-discriminating joint interventions and plot edge-level F1 vs. ground truth against intervention count.
why: The field's own 2026 retrospective ranks the dual-basis/faithfulness problem first and lacks any agreed numerical target for explanation quality; the problem is now empirically demonstrated but only from the negative side (toy non-identifiability, ablation-methodology sensitivity, template variance, limits of single-site patching), while no one has measured the equivalence class left open by standard pipelines, framed identification as budgeted intervention design, or validated a protocol against ground truth — and every downstream safety claim (monitors, steering, auditing, unlearning) inherits the currently unconstrained choice among behaviorally-equivalent mechanisms.

direction: Rank rival behavior-equivalent mechanistic decompositions by held-out interventional predictive accuracy under distribution shift, and validate that criterion on models with known ground-truth mechanisms before applying it to natural models.
project: Interventional Generalization: A Ground-Truth-Validated Criterion for Choosing Among Behavior-Equivalent Decompositions
question: Can a non-circular quantitative criterion — how accurately a decomposition's attribution graph predicts the model's response to held-out and composed interventions on unseen, distribution-shifted inputs — discriminate among rival decompositions that equally explain in-distribution behavior, and does its ranking track the true planted algorithm and downstream utility?
first_experiment: Build ≥6 rival decompositions (multiple SAE seeds, TopK vs JumpReLU, SVD basis, ACDC/EAP-IG circuit) on one InterpBench SIIT transformer with a known circuit and on Pythia-160m with public SAEs; score each attribution graph by predicted-vs-measured effects of a battery of held-out interventions on ID and OOD inputs; test whether the criterion discriminates rivals, recovers the ground-truth-aligned decomposition, and adds information beyond in-distribution sufficiency.
why: It targets the open problem the field's own 2026 assessment ranks first (the dual-basis problem and faithfulness-as-a-number), is tractable on open models and public SAE releases where frontier-scaling and universality directions are not, and is not already done — the closest work (iSAE identifiability, margin-graph linearization fixes, Certified Circuits, observational OOD prediction à la Li et al., and unreliable SAE benchmarks) all stop short of a ground-truth-validated selection criterion among rival decompositions; and both outcomes (validation or quantified failure) are publishable and consequential for safety applications.

direction: Build the missing validation layer for mechanistic interpretability — a held-out "mechanism-separating" evaluation that quantitatively distinguishes decompositions which track a model's true computation (e.g., genuine multi-hop circuits) from decompositions that merely reproduce in-distribution behavior (e.g., feature-skipped shallow lookups), and use that signal to make decompositions faithful by construction.
project: Held-Out Mechanism Discrimination: A Non-Circular Faithfulness Metric and Benchmark for Circuit Decompositions
question: When multiple circuit decompositions (CLT features, per-layer transcoders, SAE circuits, MLP-neuron attribution) reproduce a model's behavior equally well in-distribution, does the decomposition whose replacement model correctly predicts the base model's behavior on held-out inputs specifically constructed or selected to separate candidate mechanisms (novel compositions, interventions on intermediate representations) track the model's actual computational mechanism — and can this held-out mechanism-prediction gap serve as the field's first quantitative, non-circular faithfulness measure for decompositions, and as a training signal to eliminate feature-skipping?
first_experiment: The "multi-hop dissociation test" in a controlled setting. Train small transformers on a synthetic two-hop recall task (contexts define A→B and B→C maps; query asks for A→C) under two regimes: (a) a composition regime where A→C never co-occur, and (b) a coextensive regime where direct A→C mappings appear alongside compositional ones, so both a two-hop circuit and a one-hop lookup are objective-compatible across seeds (following the "Shortcut Before Circuit" identifiability construction). Train CLTs and PLTs on each model using the open-source circuit-tracer settings, then compare the standard in-distribution replacement score against a new held-out mechanism-prediction score: KL divergence between base-model and replacement-model outputs on (i) unseen A→C compositions and (ii) inputs where the intermediate B-representation is patched to held-out values. Prediction: feature-skipped decompositions will match in-distribution scores but diverge sharply on the separating set, yielding a large "mechanism generalization gap" that tracks the presence/absence of intermediate-node edges in the graphs — validating the metric against known-unfaithful decompositions before scaling it to real models (Llama-3.1-8B / Gemma-2 on the Lindsey et al. multi-hop city–state tasks, comparing CLT vs. PLT vs. neuron-basis pipelines), and then using the held-out signal as a regularizer to train faithful-by-construction transcoders.
why: It targets the gap that three independent sources — the 2026 state-of-field review (ranking attribution-graph faithfulness the top open problem), the ICML 2026 feature-skipping result (demonstrated, no metric, no fix), and the Oct 2026 context-distortion result (current metrics actively misrank) — all independently identify as the field's bottleneck, and it converts the recent identifiability theory (Méloux et al. ICLR 2025; "Shortcut Before Circuit") into a practical evaluation rather than leaving it a toy-model curiosity. It has the highest leverage per unit of effort because it multiplies the value of all existing SAE/CLT/neuron-basis infrastructure instead of adding another unvalidated method, it directly enables the reasoning-vs-lookup and deception-monitoring use cases the field deems existential-risk-relevant, and its scoring is cheap (forward passes, not attribution), partially answering the compute-efficiency complaint. It has not been done because the pieces only crystallized in the last nine months (feature skipping: Feb 2026; metric failure: Oct 2026; neuron-basis rivalry: Jan 2026), the institutional incentive runs toward scaling graphs to bigger models and new phenomena (the "coverage" axis) rather than verification infrastructure, the multi-org replication project evaluated everything with in-distribution replacement scores and listed validation only as "automate human practice," and constructing mechanism-separating eval distributions requires deliberately breaking the coextensiveness that natural data and standard benchmarks preserve — a step no one has yet taken for decomposition-level (as opposed to component-level) faithfulness.

direction: Shift circuit tracing from per-prompt execution traces to population-level analysis — distilling families of attribution graphs over a prompt distribution into general, mixture-structured circuits validated by out-of-sample prediction of intervention effects.
project: Population Circuit Tracing: From Execution Traces to General Algorithms
question: When attribution graphs are traced across a distribution of prompts for a task, does distilling the graph family into a general circuit (with mechanism-level mixtures) recover the model's underlying algorithm — measured by whether the distilled circuit predicts which feature-edge pathways carry influence and what intervention effects will be on held-out prompts, beyond what any single per-prompt graph can?
first_experiment: Using the released cross-layer transcoders and Circuit Tracer on Gemma-2-2B (or Llama-3.2-1B), trace per-prompt attribution graphs for ~120 prompts of the greater-than task and two-operand addition, split 80/40 train/test; then (1) align features across the family via co-activation clustering and measure cross-prompt edge-set stability, and (2) distill a population circuit via stability selection over prompt subsamples and test on held-out prompts whether its predicted intervention effects (sign/magnitude of feature ablations) match measured effects better than baselines: best single-graph transfer, CIRCUS-style config consensus per prompt, pooled edge-frequency, and CircuitLasso — with the addition case study as the headline test of whether cyclic number structure emerges globally where per-prompt traces show only lookup-table heuristics.
why: It attacks the one limitation the creators of the field's dominant artifact explicitly flagged as unsolved — "graphs show how the model computes 57+39 but not x+y; can we merge attribution graphs into a more global picture?" — which my targeted searches confirm remains unaddressed as of November 2026: adjacent work is either single-prompt (CIRCUS, ADAG, Circuit Oracle, Anthropic's own case studies), component-level rather than attribution-graph-level (MIB, DCD), theory rather than practical distillation (Koopman identifiability, certified circuits), or structurally validated without held-out interventional prediction (CircuitLasso, HAGD — the latter admitting "ablation-based validation circularity"). It is the most promising because it converts the field's instability diagnosis (Méloux et al.) into its cure — a distribution-level estimator with held-out predictive adequacy as a non-circular resolution of the dual-basis problem; it produces monitors and audits that can survive distribution shift rather than per-prompt anecdotes; and it is feasible now with open CLTs and modest compute, where the rival big bets (frontier scaling, cross-architecture universality) are neither affordable nor unclaimed.

direction: Build the missing validation layer for mechanistic interpretability — an active, statistically grounded procedure that discriminates among competing candidate explanations (circuits/attribution graphs) by searching for the inputs and interventions where their predictions diverge, replacing "aesthetic" selection among non-identifiable decompositions with principled elimination.
project: Cross-Examination: Active Model Discrimination Among Candidate Mechanistic Explanations
question: When multiple candidate explanations of a model behavior are statistically indistinguishable on the distribution they were extracted from, can disagreement-targeted testing (selecting inputs and interventions that maximize inter-candidate predictive divergence, evaluated with anytime-valid sequential statistics) efficiently identify which explanation — if any — actually tracks the model's computation, and does failure of all candidates constitute a usable mechanistic anomaly signal?
first_experiment: On the InterpBench semi-synthetic IOI transformer (ground-truth circuit known), construct a candidate set that hides the truth: the SIIT ground-truth circuit plus decoys generated to agree on the training distribution (ACDC and EAP-IG outputs, and a transcoder/SAE-feature attribution graph from a different random seed). First, measure on-distribution statistical indistinguishability of all candidates under a shared protocol (KL faithfulness with paired e-processes). Second, run the discrimination loop: gradient-guided and template-perturbation search (repeated names, distractor counts, rare-object subpopulations) for inputs maximizing inter-candidate predictive divergence; run the real model on the top divergence tests; update pairwise anytime-valid tests; iterate. Success metric: does the loop recover the true circuit with fewer interventions than passive sampling, and does it correctly eliminate or flag decoys? This is a single-GPU, few-day experiment that decides whether the whole program works; the immediate follow-up repeats the bake-off with no ground truth on GPT-2 small's published IOI circuit versus discovered alternatives.
why: Two independent state-of-the-field assessments (the open-problems review and its 2026 retrospective) place explanation validation and the dual basis problem at the top of the field's agenda, yet the literature contains only the problem's ingredients, not the loop: non-identifiability is established (Méloux 2025; Paulo & Belrose 2025; "Many Circuits, One Mechanism" 2026), faithfulness metrics are known to misrank (Objective-Level Recovery Gaps 2026) and to miss errors (2026), single-circuit adversarial probing exists (uit de Bos & Garriga-Alonso 2024), and statistical certification machinery exists (CIF 2026) — but nobody has combined candidate sets, divergence-targeted experiment design, and sequential hypothesis testing into a selection procedure, and no one has quantified how often real-model candidate explanations that agree on-distribution diverge off-distribution. It has not been done because the field's energy went into scaling labeling and attribution-graph automation, leaving verification as the acknowledged bottleneck; the testbeds and statistics that make the loop tractable only matured in the last 12–18 months; and it is most promising because it is foundational (every monitoring, steering, auditing, and editing application inherits its reliability from validated explanations), cheap (small models + existing open infrastructure), and each possible outcome — unique survivor, characterized equivalence class, or universal failure — is a decision-relevant result rather than a dead end.

direction: Extend the field's best-understood safety mechanism — the single-turn refusal circuit — into the deployment-realistic multi-turn setting, to causally test how conversation history (especially the model's own prior responses) gates that circuit and whether internal safety monitors trained on single-turn data survive multi-turn jailbreaks.
project: Context-Gated Refusal: Causal Mediation and Monitoring of Multi-Turn Safety Failures
question: Does the single-turn refusal mechanism (diff-in-means direction / refusal SAE features) still causally mediate refusal at every turn of a multi-turn conversation — and if its effect is attenuated, which conversational sources (the model's own prior partial-compliance responses vs. user turns) write the suppression — and do internal monitors trained on single-turn activations retain detection power in multi-turn traces?
first_experiment: On Gemma-2-2B-it (SAEs + circuit-tracer available) and Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct, compute the single-turn refusal direction on AdvBench-style data only, then run Crescendo-style escalating conversations plus matched single-turn controls and, per turn, (a) measure the refusal-direction projection and refusal-feature activations at the decision token, and (b) causally ablate the direction at each turn to test whether it still flips refusal→compliance as a function of turn number — with pre-registered predictions separating "same circuit, context-suppressed" from "different mechanism" outcomes.
why: It targets two problems the field itself declares open — monitoring/mechanistic anomaly detection and multiturn/agentic interpretability — at the intersection where the strongest existing mechanistic foundation (the refusal direction) has never been tested, so it is simultaneously cheap, falsifiable, and safety-critical; existing work stops at representation reading (Microsoft RepE), probe-level drift (STAR), single-turn causal screens (NeurIPS 2026), or behavioral attacks, and none performs causal mediation of multi-turn refusal by the single-turn mechanism, localizes which prior turns supply the suppression (adoptable commitment-juncture resampling), or quantifies the single-turn→multi-turn transfer failure of internal monitors — so the core result is unclaimed, and either outcome (persistence or mechanism-swap) is a publishable mechanistic finding with a direct monitoring and defense application.

direction: Build a non-circular, held-out **predictive validation protocol for circuit explanations** — scoring mechanistic hypotheses by their ability to make risky, falsifiable predictions about model behavior under novel inputs and interventions, in settings where rival decompositions agree on-distribution — because faithfulness/verification of attribution-graph explanations is the field's self-identified top open problem and everything downstream (global circuits, cross-model transfer, deployment monitors, automated interp agents) currently rests on unvalidated foundations.
project: Predictive Faithfulness: Adjudicating Rival Circuit Explanations by Held-Out Risky Predictions
question: When multiple circuit explanations of the same behavior agree on-distribution (the dual-basis problem), can a battery of held-out predictive tests — novel-input logit prediction, targeted structural interventions, perturbation-coupling (chart-rank) signatures, cross-seed recurrence, and error agreement — quantitatively separate mechanistically-correct explanations from degenerate look-alikes, and which methodological choices of the attribution-graph pipeline (sparsity penalty, transcoder type, pruning threshold, prompt selection) produce explanations that survive these tests?
first_experiment: Train the standard grokking modular-addition transformer (p=113, known Fourier/trig ground-truth mechanism, minutes of compute); build a "decomposition zoo" of per-layer and cross-layer transcoders across seeds, sparsity penalties, and pruning thresholds, generating attribution graphs for the task; verify that all zoo members pass standard on-distribution replacement-score checks while implying distinct mechanisms (expecting lookup-table-style decompositions, as the landscape doc reports); then run the held-out predictive battery — held-out operand pairs, targeted Fourier-frequency ablations with hypothesis-specific predicted error patterns, chart-rank perturbation-coupling tests, and cross-seed recurrence — scoring each candidate explanation by predicted-vs-actual intervention outcomes on held-out items, yielding a "Predictive Faithfulness Score" and evidence for which pipeline knobs track it. Extension: apply the protocol to the near-disjoint IOI circuit zoo on GPT-2 (where 73% claim-flip instability is documented) and to two-hop factual recall on Gemma-2-2B using released CLTs.
why: It directly attacks the problem that a 2026 state-of-the-field review ranks first — no agreed, non-circular faithfulness measure exists while the field's outputs (attribution graphs) have become the standard artifact and safety monitors increasingly depend on them — and it converts a diagnosed failure mode into a constructive, quantitative method. It has not already been done: the closest works are each only fragments — Miller et al. (2024) show metric fragility but stay within ablation-on-training-prompts; Méloux et al. (2025) prove non-identifiability but propose no empirical discriminator for real models; InterpBench evaluates component-level discovery methods against planted circuits but predates the transcoder/attribution-graph pipeline and never tests held-out prediction; Zhang et al. (2026) add error agreement within one distribution; Mahale (2026) measures claim instability but explicitly proposes no remedy; the chart-rank theory (2026) discriminates mechanisms of raw models, not explanations produced by interpretability pipelines; and the ICML 2026 CLT result documents unfaithfulness in a toy setting without a general detection or ranking protocol. The integration — decomposition zoos plus risky-prediction batteries plus a validated community metric, instantiated where ground truth is known (grokking addition, where the true trigonometric mechanism and its documented lookup-table degenerate twin give a clean positive and negative control) and then stress-tested on real-LM tasks — is precisely the missing verification layer, is feasible at small-model scale with existing open tooling, and would give the field the "faithfulness score as top-1 accuracy" that its own 2026 retrospectives say it lacks.

direction: Build a ground-truth-anchored "adjudication" benchmark and protocol that discriminates between rival circuit/decomposition hypotheses which are indistinguishable in-distribution, by scoring them on held-out distribution-shift intervention batteries — operationalizing the dual-basis problem the field has named but not yet measured.
project: The Adjudication Benchmark: Ground-Truth-Anchored, Held-Out Validation of Rival Mechanistic Hypotheses
question: When multiple circuit hypotheses (from different discovery methods, or deliberately constructed adversaries) are equally faithful to a model on the task distribution used for discovery, does held-out distribution shift — paraphrase families, numeral/lexical format shifts, compositional recombinations, model errors, planted-mismatch batteries — separate them, and does the hypothesis matching the known (canonical or planted-by-construction) mechanism systematically win, yielding the field's first standard metric for identifying *the* mechanism rather than *a* mechanism?
first_experiment: On greater-than in GPT-2 small (canonical circuit known from Hanna et al. 2023, including their ready-made adjective/noun battery that separates the true mechanism from the lexical-heuristic confound): (1) extract circuits via three-plus methods (ACDC, EAP-IG, activation-patching ground truth, plus a CLT attribution-graph pass replicating Goodfire's setup) and verify they form an in-distribution equivalence class (~equal faithfulness); (2) evaluate every candidate on held-out batteries — Hanna's disjoint adjective/noun split, numeral-format extrapolation (Roman numerals, word-form years, years outside 1700–1799), paraphrase template families, and exact model-error agreement; (3) quantify the "adjudication gap": how sharply in-distribution twins diverge out-of-distribution, and whether component-level recovery of the canonical circuit predicts held-out agreement. GPT-2 scale, open tooling (TransformerLens, MIB harness, circuit-tracer), a few GPU-days — and it generalizes immediately to Tracr-compiled organisms and trained synthetic organisms where ground truth is exact.
why: It attacks the problem that the field's own 2026 state-of-field review ranks first — "how do you know an attribution graph faithfully describes the model versus being one of many decompositions that fit the same behavior?" — at the exact moment the problem has been articulated but not operationalized: the critique strand (variance, error-agreement, breadth, metric non-robustness) has produced only deflationary results with no ground-truth anchoring, while the benchmark strand (MIB, AuditBench) anchored to same-distribution faithfulness or black-box auditing. The closest works each stop short: the Groundless series is a toy-scale blog investigation without organisms or a reusable battery; "Many Circuits, One Mechanism" tests one input axis (token frequency) and explicitly declines to build ground truth; the unit-tests protocol handles intervention specificity, not decomposition identity; Goodfire's CLT replication is qualitative and single-prompt; FlyHack does stress-testing only in a vision connectome model. Meanwhile SAE-feature validation — the obvious alternative direction — already crowded in 2026 (anytime-valid hypothesis testing, SHAP causal faithfulness, cross-family causal-necessity audits). This direction is uniquely cheap to start (GPT-2 + existing tooling), uniquely scalable along the organism axis (Tracr variants, grokking organisms, planted auditing organisms), directly serves the missing verification infrastructure for deployed circuit-derived safety monitors, and has high information value in both directions: if the ground-truth member wins, the field gains its first principled metric for ranking decompositions; if it loses, that is a bombshell negative result about canonical circuits themselves.

direction: Build the field's missing evaluation standard for feature-level circuit explanations — systematic held-out and adversarial stress testing of attribution-graph decompositions, using disagreement between independently-trained decompositions as a cheap trust signal, validated against known-mechanism organisms.
project: When Do Circuit Explanations Break? A Held-Out Faithfulness Standard for Attribution Graphs
question: Under what input conditions do transcoder-based attribution-graph explanations of a behavior stop predicting the model's behavior, and can cheap signals — decomposition-ensemble disagreement (across seeds, sparsity levels, and CLT-vs-per-layer-transcoder families) plus held-out sufficiency of the pruned graph under a fixed protocol — (a) predict where explanations fail and (b) constructively rank competing decompositions, resolving the dual-basis problem at feature level?
first_experiment: On GPT-2 Small's greater-than task (known ground-truth mechanism from Hanna et al.; Goodfire has released reference CLTs): train an ensemble of CLTs differing in seed, sparsity, and family (CLT-Forge / circuit-tracer), build attribution graphs on a fixed discovery prompt set, extract each graph's implied suppress/boost algorithm, then measure (i) graph-held-out sufficiency (KL of pruned replacement model vs. true model) and (ii) cross-decomposition disagreement on held-out subpopulations where candidate explanations diverge — digit-decomposition variants (17XX vs. 19XX vs. 20XX), paraphrase/distractor variants, token-frequency-band shifts, and inputs found by optimizing for graph–model logit divergence. Deliverable of the first experiment: does ensemble disagreement predict behavioral-prediction failure (a cheap warning light), and does held-out sufficiency + disagreement rank the faithful decomposition above known unfaithful rewrites (e.g., the ICML 2026 deep→shallow mode, tested in a multi-hop Boolean organism and in multi-hop factual recall on Gemma-2 with Gemma Scope 2 transcoders)?
why: It is the field's own consensus top-priority gap, three times over: Sharkey et al. (2025) flag faithfulness/verification as the central open problem; the 2026 retrospective explicitly places attribution-graph faithfulness and the dual-basis problem first ("the open problem I would put at the top of any new survey"), noting the bottleneck moved from labeling to verification; and the method's own authors (Circuits Research Landscape, Aug 2025) call for systematic validation, more global/mergeable circuit pictures, and "downstream tasks for measuring understanding." It has not been done because the artifact is new — the diagnostic toolkit that matured for component-level circuits (non-identifiability, misranking, phantom specialization, certification) simply has not been ported to feature-level graphs, and the one paper that touches it (ICML 2026) is a toy-model demonstration whose real-model extension it explicitly leaves "preliminary," while Goodfire's check is one qualitative prompt. It is the highest-leverage direction because everything downstream — deception monitors, sandbagging audits, mechanistic anomaly detection, alignment auditing games — currently inherits unverified decompositions, and the 2025–2026 results on evading probes and latent monitors show that gap will be exploited; a standardized stress-test metric is the prerequisite that makes those safety claims falsifiable. And it is newly tractable: open transcoders, open circuit-tracing libraries, known-mechanism organisms, and the MIB infrastructure all landed in the last twelve months, so the first experiment needs only modest compute and open artifacts. Alternatives I weighed — auditing-game benchmarks (heavy, multiple groups moving), mechanism-level anomaly detection (blocked on exactly this metric), weights-first decomposition (deeper but a multi-year agenda) — either depend on this result or duplicate active community efforts; this is the keystone with a crisp first step.

direction: Shift circuit tracing from per-prompt execution traces to algorithm-level understanding by building methods that aggregate families of attribution graphs across many prompts into a global circuit that captures the shared mechanism, its input-conditional variants, and predicts held-out behavior.
project: Algorithm Circuits: Distilling Global Mechanisms from Families of Attribution Graphs
question: Given a distribution of per-prompt attribution graphs (shared CLT feature basis) for a task, can we recover a global circuit — an invariant algorithmic core plus prompt-conditional subgraphs — that (a) matches known aggregate mechanisms, and (b) predicts behavior and intervention outcomes on held-out prompts better than any single-prompt circuit?
first_experiment: On Gemma-2-2B (open CLTs via Circuit Tracer), generate ~200 attribution graphs over a two-hop factual-recall family (e.g., "The capital of the state containing Dallas is…"), where single-prompt graphs show a "Dallas→Texas→Austin" hop plus "Dallas→Austin" shortcut paths; align the graphs in the shared CLT feature space, cluster them into an invariant core and route-specific subgraphs, then test on held-out prompts whether the distilled global circuit predicts (i) which route dominates per prompt and (ii) the model's output distribution, and whether ablating the distilled core degrades the task on held-out prompts more than ablating any single-prompt circuit — with a second task family (multi-digit addition, where per-prompt graphs show lookup tables but the known aggregate algorithm is trigonometric) as a replication with existing ground truth.
why: It is the most promising because it is the explicit, thrice-flagged "next step" from the attribution-graph originators; it converts three 2026 diagnostic results (circuit inconsistency, equivalence-class sampling, phantom specialization) into a constructive method; it simultaneously attacks the two documented failure modes of the field's dominant tool (locality and shattered geometry); it has a clean falsifiable first experiment with known ground truth and modest compute; and its output is a methodological multiplier that every downstream application (monitoring, audits, capability prediction, reasoning-model biology) consumes. It has not been done: my searches found no cross-prompt distillation method for feature-level attribution graphs — the closest works only measure consistency across prompts (Li & Subramani 2026), show structural variability is deceptive (Bayat Makou et al. 2026), compare graphs for factual-edit localization (Circuit-Diff), compute pairwise graph-similarity kernels, or ensemble pruning thresholds on a single prompt (CIRCUS) — all diagnostics or tooling, none a distillation-and-held-out-validation method; the capability to do it (shared-basis CLTs, Circuit Tracer, open graph corpora) only materialized in mid-2025, and the field's attention has since flowed to faithfulness critique and automated graph interpretation rather than this constructive gap.

direction: one sentence — Replace broken ablation-based faithfulness with a context-preserving, interchange-based evaluation objective for recovered mechanisms, validated and standardized on an adversarial-pairs benchmark with known ground-truth circuits.
project: In-Context Mechanism Evaluation: Interchange-Based Validation of Recovered Circuits (with ContextBench)
question: Does context-preserving interchange evaluation (mechanism values patched into the intact model on held-out/shifted prompts + internal consistency + error tracking) correctly rank known-reference mechanisms over adversarial alternatives where standard faithfulness misranks 13–41%?
first_experiment: On IOI/GPT-2 + two InterpBench tasks, compute the three context-preserving scores for reference circuits, controlled-edit candidates, and EAP/EAP-IG/ACDC/Edge-SP outputs, and measure misranking rates on the published pair pools where KL faithfulness fails.
why: It is the field's self-identified #1 open problem (Sharkey et al. 2025; 2026 retrospective), freshly made acute by the Oct 2026 context-distortion result, yet no one has built the constructive replacement — existing work only diagnoses, standardizes the broken metric, or solves a different axis — while the needed ground-truth infrastructure already exists, the compute is small-model scale, and a trustworthy evaluator upgrades the validity of every downstream interpretability and safety claim.

direction: Move mechanistic circuit analysis from per-prompt "execution traces" to distribution-level, generalization-validated explanations — merging attribution-graph circuits across prompt families and scoring them by held-out causal validity, thereby attacking the dual-basis/faithfulness problem the field ranks as its top open methodological question.
project: From Execution Traces to Algorithms: Measuring and Closing the Generalization Gap of Attribution-Graph Circuits
question: Do feature-level circuits discovered on individual prompts encode properties of the model or artifacts of the analyzed prompt — and can cross-prompt merging of attribution-graph circuit hypotheses, validated by held-out causal prediction on both model successes and errors, recover general algorithmic explanations that survive distribution shift?
first_experiment: A "circuit generalization gap" audit on Gemma-2-2B and Llama-3.2-1B with Circuit Tracer cross-layer transcoders: trace attribution graphs on ~100 prompts from one well-defined family (two-hop factual recall; then greater-than), extract per-prompt circuits under a fixed pruning protocol, and measure (a) cross-prompt feature/edge overlap, (b) held-out causal validity — transplanting each circuit to unseen prompts via replacement-score and activation-patching, including error reproduction — and (c) whether a frequency-weighted merge of the per-prompt graphs predicts held-out interventions better than any single-prompt circuit; replicate the same protocol on the Sparse Transformer/InterpBench testbeds, where the true neuron basis and circuit are known, to check whether merging recovers ground-truth structure (e.g., the trigonometric addition algorithm that per-prompt graphs are known to shatter).
why: It targets the exact question the field's own 2026 state-of-field review puts at the top of any new survey (dual basis problem, faithfulness as a numerical target) and the explicit open item in the Anthropic/DeepMind/EleutherAI/Goodfire circuits landscape ("merge attribution graphs for a global circuit picture"), yet nothing in the literature occupies the niche: CIRCUS varies only pruning configs on one prompt, Certified Circuits certifies component-level (not feature-level) circuits without algorithmic recovery, and the error-reproduction and ground-truth testbed results (Sep–Oct 2026) are symptoms waiting for precisely this diagnosis-and-fix — while the recent availability of open CLTs, thousands of pre-generated graphs, and ground-truth models makes it tractable now, for a cost of days rather than the six-figure budget of prior circuit studies, with a publishable and field-relevant result whichever way the generalization gap lands.

direction: Develop and validate a context-distortion-free faithfulness objective for circuit and attribution-graph evaluation, fixing the newly demonstrated objective-level misranking in mechanistic interpretability's standard of evidence.
project: Grounded Faithfulness: Distortion-Free Evaluation Objectives for Circuits and Attribution Graphs
question: Can a practical evaluation objective rank candidate circuits/decompositions by true recovery of intact-model behavior — eliminating context-distortion misranking — and extend into a consensus, cheap, non-circular faithfulness score for attribution graphs?
first_experiment: Reproduce the published misranked IOI/Greater-Than circuit pairs in GPT-2 small, then benchmark three candidate distortion-free scores (fully restored-context evaluation, upstream-only patching, and an intervention-free held-out completeness readout) against standard KL faithfulness on repair rate, false-inversion rate, and compute cost.
why: It is the field's own top-ranked methodological problem, freshly diagnosed (Oct 2026) with an explicit call for a fix that no one has supplied; it upgrades the standard of evidence for the field's dominant artifact, is verifiable on public known-mechanism benchmarks at single-GPU cost, and is not already done — the existing result is a diagnosis with diagnostic restoration search, not a deployable metric.

direction: Turn mechanistic explanation from an aesthetic choice into a falsifiable science by adjudicating the equivalence class of candidate circuits through their ability to predict model behavior under adversarial and distribution-shifted inputs, validated against newly available ground-truth models and then converted into a robustness-optimizing discovery objective.
project: Falsification-First Circuit Discovery: Adjudicating the Equivalence Class by Adversarial Behavioral Prediction
question: When multiple candidate circuits are statistically indistinguishable under standard in-distribution faithfulness, does the model's behavior on held-out, adversarially shifted, and error-prone inputs discriminate among them — and can that signal (a) reliably identify the true mechanism, as validated on ground-truth models (InterpBench, Sparse Transformer), and (b) be converted into a discovery objective whose circuits predict behavior under distribution shift where current circuits fail?
first_experiment: On IOI in GPT-2 small, collect ~15–30 candidate circuits from all public discovery methods (manual Wang et al., ACDC, EAP, EAP-IG, subnetwork probing) plus seed/data-distribution variants; verify they are indistinguishable in-distribution under a fixed ablation methodology; then measure each candidate's exact answer agreement and KL divergence against the full model on adversarial suites (duplicated names, flipped order, repeated-token distractors, unseen templates), model-error subsets, and length-shifted inputs — quantifying (i) how many in-distribution-equivalent candidates are falsified OOD, (ii) whether the OOD ranking is stable across suites, and (iii) whether surviving candidates share a structural core; replicate the same protocol on InterpBench's SIIT-IOI model where the true circuit is known, testing whether OOD adjudication ranks the true circuit above impostors better than in-distribution faithfulness does.
why: It attacks the problem that the field's leadership, an 18-month retrospective, and four independent 2024–2026 papers all independently identify as the central blocker — multiple decompositions pass all current criteria and choosing among them is aesthetic — while the field's own definition of understanding (predict behavior on arbitrary inputs) is never actually tested; prior adversarial-evaluation work was destructive-only on three published circuits before ground-truth models existed, the equivalence-class and error-reproduction papers are diagnostic-only and in-distribution, and the patching-limits work formalizes the failure without building the constructive remedy — so the combination (equivalence-class collection → OOD falsification → ground-truth validation → robust discovery objective) is genuinely unclaimed, runs entirely on small public models with released tooling, and directly serves deployment-grade monitoring, whose circuits must survive exactly the distribution shift this program optimizes for.

direction: Establish distribution-shift predictive validity — the ability of a circuit hypothesis to predict the intact model's behavior on held-out, naturally perturbed inputs — as the principled, quantitative criterion for selecting among equally-faithful circuit/decomposition hypotheses (the "dual basis problem"), and ship it as a standardized stress-test benchmark for component-level circuits and feature-level attribution graphs.
project: Circuit Stress Tests: Distribution-Shift Predictive Validity as a Criterion for Circuit Hypotheses (MGG — the Mechanistic Generalization Gap)
question: When two circuit hypotheses (or attribution-graph decompositions) are equally faithful on the discovery distribution, does their predictive validity under natural distribution shifts (entity swaps, paraphrases, distractors, length/position changes) discriminate the true mechanism from spurious members of the equivalence class — and can this be standardized into a metric and benchmark that the field agrees to report?
first_experiment: On GPT-2-small IOI and greater-than (plus one Gemma-2-2B attribution graph via the open circuit-tracer), assemble a candidate set of matched-size circuit hypotheses — the published reference circuits, automated EAP-IG/ACDC circuits, and deliberately confounded circuits refit on a restricted discovery split (à la Geng et al.'s controlled edits) — all of which tie on in-distribution CPR/CMD within noise; then run each candidate through a battery of natural shifts and measure whether the intact model's outputs and intervention effects on shifted inputs are predicted by the candidate (interchange-intervention accuracy per shift axis), checking against the known reference/InterpBench ground truth whether the OOD ranking picks the true mechanism where in-distribution faithfulness ties. If discrimination succeeds, build the benchmark and metric ("Circuit Stress Test" suite); if canonical circuits are themselves brittle OOD, publish that negative result as the calibration the field explicitly says it lacks.
why: It attacks the field's self-identified #1 open problem — verification of attribution graphs and the dual basis problem — at the moment it has become acute: non-identifiability is proven (Méloux et al., phantom specialization), in-distribution faithfulness is proven unreliable (Geng et al. misranking; error-reproduction failures), and the OOD-validation objective has been blessed as a proof-of-concept on toy models (Li et al. 2025) but never executed for circuit-level hypotheses in real LMs or for attribution graphs; the Neuronpedia future-work list explicitly requests OOD-input hypothesis validation and nobody has delivered it. It is cheap (small open models, existing tooling, ground-truth organisms), it has an informative result either way (a new agreed metric, or the brittleness negative result the field says it needs), and it is upstream of every deployment-grade safety monitor that currently trusts unvalidated features.

direction: Build a falsification-first validation layer for feature-level circuit hypotheses (attribution graphs / sparse feature circuits) on open-weight LLMs — automated search for the inputs and interventions where a circuit hypothesis maximally diverges from the real model's behavior, scored by a causal-abstraction error metric, used both to stress-test published circuit claims and to empirically adjudicate between competing decompositions that fit the discovery data equally well.
project: Circuit Breaker — Automated Falsification and Adjudication of Attribution Graph Hypotheses
question: When a circuit hypothesis reproduces model behavior on the distribution where it was discovered, does an automated search for maximally-diverging natural-language inputs and interventions falsify it — and when two competing decompositions (e.g., an edge-level EAP-IG circuit vs. a transcoder attribution graph) both fit the discovery distribution, does the divergence-maximizing test empirically determine which (if either) is the mechanism, converting the dual-basis problem from an aesthetic judgment into a measurable one?
first_experiment: A two-horse race on IOI, calibrated against a known failure mode: (1) reconstruct the published Wang et al. edge circuit and an EAP-IG edge circuit on GPT-2 small, plus a feature-level IOI attribution graph from the open circuit-tracer library on Llama-3.2-1B; (2) confirm all pass standard i.i.d. replacement-score thresholds on the discovery distribution; (3) run a divergence-maximizing search — seeded with the "romantic object" subpopulation ACE found by hand, then extended by constrained gradient-guided token-space optimization and LLM-guided paraphrase generation — to maximize KL(replacement model ‖ full model) and KL between the two hypotheses' replacement models under resample ablation; (4) on the top-K divergent inputs, score each hypothesis with a CAE-style interventional violation metric (including faithfulness testing over unmapped variables) to determine which decomposition's predictions match actual model behavior. Either outcome is decisive: hypotheses that fail yield the first circuit-adversarial benchmark for attribution graphs; a hypothesis that survives everywhere yields the first empirical equivalence certificate between decomposition paradigms.
why: It is the one direction named as the field's top priority by essentially every authoritative source — Sharkey et al.'s faithfulness flag, the 2026 retrospective's "dual basis problem" and verification-bottleneck diagnoses, and the attribution-graph builders' explicit call for automated OOD interventional validation — while remaining unclaimed: the nearest neighbors each cover only a fragment (sampled-not-optimized worst cases on component-level circuits; inclusion-stability certification; metrics validated only on toy systems; single-feature statistical tests), and the combination — optimization-driven falsification of graph-level hypotheses on real LLMs, doubling as a decomposition discriminator — appears nowhere in the 2025–26 literature. It is also the highest-leverage direction for safety: interpretability-derived monitors are already in production but unvalidated circuits fail silently under exactly the distribution shifts that adversarial pressure exploits, and audit-game benchmarks (AuditBench, hidden-object organisms) cannot function without circuits that survive hostile conditions. Finally it is unusually tractable: everything needed — open-weight models, public transcoders/SAEs, reference circuits with known failure modes to calibrate against, and published metrics to port — is open and single-GPU-scale, so the marginal cost is low while the information value for the field's central methodological question is high.

direction: Build automated counterfactual-simulatability evaluation for mechanistic explanations — using held-out behavioral prediction on distribution-shifted inputs and explanation-aware discriminating interventions to select among competing circuit decompositions, resolving the identifiability/dual-basis problem that in-distribution faithfulness metrics provably cannot.
project: Circuits That Predict: Counterfactual Simulatability as a Selection Criterion for Mechanistic Explanations
question: When multiple mechanistic explanations of the same behavior are statistically indistinguishable under standard in-distribution intervention faithfulness, can automatically generated counterfactual tests (held-out input families plus explanation-aware intervention probes) separate them, and does predictive accuracy on those tests reliably select the true mechanism?
first_experiment: On GPT-2-small IOI and the InterpBench model with a known IOI mechanism, construct a pool of candidate circuits (published circuit, seed/threshold variants from EAP-IG/ACDC, controlled same-size edits) verified to tie on in-distribution KL faithfulness; for each candidate derive its predicted behavioral sensitivity profile over ~20 parameterized perturbation families (role swaps, novel objects, distractors, repetitions, name/position manipulations); compare each profile to the intact model's actual behavior on those families; measure (a) the tie-breaking rate — fraction of in-distribution-tied pairs separated OOD — and (b) selection accuracy against InterpBench's ground-truth circuit, benchmarked against the in-distribution faithfulness ranking's misranking rate.
why: It attacks the gap that the field's own 2026 retrospectives rank first — verification and the dual basis problem — where three independent lines (non-identifiability theory, demonstrated faithfulness misranking, and leaders' explicit request for automated OOD validation of hypotheses) converge, yet no existing work applies simulatability-style held-out behavioral prediction to select among mechanistic decompositions: adversarial circuit evaluation, Certified Circuits, and CIRCUS each evaluate a single explanation's stability rather than discriminating between candidates, and counterfactual simulatability exists only for verbal explanations. InterpBench's ground-truth mechanisms — available only since late 2024 and not yet used this way — finally make the central claim falsifiable rather than philosophical, the experiment is tractable at GPT-2 scale on one GPU, and success would give the field the missing "perplexity-like" quantitative target for explanation quality that safety-critical monitors built on circuits currently lack.

direction: Build predictive distribution-level circuit models — merge per-prompt attribution graphs into compact, context-conditioned global circuit models whose generality is validated by held-out prediction of both circuit structure and model behavior, providing the field's missing non-circular faithfulness criterion.
project: Circuit Atlas — From Per-Prompt Attribution Graphs to Predictive, Held-Out-Validated Global Circuit Models
question: When per-prompt attribution graphs are extracted across a controlled distribution of prompts for a task, do they compose into a compact context-conditioned global circuit model that (i) predicts the per-prompt graph structure and (ii) predicts the model's behavior — including its errors — on held-out and shifted prompts; and can this framework distinguish genuine context-conditioned mechanism switching from sampling within an equivalence class of behaviorally equivalent decompositions?
first_experiment: On GPT-2-small (fast, best-studied) and Gemma-2-2B (open Circuit-Tracer replacement models), extract per-prompt feature-level attribution graphs for ~200 IOI prompts spanning 5 template families × controlled name/order/distractor variations, plus a held-out set and shifted templates. First measure edge/feature stability within vs. across template families (Jaccard overlap, weight correlations) to quantify the instability the 2026 papers report at feature level. Then, using only 4 of 5 template families, fit a single merged graph annotated with per-edge context-conditional statistics (activation frequency and weight as functions of prompt features), and test whether it predicts (a) held-out per-prompt graph structure (edge-level AUC) and (b) held-out circuit-replaced behavior including error reproduction, against three baselines: a single-template task circuit, a CIRCUS-style consensus circuit, and an equivalence-class random null. If held-out prediction beats the single-circuit baseline, the conditional global model is real; where it fails, classify each failure as phantom (structure changes, behavior preserved) or functional (behavior changes) — the taxonomy the field currently lacks.
why: It is the exact convergence point of the field's strongest 2025–2026 signals: leaders explicitly asked for "merging attribution graphs into a global circuit picture" (Nanda/Lindsey), the validation chapter demands "predictions on held-out behaviors," the 2026 retrospective names decomposition choice as the top open problem, and five independent papers proved single-task circuits are unstable without offering the constructive fix. It is not already done: the closest works either certify a robust *single* circuit (Certified Circuits, CIRCUS), document variance and stop (Demystifying Variance, Explanation Multiplicity), transfer-test one input axis at component level without prediction (phantom specialization), cluster per-prompt circuits observationally (ACC++), or remain position papers (ModCirc) — no work builds a feature-level, multi-axis, context-conditioned global model validated by held-out prediction of structure *and* behavior. It is also the most safety-relevant methodology gap: it quantifies monitor coverage (on which inputs the monitor's circuit actually governs behavior), detects mechanism switching central to deception/sandbagging monitoring, predicts where steering/ablation interventions will fail under distribution shift, and its method is tractable with existing open tooling on modest compute, with each milestone (stability atlas → conditional model → failure taxonomy) independently publishable.

direction: Develop and validate a principled disambiguation framework for the dual basis problem — selecting among competing mechanistic decompositions (circuits/feature bases) that are equally faithful on-distribution, using divergence of their behavioral predictions under held-out distribution shift as the discriminating signal.
project: Separating the Equivalence Class: Distribution-Shift Divergence as a Selection Criterion for Competing Circuit Explanations
question: When multiple structurally distinct circuit explanations of the same behavior are statistically indistinguishable under standard on-distribution faithfulness criteria, do their behavioral predictions diverge under a pre-registered family of distribution shifts — and can shift-generalized faithfulness (plus targeted interventions at points of maximal predicted divergence) recover the ground-truth mechanism, where on-distribution faithfulness cannot?
first_experiment: On GPT-2 small (IOI, Greater-Than) and one InterpBench model with a known ground-truth mechanism: (1) generate a candidate set using ACDC, EAP-IG, and edge-masking across a pre-registered multiverse grid (seeds × corruption types × metrics × thresholds), retaining candidates that pass standard faithfulness on-distribution yet are structurally near-disjoint (median pairwise Jaccard < 10%, following Mahale's protocol); (2) evaluate each candidate's KL faithfulness across a pre-registered shift family (name-pool and rare-name shifts, repeated-name adversarial variants, length/position shifts, token-frequency bands per Bayat Makou, distractor composition); (3) test three pre-registered hypotheses — H1: on-distribution-tied candidates diverge monotonically with shift magnitude; H2: ranking by shift-averaged faithfulness recovers the reference/InterpBench circuit better than on-distribution faithfulness; H3: interventions designed at points of maximal candidate-predicted divergence discriminate better than random interventions. All code, candidates, and shift families released; the outcome grounds the selection framework if confirmed, or bounds the dual basis problem's practical severity if refuted.
why: It is the field's own top-ranked open problem (the 2026 state-of-the-field assessment places the dual basis problem above all others), it gates the reliability of everything downstream — safety monitors that fail under distribution shift, EU-AI-Act-grade circuit claims that flip across analysts, model edits and transfers built on possibly-wrong subgraphs — and 18 months of work has produced only diagnostics (non-uniqueness proofs, multiverse flip rates, misranking analyses, phantom specialization) while the selection problem itself stands untouched: Certified Circuits certifies stability but cannot choose among stable candidates, the only identifiability theorem applies to a non-legible spectral primitive, and the "Which Circuit is it?" sequence is still at the conceptual stage. The timing is ideal — the diagnostics matured in 2026, ground-truth infrastructure (InterpBench, reference circuits, Gemma Scope) exists, the experiment runs on open models for a small compute budget, and every outcome is informative: success yields the first validated, non-aesthetic criterion for saying which decomposition is the mechanism, and failure yields the field's first quantitative bound on how much the dual basis problem actually matters off-distribution.

direction: Empirically adjudicate the "dual basis problem" — competing circuit decompositions (raw-neuron RelP circuits vs. SAE-feature circuits vs. transcoder/CLT circuits) that are equally faithful in-distribution — by testing which decomposition's causal predictions generalize under distribution shift and novel interventions, with ground-truth validation on InterpBench's known-mechanism models.
project: "Adjudicating the Dual Basis: Predictive Adequacy of Competing Circuit Decompositions under Distribution Shift"
question: When two or more decompositions of the same model behavior are equally faithful on the extraction distribution, do their causal predictions diverge under held-out conditions (paraphrase shift, token-frequency-band shift, matched negatives, novel interventions not used during extraction), and does the divergence pattern identify which decomposition tracks the model's actual computation rather than a behaviorally equivalent rewrite?
first_experiment: On Gemma-2-2B (public SAEs via Gemma Scope; RelP neuron-basis pipeline open-source), extract two circuits for the same behavior (two-digit addition and subject-verb agreement, both with published reference structure) at matched in-distribution faithfulness — one in the neuron basis (RelP on MLP activations), one in the SAE-feature basis — then re-evaluate both circuits' faithfulness and intervention-prediction accuracy on held-out shift families: paraphrase/lexical rewrites, token-frequency-band re-sampling (Bayat Makou protocol), matched negative controls (unit-test protocol), and one novel intervention (cross-prompt activation patching), computing each basis's "explanation transfer gap" (drop in predictive adequacy from in-distribution to shifted conditions). If the bases diverge under shift, that is the first empirical handle on the dual basis problem; if they do not, that is strong evidence cheap neuron-basis circuits can replace expensive SAE pipelines for deployment-grade monitoring.
why: It attacks the field's top-ranked open problem — named by the 2026 retrospective as what belongs at the top of any new survey, and newly made acute by three 2026 papers showing decompositions are non-unique, misranked by standard faithfulness, and sometimes incentivized to be unfaithful — while remaining feasible with open artifacts and modest compute. It has not already been done because the existing work is complementary, not overlapping: the CLT-unfaithfulness paper detects the problem only in a Boolean toy model; the misranking paper stays within a single basis; the Transluce neuron-vs-SAE comparison is in-distribution only; ObserverBench evaluates decision adequacy, not mechanism identity; and "Many Circuits, One Mechanism" does cross-condition transfer within one method and explicitly calls for the broader evaluation I propose. Every outcome is informative: divergence yields the first principled, non-aesthetic criterion for ranking decompositions ("predictive adequacy under shift" — the field's missing analog of top-1 accuracy or perplexity), while non-divergence validates SAE-free circuit monitoring for the deployment constraint the retrospective flags. Safety-wise, trust in circuit-based monitors and steering rests entirely on the assumption that the decomposition tracks the real computation rather than an ID-equivalent rewrite — and in-distribution-only explanations are precisely the ones obfuscation attacks can exploit, so this is the trust test the field currently lacks.

direction: Build a systematic interventional adjudication protocol and quantitative faithfulness metric for attribution graphs, which validates and ranks competing mechanistic explanations (hop vs. shortcut, CLT vs. PLT, algorithm vs. lookup) by testing their intervention-response predictions on constructed input distributions where those predictions diverge.
project: Crucial Experiments for Circuit Hypotheses: Dissociation-Based Validation and Adjudication of Attribution Graphs
question: When two attribution graphs (or two pathways within one graph) propose different causal mechanisms for the same behavior, do their interventional predictions diverge on held-out input distributions constructed to dissociate them — and can the graph whose predictions match the model's actual counterfactual behavior be identified quantitatively, yielding a non-circular faithfulness score for the field's standard artifact?
first_experiment: On Gemma-2-2B with the publicly released cross-layer transcoders (circuit-tracer), take the published two-hop factual-recall case ("The state containing Dallas has its capital in" → Austin), whose attribution graph shows both an intermediate-hop path (Dallas → state features → capital features) and a direct shortcut path; construct a dissociating prompt suite — counterfactual-context prompts that make the hop and shortcut predict different answers (e.g., contexts establishing Dallas is in Oklahoma, ambiguous multi-state entities, paraphrase families), plus neutral controls — then (a) suppress/patch the graph-nominated intermediate "state" features under each prompt family and measure whether the hop path's claimed mediating role holds exactly when the graph says it should, (b) compute the Interventional Prediction Gap (graph-predicted vs. actual post-intervention behavior) per path, and (c) repeat under the PLT decomposition to test whether the two decompositions' conflicting mechanistic stories are behaviorally resolved. This uses only open artifacts (released CLTs/PLTs, Neuronpedia reference graphs, CounterFact-style prompt construction) and directly tests the ICML 2026 unfaithfulness finding at language-model scale.
why: It attacks the single most acute, freshly-diagnosed bottleneck in the field — the verification gap behind attribution graphs, which a major 2026 retrospective ranks as the top open methodological problem ("the bottleneck in 2026 is verification, not labeling") — and it has three force-multiplying properties: (1) leverage, because attribution graphs are now the standard substrate for safety monitors, audits, and model-biology claims, so a validated adjudication protocol upgrades every downstream consumer; (2) tractability, because released CLTs/PLTs for small models and existing replication infrastructure make rigorous intervention experiments feasible without frontier-scale compute; and (3) decisiveness, because it converts the field's known ambiguity (PLT/CLT disagreement, hop/shortcut coexistence, lookup/algorithm confusion) into falsifiable, quantifiable comparisons. It has not been done: all existing faithfulness work targets component-level circuits (Hanna, Shi, Miller, Certified Circuits), the unfaithfulness result is diagnosis-only in a toy model, edit-based interventions serve discovery rather than adjudication, identifiability theory proved the underdetermination without building the protocol, and while field leaders explicitly call for "automated intervention experiments and synthetic/OOD inputs used for hypothesis validation," no one has built the dissociation-based protocol, the metric, or the benchmark that answers that call — making this the highest-leverage, clearly unoccupied niche in mechanistic interpretability today.

direction: Develop and ground-truth-validate distribution shift as a principled, non-circular discriminator for mechanistic explanations — testing whether behaviorally-equivalent circuit explanations (e.g., transcoder attribution graphs) can be ranked by how well their counterfactual predictions survive controlled distribution shifts.
project: Faithfulness Under Shift: Discriminating Dual Decompositions with Controlled Distribution Shift
question: When two mechanistic explanations (e.g., a deep multi-hop attribution graph vs. a shallow rewrite, both matching the model on the training distribution) imply different behaviors under controlled input shifts, does agreement between each explanation's predicted shifted behavior and the model's actual shifted behavior reliably identify the true mechanism — and can this "shift-agreement" criterion be quantified and validated against planted ground-truth circuits in semi-synthetic transformers before being applied to real language models?
first_experiment: Build a planted-circuit testbed: take an InterpBench-style SIIT transformer (or train one with public SIIT code) implementing a genuinely 2-hop compositional algorithm whose training distribution admits a behavioral shortcut (a single-hop correlate that predicts outputs comparably well on-distribution); verify the dual-basis phenomenon by demonstrating both explanations achieve statistically matched on-distribution behavioral agreement; then generate a family of "decoupling" shifts (inputs where the shallow correlate and the deep mechanism diverge) and measure each explanation's predicted-vs-actual behavior on them, plus edge-level recovery against the planted circuit — establishing whether the shift signal cleanly separates the true mechanism before any transcoder machinery is involved; only then train a cross-layer transcoder with CLT-Forge on the same model and repeat the discrimination test at the attribution-graph level, measuring shift-agreement (a proposed metric: Explanatory Shift Agreement) against ground truth.
why: It attacks the field's self-diagnosed #1 gap — the verification asymmetry that left attribution graphs, the standard artifact since March 2025, almost entirely unvalidated — and directly operationalizes the "dual basis problem" that the mid-2026 state-of-field review named as the top problem for any new survey. It has not been done: non-identifiability work (Méloux et al. ICLR 2025) only established the problem in tiny Boolean MLPs without proposing a selection criterion; the ICML 2026 transcoder-unfaithfulness paper documented the shallow-rewrite failure in a Boolean toy but offered no detection protocol or realistic-model study; InterpBench's planted-circuit models have only ever been used for on-distribution evaluation of node/edge circuit discovery; all faithfulness-metric work (Hanna et al. 2024, error-agreement evaluation 2026, intervention unit tests ICML 2026) stays on-distribution; and SAE feature validation (anytime-valid testing, causal auditing) is feature-level and on-distribution — no work ranks *competing mechanistic explanations* by off-distribution behavioral prediction, and Anthropic's own August 2025 future-work list lists "synthetic / out-of-distribution inputs used for hypothesis validation" as an open question. It is the most promising because it is foundational (validation is the bottleneck all downstream applications — monitors, auditing, model editing — depend on), safety-critical (shallow-correlate explanations fail exactly under the distributional shift where monitoring matters most), immediately tractable with open tools at single-GPU scale, and yields a reusable metric and benchmark rather than another case study — while any negative result (e.g., shifts failing to discriminate) would itself be publishable evidence about the limits of the field's dominant artifact.

direction: Mechanistically trace, at the feature level, how an RL-trained reasoning model's chain-of-thought causally mediates (or bypasses) the computation of its final answer — turning CoT-monitorability from an empirical detector game into a causal understanding of when thinking tokens are load-bearing versus decorative.
project: Is the Thinking Thinking? Feature-Level Circuit Analysis of the Reasoning-to-Answer Pathway in RL Reasoning Models
question: In reasoning models like DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen, what fraction of the causal ancestry of the final answer flows through features that read and process the thinking tokens versus bypass features, does that "CoT mediation score" distinguish faithful derivation from pre-committed/rationalized answers (e.g., hint-induced flips), and does it explain why probe-based unfaithfulness detectors succeed or fail across models?
first_experiment: On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B (plus the released 7B transcoder adapters), on GSM8K/MMLU subsets: (1) train linear probes at the last prompt token and at each thinking position to decode the final answer, replicating the pre-commitment finding on a reasoning model and locating a persistent "answer register" along the trace; (2) run circuit-tracer attribution graphs from the final-answer logits on ~50 paired traces (probe-decoded-pre-CoT vs. not; hinted-flip vs. clean), and compute the share of causal ancestry routed through thinking-token features versus direct/bypass paths; (3) pre-register one interventional prediction per pair (ablating the dominant bypass features should flip pre-committed answers but not mediated ones) and test it before inspecting the graphs. A null on step (1) is itself a decisive result separating reasoning models from prompted-CoT instruction models.
why: It directly operationalizes the field's own top-listed open question (causal importance of CoT, from Nanda/Lindsey's future-work list) in the model class where CoT monitoring is the primary safety lever, and it supplies the mechanistic explanation that the crowded detection literature (probes, circuit-fingerprint classifiers, circuit scores) conspicuously lacks — "Two Regimes" shows detector failures are model-dependent and unexplained, which is exactly the gap a causal circuit account closes. It is tractable now for the first time because feature-level tooling for reasoning models only became available in early 2026 (transcoder adapters with public checkpoints, Qwen-Scope), prior circuit work deliberately avoided reasoning traces as too convoluted (CRV), behavioral causality work explicitly disclaims the internal mechanism (Jia & Mu), and the nearest mechanistic work on R1-distills stopped at attention heads and hesitation tokens — so the core object (feature-level mediation of answer computation by thinking tokens, including bypass pathways in unfaithful cases) is unclaimed, while producing a reusable metric (CoT mediation score) that plugs into the field's rigor agenda via pre-registered interventional validation.

direction: Extract validated, generalizable algorithmic circuit structure from families of per-prompt attribution graphs, replacing execution traces with invariant, conditionally-routed circuit models tested by predicting held-out behavior and interventions.
project: From Execution Traces to Algorithms: Validated Global Circuits from Families of Attribution Graphs
question: What structure of attribution graphs over a prompt family is invariant vs. prompt-specific, and does that invariant algorithm graph predict held-out behavior and ablation effects better than single-prompt traces, robustly across alternative feature decompositions?
first_experiment: Generate ~60 attribution graphs on Gemma-2-2B (public CLTs, circuit-tracer) for a two-hop factual-recall prompt family with a 40/20 train/held-out split; measure node recurrence, edge-weight consistency, and topology clustering against a null prompt family, then test whether the family-aggregated graph predicts held-out per-feature ablation effects better than single-prompt, activation-ranked, and random baselines.
why: It directly attacks the attribution-graph authors' own top open item (merging graphs into a global picture), operationalizes faithfulness as falsifiable held-out prediction, and offers the first principled answer to the dual-basis problem via decomposition-robust invariant structure — a combination no prior work touches: graph-family merging remains unevaluated tooling, consistency was measured only with patching-based scores without attribution graphs or held-out intervention tests, and certification work addresses dataset-perturbation stability rather than algorithm extraction, all while the required tooling (public transcoders, MIT-licensed tracer, one-GPU feasibility) only recently became available.

direction: Characterize the computation that lives in the unexplained residual of learned feature decompositions (SAE/transcoder error terms), formalize "intervention completeness" — whether an intervention is a true behavioral bottleneck or merely blocks one route — and use recovery-proofness as the first principled selection criterion among competing decompositions and as a hardening target for safety-critical interventions.
project: Residual Computation and Intervention Completeness: When Is a Feature Intervention a Real Bottleneck?
question: When we suppress a behavior by intervening on a set of learned features, what computation in the decomposition residual carries the recoverable behavior (is it neuron-sparse, cross-layer superposition, or prompt-specific noise), how can intervention completeness be formalized and measured, and does ranking decompositions by recovery-proofness resolve the dual-basis problem while yielding hardened, bypass-resistant safety interventions?
