first_experiment: On Gemma-2-2B with Gemma Scope SAEs, replicate post-intervention recovery for two behaviors (refusal steering and indirect object identification), then decompose each recovered perturbation by projecting it onto (a) the neuron basis, (b) SAE decoder directions at other layers, and (c) error terms at other layers — directly testing the unrun cross-layer-superposition hypothesis and producing a "recovery atlas" that establishes whether residual computation is structured (go) or diffuse (kill signal) before building the formal completeness metric.
why: It sits at the exact intersection of the field's three most-acknowledged 2026 gaps — attribution-graph faithfulness, the dual-basis problem, and deployment-grade safety — because feature-level defenses (SAE clamping, SAE-based unlearning) are already being relied upon while demonstrably bypassable through the residual; it is not already done because the recovery paper only demonstrated the vulnerability with a single attribution analysis, the cross-layer-superposition MVE from 2025 was left unrun, the completeness literature (AND/OR/ADDER gates) treats redundancy within a basis rather than the unexplained residual, the identifiability work proved non-uniqueness without offering a selection criterion, and the neuron-basis paper suggests a fix without a metric or safety connection; and it is unusually cheap and falsifiable — it runs on open models and open SAE dictionaries with optimization-based diagnostics, so the first experiment can be executed in days and its outcome (structured vs. diffuse residual computation) decisively shapes or kills the rest of the program.

direction: Mechanistic causal provenance of reasoning models' final answers — determining per example whether the emitted answer is copied from a specific chain-of-thought occurrence, recomputed from the prompt, or read out of a pre-committed internal state, and building ground-truth-validated, cheap internal detectors of that provenance as a monitoring primitive.
project: Where Does the Answer Come From? Causal Provenance of Final-Answer Emissions in Reasoning Models, Validated on Provenance-Controlled Model Organisms
question: When a reasoning model emits its final answer, what is the token-level causal origin of that answer — copy from a specific CoT occurrence (and which one, when several appear), fresh recomputation from the prompt, or readout of a pre-committed internal state formed mid-CoT — and can per-example provenance mode be reliably detected from cheap internal signals, validated against organisms with controlled provenance?
first_experiment: On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B over ~500 GSM8K/MATH-500 trajectories containing ≥2 answer emissions (in-think and post-think), run a three-probe battery: (1) a logit-lens scan of the residual stream at every position to map when and where the answer value first becomes decodable (the pre-commitment map); (2) attention-mask each CoT answer occurrence during the final answer pass and measure per-occurrence final-answer flip rates, identifying the "operative" occurrence (the line-8-vs-line-11-vs-line-13 problem); (3) corrupt the first CoT answer occurrence (replace the digit) with a constrained on-policy continuation and measure whether the final answer follows the corruption (copy) or reverts (recompute/self-repair). Output: the first per-example provenance taxonomy plus flip-rate statistics deciding which mode dominates and where divergences (wrong answers, self-corrections) concentrate — one GPU, days of compute — followed by organism training (forced-copy, forced-recompute-with-distractor-CoT, cached-commitment SFT/RL models) to validate detectors against known ground truth.
why: It attacks the one reasoning-model interpretability problem that the field's own flagship agenda flags as unsolved and central — "the answer likely came from copying the thoughts, or maybe it was computed anew... Who knows" — and which ten months of fast-moving 2026 work has skirted but not answered: existing papers provide only behavioral counterfactuals (Thought Anchors, Commitment Boundary), correlational attention patterns (self-reading analysis), aggregate information-flow metrics (Faithfulness as Information Flow), or probability-trajectory evidence of early commitment (Halt Vector), none of which deliver a causal, mechanism-level, per-example account of the answer-emission computation. It has a direct safety theory of change (per-example CoT-monitoring diagnostics and incriminating/exonerating flagged behavior in the science-of-misalignment agenda), it answers the open-problems review's demand for ground-truth benchmarks via provenance-controlled organisms that make the method falsifiable rather than anecdotal, it is genuinely tractable with open small reasoning models and public tooling on modest compute, and it builds the atomic primitive ("which forward passes actually matter") that the still-unsolved trajectory-level circuit analysis needs — while its negative-result branches (e.g., answers are always recomputed, or provenance is undetectable from internals) would themselves be important, publishable calibration results for how much CoT monitoring can be trusted.

direction: Build a quantitative, non-circular framework that adjudicates among behaviorally-equivalent mechanistic explanations (circuits, attribution graphs, SAE-feature decompositions) by their divergent predictions under held-out inputs and interventions.
project: Held-Out Divergence as the Arbiter of Mechanistic Explanations (HODGE)
question: Do candidate decompositions that are indistinguishable in-distribution diverge systematically under carefully chosen held-out inputs and interventions, and can that divergence serve as a principled metric for which explanation is the mechanism the model actually uses?
first_experiment: On GPT-2 small IOI, take manual, ACDC-discovered, and pruned circuit candidates matched on base-distribution KL, then evaluate success-agreement, error-agreement, and intervention-transfer on DoubleIO/TripleIO variants, negation/lexical nuisances, and random perturbations, testing whether in-distribution-equivalent candidates separate reproducibly under held-out divergence.
why: It targets the field's own top-ranked unresolved methodological problem (decomposition choice is currently "an aesthetic decision"), sits at the constructive frontier beyond mature diagnoses (non-identifiability proofs, non-robust faithfulness metrics, unit tests, error-reproduction evaluation, structural identifiability theory that is explicitly not legible), is feasible on small models with public infrastructure, directly underpins the distribution-shift failure of interpretability-derived safety monitors, and remains unoccupied because each adjacent line holds only one piece of the puzzle.

direction: Audit models whose behavioral evaluations look clean after standard emergent-misalignment mitigations, using white-box signals, to determine whether dormant conditional misalignment is visible in activations, only under cue-adjacent contexts, or only in the weights.
project: Dormant but Detectable? White-Box Auditing of Conditionally Misaligned Models
question: When standard mitigations (benign-data mixing, post-hoc HHH finetuning, inoculation prompting) suppress emergent misalignment on behavioral evaluations, does the resulting model retain a detectable internal signature of its dormant conditional misalignment — in activation space on held-out benign prompts, only under benign cue-adjacent contexts, or exclusively in the weights — and can such a signature be separated from benign format/style drift?
first_experiment: Using the public insecure-code dataset, LoRA-finetune Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct into an EM organism (multi-seed), verify EM behaviorally, then apply post-hoc HHH finetuning (the mitigation known to leave conditional misalignment) and verify behavioral cleanliness on standard evals; extract the mean-diff misalignment direction from the un-mitigated organism (cross-checked against Soligo et al.'s released direction); then measure projection of that direction onto activations across all layers for held-out benign prompts under three regimes — generic prompts, cue-adjacent benign framings (Python-string format, educational framing, coding system prompt), and matched controls (base model, secure-code finetune, HHH-only finetune) — testing whether any regime separates mitigated-EM models from controls at seed-level significance (AUC/effect size) before any misalignment-eliciting prompt is used; depending on the branch, extend to SAE-feature and persona-vector detectors, or to weight-space readouts (rank-1 adapter scalars, LoRA spectral deltas) to localize where the dormant state lives.
why: It attacks the single most deployment-relevant open failure mode in the interpretability-for-safety pipeline: mitigations that pass standard evals while leaving context-gated misalignment (Dubiński et al. 2026) were discovered behaviorally and left unexamined internally, even though activation monitors are exactly what labs currently rely on; the 2026 retrospective explicitly names "behaviors generated only under distributional shift" as beyond monitor coverage, and this project measures that boundary on a safety-critical anomaly class. It has not been done: the nearest works each stop short — trait-space monitoring (Nghiem et al. 2026) detects EM during training on training-like distributions, persona vectors (Chen et al. 2025) monitor shifts during finetuning, AuditBench (2026) hunts elicitable hidden behaviors with agents, MAD methods (Anthropic 2025; functional attribution 2026) require known triggers, and the persona-subspace paper (2026) studies un-mitigated organisms and intervention failures, not audits of mitigated models. It is uniquely decisive because all three outcomes are publishable and consequential, it is computationally tractable with open weights, released organisms and datasets, and single-GPU LoRA finetunes, and it bridges the EM-mechanism literature to the monitoring/auditing community with both a method (an audit protocol with format-matched controls separating intent from style) and a mechanistic localization result (where dormant misalignment lives).

direction: Mechanistic interpretability of internal task-state tracking in multi-turn agentic LLMs — locating where an agent's representation of task progress/state lives, how tool observations write to it, and why it degrades or is corrupted across turns — the "cross-scope continuity" gap explicitly named as unresolved by the field's own 2026 review and by DeepMind's pragmatic vision, while all adjacent work stops at probing, steering, or system-level positions.
project: Where Is the Working Memory? A Mechanistic Account of Task-State Representation, Update, and Degradation in Multi-Turn Tool-Using Language Models
question: Do instruction-tuned LLM agents maintain a persistent, decodable internal task-state representation across an agentic trajectory (and if so, at which positions/layers is it written and read, and via what circuit mechanism do tool observations update it), or do they recompute state from the raw transcript each turn — and does this representation mechanistically degrade or get corrupted as trajectories lengthen or when harness summaries replace raw history?
first_experiment: On Gemma-2-2B-it (and Llama-3.1-8B-it for generality) running a controlled tool-use environment with ground-truth state (a simulated file system with create/read/write/delete), generate ~1k agent trajectories; train linear probes on residual-stream activations at every layer/position (after tool-result tokens, at pre-action positions) to decode state variables (files modified so far, current subgoal, next intended action); then run activation patching on contrastive trajectory pairs (same surface history, different true state, and vice versa) to localize where state is written and read — distinguishing "maintained compressed state" from "recomputed from transcript," with a trajectory-length sweep and a summary-substitution condition as the second step.
why: (1) Importance — it targets the central unresolved gap named by the field's own most recent review (Oct 2026: "cross-scope continuity"), is listed as out-of-reach by Google DeepMind's pragmatic vision, and sits where deployment risk is actually growing (irreversible agentic actions, goal drift, long-horizon failure), where internal state monitors would be a cheap complement to fragile CoT monitoring; (2) tractability — feasibility is proven by adjacent work (tool-need/risk/capability probes work pre-action; state tracking is mechanistically understood within single contexts; circuit-tracer + Gemma Scope run on one GPU), but no one has connected these into a mechanistic account across turns; (3) not already done — existing agentic-internal work is probing/monitoring (Beyond the Black Box, TACIT, agent-confidence), steering (Agent MechSuits), or system-level positions (ATLIS), all of which explicitly leave "internal model mechanisms" unexplained, because the field's pipelines were built around single prompts, harness confounds deterred researchers, and open circuit-tracing tooling only became available mid-2025; (4) leverage — the result is foundational either way: a persistent state representation would give the field a new, cheap, deployment-grade monitoring object for agents, while its absence would mechanistically explain long-horizon degradation and reveal a core architectural fragility (state recomputation) that agentic training and harness design would need to fix.

direction: Make mechanistic explanations earn their status by out-of-distribution prediction — build the automated protocol that compiles competing explanations of a model behavior into falsifiable predictors, actively searches for the inputs that discriminate them, and certifies the survivors with anytime-valid statistics.
project: The Explanation Tribunal: Active Discrimination and Statistical Certification of Competing Mechanistic Explanations
question: When two mechanistic explanations (e.g., a hand-drawn IOI circuit vs. an ACDC circuit vs. a transcoder attribution graph) both replicate a model's behavior in-distribution, does automated search over held-out inputs and interventions statistically separate them, and can the survivors be certified as faithful predictors of the model?
first_experiment: On GPT-2 Small and IOI, register four competing explanations (Wang et al. circuit, ACDC circuit, minimal S-inhibition+name-mover variant, shuffled null circuit), compile each into a predictor via its resample-ablation policy, confirm they fit comparably on 10k in-distribution inputs, then maximize predictor-vs-predictor KL over on-task token space (straight-through Gumbel search on template slots + genetic/LLM-guided paraphrases), query the real model at the top discriminating inputs, and rank/eliminate/certify candidates with betting-style anytime-valid confidence sequences.
why: It is the concrete synthesis of the field's self-identified #1 open problems (faithfulness-as-a-number and the dual basis problem), the enabling pieces (runnable transcoder replacement models, CIF's statistical layer, ISS's active-separation template) only matured in the last 12 months and have never been joined, and it has been left open because discovery has been more publishable than verification, discriminating-input search between explanations requires a novel objective distinct from standard adversarial attacks, and frontier-lab incentives make thousands of intervened forward passes per query unattractive — a foundational, cheap, safety-relevant slot an independent researcher can occupy.

direction: Operationalize the "dual basis problem" by building and validating a decomposition-selection criterion — held-out interventional prediction under distribution shift — that discriminates among mechanistically equivalent decompositions, using model organisms with known ground-truth algorithms.
project: Decomposition Stress Tests: Held-Out Interventional Prediction as a Selection Criterion for Equivalent Mechanistic Explanations
question: When multiple mechanistic decompositions of the same model are equally faithful on the discovery distribution, does held-out interventional prediction (novel ablations and patching interventions × shifted input distributions) discriminate the decomposition that tracks the model's actual algorithm — and is on-distribution faithfulness demonstrably insufficient for this?
first_experiment: Train ~25 seeds of the standard 1-layer attention-only transformer on modular addition (p=97); establish each seed's ground-truth algorithm family via established Fourier key-frequency analysis and ablation signatures; generate an ensemble of on-distribution-faithful decompositions per seed (SAEs across widths/sparsity/seeds, transcoders, ACDC/EAP-IG edge circuits across thresholds); then run a held-out interventional stress test in which each decomposition must predict the outcomes of ablations, path-patching, and restricted-operand-distribution inputs it was never fit on, and test two hypotheses: (H1) on-distribution faithfulness does not predict off-distribution interventional accuracy among near-tied decompositions (rank flips), and (H2) interventional transfer accuracy recovers the ground-truth algorithm family per seed. Scale-up: apply the identical protocol to a published real-LM circuit (IOI / greater-than in GPT-2 or Gemma) as a demonstration.
why: It targets the field's top-ranked open problem (faithfulness/verification, the dual basis problem) at the moment the diagnosis is complete but the cure is missing — Méloux et al. stopped at non-identifiability plus discussion of predictive standards, the Dead Salmons paper calls for hypothesis-testing framing without building it, Bayat Makou et al. demonstrated equivalence classes without a selection criterion and explicitly excluded the feature level, Wu et al. documented that steering outcomes are unpredictable on unseen templates without a remedy, and Guo et al. handle feature selection within a single decomposition rather than choice between decompositions. It has not been done because it falls between two sub-communities (feature-level SAE validators and edge-level circuit discoverers) and the enabling diagnostic results only matured in 2025–2026. It is the most promising direction because it is cheap and rigorous (ground-truth model organisms on one GPU), every outcome is publishable (if on-distribution faithfulness suffices, that is reassuring; if not, we get the field's first validated, non-aesthetic decomposition-selection metric), it yields an adoptable community protocol analogous to what perplexity did for LMs, and it directly addresses the safety-critical deployment gap: interpretability-derived monitors are only trustworthy off-distribution if built on the decomposition that survives distribution-shift stress tests.

direction: Build a validated protocol that adjudicates between competing mechanistic explanations (the dual-basis/proxy-fidelity problem) by actively generating held-out causal tests that maximize disagreement among candidate explanations, validated on substrates with planted ground-truth mechanisms.
project: DisCrim — Discriminating Causal Tests for Competing Mechanistic Explanations
question: When two candidate mechanistic explanations of the same behavior are indistinguishable under standard in-distribution ablation-based evaluation, can an actively designed battery of held-out causal tests (novel inputs and interventions chosen to maximize predicted disagreement between the candidates) reliably identify which candidate reflects the model's true computation — and what is the empirical law connecting a decomposition's reconstruction quality to how easily it survives such adjudication?
first_experiment: On a known-mechanism substrate (an InterpBench multi-hop task, or the small boolean multi-hop transformer setup from the Feb 2026 CLT-unfaithfulness work), construct the canonical candidate pair: (A) the ground-truth mechanism, (B) a deliberately shallow "skip" rewrite that reproduces input–output behavior but bypasses intermediate computation. First, show both pass standard in-distribution faithfulness (KL/logit-diff under resampling and mean ablation, with CIF-style confidence sequences) — i.e., the existing criterion cannot tell them apart. Then make each candidate an executable predictor of outputs, intermediate activations, and intervention outcomes; search over held-out inputs and interventions (novel compositions requiring intermediate nodes; patches confined near the natural manifold) to maximize the two candidates' predicted divergence; run that test battery on the real model; and measure held-out causal agreement for each candidate. Success criterion: the discriminating-test battery separates truth from mimic with high accuracy while in-distribution faithfulness shows no separation. If it works, extend to candidate sets from real decomposition bases (CLT vs. per-layer transcoder vs. component-level vs. neuron-level circuits on IOI/Greater-Than/Gemma-Scope SAEs) and to behavior-matched model organisms with and without planted mechanisms.
why: It is the actionable response to the two problems that both major 2026 field assessments rank at the top (dual basis; proxy fidelity) and to the "evaluation and benchmarking" gap (§14.2) — every recent paper misranks, error-blinds, or phantom-circuits the current criteria, and each explicitly calls for a rethink without proposing one. It has not been done because it only became possible in the last ~18 months, when its required ingredients separately matured: proof of non-identifiability (2025), quantified misranking and error-blindness (late 2026), ground-truth substrates (InterpBench, validated model organisms with released checkpoints), and certified adaptive interventional statistics (CIF, July 2026) — but no work combines them into a discrimination protocol, and the closest precursors either test one hypothesis against the model rather than hypotheses against each other, or use held-out prediction only correlatively at the behavioral level. It is feasible at academic compute on open models and releases, it directly upgrades safety auditing (distinguishing "the model truly computes X" from "behaviorally mimics X" — precisely the distinction that matters for deception detection and monitoring, and the one CLT feature-skipping is known to obscure), and it yields three concrete artifacts: a falsification-first evaluation protocol, a non-circular held-out causal score, and a benchmark of candidate pairs with ground-truth labels (including planted mimics) that the field can use to rank future decomposition methods. Its main risk — that discriminating tests merely probe OOD artifacts rather than the natural computation — is itself measurable and mitigable by manifold-constrained interventions and the ground-truth validation loop; and "indistinguishable within test budget" is an honest, useful outcome, converting unicity intuitions into explicit, quantified bounds on what current evidence can establish.

direction: Build an automated "crucial experiment" method for mechanistic interpretability that adjudicates between competing circuit hypotheses by exploiting the fact that extracted circuits are executable surrogate models — actively searching for inputs where rival hypotheses make divergent behavioral predictions and testing which prediction the real model follows — validated on ground-truth testbeds and applied to attribution graphs in real LMs.
project: Crucial Circuits: Adjudicating Competiting Circuit Hypotheses by Divergent-Prediction Input Search
question: When two circuit hypotheses for the same model behavior both match the model on the discovery distribution (the "dual basis" / depth-rewriting problem), can an automated protocol that searches for inputs maximizing the behavioral divergence between the candidate circuits reliably identify which hypothesis tracks the model's true computation — and does this adjudication power survive distribution shift where on-distribution faithfulness cannot discriminate at all?
first_experiment: On an InterpBench semi-synthetic transformer with a known ground-truth grafted circuit, construct a competitor hypothesis (a shallow "depth-rewritten" variant, plus sparsity/ablation variants of standard discovery outputs from ACDC/EAP-IG) verified to match ground-truth behavior on the task's training distribution; implement the divergence search — run both candidate circuits as surrogate models and optimize/generate prompts maximizing the KL divergence between their output distributions; then test whether (a) such inputs are reachable at scale, and (b) the real model's behavior on them matches the ground-truth circuit rather than the rewrite, quantifying discrimination accuracy against on-distribution faithfulness (which should be indistinguishable between candidates). Success criterion: significantly better-than-chance adjudication, and a measured "discrimination budget" (number/diversity of inputs needed per bit of hypothesis selection). If this works, replicate the CLT-vs-per-layer-transcoder disagreement (the ICML 2026 depth-rewriting finding) on a real open model's attribution graphs.
why: It attacks the field's own #1-ranked bottleneck — the verification/faithfulness gap, which the 2026 state-of-the-field review puts above all other open problems and which Geng et al. explicitly call for rethinking — and it is the first *positive adjudication method* in a literature that currently only diagnoses the problem: non-identifiability was proven in toys (Méloux et al. 2025), faithfulness metrics were shown non-robust (Miller et al. 2024) and misranking (Geng et al. 2026), and transcoders were shown incentivized toward unfaithful depth-rewrites (ICML 2026), but no method exists that decides *which* of several behavior-matching decompositions is the real mechanism. The key technical move is genuinely unexploited: transcoder/CLT graphs are runnable surrogate models, so rival hypotheses can be differentially tested by adversarially searching for inputs where they disagree — a "crucial experiment" generator, which the multi-org roadmap explicitly requests under "automate intervention experiments and synthetic/OOD inputs for hypothesis validation" but which nobody has built. The nearest prior art falls short in different ways: mechanistic unit tests use hand-written negatives for claim *specificity*, not structural *adjudication*; causal scrubbing tests one hypothesis at a time under hypothesis-preserving ablations rather than seeking discriminating inputs; MIB evaluates on fixed task distributions; InterpBench supplies ground truth but no discriminating protocol; and the FlyHack-style stress-testing is domain-scoped claim-auditing in a connectome model, not input-search adjudication in LMs. The payoff is direct and safety-relevant: every deployment monitor and audit built on features or circuits currently inherits whatever decomposition the discovery method happened to emit, and an adjudication primitive plus a MIB-style OOD track would make "validated circuit" a measurable claim instead of an aesthetic one.

direction: I will build an automated input-design and discrimination procedure that decides between competing circuit hypotheses by their held-out behavioral predictions, validated on known-answer cases and deployed on live attribution-graph disagreements.
project: Circuit Tribunal: Discriminative Validation of Competing Circuit Hypotheses via Designed Test Inputs
question: When two mechanistic accounts of the same behavior both fit the discovery distribution, can automated design of held-out and separator inputs — the inputs where the accounts' predictions maximally diverge — reliably identify which account the model actually implements, and does the winner also better predict intervention outcomes?
first_experiment: Planted-river known-answer test on GPT-2 small (IOI + greater-than): reconstruct published circuits, build plausible mis-specified rivals matched on the discovery distribution, generate natural-variation and optimized separator inputs maximizing inter-account KL, and verify the discriminator picks the true account with paired win-rates — then scale to the live CLT-vs-neuron disagreement on greater-than and the two public Gemma-2-2B decompositions.
why: It is the field's top-ranked open problem (the dual basis / validation gap, per the Open Problems review and its 2026 retrospective), the phenomenon is proven real by three 2025–2026 papers and a live Goodfire disagreement, all adjacent work (adversarial falsification, unit tests, certified stability, e-process feature validation, MIB scoring, IIA on fixed datasets) stops short of comparative selection between accounts on real models, and the whole loop runs cheaply on public one-GPU artifacts — while its failure modes are themselves informative results.

direction: Rank competing mechanistic decompositions of the same model by their out-of-distribution interventional prediction error — treating each decomposition (attribution graph, circuit, dictionary) as a predictive model of the model's response to interventions — to turn faithfulness into a non-circular numerical target and resolve the dual basis problem pragmatically.
project: Interventional Out-of-Distribution Faithfulness (IODF): A Metric and Benchmark for Ranking Competiting Mechanistic Decompositions by Held-Out Intervention Prediction
question: Do mechanistic decompositions that are indistinguishable under current in-distribution faithfulness criteria (behavior replication, ablation KL, IIA, label readability) become separable — and correctly rankable — by their ability to predict the model's response to interventions on held-out inputs, held-out intervention magnitudes, and held-out intervention families (ablation → rescaling → steering → interchange)? And does this metric preferentially reject known unfaithful decomposition modes (e.g., shallow rewrites of deep multi-hop circuits, seed-unstable graphs)?
first_experiment: On GPT-2 small / Indirect Object Identification with public residual-stream SAEs, build four competing decompositions of the same behavior — (a) the standard fixed-support SAE attribution graph, (b) the same graph from a second SAE seed and architecture, (c) a neuron-basis baseline, and (d) a deliberately constructed "shallow rewrite" graph (direct input→output shortcut edges fit to reproduce in-distribution behavior, mimicking the CLT unfaithfulness mode) — then measure each graph's prediction error on the model's output change under (i) held-out single-feature ablations, (ii) magnitude-sweep and multi-feature ablations, and (iii) intervention-type shift (rescaling, steering, interchange patching) and input-distribution shift (novel templates, distractors), comparing the resulting rankings against current in-distribution faithfulness metrics and against the known IOI circuit as a platinum reference; ~2 GPU-days, with CIF-style anytime-valid intervals on the reported separations.
why: It attacks the field's self-identified top bottleneck — verification infrastructure, whose gap has widened while labeling got automated — and the dual basis problem, the most important unresolved methodological question of 2026 per the field's own retrospective. It has not been done because the necessary pieces only matured in the last 18 months (multi-layer public dictionaries, transcoders, causal-statistics tooling, the Méloux non-identifiability result, and documented unfaithfulness modes), and because every nearby line of work stopped short: e-process validation works feature-by-feature, CIF wraps existing estimands without proposing one, margin graphs fix linearization at clean inputs rather than testing generalization, SAEBench/InterpBench score reconstruction or synthetic-model discovery rather than real-model decomposition ranking, and the causal-abstraction/transportability theory has never been operationalized as a scalable ranking metric. It is foundational and bidirectionally valuable: if OOD interventional prediction separates decompositions, the field gains its "top-1 accuracy" — a principled selection criterion that upgrades SAE research, circuit auditing, and deployment-grade safety monitors; if it does not, that negative result caps what interpretability-derived monitors can be trusted to guarantee under distribution shift, which is itself a first-class safety finding. And it is tractable now on small open models with public dictionaries, with a clear scaling path toward the frontier models where verification matters most.

direction: Make mechanistic explanation selection falsifiable by actively designing inputs that separate rival circuit/attribution-graph explanations, so that "the circuit" is whichever hypothesis survives adversarial discriminating tests rather than whichever looks prettiest.
project: DISCRIMINATE — Adversarial Differential Testing of Rival Mechanistic Explanations
question: When multiple mechanistic explanations (circuits, attribution graphs, transcoder replacement models) reproduce a model's behavior equally well on the observed distribution, can an automated protocol that (i) computes the input regions where rival explanations' predictions diverge, (ii) actively searches/optimizes for high-divergence inputs (compositional, OOD, and error-prone regions), and (iii) adjudicates against the true model, reliably identify the faithful explanation — and can this be distilled into a quantitative "discrimination score" that ranks decompositions non-aesthetically and predicts their OOD failure modes?
first_experiment: In a ground-truth sandbox (a grokked modular-addition transformer and/or InterpBench semi-synthetic models with known algorithms), construct rival explanation pairs — the known-faithful circuit vs. a deliberately "shortcut" rival built via the CLT feature-skipping recipe (deep multi-hop rewritten as shallow input→output edges), plus capacity-matched random and shuffled-edge controls. First show that standard on-distribution metrics (circuit error, exact-match agreement on successes, IIA) cannot separate the rivals. Then implement the minimal discriminative loop: enumerate candidate inputs (combinatorial template search plus, later, an LLM agent), forward both replacement models to find maximal-prediction-divergence inputs, and test top-K inputs against the real model. Success criterion: the true model's outputs side with the faithful explanation on the searched discriminating set (e.g., ≥90% agreement) while the shortcut rival collapses, quantified as a "discrimination gap" that is ~0 for hand-crafted fixed test sets. Second step: apply the same protocol to three real rival explanations of one behavior (e.g., IOI via ACDC, per-layer transcoder attribution graphs, and CLT attribution graphs on GPT-2/Gemma with Gemma Scope).
why: It attacks the field's two self-declared top gaps — the verification bottleneck ("faithfulness as a numerical target") and the dual-basis problem — named by both the 2025 Open Problems coalition and the 2026 retrospective, and verification is the prerequisite for every safety application (deception audits, CoT-trust, model editing) that currently rests on unvalidated explanations. It has not been done: identifiability work only proves the problem; error-agreement and unit-test protocols are static or hand-crafted and evaluate one explanation at a time; agentic explainers lack any principled rival-discrimination objective and report validation as their key obstacle; auditing benchmarks test auditor performance, not explanation adjudication. It is newly tractable because ground-truth model organisms (InterpBench, grokked models), CLT infrastructure, and public transcoders only became available in the last 18 months — and the recent CLT-unfaithfulness result doubles as a constructive generator of realistic unfaithful rivals, turning a discovered weakness of the dominant method into the test bed for its fix. The first experiment is cheap (toy models, one GPU, TransformerLens) yet decisive, and the deliverable — a protocol, a metric, and a rival-explanation benchmark — is infrastructure the whole field would use, in the same way perplexity standardized language modeling.

direction: Build a quantitative framework for the decomposition-underdetermination ("dual basis") problem — showing that feature decompositions of the same model that are behaviorally equivalent in-distribution diverge under distribution shift, and deriving a label-free out-of-distribution fidelity metric that selects the decompositions whose circuit claims and safety monitors actually survive the shift.
project: Equivalence Is Not Identity: Stress-Testing Feature Decompositions of Language Models Under Distribution Shift
question: When multiple feature decompositions of the same model (SAE seeds/widths/training distributions, transcoders, neuron bases) are behaviorally equivalent on in-distribution prompts, how much do they diverge in out-of-distribution replacement fidelity and in the causal claims (feature interventions, monitor verdicts) they license — and does a label-free shifted-fidelity metric predict which decomposition's interventions and monitors survive the shift?
first_experiment: On GPT-2 small (greater-than and IOI tasks) using pretrained CLTs from the circuit-tracer ecosystem plus multiple SAELens dictionaries and the raw neuron basis: (1) verify in-distribution behavioral equivalence by computing each decomposition's replacement score/KL on the standard task prompt families; (2) compute the same fidelity on uit-de-Bos-style shifted/adversarial inputs (paraphrased templates, romantic objects for IOI, injected cue tokens à la Ma et al. 2026) to quantify pairwise divergence between decompositions that agree in-distribution; (3) for the same claimed mechanism (e.g., the greater-than suppression/boost mechanism vs. the parity-heuristic mechanism Goodfire reported), ablate/steer the corresponding features under each decomposition and compare behavioral effects on shifted inputs — establishing whether in-distribution-equivalent decompositions license conflicting causal interventions, before scaling the ensemble and building the ranking metric.
why: It attacks the problem the field itself ranks first but hasn't occupied: the 2026 state-of-the-field review calls decomposition choice an "aesthetic decision" and faithfulness verification the top gap; the only adversarial circuit evaluation predates feature-level attribution graphs and covers three hand-derived head-level circuits; the CLT-unfaithfulness work is a single toy-model mode with preliminary real-model evidence; and the feature-consistency literature measures seed agreement, not behavioral equivalence classes or OOD-conditional causal validity. Meanwhile every 2026 safety application (production feature monitors, auditing tools that "mid-pack" in AuditBench, cross-model transfer failures) silently depends on the answer — so the result is load-bearing whether it comes out negative (false assurance demonstrated) or positive (current practice vindicated), and it is tractable now on public small models without frontier compute.

direction: Solve the dual-basis problem for attribution graphs by treating each candidate circuit hypothesis as a cheap surrogate algorithm, automatically searching for inputs where candidate graphs' predictions diverge, and adjudicating faithfulness by testing the real model on those inputs.
project: Discriminating Circuits — Active Counterfactual Stress-Testing of Attribution Graphs
question: When two attribution graphs (extracted under different legitimate choices — pruning threshold, transcoder architecture, extraction-distribution) explain the same behavior equally well on the extraction prompt, which — if either — is faithful to the model's actual algorithm, and can this be decided automatically by finding inputs on which their surrogate predictions diverge and checking the model's actual behavior there?
first_experiment: On the greater-than task in GPT-2 (or two-hop facts in Gemma-2-2B) using open CLTs/PLTs via Circuit Tracer, extract K attribution graphs for the same prompt under different standard extraction settings; (1) confirm they are statistically indistinguishable on-distribution (matching replacement scores and behavior) — instantiating the dual-basis problem on real graphs; (2) for each graph, compute its implied surrogate next-token predictions on a battery of off-distribution inputs (century-boundary years, carries, alternate formats), then use surrogate gradients to search for maximally-diverging inputs within natural-language perturbation families; (3) run the real model on those inputs and measure which graphs' predictions track it. Success = graphs indistinguishable on-distribution become reliably separable off-distribution, with a consistent winner; failure = an important quantification of how far execution traces are from algorithms.
why: It attacks the problem that an independent 2026 state-of-field review ranks #1 (faithfulness/dual-basis) and that the attribution-graph builders themselves list as an open direction ("automating intervention experiments and synthetic/OOD inputs for hypothesis validation") — so it is the binding constraint on every downstream safety use (monitors, audits, steering) that inherits unvalidated graphs, and it converts ~7,000 existing unvalidated graphs from liabilities into testable hypotheses. It is genuinely not done: everything published through late 2026 is diagnosis (non-identifiability, metric non-robustness, equivalence-class sampling, extraction-choice dependence) or on-distribution single-hypothesis testing (causal scrubbing, MIB, Certified Circuits, replacement scores) — none uses the surrogate-as-simulator to *design discriminating inputs*, which is the key inversion that makes validation cheap and principled rather than aesthetic. It is newly tractable only because open CLTs/PLTs, Gemma Scope, and Circuit Tracer matured in 2025–2026, and it is executable at individual-lab scale on GPT-2/Gemma-2-2B.

direction: Develop a distribution-shift-based diagnostic that separates genuine mechanism change from decomposition-method artifacts in feature-level circuit explanations, and test whether it predicts the out-of-distribution failure of interpretability-derived safety monitors.
project: Phantom or Reorganization? A Distribution-Shift Diagnostic for the External Validity of Feature-Level Circuits
question: When a feature-level attribution graph or circuit discovered on distribution D disagrees with the one discovered on distribution D′, can behavioral-change-conditioned intervention transfer plus cross-method triangulation determine whether this reflects a genuine change in the model's computation or an artifact of the decomposition method — and does that classification predict when interpretability-derived monitors fail out-of-distribution?
first_experiment: Extract attribution graphs with the open-source circuit-tracer on Gemma-2-2B (public transcoders) for ~30 refusal-inducing prompts under a four-rung shift ladder (vanilla English → paraphrase → French translation → domain-shifted harmful requests); match features across the graphs and compute (a) structural agreement (matched-feature edge overlap), (b) functional agreement (does ablating the D0 refusal circuit's top features still suppress refusal on Di prompts?), and (c) behavioral change (refusal rate Di vs D0) — then classify each disagreement into robust core (stable structure + transferred interventions), phantom specialization (structure differs, function transfers), genuine mechanism reorganization (structure differs, interventions fail, behavior changes), or incomplete extraction (structure stable, interventions fail), cross-validating the "genuine" labels with an independent decomposition method (head-level EAP-IG / attention-feature SAEs).
why: It attacks the field's own top-ranked open problem — the dual-basis/faithfulness gap, where choosing between decompositions is currently "an aesthetic decision" — at the moment the 2026 variance literature (CIRCUS, Certified Circuits, Many Circuits One Mechanism, Demystifying Variance) has established that the phenomenon is real and widespread but none of them offers a principled separating diagnostic, and none works at the feature level on realistic shifts or models. It has not been done because the stability papers treat instability as noise to abstain from rather than evidence to interpret, the phantom-specialization result is confined to head-level toy tasks with token-frequency shifts only, and the safety community measures OOD monitor failure behaviorally without connecting it to decomposition instability. The direction is maximally timely (attribution graphs are now the dominant artifact and their trustworthiness is the field's stated worry), safety-critical (it would give the first mechanistic explanation and leading indicator for the documented OOD failure of feature-based monitors, and test whether stable refusal *behavior* masks shift-dependent refusal *mechanisms* — a failure mode single-direction monitors cannot see), and feasible for a single researcher with a free-GPU-scale setup and public artifacts, with a publishable result whatever the outcome: either a reassuring external-validity extension of the dominant artifact or a demonstration that published circuits are distributionally contingent in ways that explain real monitor failures.

direction: Build an operational identifiability program for mechanistic explanations — replace on-distribution faithfulness (which provably cannot discriminate between competing mechanisms) with out-of-distribution predictive validity as a ground-truth-validated selection criterion for circuit-level explanations, starting with model organisms that contain deliberately confounded, dissociable mechanisms.
project: Dissociate: Out-of-Distribution Predictive Validity as a Test of Whether an Attribution Graph Is the Mechanism (or Just One Consistent Story)
question: When multiple circuit-level explanations of a model's behavior are equally faithful on the task distribution, does their ability to predict the model's behavior on systematic distribution shifts and mechanistically-implied interventions reliably identify the actually-implemented mechanism — and how often do standard pipelines (EAP-IG, ACDC, attribution graphs) produce explanations that pass on-distribution faithfulness but fail this test?
first_experiment: Train a population of small "twin organisms" (2–4 layer transformers, Li et al. scale) on tasks where a planted mechanism M1 and a shortcut M2 are behaviorally confounded in-distribution — e.g., modular arithmetic where a Fourier-style algorithm and a frequency-restricted lookup algorithm agree on the training operand distribution — with known, divergent predictions on held-out operand combinations and counterfactual interventions. Run standard circuit discovery (EAP-IG, ACDC, and transcoder-based attribution graphs) on each model; for every recovered hypothesis measure (a) standard on-distribution faithfulness and (b) OOD-predictive validity against the planted ground truth. The decisive outcome: on-distribution faithfulness is statistically indistinguishable between true and confound hypotheses (empirically demonstrating the dual-basis failure in a real pipeline, beyond Boolean toys) while OOD-predictive validity separates them.
why: It attacks the gap that both the field's canonical open-problems document and its 2026 retrospective rank first (verification/faithfulness; the "dual basis problem"), yet it is unoccupied rather than merely young: Méloux et al. established non-identifiability but stopped at discussion of the predictive stance; Li et al. opened OOD prediction only as a whole-model observational proof-of-concept, never for circuit-level artifacts or explanation selection; statistical validation is per-feature and on-distribution; formal verification gives only continuous-perturbation guarantees for vision classifiers; and model-organism work (e.g., "How to train your model organism," Oct 2026) builds testbeds for recovering *behaviors*, not for adjudicating between *mechanistically competing explanations*. It is feasible on one GPU with open tooling (TransformerLens, EAP-IG, circuit-tracer on Gemma-2-2B/Llama-3.2-1B), it produces publishable results either way (a positive result gives the field its first validated faithfulness metric — the "top-1 accuracy" of interpretability the field says it lacks; a negative result is an urgent safety-relevant warning that deployed attribution-graph-based audits and monitors rest on underdetermined stories), and success directly unblocks the downstream problems I rejected as premature: cross-model transfer, deployment-grade monitors, and auditing of deception and backdoors, all of which require knowing that an explanation is the mechanism rather than merely consistent with it.

direction: Causally dissect the evaluation-awareness pathway in open-weight LLMs — from internal "being tested" representations to behavioral changes — and convert it into a causally validated monitor and deployment-restoring intervention.
project: From Representation to Reaction: A Causal Circuit Account of Evaluation Awareness in Language Models
question: Is the linearly decodable "I am being evaluated" representation causally upstream of eval-conditioned behavior changes (verbalized and unverbalized), which components compute and read it, and can interventions on this pathway both detect unverbalized evaluation-conditioned cognition and restore deployment-like behavior under evaluation?
first_experiment: Subspace-restricted interchange patching between ~300 paired evaluation/deployment prompt pairs in OLMo3-7B and Qwen3-8B, swapping activations restricted to the probe's low-rank subspace across layers and measuring behavioral flips against rank-matched and shuffled-pair controls, yielding a layer-resolved causal-effect curve.
why: Evaluation awareness is breaking every eval-based safety pipeline now (METR/Apollo flagged it as their top concern; Mythos showed unverbalized awareness), the field's white-box toolkit for it is entirely correlational or verbalization-focused, and the specific causal link — representation → behavior — has never been tested or localized, despite all needed ingredients (open weights, released code, paired-prompt data, mature attribution tooling) being in place; the existing systematic study (Heidari et al. 2026) explicitly stopped at representation, verbalization, and steering of what models say, the sandbagging-circuit work covers only deliberately-installed downstream intent axes, and concept-targeted attribution graphs have never been aimed at a safety-critical context representation or at behavior change rather than next-token logits.

direction: Build an automated discriminating-input search protocol that adjudicates between behaviorally-equivalent competing mechanistic explanations by finding where their interventional predictions diverge and letting the model's actual behavior arbitrate, yielding a non-circular faithfulness metric.
project: Adjudicator: Active Discrimination of Competing Mechanistic Explanations
question: Can automated search over inputs and interventions find distributions that separate candidate explanations that agree in-distribution, and does model behavior there reorder faithfulness rankings and predict which explanations survive distribution shift?
first_experiment: On GPT-2 small IOI, pit the manual circuit against an ACDC circuit (both near-identical on standard faithfulness) as behavioral predictors, optimize a benign input-variant family to maximize their predicted-behavior divergence, then check which candidate's predictions track the real model on the discovered discriminating inputs.
why: Verification — not labeling — is the field's diagnosed #1 bottleneck in 2026; four 2025–2026 papers plus Anthropic's own open-problems list demonstrate or demand exactly this adjudication capability and none builds it; it is cheap to start, non-circular by construction, fails informatively, and directly enables distribution-robust safety monitors.

direction: Treat competing mechanistic explanations as predictive causal models and adjudicate them by held-out counterfactual agreement on distribution-shifted inputs, replacing aesthetic choice among decompositions with a principled selection criterion.
project: Explanation Test Sets: Held-Out Counterfactual Adjudication of Mechanistic Explanations
question: Can held-out counterfactual agreement — the match between an explanation's predicted intervention effects and the full model's behavior on novel inputs never used for discovery — serve as a principled, quantitative criterion for selecting among circuit explanations that are indistinguishable on the eliciting distribution?
first_experiment: On the Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct multi-hop city→state→capital task, build the same behavior's explanation in three bases (CLT attribution graph via circuit-tracer, RelP neuron-basis circuit via the Transluce pipeline, SAE-feature circuit) and measure each one's counterfactual agreement on eliciting prompts versus held-out novel-entity and recomposed-chain variants where shallow-rewrite and deep-path hypotheses diverge, scoring with anytime-valid confidence sequences to compute each basis's generalization gap.
why: The 2026 state-of-the-field retrospective names the dual basis problem the field's top open problem, and the diagnosis literature (non-identifiability, explanation multiplicity, metric sensitivity, CLT unfaithfulness) is complete while the constructive selection criterion it calls for has not been built — the nearest works (MIB, Certified Circuits, CIF, error-reproduction evaluation, the Transluce basis comparison) each address a different fragment, all required artifacts are public, and either experimental outcome (bases separate, or all explanations fail OOD) produces a load-bearing result for safety-critical interpretability claims.

direction: Measure whether attribution-graph circuits discovered on one prompt distribution predict intervention outcomes on held-out and shifted inputs, and use this out-of-sample predictive faithfulness as the first principled, non-aesthetic criterion for ranking the field's competing decomposition bases (CLT vs per-layer SAE vs neuron basis).
project: Held-Out Faithfulness — Out-of-Sample Intervention Prediction as a Ranking Criterion for Attribution Graphs
question: Do attribution graphs built over transcoder/SAE features on a training distribution of prompts generalize as predictors of model behavior under ablations and swaps on unseen entities, paraphrases, distractors, and template shifts — and which decomposition basis (cross-layer transcoders, per-layer SAEs, MLP-neuron basis) retains the most out-of-sample predictive faithfulness?
first_experiment: Using Gemma-2-2B with the public CLT dictionary (circuit-tracer) and the Birardi & Paulo two-hop factual-recall harness, build pruned attribution graphs on ~20 seed prompts; extract each graph's predicted Δlogit/Δbehavior for supernode ablations and entity swaps; run the actual interventions on (i) in-distribution held-out entities, (ii) paraphrased templates, (iii) distractor-augmented prompts, (iv) template-shifted variants; report the in-distribution vs. out-of-distribution predictive correlation, with influence-matched random feature sets as controls. Then repeat the identical protocol with Gemma Scope per-layer SAEs and the RelP neuron-basis pipeline to produce the first cross-basis OOD faithfulness ranking.
why: It attacks the field's most foundational self-identified weakness — the faithfulness/verification gap and the dual basis problem — at the level of its dominant artifact, in exactly the way its leaders have called for ("automate intervention experiments and synthetic/OOD inputs for hypothesis validation"), and it operationalizes the pragmatic standard (predictive/manipulability power) that the identifiability literature (Méloux et al. ICLR 2025; Dead Salmons) says the field must adopt. It is not already done: the closest works each stop short of it — MIB evaluates localization on fixed tasks, not graph-level OOD prediction; Certified Circuits certifies discovery stability under dataset edits, not intervention-predictive validity; Li (2026) measures seed fragility only in-distribution on Pythia-160m; Birardi & Paulo validate labels only on seed prompts; Duan (2026) predicts per-feature steering side effects, not graph structure; Arora et al. compare bases only in-distribution. It is feasible with inference-only compute on open weights and public dictionaries, fully automatable by an agent, safety-relevant (feature-based monitors must survive distribution shift), and valuable either way: OOD collapse would be a headline cautionary result constraining how much feature-level monitors can be trusted, while OOD robustness would give the field its first cheap, non-circular validation lever and a principled basis-ranking metric.

direction: Build an active "discriminator search" method for mechanistic explanations — treat attribution graphs / transcoder circuits as competing hypotheses that make counterfactual predictions, automatically search compositional inputs and internal interchange interventions for experiments that separate behaviorally-equivalent explanations, and use the discriminators to rank, refute, repair, or certify their domains of validity.
project: Breaking the Tie: Adversarial Discrimination of Behaviorally Equivalent Circuit Explanations
question: When two circuit explanations of a model behavior are indistinguishable on the training distribution (the dual-basis ambiguity), can an automated search over compositional inputs and internal interchange interventions find a small set of discriminating experiments that separates them — and can those discriminators be used to rank competing decompositions, repair unfaithful ones (e.g., restore multi-hop edges removed by sparsity pressure), and output certified domains of validity?
first_experiment: In a Boolean toy model with known ground truth (following the ICML 2026 shallow-rewrite setup), train a small transformer on a deep multi-hop task, train transcoders/CLTs with standard sparsity penalties to reproduce the unfaithful shallow rewrite, verify that ground-truth-shaped and shallow explanations tie on on-distribution fidelity and interchange-intervention accuracy, then implement the discriminator search — optimize over compositional input generation and node-level interchange interventions to maximize prediction divergence between the two explanations — and measure (a) whether it separates the tied explanations, (b) how many experiments it needs, and (c) whether found discriminators generalize to held-out related inputs.
why: It attacks the problem the field itself ranks first: the 2026 state-of-the-field review names the dual-basis problem and faithfulness scoring as the top open methodological questions, and notes that verification has fallen catastrophically behind labeling. The diagnoses are all recent (Méloux's non-identifiability proof at ICLR 2025; the CLT shallow-rewrite result at ICML 2026), which means the problem is live and unsolved — but every existing response is either passive (CIF's statistics on a declared estimand, Bucketing's region mapping, IIA on fixed distributions) or at the wrong level (CHIVE does prompt-level behavioral counterfactuals and explicitly excludes internal computation; ISS does active separating interventions but for abstract causal models on perceptual edits, not MI's attribution-graph artifacts, with no repair loop). Nobody has operationalized "which decomposition is the circuit?" as an empirical question with an active experiment search. It is upstream of everything else: attribution graphs are now the standard artifact and interpretability-derived safety monitors will fail exactly on the distribution shift that unfaithful explanations can't anticipate — CHIVE's finding that interpretability tools give zero counterfactual-prediction uplift is the evidence that this gap is real and damaging. And it has not been done because the field's energy went into scaling explanation *generation* (labels, graphs, automation), not into building the discriminating infrastructure that generation now desperately needs.

direction: Make faithfulness a measurable competition rather than an aesthetic judgment — rank rival mechanistic explanations (circuits, SAE dictionaries, attribution graphs) of the same behavior by their statistically certified predictive power on interventions over held-out, disagreement-maximizing inputs.
project: Explanation Trials: Adversarial, Anytime-Valid Discrimination of Rival Mechanistic Explanations by Held-Out Interventional Prediction
question: When two or more mechanistic explanations of the same model behavior fit equally well on the distribution they were derived from, can their counterfactual commitments — predicted behavior under a shared menu of interventions on novel inputs, actively selected to maximize disagreement between the rivals — be used to select the more faithful explanation with statistical validity and without circularity, and how much residual underdetermination remains after the discriminating-test space is exhausted?
first_experiment: On an InterpBench semi-synthetic transformer with a known ground-truth IOI circuit, plant decoy rivals — alternative subgraphs/decompositions engineered to match the true circuit's behavior on the training distribution but with different internal structure — then run the discrimination protocol: compute each rival's predicted outputs under a shared intervention menu (edge/feature ablations, activation patches) over a held-out input pool, auto-select the K input–intervention pairs with maximal inter-rival predicted divergence, execute them on the model, and score each rival with CIF-style anytime-valid confidence sequences over its counterfactual log-loss. Success criterion: the ground-truth circuit is significantly separated from every decoy at a controlled false-alive rate; persistent ties are themselves the result — a precise map of where the equivalence classes lie — and tell us how to enrich the test space before scaling to real-model rivals (GPT-2/Gemma-2-2B IOI and Greater-than: ACDC vs EAP-IG vs hand-built vs cross-seed SAE circuits), then to attribution-graph rivals via CLT-Forge, and finally to downstream value: whether the tournament winner yields more robust steering and monitoring under distribution shift.
why: It is the field's own top-ranked self-diagnosed gap — the generalized dual-basis problem elevated to first place by the 2026 state-of-the-field review, with the labels-vs-verification asymmetry explicitly flagged as having *widened* since 2024 — and it is the natural empirical complement to three 2025–2026 results that jointly changed the rules: explanations are provably non-unique (Méloux et al.), non-uniqueness is structural rather than algorithmic (Koopman spectral identifiability), and rival decompositions of real models now exist at scale (seed-dependence studies). Everyone proved or documented the problem; nobody has operationalized the "pragmatic selection criterion" those papers call for. It has not been done because the pieces only matured recently — ground-truth models (InterpBench), released rival pools, an anytime-valid statistical layer (CIF), and automated attribution-graph tooling all date from 2024–2026 — because field momentum went into building better decomposers and cheaper labeling rather than verification, and because the closest existing efforts each stop short by design: CIF certifies single claims over declared distributions rather than ranking rival explanations, feature-validation work is feature-level not decomposition-level, Certified Circuits guarantees discovery stability rather than explanation validity, and MIB compares methods on fixed tasks rather than actively synthesizing discriminating tests. The payoff compounds: every downstream use of interpretability — safety monitors, audits, steering, model editing, cross-architecture transfer — currently inherits an arbitrary, unverified choice among decompositions, and this gives them a principled, cheap, reusable way to make it.

direction: Replace aesthetic and in-distribution validation of attribution graphs with held-out mechanistic validation — treat every traced circuit as a falsifiable hypothesis whose ablation/steering predictions must generalize to held-out prompts, and use out-of-sample mechanistic accuracy as the field's standard, non-circular metric for faithfulness and for selecting among behaviorally-equivalent decompositions.
project: Circuits Must Predict: Held-Out Mechanistic Validation for Attribution Graphs
question: Do attribution-graph circuit hypotheses generated on a discovery distribution predict model behavior under intervention on held-out prompt families (novel templates, novel entities, deeper compositional chains, distractors) — and when two decompositions are behaviorally equivalent in-distribution, does held-out mechanistic accuracy discriminate the true mechanism from shallow-rewrite artifacts?
first_experiment: Using the open-source circuit-tracer library with pretrained CLTs for Llama-3.2-1B (then Gemma-2-2B), trace attribution graphs for synthetic 2-hop factual-recall prompts (50 discovery prompts, 2 templates); then measure (a) replacement score and (b) the causal effect of ablating the graph's top nodes/edges on 10× held-out prompt families — paraphrased templates, unseen entity chains, and 3-hop chains — quantifying the "mechanistic generalization gap" (in-distribution vs. held-out intervention-prediction accuracy), and specifically testing whether graphs traced in-distribution behave like shallow rewrites that fail to predict the deep pathway exactly on held-out 3-hop inputs.
why: It is the field's own top-diagnosed open problem (the 2026 retrospective's "dual basis problem," Circuit Oracle's admitted evaluation gap, and the Neuronpedia landscape's call to "automate intervention experiments and out-of-distribution inputs for hypothesis validation"), and it is upstream of everything downstream — safety monitors, audits, and cross-model transfer all inherit whatever validity the graphs have. It has not been done because the validation infrastructure never kept pace with automated labeling (the "verification asymmetry"), because existing benchmarks and adversarial evaluations (MIB, Certified Circuits, Adversarial Circuit Evaluation) all operate at the component level with pre-2025 methods rather than on feature-level attribution graphs, because the field's automation energy went into reading graphs (ADAG, probe prompting, Circuit Oracle) rather than testing them, and because the toy-model proof that CLTs learn unfaithful shallow rewrites is only months old — quantifying and discriminating that failure mode on real models with held-out tests is the obvious, high-leverage next step that no one has yet taken.

direction: Merge per-prompt attribution graphs into predictively-validated global circuit templates to convert mechanistic interpretability from local anecdotes into cumulative, testable knowledge.
project: Graphs to Atlas: Predictively-Validated Global Circuit Templates from Attribution Graphs
question: Can per-prompt attribution graphs for a task family be merged into a few task-level circuit templates that predict which features and edges carry behavior on held-out prompts (without re-tracing), recover known hand-analyzed circuits where ground truth exists, and whose per-prompt deviation reliably flags anomalous computation?
first_experiment: Trace ~50 IOI prompts in GPT-2-small with circuit-tracer cross-layer transcoders, cluster the graphs over the shared feature space, extract a position-relative weighted edge core as the template, and test whether it achieves ≥90% of per-prompt graph replacement score on 100 held-out IOI prompts while matching the Wang et al. reference motif and its known failure cases — a decisive either/or result at single-GPU cost.
why: It addresses the biggest structural limitation of attribution graphs — their locality, which caps both validation (no held-out test possible) and deployment (no reusable reference for monitoring) — and was explicitly flagged as open by the circuit-tracing creators in August 2025; it has not been done: the closest works (ACC++ per-prompt circuit clustering, "Many Circuits, One Mechanism," non-identifiability and faithfulness critiques) characterize or critique the problem without constructing validated global templates, the safety-specific CAP paper covers only a slice of the adjacent suppression problem, and the sole paper claiming hierarchical global extraction is not credible — while the 2026 critique literature supplies exactly the evaluation protocol (edge-level metrics, cross-condition transfer, context-preserving interventions) that makes a constructive attempt finally defensible, on fully open tooling and one GPU.

direction: Build a planted-ground-truth testbed that quantitatively measures whether the modern transcoder-based attribution-graph pipeline recovers known mechanisms in language models, and use mechanism-level out-of-distribution interventions to adjudicate between competing decompositions — turning interpretability faithfulness from an aesthetic judgment into a measurable, non-circular score.
project: TraceProof — Ground-Truth-Planted Evaluation and Dual-Decomposition Adjudication for Attribution-Graph Circuit Tracing
question: When a language model's behavior is produced by a mechanism known by construction, does the attribution-graph pipeline recover that mechanism (rather than an observationally equivalent decomposition), and can held-out intervention agreement — measured on inputs where the planted mechanism makes divergent predictions — serve as a non-circular criterion for selecting among multiple decompositions that all pass standard in-distribution faithfulness checks?
first_experiment: Take one small model with exact ground truth — a SIIT/InterpBench transformer (and, in parallel, GPT-2 small on greater-than, where the Hanna et al. circuit is the reference, replicating Goodfire's setup) — train cross-layer transcoders with Anthropic's open-source circuit-tracer, generate pruned attribution graphs for eval prompts, and score recovery at three levels: (1) abstraction-level interchange-intervention accuracy, i.e., whether graph nodes patched per the planted high-level causal model reproduce its I/O behavior (IIA); (2) structural precision/recall of recovered edges against the planted circuit where expressible; (3) standard in-distribution replacement score and held-out answer agreement for comparison. This is cheap (single-model, GPT-2 scale), uses only existing public artifacts, and every outcome is informative: high recovery validates the metric machinery and gives the field its first baseline; low recovery localizes exactly where the pipeline's verification gap bites (error nodes, pruning, superposition), which sets up the follow-up dual-decomposition experiment with independently-seeded CLTs and compositional-OOD planted mechanisms (e.g., SDF-planted two-hop fact chains with novel transitive queries).
why: It attacks the problem that both the field's own 2026 retrospective (attribution-graph faithfulness + dual basis problem, called "the open problem I would put at the top of any new survey") and its empirical alarm bells (Geng et al.'s misranking, Méloux et al.'s non-identifiability) identify as the central methodological gap, while also answering the multi-org landscape's explicit call for objectively verifiable understanding benchmarks. It has not been done: InterpBench predates the transcoder pipeline and evaluates only component-level discovery (ACDC/EAP/SP); Geng et al. evaluate only component-level circuits against hand-found references, not planted mechanisms; Goodfire's CLT-vs-known-mechanism work is a single qualitative case study with no recovery metric, no planted mechanisms trained on natural data, and no test of whether competing decompositions can be discriminated; AuditBench plants behaviors, not mechanisms, and measures behavioral auditing rather than mechanistic recovery; and all 2025–2026 attribution-graph papers (ADAG, Circuit Oracle, hierarchical graph decomposition, DifFRACT) automate generation or interpretation, not verification. The direction is feasible for me now (small open models, public circuit-tracer and InterpBench code), tolerates negative results as findings, and compounds: a verified, ground-truth-calibrated evaluation layer is the prerequisite infrastructure for trusting any interpretability-derived safety claim — monitors, audits, and CoT-faithfulness tools alike.

direction: Hold-out distribution shift should become mechanistic interpretability's standard validation axis — measuring and then explaining how circuits, features, and attribution graphs degrade across shift families, and using that divergence to select among competing decompositions of the same behavior.
project: Circuits That Survive the Shift: held-out distributional shift as a validation standard for mechanistic explanations
question: When a mechanistic explanation (circuit/feature set/attribution graph) validated in-distribution is tested under realistic distribution shifts (paraphrase, entity/domain, format, compositional, adversarial shifts), how much interventional fidelity and steering efficacy does it lose, which components are shift-robust versus shift-fragile, and does cross-shift divergence empirically discriminate between competing decompositions that are equally faithful in-distribution?
first_experiment: On GPT-2-small and Gemma-2-2B IOI (plus greater-than), build four competing explanations of the same behavior — the manual Wang et al. edge circuit, an EAP-IG automated edge circuit, a neuron-basis circuit (pre-activation MLP neurons with modern attribution à la Transluce), and an SAE-feature-basis circuit (Gemma Scope where applicable) — verify all pass standard in-distribution faithfulness thresholds, then run a benchmark of ~5 programmatically generated shift families (paraphrase templates, entity swaps, prompt-format/context shifts, distractor variants like DoubleIO, compositional embedding) measuring per-family faithfulness, error agreement, steering efficacy, and component-level survival rates for each basis.
why: It directly attacks the field's most severe, cross-cutting diagnosed problems — the verification asymmetry (explanations are generated far faster than they are verified), the dual-basis problem (no principled way to choose among decompositions that fit equally well), and the deployment gap (monitors and steering must survive the very distribution shifts that eval-awareness and monitor-evasion work shows models respond to) — while each nearby existing work stops short: Demystifying Variance documents template-dependent circuits but explicitly declines to construct a fix; Certified Circuits only certifies inclusion stability under dataset resampling/edit distance, not held-out shift families nor decomposition choice; the error-agreement paper tests held-out errors but stays in-distribution; Adaptive Circuit Behavior explores one task in one model in one basis; MIB evaluates same-distribution test splits; and the non-identifiability line is theory plus toy MLPs. Nobody has built a multi-shift, multi-basis, quantitative stress test of mechanistic explanations in real LLMs — and the experiment is tractable on open-weight models with existing tooling, yields publishable findings whichever way the results fall, and generalizes immediately to safety-critical use cases (do deception/refusal/eval-awareness monitors validated on one distribution still detect the behavior after shift?).

direction: Mechanistic interpretability's safety case is bottlenecked by audits that fail silently against hidden mechanisms, so the most promising next direction is the measurement science and defense of audit reliability — quantifying the detection power and coverage of white-box audits and building randomized, dictionary-free detectors that cover the low-dimensional subspace-hiding evasion vector demonstrated by Neural Chameleons and the auditing-game failures.
project: Covering the Blind Spot: Quantified Detection Power and Randomized Dictionary-Free Audits for Adversarially Hidden Mechanisms
question: When a white-box audit of a language model finds no hidden behavior, what is the probability that one exists anyway as a function of audit method, training methodology, and obfuscation — and can a randomized dictionary-free battery (behavioral divergence under random-direction ablations, plus SAE-dark-matter residual statistics) achieve quantified coverage, i.e., detection probability ≥ 1−ε against any hidden mechanism implemented as an activation manipulation of effective rank ≤ k?
first_experiment: On the released Neural Chameleon organism (Gemma-2-9b fine-tuned to zero-shot evade unseen monitors by moving activations into a low-dimensional subspace) with quirk-matched benign controls from the Model Organism Lottery suite, run at matched false-positive rate: (a) standard detectors — linear and MLP probes, probe ensembles, Gemma-Scope SAE monitors — and (b) a randomized battery of n random unit directions per layer with behavioral-divergence readouts under directional ablation plus dark-matter residual statistics, sweeping n to produce the first empirical detection-power/coverage curves and testing whether randomized coverage detects what probes and SAEs provably miss.
why: It targets the single most empirically validated open problem in the field — at least six independent 2025–26 results show white-box audits failing quietly (auditing games 1/5, ICML 2026 "none reliably surface backdoors," AuditBench's tool-to-agent gap, Neural Chameleons, Pando, SAE-intervention unreliability), and the Nov 2026 field survey names false confidence from unfaithful analysis its "most insidious risk" while leaving quantified coverage as an unimplemented "potential approach." It is not already done: existing benchmarks measure aggregate audit success or benchmark realism (AuditBench, Model Organism Lottery, Pando) but nobody reports per-method detection power at controlled FPR, coverage statements for negative audits, or dictionary-free randomized detectors against subspace-hiding — the closest precedent (ad hoc "fuzzing" in the sandbagging game) was abandoned as ambiguous rather than formalized, and the coverage mathematics exists only in the compressed-sensing/randomized-smoothing literature, which mech interp has never imported. It is newly tractable because every needed testbed with ground truth was released in the last twelve months, at 1B–70B scale with no frontier access required; and it is valuable in both directions — a working coverage-certified audit design directly strengthens deployment monitoring and agentic auditing, while a demonstrated power floor would, for the first time, put hard numbers on what "no deception circuit found" is worth, disciplining the field's safety claims and informing where interpretability investment should go next.
