direction: Make attribution graphs trustworthy by fixing the training objectives that make cross-layer transcoders collapse genuine multi-step computation into unfaithful shortcuts — the field's dominant artifact currently cannot distinguish real reasoning from lookup, and every proposed fix has been left untested.
project: Faithful-by-Construction Circuit Tracing: Eliminating Feature-Skipping in Cross-Layer Transcoders
question: Can cross-layer transcoder training objectives be modified (separated decoder-norm sparsity penalties, decoder-span limits, auxiliary intermediate-reconstruction losses) so that attribution graphs faithfully preserve multi-step circuits — distinguishing genuine cross-layer superposition from shortcut collapse — without sacrificing reconstruction quality or the efficiency gains that motivated CLTs?
first_experiment: Replicate the feature-skipping baseline on the Boolean toy model with known ground truth plus one InterpBench semi-synthetic transformer with a known multi-hop circuit, then train the standard CLT against a CLT with the separated per-layer decoder-norm sparsity penalty (the modification its own proponents identified as "most promising" but never ran) and measure three quantities: intermediate-feature recovery rate (does the graph include the true intermediate computation steps?), replacement score, and preservation of genuinely persistent cross-layer features — a decisive go/no-go signal on a single GPU that determines whether the objective-geometry explanation of unfaithfulness is actionable.
why: It targets the single highest-leverage artifact in mechanistic interpretability — attribution graphs — at its most damaging failure mode: the Feb 2026 finding that CLTs rewrite multi-hop circuits into shallow sums "obscuring the actual computational pathway," meaning current tracing cannot distinguish genuine reasoning from memorization, which is precisely the distinction CoT-monitoring and deception-detection applications need. Every retrospective ranks explanation validation/faithfulness as the field's top open problem and notes that no agreed quantitative measure exists, yet the four proposed mitigations remain explicitly untested ("we have not yet systematically tested mitigations"), and the field's own landscape document lists the relevant architectural questions ("why are cross-layer connections helpful," "restricting the layer range that a feature can write to") as open while their one attempted fix (end-to-end KL finetuning) made replacement scores worse — so the obvious cheap interventions are not already done. It is also the practical foothold on the deeper dual-basis problem the literature says is unsolved: faithfulness to intermediate computation becomes a principled criterion for ranking competing decompositions, rather than an aesthetic one. It has not been done because the failure was only demonstrated seven months ago by a small SPAR cohort without resources to run controlled training comparisons, because no ground-truth substrate (InterpBench/SIIT models, Tracr) has yet been aimed at transcoder training objectives, and because attribution-graph work has raced toward scaling and automation (Circuit Oracle, hierarchical graphs, deception analyses) while treating the graphs' reliability as an assumption rather than a result — leaving the load-bearing problem vacant.

direction: Establish distribution-shift-aware certified interventional fidelity as the standard for validating mechanistic explanations and adjudicating competing decompositions.
project: Fidelity Under Shift (FUS)
question: How does certified interventional fidelity of competing decompositions (SAE seeds/widths vs. neuron basis vs. transcoders) of the same model and behavior decay along a controlled ladder of distribution shifts, can cheap in-distribution statistics predict the decay, and does shift-aware fidelity produce a consistent ranking where in-distribution faithfulness ties?
first_experiment: Build attribution graphs for IOI/greater-than/multi-hop recall on Gemma-2-2B from two SAE seeds, two widths, and the neuron basis; pre-register each graph's predicted ablation effects; realize the ablations on held-out prompts across a five-rung shift ladder; score each decomposition with CIF-style confidence sequences and test whether seeds that tie in-distribution diverge under shift.
why: It targets the field's self-identified top open problem (dual basis + unverified explanations) in the regime where safety monitors actually fail (OOD), it composes existing isolated pieces (CIF, margin graphs, seed-divergence findings, neuron-basis circuits) rather than duplicating any of them, and it yields a decisive and useful result either way.

direction: Developmentally track how RLVR reshapes the internal knowledge-boundary circuitry underlying the hallucination tax, to determine whether RLVR erases or merely suppresses the model's internal representation of what it doesn't know, and localize the mediating components.
project: The Anatomy of the Hallucination Tax: How RLVR Rewires (or Preserves) Knowledge-Boundary Circuitry in Reasoning Models
question: Does outcome-only RLVR that incentivizes guessing destroy a model's internal representation of its own knowledge boundary, or preserve it while rewiring downstream circuitry that converts uncertainty into abstention vs. confident guessing — and which components implement the change?
first_experiment: GRPO-train Qwen2.5-1.5B on GSM8K with saved checkpoints; at each checkpoint measure abstention rate on the SUM unanswerable-math set alongside linear-probe decodability of "solvable vs. under-specified" from hidden states, then plot behavior vs. representation across training to decide between signal-suppression and signal-erasure.
why: It fills a verified, unoccupied gap at the intersection of the behavioral hallucination-tax literature, the static overconfidence-circuit literature, and the RLVR-training-dynamics literature, it offers a cheap falsifiable test whose both outcomes are decision-relevant for whether internal uncertainty monitors can be trusted on RLVR-trained deployed models, and it is tractable with open models and public data while doubling as the first developmental-interpretability study of RL post-training — an area the field's own roadmap flags as under-worked.

direction: Make circuit tracing trustworthy by measuring, detecting, and preventing "shallow-rewrite" unfaithfulness in cross-layer-transcoder attribution graphs — the dominant artifact of modern mechanistic interpretability, which was just proven (ICML 2026) capable of systematically hiding real multi-hop mechanisms in toy models with no metric, benchmark, or fix yet existing for real language models.
project: Faithful by Construction: Detecting and Preventing Shallow-Rewrite Unfaithfulness in Cross-Layer Transcoder Circuit Tracing
question: When and why do cross-layer transcoders rewrite deep multi-hop computations into shallow single-hop circuits in real language models, can this unfaithfulness be detected without ground truth, and can transcoders be trained (via end-to-end behavioral objectives or depth-preserving regularization) so that their traced circuits are faithful by construction — with faithful graphs yielding interventions (steering, ablation, unlearning) that generalize off-distribution while shallow-rewritten ones fail?
first_experiment: Build a ground-truth model organism on GPT-2-small scale: inject a known two-hop factual chain (fact A→bridge B, bridge B→answer C) via fine-tuning so the true mechanism is known by construction, train cross-layer transcoders across a sweep of sparsity penalties (following Anthropic's circuit-tracer recipe), and trace attribution graphs on multi-hop prompts — measuring a Path Recovery Score (does the graph contain the true bridge-feature chain, or a direct shortcut edge skipping the bridge?), validated causally by ablating bridge features (a faithful graph predicts output collapse; a rewritten one does not), then checking whether the same statistic predicts intervention generalization on held-out prompt formats.
why: It attacks the problem that two independent 2026 assessments (the Sharkey et al. retrospective and DeepMind's pragmatic-vision debate) rank as the field's most important methodological gap — explanations that match behavior while obscuring mechanism — at the moment a new, concrete failure mode has been diagnosed in toys but left unmeasured, undetected, and unfixed in real models; every safety application built on attribution graphs (auditing, unlearning, editing, monitoring) inherits the risk, so a validated faithfulness metric plus a training fix raises the reliability of the entire pipeline. It has not been done: the ICML 2026 result is diagnosis-only with preliminary real-model evidence, the multi-org replication tried reconstruction-oriented finetuning (not mechanism-level faithfulness) and abandoned it, Goodfire's known-mechanism study is qualitative on a single task, Miller et al. 2024 covers only head-level circuits' ablation sensitivity, and the automated-graph-analysis literature (ADAG, Circuit Oracle, probe prompting) automates *reading* graphs while silently assuming graphs are faithful in the first place — while the required infrastructure (circuit-tracer, public Gemma CLTs, Tracr, TransformerLens) makes it tractable at single-lab scale.

direction: Detect, quantify, and fix the "shallow rewrite" unfaithfulness of cross-layer transcoder circuit tracing.
project: Deep or Shortcut? A Ground-Truth Stress Test for Transcoder Circuit Tracing
question: When a model computes a behavior via a deep multi-step pathway, how often does CLT-based circuit tracing substitute a behaviorally-matching shallow rewrite, can this be detected without ground truth, and can training or selection criteria prevent it?
first_experiment: Train PLTs/CLTs with varied sparsity penalties on known-depth testbeds (two-hop composition transformers + InterpBench compiled models), trace attribution graphs, and measure rewrite incidence via interventions that discriminate shallow from deep hypotheses (e.g., intermediate-representation patching), producing a validated graph-vs-actual divergence statistic.
why: It attacks the newly documented but unaddressed structural flaw in the field's dominant artifact (attribution graphs), which every downstream safety application inherits; the only adjacent work is a July 2026 toy-model diagnosis that explicitly leaves detection and mitigation open, all neighboring clusters (validation metrics, steering prediction, self-repair, universality) target different failure modes, and the builders' own fix attempt failed and was abandoned — making this the highest-leverage, verifiably unclaimed problem I can start on with open tools today.

direction: Operationalize the "dual basis problem" by testing whether behaviorally equivalent decompositions of a language model diverge in the validity of their interventional predictions under distribution shift, and identify which decomposition properties predict that divergence.
project: Many Explanations, One Model: Ranking Mechanistic Decompositions by Interventional Faithfulness Under Distribution Shift
question: Among decompositions (SAE dictionaries of differing seeds/architectures/hyperparameters, component- and neuron-level circuits) that are statistically indistinguishable by in-distribution faithfulness criteria, does interventional prediction validity (predicted vs. actual ablation/steering effects) diverge on held-out distributions, and which intrinsic decomposition properties (support stability, TopK margin distributions, feature frequency, split/merge structure, cross-seed basis alignment) predict the divergence?
first_experiment: Using GPT-2 small, the well-characterized IOI circuit, and ~6–8 public residual-stream SAE dictionaries (multiple seeds, TopK/JumpReLU/ReLU variants) plus ACDC/EAP-IG component circuits, derive feature-ablation predictions on the in-distribution IOI prompt set, then measure predicted-versus-actual logit changes along a pre-registered shift ladder (name swaps, distractor clauses/DoubleIO, template paraphrases, typos, length extrapolation) to test whether in-distribution-tied decompositions separate out-of-distribution, regressing that separation on the candidate decomposition properties.
why: The 2026 state-of-field review names the dual basis problem the field's top open methodological question and identifies a severe verification bottleneck (labels scaled, validation didn't), while deployment safety monitors are admitted to fail under distribution shift — yet a systematic sweep shows every adjacent work stops short of this slice: Méloux et al. (ICLR 2025) proved non-identifiability only in Boolean toys without a constructive ranking criterion; Nainani et al. (2024) tested a single circuit under prompt variants and found generalization rather than comparing rival decompositions; MIB/InterpBench evaluate in-distribution or synthetic ground truth; Li (2026) covers SAE-seed fragility but not distribution shift; "Edge of Understanding" (2026) detects OOD inputs instead of validating explanations; and no standard perplexity-like metric exists for ranking decompositions by interventional OOD validity — while public models and dictionaries now make the first experiment a single-GPU project whose two possible outcomes (separation or uniformity) are both significant findings for interpretability methodology and safety auditing.

direction: Extend mechanistic interpretability beyond the single forward pass by reverse-engineering how LLM agents compute, maintain, and update their internal task state across multi-turn tool-using episodes ("contextual recurrence"), as the missing substrate for causally grounded agent monitoring.
project: Contextual Recurrence — A Mechanistic Account of Task-State Maintenance in LLM Agents
question: When an LLM agent acts over multiple turns, where and how does it internally represent the evolving task state (object locations, inventory, completed subgoals, plan stage), which components write and read that state as tool outputs and its own actions arrive, and can causally validated state representations support monitors that read what the agent actually believes rather than what it says — including when stated reasoning diverges from internal state?
first_experiment: Build a deterministic miniature tool-use environment (gridworld with a ~3-bit ground-truth state: agent position, key-carried, door-open) and collect 2–5k multi-turn rollouts from Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct (plus Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct as a second model); train linear probes and small SAEs on residual-stream activations to decode the true state at each turn's action position, with recency-controlled evaluation (state-changing events ≥K turns back, no recent mention) and shuffled-state baselines to exclude context-copying; if decodable, run cross-trajectory activation patching (state-A activations into state-B contexts) to test whether the agent's next tool call follows the patched state rather than the true context, and localize the update sites (layers/heads/latents) that write state after tool observations via path patching.
why: It attacks a gap every 2026 survey and frontier paper acknowledges but none occupies — the field's tools are single-pass, its deployment-relevant applications (monitoring, mechanistic anomaly detection, CoT-faithfulness) are multi-turn, and the current probe-based agent monitors are explicitly correlational and already being evaded, while the mechanism-level question of where agent state lives and how it updates has no published mechanistic answer (entity-tracking work covers narrative-stated changes, agent-MI papers decode safety labels, theory papers argue limits abstractly). It is the most promising because it is foundational rather than duplicative: the crowded agent-monitoring wave needs exactly this substrate to explain when and why monitors work or fail, it is decisively testable at small scale with ground-truth state (both outcomes are publishable findings), and it converts mechanistic interpretability's comparative advantage — reading cognition, not just behavior — into the regime where deployment risk is now concentrated.

direction: Empirically resolve the dual-basis problem for attribution graphs by testing whether causal circuit accounts from equally-faithful decompositions diverge under distribution shift, and whether out-of-distribution causal fidelity is a principled criterion for identifying "the real circuit."
project: Many Graphs, One Model: OOD Causal Fidelity as a Selection Criterion for Feature Decompositions
question: When multiple transcoder/SAE decompositions of the same model each yield attribution graphs that faithfully reproduce the model's behavior on the training distribution, (a) how much do their structural and causal predictions diverge under paraphrase, entity-swap, format, and compositional-novelty shift, and (b) does divergence-under-shift rank decompositions consistently enough to serve as a non-aesthetic, certifiable criterion for choosing which circuit account to trust?
first_experiment: On Gemma-2-2B (and Llama-3.1-8B), build attribution graphs for two behaviors (one algorithmic, e.g. greater-than/IOI-style; one multi-hop factual recall) using ≥4 decompositions — Anthropic's open-source circuit-tracer transcoders plus independently trained transcoders/CLTs varying seed and width (CLT-Forge / EleutherAI tooling). Verify in-distribution faithfulness parity (replacement scores within anytime-valid CIF bounds), then run a single shift family (paraphrase + entity swap) and measure, per graph: faithfulness to the full model under mirrored feature/edge interventions, and cross-decomposition divergence of those intervention predictions. Divergence above the certification bound on this minimal setup justifies the full behavior × shift × decomposition grid.
why: It targets the problem the field's own retrospective ranks first — the dominant artifact (attribution graphs) is deployed for safety monitoring but its causal claims have never been validated out-of-distribution, nor has anyone compared circuit accounts across equally-valid decompositions. It is not already done because every neighboring line stops short: 2026 feature-validation work is feature-level, seed-dependence work stops at subspaces without whole-graph causal divergence, 2024 faithfulness-robustness work predates transcoder graphs and varied ablation method rather than input distribution, identifiability work is theoretical and non-legible, CHIVE explicitly excluded internal explanations (while its null result makes the question urgent), and CIF has only a single-circuit demo. The project is cheap (inference-heavy, open artifacts), safety-relevant (monitors built on decomposition artifacts will silently fail under shift), and informative in both directions — divergence yields the field's first faithfulness-under-shift benchmark and a principled decomposition selector (testable against cheap intrinsic signals like cross-seed feature stability); its absence would be the first robustness license for scaling circuit accounts to monitoring frontier models.

direction: Diagnose and close the "tool-to-agent gap" — the replicated finding that white-box interpretability tools fail to improve agentic audits — by quantifying how much transcript-unrecoverable information each white-box signal actually carries and building calibrated, confound-controlled evidence interfaces that deliver it to investigator agents.
project: Beyond the Transcript: Diagnosing and Closing the Tool-to-Agent Gap in Agentic Alignment Audits
question: When an investigator agent audits a model with an implanted hidden behavior, why does white-box evidence fail to help — is the relevant information absent from activations, text-recoverable, or lost in delivery to the agent — and can an evidence interface that separates text-novel from text-recoverable signal, with calibrated confidence and hypothesis-directed queries, convert activation information into audit success?
first_experiment: On AuditBench's 12 held-out development models (6 behaviors × 2 instillation methods), run the default interaction protocol to collect transcripts, then collect each white-box tool's outputs on the same activations (SAE top-features, activation-oracle QA, logit-lens KL, steering deltas). Train three behavior-identification readouts per model: transcript-only, white-box-only, and combined; report the conditional lift of white-box over transcript. Then test text-invertibility by training a text-only model to predict each tool's output, splitting white-box signal into text-recoverable vs. text-novel components. Gate on the 2×2 outcome: text-novel signal present + agent failure → build the interface and re-run investigator agents on AuditBench's full 56-model suite; text-novel signal absent → document that activations don't carry it and redirect tool investment.
why: Mechanistic interpretability's comparative advantage is auditing and monitoring, and auditing for hidden behaviors is its most safety-critical concrete application — yet two independent 2026 benchmarks just showed the field's flagship white-box tools lose to scaffolded black-box prompting inside the audit loop. The gap is named but unexplained: AuditBench's three failure-mode hypotheses are explicitly untested, no work has quantified the conditional (transcript-independent) information content of white-box evidence for unknown-behavior audits, existing "black-to-white boost" work covers only static known-behavior probes, and the activation-oracle line is being fixed at the tool level (calibration, hallucination) without ever evaluating agentic audit value. The benchmark, models, agent, and proxy harness are all released, making this immediately actionable on open weights — and the question cuts to the field's deepest unresolved issue (what activations encode beyond tokens) while producing a decision-relevant answer either way.

direction: Build suppression-aware circuit tracing — a general method, metric, and taxonomy for the suppressive computations that attribution-graph construction and pruning systematically omit, making circuit explanations counterfactually faithful.
project: The Suppression Channel: Counterfactually Faithful Attribution Graphs
question: Which suppressive edges/features are causally important to model behavior, does standard attribution-graph pruning systematically omit them, and can a suppression-aware extension recover a more faithful account of the computation?
first_experiment: Compute signed, unpruned attribution graphs on GPT-2 Small (then Llama 3.2 1B with public transcoders) over competitor-suppression testbeds (factual recall with distractors, IOI, refraction), and test whether (H1) negative-influence edges form identifiable suppression chains, (H2) standard absolute-influence pruning drops most counterfactually-important suppressive edges, and (H3) amplifying/ablating top suppressor features produces predicted resurfacing/deepening of suppressed alternatives.
why: It's the explicitly-flagged-but-unclaimed gap in the field's dominant tool, independently corroborated by the 2026 state-of-the-field literature as the top open methodological problem; prior work treats suppression only as scattered special cases, the crowded 2026 effort went to graph annotation and refusal directions instead, and fixing it upgrades the faithfulness of every circuit claim downstream while mapping the mechanism of safety-critical withholding (refusal, jailbreaks, rationalized CoT).

direction: Turn the "dual basis problem" from an aesthetic choice into an empirical science by using designed input-distribution shifts as a discriminating instrument among behaviorally-equivalent mechanistic explanations — validated on models with planted ground-truth algorithms and decoy accounts, then applied to the community's documented open cases (trig-addition vs. lookup tables, hop vs. shortcut, heuristics vs. algorithm).
project: Stress-Testing the Circuit: Adjudicating Competing Mechanistic Explanations by Their Predictions Under Distribution Shift
question: When two or more mechanistic explanations (e.g., transcoder attribution graphs vs. structured-algorithm accounts) are equally faithful on-distribution, do their divergent predictions under targeted input-distribution shifts and matched interventions identify the account that actually tracks the model's computation — and can this selection procedure be certified against planted ground truth before being trusted on real models?
first_experiment: Train a 1–2 layer grokked transformer on modular addition (known ground truth: Fourier-rotation/trig algorithm), extract transcoder-based attribution graphs that — per published replication — recover "lookup table" features instead, verify both accounts achieve statistically indistinguishable ablation faithfulness on held-out in-distribution prompts, then run a stress battery (unseen operand ranges, phase-structured operand pairs that only a trig algorithm must handle systematically, Fourier-direction vs. random embedding perturbations) and measure which account predicts the model's actual behavior and intervention effects off-distribution; include a control arm (a Tracr-compiled or data-restricted model that genuinely implements a lookup table) to confirm the instrument picks the right winner in both directions.
why: It attacks the field's self-diagnosed #1 problem — verification and the dual basis problem — at the point of maximum leverage, just as attribution graphs became the standard artifact and are being deployed in safety monitors whose validity under shift is the binding constraint on all downstream claims. It has not been done because the adjacent lines each stop one step short: non-identifiability work proves the problem without a remedy; certification work conditions on a declared distribution rather than exploiting shifts to discriminate; OOD-prediction work (Li et al.) operates at the population-signature level, not on circuit-level accounts of a single model; and the community documents the ambiguous cases (lookup vs. trig, parity detectors, hop vs. shortcut) as open observations without an adjudication method. Meanwhile it is cheap, falsifiable, composes with the 2026 rigor literature rather than competing with it, and its failure mode (irreducible non-identifiability even under shift) would itself be a publishable sharpening of non-identifiability theory.

direction: Arbitrate competing circuit explanations by adversarially searching for out-of-distribution inputs where their executable surrogates diverge and using the model's actual behavior there as a principled faithfulness criterion and domain-of-validity map.
project: Disagreement Probing: Arbitrating Competing Circuit Explanations by Their Out-of-Distribution Divergence
question: Can out-of-distribution surrogate disagreement, arbitrated by the model's real behavior, serve as a non-circular quantitative measure of circuit faithfulness that selects among competing decompositions and certifies where circuit-based explanations and monitors remain valid?
first_experiment: On GPT-2 small IOI, pit three executable circuit surrogates (published Wang et al. circuit; ACDC circuit; a deliberately shallow rewrite) against the full model under constrained adversarial input search — embedding-space gradient descent with LM-likelihood naturalness regularization plus structured IOI prompt variants — and test which surrogate's predictions track GPT-2's actual outputs on the discovered disagreement set, with the prediction that the faithful circuit survives while the shallow rewrite fails on inputs requiring multi-hop composition.
why: It converts the field's top-ranked open problem (dual basis / no numerical faithfulness standard) into a falsifiable experiment, exploits a just-documented failure mode (sparsity-incentivized shallow circuit rewrites), extends the proven OOD-prediction objective to real-model circuit decompositions where its authors left off, directly serves safety by certifying the domain of validity of feature-based monitors, and remains undone because the required ingredients — executable attribution-graph surrogates, cheap adversarial search, and a concrete unfaithfulness target — only became available together in the last year, while the field's effort has flowed into building new decompositions rather than stress-testing the ones it already trusts.

direction: Build adversarial separation testing — automatically constructing behaviorally-equivalent decoy mechanisms and searching for the distributions/interventions that discriminate them — to convert circuit-explanation non-identifiability into a measured "identification coverage" certificate for attribution graphs and feature circuits.
project: Decoy Mechanisms: Adversarial Separation Testing and Identification Coverage for Circuit Explanations
question: Given two mechanistic explanations that reproduce a model's behavior equally well on the validation distribution, can an automated search over distributional and interventional stress tests find targeted tests that separate them, and can we quantify — as a falsifiable, anytime-valid certificate — the range of distributions over which a candidate explanation is actually identified rather than merely consistent?
first_experiment: On GPT-2 small IOI, construct behaviorally-equivalent decoy explanations of the canonical IOI circuit (positional-heuristic, copy-suppression-only, and subspace-abstraction decoys), verify equivalence on the base-prompt distribution, then run an automated search over IOI's known distributional knobs × intervention types to find minimal separating test sets — validating that the search rediscovers known human findings (Makelov's subspace illusion, S2 hacking) and calibrating true-vs-decoy discrimination on InterpBench's planted-ground-truth SIIT-IOI model.
why: It targets the problem the field's own 2025–2026 reviews rank first (attribution-graph faithfulness and the dual-basis problem, where "validation is not identification" and mechanism choice among equivalent decompositions is still aesthetic), synthesizes four mature-but-unconnected pieces that only recently became available (non-identifiability proofs at tiny scale, single-hypothesis statistical certification, planted-ground-truth models, manually-discovered OOD mechanism shifts), directly serves safety deployment by certifying what interpretability-derived monitors actually cover, and remains undone because the field's incentives reward discovering circuits rather than stress-testing them — making it foundational, tractable at solo scale on 1B-parameter open models, and genuinely novel.

direction: Solve the attribution-graph dual-basis problem by building ground-truth model organisms with known computational-pathway depth in open LLMs and an out-of-distribution interventional faithfulness metric that can select the true mechanism among behaviorally-equivalent circuit explanations — turning faithfulness from an aesthetic judgment into a measured, reportable quantity.
project: "The Dual-Basis Benchmark: Out-of-Distribution Interventional Validation of Attribution Graphs"
question: When multiple circuit decompositions (CLT vs. per-layer transcoders vs. different sparsity/threshold configurations) all reproduce a model's behavior in-distribution, which interventional predictions diverge out-of-distribution, and does the divergence identify the decomposition that matches the model's true (planted, ground-truth) computational pathway — in particular, does sparsity-incentivized "depth rewriting" (deep multi-hop mechanisms explained as shallow sums) systematically evade detection?
first_experiment: Fine-tune Gemma-3-270M on a synthetic multi-hop lookup task (chains of k=2–4 relational hops, with distractors) so the ground-truth mechanism — carrying intermediate entity states across layers — is verifiable by construction via activation patching of intermediate variables; then run circuit tracing under ≥4 decomposition configurations, confirm all recovered graphs are behaviorally equivalent in-distribution (matched KL to model output), and measure each graph's Interventional Faithfulness Gap: the divergence between the graph-predicted and the model's actual response to interventions (patching/ablating predicted intermediate features) on held-out OOD stress inputs — perturbed intermediate entities, longer-than-trained chains, paraphrased relations. Prediction: shallow-rewrite graphs pass in-distribution but fail the OOD interventional test; pathway-tracking graphs pass both.
why: It attacks the field's self-identified top open problem — the 2026 state-of-field review calls the dual-basis problem and the missing agreed faithfulness metric the most important methodological questions, and notes verification has fallen ~3 orders of magnitude behind labeling. It has not been done because (a) the tooling only became available recently (Gemma Scope 2's open cross-layer transcoders, Dec 2025; CLT-Forge, Mar 2026), (b) the specific failure mode — sparsity-penalized depth rewriting — was only demonstrated in a toy model in 2026 with "preliminary" LM evidence, and (c) validation work is structurally under-incentivized: graphs are judged by readability, and no one owns the metric. Adjacent efforts (CIRCUS, Certified Circuits, MIB, Have Faith in Faithfulness, the Goodfire/Dunefsky-style planted-mechanism replications) each stop short of a feature-level, OOD-interventional, ground-truth-validated selection criterion. The payoff is a trust layer for the entire attribution-graph paradigm — the artifact on which mechanistic audits, production safety monitors, and "interpretability as evidence" all rest — and it specifically targets the deep multi-hop computations where shallow decompositions would most dangerously mislead safety applications, using fully open models and tools.

direction: Make circuit explanations falsifiable predictive theories by validating them out-of-distribution and using those tests to adjudicate between competing decompositions of the same behavior.
project: Circuits as Predictive Theories: Out-of-Distribution Falsification of Attribution-Graph Explanations
question: When two circuit explanations are both faithful on extraction prompts but diverge on held-out and shifted inputs, which describes the mechanism the model actually uses — and can held-out predictive + interventional accuracy become the field's first non-circular faithfulness measure?
first_experiment: On Gemma-2-2B with public transcoders, trace attribution graphs over ~100 two-digit addition prompts, extract the competing "operand-identity lookup table" vs. "helix/rotation algorithm" hypotheses they imply, and score both hypotheses' pre-registered predictions — feature activations and intervention effects — against the real model on ~100 held-out, out-of-range, and format-shifted prompts.
why: It targets the #1 ranked open problem in the field's own June-2026 retrospective (non-circular faithfulness of attribution graphs / the dual basis problem), answers an explicit 15-month-old future-work call from the field's leaders (merging per-prompt graphs into a global circuit picture), and converts 2026's pathology results (CLT shallow-rewrite incentives, phantom specialization, success-without-error faithfulness, toy-model non-identifiability) into the missing positive methodology — unclaimed because per-prompt tracing only became cheap and open with public transcoders and circuit-tracer in mid-2025, while all adjacent work (error-agreement evaluation, dataset-edit certification, head-level structural equivalence) addresses a different axis on pre-transcoder artifacts; it is foundational for every safety application of circuits, has a ready-made ground-truth conflict to adjudicate (trigonometric addition vs. lookup-table features), and is executable on open-weight models with a single GPU.

direction: Build "mechanism organisms" — plant known, node-level multi-hop computational mechanisms into real pretrained LLMs to create the first true positive-control testbed for verifying that circuit-tracing pipelines recover genuine mechanisms rather than shallow rewrites.
project: MechanismBench: Circuit Implantation as Ground Truth for Mechanistic Interpretability
question: When circuit-tracing pipelines (CLTs + attribution graphs, SAE feature circuits, EAP/ACDC) are applied to a real pretrained language model whose internal mechanism for a behavior is known by construction — because we implanted it — do they recover the true mechanism's nodes, edges, and hop structure, or do they produce behaviorally-equivalent shallow rewrites, and can a recovery-validated faithfulness metric distinguish the two?
first_experiment: Take Gemma-2-2B-it (Gemma Scope available) or Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct; select a fictional-universe two-hop conditional factual task the base model provably cannot solve; install the mechanism via sparse TopK-LoRA fine-tuning restricted to causally identified MLP sites so hop 1 (entity→bridge) and hop 2 (bridge→answer, composing into the output) live in known, disjoint weight blocks; verify installation with behavioral tests plus necessity/sufficiency ablations of the planted blocks (and capability-preservation checks per "How to Train Your Model Organism"); then train per-layer transcoders/CLTs on the edited model and check the first falsifiable prediction: whether the recovered attribution graph contains the planted bridge node as an intermediate cause, or collapses the two hops into a one-edge shortcut — the shallow-rewrite failure mode predicted for CLTs but never tested against ground truth in a real LLM.
why: Verification of interpretability outputs is the field's self-identified #1 bottleneck in 2026 — labeling scaled, validation didn't; attribution graphs are treated as reliable descriptions despite documented unfaithfulness (CLT shallow rewrites, context-distortion misranking, non-robust metrics), and every downstream use (safety monitors, audits, model editing) inherits that doubt. A positive control with known mechanism-level ground truth is the missing instrument that would (a) settle whether flagship circuit-tracing methods find real mechanisms, (b) arbitrate contested hypotheses like hop-aligned vs. layer-order-inverted multi-hop computation, and (c) let the community calibrate a non-circular faithfulness metric by checking which behavioral scores actually track mechanism recovery. It has not already been done because existing ground-truth approaches are all compromises: Tracr/InterpBench compile synthetic models from scratch (unrepresentative of natural LLMs), model organisms plant behaviors whose mechanisms are unknown by construction, knowledge-editing work installs facts rather than composed algorithmic mechanisms and evaluates behaviorally, and the ICML 2026 CLT-unfaithfulness result was demonstrated only in a Boolean toy with "preliminary" real-model evidence — leaving the controlled real-LLM experiment, which this project runs, undone.

direction: Mechanistic anomaly detection via circuit-path fingerprints validated on planted-ground-truth model organisms, targeting obfuscation- and distribution-shift-robust monitoring where feature-level detectors demonstrably fail.
project: PathGuard: Obfuscation-Robust Mechanistic Anomaly Detection with Circuit-Path Fingerprints and a Planted-Mechanism Benchmark
question: Do distances between attribution-graph fingerprints against a trusted reference distribution detect anomalous internal mechanisms (including adversarially obfuscated ones) with high AUROC and low false positives under benign distribution shift, where probe/SAE/activation baselines collapse?
first_experiment: Plant a known, ablation-verified backdoor circuit in a small transformer (InterpBench model, then Gemma-2-2b + circuit-tracer), extract attribution-graph fingerprints on trusted-clean vs. triggered inputs, and benchmark fingerprint-distance detection against linear probes, SAE-latent, Mahalanobis, and influence-function baselines — first normally, then with the backdoor adversarially regularized to keep activations in-distribution.
why: It unifies the field's top-ranked open problems (verification/ground truth, OOD-robust monitoring, mechanistic anomaly detection) in a niche with exactly one prior method paper, is newly tractable thanks to cheap open circuit-tracing infrastructure from 2025–2026, is justified by non-identifiability theory as needing discrimination rather than uniqueness, and remains publishable as a benchmark or as a negative result either way.

direction: Reframe circuit discovery from point estimation of "the circuit for a task" to statistically estimating and causally validating the *conditional distribution* of circuits over inputs — a validated circuit atlas — thereby solving the field's top-ranked faithfulness/dual-basis problem and creating the first global, monitorable circuit picture.
project: Circuit Atlases: From Prompt-Local Attribution Graphs to Validated Global Mechanisms
question: Do circuit variations across inputs follow a predictable conditional structure — and does a model of that structure (an atlas mapping input features → pathway distributions) yield circuits that are causally sufficient and necessary on *held-out, distribution-shifted* inputs where any single task-level circuit is known to fail?
first_experiment: On GPT-2 small (then Pythia-160M/1.4B) using EAP-IG with certified subsampling, extract per-prompt circuits for IOI and greater-than across a controlled grid of ~1,000 prompts varying template format, token-frequency band, and name/entity rarity (all public tooling: TransformerLens, Circuit Tracer, one GPU, days not months). Then: (1) verify the "many circuits, one mechanism" regime by clustering per-prompt circuits and measuring structural vs. functional (interchange-intervention) divergence; (2) fit a simple multinomial model predicting circuit-family membership and edge-inclusion probabilities from interpretable input features; (3) the kill-or-confirm test — for 200 held-out prompts including rare templates where the canonical IOI circuit is documented to fail, compare sufficiency (ablate complement, behavior preserved) and necessity (ablate predicted edges, behavior destroyed) of *atlas-predicted* circuits vs. the task-level circuit vs. circuits discovered directly on each prompt. If atlas-predicted circuits match or beat directly discovered ones on held-out causal sufficiency, the atlas is real; if not, conditionality is unpredictable from input features — itself a decisive negative result that settles the "task circuit vs. template circuit" debate the field is currently stuck on.
why: It is the unique convergence of (a) the field's top self-identified open problem (faithfulness of the standard artifact, dual-basis), (b) a wave of 2025–2026 diagnostic results that establish the phenomenon but leave the constructive step unclaimed, (c) an explicit request on the attribution-graph community's own roadmap ("merge graphs into a global circuit picture," "automate the validation loop"), and (d) the deployment gap — monitors need distribution-aware mechanisms, and a validated atlas is exactly what a production monitor consumes (predicted pathway per input; anomaly = model deviates from atlas). It has not been done: per-prompt tracing (ACC++) is descriptive only; Certified Circuits stabilizes a single point-estimate circuit; feature-level e-process validation tests features, not conditional circuit structure; ADAG automates description, not prediction or causal validation; the EPFL variance work diagnoses template-dependence and stops at pessimism; the Koopman theorem gives an identifiable but non-legible primitive, leaving the legibility-validation bridge unbuilt. It is feasible for a small team with public models, dictionaries, and tooling — and it is falsifiable within weeks, with both outcomes (atlas holds / conditionality unpredictable) materially advancing the field.

direction: Build the missing empirical foundation for the "dual basis problem": measure, predict, and exploit when observationally equivalent feature decompositions of the same model diverge in their interventional predictions under distribution shift, yielding the field's first decomposition-selection criterion and an interventional-OOD validation benchmark.
project: The Decomposition Gauntlet — Auditing and Selecting Feature Decompositions by Out-of-Distribution Interventional Validity
question: When multiple sparse decompositions (different seeds, widths, sparsities, objectives) of the same activations are observationally equivalent — matching reconstruction, interpretability scores, and even first-order causal similarity — are they interventional-equivalent out-of-distribution, and what measurable property of a decomposition (per-feature causal-necessity profile, cross-seed stability, frequency coverage, anti-aliasing margin) predicts the OOD validity of its ablation, steering, and editing predictions well enough to serve as a non-circular selection criterion?
first_experiment: In a synthetic superposition model with planted features and a known compositional input→feature→output causal graph, train an SAE ensemble (≥5 seeds × 3 widths × 3 sparsities × TopK/JumpReLU/Matryoshka) at one site, then hold out entire families of feature combinations and measure how accurately each decomposition predicts the model's actual output change under ablation, amplification, and swap interventions — single and composed, weak and strong — testing the hypothesis that in-distribution metrics (including first-order causal similarity) fail to predict OOD interventional divergence while a causal-necessity profile does; follow with the same battery on GPT-2/Pythia IOI using a multi-variant SAE suite, then a case study testing whether probe-able "knowledge" directions behind the 98%-AUROC-but-unsteerable knowledge-action gap are read-inert.
why: The field's own 2026 assessment ranks decomposition faithfulness/selection as its top methodological problem ("which attribution graph is the circuit?" is currently settled by aesthetics), and three independent 2026 negative results (random baselines matching trained SAEs, causal inertness at cosine ≈ 1, probes that read what steering cannot touch) show the existing metrics cannot answer it; yet the closest prior work stops at per-feature in-distribution validation, first-order Jacobian similarity, stability-without-intervention, or protocol-critique theory without a constructive criterion — so decomposition-level, OOD, interventional selection is verified as unclaimed, newly tractable thanks to the convergence of validation statistics and multi-variant SAE releases, and upstream of monitoring, steering, auditing, and transfer, with a decisive first experiment whose both possible outcomes advance the field.

direction: Build ground-truth trained model organisms to measure — and then close — the gap between on-distribution faithfulness and interventional generalization of mechanistic explanations, i.e., solve the dual-basis selection problem empirically.
project: The Dual-Basis Gap: Ground-Truth Testbeds for Selecting Among Equivalent Mechanistic Explanations
question: When multiple circuit/feature decompositions of the same trained transformer all faithfully explain its behavior on the training distribution, how sharply do their predictions diverge under held-out interventions and distribution shift — and can practical criteria (mechanistic description length, adversarially-averaged faithfulness, seed/spec-ensemble consensus, local learning coefficient) identify which explanation tracks the model's true mechanism?
first_experiment: Train ~20 seeds of small (1–2 layer) transformers on modular addition (a·b mod p) to grokking, where the generalizing mechanism (discrete Fourier / trig-identity algorithm, Nanda et al. 2023) is known and the pre-grok memorization circuit is a natural impostor; then construct an ensemble of matched on-distribution-faithful decompositions (hand-derived Fourier circuit, SAE-feature circuits at multiple widths/seeds, EAP/ACDC head circuits, and the memorization-style circuit) and compare each one's predicted ablation/patching/steering effects against the model's actual behavior on held-out operand pairs and shifted input distributions, computing for every decomposition an "interventional generalization gap" and testing whether any criterion ranks the true mechanism above its impostors.
why: It attacks the single bottleneck that the field's own 2025 review and 2026 retrospective rank highest — explanation validation and the dual-basis problem — at the moment the enabling pieces (non-identifiability evidence, certification tooling, cheap small-model training, mature SAE/patching infrastructure) have just come together but the selection question itself is unclaimed. It has not been done: existing ground-truth testbeds (InterpBench, TracrBench, SynthSAEBench) evaluate compiled or data-synthetic models on-distribution only; Paulo & Belrose compare dictionaries without ground-truth mechanisms or OOD interventions; Méloux et al. establish non-identifiability but in untrainable-scale MLPs and propose no criteria; Explanation Multiplicity documents instability without a path to adjudication; Adaptive Circuit Behavior tests one circuit's format robustness, not equivalence-class selection. It is uniquely tractable for me — tiny models, cheap interventions, falsifiable metrics — and every partial result is valuable: quantifying the gap justifies the pragmatic stance if small, or forces decomposition reform if large, and the resulting benchmark plus validated selection criterion is precisely what monitoring under distribution shift, model editing, and audit-grade interpretability need next.

direction: Build the missing global layer of circuit tracing — aggregate many prompt-local attribution graphs into a validated "circuit atlas" that separates a task's invariant mechanism from prompt-specific peripheral strategies, and use out-of-sample prediction as a non-circular faithfulness test.
project: From Prompt-Local Graphs to a Global Circuit Atlas: Aggregating and Validating Attribution Graphs Across Prompts
question: For a fixed task, is there an invariant core of feature-level circuits — and if so, can an atlas built from a finite sample of prompts (a) predict the circuit structure and behavior on held-out prompts and unseen templates, (b) be decomposed into invariant-core vs. template/context-dependent-periphery components whose causal roles differ under intervention, and (c) transfer across model families — or does the 2026 "no comprehensive task circuit exists" pessimism hold at feature granularity too?
first_experiment: Take the greater-than task on GPT-2 small with publicly available pretrained cross-layer transcoders (Goodfire/Anthropic circuit-tracer tooling; a second replication on Gemma-2-2B with circuit-tracer's shipped transcoders). Generate attribution graphs for ~200–500 prompts that systematically vary year, noun, and sentence template. Then: (1) quantify edge- and feature-overlap statistics and cluster the graphs into families, testing whether the component-level template-variance result reproduces at feature granularity; (2) construct a first-cut aggregate atlas (aggregate weighted feature→feature edges over prompts, threshold into a candidate "core"); (3) the decisive test — evaluate the untuned core's faithfulness (necessity/sufficiency via ablation in the local replacement model) on held-out prompts and templates it was never built from, and check it recovers Hanna et al.'s known greater-than mechanism without per-prompt selection.
why: It attacks the top-ranked open problem of 2026 (non-circular faithfulness/verification) via the field's dominant artifact, and answers an open question the attribution-graph creators themselves explicitly posed ("can we merge attribution graphs for a more global picture?") that has not been attempted: adjacent 2026 work is either purely diagnostic at component level (phantom specialization, variance demystification), theory-only identifiability (spectral/formal guarantees), or automates interpretation of a single graph (ADAG, Circuit Oracle) — none builds, validates, or releases an aggregated global object. It also amortizes interpretability cost (a flagged unsolved problem): once an atlas exists, explaining a new prompt reduces to cheap lookup plus residual tracing, and the same atlas construction is the cleanest instrument yet for testing feature-level universality across models. It has not been done because the field only recently got reusable pretrained transcoders and drifted to single-prompt analysis, and because the pessimistic 2026 variance results discouraged rather than provoked the constructive attempt — while success or failure both resolve a question that currently gates whether task-level (rather than prompt-level) interpretability claims are justified.

direction: Develop held-out validation and prompt-distribution-stable consensus construction for attribution graphs, the field's dominant circuit artifact.
project: Held-Out Circuits: Stress-Testing the Faithfulness of Attribution Graphs Beyond Their Construction Prompts
question: Do attribution graphs remain stable and causally faithful beyond the prompts they were built from, and can stability selection over diverse prompt subsamples produce consensus graphs whose circuit claims transfer out-of-distribution?
first_experiment: Build attribution graphs for ~100 construction prompts of one behavior (released transcoders on Gemma-2-2B/Llama-3.2-1B plus a synthetic multi-hop-facts model organism), then compare in-distribution vs. held-out (paraphrase / novel-entity / novel-composition / longer-chain) replacement scores, cross-prompt graph agreement, and causal node-ablation effects — producing the first stress-test table for the standard artifact.
why: It is the field's own top-ranked open methodological problem (attribution-graph faithfulness / dual-basis), sits in the exact gap left by CIRCUS (threshold-only uncertainty, single prompt), Certified Circuits (neuron/edge circuits only), and the 2026 automation papers (assume validity), is named as open by the method's original authors, directly de-risks safety applications that rely on graphs, and is fully executable with open tooling and modest compute.

direction: Build the missing out-of-distribution validation science for mechanistic decompositions — measuring whether circuits/feature decompositions generalize beyond their discovery distribution and using that to discriminate dual decompositions.
project: Overfit Explanations: A Validation Split for Mechanistic Interpretability (Generalized Faithfulness under Shift)
question: Does a decomposition that faithfully reproduces model behavior on its discovery distribution remain valid under distribution shift, and can cheap held-out intervention tests identify which of several equally-faithful candidate decompositions is real?
first_experiment: Discover three matched-faithfulness decompositions (canonical IOI circuit, ACDC/EAP circuit, SAE-feature circuit) for GPT-2-small/IOI and a Gemma-2-2B multi-hop task, then measure their faithfulness and divergence under paraphrase, distractor, repeated-name, length, and mixed-mechanism shifts.
why: It is the field's own #1-ranked open methodological problem (faithfulness/dual-basis), it gates the safety value of deployed interpretability monitors, it unifies recent negative results as overfitting of explanations, it is tractable with open models and existing tooling, and no prior work goes beyond in-distribution, run-to-run, cross-model, or tiny-vision-scale validation.

direction: Turn the dual basis problem from a philosophical worry into an empirical decision procedure — rank behavior-equivalent mechanistic decompositions (attribution graphs, CLT vs. per-layer transcoders, SAE dictionaries) by their out-of-distribution and held-out-intervention predictive adequacy, using the deep-multi-hop-vs-shallow-rewrite confound as the flagship discriminating case.
project: Circuit Stress Tests: Discriminating Behavior-Equivalent Decompositions by Out-of-Distribution Predictive Adequacy
question: When two feature-level decompositions of a language model both account for a behavior in-distribution (e.g., a cross-layer-transcoder attribution graph and a per-layer-transcoder composition), do their implied predictions about the model's behavior under distribution shift and off-manifold interventions diverge — and does the decomposition whose predictions match the model's actual OOD/intervention behavior correspond to the true underlying mechanism (validated in synthetic settings with known ground truth), thereby providing a non-aesthetic ranking criterion for the dual basis problem?
first_experiment: Train a zoo of small transformers (2–3 layers) on a synthetic two-hop composition task with a known ground-truth SCM (edge triples A→B, B→C, queried A→C; hold out bridge entities and unseen compositions). Fit both cross-layer transcoders and per-layer transcoders/SAEs to each model, build attribution graphs, and verify the decompositions are behavior-equivalent in-distribution (comparable circuit error). Then run a discriminator battery derived from each decomposition's causal claims — ablate/patch predicted bridge-entity features on held-out compositions, corrupt bridge representations, interchange interventions on predicted intermediate subspaces — scoring each decomposition's predicted behavioral deltas against the model's actual deltas with CIF-style anytime-valid confidence sequences. Success criterion: the ID-equivalent decompositions make measurably divergent OOD/intervention predictions, and the one matching ground truth is consistently selected. (Then replicate on Gemma-2-2B with the open-source circuit-tracer on two-hop factual recall, where the "curse of two-hop reasoning" provides a natural behavioral anchor.)
why: It targets the field's own top-diagnosed open problem — the 2026 retrospective calls the dual basis problem the issue a new survey should put first, noting decompositions are currently ranked "by how readable their labels are" — and it is the direct synthesis of four converging threads that each stop one step short: Méloux et al. diagnose non-identifiability only in toy MLPs; the ICML 2026 result shows CLTs learn behavior-matching shallow rewrites but provides no way to tell which decomposition is right; Li et al. show internals can predict OOD behavior only at the whole-model attention-pattern level, never for circuit/feature decompositions; and CIF supplies the statistics but no discriminating criterion. Nobody has built the OOD-ranking framework, the stress-test battery, or the ground-truth validation for feature-level decompositions on real models. It matters because safety monitors and audits inherit whatever decomposition the analyst fit — a shallow-rewrite decomposition that passes ID faithfulness checks will silently mispredict intervention effects precisely under distribution shift, which is where monitors fail. And it is cheap and tractable now: synthetic tasks give oracle ground truth, open tooling (circuit-tracer, Gemma Scope, TransformerLens/nnsight) covers the decomposition layer, and the deliverables (a stress-test benchmark plus a validated ranking criterion) are the kind of standardizable artifact the field's "downstream tasks for measuring understanding" agenda explicitly requests.

direction: Build the validation layer for feature-level circuit tracing — a ground-truth-anchored, held-out/distribution-shift framework that adjudicates between competing attribution-graph explanations that are indistinguishable on-distribution.
project: Adjudicating Circuits: Ground-Truth-Anchored, Held-Out Validation for Attribution Graphs
question: When multiple feature-level circuit explanations (e.g., PLT- vs CLT-derived graphs, or graphs rewritten deep-to-shallow) account equally well for model behavior on the observed prompts, do standard on-distribution metrics (replacement score, ablation faithfulness) fail to identify the one matching the model's actual mechanism — and can a battery of held-out discriminative tests (prompt-variant agreement, novel-intervention transfer, error agreement) reliably separate the faithful explanation from unfaithful ones, measured against models with known ground-truth mechanisms?
first_experiment: Train per-layer and small cross-layer transcoders on InterpBench's SIIT models (known ground-truth circuits, e.g., IOI), build attribution graphs for the task, and measure (a) whether the pruned feature graph recovers the known circuit at the algorithm level, (b) whether controlled alternative explanations (shallow rewrites, shortcut splices, critical-edge prunings) match on-distribution replacement score/faithfulness while differing mechanistically, and (c) which candidate explanations survive held-out tests: stress prompt variants, novel feature ablations/steering, and error agreement.
why: It targets the field's self-identified #1 open problem — attribution graphs are now the dominant artifact, deployed in production safety monitors, yet they are validated almost solely by on-distribution replacement score, and 2024–2026 results (non-identifiability, metric fragility, context-distortion misranking, error-blindness, CLT unfaithfulness) show on-distribution fit cannot select among competing explanations. It has not already been done because every existing validation effort targets head/edge-level circuits (InterpBench was built for ACDC/EAP-style discovery, never transcoder recovery), the CLT-unfaithfulness result stopped at a Boolean toy with preliminary LM evidence, and no feature-level known-mechanism benchmark or held-out validation protocol exists — the infrastructure (public CLTs, InterpBench, Circuit Tracer, established natural-model mechanisms) only matured in the last 18 months, and the field's incentives still favor discovery over verification. It is upstream of all downstream applications (auditing, monitoring, transfer, model editing), tractable at GPT-2 scale, and would produce the standard faithfulness-scoring protocol the field currently lacks.

direction: Mechanistic model diffing of RLVR post-training: a longitudinal, causally validated feature-level account of what GRPO changes in a base model's computation.
project: Reweight or Rewire? A Checkpoint-by-Checkpoint Circuit-Level Account of What RLVR Does to a Base Model
question: Is the pass@1 gain and diversity collapse produced by RLVR implemented as reweighting of pre-existing features (causally reconstitutable in the base model by feature steering alone) or as new computation, and does the transition timeline predict RLVR's monitorability/faithfulness decay?
first_experiment: GRPO-train Qwen2.5-0.5B on GSM8K in verl with 50-step checkpoints, then diff every checkpoint against the base model using frozen SAEs/crosscoders (swap-readout firing-rate deltas + reconstruction-error growth) alongside pass@1/pass@128/entropy measurements, and regress the behavioral trajectories on the reweighting and unexplained-computation components.
why: It occupies an explicitly named, verified-unclaimed open problem (model diffing for RL post-training), resolves a live contradiction between the 2026 OPD-reweighting result and the GRPO hint-hiding new-computation result, mechanistically explains two hot behavioral phenomena (pass@k narrowing and monitorability decay) that only have entropy-level accounts, builds in causal validation that the field's 2026 retrospectives rank as its top methodological gap, and is fully tractable on open ≤1.5B models with tooling and protocols that only matured in late 2026.

direction: Build a head-to-head adjudication methodology for competing mechanistic explanations — treat each candidate explanation (circuit, feature decomposition, attribution graph) as making counterfactual predictions over input families, construct families where candidates diverge, and rank them empirically by how far their behavioral validity extends beyond the distribution they were built on.
project: Explanatory Reach — Adjudicating Competiting Mechanistic Explanations by Differential Predictions (title: "Which Circuit? Adjudicating Competing Mechanistic Explanations by Designed Discriminating Distributions")
question: When multiple mechanistic explanations all pass current validity criteria on a behavior's construction distribution, can we construct input distributions on which they make divergent predictions, and does adjudicating them there (a) yield a stable, principled ranking that differs from what standard faithfulness selects, and (b) produce a quantifiable "explanatory reach" — the measure of input space over which each explanation's predictions remain valid?
first_experiment: On GPT-2 small / indirect-object identification, evaluate three public candidate circuits that all pass standard faithfulness — the Wang et al. manual circuit, an ACDC circuit, and an EAP-IG circuit (from MIB) — under a single fixed resample-ablation policy. Over a parametric grid of controlled IOI prompt families (name-order swaps, repeated-subject position, distractor count/placement, object semantic category including the known "romantic object" slice, name-frequency bands, error-rich slices), (1) measure the pairwise KL divergence between candidates' output distributions to verify discriminating families exist where all candidates are individually "faithful" on the canonical distribution, then (2) on the highest-divergence families, measure which candidate's output distribution tracks the full model's, yielding a first "who wins where" adjudication table and a prototype reach metric (fraction of families where a candidate matches the model within a KL threshold), replicated across seeds and ablation-policy variants to check the ranking's robustness.
why: It is the most promising because it attacks the one problem the field itself ranks first (the dual-basis / "which decomposition?" question and faithfulness-as-a-numerical-target), in the exact window where a 2024–2026 wave of negative results (non-identifiability, multiverse instability, phantom specialization, error-blindness) has established demand but supplied only measurement, not method — and because it is tractable now that circuits, ablation protocols, task generators, and SAE dictionaries are all public artifacts. It has not already been done because every adjacent paper stops short of head-to-head adjudication: adversarial evaluation (uit de Bos & Garriga-Alonso 2024) tests one circuit against the model, Certified Circuits (Anani et al. 2026) certifies stability of a single discovery run, error-reproduction testing (Zhang et al. 2026) evaluates each method separately, phantom specialization (Bayat Makou et al. 2026) shows structural differences are not functional differences but does not select within the equivalence class, and the identifiability work (Méloux et al. 2025; Dhor & Chen 2026) demonstrates non-uniqueness or finds non-legible invariants without ranking legible candidates — the systematic construction of *discriminating* input families and the reach metric that turns explanation choice from an aesthetic decision into an empirical one remain unoccupied.

direction: Develop and validate interventional generalization — held-out out-of-distribution interventional predictiveness — as the first quantitative, non-circular criterion for selecting among behaviorally-equivalent decompositions of a model, resolving the dual basis problem that currently makes decomposition choice an aesthetic decision and causes feature-based safety interventions to fail under distribution shift.
project: Interventional Generalization: A Selection Criterion for Behaviorally-Equivalent Decompositions in Mechanistic Interpretability
question: When multiple decompositions of the same model are statistically indistinguishable in-distribution, do their feature-level interventions make divergent predictions on shifted distributions, and does out-of-distribution interventional generalization identify the decomposition whose causal claims hold at deployment?
first_experiment: On Gemma-2-2B layer 12, assemble ~8 decompositions (Gemma Scope SAEs at multiple widths/L0s, three self-trained SAE architectures/seeds, one matryoshka SAE, one cross-layer transcoder); verify overlapping in-distribution evals (FVU, sparsity, MIB-style sufficiency across 5 behaviors with bootstrap CIs), then measure cross-decomposition agreement of matched feature-ablation/patching effects on the base distribution vs. three shifted distributions (language, domain, adversarial paraphrase), testing whether interventional rank agreement collapses under shift.
why: The field's own 2026 retrospective, the Open Problems coalition, and a convergent wave of negative results (non-canonical SAEs, dead-salmon non-identifiability, unreliable SAE interventions, identifiable-but-not-legible invariants) all nominate decomposition selection/faithfulness as the top open methodological problem, yet every adjacent 2025–26 paper stops one step short — selecting features within a fixed decomposition, comparing codes on one dictionary in-distribution, certifying edge-circuit stability, or checking equivalence across models — leaving the within-model, OOD, ground-truth-validated selection criterion unbuilt; it is foundational for safety (monitors currently inherit arbitrary decompositions and demonstrably fail under shift), and it is tractable now because public multi-width SAE releases, transcoders, MIB, and InterpBench ground-truth models only became available in the last 18 months, making the first experiment cheap, decisive, and informative in either outcome.

direction: Adjudicate whether the template-induced "different circuits for the same task" phenomenon is phantom specialization (one mechanism, redundantly implemented) or genuine mechanism multiplicity, by applying the functional-equivalence battery of cross-condition transfer, shared-core recovery, and interchange interventions to template variation — thereby determining whether "the task circuit" is a coherent object and whether circuit-derived monitors/steering can be trusted under template shift.
project: Phantom or Real? A Functional Adjudication of Template-Induced Circuit Multiplicity in Language Models
question: When different prompt templates of the same task activate structurally distinct circuits (as Wu et al. 2026 and Franco et al. 2026 report), do those circuits implement the same abstract computation via interchangeable components (phantom specialization, as Makou et al. 2026 showed for token-frequency variation), or genuinely distinct mechanisms — and does structural circuit concentration validly predict whether interventions transfer to unseen templates?
first_experiment: On GPT-2 small and Pythia-160M, use MIB's IOI/SVA/greater-than data split into ~30 template families; discover per-template circuits with CEAP and EAP-IG (4 subsamples per template to control within-template discovery variance, following Makou et al.'s protocol); then run the four-part functional battery on every template pair — (a) cross-template edge transfer (unfaithfulness of template A's circuit on template B's data vs. size-matched within-template and random controls), (b) shared-core recovery across all templates, (c) interchange interventions swapping task-relevant intermediate representations across templates to test whether one abstract algorithm covers all templates, and (d) cross-template steering/patching transfer vs. the documented failure case — and finally regress functional invariance on structural concentration (pairwise Jaccard) to validate or falsify the proposed confidence proxy.
why: It targets the field's most consequential live contradiction — whether the "task circuit" exists at all — at the exact point where three 2026 papers (EPFL, Boston University, TU Darmstadt) give conflicting answers and each explicitly defers the missing test; it operationalizes the dual-basis/verification gap that the 2026 retrospective of Sharkey et al. ranks as the field's top open problem; it is safety-critical because interpretability-derived monitors and steering are validated only on their discovery distribution, and this project yields a validated, cheap diagnostic (a template stress test extendable into a new MIB track) for whether they survive shift; it is tractable at toy-to-1B scale with public tooling and standard causal batteries; and it has not been done because the template-variance observation is only months old, the functional-equivalence methodology was only published in June 2026 for a different input axis (token frequency), the disagreement spans three non-communicating sub-communities (optimization, attention-signal tracing, NLP circuit discovery), and the required controls (discovery-variance confounds, size-matched transfer baselines) raise the effort above a quick structural-overlap comparison that no incentive structure has yet rewarded.

direction: Shift mechanistic interpretability from task-specific structural circuits to causally-defined functional units, resolving the just-discovered consistency–specificity/equivalence-class crisis that currently undermines targeted interventions, model editing, and cumulative understanding.
project: Operators, Not Circuits: Discovering Causally-Defined Reusable Computational Units in Language Models
question: Is there a decomposition of an LLM's computation into a small library of causally-defined functional "operators" that is simultaneously consistent across inputs, specific across tasks, and stable across input-distribution shifts — and can task behavior be predicted and intervened upon as a composition of these operators, where structural circuits cannot?
first_experiment: On Llama-3.2-1B (plus Gemma-2-2B for SAE-feature replication), extract per-instance circuits with EAP-IG for 5 structurally matched tasks (IOI, Greater-Than, Addition, subject–verb agreement, CopyColors-MCQA) and reproduce the "consistent but not specific" failure; then compute for each shared-core MLP block a *causal fingerprint* — its causal effect vector across a factorial battery of controlled counterfactual edits (subject/object swap, binding break, quantity edit, negation, reorder, distractor injection) — and test whether (a) fingerprint clusters are stable across tasks and across token-frequency bands (Bayat Makou's transfer test), (b) task identity becomes separable from cluster-usage profiles where it is not from structural circuits, and (c) ablating/scaling a single operator cluster produces predictable, task-targeted behavioral effects that capacity-matched random structural ablations do not.
why: It attacks a field-level bottleneck rather than an incremental method tweak: two independent 2026 results just showed the standard "task circuit" object is unreliable exactly where safety and editing applications need it, and the field's own open-problems agenda lists "what is the right unit of analysis" as unresolved. It is timely (the constructive follow-up window opened only months ago), solo-tractable (1–3B open models, existing tooling, standardized metrics from MIB and the consistency/specificity protocol), and demonstrably not already done — existing work is diagnostic (Li & Subramani; Bayat Makou), structural-reuse documentation (Merullo; Circuit Compositions), representational/comparability infrastructure (CFS/ILP), or training-time (quanta), and none discovers or validates a causally-defined task-general operator basis. A positive result restores the theoretical basis for targeted safety interventions; a rigorous negative result (operators fail the same tests) is equally publishable and would sharpen the field's foundational commitments — either branch moves the field.

direction: Build an automated adversarial adjudication framework that separates competing mechanistic explanations (circuits/attribution graphs) by searching for held-out inputs and interventions where their causal predictions maximally diverge, then testing the real model — converting explanation choice from an aesthetic judgment into a quantitative, non-circular, out-of-sample science.
project: Crucible: Adversarial Adjudication of Competiting Circuit Hypotheses via Held-Out Differential Prediction
question: When two or more circuit/decomposition hypotheses replicate the same model behavior equally well on the discovery distribution, can automated search over held-out inputs × interventions (ablations, patching, steering) find cases where their interventional predictions diverge — and does the hypothesis that empirically survive correspond to the true mechanism, with rankings that are invariant across ablation methodologies (repairing the non-robustness found by Miller et al. 2024) and transferable from ground-truth model organisms to real open-weights LLMs?
first_experiment: On a model organism with known mechanism (Grokking modular addition's Fourier circuit, and/or a tracr-compiled transformer with a known ground-truth circuit), construct the true hypothesis plus 3–5 plausible decoys (wrong-feature variants, subsampled circuits, adversarially chosen decoy graphs) chosen so that all achieve statistically indistinguishable circuit error / replacement score on the discovery distribution; then implement the Crucible harness — for each competing pair, compute predicted post-intervention logits across a grid of held-out inputs and intervention types, run gradient-based search for the maximum predicted-divergence test case, execute it on the real model, and score — with success defined as: the harness ranks the true mechanism first while discovery-distribution faithfulness cannot separate the candidates, and the ranking is invariant across at least three ablation methodologies.
why: It attacks the problem that a mid-2026 state-of-the-field review ranks first among all open methodological questions — the dual-basis/faithfulness problem, where "choosing among decompositions is currently an aesthetic decision" and verification lags labeling by orders of magnitude — and it is the constructive response the field's own leaders have explicitly requested ("automate intervention experiments and synthetic/OOD inputs for hypothesis validation," Nanda & Lindsey, Aug 2025) but nobody has built: every existing effort stops short (per-feature tests that all fail in the NeurIPS 2026 case study, non-identifiability demonstrations without a selection criterion, qualitative virtue frameworks, faithfulness-metric non-robustness diagnoses, and domain-specific stress tests in fly vision), because the required synthesis — treating competing explanations as theories that are adjudicated by automated search for maximally discriminating held-out interventions, à la crucial experiments in science — sits at an unfashionable intersection of philosophy of science and systems engineering that neither the theory nor the tooling camps have claimed; it is tractable with open models, open SAE/transcoder releases and circuit_tracer on modest compute, it upgrades every downstream consumer of attribution graphs (safety monitors, auditing games, feature validation) rather than one model or one circuit, and its first experiment has a decisive, ground-truth-verifiable success criterion, so it cannot degenerate into another circular faithfulness metric.
