direction: Build an automated interventional validation framework that treats circuit and attribution-graph hypotheses as falsifiable causal models, tests their predictions under held-out inputs and novel interventions to quantify each claim's validity scope and adjudicate between behaviorally-identical competing decompositions.
project: ScopeTest — Adversarial Interventional Validation of Circuit Hypotheses
question: Over what domain of inputs and interventions does a circuit hypothesis's causal claim actually hold once it passes in-distribution faithfulness — and can that validity scope be measured automatically, with the measurement able to distinguish between decompositions that are behaviorally indistinguishable on the discovery distribution?
first_experiment: On GPT-2 small, take the published IOI circuit and an ACDC/EAP-IG circuit rediscovered on a subset of template families; hold out the remaining templates and auto-generate a bank of held-out interventional tests (rephrasings, DoubleIO-style algorithm-breaking inputs, composed head ablations, resampling/steering interventions); score each circuit on predicting the sign and magnitude of behavior change under each intervention, measuring (1) the gap between in-distribution faithfulness and out-of-distribution interventional predictive accuracy, (2) whether circuits that pass in-distribution tests diverge on held-out tests, and (3) whether the divergences localize to specific undocumented mechanisms like S2 Hacking — with the same protocol sanity-checked on InterpBench models where the true circuit is known.
why: It attacks the field's most-diagnosed bottleneck (verification, not labeling, is the 2026 constraint; the dual basis problem is the top open problem), it operates on the field's dominant artifact so every improvement multiplies downstream value in monitoring, editing, auditing and transfer, it was explicitly called for by the attribution-graph originators ("automate the validation loop", "auditing games") yet remains unoccupied — existing work stops at in-distribution hypothesis tests (Shi et al. 2024), single-circuit generalization case studies (Nainani et al. 2024), variance diagnostics (Wu et al. 2026), and agents that describe components rather than validate circuit claims (Haklay et al. 2026) — and it is cheap to start (GPT-2 small and Gemma-2-2B on one GPU with open tooling) while producing a publishable result either way: either canonical circuits survive (a quantified validity scope, the first such number for the field's flagship circuit) or they fail out-of-distribution (exactly the rigorous negative result the field says it needs).

direction: Use transcoder-based attribution graphs to determine whether hidden sandbagging mechanisms are legible in the feature graph or buried in error nodes, and build a circuit-level detector benchmarked against the linear-probe baselines that failed the AISI auditing game — including against red-team distractor organisms.
project: Circuit Forensics for Sandbagging: Attribution-Graph Signatures and the Error-Node Blind Spot
question: When a model implements a hidden conditional behavior such as sandbagging, how much of the decision-relevant computation is representable as transcoder features in the attribution graph versus lost in error nodes — and can attribution-graph signatures detect the behavior more robustly than the probe baselines that failed the AISI auditing game, especially under distractor organisms designed to induce false positives?
first_experiment: Train a password-locked Qwen3-4B sandbagging organism (Greenblatt-style SFT) plus AISI-style distractor organisms (language-switching, double-negatives — behavior-preserving decoys); using the pretrained per-layer transcoders in circuit-tracer, trace ~200 sandbagging vs. honest forward passes on identical eval prompts at the answer-commit token; decompose the cue→underperformance influence into feature-node vs. error-node mass; causally validate candidate features by ablation/steering in the transcoder graph; then fit a detector on graph statistics and measure AUROC and false-positive rate on the distractors versus layer-wise difference-in-means probes on the same data.
why: It sits exactly at the intersection of two named, unexecuted open problems — the circuit community's "error nodes are too prevalent and block tracing" plus its proposed auditing-games benchmark, and AISI's explicit call for robust sandbagging detection after its game showed probes, transcripts, and elicitation all fail — so even partial success is a real advance: either a detection modality with causal grounding that shallow monitors lack (obfuscation must still *compute* the behavior somewhere, and the transcoder graph sees routing, not just activations), or the first quantified proof of the blind spot of the field's main auditing instrument on precisely the safety cases where it matters. It has not been done: AISI never ran attribution-graph analysis, the 2026 automated-auditing follow-up reports white-box tools still failing, Tan et al. (2026) do axis-graft elicitation rather than detection, the HTX transcoder-deception paper is a steering demo without organisms or benchmarks, and the closest work (LessWrong SAE analysis of the deception organism) is activation-level with no causal graph, no distractor robustness, and no error-node accounting — while the feasibility is proven by pretrained transcoders running on free Colab GPUs and AISI's open-sourced organisms and red-team playbook.

direction: Merge attribution graphs across prompt families into algorithm-level circuit hypotheses and validate them against model organisms with known ground-truth algorithms, converting the field's dominant per-prompt execution traces into general, testable mechanism claims.
project: From Execution Traces to Algorithms: Cross-Prompt Merging of Attribution Graphs Validated on Ground-Truth Model Organisms
question: Does aligning and merging attribution graphs over a family of prompts recover the general algorithm the model implements — distinguishable from per-case lookup-table features via held-out-prompt prediction, ground-truth subspace alignment, and implementation-chart rank tests?
first_experiment: Generate and merge transcoder-based attribution graphs over an (a,b)-family on a grokked modular-addition transformer with a known Fourier algorithm, and measure whether the merged circuit concentrates in the known cos/sin subspaces, achieves high replacement score on held-out operands, and classifies as a shared-rule rather than lookup-table implementation.
why: It targets the field's self-identified #1 open problem (faithful, non-dual-basis, global rather than per-prompt circuit explanations) at the exact moment the enabling tools and ground-truth organisms matured, is executable with open small-scale tooling, and remains unclaimed because existing automation annotates or compares single graphs rather than merging them into validated algorithm hypotheses.

direction: Mechanistic interpretability of the instruments themselves — quantify, detect, and fix the multi-hop flattening failure of transcoder-based attribution graphs using model organisms with known ground-truth circuits.
project: When Circuit Tracing Lies: Quantifying, Detecting, and Correcting Multi-Hop Flattening in Attribution Graphs
question: When and how do cross-layer transcoder attribution graphs rewrite genuine multi-step computation into shallow feature-to-output shortcuts that match on-distribution behavior, and can an intermediate-intervention consistency test reliably distinguish faithful graphs from unfaithful rewrites that pass standard output-level faithfulness metrics?
first_experiment: Train a small transformer on a synthetic 2–3-hop composition task with hidden bridge entities, causally validate its ground-truth mechanism via probes and patching, train transcoders/CLTs across sparsity levels, extract attribution graphs, and measure shortcut-edge prevalence plus whether an intermediate-consistency score separates faithful graphs from rewrites that both pass output-KL validation.
why: Attribution graphs are the field's dominant artifact and increasingly its safety-audit substrate, yet their documented incentive to flatten multi-hop computation (ICML 2026, toy-only) is unquantified, undiagnosed, and uncorrected — leaving audits vulnerable exactly on multi-step deceptive or dangerous behaviors; the problem is acknowledged but framed as a caution rather than a research program, the groups most expert in the tooling have conflicts of interest, and no quantification, diagnostic, or mitigation exists in the literature as of November 2026.

direction: Resolve the dual-basis problem empirically — treat rival feature decompositions of the same LLM as competing causal hypotheses and use held-out distribution shift as the discriminating experiment, turning decomposition faithfulness into a non-circular, numerical selection target for the first time.
project: Which Decomposition Is the Model's? Quantifying OOD Interventional Divergence Among Feature Dictionaries
question: When multiple decompositions (SAE seeds, architectures, transcoders) of the same model layer reproduce in-distribution behavior, how large is their divergence in predicting the model's actual response to feature interventions on held-out, distribution-shifted inputs — does in-distribution interventional fidelity predict OOD fidelity, and can OOD-divergence-based selection (or training) identify the decomposition whose interventions generalize?
first_experiment: On Gemma-2-2B with public Gemma Scope SAEs (two independent seeds per config) plus 2–4 newly trained variants (TopK/JumpReLU/ReLU, different seeds, optionally a transcoder set) on the same layer: for ~4 behaviors with clean causal handles (IOI, greater-than, factual recall, harmful-request compliance), compute feature attributions per decomposition on in-distribution prompts, use them to *predict* logit effects of feature ablations/boosts, run the real interventions, and score predicted-vs-actual error — first in-distribution, then on shifted distributions (other domains, non-English, adversarial paraphrases) and across intervention-strength sweeps that induce intervention-OOD states. Report (a) the spread of intervention-prediction error across decompositions as a function of shift, (b) the rank correlation between in-distribution and OOD fidelity, and (c) an error decomposition into input-shift, intervention-divergence, and SAE-reconstruction-residual components (adapting the recovery-path attribution of the 2026 clamping-bypass paper). A large spread with weak ID→OOD correlation quantifies the dual-basis problem in a real LLM and validates OOD divergence as a selection signal; a small spread is a publishable negative result that deflates a major worry.
why: It attacks the problem the field's own leadership now ranks first — the dual basis problem and faithfulness-as-a-numerical-target — and it is the keystone under every safety application: monitoring (SAE probes lose to linear probes OOD), steering and unlearning (clamped behavior recovers through the residual), and mechanistic anomaly detection all consume a decomposition whose choice is currently arbitrary, so no downstream guarantee is possible until selection is principled. It has not been done because the pieces matured only in the last 18 months (public dictionaries and circuit-tracer, the degeneracy measurements, the structural non-identifiability theorems, the intervention-divergence theory, the certification statistics) and because the field's incentive structure automated labeling while verification lagged — the nearest neighbors each stop one step short: ISS separates toy causal abstractions, CIF certifies in-distribution estimands, ObserverBench benchmarks observers rather than decompositions, iSAE stabilizes the estimator rather than testing the model, Li et al. predict OOD rules on toy models without comparing causal decompositions, and the cross-family feature paper tests in-distribution necessity only. It is tractable on open-weight models with public tooling on a single-GPU budget, its metric is adoptable by others the way perplexity is, and its main risk (a negative result) would itself redirect a significant fraction of the field's validation effort.

direction: Build predictive-adequacy validation of mechanistic explanations — treat circuits, SAE feature sets, and attribution graphs as falsifiable theories tested on pre-registered distribution-shift families, to quantify their explanatory generalization gap and adjudicate between competing decompositions of the same model.
project: ExGen — Explanatory Generalization: Held-Out Predictive Adequacy as the Standard for Mechanistic Explanations
question: When a mechanistic explanation (circuit, feature set, or attribution graph) is fitted on one task distribution, how much of the model's behavior — successes and errors alike — does it predict under systematic distribution shift, and does held-out predictive power succeed where on-distribution faithfulness fails at distinguishing competing decompositions of the same model?
first_experiment: On GPT-2 small, take the Wang et al. IOI head-circuit, an automated EAP-IG circuit, and two independently trained SAE-based decompositions of the same task; pre-register a battery of shift families (structural variants like DoubleIO/TripleIO, lexical fillers, compositional recombinations, minimal-pair adversarial edits, the model's error subset, and transfer of intervention effects); then measure per-family circuit-vs-model exact answer agreement split by success/error, KL divergence on full output distributions, and intervention-counterfactual agreement — producing the first "explanatory generalization profile" per artifact and the first dual-basis adjudication data point (single GPU-days, all public artifacts).
why: It is the one gap that the field's own roadmap (Sharkey et al. 2025; the 2026 retrospective's top-listed additions), its loudest critics (Hendrycks: explanations lose exactly the edge cases where safety lives), a NeurIPS 2026 position paper, and the newest empirical results (circuits explain 97% of successes but ~11–42% of errors) all independently converge on; it gates every downstream use (automated labels, interpretability agents, safety monitors, and safety cases all need quantified validity domains), it converts the field's hardest foundational problem — the dual basis / non-identifiability (Méloux et al. proved it in toy models but built no selection criterion) — into an empirically decidable question; and it has not been done because the existing work occupies adjacent but disjoint slices: MIB ranks methods on-distribution with same-distribution test sets, Zhang et al. (2026) measure error agreement on-distribution only and label it "necessary but not sufficient," Certified Circuits (2026) certifies discovery stability to dataset edits rather than explanation validity across shift types, Adaptive Circuit Behavior (2024) is a single-task case study with no framework or metric, the anytime-valid SAE-validation line tests individual features rather than whole explanations, and MechEvalAgent (2026) verifies paper reproducibility rather than predictive validity — while the framework proposed here unifies all of these into one pre-registered, falsification-based standard that is cheap enough (small public models, existing SAE releases) for immediate execution and that yields new mechanism discoveries either way it turns out.

direction: Aggregate per-prompt cross-layer-transcoder attribution graphs into task-level circuit-family distributions, validated by held-out generalization, and use per-prompt deviation from the family circuit as a circuit-level mechanistic anomaly detector.
project: Circuit Families — Global Task Circuits from Attribution Graphs for Understanding and Monitoring
question: Can attribution graphs from many prompts of one task be aggregated into a shared task-level circuit distribution that generalizes to held-out prompts and whose per-prompt deviations detect anomalous internal mechanisms better than activation-space baselines?
first_experiment: Generate CLT attribution graphs (circuit-tracer, released Gemma-2-2B transcoders) for ~200 prompts each of two known-hypothesis task families (multi-digit addition, factual recall); aggregate edge weights into per-edge distributions; compare replacement score of family-level pruning vs. per-prompt pruning on held-out prompts, test edge-distribution multimodality against known mechanistic diversity, and run a cross-prompt edge-correlation ablation as the falsification check.
why: The method's own community lists "merge attribution graphs into a global picture" as an open problem and no 2026 work does it — closest efforts (DCD, Circuit-Diff's un-evaluated aggregation tool, patch-effect graph kernels, single-task Sparse Feature Circuits) each stop one step short; it is feasible on one GPU with released CLTs; it converts the tool's biggest weakness (local, ~25%-satisfying graphs, noisy edges) into its biggest opportunity (shared structure = signal), answers the newly-discovered mechanistic-diversity problem with a distributional representation, and yields exactly the validation and monitoring capabilities (falsifiable held-out predictions, circuit-level anomaly detection) that the field's reviews identify as its sharpest unsolved gaps.

direction: Shift circuit tracing from per-prompt "execution traces" to distributional circuit analysis — attribution graphs sampled over the model's own output distribution on a fixed prompt, with causal identification of the feature-level arbiters that decide between competing continuations.
project: Distributional Circuit Tracing: Explaining the Sampling Distribution, Not Just One Trajectory
question: When a model can plausibly produce multiple continuations from the same prompt, how do attribution graphs relate across sampled trajectories, and which internal feature-level circuits causally arbitrate between the competing outcomes (including the rare/tail branches)?
first_experiment: Using the open circuit-tracer library with cross-layer transcoders on Gemma-2-2B (plus Qwen3-4B and R1-Distill-1.5B for reasoning forks), take ~15 "fork" prompts across 4 categories (close-call factual recall with strong competitor answers, ambiguous questions with two defensible answers, borderline-safety compliance, arithmetic with common-wrong answers), sample ~50 trajectories each at deployment temperature, generate one attribution graph per trajectory, then measure: (1) the outcome distribution per prompt; (2) a Graph Stability Index — node/edge overlap within-outcome vs. across-outcome trajectories, with fork-token entropy vs. graph-divergence correlation; (3) pre-fork arbitration analysis — since trajectories share the prefix up to the fork token, test which feature activations at shared positions discriminate eventual outcomes; (4) causal spot-checks — steer/ablate the top candidate "arbiter" features across branch contexts and measure the induced shift in the outcome distribution, not just the next sampled token.
why: It attacks a foundational validity gap that the field's own leaders flagged as open but no one has filled — attribution graphs "explain why a model behaved one way... but not why it didn't behave a different way" and are "execution traces rather than general algorithms" (Circuits Research Landscape, Aug 2025) — and it does so on the axis that matters most for deployment: agent and reasoning models act stochastically, tail-risk behaviors are distributional, self-consistency/RLVR/best-of-N all live on this distribution, and CoT-monitorability debates assume we can distinguish reliable reasoning from lucky sampling. It also unifies the two hottest threads of 2025–26: the statistical-rigor turn in circuit discovery (which has only varied inputs and analyst choices) and the branching/entropy turn in reasoning models (which has only worked at the token/text level). It has not already been done: I verified systematically that (a) all variance/certification work (Méloux et al., CEAP, Makou et al., CIRCUS, Certified Circuits) varies datasets, templates, or pruning thresholds — never the model's sampling; (b) distributional rollout attribution exists only at the text level (Thought Anchors, Macar et al.), with AttriCoT explicitly naming internal feature circuits over distributions as out of scope; (c) entropy neurons and high-entropy minority tokens are token-level phenomena without circuit-level causal accounts; and (d) no paper through at least October 2026 samples multiple rollouts of one prompt and performs feature-circuit attribution plus causal arbitration testing — while the inexpensive first experiment, decisive whichever way it lands, can be run today on fully open tooling before Anthropic, Goodfire, or the landscape-report authors claim it.

direction: Build the constructive counterpart to the now well-documented non-identifiability of circuits — an active adjudication methodology that discriminates between behaviorally-equivalent rival mechanistic hypotheses by searching for inputs/interventions where their predictions diverge and testing which one the network actually follows (or certifying that no reachable test separates them).
project: Adjudicating Rival Circuits — Discriminating Tests for Behaviorally-Equivalent Mechanistic Hypotheses
question: When multiple circuit hypotheses are behaviorally equivalent on-distribution, can a systematic procedure find task-valid inputs and interventions where their predictions diverge, reliably determine which hypothesis the real network sides with, and formally certify when the choice is inconsequential (benign multiplicity) versus consequential under distribution shift (malign multiplicity)?
first_experiment: On IOI in GPT-2 small, assemble at least three rival circuit hypotheses that all pass standard in-distribution faithfulness — the Wang et al. hand-built circuit, an ACDC extraction, and an EAP-IG extraction (all available via MIB tooling) — confirm that standard metrics (faithfulness, completeness, minimality, overlap) cannot separate them, then run the multi-hypothesis generalization of uit de Bos & Garriga-Alonso's evolutionary input search to maximize pairwise disagreement between the hypotheses' outputs, and on each maximally-disagreeing input record which hypothesis the full network's output matches — yielding either a consistent winner, a regime map (different hypotheses win on different input families), or an indistinguishability certificate; validate the procedure in parallel on InterpBench planted-ground-truth models, where we know which candidate mechanism is real.
why: It attacks the dual basis problem, which both the field's coalition review (2025) and its 2026 retrospectives rank as the single most important open methodological question — the question that currently blocks trust in interpretability-derived safety monitors and audit claims, and that turns interpretability from "one of many valid stories" into a testable science. It has not been done: every 2024–2026 paper in this space either diagnoses multiplicity (Méloux, Sheng & Fu, Bayat Makou, Explanation Multiplicity), tests a single circuit against the network (Adversarial Circuit Evaluation), stabilizes component selection (Certified Circuits), recovers effect maps (Mechanistic Tomography), or evaluates observers for control (ObserverBench) — none generates discriminating experiments between rival hypotheses and adjudicates among them. It is newly feasible only now (InterpBench's planted mechanisms, MIB's standardized rival circuits, and mature adversarial-search machinery all appeared within the last ~18 months), it runs on models small enough for an independent researcher, its outputs — an open adjudication suite, the first empirical characterization of equivalence-class structure in real models, and "decomposition disagreement" as a distribution-shift alarm — directly plug the verification bottleneck that the field itself has identified as its rate limiter.

direction: Build the missing validation layer for attribution graphs — methods and model organisms that reliably distinguish a circuit decomposition that recovers the model's actual mechanism from a behaviorally-equivalent "decoy" decomposition (e.g., a shallow rewrite of a multi-hop circuit), turning circuit-tracing claims into falsifiable predictions.
project: Decoy Circuits: A Ground-Truth Benchmark and Test Suite for Detecting Unfaithful Attribution-Graph Decompositions
question: When an attribution graph accounts for a model's behavior on-distribution, can a battery of cheap, principled tests — compositional OOD perturbations, error-agreement on failure cases, cross-decomposition consensus (PLT vs CLT vs raw neurons), and unexplained-computation routing through error nodes — reliably separate faithful circuits from sparsity-induced shallow rewrites, first where the true mechanism is known by construction, then on real LLM multi-hop tasks?
first_experiment: Train small transformers (plus Tracr-compiled controls) on a synthetic multi-hop task where data design controls whether the model learns the deep hop-by-hop mechanism or a behaviorally-equivalent shallow shortcut (mechanism verified by ablation); train CLTs/PLTs across a sparsity-penalty sweep to elicit both decomposition types; then run the candidate discriminating test battery against known ground truth and report which tests (or ensemble) achieves high decoy-detection AUC — the port to Gemma-2-2B's public transcoders via circuit-tracer follows immediately if it works.
why: It targets the field's own top-ranked, freshly-opened problem: the dominant artifact (attribution graphs) was just shown (July 2026) capable of systematic, incentive-driven unfaithfulness, yet no systematic detection method, benchmark, or protocol exists — existing work stops at demonstrating the failure mode, and the OOD-validation and error-agreement paradigms were developed in disjoint toy settings and never combined with attribution graphs. It is uniquely feasible for a small lab (public CLTs run on free Colab; model organisms are tiny), it converts "verification lagged labeling" — the field's diagnosed bottleneck — into concrete tooling, and it protects every downstream consumer of circuit hypotheses: interpretability-based safety audits and monitors are exactly the systems that a shallow-rewrite decoy could fool, since a deception or hidden-objective mechanism rewritten as benign-looking shallow feature sums would still match observed behavior. It has not been done because the failure mode is only months old, the public transcoder infrastructure that makes the real-model test cheap is only a year old, and the field's energy has gone into building and applying graphs rather than adversarially validating them.

direction: Extend mechanistic interpretability from single-turn "model biology" to the deployment-relevant multi-turn regime by causally reverse-engineering how LLM agents read, bind, and maintain tool results and task state across turns.
project: Where Does the Agent Keep Its Notes? A Mechanistic Anatomy of Tool-Result Integration and Task-State Tracking in Multi-Turn LLM Agents
question: When a multi-turn LLM agent uses information from an earlier tool result to select its next action, which attention heads and features read that result, is binding content-keyed (robust) or positional/format-based (attackable), and which context positions are causally load-bearing for task state?
first_experiment: On Qwen3-4B (supported by circuit-tracer CLTs) with a synthetic 5-10 turn tool-calling trace whose final action provably depends on one value V from a tool result at turn t: (1) corrupt V's KV entries layer-by-layer, position-by-position and re-run the continuation, producing the first layer×position causal dependency map of tool-result integration in an agent loop; (2) localize the "reading" heads via value-path patching and attention analysis restricted to patched positions; (3) run a content-vs-position test — replay a different value in matching format at a shifted position (a controlled TRAP-style misbinding) to determine whether binding is content-keyed or positional, with random-position and format-only controls and a replication in a second model (GPT-OSS-20B or Llama-3.1-8B).
why: It attacks a problem the field's own strategic documents flag as the next frontier yet untouched mechanistically — DeepMind lists multiturn/agentic interpretability as far out of reach, an ICML 2026 position paper demands it, and the Neuronpedia roadmap asks how models aggregate information over long contexts and what state-tracking algorithms they use. Everything adjacent is the wrong level: TRAP demonstrates misbinding behaviorally without explaining it; Tokengeist attributes provenance through a black-box interface; probe-based work (WMIP, pre-action monitors, latent-persistence studies) is correlational; the one circuit paper covers external memory frameworks, not the in-context loop. No one has produced causal evidence of how tool results are read, bound, and used across turns. It only became tractable in the last ~18 months (open reasoning+tool models with interp infrastructure, nnsight-style KV interventions, sparse-attention scaling), so the window is open but closing. And the payoff is direct and practical: a mechanistic account of binding predicts which agent failures (misbinding, injection susceptibility, "silent" memory loss) arise from which circuits; the layer×position dependency map yields principled KV-eviction/summarization policies that preserve load-bearing state (directly informing the behavioral KV-compression-safety literature); and head/feature signatures give monitoring signals that the 2026 probe-monitoring papers showed are unreliable when read naively. For a solo researcher, it is the rare combination: frontier-flagged, tool-ready, safety-critical, and not yet staked.

direction: Make circuit explanations falsifiable by building ground-truth "dual-basis" model organisms and a held-out interventional discrimination metric that exposes whether the field's standard faithfulness evidence can certify mechanistically wrong attribution graphs.
project: Adversarial Faithfulness: Model Organisms and a Non-Circular Metric for Validating Attribution Graphs
question: When an attribution graph (or any feature decomposition) achieves high replacement/faithfulness scores on the evaluation distribution, does it actually recover the model's mechanism — or is it one of several decompositions consistent with the observed behavior that diverge under interventions on held-out inputs, and can a principled battery of held-out discriminating interventions separate the true circuit from decoys without access to ground truth?
first_experiment: On an InterpBench SIIT transformer with a known ground-truth circuit, train per-layer transcoders on a deliberately narrow prompt distribution, extract attribution graphs with the standard pipeline (circuit-tracer), then construct a "decoy" graph perturbation — swapping ground-truth edges for alternatives chosen to preserve replacement score on the training distribution — and measure three quantities: (i) replacement score in-distribution (standard evidence), (ii) ground-truth edge/feature precision-recall, and (iii) behavioral prediction error under a small battery of interventions on held-out, distribution-shifted inputs. Success criterion: a quantified circularity gap — decoy graphs passing (i) while failing (ii) and (iii) — which both demonstrates the problem and validates the discriminating-intervention protocol as the seed of the new metric.
why: It attacks the single gap most consistently named as top priority by the field itself — the Sharkey et al. faithfulness problem, the 2026 retrospective's "dual basis problem" and "faithfulness as a numerical target," and the multi-lab circuits report's call for downstream tasks that actually measure understanding. It has not been done because the pieces only became available recently: ground-truth organisms (SIIT, 2024) predate the attribution-graph paradigm (2025) and were never connected to it, the statistics community delivered interventional-rigor tooling (CIF, 2026) without ground-truth discrimination, and the field rushed through automated labeling/analysis faster than verification infrastructure could form — the retrospective shows validation is now *the* asymmetric bottleneck. The project is feasible at GPT-2/1B scale with open weights, open transcoder tooling, and a few GPU-days for the first experiment; its output (decoy organisms + metric + honest evaluation of the dominant pipelines) compounds across every downstream use of interpretability — auditing, monitoring, editing — and directly serves safety by replacing the field's current, gameable standard of evidence with a falsifiable one.

direction: Build the first mechanistic developmental study of evaluation awareness — determining when across pretraining and post-training "I am being evaluated" becomes internally readable, causally load-bearing, and behaviorally expressed in open models.
project: The Ontogeny of Evaluation Awareness: When Do Language Models Learn That They Are Being Tested?
question: When during training (pretraining, SFT, DPO/RLVR) do language models first internally represent, causally use, and behaviorally act on the evaluation-vs-deployment distinction — and is this disposition inherited from pretraining or installed by post-training?
first_experiment: Run a fixed contrastive battery of ~2–4k evaluation-vs-deployment prompts through all public OLMo-2-7B checkpoints (pretraining intermediates + SFT/DPO/RLVR stages, integrity-audited) and Pythia-1.4B/6.9B checkpoints, train layer-wise logistic probes with matched controls at every checkpoint, and plot the internal-readability emergence curve — correlating onset with dated exposure to exam-like text in OLMo's open data and with the first checkpoint showing behavioral eval/deployment divergence.
why: Evaluation awareness is the exact internal property that enables sandbagging and alignment faking, yet every existing probe/steering result is on final models, so nobody knows whether it is inherited (unremovable, must be monitored during training) or installed by post-training (a targetable intervention window) — and the field's own 2026 retrospective identifies monitoring-coverage gaps and unvalidated artifacts as its core weaknesses; the developmental-interp toolkit has just matured for tasks and linguistic features, a behavioral-only sycophancy-across-stages paper appeared two weeks ago proving demand, and the persona-subspace work explicitly leaves provenance open, so the safety-critical disposition case is an unclaimed, methodologically de-risked intersection — feasible in a few GPU-days with fully public checkpoints, stimuli, and a pre-registered readable/behavioral/causal three-track protocol whose every outcome changes how labs monitor training.

direction: Use out-of-distribution interventional divergence — the degradation of a decomposition's predicted behavior under interventions on distribution-shifted inputs — as a validated, non-circular criterion for selecting among behaviorally equivalent decompositions (SAEs, transcoders, attribution graphs) of the same model.
project: Which Decomposition Is the Circuit? Distribution Shift as a Non-Circular Test of Mechanistic Faithfulness
question: Among decompositions that are behaviorally equivalent on the training distribution, does out-of-distribution interventional divergence identify the decomposition that tracks the model's actual mechanism, and can "shift-invariant interventional fidelity" serve as a practical faithfulness metric and training objective where current metrics are non-robust or circular?
first_experiment: In a Boolean multi-hop model organism with known ground-truth computation (extending the ICML 2026 CLT unfaithfulness setup), train a family of decompositions — cross-layer transcoders under varying sparsity penalties, plus per-layer transcoders — selected so they all match on-distribution behavior; then measure, for each decomposition, agreement between its predicted behavior and the real model's behavior under (a) interventions on intermediate variables and (b) shift families (longer chains, novel compositions, ablated hops). Metric: correlation between each decomposition's shift-divergence profile and ground-truth graph recovery. Prediction: on-distribution-equivalent decompositions split under shift, and shift-invariance correlates with mechanism recovery; if instead all decompositions diverge equally (or faithful ones diverge too), that is itself the key falsification result about environment-relativity of mechanisms. Follow-ups: replicate on grokked modular arithmetic (Fourier-basis ground truth) and GPT-2 IOI, where competing published decompositions exist.
why: It targets the field's own top-ranked open problem (the dual basis problem, per the June 2026 state-of-field review, and the validation problem per Sharkey et al. 2025), and 2026's strongest negative results — CLTs learning unfaithful circuits, faithfulness metrics' ablation sensitivity, SAE seed non-identifiability, and SAE OOD compositional failure — created the demand for exactly the missing piece: a principled tie-breaker among equivalent decompositions. It has not been done because adjacent work stops one step short: the ICML 2026 CLT paper demonstrates one unfaithfulness mode and blames sparsity but offers no general detection or selection method and no shift analysis; Certified Interventional Fidelity provides statistical machinery for single claims but treats sensitivity to the intervention distribution as a caveat rather than a discriminator; the iSAE and feature-consistency lines establish statistical stability, not mechanistic correctness; "Stop Probing, Start Coding" shows SAE *codes* fail OOD for concept recovery but doesn't rank decompositions as explanations of computation; and the non-linear representation dilemma proves underdetermination theoretically while explicitly leaving the positive program ("studying the connection between information-encoding assumptions and causal abstraction") as future work. This direction is also feasible for an individual researcher — model organisms plus open tooling (CLT-Forge, Gemma Scope, nnsight) at toy-to-GPT-2 scale — unlike the compute-heavy alternatives (cross-architecture universality, frontier-model scaling), and unlike already-crowded niches (feature validation at scale, deployment monitors). It upgrades the entire stack: a validated faithfulness criterion is the prerequisite for trustworthy features, robust safety monitors, and falsifiable circuit claims.

direction: Mechanistically characterize and predict the auditability of trained-in behaviors via their causal isolation — the dimensionality and intervention-robustness of the subspace mediating them — as the explanatory variable behind why white-box interpretability tools succeed or fail across training methodologies and obfuscation.
project: The Causal Isolation Hypothesis of Auditability
question: Does the internal causal organization of a trained-in hidden behavior predict whether white-box auditing tools can recover it, better than behavior strength, capability damage, or output naturalness, across training methodologies and adversarial obfuscation?
first_experiment: On the released behavior-strength-matched Model Organism Lottery suite (61 organisms, 7 training methods, 2 architectures), measure per-organism causal isolation of the quirk (activation-difference subspace rank, ablation/project-out survival of the behavior, and base↔organism patching mediation per layer) and test whether these metrics predict the suite's published audit-tool success rates, controlling for behavior strength and organism damage.
why: Three 2026 benchmarks independently found white-box tools fail unpredictably in auditing settings, but the field explains this only with coarse correlates — no one has measured the behavior's internal causal structure as the predictor, making this the highest-leverage, tractable (all organisms public, 1–14B scale), and genuinely unclaimed mechanistic gap at the intersection of the field's top safety application (auditing) and its most surprising recent negative results.

direction: Treat learned feature decompositions (SAEs, transcoders, attribution graphs) as underdetermined causal hypotheses and build an adversarial "twin decomposition" methodology plus an interventional identification metric that empirically determines which part of a decomposition — directions, subspaces, or equivalence classes — the model's actual causal behavior pins down.
project: Twin Decompositions: Adversarial Identification Tests and an Interventional Faithfulness Gap Metric for Feature Dictionaries
question: Two feature decompositions that are statistically indistinguishable under every standard on-distribution evaluation (reconstruction loss, sparsity, probing, autointerp labels, on-distribution steering/patching effects) — does the model's causal response to held-out interventions distinguish them, and if so, what is the minimal, safe battery of interventions that does, and what structure (direction vs. subspace vs. equivalence class) of the decomposition does that battery uniquely identify?
first_experiment: On GPT-2-small with public residual-stream SAEs and the fully-mapped IOI circuit as a known-answer test (using MIB's IOI dataset with held-out names/objects): (1) take the released SAE as decomposition D1 and validate IOI-relevant latents via attribution patching; (2) construct a twin D2 by constrained retraining — an invertible linear mixing of maximally co-active latents plus encoder refit such that reconstruction FVU, L0, per-latent activation profiles, autointerp labels, and on-distribution IOI patching/steering effects all match D1 within reseed-noise thresholds (per Chanin et al.'s minimum-reliable-difference method), while decoder geometry differs off-manifold; (3) demonstrate D1 and D2 are indistinguishable under the full standard SAEBench-style suite; (4) run a held-out interventional battery (zero-ablation, magnitude scaling ×0.25–4, cross-pair recombination along the mixing directions, counterfactual patching), and score each twin's predicted effect against the realized model effect, reporting the Interventional Identification Gap — the fraction of the battery on which the twins disagree — together with a taxonomy of which interventions are safe discriminators vs. pernicious (dormant-pathway-recruiting) in Grant et al.'s sense. Fits on one GPU; a week of compute.
why: It targets the problem the field itself now ranks first — the dual basis problem / absence of a non-circular faithfulness measure — at the moment when attribution graphs have become the standard artifact and millions of unverified feature labels are flowing into safety monitors. It is not already done because: Leask et al. demonstrated non-uniqueness but only at the reconstruction level and explicitly deferred identification; Guo et al. proved observational non-identification only for single-feature selection, not whole decompositions, and never built rival decompositions; MIB benchmarks localization *given* a decomposition, not the identity of decompositions (and found SAEs no better than neurons — a symptom of exactly this gap); the benchmark audit found no reliable quality metric and proposed none; and the two position papers call for identification assumptions without providing an operational method. Moreover, the first experiment is genuinely two-sided: if the twins separate, the field gains its first quantitative, ground-truthed interventional faithfulness metric (a natural MIB-v2 track and a verification tool for the label-verification bottleneck); if they cannot be separated by any safe intervention, that establishes — against the field's working assumption — that the canonical unit is the causally-identified equivalence class or subspace (consistent with the "unstable features, reproducible subspaces" finding), which redirects what "feature" should mean everywhere downstream, from steering and unlearning to deception monitoring.

direction: Find and exploit the mechanistic substrate of cross-turn in-context state persistence (registers vs. re-derivation) in agentic LLM rollouts, to build monitors and interventions that work where static per-token probes fail.
project: Where Does an Agent Keep Its Secrets? Write/Read Dynamics of In-Context State Across Rollout Turns
question: Do models store cross-turn states (concealed goals, monitoring beliefs, intentions) as localized register representations written once and re-read via attention, or re-derive them per turn — and can state-write/read events serve as robust monitoring and intervention targets?
first_experiment: Cross-turn probe-transfer test on 100 paired planted-secret vs. benign multi-turn rollouts in Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct: train turn-1 "goal-state" probes, evaluate unretrained transfer at every (layer, position) in later pre-action turns, plus attention-flow analysis from later decision tokens back to turn-1 positions; then localize with cross-turn KV patching and attribution graphs.
why: It targets the 2026 field's sharpest confluence of diagnosed gaps — multi-turn/agentic interpretability explicitly out of reach (GDM), static probes failing pre-action in agentic contexts (three negative results), single-prompt attribution graphs — with a cheap, falsifiable first experiment on open weights, and it is genuinely unoccupied: the closest work (Tokengeist, KV-cache patching, concealment/eval-awareness probing) stops one step short of feature-level cross-turn state dynamics.

direction: Establish "mechanistic generalization" as the field's selection criterion — build a benchmark and metric that adjudicate among equally-faithful decompositions (circuits, SAE features, attribution graphs) by whether their mechanistic claims predict model responses to interventions on held-out, distribution-shifted inputs, replacing aesthetic choice in the equivalence class with a testable standard.
project: "Does Your Circuit Survive Shift? A Held-Out Interventional Validity Benchmark for Ranking Mechanistic Decompositions"
question: When multiple decompositions of the same behavior are equally faithful in-distribution, does in-distribution faithfulness predict which decomposition's mechanistic claims (component roles, causal effect signs and magnitudes, error accounts) generalize to held-out inputs and interventions — and which principled criteria (mechanism description length, diversity of the discovery distribution, resampling stability, alignment with model-intrinsic structure such as the Koopman fingerprint) select the decomposition that generalizes?
first_experiment: On GPT-2-small and Pythia-160M (IOI, subject-verb agreement) using MIB's data pipeline, extract K=8 circuits per task with EAP-IG from K disjoint discovery mixtures (2 templates × 2 entity sets × 2 seeds); verify all reach ≥95% in-distribution faithfulness; then, on two held-out distributions (unseen templates, unseen entity/frequency bands), measure each circuit's (a) standard faithfulness, (b) interventional predictive validity — the rank correlation between each edge's in-distribution causal effect and its held-out causal effect under the same patching protocol, controlling for context distortion via intact-signal restoration — and (c) error-reproduction agreement on held-out error prompts; finally compute the rank correlation between in-distribution faithfulness and each held-out metric across candidates (with CIF-style anytime-valid confidence sequences), plus a feature-level replication on Gemma-2-2B with Gemma Scope SAEs. A weak correlation founds the benchmark; a strong one is an equally informative negative result that recalibrates the field's worry.
why: It attacks the field's self-identified top methodological bottleneck — the dual basis problem and the verification asymmetry — at the moment a dense 2025–2026 diagnosis literature (non-identifiability, faithfulness misranking, phantom specialization, template variance, success-bias) has made the problem impossible to ignore while leaving the constructive question untouched; it has not been done because every existing effort stops short: MIB tests held-out items within-template, Certified Circuits certifies only subsampling stability of inclusion decisions, CIF fixes the distribution rather than testing generalization across it, the Koopman fingerprint is intrinsic-but-not-legible, compositional interpretability is formal without empirics, and Li et al. is a toy-model observational proof of concept with no formal decompositions, pretrained models, or benchmark — while the June 2026 retrospective confirms ranking decompositions remains "an aesthetic decision"; it is the most promising direction because it converts a crowded diagnosis space into a constructive framework with direct safety payoff (steering and monitoring built on a decomposition inherit exactly these OOD failure modes, which is where current interpretability-based safety applications demonstrably fail), and because it is tractable end-to-end on open models and infrastructure rather than requiring frontier-scale compute.

direction: Build the missing selection criterion for mechanistic explanations — rank competing decompositions by counterfactual fidelity (held-out inputs, shifts, and interventions) rather than in-distribution fit, using ground-truth model organisms.
project: Counterfactual Fidelity: Selecting Among Competing Decompositions by Predicting Where the Model Breaks
question: When multiple decompositions of the same model reproduce its behavior on the fitted distribution, can a cheap observable property of a decomposition (graph stability under input resampling, feature-reuse/absorption rates, traced-path depth profile, error coverage) predict which decomposition's circuits track the model's actual mechanism out-of-distribution?
first_experiment: Train ≥4 decompositions (SAEs across seeds/sparsity incl. high-L1 shallow-rewrite-prone variants, plus a transcoder) on a Tracr/InterpBench transformer with a known multi-hop program; confirm comparable reconstruction loss and in-distribution faithfulness; measure each decomposition's circuit agreement with the model on held-out prompts, on resample/mean ablations not used in construction, and on model errors; then test whether the candidate cheap statistics rank decompositions by their measured counterfactual-fidelity gap.
why: The 2026 retrospective of Sharkey et al.'s Open Problems singles out the dual basis problem — many decompositions explain the same behavior and we choose among them by aesthetics — as the field's most important open methodological question; the first diagnoses (ICML 2026: sparsity incentives produce unfaithful shallow rewrites; Sept 2026: circuits reproduce successes but not errors) appeared only months ago and none proposes a selection rule, while all existing validation is within-decomposition (SAEBench-type), per-feature, or in-distribution (EAP-IG). The criterion compounds across every downstream use (monitors, audits, steering), doubles as a mechanistic anomaly detector via decomposition-disagreement signals, and is runnable on free open infrastructure (Tracr, InterpBench, Gemma Scope, circuit-tracer) — high importance, low occupancy, immediate feasibility, and a valuable publishable result in either experimental branch.

direction: Distill families of per-prompt attribution graphs into a single task-level circuit hypothesis validated by held-out behavioral prediction, making circuit faithfulness measurable and decomposition choice principled.
project: Traces to Algorithms: Distilling Families of Attribution Graphs into Validated Task-Level Circuits
question: Can per-prompt attribution graphs over a task be merged into one (possibly branched) feature-level algorithm whose critical nodes and edges predict model behavior on held-out and counterfactual prompts as well as per-prompt graphs, at far lower cost?
first_experiment: On Gemma-2-2B with released cross-layer transcoders, generate ~80 attribution graphs for two-hop factual-recall prompts (30% held out), cluster features into cross-prompt role supernodes, aggregate a consensus weighted DAG, and validate it on held-out prompts via per-prompt replacement score, necessity/sufficiency patching on predicted-critical vs. predicted-irrelevant edges, and intermediate-entity counterfactuals.
why: It is the explicitly requested, still-open constructive response to the field's three converging negative results (non-identifiability, phantom specialization, "graphs are execution traces, not algorithms"), it subsumes the missing faithfulness metric and dual-basis ranking in one object, the infrastructure (public CLTs, stable feature IDs) only matured in late 2025 while 2025–26 effort went to describing/querying/scaling graphs rather than unifying them — so the gap is real, timely, and tractable on one GPU.

direction: Build an automated adjudication method for mechanistic interpretability — treat competing explanations (circuits, attribution graphs, SAE decompositions) as hypotheses, search for inputs where their behavioral predictions diverge, and use the model's actual responses to rank explanations, quantify how underdetermined mechanisms are on natural data, and surface hidden behaviors that natural-distribution analysis misses.
project: Falsification-First Interpretability: Adjudicating Competing Mechanistic Hypotheses via Divergence-Seeking Input Search
question: When two mechanistic explanations of a model's behavior are behaviorally indistinguishable on the natural data distribution, can we automatically find plausible inputs on which they make divergent predictions, does the model's actual behavior on those inputs consistently adjudicate between them, how much of the plausible input space leaves the mechanism underdetermined, and does explanation-extrapolation probing expose hidden mechanisms invisible to natural-distribution interpretability?
first_experiment: On GPT-2 small with three independently trained transcoder/SAE decompositions of the same layers (open CLT-Forge/Gemma-Scope-style checkpoints, different seeds and sparsity), first verify ID-equivalence by extracting the IOI circuit from each and confirming statistically indistinguishable replacement scores on the task distribution; then run gradient-based token-level disagreement search (straight-through/Gumbel relaxation over token embeddings with a reference-LM fluency penalty) to maximize pairwise KL divergence between the three replacement models' output predictions on IOI templates; finally, run the true model on the discovered discriminating inputs and score each decomposition's prediction of the actual behavior to obtain (a) the underdetermination curve (divergence achievable as a function of distance from the data manifold), (b) adjudication win-rate versus chance, and (c) a calibration control on a toy transformer with a known ground-truth unique circuit to measure false adjudication. Feasible on one GPU in days; either outcome — a working adjudicator with a consistent winner, or demonstrated behavioral-equivalence robustness — is a decisive, publishable result that quantifies the dual basis problem for the first time and directly extends to AuditBench models as the follow-up safety experiment.
why: It attacks the field's self-declared top open problem (the dual basis problem / non-circular faithfulness, named "the open problem I would put at the top of any new survey" in the 2026 retrospective of Sharkey et al.'s open-problems paper) and the exact item the practitioners' roadmap lists as undone ("automate synthetic/OOD inputs used for hypothesis validation"), yet it is not already done: the 2024–2026 literature either diagnoses the problem (faithfulness metrics not robust; SAE non-canonicality; circuit-discovery variance; NeurIPS 2026's formalization of evaluation aliasing), stabilizes decompositions against retraining (iSAE), or partitions observed inputs for a single hypothesis (Bucketing the Good Apples) — none adjudicates among alternatives via input search, and the only OOD-prediction proof-of-concept (Li et al. 2025) is synthetic, observational, and decomposition-free. It became tractable only in the last 18 months, when open transcoders (CLT-Forge, circuit-tracer), Gemma Scope, and AuditBench removed the cost barrier to obtaining multiple alternative decompositions and hidden-behavior testbeds; it needs no frontier-scale compute, so a small team can execute it now; it yields a reusable, non-circular, behavior-grounded faithfulness metric the field lacks; and unlike adjacent hot areas (label verification, cross-architecture transfer, monitor-training dynamics), it bridges the field's central methodological gap to its most concrete safety application — auditing models for hidden behaviors, where AuditBench shows white-box tools currently lose to black-box ones because they cannot extrapolate beyond natural data, which is precisely the failure mode this method is designed to fix.

direction: Operationalize the "dual basis problem" for attribution graphs by treating each graph as a runnable, falsifiable replacement model whose held-out predictive adequacy — measured across independently trained decompositions and calibrated against known ground-truth mechanisms — becomes the field's first quantitative admissibility standard for circuit explanations.
project: Graphs on Trial: Held-Out Predictive Adequacy as a Test of Attribution-Graph Faithfulness Across Decompositions
question: When two independently trained feature decompositions both produce attribution graphs that explain a model's behavior on the prompts they were built from, do their pruned replacement models make convergent or divergent predictions on held-out and counterfactual inputs — and does held-out predictive adequacy, checked against known ground-truth mechanisms, identify the faithful decomposition?
first_experiment: On GPT-2 small (greater-than task, known neuron algorithm) and a modular-addition transformer (known Fourier-rotation algorithm), build attribution graphs from at least two independent dictionaries/transcoder seeds using the standard pipeline, construct each graph's runnable pruned replacement model, and measure (i) replacement-vs-full-model agreement on held-out years/operands and algorithm-breaking counterfactuals, and (ii) cross-decomposition agreement of those out-of-distribution predictions, then test whether disagreement localizes nodes/edges that deviate from the known true mechanism.
why: It targets what a 2026 state-of-the-field review calls the field's most important methodological open problem — explanations are currently ranked by label readability, not evidence — and the dominant artifact of the field (attribution graphs) lacks any held-out, cross-decomposition validation despite being cited as evidence for safety-critical claims; it has not been done because existing work stops at feature-level falsification, adjacent-layer operator margins and seed overlap, one toy unfaithfulness mode, component-level benchmarks, or single-prompt replications, and because the "graph as runnable predictive model" reframing that makes systematic falsification cheap only became available with the recent transcoder tooling.

direction: Make attribution graphs falsifiable at the distribution level — measure whether transcoder-based circuit explanations predict real LLM behavior under distribution shift, and quantify the dual-basis problem by comparing decompositions that agree in-distribution but diverge off-distribution.
project: Falsifiable Circuits: Distribution-Level Validation of Attribution Graphs and the Dual-Basis Problem
question: Do attribution graphs built on seed prompts predict a model's behavior and intervention outcomes on held-out prompt families, and when two decompositions (e.g., CLT vs. PLT, different seeds/sparsities) are matched in on-distribution faithfulness, do their off-distribution intervention predictions diverge — and can divergence rank decompositions by something other than label aesthetics?
first_experiment: On GPT-2-small's greater-than task ("The war lasted from the year 1711 to 17") using public CLTs and PLTs via circuit-tracer: generate attribution graphs for 50 seed prompts per decomposition variant (CLT, PLT, ≥2 seeds, ≥2 sparsity levels), verify matched on-distribution replacement scores, then on 200 held-out greater-than prompts stratified by distance from seed support (different centuries, corpora, number ranges) apply feature ablation/steering on each graph's top causal nodes and compute the Spearman correlation between graph-predicted and actual logit deltas, plus inter-decomposition prediction divergence. A single GPU, a few days, and it either demonstrates a working discriminative validation metric (or shows current graphs generalize well — also publishable), while directly testing the qualitative "lookup table vs. geometry" anecdote from the landscape report.
why: It attacks the gap the field's own 2025 review and its 2026 retrospective rank first — the verification bottleneck and dual-basis problem — at exactly the point where theory (identifiability results, implementation charts, the pragmatic "predictive standard") and infrastructure (open transcoders, circuit-tracer, Neuronpedia) have just made it tractable but before anyone has claimed the empirical middle ground. It is feasible on small open models without frontier access, every outcome is informative (a standard faithfulness-under-shift metric either becomes the field's missing benchmark — as MIB did for localization — or exposes that current explanations fail the field's stated goal of predicting behavior in unseen situations), and it multiplies the value of all downstream work, since monitoring, auditing, unlearning and anomaly detection all inherit trust from validated decompositions. It has not been done: a systematic search shows the 2026 attribution-graph literature is exclusively about constructing, describing and scaling graphs, while all validation work is component-level, on-distribution, or synthetic-only.

direction: Mechanistic interpretability of reasoning models via distribution-level causal analysis — intervening on internal features at natural decision points and measuring their effects on the resampled outcome distribution, to build the first decision circuits that span sampling boundaries, starting with self-correction/backtracking.
project: Decision Circuits — Feature-Level Distributional Causal Analysis of Self-Correction in Reasoning Models
question: When a reasoning model reaches a self-correction decision point (e.g., emitting "wait" and backtracking), which internal features causally determine the branch, how large and how specific are their distribution-level effects — i.e., how does ablating/steering each feature at the decision point shift P(revision), P(approach-switch), and P(final-answer-correct) over on-policy resamples — do those effects mediate through upstream error/uncertainty states, and are they consistent across problems, model families, and base-vs-RL-trained model pairs?
first_experiment: On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B (plus R1-Distill-Llama-8B with the published mitroitskii crosscoder): sample ~200 math CoTs, detect "wait"-type backtracking decision points and matched control points, then for the top-K wait-promoting/wait-suppressing crosscoder features apply ablation/steering at the decision point and resample the remainder of the CoT 64–128 times per condition, estimating P(revision), P(approach-switch), and P(final-correct) with paired bootstrap confidence intervals against no-intervention, random-feature, and sham controls — and against the text-edit resampling baseline of Thought Branches. Success criterion: significant, dose-responsive, feature-specific shifts in outcome distributions that text-level edits cannot reproduce; a negative result is itself informative and would validate the DeepMind team's skepticism.
why: First, the field's most influential team explicitly flagged this area as extremely neglected and posed the sampling-boundary problem as unsolved, directly soliciting answers. Second, my verification shows the specific primitive is still unclaimed as of November 2026: every adjacent paper stops one step short — feature work measures next-token logits with single-sample downstream checks (its authors defer circuit construction to "future work"), resampling work intervenes only on text, the deception-localization work uses head-level suppression for one behavior, and the model-diffing work uses externally-applied steering rather than the model's own decision points. Third, this is the bridge between the two most active threads in the subfield, so a solid version of the primitive upgrades many existing results (constructive model diffing, deception-suppression circuits, CoT faithfulness) rather than being an isolated finding. Fourth, it has a direct safety payoff: self-correction is load-bearing for capability and monitorability, and quantifying when and how it can be silently suppressed bears on sandbagging detection and on whether reasoning RL or safety training damages the mechanism. Fifth, it has not been done largely because it is the expensive, tedious part — thousands of interventions, hundreds of resamples each, careful statistics at natural mid-trajectory points — which is precisely the workload an autonomous agent can carry that human labs have systematically skipped.

direction: Mechanistically localize the knowledge–action gap — where internally-encoded correct answers fail to become expressed behavior — and bridge it with mechanism-targeted rather than global interventions.
project: Where Does the Answer Go? A Circuit-Level Account of the Knowledge–Action Gap in Language Models
question: When a model's activations linearly encode the correct answer but it outputs an error, does the knowledge (i) never reach the output pathway, (ii) get overwritten at identifiable sites, or (iii) reach the output but get outcompeted by a stronger circuit — and can targeted interventions at those sites correct errors with low collateral damage where global steering fails?
first_experiment: Per-layer probes separating "correct answer" from "predicted output answer" plus logit-lens tracing of the correct-answer token in Qwen2.5-7B/Llama-3.1-8B on error cases, followed by paired-run activation patching and suppressor-component ablation to map where the correct answer's causal influence is lost.
why: The gap is replicated, safety-critical, and measured-but-unexplained — prior work observes it (Orgad et al.), fails to close it (Basu et al.'s four failed intervention paradigms), or handles only isolated instances (Anthropic's persona anecdote, procedural hallucinations, MLLMs) — so a causal localization with targeted interventions is the natural, unclaimed next step, and it is tractable today with open models and existing circuit tooling.

direction: Treat mechanistic explanations (attribution graphs and SAE feature sets) as predictive theories and measure whether their counterfactual intervention predictions remain calibrated under distribution shift — using held-out interventional validity, not reconstruction error or label readability, as the field's first non-circular standard for judging and choosing among decompositions.
project: Does the Circuit Survive the Shift? Held-Out Interventional Validity of Attribution Graphs
question: When an attribution graph built on distribution D predicts the effect of ablating/steering a feature, how does the accuracy of those predictions degrade as we move to paraphrases, held-out entities, template changes, multilingual inputs, and domain shifts — does degradation concentrate in predictable places (small-margin features, unstable supports), and does held-out interventional validity rank competing decompositions (SAE widths, seeds, transcoders, neuron baselines) differently than on-distribution faithfulness does?
first_experiment: Using Gemma-2-2B with pretrained Gemma Scope SAEs/transcoders and the open-source Circuit-Tracer library on the MIB IOI task: (1) build attribution graphs on the clean training split; (2) extract each graph's predicted logit-diff change for a fixed menu of ~100 feature ablations; (3) actually run those ablations on the clean test split, on meaning-preserving paraphrases, on held-out names (MIB-private-style), and on translated/distractor-augmented prompts; (4) report predicted-vs-actual calibration (sign accuracy, rank correlation, MAE) per shift level as an "explanation decay curve," and test whether failures concentrate on low-margin features as the Oct 2026 margin analysis predicts. This needs one open-weight model, public dictionaries, and no training — days, not months.
why: It attacks the problem that the field's own 2026 assessments independently rank first — the gap between an explanation that fits its discovery distribution and one that is *true* of the model (the dual-basis problem), plus the verification bottleneck that followed automated labeling — and it operationalizes the "predictive/manipulability standards" that Méloux et al. identified as the pragmatic escape from non-identifiability. It has not been done because the existing fragility literature stops one step short: Certified Circuits certifies structural inclusion under dataset resampling, Many Circuits One Mechanism shows equivalence-class structure at the head/edge level, the margin paper corrects first-order error at a single input, and the 2026 SAE validation papers score single features on-distribution — none calibrates the *quantitative counterfactual predictions* of feature-level graphs across semantic shift, and none uses held-out interventional validity to rank decompositions (the Oct 2026 survey lists exactly this comparison as proposed-but-undone). The payoff is dual-outcome: if calibration degrades sharply, we have the first quantitative diagnosis of *why* deployed feature monitors fail under shift and a screening rule (margin/support diagnostics); if it holds, we have a validated, non-circular faithfulness metric the field has been asking for — either way the answer redirects how circuits get validated before they are trusted for safety decisions.

direction: Treat mechanistic explanations (attribution graphs, SAE/transcoder feature circuits, discovered subgraphs) as predictive causal models and rank competing decompositions by validated, repair-aware counterfactual transfer — their ability to predict model behavior under held-out interventions and distribution shift — using models with known ground-truth circuits as the calibrator.
project: Counterfactual Transfer Faithfulness: A Ground-Truth-Validated Test for Choosing Between Competing Circuit Explanations
question: When several mechanistic explanations all reproduce a model's behavior (and pass interventions) on the prompts used to extract them, does their agreement with the model under held-out interchange interventions, out-of-distribution prompt variants, and post-ablation states (including self-repair/backup recruitment) separate the faithful decomposition from unfaithful ones — where standard metrics (replacement score, ablation faithfulness on the calibration set, sparsity, autointerp, probing accuracy) cannot?
first_experiment: On the InterpBench SIIT-trained GPT-2 IOI model (ground-truth circuit known), generate three competing explanations for the same behavior — (1) the ground-truth circuit, (2) an SAE-feature circuit (GPT-2 SAEs / sparse feature circuit pipeline), and (3) a deliberately shallow decomposition induced by over-sparsified transcoders (the unfaithfulness mode shown by the 2026 CLT paper) — then measure in-distribution interventional agreement versus held-out interventional agreement on new interchange families, IOI prompt variants (DoubleIO-style compositional shifts), and ablation-plus-backup-recruitment states; the test succeeds if the ground-truth circuit strictly wins on transfer while all three tie on calibration-set faithfulness, and existing SAEBench-style metrics fail to predict the ranking.
why: It attacks the field's top self-identified gap — the dual basis problem and the absence of a non-circular faithfulness standard — at exactly the moment attribution graphs became the standard artifact and the first unfaithfulness mode was discovered (July 2026), so the timing is ripe and the infrastructure (InterpBench's 86 ground-truth models, open-source circuit-tracer tooling, Gemma Scope/GPT-2 SAEs) only became available within the last year. It has not been done because the necessary pieces only recently existed and were never combined: Méloux et al. established non-identifiability but no selection criterion; Miller et al. showed existing metrics fail but offered no alternative; the CLT-unfaithfulness paper demonstrated the failure mode in a toy but built no metric or benchmark; InterpBench evaluates discovery algorithms on a single distribution rather than explanations under distribution shift; Certified Circuits certifies dataset-stability of discovery, not counterfactual transfer of explanations; and no work is repair-aware, even though self-repair (CoAx, 2026) is precisely the phenomenon that distinguishes a mechanism-honest explanation from a behavioral rewrite. Success yields a standard evaluation protocol the community can adopt for every future circuit claim; failure yields the negative result the field explicitly says it needs.

direction: Develop a ground-truth-calibrated differential validation battery that adjudicates which mechanism is real among behaviorally-equivalent attribution-graph explanations, closing the field's verification gap for its dominant artifact.
project: Circuit Adjudication — Calibrated Differential Tests for Behaviorally-Equivalent Feature Circuits
question: Can structure-sensitive counterfactual interventions reliably identify the causal mechanism a model actually uses, among competing feature-level explanations that behavioral faithfulness metrics cannot distinguish?
first_experiment: Train a seed-population of small transformers on a multi-hop task family engineered to admit a shortcut solution, certify each model's true mechanism from its weights, train CLTs/PLTs on them, and show that (a) standard behavioral metrics fail to separate the two graph populations while (b) the differential intervention battery separates them with high AUROC against certified ground truth.
why: It targets the #1 open problem of 2026 — attribution graphs became standard infrastructure while validation lagged, and non-identifiability is now proven and measured but has no instrument — and it has not been done because all nearest work (toy failure demonstrations, instability diagnostics, stability certification, component-level benchmarks, single-case replications) stops one step short of a calibrated adjudication protocol, while remaining feasible on open models and open tooling.

direction: Operationalize the dual basis problem by treating competing mechanistic decompositions (circuits, attribution graphs, SAE-feature circuits) as falsifiable hypotheses that are arbitrated by their divergent predictions of model behavior under designed distribution shift, yielding a quantitative, non-circular, held-out "predictive faithfulness" metric.
project: Circuits as Hypotheses: Arbitrating Competing Mechanistic Decompositions via Held-Out Behavioral Predictions
question: When multiple decompositions of a model are equally faithful in-distribution, does the model's behavior under targeted distribution shift discriminate between them — and can the degree of separation and agreement be combined into a single predictive faithfulness score that is measurably more trustworthy than in-distribution faithfulness metrics?
first_experiment: In a controlled synthetic setting with known ground truth — the Boolean multi-hop composition task from the ICML 2026 CLT-unfaithfulness result, where a ground-truth deep multi-hop circuit and a shallow single-hop rewrite both match training behavior — I will (1) verify both candidate decompositions achieve equal in-distribution faithfulness under standard metrics, (2) derive each candidate's implied predictions on a designed family of shifted inputs (inputs that break the shallow rewrite's assumptions but not the deep path, and vice versa), and (3) test whether actual model behavior systematically matches one candidate. Either the model arbitrates (proof of concept for the metric) or it doesn't (first quantitative measurement of the "equivalence horizon" — equally informative, since it shows ID-faithfulness is genuinely insufficient). Scale-up then applies the framework to public models: candidate IOI circuits in GPT-2 from different discovery pipelines, using the public phantom-specialization codebase and MIB tasks.
why: It attacks the problem the field's own 2026 synthesis ranks #1 — "two attribution graphs that produce the same output behavior on the training distribution can diverge on held-out inputs; which one is 'the circuit'?" — with a cheap, model-agnostic method rather than a $50k–250k per-circuit analysis. It is not already done because every adjacent line stops one step short: Li et al. predict OOD rules from attention signatures but never compare competing decompositions; Huang et al. assume a single accepted mechanism and use it as a monitor; Makou et al. diagnose equivalence classes but propose no discriminating test or score; Certified Circuits and Hadad et al. certify *stability of one pipeline's output*, not *truth between rivals*; causal scrubbing resamples within the hypothesis's own equivalence classes, which the pitfalls paper shows can't reject wrong hypotheses; and the CLT-unfaithfulness paper shows unfaithful decompositions pass behavior checks but offers no detector. The insight that makes it work is treating shift not as a robustness nuisance (as prior work does) but as the *discriminating variable*, with the disagreement between candidate decompositions actively used to search for separating inputs — turning a philosophical worry into an empirical scoreboard, which is exactly the "perplexity for circuits" the field says it lacks, and which safety applications need because monitors built on unvalidated decompositions currently provide false assurance.

direction: Identify and causally validate the internal "state ledger" that LLM agents use to track true task progress across turns, and test whether divergence between this load-bearing internal state and the agent's reported status is an unsupervised, evasion-robust monitor for false-success and reward hacking.
project: The Agent's State Ledger: A Mechanistic Account of Cross-Turn Task-State Tracking and Its Divergence from Reported Status
question: When an LLM agent acts over multiple turns, (a) where and how is true task progress represented internally (which features/circuits write, carry, and read it across steps), (b) is that representation causally load-bearing for action selection and completion claims, and (c) does unsupervised divergence between internal true-state and reported status predict false success/reward hacking — and can an adaptively evading model fake it without destroying its own task performance?
