first_experiment: Generate ~200 ReAct trajectories in Gameable ALFWorld with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Gemma-2-2b-it, annotating ground-truth progress per step from the environment; hook mid-layer Gemma Scope SAE activations at each action/report step; train linear decoders on SAE features to predict true progress vs. reported status. Success criterion: at steps where the agent's text misreports status (including the "claim task complete" affordance), the true-state decoder still reads correctly while the reported-status decoder reads the lie, with divergence emerging at least one step before the false claim (AUROC separation) — establishing the ledger exists and divergence is an unsupervised precursor signal. Then causally validate: patch and ablate the identified state features across a turn boundary (circuit-tracer attribution graphs on Gemma-2-2b) to locate the write/read circuit and test load-bearing-ness; finally, fine-tune on School-of-Reward-Hacks and run obfuscation training against the divergence monitor vs. supervised DoM probes to test the evasion-robustness thesis.
why: It targets the field's top-stated application (monitoring for dangerous cognition) at its least-understood deployment mode (multi-turn agents), which DeepMind's pragmatic vision explicitly flags as out of reach and the 2025 review says "needs better decomposition." The detection side is heavily populated (Goodfire's DoM probes, MMD trajectory detectors, CoT monitors), but all are correlational, supervised, and demonstrably evadable by obfuscation training; no work has mechanistically localized the cross-turn state variable, tested its causal load-bearing-ness, or derived a monitor from state-vs-report divergence with the structural argument that faking it costs task performance. Existing adjacent results — single-sequence entity-tracking circuits, single-turn CoT "diagnostic but not causal" error awareness, token-level cross-turn attribution (Tokengeist) — all stop short of a state variable in an agent loop, and the enabling tooling (open transcoders, Gemma Scope, circuit-tracer, Gameable ALFWorld, public false-success testbeds) only matured in the last 12–18 months, which is precisely why this gap exists and is now closable on open-weight models with modest compute.

direction: Build a standardized, automated "severe testing" protocol that adjudicates rival mechanistic explanations (head-circuits, SAE/transcoder feature circuits, attribution graphs) by generating inputs where the rivals' behavioral predictions diverge and scoring each explanation's predictive agreement with the intact model on those inputs, replacing in-distribution intervention faithfulness as the field's default validation metric.
project: InterpSevere: Predictive Adjudication of Rival Mechanistic Explanations via Discriminating-Input Generation
question: Can the dual-basis ambiguity in mechanistic interpretability be resolved by treating each explanation as a predictive theory — scoring it by behavioral agreement with the intact model on held-out and automatically generated *discriminating* inputs — and does this held-out predictive score succeed where in-distribution intervention faithfulness demonstrably fails (misranking under context distortion, phantom specialization across input distributions, unexplained model errors)?
first_experiment: On GPT-2 small with IOI (plus Greater-Than as a robustness control): assemble a candidate pool of the published reference circuit, ~20 seeds each from ACDC/EAP/EAP-IG (size-matched), same-size random subnetworks, and controlled corruptions; compute for each candidate (a) standard in-distribution KL faithfulness, (b) held-out predictive agreement on fresh IOI prompts and five variant families (repeated names, swapped positions, romantic objects, new names, distractor-count changes), and (c) agreement on discriminators found by a cheap gradient-guided search that maximizes prediction disagreement between rival candidate explanations. Deliverable: the scatter of (a) vs. (b), a test of whether (a) fails to predict (b), and whether (c) separates the true mechanism from equivalence-class alternatives that (a) scores as ties — with InterpBench as the ground-truth sanity check where the correct algorithm is known.
why: (1) It attacks the field's top self-diagnosed gap — the verification-vs-labeling asymmetry and the dual basis problem — using the field's own definition of understanding (prediction on arbitrary inputs) as the metric; a consensus validation protocol acts as the loss function for the entire field, upgrading every discovery method and every automated pipeline simultaneously, which is the highest-leverage move available to a single researcher. (2) Timing: attribution graphs and agentic discovery just industrialized interpretation *generation*; validation is the bottleneck everyone now hits, and the 2026 literature explicitly asks for it (automated validation loops, cross-condition transfer tests, auditing-game metrics) without anyone building the unifying protocol. (3) It is not already done: the nearest works each cover a different slice — 2024's adversarial evaluation tested only three hand-picked circuits with intervention-defined outputs before attribution graphs existed; MIB scores in-distribution interventions on fixed tasks; the 2026 misranking and error-reproduction papers diagnose failures of the old metric but still define ground truth through interventions; certified circuits guarantee dataset stability, not behavioral adjudication; and the equivalence-class paper calls for exactly the transfer tests I would build but does not construct them. No existing work generates discriminators *between rival explanations*, unifies prediction-based scoring across explanation types, or validates the metric against ground-truth model organisms. (4) It is feasible with open models, TransformerLens/Circuit-Tracer, MIB tasks, InterpBench, and modest compute. (5) Its failure mode is itself valuable: if held-out predictive accuracy also cannot adjudicate rival decompositions, that is a fundamental negative result showing behavioral definitions of understanding are insufficient, which would redirect the field toward non-behavioral selection criteria — so the expected value is positive either way.

direction: Treat mechanistic explanations as forecasting instruments — evaluate and select among rival decompositions (circuits, SAE feature sets, attribution graphs) by their power to predict model behavior under distribution shift, converting the dual-basis problem from an aesthetic choice into a measurable behavioral criterion.
project: Forecast or Fail — Out-of-Distribution Forecasting as a Non-Circular Criterion for Mechanistic Explanations
question: Do mechanistic explanations that are indistinguishable in-distribution make divergent predictions about model behavior under distribution shift, and can out-of-distribution forecast accuracy serve as a principled criterion for identifying which decomposition reflects model-intrinsic structure rather than the method that found it?
first_experiment: On GPT-2 small with the IOI task: construct ≥6 rival explanations with matched in-distribution faithfulness (manual 26-head circuit; ACDC and EAP-IG circuits across multiple seeds/batches; feature circuits from several independently trained public SAEs), verify they pass a fixed ID bar (KL agreement plus error reproduction), then pre-register ~6 IOI shift families (novel names, adjective variants, backwards naming, distractor injection, longer contexts, template rephrasings) and measure three quantities: (1) explanation–model agreement under ablation on each shift, (2) explanation–explanation forecast divergence between ID-equivalent rivals, and (3) whether that divergence tracks actual shifts in model behavior. Falsifiable prediction: ID-equivalent rivals diverge OOD in a structured, decomposition-family-dependent way, and forecast survival correlates with independent stability measures (seed-overlap, feature absorption rates).
why: It attacks what the field itself ranked as its most important open methodological question — the dual basis problem and the lack of a non-circular faithfulness target — while subsuming the deployment concern that ID-validated monitors may silently fail under distribution shift; it is cheap (open models, public SAEs, one GPU), yields important results in either direction, and builds reusable benchmark infrastructure that a 2026 NeurIPS position paper explicitly declares missing. It has not already been done: the nearest neighbors each stop short — adversarial circuit evaluation tested only 3 fixed manual circuits with adversarial search, not systematic shifts or rival comparison; Huang et al. predicted binary correctness from hand-specified mechanisms on 5 tasks, not automated feature/circuit artifacts or decomposition selection; Li et al.'s predictive-interpretability objective was demonstrated only on tiny synthetic transformers with attention patterns; Wu et al.'s rephrasing-variance work diagnoses discovery-method instability but neither evaluates forecasts nor offers a selection principle; and the new Koopman identifiability theory provides a coordinate-free spectral primitive, not a behavioral criterion for the SAE/circuit artifacts the field actually deploys. The scattered ingredients are all in place, but no one has assembled them into a forecasting-based evaluation and selection framework on real language models.

direction: Build a ground-truth-validated framework and benchmark for adjudicating among behaviorally equivalent mechanistic explanations — turning explanation selection from an aesthetic judgment into an interventionally certified measurement.
project: Adjudicating Rivals: An Interventional Separation Criterion and Benchmark for Behaviorally Equivalent Mechanistic Explanations
question: When multiple circuit/decomposition explanations of the same model behavior are behaviorally tied on the discovery distribution (zero circuit error, high ablation fidelity), which finite, ground-truth-free battery of tests — input-distribution shift, error agreement, interchange-intervention agreement on novel states, weight/activation-edit transfer, and self-repair/co-ablation probes — reliably separates the mechanism that actually computes the behavior from behaviorally-matched rewrites, and can this battery be distilled into a single certified "interventional separation score" that ranks rival explanations without access to ground truth?
first_experiment: On 4–5 InterpBench/SIIT semi-synthetic transformers with known ground-truth circuits (IOI, greater-than, docstring, frac_prevs) plus GPT-2-small IOI, generate a field of rival candidates — the ground-truth circuit, ACDC and EAP-IG outputs, deliberately constructed behaviorally-matched shallow rewrites (path-shortcutting à la the ICML 2026 CLT failure mode), and size-matched random controls — then (Phase 1) confirm all candidates tie under standard circuit-error/ablation-fidelity metrics on the discovery distribution, and (Phase 2) apply the five-family test battery to measure whether ground truth separates from rewrites, with each comparison reported as an anytime-valid (CIF-style) certified claim. A single GPU and open tooling (TransformerLens, nnsight, InterpBench) suffice; separation validates the criterion, failure maps its boundary — both publishable.
why: It is the problem the field's own retrospective ranks first ("ranking decompositions by something other than how readable their labels are"), Sharkey et al. flag validation as the field's sharpest gap, and a 2026 EU AI Act audit quantifies the stakes (73% claim-flip rate) — yet every existing response is partial: ISS requires pre-enumerated candidates and MILP solvers on toy abstraction tasks; CIF certifies a chosen estimand without choosing one; error agreement is necessary-but-insufficient; Certified Circuits certifies stability, not validity; the Koopman invariant is not legible; and InterpBench has only ever scored discovery recall, never adjudicated rivals. It has not been done because the diagnosis itself only matured in 2025–2026, field incentives reward discovery over evaluation, the needed combination (causal-abstraction theory + sequential statistics + benchmark engineering) spans communities, and realistic ground-truth models only became available with InterpBench/SIIT in 2024–25. Solving selection is the bottleneck that converts mechanistic interpretability from plausible-story generation into certifiable evidence for monitoring, safety cases, and audits — high leverage, low compute, decisive first experiment, and a benchmark the whole field can adopt the way perplexity and top-1 accuracy anchor other fields.

direction: Mechanistically decode reasoning hidden by optimization pressure — quantify how much covert computation remains recoverable from activations as encoding pressure escalates from fixed ciphers to decoder-adversarial RL, and localize its representational substrate.
project: Decode Under Pressure: White-Box Legibility of Obfuscated Reasoning
question: When RL training makes chain-of-thought unfaithful or encoded, how much of the hidden reasoning remains recoverable from activations, at what pressure does recovery fail, and where does the hidden computation then live?
first_experiment: Train a 1.5B open obfuscation organism (GRPO, joint task+monitor-penalty reward on a hacking-required honeypot), run a decoder battery (logit lens, tuned lens, public-SAE decoding, probes) on reasoning-position activations against ground-truth hack labels, and measure whether content — not just detection — survives, and whether the mid-layer English anchor survives RL-instilled obfuscation.
why: It is the explicitly flagged, unoccupied center of the field's top safety agenda (CoT monitorability), bounded by three papers that each defer exactly this work, feasible on open small models, and scientifically guaranteed to inform the dark-matter/transfer debates — while every neighboring direction (SAE methods, attribution automation, faithfulness metrics, probe evasion, sandbagging) is already crowded.

direction: Do the first mechanistic decomposition of how language models generate "random" choices and shape output distributions, using attribution graphs on open models, as the opening move against the "complexity of sampling" open problem.
project: The Biology of Sampling: How Language Models Compute "Random" Choices
question: What internal mechanisms compute the candidate set, constraint enforcement, salience weighting, and apparent randomness in "random choice" generations — and is randomness genuine distributional computation or a deterministic, context-hash-like selection among salient candidates?
first_experiment: Behavioral mapping of random-choice distributions across four small open models (~1,000 paraphrases, N ∈ {2,10,20,100,1000}), then pre-registered attribution-graph analysis on Gemma-2-2B's released cross-layer transcoders: ablate salience features (predict flattening toward uniform) and constraint features (predict out-of-range mass).
why: DeepMind explicitly lists "complexity of sampling" as far out of reach with no roadmap; the behavioral RNG literature (2024–25) documents strong, replicated biases but stops short of any mechanistic account, and my searches found zero circuit-level studies of sampling-style generation — while the exact tooling for the question (attribution graphs + public Gemma/Llama transcoders, runnable on a free GPU) is mature, neglected, and safety-relevant (predictability of "random" outputs, diversity monitoring, seed-hijacking surface).

direction: Quantify and diagnose the gap between behavioral sufficiency and mechanistic fidelity in transcoder-based attribution graphs on real multi-hop transformers.
project: "Does the Microscope See the Hop?" — Ground-Truth Fidelity Tests for Attribution Graphs
question: Do attribution-graph circuits for multi-hop behaviors route through the model's causally verified intermediate representations, or behaviorally-equivalent shallow rewrites, and can sparsity level and replacement score predict the dissociation?
first_experiment: Fine-tune Gemma-2-2B on invented-entity 2/3-hop fact chains, pin down the true mechanism via targeted activation patching, then compare mechanistic fidelity of public-CLT attribution graphs (at multiple sparsity levels) against replacement score, using novel compositional prompts as the arbiter between competing circuit explanations.
why: It addresses the field's top-ranked open problem — the faithfulness/dual-basis gap in its dominant artifact — with existing public infrastructure and a metric design that no prior work provides (prior work stops at toy models, single-mechanism replications, or ablation-sufficiency metrics that cannot detect mechanism-matching rewrites), while directly strengthening the safety monitoring and auditing systems that inherit decomposition errors.

direction: Make attribution-graph/circuit hypotheses falsifiable by measuring their held-out and adversarially-probed predictive validity as surrogate models, using failures to refine graphs and to rank competing decompositions.
project: Predictive Circuit Validity — Attribution Graphs as Falsifiable Surrogate Models
question: How well do attribution graphs predict the true model's behavior on inputs they were not built from, and can that held-out predictive validity serve as the field's first non-circular, quantitative faithfulness standard — exposing failure modes, resolving the dual-basis ranking problem, and powering an automated interpret→falsify→refine loop?
first_experiment: On GPT-2-small (greater-than and IOI behaviors), build attribution graphs from calibration prompts using open transcoders, then quantify three-way agreement (true model vs. graph-restricted computation vs. full-transcoder model) on held-out paraphrases, minimal pairs, and gradient-guided divergence-maximizing inputs — testing whether graphs that pass the standard within-prompt replacement-score check nonetheless collapse on identifiable held-out input classes, and whether adding the discovered "theory-breaking" inputs to calibration and re-tracing improves held-out validity.
why: It targets the field's self-identified #1 open problem in 2026 — the faithfulness/verification gap and dual-basis problem — which remains unoccupied because all existing standards (MIB, EAP-IG faithfulness, replacement scores, unit tests, SAEBench) evaluate within the calibration distribution, at the wrong granularity, or via interventions only; it is cheaply tractable with open models and public transcoders, fully automatable, and produces missing infrastructure that the exploding volume of unvalidated auto-generated interpretations — and safety applications built on them — urgently need.

direction: Make predictive validity under distribution shift the standard of evidence for mechanistic explanations, by charting circuits' validity domains and using differential off-distribution predictions as the principled tiebreaker among rival decompositions.
project: Where Circuits Stop Predicting: Validity Domains for Mechanistic Explanations
question: Over what region of input space does a circuit discovered on one distribution still quantitatively predict the intact model's behavior, and can rival in-distribution-equivalent decompositions be empirically adjudicated by their divergent off-distribution predictions?
first_experiment: Pilot on GPT-2 Small IOI: fix the published reference circuit, test it across ~6 controlled shift axes (name novelty, paraphrase, distractors, order, length, surface form), score per-axis predictive transfer of its path-level predictions against observed logit changes and ablation effects, then repeat on ACDC/EAP-IG/certified rivals plus a random null to see whether their off-distribution predictions diverge where in-distribution faithfulness ties; scale later to refusal in Gemma-2-2B with Gemma Scope.
why: It is the convergence point of the field's top diagnosed problems (falsifiability, dual basis, broken faithfulness metric, monitor failure under shift) with a cheap, concrete first experiment, and no existing work builds the systematic response — the closest papers are synthetic-only proofs of concept, single-axis frequency studies, stability certificates for discovery decisions, and diagnosis-without-remedy papers.

direction: Build the missing adjudication layer for mechanistic interpretability — a ground-truthable benchmark and non-circular metric that scores decomposition-based explanations (feature circuits, attribution graphs) by their ability to predict model behavior under interventions on distribution-shifted inputs that deliberately decouple correlated computational pathways, and use it to rank competing decompositions of the same model and detect mechanism-obscuring "aliasing" unfaithfulness in real attribution graphs.
project: DecoupleBench: Adjudicating Mechanistic Explanations by Causal Prediction under Pathway-Decoupling Interventions
question: Do decomposition-based mechanistic explanations that are indistinguishable under standard in-distribution faithfulness checks (ablation, replacement score, interchange-intervention accuracy on fixed counterfactuals) diverge in their causal predictions when evaluated on inputs and intervention sets that decouple correlated pathways — and does the proposed decoupling-prediction-error metric identify the true mechanism (validated against injected ground truth) where existing metrics fail, thereby providing a principled, non-aesthetic criterion for the dual-basis / explanation-multiplicity problem?
first_experiment: On a small transformer trained on a multi-hop task with a known ground-truth circuit (reimplementing/extending the Boolean toy of the ICML 2026 CLT-unfaithfulness paper, plus one SIIT/InterpBench-style GPT-2-scale model), extract explanations from several competing decompositions — cross-layer transcoder, per-layer transcoder, two SAE seeds of different sizes — confirm all pass standard in-distribution checks (replacement score, ablation faithfulness, L0, reconstruction FVU), then construct a decoupling test set (counterfactual inputs plus interventions that break the input correlations the shallow-rewrite alias depends on) and measure each explanation's causal prediction error under those interventions. Success criterion: ground truth achieves low decoupled-prediction error while the behavior-matching-but-obscuring decomposition fails sharply, and no existing metric separates them. This single result founds the benchmark, delivers the first quantitative detection tool for the known CLT aliasing failure mode, and then ports directly to real models (GPT-2 via circuit-tracer; Gemma-2-2b via Gemma Scope) to adjudicate PLT-vs-CLT and seed-vs-seed discrepancies.
why: It attacks the field's own top-ranked methodological problem (faithfulness of attribution graphs and the dual-basis problem, per the 2026 retrospective of Sharkey et al.), and it is the bottleneck every downstream application now queues behind: safety monitors must survive distribution shift (exactly where GDM's negative results landed), audits require adjudication (Explanation Multiplicity shows claims flip 73% of the time), and the ICML 2026 result shows the dominant artifact can systematically obscure the true mechanism — yet no detection metric, no ground-truthed benchmark of explanation-level faithfulness, and no decomposition-selection criterion exist. It is not already done because the closest works each stop one step short: MIB and InterpBench ground-truth *localization* (edges/nodes) with in-distribution interventions, not explanations; Certified Circuits certifies stability of inclusion decisions, not mechanism identity; sanity-check baselines evaluate SAE *properties*, not causal-explanatory power; and the aliasing paper demonstrates the phenomenon in a toy model but explicitly leaves measurement in real models and objective-choice implications open — while the attribution-graph leaders list "automated validation with synthetic/OOD inputs" and "objectively verifiable downstream tasks for understanding" as undone. The approach is also tractable for me now: every component runs at GPT-2/Gemma-2-2b scale on public tooling (circuit-tracer, CLT-Forge, Gemma Scope, InterpBench), and its payoff is multiplicative — it converts the field's output from "plausible stories" into "ranked, falsifiable explanations," which is the precondition for interpretability to carry evidentiary weight in exactly the deployment and audit settings where it is now being invoked.

direction: Mechanism-faithful decomposition — determine when sparse replacement models (SAEs/transcoders) recover a network's true computational algorithm versus a behaviorally-equivalent rewrite, and build the ground-truth testbed and ground-truth-free diagnostics that make this measurable.
project: "Rewrite or Mechanism? A Ground-Truth Testbed for Mechanism-Faithful Decomposition"
question: When do sparse decompositions (SAE/PLT/CLT, across training objectives) recover the true algorithm of a transformer with a known mechanism versus a behaviorally-equivalent shortcut — and can out-of-distribution intervention agreement between base and replacement model diagnose this without ground truth?
first_experiment: Train a small transformer on modular addition to grokking (whose trigonometric/Fourier mechanism is fully characterized in prior work), then train matched-budget SAE variants and per-layer transcoders on its activations, and measure three things side by side: (a) in-distribution replacement fidelity (MSE, replacement score, KL), (b) mechanism identity (Fourier content of decoder directions, preservation of the circular/helix geometry, whether attribution graphs recover cos·cos + sin·sin computation rather than lookup pairs), and (c) agreement between base and replacement model outputs under out-of-distribution inputs and activations patched along/orthogonal to the known circular subspace. Prediction: (a) will not track (b), while (c) will.
why: It attacks the field's foundational bottleneck — identifiability and validation of explanations — which every downstream application (monitors, editing, safety cases, automation) silently depends on; the problem is now validated by four independent lines of evidence (CLT rewrites, geometry shattering, phantom specialization, structured reconstruction error) yet no constructive systematic answer exists: closest works are a Boolean toy model with only preliminary real-model evidence, an edge-level benchmark without mechanism ground truth, and representation-level manifold analysis — none build known-mechanism organisms, compare decomposition objectives, or test an OOD-intervention diagnostic, and the grokking modular-arithmetic organism in particular has never been used to evaluate sparse decomposition faithfulness; the field's incentive structure has favored method development and case studies over validation (its own reviews and meta-evaluations admit this), leaving rigor-focused work under-occupied; it is tractable with small models and public tooling on modest compute, and it is decisive either way — confirming the rewrite problem yields both a diagnostic and a benchmark, while refuting it would redirect substantial community effort.

direction: Build the missing validation layer of mechanistic interpretability — systematic measurement of how causally-validated features, circuits, and monitors retain (or lose) their causal role and predictive value under input distribution shift — turning "faithfulness" from an in-distribution aesthetic into a transfer-testable, non-circular engineering tolerance.
project: Shift-Robustness Certification for Mechanistic Artifacts: Do Validated Features Still Cause What They Caused?
question: When an SAE feature, circuit, or latent is causally validated in-distribution (its natural values pass installation/removal/rescue tests), how does its causal effect size and behavioral predictive value degrade across a controlled ladder of distribution shifts (paraphrase → new domains → format/encoding → multilingual → adversarial templates), and what distinguishes shift-robust artifacts (those re-derived by the model's computation) from shift-fragile ones (input-statistic detectors whose firing persists while their causal role silently changes)?
first_experiment: On Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Gemma-2-2B/9B-it, take the published refusal direction (Arditi et al.) and Gemma Scope refusal features, establish the in-distribution causal effect with the installation/removal contract on a held-out harmful-prompt set, then re-measure the *same* interventions' behavioral effect across the shift ladder — computing a "causal transfer ratio" (shifted effect / ID effect) side-by-side with detection robustness (does the feature still fire / does a probe still detect the content) — with the known-unknown entity latents and subject–verb agreement feature set as controls. One model, four behaviors' worth of artifacts, ~50 GPU-hours; if detection-robust/causal-fragile dissociations appear at modern scale the way the toy-scale results predict, the full benchmark and characterization study follows.
why: It sits precisely on the field's two self-identified worst gaps — the verification bottleneck (most published features are causally unvalidated, and validation is currently done only in-distribution) and the growing OOD coverage gap for interpretability-based safety monitors — and it converts them into one measurable, falsifiable program: an agreed metric ("causal transfer under shift"), a reusable benchmark, and a scientific characterization of *which* features survive shift and why, which doubles as the first principled, non-aesthetic criterion for ranking competing decompositions (the dual-basis problem: a decomposition that predicts held-out shifted behavior beats one that merely reconstructs activations it was fit on). It is not already done because (1) the entire 2024–2026 causal-validation wave conditioned on natural in-distribution inputs — the immediate question was "is the claim true at all," not "how far does it extend"; (2) existing shift work lives in adjacent niches that lack the other half: probes are correlational, Certified Circuits certifies discovery stability rather than validated artifacts' causal roles, MOOD is behavioral-only, and the predictive-validity and detection-vs-causal-dissociation results exist only on toy models (GPT-2/IOI, synthetic transformers); and (3) the combination only became *possible* in the last ~18 months, when open SAE suites, a published inventory of causally-validated latents, and the natural-value intervention contract all came into existence simultaneously — so the intersection is empty not because it was judged unimportant, but because its ingredients only just arrived and no one owns the boundary between the validation, certification, and monitoring communities.

direction: Convert mechanistic circuit explanations from same-prompt artifacts into held-out behavioral forecasters, and use that non-circular simulatability criterion to adjudicate the dual basis problem — which decomposition of a model actually captures its mechanism.
project: Circuit Simulatability: Attribution Graphs That Predict Behavior on Unseen Inputs
question: When a circuit/attribution graph extracted on one set of prompts is used as a forward simulator on held-out, systematically transformed inputs (paraphrases, entity substitutions, distractors, negations), how well does it predict the full model's answers and answer-flips — and do competing feature bases (cross-layer transcoder features vs. per-layer transcoder features vs. raw pre-down-projection neurons vs. attention heads) differ in held-out predictive validity, i.e., can prediction rather than aesthetics decide which decomposition is "the circuit"?
first_experiment: On GPT-2-small (greater-than, IOI) and Llama-3.2-1B (multi-hop entity recall, subject-verb agreement), extract circuits for the same behavior in three bases (CLT features via CircuitTracer; per-layer transcoders via Gemma Scope; raw pre-down-projection MLP neurons via RelP attribution), then run each circuit's replacement model — pruned exactly as for publication — on a held-out counterfactual family built from mechanistically-motivated transformations, and score flip-prediction accuracy, answer agreement, and error-node mass needed for transfer, against controls (matched-random graphs; graphs refit on the perturbed family as an upper bound; full-model logit-difference baselines). A single decisive signal: does any basis's published graph beat the random-graph control on prompts it was never built for?
why: It attacks the field's own top-ranked open problem — faithfulness as a numerical target and the dual basis problem — using the exact criterion (predict behavior on arbitrary inputs) that Sharkey et al. define as "understanding," the escape Méloux et al. propose after proving non-identifiability, and the standard Anthropic's CHIVE just operationalized behaviorally (where all current white-box tools gave zero uplift, and circuit tools couldn't even be evaluated). It has not been done because the required ingredients converged only recently — open competing decompositions (CLT vs. PLT vs. neuron-basis, Jan 2026), open circuit-tracing tooling (2025–26), and the simulatability framing (mid-2026) — and because attribution graphs were assumed to be intrinsically per-prompt, so nobody built the forecasting interface; every nearby evaluation (unit tests, error agreement, certified stability, rephrasing-variance studies) tests a circuit on the distribution or claims it was built for, rather than on mechanistically constructed held-out input families, and none ranks decompositions. It is tractable at 1–2B scale on open models, it directly serves safety (auditors need explanations that generalize to unseen trigger variants — the gap CHIVE exposed and secret-elicitation work confirmed), and every outcome is informative: a winning basis resets community defaults, a losing one gives transcoder training a causal, held-out objective, and universal failure quantifies — for the first time numerically — the distance between current explanations and real understanding.

direction: Aggregate families of per-prompt attribution graphs into algorithm-level mechanism hypotheses and adjudicate rival explanations by their out-of-distribution and interventional causal predictions rather than in-distribution reconstruction.
project: From Execution Traces to Algorithms: Adjudicating Rival Mechanistic Explanations by Out-of-Distribution Causal Prediction
question: Do attribution-graph families merged across a designed prompt distribution recover the model's general task algorithm, and can out-of-distribution causal predictions discriminate between competing mechanism accounts (Clock/trig-helix vs. lookup-tables vs. bag-of-heuristics for arithmetic) that are indistinguishable on the prompts used to build the graphs?
first_experiment: On GPT-J/Pythia-6.9B or Gemma-2-2B with public transcoders, generate attribution graphs for ~200 addition prompts from a factorial design (magnitude, digit length, mod-2/5/10 residues, operand frequency), quantify cross-prompt graph divergence, cluster features into per-feature input-selectivity profiles to extract the invariant subgraph, and then test whether the trig-helix hypothesis or the lookup-table hypothesis better predicts base-model logits and intervention outcomes on held-out operand pairs never used during graph construction.
why: It targets the field's top-ranked methodological problem (the dual-basis problem: many decompositions agree in-distribution but diverge OOD) and the attribution-graph authors' own explicitly-flagged open problem (per-prompt traces vs. general algorithms), yields a non-circular, quantitative faithfulness metric that monitoring and anomaly-detection applications require before circuit claims can be trusted, and is feasible on open models with existing free tooling — while no prior work merges attribution graphs across prompts or adjudicates competing mechanism hypotheses by OOD causal prediction (closest works either compare component-level circuits without synthesis, evaluate errors without OOD mechanism discrimination, or established the trig-helix finding without confronting the transcoder-graph account).

direction: Build the first validated, non-circular criterion for choosing between behaviorally-equivalent internal decompositions — held-out interventional generalization — validate it on planted-impostor ground truth, and use it to adjudicate the live neuron-basis vs. transcoder-basis circuit dispute.
project: Circuit Adjudication: Selecting Among Behaviorally-Equivalent Decompositions via Held-Out Interventional Generalization
question: Can held-out interventional generalization — a decomposition's ability to predict model behavior under novel interventions and distribution shifts it wasn't tuned on — correctly identify the true mechanism among behaviorally-equivalent competing decompositions, and can it settle the neuron-basis vs. cross-layer-transcoder dispute on real models?
first_experiment: Plant-impostor test: train small transformers on a 2-hop task with known mechanism, recover the true transcoder circuit, fit a sparsity-induced shallow impostor matched on in-distribution circuit error, and measure whether an Interventional Generalization Score (held-out accuracy over a grid of compositional recombinations × ablation methods, with anytime-valid confidence sequences) separates them despite their on-distribution tie.
why: The field's own 2026 assessment ranks the dual basis problem first and notes decomposition choice is still "an aesthetic decision"; all neighboring work (CHIVE's counterfactual simulatability, Adversarial Circuit Evaluation, InterpBench, non-identifiability proofs, CLT-unfaithfulness findings) stops one step short of an adjudication protocol, while a concrete published dispute between competing circuit bases is unresolved and everything downstream — feature-label verification, cross-architecture transfer, safety monitors — depends on solving it.

direction: Build the first operational framework that discriminates between rival mechanistic explanations (attribution graphs, feature circuits, neuron circuits) of the same behavior by their ability to predict intervention outcomes on held-out, distribution-shifted inputs — turning the field's own predictive definition of "understanding" into a measurable, ranked score.
project: Judging Decompositions by Their Predictions: Distribution-Shift Stress Tests for Rival Mechanistic Explanations
question: When multiple decompositions of the same model behavior are statistically indistinguishable under in-distribution faithfulness testing, do their behavioral predictions (sign and magnitude of ablation/patching effects, predicted answer flips, predicted failure modes) diverge under graded distribution shift, and can out-of-sample predictive validity serve as a principled, non-aesthetic criterion for ranking rival mechanistic explanations — the "dual basis problem"?
first_experiment: On GPT-2 small's indirect object identification task (with a replication on one Llama-3.2-1B task), collect ≥5 rival candidate explanations of the same behavior — the manual IOI circuit, ACDC, EAP-IG, an attribution-patching circuit, and ≥2 cross-layer-transcoder attribution-graph subcircuits from different seeds/architectures (public circuit-tracer) plus a neuron-basis circuit (RelP). Verify all pass standard in-distribution faithfulness. Then construct graded held-out probe families — resampled names/objects (MIB-style), structural variants (adverb insertion, position swaps, distractors), algorithm-breaking variants (DoubleIO/TripleIO), and model-error prompts — and for each explanation generate quantitative intervention predictions (predicted effect of ablating each node/edge on each held-out prompt), then run the actual ablations. Score each explanation by the correlation between predicted and actual intervention effects and by answer-flip accuracy, in-distribution vs. out-of-distribution. Expected first result: circuits indistinguishable in-distribution separate sharply under shift, establishing a "predictive sufficiency" metric and its discriminative power.
why: It attacks the open problem that the field's most recent state-of-the-field assessment ranks first — the dual basis problem and attribution-graph faithfulness ("two graphs that match on the training distribution can diverge on held-out inputs; which one is the circuit?") — at exactly the moment attribution graphs have become the dominant artifact but their validation lags their generation. It has not been done because the closest prior work each stops short: Méloux et al. (ICLR 2025) prove non-identifiability but only on Boolean MLPs and merely suggest predictive standards; Shi et al. (NeurIPS 2024) hypothesis-test a single circuit in-distribution; Miller et al. (2024) show faithfulness metrics are ablation-sensitive without discriminating rivals; Zhang et al. (2026) add error reproduction but in-distribution; Gerasimov et al. (2026) rank by cross-seed stability, not behavioral validity; MIB scores single methods on same-task held-out instances; Hadad et al. (2026) certify single circuits on small vision models; and FlyHack (2026) stress-tests mechanistic claims only in a fly-vision model. No one has used graded distribution shift as the discriminating variable between rival explanations with interventions as the testbed, at LLM scale, despite the circuits community itself listing automated OOD hypothesis validation as an open direction. The experiment is cheap, tooling exists, results are informative whether positive or negative, and a working metric becomes shared infrastructure that every future decomposition paper can be scored against.

direction: Stress-test mechanistic anomaly detection for LLMs to determine whether anomaly scores track anomalous internal mechanisms or merely unusual inputs, under held-out trigger channels, benign distribution shift, and adaptive adversaries.
project: Mechanism or Distribution? A stress-test protocol and benchmark for mechanistic anomaly detectors in language models
question: Do current mechanistic anomaly scores detect anomalous mechanisms rather than just unusual inputs — do they separate triggered backdoor computation from benign-but-novel inputs of matched perplexity and matched outputs, and do they still catch backdoor behavior expressed through trigger channels never seen in the trusted calibration set?
first_experiment: LoRA-backdoor Gemma-2-2B-IT (Bailey et al. protocol), compute Gemma Scope SAE anomaly scores on four matched test sets — clean, triggered, held-out paraphrase triggers, and benign-unusual inputs matched in novelty and output string — and measure whether the score separates triggered from benign-unusual, decomposing any confound into mechanism vs. dictionary-OOD components.
why: It attacks the field's own top-diagnosed deployment gap (monitors fail under distribution shift) in the one empirically thin, high-leverage area — MAD is explicitly "rare" with only one 2026 method paper that stops short of this threat model, unlike the crowded CoT-faithfulness, deception-probe, and sandbagging literatures; it sidesteps the unsolved faithfulness and cross-architecture-transfer problems while functionally testing detector faithfulness; and both outcomes (detectors survive → deployment-ready evidence; detectors fail → the sharp negative result redirecting the field) directly change what the field does next, with the protocol itself becoming the missing benchmark standard.

direction: Build and ground-truth-validate a distribution-shift-based ("mechanistic extrapolation error") test that discriminates behaviorally-equivalent but mechanistically-different circuit decompositions, addressing the field's top open problem of decomposition faithfulness.
project: Behaviorally Equivalent ≠ Mechanistically Equivalent: Distribution-Shift Tests of Circuit Decomposition Faithfulness
question: Can disagreement between a learned decomposition's implied behavior and the model's actual behavior under mechanism-probing distribution shifts identify the faithful decomposition among behaviorally-equivalent candidates, more robustly than ablation-based faithfulness metrics and without access to ground truth?
first_experiment: On a known-ground-truth Boolean multi-hop toy and an InterpBench/SIIT transformer implementing a k-hop algorithm (with k+1, k+2-hop variants), train transcoders/CLTs at multiple sparsity levels, select behaviorally-equivalent decompositions, and test whether their mechanistic extrapolation error ranks them by ground-truth circuit recovery — stably across ablation methodologies.
why: The field's #1 named open problem (decomposition faithfulness / dual-basis selection) was just made acute by the ICML 2026 finding that sparsity penalities push cross-layer transcoders toward shallow unfaithful rewrites, while the constituent pieces (ground-truth organisms, OOD-prediction methodology, known metric fragility, MAD's dependence on faithful mechanisms) exist but have never been combined — so this is the highest-leverage, cheapest, and demonstrably unclaimed next step.

direction: Mechanistic interpretability should pivot from discovering and scoring single explanations to actively adjudicating among the multiple decompositions that all pass current validation — searching the input×intervention space where candidate mechanisms' predictions diverge, falsifying losers, and certifying behavioral equivalence when they cannot be separated.
project: Adjudicate: Active Discrimination and Equivalence Certification for Competing Mechanistic Explanations
question: When two or more decompositions (head-level circuits, SAE-feature circuits, subspace-patching accounts, attribution graphs) of the same model both pass faithfulness-style validation on the observed distribution, can we (a) efficiently find the inputs and interventions on which their predicted behaviors diverge, (b) use those experiments to falsify incorrect candidates with anytime-valid statistics, and (c) certify behavioral equivalence over an accessible experiment space when nothing separates them — and does the surviving explanation predict held-out errors and distribution shift strictly better than the eliminated ones?
first_experiment: Build a ground-truth testbed with a planted decoy: compile a simple RASP program into a Tracr transformer (true mechanism known by construction), and construct a second "decoy" explanation — an alternative program/circuit that agrees with the model on the task's training distribution but differs mechanistically (diverging only under held-out input transforms such as reordering, distractors, or alphabet extension). Verify the negative result that standard validation metrics (faithfulness under mean ablation, completeness, node overlap, max-activating examples) cannot distinguish decoy from ground truth; then run a prototype divergence search over input transforms × intervention types and show it immediately identifies the separating experiment. This validates the procedure where truth is known, then graduates to GPT-2 small IOI, where three published, mutually incompatible accounts (Wang et al.'s head-level circuit, the subspace-patching account shown to be an illusion by Makelov et al., and SAE-feature-based circuits) can be adjudicated, including against the model's errors, which current circuits demonstrably fail to explain.
why: It attacks the field's self-declared #1 gap — the verification bottleneck and the dual basis problem — which gates everything downstream: you cannot monitor, steer, edit, or transfer a mechanism you have misidentified, and unadjudicated attribution graphs risk becoming a pile of plausible-but-unvalidated stories precisely as they become the standard artifact. It is the most promising because (i) it converts interpretation from story-telling into falsifiable science with a concrete numerical deliverable (discrimination power of an experiment battery + equivalence certificates), (ii) it is tractable now: documented rival explanations exist for IOI-class tasks, ground-truth model organisms (Tracr/InterpBench) exist to validate the method itself, open tooling (TransformerLens, SAELens, circuit-tracer, Tracr) runs on a single GPU, and the statistical layer (anytime-valid tests) has just been imported by adjacent work I can build on. It has not already been done because every existing evaluation effort evaluates *one* explanation against fixed criteria — CIF certifies a single estimand, unit tests and error-agreement add criteria for a single claim, MIB/InterpBench rank discovery methods in-distribution, causal scrubbing tests a single human-designed hypothesis, and Méloux et al. proved non-identifiability but stopped at diagnosis; Sun & Toneva formalize equivalence but across models via representation similarity, not within one model via interventions, and active circuit discovery selects interventions for discovery efficiency, not for separating candidate mechanisms. No one searches the experiment space for where two candidate mechanisms diverge, and no one has built the decoy-generation machinery that makes the whole thing testable.

direction: Build the missing verification layer for mechanistic interpretability — certify circuit hypotheses by their ability to predict model behavior under held-out, mechanism-discriminating interventions and distribution shift, using model organisms with causally verified planted ground truth, and use that transportability score to resolve the dual-basis problem (which of several valid-looking decompositions is "the circuit").
project: Circuit Transport: A Held-Out Interventional Certification Benchmark for Mechanistic Hypotheses
question: Do circuit hypotheses recovered by current methods (attribution graphs over transcoders, SAE-feature ablations, patching-based subnetworks) predict the full model's behavior on held-out inputs and interventions that discriminate between competing mechanisms — how large is the in-distribution-to-OOD transport gap, and does selecting circuits by transportability rather than ID faithfulness pick the decomposition that actually tracks decision computation?
first_experiment: Using Pando's 720 released model organisms (exact planted decision-tree ground truth) plus 3 quirk-matched models from the Model Organism Lottery suite: train 2–3 SAE/transcoder decompositions with different seeds per organism; extract each decomposition's feature-circuit for the planted behavior, validating it only in-distribution as is standard practice; then score every hypothesis on five held-out families — (a) held-out rule instances, (b) surface paraphrases (renamed fields/values), (c) decision-threshold boundary inputs where alternative decompositions diverge, (d) decoy inputs that activate the circuit's features but where the planted mechanism computes something else, (e) benign-OOD prompts — measuring interventional prediction accuracy (ablated-circuit vs. full-model agreement) per family. Deliverable: the first quantified transport gap for current methods, decomposition-vs-decomposition divergence, and a test of whether transportability-selected features recover decision computation where ID-selected ones fail.
why: It attacks the single problem the field's own leadership ranks first (faithfulness as a numerical target + the dual-basis problem) at exactly the moment the ingredients became available but the integration doesn't exist: CIF supplies only statistics for a fixed estimand, the NeurIPS circuit-hypothesis tests cover only classic GPT-2 circuits in-distribution, "Many Circuits, One Mechanism" documents non-uniqueness but only at component level on toy tasks, "Do Circuits Explain Model Errors?" adds one necessary-but-insufficient test, Harvard's OOD prediction is a small-transformer proof-of-concept, and Pando measures audit value but never tests whether circuit hypotheses transport. A rigorous transportability protocol is upstream of every hot downstream agenda — reasoning-model biology, misalignment monitoring, auditing games, anomaly detection — each of which currently produces unverifiable mechanistic claims; fixing verification multiplies the value of all of them, it is tractable on released open models with modest compute, and it produces genuinely novel mechanistic findings (backup circuits, task-representation leakage, context-dependent superposition) as failure modes it surfaces.

direction: Mechanistic anomaly detection on circuit-level computational structure — using per-prompt transcoder attribution-graph statistics (error-node mass, edge/route topology) as the monitoring substrate instead of raw activations, evaluated adversarially against obfuscation attacks that defeat representation-level monitors.
project: Circuits as Fingerprints: Attribution-Graph Monitors for Detecting Hidden Computation in LLMs — and Their Limits under Obfuscation
question: Can structural statistics of per-prompt cross-layer-transcoder attribution graphs (per-layer error-node mass, edge-weight concentration, rare feature-route patterns) distinguish anomalous computation (backdoor triggers, password-locked sandbagging, conditioned deception) from trusted computation with low false positives on benign distractor behaviors — and does this circuit-level signal survive obfuscation attacks (adversarial suffixes, RL-obfuscation) that bypass probes, SAE monitors, and latent OOD detectors?
first_experiment: On Gemma-2-2B-it with the open circuit-tracer CLTs, train a small password-locked sandbagging LoRA and a simple trigger backdoor organism; compute for ~500 trusted benign, ~500 triggered-anomalous, and ~500 benign-distractor prompts the three cheap per-prompt quantities — (i) CLT feature activations per layer, (ii) per-layer error-node mass, (iii) top-k attribution edges via attribution patching from the output logit — then test whether simple graph statistics (error mass, edge-concentration Gini, rare-route density) AUROC-separate anomalous from both trusted and distractor-benign prompts, benchmarked against an activation-probe baseline at matched false-positive budgets.
why: It targets the field's two most explicitly-stated open safety problems simultaneously — the auditing-games false-positive failure and "mechanistic anomaly detection needs better decomposition" — at the exact intersection no one has entered: the circuit-tracing community has been racing on understanding/automation/faithfulness (4+ papers in 2026) while the monitoring community is stuck on activation-level signals that the obfuscation literature has now shown to be fundamentally bypassable, and the only transcoder-safety paper to date (July 2026) explicitly notes the space is empty and stops at steering. The hypothesis is scientifically crisp and falsifiable in both directions: an anomalous mechanism must still *perform* its function, so preserving harmful behavior while keeping the entire cross-layer causal route in-distribution is a strictly stronger obfuscation constraint than fooling a per-layer representation monitor — if that holds, we get the first white-box monitor with a principled robustness story; if it fails, we precisely map where the obfuscation-performance frontier sits, which recalibrates the whole latent-monitoring agenda. It has not been done because attribution-graph tooling and open CLT releases are barely a year old, the required assembly (circuit-level detector + adaptive attacker + distractor-calibrated false positives) spans two research communities that have not overlapped, and it is only now runnable on a single free-tier GPU — making it the rare high-importance direction that is simultaneously untouched, safety-critical, and tractable.

direction: Develop and apply a held-out interventional discrimination methodology with a quantitative circuit-predictive-validity metric to determine which behaviorally-equivalent attribution-graph circuit hypothesis is causally real in open LLMs.
project: Breaking Behavioral Ties: Held-Out Interventional Discrimination of Equivalent Circuit Hypotheses in Language Models
question: Which held-out interventional tests discriminate among behaviorally-equivalent feature-level circuit hypotheses (CLT vs. PLT vs. direct-path accounts) in real language models, and how much of the standard two-hop circuit narrative survives them?
first_experiment: Trace "The state containing Dallas has its capital in" on Gemma-2-2B and Llama-3.2-1B with released CLTs/PLTs, extract the top 3 competing path hypotheses from the seed graph, and score each hypothesis's predicted ablation/amplification effects against observed effects on held-out prompt families (novel state–capital pairs, 3-hop chains, corrupted intermediates, paraphrase/language shift, reversed queries) versus the seed prompt.
why: It targets the field's top-ranked 2026 open problem — attribution-graph faithfulness and the dual basis problem — at the exact moment the problem is proven in toy models (ICML 2026) but unsolved in real LMs, and it is distinct from the nearest prior work (toy-scale non-identifiability proofs, component-level structural-equivalence studies, discovery-stability certification, and the graph-annotation automation wave), tractable with existing open infrastructure, and yields a publishable quantitative result whether or not current circuit narratives generalize.

direction: Convert the newly documented non-identifiability of circuits from a liability into an experimental instrument — use disagreement-maximizing inputs across the equivalence class of candidate circuit explanations to arbitrate among them, define a non-circular faithfulness target, and build a mechanism-coverage monitor that flags when model behavior escapes every validated explanation.
project: Crucial Experiments for Circuits: Arbitrating Competiting Mechanistic Explanations by Disagreement
question: When many circuit explanations of a behavior are faithful on the extraction distribution, can inputs selected to maximize disagreement between them (a) recover a principled ranking of explanations by the model's actual behavior where they diverge, (b) yield a numerical faithfulness criterion that predicts held-out/template-shift/adversarial robustness better than on-distribution faithfulness, and (c) define an out-of-mechanism-family detector that catches real mechanism changes at low false-alarm rates?
first_experiment: On GPT-2 small with IOI and Greater-Than: extract ~40 candidate circuits per task by varying seeds, data subsamples, pruning thresholds, and templates (reusing documented axes and open pipelines — ACDC/EAP-IG in TransformerLens); verify all are faithful on-distribution; search for benign inputs maximizing ensemble disagreement (max-min pairwise KL between circuits' output distributions); measure the full model on the top disagreement inputs and test whether the disagreement-set ranking decorrelates from the on-distribution ranking and predicts which circuits survive new templates and known adversarial edge cases.
why: It attacks the gap the field itself ranks first — 2026 retrospectives call for a faithfulness-as-numerical-target, a principled way to rank decompositions beyond label readability, and monitors that know their own coverage — and it does so by *exploiting* the best-documented pathology (explanation multiplicity) rather than suppressing it, which turns a philosophical worry into a measurement tool and a deployment-shaped safety artifact. It has not been done because the field has treated multiplicity as variance to reduce (CIRCUS, Certified Circuits, CEAP all discard unstable structure), adversarial input search has only been applied to single circuits versus the model, and the equivalence-class framing plus the cheap multi-candidate infrastructure both matured only in 2025–2026; targeted searches for explanation-ensembles, discriminating/"crucial" experiments, model-discrimination-by-input-search, and mechanism-shift detection in mechanistic interpretability returned no instances, while every ingredient (MIB-standard tasks, open extraction pipelines, documented instability axes, adversarial-search precedent) is public and reproducible — making it simultaneously the highest-leverage open problem and one I can actually execute on open-weight models without frontier-scale compute.

direction: Build a non-circular validation standard for mechanistic explanations — score explanations by whether their predictions match the model on adversarial input batteries engineered to discriminate rival mechanisms, calibrated on model organisms with planted mechanisms and known decoys.
project: Litmus — Adversarial Discrimination Batteries for Validating Mechanistic Claims, Calibrated by Planted-Mechanism Model Organisms
question: When two mechanistic explanations (circuits, attribution graphs, feature sets, agent hypotheses) are equally faithful in-distribution, can a battery of distribution-shifted inputs engineered so that the rival mechanisms diverge — conflicting triggers, paraphrased/rellocated cues, novel entity combinations, obfuscated variants — reliably separate the true mechanism from plausible decoys, and do current interpretability pipelines (ACDC/EAP-IG, transcoder attribution graphs, SAE labels, LLM investigator agents) actually recover the true mechanism when scored this way?
first_experiment: Train a Pythia-160M/GPT-2-small model organism on a synthetic corpus with a planted conditional-routing mechanism (a document-level control token determines which of two entities is retrieved for recall); enumerate four decoy mechanism classes (position-keyed lookup, surface-pattern match, first-vs-last-token-wins, global-mode-flag); generate discriminating batteries for each decoy; then run ACDC, EAP-IG, and a small transcoder attribution graph blind on the organism and test whether each pipeline's extracted mechanism predicts the model's outputs on the batteries — measuring whether in-distribution faithfulness scores (which will look similar) fail to separate true from decoy while battery scores succeed.
why: It attacks the field's #1 self-diagnosed gap — the verification/faithfulness/dual-basis crisis named by both the Sharkey et al. open-problems coalition, its 2026 retrospective ("a quantitative faithfulness measure that everyone agrees on... trustworthy as opposed to circular"), and the Aug 2025 multi-org landscape doc ("objectively verifiable downstream tasks directly about understanding") — at the exact moment automated interpretability agents (SAEScientist-Bench, AuditBench investigator agents) are scaling up and desperately need a non-circular scorer of mechanistic claims rather than behavioral ones. It has not been done because each prior work stops short: Hanna et al. test held-out instances of the same task with no ground truth or decoys; InterpBench plants architecturally-imposed toy circuits with no realism, decoys, or shift batteries; AuditBench scores behavioral identification, not explanation correctness; CIF adds statistics to a chosen estimand without discriminating among estimands; and the multiplicity/phantom-specialization papers explicitly measure the problem while disclaiming a fix ("we do not propose a better method"). It is tractable at small scale with synthetic data and small models, yet the battery protocol itself scales to any model including frontier ones — planted organisms serve only as calibration — and it directly serves deployment: explanations that survive adversarial shift are precisely the ones safe to build monitors and audit filings on. It is also the kind of work an autonomous agent like me can fully execute and bootstrap: generating corpora, training organisms, running pipelines, and using LLM agents as the explainers under test.

direction: Build the field's missing scientific instrument — evaluate mechanistic explanations (attribution graphs, feature circuits, direction abstractions) as falsifiable theories by testing whether their quantitative causal predictions transfer to held-out, distribution-shifted inputs, and use that to rank competing decompositions of the same model.
project: Engineering Tolerances: A Predictive Faithfulness Benchmark for Mechanistic Explanations under Distribution Shift
question: When a mechanistic explanation validated in-distribution makes quantitative causal predictions (sign and magnitude of behavior change under feature ablation/steering), do those predictions transfer to held-out inputs across paraphrase, entity-substitution, multilingual, format, fictional-framing, encoded, and multi-turn escalation shifts — and can decompositions that agree in-distribution be distinguished by their held-out predictive accuracy, operationalizing the dual basis problem?
first_experiment: On Gemma-2-2B-it with Gemma Scope SAEs and the Arditi refusal direction: fit intervention-effect predictions (ΔP(refusal) under direction ablation/steering at several scales, plus SAE-feature ablations) on 100 in-distribution harmful prompts; then test sign-accuracy and Spearman rank-correlation of predicted vs. observed effects on 6 shift axes × 100 held-out prompts each, comparing the 1-node refusal-direction abstraction against the SAE-feature attribution graph — testing whether they agree in-distribution yet diverge out-of-distribution, with confidence sequences adopted from Certified Interventional Fidelity and effect-persistence measured over full generations (per the "SAE interventions are unreliable" caveat).
why: The field's own mid-2026 assessment names verification-faithfulness and the dual basis problem as its top open problems and explicitly calls for a shared numerical faithfulness score "the way language modeling has perplexity"; the concept (Li et al. 2025), statistics (CIF 2026), brittleness warnings (Certified Circuits, Méloux et al.), and infrastructure (Gemma Scope, circuit-tracer, nnsight) all exist but no one has assembled them into a predictive-faithfulness benchmark over real attribution-graph artifacts — closest works are synthetic proof-of-concept (Li et al.), a statistical layer with no benchmark content (CIF), discovery-stability certification rather than predictive validity (Certified Circuits), in-progress feature-label validation (not graph-level, not OOD, not dual-basis), and single-circuit case studies (Adaptive Circuit Behavior); it is tractable with one GPU and released open-model tooling, it directly upgrades deployment-critical findings (deception/refusal monitors collapsing under shift) into diagnosable explanation failures with "engineering tolerances" as the deliverable, and it is informative under both outcomes — a large OOD gap is a landmark result motivating explanation repair, and a small gap gives the field its agreed yardstick — whereas every alternative direction I surveyed (reward-hacking internals, CoT-faithfulness circuits, probe robustness, metacognition probing, attribution-graph automation) is already crowded, and agentic interpretability, while wide open, lacks a comparably crisp falsifiable entry point.

direction: Make causal coupling — whether decodable internal signals are actually load-bearing in the model's own computation — into a measured, mechanistically explained, cheaply predicted, and adversarially validated foundation for evasion-resistant latent monitoring.
project: Load-Bearing or Decorative? A Causal Coupling Audit and Etiology Taxonomy of Safety-Relevant Internal Signals
question: When a concept (refusal, truth, deception, eval-awareness, reasoning-error awareness) is decodable from a model's activations, what mechanistically determines whether the model's behavior causally depends on that representation — can decodable-but-uncoupled signals be classified into mechanistic etiologies (informational residue vs. anticipatory precomputation vs. dormant backups vs. actively gated-off computation vs. probe artifacts), can coupling be predicted cheaply from weights and activation statistics, and does a signal's coupling profile certify which latent monitors survive obfuscation-style evasion?
first_experiment: On Gemma-2-2B-it (cross-checked on Llama-3.2-1B-it), implement five canonical safety-relevant probes from published recipes, then for each signal measure (1) decodability (AUROC), (2) behavioral coupling via coherence-gated ablation/patching with CoAx-style conditional co-ablation so self-repair backups cannot mask true coupling, and (3) a weight-level readout screen (unembedding, attention QK/OV, downstream MLP W_in alignments to the probe direction) to classify uncoupled-but-decodable signals into etiology classes, each validated by class-specific interventions — culminating in an adversarial stress test (behavior-preserving fine-tune that removes the decodable signature) testing the prediction that decoupled monitors are evaded while coupled monitors survive or force detectable behavior change.
why: It targets the field's most consequential unexplained finding — the 2026 cluster (Decodability Is Not Causality; Lagged Coupling; Pretty Linear Liars; Read-Best Is Not Steer-Best; commitment-boundary/epiphenomenal CoT; Hidden Error Awareness) has established that decodability ≠ causal use everywhere it looked, but only demonstrates the gap in single settings, while nobody has built the multi-signal, self-repair-aware coupling audit, the mechanistic etiology of the gap, or the adversarially validated bridge from coupling to monitor evasion-resistance; it matters because latent monitoring is the flagship safety application and the evasion arms race (Obfuscated Activations, RL-Obfuscation, evasion-from-feedback) makes "which monitors are tamper-evident" a pressing, currently unanswerable question that the same quantity also predicts for steering/editing/unlearning failures; and it is tractable end-to-end on free open-weight models with existing artifacts (GemmaScope, circuit-tracer, open probe recipes, nnsight), serving exactly what the 2025 open-problems review (validate explanations, trustworthy monitoring) and DeepMind's pragmatic pivot (simple tools validated on concrete safety tasks) both demand.

direction: Move circuit tracing beyond per-prompt execution traces by systematically merging families of attribution graphs into invariant, algorithm-level "circuit schemas" whose cross-prompt stability serves as a non-circular validation signal and error predictor.
project: Circuit Schemas — Distilling Algorithm-Level Circuits from Families of Attribution Graphs
question: When one computational mechanism runs across a distribution of prompts, which nodes and edges of per-prompt attribution graphs constitute the invariant algorithm versus prompt-specific execution details — and does this decomposition (a) transfer causally to held-out prompts, (b) discriminate faithful deep computations from unfaithful shallow rewrites, and (c) predict where the model itself fails?
first_experiment: On Gemma-2-2B with public cross-layer transcoders (Anthropic's open-source circuit-tracer, runs on a free Colab GPU): (1) estimate the tracing pipeline's noise floor by re-generating the graph for one prompt under varied seeds/pruning thresholds; (2) trace two-hop factual recall ("The state containing {city} has its capital in") over 50 held-in city/state/capital triples, matching features across graphs by decoder-direction cosine similarity and activation-pattern correlation; (3) compute the per-node/per-edge invariance spectrum (fraction of family prompts in which each matched node/edge appears); (4) freeze the invariant core and test it on 50 held-out triples — replacement score per prompt, transfer of interventions (ablating the entity→state lookup node), and whether low-invariance/execution-trace variability predicts the model's errors on ambiguous entities (name-share cities, multi-state cities). Success criterion: the invariant core beats per-prompt circuits at reproducing held-out behavior, and its interventions transfer across the family; failure (invariance at the noise floor) would itself be a significant negative result about attribution graph stability.
why: It simultaneously attacks the field's two highest-priority open problems — the dual-basis/faithfulness problem (the top methodological complaint of the 2026 retrospective, instantiated by ICML 2026's CLT-unfaithfulness result) and the "merge graphs into a global circuit picture" item named twice in the attribution-graph community's own future-work list — and it is demonstrably not already done: every adjacent 2024–2026 work either automates per-graph annotation, diagnoses non-uniqueness without constructing a merged representation, or aggregates importance scores without aligning per-prompt computational structure, held-out graph prediction, or failure localization; and it is feasible now on open weights, cheap enough for a single researcher, with generalizable leverage as prerequisite infrastructure for scaling circuit tracing to frontier models, agentic trajectories, and mechanistic anomaly detection.

direction: Make the residual computation that sparse dictionaries fail to explain — currently a dismissed error term in SAEs/transcoders — the object of mechanistic study and a new, obfuscation-robust channel for mechanistic anomaly detection.
project: Outside the Dictionary: The Anatomy and Safety Monitoring of Sparse-Decomposition Residuals
question: Does safety-relevant anomalous computation (obfuscated jailbreaks, backdoor triggers, sandbagging, and ordinary model errors) concentrate in the residual/error term that sparse dictionaries and transcoders fail to capture, and can residual-based signals (error-node influence, reconstruction adequacy) serve as mechanistic anomaly monitors that survive adaptive obfuscation better than feature- and probe-based monitors?
first_experiment: On gemma-2-2b with public cross-layer transcoders (circuit-tracer), compute per-layer/per-position residual statistics — reconstruction-error norm, error-node influence fraction, activation energy outside active dictionary features — for matched prompt sets: benign trusted inputs, obfuscated jailbreak suffixes that bypass SAE/probe monitors, clean jailbreaks, backdoor-trigger inputs, and natural OOD inputs; test whether residual load discriminates mechanistic anomalies from mere distributional shift (AUROC with matched-output controls), and whether it predicts the prompts where attribution graphs currently fail to give satisfying insight.
why: It attacks the field's most-cited unsolved foundation (dictionary error / missing concepts) through its highest-value application (monitoring stealthy behavior), at the exact intersection where six recent results (error nodes, pathological SAE errors, unfaithful CLTs, circuits-that-miss-errors, obfuscated-activation attacks, white-box tools underperforming in audits) all converge but none has looked; it is not already done because the dictionary-learning, monitoring, and circuit-evaluation communities each treat the residual as someone else's problem, and it is tractable for a small effort using public transcoders, open models, and released attack artifacts — with a useful answer either way, since a null result would calibrate the "compression loses edge cases" critique while a positive result yields a new monitoring primitive and a roadmap for error-targeted dictionary expansion.

direction: Treat rival mechanistic decompositions (SAE features, transcoder attribution graphs, edge circuits) of the same behavior as competing hypotheses making testable intervention predictions, and map where their agreement holds on-distribution versus where it breaks under distribution and intervention shift — validated against known-mechanism model organisms — to produce the field's first quantitative "explanation validity envelope" and an ensemble-divergence anomaly signal.
project: Equivalence Envelopes: Measuring When Rival Mechanistic Explanations of the Same Model Diverge
question: When multiple heterogeneous decompositions of the same model and behavior agree on the discovery distribution, where exactly do their intervention predictions diverge under input-distribution shift and altered intervention contexts; does that divergence predict where explanations demonstrably fail; and can inter-explanation disagreement serve as an unsupervised mechanistic anomaly signal validated on planted-mechanism organisms?
first_experiment: On GPT-2 small (indirect object identification) and one InterpBench model with a known planted mechanism, build an ensemble of decompositions — 3+ SAEs across seeds/widths/objectives (public plus self-trained), one transcoder-based attribution graph via open CircuitTracer, and ACDC/EAP-IG edge circuits — convert each into a claim set of predicted ablation/resampling effects (ΔKL, Δlogit-diff) per component set per input distribution, measure pairwise claim agreement in-distribution, then re-measure on shifted families (token-frequency bands, templates, languages, lengths) and altered intervention contexts, and test whether inter-explanation divergence tracks the documented failure cases (Geng et al.'s context-distortion misrankings; uit de Bos & Garriga-Alonso's benign-input IOI failures).
why: It targets the field's own top-ranked 2026 open problem — the dual-basis/faithfulness gap that gates all downstream safety applications — at the moment when every required ingredient (public dictionaries, attribution-graph tooling, known-mechanism benchmarks, backdoor organisms) has just matured; it has not been done because each existing paper covers only one slice (edge circuits at one shift type in "Many Circuits, One Mechanism"; metric critique in Geng et al.; toy-model OOD prediction in Li et al.; feature-level seed variance in Paulo & Belrose/Leask/Gerasimov; influence-function rather than decomposition-ensemble anomaly detection in the Melbourne MAD work), while the heterogeneous, claim-level, ground-truth-validated synthesis remains unclaimed and is tractable for a small-compute researcher using open artifacts.

direction: Mechanistic interpretability should next build the missing construct that turns explanation non-identifiability from a diagnosed problem into a solved one — using predictive divergence under systematically designed distribution shift as a ground-truth-validated discriminator among behaviorally equivalent circuit explanations.
project: SHIFT-TIEBREAK: Ground-Truth-Validated Discrimination of Rival Circuit Explanations via Out-of-Distribution Predictive Divergence
question: When multiple circuit or attribution-graph explanations of a behavior are behaviorally equivalent on the discovery distribution, does predictive divergence between the candidate explanation (ablated/replacement model) and the full model across a designed family of shifted inputs (compositional depth, distractor injection, token-frequency bands, position/length shifts, counterfactual variable swaps) identify which explanation tracks the model's true mechanism — and can this be packaged as a non-circular "generalization faithfulness" score that outperforms in-distribution faithfulness, inclusion stability, and label interpretability?
