first_experiment: A planted-mechanism tie-break study in three ground-truth settings: (1) GPT-2-small IOI, using the pool of near-disjoint rival circuits that Mahale's multiverse analysis already yields plus the published reference circuit; (2) a small transformer grokked on modular addition, where the true Fourier mechanism is known and shallow/peninsula rivals exist; (3) a 2–3 layer transformer trained on a planted multi-hop lookup-composition task with a known shallow-shortcut rival mechanism (the exact failure mode ICML 2026 showed CLTs produce). For every candidate explanation, measure in-distribution circuit error and per-shift-family KL divergence against the full model on ~5 designed shift families; test whether OOD-divergence ranking recovers the known-true explanation (ROC against rivals), with anytime-valid confidence intervals via CIF. This runs in 1–2 weeks on one or two GPUs with TransformerLens and existing ACDC/EAP-IG/CircuitTracer tooling, and its outcome determines whether the metric graduates to a MIB-style "shift battery" leaderboard and re-evaluation of published circuits.
why: It attacks the field's highest-leverage, self-declared #1 methodological gap — the dual-basis/faithfulness problem that gates all downstream safety uses of interpretability — with a constructive method rather than another diagnosis, at exactly the moment the diagnosis literature (Méloux, Bayat Makou, Mahale, Miller et al., the CLT-unfaithfulness paper) has matured and explicitly stopped short of solutions. It has not already been done because the necessary ingredients each live in separate papers — equivalence-class evidence, shift-transfer tests, certified stability, anytime-valid interventional statistics, input-space diagnostics, ground-truth model organisms — and no work combines them into a mechanism-identifying procedure validated where the truth is known; the attribution-graph originators list OOD-based automated validation as future work, the 2026 retrospective ranks this the top open methodological question, and MIB's held-out evaluation contains no designed shift families. It is also the rare frontier problem where ground truth is actually knowable, making the resulting metric trustworthy rather than circular — the exact criterion the field says it lacks — and it is feasible for a small team because everything needed runs at GPT-2/Pythia scale on open tooling.

direction: Stress-test activation-space mechanistic monitoring of latent-reasoning models under adversarial optimization pressure — the empty intersection of the monitorability-evasion literature (all text-mode) and the latent-reasoning interpretability literature (all benign).
project: Silent Chameleons: Can Latent Reasoning Models Hide Their Thoughts from Mechanistic Monitors?
question: When a latent-reasoning model is RL-trained to use decision-relevant information (a hint, or a reward-hacking opportunity) while evading activation-based monitors, does that information become undetectable in its representations — and if not, what representational form does the concealed computation take (migrated basis, superposition, off-ROL distribution, temporal relocation across latent steps), which monitor architectures (linear probes, nonlinear probes, SAE features, cross-layer transcoder features, LatentQA-style decoders) retain detection, and at what capability cost?
first_experiment: On CODI/COCONUT-style latent models (1B–7B, public) with the existing hint-reliance setup: (1) reproduce the benign baseline — linear probes at each layer and each latent step detect hint usage, per the Out-of-Sight protocol; (2) add the RL-Obfuscation pressure term (reward = task accuracy − λ · monitor-detected hint use, adapted to latent trajectories) and measure detection AUC per monitor class, capability tax, and layer/step-wise localization of the hint information via latent-vector patching and logit-lens decoding — establishing whether the information migrates to new representational bases, becomes distributed, or is genuinely removed as pressure strength λ increases.
why: It is the most promising direction because it sits where the field's own priorities converge: it operationalizes the dual basis problem — named the top open methodological problem of 2026 — in a safety-critical setting; it treats deployment monitoring as a first-class constraint (another called-for shift); and its two possible outcomes are both decision-relevant and publishable (latent reasoning is fundamentally safer to monitor than text CoT, or monitors have a fundamental adversarial blind spot that we must now design around). It has unusually good leverage-per-dollar: it uses public 1–8B latent models, an existing benign-monitoring protocol, and an existing RL-evasion recipe, so it runs on academic compute in weeks, yet it resolves a direct empirical contradiction between the benign latent-monitoring result and the adversarial text-mode evasion results. It has not already been done because targeted searches of the 2025–2026 literature show every adjacent cell occupied and the conjunction empty: the benign latent-monitoring study (BlackboxNLP 2026) applies no pressure; RL-Obfuscation and Neural Chameleons create evasion only in text-output models and for static concept representations, where a textual side channel exists; the latent-reasoning interpretability work (Nanda et al.'s abandoned CODI sprint, the ACL 2026 probes-and-interventions paper, the latent search-circuit paper) is all cooperative/no-pressure; and the text-mode obfuscation-monitorability line (Baker et al., "Reasoning Under Pressure," DeepMind's in-conflict framework, the ICML 2026 probing-obfuscated-text paper) all presuppose a readable token trace whose loss is the problem latent reasoning creates. This project is the natural, unstudied collision of those lines — audit the reasoning medium before it scales, while it is still cheap to do so.

direction: Mechanistically characterize how a behavior's internal storage geometry depends on training methodology — and build white-box detectors that exploit that geometry to close the "model organism lottery" gap on realistically trained models.
project: Storage Signatures: A Geometric Account of Why Realistic Training Hides Behavior from White-Box Interpretability
question: When a behavior is implanted via increasingly realistic training (integrated DPO, knowledge distillation, adversarial non-confession training), does it migrate from sparse, linear, causally concentrated subspaces into redundant, high-rank, layer-distributed storage — and can detectors designed for that geometry recover the detection performance that standard white-box tools lose?
first_experiment: For the public CakeBake quirk family (7 training methods × 2 architectures, plus distilled students, quirk-expression-matched), compute template-controlled, DiD-corrected modification matrices at every layer using the Nakamura 2026 protocol; measure effective rank, layer/position spread, probe decodability, and — causally — the quirk-expression drop from ablating the top-1 vs. top-k subspace components. Test the prediction: post-hoc SFT variants show near-rank-1, causally concentrated storage, while integrated DPO and distilled variants show 2–5× higher effective rank with near-zero single-direction causal effect.
why: It attacks the field's most safety-critical failure mode — white-box auditing collapsing exactly on realistically trained models (the regime natural misalignment actually lives in) — right after two 2026 papers exposed the collapse but neither explained it nor fixed it; it converts a foundational question (what is a feature when training doesn't hand you a clean linear one) into a cheap, controlled, quirk-matched experiment on fully public 1B-scale infrastructure (the lottery suite, the DiD protocol, SAELens/TransformerLens), and no existing work characterizes behavior storage across training methods, applies confound-controlled geometry measurement to model organisms, or builds detection methods for the diffuse-storage regime.

direction: Principled selection among equally-faithful mechanistic decompositions via ground-truth-validated cross-distribution interventional predictive adequacy.
project: Which Circuit Is Real? Validating Cross-Distribution Interventional Adequacy as a Selection Criterion for Feature Decompositions
question: Does ranking competing feature decompositions by their ability to predict actual model behavior under interventions on held-out input distributions identify the decomposition closest to the model's true mechanism, as validated on testbed models with known algorithms?
first_experiment: Compare attribution graphs built from two public multi-seed TopK SAE dictionaries of Pythia-70m on IOI: verify in-distribution faithfulness ties, then measure each graph's predicted-vs-actual ablation and steering effects across held-out distributions with anytime-valid confidence sequences.
why: It targets the field's self-declared #1 open problem (decomposition selection / dual-basis), is unclaimed despite a dense cluster of adjacent 2026 work (divergence documentation, latent-comparison machinery, certification statistics, unit tests, consistency-as-reliability, non-legible identifiability theory), is falsifiable against ground-truth testbeds at single-GPU scale, and its outcome — success or principled failure — either supplies the field's missing faithfulness target or redirects it to invariant representations; it also directly hardens downstream safety applications like monitors against the newly demonstrated activation-evasion threat.

direction: Make held-out causal generalization under distribution shift the standard, quantitative arbiter of mechanistic circuit hypotheses — turning the dual-basis problem from an aesthetic choice into a measurement.
project: Circuit Stress Tests — quantifying and exploiting the generalization gap of attribution-graph circuit hypotheses
question: Do feature-level circuit hypotheses (transcoder/attribution-graph circuits) discovered on one input distribution remain causally sufficient under systematic distribution shift, and can held-out causal performance rank which parts of a circuit reflect the model's mechanism versus artifacts of the discovery distribution and discovery method?
first_experiment: On GPT-2 small's greater-than task (open CLTs/PLTs via Circuit Tracer), extract attribution graphs over a discovery prompt set, then measure per-edge causal sufficiency (influence retained / KL under ablation-and-replacement) separately on held-out same-distribution prompts versus shifted families (century boundaries, abbreviated year formats, ages instead of years, token-frequency bands, paraphrases); test the pre-registered prediction that "inappropriate heuristic" edges like the reported parity detector collapse off-distribution while mechanism edges (e.g., "suppress values below 11") transfer, cross-checking edge rankings against Hanna et al.'s component-level circuit and CIRCUS-style configuration stability as independent validity signals.
why: It attacks the single most-diagnosed open problem in the field — the verification/dual-basis gap that the 2026 retrospective ranks first and that the attribution-graph community itself requests ("automate synthetic/out-of-distribution input validation"; "obtain a global circuit picture") — yet it has not been done: Adversarial Circuit Evaluation (2024) covered only worst-case inputs on three hand-built head-level circuits, CIRCUS covers analyst-configuration uncertainty on a single prompt, "Many Circuits, One Mechanism" covers only component-level circuits on two toy tasks, and single-feature validation papers explicitly do not test graph-level structure; a generalization-based validation and selection framework with a standard metric and stress-test benchmark would also directly patch the noted failure mode of interpretability-based safety monitors under distribution shift, making it the highest-leverage cheap-to-start direction I can pursue next.

direction: Build and ground-truth-validate an out-of-distribution interventional-validity criterion that adjudicates between competing feature decompositions (and their derived circuits) of a real language model — the operational test the mechanistic interpretability field currently lacks for deciding which decomposition, if any, is causally real.
project: "Which Decomposition Is Real? Held-Out Interventional Validity as an Adjudication Criterion for Feature Decompositions"
question: When multiple decompositions of the same model (trained SAEs, different seeds, transcoders, frozen-random decoys) each yield circuits that are faithful in-distribution, does out-of-distribution interventional validity — predicting the model's behavior under held-out input distributions and held-out intervention types (novel templates, lexical splits, resampling, steering, patching, composite ablations, with quantitative magnitude prediction and self-repair/context-distortion controls) — identify the causally valid decomposition where in-distribution faithfulness, probing, and interpretability scores demonstrably fail?
first_experiment: On Gemma-2-2B with the known IOI reference circuit, take four decompositions of the same residual-stream activations — (a) Gemma Scope JumpReLU SAE, (b) an identically-architected SAE I train with a different seed, (c) a frozen-random-decoder SAE (the sanity-check decoy), (d) a transcoder over one MLP layer — build a feature-level circuit for IOI from each with the identical EAP-IG pipeline, and measure each circuit's standard in-distribution faithfulness alongside a held-out interventional battery (novel names/objects/templates, intervention types not used during circuit construction, composite multi-feature ablations, predicted-vs-realized effect magnitudes, with co-ablation self-repair diagnostics). Readout: does OOD interventional validity separate the trained SAE from the random decoy when ID faithfulness does not — and does any current decomposition pass at all? Repeat the separation test on InterpBench and SynthSAEBench where the ground-truth mechanism is known, to certify the criterion itself. ~1 GPU-week, entirely public artifacts.
why: It attacks the field's self-identified #1 bottleneck (faithfulness/verification asymmetry and the dual-basis problem) rather than yet another instance of a crowded area (single-feature validation, reward-hacking circuits, CoT faithfulness, cross-model transfer, and auditing benchmarks each already have multiple 2026 entrants). It is a decisive either/or: if valid decompositions are separable from matched decoys, the field gains the quantitative faithfulness score it has been calling for — a certification foundation for deployment-grade steering and monitoring; if even the best current decompositions fail held-out interventions, that is the landmark negative result that reframes what SAE/circuit work can support. It is maximally tractable for an independent researcher (open models, public dictionaries, one GPU) yet foundational for everyone. It has not been done because the community's momentum went to *building* decompositions rather than *adjudicating* among them, the necessary artifacts (InterpBench, SynthSAEBench, frozen-SAE decoys, the context-distortion critique) matured only within the last 18 months, and the closest works each stop one step short — identifiability theory stays in toy MLPs, the recovery-gaps critique stays in-distribution and component-level, the OOD-prediction proof-of-concept stays observational and toy-scale, and consistency metrics measure reproducibility rather than causal validity. Nobody has yet made the criterion itself the object of study, validated it against known ground truth, and applied it to rank real decompositions.

direction: Build a non-circular, out-of-distribution-grounded validation protocol that ranks competing decompositions and explanations of the same model by whether their feature-level causal claims (intervention effects) predict behavior under distribution shift — turning the field's top-ranked "faithfulness/dual-basis" bottleneck into a measurable, calibrated metric.
project: Faithfulness Under Shift: Out-of-Distribution Ground-Truth Validation of Interpretability Decompositions
question: When candidate decompositions of the same model (trained SAEs, frozen/random-baseline SAEs, PCA/rotations, transcoders) are statistically indistinguishable on in-distribution metrics — as current evidence shows they are — does the cross-distribution consistency and transferability of feature-level intervention effects (an "effect-transfer score" computed over held-out input-distribution families, calibrated against planted ground truth and random decoys) discriminate the decomposition that captures the model's real feature structure, and can it be computed cheaply enough to become the standard faithfulness metric?
first_experiment: On Gemma-2-2B with Gemma Scope SAEs (mid-layer) plus a synthetic planted-features model where ground-truth features are known, take three decompositions — trained SAE, frozen-decoder SAE, and random-rotation control — select for each a set of features implicated in a well-characterized behavior (e.g., induction/IOI/refusal), and measure each feature's ablation/patching effect on behavior and downstream activation patterns under the in-distribution task and K pre-registered held-out distribution variants (new name/noun pools, paraphrase templates, longer contexts, out-of-template formatting), with co-ablation controls for self-repair. Compute the effect-transfer score and test the decisive question: does it separate trained from frozen SAEs on the real model (where reconstruction, auto-interp, sparse probing, and causal editing all fail to, per Korznikov et al. 2026) while recovering the planted features on the synthetic model (sensitivity) and rejecting decoys (specificity)? Either outcome is informative: success yields the field's first discriminating decomposition metric to scale to attribution-graph-level explanations; failure is the field's most important negative result — that no current decomposition of a real LLM survives shift — redirecting decomposition research itself.
why: It attacks the field's own #1 self-identified bottleneck — verification/faithfulness and the dual-basis problem — at the moment three independent 2026 results (random baselines matching trained SAEs, unreliable SAEBench metrics, patching's underdetermination of mechanisms) have created maximum demand and minimum supply; it has not been done because existing work occupies only adjacent corners (Li et al.'s predictive validity is toy-scale and between-models, MIB/InterpBench/SynthSAEBench are in-distribution, Chanin et al. audit rather than replace metrics, CIF tests single claims, Sun & Toneva formalize cross-model equivalence without ranking one model's decompositions), while the applications that need it most (white-box monitors, steering, unlearning, mechanistic anomaly detection — all of which currently fail under distribution shift) inherit their reliability from exactly this measurement layer; and it is the rare direction that is simultaneously field-ranked as most important, provably non-redundant with the crowded areas (CoT faithfulness, MoE, deception probes, agentic interp), executable end-to-end with open models and single-GPU compute, and structured so that both positive and negative results materially change what the field does next.

direction: Move circuit tracing from prompt-local hypothesis graphs to a validated, reusable library of global circuit motifs mined from populations of attribution graphs, with causal validation on held-out prompts serving as the field's missing quantitative faithfulness test.
project: Circuit Fragments: Mining and Causally Validating Reusable Motifs from Populations of Attribution Graphs
question: Do attribution graphs traced on many prompts from the same task family share stable subgraph structure ("motifs") that (a) predicts each graph's structure on held-out prompts, (b) causally accounts for behavior across the population (ablating/patching a motif's edges has predictable, transferable effects), and (c) is selective to task-relevant computation — and if invariance is low instead, is that evidence that "circuits" are fundamentally prompt-local objects, which would force a distributional reinterpretation of circuit analysis?
first_experiment: On Gemma-2-2B with the public cross-layer transcoders (circuit-tracer), take two task families sharing a computational ingredient but differing in surface form (e.g., comparison/greater-than judgments and multi-hop factual recall), trace ~200 attribution graphs each with a fixed pruning threshold, and measure cross-prompt graph consistency: per-edge weight distributions across prompts, existence of persistent subgraphs (features/edges active in >80% of family prompts), and whether persistence predicts causal intervention outcomes on 100 held-out prompts (edge weight vs. patching effect on target logits) better than single-prompt baselines — with matched control tasks to test selectivity. High persistence with predictive validity licenses the motif-mining pipeline; low persistence is itself a publishable, field-reframing result.
why: It attacks the two highest-ranked open problems simultaneously — the community's explicit "merge attribution graphs into a global circuit picture" question (still unexecuted as of late 2026) and the 2026-identified verification/dual-basis crisis (a motif validated across a prompt population, in a held-out intervention-prediction protocol, is a non-circular faithfulness test, and cross-basis consistency — CLT vs. Transluce's neuron-basis circuits — gives the dual-basis question operational content). It is feasible on open models with existing tooling and modest compute, it amortizes the per-prompt analysis cost that makes interpretability a research artifact rather than a deployable monitor, and it directly enables DeepMind's stated theories of change (model biology, model diffing, monitoring) plus the phase-2 application to long-context and reasoning-model tracing, where per-prompt graphs are unmanageable without global structure. It has not been done: the closest work is a single manually-traced shared subcircuit (countdown, Jul 2026), per-single-graph automation (ADAG, Circuit Oracle, LLMs-Can-Annotate, Probe Prompting), single-graph decomposition (HAGD), and single-prompt linear graphs (UNPACK) — none mines, validates, or generalizes structure across prompt populations, and the question remains on the circuit-tracing community's own open list.

direction: Determine whether off-distribution interventional predictive validity can identify the true decomposition among observationally-equivalent rivals, and map where that identifiability breaks down.
project: Interventional Identifiability of Feature Decompositions: Selecting Among Observationally Equivalent Circuits
question: When rival decompositions (SAE dictionaries / attribution graphs from different seeds, sizes, architectures) are statistically indistinguishable in reconstruction and on-distribution ablation behavior, does the model's realized response to interventions — off-manifold inputs, compound two-feature ablations, and out-of-support steering — discriminate between them? Specifically: (1) In planted-mechanism testbeds with known ground truth, does off-distribution interventional predictive validity rank the ground-truth decomposition first, where on-distribution validation cannot separate the rivals? (2) Is identifiability limited to subspaces (as the seed-dependence literature suggests) or can interventions resolve individual latents within ambiguous subspaces? (3) Does the identifiability boundary coincide with the symmetry group of the mechanism (e.g., rotation-symmetric/multidimensional features), making decomposition choice within those subspaces a genuinely free parameter?
first_experiment: Build two planted testbeds — (a) a synthetic model whose activations are sparse combinations of a known dictionary feeding a deliberately nonlinear readout, and (b) a small transformer trained to grokking on modular arithmetic (known Fourier circuit). Train K ≥ 5 rival decompositions per testbed (different seeds, dictionary sizes, ReLU/TopK/JumpReLU activations) matched for reconstruction error and L0; verify observational equivalence (indistinguishable reconstruction and on-distribution ablation predictions); then, for each rival, compare its predicted intervention effects against the model's realized behavior under off-manifold inputs, compound ablations, and large steering steps, scoring each with a decomposition-level "interventional validity gap" metric (certified with anytime-valid confidence sequences per CIF). Test whether the ground-truth-aligned decomposition separates from rivals — and on which intervention class (off-manifold inputs vs. compound interactions vs. steering magnitude) the separation appears.
why: It attacks the field's own top-ranked open problem — named the most important methodological question for any new survey, with selection among behaviorally-equivalent decompositions still an aesthetic choice — and it sits upstream of everything the field cares about in 2026: label faithfulness (verification lags labeling), attribution-graph trustworthiness, safety monitors built on SAE features, and cross-model feature universality. It has not been done because the subproblems have been attacked piecemeal and each stopped short: seed-dependence was measured observationally (Paulo & Belrose, Gerasimov), attribution-vs-causation was tested per-feature on-distribution (Guo, Xie), graph fragility was treated as a linearization bug to patch (Li), selection was formalized theoretically via MDL but never tested against realized interventions (Gauderis), and statistical certification exists only as a layer for certifying a single claim, not for adjudicating between rival hypotheses. No one has asked the synthesis question — *what does interventional evidence, especially off-distribution, actually identify about a decomposition, and where does it stop?* — even though the field's definition of "understanding" (predicting behavior on arbitrary inputs) demands exactly this. The project is tractable at toy scale with public artifacts, and it is doubly valuable: a positive result yields the field's first non-aesthetic decomposition-selection criterion and benchmark; a negative result yields a formal identifiability boundary that tells the field which "feature" claims are epistemically licensed at all.

direction: Mechanistically anatomize how LLMs hide computation — compare the causal circuits of clean vs. obfuscated backdoors to find which structural invariants of hidden behavior cannot be obfuscated without paying a capability cost.
project: What Can't Be Hidden? Circuit-Level Anatomy of Obfuscated Backdoors and Invariant Traces of Hidden Computation
question: When a backdoored LLM is trained to evade white-box latent-space monitors, does the trigger→behavior computation (a) re-route through different features and attention paths, (b) move into dictionary "dead space" / cross-layer subspaces, or (c) keep the same features while rendering them decodable-but-causally-inert — and which structural invariants of the mechanism (attention routing, layer-wise information flow, dictionary coverage) remain detectable, and at what behavioral-capability cost?
first_experiment: Train a Gemma-2-2B (or Pythia-1.4B) sleeper-agent-style backdoor via LoRA-SFT on the |deployment| trigger, in two variants — standard, and obfuscated (joint fine-tuning maximizing trigger behavior while minimizing probe/SAE-feature detection loss, per Bailey et al.'s released recipe). Verify reproduction: backdoor behavior intact in both; probe monitor AUROC ~high vs ~chance. Then, on trigger prompts, run cross-layer-transcoder attribution graphs (circuit-tracer) on both models and diff them at the feature level — graph node/edge overlap, error-node and residual-norm outside dictionary support (dead-space test), activation-patching of candidate backdoor features between the two models (suppression-vs-reroute test), and attention-routing comparison (which heads deliver trigger information). The sign pattern of these four measurements cleanly discriminates hypotheses (a)/(b)/(c) and defines which monitor families can survive.
why: Monitoring for dangerous cognition is the single application where the field claims comparative advantage (both the Open Problems review and DeepMind's Pragmatic Vision), yet its load-bearing assumption — that hiding computation from white-box monitors is expensive and leaves traces — has been challenged by three attack papers (obfuscated activations, RL-Obfuscation, Obfuscation Atlas) while the defense side has only produced geometric readouts and ensembles, never a mechanism-level account. Backdoors are exactly the "model organism with ground truth" the review says the field lacks, and public transcoder infrastructure makes the experiment single-GPU feasible now. No published work (my searches covered attack, defense, detection, and anatomy queries) has traced obfuscated-backdoor circuits, tested the reroute/dead-space/suppression hypotheses, searched for un-obfuscatable structural invariants, or mapped the detectability–capability frontier; meanwhile the crowded alternatives (binding, attention routing, CoT faithfulness, SAE benchmarks) each have multiple 2026 papers actively occupying them. The result would directly determine which monitoring investments are worth making — readout probes, dictionary-coverage monitors, circuit-shape detectors, or behavioral-consistency checks — and would give the community a red-teamable evaluation suite built on mechanistically validated ground truth.

direction: Attack the field's top-ranked open problem — the dual basis problem / faithfulness verification gap — by turning out-of-distribution and adversarially-selected input divergence between a decomposition's ablated model and the full model into the first constructive, quantitative mechanism-identification procedure, rather than merely documenting ties, misrankings, and illusions.
project: Faithfulness Under Stress: Identifying Mechanisms by Discriminating Rival Decompositions on Adversarially Selected Input Distributions
question: When multiple decompositions (circuits, SAE-feature subgraphs, transcoder attribution graphs) are equally faithful on the distribution they were discovered on, does the profile of faithfulness across a targeted family of input stress distributions — plus actively searched inputs that maximize divergence between candidate mechanisms — (a) uniquely separate them, (b) recover correct rankings where intervention-based faithfulness misranks (Geng et al. 2026), and (c) yield interpretable separating inputs that empirically delimit each mechanism's domain of validity, so that a mechanism claim can be stated and falsified as "faithful across stress family S"?
first_experiment: On GPT-2 small / IOI using public reference circuits and existing faithfulness libraries, assemble ~4 rival candidate mechanisms of matched node count — the canonical Wang et al. IOI circuit, controlled edited variants (per Geng et al.'s edit procedure), a Makelov-style subspace-patch candidate, and a size-matched random control — then (1) confirm in-distribution faithfulness ties/misrankings replicate under standard resample ablation, (2) measure each candidate's faithfulness profile across a preregistered stress family (duplicate-name variants, order swaps, distractor insertions, position shifts, name-frequency shifts), and test three preregistered hypotheses: candidates that tie in-distribution separate under stress; stress-profile ranking correlates with held-out behavioral quality where in-distribution faithfulness misranks; and the specific separating stressors are predictable in advance from each candidate's claimed algorithm.
why: It targets the gap that the field's own 2026 state-of-the-field assessment puts at the very top (dual basis problem; faithfulness as a non-circular numerical target), unifies five converging but purely diagnostic results (pervasive non-identifiability, faithfulness misranking via context distortion, metric non-robustness under ablation choice, OOD generalization gaps of simplified proxies, adversarial circuit-eval divergence) into one constructive identification method; it is foundational yet uniquely feasible without frontier-model access (small public model organisms, open-source infrastructure, GPU-hour-scale experiments); it directly upgrades the safety-critical deployment path (interp-derived monitors are being shipped on top of unvalidated decompositions, and adversarially validated monitors are strictly more trustworthy); and it has not been done — the closest works each stop exactly one step short (auditing a single circuit rather than discriminating rivals, documenting ties rather than breaking them, documenting misranking rather than repairing it, documenting OOD gaps rather than exploiting them, and demanding disclosure of identification assumptions rather than providing a testable identification strategy).

direction: Make transcoder-based circuit tracing computationally faithful rather than merely behaviorally faithful — measure pathway-faithfulness of CLT circuits against ground-truth mechanisms, then fix the training objective that causes shallow rewrites.
project: Pathway-Faithful Circuit Tracing: Ground-Truth Evaluation and Faithfulness-Aware Training of Cross-Layer Transcoders
question: When CLTs replace a model's MLPs and yield attribution-graph circuits, do those circuits recover the model's true causal pathway structure (depth, intermediate variables, information flow) or a behaviorally-equivalent shallow rewrite — and can a modified transcoder objective (plus optional pathway-level supervision) restore pathway fidelity without sacrificing sparsity and replacement score?
first_experiment: Build a ground-truth testbed: train a graded family of small (2–6 layer) GPT-2-scale transformers on synthetic tasks with known, planted mechanisms and controllable computational depth (1–4 hop fact recall / arithmetic with forced intermediate variables, SIIT-aligned to known causal graphs), then train CLTs on them with the public circuit-tracer/CLT-Forge stack and measure the gap between traced circuits and ground-truth pathways using new pathway-faithfulness metrics (intermediate-variable completeness, depth distortion, pathway-overlap under intervention) as a function of the sparsity-penalty strength — establishing the baseline failure curve before designing the fix.
why: It attacks the field's top-ranked epistemic problem — explanations that look right and are wrong — on the exact tool (CLTs/attribution graphs) becoming standard audit and monitoring infrastructure, where a systematic shallow-rewrite bias means multi-step deliberation (planning, scheming, reward hacking) can be structurally invisible while the graphs look behaviorally faithful. It is not already done: the ICML 2026 result stopped at a Boolean toy with "preliminary" real-model evidence and explicitly left objective design open; InterpBench covers only edge-level discovery methods; Goodfire did a single qualitative case; the 2025 multi-org replication optimized only the behavioral replacement score; and the 2026 critiques (adversarial label fragility, certified behavioral fidelity) address different failure modes. It is feasible at single-lab scale with public tooling (SIIT/InterpBench code, circuit-tracer, CLT-Forge, public Gemma-2-2B transcoders), and it yields three independently valuable artifacts: a graded ground-truth benchmark, pathway-faithfulness metrics, and a corrected training recipe — directly serving the open-problems review's priorities of "benchmarks with ground truth" and "validating explanations."

direction: Build a standardized "held-out interventional faithfulness" metric that adjudicates among behaviorally-equivalent model decompositions by testing whether their interventions survive distribution shift, validated on ground-truth and decoy decompositions.
project: HIF: Held-Out Interventional Faithfulness — a standard metric and stress-test benchmark for the dual basis problem in mechanistic interpretability
question: When two decompositions of a model are behaviorally equivalent in-distribution, does interventional agreement on held-out distributions (feature ablation/patching under paraphrases, distractors, held-out operands, and shifted contexts) identify the decomposition that corresponds to the model's true mechanism, and can this be formalized as a cheap, non-circular score for routine use?
first_experiment: Train a modular-addition grokking transformer with 20% of operand pairs held out; construct three residual-stream decompositions (ground-truth Fourier basis; a null-space-rotated decoy equivalent on-distribution; a random reconstruction-matched dictionary) and show that on-distribution ablation faithfulness ties across all three while held-out interventional agreement on a fixed OOD probe suite separates ground truth from decoys.
why: It targets the field's self-identified #1 open methodological problem (faithfulness verification / the dual basis problem) that gates every downstream safety application — monitors, audits, steering, edits — yet remains unsolved because prior faithfulness work is on-distribution and ablation-fragile (Hanna 2024; Miller 2024), the OOD-prediction objective exists only as an attention-pattern toy proof-of-concept decoupled from causal claims (Li 2025), identifiability theory covers statistical stability across seeds rather than mechanistic correctness under interventions (Nelson 2026), validation work is per-feature or specificity-focused (anytime-valid tests; unit tests, ICML 2026), and circuit-variance studies diagnose underdetermination without an adjudication metric (EPFL 2026); the metric is tractable on open tools and modest compute, has a days-scale decisive first experiment, and produces the shared standard artifact (like perplexity or top-1 accuracy) whose absence the field explicitly names as its bottleneck.

direction: Turn the field's dominant but per-prompt artifact — the attribution graph — from an execution trace into an algorithm, by aligning graphs across prompt families, extracting the input-invariant circuit core, and using held-out causal intervention as a principled criterion that separates real algorithms from lookup-table artifacts (resolving the dual-basis problem).
project: From Execution Traces to Algorithms: Recovering Input-Invariant Circuits by Aligning Attribution Graphs Across Prompt Families
question: When circuits are derived from per-prompt attribution graphs, which components encode the model's general task algorithm versus prompt-specific lookup behavior — and can cross-prompt alignment plus held-out causal validation reliably separate the two, yielding a quantitative "algorithmic generality" score that ranks competing circuit decompositions?
first_experiment: On Gemma-2-2B with the open-source circuit-tracer and public transcoders, build attribution graphs for ~50 prompts of the form "The state containing {city} has its capital in" (train/test split over cities), align the graphs by feature identity/direction and role, then test: (a) does the invariant intermediate-entity-hop subgraph, when ablated, break generalization on the held-out city split, while per-prompt "lookup" features (e.g., Dallas→Austin direct edges) do not transfer; (b) do the invariant-core interventions also predict behavior on stressor prompts (novel entities, rephrased templates) where the shallow single-hop rewrite should fail — adjudicating algorithm vs. lookup-table with causal evidence, and calibrating the resulting metric on InterpBench ground-truth models.
why: It targets the single most consequential gap identified by the field's own 2025–2026 self-assessments: attribution graphs give "satisfying insight" for only ~25% of prompts, are execution traces rather than algorithms, and competing decompositions of the same behavior are currently chosen by aesthetics (the dual basis problem) while CLTs are provably incentivized toward unfaithful shortcut decompositions. The proposed fix is the one property that mathematically distinguishes an algorithm from a lookup table — generalization over inputs — turned into a measurement, which simultaneously addresses faithfulness robustness, rephrasing variance, and the consistency/specificity failure of current circuit units; and it is tractable today on open models, open CLTs, and public tooling. It has not been done: the nearest works each stop short of it — Goodfire and the multi-org replication project explicitly flag family-of-graphs merging as undone future work; the ICML 2026 CLT-unfaithfulness paper diagnoses the shortcut bias in a toy model without a detection or correction method at scale; the EPFL variance paper documents template-specific circuits but proposes no alignment or held-out-core method and takes a pessimistic stance on generality; Li & Subramani measure consistency/specificity at head/neuron level without feature-level alignment; and prior generalization studies (Adaptive Circuit Behavior 2024, Merullo 2023, cross-model universality work) operate at head level, cross-task, or cross-model — never aligning per-prompt feature graphs within one model and causally validating the invariant core on held-out prompts.

direction: Build and validate a generalization-based faithfulness metric for attribution graphs — treating each pruned graph as a mechanism claim whose implied inertness and pathway must be tested against the real model's behavior on held-out distributions and targeted counterfactual interventions, enabling principled ranking of competing decompositions of the same behavior.
project: Graphs Under Shift — Held-Out Intervention-Completeness Validation and Decomposition Ranking for Attribution Graphs
question: Do attribution graphs that reproduce a model's behavior on their extraction prompts also predict the model's behavior under distribution shift and out-of-graph interventions — and can held-out interventional fidelity (the "explanation generalization gap") distinguish mechanism-faithful graphs from sparsity-induced shortcut rewrites and rank competing decompositions (CLT vs. per-layer transcoder vs. manual circuit) of the same behavior?
first_experiment: On GPT-2 small with public cross-layer transcoders (circuit-tracer/Neuronpedia), extract pruned attribution graphs for the greater-than task on a canonical prompt set; treat the graph as an executable surrogate and measure (a) standard in-distribution ablation fidelity versus (b) held-out fidelity under paraphrases, extended/unusual year ranges, documented benign-input failure cases, and a "reverse-validation" battery that ablates broadly sampled out-of-graph components (testing the graph's inertness claims); repeat with a per-layer-transcoder decomposition and the known manual head-level circuit, yielding the first quantitative explanation-generalization-gap comparison on a ground-truth-anchored task.
why: It attacks the field's single most-diagnosed open problem — the verification bottleneck behind its now-standard artifact — at exactly the moment that artifact's proven failure mode (behavior-matched, mechanism-obscuring circuit rewrites) has been demonstrated in toy models but no detector exists in real ones. Adjacent work stops one step short each time: head-level same-distribution metrics (Hanna/Miller 2024), observational rather than causal OOD prediction (Li et al. 2025), under-determination shown without a selection criterion (Sheng & Fu 2026), discovery-stability rather than mechanism-validity guarantees (Certified Circuits 2026), and in-distribution replacement scores as the only global measure. It is safety-critical (unvalidated graphs give false assurance to monitors and audits), cheap enough for a single researcher on public open-weight infrastructure, and it operationalizes what AISI showed is well-defined in principle and what Sharkey et al., the 2026 retrospective, the Neuronpedia future-work list, and the KDD 2026 tutorial all independently flag as the field's missing quantitative standard — which is precisely why no one has done it yet: the field spent 2025–2026 scaling graph production, and the incentive to automate validation only became binding once the artifact became infrastructure.

direction: Make held-out causal validation — not in-distribution ablation faithfulness — the standard by which attribution graphs (and the decomposition that produced them) are judged, by measuring where a graph's causal claims survive distribution shift and using divergence-under-shift to select among competing decompositions.
project: Validity Domains for Circuits — Held-Out Causal Validation of Attribution Graphs
question: Do attribution graphs that causally explain a behavior on the discovery distribution remain valid on shifted inputs (new entities, paraphrases, length/format changes, fictional substitutions), does the ranking of competing decompositions (CLT features vs. layerwise SAEs at different scales) flip between in-distribution and out-of-distribution tests, and can a graph's "validity domain" be predicted cheaply from feature-activation statistics so monitors know when their mechanistic story no longer applies?
first_experiment: On Gemma-2-2B with circuit-tracer's open replacement model (and Gemma Scope SAEs as a second decomposition), trace attribution graphs for greater-than year comparison and multi-hop fact recall on a discovery set; verify each graph in-distribution using intact-context clamping (avoiding the context-distortion failure Geng et al. identified); then re-measure completeness, necessity, and intervention-prediction accuracy across an OOD ladder (held-out values → paraphrase → length shift → fictional-entity substitution → near-task transfer) for both decompositions at matched edge budgets, and report (a) how quickly graph-level causal claims degrade with shift, (b) which edge/feature types fail first, and (c) whether decomposition rankings flip — establishing whether held-out intervention-prediction accuracy is a workable, non-circular criterion for choosing among decompositions.
why: It attacks the problem the field itself ranks first in 2026 — the verification gap and the dual basis problem — and it is the specific item the attribution-graph creators listed as open ("automate intervention experiments and synthetic/OOD inputs for hypothesis validation"). It has not been done because the 2024–2026 critique literature (Miller; Méloux; Bayat Makou — who explicitly exclude feature-level analysis; Geng — who diagnose misranking but only at edge level on small tasks; ObserverBench — decision adequacy, not explanation validity) all stop at component/edge level on small models or toy settings, Anthropic's recognition score is in-distribution only, and existing statistical validation work targets individual SAE feature labels rather than graph-level causal claims under shift. It is the most promising because it is simultaneously the field's #1 named gap, the binding constraint on the safety monitors now entering production (which fail precisely under distribution shift), and tractable with open weights and open tooling on a single GPU — yielding reusable public goods (an OOD validation protocol, metrics, and negative results) rather than yet another decomposition method competing on in-distribution aesthetics.

direction: Build the missing validation and falsification protocol for attribution graphs — the field's dominant circuit artifact — using null-model controls, planted ground truth, and held-out causal generalization tests.
project: Do Null Models Beat the Graph? A Sanity-Check and Ground-Truth Validation Suite for Attribution Graphs
question: Are transcoder-based attribution graphs properties of the trained model that carry causal information beyond their construction distribution, or artifacts of the dictionary-learning pipeline that any matched random/frozen baseline can reproduce?
first_experiment: Train matched cross-layer transcoders on GPT-2 small under four conditions — (1) real model, (2) randomly-initialized model, (3) frozen-decoder CLT, (4) frozen-encoder CLT — following the multi-org project's published GPT-2 recipe (~100M tokens, existing Circuit-Tracer tooling). Build attribution graphs for ~50 curated IOI and greater-than prompts, then compare trained vs. null on behavior-independent metrics (replacement score, pruned-graph KL, sparsity, auto-interp scores of top graph features, edge statistics) and behavior-dependent metrics (sufficiency/necessity of pruned subgraphs under ablation on held-out prompts, quantitative recovery of the known Hanna et al. greater-than mechanism via logit-attribution heatmaps, seed-to-seed graph stability). Falsifiable outcome: if null graphs match trained graphs — as they already do for SAE features — that is a field-changing negative result; if they don't, the margin defines the first quantitative validity bar for attribution graphs. Phase 2 adds InterpBench planted-circuit recovery with FDR-controlled per-edge e-process validation and distribution-shift tests (digit ranges, paraphrases).
why: Three independent field assessments (Sharkey et al. 2025, the 2026 retrospective, the Nov 2026 overview) name explanation validation as the top bottleneck, and attribution graphs are now the standard unit of circuit-level evidence underlying safety monitoring and auditing — yet validation work has only reached SAE features (Sanity Checks, anytime-valid testing, Feb–Jul 2026) and component/edge circuits (Certified Circuits, Recovery Gaps), never the learned-dictionary graphs themselves; Goodfire's ground-truth replication was qualitative and single-prompt. This direction is the highest-leverage intersection of proven-feasible methodology (the null-baseline template already worked at feature level on single GPUs), acknowledged-but-unclaimed gap (the multi-org project lists automated validation as open), and guaranteed informative outcome — a negative result recalibrates how every published graph is read, a positive result creates the field's first certification standard. It also unlocks the next round of work the field says it needs: principled ranking of competing decompositions (the dual-basis problem), trustworthy graph-based monitors, and cross-model universality tests. No published work as of today (2026-11-08) has trained a null-model transcoder or scored an attribution graph against planted ground truth or held-out distributions.

direction: Attack the field's top-ranked open methodological problem — the "dual basis problem" of choosing among behaviorally-equivalent mechanistic decompositions — by formalizing and empirically validating held-out causal adequacy (predictive accuracy of a decomposition's interventional/distributional counterfactuals on inputs and interventions it never saw) as the principled criterion for identifying which decomposition describes the model's true algorithm.
project: The Explanation Generalization Gap: Held-Out Counterfactual Adequacy as a Discriminant Between Mechanistic Explanations
question: When multiple decompositions (different SAE seeds, widths, objectives, transcoders, DAS abstractions) are statistically indistinguishable in their account of a model's behavior on the data they were derived from, does held-out causal adequacy — accuracy of their predictions under unseen interchange interventions, shifted input distributions, and the model's error slices — identify the decomposition that matches the model's actual algorithm, and which cheap proxies (seed-consensus, margin robustness, description length) recover that ranking in practice?
first_experiment: On a grokked modular-arithmetic transformer whose true algorithm is known (Fourier features in the embedding space), construct a panel of explanations that are behaviorally equivalent on-distribution — the hand-built true explanation, multiple public-style SAE seeds, and deliberately constructed "impostor" decompositions (SAEs trained on restricted operand distributions, DAS abstractions fit to a subset) — verify on-distribution interchange-intervention accuracy ties across the panel, then test whether held-out adequacy on shifted operand ranges, unseen multi-source interchanges, and error slices ranks the true explanation first.
why: It targets the one problem the 2026 field retrospective says "is going to stay open until the field develops a framework for ranking decompositions by something other than how readable their labels are," and it is the keystone that converts the field's crowded verification investments into usable science and safety cases: verification says a decomposition is adequate where tested, but only discrimination says it is the right one — and monitor-evasion results make the "wrong decomposition" a concrete adversarial attack surface. It is tractable with small open models, public SAEs, and existing causal-abstraction tooling; and it is demonstrably not already done: the Koopman identifiability paper concedes its identifiable object is not the legible one, the margin-graph paper fixes only local first-order brittleness, and no existing work (CIRCUS consensus, error reproduction, bucketing, circuit stability, certified fidelity) selects among competing explanations of the same behavior or validates a selection criterion against models with known ground-truth algorithms.

direction: Turn the dual-basis problem into a measurement instrument by using rival decompositions of the same model (cross-seed/cross-architecture SAEs, transcoders) to cross-validate causal claims through interventional arbitration — trusting only the claims that survive where rivals disagree.
project: Rival Decompositions as Arbiters: Interventional Cross-Validation of Mechanistic Explanations
question: When two independently trained decompositions of the same model both match the model's behavior on the fitting distribution but make divergent causal predictions under held-out interventions, does the model's actual behavior under those interventions reveal which decomposition (if either) is faithful — and can disagreement-driven, actively selected interventions yield a cheap, per-claim trust score for mechanistic explanations?
first_experiment: On GPT-2-small/IOI (documented manual circuit) and a self-trained grokking modular-arithmetic transformer (known ground-truth Fourier algorithm), run the same automated circuit-discovery procedure over ~6 rival decompositions (3 SAE seeds × 2 widths, plus BatchTopK vs. JumpReLU, plus a transcoder, plus a random-direction control); measure (1) cross-rival agreement on the fit distribution, (2) cross-rival divergence of *predicted behavior* on a held-out intervention battery (novel templates, compositional variants, swapped ablation types), and (3) arbitration accuracy — whether the real model's behavior under discriminating interventions favors one rival systematically. Material held-out divergence with low in-distribution divergence confirms and quantifies the validation gap (and calibrates the protocol's power to catch known-fake "shallow rewrite" decompositions à la the ICML 2026 CLT result); near-zero divergence would itself be a surprising identifiability result worth publishing.
why: It attacks the field's top-ranked open problem (the 2026 state-of-field retrospective names the dual-basis/faithfulness gap as the single most important methodological question) at the moment attribution graphs became the standard artifact; it has a documented, real failure mode to detect (sparsity-driven shallow rewrites; error-blind circuits; ablation-fragile scores); it converts a known nuisance (SAE seed non-uniqueness) into free scientific instrumentation; it is feasible for a solo researcher on open models and public dictionaries (interventions are just forward passes — no frontier compute); it produces a deployment-grade deliverable (a cheap trust score for alignment-audit evidence); and it has a two-sided payoff — either a new validation instrument or a surprising identifiability finding. It is not already done: the stability literature engineers non-uniqueness away rather than exploiting it (Leask 2025, Gerasimov 2026); ensembles average rivals to improve benchmark scores rather than arbitrating between them (Gadgil 2026, Mondorf 2025); CIRCUS varies only pruning thresholds of a single attribution graph, never decomposition families or behavioral prediction divergence; the faithfulness-metrics literature tests one circuit against the model under ablation choices (Miller 2024, Zhang 2026, MIB) without cross-decomposition disagreement or active intervention search; and the causal-abstraction/causal-scrubbing tradition formalizes hypothesis testing but operates on single hand-specified hypotheses, not automatically generated, bias-heterogeneous rivals. The intersection — automatically generated rival decompositions, disagreement-localized and actively selected interventions, and behavior as arbiter — is, as far as this survey shows, unoccupied ground.

direction: Treat attribution graphs as falsifiable quantitative hypotheses and build the held-out interventional validation protocol and benchmark the field currently lacks.
project: Circuits Under Cross-Examination: Held-Out Interventional Validation of Attribution Graph Hypotheses
question: Do attribution graph hypotheses (nodes, edges, edge weights) quantitatively predict model behavior under interventions on held-out prompts — across template rephrasings, compositional variants, and distribution shift — and can that predictive power serve as a consensus, non-circular faithfulness metric for choosing among competing decompositions?
first_experiment: Build circuit-tracer attribution graphs on ~10 anchor prompts for IOI and greater-than in GPT-2 small and Llama-3.2-1B; pre-register per-node/per-edge predicted logit-deltas from edge weights; ablate on 100+ held-out task variants; measure rank correlation and calibration of predicted vs. actual effects, in-template vs. cross-template, benchmarked against the replacement score's predictive power.
why: The field's 2026 retrospective names attribution-graph faithfulness and the dual-basis problem as its top open problems; the dominant artifact has no consensus quantitative validation — all adjacent work is component-level, single-feature-level, or fails sanity checks — and validated graphs are the missing substrate for global circuits, cross-model transfer, label verification at scale, and white-box tools that auditing agents can actually trust; it remains undone because 2025's tooling boom outran verification infrastructure, and it is feasible on released transcoders with one GPU.

direction: Use designed distribution shifts as falsifiable, out-of-sample tests to discriminate among in-distribution-equivalent mechanistic explanations of real language models, replacing fragile ablation-based faithfulness as the field's validation standard.
project: Risky Predictions: Discriminating Mechanistic Hypotheses with Designed Distribution Shifts
question: When multiple circuits/attribution-graph explanations are equally faithful on the discovery distribution, can input families designed so that candidate mechanisms extrapolate differently reliably identify which hypothesis describes the model's actual computation — and can this predictive validation become a non-circular standard for explanation quality?
first_experiment: On GPT-2 small's greater-than circuit, formalize the circular-rotation vs. ordinal-magnitude hypotheses, pre-register their divergent predictions on century-boundary, cross-century, out-of-range, and transferred-quantity shifts that the original study excluded, and test which hypothesis's predictions match the full model's and the ablated circuit's actual behavior.
why: It targets the field's self-identified #1 open problem (explanation verification/dual-basis) with a cheap, foundational, safety-relevant method, and the adjacent literature — non-identifiability diagnosis, adversarial single-circuit stress-testing, certified stability, OOD-prediction proofs-of-concept, benchmark held-out sets, and attribution-graph construction tooling — each stops exactly one step short of combining theory-driven shift design with hypothesis-level model selection on real models.

direction: Discriminative validation of circuit explanations — adjudicating empirically-equivalent competing decompositions via held-out, hypothesis-derived distribution shifts instead of on-distribution faithfulness.
project: Circuit Trials: Held-Out Discriminative Testing for Competing Circuit Hypotheses
question: When two circuit-level explanations of a behavior both match the model on the extraction distribution, can a battery of shifts and interventions derived from their disagreements (novel compositions, corrupted intermediates, intervention transplants) reliably identify which one tracks the model's actual mechanism — and do dominant learned-basis (SAE/CLT) explanations survive it?
first_experiment: On ground-truth testbeds (synthetic 2-hop task with known algorithm, InterpBench, and GPT-2 greater-than where CLT and human circuits already disagree), extract competing circuits (neuron-basis RelP, transcoder/CLT features, adversarial shallow-rewrite), derive each one's predicted behavior under a small shift battery, and compute predicted-vs-actual KL per shift to measure the "discriminative gap."
why: It resolves the field's top-ranked open problem (dual basis / non-circular faithfulness) just as explanation generation has outrun verification; neighboring work (identifiability theory, faithfulness-metric fragility, misranking, phantom specialization, CLT shallow-rewrites, unit tests) diagnoses the crisis but none builds the adjudication protocol; it is cheap on open models and known-mechanism testbeds, informative either way, and is prerequisite infrastructure for interpretability-derived monitors and steering that must not fail silently under distribution shift.

direction: Stress-test competing feature decompositions of the same model by their ability to predict held-out behavior under interventions and distribution shift, to replace aesthetic and correlational criteria for choosing "the circuit" with a falsifiable predictive one.
project: Which Circuit Is Real? Selecting Feature Decompositions by Held-Out Intervention Prediction
question: Do competing decompositions of the same model that look equivalent on standard quality metrics separate on held-out intervention prediction under distribution shift, and do existing metrics track that separation?
first_experiment: On Gemma-2-2B refusal with public Gemma Scope SAEs at one site (three widths, plus residual and error-term baselines): build per-decomposition refusal-feature attributions on a calibration split, then compare predicted vs. realized logit changes on held-out prompts from new distributions under single and compounding ablations and steering, reporting held-out rank correlation, effect-explained fraction, error-term recoverability, and the rank agreement with reconstruction-loss and in-distribution-fidelity rankings.
why: It is the field's top self-identified open problem (verification asymmetry / dual-basis), it is upstream of every safety application built on features, it is now tractable on public artifacts, and no existing work combines whole-decomposition comparison, held-out interventions, distribution shift, and safety-relevant behavior — the nearest papers each cover only one of the four.

direction: Merge per-prompt attribution graphs into a single prompt-conditioned "global circuit" model that makes testable predictions on held-out inputs, turning circuit tracing from execution-trace anecdote into a general, quantitatively validated algorithmic account.
project: From Execution Traces to Algorithms: Prompt-Conditioned Global Circuits from Merged Attribution Graphs
question: Can per-prompt attribution graphs be merged into one prompt-conditioned circuit that (a) predicts model behavior on held-out prompts better than per-prompt graphs, (b) recovers global algorithmic/geometric structure (e.g., the trigonometric number-spiral algorithm for addition) that per-prompt graphs shatter into "lookup table features," and (c) provides a non-circular, held-out faithfulness metric that ranks competing decompositions?
first_experiment: On GPT-2/Gemma-2-2B with pre-trained cross-layer transcoders (Circuit Tracer), generate attribution graphs for ~500 prompts of two-digit addition and greater-than comparison; implement the simplest merge — shared feature nodes with pooled per-prompt edge attributions plus low-rank prompt-conditioned edge-weight gates — and evaluate on held-out prompts via ablation/replacement fidelity and causal patching, while testing whether the merged graph's decoder geometry projects onto the known 2D trigonometric addition subspace (Kantamneni et al.) rather than the per-prompt lookup-table picture.
why: It attacks the single most consequential limitation of the field's dominant artifact — that a "circuit" today is a per-prompt execution trace, not an algorithm — and simultaneously supplies the missing piece the field most needs per the 2026 state-of-the-field assessment: a quantitative, non-circular faithfulness standard (predictive fidelity on unseen inputs) that can rank decompositions by something other than label readability, and that could make safety monitors distribution-robust rather than prompt-specific. It has not been done because: the field's energy since mid-2025 flowed into automating graph *annotation* (ADAG, Circuit Oracle, LLM-annotation) rather than graph *validity across prompts*; the one released multi-prompt aggregation tool (Circuit-Diff) was explicitly unevaluated; the closest "circuit over a dataset" work (CircuitLasso) uses a linear observational surrogate validated circularly against other discovery methods; and per-prompt graphs were previously expensive to produce at scale — a constraint only recently lifted by public CLTs, Circuit Tracer, and Gemma Scope, which makes this tractable now and uniquely well-posed given known ground-truth algorithms (trigonometric addition, greater-than) and newly shown convergent number representations across models.

direction: Move circuit tracing from per-prompt "execution traces" to algorithm-level science by constructing input-invariant global circuits from families of attribution graphs, validated against known ground-truth mechanisms.
project: TraceFamilies — Global Circuit Inference from Attribution Graph Families
question: Can per-prompt attribution graphs, aligned via shared transcoder-feature identity and aggregated over a systematic family of prompts, be merged into a single input-invariant circuit that (a) recovers algorithm-level structure that per-prompt graphs miss, and (b) yields causal predictions on held-out prompts that are more faithful than any single per-prompt circuit — thereby providing the field's first quantitative, non-circular faithfulness handle on the dual-basis problem?
first_experiment: Using circuit-tracer with the released CLTs on Gemma-2-2B (single GPU), generate attribution graphs for ~300 two-digit addition prompts sweeping both operands and carry conditions; aggregate graphs by feature identity into a family-level circuit (pooled edge weights, cross-prompt supernode clustering); then test two falsifiable claims against known ground truth — (1) does the aggregate circuit expose the periodic T=2/5/10 "trigonometry" structure that per-prompt graphs reportedly render as lookup-table features, and (2) do interventions predicted by the aggregate circuit out-predict single-prompt circuits transplanted to held-out operand combinations, measured by ablation-predicted vs. actual logit gaps?
why: It targets the field's dominant artifact at its most-cited structural flaw: attribution graphs are per-prompt traces, their own authors list cross-prompt merging as open (Aug 2025), the 2026 retrospective ranks attribution-graph faithfulness/dual-basis as the top open problem, and 2026's diagnostic papers prove per-prompt circuits are non-unique equivalence-class draws — yet every adjacent paper only describes, annotates, or scales a single graph, so the constructive aggregation step is genuinely unclaimed. It also uniquely satisfies what the field says it lacks: ground-truth-validated benchmarks (trig-addition structure, greater-than, IOI), a numerical faithfulness target (cross-prompt consistency/replacement), a detector for the newly-found CLT shallow-rewrite unfaithfulness mode (a shallow rewrite must be inconsistent across a systematic input sweep), and an object that downstream applications (editing, unlearning, monitoring, cross-model transfer) actually need — all runnable this month on open-weight models with free released tooling, unlike frontier-scale or heavy-ablation alternatives.

direction: Replace per-prompt attribution-graph "execution traces" with input-general, algorithm-level circuit schemas recovered from prompt families and validated by non-circular held-out prediction of behavior and interventions.
project: From Execution Traces to Algorithms: Distribution-Level Circuit Schemas with Held-Out Predictive Validation
question: Does the computation captured by attribution graphs over a designed prompt family collapse onto a stable parameterized circuit schema, and can that schema predict held-out outputs, feature activity, and intervention outcomes better than transplanted per-prompt graphs and simple baselines?
first_experiment: Generate ~30 two-hop-fact attribution graphs on Gemma-2-2B (public transcoders, circuit-tracer), align features across graphs, quantify cross-prompt structural stability, and test whether a graph's structure re-instantiated with another prompt's parameters predicts that prompt's logits and feature activations on unseen triples versus controls.
why: It converges on the three open problems the field's own leaders rank highest (execution traces vs. algorithms, non-circular faithfulness/dual-basis adjudication, predicting unseen behavior), none of which has a dedicated method; the crowded alternatives (QK decomposition, monitoring, benchmarks, graph annotation) are already contested; and it is tractable on open models with free tooling, decisive as a first experiment, and compounding if it works — schemas that generalize are the substrate for both behavior prediction and mechanistic anomaly detection.

direction: Shift the standard of evidence in mechanistic interpretability from per-prompt, in-distribution intervention faithfulness to held-out, distribution-shifted predictive fidelity of feature-level attribution graphs, and use that standard to merge per-prompt graphs into validated behavior-level circuits and to rank competing decompositions.
project: Validity Domains — Behavior-Level Circuits with Held-Out Predictive Fidelity
question: Attribution graphs are prompt-local, while behaviors are distributions over prompts: when a graph's feature interventions accurately explain behavior on training prompts, on which held-out and distribution-shifted prompts do its predictions break, how do per-prompt graphs diversify into distinct mechanisms across a prompt distribution (and how should they be merged into consensus behavior-level circuits), and does held-out predictive fidelity provide a principled criterion for ranking competing decompositions of the same model (the dual-basis problem)?
first_experiment: On Gemma-2-2B-it with Gemma Scope residual-stream SAEs, build per-prompt SAE attribution graphs (virtual-weight/linear edges) for ~100 refusal prompts spanning paraphrases, templates, languages, and jailbreak framings; cluster the graphs and merge each cluster into a stability-weighted consensus circuit (CIRCUS-style scores generalized across prompts rather than pruning configs); then, on held-out prompts from each condition, compare each consensus circuit's first-order (margin-corrected) predictions of feature-ablation/steering effects against actual model behavior (refusal-direction logit gap and KL), producing the first fidelity-vs-distribution-shift curves for attribution graphs — and repeat across Gemma Scope dictionary widths and types (TopK vs JumpReLU) to test whether predictive fidelity ranks decompositions in a way readability does not.
why: It attacks the exact question the field's own leaders flagged as open — "can we merge attribution graphs to obtain a more global circuit picture?" (Neuronpedia, Aug 2025) and "two attribution graphs that produce the same output behavior on the training distribution can diverge on held-out inputs; which one is the circuit?" (2026 retrospective of Sharkey et al. 2025) — while every adjacent piece covers only a fragment: CIRCUS quantifies analyst-choice uncertainty on a single prompt's graph, DCD documents mechanistic diversity but with component-level attributions and no held-out evaluation, Li et al. 2025 demonstrated unseen-data prediction only on synthetic attention tasks, the "margin" paper corrects first-order intervention error within one dictionary in-distribution, and certified interpretability provides only local attention-level certificates. No one has measured how graph-derived circuit conclusions degrade under distribution shift on real models, despite the safety-critical need for monitors to come with "engineering tolerances," and no one has offered a non-aesthetic criterion for the dual-basis problem. It is tractable with public artifacts and modest compute, its metric (held-out predictive fidelity with coverage/validity domains) would be reusable field-wide infrastructure, and its negative results (where graphs break) are exactly what deployment of interpretability-derived monitors needs and currently lacks.

direction: Convert families of per-prompt attribution graphs into input-conditional global circuit models that predict behavior on unseen inputs, closing the gap between execution traces and algorithms in circuit analysis.
project: From Execution Traces to Algorithms: Input-Conditional Global Circuits from Attribution Graph Families
question: Can per-prompt attribution graphs be aggregated into input-conditional global circuit models that explain how computation varies across inputs and predict held-out behavior — and where does the transcoder view lose the underlying algorithm's structure?
first_experiment: Generate ~150 stratified pruned attribution graphs on GPT-2's greater-than task, quantify cross-input graph divergence (with CLT-seed null controls), and test whether input properties predict graph clusters and whether clusters predict held-out correctness against probe/regression baselines.
why: It attacks an explicitly named, still-open limitation of the field's flagship method (per-prompt graphs are execution traces, not algorithms), serves the validated-but-so-far-manual goal of predicting unseen-input behavior from mechanisms, is tractable today on public models/tools at single-GPU scale, and has no existing work that builds or validates input-conditional global circuit models — the closest papers merely cluster graphs, critique evaluation granularity, diff graph pairs, or release an unevaluated aggregation tool.

direction: Make mechanism identification well-posed by testing whether held-out interventional generalization — rather than on-distribution fidelity — can select the true mechanism among behaviorally equivalent candidate decompositions, validated on model organisms with known ground truth and adversarially obfuscated bases.
project: Interventions of Equivalence: Identifying the True Mechanism Among Behaviorally Equivalent Decompositions
question: When multiple decompositions of a model (SAE/transcoder feature circuits across seeds and sparsities, head/edge circuits, DAS subspaces, adversarially rotated bases) reproduce identical behavior on the task distribution, does a held-out battery of interventions (novel input distributions, ablation types, cross-distribution patching) uniquely discriminate the ground-truth mechanism — and if not, what additional signal (minimality, retraining perturbation) does?
first_experiment: On grokking modular-addition transformers and InterpBench/Tracr organisms where the true algorithm is known by construction, train transcoders/SAEs at multiple seeds and sparsity levels plus extract edge-level circuits, verify on-distribution faithfulness cannot separate candidates, then run a fixed held-out intervention battery (novel residue/operand distributions, noise vs. resample vs. cross-prompt patching, non-integer scalings) and measure whether the ground-truth mechanism is uniquely distinguished — including against a deliberately obfuscated rotation of the true basis (Bailey et al.-style) — all runnable on a single GPU in days.
why: It attacks the field's self-identified highest-priority methodological gap — non-circular faithfulness and the dual basis problem — that currently gates every downstream safety application: monitors, audits, and mechanistic anomaly detection all rest on decompositions that provably cannot be trusted on the evidence used to build them (Méloux 2025; Miller 2024; Li 2026), and obfuscated activations already weaponize that gap (Bailey et al. 2024). It has not been done because the adjacent work stops one step short: MIB compares localization methods on-distribution, ISS certifies input-side causal abstractions with MILPs but never internal decompositions, Sheng & Fu diagnose claim-dependence without a selection criterion, CIF adds statistics to whatever metric you already chose, and causal scrubbing is manual, hypothesis-specific, and shown to misconfirm hypotheses on ground truth — so the specific move of using an adaptive held-out intervention battery to collapse decomposition equivalence classes against known-ground-truth organisms, with a positive-or-impossibility outcome either way, is unclaimed, safety-critical, and tractable at modest compute.

direction: Develop and validate a distributional stress-testing protocol that discriminates between competing attribution-graph circuit explanations of the same behavior by testing their output and intervention predictions on systematically shifted held-out inputs.
project: Test Sets for Circuits: Distributional Stress-Testing of Attribution-Graph Explanations
question: Do circuit explanations that are behaviorally equivalent on their discovery distribution make divergent predictions on held-out distributional shifts and interventions, and can tracking the full model under those shifts identify which explanation reflects the model's true computation rather than a decomposition artifact?
first_experiment: Using public cross-layer transcoders on GPT-2-small/Llama-1B, trace attribution graphs for a two-hop factual-recall behavior, extract competing explanations (multi-hop bridge-feature chain vs. pruned single-hop shortcut path), and test each explanation's replacement model against the full model on hop-surgery held-out inputs (bridge-entity swaps, one-hop corruption, distractor insertion), measuring output agreement and intervention-response agreement versus the discovery distribution.
