why: Validation of explanations is the field-acknowledged top bottleneck (2026 retrospective's "dual basis problem"; Neuronpedia 2025 open-question list), recent results prove current evaluation inadequate (non-identifiability at ICLR 2025, CLT unfaithfulness at ICML 2026, non-robust faithfulness metrics, circuits that reproduce successes but not errors), and no prior work uses held-out natural distribution shifts to *discriminate* competing feature-level explanations or extends validation to intervention predictions — while public CLT infrastructure makes the first experiment cheap, concrete, and immediately informative.

direction: Systematically diagnose, benchmark, and fix the "shallow-rewrite" unfaithfulness in transcoder-based circuit tracing — where attribution graphs explain behavior while silently bypassing the model's true multi-step computational pathway.
project: Honest Graphs: A Ground-Truth Audit and Repair of CLT-Based Circuit Tracing
question: When and why do cross-layer-transcoder attribution graphs replace a model's genuine multi-hop computational pathway with a behaviorally-equivalent shallow shortcut, can this be quantified on model organisms with known ground-truth circuits, and can training objectives or pruning criteria be designed that eliminate the shortcut without sacrificing sparsity or replacement score?
first_experiment: Train a small (2–4 layer) transformer from scratch on a synthetic two-hop recall task ("A's friend is B; B's manager is C" → C) where A→C pairs never occur in training, so composition is forced; verify with path patching that the model uses a causally necessary intermediate "bridge" representation; then train CLTs (via open-source circuit-tracer/CLT-Forge) across a sweep of sparsity penalties and generate pruned attribution graphs; measure Bridge Recovery Rate — the fraction of ground-truth load-bearing bridge components that remain load-bearing nodes in the graphs — and run knock-out interventions on graph nodes to detect shortcut explanations, replicating and quantifying the toy-model failure mode on a real transformer.
why: It attacks the field's newly standardized core infrastructure at the moment of maximum leverage: every attribution-graph finding about safety-relevant behavior (planning, deception, hallucination) depends on CLT faithfulness, yet the only evidence of systematic unfaithfulness is a Boolean toy model with "preliminary" real-model hints, and the standard evaluation metric (replacement score) provably rewards the failure mode — so the field is scaling a tool it cannot yet trust. It is cheaply tractable (GPT-2-scale open models, known-circuit model organisms like IOI and grokking modular addition as follow-up testbeds, existing open-source CLT tooling) and yields incremental wins (diagnostic → benchmark → fix). It has not been done because the unfaithfulness result is only four months old and confined to a toy; the Aug 2025 landscape project evaluated CLT variants only on replacement score, not ground-truth path fidelity; prior faithfulness critiques ("Have Faith in Faithfulness," "Transformer Circuit Faithfulness Metrics are not Robust") target edge-level ACDC-style circuits rather than the CLT replacement-model pipeline; and the formal-guarantees work is vision-only and verifier-based; moreover the field's validation culture explicitly admits ground-truth hypothesis testing is rare and costly — precisely this gap.

direction: Build the first mechanistic account of how a trained hidden objective persists across multi-turn LLM-agent conversations — testing whether it lives as re-derived per-turn state or as carried internal state — and turn that account into an early-detection monitor.
project: Where Do Hidden Objectives Live? Cross-Turn State, Context Surgery, and Detection of Latent Agent Intent
question: When a model acts on a hidden objective that was specified turns earlier and never re-mentioned, is that objective (a) re-derived each turn from situational trigger features, or (b) carried as persistent internal state in activations/KV cache — and in either case, can we causally locate it and detect it before it is expressed?
first_experiment: Train (or obtain from open releases) a small model organism (~2–7B, synthetic-document fine-tuning following the validated Hua et al. 2025 / organism-validation recipes, with installation + capability-preservation + naturalness checks) whose hidden objective fires only in a later turn of a multi-turn tool-use conversation; then run the decisive cheap test before any decomposition work — a context-surgery battery that paraphrases, reorders, and deletes the original instruction at the expression turn, plus KV-cache lesioning of the instruction's span mid-conversation (nnsight), measuring whether the hidden behavior survives. Survival under deletion but not under KV lesion ⇒ carried state; survival of neither ⇒ re-derivation; then verify whichever claim with cross-turn activation patching (patch turn-boundary activations from expressing vs. control runs) and attribution graphs at the expression turn.
why: It attacks the field's named out-of-reach goal (multiturn/agentic interpretation) with its first tractable slice, directly serves interpretability's comparative advantage (monitoring for dangerous cognition in agents, where scheming/hidden objectives are the frontier threat), and every adjacent line stops just short of it: hidden-objective organisms are only audited behaviorally (Anthropic 2025, Pando 2026, AuditBench 2026), the sandbagging causal model handles a single-context conditional state, goal-drift probes target task goals rather than misaligned intent, latent-state-persistence work used untrained models with no mechanism analysis, CoT-monitoring papers operate on text, and KV-cache studies are security/systems work without causal anatomy. It has not been done because the field's tools matured (open circuit tracer, KV-cache intervention support, validated organism recipes) only within the last year, and attention went to single-pass features and text-level monitors — leaving the temporal substrate of agentic behavior unstudied; my version is feasible on one GPU, uses established methodology with built-in validation, yields a reusable instrument (cross-turn patching/context surgery), and is decision-relevant either way: re-derivation means per-turn trigger-feature monitors suffice, while carried state means monitors must track cross-turn state and editors can target the specific components that hold it.

direction: Make the "dual-basis problem" empirical by developing automated search for inputs and interventions that discriminate between competing mechanistic explanations of the same model behavior, replacing aesthetic choice among decompositions with evidence-based selection.
project: Splitting the Basis: Automated Discrimination of Competing Mechanistic Explanations of LLM Behavior
question: When two independently-derived decompositions (e.g., a published attention-head circuit, an ACDC/EAP-IG rediscovered circuit, and a transcoder/SAE-based attribution graph) each faithfully reproduce the model's behavior on the validation distribution, where in input space do they make different predictions, can targeted input/intervention search find and quantify that divergence, and does the decomposition the model actually "sides with" off-distribution tell us which explanation a deployed monitor should trust?
first_experiment: On GPT-2 small (IOI) and Gemma-2-2B (greater-than, factual recall), construct three competing decompositions of each behavior — the published circuit, an automated-discovery circuit, and a transcoder/SAE-attribution graph — verify each is faithful on the standard evaluation distribution, then measure pairwise divergence between explanations (and each vs. the full model) across a battery of controlled benign shift suites (name permutations, repeated-name breaks, distractor insertion, paraphrases, compositional recombination), producing the first "separability profile" showing whether explanation equivalence is distribution-relative and whether the model's endorsement of a mechanism varies by input region.
why: The field's most credible state-of-the-field review calls ranking decompositions "the open problem I would put at the top of any new survey," and notes it remains aesthetic; identifiability failure is proven only in toy models, and every nearest neighbor (Adversarial Circuit Evaluation, ISS, Bucketing the Good Apples, CIF, Certified Circuits) handles only one explanation at a time, hand-specified candidates, or toy scales — none pit learned decompositions of a real LLM behavior against each other via targeted search, and none ties the outcome to monitor deployment, where in-distribution validation is known to be insufficient and safety-monitor coverage is documented as narrow; it is cheap relative to frontier-scale circuit work (open models, public SAEs, existing benchmarks and statistical tooling), generates reusable artifacts (separability suites, search method), and is doubly informative since a null result would itself resolve whether identifiability is a practical or merely theoretical concern.

direction: Establish out-of-sample behavioral validation as the standard test for attribution-graph circuit hypotheses, quantifying and benchmarking the "dual basis problem" — that many decompositions can explain the same on-prompt behavior while diverging on held-out inputs.
project: Circuits That Don't Lie Out of Sample: Held-Out Behavioral Validation of Attribution Graphs
question: When an attribution graph accounts for a model's behavior on the prompts used to derive it, does its underlying replacement model also predict the model's behavior on held-out and adversarial inputs — and do multiple independently-trained decompositions of the same model that agree in-distribution diverge out-of-distribution in ways that matter for audits and safety monitors?
first_experiment: With the public Circuit-Tracer library and released cross-layer transcoders for Gemma-2-2B and Llama-3.2-1B, derive attribution graphs for three well-studied behaviors (multi-hop fact recall, arithmetic, pronoun binding) on a fixed derivation prompt set; measure standard on-prompt validity (influence retention, replacement KL), then evaluate the same graphs' replacement models on held-out sets (same-distribution resamples, rephrased templates, minimal-pair counterfactuals with entity swaps and distractor insertion, near-threshold prompts) to quantify how validity degrades out-of-sample; finally, independently train 4–6 CLT decompositions (varying seed, width, TopK) with an identical graph-construction pipeline and test whether "decoy graphs" exist that pass all on-derivation checks yet diverge out-of-distribution — yielding the first empirical estimate of the dual-basis failure rate plus a draft Held-Out Circuit Validity metric.
why: It targets the gap that the field's own retrospectives now rank first — labeling was automated in 2025 but verification was not, so most published feature labels and circuit claims are causally unvalidated while safety monitors and audits are being built on top of them — and it does so in a space that is methodologically central yet nearly unclaimed, because every adjacent effort stops one step short: CIRCUS (Feb 2026) varies only pruning thresholds on a single graph, circuit-discovery variance studies (e.g., CEAP, June 2026) operate at the component level before cross-layer transcoders existed, the Koopman identifiability theory (Aug 2026) deliberately yields a non-legible fingerprint rather than validating legible graphs, MIB benchmarks component-level circuits on synthetic tasks, and the model-organism literature builds better testbeds without using them to test graph validity; meanwhile the crowded frontiers (SAE/transcoder engineering, graph-annotation automation, CoT faithfulness, RL-reasoning biology, eval-awareness) are absorbing the field's headcount. The work is newly tractable thanks to public transcoder artifacts and 1–2B open-weight models (a few GPU-days for the first experiment), it converts a philosophical worry into a measurable number and a benchmark the field explicitly said it lacks, and it imports the one scientific practice mechanistic interpretability has not yet adopted — out-of-sample testing of mechanistic hypotheses — which is the precondition for trusting any interpretability-derived audit, monitor, or safety argument.

direction: Build an unsupervised, causally validated "mechanism repertoire" audit for language models — mapping a model's behavior modes from internal activations without task priors — and use it both to detect planted hidden behaviors at calibrated false-positive rates and to map exactly which evasion strategies can still hide an anomalous mechanism.
project: Repertoire: Prior-Free Mechanism-Level Auditing and the Detectability Frontier of White-Box Monitors
question: Can a model's internal behavior repertoire be discovered without knowing what to look for, such that hidden behaviors surface as statistically anomalous modes (with controlled false-alarm rates on benign models), and what must an anomalous mechanism preserve — activation patterns, SAE latents, reconstruction residual, co-firing composition, or weights — to remain undetectable?
first_experiment: On a small open model with public SAEs (e.g., Gemma-2-2B or Qwen3-8B + Gemma Scope/SAE Lens), sample continuations over a broad corpus, build a feature co-firing/attributions signature per behavior candidate, cluster into candidate modes, causally validate the top modes via steering/ablation with LLM-judged coherence, and calibrate against null controls (permuted-feature and base-model baselines) — then freeze the pipeline and run it unchanged on 5–10 released AuditBench organisms (SDF-trained, transcript-distilled, and adversarially trained variants), measuring whether planted behaviors emerge as anomalous modes with detection AUROC and FPR, using latents plus reconstruction-residual and co-firing-composition channels (since 2026 recovery results show behavior hides in the residual).
why: It targets the field's one empirically demonstrated failure (white-box tools lose to black-box in auditing, per AuditBench's tool-to-agent results) in the application where interpretability has comparative advantage over behavioral evals — detecting cognition the model is trained to hide — and every component matured only in the last year (planted-behavior organism benchmarks in Feb 2026, functional-attribution MAD in Apr 2026, unsupervised mode discovery in Jun 2026, evasion/recovery results Jun–Sep 2026), so the integration — repertoire-level, prior-free, null-calibrated, adversarially stress-tested, spanning latents and residuals rather than SAE features alone — has not been done, while the alternative directions I surveyed (SAE variants, seed consensus, circuit-tracing automation, model diffing, coverage metrics, CoT faithfulness) are each already crowded with 2025–2026 papers, and even a negative result here (planted behaviors invisible to the full pipeline) would deliver the first systematic characterization of the detectability frontier that all future monitoring work needs.

direction: Build a quantitative ground-truth evaluation and metric suite for attribution-graph circuit tracing — testing whether cross-layer-transcoder decompositions faithfully recover known multi-hop algorithms, and identifying which sparsity/training choices make them unfaithful.
project: Are Attribution Graphs Telling the Truth? A Ground-Truth Benchmark for Transcoder Circuit Tracing
question: When and why are CLT-derived attribution graphs unfaithful to a model's known computation — specifically, do standard sparsity penalties cause the "deep-multi-hop-to-shallow-shortcut" rewrite predicted by recent toy-model results, and can non-circular, intervention-based metrics detect and rank decompositions that are behaviorally indistinguishable?
first_experiment: Train cross-layer transcoders with CLT-Forge on 2–4 public SIIT/InterpBench transformers implementing known multi-hop algorithms (e.g., IOI plus a synthetic 2–3-hop composition task), extract attribution graphs with the standard pruning pipeline, and measure node-, edge-, and path-level precision/recall against the known ground-truth causal graph while sweeping the L1 sparsity coefficient — directly testing whether stronger sparsity increases shortcut edges that replace true multi-hop paths.
why: Attribution graphs have become the standard evidentiary artifact of mechanistic interpretability and are already feeding safety audits and monitors, yet their verification has not kept pace — the field's own 2026 retrospective ranks faithfulness scoring and decomposition selection as its top open problems, an ICML 2026 result shows the tooling has an incentivized failure mode, and the closest prior work is either a Boolean toy model (no realistic transformer, no metrics), a component-granularity benchmark that predates CLTs (InterpBench), or a single qualitative replication (Goodfire); nobody has connected semi-synthetic ground-truth models to feature-level circuit tracing, because CLTs only emerged in 2025 and are expensive at frontier scale — but InterpBench models are small enough to make this tractable, the community already trusts both infrastructure pieces, and the result matters either way: quantifying a real failure mode forces downstream work to validate its claims, while a clean validation would be the first rigorous license to trust published circuits.

direction: Mechanistically characterize how long-horizon LLM agents internally represent and causally maintain their task/goal state across an episode, and use that representation for early drift detection and control.
project: The Running State — A Causal Account of Task-State Representations in Long-Horizon Language-Model Agents
question: Do transformer agents implement a compact, causally efficacious abstract task-state representation that is re-instantiated at each step of an episode (and can it be transplanted between episodes to override textual history), or is behavior reconstructed from raw context each step with no monitorable state?
first_experiment: Build a text grid-world "messenger" model organism (~500 paired episodes of 20–60 turns differing only in the assigned goal/constraints), then run cross-episode activation patching on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (and Gemma-2-9B-it with Gemma Scope): at each turn boundary, swap activations between goal-A and goal-B episodes at every layer and readout position, measuring how often subsequent goal-directed actions flip; then test whether the minimal SAE feature set at the highest-flip site (a) decodes the true state, (b) flips behavior when feature-patched (vs. random-feature controls), and (c) tracks state under paraphrase-based distribution shift — establishing whether a causally validated "running state" subspace exists.
why: It targets the intersection of the field's strongest tool (causal feature circuits) and its biggest unexplored territory (long-horizon agent state), where 2026's self-diagnosed gaps — narrow monitorability, distributed-circuit behaviors, OOD-fragile probes, and the documented "horizon gap" in agent failures — all converge; adjacent work is probing-only (ICML 2026 goal-directedness), token-attribution-only (multi-turn tracing), or confined to single-pass synthetic state tracking, so the causal, feature-level, across-turn question is genuinely unclaimed, and every outcome — a state subspace (enables drift monitors and control) or its absence (a fundamental limit on feature-based agent monitoring) — is publishable and safety-relevant.

direction: Build a principled, statistically certified criterion that ranks competing mechanistic decompositions (CLT/transcoder/SAE/neuron-based circuits) by their agreement with the model under pre-registered held-out interventions and distribution shifts — turning the field's "dual basis problem" into a solvable benchmark-and-metric agenda, validated against ground-truth circuits and then applied to real models.
project: Dual Basis Testbed — Pre-Registered Interventional Discrimination of Circuit Explanations
question: When multiple sparse decompositions faithfully reproduce a model's in-distribution behavior, can a pre-registered battery of held-out interventions (compositional edge/path ablations, tail-distribution inputs, abstract counterfactuals, adversarially searched interventions) identify which decomposition tracks the model's actual computation, and does a tractable "interventional disagreement score" (with anytime-valid confidence sequences) recover ground-truth faithfulness where standard metrics (reconstruction FVU, replacement KL, sparsity, interpretability ratings) cannot?
first_experiment: Train small transformers on a controlled 2–3-hop relational composition task whose deep circuit is verifiable by construction and exhaustive ablation; train 8–16 cross-layer transcoders across seeds, widths, and sparsity penalties (some expected to learn the known shallow-rewrite failure mode); demonstrate that standard in-distribution metrics fail to separate ground-truth-faithful from shallow-rewrite decompositions; then run a small pre-registered held-out intervention suite and test whether interventional disagreement separates them. Compute cost: days on one GPU node; a negative result (no intervention family discriminates) is itself a field-relevant finding that redirects attention to weight-space or identifiable primitives.
why: It is the field's own top-ranked gap — the Open Problems follow-through names faithfulness scoring and the dual basis problem as the central unfinished agenda, and every downstream safety use (monitors, audits, anomaly detection) currently inherits method contingencies. It is not already done: the ICML 2026 paper only diagnoses one failure mode without a criterion ("preliminary evidence"); CIF provides statistics for a fixed estimand but explicitly not intervention-distribution design or decomposition selection; Li et al. is an observational proof-of-concept on toy classifiers; MIB/SAEBench/AuditBench evaluate localization, SAE quality, and behavior elicitation — not mechanism-identification among behaviorally equivalent decompositions; and the Anthropic "neurons in disguise" paper calls for better attribution of non-neuron structure without providing a selection method. Meanwhile all prerequisites (public CLTs, controlled testbeds, certification statistics) matured only in 2025–2026, so the agenda is now tractable at academic scale, the validation methodology avoids the model-organism fragility problem, and success would convert the field's growing pile of unverified decompositions into certified science — while even a clean negative result would redirect the field productively.

direction: Make decomposition choice scientific by scoring feature-level attribution graphs on held-out, out-of-distribution interventional predictive adequacy and using that metric to adjudicate rival decompositions of the same model.
project: Held-Out Interventional Adequacy: Adjudicating Rival Decompositions of the Same Model
question: Do attribution graphs from rival decompositions that are indistinguishable in-distribution make divergent interventional predictions under distribution shift, and does held-out interventional predictive adequacy yield a stable, non-circular faithfulness ranking of decompositions across behaviors, models, and shift types?
first_experiment: On Gemma-2-2B with public SAEs (two seeds) and a transcoder, build attribution graphs for IOI and greater-than, then compare each graph's predicted vs. actual ablation effects on 100 in-distribution vs. 400 held-out shifted prompts to test whether in-distribution-equivalent graphs diverge out-of-distribution.
why: It converts the field's self-diagnosed #1 gap of 2026 — verification of feature-level explanations and the dual-basis ambiguity — into a falsifiable, compute-cheap benchmark using only public models and dictionaries, and no existing work combines OOD interventional adequacy with cross-decomposition adjudication on real models: the nearest papers stop at component-level circuits, seed-stability without shift, toy-model diagnosis, or null-model calibration.

direction: Build a quantitative, held-out validation standard for mechanistic explanations — score attribution graphs by how well their structure predicts model behavior under interventions and inputs *not* used during discovery, making "explanation quality" a measurable generalization property instead of an aesthetic one.
project: Held-Out Interventional Adequacy (HIA): Out-of-Sample Validation for Attribution Graphs
question: Does an attribution graph's fit on its discovery distribution predict its ability to quantitatively predict the model's behavior on held-out inputs and held-out intervention classes — and if not, where do explanations fail first (which nodes, which edge types, which kinds of shift)?
first_experiment: On GPT-2 small (IOI, Greater-Than — both with reference circuits) and Gemma-2-2B with Gemma Scope, construct attribution graphs for each behavior using at least two methods (e.g., EAP-IG edge circuits and transcoder-based graphs via the open-source circuit tracer). Interpret each graph as a linear path-effect model that predicts Δlogit under any intervention. Then evaluate on a battery the graph never saw: (i) novel inputs — new entities, paraphrased templates, changed formats; (ii) novel intervention classes — graded/noise ablations, joint multi-component ablations, context-length shifts; (iii) negative controls — ablating components the graph claims are irrelevant. Report per-graph predictive R² against the real model, localize error by node/edge, and correlate in-distribution faithfulness (the standard metric) with held-out adequacy. Either outcome is decisive: collapse demonstrates the field-level overfitting problem and motivates the metric; robustness establishes the first trustworthy cheap certification for circuit claims.
why: It targets the bottleneck the field's own 2026 retrospective puts at the very top of the list ("the most important methodological question of 2026"), the gap that four independent lines of work (ablation sensitivity, statistical instability, CLT unfaithfulness, ID/OOD ablation decorrelation) all converge on without closing: existing work measures in-distribution ablation fidelity (Hanna et al.), instability (Méloux et al.), intervention specificity (unit tests), or synthetic ground truth (InterpBench) — but nobody scores real-model attribution graphs on held-out interventions and distribution shift as a standard, decomposable metric, and nobody has tested whether published in-distribution faithfulness predicts out-of-sample validity (early evidence says it doesn't). It is also principled leverage on the dual-basis problem — ranking competing decompositions of the same model by held-out predictive adequacy rather than readability — and it is a prerequisite for the deployment use case that matters most for safety: interpretability-derived monitors must be certified under exactly the distributional shift where the 2026 retrospective says they currently fail. It is tractable without frontier compute (small open models, public SAE/transcoder artifacts), the first experiment is cheap and produces a publishable result either way, and the timing is right: attribution graphs just became the standard artifact, so defining their evaluation standard now shapes how the next generation of circuit claims is graded.

direction: Build a constructive, adversarial discrimination methodology for mechanistic explanations — treat competing candidate explanations (circuits, attribution graphs, transcoder decompositions) of the same behavior as hypotheses, actively search input space and intervention families for regions where their predictions diverge, and use the full model's behavior there to select, merge, or falsify them and to map mechanism regimes.
project: DIVERGE — Adversarial Discrimination of Behaviorally-Equivalent Mechanistic Explanations
question: When two or more candidate explanations of the same model behavior are indistinguishable under standard faithfulness metrics on the task distribution, can we systematically find inputs (and joint interventions) where their implied predictions diverge, and does the model's actual behavior in those divergence regions provide a statistically powerful, non-circular signal for adjudicating which mechanism the model really implements — or for discovering that the behavior is a mixture of mechanisms across input regimes?
first_experiment: On GPT-2 small IOI, take four published candidate explanations — the manual Wang et al. circuit, an ACDC-discovered circuit, an EAP-IG circuit, and a copy-suppression-only alternative — verify they are statistically indistinguishable on the standard task distribution under a fixed resample-ablation protocol, then (1) compute pairwise inter-explanation divergence over a large natural prompt corpus (template × name × object × order factors), (2) extend it with an automated search (discrete template search plus gradient-guided search in embedding space) to maximize inter-explanation divergence, and (3) test each candidate's agreement with the full model (exact-choice agreement on both successes and errors, plus KL) in the top-divergence regions — checking whether the search automatically rediscovers known edge cases (romantic objects, S2-hacking regimes) and rejects at least one candidate that standard metrics score equally, with the whole procedure validated against InterpBench's ground-truth circuits.
why: It is the field's own top-ranked, still-unclaimed gap — the constructive response to the dual-basis problem that the 2026 literature diagnoses but does not solve: Méloux et al. proved non-identifiability but only called for discriminative criteria; the NeurIPS 2026 reachable-state-geometry paper measures when evidence is blind but does not optimize inputs to break ties; uit de Bos & Garriga-Alonso adversarially tested circuits against the model on hand-picked variants, not explanations against each other; Shi et al. tested each circuit individually against idealized properties; the ICML 2026 CLT paper showed competing interpretations exist without adjudicating them; and Zhang et al. added another single-circuit metric rather than a comparative one. No work formalizes inter-explanation divergence over input space, searches for it, or uses model behavior there as the adjudication signal and mechanism-regime map. It is the most promising direction because it is leverage rather than another decomposition: SAEs and transcoders are now mass-produced infrastructure whose outputs are candidate explanations that currently cannot be rigorously ranked, so a discrimination methodology multiplies the value of every other tool in the field; it directly supplies the "faithfulness as a numerical target" the field says it needs, in a form (comparative, model-adjudicated, protocol-fixed) that sidesteps the known fragility of absolute faithfulness scores; its outputs (validated explanations and their failure regions) are the prerequisite for mechanistic anomaly detection and deployment-grade monitors, the narrow-but-growing safety application; it is executable end-to-end now, at GPT-2/Gemma-2-2B scale, using open tooling (TransformerLens, circuitry, AdversarialCircuitEvaluation, MIB, InterpBench) that only matured in the last two years; and the diagnostic papers landing in the last twelve months make it maximally timely, before someone assembles these existing pieces into the same framework.

direction: Build the missing validation layer for mechanistic interpretability — a pipeline and benchmark that compiles attribution-graph (circuit) explanations into registered, quantitative predictions of model behavior on held-out counterfactual inputs, and measures whether circuit-level understanding gives predictive uplift over black-box and activation-reading baselines, on successes, errors, and model organisms with known implanted mechanisms.
project: Simulatability for Circuits: Turning Attribution Graphs into Testable Predictions
question: Do circuit-level mechanistic explanations (attribution graphs from cross-layer transcoders), compiled into structured "mechanism cards," predict model behavior on counterfactual inputs better than behavior-only agents and activation-reading tools — and do discriminative transformation batteries separate the true circuit from superficially equivalent alternative decompositions?
first_experiment: On the greater-than task in GPT-2 small (using Goodfire's public CLT recipe) and one comparable task on Gemma-2-2b with released circuit-tracer CLTs: (1) generate an attribution graph for a seed prompt, auto-group supernodes, and hand-compile a mechanism card (typed variables + composition rules, e.g., "input-year feature suppresses years < YY; abstract 'greater-than' feature promotes years > YY"); (2) pre-register, before running the model, its predicted outcome distributions across 6–8 transformation families (century/digit changes, non-year numbers, boundary years, paraphrase, distractors, error-inducing prompts); (3) score registered predictions (flip accuracy, log-score) against actual behavior, including error cases; (4) compare against a behavior-only LLM agent and an SAE-feature-summary baseline to measure mechanistic uplift; (5) run the same battery on a competing "shortcut" mechanism card (e.g., memorized-year mapping) to test discriminative separation. Success = measurable uplift on boundary/error families where behavior-only agents fail; either result updates the field's central metric.
why: It attacks the field's own top-ranked open problem — faithfulness of circuit explanations as a numerical target and the dual-basis problem ("which one is *the* circuit?") — with an objective, replication-proof metric (measured counterfactual outcomes, not expert agreement), directly answering the circuit-tracing community's explicit call to automate the validation half of the hypothesis loop. It is not already done because: CHIVE tested only read-only activation tools and deliberately excluded circuit and intervention-based explanations; the simulatability literature (ALMANACS, ConSim, self-explanation papers) has never evaluated internal circuit hypotheses; the entire 2026 circuit-tracing literature optimizes internal replacement scores and automates *description* (ADAG, Circuit Oracle, graph annotation) rather than *predictive testing*; and Zhang et al.'s error-agreement result is a static critique on toy circuits, not a predictive evaluation method. The infrastructure (public CLTs, AuditBench's 56 known-mechanism models, released CHIVE datasets, MIB) only converged in the last year, making this newly tractable at single-GPU scale. And the expected value is symmetric and enormous: uplift validates the circuit-tracing paradigm and gives auditors/monitors a principled tool for choosing among explanations (feeding mechanistic anomaly detection and AuditBench-style audits), while a null result — extending CHIVE's no-uplift finding to mechanism-first methods — would be the decisive evidence behind the field's pragmatic turn.

direction: Develop and validate held-out interventional generalization as the first principled, non-circular selection criterion for competing mechanistic decompositions (circuits/attribution graphs), directly attacking the field's "dual basis problem" at feature level.
project: Tied, Then Tested: Ranking Mechanistic Decompositions by Held-Out Interventional Generalization
question: When multiple feature-level decompositions of the same model behavior are matched on standard validation faithfulness (the dual basis regime), do they make divergent predictions about the model's response to interventions on held-out inputs and unseen intervention types — and can interventional predictive accuracy on those held-out tests serve as a principled criterion for selecting among decompositions that the standard metric cannot distinguish?
first_experiment: On Pythia-160m's IOI task (reference circuit from MIB), construct ≥6 competing feature-level decompositions tied on the standard validation metric — attribution graphs over public TopK SAEs at widths 4k/16k/65k, three SAE seeds, a transcoder-based graph (CLT-Forge), and an EAP-IG head-edge baseline, each pruned to ~90% validation faithfulness — then measure each decomposition's predicted-vs-actual counterfactual KL divergence on a held-out suite of (a) input-shifted prompts (new templates, frequency-band shift) and (b) intervention-shifted ablations (strengths unused in pruning, support-crossing ablations, compound two-feature interventions), with CIF-style anytime-valid confidence sequences, testing three falsifiable claims: (1) tied decompositions diverge beyond error bars out-of-sample, (2) the interventional-generalization ranking differs from the validation-faithfulness ranking, and (3) the ranking is stable across a second behavior and on Gemma-2-2B with Gemma Scope dictionaries.
why: It targets the problem the 2026 state-of-field review independently ranks as the field's top methodological gap ("how do you know an attribution graph faithfully describes the model, as opposed to one of many decompositions that account for the same behavior... which one is 'the circuit'?"), and it converts a currently aesthetic choice into an empirical, falsifiable one — which matters for safety because monitors and audits built on any single decomposition are unsound if tied decompositions diverge under distribution shift. It is feasible now because every enabling piece has just matured (public dictionaries, open attribution-graph tooling, certified-estimand statistics, reference circuits) while the synthesis itself is missing: Méloux proved non-uniqueness only in toys without a ranking metric; Geng demonstrated the standard metric misranks but offered no replacement criterion; Bayat Makou showed equivalence classes at head level without held-out interventional prediction; Li fixed linearization within a fixed dictionary without ranking dictionaries or testing input shift; CIF certifies a chosen estimand without choosing among candidates; MIB evaluates in-distribution localization only; and Koopman identifiability yields an object that is explicitly not legible. The constructive selection framework — decompositions as interventional predictors, ranked by held-out counterfactual accuracy with certified error bars — has not been built, and it generates the natural next steps (interventionally-robust dictionary training, the cross-architecture transfer program, and deployment-grade monitors) rather than competing with them.

direction: Build an empirical science and benchmark for the out-of-distribution generalization of mechanistic explanations — treating circuits, SAE features, and attribution graphs as predictive causal models whose causal claims must be validated, compared, and selected by their interventional agreement under controlled distribution shift rather than in-distribution faithfulness.
project: EXPLAIN-SHIFT: Stress-Testing and Selecting Mechanistic Explanations Under Distribution Shift
question: When a mechanistic explanation (circuit, feature set, or attribution graph) discovered and validated on distribution D makes causal claims that agree with the model's behavior on D, how well do those causal claims predict the model's interventional behavior on systematically shifted distributions D′ — and can shift-divergence serve as a principled, non-circular criterion for selecting among behaviorally equivalent candidate explanations of the same behavior?
first_experiment: The pilot stress test. In GPT-2 small (and one feature-level case in Gemma-2-2B with Gemma Scope), take three published explanations — the IOI circuit, the greater-than circuit, the docstring circuit — plus 3–5 causally validated SAE features with known steering effects. Construct an ordered ladder of controlled shift families per task (paraphrase templates → name/entity substitution → distractor clauses → algorithm-breaking structural variants à la DoubleIO → language/format switch), and for each rung measure: (1) behavioral invariance of the full model, (2) the explanation generalization gap — agreement between the base-distribution circuit and the full model under ablation on shifted inputs (KL/logit-diff), (3) causal-structure drift — Spearman correlation and top-k Jaccard between per-edge/per-head patching effects measured on-distribution vs. shifted, and (4) feature steering dose-response consistency on vs. off distribution. Prediction to falsify: agreement decays with shift severity in an ordered way, with a stable causal "skeleton" and a fragile lexical periphery, and different explanation types (edge circuits vs. feature steering) degrade at different rates. One GPU, roughly a week, using TransformerLens/AutoCircuit/nnsight; positive controls (the refusal direction, known to transfer) confirm the benchmark can distinguish robust from fragile explanations rather than uniformly reporting failure.
why: It attacks the field's self-diagnosed #1 bottleneck — verification of explanations at scale, the dual basis problem, and shift-fragile monitors — with infrastructure and empirical laws rather than philosophy, and every ingredient is now in place (released SAEs, standard models, mature patching tooling) but unassembled. It is not already done: the closest works each occupy only one facet — toy-scale proof-of-concept (Li et al., synthetic Dyck-1), a single circuit across two prompt variants (Nainani et al.), worst-case adversarial input search without shift taxonomy, feature level, or selection (uit de Bos & Garriga-Alonso), certification of component inclusion under dataset subsampling rather than explanation quality or selection (Certified Circuits), in-distribution error agreement (Zhang et al.), methodological-axis robustness of faithfulness metrics (Miller et al.), and pure theory showing legible ≠ identifiable (Koopman-spectral work). None delivers a shift-ladder benchmark, an explanation-level generalization metric, or shift as a discriminator among competing decompositions on real LLMs. The payoff is threefold: the first quantitative "engineering tolerances" for interpretability-derived monitors (directly addressing the growing deployment coverage gap), a principled answer to which decomposition is "the circuit" — replacing aesthetic choice with out-of-sample interventional prediction — and a compounding community benchmark that makes all downstream claims, from universality studies to mechanistic anomaly detection, verifiable rather than merely labeled.

direction: Build a distribution-shift validation harness for attribution-graph circuit explanations that tests whether their causal predictions survive controlled semantic distribution shift, using shift-robustness as the first principled discriminator between competing decompositions of the same behavior.
project: Stress-Testing the Circuit: Distribution Shift as a Discriminating Test for Mechanistic Explanations
question: When a transcoder-based attribution graph reproduces model behavior in-distribution, are its causal claims (which features matter, with what sign and magnitude) preserved across semantic distribution shift, and does preservation under shift separate the genuine mechanism from impostor decompositions that merely fit the training distribution?
first_experiment: Using pre-trained cross-layer transcoders (Circuit Tracer) on GPT-2 small's "greater-than" task — where the literature already documents both a genuine magnitude-comparison mechanism and narrow impostor heuristics (a parity detector, a year-range detector) within the same CLT graphs — generate attribution graphs over ~500–1,000 prompts stratified across in-range years (1100–1599) and shifted subpopulations (out-of-range years, non-year numerals, distractor contexts), extract each graph's signed causal predictions on candidate-number logits, then measure (1) feature/edge consistency across subpopulations, (2) predicted-vs-actual logit changes under targeted feature ablations in-distribution vs. shifted, and (3) whether the documented impostor features lose causal power or flip under shift while core ordering features persist.
why: Attribution graphs are now the field's dominant artifact and the substrate for emerging safety monitors, yet the field's own 2026 assessment names the dual basis problem — many decompositions fit in-distribution, and choosing among them is aesthetic — as its top open methodological question; meanwhile all adjacent work occupies different niches (2025–26 attribution-graph papers automate generation/description but not validation, faithfulness-robustness work varies ablation but holds inputs fixed, error-agreement work tests the same distribution, formal verification certifies only L∞-style feature stability on small vision models, identifiability theory proves the underdetermination without resolving it, and the attribution-graph authors themselves list OOD-based hypothesis validation and global circuit pictures as open future work). It is simultaneously foundational, safety-relevant as the prerequisite for shift-robust monitors, and tractable with fully open tooling on small models.

direction: Build an automated "cross-examination" protocol that treats rival mechanistic explanations (circuits, transcoder subgraphs, algorithmic hypotheses) as competing hypotheses, actively searches the input-and-intervention space for traces where their predictions maximally diverge, and uses the full model's actual behavior at those traces to adjudicate, rank, and improve them.
project: Cross-Examination: Adversarial Adjudication of Competing Mechanistic Explanations
question: When multiple mechanistic explanations reproduce a model's behavior on its natural distribution, can divergence-seeking search over inputs and interventions automatically identify where their predictions part ways, and does the model's true behavior at those points reliably and non-circularly select the correct explanation?
first_experiment: On GPT-2 small's IOI task, fit the documented rival circuits (manual Wang et al. circuit, ACDC/edge-pruning circuits, attribution-patching circuit, plus the documented backup branch), confirm they are all faithful on-distribution, then run a divergence-finder (template-grammar perturbations in the style of DoubleIO/TripleIO plus evolutionary/gradient search over prompts and ablation regimes) to locate the top-k points where circuit predictions split; measure (i) the abundance of divergence points, (ii) adjudication accuracy — how well full-model behavior at those points ranks the circuits versus on-distribution faithfulness metrics, validated against literature-established ground truth (S2 hacking, backup heads), and (iii) discovery yield — whether any divergence point exposes a mechanism not in any candidate circuit.
why: It attacks the field's top-ranked open problem of 2026 — faithfulness and the dual-basis problem — with a constructive, automatable method rather than another diagnostic metric, exactly the "verification infrastructure" that the Open Problems review, the 2026 retrospective, and the Dead Salmons critique all demand but none deliver. It has not been done: Méloux et al. (ICLR 2025) only demonstrate non-identifiability in toy Boolean MLPs; the Dead Salmons paper calls for hypothesis-testing against alternatives without building the engine; mechanistic unit tests (ICML 2026) use fixed negative controls rather than searched discriminating traces; Rethinking Circuit Evaluation (Sep 2026) uses naturally occurring errors with no search and no rival adjudication; CIRCUS quantifies analyst-choice uncertainty, not input-space divergence; and the one instance of variant testing (Adaptive Circuit Behavior, 2024) is manual, single-circuit, and found real mechanisms precisely where my protocol would search systematically. It is feasible on open models with modest compute, and unlike pure validation work it produces discoveries as a byproduct (divergence points are where backups, compensation, and unmodeled machinery live), while directly serving safety applications that currently rest on unvalidated mechanisms — mechanistic anomaly detection, monitoring, and auditing feature-level claims like "this is the deception circuit."

direction: one sentence — see above: map and predict the evasion-tax frontier of internal activation monitoring from the causal indispensability and encoding redundancy of monitored concepts.
project: The Evasion Tax: When Can a Neural Network Not Hide What It Computes?
question: What determines the minimum capability cost for a model to evade monitors on a concept C during task T, and can it be predicted from C's causal indispensability to T and the redundancy of C's encodings?
first_experiment: Adversarial fine-tuning of open sandbagging/chameleon organisms against probe ensembles, sweeping the capability-preservation constraint to trace the recall-vs-capability Pareto frontier, then regressing frontier position on measured causal indispensability and encoding redundancy of each monitored concept.
why: Monitoring is interpretability's deployed safety application, its failure modes are freshly demonstrated and worsening, existing defenses are unprincipled, and the enabling law — indispensable information is expensive to hide — is suggested by scattered results but has never been formalized, tested, or turned into monitor-design principles.

direction: Build an automated adversarial falsification engine that turns attribution-graph circuit hypotheses into discriminating experiments — generating minimal pairs, nuisance rewrites, OOD prompts, and targeted interventions where rival circuit hypotheses diverge — thereby providing the field's first calibrated, non-aesthetic standard for validating and ranking circuit explanations.
project: Circuit Tribunal: Automated Adversarial Validation of Attribution-Graph Hypotheses
question: When multiple attribution graphs (or component circuits) are equally faithful to a model's behavior on the observed prompt, which adversarially generated tests — held-out inputs and interventions chosen to maximize divergence between rival hypotheses — reliably discriminate the true mechanism from the equally-consistent alternatives, and what false-confirmation rate does standard validation practice incur when measured against model organisms with planted, ground-truth mechanisms?
first_experiment: On Gemma-2-2B with Gemma Scope cross-layer transcoders and the open-source circuit-tracer, generate ~20 attribution graphs for the same behavior (IOI plus one natural multi-step behavior) varying only transcoder seed, pruning threshold, and graph-construction choices; verify they are indistinguishable by standard on-prompt faithfulness (replacement score / circuit error); then run a hand-built battery of ~50 discriminating tests per hypothesis pair (minimal pairs, paraphrases, targeted edge ablations, feature-direction steering) to measure (a) how badly the graphs disagree out-of-sample, and (b) the gap between on-prompt faithfulness and held-out interventional predictive accuracy — the baseline numbers that justify automating the test generator and calibrating it against AuditBench model organisms.
why: It attacks the field's self-identified #1 bottleneck — the verification asymmetry and the dual-basis problem — named by the Sharkey et al. open-problems coalition, re-flagged as top-priority by the 2026 retrospective, and listed as an explicit unfilled call ("automate intervention experiments and synthetic/OOD inputs for hypothesis validation") by the authors of the attribution-graph methodology themselves. It has not been done because the nearest neighbors each cover only one slice: ICML 2026's "unit tests" handle specificity only with a distilgpt2 pilot and no rival-hypothesis discrimination, automated tooling (ADAG, Circuit Oracle, LLM annotators) automates description rather than falsification, the ACD agent selects interventions per-prompt without hypothesis-level comparison or ground truth, MIB benchmarks discovery methods on static tasks, and causal scrubbing remains manual, component-level, and error-prone. Meanwhile the model-organism infrastructure needed to calibrate it (AuditBench, auditing-game replications) only matured in 2025–26. Crucially, this direction multiplies the value of every competing research program — reasoning-model CoT claims, cross-architecture universality, and safety monitors all currently rest on unvalidated circuit hypotheses — so it is the highest-leverage place for me to work next, and it is executable on open-weight models with public tooling rather than requiring frontier-lab access.

direction: Build and validate a counterfactual, prompt-family-level protocol that distinguishes generalizable algorithmic circuits from per-prompt execution traces in transcoder-based attribution graphs, using ground-truth mechanisms as the reference standard.
project: Trace or Algorithm? Counterfactual Validation of Attribution Graphs Across Prompt Families
question: When a transcoder attribution graph built on a single prompt achieves a high replacement score, is its implied circuit an algorithm that predicts feature activations and intervention outcomes on held-out variants of the task — and can per-prompt graphs be aggregated into a global circuit hypothesis that recovers the model's true mechanism rather than a behaviorally equivalent lookup-table decomposition?
first_experiment: Using Circuit Tracer with open transcoders on GPT-2 small (cross-check on Llama-3.2-1B), generate attribution graphs for the greater-than task; extract each graph's testable causal claims (active feature set, claimed input-selectivity of each feature, claimed direction of effect on candidate tokens); construct a held-out family of ~200 year/template variants; then measure (i) agreement between graph-implied and actual feature activations across the family, (ii) graph-predicted vs. measured logit changes from ablating each graph feature on held-out prompts (graph counterfactual error), and (iii) out-of-distribution replacement score, comparing single-prompt graphs, merged family graphs, and size-matched random-feature controls — with a planned follow-up on grokked modular addition, where the known Fourier mechanism provides hard ground truth for whether family-merging recovers the algorithm or the documented lookup-table shadow.
why: It targets the field's self-identified #1 open problem — validation/faithfulness of attribution graphs, the dual-basis problem — exactly when attribution graphs have become the dominant artifact and verification infrastructure has fallen behind generation; the attribution-graph community itself explicitly flags "families of attribution graphs" and "merging graphs into a global circuit picture" as undone future work. It is not already done: the 2025–26 automation wave (ADAG, Circuit Oracle, LLM annotation, probe-prompting) automates graph description rather than causal validation; the faithfulness critiques (Miller et al. 2024, Geng et al. 2026, Sheng & Fu 2026) concern scoring protocols and component-level circuits on fixed tasks, not held-out generalization of transcoder graphs; the recent mechanism-geometry theory evaluates only pre-specified hypotheses and does not infer mechanisms from attribution graphs; and the closest prior work (IOI generalization, 2024) predates attribution graphs, uses head-level circuits, one task, and no validation metrics. It is safety-critical — interpretability-derived monitors built on trace-level circuits fail silently under distribution shift, so a certified trace/algorithm criterion tells us when circuit claims can be trusted off-distribution — and it is feasible at single-GPU scale on open models with existing tooling and known ground-truth mechanisms, unlike frontier-scale validation work.

direction: Build the missing evaluation layer for mechanistic interpretability — a quantitative, automated "held-out causal agreement" protocol that scores attribution graphs (and competing feature-level decompositions of the same behavior) by how well their causal predictions survive out-of-distribution prompts and targeted interventions, turning faithfulness from an aesthetic judgment into a measurable number.
project: How Far Does a Circuit Reach? A Held-Out Causal-Agreement Standard for Attribution Graphs
question: Does an attribution graph's causal story predict model behavior beyond the prompt distribution it was built on — and can held-out causal agreement serve as the field-standard metric that ranks competing decompositions (PLT vs. CLT vs. SAE-feature circuits, varying sparsity and pruning thresholds) by something other than interpretability aesthetics?
first_experiment: On GPT-2 small and Llama-3.2-1B, using open CLT/PLT tooling, build attribution graphs for two well-studied behaviors (greater-than comparison; two-integer addition) on a development distribution. Freeze each graph, then generate a graded battery of ~1,000 held-out probes: same-family held-out samples, paraphrases, distractor insertions, longer contexts, and composed two-instance prompts. For each, (a) run the graph as a replacement model and score answer-agreement on successes *and* errors, and (b) ablate/patch the graph's top features and compare predicted logit-deltas (edge-derived) against actual model deltas, including edges with negative (suppressive) influence. Report a "generalization gap" — in-distribution vs. held-out causal agreement — and test whether replacement score, sparsity level, or dictionary type predicts it. Either a large, systematic gap (the metric discriminates; the instrument is validated and immediately publishable with findings) or a small gap (strong positive evidence that attribution graphs are faithful infrastructure — equally publishable). ~1 GPU-week, no frontier-model access required.
why: It attacks the problem the field's own leadership ranks first — attribution-graph faithfulness and the dual-basis problem — at the moment when automated generation (ADAG, Circuit Oracle, LLM graph agents) is massively outpacing verification, so the instrument's value compounds with everything downstream (safety monitors, model editing, automated auditing). It synthesizes four established but siloed results — adversarial fragility (uit de Bos 2024), non-robust metrics (Miller et al. 2024), phantom equivalence classes (Makou 2026), and incentivized unfaithful CLT rewrites (ICML 2026) — into the first scored, generalization-based test that works on the feature-level attribution graphs that are now the field's standard artifact. It has not been done because the artifact is barely 20 months old, the open tooling (CLT-Forge, circuit-tracer, Gemma Scope 2) only matured in late 2025–2026, the evaluation community's machinery (MIB lineage) was built for head-level in-distribution circuit *discovery* rather than explanation *validation*, and benchmark-and-metric work carries less incentive gradient than new discovery methods — the exact asymmetry the 2026 field review documents. Both outcomes of the first experiment are decisive results, which is the hallmark of a direction with information value rather than sunk-cost risk.

direction: Pursue unsupervised, output-conditioned mechanistic anomaly detection using sparse features to catch hidden model behaviors without behavioral labels, and stress-test it against monitor-evading training.
project: Conditional Feature Fingerprints: Unsupervised Mechanistic Anomaly Detection for Hidden Behaviors in LLMs
question: Can an SAE-feature anomaly score conditioned on the model's output, fit only to trusted benign data, detect hidden behaviors (backdoors, planted personas, sandbagging) with low false positives, distinguish "same output, anomalous mechanism" from normal computation (the recognition-vs-causation problem), and survive RL-Obfuscation-style evasion training that defeats supervised probes?
first_experiment: On one small public organism (≤14B, e.g., a released backdoored/audit-game model) with open mid-layer SAEs: fit a local density model over trusted benign output-position feature activations, then score triggered vs clean inputs and the control set of clean inputs that naturally produce the backdoored output; report AUROC/FPR@95 for output-conditioned vs input-only scoring, feature-space vs raw-activation Mahalanobis, perplexity, and a supervised probe upper bound — the decisive readout being the output-conditioned feature-space gap over all baselines.
why: White-box monitoring is the field's top-priority application (Open Problems §3.2.1) with direct regulatory/safety-case pull, yet MAD has only one empirical method (influence functions, no features, no output-conditioning), unsupervised SAE detection has only been applied to unsafe inputs, the recognition-vs-causation false-positive problem named in the roadmap is unsolved, and the evasion-attack literature and public hidden-behavior organisms are too recent for anyone to have combined them — so the conjunction is unoccupied, important, and tractable with open models and inference-scale compute.

direction: Develop "differential validation" of mechanistic explanations — treating multiple equally-faithful circuit candidates for one behavior as competing hypotheses that are adjudicated by their predictive divergence under controlled distribution shift, turning the field's dual-basis problem from an aesthetic choice into a measurable, safety-relevant test.
project: One Behavior, Many Circuits: Distribution Shift as a Discriminating Test of Competing Mechanistic Explanations
question: When several circuit candidates for the same model behavior are statistically indistinguishable in faithfulness on the training distribution, where and why do their behavioral predictions diverge from each other and from the model under controlled distribution shifts — and can shift-induced divergence serve as a non-circular criterion for adjudicating which candidate tracks the model's actual computation rather than a re-description of the test distribution?
first_experiment: On GPT-2 small (and replicating one result on Llama-3.2-1B or Gemma-2-2B with public dictionaries), take the IOI and greater-than tasks and construct ≥5 circuit candidates that each pass the standard faithfulness bar (≥90% logit-diff recovery / replacement score ≥0.8) yet come from different pipelines — the manual canonical circuit, ACDC, EAP-IG/CEAP, subsample-certified variants, different ablation bases (mean vs. resampling vs. optimal), and different SAE/transcoder seeds. First verify pairwise in-distribution equivalence using the equivalence tests from the circuitry package; then sweep controlled shifts (novel/unseen entity names, template rephrasings, added distractor subjects à la IOI-hard, length and context shifts) and measure, per axis: each candidate's agreement with the full model, pairwise candidate-vs-candidate prediction divergence, and (via targeted patching) which components mediate the divergence. The headline output is each candidate's "divergence profile": whether circuits that are interchangeable in-distribution decorrelate out-of-distribution, and whether divergence concentrates in a small set of components — those components being validated as genuinely load-bearing in a way in-distribution ablation cannot show.
why: It attacks the two problems the field itself ranks highest — faithfulness verification and the dual-basis problem — with a single empirical program that is cheap (public open-weight models and Gemma Scope/Llama Scope dictionaries, no frontier access needed) and composes with, rather than competes against, the crowded adjacent work: Méloux et al. and Wu et al. diagnose non-uniqueness and variance but stop at diagnosis (Wu et al. explicitly conclude comprehensiveness is unattainable without proposing what to do instead); Shi et al. test circuits only at a fixed distribution; Anani et al. certify component-level stability under dataset subsampling, not predictive divergence of whole explanations under shift; Zhang et al. add an error-agreement axis on-distribution; Dhor & Chen's identifiable object is by their own admission not legible, leaving the legible-decomposition adjudication open. Nanda and Lindsey flag synthetic/OOD inputs for hypothesis validation as an open direction, and the 2026 field retrospective states that ranking decompositions is "currently an aesthetic decision" — so the constructive, quantified version of this question is claimed by no one, while being simultaneously the top methodological gap and directly safety-relevant: a monitor or audit built on a decomposition that diverges from the model under shift is a monitor that fails exactly when deployed, so divergence profiles double as a deployment-gating signal for interpretability-derived monitors.

direction: Build an automated "crucial experiment" protocol for mechanistic interpretability that adjudicates between competing circuit hypotheses (from different methods, seeds, or architectures of decomposer) by deriving the input distributions and interventions where their predictions diverge, testing those predictions against the real model, and calibrating the resulting adjudication score on model organisms with planted, known mechanisms.
project: Adjudicator — Ground-Truth-Calibrated Discrimination of Competing Circuit Hypotheses
question: When two circuit explanations of the same behavior are behaviorally indistinguishable in-distribution, can their interventional predictions on automatically-searched distribution-shifted and adversarial inputs empirically discriminate which one reflects the model's actual mechanism — and does that discrimination score, validated against planted ground truth, fix the faithfulness measurement gap (the "dual basis problem")?
first_experiment: Build a small (2–4 layer) TransformerLens-compatible model organism on a synthetic three-hop relational-chain task in two training regimes — one admitting only a genuine multi-hop mechanism (held-out compositions) and one also trained on direct shortcut pairs that admits a shallow single-hop rewrite; train per-layer transcoders and a small CLT (multiple seeds) on both; extract attribution graphs that all achieve high in-distribution replacement score; then compute, for each candidate hypothesis, the agreement between its predicted intervention effects (feature/edge ablations and resampling) and the actual model on (a) in-distribution prompts, (b) held-out chain compositions, and (c) prompts where the deep and shallow mechanisms diverge — checking whether the adjudication score separates the true planted mechanism from the shallow rewrite where standard faithfulness ties. Success = the protocol ranks the data-installed mechanism above the rewrite on discriminating sets while replacement score cannot.
why: It attacks the single most-cited methodological bottleneck of 2025–2026 — verification and adjudication of circuit explanations, the "dual basis problem" — which gates every downstream use of interpretability (monitoring, auditing, model editing, safety cases), so fixing the measurement multiplies the value of everything else in the field; it is an empirical escape from the proven in-distribution non-identifiability result (ICLR 2025), converting a philosophical problem into a testable one; it directly answers three separately-posed open questions from the field's own roadmaps (automated OOD validation, faithfulness as a numerical target, circuit-evaluation benchmarks); and it has not been done because until mid-2025 the field lacked cheap hypothesis generation at scale (there was little to adjudicate), the negative-results literature (Miller 2024, uit de Bos 2024, Méloux 2025, ICML 2026) attacked only single facets — single-circuit stress tests, exhaustive toy enumeration, CLT unfaithfulness diagnosis — without building the hypothesis-vs-hypothesis protocol, and the remaining work is compute-light and methodology-heavy rather than scale-heavy, leaving it unclaimed by frontier labs while being tractable with public models (GPT-2/Gemma-2-2B + Gemma Scope, TransformerLens, CLT-Forge, pyvene) and small self-trained organisms with verifiable ground truth.

direction: Build an automated, ground-truth-calibrated "differential diagnosis" protocol that adjudicates between competing circuit-level explanations of the same model behavior by searching for held-out input distributions and interventions where their predictions diverge, then testing which one the real model actually follows.
project: Dueling Decompositions — Falsification-Driven Adjudication of Attribution Graphs
question: When two circuit explanations (e.g., a cross-layer-transcoder attribution graph and a per-layer-transcoder/SAE-patching graph) both achieve high behavioral faithfulness on the distribution they were built on, can a systematically designed family of held-out interventions and input shifts reliably identify which graph matches the model's actual mechanism — and which decomposition pipelines produce genuine mechanisms versus behavior-mimicking "shallow rewrites"?
first_experiment: On a setting with known ground truth — an InterpBench semi-synthetic transformer plus a small transformer trained on a synthetic multi-hop task whose true mechanism is known by construction — I will train a cross-layer transcoder and per-layer transcoders with CLT-Forge, extract attribution graphs for the same behavior from both pipelines, verify both score ~equally on standard on-distribution faithfulness, then compute each graph's interventional predictions under a designed family of tests (suppressing intermediate-hop features, ablating early-layer components under shifted input distributions, cross-prompt activation swaps) and check which graph's predictions match the true model's responses. Success criterion: the protocol correctly recovers the known deep mechanism and identifies the minimal intervention family that falsifies the behaviorally-equivalent shallow rewrite; the immediate follow-up applies the same protocol to multi-hop factual recall in Gemma-2-2B, where the ICML 2026 result predicts CLT graphs will fail.
why: It attacks the field's self-identified #1 open problem — attribution graphs are the dominant artifact yet are validated by readability rather than measurement, and 2026's own papers prove standard metrics cannot tell mechanisms from behavior-mimics. It is not already done: the ICML 2026 unfaithfulness paper stops at toy models plus "preliminary evidence"; the misranking and patching-limits papers only diagnose; CIF adds statistics to a fixed estimand without discriminating hypotheses; causal scrubbing is human-guided and subject to the same context-distortion critique; the POMDP active-discovery work ranks features rather than adjudicating whole competing graphs; and no ground-truth-calibrated, multi-hypothesis, held-out-intervention protocol exists for real models. It is timely (four 2026 papers create the demand, CLT-Forge/InterpBench/circuit-tracer supply the means), feasible on open ≤9B models without frontier access, and maximally leveraged: an evidentiary standard for attribution graphs upgrades every downstream claim in auditing, monitoring, model editing, and CoT-faithfulness — the safety-critical consumers of this research — rather than adding one more circuit to the pile.

direction: Build a causal, feature-pathway account of when chain-of-thought is the computation versus post-hoc theater in open reasoning models, replacing confounded behavioral CoT-edit tests with internal circuit-level measurement.
project: Anatomy of Reasoning Theater: Circuit-Level Causal Paths Between Verbalized Steps and Answers in Reasoning Models
question: When a reasoning model verbalizes a chain-of-thought step, does the internal computation that produces the final answer flow through the features instantiating that step, and what circuit-level differences distinguish genuine stepwise computation from rationalization of a pre-committed answer, honest mistakes, shortcuts, and last-minute answer flips?
first_experiment: On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B (and spot-checks on Qwen3-4B), run ~500 multi-hop factual questions under three conditions — no hint, wrong-answer hint, correct-answer hint (Chen et al. biasing paradigm) — segment each generated trace into steps, extract per-step feature sets via neuron-basis RelP attribution at step-final positions, and compute a "load-bearing ratio" (fraction of attribution flow to final-answer logits routed through each step's features versus bypassing them), together with a pre-CoT answer-commitment probe. Prediction: hint-condition traces that adopt the hinted answer without verbalizing it will show pre-commitment plus near-zero answer-path routing through early CoT steps, while unhinted traces show high routing. Validate the internal measure against the labeled FINE-CoT unfaithfulness benchmark and against thought-anchors-style behavioral resampling, establishing convergence and known-confound divergences between internal and behavioral tests — roughly one to two A100-days of compute.
why: It targets the single sharpest open question the attribution-graph community itself flagged three times in its 2025 roadmap, and it is safety-critical: CoT monitoring — the most deployable near-term oversight channel — silently fails exactly where CoT is theater, and "Drop the Act"-style mitigations presuppose detection that currently lacks any mechanistic grounding. It has not been done because the necessary ingredients only recently converged (public attribution tooling that avoids proprietary cross-layer transcoders, open RL-trained reasoning models, labeled unfaithfulness benchmarks), and every adjacent line stops short: Anthropic's rationalization findings were qualitative case studies on proprietary models; probing work (pre-CoT answer decoding, "wait"-token states) is correlational; CIE-Scorer scores discrepancy with supervised graph distances but explains no mechanism; behavioral causal tests (Thought Anchors, decorative-vs-load-bearing continuation patching) are confounded by off-distribution edits in the very way the community roadmap warns; and the closest circuit-anatomy work (the commit–abstain circuit) addresses hallucination, not CoT load-bearing-ness. A positive result yields the first open, causal account of CoT-computation divergence plus a label-free per-step faithfulness metric; a negative result — that verbalized steps and answer paths are always tightly coupled — would itself be a major, publishable validation of CoT monitorability.

direction: Build a mechanism-discriminating distribution-shift instrument that detects and ranks "impostor" circuit decompositions — those matching behavior in-distribution while misrepresenting mechanism — by scoring their predictions of model behavior on distributions designed to separate competing mechanistic accounts, starting with addition in GPT-2/Gemma-2-2B where lookup-table and trigonometric accounts diverge.
project: Impostor Circuits: Crucial Experiments for Mechanistic Explanations via Designed Distribution Shift
question: When a transcoder-derived circuit or SAE decomposition reproduces a model's behavior in-distribution, how often is it a mechanistically false "impostor," and can designed input distributions that separate competing mechanistic hypotheses serve as a non-circular criterion for detecting and ranking such impostors?
first_experiment: Run pretrained cross-layer transcoders (circuit-tracer) on two-digit addition in GPT-2 small and Gemma-2-2B, construct hypothesis-discriminating distributions from the known divergence between the trigonometric-manifold and lookup-table accounts (out-of-range operands, format perturbations, intermediate-value carry probes), and test whether the attribution graph's implied mechanism fails to predict the real model's behavioral changes where the manifold account succeeds.
why: It targets the field's self-identified top open problem (the dual-basis/non-circular faithfulness gap in its dominant artifact, flagged by both the 2025 open-problems review's 2026 retrospective and the tool-builders' own future-directions list), unifies four confirmed but scattered findings (geometry shattering, sparsity-incentivized shallow rewrites, proven non-identifiability, ablation-fragile faithfulness metrics) that no paper has assembled, and remains unoccupied because the necessary ingredients (standardized attribution graphs, feasible OOD-behavioral prediction, known competing mechanisms with ground-truth benchmarks like InterpBench) only matured in the last 18 months while field incentives steer effort toward building new decomposers scored by reconstruction rather than adversarially testing the ones we already trust.

direction: Ground the validation of mechanistic explanations in held-out predictive validity — treat circuits and attribution graphs as scientific theories to be tested and ranked by how well they predict model behavior on novel input distributions, novel interventions, and model errors, with the metric calibrated against models whose true mechanisms are known.
project: Circuits as Theories: A Predictive-Validity Standard for Mechanistic Explanations
question: Can a generalization profile — agreement between an explanation's behavior and the model's behavior across a ladder of held-out distributions, intervention types, and model errors — serve as a quantitative, mechanism-sensitive faithfulness metric that (a) separates faithful explanations from merely behavior-matching ones where ground truth is known, and (b) resolves the dual basis problem by ranking competing decompositions (SAE seeds/sparsity, PLT vs CLT, head-level vs feature-level) in ways on-distribution faithfulness cannot?
first_experiment: The "shattering test" on grokking modular arithmetic. Train small transformers on modular addition (true algorithm known: trigonometric operations over structured embeddings); extract per-layer transcoders and SAEs across multiple seeds and sparsity levels; build attribution graphs with Circuit Tracer; then compute each extracted circuit explanation's agreement with the full model across a held-out ladder (operands beyond the trained range, unseen operand combinations, transfer to a related operation) plus on errors. Test: does held-out predictive validity demote the "lookup table" explanations that shatter the true trig mechanism — and demote deliberately planted shallow rewrites (the ICML 2026 failure mode) — while on-distribution replacement score rates them all equally? Include InterpBench semi-synthetic models for calibration and real-LM tasks (IOI, greater-than, Gemma-2-2B two-hop reasoning with public SAEs/CLTs) as the extension. All runnable with public tooling on a few GPUs.
why: It attacks the field's #1 self-identified bottleneck — Sharkey et al. flag faithfulness; the 2026 retrospective says verification infrastructure is the thing that fell behind and names the dual basis problem as the top open methodological question; Anthropic/GDM/Goodfire/EleutherAI's own future-work list explicitly requests automated validation with synthetic/OOD inputs and "objectively verifiable downstream tasks for understanding."
