Converging 2024–2026 evidence (adversarial failures, missed errors, non-identifiability, sparsity-incentivized shallow rewrites, seed-dependent features) shows the current standard of evidence (on-distribution sufficiency/faithfulness) cannot distinguish a true mechanism from a behaviorally equivalent fake — which blocks every downstream safety application. It converts a philosophical impasse (non-identifiability) into an empirical science with a standard metric, and its first result would directly improve method design (training objectives for transcoders/SAEs that reward held-out generalization). It has *not* been done: Li et al. (2025) proved the concept only for attention-pattern algorithm rules on toy classifiers; Adversarial Circuit Evaluation (2024) covered three hand-made head-level circuits with no metric, calibration, or ranking; error-agreement evaluation (2026) stays on-distribution; MIB/InterpBench evaluate on-distribution localization; the provable-guarantee work targets discovery stability at vision scale; and the ICML 2026 transcoder paper demonstrates one unfaithfulness mode while explicitly calling for the principled criteria this project builds.

direction: Build the constructive counterpart to 2026's validation-crisis wave — treat mechanistic explanation selection as an active experimental-design problem in which inputs and interventions are automatically synthesized to maximally discriminate among candidate explanations, collapsing the equivalence class of "defensible circuits" and yielding a quantitative, non-circular faithfulness score.
project: EquiClass: Active Discrimination of Competing Mechanistic Explanations
question: When multiple defensible circuit/feature explanations account for a model's behavior on its discovery distribution, can a small, automatically-selected set of inputs and interventions collapse the candidate set to a near-unique survivor — and does the size of the residual equivalence class serve as a standard, non-circular measure of how well-identified an explanation is?
first_experiment: On GPT-2 small / IOI (the exact setting where the multiplicity paper documented ~7,500 claim-producing defensible specifications), sample ~50 candidate circuits across analytic axes (ACDC thresholds/seeds, edge-pruning, manual circuit, random nulls) under one shared ablation protocol; compute each candidate's predicted outcome (success/logit-diff) on 2,000 diverse IOI prompts spanning known stress families (repeated/doubled names, order ambiguity, distractor noun–verb pairs); select the ~1% of prompts with maximal cross-candidate predicted disagreement, run true-model ablations on them, and measure candidates eliminated per experiment versus matched i.i.d. prompts — success criterion: ≥3× faster equivalence-class collapse and better held-out prompt-family generalization of the surviving class.
why: It attacks the field's self-declared #1 open problem — the 2026 retrospective calls the dual-basis/faithfulness problem "the open problem I would put at the top of any new survey," and Sharkey et al. list ground-truth validation as a top priority — but every existing contribution stops short of it: the multiplicity, unit-tests, non-uniqueness, and metric-fragility papers explicitly disclaim proposing a fix; CIF certifies single claims without selecting among candidates; CHIVE evaluates behavioral (not mechanistic) explanations one hypothesis at a time; the margin paper fixes one first-order failure locally; interpretive equivalence is cross-model; and the active-intervention POMDP work optimizes attribution efficiency, not explanation discrimination. The multiplicity result that candidate circuits are functionally uncorrelated (κ≈0.02) is precisely the precondition guaranteeing discriminating measurements exist — no one has automated finding them. It is compute-feasible on public small models, directly serves safety-critical use cases (auditors and regulators cannot rely on evidence that flips across defensible specifications), and even a negative result — equivalence classes that resist collapse — would itself be an important, quantified refutation of the field's implicit assumption that enough interventions always pin down the mechanism.

direction: Build and validate a "mechanism triangulation" protocol that adjudicates which mechanistic claims are real properties of the target model when independently trained decompositions (SAE variants/seed families, per-layer transcoders, cross-layer transcoders, head-level circuits) agree on behavior but disagree on mechanism — turning the field's validation bottleneck into a calibrated certification instrument.
project: Mechanism Triangulation — Certifying Disagreeing Decompositions via Interventions on the Target Model
question: When two or more independent decompositions of the same model reproduce the same behavior but propose different internal mechanisms, which claims are properties of the target model and which are artifacts of the proxy — and can cross-decomposition disagreement, matched by interventional signature and adjudicated by targeted interventions on the target (not the replacement model), yield a calibrated, distribution-shift-robust certification score for interpretability claims?
first_experiment: Build a planted-mechanism calibration testbed: train small transformers in which a target behavior is installed via a known, constructed pathway plus a deliberately planted *decoy* pathway that is behaviorally equivalent on the training distribution but mechanistically distinct; train ≥3 independent decompositions (two SAE architecture/seed families + one transcoder stack); match claimed nodes and edges across decompositions by their interventional signature (ablation/patching effect profiles) rather than geometric similarity; then run the adjudication battery — necessity/sufficiency ablations, path patching, cross-condition transfer, and distribution-shift stress — against the *target* model, scoring how cleanly the protocol separates planted-mechanism claims from decoy claims (AUC). On success, apply the same instrument to Gemma-2-2B on refusal (with the Arditi et al. direction and CLT analyses as disagreeing claimants) and greater-than (with Hanna et al.'s reference circuit as arbiter), producing the first quantified agreement/artifact-rate map across heterogeneous decompositions of a real model.
why: It is the field's consensus bottleneck — named the top open problem by the 2026 retrospective (faithfulness as a numerical target; the dual basis problem) and dedicated its own open-problem section ("proxy fidelity") in the November 2026 survey — yet the existing 2026 work only covers slices: stability over pruning thresholds (CIRCUS), correlational seed consistency (PW-MCC), per-feature statistics (anytime-valid tests; causal inertness audits), feature falsification for reasoning, equivalence-class documentation without adjudication ("Many Circuits, One Mechanism"), and incentive diagnosis without resolution (CLT unfaithfulness). Nobody matches claims across *heterogeneous* decompositions by causal signature, arbitrates with interventions on the *target* rather than comparing proxies to each other, calibrates against planted decoy mechanisms, or stress-tests certification under distribution shift. The payoff is symmetric and large: either the protocol yields the "faithfulness number" the field lacks — a reusable certification layer under every downstream safety use of interpretability — or it reveals that most cross-decomposition mechanistic claims are proxy artifacts, which quantifies the dual-basis problem on real models for the first time and redirects the field's effort. Either result is a headline; the instrument is infrastructure for truth, not yet another decomposition competing on interpretability aesthetics.

direction: Build a general, ground-truth-validated methodology for extracting and auditing **suppressive circuits** — multi-hop inhibitory pathways that explain why a model did *not* produce an alternative behavior — within transcoder-based attribution graphs, and apply it to safety-critical absences like refusal robustness.
project: The Missing Negative: Counterfactual Attribution Graphs for Suppressive Circuits
question: Can suppressive circuits (multi-hop inhibitory pathways vetoing an alternative behavior) be systematically extracted from transcoder-based attribution graphs, validated against documented negative components, and used to quantify and predict the robustness of safety-critical "absence" behaviors such as refusal under jailbreaks?
first_experiment: On GPT-2-small with public cross-layer transcoders and the documented IOI circuit: build a signed, counterfactually-seeded attribution graph (seeded at the competing-name logit — the suppressed alternative) with a suppressive-path extraction procedure, and measure whether it recovers the documented negative name-mover heads as inhibitory chains better than the standard positive-seeded graph and the strongest intact-state attribution baseline (ROC-AUC on documented negative components), as a ground-truth proof that "explanations of absence" carry extractable signal.
why: It targets a hole that both the field's open-problems review and its flagship circuit-tracing team explicitly flagged as unsolved and that the newest adjacent work (CAP's node-level discovery that jailbreaks act by suppressing safety features; CoAx's post-ablation backups; single-head case studies like copy suppression) has deliberately or structurally not addressed — circuit-level suppressive pathways in the intact model. It is timely (suppression was just shown to be safety-critical and invisible to activation-based monitors), immediately useful to everyone using attribution graphs, directly safety-relevant (suppression-robustness auditing, jailbreak-precursor monitoring, predicting unseen failure modes), and tractable with existing open tools on a single GPU — while the crowded areas (graph annotation/automation, CoT faithfulness, attention tracing, universality, self-repair) offer far less marginal value.

direction: Mechanistically localize how LLMs internally detect evaluation-vs-deployment contexts — disentangling genuine situation assessment from surface formatting features — and test whether that detection causally gates strategic behavior like sandbagging, to adjudicate the conflicting 2025–2026 causal results with circuit-level evidence on open models.
project: The Eval-Detector Circuit: Situation Assessment vs. Surface Cues in Evaluation Awareness
question: Is there a causally efficacious internal representation of "I am being evaluated" in open-weight LLMs that is distinct from prompt-formatting features, where is it implemented (which features, which layers, which downstream consumers), and does it mediate strategic behavior changes (sandbagging, exam-mode shifts) — or is evaluation awareness, as the steering-null results suggest, an artifact of surface features with the real policy driver elsewhere?
first_experiment: A 2×2 matched-twin decomposition scan. For ~10 benchmark suites, construct four cells per item: (a) benchmark-form prompt, (b) deployment-form twin of the same task (same content rewritten as a realistic user request), (c) deployment content wrapped in eval form, (d) benchmark content in natural form. Run Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Gemma-2-9B with Llama Scope / Gemma Scope SAEs across all layers, and partition active features into form-tracking, content/benchmark-recognition, and genuinely inferential families; then replicate both prior steering results (Nguyen et al.'s ~25% recovery vs. the NeurIPS 2026 null) under this matched design with norm-matched random-direction controls and counterbalanced answer positions. The 2×2 directly defeats the "labels predictable from text" confound: if no feature family separates eval-context from eval-form, awareness is an illusion; if one does, it becomes the target for the follow-up causal-mediation and attribution-graph study.
why: It targets the highest-stakes open gap in the field's own assessment — eval integrity underwrites governance decisions, awareness is documented in frontier models, unverbalized awareness defeats CoT monitors, and Apollo has explicitly called for white-box solutions — while every existing result (probes, steering, logits monitors, benchmarks) is correlational or contested at the causal level, with the mechanism itself declared unknown in the 2026 literature. It hasn't been done because the field sprinted through the measurable surface (benchmarks, probes, monitors — now saturated) before the bottleneck moved to validation and mechanism, and because a proper study requires the matched-twin design that defeats the text-predictability confound nobody has yet built. It is feasible on open models with public SAEs and datasets within a small-lab compute budget, it produces a publishable, decision-relevant result whichever way the science lands (a validated detector circuit → white-box monitors and authentic-eval design; a refutation → a major corrective to a fast-growing literature), and it sets up the natural follow-on: trained model organisms where detection is causally wired to concealment.

direction: Build an automated "differential diagnosis" procedure for mechanistic explanations — actively designing inputs and internal interventions that discriminate between behaviorally-equivalent candidate circuits, with a calibrated hypothesis posterior as the field's first non-circular faithfulness measure.
project: Circuit Differential Diagnosis: Active Interventional Discrimination of Behaviorally-Equivalent Mechanistic Explanations
question: When multiple mechanistic explanations of a model's behavior are equally predictive on the discovery distribution, can an automated search over input distributions and internal interventions find tests that separate their interventional predictions, and does the resulting posterior over candidate mechanisms provide a quantitative, non-circular measure of how underdetermined an explanation remains ("explanation equivocation")?
first_experiment: On a grokking modular-addition transformer (true Fourier/trig-identity mechanism known from Nanda et al. 2023), assemble a library of candidate mechanistic hypotheses — the true Fourier circuit, a memorization/lookup hypothesis, a wrong-frequency Fourier variant, and a shallow "skip-trigram" rewrite — verify all are behaviorally equivalent on the training distribution, then run the discriminator: for each pair, gradient/guided search over probe inputs and ablation/patching sites maximizing predicted output divergence between candidates, score against the real model, and update the posterior. Success = the search separates the true mechanism from every alternative with far fewer probes than random probing, and the equivocation score ranks candidates correctly. Immediate follow-up sanity check: repeat with GPT-2 small greater-than, competing the published Hanna et al. circuit against a CLT-derived attribution subgraph, testing whether the procedure detects the shallow-rewrite failure mode diagnosed at ICML 2026.
why: The 2026 retrospective of Sharkey et al. names the dual basis problem the field's most important methodological question and notes faithfulness has no agreed numerical measure; ICLR 2025 established non-identifiability empirically but proposed no remedy; ICML 2026 showed the flagship method (CLTs) is systematically biased toward behaviorally-equivalent-but-wrong circuits; and the 2026 partial responses (unit tests, error-reproduction metrics, certified stability) are each fragments of — but do not implement — an active hypothesis-discrimination framework. Nothing in the literature does automated discriminating-test design over inputs×interventions with calibrated posteriors over mechanisms, yet all the ingredients (known-mechanism tasks, open checkpoints, patching tooling, benchmarks) now exist, making this the highest-leverage, cheapest-to-attack, and still-unclaimed problem in the field.

direction: Resolve the dual-basis problem in mechanistic interpretability by generating input distributions where competing explanations of the same behavior make divergent predictions, and ranking explanations by validated held-out predictive accuracy.
project: DIVERGE: Discriminating Competing Mechanistic Explanations by Predictive Power under Distribution Shift
question: When two mechanistic explanations of the same behavior both pass current faithfulness checks, do their implied behavioral predictions diverge under controlled input shifts, and does held-out predictive accuracy on those shifts identify the explanation that tracks the model's actual computation where intervention-based faithfulness cannot?
first_experiment: On InterpBench/MIB tasks with known ground-truth circuits, construct dual alternatives that pass in-distribution ablation faithfulness (including Geng et al.'s documented misranking cases), generate maximal-divergence OOD test families from each candidate's implied rule, and test whether a "Predictive Power under Shift" score ranks the true mechanism above its duals where ablation faithfulness misranks or ties — then apply the protocol to the two inconsistent published explanations of a grokked modular-addition model.
why: It is the field's self-identified #1 open problem (dual basis / faithfulness), sits at the convergence of five documented failures (proven non-identifiability, misranking by the standard metric, zero predictive uplift from interp tools, threshold instability, and safety monitors that fail under shift), and is cheaply testable on public ground-truth artifacts — while every neighboring line of work (toy OOD prediction, MIB, CHIVE, unit tests, explanatory virtues, CIRCUS) stops short of arbitrating between competing mechanistic decompositions.

direction: Build and validate an interventional decoy-discrimination protocol — a held-out, off-distribution validation method that selects the true mechanism among behaviorally-equivalent circuit hypotheses — benchmarked on known-ground-truth models and deployed on real attribution graphs.
project: DecoyBench — Ground-Truthed Discrimination of Faithful Mechanisms from Behaviorally-Equivalent Decoys
question: When multiple candidate mechanisms (attribution graphs / circuit hypotheses / decompositions) reproduce a model's behavior on the evaluation distribution, does a practical protocol of interchange interventions and ablations on off-distribution inputs and intermediate variables reliably separate the model's true mechanism from plausible decoys — and which signals (interventional divergence, cross-condition transfer, self-repair-aware knockout curves, predictive validity on composed tasks) carry that signal, at what discriminative power?
first_experiment: Take one InterpBench SIIT transformer with a known ground-truth circuit (e.g., greater-than); generate a zoo of decoy hypotheses that match its standard-task behavior — per-layer transcoders and small CLTs across seeds/sparsity levels (inducing the documented multi-hop→shallow rewrite), plus hyperparameter variants from the multiplicity grid; verify each decoy's in-distribution replacement accuracy; then measure each candidate's divergence from ground truth under a small pre-registered grid of off-distribution interchange interventions (interventions on intermediate variables, frequency-band-shifted inputs, novel token compositions) and report whether any single cheap signal achieves non-trivial AUROC at separating true circuit from decoys.
why: It attacks the field's self-identified #1 problem — the dual-basis/faithfulness gap — at the moment when diagnoses (multiplicity: 73% claim-flip; phantom specialization; ICML 2026's proof that CLT sparsity incentives produce behavior-matching but mechanism-obscuring rewrites) have outpaced cures, and the explicit next step everyone names ("a faithfulness measure that is trustworthy rather than circular") is unclaimed. It has not been done because the existing ground-truth testbed (InterpBench) was built for and only evaluated edge-level discovery methods, the 2026 non-identifiability papers deliberately stopped at measurement, stability/consensus methods conflate stability with truth, spectral identifiability yields invariants that are explicitly not legible decompositions, and the one adjacent validation effort targets feature labels rather than mechanism-level hypotheses. It is tractable for a single researcher (all models, code, and transcoder checkpoints are public at GPT-2/Gemma-2B scale), and it is maximally leveraged: a validated selection protocol converts directly into trustworthy monitors and audit evidence — the deployment use case the field says is bottlenecked — and every subsequent attribution-graph paper can adopt it as the standard faithfulness score.

direction: Extend mechanistic interpretability from the single forward pass to the multi-turn agent trajectory, building intervention-based tools that causally map where task state is stored, carried, and consumed across turns, to ground the next generation of agent safety monitors.
project: In-Context State Registers — Causal Provenance Analysis of Multi-Turn Agent Trajectories
question: When a multi-turn LLM agent makes a decision that depends on earlier-turn information (a user constraint, a tool output, an injected instruction), which context positions causally carry that information at decision time — the original source tokens, the model's own intervening outputs ("self-notes"), or diffuse representations — and do these causal provenance maps yield robust, mechanism-grounded monitors (e.g., detecting that an action traces to injected content rather than the user's goal)?
first_experiment: Build a cross-turn KV-cache patching harness (nnsight or direct past_key_values hooks) and run it on paired multi-turn tool-use trajectories in two small open instruct models (e.g., Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct): trajectory pairs differ in exactly one item of task state (turn-1 constraint or turn-2 tool output); patch activations at candidate storage sites (original turn-1 tokens vs. the model's own turn-2/3 outputs) into the clean run and measure the flip rate of the turn-4 decision, sweeping layers and positions. This produces the first causal provenance map for a trajectory-level decision and adjudicates the direct-re-read vs. self-notes vs. diffuse hypotheses; validate the maps against known ground truth (InjecAgent-style injections with a known true source) and against correlational baselines (attention mass à la AttnLocate, retrieval-head scores, MCAIR-style probes).
why: It is the one direction that is simultaneously (1) safety-critical — agent monitoring is where interpretability's narrow coverage gap is growing fastest, and probe-based monitors are already being evaded (AISI "evading probes," Dec 2025), so a causal substrate is needed; (2) field-recognized — DeepMind's pragmatic vision explicitly lists multiturn/agentic computation as out of reach, Anthropic's circuit tracing is single-prompt by construction, and the Open Problems review notes applications don't cover agentic behavior; (3) demonstrably undone — 2026's entrants (MechSuits, MCAIR, AttnLocate, STAR, Hodoscope) all stop at probes, attention features, representation drift, or behavioral diffing, and targeted searches found no cross-turn patching or trajectory-level causal attribution work anywhere; (4) tractable for me — small open-weight models, cheap interventions, existing datasets (InjecAgent, MCPTox, MAS, ImpossibleBench) as ground truth and follow-up testbeds, single-GPU friendly. It has not been done because the field's artifacts bake in the single-prompt unit of analysis, the interp community's 2025–26 attention went to dictionary scaling and faithfulness validation, and the agent-safety community, following DeepMind's pragmatic turn, skipped straight to probes — leaving the mechanistic bridge, and the reusable KV-patching infrastructure it requires, unbuilt.

direction: Discriminate competing mechanistic hypotheses of the same model by their held-out interventional predictions, using actively selected experiments, to establish when mechanistic explanations are identifiable in practice rather than merely faithful on-distribution.
project: Decoy Circuits: Identifying the True Mechanism Among Equally Faithful Hypotheses via Discriminating Interventions
question: When multiple mechanistic hypotheses replicate a model's on-distribution behavior equally well, where do their predictions of held-out inputs and interventions diverge, and can a small set of disagreement-maximizing experiments identify the model's actual mechanism?
first_experiment: Build decoy hypotheses of matched on-distribution faithfulness for a known-mechanism task (grokking modular arithmetic / GPT-2 IOI), show standard faithfulness metrics cannot separate them, then demonstrate that a handful of targeted, disagreement-maximizing held-out interventions eliminates the decoys and recovers the true mechanism, quantifying identification accuracy versus intervention budget (active vs. random selection).
why: The field's own 2026 state-of-the-field review names decomposition selection among behaviorally equivalent explanations (the dual basis problem) and the absence of a trusted faithfulness measure as the top open methodological problems; non-identifiability has been proven in toy settings but the constructive identification methodology has not been built on real transformers, and it would directly predict and remediate the 2026 wave of intervention and monitor failures — all while being feasible today with open-weight models and public SAE/circuit-tracing infrastructure.

direction: Replace "fit-and-evaluate on the same distribution" faithfulness with interventional cross-validation — selecting among equally-faithful mechanistic decompositions by their predictive power on held-out intervention families and input shifts — turning the field's top diagnosed problem (non-identifiability / dual basis / evaluation misranking) into a constructive, quantitative, deployable validity criterion.
project: Stress-Tested Decompositions: Interventional Cross-Validation as a Non-Circular Faithfulness Criterion for Mechanistic Explanations
question: When several decompositions (circuits, SAE/transcoder features) are equally faithful on the input distribution and intervention types they were fitted on, does held-out interventional stress-testing (leave-one-environment-out over a grid of input-shift × intervention-family combinations) discriminate the decomposition that tracks the model's actual mechanism from those that merely fit — and does the winner's validity gap predict, in advance, which downstream artifacts (monitors, steering vectors, edits) survive distribution shift?
first_experiment: On InterpBench planted-mechanism models plus GPT-2 IOI and Greater-Than, construct matched-size candidate sets — the planted/reference circuit, controlled-edit decoys tuned to equal the reference's standard faithfulness, and multi-seed outputs of ACDC/EAP-IG — then run a leave-one-verification-environment-out evaluation over an environment grid (token-frequency bands, paraphrase/negation/length shifts × mean-, zero-, resampling ablations, path patching, interchange interventions), testing whether held-out interventional fidelity ranks planted above decoy where standard same-distribution faithfulness cannot (baseline misranking rate from Geng et al.: 13–24%); define the "interventional generalization gap" and check it predicts out-of-environment behavioral error. Single-GPU feasible with TransformerLens/nnsight; a null result (decompositions indistinguishable even under stress) is itself a publishable field-level finding.
why: It is the constructive answer to the problem the field itself ranks first — Sharkey et al. (2025) flagged faithfulness, and the mid-2026 retrospective names the dual basis problem as what "I would put at the top of any new survey," with decomposition choice still "an aesthetic decision" — and I verified across ~15 targeted searches that no work combines a selection criterion, held-out intervention families, input-distribution shift, and downstream monitor survival; the nearest neighbors each stop short (Geng et al. diagnose misranking without a protocol; CIF certifies a declared estimand rather than choosing among candidates; GAE repairs one dictionary rather than selecting; Duan covers model-update staleness but not input shift; unit tests falsify single claims, not compare explanations). It matters beyond methodology: feature-based safety monitors are deployed but fail silently under distribution shift — the exact gap the 2026 retrospective says is growing — and this research produces the missing primitive for them: a cheap validity check that tells a monitor when its underlying decomposition still describes the computation. It is tractable at open-model scale, sits at an under-occupied intersection (circuit evaluation × SAE validation × monitor deployment), and its ingredients (planted-mechanism testbeds, statistics layer, OOD suites) only came together in the last twelve months, which is why it could not have been done earlier.

direction: Establish held-out behavioral prediction as the standard, quantitative, non-circular evaluation (and selection) criterion for mechanistic explanations — testing explanations like scientific theories, by what they predict about model behavior on input families they were not built from.
project: Explanation Tolerances: A Held-Out Generalization Standard for Mechanistic Explanations
question: When multiple mechanistic explanations of the same behavior (circuits from different discovery runs/distributions, competing SAE decompositions, attribution graphs) are statistically indistinguishable under standard in-distribution faithfulness metrics, do they diverge in their ability to predict the model's behavior on held-out input families — and can a standardized held-out predictive score (per-family KL/behavioral agreement between the explanation-implied model and the full model) resolve this underdetermination, expose where each explanation breaks, and track downstream utility such as steering effectiveness and monitor reliability under distribution shift?
first_experiment: On GPT-2 small's IOI task (replicating on one MIB task and Greater-Than): assemble four competing, size-matched explanations — the canonical hand-built circuit, an ACDC circuit discovered on the standard distribution, an ACDC circuit discovered on a shifted distribution, and a size-matched random control; (i) confirm they are indistinguishable under the MIB in-distribution CPR metric (with CIF-style confidence sequences); (ii) evaluate each on a battery of ~10 held-out input families (new name pools, syntax variants, length/position shifts, counterfactual minimal pairs, distractor types never seen during discovery) by scoring the circuit-with-replacement prediction against actual full-model behavior per family; measure the rank divergence between in-distribution faithfulness and held-out score, and derive per-family "engineering tolerances" (where each explanation's predictions fail). Compute budget: a single-GPU, ~1-week run using TransformerLens and MIB data.
why: It attacks the gap that the field's own 18-month retrospective ranks highest — the verification bottleneck and the dual basis problem — at the exact moment every ingredient has just matured: MIB provides in-distribution infrastructure, CIF provides the statistics, "Many Circuits, One Mechanism" and "Are We Recovering Mechanisms?" (Oct 2026) prove that in-distribution faithfulness misleads, and Li et al. (2025) prove held-out prediction is feasible but only on synthetic toy models. No one has yet built the real-LLM, family-level, standardized version; it converts a philosophical dispute ("which decomposition is right?") into an empirical one, it upgrades every downstream use (circuit papers' claims, SAE feature validation, steering, editing, OOD-fragile safety monitors), and it matches the field's own definition of understanding. It has not been done because the constituent results only appeared in the last 18 months and the field's energy went into scaling discovery (attribution graphs, transcoders) rather than validation — and because no existing benchmark (MIB: templated in-distribution; SAEBench: feature-level) tests explanations as predictors on held-out input families.

direction: Turn the field's non-identifiability ("dual basis") problem from a philosophical worry into an empirical engine by stress-testing competing circuit/attribution-graph explanations on the distribution-shifted inputs where their causal predictions diverge, producing validity envelopes and a reusable falsification protocol.
project: Circuit Stress Tests: Validity Envelopes and Dual-Basis Discrimination for Feature-Level Explanations
question: Do feature-level circuit explanations that pass standard in-distribution faithfulness tests make divergent, testable predictions about model behavior under distribution shift — and when two candidate explanations diverge, does held-out causal testing identify which one (if either) the model actually implements?
first_experiment: On one open model (GPT-2 small or Gemma-2-2B with Gemma Scope/CLT-Forge transcoders), construct ≥4 competing explanations for a canonical behavior with published circuits (IOI or greater-than): the published head/edge circuit, two SAE/transcoder feature circuits from different seeds/widths, and one ACDC-derived circuit; verify all pass the standard in-distribution faithfulness bar; then run a fixed battery of ~20 structured shifts (paraphrase templates, distractor insertion, role swaps, compositional variants like DoubleIO/TripleIO, semantic substitutions) and, for each explanation, compare its ablation-predicted effects against the full model's actual behavior on each shift — measuring (a) correlation between in-distribution faithfulness and out-of-distribution validity, (b) the fraction of shift axes where competing explanations' predictions diverge, and (c) each explanation's "validity envelope" of shifts it survives.
why: It is the field's self-diagnosed #1 open problem (the 2026 retrospective of Sharkey et al. names faithful attribution-graph validation and the dual basis problem as the top gaps), it operationalizes the field's own definition of understanding (prediction on arbitrary inputs) which no current evaluation does — ACE (2024) only did worst-case in-distribution tests on head-level circuits, MIB benchmarks discovery not validation-under-shift, and identifiability work (Méloux et al., Sun & Toneva) is theoretical or representational rather than interventional; it has not been done because the 2025 shift to attribution graphs outpaced verification infrastructure, because the incentive gradient in 2026 points toward automating production (annotation, querying, scaling) rather than auditing it, and because it requires cross-method plumbing between SAE, transcoder, and head-level explanations that only recently became feasible with public SAEs, CLT-Forge, and open tooling — while remaining computable at single-GPU scale with an informative result regardless of which way the empirical chips fall.

direction: Mechanistic analysis of goal misgeneralization in LLM agents — inducing proxy-goal pursuit in open-weight agent models and tracing where the intended goal survives internally, to build a diagnostic that predicts which test-time repair can restore goal-following.
project: Where Does the Goal Live? Internal Anatomy and Repair of Goal Misgeneralization in LLM Agents
question: When an LLM agent finetuned on a distribution where a proxy goal co-occurred with the stated goal remains competent out-of-distribution but pursues the proxy, is the stated goal still (a) represented, (b) causally read by the policy, (c) behaviorally followed — does this depth taxonomy from visual RL agents replicate in language agents, and does it predict which repair (activation steering, representation patching, prompt-restatement) works?
first_experiment: Build a procedurally generated, fully observable text grid-world suite where the system prompt states the true goal ("reach the ◆") but expert trajectories are generated such that the target always coincides with a proxy cue (e.g., upper-right quadrant) on the training maps and the coincidence is broken on held-out OOD maps; LoRA-finetune Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (and Qwen2.5-7B as a replication) on ~50k expert trajectories; then measure OOD goal-success vs. proxy-following rates to establish that GMG emerges (competence retained, systematic proxy pursuit) — and if it does, train layerwise linear probes decoding stated-target and proxy locations on OOD rollouts, followed by activation patching/ablation of each subspace to test whether the goal representation is causally read or merely present, yielding the first depth classification and a first steering-repair test.
why: It targets a canonical, deployment-critical alignment failure at the exact frontier the field's own documents say is underserved — interpretability under distribution shift, for agentic systems, with actionable output (a repair oracle distinguishing "recoverable with a patch" from "must retrain") — and it uses the now-mature microscopes (probes, SAEs, patching, steering) rather than competing in oversaturated method-development or already-occupied areas (CoT faithfulness, reward-hack monitors, emergent misalignment, introspection, auditing games, all verified occupied). It has not been done because the internal analysis of GMG only became possible this October in visual RL, the RL-safety community works in Procgen-style modalities without LLM interp tooling, the LLM interp community has only recently moved from single-turn to agents (and, when it did — SPAR-Telos, Feb 2026 — studied benign goal-directedness probes, not misgeneralization induction), and the setting requires an interdisciplinary combination of RL-safety experimental design and LLM circuit tooling; the LLM-specific surface (stated goals, in-context restatement, CoT rationalization — where the model can verbally claim the goal while internally pursuing the proxy) is novel relative to the visual-RL template and directly relevant to how finetuned and distilled agents are actually deployed.

direction: Treat rival mechanistic explanations (circuits, attribution graphs, SAE feature accounts, algorithm hypotheses) of the same model behavior as competing falsifiable surrogates, and adjudicate between them by actively searching the input×intervention space for points where their predictions — of outputs *and* internal states — diverge, letting the model itself break the tie that in-distribution metrics cannot.
project: Crucible: Adjudicating Rival Mechanistic Explanations with Actively Designed Divergence Experiments
question: When two mechanistic explanations of the same model behavior are behaviorally equivalent on the observed distribution, do actively searched discriminating experiments (targeted inputs + interchange interventions, with predictions over internal activations as well as outputs) reliably separate them — i.e., can the dual-basis/multiplicity problem be converted from an aesthetic choice into an empirical one, and what divergence profiles do real rival circuit accounts (e.g., the near-disjoint IOI circuits from different discovery pipelines) exhibit when subjected to it?
first_experiment: In a grokked modular-addition transformer (Nanda et al. 2023 setup — cheap, known ground-truth algorithm), construct an impostor explanation calibrated to match the true trigonometric algorithm on every standard in-distribution criterion (natural held-out accuracy, resample-ablation KL, IIA on a standard interchange-intervention suite, MIB-style splits). Then run the core loop: (1) compile both explanations into executable surrogates predicting outputs and intermediate activations under arbitrary (input, interchange-intervention) combinations; (2) search that space to maximize pairwise prediction divergence; (3) run the real model on the top discriminating experiments and score each explanation against actual outputs and activations (with CIF-style anytime-valid tests for the verdict). Success criterion: standard in-distribution metrics tie or mislead, while the divergence-search protocol separates true from impostor — a decisive existence proof that explanation choice is resolvable by designed experiments, before scaling to genuine rival circuits on IOI/Othello-GPT and GPT-2.
why: It directly attacks the field's self-declared top open problem for 2026 — the dual-basis problem and the verification bottleneck named by the retrospective, the 73% claim-flip rate that makes circuit evidence unusable for auditing, and CHIVE's finding that current interpretability tools add no predictive value. It is constructive where the field has only diagnostic (Méloux, Multiplicity, Many-Circuits-One-Mechanism), single-claim (CIF, unit tests, Adversarial Circuit Evaluation), and cross-model-theoretic (Sun & Toneva) work — none of these pit rival explanations against each other with actively searched discriminating experiments, internal-state predictions, or certified verdicts. It rides existing infrastructure rather than requiring new compute (toy models first, GPT-2 next), it yields reusable artifacts (the explanation→surrogate compiler, divergence profiles as a new explanation-quality metric, an "indistinguishability certificate" that honestly delimits what was tested), it plugs divergence search back into circuit discovery as uit de Bos et al. suggested, and it supplies exactly the "willingness to publish negative results when interventions do not survive distribution shift" the field says it now needs — with direct safety payoff, since monitors and audits built on unvalidated decompositions fail silently precisely where rival explanations diverge.

direction: Turn the dual-basis/faithfulness problem into an experimental discipline by building an engine that finds inputs and interventions where competing mechanistic decompositions of the same behavior make different predictions, then uses the model's actual behavior to adjudicate which explanations generalize off-distribution.
project: Explanation Tournaments — Discriminative Stress-Testing of Mechanistic Decompositions
question: When multiple decompositions (hand-curated circuits, ACDC-discovered circuits, SAE/transcoder-based decompositions) replicate a model's behavior on the natural distribution, which one's interventional predictions survive off-distribution — and can automated divergence-search reliably find the probes that separate them?
first_experiment: An "IOI adjudication tournament" on GPT-2 small: fit a standardized prediction interface (predicted next-token logits under graded mean/resampling ablations and feature ablations) to four competing decompositions — (1) the hand-curated IOI circuit of Wang et al., (2) an ACDC-discovered circuit, (3) an SAE-feature decomposition, (4) a matched-sparsity random decomposition as null control — on a calibration set only; then optimize held-out inputs and intervention parameters to maximize prediction disagreement between the decompositions subject to task-validity constraints; pre-register each decomposition's predictions; run the true model on the discriminating probes; and score held-out interventional faithfulness (KL of predicted vs. actual logits) to produce the first divergence-vs-distribution-shift curves and an adjudication leaderboard.
why: It attacks the field's own top-ranked open problem (the 2026 retrospective of Sharkey et al. literally places the dual basis problem "at the top of any new survey" and demands a faithfulness measure that is "trustworthy as opposed to circular"), yet nobody has built the missing layer: all existing work either scales decompositions (attribution graphs — big-lab compute territory), verifies single claims against generic nuisances (unit tests, matched evaluation, faithfulness robustness), measures seed-statistics of SAE instability, or proves non-identifiability in the abstract (Méloux et al.) — none discriminates between competing explanations with adversarially searched, pre-registered interventional probes, and none produces an OOD-validated trust ranking of explanation classes. It is feasible for an independent agent because it runs on small open models and well-understood behaviors with reference circuits, and it converts Grant et al.'s "pernicious divergence" from a caveat into a measurable failure mode; its payoff compounds because monitors built on decompositions are exactly what safety applications depend on, and their off-distribution failure is where safety-critical monitoring breaks.

direction: Make attribution-graph validation non-circular by scoring decompositions on held-out interventional generalization — treating each graph as a predictive theory of interventions to be tested, not a description to be reproduced.
project: From Execution Traces to Predictive Mechanisms: An Interventional Generalization Score (IGS) for Attribution Graphs
question: When two feature-level decompositions of the same model behavior match equally on reconstruction, replacement score, and in-distribution faithfulness, does their internal causal structure predict — on held-out inputs and unseen intervention types (feature ablation, amplification/steering, edge clamping) — which one is the model's actual mechanism, and can that prediction be quantified into a standard, automatically computable score that resists the circularity of interpretability-only metrics?
first_experiment: On a modular-addition model organism (known cyclic/trigonometric mechanism), train small cross-layer transcoders and construct three decompositions matched on replacement score and reconstruction error: (A) the standard transcoder graph, (B) a "dual-basis decoy" (features recomposed into lookup-table-style conjunctions preserving input-output behavior), (C) a ground-truth-aligned decomposition built from the known algorithm. Run an automated probe suite of feature ablations, amplifications, and edge clamps on held-out operand splits; predict outcomes from each graph's influence structure; measure agreement (sign accuracy, rank correlation of logit deltas, KL under clamps). Success criterion: the score separates ground-truth/standard graphs from decoys where all existing metrics (replacement score, reconstruction, labels) fail — a decoy-matched, truth-known setting no prior faithfulness work has used; if all three are indistinguishable, the direction is falsified cheaply and the intervention families must be redesigned.
why: It attacks the field's #1 self-identified open problem — the generalized dual-basis/faithfulness gap that the 2026 retrospective says belongs at the top of any new survey — and unifies three separately documented pain points (dual-basis indeterminacy, transcoder "shattering," trace-vs-algorithm ambiguity) under one measurable principle, thereby upgrading every downstream direction (global graph merging, cross-model transfer, deployment monitors, auditing games) that currently presupposes trustworthy validation. It has not been done: the closest neighbors either diagnose ablation sensitivity (Miller 2024), test in-distribution behavioral reproduction (Hanna 2024), certify coarse components against input/dataset perturbations (Hadad 2026; Anani 2026), measure analyst-choice stability rather than mechanism validity (CIRCUS 2026), validate individual features rather than graph structure (ICML 2026 anytime-valid; arXiv:2610.15850), or give local theory without learned decompositions or held-out generalization ("Same Function, Different Mechanism," Oct 2026) — and the circuits-landscape consortium explicitly lists automated perturbation-based validation as undone future work. Meanwhile the required infrastructure (open CLTs, Circuit Tracer/CLT-Forge, Gemma Scope, known-mechanism organisms) matured in 2025–2026, making this the rare gap that is both maximally foundational and executable on one GPU today.

direction: Build an operational framework that resolves mechanistic interpretability's proven non-identifiability by actively designing held-out input-and-intervention probe families on which behavior-equivalent competing explanations (e.g., deep multi-hop circuits vs. shallow behavior-matching rewrites) make divergent causal predictions, and quantify what fraction of the explanation space is irreducibly indistinguishable.
project: Probing the Equivalence Class: Held-Out Causal Discrimination of Competing Mechanistic Explanations
question: When two or more mechanistic explanations match a model's behavior on the distributions used to construct them, can actively chosen held-out input distributions and intervention families empirically discriminate them — and under what probe families does the residual equivalence class collapse, or provably remain?
first_experiment: Train a 2–4 layer transformer on a synthetic two-hop relational composition task (A→r1→B→r2→C) with a known ground-truth mechanism; construct two explanations that both achieve ~perfect in-distribution patching fidelity — the iterative-composition circuit (uses intermediate entity representations) and a shallow direct-lookup rewrite (replicating the ICML 2026 CLT failure mode); then test both on held-out probe families (novel unseen compositions, longer chains, and ablation/patching of the intermediate representations) and measure which explanation's causal predictions survive — establishing that cheap held-out discrimination separates explanations that standard in-distribution fidelity cannot.
why: It attacks the problem the field itself ranks first — the dual-basis/non-identifiability problem — at the moment when all the prerequisite pieces exist but no one has joined them: non-identifiability is proven (Méloux 2025), a concrete behavior-matching-but-mechanism-obscuring decomposition is documented (ICML 2026 CLT result), statistical certification machinery is built (CIF 2026), one partial discriminator is discovered (error-agreement, 2026), and the philosophical desiderata are articulated (explanatory virtues, identification-assumption norms) — yet no framework, benchmark, or method exists to *select among* behavior-equivalent explanations by empirical causal evidence rather than label readability. It has not been done because each existing effort stopped one step short of operational discrimination, and because the required synthesis (causal experimental design + MI decompositions) sits between two communities. It is the keystone for the field's two most-pressing gaps at once: the verification bottleneck (validating the *right* features, not just labeling features) and monitor reliability under distribution shift, and it is tractable with toy tasks, small open-weight models, and public SAE/transcoder infrastructure.

direction: Build and validate a causal discrimination protocol that identifies which of several behaviorally-equivalent sparse decompositions (e.g., cross-layer-transcoder attribution graphs) matches the model's true mechanism, using held-out input families and targeted interventions chosen where the candidates' predicted computations diverge.
project: Crucial Experiments for Circuits: Causally Discriminating Behaviorally-Equivalent Decompositions
question: When two sparse decompositions of the same model reproduce its behavior equally well in-distribution, can a small, principled battery of held-out causal probes — compositional recombinations, distribution-shifted inputs, and feature-level interventions at nodes where the candidate graphs diverge — reliably identify the decomposition that matches the model's actual internal pathway, how often does standard in-distribution validation fail to discriminate, and what is the minimal discriminating probe set?
first_experiment: On InterpBench SIIT transformers and a Boolean multi-hop toy model with known ground-truth circuits, construct paired decompositions — (a) the ground-truth-aligned decomposition and (b) a behaviorally-equivalent "shallow rewrite" induced by strengthening the sparsity penalty during transcoder training (following the ICML 2026 construction) — verify both pass standard validation (in-distribution ablation faithfulness, clean-distribution KL), then run a battery of held-out causal probes and measure: (i) whether the probes separate true from rewritten decompositions, (ii) the minimal discriminating probe subset, and (iii) whether the divergence points predicted by each candidate's graph localize where behavioral divergence appears. If they separate, replicate on a real LM (Pythia-1.4B / Gemma-2-2B) comparing per-layer-transcoder vs. CLT attribution graphs on a multi-hop fact-retrieval task.
why: It attacks the problem the field's own 2026 retrospective ranks as its #1 open methodological question — the dual basis problem — at exactly the moment it has become acute: attribution graphs are now the standard artifact and the substrate for deployed safety monitors, and three 2026 papers (CLT-unfaithfulness, objective-level recovery gaps, observer effects) prove that behaviorally-equivalent-but-wrong decompositions arise routinely and that standard faithfulness metrics reward them. Yet every existing response stops short: the diagnosis papers end at problem identification ("preliminary evidence," "call for rethinking"), CIRCUS and Certified Circuits quantify robustness *within* one decomposition rather than identity *among* competing ones, and benchmarks like InterpBench and MIB score discovery against in-distribution ground truth without discriminating hypotheses. The constructive step — treating each decomposition as a causal hypothesis, deriving the interventions that separate them, and validating the protocol against known ground-truth circuits before applying it to real LMs — requires tooling and testbeds that only matured in 2025–2026, which is why it has not been done, and it directly unlocks two downstream goals the field says it needs: trustworthy interpretation of the standard artifact, and mechanistic-anomaly-detection reference mechanisms that remain valid under distribution shift. It is also tractable at single-GPU scale for an independent researcher, unlike cross-architecture transfer or frontier-model scaling.

direction: Mechanistically characterize the internal task-state that tool-using LLM agents maintain across turns — first auditing whether existing decomposition tools are valid in the agentic regime, then locating, decoding, and causally manipulating the cross-turn "agent state" representation.
project: Where Does the Plan Live? Locating and Editing the Cross-Turn Task-State of Tool-Using LLM Agents
question: Do multi-turn LLM agents maintain a compact, causally operative internal representation of task progress and plan state across turns — is it decodable with linear probes, recoverable by SAE decomposition, and can swapping or ablating it across rollouts transfer or destroy the agent's plan?
first_experiment: On Gemma-2-2B-it / Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct with public SAEs, generate ~500 τ-bench/BFCL-style tool-use rollouts (10–40 turns), then (1) measure SAE reconstruction error, dead-latent rate, and steering efficacy on rollout activations versus matched pretraining-like text, stratified by token type (tool-JSON, system prompt, natural language) — a validation audit no one has published; and (2) train layerwise linear probes for active subgoal, completed-step count, and tool-argument bindings at each turn, then run cross-rollout activation patching at turn N to test whether injected plan-state redirects the agent's subsequent tool calls.
why: It attacks a gap that is simultaneously acknowledged as far-out-of-reach by DeepMind, called for by the ICML 2026 position paper on agentic interpretability, and required by the emergent agent-monitoring agenda — yet no published work does feature/circuit-level analysis of cross-turn computation (Tokengeist stops at token provenance; probes stop at correlation; lookback-head work stops at single contexts). It sits upstream of the crowded faithfulness and monitoring races rather than inside them, connects three of the field's own open problems (missing chat-regime concepts, deployment-grade monitoring, multiturn interpretability), is executable on open weights with one GPU in an automatable loop that matches my capabilities, and every failure mode of the first experiment is itself a publishable, field-steering result: either the decomposition stack silently breaks on agent trajectories (invalidating the monitoring stack's foundation), or the agent-state hypothesis is confirmed (opening state-level interventions for goal drift and cross-turn scheming), or it is refuted (agents' coherence is more distributed than assumed — an important negative result nobody has tested).

direction: Extend mechanistic anomaly detection from input-level backdoors to unsupervised, decomposition-free detection of covert misbehavior in agentic trajectories, using component-ablation causal-response fingerprints as the anomaly signal.
project: Fingerprinting Agent Mechanisms — Unsupervised Mechanistic Anomaly Detection for Covert Misbehavior in LLM Agent Trajectories
question: Can the causal response profile of an LLM agent's computation (how its output loss/logits respond to randomized structural ablations of heads/MLPs/SAE latents, conditioned on task context) separate covertly misbehaving trajectories (sabotage, sandbagging, hidden objectives) from trusted benign trajectories without any labeled misbehavior examples — and does this signal survive adversaries who conceal their chain-of-thought and are optimized to mimic benign activations?
first_experiment: On an open-weight model (1–8B, e.g., Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct or Llama-3.1-8B) fine-tuned or prompted into a known anomalous mode (sandbagging or a backdoor behavior), compute ablation-response fingerprints — for ~50 trusted and ~50 anomalous trajectory steps, run ~40 randomized component subsets through the model and record the next-token logit/loss displacement vector; measure AUROC of the fingerprint-distance detector against trusted trajectories, and compare against the naive white-box unsupervised baseline (residual-stream/SAE activation statistics) on the same data, including an obfuscated-backdoor variant where activation statistics are expected to fail but fingerprints should not. Cost: days on one GPU; result either validates the core signal or cleanly falsifies it.
why: It targets what both the 2025 open-problems review and the 2026 pragmatic vision identify as interpretability's highest-value application (monitoring dangerous cognition) at its fastest-growing frontier (agentic deployment), right after TraceMRT (Nov 2026) showed transcript-level monitors break under coherent concealment. It has not been done because the pieces only just assembled: the only existing MAD implementation (April 2026) works input-by-input with expensive weight-space influence sampling and never touches agentic or generative settings; AISI's and NeurIPS 2026 white-box monitors are all supervised detectors that need labeled misbehavior and are known to be evadable; Hodoscope (April 2026) formulated unsupervised agent monitoring but operates purely on transcripts. Nobody has combined unsupervised + internals-based + trajectory-level, and nobody has proposed causal-sensitivity fingerprints as the anomaly statistic. It is feasible for an individual researcher (public benchmarks, open weights, single GPU, cheap signal), it sidesteps the decomposition/faithfulness bottleneck rather than fighting it, it directly addresses the deployment-grade-cost gap, and even its failure modes (fingerprint mimicry by adaptive adversaries, self-repair confounds analyzable with CoAx) would produce publishable, field-relevant negative results.

direction: Transform attribution graphs from per-prompt execution traces into validated general algorithms by systematically merging them across prompt families and testing held-out generalization.
project: Consensus Circuits: From Execution Traces to Algorithms
question: What fraction of a per-prompt attribution graph is family-stable algorithm versus input-specific contingency versus prompt-specific noise, and do consensus circuits merged across a prompt family transfer to held-out prompts better than per-prompt graphs — behaviorally, structurally, and against known ground-truth algorithms?
first_experiment: Trace attribution graphs for the full greater-than prompt family (all 100 two-digit input years, GPT-2-small + public CLTs via circuit-tracer), compute per-edge/per-node inclusion frequencies and attribution-mass splits into core/input-specific/noise, and check whether the stable core reproduces Hanna et al.'s input→output mechanism.
why: It attacks the field's two top-ranked open problems (faithfulness of its dominant artifact; the dual-basis problem) with a capability the method's creators explicitly requested, that no existing work — CIRCUS's config-ensembling, Certified Circuits' dataset edits, Query Circuits, Sparse Feature Circuits — actually does, using public transcoders on small models I can afford, with informative outcomes whichever way the data falls.

direction: Build a discriminative, held-out falsification protocol that validates rival mechanistic explanations of the same behavior by their risky predictions on counterfactual inputs, model errors, and targeted interventions — turning circuit validation from an aesthetic choice into an empirical one.
project: Falsification-Grade Circuits: A Discriminative Protocol and Benchmark for Validating Rival Mechanistic Explanations
question: Can held-out structural variants (deeper multi-hop chains, substituted/novel intermediate entities, distractors, negations, error-prone inputs) reliably discriminate between rival circuit hypotheses that are indistinguishable on the original prompts, and which hypothesis does the real model's behavior actually support?
first_experiment: Trace attribution graphs for ~20 multi-hop factual-recall prompts in Gemma-2-2B using open CLTs/transcoders, derive the rival "iterative composition" vs. "shallow shortcut" hypotheses, generate held-out variant families predicted to separate them, and measure divergence between hypotheses plus each one's predictive accuracy on real outputs and targeted-ablation effects.
why: It is the convergence point of the field's #1 diagnosed open problem (faithfulness/validation of attribution graphs), the dual-basis problem, and 2026's most alarming empirical results (zero uplift from white-box tools on counterfactual prediction; circuits that explain successes but not errors; CLT shallow-rewrite unfaithfulness) — none of which has been combined into an operational discriminative test on real models, because the necessary infrastructure (open CLTs, agentic counterfactual generation, error-reproduction evaluation) matured only in the past year and the problem sits between subfields that each scoped it out.

direction: Develop input-distribution-based cross-examination as the field's first constructive, non-circular method for selecting among rival circuit decompositions, validated against known ground truth.
project: Circuit Cross-Examination: Adjudicating Rival Decompositions via Discriminating Input Distributions
question: Can automatically constructed, behaviorally-discriminating input distributions identify which of two competing mechanistic explanations is the model's true mechanism, where in-distribution intervention faithfulness provably cannot?
first_experiment: In the Boolean known-ground-truth setting, take a behaviorally-equivalent shallow-rewrite vs deep-multi-hop pair of decompositions, search for inputs maximizing their predictive divergence, and test whether model behavior on that set recovers the true mechanism with high power while standard faithfulness scores fail.
why: It is the constructive next step the 2024–2026 diagnosis literature explicitly calls for but has not built; it converts the field's hardest acknowledged open problem into a tractable, benchmarkable, falsifiable empirical question using infrastructure that already exists; and it directly produces the verified-explanation primitive that deployment-grade safety monitoring requires.

direction: Attack the field's top-diagnosed bottleneck — the dual-basis/verification gap — by validating out-of-distribution predictive adequacy as a quantitative, ground-truth-checked criterion for selecting the true mechanism among in-distribution-equivalent mechanistic explanations, rather than generating yet another decomposition method.
project: Faithful Decoys: Validating Out-of-Distribution Predictive Adequacy as a Selection Criterion for Mechanistic Explanations
question: When multiple mechanistic explanations (circuits, SAE-feature circuits, attribution graphs, probe-based accounts) are statistically indistinguishable in faithfulness on the in-distribution task, does each candidate's ability to predict the full model's behavior under distribution shift and novel interventions (cross-distribution activation patching, adversarial inputs, self-repair-inducing ablations) reliably rank explanations by closeness to the model's true underlying algorithm — and can this be turned into a standardized, statistically certified metric (with CIF-style anytime-valid tests) that doubles as a mechanistic anomaly detector?
first_experiment: On ground-truth organisms where the true algorithm is known (InterpBench compiled transformers; group-operation/modular-addition transformers with known Fourier vs. non-Fourier algorithms; planted-feature/backdoor organisms), generate ≥3 candidate explanations per behavior that all achieve ~95%+ in-distribution faithfulness — including at least one "decoy" implementing a different but in-distribution-equivalent algorithm — then measure each candidate's KL divergence from the full model on held-out OOD input families and counterfactual patches, testing whether the known-true explanation separates from decoys only out-of-distribution while being indistinguishable in-distribution (AutoCircuit/TransformerLens/circuit-tracer on GPT-2-scale models, single GPU).
why: It directly converts the field's #1 open problem — "which of several behaviorally-equivalent explanations is the mechanism?" (flagged by Sharkey et al. as benchmarks-with-ground-truth and faithfulness, named the top problem by the 2026 retrospective, proven non-identifiable by Méloux et al., quantified as a 73% claim-flip rate by the 2026 Explanation Multiplicity study) — from an aesthetic judgment into a measurable, falsifiable one, which is exactly what the DeepMind pragmatic turn says progress measurement needs but nobody has built. It has not already been done because the nearest works each stop one step short: Li et al. (2025) prove OOD prediction from internals is possible but use observational attention signatures on synthetic Dyck-1 classifiers and explicitly call it proof-of-concept, without competing mechanistic explanations, decoys matched on in-distribution faithfulness, or ground-truth ranking; uit de Bos et al. (2024) and Miller et al. (2024) show existing circuits and metrics are fragile but propose no selection criterion; MIB and InterpBench evaluate discovery methods in-distribution only; GAE (NeurIPS 2026) fixes dictionary-projection faithfulness under shift rather than discriminating among explanations; CIF (2026) provides uncertainty quantification for interventional claims but no selection principle; and the MAD-via-functional-attribution paper (2026) detects anomalies in parameter space without any explanation-level mechanism-identity test — leaving the synthesis unclaimed, with compounding payoff: a validated metric becomes shared infrastructure for every downstream use (label verification, audit reliability, monitor trust), and a negative result would itself calibrate how much OOD-generalization evidence is worth, both of which the field currently lacks.

direction: Turn per-prompt attribution graphs into input-general, interventional-ly validated algorithmic circuits by merging graph families across parametric input sets.
project: From Traces to Algorithms: Recovering Input-General Circuits by Aggregating Families of Attribution Graphs
question: Can attribution graphs generated across a family of related prompts (e.g., many (a,b) addition pairs) be aligned and merged into a parameterized algorithmic circuit that predicts held-out interventional effects better than single-prompt graphs or dataset-averaged circuits, and do per-prompt "lookup table" features compose into known algorithmic structure (e.g., the trigonometric addition mechanism) once analyzed across the family?
first_experiment: Generate ~500 attribution graphs for two-operand addition in GPT-2 small with public cross-layer transcoders, fit per-feature tuning curves over input parameters to align features across graphs, fit parametric edge-influence models, and test on held-out (a,b) pairs whether the merged graph predicts actual ablation effects better than transplanted single-prompt graphs, dataset-averaged sparse feature circuits, and L0-matched random baselines — checking for recovery of carry logic and Fourier-summation substructure invisible per-prompt.
why: It attacks three documented, still-open gaps simultaneously — the "execution trace vs. algorithm" limitation, the dual-basis problem (cross-input consistency as a principled, non-aesthetic selection criterion), and the validation bottleneck (merged graphs make many preregistered falsifiable predictions) — using a task with known ground-truth algorithms, open models and tooling, and batch-scale automation that is my comparative advantage; and it remains unoccupied 15 months after being explicitly listed as an open problem by the attribution-graph authors themselves.

direction: Pivot mechanistic interpretability's center of gravity from generating circuit hypotheses to actively falsifying them — using attribution graphs themselves to guide automated counterfactual input/intervention search that measures faithfulness non-circularly, adjudicates between equivalent decompositions, and discovers the suppressive mechanisms that realized-behavior graphs structurally miss.
project: Break the Graph — Automated Counterfactual Falsification of Attribution-Graph Hypotheses
question: Do attribution graphs generalize as causal predictions beyond the prompt they were built on — and can a systematic, graph-guided counterfactual search convert faithfulness into a quantitative, non-circular measure while recovering the suppressive edges and hidden mechanisms that graphs of the realized behavior cannot reveal?
first_experiment: On an open model with public transcoders (Gemma-2-2B via circuit-tracer/CLT-Forge, plus Gemma Scope), build attribution graphs for ~20 prompts of one templated behavior (multi-hop factual recall plus a bias case), generate ~200 systematic semantic mutations (entity swaps, distractor insertion, counterfactual context), and measure: (a) the full model's flip rate per mutation, (b) whether the graph-replacement (pruned-circuit) model flips on the same subset, (c) whether the graph's claimed feature-firing patterns track the mutations as it predicts — repeating across ≥3 transcoder bases (different seeds/TopK) to test whether divergent decompositions are separated by the same inputs. Pilot success = graphs disagree with each other and with the full model on a measurable, targeted subset of mutations, establishing that faithfulness is input-dependent and discriminable before scaling to the full automated falsification agent, validated against planted-behavior model organisms (e.g., the open-source auditing-game organism) where the true mechanism is known.
why: It attacks the field's #1 self-diagnosed bottleneck using the field's own definition of understanding — everyone agrees verification is the bottleneck (the 2026 retrospective names attribution-graph faithfulness and the dual-basis problem as the top open problems; Sharkey et al. defines understanding as predicting behavior on arbitrary inputs), yet all 2026 attribution-graph work is descriptive and all faithfulness work is passive/metric-based. It has not been done because: the identifiability critique (2025) stopped at the conceptual argument; Adversarial Circuit Evaluation (2024) is head-level, on three toy circuits, and predates attribution graphs, so it could not use the graph to *target* the input search; the 2026 graph papers (ADAG, Circuit Oracle, probe prompting, Circuit-Diff) describe, annotate, and query graphs rather than attack them; and the 2026 agent-interpretability wave automates hypothesis *generation*, not mechanism-targeted falsification (the only adjacent stress-testing work, FlyHack, is in a connectome-constrained visual model). The payoff is twofold: a standard, ablation-method-independent faithfulness score the whole field can adopt, and discovery of suppressive edges — the mechanistic account of what keeps harmful behavior suppressed and of exactly where circuit-derived safety assurances will break under distribution shift, the precise gap the 2026 field review says is growing as models become more capable. It is also feasible for a small effort: public transcoders and CLT tooling exist for 1–9B open models, planted-behavior organisms released Dec 2025 provide ground truth, and the pilot runs on a single GPU.

direction: Mechanistic interpretability's bottleneck has shifted from finding decompositions of a behavior to choosing between the many decompositions that fit it, so I will build an automated falsification-tournament framework that selects among competing decompositions by their intervention-conditional, out-of-distribution predictive track record — turning decomposition choice from an aesthetic judgment into a measured, non-circular number.
project: Circuit Court — Falsification Tournaments for Competing Mechanistic Decompositions
question: When two or more decompositions of the same model+behavior (e.g., a hand-built circuit, an ACDC/edge-pruned circuit, a transcoder attribution graph, an SAE-feature circuit, a probe-based description) all reproduce the behavior on the distribution where they were discovered, which of them keeps predicting the true model's behavior under interventions on automatically searched discriminating inputs — and does the tournament winner also win where it matters downstream: OOD monitoring, steering, and anomaly-detection utility?
first_experiment: On GPT-2-small IOI, implement the two published, both-"faithful" decompositions (Wang et al.'s hand-built IOI circuit and Conmy et al.'s ACDC circuit) as runnable pseudo-models via their resample-ablation policies; search five pre-specified distribution-shift families (name corruption, repeated-subject, distractor insertion, order permutation, template paraphrase) for inputs where the two hypotheses' predicted outputs diverge; measure each hypothesis's KL against the full model there; then pre-register and test the key claim — the hypothesis that tracks the model better on the searched discriminating families also tracks it better on two held-out families never used in the search. Days of single-GPU compute, and decisive in both directions: disagreement found proves the dual-basis wedge is real and measurable; universal agreement yields a rigorous positive control before scaling to feature-level decompositions (Gemma-2-2B SAE-circuit vs. transcoder graph), where planted "decoy" decompositions in Tracr/InterpBench models will validate that the tournament picks the true mechanism over a behaviorally-equivalent impostor.
why: It attacks the gap that the field's own 2025–2026 self-assessments rank first — explanations are generated millions of times faster than they are validated, and choosing between behaviorally equivalent decompositions is "an aesthetic decision" with no principled framework — while staying clear of the saturated adjacent territory (CoT faithfulness, emergent misalignment, crosscoder diffing, deception probes). It has not been done because the closest prior work all stops one step short: Adversarial Circuit Evaluation and Hypothesis Testing test single hypotheses with no automated search for between-hypothesis disagreement, no selection rule, and no ground-truth validation; Certified Interventional Fidelity provides statistics for a given claim but no adversarial experiment generation or ranking; InterpBench/Tracr ground-truth discovery methods, not selection among decompositions; and the 2026 retrospective states explicitly that ranking decompositions "by something other than how readable their labels are" remains open. The project is tractable on fully open tooling at single-GPU scale, produces compounding infrastructure (a reusable tournament algorithm, the first planted-decoy selection benchmark, and a candidate standard faithfulness number every future decomposition paper can report), and carries direct safety payoff: every internal-behavior monitor is a bet on one dual basis, and this framework is how you find out before deployment whether that bet is a theory or a curve-fit.

direction: Build a ground-truth audit of the SAE/transcoder circuit-tracing pipeline — measuring how much of a trained network's known algorithm, especially computation performed in superposition, its discovered "circuits" actually recover — and use that non-circular metric to quantify what hides in error nodes and to drive computation-aware decomposition methods.
project: Blind Spot Benchmark: Ground-Truth Computation-Recovery Audits of Feature-Decomposition Circuit Tracing in Superposition
question: When a trained network implements a known algorithm — including algorithms computed natively in superposition (binary-codeword compressed computation, U-AND circuits, multi-task grokking) — what fraction of the algorithm's causal computation is recovered by the standard pipeline of SAE/transcoder decomposition → attribution graphs → pruning, which parts are irrecoverably buried in error terms, and can a ground-truth "Computation Recovery Score" distinguish decompositions that currently look equally good by reconstruction and replacement-score metrics (the dual basis problem)?
first_experiment: Train (from the released code) the L4-loss compressed-computation network (100 sparse input features → 50 ReLU neurons → ReLU targets; ground truth = extracted binary codeword matrix M plus its 3-parameter description recovering ~1.13× loss). Train standard TopK/JumpReLU SAEs and a per-layer transcoder on the 50-dim hidden activations at several budgets, build attribution graphs with standard pruning thresholds, and compute against the ground-truth computation graph (input i → codeword neurons → output i, plus known interference edges): (a) function recall — fraction of the 100 computed functions matched by a causally-firing latent; (b) edge precision/recall of the traced circuit vs. ground truth at matched edge budgets, standard pruning vs. ground-truth-optimal pruning; (c) error-node mass — how much task-relevant computation flows through error terms, and whether error directions are predictable from codeword-overlap structure (structured CiS) versus noise.
