why: It attacks the three open problems that the field's own 2025–2026 retrospectives rank highest — the dual basis/faithfulness problem (a decomposition can reconstruct well yet be causally wrong; ground-truth algorithms break the circularity that afflicts every faithfulness metric on real models), error-node prevalence ("too prevalent... blocking us from tracing the important circuits," with nobody knowing whether error mass is noise or hidden computation), and computation in superposition (flagged by Sharkey et al. as the least-worked foundational gap). It has not been done because the ingredients only recently converged and sit in disjoint communities: exact known-solution CiS toy models matured only in mid-2025–2026 (Braun → Bhagat → Gibson → da Silva & Heimersheim; U-AND), the transcoder/attribution-graph pipeline only became standard and open-sourced in 2025–2026 (Circuit Tracer, clt-training, CLT-Forge), the ground-truth benchmark efforts chose different objects (InterpBench = planted circuits with no superposition at edge level; SynthSAEBench and feature-audit work = representation-level recovery in untrained synthetic models), and the theory groups studying CiS analyze the models rather than the tools. It is cheap (50-neuron networks, one GPU), falsifiable in both directions, and produces a metric the benchmark community demonstrably wants; the expected finding — that linear readouts are recovered while nonlinear superposed encoding lands in error terms — would redirect method development (computation-aware objectives, error-term decomposition, end-to-end training) toward the exact blind spot that safety monitoring coverage ("behaviors emerging from distributed circuits with no clean feature representation") currently depends on.

direction: Develop a quantitative, non-circular methodology for testing the identifiability and cross-prompt validity of attribution-graph circuit hypotheses — adjudicating between multiple decompositions of the same behavior using held-out prompts and interventions — to solve the field's top-ranked open problem (the "dual basis problem" / attribution-graph faithfulness).
project: Which Graph Is the Circuit? Discriminating Competing Attribution-Graph Hypotheses Under Distribution Shift
question: When multiple circuit hypotheses derived from different decomposition bases (cross-layer transcoder features, MLP-neuron basis, SAE features, and different pruning thresholds/seeds) are equally faithful on the distribution they were fit to, do they make divergent predictions on held-out prompt distributions and targeted interventions — and can a "predictive validity" score built on those divergences serve as a non-circular, standardized faithfulness metric for attribution graphs?
first_experiment: In Gemma-2-2B on a well-understood behavior (IOI and multi-hop factual recall from MIB, both with public reference data), generate three-plus circuit hypotheses for the identical behavior using (a) an open cross-layer transcoder graph, (b) a neuron-basis graph with RelP attribution, and (c) transcoder graphs at different pruning thresholds/seeds; confirm all reach comparable in-distribution faithfulness (replacement score / MIB faithfulness AUC); then measure hypothesis divergence on (i) held-out prompts with unseen entities and paraphrase/structural variants, and (ii) interventions (ablations/steering) on edges and features unique to each hypothesis — computing a pairwise "discrimination rate" to establish, empirically, whether the dual-basis problem is consequential and how much held-out evidence is needed to single out the true mechanism.
why: It attacks the question that two independent 2025–2026 state-of-the-field assessments rank as the field's most important unresolved problem, at the moment when automation has made the problem acute (millions of labeled features and auto-generated graphs, verification rate flat); it converts a philosophical worry into a measurable quantity; and it is demonstrably not already done — every adjacent line (faithfulness of single circuits, certified stability of one algorithm, verification of vision-model circuits, single-circuit generalization case studies, MIB's in-distribution scoring) either evaluates one hypothesis in isolation or certifies robustness rather than discriminating among mechanistic alternatives, and no cross-prompt consistency study of attribution graphs exists in the literature I surveyed. It is also directly safety-relevant: deployment monitors and audits inherit circuit claims, and unvalidated graphs are the documented reason those applications remain "real but narrow."

direction: Build the missing verification layer for mechanistic interpretability — a quantitative, held-out causal-validation standard for attribution-graph circuit hypotheses that also arbitrates between competing decompositions, calibrated on model organisms with known ground-truth mechanisms.
project: GraphFaith: Held-Out Causal Validation and Dual-Basis Arbitration for Attribution Graphs
question: Does the causal structure of an attribution graph computed on one prompt family — its nodes, edges, and importance weights — actually predict the model's causal response to interventions on held-out and distribution-shifted prompts, and do competing decompositions of the same model (CLT vs. per-layer transcoder vs. different SAE seeds) make divergent held-out predictions that held-out testing can principledly adjudicate?
first_experiment: On an open ~2B model with pretrained cross-layer transcoders (circuit-tracer) and Gemma Scope SAEs, build attribution graphs for ~200 two-hop factual-recall prompts; then on 200 held-out prompts, run graph-guided vs. random vs. magnitude-matched ablations and score how well ID-derived node/edge importance predicts actual causal effect (rank correlation and AUC), under three shifts (paraphrase, entity swap, distractor injection); repeat identically with a second decomposition to quantify dual-basis divergence; run the same protocol once on a known-mechanism organism (a model fine-tuned with a planted, verified multi-hop retrieval chain) to calibrate the metric's sensitivity.
why: It is the field's own top-ranked open problem — the June 2026 state-of-the-field retrospective identifies verification (not labeling) as the unsolved bottleneck, notes most published feature claims are causally unvalidated, and names attribution-graph faithfulness plus the dual basis problem as what a new survey would lead with — yet no work delivers it: every recent attribution-graph paper automates *reading* the graph (ADAG, Probe Prompting, Circuit Oracle, Circuit Oracle-style agents), the faithfulness literature predates attribution graphs and works at head/MLP granularity on single tasks, existing benchmarks target component-level circuit discovery (InterpBench) or behavior-level auditing (AuditBench), and the only ground-truth study of decomposition unfaithfulness is a Boolean toy model with "preliminary" real-model evidence. Meanwhile the failure mode is proven consequential: decompositions can match behavior while hiding the true computational pathway, which means attribution-graph-derived safety audits and production monitors can greenlight exactly the behaviors they claim to rule out. It is maximally leveraged — fixing verification upgrades every downstream artifact (audits, monitors, model-organism science, automated-annotation agents) — and it just became feasible with open tooling and modest compute, so the window is open now, before someone else turns it into a framework paper.

direction: Establish held-out interventional fidelity as the standard metric for validating and ranking non-identifiable mechanistic decompositions, by testing whether frozen attribution graphs predict intervention outcomes on novel prompts, novel interventions, and shifted distributions.
project: Explain-then-Predict: Held-Out Interventional Fidelity as the Standard for Validating and Ranking Mechanistic Decompositions
question: How well does a frozen decomposition + attribution graph, built on a calibration set, predict the model's behavior under interventions on inputs and intervention types it was not built on — and which decomposition properties (seed stability, reconstruction error, feature margins, granularity) predict that held-out fidelity?
first_experiment: Build margin-corrected attribution graphs with public Gemma Scope SAEs and open circuit-tracer on ~20 calibration prompts of a factual-recall behavior in gemma-2-2b, freeze them, then compare predicted vs. realized effects of single/combined ablations and steering on calibration prompts, 200 held-out paraphrases, and shifted inputs across ≥3 SAE seeds and 2 expansion factors, scoring held-out interventional fidelity with anytime-valid confidence sequences and self-repair-aware conditional tests.
why: It attacks the field's self-identified top open problem — the validation/dual-basis gap left by asymmetric scaling of labeling over verification — at the moment (late 2026) when public transcoders, open circuit-tracer, and the margin/CIF/stability/CoAx corrections have just made the required held-out interventional sweeps cheap; adjacent 2025–26 work each covers one slice (same-prompt margins, membership stability, statistics, self-repair, cross-seed matching) but no protocol scores explanations as intervention-predictors on novel inputs or ranks alternative decompositions of the same network by anything but label readability, which is precisely what non-identifiability results (ICLR 2025) and the NeurIPS 2026 evaluation-paradigm position paper say the field now needs, and what safety deployment (monitors and audits that must work off-distribution) cannot proceed without.

direction: Build a predictive, non-circular validation and selection framework for mechanistic decompositions — an "interventional adequacy under distribution shift" standard that identifies which of several equally adequate competing circuit hypotheses actually tracks the model's real behavior off-distribution.
project: The Dual-Basis Testbed — Held-Out Interventional Adequacy for Competing Mechanistic Decompositions
question: When multiple decompositions (across SAE seeds, dictionary sizes, methods, thresholds) all adequately explain a behavior on its discovery distribution, how much do they diverge in their behavioral predictions under distribution shift, and which selection principles — validation-set breadth, cross-seed/dictionary invariance, stability pooling, weight-space grounding via parameter decomposition — computed at discovery time predict which decomposition's counterfactual claims generalize?
first_experiment: On GPT-2 small + IOI (matching the 2026 multiplicity study for comparability) and pythia-160m with public TopK SAEs: extract ≥4 competing circuit hypotheses for the same behavior (different SAE seeds, different dictionary sizes, an edge-level ACDC circuit, and the textbook head-level circuit); verify all reach equal adequacy (≥95% of the full model's effect) on the discovery distribution; then measure each hypothesis's predicted-vs-actual behavior (KL on next-token distributions under its own prescribed ablations) on a pre-registered shift battery (template paraphrases, argument-order swaps, name/entity swaps, distractor insertion, negation, format change), producing the first "dual-basis divergence curve" and testing whether validation breadth at discovery time predicts out-of-distribution adequacy — roughly 2–3 GPU-days with TransformerLens/nnsight and public SAE checkpoints.
why: It attacks the one bottleneck that six independent, recent, high-credibility sources (Sharkey et al. 2025, the 2026 retrospective, the NeurIPS 2026 position paper, Méloux et al. 2025, Mahale 2026, Li et al. 2025) all identify as blocking — the field's claims are non-identifiable and their verification lags their generation — and it is the *constructive* step no one has taken: prior work measures instability (claim flips, seed divergence, margin crossings) or provides falsification layers (unit tests, anytime-valid statistics), but none quantifies behavioral divergence between equally adequate decompositions under shift, and none tests selection principles that turn validation from per-claim audit into a predictive, normalizable standard; it multiplies the trustworthiness of every downstream application (safety monitors, audits, model edits) rather than adding one more artifact to an already crowded methods space; and it has a two-sided payoff — if no selection principle works, that is a major, publishable result forcing shift-specific validation of deployed monitors, and if one does, interpretability claims finally become falsifiable and comparable, which is exactly the "perplexity moment" the field says it needs.

direction: Establish held-out counterfactual predictive validity — predicting the real model's outputs under novel prompts and novel feature interventions — as the quantitative, non-circular standard for validating and ranking feature-level decompositions (SAEs/transcoders and their attribution graphs), empirically adjudicating the dual basis problem.
project: Graph on Trial — Held-Out Counterfactual Validation of Attribution Graphs
question: When several decompositions (SAEs of different widths/seeds/architectures, cross-layer transcoders, raw-neuron baselines) all produce plausible attribution graphs for the same behavior on the same prompt, do their graphs agree on the model's behavior under held-out counterfactuals — novel prompts and feature ablations/scalings not used to build the graph — and which decomposition choice maximizes that agreement, independently of how readable its labels are?
first_experiment: On Gemma-2-2B with Gemma Scope SAEs (16k/65k/262k/1M widths, both released seeds) and the open-source cross-layer transcoders, take a compact multi-step behavior (two-hop factual recall or state tracking) with programmatically variable surface forms. Build attribution graphs on K source prompts, then extract each graph's quantitative predictions for a pre-registered battery of held-out counterfactuals: (i) the output distribution shift predicted when ablating or 2×-scaling each top-path feature, (ii) the predicted output on entity-swapped / reordered novel prompts, (iii) the predicted dominant path under those counterfactuals. Run the real model on every counterfactual and score predictions with KL/total-variation distance and rank correlation. Headline readout: how much do graphs that fully agree on the source prompt diverge in held-out predictive validity (the dual basis problem made empirical), and does predictive validity rank decompositions differently than label-readability does? Fits on 1–4 GPUs with fully open artifacts, and scales the Li 2026 margin-analysis result from Pythia-160m to real models and naturalistic behaviors.
why: It attacks the field's own self-diagnosed #1 gap (2026 retrospective: faithfulness verification and the dual basis problem, with no agreed non-circular metric) at the feature level where the field actually operates post-attribution-graphs. It converts a philosophical worry ("which decomposition is real?") into a measurable one, and its output — a validity metric plus a benchmark battery — would discipline every downstream use (monitors, audits, edits) currently built on unvalidated features. It has not already been done because the closest work each stops one level short: Miller et al. 2024 and the phantom-specialization paper operate at the component level and never test held-out predictions across decompositions; Li 2026 fixes a linearization artifact in toy models but builds no ranking framework; Certified Circuits and InterpBench certify stability or use synthetic ground truth rather than adjudicating decompositions on real models; AxBench/SAE Bench evaluate steering utility, not counterfactual explanatory validity; and the incentive structure (mechanism discovery over metrology, labeling outpacing verification) has left validation as the hole in the middle of the field's fastest-growing artifact.

direction: Establish and ground-truth-validate out-of-distribution intervention consistency as the principled criterion for selecting the true mechanism among behaviorally equivalent mechanistic explanations, ending the field's reliance on aesthetics to choose between circuits.
project: Which Circuit Is Real? Ground-Truth-Validated Selection Principles for Behaviorally Equivalent Mechanistic Explanations
question: When multiple circuit or feature explanations of the same behavior are behaviorally equivalent in-distribution, which intrinsic property identifies the member matching the model's actual mechanism — and does out-of-distribution intervention consistency separate the true mechanism from artifact members where in-distribution faithfulness cannot?
first_experiment: Generate ≥40 behaviorally-equivalent candidate explanations (varying discovery method, seed, pruning threshold, and decomposition basis) of grokking transformers on modular addition, verify in-distribution equivalence, then measure each candidate's interventional faithfulness under controlled distribution shifts (larger modulus, unseen operands, permuted vocab, cue-decoupling perturbations) and correlate candidate selection scores (OOD consistency, MDL, seed-stability, interventional agreement) with ground-truth recovery against the known Fourier circuit; replicate on the Sparse Transformer natural-language testbed with its known sparse-MLP basis.
why: It targets the field's self-identified top open problem — behaviorally-equivalent explanations are non-identifiable and claims flip under defensible analytic variation (73% flip rate across 15,840 specifications) — yet 2026's responses are either purely diagnostic (multiplicity surveys, recovery-gap audits) or procedural heuristics (consensus ensembles, dataset-edit certification) that never validate whether the selected member is the true mechanism; no study compares selection principles head-to-head on testbeds with known ground truth, because such testbeds (Sparse Transformer, InterpBench) only became available in the last month and the interventional-agreement criterion has only been formalized in classical causal models, never imported into neural decomposition. Solving selection is upstream of all safety applications — monitors, audits, and edits fail under distribution shift exactly when built on the wrong equivalence-class member — and the tooling, released testbeds, and motivated audience exist right now, making this the highest-value, least-claimed lane in mechanistic interpretability today.

direction: Build automated discriminating-experiment synthesis — a method that takes two or more competing mechanistic hypotheses (circuits, attribution graphs, or SAE bases) and automatically designs, runs, and statistically certifies the intervention distribution that maximally separates their predicted behaviors, converting mechanistic claims from consistency scores into certified hypothesis tests.
project: Separation by Design: Certified Discrimination of Competing Mechanistic Hypotheses via Optimized Interventions
question: Given a declared intervention family and two competing mechanistic hypotheses that are behaviorally consistent on the evaluation distribution used to develop them, can we automatically synthesize a (joint, distribution-shift-safe) intervention set that maximizes predicted behavioral divergence between them — and does adaptive use of that set, under anytime-valid sequential testing, correctly certify the true mechanism and quantify when hypotheses are behaviorally equivalent?
first_experiment: On a grokking modular-addition transformer with a known trig-identity algorithm, construct the two published rival high-level hypotheses (trig-integral computation vs. piecewise-linear case analysis); compute each hypothesis's predicted patching responses across the reachable-state geometry, solve for the maximally separating joint intervention distribution, and show that (i) standard single-site/mean ablations cannot separate them, replicating known blindness, while (ii) the designed joint interventions separate them at small budget with anytime-valid confidence, selecting the true algorithm — then repeat the protocol on InterpBench's known-mechanism models and on cross-seed SAE basis pairs from Gemma Scope.
why: It attacks the problem the field itself ranks first — the 2026 retrospective calls the dual-basis/faithfulness question "the open problem I would put at the top of any new survey," and five independent 2024–2026 results prove current evaluation cannot distinguish mechanisms — yet the constructive step is missing: existing work is either diagnostic (blind-spot audits, misranking findings, illusion papers), statistical-but-passive (CIF certifies only pre-declared estimands), or estimation-of-a-single-map (mechanistic tomography starts after the basis is chosen). Assembling prospective blind-spot geometry, classical model-discrimination experimental design (never imported into interp), and CIF's anytime-valid statistics into an active, certified discriminator is newly actionable (the enabling papers are all from July–December 2026), testable on ground-truth suites at single-GPU cost, and delivers a practical artifact — automated adversarial tests for interpretability-derived monitors and a measurable, non-aesthetic criterion for choosing among decompositions.

direction: Establish a quantitative, distribution-shift-aware validation framework — with ground-truth calibration and an agreed trust metric — for attribution-graph circuit explanations, the field's now-dominant but least-verified artifact.
project: Credible Circuits: Stress-Testing the Faithfulness of Attribution-Graph Explanations Under Distribution Shift
question: When and under what distribution shifts do attribution-graph circuit explanations make *correct counterfactual predictions* about a model's behavior — and can a single calibrated trust score, validated against ground-truth algorithms and the model's errors, predict where those explanations will fail before they are deployed as safety evidence?
first_experiment: Train a cross-layer transcoder on GPT-2-small with CLT-Forge (Goodfire recipe, ~100M FineWeb tokens), build attribution graphs for 30–50 prompts each on the greater-than and IOI tasks (both have independently established mechanisms), then run three falsifiable tests: (1) *graph stability* — node/edge overlap and role consistency of top features across prompt resamples, quantifying prompt-locality; (2) *intervention transferability* — ablate/steer the top features identified on 5 calibration prompts and measure, on held-out shifted prompts (unseen entity categories, unseen year ranges, paraphrases, distractors), the rank correlation between attribution-predicted and true logit deltas as a function of shift severity; (3) *error agreement* — the fraction of the model's own errors reproduced by the graph-restricted computation, compared to successes, adapting the 2026 error-agreement protocol from component circuits to feature-level graphs. Calibrate all three against a Tracr/InterpBench compiled greater-than model where the true circuit is known, giving precision/recall of recovered edges and a sanity ceiling.
why: It attacks the single highest-leverage, self-diagnosed bottleneck of the field: verification infrastructure collapsed under the automation wave, the dual-basis problem (which of many decompositions is "the circuit"?) has no principled criterion, and interpretability-derived monitors and safety cases are already being deployed on top of unvalidated graph claims — a false-assurance risk the Open Problems paper flags but nobody has quantified. It has *not* already been done because the existing validation literature covers only the older component-circuit paradigm (Certified Circuits, ICML 2026; error-agreement, 2026; faithfulness-metric robustness, 2024), while for CLT attribution graphs the entire evidence base is one single-prompt replication (Goodfire 2025) plus a theory paper on incentive misalignment (ICML 2026); no one has built the shift-aware, error-aware, ground-truth-calibrated trust metric the field's own leaders list as the top open problem. It is feasible on open weights and open tooling with modest compute, it is upstream of global-circuit and reasoning-model work (which cannot be trusted without it), and it produces decisive results either way: if graphs transfer, the field gains its first calibrated certificate of trust; if they fail systematically, the field learns exactly where its dominant artifact misleads — which is precisely the "willingness to publish negative results" the 2026 retrospective says is now needed.

direction: Build a systematic "discriminating experiments" framework that treats competing circuit explanations (attribution graphs from different decomposition stacks) as falsifiable hypotheses and arbitrates them by which one better predicts the model's behavior, internal activations, and intervention effects on held-out and adversarially constructed inputs.
project: Circuit Arbitration: Falsifying Attribution Graphs with Discriminating Experiments
question: When two circuit-level explanations of the same model behavior (e.g., a cross-layer-transcoder attribution graph vs. a per-layer SAE/attention-feature graph) both reproduce the model's behavior on the eliciting distribution, can experiments designed from their points of disagreement — input families where the graphs make divergent predictions about latent firings, ablation effects, and outputs — reliably discriminate them, yielding a non-circular, held-out measure of mechanistic faithfulness that ranks decompositions?
first_experiment: On Gemma-2-2B (free-tier GPU), generate attribution graphs for the same multi-hop factual-recall prompts using two independently trained decomposition stacks (Anthropic circuit-tracer CLTs vs. the OpenMOSS LM-SAE engine, plus a Gemma Scope feature-level graph as a third competitor); extract each graph's implied mechanism (intermediate nodes, predicted ablation effects, firing conditions); pre-register each graph's predictions on ~5 constructed input families where the graphs disagree (wrong-intermediate-fact, negated intermediate, entity-property paraphrase, distractor injection, and suppression/steering of the disputed node); then score which hypothesis the model's actual behavior and measured causal effects vindicate. Either outcome is decisive: a demonstrable arbitration win establishes the framework, and systematic failure quantifies the dual-basis crisis with actionable failure modes.
why: It attacks the field's self-identified #1 problem — the dual-basis/faithfulness gap, explicitly named as the top open methodological question in 2026 and still unclaimed — at the exact moment attribution graphs have become the standard artifact and public tooling has made competing decompositions of the same open model trivially available. It has not been done: non-identifiability was only shown in toy MLPs (Méloux et al. 2025) without operationalizing arbitration; adversarial circuit evaluation stress-tested single published circuits rather than comparing alternatives; certified/verified circuit work (2026) provides robustness for one circuit, not discrimination between hypotheses; the ICML 2026 transcoder-unfaithfulness paper documented that competing graphs diverge but stopped at "preliminary evidence"; per-feature validation handles features, not graph-level mechanistic structure; and MIB measures on-distribution sufficiency, not held-out mechanistic prediction. It is also the highest-leverage move available: every downstream use of interpretability — monitoring, auditing, model diffing, cross-model transfer — currently rests on unverified, non-unique decompositions, and this is the cheap (single-GPU), method-agnostic layer that makes all of them trustworthy, while feeding concrete failure modes back into decomposition research (e.g., whether sparsity penalties incentivize predictively wrong circuits).

direction: Predicting when feature-space interventions form true behavioral bottlenecks — a cheap pre-deployment "route coverage" audit for latent-space defenses that doubles as a principled, non-circular criterion for ranking competing decompositions.
project: Certified Bottlenecks: Predicting Re-Elicitation of Suppressed Behavior from Decomposition Coverage
question: Can the recoverability of a behavior after feature-level suppression (ablation/clamping) be predicted in advance from cheap first-order statistics — specifically, how much of the behavior's causal effect energy lies inside vs. outside the intervened decomposition's span, plus conditional backup growth and reconstruction-error magnitude — validated against actual adversarial re-elicitation across behaviors, models, and SAE dictionaries?
first_experiment: On Gemma-2-2B-it with Gemma Scope residual-stream SAEs: (1) suppress refusal by ablating top-k refusal features (k ∈ {10, 50, 200}, several layers and selection methods), measuring coherent suppression with a two-judge protocol; (2) run constrained residual-space re-elicitation (projected gradient descent orthogonal to selected encoder directions, per Cui et al. 2026) to measure actual recovery rates; (3) compute the candidate cheap predictors — one-backward-pass decomposition of the compliance-logit gradient energy into the selected-decoder span, the unselected-feature span, and the SAE error residual, plus conditional effect growth and reconstruction error; (4) test whether predicted coverage rank-correlates with measured recovery across all (behavior, k, layer, selection) conditions, replicating the validation on WMDP unlearning and on Llama-3.1-8B + Llama Scope. Falsifiable either way: a validated AUC-thresholded audit, or a documented map of what the first-order statistic misses (pointing to second-order/backup structure).
why: It sits at the intersection of the three problems the field itself ranks highest in 2026 — faithfulness/verification ("labels are produced too easily and verification has not kept pace"), the dual-basis problem ("choosing among decompositions is currently an aesthetic decision"), and the growing coverage gap in safety monitoring ("monitors do not work for behaviors that emerge from distributed circuits") — and it converts the June/July 2026 *diagnostic* papers (recovery attacks, backup discovery, faithfulness non-robustness) into a *predictive, deployable certificate*. It has not been done because the necessary pieces live in disjoint literatures (adversarial robustness, circuit-completion methodology, dictionary learning) that haven't been integrated: Cui et al. attack but don't predict; CoAx finds backups among heads via expensive per-component interventions and excludes the residual channel; MIB and faithfulness metrics are in-distribution only; steering-side-effect predictors address the forward direction, not suppression completeness. It is feasible on open models with public SAE suites on a single GPU, its first experiment is cheap and falsifiable, and — whether or not the predictor validates — the answer directly determines whether the latent-space defenses now being deployed can ever be made sound, and what structure (residual, backups, interference) must be added to decompositions to close the routes.

direction: Make attribution graphs falsifiable scientific hypotheses by developing and stress-testing held-out interventional predictive validation — the standard that a circuit hypothesis counts as a mechanism only if it predicts model behavior under interventions and inputs it was not built on, including against deliberately constructed competing decompositions that are equally faithful in-distribution.
project: Mechanism or Mimic? Held-Out Interventional Validation for Attribution Graphs
question: When two or more circuit decompositions of the same model behavior are equally faithful in-distribution (the dual basis problem), can held-out interventional prediction — the graph's ability to forecast behavioral change under novel node ablations, feature-flip patches, paraphrases, and unseen-entity inputs — discriminate the true mechanism from co-faithful mimics, and which properties of a validation battery make that standard non-circular and reliable?
first_experiment: On an open small model (GPT-2 small with open transcoders, or Gemma-2-2B with Gemma Scope), build attribution graphs for a task with rich held-out structure (IOI or colored-objects MCQA from MIB) on a fitting split; construct at least two "decoy" graphs with statistically matched replacement scores (independent transcoder seeds/architectures plus adversarially perturbed edge sets that preserve on-distribution behavior); then compute interventional predictive accuracy for true vs. decoy graphs on held-out instances — predicted vs. actual behavioral change under ablations and causal-chain-consistent patches (upstream flips should propagate as the graph claims). A grokked modular-arithmetic model with a known solution algorithm serves as the planted ground-truth organism to calibrate whether the metric identifies the true mechanism rather than just any coherent story.
why: It attacks the gap that three independent sources — the field's own 2025 open-problems review, the 2026 state-of-the-field retrospective (which ranks the dual basis problem first and notes verification has not kept pace with labeling), and the multi-organization replication project — all identify as the current bottleneck; it converts the only existing demonstration of non-identifiability (toy Boolean nets, ICLR 2025) into a real-model, quantitative protocol; it complements rather than duplicates 2024–2026 prior art, which covers ablation-faithfulness (Hanna et al.), localization benchmarks with held-out instances (MIB), intervention specificity (mechanistic unit tests, ICML 2026), and formal-but-unoperationalized criteria (compositional interpretability), while every 2026 attribution graph paper advances construction/automation rather than validation; and it is tractable — small open models, public transcoders, and the open circuit-tracer library put the decisive experiment within reach, with both a positive outcome (a practical, standardizable validation battery the field has said it lacks) and a negative outcome (co-faithful mimics are indistinguishable — a humbling result that would discipline the field's mechanistic claims) being genuinely publishable.

direction: Build a differential-diagnosis validation standard for mechanistic circuit claims — turn competing circuit/attribution-graph hypotheses into runnable predictors, construct held-out input families where their implied algorithms make divergent predictions, and use behavioral agreement there as the field's first non-circular faithfulness metric that can discriminate between decompositions the current on-distribution ablation paradigm cannot tell apart.
project: Differential Diagnosis for Circuits: Discriminating Competing Mechanistic Hypotheses by Out-of-Distribution Behavioral Prediction
question: Do circuit hypotheses that are statistically indistinguishable under on-distribution ablation faithfulness make divergent behavioral predictions on held-out "discriminating" input families, and can a simulatability score on those families rank rival decompositions (manual vs. ACDC vs. EAP-IG circuits; CLT vs. PLT attribution graphs) by true mechanistic fidelity — replacing circular ablation-fidelity as the field's standard faithfulness metric?
first_experiment: On GPT-2-small IOI and greater-than, freeze each published rival circuit (Wang et al. manual, ACDC, EAP-IG — which differ in edges yet all report high faithfulness) as a runnable replacement model, then measure exact-answer agreement and logit correlation with the full model on (a) the discovery distribution, (b) held-out same-template prompts, and (c) algorithmically parameterized discriminating families where the implied algorithms diverge (DoubleIO/TripleIO, role swaps, duplication shifts — extending Nainani et al.'s variant analysis). Deliverable: the separation between hypotheses' agreement scores on (c) versus (a)/(b), i.e., whether on-distribution faithfulness rank decorrelates from OOD-predictive rank. All inputs are public artifacts (TransformerLens, published circuits, nnsight), runnable on one GPU in days; success criterion is confident discrimination between at least two circuit pairs that ablation-faithfulness cannot distinguish.
why: Every independent assessment of the field — the 2026 retrospective of the canonical open-problems paper (faithfulness-as-numerical-target and the dual basis problem ranked top), the attribution-graph inventors' own directions list (validation of circuit hypotheses, downstream tasks measuring understanding), and the 2024–2026 empirical literature (metric fragility in Miller et al., error-blindness in Zhang et al., CLT shallow-rewrite unfaithfulness at ICML 2026, decoupling of predictive value from causal faithfulness in Li et al.) — converges on the same gap: we certify circuit explanations on the distribution where they were found, so rival explanations that fit it are unresolvable "aesthetic choices," and safety-relevant extrapolation of circuit-derived monitors is unquantified. The nearest prior work each stops one step short: none constructs discriminating input families designed so rival *mechanistic* hypotheses diverge, runs the hypotheses as predictors rather than ablating the model, or proposes the resulting score as a general metric on real LLMs — the toy-model CLT paper explicitly diagnoses the problem without supplying the test, and Li et al. establish the OOD-prediction objective without circuits or real models. It is therefore open, foundational (every downstream use of circuits — auditing, monitoring, model editing, benchmarking interpretability agents — inherits its validity domain), cheap relative to its leverage, and produces valuable results whichever way the experiments resolve.

direction: Mechanistic interpretability should move from single forward passes into multi-turn computation — characterizing, causally intervening on, and repairing the internal "task state" that persists (and decays) across conversation turns.
project: Where Does the Task Go? A Causal Account of Task-State Decay and Pre-Commitment in Multi-Turn Conversation
question: Why do LLMs irrecoverably lose instructions across turns — is the constraint-laden task state (a) actively overwritten in the residual stream, (b) still present but no longer read (a read-out failure, i.e., "ignoring" rather than "forgetting"), or (c) locked into an early-turn "commitment anchor" that later turns read instead of the instruction — and can state-level interventions at turn boundaries causally restore instruction-following where text reminders fail?
first_experiment: On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, reproduce the Laban et al. sharded-instruction protocol (two constrained generation tasks with quantifiable constraints). At every turn boundary and layer, train linear probes on the residual stream to decode each active constraint (format, length, content slots, persona), comparing decodability over turns in the sharded condition against the identical state in the fully-specified single-turn condition; in parallel, measure attention from each turn's first planning tokens back to instruction tokens versus to the model's own earlier output tokens. This single run dissociates the hypotheses (probe decay ⇒ state overwriting; intact probes + attention drifting to self-generated tokens ⇒ read-out failure/anchor lock-in), and I immediately follow it with the causal test: patch the task-state positions between sharded and full-context runs at turn boundaries (and refresh instruction KV-cache entries) and measure whether compliance recovers — a result either way is a finding, and it costs only a few GPU-days.
why: It targets the field's biggest unclaimed territory at exactly the right moment: the flagship behavioral phenomenon is established and widely cited but has no mechanistic account; signal-level neighbors (Abdelnabi et al.'s activation-delta detection, Goal-Drift Probes, hidden-state trajectory tracking) prove the internal signal exists while explicitly stopping short of mechanism, causality, or repair; "When Agents Commit Too Soon" names the commitment problem but admits its measure "cannot by itself establish that commitment was premature"; and MechSuits/Asking Forever cover adjacent failure modes (harm states, clarification-seeking), not task-state persistence. It is safety-critical (agents ignoring constraints over long horizons is a top deployment risk, and the forgetting-vs-ignoring dissociation is exactly what auditors and monitors need), mechanistically novel (cross-turn KV read-out and commitment anchors are new objects — all current circuit work is single-pass), highly tractable with open 7–9B models and standard tooling (nnsight/TransformerLens, since multi-turn is full-context concatenation — no new infrastructure needed), and it produces deployment-grade deliverables: a drift monitor grounded in a causal model of the failure, plus a state-level repair that outperforms text reminders. Its main risks — that the mechanism is just "attention dilution," or that probes fail to generalize — are themselves testable in the first week, and either answer redirects rather than dead-ends the program.

direction: Establish predictive faithfulness as a quantitative, non-circular standard for mechanistic explanations — scoring circuits, SAE decompositions, and attribution graphs by their ability to predict the model's behavior on held-out inputs, distribution shifts, and novel interventions — and use it to adjudicate between competing decompositions that are equivalent in-distribution.
project: Predictive Faithfulness: Validating and Adjudicating Mechanistic Explanations by Held-Out Behavioral Prediction
question: When multiple mechanistic explanations of the same behavior are observationally (and even interventionally) equivalent on the distribution they were discovered on, does their predictive faithfulness under distribution shift and novel interventions diverge — and can that divergence serve as a principled, non-circular criterion for verifying explanations and ranking competing decompositions?
first_experiment: An OOD faithfulness audit of the canonical IOI circuit in GPT-2 small: measure standard in-distribution ablation faithfulness across multiple ablation methodologies, then re-measure the same full-model-vs-circuit agreement on a ladder of shifts (held-out names/objects à la MIB private test, DoubleIO/TripleIO prompt variants where S2-Hacking lives, corrupted-prompt variants), producing the first quantified "faithfulness gap" curve and localizing divergences to specific mechanisms — a one-GPU, weeks-scale experiment whose outcome decides whether to extend to matched-faithfulness competing SAE decompositions via Gemma Scope.
why: It targets the gap that the field's own 2026 retrospective ranks above all others ("the open problem I would put at the top of any new survey") — faithfulness verification has lagged automated labeling, and the dual basis problem currently gets resolved by aesthetic choice. It is not already done because every adjacent effort stops short: Miller et al. showed in-distribution metrics are fragile without proposing a replacement; MIB is in-distribution; Certified Circuits and Formal MI certify discovery stability and local neighborhoods, not distribution-level predictive adequacy; Nainani et al. is one circuit's case study with no metric; simulatability metrics (NSG) cover only natural-language self-explanations; and the non-identifiability result (Méloux et al.) diagnoses the problem and gestures at predictive/manipulability standards without building them. This direction is a keystone: a shared, exact-simulatability scoreboard would discipline SAE defaults, circuit discovery, and attribution graphs simultaneously, directly enables deployment-grade monitoring under shift, and is executable end-to-end on open models and tooling — maximum field-shaping impact per unit of compute.

direction: Pursue distribution-shift-based discrimination of in-distribution-equivalent mechanistic explanations as the field's first principled, quantitative criterion for choosing among competing decompositions.
project: Explanatory Transfer: Discriminating Competing Decompositions Under Distribution Shift
question: Which of several decompositions that are statistically indistinguishable in-distribution remains a valid causal explanation of model behavior under distribution shift and novel interventions, and is that property predictable from legibility or in-distribution fidelity?
first_experiment: Certify in-distribution equivalence of four IOI explanations in GPT-2 small (Wang head circuit, matched EAP-IG circuit, SAE-feature circuits from two seeds) with anytime-valid tests, then compare their ablation divergence from the full model, novel/composed-intervention prediction accuracy, and complement-coverage across a natural-shift ladder (paraphrase, lexical, distractor, compositional, position shifts).
why: The dual basis problem is the field's self-identified top open problem and faithfulness-lacks-a-metric its top methodological gap; this direction operationalizes both with existing public tooling, is unoccupied (all prior work evaluates single decompositions, in-distribution, or worst-case only), yields an informative result either way, and directly determines when interpretability-derived monitors can be trusted under the distribution shift where they are needed most.

direction: Build a method-agnostic "explanation discrimination" layer for mechanistic interpretability that treats competing decompositions (CLT vs. per-layer transcoders vs. neuron-feature circuits) of the same behavior as rival causal hypotheses, automatically designs the input shifts and interventions that maximally separate their predicted behaviors, and ranks them by off-distribution predictive adequacy — validated on tasks with known ground-truth mechanisms.
project: Adjudicating Rival Circuits: Designed Discriminating Tests for Competiting Mechanistic Decompositions
question: When multiple decompositions of the same model behavior are behaviorally adequate in-distribution, can experiment design — input and intervention distributions synthesized to maximize divergence between the decompositions' predicted behaviors — distinguish the decomposition that describes the model's actual mechanism from ones that merely reproduce its training-distribution behavior, and does the winner on designed tests correspond to the known ground-truth mechanism?
first_experiment: On GPT-2 small with the greater-than task (known manual circuit, Hanna et al. 2023; public CLT replication recipe from Goodfire), extract two rival decompositions — a cross-layer transcoder and per-layer transcoders (via CLT-Forge) — and verify both pass standard in-distribution fidelity. Then compute, on a family of natural shift inputs (years far outside the training range, digit-boundary cases, prior-shifting noun contexts), where the two replacement models' predicted output distributions diverge most, and test which replacement model tracks the true model (KL to the real model plus agreement on model errors) on the top-k discriminating inputs — checking specifically whether the decomposition whose structure matches the known year-gating MLP mechanism wins, and pairing the evaluation with anytime-valid statistics so adaptive test selection cannot overfit.
why: It attacks the problem the field's own 2026 retrospectives rank first — the dual basis problem / faithfulness of decompositions — at the moment when enabling infrastructure has just matured and the failure modes (CLT shallow rewrites, seed variance, error blindness, exhaustive non-identifiability) have just been documented but left without remedy. Every adjacent 2025–2026 contribution stops one step short: Méloux et al. prove non-identifiability without remedy, CIF certifies estimates for fixed experiments rather than designing experiments, error-reproduction uses one static test set on one circuit, MCT tests state abstractions rather than rival circuit explanations, Koopman offers an identifiable primitive that is deliberately not legible, and FlyHack stress-tests single claims in a fly-vision ensemble rather than adjudicating between decompositions. Nobody has built the active, hypothesis-testing layer that ranks decompositions by something other than label readability — the explicit gap named in the retrospective — and doing so is cheap (GPT-2-scale, public artifacts), falsifiable, informative under both success (a validated ground-truth-free discriminator, usable on frontier models where no ground truth exists) and failure (evidence that natural shifts underdetermine mechanisms, sharpening what primitives the field must change), and it compounds across all future decomposition methods rather than competing with any of them.

direction: Build the missing global layer of circuit tracing — aggregate thousands of prompt-local attribution graphs over a prompt distribution into a causally validated, distribution-level circuit model ("circuit atlas") and test whether it predicts behavior and circuit structure on held-out prompts.
project: From Prompt-Local Graphs to a Global Circuit Atlas: Distribution-Level Validation of Transcoder Circuit Tracing
question: Is there a stable, feature-level global circuit structure underlying a model's behavior across a prompt distribution — and can a circuit atlas aggregated from per-prompt attribution graphs (i) predict per-prompt attribution graphs on held-out prompts, (ii) predict model behavior under interventions better than prompt-local circuits, and (iii) distinguish faithful global mechanisms from unfaithful shallow rewrites (per the ICML 2026 CLT unfaithfulness result)?
first_experiment: Using the open circuit-tracer release with pretrained CLTs on Gemma-2-2B, trace ~200 prompts consisting of paraphrase clusters of the same underlying task (e.g., two-hop factual recall) plus distinct questions; compute within-paraphrase vs. between-question stability of feature-edge sets (edge-Jaccard and edge-weight rank correlation), and causally patch a sample of the edges that look stable on held-out prompts. Outcome: if paraphrase clusters share stable edge structure, a global atlas is possible and I proceed to aggregation + held-out prediction; if they don't, that is itself a publishable negative result showing attribution graphs are largely prompt-idiosyncratic and must be treated as local samples, not circuit recoveries.
why: (1) It is explicitly listed as an open problem by the attribution-graph method's own creators (Lindsey, Nanda, McGrath et al., Aug 2025 multi-org landscape), the highest-signal possible endorsement of value, and it remains unsolved as of November 2026 under every phrasing I searched — closest work is either component-level, single-task, single-graph automation, or patching-similarity pipelines, none of which builds a validated feature-level global model. (2) It compounds with the field's dominant artifact rather than competing with it, and it operationalizes three diagnosed field-level gaps at once: faithfulness verification (distribution-level causal tests are built into the evaluation), the dual basis problem (cross-prompt stability is a principled, non-aesthetic criterion for ranking decompositions), and behavior prediction on arbitrary inputs (Sharkey et al.'s own definition of "understanding"). (3) It is feasible for an independent researcher: mature open tooling (circuit-tracer, CLT-Forge, Gemma Scope 2), 2B-scale models, cheap graph analysis, with a decisive cheap first experiment whose both branches produce publishable knowledge. (4) It directly stress-tests the newest known failure mode (CLT shallow-rewrite unfaithfulness) by making prompt-stability a measurable diagnostic of decomposition faithfulness, and it naturally extends to suppressive/inhibitory edges — the other listed open problem — since predicting "why the model didn't do X" requires signed edges in the global picture.

direction: Mechanistic analysis of suppressive computation — building the counterfactual attribution methods and ground-truth "suppression model organisms" needed to explain, detect, and fix why language models fail to act on knowledge they demonstrably represent internally.
project: "The Road Not Taken: Ground-Truth Model Organisms and Counterfactual Attribution Methods for Suppressive Computation in Language Models"
question: When a language model fails to produce a behavior it internally represents (the correct answer, a refusal, a hazard flag), which components actively suppress that behavior — and do existing circuit-discovery and attribution methods find them?
first_experiment: Train a small (2–4 layer) transformer on a synthetic cue-triggered suppression task whose inhibitory circuit is known by construction (the model computes the contextually-supported token in early layers but must emit a distractor whenever a cue appears, forcing a planted veto pathway; verify the pathway by targeted ablations). Then run the standard pipelines on it — attribution patching, path patching, ACDC, and a CLT attribution graph trained with the community-recommended recipe, anchored on the realized output — and measure each method's "suppression recall" (does the true suppressor appear in the discovered circuit at all, with what rank and sign?). The expected quantified miss-rate of standard tools is the paper's headline number and directly motivates the fix: counterfactual-anchored attribution (attributing the realized-vs-counterfactual logit difference with ablation-based, sign-preserving edge scores), validated on the organisms and then applied to a real knowledge-action failure in Gemma-2-2B using public cross-layer transcoders.
why: It is (1) *explicitly* named as unresolved by the attribution-graph authors themselves ("why didn't the model do X?" / suppressive edges) and by the field's consensus open-problems review, which notes negative and backup components are missed by methods that maximize task performance; (2) verified empty — 18 months of explosive automation around attribution graphs (labeling, describing, merging, querying) have not produced a general suppression-attribution method or ground-truth benchmark, while every adjacent niche (sycophancy, CoT faithfulness, evaluation awareness, steering, anomaly detection) is crowded; (3) high-leverage: it mechanistically underpins the field's declared comparative advantage — auditing unsafe cognition (deception, sandbagging, sycophancy) — and offers the first mechanistic diagnosis of the 2026 "interpretability without actionability" result, potentially overturning its pessimistic conclusion by showing naive steering targets the wrong node while suppressing the actual veto pathway fixes behavior with less collateral damage; (4) it simultaneously attacks the field's #1 methodological gap (validation) via constructible ground-truth organisms, borrowing proven silent-pathway planting methodology; and (5) it is tractable now — open weights, public transcoders, and cheap interventions on a single GPU. It has not been done because attribution graphs are anchored on the realized output, their pruning and gradient attribution inherit a bias toward the actual answer's positive pathways, and the field's energy has flowed to automating positive-path explanations — leaving "the computation that didn't happen" systematically unexamined.

direction: Attack the field's acknowledged #1 bottleneck — the dual basis problem — by turning mechanistic explanation validation into active model discrimination: design inputs and interventions that maximally dissociate competing circuit hypotheses, and rank decompositions by held-out dissociation accuracy instead of aesthetics.
project: Adversarial Decomposition Discrimination — Circuit Hypotheses as Falsifiable Predictions
question: When multiple decompositions of the same model equally reproduce behavior on the distribution they were discovered on, can actively designed inputs and interventions dissociate their behavioral predictions, and does "dissociation accuracy" — predictive accuracy on constructed discriminating experiments — provide a principled, non-circular standard for ranking mechanistic explanations of a model?
first_experiment: On GPT-2 small with IOI (TransformerLens + public artifacts), formalize four competing circuit hypotheses — the Wang et al. IOI circuit, an ACDC-extracted circuit, an EAP-IG circuit from MIB, and a transcoder-based attribution-graph circuit — as behavioral predictors of intervention outcomes; run a structured search (over names, orderings, distractors, repeated names, and templates) to generate input sets that maximally separate these hypotheses' predicted ablation/patching effects; then measure each hypothesis's real predictive accuracy under intervention on its dissociating sets. Outcomes: hypotheses that tie on-distribution but split on designed inputs establish the dual basis problem as empirically consequential and give the field its tie-breaker; hypotheses that agree everywhere is an equally publishable robustness result. Either way, the metric and dissociating test sets become the deliverable, extensible next to Greater-Than, Arithmetic, and attribution-graph hypotheses on Llama-3.2-1B.
why: It targets the problem that both the Sharkey et al. review (via its own definition of understanding as prediction on arbitrary inputs) and the 2026 state-of-field review place at the very top — the validation/verification gap and the dual basis problem — while every adjacent work stops short of it: MIB benchmarks methods on fixed tasks and fixed counterfactuals; Certified Circuits certifies one algorithm under dataset edits; Méloux et al. prove non-identifiability in toy models and call for predictive/manipulability standards without constructing them on real LMs; Bucketing and the variance papers passively diagnose single hypotheses on natural inputs; none imports experimental-design theory to actively discriminate between decompositions, which is precisely the gap between "many circuits, one mechanism" being observed and the field having any principled way to choose among them. It is cheap to start (GPT-2, public circuit artifacts), it directly serves safety (monitors and steering built on unvalidated decompositions are the field's live liability, as the CLT-unfaithfulness result shows), and its artifacts — a standard metric plus reusable dissociating test sets — are immediately adoptable by MIB, the auditing-games community, and attribution-graph practitioners alike.

direction: I will work on making mechanistic (latent-space) monitoring robust to adaptive evasion — or determining rigorously that it cannot be — by building an escalating suite of evasion model organisms, mapping the capability–evasion–detectability frontier, and developing label-free "meta-monitors" that detect the act of hiding itself.
project: Catching the Hider: Label-Free Detection and the Price of Adaptive Evasion of Mechanistic Monitors
question: When a model adapts to evade latent-space monitors, is the act of hiding itself detectable — do structural signatures of evasion (verdict/context-conditioned activation edits, migration into low-dimensional subspaces, residual excess computation) yield a label-free meta-monitor that stays robust as evasion organisms escalate, and what does evasion cost in capability as monitor diversity and task difficulty grow?
first_experiment: Reproduce the cheapest evasion organism with public code (Neural-Chameleon-style rank-1 LoRA or RL-Obfuscation on Qwen2.5-1.5B/Llama-3.2-1B), train the standard monitor suite (linear, max-pool, attention-pool, MLP probes), confirm evasion success and capability retention; then, on the same organism, run the cheapest label-free meta-monitor — a probe on context-conditional activation sensitivity (same forced response content, trigger/verdict context present vs. absent) — and test whether it flags evasion attempts at 1% FPR on benign traffic, including on the OOD-stealthy organism variant that defeats refit monitors and OOD detection.
why: Monitoring dangerous cognition is the review's top application goal and the one safety decision-relevant capability interpretability currently offers, yet its entire paradigm is being dismantled wave-by-wave by an attack literature while the defense side has only three uncoordinated papers and one explicit, unresolved chicken-and-egg problem (detecting evasion without evasion labels) left open in the newest work. It is tractable for me: organisms at 1–9B scale with published recipes and ground-truth labels (we know exactly which mechanism is hidden), which simultaneously supplies the field's missing validation-with-ground-truth. It has not been done: no standardized escalation benchmark of evasion organisms exists (each paper attacks only its own predecessors), no label-free meta-monitor has been built or adversarially stress-tested (SafetyNet covers only within-family activation geometry; AWM is still evadable; functional-attribution MAD has never been attacked), and the capability–evasion frontier is unquantified with contradictory scattered evidence ("negligible tax" vs. the SQL tax). Either outcome changes real decisions: a working meta-monitor and quantified evasion costs justify continued investment in latent monitoring; their failure tells labs to stop deploying probes as a primary defense and pivot to weight-space/functional and control-based approaches — and both results would come with a mechanistic account of *why* hiding works, i.e., which invariances between computation and representation monitors read and which models can exploit.

direction: Turn the field's top-ranked open problem — the "dual basis"/equifinality problem, where multiple decompositions of the same model each account for the same behavior in-distribution — into a quantitative science by adjudicating competing decompositions (SAE, transcoder, MLP-neuron, probe-subspace) through the divergence of their interventional predictions under distribution shift, and validating a selection criterion ("distributional interventional stability") against models with known ground-truth algorithms.
project: Adjudicating Equifinality: Ranking Competent Decompositions by Distributional Interventional Stability
question: When two or more feature decompositions of the same model each faithfully explain the same behavior on the observed distribution, (a) how much do their interventional predictions (component rankings, patching effects, monitor readouts) diverge on held-out and distribution-shifted inputs, and (b) can "distributional interventional stability" — the invariance of a decomposition's interventional component rankings across shift — serve as a principled, ground-truth-validatable criterion for selecting the decomposition that reflects the model's real mechanism rather than one admissible account among many?
first_experiment: On Gemma-2-2B (Gemma Scope SAEs) and Llama-3.1-8B, take the two behaviors where competing explanations already coexist in the literature — multi-hop city→state recall and subject–verb agreement — and re-derive the circuit for each behavior in at least three bases (residual/MLP SAE features via attribution patching; MLP pre-activation neurons via the public Transluce pipeline; supervised probe subspaces). Certify comparable in-distribution fidelity for all of them using a CIF-style anytime-valid metric, then run a fixed shift battery (template paraphrase, language swap, distractor insertion, entity substitution, compositional chain-lengthening) and measure, per decomposition: faithfulness decay, rank correlation of component importances across shifts, and agreement of behavioral readouts under identical interventions. The deliverable is the first quantitative "equifinality in-distribution, divergence under shift" curve across decomposition bases in a real transformer.
why: It attacks the single gap that the field's own 2026 retrospectives rank first: attributions graphs and feature monitors are being adopted as safety infrastructure while the choice among competing decompositions remains "an aesthetic decision." It is not already done: the non-identifiability result exists only for toy Boolean MLPs with no real-network equifinality measurements and no selection criterion (Méloux et al. 2025); faithfulness fragility was shown within a single basis, not between bases (Miller et al. 2024); CIF supplies uncertainty quantification but explicitly stops short of comparing decompositions across input distributions (Asiaee 2026); the neuron-basis paper demonstrates a rival basis but never head-to-head tests its divergence under shift against SAE/transcoder accounts (Arora et al. 2026); SAE consistency work covers only seed variance (ACL 2026); and existing validation efforts target individual feature labels, not whole decompositions. The payoff is concrete: it explains *mechanistically* why feature-level monitors fail out-of-distribution (the behavior-level MOOD finding), and yields a cheap, model-organism-validatable selection principle that makes monitors and attribution graphs trustworthy under shift — exactly the rigor the field says it now needs, runnable today on open models with public SAE releases and existing pipelines.

direction: Build the first causal, circuit-level account of how multi-step agents represent and update task state across trajectory steps, via cross-trajectory activation patching at step boundaries in open tool-using models.
project: Trajectory-State Circuits: A Causal Account of Task-State Tracking in Multi-Step Agents
question: Do tool-using LLM agents maintain a causally load-bearing internal task-state representation (subgoal, inventory, tool outcomes, progress) that persists across steps and drives later actions — or is state recomputed from scratch from re-encoded context each step — and which components write and read it?
first_experiment: Run Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on a controllable synthetic multi-step tool environment (key → door → locked chest grid-world in text form); extract residual-stream activations at each assistant-turn boundary; train linear readouts for ground-truth state variables; then cross-trajectory activation-patch candidate state-carrying positions/subspaces at step k and test whether the next action follows the donor's state or the recipient's context — a loaded state buffer, or a null showing per-step recomputation (itself a novel mechanistic explanation of long-horizon fragility).
why: Agent-level interpretability is today only correlational probe/SAE monitoring (tool-need, reward-hack, risk states) plus one security-specific causal study on prompt-injection role; attribution graphs and reasoning-trace work don't span trajectory steps, and behavioral work shows state persistence is exactly where agents break. The field's own 2026 review says safety-monitoring coverage is weakest under distribution shift and long horizons — this direction grounds agent monitors and interventions (e.g., state repair) in mechanism, uses mature tools on open models in an unexplored regime with a decisive first experiment, and produces reusable cross-step patching methodology; nobody has yet run the general program, so it is the highest-impact gap I can open before the field converges on it.

direction: Develop and empirically validate a *discriminative selection principle* for mechanistic explanations — treating explanation choice as hypothesis testing solved by "crucial experiments" (designed distribution shifts and interventional probes under which behaviorally-equivalent candidate mechanisms make divergent predictions), validated against organisms with known planted mechanisms, thereby converting the field's "dual basis problem" from an aesthetic choice into a measurable one.
project: Crucial Experiments for Mechanistic Explanations: Identifying the True Mechanism Among Behaviorally Equivalent Candidates
question: When multiple mechanistic explanations replicate a model's behavior equally well in-distribution, can designed distribution shifts and counterfactual interventions uniquely identify the true underlying mechanism — and what is the "identifiability curve" (how much discriminating power does each designed experiment buy, in-distribution faithfulness being known to fail)?
first_experiment: Train small attention-only transformers on modular addition (a+b mod p) with varying data fractions, where memorization (lookup table) and the Fourier trig-identity algorithm are exactly behaviorally equivalent on the training set and ground truth is verifiable by direct Fourier analysis of the QK/OV circuits; enumerate the equivalence class of candidate explanations — explicit algorithm hypotheses plus subgraph candidates from standard pipelines (ACDC, EAP-IG, CLT-style attribution) — then run a battery of designed discriminating conditions (unseen operand pairs, operand-frequency shifts, input noise, cross-modulus transfer, counterfactual simulation of internal variables like phase/lookup-key) and measure which selection criterion recovers the true mechanism where in-distribution faithfulness misranks.
why: It attacks the field's self-identified top methodological problem — the 2026 retrospective ranks it first, calling selection among decompositions "an aesthetic decision" — and uniquely sits in the gap between a saturated diagnosis literature (non-identifiability, equivalence classes, faithfulness misranking) and an empty solution literature: existing work either documents multiplicity (Méloux, Bayat Makou, Mahale), certifies a method's stability (Anani, July 2026 e-values), or predicts OOD behavior from one hand-picked mechanism (Huang) — none discriminates among competing mechanisms against known ground truth. It is directly load-bearing for safety: audits with a 73% claim-flip rate, deployed activation monitors, and evasion-vulnerable monitor structures all fail or succeed depending on whether the claimed mechanism is the true one; and it is tractable — small models, the grokking fruit-fly setup, existing InterpBench/MIB-style infrastructure, and a cheap first experiment with a crisp, publishable outcome either way (if OOD-discriminative power selects the true mechanism, we have the field's first validated faithfulness-adjacent metric; if it doesn't, we have the first quantified evidence that mechanisms are underdetermined even under designed shifts, which is equally important).

direction: Build and ground-truth-validate an adjudication protocol and scoring rule for mechanistic explanations — a way to choose, by measurement rather than aesthetics, among multiple distinct decompositions/circuits/attribution graphs that all pass standard faithfulness on the same behavior.
project: Adjudicating Degenerate Mechanisms: A Ground-Truth-Validated Protocol for Choosing Among Competing Interpretability Explanations
question: When multiple distinct explanations of the same model behavior (component circuits from different thresholds/seeds; feature-level attribution graphs from different SAE seeds, widths, and gate functions; transcoder graphs) all pass standard intervention faithfulness on the evaluation distribution, which discriminating criteria — out-of-distribution faithfulness, error reproduction, intervention specificity, robustness to nuisance rewrites, cross-condition transfer, and principled parsimony — reliably identify the model's true mechanism, and can they be combined into a single validated "mechanism recovery score" that dominates faithfulness alone?
first_experiment: A controlled degeneracy study with known ground truth: take GPT-2-small on IOI (known manual circuit, MIB task) plus one InterpBench model with a planted mechanism, and build a panel of ≥15 rival explanations that all pass standard KL/logit-diff faithfulness — ACDC/EAP-IG circuits under varied thresholds, bootstrap resamples and ablation settings; attribution graphs from ≥5 SAE checkpoints (different seeds, widths, TopK/JumpReLU/ReLU); and equally-sized controlled-edit variants. Then run the discriminating battery (error agreement on the model's failures, negative-control specificity tests, token-frequency-band and paraphrase transfer tests, cross-seed graph-operator comparison via the margin protocol) and score every candidate structurally and causally against the known mechanism, measuring how often each criterion ranks the true mechanism first. Falsifiable prediction: standard faithfulness ranks the true mechanism first well under 50% of the time among passing candidates, while the composite does substantially better.
why: It is the field's own top-priority open problem — the generalized dual basis problem and the missing standard faithfulness score — named as such in the 2026 state-of-field review, and it directly gates safety value, since production feature-level monitors inherit an arbitrary decomposition choice. It has not been done because the adjacent works each stop one step short: non-identifiability is proven only in toy models without a real-model protocol; instability and seed-dependence studies quantify the disease but never adjudicate; the misranking and error-reproduction papers expose single metric pathologies rather than building a validated multi-criterion rule; consensus/ensemble methods aggregate without ground truth; the explanatory-virtues framework is conceptual without operationalization; and discovery benchmarks (MIB, InterpBench) validate discovery methods, never selection among passing explanations. Degeneracy is also structurally invisible to researchers who use a single decomposition, and the ground-truth infrastructure needed to make adjudication an empirical question (InterpBench, MIB, controlled-edit machinery) only matured in 2024–2026 — making this both the highest-leverage and the newly-answerable gap.

direction: Develop and validate a ground-truth-anchored, intervention-based adjudication protocol that distinguishes genuine circuit mechanisms from counterfeit decompositions of the same behavior, replacing ablation-faithfulness as the field's evaluation objective for mechanistic claims.
project: Circuit Adjudication — Held-Out Interventional Discrimination of Genuine vs. Counterfeit Decompositions
question: When multiple decompositions of a model all reproduce its behavior on the construction distribution, can a pre-registered family of structurally-targeted held-out interventions — chosen by structural divergence between rival causal graphs, not by their scores — reliably identify the decomposition that tracks the model's actual computation, and can that judgment be certified with anytime-valid statistics?
first_experiment: Reproduce the counterfeit phenomenon in a Boolean toy model with known ground truth (train a cross-layer transcoder under sparsity penalties to induce the shallow rewrite of a deep multi-hop circuit), then test the core hypothesis: standard replacement-score faithfulness fails to separate genuine from counterfeit (in-distribution blindness), while interventions targeting the intermediate variable of the deep pathway — present in the genuine graph, absent from the counterfeit — cleanly separate them; validate the metric's discriminative power against ground truth on InterpBench before extending to GPT-2 IOI/Greater-Than and CLT-based attribution graphs on Gemma-2-2B.
why: It is the constructive response to the field's single most-identified open problem — attribution-graph faithfulness and the dual-basis/identification gap, flagged by the consensus Open Problems paper, elevated to top priority by the 2026 retrospective, empirically exposed by Miller 2024, Makelov 2024, Geng 2026, Li & Subramani 2026, and the ICML 2026 CLT-unfaithfulness result, and demanded as a norm by the 2026 position paper on identification assumptions — yet every one of those works stops at diagnosis, and the adjacent constructive work (iSAE identifiability, CIF statistics, MIB localization, unit-test specificity, per-feature validation) targets different objects, leaving the between-decomposition adjudication protocol unclaimed. It is tractable with open tooling and modest compute, its results upstream and strengthen nearly every other interpretability application (auditing, monitoring, editing, cross-model transfer), and it converts "validation is not identification" from a warning into a working identification strategy.

direction: Build and ground-truth-validate an "explanatory generalization" score that adjudicates among equally in-distribution-faithful competing mechanistic explanations by testing each candidate's algorithmically-derived predictions about model behavior on held-out inputs and interventions outside its discovery distribution.
project: Breaking the Tie: A Ground-Truth-Validated Explanatory Generalization Score for Competing Mechanistic Explanations
question: When two circuits or attribution graphs are statistically indistinguishable in faithfulness on the distribution they were discovered on, does a pre-registered battery of out-of-distribution prediction tests (algorithm-derived prompt variants, token-distribution shifts, interchange interventions on held-out algorithm-variable values, and exact model-error reproduction) reliably rank the true mechanism above impostor candidates — and can this be packaged as a calibrated, anytime-valid score that would have caught the field's known failures (romantic-object IOI failures, S2-hacking, unreproduced errors, misranked discovery outputs)?
first_experiment: The impostor test: take the GPT-2 small IOI reference circuit and an InterpBench planted-mechanism model; generate ~50 size-matched impostor circuits via controlled edge edits optimized to match in-distribution KL faithfulness; verify reference-vs-impostor in-distribution faithfulness ties with confidence sequences; run a four-family battery (frequency-band shifts, prompt-variant matrix plus DoubleIO/TripleIO, held-out-variable interchange interventions, exact-error agreement) and measure true-vs-impostor classification — hypothesis: in-distribution faithfulness alone is at chance while the battery separates them.
why: It targets the problem the field's own 2025 coalition document and its 2026 retrospective rank first (the dual-basis problem, faithfulness as a non-circular numerical target), at the moment a dense wave of 2024–2026 papers — Méloux et al.'s non-identifiability proof, phantom specialization, explanation multiplicity, faithfulness misranking, error-blindness, metric non-robustness — has each diagnosed the problem and explicitly stopped short of a validated solution; the closest works are disjoint (Li et al.'s predictive objective is observational and toy-scale, unit tests cover specificity not predictive adequacy, CIF supplies statistics without a criterion, MIB/InterpBench supply an unused validation substrate), so the synthesis — a criterion validated where ground truth is known, then applied to re-adjudicate published-circuit disputes — is unclaimed, cheap to run on existing tooling, and produces a reusable community artifact that turns explanation selection from an aesthetic choice into a measured, certifiable one.
