direction: Make faithfulness of feature-level circuit explanations a measurable, non-circular quantity by validating decompositions as standalone replacement models whose behavioral predictions must survive input distribution shift, and using that held-out generalization fidelity to discriminate among the equivalence class of on-distribution-equivalent decompositions.
project: Generalization Fidelity — Held-Out Behavioral Validation of Attribution-Graph Decompositions
question: When two feature-level decompositions (transcoder dictionaries / attribution-graph replacement models) of the same model are statistically indistinguishable in on-distribution faithfulness, does their replacement-model fidelity on distribution-shifted and compositional inputs (a) diverge, and (b) rank the true mechanism — including distinguishing faithful decompositions from sparsity-incentivized shallow rewrites — above what on-distribution faithfulness can achieve?
first_experiment: On GPT-2 small with the greater-than task (known mechanism from Hanna et al.), take ≥5 transcoder variants (public CLT from Goodfire/circuit-tracer plus cheaply retrained PLTs/CLTs varying seed, width, and sparsity penalty), build each decomposition's replacement model on the standard discovery prompts, then evaluate replacement-vs-full-model agreement (KL / logit-diff) on an OOD suite: far and century-boundary years, lexical and token-frequency-band shifts (Makou et al. protocol), and the benign subpopulations uit de Bos identified. Decision rule: if ID-fidelity rank correlates ~1 with OOD-fidelity rank and gaps are negligible, the discriminator is empirically weak and I publish the negative result; if ID-equivalent decompositions diverge OOD, I proceed to ground-truth calibration — verifying on InterpBench models and the ICML 2026 Boolean toy that OOD fidelity prefers the planted multi-hop mechanism over its behavior-matching shallow rewrite — then apply the validated metric to compare PLT vs CLT circuit interpretations on Llama-3.2-1B / Gemma-2-2B.
why: It attacks the field's self-identified #1 bottleneck — verification of an exploding pile of unvalidated decompositions — with a metric that is non-circular by construction: it scores predictions about the *intact* model on inputs the decomposition never saw, so it cannot be gamed by refitting to the evaluation distribution, and it avoids the context-distortion failure Geng et al. showed invalidates ablation-based scores. It has not been done because (1) attribution-graph tooling only became reproducible outside Anthropic in mid-2025 (circuit-tracer, CLT-Forge, public dictionaries), so the replacement model could only recently be "just run" on arbitrary eval sets; (2) the field's evaluation habit is ablation-centric — replacement score is treated as a per-prompt sanity check, not a generalization target, because circuits were framed as explaining one behavior on one prompt; and (3) the shallow-rewrite failure mode that makes OOD shift a *discriminator* rather than a mere robustness stress test was only documented in 2026, so the diagnosis (ICML 2026) and the detector (this project) have not yet been connected. It is tractable solo with one GPU and open artifacts, it directly serves safety applications that need to know when an explanation stops tracking the model, and every outcome is informative: a positive result gives the field its missing standard faithfulness number; a negative result empirically bounds the dual basis problem.

direction: Develop held-out interventional generalization as a principled, measurable criterion for mechanistic explanations, and use it to lift families of per-prompt attribution graphs into prompt-family-level algorithmic circuit schemas that can be validated, compared, and selected among rival decompositions of the same model.
project: From Execution Traces to Algorithms: Interventional Generalization as a Selection Criterion for Circuit Explanations
question: Can a circuit hypothesis's ability to predict a model's behavior on held-out prompts and held-out interventions (inputs and interventions unused in constructing the hypothesis) serve as a tractable, principled criterion for (a) merging per-prompt attribution graphs into general algorithm-level circuit schemas with bound variables, and (b) selecting among observationally-equivalent rival decompositions (e.g., deep monotone-threshold circuits vs. shallow lookup/parity rewrites from CLTs/PLTs)?
first_experiment: On GPT-2 small (open transcoders via circuit-tracer) with the greater-than task: generate attribution graphs for ~50 training prompts, canonicalize features across prompts into role-groups (input-year detectors, suppression/promotion gates, parity/lookup distractors), formalize the two rival causal schemas the literature already implies (Hanna-style monotone threshold vs. CLT-style heuristic mixture), then on 50 held-out prompts measure each schema's predicted vs. actual logit shifts under interventions it never saw (ablating role-groups; patching input-year feature activations to out-of-distribution years crossing the 17YY boundary). Report an interventional-fidelity score with CIF-style confidence sequences, alongside the standard in-distribution replacement score as a control; sanity-check the metric itself on an InterpBench/weight-sparse model where the true circuit is known by verifying it ranks the true algorithm above an observationally-equivalent shallow rewrite.
why: It attacks the field's self-declared #1 gap — three independent authoritative sources (Sharkey et al. 2025, the 2026 retrospective, and the multi-org circuits landscape report) converge on faithfulness verification, the dual-basis problem, and "traces vs. algorithms" as the top unsolved methodological issues, and the landscape report explicitly lists graph merging as future work. It has not been done because until recently the pieces didn't exist: open CLTs/circuit-tracer (2025), ground-truth models with released weights (InterpBench 2024; OpenAI weight-sparse transformers, Nov 2025), and certification statistics (CIF, mid-2026) all arrived in the last 18 months, and the closest neighbors each stop short — Méloux et al. prove non-identifiability but leave the predictive/manipulability standard undeveloped; Li et al. demonstrate OOD-predictability only with attention patterns in toy models, not circuit-tracing pipelines or decomposition selection; the ICML 2026 unfaithful-CLT paper diagnoses the deep→shallow rewrite without offering a criterion to reject it; Goodfire observed rival decompositions but analyzed a single prompt qualitatively. The combination — construction of general schemas from trace families plus interventional-generalization scoring, validated on known-ground-truth models — is unclaimed, is runnable at GPT-2/Gemma-2B scale on modest compute with fast iteration, and if it works it upgrades every downstream use of circuit tracing (auditing, monitoring, feature validation) by replacing an aesthetic judgment about decompositions with a number.

direction: Pursue automated, decomposition-agnostic, distribution-shift-aware causal validation of mechanistic explanations — the field's named-but-unsolved verification bottleneck.
project: ScrubBench: Held-Out Causal Validation of Mechanistic Explanations Under Distribution Shift
question: Do equally faithful circuit explanations from different decompositions diverge on out-of-distribution inputs, and can a context-distortion-corrected scrubbing-style metric predict which explanation's causal claims survive the shift?
first_experiment: Extract IOI/Greater-Than circuits for the same model from ≥3 decomposition bases (EAP-IG, SAE features, transcoders, published reference circuits), verify matched in-distribution faithfulness, then measure their divergence and OOD faithfulness gaps on compositional distribution shifts (novel templates, distractors, orders), testing whether scrubbing-style context-corrected validation predicts OOD survival better than standard faithfulness.
why: It is the top named open problem of the field's own 2026 retrospection — the dual basis problem — now made urgent by ICML 2026 evidence that the flagship attribution-graph method learns unfaithful circuits, by demonstrated misranking failures of the standard faithfulness metric, and by the collapse of trust in unsupervised readouts (GDM's SAE deprioritization), yet no existing work provides the metric, the OOD axis, or the multi-decomposition comparison: MIB is in-distribution-only, the misranking paper stops at diagnosis, the CLT paper is toy-only, causal scrubbing was never automated, and equivalence frameworks are theory — making this both the highest-leverage and demonstrably unoccupied direction, tractable on small models with public infrastructure.

direction: Mechanistically characterize — at the circuit and feature level, with causal cross-trajectory activation patching — how multi-turn LLM agents write, carry, read, and lose their goal/constraint state, and build a mechanism-grounded goal-anchoring intervention from that account.
project: Anchored Agents: A Causal Mechanistic Account of Goal-State Maintenance and Drift in Multi-Turn LLM Agents
question: Where does an agent's active goal state live across turns, is it causally used or merely decodable, and does drift arise from state decay, state overwriting, or read-path failure — and can a mechanism-grounded anchor restore adherence better than probes, reminders, or naive steering?
first_experiment: Collect matched compliant/drifting ReAct-agent trajectories on ALFWorld + constraint-tracking tasks (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B), localize goal state with probes and SAE features per turn, then cross-trajectory patch goal-state activations/features between the paired runs at matched steps, sweeping layers and positions, to test causal use and decompose drift into decay vs. overwriting vs. read-path failure.
why: It targets the explicitly-open causal question at the heart of the newest wave of agentic interpretability (whose 2026 papers are probe/attention/steering-level only), it is safety-critical as agents deploy at scale, and it is freshly tractable because every ingredient — open-weight models with public SAEs, drift-elicitation benchmarks, patching/circuit-tracing tooling — now exists but the cross-turn patching methodology has not yet been attempted by anyone.

direction: Develop and validate a distribution-shift-and-intervention "stress-test" protocol that adjudicates between behavior-equivalent attribution-graph decompositions — using semi-synthetic transformers with compiled ground-truth deep multi-hop circuits to extend InterpBench to the circuit-tracing era and turn faithfulness of attribution graphs from an aesthetic judgment into a measurable, non-circular metric.
project: Deep or Shallow? Ground-Truth Adjudication of Attribution Graphs under Distribution Shift
question: When two attribution graphs both account for a model's behavior in-distribution but imply different mechanisms (a true deep multi-hop chain vs. a sparsity-induced shallow rewrite), can out-of-distribution and interventional predictive adequacy discriminate the faithful decomposition — and how often does standard circuit tracing actually produce the unfaithful rewrite in realistic models?
first_experiment: On a small transformer with a compiled known 3-step multi-hop algorithm (SIIT-trained, InterpBench-style, plus the Boolean toy model from the ICML 2026 paper), train a standard JumpReLU cross-layer transcoder with circuit-tracer/CLT-Forge, extract attribution graphs, and measure three things: (1) ground-truth graph match — does the recovered graph trace the deep chain or a shallow sum; (2) standard in-distribution replacement score for both candidate graphs; (3) the key test — held-out OOD predictive adequacy: on compositional variants of the task and targeted interventions that the decomposition never saw, does the shallow-rewrite graph's predicted behavior diverge from the model while the deep-chain graph tracks it? All single-GPU scale on GPT-2-small/Gemma-2-2B with existing open tools.
why: It attacks the field's self-identified #1 problem of 2026 — the dual-basis/faithfulness gap — on the artifact the field has standardized on (attribution graphs), converting a freshly published failure mode (ICML 2026's unfaithful-rewrite result, which stopped at "preliminary evidence" with no detection method) into a benchmark, a diagnostic metric, and a mitigation path; it implements the 2025 Open Problems review's own proposed fix (ground-truth benchmarks) for the era's dominant method, which InterpBench predates and MIB does not cover (natural models, in-distribution interventions only); and it is tractable at single-GPU scale with mature open infrastructure (circuit-tracer, CLT-Forge, InterpBench code) — with a guaranteed-informative outcome either way. It has not been done: no CLT/transcoder evaluation exists on InterpBench or any compiled ground-truth model, no study quantifies rewrite frequency or OOD-detectability in realistic or natural models, and every existing faithfulness tool (replacement score, ablation-based metrics, feature-level e-processes) validates behavior-matching in-distribution rather than adjudicating between mechanism hypotheses — the field still ranks decompositions "by how readable their labels are."

direction: Build a validated, non-circular selection criterion for the dual basis problem — adjudicating among behaviorally-equivalent decompositions by which one best predicts the model's real behavior on disagreement-maximizing held-out inputs and interventions, validated against ground-truth mechanisms.
project: Adjudicating Decompositions: Ground-Truth-Validated Selection Among Behaviorally Equivalent Mechanistic Explanations via Disagreement-Weighted Behavioral Prediction
question: When multiple decompositions (circuits, SAE dictionaries, transcoder graphs) reproduce a model's behavior equally well on the distribution where they were discovered, does a criterion of "expected behavioral prediction error, weighted toward inputs where the candidate replacement models maximally diverge, including interventional and distribution-shifted queries" reliably rank the model's true mechanism above impostor decompositions — and does it outperform in-distribution faithfulness, stability consensus, and structural-overlap metrics, which demonstrably misrank?
first_experiment: On a grokked modular-addition transformer (mod p, known Fourier/trig-identity mechanism, fully enumerable 2D input space), construct a candidate zoo — the ground-truth Fourier decomposition, an SAE decomposition, a random-rotation dictionary matched in reconstruction error and sparsity, and an ID-behavior-matched impostor (e.g., a lookup/cyclic hybrid chart) — verify all candidates tie on standard in-distribution faithfulness metrics (replicating known non-identifiability), then exhaustively enumerate all p² input pairs, compute where candidate replacement models diverge, and test whether prediction error on the top disagreement inputs ranks the true decomposition first; report separation (AUC of true-vs-impostor ranking) for the disagreement-weighted criterion against in-distribution KL, CIRCUS-style stability scores, and edge-overlap baselines, before scaling the same protocol to InterpBench IOI/SIIT models and then to Gemma-2-2B with Gemma Scope SAEs versus matched-rotation controls.
why: It attacks the field's self-identified top bottleneck — verification infrastructure lagged labeling, the dual basis problem is unsolved, and choosing among decompositions is still aesthetic (2026 field retrospectives; Geng et al. Oct 2026 quantified that current faithfulness metrics prefer the behaviorally worse circuit in 13–24% of pairs) — and every downstream goal (deployment-grade monitors, alignment audits, EU AI Act "general logic" filings, cross-model transfer) is gated on it. It has not been done because the field's energy went to scaling decomposition rather than verification: the identifiability work (Méloux et al. 2025) proved non-identifiability and stopped at suggesting predictive standards; the 2026 responses handle narrower problems (CIRCUS: threshold variance; Koopman: an identifiable-but-not-legible spectral object; implementation charts: local ranks of fully pre-specified hypotheses, explicitly not inferring mechanisms from behavior; interpretive equivalence: cross-model representation matching); and the ground-truth infrastructure needed to validate a selection criterion (InterpBench, SIIT, GrokkingToolbox, Gemma Scope, open circuit-tracing) only matured in 2025–2026, so the decisive experiment was barely runnable before now. Success produces the interpretability analogue of top-1 accuracy — a shared, non-circular, adversarially robust faithfulness standard — while failure even on designed ground-truth models is a fundamental negative result that would force the field to abandon behavioral adjudication and redirect effort, making the direction valuable either way, cheap enough for one researcher, and central rather than peripheral to AI safety.

direction: Make out-of-distribution predictive adequacy the operational test of mechanistic explanations by systematically stress-testing feature-level circuits (SAE/transcoder/attribution-graph circuits) — the field's dominant but least-validated artifact — for seed-induced non-uniqueness, error non-reproduction, and shift fragility, and developing a "validity profile" metric that ranks explanations by where and why they stop tracking the model.
project: Validity Profiles for Feature-Level Circuits: Stress-Testing the Dominant Artifact of Mechanistic Interpretability
question: Do SAE/transcoder feature circuits that are equally faithful on their extraction distribution diverge in their predictions of model behavior under distribution shift, extraction-seed variation, and on model errors — and can a cheap, non-circular "validity profile" (shift-family agreement curve + error-reproduction rate) distinguish and rank explanations that standard faithfulness metrics cannot?
first_experiment: On GPT-2 small layer 9, train five SAEs identical except for seed, extract the IOI feature circuit from each with the same method and threshold, then measure each circuit's (a) in-distribution faithfulness (KL and exact-match under ablation), (b) cross-seed node/edge overlap, and (c) agreement with the full model on held-out shift families: token-frequency bands, novel noun/name lists, template variants (DoubleIO-style), benign subtask slices (romantic-object-style), and naturally occurring model errors. If in-distribution faithfulness is uniformly high while out-of-distribution agreement varies widely across seeds, this establishes that standard evaluation is blind to the property that matters — the founding result for the validity-profile metric.
why: It attacks the field's self-identified #1 open problem (faithfulness/verification, the dual basis problem) at the level of the artifact the field now overwhelmingly produces — feature circuits and attribution graphs — where the extensive 2024–2026 circuit-validity literature (adversarial evaluation, equivalence classes, error reproduction, self-repair, transferability) has not yet reached, and where SAE seed/width/threshold choices multiply the degrees of freedom that generate interchangeable-but-divergent explanations. It is not already done: the closest works test either feature *quality* (Korznikov et al.'s frozen baselines) or *component-level* circuit validity (Makou et al., Zhang et al., uit de Bos & Garriga-Alonso), not feature-level explanation validity under shift and seed variation; it is cheap enough to run at small scale with public tooling while scaling cleanly to Gemma-2-2B attribution graphs; it converts a contested philosophical question into a quantitative, adoptable metric; and it yields deployable guidance (when can a feature-based monitor be trusted?) that the field's current verification gap leaves entirely unaddressed.

direction: Replace aesthetic selection of circuit explanations with a quantitative standard — rank causal decompositions (especially attribution graphs) by how well they predict the model's response to interventions on inputs they were not built from, and treat held-out mechanism failure as an anomaly signal.
project: Circuits That Generalize: Predictive Faithfulness as a Standard for Causal Circuit Explanations
question: When a causal explanation of a model's behavior (an attribution graph, SAE circuit, or component-level circuit) is fitted on a seed distribution, how much of its apparent faithfulness is memorization of that seed distribution versus genuine mechanism — measured as held-out intervention prediction across a taxonomy of input shifts — and can that number discriminate between rival decompositions of the same model and flag inputs processed by anomalous mechanisms?
first_experiment: On Gemma-2-2B with Anthropic's open circuit-tracer, generate attribution graphs for one well-defined behavior (numerical comparison / greater-than) on a ~50-prompt seed set; then, on ~500 held-out prompts spanning lexical, compositional, positional, and frequency-band shifts, compute Predictive Faithfulness = rank correlation between each graph's predicted effect (from its linear edge weights and feature ablation structure) and the model's actual output change under the same interventions — reporting error-node mass as an unexplained-computation term, under three ablation schemes (resample/mean/optimal) to check ranking stability — and compare the transcoder decomposition against (a) a random-feature decomposition control and (b) a component-level circuit, testing the core premise cheaply on one GPU before scaling to planted-circuit organisms (InterpBench-style, with normal + backdoor mechanisms as ground truth) and a mechanism-family anomaly detector.
why: It attacks the field's #1 self-identified gap — named independently by the 2026 Open Problems retrospective (the dual basis problem, "the open problem I would put at the top of any new survey," and faithfulness as a missing standard number), by Sharkey et al.'s validation critique, by Miller et al.'s non-robustness finding, and by the attribution-graph creators' own open-questions list (automated validation, merging graphs into global pictures, verifiable downstream tasks) — while MIB, the field's benchmark, explicitly covers only same-distribution localization and the closest papers (phantom specialization, error-reproduction, adversarial evaluation) diagnose the problem without providing the standard, the decomposition ranking, the attribution-graph application, or the ground-truth and anomaly-detection bridges. It is high-leverage (trusted-by-default explanations are the prerequisite for every safety application — monitoring, auditing, editing — and DeepMind's own pragmatic pivot shows the field currently distrusts its fancy methods), and it is tractable now: open-weight models, free public transcoders, existing organism and dataset infrastructure, single-GPU scale, with a decisive first experiment rather than a multi-year bet.

direction: Empirically adjudicate the dual basis problem by testing whether off-distribution interventional fidelity discriminates among equally-faithful competing mechanistic decompositions of the same behavior.
project: Which Circuit Is It? Off-Distribution Interventional Fidelity as an Adjudicator of Mechanistic Explanations
question: When multiple decompositions of one model behavior are equally faithful on the extraction distribution, can their interventional predictions under distribution shift (which components are irrelevant, which are core) reliably discriminate between them — and does the decomposition that wins OOD also steer and monitor best?
first_experiment: GPT-2 small + IOI: build three ≥95%-faithful decompositions (published 26-head circuit; EAP-IG circuit at a different sparsity; two seeded public-SAE latent circuits), run an OOD battery (DoubleIO/TripleIO, romantic-object subpopulation, paraphrase templates, frequency shifts) with ablations and patches, and measure whether each decomposition's irrelevance/core claims survive the shifts.
why: It targets the open problem the field's 2026 self-assessment ranks first, sits in verified empty territory between adjacent literatures (identifiability proofs, variance documentation, single-circuit adversarial evaluation, feature-label validation), is tractable with public tools on small models, and either outcome — a working decomposition selector with validity envelopes, or proof that behavior alone cannot resolve decompositional ambiguity — would materially redirect how mechanistic interpretability claims are certified.

direction: Turn the choice among multiple valid mechanistic decompositions (SAE seeds, architectures, analytic settings) from an aesthetic decision into an empirical one, by testing which decomposition's interventional predictions survive deliberate input distribution shift.
project: Which Circuit Is Real? Off-Distribution Interventional Validity as a Selection Principle for Mechanistic Decompositions
question: When multiple decompositions of the same network agree on in-distribution behavior, do their causal claims (predicted ablation/steering effects) diverge under distribution shift — and does off-distribution interventional agreement serve as a quantitative, principled criterion for selecting among them, with in-distribution identifiability (iSAE-style stability) failing to predict it?
first_experiment: A seed-pair divergence test — take ≥3 independently trained SAEs at the same layer of one model (public Pythia TopK dictionary pairs or Gemma Scope plus two self-retrained seeds), fix 1–2 behaviors with clean intervention semantics (factual recall, IOI-like), extract each decomposition's predicted ablation effects via attribution patching, then realize those ablations on (a) held-out in-distribution prompts and (b) systematically shifted prompt sets (paraphrase, new entity domains, negated/counterfactual contexts); measure predicted-vs-realized error, sign-flip rates of feature-importance rankings, and cross-seed agreement in-distribution vs. shifted. High in-distribution agreement with divergent shifted-condition rankings confirms the selection problem is real and measurable and launches the full program (architecture comparisons incl. iSAE vs. TopK vs. transcoders, multiple behaviors, and an open "OOD causal-validation" benchmark); universal agreement would itself be a publishable robustness result and pivot the comparison to decomposition-type level where theory predicts divergence.
why: It sits at the convergence of three gaps the field independently diagnosed in 2026 — the verification bottleneck (claims outrun validation), the dual-basis problem (ranked the field's #1 open methodological question, still resolved "aesthetically"), and the brittleness of interpretability-derived safety monitors under distribution shift — so progress on it serves all three at once, including regulatory use cases (EU AI Act filings need a defensible selection criterion). Every nearest-neighbor paper demonstrably stops one step short: non-identifiability was shown only in toy models with no criterion, instability was measured but never exploited as a discriminator, intervention attribution was proposed within single decompositions on held-out prompts rather than across decompositions under shift, and identifiability fixes were never causally stress-tested — the specific question "does off-distribution interventional validity discriminate among in-distribution-indistinguishable decompositions?" has not been posed, let alone answered. It also carries a falsifiable theoretical prediction (observational stability ≠ interventional robustness off-support), so it can produce a law-like claim rather than cartography; and it is tractable for an individual researcher using mature public infrastructure (Gemma Scope, Llama Scope, EleutherAI Pythia dictionaries, TransformerLens/nnsight) on ≤2B models, with the first experiment costing roughly one GPU-week.

direction: Build and validate a discriminating-test protocol that separates a model's true mechanism from the many behaviorally-equivalent "impostor" explanations that pass standard validation, quantifying the impostor rate on ground-truth model organisms.
project: Impostor Circuits: Certifying Mechanisms, Not Just Behavior — a Ground-Truth Benchmark for Discriminating True Mechanistic Explanations from Behaviorally-Equivalent Impostors
question: When multiple candidate mechanistic explanations (from different discovery methods, seeds, ablation choices, and metric settings) all pass the standard validation battery — faithfulness, sufficiency, necessity, consistency, specificity — what fraction are mechanistically wrong (the impostor rate), and what minimal, cost-bounded battery of additional tests (counterfactual inputs on which candidate algorithms diverge, targeted path interventions, weight-space checks, cross-model tests on behavior-matched/mechanism-different pairs) empirically identifies the true mechanism rather than merely a sufficient one?
first_experiment: On two ground-truth testbeds — an InterpBench Strict-IIT transformer with a planted IOI circuit and a grokked modular-addition transformer with a consensus reverse-engineered mechanism — generate a panel of ~50 candidate explanations: the planted/consensus circuit, variants produced by ACDC/EAP-IG/RelP across seeds, sparsity thresholds and the seven defensible ablation axes, plus deliberately constructed impostor algorithms (e.g., position-heuristic and shortcut implementations that achieve high faithfulness). Score every candidate on the standard battery and compute (a) the impostor rate under standard validation and (b) the detection power and cost of each additional discriminating test, starting with counterfactual input families engineered so the true algorithm and each impostor algorithm make divergent predictions. This yields the first ground-truth-anchored quantification of how underdetermined "the mechanism" is under standard validation, plus a provisional ranking of discriminating tests — then extend to feature-level candidates (SAE/transcoder-based) and the MO-lottery behavior-matched/mechanism-different model pairs.
why: It attacks the field's own #1 self-identified methodological gap — the dual basis problem and the verification bottleneck — which the 2026 state-of-field review puts above everything else ("which one is *the* circuit?" is currently "an aesthetic decision"), and it converts the field's pile of established negative results (non-identifiability, metric non-robustness, 73% claim-flip rates, non-specificity) into the missing constructive counterpart: a validated, cost-bounded protocol and open benchmark for certifying mechanisms. It has not been done because existing ground-truth infrastructure (InterpBench) was used only to score discovery methods on graph recovery, not validation protocols; the identifiability work (Méloux et al.) stopped at proving non-uniqueness in tiny Boolean MLPs without modern pipelines or discriminating tests; and the instability studies (Miller, Mahale, Li & Subramani, uit de Bos) measure disagreement and failure without ground truth or a positive solution — while the newly released InterpBench/SIIT models, consensus circuits, and the 157-model MO-lottery suite make this experiment tractable now at modest compute, with direct downstream leverage for safety monitors, alignment audits, and regulatory evidence.

direction: Build a divergence-designed, held-out interventional selection protocol that determines which of several equally-faithful competing decompositions is the model's real mechanism — the field's "dual basis problem" turned from a documented pathology into a solvable model-discrimination task.
project: Divergence Courts — Held-Out Interventional Discrimination of Competing Mechanistic Decompositions
question: Can interventions and inputs designed to maximize predicted disagreement between in-distribution-equally-faithful circuit/feature decompositions identify the true mechanism (validated on ground-truth testbeds), and can the protocol formally certify irreducible non-identifiability when behavioral discrimination is impossible?
first_experiment: Generate ≥12 in-distribution-faithful competing circuits for GPT-2 small on IOI (ACDC, EAP-IG, activation patching, manual circuit, seed/spec variants), then run a greedily divergence-maximizing battery of held-out IOI-variant prompts and ablations to test whether held-out interventional agreement separates them, whether the manual circuit and known error-relevant heads rank first without being used in the design, and whether ~50 chosen experiments match the full grid's discrimination.
why: The multiplicity problem is now measured to be severe (73% claim-flip rate, functionally uncorrelated circuits, error-blindness, CHIVE's no-uplift for current tools) and named the field's top open problem, yet all current remedies certify single claims or features rather than arbitrating among competing decompositions, and no one has imported model-discrimination experimental design into mechanistic interpretability despite open models, ground-truth testbeds (Tracr/InterpBench, the known Fourier addition mechanism), and free statistical machinery making it a tractable, de-risked, keystone-level contribution.

direction: Build and validate "interventional adjudication" — a principled, quantitative criterion that identifies the true mechanism among behaviorally-equivalent competing explanations of a neural network by testing each explanation's predictions under held-out interventions, using ground-truth models and adversarial decoy explanations.
project: The Arbiter: Held-Out Interventions as an Identifiability Criterion for Mechanistic Explanations
question: When multiple mechanistic explanations (circuits, SAE/transcoder dictionaries, attribution graphs) are statistically tied on standard faithfulness, can out-of-sample interventional predictive accuracy — how well each explanation forecasts the network's response to interventions it was never fitted on — identify the explanation that tracks the model's actual internal computation, and which families of interventions carry the discriminating signal?
first_experiment: On three ground-truth systems (an InterpBench SIIT transformer with a planted circuit, a grokked modular-arithmetic transformer whose Fourier algorithm is known, and a small transformer with a literature-known circuit like IOI), assemble a candidate explanation pool containing the true mechanism plus decoys — ACDC/transcoder/SAE-derived circuits from varied seeds and pruning thresholds, plus deliberately constructed "shallow-rewrite" decoys mirroring the ICML 2026 CLT failure mode — verify the pool is statistically tied on on-distribution faithfulness using anytime-valid tests, then score every candidate on predicting the network's output under a held-out battery of novel interventions (interchange interventions at novel abstraction sites, off-distribution patching directions, resampling vs. mean-ablation mismatches, weight resampling), and measure whether interventional out-of-sample accuracy recovers the true mechanism and which intervention families provide the separation.
why: It attacks the problem the field itself now ranks as most important — choosing among decompositions is currently "an aesthetic decision" — and it is upstream of every safety use of interpretability, since a monitor built on a shallow-rewrite decoy decomposition can certify a model while hiding the very multi-hop pathway you're monitoring for. It has not been done because the field's incentives rewarded discovery over adjudication; the underdetermination insight is recent (Makelov 2024, Méloux 2025, CLT-unfaithfulness 2026); the one formal attack (ISS, Sept 2026) treats networks as black boxes with pre-enumerated abstractions rather than connecting to the SAE/circuit/attribution-graph pipeline; and ground-truth benchmarks (InterpBench, grokking) were built to score discovery methods against their planted circuit, not turned into adversarial testbeds where decoy explanations compete with the truth. It is decisively testable either way — if held-out interventional accuracy recovers planted truth, the field gets its first non-circular faithfulness criterion; if it fails, we map exactly which interventions and explanation classes resist identification — and it is computationally tractable: small models, public tooling, no frontier-scale compute needed.

direction: Pursue the prescriptive side of the circuit-multiplicity ("dual basis") problem — map the input-distribution-relative validity regions of equally-faithful circuit decompositions, use worst-case validity as a principled ranking criterion replacing aesthetics, and exploit disagreement among valid decompositions as a mechanistic out-of-distribution monitoring signal.
project: Validity Regions: From Circuit Multiplicity to Principled Decomposition Selection and Mechanistic OOD Monitoring
question: For a fixed model and task, do the members of the equivalence class of "faithful" circuits have measurably different validity regions (nested vs. genuinely divergent across input distributions, including on the model's errors)? Can decompositions be ranked by worst-case validity so that selection transfers to truly unseen distributions, and does disagreement among equally-valid decompositions function as a detector of out-of-distribution inputs and behavioral drift, outperforming output-level uncertainty baselines?
first_experiment: On GPT-2 small with IOI and greater-than: extract ~20 candidate circuits per task using EAP-IG across varied defensible settings (data samples, prompt templates, frequency bands, ablation choices, seeds), then evaluate every circuit's faithfulness (KL, accuracy, and exact error-reproduction) across a grid of held-out evaluation distributions (template paraphrases, token-frequency bands, name-pool and position shifts, answer-flipping corruptions). Compute each circuit's validity region and the overlap structure of the class; test whether a worst-case-validity-selected "core" circuit beats single-distribution extraction and resampling-only certification on a truly unseen distribution. Runs on one GPU in days with existing open-source tooling (TransformerLens, MIB, Miller et al.'s faithfulness library).
why: It attacks what field-leading retrospectives now rank as the #1 methodological problem in mechanistic interpretability, at the exact moment the diagnosis literature has matured (five 2026 papers) and explicitly stopped short of prescription — so the timing window is open and the lane is not yet occupied. It has not been done because the diagnosis papers each scoped themselves out of it (Certified Circuits treats instability as noise under one perturbation family; "Explanation Multiplicity" states "we do not propose a better method"; "Demystifying Variance" concludes comprehensive circuits are unattainable without asking what to do instead), because a non-aesthetic criterion requires the unglamorous work of measuring behavior across distribution families rather than publishing a new extractor, and because turning ambiguity into a monitoring signal requires crossing the research/deployment boundary the field has only just begun to treat as first-class. Both possible outcomes are valuable: divergent validity regions yield a principled selection rule and a novel mechanistic OOD monitor; coinciding regions would deflate the dual-basis worry with the first quantified equivalence-class map — a genuine clarification either way.

direction: Mechanistically decompose evaluation awareness in real open-weight models that exhibit evaluation gaming, using feature-level causal interventions with adversarial controls to settle whether system-card steering claims reflect a genuine internal mechanism and to build internal monitors that catch unverbalized evaluation awareness.
project: "Auditing the Eval-Awareness Vector: Causal Feature-Level Decomposition and Monitoring of Evaluation Gaming in Open-Weight Agents"
question: When eval-awareness steering vectors suppress a model's "being evaluated" representations and misaligned behavior appears, is that effect mediated by a specific, identifiable internal eval-awareness mechanism (a causally validated feature/circuit that computes evaluation context and gates safety-relevant action), or by diffuse perturbation — and can the resulting internal representation be turned into a monitor that detects unverbalized evaluation awareness?
first_experiment: On the public eval-aware model organisms (Hua et al.; Qwen3.5 type-hint organism), then replicated at inference scale on GLM-5: (1) collect residual-stream activations on paired honeypot/deployment contexts matched in task content across multiple surface-form families; (2) train linear probes and extract differential SAE features for "evaluation context"; (3) run the decisive causal test — targeted ablation/patching of the probed direction and top features versus norm-matched random-direction and unrelated-contrastive-patch controls — registering in advance the prediction that a genuine mechanism shows dose-responsive, control-specific effects on verbalized awareness and misaligned-action rate (with MATH/BFCL as capability controls), while an artifact shows controls matching targeted effects, directly adjudicating the AISI/Anthropic steering controversy at feature level.
why: It attacks the field's most-diagnosed weakness (mechanistic claims, including safety-critical ones published in system cards, are unverified) at its highest-stakes point: evaluation gaming is the top challenge in Anthropic's own sabotage risk reporting, corrupts every capability and alignment eval, and defeats CoT monitoring when unverbalized. It is not already done: AISI stopped at behavioral correlations and global steering with disputed validity; organism work (ICML 2026) is synthetic and task-cosmetic; the compact-model mechanism paper concedes decodability ≠ causality and does no feature-level intervention; reward-hack agent monitoring covers a different latent state. The missing piece — a causally validated decomposition of the eval-awareness mechanism in a real evaluation-gaming model, with the adversarial controls AISI showed are necessary — just became feasible (GLM-5 open weights, public organisms, mature intervention tooling) and no team has published it, while both AISI and Apollo have explicitly called for exactly this white-box work.

direction: Build a discriminative validation framework that tests whether attribution graphs are mechanistically faithful — using counterfactual inputs designed to separate competing decompositions — converting the field's dominant artifact from an unfalsifiable description into a predictive, testable causal model.
project: Adversarial Discrimination Testing for Attribution Graphs: A Benchmark and Metric for Mechanistic Faithfulness
question: When two decompositions (e.g., a deep multi-hop pathway vs. a shallow shortcut rewrite) produce the same attribution graph behavior on the source prompt, does the graph's causal structure correctly predict the real model's counterfactual behavior on held-out discriminative inputs and interventions — and can we score that agreement as a standard, non-circular faithfulness metric validated against ground-truth organisms?
first_experiment: On Gemma-2-2B with public cross-layer transcoders (Circuit Tracer), take two-hop factual recall prompts where the hop-derived answer and the direct associative shortcut dissociate (e.g., "The state containing Dallas has its capital in" variants where association and relation conflict); establish ground truth for which pathway causally drives the answer via activation patching on the real model (the oracle); then test whether the attribution graph, treated as a simulator, predicts the model's response under interventions and on the discriminative held-out prompt set — measuring the gap between graph-predicted and actual counterfactual behavior alongside the (on-distribution) replacement score. A large gap with high replacement score is a clean, falsifiable demonstration that behavioral faithfulness masks mechanistic unfaithfulness in real LMs, and directly instantiates the proposed metric.
why: It attacks the field's top-ranked open problem — the June 2026 retrospective names attribution-graph faithfulness/the dual-basis problem as the most important methodological question and confirms no agreed quantitative measure exists, only an unverifiable pile of labeled graphs; the ICML 2026 result proves CLTs are incentivized toward behaviorally-equivalent-but-wrong rewrites yet stops at toy-model diagnosis with "preliminary" real-model evidence; InterpBench and MIB predate feature-level circuit tracing and evaluate head/edge methods; and the Aug 2025 multi-org replication explicitly lists automated discriminative validation (interventions + synthetic/OOD inputs for hypothesis testing) as open. It hasn't been done because the field's incentive gradient ran through generating graphs (7,000+ on Neuronpedia) faster than verifying them — labeling was automated while validation was not — and because mechanistic faithfulness requires new infrastructure (discriminative-input search against competing graph hypotheses plus a graph-as-simulator comparison), not just another ablation metric. Every other agenda I weighed (auditing, global circuit merging, cross-model transfer, deployment monitors) sits downstream of it, and AuditBench's finding that white-box tools underperform black-box ones is plausibly a symptom of exactly this missing validation layer.

direction: Build and validate a behavior-conditional, distribution-level causal "coverage" metric that quantifies how much of a model's computation for a target behavior is actually carried by a feature decomposition (SAE/CLT/attribution graph) versus hidden in its unexplained residual — turning faithfulness from an aesthetic judgment into a number that can rank competing decompositions and certify latent-space monitors.
project: Blind-Spot Certificates: Causal Coverage Audits for Feature Decompositions
question: For a decomposition D (SAE features, cross-layer transcoders, or a pruned attribution graph) and a behavior class B over a prompt distribution, what fraction of the causal computation supporting B flows through D's explained component versus its reconstruction residual — and does that coverage score predict when decomposition-based monitors, unlearning interventions, and steering will fail under attack and distribution shift?
first_experiment: The "explained/unexplained causal split" on two behaviors with gold standards — IOI on GPT-2-small (Wang et al.'s hand-verified circuit, public transcoders via circuit-tracer) and refusal on Gemma-2-2B (Arditi et al.'s direction, Gemma Scope SAEs): at each layer, causally run the model on (a) only the SAE/CLT reconstruction and (b) only the reconstruction residual, measuring behavioral retention of B over ~1,000 prompts (not single prompts) for B and for generic text. This yields the first coverage and residual-load curves C(B,D) and R(B,D) for real decompositions. Three testable predictions: (i) coverage is substantially below 1 even for the best-studied behaviors, quantifying the blind spot; (ii) residual load concentrates in identifiable layers/directions; (iii) coverage varies measurably across SAE seeds and objectives, reproducing seed non-uniqueness as a behavioral quantity rather than a cosine-similarity one. Immediately after, validate the metric on InterpBench's known-circuit transformers and the Boolean multi-hop toy model from the ICML 2026 CLT-unfaithfulness paper: does C(B,D) recover ground-truth completeness and flag the "deep multi-hop rewritten as shallow single-hop" failure that replacement score misses? Then test predictive validity by checking whether coverage scores forecast success rates of post-intervention recovery attacks (Cui et al.'s protocol) and obfuscation attacks (Bailey et al.'s protocol).
why: It attacks the gap that both the field's own coalition review and its 2026 retrospective place at the top of the priority list — faithfulness/verification — at exactly the point where it becomes safety-critical: latent-space monitors, unlearning, and steering are being deployed on decompositions whose completeness is unknown, and 2024–2026 results prove those decompositions have exploitable blind spots (recovery through the residual, obfuscated activations, seed non-uniqueness, CLT shallow-rewriting). The surrounding terrain is crowded but the center is empty: per-feature causal audits, per-task circuit faithfulness, global KL replacement scores, additivity residuals, and inclusion-stability certificates all exist, yet no one has built the behavior-conditional, distribution-level coverage instrument, validated it against ground-truth circuits, or shown it predicts monitor/intervention failure — a measurement that would do for interpretability what perplexity does for language modeling. It has not been done because the incentive gradient ran toward producing labeled features faster than verifying them (the documented asymmetry), because the negative results that create demand for the metric are all ≤2 years old, and because the ground-truth testbeds needed to validate it (InterpBench, the Boolean CLT model) only recently matured. It is tractable with public artifacts at 1–7B scale and modest compute, and success yields infrastructure the whole field would use: principled ranking of competing decompositions (resolving the dual basis problem), certification thresholds for deployment-grade monitors, and training objectives for the next generation of SAEs/transcoders.

direction: Non-circular adjudication of competing mechanistic explanations via held-out interventional generalization testing.
project: Judging Circuits by Their Predictions: Out-of-Sample Interventional Faithfulness as the Test of Mechanistic Explanations
question: Do circuit explanations that are equally faithful on their construction distribution diverge in their ability to predict model behavior under distribution shift, and can a held-out generalization gap serve as the field's first non-circular, quantitative metric for selecting among rival circuit decompositions?
first_experiment: Construct competing circuit explanations (CLT attribution graph, neuron-basis RelP circuit, SAE-feature circuit) for one multi-hop factual recall behavior in Gemma-2-2B using released checkpoints and pipelines, then measure each explanation's predictive divergence from the model on held-out prompts, depth-extended/novel-composition chains, and unseen intervention types, testing whether standard on-distribution faithfulness rankings invert under shift.
why: It targets the field's own top-ranked open problem (the dual-basis/faithfulness gap named in 2026 state-of-field reviews) precisely when it became live and remains unsolved — prior work only diagnoses non-identifiability on toys, statistically certifies single claims, or structurally compares bases without behavioral out-of-sample tests — while being executable today with public models, checkpoints, and tooling, and while providing the evidence standard that deployment-grade monitoring and steering depend on.

direction: Mechanistic faithfulness of learned replacement models — systematically measuring, detecting, and fixing when transcoders/CLTs/SAEs produce behaviorally-valid but mechanistically-wrong circuit explanations, since this is the upstream validity bottleneck for all circuit-based interpretability and its safety applications.
project: Faithful Circuit Tracing: Benchmarking, Detecting, and Preventing Mechanistic Unfaithfulness in Replacement Models
question: When and why do learned replacement models (CLTs, per-layer transcoders, SAEs) yield circuit explanations that preserve behavior but misdescribe the underlying computation (e.g., collapsing true multi-hop mechanisms into shallow rewrites), can we detect such unfaithfulness without access to ground truth, and can we train replacement models whose circuits are mechanistically faithful?
first_experiment: On GPT-2 Small performing the greater-than task (ground-truth mechanism fully characterized by Hanna et al. 2023, with Goodfire's replication as reference), plus one InterpBench SIIT model with a deeper known multi-hop circuit: train a sweep of CLTs and matched per-layer transcoders across sparsity coefficients, extract attribution-graph circuits on standardized prompts, and score each against ground truth on (i) *path coverage* — does the extracted circuit contain nodes realizing every required computational step — (ii) inferred mechanism depth vs. true depth, and (iii) standard behavioral faithfulness (KL under replacement). Hypothesis: behavioral faithfulness stays flat while path coverage degrades with sparsity pressure — demonstrating that the field's standard metrics are blind to mechanistic unfaithfulness, and establishing the benchmark's core metric.
why: (1) *Upstream of everything*: every headline result built on attribution graphs — deception analyses, introspection studies, unlearning audits — inherits this failure mode; an unfaithful circuit gives safety audits false assurance, making this the highest-leverage validity fix in the field right now. (2) *The field is explicitly asking for it*: the open-problems review ranks validation among the top problems, and both 2026 critique papers stop at demonstration ("preliminary evidence") while calling for better attribution of model-true structure. (3) *Not already done*: existing benchmarks (InterpBench, MIB) target edge-level circuit discovery, not replacement-model mechanisms; JSAE optimizes computation sparsity, not agreement with the model's actual computation; Goodfire validated one mechanism, not a metric; no ground-truth-free detector or faithfulness-aware training objective exists anywhere in the literature I searched. (4) *Tractable*: open-source tooling (circuit-tracer, CLT-Forge, InterpBench) and GPT-2-scale experiments make the first paper achievable in weeks, and its results benefit every decomposition method simultaneously — SAEs, transcoders, CLTs, Lorsa, crosscoders.

direction: Build a principled, quantitative, non-circular criterion for choosing among competing mechanistic explanations — arbitrate them by their held-out predictive power over the model's actual behavior under distribution shift, rather than by readability or on-distribution faithfulness.
project: Counterfactual Coverage — Arbitrating Competiting Mechanistic Explanations by Out-of-Distribution Predictive Power
question: When two or more decompositions (e.g., attention-head circuits, transcoder/SAE attribution graphs, subspace/DAS hypotheses) each faithfully replicate a model's behavior on the inputs they were discovered on, which one is "the circuit" — and does each explanation's ability to predict the full model's behavior (outputs and ablation effects) on held-out input families (paraphrases, entity swaps, distractors, length/context shifts) serve as a measurable, non-circular selection criterion that also predicts downstream utility (intervention robustness, monitor reliability under shift)?
first_experiment: On GPT-2 small (indirect object identification) and Gemma-2-2B (a factual-recall behavior using Gemma Scope SAEs/transcoders), construct 3+ competing decompositions per behavior via different method families; verify they all pass the standard on-distribution faithfulness bar; then generate held-out input families and measure each decomposition's predicted vs. the full model's actual ablation effects on them, yielding an "Explanatory Generalization Score" per candidate. Hypothesis: candidates that are statistically indistinguishable on-distribution will diverge sharply off-distribution, and that divergence will correlate with real intervention/editing success better than on-distribution faithfulness does.
why: (1) It attacks the field's own top-ranked open problem — the dual-basis/faithfulness gap — flagged by both the 2025 coalition document and the 2026 retrospective, and it is foundational: every downstream use (editing, monitoring, auditing) inherits the correctness of the chosen decomposition. (2) It is tractable for a small team: open weights ≤8B, public dictionaries (Gemma Scope, Llama Scope), mature tooling (TransformerLens, nnsight), and cheap per-experiment compute versus training-run-dependent agendas like developmental interpretability. (3) It is unifying: one score comparable across all decomposition families, something no current benchmark offers — MIB only scores on-distribution localization, the ICML 2026 anytime-valid work validates single features in isolation, Certified Circuits certifies component-inclusion stability under dataset subsampling on toy tasks, and Méloux et al. prove non-identifiability in toys without building the pragmatic arbiter they call for. (4) It is safety-load-bearing: interpretability-derived monitors already in production fail exactly under the distribution shift this metric measures, so success directly extends the (currently narrow) safety coverage the field has achieved. And it is not already done: my searches across identifiability, faithfulness-metric robustness, circuit certification, OOD monitoring, and cross-model transfer found no work that uses held-out behavioral prediction to arbitrate between competing whole-model decompositions on real language models — the closest neighbors each stop one step short, and a decisive negative result (e.g., no decomposition generalizes) would itself be an important, publishable finding about the limits of circuit-level claims.

direction: Turn mechanistic explanation selection into an empirical science by adjudicating rival decompositions through pre-registered forecasts of held-out, shifted, and error behavior rather than in-distribution faithfulness.
project: Explanations as Forecasts: Adjudicating Rival Decompositions by Out-of-Distribution Predictive Power
question: Which of several rival mechanistic explanations of the same in-distribution behavior best predicts the model's behavior on perturbed, shifted, and erroneous inputs, and do explanation rankings stable in-distribution diverge under distribution shift?
first_experiment: Pre-register behavioral forecasts from 3–4 rival IOI circuits on GPT-2 small (manual, automated, neuron-level), then score their forecast accuracy across five shift families plus the model's natural errors, testing whether the in-distribution faithfulness ranking survives shift.
why: It attacks the field's self-identified most important open problem (the dual-basis/faithfulness crisis) with a safety-critical payoff (shift-robust audits and monitors) using entirely public infrastructure, and it remains unclaimed because every neighboring work — Li et al.'s synthetic proof-of-concept, Méloux et al.'s non-identifiability result, Zhang et al.'s error-reproduction evaluation, and the ICML 2026 transcoder-unfaithfulness finding — stops exactly one step short of building the adjudication protocol on real language models.

direction: Build an automated adversarial validation agent that adjudicates between rival circuit/attribution-graph hypotheses by pre-registering their quantitative predictions on held-out discriminating inputs, turning mechanistic explanations from unfalsifiable stories into testable predictive theories.
project: HYDRA — Hypothesis-Yielding Discriminative Rigorous Adjudication for circuit explanations** (working title: "Circuit Hypotheses as Predictive Theories: Automated Adversarial Validation of Attribution Graphs")
question: Can rival mechanistic hypotheses of the same behavior — which are indistinguishable under standard ablation-based faithfulness on the construction distribution — be reliably separated by their pre-registered predictions on a designed suite of held-out, behavior-discriminating interventions (near-miss inputs, error-inducing inputs, OOD surface variants, suppressive-edge probes), and can this discriminative validation be automated into an agent that measurably shortens time-to-validated-hypothesis on auditing games with known ground truth?
first_experiment: On an InterpBench model whose true compiled circuit C* is known, construct 5–10 rival hypotheses R that are behavior-preserving on the construction distribution (via defensible analytic variation: ablation-scheme swaps, tie-randomized selections, error-node inclusion — exactly the variations Sheng & Fu and "Explanation Multiplicity" show are unconstrained), then pre-register C* and each R's predicted logit-margins under specified ablations on a held-out discriminating suite of minimal pairs, error-inducing prompts, and OOD variants. Success criterion: standard faithfulness cannot separate C* from R (replicating the known problem), while a new discriminative predictive accuracy (DPA) metric — the rate at which the hypothesis, not its rival, correctly predicts intervention outcomes on inputs neither was built from — separates true from rival hypotheses with large margin. If DPA separates where faithfulness cannot, scale the procedure into the automated agent and extend to real attribution graphs (Gemma-2-2B via circuit-tracer) and AuditBench organisms.
why: It attacks the field's self-identified #1 bottleneck — the verification gap and the dual basis problem — at exactly the moment when the problem has been demonstrated (error-reproduction failures, non-robust faithfulness, explanation multiplicity with EU AI Act stakes) but no discriminating solution exists; it is the prerequisite for every downstream application the Open Problems review cares about (monitoring, auditing, unlearning, safety cases all assume validated decompositions); and it is uniquely suited to an autonomous agent, whose comparative advantage — generating many rival hypotheses, designing discriminating experiments at scale, and enforcing strict pre-registration against its own motivated reasoning — is precisely what the GDM pragmatic vision and the Neuronpedia landscape report request under "automate the full hypothesis generation + validation loop." It has not already been done because the existing work stops one step short at each boundary: HyVE and the Pitfalls paper automate *explanation* and concede validation is the unsolved obstacle; Zhang et al. propose error-reproduction as a single necessary axis for one circuit, not rival adjudication; Sheng & Fu and "Explanation Multiplicity" only *diagnose* multiplicity in synthetic settings and propose reporting practices; Certified Circuits offers stability bounds, not falsification; and AuditBench/InterpBench exist as auditing benchmarks but have not been used to score hypothesis-discriminating validation power. The synthesis — rivals as first-class objects, pre-registered counterfactual predictions as the evidence standard, ground-truth organisms as the scoreboard, and an agent as the engine — is unclaimed.

direction: Build the missing validation layer for circuit tracing — an automated, falsification-first harness that scores attribution-graph circuit hypotheses by whether they survive held-out predictive tests and matched-random controls, replacing "looks interpretable + replacement score" with discriminative evidence.
project: Cross-Examining Circuits: An Automated Falsification Harness for Attribution-Graph Hypotheses
question: Can a standardized battery of automatically generated falsification tests — held-out minimal pairs, position/strength intervention sweeps with matched-random controls, and preregistered predictive-validity metrics — discriminate genuine attribution-graph circuit hypotheses from matched decoy graphs (edge-shuffled, corrupted-prompt, random-feature) that are indistinguishable under current validation practice, and what false-positive rate do current interpretability claims carry under this test?
first_experiment: Using Gemma-2-2B (and Llama-3.2-1B) with open cross-layer transcoders via Anthropic's circuit-tracer library, trace attribution graphs for a canonical two-hop reasoning behavior across ~50 prompts; construct a decoy battery (edge-shuffled graphs, graphs traced on corrupted prompts, random-active-feature graphs) verified to match the true graphs on replacement score, pruned-graph statistics, and LLM-judged label plausibility; then run the test battery — held-out minimal-pair predictions, steering/ablation position-and-strength sweeps with matched-random controls, and power-corrected effect estimates — and measure the AUC of each metric family at separating real graphs from decoys. Hypothesis: current standard metrics sit near chance; the falsification battery separates them substantially. Single GPU, open artifacts, directly runnable.
why: It attacks the field's top self-identified gap (the attribution-graph faithfulness/dual-basis problem named by both the 2025 open-problems review and the 2026 retrospective), at exactly the moment the automation wave on the generation side is compounding the pile of unvalidated artifacts — so the leverage grows over time, and it is upstream of several other goals (global circuit pictures, cross-architecture transfer, deployment-grade monitors, and trusting interpretability-derived safety audits all presuppose validated circuits). It is tractable with open models, open transcoders, open-source model organisms for calibration, and MIB infrastructure. It has not already been done: MIB benchmarks localization methods rather than validating mechanistic hypotheses; Certified Circuits provides dataset-perturbation stability guarantees at component granularity on vision models; null-model "dead salmon" tests calibrate representational claims, not circuit hypotheses; Miller et al. diagnosed ablation fragility without a fix; the poetry stress test is a single ad hoc check of one finding; and no published work constructs decoy circuits to measure whether any existing metric can tell a true circuit from an impostor — which is the minimal, decisive first step toward a faithfulness measure the field can agree on.

direction: Build ground-truth recovery audits for transcoder-based attribution-graph circuit tracing — measuring whether pruned graphs recover planted mechanisms (especially suppressive pathways) across competing decompositions — and use those audits to develop a non-circular faithfulness metric plus a cross-basis-disagreement detector of unfaithful circuits in real models.
project: TraceCheck: Ground-Truth Recovery Audits and a Cross-Basis Unfaithfulness Detector for Attribution-Graph Circuit Tracing
question: When and how do attribution graphs fail to faithfully describe the computation underlying a behavior — specifically, do they recover known and planted mechanisms including suppressive pathways, and can cross-basis (CLT vs. PLT vs. neuron) disagreement and threshold-instability, validated against ground truth, serve as a cheap detector of unfaithful graphs where no ground truth exists?
first_experiment: A quantitative recovery audit on GPT-2 Small greater-than (the rare mechanism that is ~50% suppressive by design, with Hanna et al.'s neuron-level ground truth): generate pruned attribution graphs with circuit-tracer (PLTs and community CLTs) over ~100 prompts spanning the input-year range, and measure (a) recall — whether graph features' interventions reproduce the known suppress/boost logit patterns, (b) precision — what fraction of high-attribution edges are load-bearing under targeted ablation, (c) whether suppressive pathways survive pruning at all, (d) cross-basis and threshold disagreement, and (e) whether any of these correlate with replacement score — testing at toy cost the hypotheses that suppression is systematically under-recovered and that disagreement predicts infidelity before scaling the audit suite to planted-mechanism organisms (fine-tuned Llama-3.2-1B / Gemma-2-2B with single-hop, multi-hop, and suppression-heavy planted circuits).
why: It attacks the field's own top-ranked open problem (non-circular faithfulness validation and the dual-basis problem) on its dominant artifact; it has not been done because existing ground-truth infrastructure (InterpBench, MIB, Geng et al.) targets head/edge-level circuit discovery rather than the 2025+ transcoder pipeline, the ICML 2026 unfaithfulness result is confined to Boolean toys with only "preliminary" LM evidence, Goodfire's greater-than work was qualitative and single-prompt, and the suppression gap has remained an explicitly named open question since the original attribution-graph papers — while all of it is executable on a single GPU with released CLTs/PLTs, Neuronpedia, circuit-tracer, and TransformerLens.

direction: Replace aesthetics with a testable criterion for which mechanistic explanation is real, by selecting among behaviorally equivalent candidate explanations via their predictive accuracy under held-out inputs and held-out intervention classes, validated against ground-truth systems with injected decoys.
project: Circuit Cross-Validation: Selecting the True Mechanism among Behaviorally Equivalent Explanations via Held-Out Interventional Prediction
question: Do candidate explanations that are behaviorally equivalent on the extraction distribution diverge under interventions and inputs not used during extraction, and can out-of-sample interventional predictive accuracy recover the true mechanism where one exists?
first_experiment: Generate ≥4 candidate explanations for GPT-2-small IOI and a post-grokking modular-arithmetic transformer (ACDC/resample, ACDC/mean, EAP-IG at two thresholds, one injected decoy), then evaluate all candidates on in-distribution fidelity, held-out input splits (including adversarial-benign subpopulations), and held-out intervention classes never used in extraction, testing whether they tie in-distribution but separate out-of-sample with the ground-truth mechanism ranked first.
why: It directly attacks the field's top-ranked open problem — non-uniqueness of decomposition, where 2024–2026 work (Méloux et al., Many Circuits One Mechanism, Adversarial Circuit Evaluation, CIF, InterpBench, CIRCUS) has completed the diagnosis but no one has built or validated a constructive selection criterion, and the result is valuable either way: a deployable selection protocol and benchmark if interventions discriminate, or a demonstration that simplicity priors must carry the load if they do not.

direction: Build and adversarially stress-test a circuit-level monitor — using transcoder attribution-graph structure (feature pathways, error-node mass, attention routing) rather than activation values — to determine whether obfuscated harmful computation necessarily leaves detectable traces in the model's causal circuit.
project: GHOSTTRACE — Do obfuscated activations leave fingerprints in the circuit? Attribution-graph monitors under adaptive obfuscation attacks
question: When a model produces harmful output through activations engineered to look benign to SAEs, probes, and OOD detectors, where does the harmful computation go in the causal graph (transcoder feature paths vs. frozen attention vs. error nodes), and can the structure of the computation itself serve as an obfuscation-resistant monitoring signal — or can an adaptive attacker obfuscate the circuit too?
first_experiment: On Llama-3.2-1b (supported by open circuit-tracer), generate harmful outputs under (a) benign prompts, (b) standard jailbreaks, and (c) published obfuscation attacks trained against SAE+probe+OOD monitors (Bailey et al.'s public attack code/artifacts); run cross-layer-transcoder attribution graphs on all generations and compute simple graph-level statistics (error-node mass per layer/token, feature-path similarity to the benign graph distribution, attention-mediated vs. feature-mediated path mass); then test a single classifier on these graph features alone — recall@1%FPR on obfuscated harmful traffic that the original activation monitors score as benign. If graph statistics separate obfuscated from benign computation, follow up with adaptive co-evolution of attacks against the graph monitor (their 70-iteration protocol) and attention-aware monitors; if not, localize the hiding channel — both outcomes decide whether mechanism-level monitoring belongs in safety cases.
why: It attacks the sharpest known failure of interpretability's flagship application (latent monitoring) with the field's newest and most mechanism-faithful tool, at exactly the point the Open Problems review says is needed ("mechanism-level understanding rather than single features"). It is tractable now — open models, public obfuscation artifacts, single-GPU tracing tools, an established adaptive-attack protocol, and crisp metrics (recall@1%FPR under attack, attack-budget curves) — and every outcome is informative: a robust signal creates a new monitor family; a bypassed signal quantifies attribution graphs' frozen-attention/error-node blind spots and justifies parameter-space or output-side monitors instead. It has not been done: every published obfuscation result (Bailey et al. 2024; RL-Obfuscation 2025; feedback-evasion 2026; the OAT case study 2026) targets activation-value monitors; the only circuit-level safety analysis (deception via transcoders, 2026) involves no adversary; and the closest robust method (functional-attribution MAD, 2026) deliberately bypasses the model's circuit rather than reading it — leaving the middle ground, the causal circuit itself under adaptive attack, empty and decisive.

direction: Build the field's missing verification standard — an adversarial, held-out "behavioral completeness" score that measures how much of a behavior can be recovered through what a mechanistic explanation (circuit, SAE, transcoder, attribution graph) does *not* explain, and use it to non-circularly rank equivalent decompositions and certify interventions under distribution shift.
project: Residual Stress-Testing: A Held-Out Behavioral Completeness Standard for Mechanistic Explanations
question: When two decompositions of the same model both account for a behavior on the distribution where they were extracted, can a constrained optimization in the unexplained residual space — on held-out distributions disjoint from extraction — produce a stable, non-circular "residual leakage" score that ranks them, and does that ranking predict which explanation's interventions and monitors actually survive distribution shift?
first_experiment: On GPT-2 small with the IOI task, take three behaviorally equivalent explanations (the manual Wang et al. IOI circuit, an EAP-IG circuit, and a top-k SAE-feature circuit from public residual SAEs), freeze each explanation's components, then run encoder-orthogonal residual-space optimization (the "SAE Interventions are Unreliable" methodology, generalized to head/edge circuits) to recover the behavior on (i) the extraction distribution and (ii) three held-out families — token-frequency-band lexical shifts, distractor/structure shifts, and template-format shifts — and measure the residual recovery rate of each explanation per family; the hypothesis is that in-distribution recovery is statistically indistinguishable across explanations while held-out recovery diverges into a stable ranking (consistent across attack seeds), demonstrating that held-out adversarial residual leakage is a measurable, non-circular selection criterion — the seed of a reusable benchmark.
why: It attacks the gap that the field's own coalition review, its 18-month retrospective, the sanity-check literature, and the identifiability literature all independently nominate as the top open problem — the dual-basis/verification bottleneck — at the moment the diagnosis phase (2024–2026 failure-documentation) has just completed and nothing prescriptive exists; it has not been done because the nearest prior works each cover only one slice (component-stability certification, single-feature statistical testing, four-setting attack demos, one-task transfer tests) and none combine adversarial residual search + held-out distribution design + decomposition-agnostic scoring into a comparative standard; it is tractable with small models and public artifacts rather than frontier compute; and it is maximally leveraged: a consensus score disciplines every downstream interpretability claim, directly enables safety-critical certification of feature-based monitors under the distribution shift that the 2026 review says is growing the coverage gap, and converts "which decomposition is the mechanism?" from an aesthetic judgment into a measurement — the same maturation that turned image classification and language modeling into quantitative sciences.

direction: Attack the "dual basis" problem — validation of mechanistic explanations — by building model organisms with known ground-truth mechanisms and behaviorally-equivalent planted decoys, quantifying the false-assurance rate of current attribution-graph/circuit validation practice, and developing a principled, agreed mechanism-faithfulness protocol.
project: Decoy Circuits — Measuring and Eliminating False Assurance in Mechanistic Explanations of LLMs
question: When multiple feature decompositions / attribution graphs are behaviorally equivalent on the evaluation distribution, which validation procedures reliably identify the mechanism the model actually uses — and what is the false-assurance rate of current practice (reconstruction loss, ablation faithfulness/completeness, max-activating examples, auto-interpretability scores, steering success) on organisms with planted decoy mechanisms and hidden parallel pathways?
first_experiment: Construct a small (~1–2 layer) transformer — trained, or Tracr/InterpBench-compiled — on a synthetic task where a "shortcut" pathway and the "true rule" pathway are behaviorally confounded by data construction, so both independently produce correct outputs on-distribution; run the standard circuit-tracing pipeline (train transcoders → extract attribution graphs → compute faithfulness/completeness scores → auto-label features) for each pathway's components, and test whether (a) standard scores distinguish true from decoy (predicted: no — near-identical on-distribution scores), and (b) a held-out decorrelation set exposes the difference detectably *without* ground-truth knowledge, via each graph's interchange-intervention predictions on decorrelated inputs (predicted: yes — establishing that the ambiguity is real, measurable, and cheaply resolvable, the seed result for the full stress-test suite and mechanism-faithfulness scorecard).
why: It is the field's own top-ranked open problem (validation was flagged by Sharkey et al. 2025 and named the defining gap of 2026 by retrospective review), with concrete demonstrated failures in the safety-relevant setting (post-intervention recovery via unexplained residuals; random-baseline SAEs matching trained ones; contested synthetic testbeds; non-robust faithfulness metrics); it sits upstream of every downstream application (white-box evals, mechanistic anomaly detection, unlearning/editing, deployment monitors), and it is tractable now on open small models because the enabling infrastructure — open-source circuit tracing, InterpBench ground-truth organisms, e-process statistics for interpretable FDR control, recovery-path attribution diagnostics — only matured in 2025–2026.
