It has not been done: existing work validates individual features (anytime-valid testing), task-level circuit localization (MIB), tiny-vision architectural circuits with robustness guarantees (Formal MI), or feature recovery in synthetic SAE setups (Sanity Checks and its rebuttal) — but no one has planted behaviorally-equivalent decoy mechanisms and hidden pathways in transformer organisms, measured how often current pipelines certify the impostor, or produced the non-circular, agreed-upon mechanism-faithfulness protocol the field now says it needs.

direction: Make mechanistic explanations falsifiable — rank competing feature bases (neurons vs. SAE features vs. transcoders) by how well their discovered circuits *predict* model behavior and internal counterfactuals on systematically shifted held-out inputs, rather than by how they explain the discovery distribution.
project: Circuits Under Shift: A Held-Out Prediction Benchmark for Ranking Mechanistic Decompositions
question: When circuits discovered on the same task by different decompositions (neuron basis, SAE feature basis, cross-layer transcoder basis) are treated as hypotheses about the model's algorithm, do they tie on in-distribution fidelity yet diverge in predictive validity on systematically shifted inputs (novel entities, paraphrase templates, distractor insertion, hop-count extension, reversed directions, task composition) — and does one basis systematically retain mechanistic validity under shift, resolving which decomposition is "the circuit" rather than merely *a* circuit?
first_experiment: On Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (public SAEs + Circuit Tracer checkpoints available), take the two-hop city→country→capital task for which both a transcoder-based attribution graph (Lindsey et al. 2025) and a neuron-basis circuit (Transluce 2026) already exist; rediscover circuits in three bases (neuron+RelP, Llama Scope SAEs, transcoders) on a fixed discovery distribution; use an LLM to auto-generate six held-out transformation families (unseen entities, paraphrases, distractor chains, 2→3-hop extensions, reversed-hop probes, composed tasks); measure each basis's predictive ablation fidelity, minimality-under-shift, and component rediscovery overlap per family, testing whether in-distribution ties break out-of-distribution.
why: Three independent authoritative sources name it the field's most important open problem — the 2026 state-of-the-field review calls the dual basis problem "the open problem I would put at the top of any new survey" and demands a faithfulness metric "the way perplexity does for LMs"; the attribution-graph creators explicitly list "automate intervention experiments and synthetic/OOD inputs for hypothesis validation" as an open project; and the first-principles doc names falsifiability of circuits as the validation problem — yet every existing effort covers only one facet: MIB is in-distribution, Certified Circuits certifies dataset-subsampling stability, the ICML 2026 unit tests check specificity of single claims, and anytime-valid tests validate individual features, none of which rank decompositions by held-out mechanistic prediction under semantic shift. The neuron-vs-SAE comparison that would make its first experiment decisive was published only in 2026 and deliberately left OOD discrimination open, so the field is actively contesting basis choice with no principled criterion while infrastructure defaults (Gemma Scope, Llama Scope) propagate unexamined — meaning the result will redirect real effort whether the learned-feature or neuron basis wins, the pipeline doubles as reusable safety infrastructure (telling practitioners whether an interpretability-derived monitor will survive deployment distribution shift), and the automated test-generation loop is precisely the kind of high-throughput comparative work an autonomous agent can execute on open models at single-GPU scale.

direction: Run the first controlled, quantitative scaling study of mechanistic understanding itself — measuring how the consistency, specificity, faithfulness, and shift-robustness of feature/component circuits change across the Gemma 3 scale ladder (270M→27B) using the uniform Gemma Scope 2 dictionary suite.
project: Does Understanding Scale? A Controlled Scaling Study of the Trustworthiness of Mechanistic Explanations
question: Using a fixed dictionary recipe (Gemma Scope 2 SAEs/transcoders) and a fixed task suite with validated metrics, how do the properties that make mechanistic explanations trustworthy — within-task consistency across examples, cross-task specificity, causal faithfulness (necessity/sufficiency coverage), cross-seed/decomposition stability, and robustness of validated causal claims to distribution shift — change as model scale increases from 270M to 27B parameters?
first_experiment: A three-scale pilot (Gemma 3 270M, 1B, 4B) replicating the Li & Subramani protocol with EAP-IG and RelP at component level, plus feature-level circuits from Gemma Scope 2 transcoders, on four tasks (Addition, IOI, CopyColors-MCQA, ARC-Easy) plus one safety behavior (refusal): compute per-example circuit overlap (consistency), cross-task overlap and cross-task ablation damage (specificity), and necessity/sufficiency effect sizes, then plot each property against scale and test the trend with statistical tests (Shi et al.-style). A collapse or improvement between 270M and 4B on any property is already a headline result and decides whether to push to 12B/27B and add the distribution-shift axis.
why: It attacks the field's most strategic untested assumption — that interpretability knowledge gained on small models transfers to capable models — which every safety argument built on model organisms, interp benchmarks, and interp-derived monitors silently relies on; the 2026 retrospective and Open Problems papers both flag it as under-researched, yet no study measures explanation properties as a function of scale. It has not been done because the enabling infrastructure is only ~11 months old (Gemma Scope 2 is the first matched-recipe dictionary suite spanning five scales — earlier cross-model work confounded scale with architecture and SAE recipe), because the validation-metric toolkit (consistency, specificity, certified fidelity, margin statistics) only matured in 2025–2026, and because the field's energy went to within-model validation rather than across-scale testing; the closest works (Li & Subramani's consistency/specificity across five mixed models, Saphra et al.'s synthetic proof-of-concept, the Pythia-160M margin study) each hold scale constant or top out at toy scale, and all explicitly leave this question open. Unlike the now-crowded faithfulness-verification cluster, this direction is connective rather than competitive: it gives those validation metrics their missing axis, it is fully runnable on open weights and public dictionaries without frontier-lab resources, and both possible outcomes (degradation or stability of understanding with scale) decisively reshape how interpretability can be used for AI safety assurance.

direction: Operationalize the dual-basis problem into a constructive, non-circular validation science: discriminate among competing mechanistic hypotheses (circuits, attribution graphs, feature sets) by their held-out predictive accuracy on inputs constructed to separate them, replacing aesthetic choice with behavioral falsification.
project: Explanation Fingerprinting — Held-Out Discriminative Validation of Competing Mechanistic Hypotheses
question: When multiple decompositions (manual circuits, ACDC/SP-discovered circuits, SAE/transcoder-derived attribution graphs) all faithfully reproduce a model's behavior on the distribution they were validated on, which decomposition actually tracks the model's mechanism — and can automatically constructed held-out "discriminating probes" separate them with a metric that standard faithfulness cannot, yielding the field's first agreed-upon numerical faithfulness score?
first_experiment: On GPT-2 small's IOI task, take the published manual circuit (Wang et al.), an automated circuit (ACDC/EAP-IG), an SAE/transcoder-derived feature graph, and a size-matched random circuit as dead-salmon control — all tuned to comparable in-distribution faithfulness (KL/logit-diff under ablation on the ABC template set). Generate a held-out suite of ~10 programmatic prompt-variant families where these hypotheses make different behavioral predictions (word-order permutations, subject-repetition structures like DoubleIO/TripleIO, name-frequency shifts, distractor insertion, pronoun substitution), ~1k prompts each. For each hypothesis and family, measure how well ablation/restoration per that hypothesis predicts the model's actual behavior, quantify hypothesis-vs-hypothesis disagreement with bootstrap CIs, and test the key claim: in-distribution faithfulness fails to predict held-out divergence, while discriminating probes separate hypotheses that standard metrics tie.
why: (1) It attacks the intersection of the two gaps the field's own 2026 retrospective ranks highest — the verification bottleneck and the dual basis problem — and turns a diagnosed-but-unoperationalized crisis into a constructive protocol, metric, and benchmark ("the way image classification has top-1 accuracy"). (2) It has not been done: identifiability work stopped at toy scale; validation work stops at same-distribution agreement, error-reproduction, per-feature causal testing, or dataset-stability certification — none ranks competing *whole decompositions* by held-out behavioral discrimination on real models, and no automated discriminating-input search exists. (3) It is high-leverage quality control for every incumbent agenda rather than competition with any: SAE features, transcoders, attribution graphs, and interpretability agents all currently ship without it, while interpretability-derived production monitors and alignment audits are exactly the artifacts that would silently fail under distribution shift or adversarial pressure if built on the wrong decomposition. (4) It is tractable on open models with Gemma Scope and published circuits — the first experiment is a few GPU-days — and prior results (S2 Hacking, error-reproduction failures) give strong priors that the discriminating signal exists to be found.

direction: Build a causal "basis arbitration" protocol that tests whether circuits discovered for the same behavior in different feature bases of the same model (raw MLP neurons, SAE features, transcoder/CLT features) describe one mechanism or basis-relative artifacts, using cross-basis intervention equivalence and distribution-shift divergence tests.
project: One Mechanism, Many Bases — Causal Arbitration of Competing Circuit Decompositions in Language Models
question: For a fixed behavior in a fixed model, do circuits discovered in independent feature bases refer to the same underlying computation — i.e., do interventions on one basis's circuit predict and reproduce the causal effects of interventions on another's, and do the bases converge or diverge under template and distribution shift — or is at least one of them a decomposition artifact?
first_experiment: On Gemma-2-2B (and replication on Llama-3.1-8B), discover circuits for subject–verb agreement (Marks et al. 2025 benchmark) in three bases — raw pre-activation MLP neurons with RelP attribution (Transluce pipeline), Gemma Scope SAE features with attribution patching (sparse feature circuits), and head/edge level EAP-IG (MIB harness) — then measure "cross-basis causal coverage": the fraction of each circuit's causal effect on the task metric that is reproduced when intervening only on the components another basis identifies, repeated across template-shifted and OOD prompt sets, with divergence locations checked against the SAE reconstruction residual.
why: It directly attacks the field's own #1 named open problem of 2026 — the dual-basis/verification gap, where choosing among decompositions is "an aesthetic decision" — at the exact moment it became empirically ripe, because 2026 delivered viable competing bases (neuron-basis circuits rivaling SAEs; transcoder features shown partly seed-unstable) with open implementations, and 2026 evidence that SAE-based interventions and monitors can silently fail through basis artifacts. It has not been done: the closest works each cover only one slice — within-basis variance and equivalence classes (Wu et al.; Bayat Makou et al., explicitly excluding feature-level analysis), within-basis dataset-edit certification (Anani et al.), weight-level feature comparison without behavior-level circuits or shift tests (Shabalin & Piotrowski; Arora et al.), SAE-residual bypass without cross-basis comparison (Cui et al.), and toy-model non-identifiability without real-LM tests (Méloux et al.) — and my searches found no cross-method, cross-basis causal arbitration study on real language models. Both outcomes are decisive: high cross-basis coverage validates the attribution-graph research program and gives safety monitors a non-circular validation gate; low coverage is the field-level warning that published circuits are basis-relative and needs the follow-on search for basis-invariant mechanisms.

direction: Operationalize the dual basis problem by turning competing, behaviorally-equivalent mechanistic explanations into falsifiable out-of-distribution predictions and letting the model's own behavior on disagreement inputs adjudicate between them.
project: Circuit Court — Adjudicating Competing Mechanistic Explanations by Their Out-of-Distribution Predictions
question: When two mechanistic explanations of the same model behavior are equally faithful on the distribution they were discovered on, does searching for inputs where they diverge from each other — and testing the full model there — produce a statistically certified, non-circular ranking of which explanation actually tracks the model's mechanism out of distribution?
first_experiment: On GPT-2 small / IOI, assemble a candidate pool of ~10 circuits (the manual Wang et al. circuit plus automated circuits sampled from the published multiverse grid) pre-screened to be ≥95% faithful on the standard IOI distribution under matched ablation; hide the model's outputs, run a genetic search over benign prompt variations (names, objects, verbs, positions, duplications) to maximize pairwise KL divergence between the circuits' predicted output distributions; then reveal the model's outputs on the top disagreement prompts and compute each circuit's agreement rate with the model there, with anytime-valid confidence bounds — establishing whether "adjudication gaps" exist at all and whether on-distribution faithfulness ties break out-of-distribution.
why: It attacks the question a mid-2026 state-of-field review ranks as the field's single most important open methodological problem, at the exact moment five 2025–26 diagnostic papers (Méloux, Bayat Makou, Sheng & Fu, Mahale, Zhang et al.) have established that multiplicity is real and severe but none has proposed a selection procedure — Mahale explicitly declines adjudication, and the closest active method (Adversarial Circuit Evaluation, 2024) falsifies single circuits within the task distribution rather than discriminating between rival explanations, so the pairwise-divergence search, the non-circularity guarantee (model outputs hidden during input search), and the certified adjudication ranking are all genuinely new. It is the most promising direction because it is cheap (small models, public artifacts and code, days not GPU-months), safety-critical (monitors and regulatory filings built on an explanation that mispredicts out of distribution are exactly the failure mode audits need to exclude), and dual-outcome: either it gives the field its missing "perplexity for explanations" — a principled, game-resistant metric for selecting among decompositions — or it proves behavioral evidence cannot identify mechanisms at all, which would force the field onto intrinsic criteria and is itself a landmark negative result.

direction: Automate the induction of global, input-conditional algorithms from families of per-prompt attribution graphs — turning circuit tracing from single-prompt execution traces into recovered, testable model-level algorithms.
project: From Traces to Algorithms: Automatic Induction of Global Circuits from Families of Attribution Graphs
question: Can the family of per-prompt attribution graphs induced by a distribution of prompts be automatically aligned and merged into a single input-conditional algorithm that predicts the model's held-out internal computation and outputs (including its characteristic failure modes), and does this global object expose per-prompt unfaithfulness (shallow rewrites, feature-splitting artifacts) that single-prompt behavioral matching cannot?
first_experiment: On 2-operand addition in GPT-2/Llama-3.2-1B using public CLTs and neuron-basis RelP circuits, generate ~200 attribution graphs for random (a, b) across the trained digit range; cluster features by attribution profiles and decoder-direction similarity, align graphs across prompts, and test four things — (1) compression: what fraction of graph structure is shared across prompts; (2) held-out prediction: does the merged graph predict feature activations and branch points (carry/no-carry, digit-range conditions) on fresh prompts; (3) ground truth: does it recover the known trigonometric/helix-and-carry structure of addition that per-prompt transcoder graphs fail to surface; (4) failure modes: does it reproduce the model's out-of-range and multi-operand (lookahead-limited) generalization boundary. Kill criterion: if per-prompt graphs share no alignable skeleton even on this most regular task, the direction fails fast and cheaply.
why: It targets the single most-repeated, most-consequential limitation admitted by the people who built attribution graphs ("execution traces, not algorithms"; "can we merge attribution graphs into a global circuit picture?"), and it is the natural answer to the 2026 faithfulness crisis: an explanation that matches behavior on one prompt proves little, but an algorithm that predicts branch structure, activations, and generalization boundaries across a prompt distribution — including out-of-distribution — is a falsifiable causal-abstraction claim that shallow rewrites and decomposition artifacts will fail. It has not been done because cross-prompt feature identity only became tractable with CLTs/RelP attribution profiles in 2025–2026, and the automation energy of 2026 went into describing single graphs and diffing models rather than inducing algorithms; adjacent work (ADAG, Circuit Oracle, CircuitLasso, DAS/bucketing, Physics-of-LM canonicalization, RASP decompilation) is all per-graph, per-task, weight-space, or restricted to purpose-trained toy models — none merges graph families into general algorithms on pretrained LLMs, and "bag of heuristics" evidence shows exactly the kind of global structure that only a family-of-graphs method can adjudicate. The first experiment is cheap, uses public checkpoints and known ground truth, and either way produces a reusable artifact: an "algorithm recovery" metric the field currently lacks.

direction: Build ground-truth-free stress tests that determine whether attribution graphs extracted from real language models describe the model's actual mechanism or a sparsity-induced shallow rewrite, using cross-dictionary disagreement and held-out interventional prediction gaps.
project: Shortcut Stress Tests for Circuit Tracing — detecting unfaithful attribution graphs without ground truth
question: When an attribution graph matches model behavior, does it describe the computation the model actually performs, or a sparsity-preferred shallow rewrite — and can the difference be detected without ground truth by (a) divergence between counterfactual predictions of graphs built from independent dictionaries of the same model, and (b) the gap between graph-predicted and measured interventional effects on held-out, distribution-shifted inputs engineered to load the deep pathway?
first_experiment: On Gemma-2-2B (fallback: Llama-3.2-1B), for a latent two-hop factual-recall task, extract attribution graphs for the same prompt set from ≥4 independent dictionaries at matched replacement score — per-layer transcoders across a sparsity-penalty sweep and seed replicates, plus off-the-shelf Gemma Scope SAEs and (if feasible) one CLT via open tooling. Then: (1) match features across dictionaries (decoder cosine/optimal transport) and measure graph-level edge divergence; (2) for each extracted edge, compare its graph-predicted ablation effect against the measured effect, on the extraction distribution versus held-out shifted inputs (entity substitutions, aliasing, intermediate-entity masking, rarity splits). Falsifiable prediction: divergence and interventional prediction gaps will concentrate in high-sparsity dictionaries and on inputs where the deep pathway is load-bearing — the first ground-truth-free demonstration (or refutation) of the shallow-rewrite failure mode in a real LM.
why: It targets the field's own top-ranked open problem (faithfulness/the dual-basis problem, flagged by Sharkey et al. 2025, ranked #1 by the leading 2026 retrospective, and listed as an open validation direction by the Anthropic/GDM/EleutherAI circuit-tracing landscape), and it is demonstrably not done: the ICML 2026 unfaithfulness result is toy-model-only with "preliminary" real-LM evidence; the NeurIPS 2026 faithfulness checks are feature-level for a single concept; Certified Circuits handles dataset robustness only at the component level; the feature-correspondence literature benchmarks feature matching, not graph-level mechanistic faithfulness. It converts the field's aesthetic judgment of decompositions ("does it look interpretable?") into a measurable, falsifiable target — the quantitative faithfulness metric everyone agrees is missing — and the outcome matters in both directions: either we get the first detection method for unfaithful circuit tracing, or we get validated evidence that attribution graphs are robust, which the field equally needs before trusting graphs for safety auditing of deception, refusal, and hidden knowledge.

direction: Build methods that aggregate families of per-prompt attribution graphs over structured input sets into algorithm-level hypotheses with held-out predictive power, turning "faithfulness of circuit explanations" from an aesthetic judgment into a quantitative, decomposition-independent criterion.
project: From Execution Traces to Algorithms: Held-Out Structural Generalization as a Faithfulness Criterion for Transcoder Circuits
question: When circuit tracing surfaces narrow, input-specific "heuristic" features, is that the model's actual computation or a decomposition artifact — and can compact algorithm-level structure, recovered by pooling circuit families across prompts, predict circuit structure on held-out inputs better than per-prompt explanations?
first_experiment: On GPT-2-small with open cross-layer transcoders (or Gemma-2-2B with Gemma Scope transcoders), generate attribution graphs for all 100 input years of the greater-than task ("The war lasted from 1711 to 17") and a grid of two-digit addition problems; stack them into a circuit-family tensor (feature activations × edge weights × prompt); then (1) fit shared parametric structure (e.g., Fourier/monotone functions of the input) and compare its description length against per-prompt heuristic fits, (2) train the family-level model on half the input grid and test whether it predicts which features and edges appear on held-out prompts, and (3) project the pooled circuit mass onto the known trigonometric addition subspace while varying transcoder sparsity penalty, architecture (PLT vs CLT), and seed, to measure whether the "algorithm fraction" is decomposition-dependent.
why: It attacks the problem that a 2026 state-of-the-field review ranks #1 (the dual-basis/faithfulness problem, with no agreed numerical metric), directly executes an open direction the Anthropic/GD/EleutherAI/Goodfire landscape doc calls out ("merge attribution graphs, or obtain a more global circuit picture"), and resolves a live dispute (Fourier algorithms vs. bag of heuristics) whose answer determines whether current circuit-tracing infrastructure can support deployment-grade monitoring under distribution shift. It has not been done because Goodfire's replication stopped at a single prompt and explicitly deferred family analysis; the automated attribution-graph papers (ADAG, Circuit Oracle, probe prompting) label individual graphs rather than pool them; sparse feature circuits (Marks et al.) discover task-level graphs via patching without recovering algorithmic structure or testing decomposition-dependence; the faithfulness-metrics and circuit-variance literature (Miller et al., CEAP) measures variability but never aggregates across prompts into algorithm hypotheses; the ICML 2026 CLT-unfaithfulness result stays in a toy Boolean model; and the implementation-chart theory explicitly declines to infer mechanisms from data — leaving the empirical bridge from per-prompt traces to validated algorithms, with known ground truth to check against, unclaimed. Either outcome is publishable: recovery of held-out-generalizing algorithm structure vindicates the tools and yields a new standard metric; robust failure across decompositions reframes the "bag of heuristics" dispute as a fact about models, not artifacts.

direction: Develop and ground-truth-validate a held-out-distribution causal validation protocol for attribution graphs that discriminates true circuits from impostors matched on in-distribution scores, converting the field's #1 open problem — non-circular faithfulness measurement and decomposition selection — into a usable metric.
project: Impostor Circuits: Held-Out Causal Validation of Attribution Graphs
question: Do attribution graphs' causal predictions survive joint interventions on held-out input distributions where impostor graphs with matched in-distribution replacement scores diverge, and can the resulting predictive-validity score select among the equivalence class of causally valid decompositions?
first_experiment: On GPT-2-small IOI and a modular-addition transformer, extract transcoder attribution graphs on distribution D₀, generate ~100 impostor graphs matched to the true graph's in-distribution replacement score/KL within ±1%, and measure whether predictive validity of joint feature interventions on ≥5 held-out distributions separates true from impostor graphs (AUC ≫ 0.5) where in-distribution score is blind by construction.
why: It is the positive counterpart the field's own 2026 review names as its top open problem (quantitative, non-circular faithfulness; the dual-basis problem), backed by a fresh wave of negative results (all four SAE faithfulness tests fail; single-site patching structurally cannot distinguish mechanisms; circuits are non-specific and sampled from an equivalence class) yet with no existing protocol at the attribution-graph level — nearest neighbors differ in kind (component-level sufficiency tests pre-attribution-graphs, correlational single-feature checks, discovery-algorithm evaluation on InterpBench, vision-only formal verification), the required infrastructure is fully open (Circuit Tracer, Gemma Scope, Llama Scope, InterpBench, known analytic circuits), and validated circuit explanations are the upstream prerequisite for the field's other priorities (deployment monitors, auditing games, cross-model transfer), which its current automation-heavy trajectory amplifies rather than fixes.

direction: Operationalize the "dual basis problem" by building an automated protocol that constructs discriminating input distributions designed to maximally separate the intervention predictions of competing circuit explanations, and selects among them by intervention-predictive validity under distribution shift — turning explanation choice from an aesthetic judgment into a severe test.
project: Severe Tests for Circuits: Discriminating Distributions as a Selection Principle for Competing Mechanistic Explanations
question: When multiple circuit-level explanations of a model behavior are equally faithful on natural data, do automatically constructed discriminating distributions — inputs chosen to maximize predicted disagreement between candidates' intervention outcomes — empirically separate them, and does intervention-predictive validity on those distributions identify the mechanism the model actually implements?
first_experiment: On GPT-2 small and indirect object identification (the task where explanation multiplicity is already documented), instantiate 3–4 competing candidate circuits drawn from different published analytic settings plus an SAE-based circuit; for each candidate compute predicted ablation/patching outcomes per input (margin-graph-style first-order predictions); search a family of input-construction operators (name/position cue conflicts, template recombination, distractor insertion) for inputs that maximize predicted disagreement between candidate pairs; run the real interventions on the top-disagreement inputs and measure per-candidate prediction error on each distribution. Deliverable: a "mechanistic discriminability score" for IOI plus a demonstration that faithfulness rankings, which are flat in-distribution, become decisive under discriminating distributions — or, if equivalence persists, the first certified underdetermination result for a canonical LM task.
why: It attacks the field's top self-identified open problem at exactly the moment its foundations crystallized — non-identifiability is proven (Méloux et al.), measured for audits (Mahale), quantified across SAE seeds (Li), and shown to be distributional in origin (Shortcut Before Circuit) — but every existing work either diagnoses multiplicity or fixes a mechanical sub-piece; none builds the constructive selection protocol, and several explicitly leave it open. It is the highest-leverage gap because the field's dominant artifact (attribution graphs) and its safety applications (monitors, audits that must survive distribution shift) both silently inherit in-distribution-alias mechanisms; a cheap, falsifiable severe-test protocol converts that failure mode into a decidable empirical question. It is tractable for me now: small open models, public dictionaries, existing tooling, canonical tasks, no frontier compute required — and its negative results (certified equivalence classes) are as publishable and as safety-relevant as its positive ones.

direction: Build the first principled, ground-truth-calibrated adjudication framework that ranks competing feature/circuit decompositions of a language model by their off-distribution interventional fidelity, turning the field's "dual basis problem" from an aesthetic decision into a measurable one.
project: Off-Distribution Circuit Fidelity: Adjudicating Competing Decompositions of a Language Model
question: When multiple decompositions (different SAE seeds and sizes, transcoder features, neuron-basis circuits) each faithfully explain a model behavior in-distribution, do they make divergent predictions under interventions on distribution-shifted inputs — and does off-distribution interventional fidelity identify which decomposition, if any, tracks the model's actual causal structure rather than a convenient reparameterization?
first_experiment: On Gemma-2-2B, extract circuits for two structured behaviors (IOI and factual recall) under five decomposition families — Gemma Scope SAE-16k, SAE-65k, an independently retrained seed, transcoder features, and a neuron-basis circuit — retain only those passing standard in-distribution faithfulness/completeness checks, then run a fixed battery of distribution-shift families (entity swaps, paraphrases, novel compositions, held-out categories) crossed with three intervention types (ablation, feature patching, clamping with frozen residual), measuring each decomposition's interventional prediction error off-distribution versus on-distribution; then calibrate the resulting metric on InterpBench-style semi-synthetic transformers with planted ground-truth circuits to verify it ranks the true decomposition first (non-circularity). ~2–4 GPU-weeks, fully open-source components.
why: It targets the field's self-diagnosed #1 open problem — the "dual basis problem," where choosing among decompositions that account for the same behavior "is currently an aesthetic decision" — and it is upstream of every safety application: SAE-based monitors fail under distribution shift, steering handles are bypassable through the SAE residual, auditing agents demonstrably prefer black-box tools over white-box ones, and cross-architecture transfer claims are untestable until decomposition validity is settled within one model. It has not been done because the verification bottleneck only emerged in 2025–2026 (labeling was automated; validation was not), because the supporting failure-mode evidence (post-intervention recovery via the residual, behavioral non-additivity, non-robust faithfulness metrics, non-replicating screen-and-ablate circuits) crystallized only in the last 18 months, and because the pieces required for a decisive non-circular test — public multi-size SAE dictionaries, standardized behaviors with known circuits, transcoder stacks, semi-synthetic ground-truth models, and anytime-valid interventional statistics — all matured only recently. The identifiability literature stops short: iSAE establishes statistical stability across seeds, and Koopman spectral analysis proves that "the identifiable object and the legible object are not the same object" without a behavioral resolution; no one has bridged that gap empirically. A positive result converts interpretability's central artifact from an aesthetic choice into a measurable, ranked claim — multiplying the value of every existing dictionary, graph, and monitor, and giving safety-critical deployments a validation protocol they currently lack.

direction: Convert per-prompt attribution graphs from single-input "execution traces" into input-general algorithm-level circuits by aggregating graphs across prompt families and validating the recovered mechanism by out-of-distribution prediction — closing the largest named gap between the field's dominant artifact and its own definition of understanding.
project: Circuit Unification: From Per-Prompt Execution Traces to General Algorithms via Attribution Graph Aggregation
question: When a transformer implements an input-general algorithm (e.g., the trigonometric "Clock" algorithm for addition), how much of that algorithm can be recovered by aggregating attribution graphs over a family of prompts, and does the aggregated, recurring subgraph predict model behavior on held-out and out-of-distribution inputs better than any per-prompt circuit — thereby providing a principled, non-circular criterion for selecting among many valid circuit decompositions?
first_experiment: Using the open circuit-tracer stack with pre-trained cross-layer transcoders on Gemma-2-2B (or GPT-2-small), generate attribution graphs for ~200 two-digit addition prompts "a + b = c"; exploit the shared transcoder feature vocabulary (feature identities are constant across prompts, making node alignment well-defined) to compute pairwise overlap, extract the subgraph recurring in ≥95% of prompts, and measure (a) its share of attribution mass versus prompt-specific "lookup-table" features, (b) its aggregated replacement score on held-out addition prompts versus single-prompt graphs and size-matched random subgraphs, and (c) whether the recurring subgraph exhibits the circular/trigonometric structure that per-prompt graphs are known to miss (Kantamneni & Tegmark's helix result as ground truth).
why: It is the most promising direction because it is a named-but-unclaimed convergence point of four things the field itself has flagged as top-priority: the merge-attribution-graphs bullet on Nanda/Lindsey's official future-work list; the transcoder geometry-shattering limitation; the dual-basis problem (aggregation + OOD generalization turns decomposition selection from an aesthetic judgment into a testable prediction criterion, complementing — not repeating — "Certified Circuits" and "Many Circuits, One Mechanism," which operate at the component level with certification/critique rather than feature-level algorithm recovery); and the deployment-grade need for predictive rather than retrospective explanations. It has not already been done because the entire 2026 attribution-graph literature optimizes single-graph analysis (automation, annotation, transfer, pruning) rather than cross-prompt unification — no published method aggregates attribution graphs over input families or scores recovered circuits by input-general predictive power — and because tasks like addition provide causally-validated ground-truth algorithms, giving the project a rare quantitative falsification target that most interpretability research lacks.

direction: Replace the field's circular "circuit vs. discovery-distribution" faithfulness test with adjudication among rival explanations — use inter-circuit divergence under automatically constructed distribution shifts as discriminating experiments, and let agreement with the full model on those shifts be the quantitative, non-aesthetic criterion for which explanation actually tracks the model's computation.
project: Rival Circuits — Adjudicating Competing Mechanistic Explanations by Discriminating Behavioral Predictions under Distribution Shift
question: When multiple circuit explanations each achieve high faithfulness on the distribution they were discovered on, do their predictions diverge under designed semantic shift families in ways that are detectable, and does "agreement with the full model on the shifts where rivals disagree" reliably identify — better than in-distribution faithfulness, circuit size, or structural overlap — which explanation tracks the model's actual computation?
first_experiment: On GPT-2 small IOI (plus greater-than and docstring as controls), assemble a panel of rival circuits — the manual Wang et al. circuit, ACDC, EAP-IG variants, and the same circuits re-extracted under different ablation schemes and extraction distributions — then measure (i) pairwise circuit-vs-circuit KL divergence under resample ablation on the base distribution versus on designed shift families (name swaps, repeated-token and DoubleIO/TripleIO variants, OOV names, romantic-object subpopulations, natural model errors), and (ii) the rank correlation between in-distribution faithfulness and shift-resolved agreement with the full model across the panel — a single-GPU experiment testing whether circuits that are behaviorally indistinguishable in-distribution separate under shift, and whether the model's verdict on those shifts is stable and non-degenerate.
why: It attacks the problem the field's own 2026 retrospectives rank first (the dual-basis/faithfulness-measurement gap named in the Sharkey et al. lineage), yet every adjacent paper explicitly declines to solve it — uit de Bos evaluates only single circuits, Zhang et al. label their error test "necessary, but not sufficient," Mahale states they "do not propose a better method," and CIF and Certified Circuits add statistical rigor to claims and discovery respectively but no selection criterion — because the field's energy went to automating explanation *generation* (labels, attribution graphs) while evaluation remained anchored to the discovery distribution, which by construction cannot distinguish members of an equivalence class; my direction is the constructive counterpart to an already-saturated diagnostic literature, it is validated against known ground truth on InterpBench where the true algorithm is known, it operationalizes Li et al.'s "predict behavior on unseen data" objective at the circuit level in real LMs, it directly produces the scope-of-validity certificates that audits and safety monitors need, and it is executable now at toy-model scale with existing open tooling and modest compute.

direction: Turn the field's "dual basis" problem into an empirical discipline — build and validate a certified, intervention-based protocol that adjudicates between competing circuit/attribution-graph explanations of the same model behavior, so decomposition choice stops being an aesthetic judgment about labels and becomes a measured, statistical decision.
project: Deciding Between Decoys: Certified Interventional Adjudication of Competing Circuit Explanations
question: When multiple decompositions (CLT attribution graphs, per-layer-transcoder circuits, SAE feature sets, ACDC/EAP-IG subgraphs) all account for a model's behavior on its discovery distribution, can actively selected held-out interventions — certified with anytime-valid statistics — reliably identify which explanation tracks the model's true computation, at what intervention budget, and which intervention/ablation families carry the discriminating information?
first_experiment: Construct a decoy-pair testbed with Strict Interchange Intervention Training: train two transformers on the same task with identical behavioral accuracy — one aligned to the true multi-hop causal graph, one to a behaviorally-equivalent shallow-rewrite decoy (mirroring the CLT shallow-rewrite failure mode) — then run standard discovery methods on both and test whether a held-out interventional battery (interchange interventions across multiple ablation families, on inputs withheld from discovery), analyzed with anytime-valid sequential tests, discriminates true mechanism from decoy, measuring discrimination power and minimum intervention budget; replicate on InterpBench models with known IOI circuits, then apply to the Gemma-2-2B two-hop case where mediated ("Dallas→Texas→Austin") and shortcut paths coexist.
why: It attacks the single most foundational open problem the field's own 2026 retrospective ranks first — ranking decompositions by something other than label readability — at the moment it became newly tractable (public CLT tooling, SIIT ground-truth models, ISS separation theory, CIF certified statistics, MIB evaluation culture). It has not been done: ISS stops at MNIST label abstractions with no transformer ground truth; CIF certifies single claims rather than separating hypotheses and declares rather than designs intervention distributions; MIB evaluates localization methods on fixed intervention schemes, not competing mechanistic stories; the ICML 2026 CLT paper diagnoses the decoy problem but only calls for different training objectives; and the crowded feature-validation work operates one level below circuit adjudication. Safety-wise it is upstream of everything: production interpretability monitors and alignment audits are only as trustworthy as the decompositions they are built on, and a shallow-rewrite decoy is exactly the object a deceptive model would exploit to hide its real computation behind a readable, "validated" explanation.

direction: Characterize and causally attribute the "non-neuron residual" — the component of LLM computation invisible to both pruned-neuron circuits and sparse dictionaries — to establish when cheap neuron-basis interpretability pipelines can be trusted and how to extend them where they fail.
project: Where the Neurons End: Mapping and Attributing Non-Neuron Computation in Language Models
question: What fraction of an LLM's task-relevant computation is not expressible in the privileged pre-activation neuron basis (i.e., is distributed/superposed), how does that fraction vary across layers, tasks, model families, and training recipes (base vs RLVR-tuned), and can the residual be faithfully attributed with a cheap complementary decomposition (residual-dictionary + local Jacobian low-rank structure) validated on toy models with ground-truth dense circuits?
first_experiment: Using open models (Gemma-2-2B, Llama-3.2-1B, Qwen3-4B), the Transluce pruned-neuron + RelP pipeline, and GemmaScope/open transcoders as the learned baseline, run a task battery spanning neuron-friendly tasks (subject–verb agreement, state capitals), geometry-dependent tasks (integer arithmetic where transcoders "shatter" the helix), attention-heavy tasks (induction), suppression-heavy tasks (refusal), and multi-hop reasoning; for each task sweep the per-layer neuron budget k and measure (i) replacement KL of the pruned-neuron model, (ii) share of attribution mass landing on error nodes vs. neurons vs. learned features, and (iii) Jacobian alignment of kept vs. pruned components — producing the first systematic "neuron-coverage map" that identifies exactly which layers × tasks × models the new cheap circuit pipelines fail on, and thereby the concrete targets for the residual-attribution method built in phase 2.
why: It is the explicit open call of the two most recent papers that define the field's current inflection point — the Aug 2025 multi-org replication ("error nodes are simply too prevalent in graphs and block us from tracing the important circuits") and the Oct 2026 NeurIPS workshop paper ("call for better methods of attributing the non-neuron structure that is used by the model") — and it is foundational rather than incremental: it determines whether the SAE/transcoder investment of three years recovered real structure or repackaged neurons, and it sets the trust conditions for the zero-training-cost circuit pipelines the field is adopting right now, including their safety-critical blind spots (a model that hides computation in distributed directions evades both neuron pruning and sparse dictionaries — the obfuscated-activation threat model). It has not been done because it only became askable in 2026: the neuron-basis result (Arora et al., Jan 2026) and its characterization (Oct 2026) are new, prior error-term work ("What is the functional role of SAE errors?", 2025) was correlational, pre-neuron-basis, single-model, and reconstruction-focused, and every existing comparison (Transluce case studies; Shabalin et al.'s dictionary-level analysis; Ye et al.'s thresholded-neuron benchmarks) tested either few "streetlight" tasks, one model, or only dictionary-level statistics — nobody has done the causal, task-level map or built a residual-attribution method with ground-truth validation, and the compressed-computation dispute (Jul 2026) shows even the existence of this regime is unsettled. The first experiment requires no training, runs on single-node GPUs with open tools, and yields a decision-relevant map whether or not large residual structure exists.

direction: Make the out-of-distribution reliability of interpretability-based safety monitors (linear probes on misbehavior) a predictable, trainable, and stress-testable property, using interventional causal validation of probe directions as the core instrument.
project: Will the Probe Fire When It Matters? Causal Validation and Stress-Testing of Safety Monitors
question: Can a linear monitor's out-of-distribution generalization be predicted — without OOD labels — from the causal engagement of its probe direction (how strongly steering/patching along it moves the actual misbehavior), and does training probes for causal engagement and alignment with stable persona subspaces yield monitors that survive distribution shift?
first_experiment: On Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (matching #34's setting), construct ~15–20 programmatic multi-agent collusion/honesty scenario families with controlled variation axes (domain, format, phrasing), plus paraphrase/format-controlled 2×2 variants (#79) and label-shuffled negative controls (#5/#18 hygiene). Train per-family linear probes at every layer; measure stratified-k-fold AUROC vs. leave-one-family-out AUROC; then, for each probe direction, measure causal engagement via activation steering/patching (±v) on held-out families and check the steering-detection confound (#78). Primary readout: Spearman correlation between causal engagement and LOFO-AUROC across all layer×family probes; secondary: decompose AUROC drop into format-shift vs. scenario-shift components.
why: (1) It targets the binding constraint of the safety-critical application layer being deployed now (#17, #36, #38), rather than adding to saturated SAE/steering/circuit clusters. (2) The corpus shows the problem is diagnosed (#34: 0.96+ → ~0.6 AUROC collapse; #79: format artifacts) but the bridge is unbuilt: no one connects causal-probing methodology, persona-vector stability (#82), mechanism-diverse training (#2), and matched-null validation (#5) into a predictor or training criterion for monitor OOD reliability; #40 warns objective-driven selection inflates non-causal effects but is never operationalized for monitors. (3) It is feasible for an autonomous agent — open 8B weights, linear probes, and interventions, no model training — with negative controls preventing self-deception. (4) It is low-regret and generalizes: a positive result yields causally certified monitors and a transferable stress-test protocol (applicable to hermeneutics readers, steering-based mitigation, and even circuit robustness); a null result yields the decomposition study the field needs before more monitors are layered onto frontier training runs.

direction: Build a causal data-to-internals pipeline connecting unsupervised training-gradient decomposition ("gradient atoms") to the features and circuits interpretability recovers, turning interpretability from post-hoc description into prediction and audit at the level of the training diet.
project: Atoms to Features — Causal Attribution of Learned Representations to Training Data
question: Do sparse gradient atoms extracted from a model's training corpus predict — and causally determine — which internal features the trained model develops, such that a model's representational content can be forecast from its data diet alone and hidden trait-carrying structure (e.g., in subliminal-learning data) can be detected?
first_experiment: Train a 2–4 layer transformer on a synthetic corpus with ~20 planted, ground-truth feature clusters (including correlated pairs); compute per-document loss gradients, decompose them into atoms via dictionary learning in the preconditioned eigenspace, and test (1) correspondence — atom↔planted-feature and atom↔SAE-feature matching vs. random splits and per-document influence baselines, (2) timing — whether an atom's cumulative gradient mass rises before its feature emerges across checkpoints, and (3) causality — retrain with one atom's document cluster removed or 2× oversampled and verify the predicted feature disappears or amplifies without collateral damage to neighboring features.
why: It forges the one junction no paper in this 88-item corpus attempts — Gradient Atoms (2026-03) does unsupervised data influence but never touches learned features, persona-vector tracing (2026-05) observes formation without data causality, dynamic weight grafting (2025-12) localizes knowledge per-fact rather than per-data-cluster, and subliminal learning (2026-08) documents a data channel that standard auditing provably misses and leaves unexplained — while delivering direct safety payoff (corpus auditing for hidden trait structure, forecasting misaligned generalization from fine-tune diets), remaining toy-scale cheap with a clean scaling path, and being causally falsifiable through diet interventions rather than merely correlational like existing TDA.

direction: Trace mechanistic circuits across the full training trajectory and test whether training-time circuit stability predicts final-circuit robustness, turning the training run itself into an independent validation axis for interpretability claims.
project: Circuit Crystallization — Longitudinal Circuit Dynamics as a Validation Criterion for Mechanistic Interpretability
question: Does the training-time stability of a task circuit (crystallization step, edge-set volatility, component functional drift) predict its robustness at the final checkpoint — measured by adversarial circuit divergence (#23 protocol), cross-format component reuse (#27 protocol), and persistence under fine-tuning/reversion (#37 protocol) — thereby providing a non-self-referential validation criterion for circuit claims?
first_experiment: On Pythia-70M and Pythia-160M across all 16 public checkpoints, discover the IOI circuit and the induction-head circuit at every checkpoint using a hybrid attribution+pruning pipeline, match components across checkpoints by functional behavior profiles (ablation-effect vectors, Hungarian/optimal-transport matching rather than index identity), compute per-circuit stability trajectories (edge-set Jaccard over checkpoints, crystallization time, late-stage volatility), then evaluate the final-checkpoint circuits under the adversarial evaluation protocol of #23 and the format-shift protocol of #27, and test the rank correlation between training stability and robustness — with the known phase-changing induction circuit as the positive control and the known-fragile IOI circuit as the critical test case, and a dense-checkpointed 6x6 OthelloGPT (~600k params, checkpoint every 100 steps) as a fine-grained model organism replicating the full track-and-stress pipeline with ground-truth board-state features.
why: It directly attacks the field's central documented wound — circuits (#23), probes (#21, #88), explanations (#39, #58), and patching objectives (#72) all fail static, self-referential validation — by introducing a fundamentally independent evidence axis (the formation history) that no item in this corpus exploits: the closest works either trace features not circuits (#5), describe formation without predicting robustness (induction-head phase-change and grokking studies), or stress-test final models without any trajectory data (#23, #27, #37). It converts scattered dynamics findings (early persona formation, safety reversion, subliminal weight transfer) into one falsifiable program, yields a cheap deployable monitor ("don't trust a circuit that is still moving") for training and distillation pipelines, is executable at near-zero compute with public checkpoints and existing tooling, and produces a decisive result either way: a predictive law of circuit robustness, or a strong negative result proving trajectory information carries no validation signal.

direction: Systematically study when linearly decodable information in LLM activations is actually causally deployed by the model's computation versus merely present ("decodable ≠ deployed"), building a cheap weight-space predictor of causal deployment and a "deployment-validated probe" standard for safety oversight.
project: Decodable but Not Deployed: Predicting When Probed Features Are Load-Bearing
question: When a concept is linearly decodable from a model's residual stream, does the model actually read and use that direction to determine its output — and can causal deployment be predicted from the weights alone (downstream consumer mass of the decoded direction) before running any intervention?
first_experiment: On Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, decode directions for four behaviors spanning the expected deployment spectrum — refusal (positive control: ablation is known to flip behavior), repeated-token counting at pre-overwrite layers (negative control per the 2026-05 dissociation), a benchmark-format feature (predicted deployed but for the wrong reason), and a truthfulness/emotion direction (unknown) — then for each direction at each layer measure (i) probe decodability, (ii) direct logit readout, (iii) output change under ablation and contrastive patching, (iv) steering dose–response, and (v) consumer mass: the normalized projection of the direction onto downstream layers' W_Q/K/V and MLP input row spaces and the unembedding; then test whether consumer mass separates deployed from passenger directions before any intervention is run.
why: It converts the corpus's most important recent thread — five independent 2026 findings (44, 53, 24, 84, 87) showing that decodable signals, learned interventions, and canonical circuits can fail to reflect actual computation — from scattered negative results into a positive, predictive program, and it directly hardens the load-bearing assumption of probe-based scalable oversight (lie detectors, collusion probes, closed-weight auditing via reader models), where paper 24 already shows AUROC alone is dangerously misleading. It has not already been done: the closest work is single-task case studies (84 covers only counting; 53 only evaluation awareness), probing critiques from the BERT era that test removal on linguistic features without a weight-space predictor or safety behaviors (control tasks, amnesic probing), pure theory without cross-behavior measurement (44), and explanation/circuit validation (12, 50, 87) rather than a systematic decodability-to-causality map — no one has built the consumer-mass predictor or proposed deployment-validated probes as a standard, and the project is feasible for a single agent on open 7–8B models with standard patching and steering tooling.

direction: Shift mechanistic interpretability's evidentiary standard for safety probes from decodability to causal consultation, via a reusable audit that classifies internal signals as consulted or shadow.
project: Consulted or Shadow? Auditing Whether Safety-Critical Probe Signals Are Wired into Model Behavior
question: For which safety-relevant internal signals does linear decodability imply causal consultation by downstream computation, and does consultation rather than probe accuracy predict when probes are trustworthy evidence and when interventions on them will work?
first_experiment: Reproduce refusal and factual self-awareness probes in Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct; score each direction's consultation via ablation with matched random-direction controls plus collateral-KL checks; predict downstream readers via static weight-alignment consumer search; validate with component-restricted directional patching against a positive control (refusal) and negative control (format-artifact probe).
why: The probe is the load-bearing but least verified primitive of the safety-oversight wave (#14, #18, #80), and three 2026 papers (#2, #62, #75) independently wound it without unifying; no existing work combines intervention-based consultation testing, static consumer prediction from weights, a multi-signal safety audit, and the Goodhart-drift hypothesis that probe-based selection converts consulted signals into shadow ones — making this the highest-leverage, lowest-cost open gap in the field.

direction: Build a validity layer for behavioral interpretability — methods that select and certify activation-space behavior directions (persona/deception/reward-hacking/eval-awareness probes and steering vectors) by invariance across scenarios, formats, and settings, so that measured effects reflect the behavior's mechanism rather than distribution artifacts, with a calibrated certificate when no such direction exists.
project: "Certified Directions: Invariant Selection and Adversarial Stress-Testing of Behavioral Monitors in LLM Activations"
question: When a linear direction is selected from a model's activations to monitor or steer a behavior, how much of its measured effect is the behavior's mechanism versus a scenario-, format-, or objective-artifact — and can invariance-across-environments selection plus causal stress tests produce monitors that survive distribution shift, or rigorously certify signal absence?
first_experiment: On 2–3 open 7–9B instruct models (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B), take standard behavioral directions (persona vectors for sycophancy/deception via diff-in-means, an eval-awareness probe, a refusal direction) and build a crossed evaluation suite: {behavior label} × {20+ scenario families} × {4+ prompt formats, benchmark-style vs. free-form} × {surface-marker decoupling}. Measure (1) in-distribution vs. leave-one-scenario-family-out vs. leave-one-format-out AUROC, (2) causal steering effect on held-out environments, and (3) the item-5 diagnostic (directional effect vs. full-activation patch) to quantify objective-inflation. Then train invariance-regularized variants (per-environment diff-in-means agreement / min-over-environments selection) and test whether artifact share drops while causal effect survives. Success = replicated artifact failures under one unified protocol plus a measured reduction (or a tight, calibrated negative result for eval-awareness).
why: It is the only direction that addresses the single failure mode independently documented by seven papers in this corpus (5, 19, 34, 41, 43, 49, 51) while the field simultaneously deploys these same fragile artifacts in RLHF oversight (19), reward-hack mitigation (27, 46), and closed-model auditing (25) — fixing it upgrades all of them at once, and a negative-certificate capability directly answers the open questions 34 and 49 explicitly leave unresolved. It has not already been done because the existing work is fragmentary by artifact type: 43 stress-tests circuits, 5 theorizes patching objectives, 34 and 49 only diagnose, 19's mitigation is data diversity rather than principled invariance, and 16 detects instability in reward models rather than selecting robust directions — no one has unified invariant selection, crossed-design decoupling, and adversarial causal validation into a constructive framework for behavioral directions, despite the invariant-learning literature being available for the importing. It is also the right risk profile for a next project: cheap compute (probing and steering on open 7–9B models), automation-friendly (exactly the kind of systematic crossed-design evaluation an autonomous agent excels at), every outcome informative (a fix, a quantified artifact-share, or a calibrated certificate are all publishable and safety-relevant), and it lays the validated foundation for the higher-compute follow-up — training-time alignment monitoring via latent drift.

direction: Determine whether fine-tuning-induced trait changes (including subliminally distilled ones) act by moving activations along trait directions that pretraining already formed, and whether projecting those changes onto that basis enables auditing and causal reversion of fine-tuned and distilled models.
project: Persona Projection — Auditing Fine-Tunes Against Pretraining-Formed Trait Directions
question: What fraction of a fine-tune's behavioral effect is carried by the span of the base model's pretraining-formed persona directions versus newly written structure — and can subtracting the projected component from activations causally revert the trait change while preserving capability?
first_experiment: On a small open model (e.g., OLMo-2-1B or Llama-3.2-1B base): (1) extract ~8 persona vectors (sycophancy, misalignment/"evil", refusal, verbosity, humor) via standard contrastive activations; (2) run ~10 LoRA fine-tunes spanning neutral (code/math), trait-targeted (sycophancy-boosting SFT data), and subliminal-learning (random-number distillation) conditions; (3) compute each fine-tune's activation shift on a fixed held-out prompt set, decompose it into the persona-basis span vs. its orthogonal complement (with matched random-subspace nulls, per #38/#81); (4) correlate persona-projection magnitude with measured trait change (sycophancy evals, refusal rates, LLM-judged persona) and orthogonal magnitude with capability change (perplexity, MMLU-lite); (5) the decisive arm: on one sycophancy-boosted fine-tune, subtract the persona-projection component from activations at inference and test whether sycophancy reverts without capability loss.
why: It is the single uncrowded intersection that collects the corpus's loosest threads: #15 establishes the basis exists before any fine-tune and survives post-training (the premise), #38 observed one special-case displacement direction, #43 found weight noise amplifies subliminal transfer (predicted by drift-along-existing-directions), #39 localizes fine-tuned information, #46 shows trait subspaces are orthogonal — yet none decomposes fine-tune updates onto a pretraining-formed trait basis or tests projection-based causal reversion. It is also the missing constructive answer to the probe-brittleness results (#26, #31): if trait changes ride a stable low-dimensional subspace, monitors should read that subspace, and auditors can flag dangerous fine-tunes or distillations from the activation delta alone — no training data, no labels, at inference cost. Feasible with open models and standard tooling at days-not-months scale, and informative either way: high explained variance yields a finetune-auditing/correction tool; low explained variance proves fine-tuning writes novel trait structure, redirecting the field toward in-training monitoring.

direction: Turn activation-space safety monitors (linear probes and steering directions) from correlational, format-entangled artifacts into causally validated, distribution-shift-robust instruments.
project: Probe Forensics: Causally Validated and Shift-Robust Safety Monitors for LLMs
question: Which components of linear safety probes causally mediate the monitored behavior, and can probes be trained to depend only on those components so they remain valid under format, scenario, and deployment shift — and cannot be evaded by surface-feature changes alone?
first_experiment: Train standard deception/collusion probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen3-4B (item 78's protocol), then jointly measure: transfer under item 65's controlled format rewrites, SAE-decomposition of probe weights into format vs. semantic feature mass, steering dose-response along the probe direction (behavior vs. surface style), and item 44's whole-vs-part effect estimator — testing whether high in-format AUROC masks format-feature confounding and weak causal control.
why: Probe monitors underpin the field's most deployable safety agenda (scaled lie detectors, hermeneutics on closed models, reward-hacking mitigation), yet three 2026 results (44, 65, 78) independently show these readouts are objective-inflated, format-entangled, and brittle under shift — and no existing work connects them into a constructive causal-validation and robust-training program; the tools (open SAEs, steering interventions, whole-vs-part theory) only just made this tractable, every outcome is informative, and the adversarial monitor-evasion angle is novel, safety-critical, and cheap to test.

direction: Build a causal, data-side account of finetuning-induced misalignment by decomposing finetuning gradients into unsupervised "atoms," testing which atoms predict emergent misalignment, and interventionally ablating the responsible documents while measuring displacement along known persona/reversion features.
project: Gradient Atoms of Misalignment: Finding the Data Directions That Bend Personas
question: Which directions in the finetuning gradient space — induced by which training documents — causally produce broad misaligned personas, and are those directions mechanistically aligned with known persona vectors, misaligned-persona SAE features, and the safety-reversion direction?
first_experiment: On Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, compute per-document gradients (or LoRA-per-document deltas) for the public emergent-misalignment finetuning datasets plus benign controls, dictionary-learn them into atoms à la Gradient Atoms, then test across a held-out panel of ~12 finetunes whether atom loading predicts emergent-misalignment eval scores — a purely predictive, intervention-free test of whether misalignment is gradient-localized before attempting any data ablation.
why: It unifies four threads that are each validated but never joined — unsupervised training-data decomposition (75), early-forming steerable persona vectors (85), released misaligned-persona SAE features (13), and reversion dynamics (84) — into a preventive, label-free safety tool that works for unknown-unknown behaviors, unlike labeled-probe and steering approaches (3, 4); and it has not been done because existing work on emergent misalignment is either representational (features found post-hoc) or hypothesis-driven data sweeps, with no unsupervised, interventionally-validated account linking data-space structure to the linear persona/reversion geometry, while the failure mode is itself informative: a null result would show misalignment is an attractor phenomenon, not data-localized.

direction: Mechanistically characterize and causally localize how LLMs detect activation steering, converting detectability from a black-box searched quantity into a predictable, localized, and validated internal mechanism.
project: Sentinel Circuits: Localizing How Language Models Detect Activation Steering
question: Is steering detection a generic anomaly monitor over residual-stream statistics (possibly via massive activations/attention sinks), a semantic readout of the injected direction, or a probe-level measurement artifact — and can a steering vector's detectability be predicted a priori from its geometry without training any probe?
first_experiment: A 3-way controlled study on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-it — unsteered vs. semantically steered vs. magnitude-matched random-vector steered, plus content-matched natural-concept prompts — with layer-wise probes split across prompts and vectors, position/head-level localization targeting sink tokens and massive-activation dimensions, and causal patching of implicated components to test whether the detection signal is actually used.
why: It addresses the newest and most consequential unexplained phenomenon in the survey (#3, two months old) that undermines both the industrializing steering literature and probe-based safety monitoring, it is genuinely unclaimed in the corpus because it requires exactly the content-matched causal controls the meta-critique papers (#9, #35, #58, #74) show are typically missing, it is highly feasible for an autonomous agent using open-weight models and programmatic sweeps, and every possible outcome — sentinel mechanism, trivial anomaly monitor, or artifact — is informative and safety-relevant.

direction: Build a general framework and ground-truth benchmark for distinguishing features that are *causally used* by a model from features that are merely *linearly decodable* in its activations — and apply it to validate the probe/steering/circuit results the safety community currently relies on.
project: Presence Is Not Use: A Causal Utilization Framework for Linear Features
question: When a feature is linearly decodable in a model's internal activations, when is it actually read by downstream computation — and can a cheap score combining static weight-readout alignment with correctly-controlled intervention effects predict causal use reliably enough to audit probes, steering vectors, and circuits before they are trusted?
first_experiment: Train a small transformer on a synthetic task with planted, architecturally-controlled ground truth: feature F1 is read by downstream layers (by construction), F2 is present in activations but never read (a guaranteed-unused direction), F3 is partially read. Then compute, for all three: (a) linear probe accuracy, (b) weight-readout alignment (projection of every downstream component's input/OV/unembedding weights onto each direction), and (c) intervention effects with #66's whole-vs-part correction. Success criterion: probe accuracy is roughly equal across F1/F2/F2-style cases while the utilization score cleanly separates used from unused — validating the metric against ground truth before applying it to the known dissociations in this survey (#49 counting, #48/#60 probe failures, #21/#57 refusal directions).
why: It attacks the field's most consequential open problem at exactly the moment seven independent papers have exposed it from different sides but none has synthesized it — #49 is one case study, #66 is theory without a metric, #65 provides ground truth for SAE recovery but not for causal use, #87/#2/#33 document circuit fragility without a diagnostic, and #60/#48 show probe failures without a general explanation. The pieces are validated as important; the synthesis is untouched. It is feasible for me now (toy models, GPT-2-scale LMs, planted features — no closed-model access or pretraining-scale compute needed), and its leverage is unusually high: every deception probe, steering mitigation, and circuit audit in the survey implicitly assumes presence implies use, so a validated utilization score would immediately upgrade monitoring reliability (#75, #46), explain when steering works or is detected (#79, #11, #25), and give SAE training (#41, #43) a principled target beyond reconstruction. Classic path-patching tools exist but were never unified into a predictive, weight-based score benchmarked on planted ground truth — that gap, not any single technique, is the opportunity.

direction: Mechanistically dissect the linear probes underpinning safety monitoring (deception, collusion, reward-hacking, evaluation-awareness detectors) by decomposing their weight vectors into SAE-feature bases, to predict and improve their robustness under distribution shift.
project: Probe Forensics — What Safety Probes Are Made Of, and When That Survives Distribution Shift
question: Can the out-of-distribution robustness of a safety-relevant linear probe be predicted from its decomposition into interpretable SAE features, and does reconstructing probes from concept-level features (purification) improve OOD reliability without sacrificing in-distribution detection?
first_experiment: On Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with the released instruct-model SAEs (#17's release), train per-layer logistic probes on a standard deception contrast dataset; project each probe's weight vector onto the SAE decoder basis to get a feature-level decomposition (concept/persona features vs. format/style features vs. noise); then evaluate the same probes under three shifts — paraphrased scenarios, format-rewritten negatives following #56's controlled rewrites, and a different task domain (reward-hacking or multi-agent collusion rollouts following #64) — and regress OOD AUROC drop on decomposition statistics, with a seed intervention test of concept-only probe reconstruction.
why: It sits at the confluence of the field's most active 2026 threads — the measurement-validity critiques (#15, #20, #56, #64), the safety-monitoring buildout (#1, #35, #63, #88), and the released interpretability artifacts (#17's SAEs, #76's persona vectors) — yet the specific intersection is unoccupied: #56 covers one concept with no SAE decomposition or fix; #64 is a single undiagnosed negative result; #17 characterizes features but never probes' OOD behavior; #35, #1, and #88 motivate the need without providing the mechanism. If the composition-robustness link holds, the result upgrades every oversight system in Cluster 4 (a pre-deployment diagnostic plus a purification method); if it fails cleanly, that is itself an important calibration result for a field claiming 0.99 AUROCs. It is also cheap: one 8B open model, public SAEs, logistic probes, and no training runs beyond the probes themselves — a first signal within weeks, with clear follow-ons (cross-model purified probes toward #35's hermeneutics, temporal analysis toward #76).

direction: Systematically quantify, predict, and modulate the gap between what LLMs linearly encode and what causally drives their outputs, converting the field's recurring "encoded-but-inert" dissociations into a theory with a cheap validity audit for probe/SAE monitors and a reactivation lever for steering.
project: Encoded but Inert: Auditing and Reopening the Encoding→Behavior Gap in LLMs
question: When behaviorally relevant information is linearly decodable from a model's activations, what determines whether it causally influences the model's output — can dormancy be predicted from measurable properties (feature frequency, carrier-token attention, readout-layer gating, whole-vs-part effect ratio), and can inert knowledge be reliably reactivated (or live knowledge suppressed) with targeted interventions?
first_experiment: Replicate the repeated-token counting dissociation (#23) in Gemma-2-2B, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, and Qwen2.5-7B — train layerwise linear probes to decode the true count, verify decodability coexists with wrong outputs, localize the overwriting MLP near 85–93% depth — then test reactivation by ablating that MLP and steering along the probe direction, scoring whether the correct count surfaces behaviorally; go/no-go criterion: above-chance reactivation in at least one model.
why: It sits at the convergence of at least six papers' independent cautionary findings (#4, #11, #22, #23, #57, #68) that are currently treated piecemeal, and it directly hardens the two fastest-growing deployment stacks in the corpus — probe-based monitors (#50, #54, #68) and steering-based control (#41, #63, #72) — both of which silently inherit the gap, with the worst failure mode occurring exactly in the adversarial suppression regime monitors exist for; it is compute-light (open models, existing tooling, no RL), has in-corpus theoretical hooks (#4's additivity theorem, #9's logit-integration view, #12/#78's feature geometry) to grow from phenomenon to theory, and has not been done because the closest prior art either studies a single behavior (#23), issues a methodological caution without a constructive program (#22), proves a fragment of theory (#4), or predates modern LLMs, SAE features, generative behavior, and monitoring applications (amnesic probing, sandbagging-elicitation work) — leaving the systematic metric, its predictors, the reactivation intervention, and the suppression-aware monitor unclaimed.

direction: Mechanistically characterize the knowing–saying gap — when, where, and how LLM outputs override correctly-encoded internal representations — and test whether "knew-but-suppressed" is itself a detectable internal state.
project: Censored But Not Forgotten: A Mechanistic Anatomy of When LLMs Override What They Represent
question: When a model's output contradicts what its representations encode, which components cause the decoupling, is the mechanism shared across tasks, and can "knew-but-suppressed" be linearly distinguished from "never knew"?
first_experiment: Replicate the repeated-token counting dissociation (per-layer probes for the true count, logit-lens crystallization point, causal ablation of the late MLP overwrite) in small open models, then train probes to distinguish override states (correct trace + wrong commit) from ignorance states (never-encoded counts) and correct-generation states, using whole-state patching and format-matched controls.
why: It unifies the corpus's most safety-relevant anomaly cluster (items 5, 22, 46, 47, 62) into one causal, cross-task question that no existing work asks — existing results are per-task, non-causal, or mechanism-free — and its cheap, automatable probe-and-ablate methodology with built-in negative results makes it both high-expected-value and executable end-to-end by an autonomous agent.

direction: Treat task behaviors as mixtures of distinct mechanisms ("circuit polymorphism"), build the first validated diagnostic for it, and test whether it explains the off-distribution and adversarial failures of canonical published circuits.
