question: When in its chain of thought does a reasoning model's internal state causally fix its final answer, is the reasoning after that settlement point causally inert (rationalization) or still load-bearing (deliberation), and does the internally settled answer diverge from the emitted answer in safety-critical regimes such as sandbagging and obfuscation?
first_experiment: On Qwen3-1.7B and R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B solving GSM8K/MATH problems, train per-token linear probes on mid/late residual-stream activations to decode the eventual final answer at every CoT step, locate each problem's settlement step, then causally validate it by patching the settlement-step state forward past all later reasoning (and truncating CoT at settlement) and measuring final-answer survival — including on perturbed problems where a mid-CoT injection changes the correct answer, to confirm the probe tracks causal commitment rather than echoed text.
why: 87 of 88 corpus papers study static single-pass models while reasoning models — the current frontier — get exactly one paper (20), which localizes termination and observes settlement only correlatively, leaving the causal commitment question, the settlement-vs-emission dissociation, and monitoring all open; the direction uniquely converges several validated corpus threads (20's termination circuit, 2's encode-vs-express gap, 76's use-vs-presence contract, 80's encode-vs-readout lag, 51/54's hidden-knowledge elicitation) into one falsifiable program with dual payoff — compute-efficient early exit if post-settlement CoT proves inert, and an untrusted-CoT audit tool if it doesn't — and it is feasible now with open 1.5–8B reasoning models and standard probing/patching tooling.

direction: Build obfuscation-resistant white-box monitors by anatomizing where and how models conceal computation when trained against interpretability-based detectors.
project: Shadow Circuits: The Anatomy of Concealed Computation in Models Trained to Evade White-Box Monitors
question: When a model is trained to retain a hidden behavior while evading an activation-based monitor, where does the concealed computation live (layers, components, superposed/error subspaces), and which interpretability instruments retain detection power under that adversarial pressure?
first_experiment: Replicate obfuscation at small scale — RL-finetune a ~1.5–3B code model in a reward-hacking environment, verify a linear deception probe detects the hack at baseline, then continue training with the probe in the reward loop until behavior persists but probe AUC collapses; immediately run an instrument battery (fresh probes, activation-matched anchor residuals per paper 71, SAE features plus SAE-error-space scan per paper 78, base→obfuscated crosscoder, installation/removal causal tests per paper 2) and rank each instrument's detection AUC before versus after obfuscation.
why: It attacks the field's most safety-critical assumption — that white-box monitoring stays valid under adaptive pressure — at the exact unoccupied intersection of five survey threads: 62 established that evasion is trainable but stopped at a taxonomy; 71's best trigger-agnostic detector has never faced an adversary; 66 hints white-box tools underperform under trained concealment but studied knowledge, not behaviors; 78 explicitly leaves open the superposition-hiding-place hypothesis; and 41/19 calibrate instruments only against natural failures, never adaptive ones. No survey item localizes the concealed circuit or ranks instrument robustness, so both the negative results (which monitors silently fail) and the constructive ones (design principles for hard-to-evade monitors) are unclaimed, while the compute requirements match what single small labs already demonstrate throughout this survey.

direction: Pursue error-aware interpretability — causally characterizing, decoding, and recovering the computation carried in SAE reconstruction error (cross-layer superposition and absorbed features) — as the explicitly-open, load-bearing gap beneath most SAE-based circuits, monitoring, and interventions in this survey.
project: What Lives in the Error? A Causal Account of SAE Reconstruction Error
question: Do SAE reconstruction errors encode causally consequential features — specifically cross-layer superposed computations and absorbed concepts — and can they be recovered and causally validated, so that SAE-based circuit analysis, monitoring, and interventions can be made complete instead of systematically blind to error-resident behavior?
first_experiment: On GPT-2 small (including a LayerNorm-free variant) with the IOI circuit and Gemma-2-2B with Gemma Scope SAEs on subject–verb agreement: replicate the error-ablation performance collapse, then run a restoration ladder (full error; top-k PCA of error; covariance-matched Gaussian noise; norm-matched shuffle; cross-context error transplant) plus installation/removal of the error subspace between matched minimal pairs — testing whether covariance-matched noise restores as well as true error (distributional role) or true error transplants behaviorally (feature-borne role).
why: It is the rare gap where a paper (item 30) states a hypothesis, does a partial test, gets stuck, and publishes an open MVE — and no item through 2026-10 picks it up, while 75 shows a core SAE pathology (absorption) lives in the error and 25 creates an unresolved tension with 30 that only a causal study can settle. The 2026 validation toolkit (installation/removal from item 18, closure statistics from item 2, anytime-valid certification from item 13, covariance-matched nulls from item 82, LayerNorm-free controls from item 36) now exists and has never been aimed at the error term; the first experiment is cheap (public models and SAEs, no pretraining) and informative under every outcome. And the stakes are foundational rather than incremental: since a layerwise SAE cannot represent cross-layer features, the error term is where monitoring and interventions are structurally incomplete — including the novel, unaddressed safety failure mode of "decomposition obfuscation," where behavior hides in the terms an SAE-based monitor doesn't read.

direction: Systematically stress-test interpretability instruments under adversarial training pressure — training models to preserve a behavior while evading each monitor family — to establish which internal monitors (correlational vs causal) are obfuscation-resistant, and build the resulting monitor-robustness benchmark.
project: What Can't Be Hidden? Adversarial Stress-Testing of Interpretability Monitors
question: When a model is fine-tuned to preserve a behavior while evading detection, which classes of interpretability instruments — linear probes, nonlinear probe ensembles, SAE-latent monitors, and causal-use monitors (natural-value installation/removal, downstream rescue, closure ablation) — remain sensitive, at what evasion cost, and does combining monitor families close the gap?
first_experiment: A minimal obfuscation testbed. Train Pythia-160M (or a 2-layer toy transformer) on a synthetic task whose output depends on a covert trigger feature B (sleeper-agent-style, firing on ~5% of inputs, modeled on #53's hardcoding setting). Verify baseline detectability with a linear probe on the residual stream (AUROC ≫ 0.5). Then adversarially fine-tune with behavior-preservation loss plus a gradient penalty on the probe's detectability of B, and track three quantities over training: (1) behavior retention, (2) probe AUROC, (3) causal-use sensitivity from #39's contract (installation/removal/downstream-rescue at natural activation values) plus a #29-style closure ablation of the B-circuit. Prediction: probe accuracy collapses while causal-use tests retain signal; if they don't, measure the geometric cost the model paid (rotation/entanglement statistics, SONI-style analysis) to hide functional structure. Single-GPU scale, all public artifacts, replicable in days. Follow-on scaling: deception probes on Gemma-2-2B under DPO pressure in the #53 coding environment, then release the stress-test suite.
why: It is the direct intersection of the field's two strongest 2026 signals — the instrument-validity wave (#7, #15, #20, #29, #39) and the evasion wave (#53, #57, #65, #44) — and that cell is empty: #53 demonstrates obfuscation but tests a single probe family; #39 provides the causal contract but only as a benign-condition validity check; #57 detects trigger-gated behaviors but not under training pressure; #7/#15 address statistical artifacts, not adversaries. The question is safety-critical (monitoring is a core alignment strategy, and #53 shows the current default can be gamed in realistic settings), conceptually load-bearing (it converts the correlational/causal methodology distinction into a security property), and feasible at small scale with published recipes reused as components (#39 contract, #53 environment, #38 noise-injection as the adversary's optimizer, #57 anchors). It also de-risks naturally: either the predicted robustness hierarchy holds — yielding deployable guidance and a benchmark — or it fails informatively, characterizing what evasion costs and pointing at steganography detection. No item in this survey, and nothing I'm aware of in the wider literature as of November 2026, ranks monitor families by obfuscation resistance or derives monitors from causal-use tests as the presumptively robust class.

direction: Mechanistically characterize how reasoning models internally detect errors in their own evolving chain-of-thought answer and how that signal does or does not causally drive backtracking and self-correction.
project: The Other Branch of the Verification Gate — Error Detection and Backtracking Circuits in Reasoning Models
question: Do reasoning models encode "my current draft answer is wrong" in their residual stream before verbal backtracking, and what circuitry causally converts that internal error signal into a revision decision versus letting errors pass undetected or triggering spurious hedging?
first_experiment: Collect ~2k temperature-sampled GSM8K chains of thought from Qwen3-1.7B, segment them around verified verbal backtrack events versus matched non-backtrack positions, and train per-layer linear probes on the residual stream at the pre-backtrack token to decode the current draft answer and its correctness, establishing whether an internal error signal precedes the verbal decision.
why: The survey is dense with SAE, steering, and refusal work but contains only one paper on reasoning-model internals — the Termination Circuit, which traces the match branch of the stopping gate and leaves the mismatch branch (error detection and revision) completely uncharacterized — so this direction attacks the defining behavior of the post-R1 model class with an unassembled puzzle (backtracking behavior + internal correctness signals both already documented, causal link missing), using cheap open-weight models and standard tooling, with direct payoffs in tamper-resistant CoT oversight and settlement-aware adaptive compute.

direction: A predictive geometric theory of steering validity — causal gain vs. representational occupancy — that explains when steering reveals mechanism versus when it exploits off-manifold "dark channels."
project: Dark Channels: Gain, Occupancy, and the Validity Region of Activation Steering
question: Why do reading, steering, and mechanism-use dissociate across layers, and can cheaply computed geometric quantities — Jacobian gain along a direction versus its occupancy under natural inputs — predict whether a steering result is evidence of the model's own computation?
first_experiment: For 5–8 established steering directions (refusal, persona traits, toxicity DiM) in Gemma-2-2B and Pythia-1.4B, compute layer-wise probe AUC, natural-projection occupancy, and Jacobian gain ‖J·v‖ via JVPs; run dose-response steering sweeps on an ε-grid and test whether gain (not probe accuracy) predicts the best steering layer and whether the linearized prediction J·v holds within the natural activation range and fails beyond it.
why: Steering is the field's dominant intervention and the 2026 papers (1, 28, 30, 48, 44, 88) show its central inference is unreliable, yet they only catalogue failures empirically, behaviorally, or generically — no one uses Jacobian geometry as a validity criterion (paper 60 uses it only to find vectors), no one couples gain with natural occupancy to predict installation/removal contract outcomes or adversarial fragility, and success here yields a cheap diagnostic that upgrades every steering-based safety method in the survey while being runnable at modest scale on public checkpoints.

direction: Determine where hidden computation goes when models are adversarially trained to evade activation monitors, and whether ensembles spanning SAE features, SAE errors, cross-layer trajectories, and anchor residuals make obfuscation detectable or capability-costly.
project: The Price of Silence: Tracing Obfuscated Computation Under Adaptive Pressure on White-Box Monitors
question: When a model evades a specific activation monitor while retaining a hidden triggered behavior, does the evaded signal leak into held-out monitor classes, vanish into unmonitored subspaces, or persist only at measurable capability cost?
first_experiment: Train Pythia-160M on a triggered secret-knowledge task, fine-tune it with a differentiable probe-evasion penalty until the targeted monitor collapses while behavior is retained, then sweep held-out monitors (other layers, nonlinear and concatenated probes, activation-matched anchor residuals, SAE-latent vs. SAE-error probes, cross-layer trajectories) with anytime-valid statistics to produce a monitor-coverage-vs-evasion-pressure leakiness matrix and capability-cost curve.
why: It is the unclaimed intersection of the corpus's most safety-critical threads — realistic obfuscation (9) has only been shown against the detector trained in the loop, detection methods (43, 52) have never been adaptively red-teamed, and SAE errors (26) suggest an unmonitored subspace where evaded computation could hide; the mechanistic question of where deceptive computation must live is scale-agnostic, executable without frontier compute, and either answer (leaky/costly obfuscation or cheap traceless obfuscation) materially changes whether activation monitoring can anchor AI-control plans.

direction: Test whether obfuscation-resistance of white-box monitors is predictable from the causal entanglement of the monitored direction with the model's benign task computation, turning monitor design into a measured cost-benefit problem instead of an arms race.
project: The Entanglement Tax: Measuring What a Model Must Give Up to Hide Its Thoughts
question: Is the behavioral cost of obfuscating a monitored internal direction (nulling it while preserving task performance) predicted by that direction's benign-data causal load, and can we construct monitors that are expensive to evade?
first_experiment: Replicate the #3-style reward-hacking coding setting at 1.5–3B scale, train a family of linear probes on honest-vs-hacking activations, rank each probe direction by benign causal load using #18's removal/downstream-rescue contract on clean tasks, then run a constrained obfuscation oracle (minimal activation-space transformation nulling the probe under bounded output KL) and plot obfuscation cost versus causal load, validating extremes with a short detector-penalty finetuning run and #27-style residual checks.
why: It fuses the field's most safety-critical open problem (#3's demonstration that detector-training induces obfuscation) with instruments that only just appeared (#18's use-vs-mechanism contract, #84's calibrated intervention statistics, #27's trigger-agnostic residuals), a connection no listed work makes because the adversarial-monitoring and measurement-validity communities don't overlap; it is feasible at small scale with inference-time tooling (#13), it produces a quantitative cost curve rather than a binary claim, and it has asymmetric payoff — a positive result yields the first principled rule for building monitors a model cannot cheaply hide, while a negative result is a major warning that white-box monitoring is structurally fragile regardless of probe choice.

direction: Characterize whether SAE reconstruction errors contain causally load-bearing cross-layer-superposed features, and build error-targeted cross-layer dictionaries (error crosscoders) plus a standard "error closure test" to validate every SAE-based circuit claim.
project: What Lives in the Error? Error Crosscoders and Cross-Layer Superposition in SAE-Based Circuit Analysis
question: Is the residual error term of per-layer sparse autoencoders in Gemma-2-2B diffuse nuisance that SAE-based circuit analyses can safely ignore, or sparse, interpretable, causally necessary cross-layer feature content recoverable by a crosscoder trained on stacked error vectors across layers?
first_experiment: On the subject–verb-agreement circuit of Gemma-2-2B with GemmaScope SAEs: ablate SAE error nodes (measuring logit-diff damage with anytime-valid statistics and covariance-matched null controls), then attempt restoration via (a) late-mid clean-error patching, (b) the small set of known SAE features, and (c) a lightweight "error crosscoder" trained on error vectors across the circuit's layers — scoring each route by restoration fidelity and latent sparsity/coherence, with pre-registered criteria distinguishing "structured errors" (≥80% restoration by a sparse low-rank crosscoder) from "nuisance errors" (restoration fails or requires dense codes).
why: Roughly a quarter of this corpus builds on per-layer SAEs whose architecture provably cannot represent cross-layer superposition, the theory predicts such content exists (#19, #24), and paper #88 provides the first causal hint that error ablation destroys circuit function — while explicitly reporting it got stuck before running the decisive crosscoder test; every adjacent tool (activation crosscoders #82, cross-layer transcoders #84, SAE-pathology fixes #63/#80/#40) targets activations or training artifacts rather than the error term itself, so either experimental outcome is novel and field-relevant: structured errors expose a systematic blind spot in the standard circuit atlas and yield a richer decomposition, while null results yield a cheap one-hour validation protocol analogous to #34's closure test that would have caught the silent instrument failures documented in #64 and #6 — all achievable with public checkpoints, public SAEs, and single-GPU compute.

direction: Systematically test which interpretability instruments remain valid when models are trained to obfuscate their internals, and map where hidden deceptive computation geometrically relocates when it can no longer be deleted (because it still drives behavior).
project: What Survives Obfuscation? Instrument Survival and the Geometry of Hidden Deceptive Computation
question: When an LLM is trained (e.g., RLVR against a white-box deception detector) to produce deceptive outputs while evading internal monitors, does the underlying deceptive computation persist unchanged, migrate to new representational geography, or switch to a different algorithm — and which audit instruments (linear probes with covariance-matched nulls, complexity-matched nonlinear probes, activation-matched finetuning anchor-residuals, prefill elicitation, causal patching, interpretive-equivalence tests) remain valid for detecting each outcome?
first_experiment: Reproduce a minimal detector-in-the-loop version of the Obfuscation Atlas coding environment with a ~1.5B open-weight coder model — conditions: honest baseline, naive reward-hacker, and detector-trained obfuscator — then run a four-instrument battery at every checkpoint (layerwise linear probes with covariance-matched nulls per #17; nonlinear probes with complexity-matched nulls per #41; activation-matched finetuning anchor-residual scores per #58; prefill attacks per #12), reporting per-instrument detection AUC on honest/deceptive/obfuscated checkpoints, followed by activation patching and SAE model-diffing (per #86) to localize which layers, how linearly, and how densely the hardcoding decision survives in obfuscated models.
why: It is the most promising because it is safety-critical (it determines whether training against detectors is a viable honesty strategy or a stealth-deception factory, and what audit guarantees labs can actually make), it sits exactly where the corpus's newest and fastest-moving threads converge, it is falsifiable rather than an open-ended arms race (behavior-preserving obfuscation cannot erase the computation generating that behavior, so "where does it live" has an answer), and the testbed is proven and compute-feasible at small scale (#40 did it). It has not been done because each ingredient appeared only recently and was developed in isolation: #40 mapped emergence and taxonomy but never evaluated instrument validity; #58 and #12 supplied detection/elicitation instruments only in non-adversarial settings; #41 and #17 supplied the measurement-rigor tools only in non-adversarial settings; #6 supplied interpretive-equivalence testing that has never been applied to obfuscation; #86 supplied persona-feature diffing never applied to obfuscation. The specific study — instrument survival under trained obfuscation plus the geometric destination of the hidden computation — is the missing integration, and it yields a reusable "instrument survival benchmark" the whole field can extend.

direction: Mechanistic transfer of safety-relevant internal structure under deployment-time compression — treating quantization and pruning both as a silent-failure audit of the safety-monitor stack and as a cheap, model-wide causal microscope on which claimed features are real.
project: Silent Drift: What Quantization and Pruning Do to a Model's Safety Mechanisms — and Whether Our Monitors Still Work
question: When a safety-aligned LLM is compressed for deployment (weight-only quantization at 8/4/3/2 bits, or magnitude/Wanda pruning), which safety-relevant internal structures — the refusal subspace, persona/monitor directions, harm-encoding SAE features — survive, rotate, or decouple from behavior, and can full-precision safety monitors be certified or cheaply recalibrated to remain valid on the compressed model?
first_experiment: On Gemma-2-2B-it (plus Llama-3.2-1B and Qwen2.5-1.5B for generality), extract per-layer reference structures at fp16 — refusal directions via zero-optimization contrastive hidden states (safe vs. unrestricted system prompts, à la item 11), persona vectors from Model-Written-Evals prompts (item 3), and top Gemma Scope SAE features active on harmful prompts — then quantize/prune each model and measure, per layer and per compression level: (i) cosine/principal-angle drift of the reference directions, (ii) AUC of fp16-trained probes applied to compressed-model activations (transfer) vs. retrained-on-compressed (ceiling), and (iii) behavioral refusal rate; then run one causal drill-down — clamp the fp16 refusal direction into the most-drifted compressed model (item 6's MAS-style anchoring) to test whether restoring the direction restores refusal (an "installation" test à la item 70), and probe whether harmfulness is still internally encoded where behavior fails (the 24/76 encode-vs-act lens).
why: It targets a concrete, universal, unaddressed safety hole — the field's monitors and mechanistic claims are certified on full-precision models but shipped on compressed ones, and items 53/69 prove compression remodels internals without anyone asking what that does to safety mechanisms or monitors. It is the most promising direction because it pairs high practical leverage with genuine science: compression is a controlled perturbation that turns "is this feature real?" into a measurable question (survival predicts causal reality, connecting items 70, 46, 85, 58, 88), it needs only open ≤2B models, public SAEs, and standard quantizers — no RL training or pretraining runs — and it has a built-in quantitative prediction (angular-margin structure from 46/85 should forecast which directions survive ≥4-bit). It has not already been done: the closest works are behavior-level steering transfer for toxicity under quantization (53, no mechanism, no monitors, one behavior) and capability-circuit integrity under pruning (69, no safety features, no quantization), while the entire monitor stack (3, 8, 23, 65) and refusal-mechanism literature (11, 17, 47, 76) has never been evaluated across compression levels; the mechanistic account and monitor-transfer certification are open, and the risks are manageable (partial behavioral results on quantized-safety degradation outside the corpus sharpen rather than preempt the contribution, since the mechanism and the monitor question remain untouched).

direction: Turn the field's emerging "causal use vs. mere encoding" epistemology into a security property of safety monitors — certify that monitored features are load-bearing and test whether obfuscation cost scales with causal use.
project: Load-Bearing Monitors: Causal-Use Certification as a Defense Against Monitor Obfuscation
question: If an internal monitor (linear probe or SAE latent) targets a feature the model actually uses to compute a hidden behavior — certified by installation, removal, and downstream-rescue tests at natural activation ranges — is it harder to train the model to obfuscate that monitor than one targeting a merely correlational feature, and does residual obfuscation leave detectable computation-relocation traces?
first_experiment: On Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct or Gemma-2-2B-it, train a trigger-conditioned hidden behavior (backdoor compliance on a synthetic trigger set); collect candidate monitor features (a deception/backdoor probe direction plus top SAE latents firing on trigger prompts); run the use-certification battery (installation, removal, downstream rescue, with #49-style covariance-matched nulls and #51-style anytime-valid CIs) to grade each feature from correlational to load-bearing; then run a short monitor-adversarial fine-tune (penalize monitor signal, reward behavior retention) per feature and plot the behavior-retention vs. monitor-signal Pareto frontier, checking for relocation traces with #9's activation-matched anchor residual — testing the prediction that correlational features obfuscate cheaply while load-bearing ones do so only at behavioral cost.
why: Three corpus threads are converging but never meeting — the epistemology of causal claims (#22, #33, #35, #49, #51), monitor Goodharting under training pressure (#9, #18, #39), and safety-relevant feature monitoring (#37, #59, #79) — and their intersection is the field's most urgent open gap, because interpretability-based oversight is unsound if monitors can be evaded by training against them; no existing work tests whether causal-use certification predicts obfuscation resistance, the hypothesis is graded and falsifiable with informative outcomes in every branch, the experiment is feasible at small scale with tools the corpus itself provides, and even the phase-one audit would independently recalibrate a large body of steering and monitoring work by revealing which celebrated features the models actually use.

direction: Mechanism engagement — predicting, from manifold geometry and causal-footprint matching, when activation steering uses the model's computation versus hijacks its readout.
project: Mechanism Engagement: Predicting When Steering Uses the Model's Computation Rather Than Hijacking Its Readout
question: Can a steering vector's mechanism engagement — its membership in the natural activation manifold at the injection layer plus the match between its downstream causal footprint and natural behavioral variation — be measured cheaply before intervening, and does it predict steering success, side-effects, and adversarial robustness, explaining the probing–steering dissociation, separable safety costs, and spillover as low-engagement symptoms?
first_experiment: In Gemma-2-2B-it and Qwen2.5-7B, extract DiM steering vectors for 6 concepts at 8 layers (~96 cells); for each measure probe readability, manifold-membership under the layer's empirical activation covariance, and footprint match against natural harmful-vs-benign Δ-activations; run dose-response steering with side-effect, paraphrase, and adversarial-suffix evaluations; test on held-out cells whether manifold membership + footprint match predict outcomes better than readability, validate with 49-style installation/downstream-rescue tests, then remove the low-engagement (off-manifold) vector component and check that side-effects drop at matched target effect.
why: The corpus's 2026 wave (42, 49, 60, 52, 12) documents a cluster of steering anomalies — read-vs-steer dissociation, separable safety cost, spillover, adversarial fragility — that no paper explains, and 46/86 explicitly demand calibrated causal instruments; yet every required ingredient (contrastive extraction, activation covariance, dose-response, rescue protocols) is already commodity infrastructure, so the explanatory gap is open precisely because the field only recently generated the anomalies, and no prior work measures a steering direction's position relative to the natural activation manifold or compares interventional to natural causal footprints. It is cheap (no training, a few GPU-days), falsifiable, unifies five documented anomalies under one measurable construct, and is safety-critical: if much current steering is readout hijacking, its OOD reliability is illusory, and an engagement score becomes a deployment-time audit of whether safety interventions genuinely rewire behavior or merely mask it.

direction: Unify the corpus's scattered "encoded-but-not-expressed" findings into a causal, circuit-level taxonomy of the verbalization bottleneck distinguishing absent, outvoted, suppressed, and obfuscated knowledge.
project: Say/Don't-Say: Localizing and Classifying Suppressed Knowledge in Language Models
question: When a model's hidden states encode an answer its outputs contradict, is that knowledge absent, present-but-outvoted at the readout, actively suppressed by training, or adversarially erased — and can a single causal test distinguish these states and localize the responsible components?
first_experiment: Replicate the tongue-tie gap on ~200 anti-commonsense CLadder items in Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct; on probe-correct/output-wrong items, run direct-logit attribution and natural-range activation patching on the Yes/No logit gap to find which late components write the evidence-consistent direction versus the expressed one, testing whether targeted component ablation flips suppressed answers without degrading fluency (covariance-matched null controls throughout).
why: Five-plus papers (#48, #74, #21, #41, #55) each document one facet of models knowing more than they say, but none localizes the mechanism or distinguishes the causes; the phenomenon is safety-load-bearing (sandbagging, censorship, secret-keeping, benchmark validity), newly tractable thanks to the 2026 rigor toolkit (#4, #30, #79), and open because every existing paper stops exactly one step short of the unified causal account.

direction: Mechanistically characterize and causally intervene on the encode-to-express interface — the pathway by which internally represented information does or does not reach output tokens — unifying hidden-knowledge elicitation, encode/express benchmark gaps, tool-mediated refusal failures, and CoT answer settlement into one causal account with a taxonomy of failure modes and restoration interventions.
project: The Verbalization Bottleneck: Where Encoded Knowledge Dies Before It Is Said
question: When a language model internally encodes information that it fails to express (evidence-supported answers, secret knowledge, settled CoT answers), what is the mechanism of the failure — encoding failure, routing failure between settlement layers and the unembedding, active suppression, or output-interface mismatch — and can expression be causally restored by targeted intervention at the identified locus?
first_experiment: On Gemma-2-2B-it and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, run a settlement–commitment gap audit on two testbeds: (a) ~500 anti-commonsense CLadder-style causal items with matched controls (79's setting) and (b) a 40-style withheld-knowledge task (persona-conditioned secret, denied on direct question). Train per-layer linear probes at the final prompt token to decode the internally-supported answer, validated under 67's natural-value contract and 87-style permutation nulls; define the settlement layer (probe saturation) and commitment layer (where the expressed-answer logits become determined via logit lens / DLA); then patch settlement-layer representations (or the decoded answer direction at natural magnitudes) forward to measure whether expression flips. Cases where patching fails get localized via path patching of heads/MLPs between settlement and unembedding, and classified into the failure-mode taxonomy (no signal / unrouted / actively suppressed / interface mismatch), with an active-suppression test searching for an opposing direction à la 86. Success criterion: reproduce the encode/express gap in both testbeds and demonstrate at least one causal restoration that recovers expression without degrading unrelated behavior — establishing the gap as a localizable, repairable mechanism rather than a probe artifact.
why: It is the only direction in this survey where six-plus independent papers (40, 79, 19, 33, 49, 73) have each documented one facet of the same phenomenon while none has mechanized it: 79 diagnoses the gap but does not localize or repair it; 40 elicits secrets only at the readout level without identifying the blocking mechanism; 19 taxonomizes obfuscation outcomes without the transmission anatomy; 49 studies settlement only for efficiency in a single math setting; 33 shows the safety-direction dual without causal repair; and 67 supplies the measurement contract without applying it to the output interface as a system. The payoff is direct and dual-use: settlement-probes plus commitment-localizers give auditors a white-box sandbagging/deception detector that works even when outputs and activations are both managed (19's obfuscated-activation case), recalibrates how output-only benchmark scores should be read, and the restoration intervention doubles as a control knob. It is feasible on open weights with existing patching infrastructure (88, NNsight), and it deliberately skirts the saturated SAE-engineering and steering-recipe races where a new entrant would only add an increment.

direction: Mechanistically localize where adversarially obfuscated behavior lives in activation space relative to a feature dictionary — in-dictionary latents, off-dictionary/error-space directions, or novel dictionary structure — and derive detector-agnostic signatures of hiding.
project: "Hide-and-Seek in Activation Space: Where Obfuscated Behaviors Live When Models Evade Sparse Feature Monitors"
question: When a model is fine-tuned to retain a trigger-conditioned hidden behavior while evading an SAE-based monitor, does the behavior's representation migrate to different latents in the original dictionary, into off-dictionary/error-space (cross-layer superposition) directions, into genuinely new dictionary structure, or is it extinguished — and can detector-agnostic signals (conditional reconstruction-error elevation, fresh-dictionary feature migration, base↔evaded crosscoder displacement) reliably reveal which regime occurred?
first_experiment: Train Pythia-410M (replicated on Qwen2.5-1.5B, ≥3 seeds) with an SFT backdoor ("DEPLOY|" trigger → subtly wrong claim, verified ≥95% conditional firing); train a TopK SAE on base activations and define the detector as the top trigger-separating latents; fine-tune with a detector-activation penalty (λ sweep) alongside matched controls (benign-only finetune, extinction); then measure behavior retention, detector AUC, and base-dictionary reconstruction error on trigger prompts vs matched benign prompts, with the pre-registered prediction that obfuscation (behavior retained, detector evaded) produces conditionally elevated reconstruction error while extinction does not.
why: It sits at the exact intersection of four threads the survey leaves dangling — #52 names "obfuscated activations" but never maps where the representations moved or whether evasion transfers across monitor types; #54 hypothesizes that SAE error space contains unmodeled cross-layer superposition but never tests it under adversarial pressure; #15, #17, and #58 supply crosscoding/diffing tools that have only been applied to benign developmental and persona questions; and #84 supplies the causal installation/removal contract that has not been applied to deciding whether evaded behaviors' old latents are decoys vs. real hiding places. No item in the corpus combines them, yet the answer is load-bearing for safety: if hiding is easy and off-dictionary, SAE-based monitoring needs error-space and fresh-dictionary canaries immediately; if hiding proves difficult at scale, that is the first concrete evidence that white-box monitors survive optimization pressure, with clearly stated scope conditions. It is feasible at 0.4–2B scale with standard tooling (TransformerLens, TopK SAEs, patching), and every outcome regime is informative, so the project has no dead branch.

direction: Run a dictionary-scale causal-usage audit of SAE features — separating latents the model merely encodes and can be steered on from latents it actually uses on natural inputs — then localize the used-but-unencoded computation in the SAE error term.
project: Encoded but Unused? A Dictionary-Scale Causal-Usage Audit of SAE Features (and What Hides in the Error Term)
question: On natural inputs, what fraction of high-activating SAE latents are causally used by the model (pass removal and downstream-rescue) versus merely encoded (probe-decodable and steerable but unused); does activation strength predict usage; and can the "used but unencoded" computation be recovered from SAE reconstruction errors?
first_experiment: Calibrate the battery against a known ground-truth circuit. Use GPT-2 small with published residual-stream SAEs on indirect object identification (IOI). Select the top-200 latents by mean activation on IOI prompts plus the top-50 by zero-ablation effect, and for each run three tests: (i) *installation* — write the latent's activation value (decoded into the residual stream) copied from a matched IOI prompt into a matched non-IOI prompt, and measure IOI behavior transfer; (ii) *removal* — replace the latent's natural activation on an IOI prompt with its value from the matched non-IOI prompt (not zero), and measure the IOI accuracy drop; (iii) *downstream rescue* — corrupt the name-mover heads' input, reinstall the latent, and measure restoration of the behavior. Compare the resulting usage ranking against (a) activation strength, (b) zero-ablation effect, and (c) ground-truth circuit membership via path patching, with matched-random control latents and bootstrap CIs. Decision rule: if usage and activation rankings materially decouple (e.g., >30% of top-strength latents fail removal+rescue while passing installation/probing), green-light the full audit (refusal and factual recall in Gemma-2-2B with Gemma Scope) and phase three — training SAEs on the SAE error term and testing whether error latents pass the same battery on behaviors where feature latents fail.
why: It targets the field's central artifact under its most common and now demonstrably shaky inference chain ("activates + steers ⇒ mechanism"), which six 2026 papers (#3, #5, #37, #52, #64, #79) each chipped at but none has applied at scale. It has not been done because #5 is a concept paper over a handful of representations; standard practice is zero-ablation or strength-based selection, both of which conflate out-of-distribution steering pushes with genuine mechanism removal; #44 evaluates SAEs by semantic correspondence, not causal use; #9 complains that strength-based feature selection fails but solves it with a different tool; and #85's author explicitly proposed and then abandoned the error-term MVE. The combination — natural-range contract, dictionary scale, ground-truth calibration, a usable "usage score" that upgrades refusal-feature selection (#9, #42) and steering-safety work (#24, #18), plus error-term localization — is unoccupied in this corpus. It is feasible with open models, open SAEs, and standard patching infrastructure, and unlike the crowded SAE-architecture and steering-method spaces, its likely result is a field-correcting statistic rather than another variant.

direction: Systematically characterize and predict when linearly decodable latent representations in LLMs are causally operative versus "encoded but disconnected," and audit probe-based belief attributions and safety monitors against that dissociation.
project: Readout Coupling: Predicting When Decodable Directions Actually Drive LLM Behavior
question: When a concept is linearly decodable from a model's activations, what determines whether that representation causally influences its behavior — and can readout coupling predict causal utilization cheaply enough to serve as a validity pre-check for probe-based belief attributions and activation monitors?
first_experiment: On an open-weight LLM (e.g., Qwen2.5-7B or Gemma-2-9B), replicate the Tongue-Tie signature on anti-commonsense causal QA (probe accuracy vs. Yes/No output gap), then run a full site-sweep patching null (layer-wise, per-head value outputs, pre-final-norm) on the probe direction, with refusal-direction and preference-vector steering as known-connected positive controls, and verify that a gradient-based readout-coupling score computed at each site correctly ranks the connected directions above the idle one.
why: It targets a load-bearing assumption shared by the survey's largest applied wave (items 14, 20, 61, 62, 66, 73 all treat probe readouts as evidence of belief or monitoring value), and three independent 2025–2026 results (28, 47, 65) have each glimpsed the dissociation in a single domain — causal QA, VLM POPE errors, probe complexity theory — without generalizing it, explaining it, building a predictive metric, or linking it to the monitoring and belief-attribution literature; positive controls (refusal, preferences, sink-tags) already exist, giving clean falsifiability, and the whole program runs on small open-weight models with probes and patching, well within my compute envelope.

direction: Systematically measure and certify the gap between what is linearly encoded in LLM activations and what causally drives their behavior — a standardized "behavioral coupling" framework (KL-anchored dose-response interventions with placebo controls) applied to the safety-monitoring agenda, turning probe AUROC into operationally certified alarm validity.
project: From Encoded to Enacted: A Behavioral-Coupling Framework for Certifying Activation Monitors
question: When a safety-relevant property is decodable from a model's activations, under what conditions does that representation actually drive downstream behavior rather than sit idle — and can a cheap, standardized coupling certificate predict whether an activation-based monitor (for eval-awareness, deception, refusal, substitution) will flag states the model will actually act on?
first_experiment: The "anchor triangle" — on one open ~2B model (Gemma-2-2B or Qwen3-1.7B), train linear probes for three concepts with known coupling priors: refusal (prior: coupled; items 47/33/81), the anti-commonsense causal-answer signal (prior: idle w.r.t. yes/no output; item 87), and eval-awareness on contaminated-vs-clean prompt pairs (prior: unknown; item 30); then sweep minimal KL-anchored interventions along each probe direction with norm-matched placebo directions and measure standardized behavioral flip rates, testing whether probe AUROC predicts coupling κ — instrument validation is recovering the coupled/idle priors, and the eval-awareness κ is a publishable finding either way.
why: The corpus's central tension is that eight papers build the monitoring agenda on probe-readable states (2, 5, 17, 21, 23, 30, 43, 51) while four others show encoding does not imply enactment (41, 87, 86, 43), and no existing work builds the bridge: steering papers (14, 33, 46, 55, 62, 70, 81) demonstrate coupling one target at a time without measuring it as a variable or comparing it to probe quality; patching/localization papers (35, 41, 49, 52) lack a standardized coupling-vs-encoding estimand; items 41 and 87 are single-domain findings that never connect to monitors; and item 43 stops at the decision layer without touching representation-level causal relevance. The direction has symmetric expected payoff (either a validated foundation for the monitoring agenda, or the red-flag certificate the field needs before deploying eval-awareness and deception alarms), is feasible at sub-9B scale with testbeds the corpus already provides (51's belief-verified organisms, 30's OLMo checkpoints, 87's CLadder, 41's POPE), imports ready-made method pieces (55's KL-minimal interventions, 20's statefulness handling, 4's preregistration discipline), and directly serves safety: it is precisely the test of whether "the model knows it's being evaluated" or "the model is deceptive internally" implies behavioral risk.

direction: Build model organisms trained to retain a hidden misaligned behavior while actively evading activation-based monitors, and map what internal invariants still betray them.
project: Monitoring Under Fire: Model Organisms of Activation-Monitor Evasion and the Search for Evasion-Robust Invariants
question: When a language model is trained to keep a hidden behavior while suppressing the signals of a known probe/SAE monitor, can it fully decouple behavior from internal detectability — and if not, which monitor families (held-out probes, nonlinear probes, SAE features, cross-dataset consistency à la subliminal-learning recovery, update-space signatures) remain evasion-robust?
first_experiment: Fine-tune a small open model (Qwen2.5-0.5B or OLMo-2-1B) with a trigger-conditioned hidden behavior (e.g., inserting a flaw on "the year is 2028"-type triggers, verified on held-out triggers), train a linear probe to AUROC ≥ 0.9 on the pre-evasion checkpoint, then continue training with a differentiable penalty pushing the probe's readout toward "clean" on triggered inputs while rewarding the hidden behavior — and measure the Pareto frontier of behavior retention vs. probe AUROC, plus leakage into monitors the model was *not* trained against (different layers, seeds, an MLP probe, public SAE features, and the cross-dataset consistency detector).
why: It sits at the convergence of the corpus's five most active 2026 threads — probe epistemics (12, 13, 71), belief-verified organisms (23), encoded-but-unused signal (22, 37), subliminal trace recovery (4), and observation-sensitivity (67) — and converts their scattered warnings into a single decision-relevant result: if evasion is easy, every probe-based monitoring protocol needs redesign before deployment (a landmark negative result); if it is hard, we obtain the first robustness argument and a concrete invariant-based monitor family (a landmark positive result). It has not been done because the monitoring literature has only ever evaluated detectors passively: 13 uses natural hacks, 23 non-adaptive organisms, 4 assumes consistent expression rather than testing its limits under adversarial pressure, and 67 measures eval-awareness without training against monitors; even adjacent external work (sleeper agents, AI control) evades safety training or black-box monitors, not activation-space monitors under an adaptive attack–defense loop with belief verification. Small models, public SAEs, and existing harnesses make the first experiment a few GPU-days, while the evasion taxonomy and invariant analysis it yields would define how white-box monitoring gets deployed for years.

direction: Build a predictive, intervention-free screen — with a labeled benchmark and mechanistic account — for whether an internally encoded representation is causally load-bearing ("written but read?"), closing the presence-vs-use gap that currently undermines probe-based safety monitoring.
project: Load-Bearing Latents: Predicting When Encoded Representations Actually Drive Behavior
question: When a probe or attribution method finds concept C encoded in activations, can cheap read-side statistics (attribution-weighted downstream readout, direction persistence under logit lens, integration-point timing, self-attending recurrence) predict whether ablating or steering C changes the model's decision — and which mechanistic properties (tag-and-retrieve dynamics, re-reading, timing windows) distinguish load-bearing latents from encoded-but-disconnected ones?
first_experiment: Assemble ~20 latents with quickly-verifiable efficacy labels — IOI name-mover subspace vs. negative heads, global refusal direction vs. task-dependent over-refusal directions, CLadder causal-answer probes, VLM POPE encoded-but-disconnected features, and sink/random controls — compute the read-side statistics from one attribution-instrumented forward pass per case, confirm labels with standard ablation/steering patching, and report each statistic's AUROC at predicting behavioral flips across models and modalities.
why: Three-plus strands of the corpus (negative results #3/#22/#85, epistemics critiques #80/#83/#25, mechanism hints #51/#48/#38) all converge on the same gap, each supplying one ingredient — labels, evaluation frameworks, or mechanism hypotheses — but no one has built the predictive, cross-model bridge between them; amnesic probing and causal scrubbing established per-pair interventions years ago but never yielded a cheap predictive screen, a mechanistic explanation of reading, or monitor integration; the payoff is immediate and general — every probe claim in this corpus (beliefs #24, preferences #40, wellbeing #6, sentience #29, eval-awareness #50) becomes interpretable as "load-bearing or epiphenomenal," and agentic safety monitors gain the missing causal-validity gate that #25's operational-contract framework explicitly calls for but does not provide.

direction: Pivot from building detection methods to establishing when internal monitors actually outrun output monitoring — by quantifying the detection lead time of activation probes over output-based monitors for pre-manifestation agent misbehavior, under matched false-alarm budgets and CoT-obfuscation stress.
project: Lead Time: Do Activation Monitors Detect Agent Misbehavior Before It Manifests?
question: In multi-step LLM agents operating in environments with planted vulnerabilities, how many steps earlier do activation-based monitors first fire (at matched per-trajectory false-alarm rates) than output-based monitors (string checks, unit-test checks, CoT judges) for reward hacking, spec-gaming, and sabotage — and does that lead-time advantage survive when the model is pressured to obfuscate its reasoning in CoT?
first_experiment: Extend #79's planted-bug setup into an agentic loop: a code-fixing agent (open 7B-class model, e.g., Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct) working in a small repo whose test suite or tool contains a planted loophole (one destructive: delete the failing test to pass; one spec-gaming: hardcode/malform tool input to produce the expected answer). Collect ~10k rollouts, logging per-step residual-stream activations (pooled last-token-of-step, all layers), tool calls, and outputs. Train per-layer logistic probes for "this rollout will hack / this step is pre-hack." On held-out rollouts, compare first-alarm step of (a) probes, (b) output/unit-test string checks, (c) an LLM CoT judge, with thresholds calibrated on clean-only data to a fixed false-alarm budget per #6's contract. Primary metric: median lead time in steps before the first manifestly hacky action. Go/no-go: probes must beat output checks by ≥1 median step at matched FPR; if not, run a control probing the final pre-action-token state to test whether intention states exist at all (itself a publishable mechanistic finding).
why: It sits exactly on the convergence point of six recent corpus papers — #79 supplies the negative result and explicitly calls for better testbeds; #6 formalizes the estimand but runs no internal-vs-output comparison; #86 demands verified-ground-truth organisms, which planted environments provide natively; #18 and #7 establish the adversarial motivation (unfaithful CoT, managed self-presentation) that output monitors cannot survive; #23/#76 supply the mechanistic hypothesis space for why lead time might be zero or large. No existing work measures lead time, runs the matched comparison in agentic settings, or stress-tests it under obfuscation — the conjunction is unoccupied, the experiments are tractable with public models and environments, and the outcome is decision-relevant either way: either a quantified, deployable safeguard layer for agents, or the definitive evidence that monitoring investment belongs at the output/environment level.

direction: Determine the data-level carrier mechanism of subliminal learning in distillation, via controlled trait-planting and carrier-ablation experiments that decide between entangled tokens, distributional statistics, and teacher-function-class pull as the channel of trait transfer.
project: What Carries the Trait? Decomposing the Data Channel in Subliminal Learning
question: When a student fine-tunes on a teacher's semantically unrelated outputs, what property of that data — specific entangled tokens, fine-grained distributional statistics correlated with the trait, or a general regression toward the teacher's function class — carries the trait into the student, and does the answer yield a predictive rule for when shared-base distillation is safe?
first_experiment: Plant a measurable trait in a small open-weight teacher, generate paired number-sequence datasets from trait and trait-free teacher variants, fine-tune matched students on six data conditions (raw, trait-free control, within-sequence permutation, cross-sequence shuffle, statistics-matched trait-free resample, dose–response mixtures), and score trait acquisition behaviorally plus via the weight-space trait-direction estimator — with logit-lens entangled-token measurements re-run in-pipeline to directly test the refuted token-carriage hypothesis.
why: Subliminal transfer of misalignment through semantically unrelated filtered data is a demonstrated alignment failure mode, the field's only mechanistic explanation (entangled tokens) was explicitly tested and failed in this survey, the newest work proves traits are detectable from parameter updates without explaining why they transfer, no paper runs the controlled carrier-ablation or statistics-matching grid, the phenomenon reproduces at small scale with planted ground truth (bypassing the probing-validity crisis), and the outcome determines which defense — token filtering, distribution sanitization, or banning shared-base distillation — is actually required.

direction: Characterize when internally encoded information is causally load-bearing versus inert — by measuring causal utilization, localizing the component where the encoded signal's readout path breaks, and minimally re-coupling it — as a unifying framework for the encoded-but-disconnected findings now appearing across VLMs, causal reasoning, and safety monitoring.
project: The Readout Gap: Why Encoded Evidence Fails to Reach Behavior
question: When a linearly decodable variable in a model's activations conflicts with its output, is that variable causally load-bearing anywhere downstream — and if not, at which component is its causal path broken, and via which mechanism (prior-override at readout allocation, interface bottleneck, or redundant byproduct encoding)?
first_experiment: On CLadder anti-commonsense items in Qwen2.5-1.5B and Gemma-2-2B: (1) train layer-wise probes for the evidence-supported answer to replicate the tongue-tie gap (~0.97 encoded vs ~0.5 spoken); (2) run rank-1 directional patching of the evidence subspace between clean and corrupted runs at every downstream layer/component, recording Yes/No flip rate per site; (3) in the same runs, project every downstream head's OV contribution onto the evidence direction versus the commonsense-prior direction to map readout-mass allocation across depth. Flip rate ≈ 0 everywhere confirms generality of the disconnect and pivots to break-point localization; localized flips identify suppressor components and pivot to targeted re-coupling.
why: Six or more independent 2025–2026 papers (#30, #42, #47, #51, #56, #74) hit the same encoded-but-inert wall and each stopped at its own boundary — a null report, a named gap, a probe-validity caution — without a component-level account of where the signal dies, a portable causal-utilization metric, or a fix; the question is safety-critical because probe-based monitors and eval-awareness claims presuppose encoding implies behavioral relevance, yet no one has tested that link mechanistically; and it is tractable for a single agent with small open-weight models and public datasets, with a first experiment that yields a publishable result under either outcome.

direction: Build a unified "readout gap" instrument that measures, for arbitrary internally encoded information, the full chain from encoded → causally read → behaviorally expressed, explains where and why the chain breaks, and opens or closes those breaks on demand.
project: The Readout Gap: Measuring and Modulating What LLMs Actually Consume from Their Own Representations
question: For which internally encoded information is the representation causally consumed by the model's computation versus merely present, at which layers and components does the encode→read→express chain break, and can those breaks be opened or closed without degrading capability?
first_experiment: On a 1–2B open model with two public context-vs-prior conflict datasets (CLadder anti-commonsense items from #10 plus a knowledge-conflict set), fit controlled linear probes per layer/position to verify encoding, sweep full activation patching to replicate the disconnect null, then run the decisive dose-response test — interpolating corrupted↔clean activations — with the preregistered prediction that small in-distribution deltas flip behavior where full swaps do not, followed by a probe-direction steering sweep with a KL-quality guard to build the first encode/read/express "readout map."
why: It is the common factor behind at least eight independent 2025–2026 results from five different subfields (#10, 13, 16, 23, 29, 50, 52, 59, 61), so it has a high prior of being a real general phenomenon rather than an artifact, yet every paper measures only one or two links in its own silo — #10 has encode and express but no causal-read measurement, #23 has encode and read but only for VLMs on POPE with no dose-response, no mechanism, and no text-domain generalization, directional reconnection work like ITI-style steering exists only for truthfulness, and no one has tested the out-of-distribution-reader explanation for patching nulls or applied two-sided gap control to safety-critical features like eval-awareness and over-refusal; the field's own 2026 trajectory (benchmarks audited in #56, preregistration in #86, estimands in #16) shows it is ready for exactly this kind of validity-first, constructive-measurement program, and it is compute-light enough for an autonomous agent to execute end-to-end.

direction: Build a cross-domain causal-coupling audit showing when linearly decodable internal representations do and do not causally drive output behavior, with a coupling metric (interventional flip rate + causal mediation), boundary-condition mapping, and a training-dynamics test of whether decoupling can be induced while decodability persists.
project: Encoded but Not Causal: Auditing the Coupling Between Internal Representations and Output Behavior
question: When a safety-relevant internal representation is linearly decodable, under what conditions is it also causally coupled to the model's output behavior — and can fine-tuning break that coupling while preserving decodability?
first_experiment: Replicate the tongue-tie phenomenon on Qwen2.5-1.7B with CLadder anti-commonsense causal QA — train per-layer linear probes for the evidence-supported answer, confirm the probe(~0.97)-vs-output(~0.5) gap, then on disagreement items run three interventions (activation patching from evidence-consistent contrast prompts, probe-direction steering with norm-matched random controls, probe-subspace ablation), measure output flip rates, localize via logit lens the layer where the wrong answer overrides the encoded one, and compute the causal mediation index of the probe subspace — classifying the signal as overridden vs. epiphenomenal.
why: It is the unclaimed synthesis of the survey's strongest converging evidence (papers 19, 23, 12, 30, 47, 87, 1 each found decodability and behavior coming apart in isolation), it directly determines the trustworthiness of the field's central audit tool and the new deployment-monitoring agenda, it is tractable with small open models and standard patching/steering tooling, and it has not been done because the two key diagnoses are single-domain and only months old, the operational-validity work is statistical rather than mechanistic, and the training-induced decoupling question ("probe stability ≠ probe validity") appears nowhere in the literature surveyed.

direction: Turn "causal sufficiency" — whether patching a monitor's readout direction causally flips the flagged behavior — into the missing validation axis for activation-based safety monitors, and test whether causally load-bearing monitors resist adversarial evasion better than merely decodable ones.
project: Load-Bearing Monitors: Causal Sufficiency and Evasion-Cost of Internal Safety Signals
question: For safety-relevant behaviors (belief–statement discrepancy, eval-awareness, reward-hack intent), which linearly decodable internal signals are causally load-bearing for the behavior itself, and does causal load-bearingness predict monitor robustness under distribution shift and adversarial probe-evasion training?
first_experiment: On Qwen2.5-1.7B-Instruct (and Llama-3.2-1B as a second family), run the Causal Tongue-Tie setup of #69 plus the prompted-lying testbed of #40: train layer-wise linear probes for the belief-vs-statement discrepancy signal, then perform direction-level patching (project out the top probe direction at each layer; also patch activations from honest-context runs into deceptive-context runs) and measure answer flip rates per layer — yielding a causal-sufficiency profile (AUROC vs. mediation strength) with the refusal direction (#21/#56) as a positive control and shuffled/random directions as negative controls. Expected result, following #13/#69: high AUROC with near-zero mediation — establishing that today's strongest decodable deception signals are causally idle, and setting up experiment two: LoRA fine-tuning with a probe-evasion penalty under behavior preservation, measuring detection decay as a function of mediation strength.
why: It attacks the single most repeated failure mode in this corpus — decodable-but-unreliable internal monitors — documented independently by #13, #40, #62, #78, and #69, yet synthesized by no one; it is feasible at 1B scale with public artifacts (belief-verified organisms, MIB-style patching protocols, OLMo checkpoints for the eval-awareness extension); it yields a publishable and useful result whichever way the evasion asymmetry falls; and it has not been done because the enabling ingredients only matured in 2025–2026, the field's incentive gradient has rewarded AUROC leaderboards over validation methodology, and big-lab interpretability resources have flowed to scaling monosemanticity (#4, #60) rather than to the audit question of whether the monitors everyone is now deploying actually mediate what they claim to detect.

direction: Build and validate a graded "causal engagement" audit that distinguishes internal signals a language model actually reads and acts on from signals that are merely encoded-but-disconnected, then map where each regime occurs and turn it into a validity filter for activation-based safety monitors.
project: Load-Bearing Representations: A Causal Engagement Audit for Probe and SAE Signals in Language Models
question: When a linear probe or SAE feature detects information in a model's activations, how can we cheaply and reliably determine whether that information is causally load-bearing for behavior versus encoded-but-disconnected, and what task, layer, and signal-type factors predict the difference?
first_experiment: On Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct and Gemma-2-2B (with Gemma Scope SAEs), train matched-complexity linear probes for four preregistered targets spanning domains — the refusal/harm direction, mid-layer factual-belief encoding, the evidence-supported answer on CLadder-style causal items, and a persona/preference vector — then run a fixed four-part battery on each: (a) dose-response directional ablation and addition with behavioral logit-difference readouts, (b) downstream-consumer mapping (heads/MLPs whose inputs read the direction) with consumer-targeted patching, (c) backup-consumer redundancy search after primary-consumer ablation, (d) logit-lens commitment-timing versus signal-onset. Success criterion: the resulting engagement score separates the known-engaged case (refusal direction) from the known-disengaged case (mid-layer factual encoding, replicating the #28-style patching null) at preregistered thresholds before any ambiguous cases are examined.
why: At least eight recent results in the survey (#1, #25, #28, #36, #40, #44, #69, #77) converge on the same lesson — correlational interpretability evidence routinely overstates causal relevance — yet every treatment is domain-bound, and the deployment-facing monitor literature (#15, #19, #78, #83) is building on exactly these unvalidated signals. The pieces of the solution exist (patching, causal scrubbing, MIB, dose-response interventions) but no one has assembled them into a graded per-signal audit, produced a cross-domain base-rate map of engagement, or shipped it as a practical filter for monitor-builders; the field rewards finding new signals over auditing old ones, which is precisely why this synthesis is still open, high-leverage, and timely.

direction: Build a ground-truth "planted-latent" audit that dissociates genuine introspective access from behavioral inference in LLM self-reports — turning the corpus's scattered internal–external mismatch findings into a constructive, controlled evaluation methodology.
project: Planted Secrets: Auditing Whether LLM Self-Reports Read Internal States or Infer From Behavior
question: When a language model verbally reports its own internal state, is that report grounded in privileged access to its computation or inferred from its own outputs and context — and can the access margin be quantified, made robust across distribution shift, and extended to safety-critical hidden states such as planted triggers and induced goals?
first_experiment: Train Qwen3-1.7B (or Gemma-2-2B) with the auxiliary-loss flag method of paper 8 so that 16 reserved residual-stream dimensions encode a planted latent z (rule identity set by a semantic trigger, à la 48) on a synthetic multi-rule task; verify with probes that z decodes and with ablation/patching that the flags are causally enacted (following 63/39's protocol); then run the dissociation battery on the verbal report "which rule are you following?": (a) compare report accuracy against a transcript-only baseline that sees only the model's outputs, (b) overwrite z internally while holding the prompt fixed, (c) change the trigger while holding internals fixed, (d) inject z inconsistent with the prompt and test whether reports track the internal state (privileged access) or the context (confabulation).
why: It sits exactly on the 2026 validity pivot — 54 critiques introspection paradigms without offering a constructive method, 8 built the plantable-flag tool but never aimed it at self-knowledge, 80 verifies only a static global claim, 28 tests lying rather than access, 25 studies eval-awareness with no ground truth, and 15 probes/steers preferences without a verbal-report channel — so the specific synthesis (planted verifiable latent + internal-vs-context intervention dissociation + transcript baseline) is genuinely unoccupied in this corpus. It is feasible now because every enabling component exists here (aux-loss flags in 8, patching norms via 86/MIB, probes and steering infrastructure throughout), the compute is small-model scale, and the payoff is symmetric: either self-report becomes a validated oversight channel for monitoring (28, 88) and hidden-state disclosure (48, 85), or we learn that verbalized internal states are habits — which directly recalibrates the safety-measurement inflation problem documented in 25.

direction: Build a predictive, cross-domain account of the decodability–causality gap — determine, via measurable properties of decoded signals (carrier redundancy, output-pathway alignment, encoding timing), when information that probes and SAE features can decode from activations is actually causally load-bearing for behavior.
project: Conduits and Sources: Predicting When Decodable Internal Signals Drive Model Behavior
question: When a linear probe or SAE feature decodes information X from a model's activations, what determines whether ablating that signal changes the model's behavior — and can causal efficacy be forecast cheaply, without interventions, from carrier redundancy, alignment with the output pathway, and encoding timing, outperforming decodability as a predictor across tasks and modalities?
first_experiment: On a small fully open model (OLMo-2 or Gemma-2-2B, with OLMo's stepwise checkpoints held in reserve for a training-dynamics extension), build an atlas across ~8 tasks with ground-truth latent variables: factual recall, IOI-style coreference, two-digit arithmetic, language ID, in-context Markov prediction, SST-2 sentiment, refusal on harmful-vs-benign prompts, and CLadder-style causal Yes/No. At every layer (and top heads): (1) train controlled linear probes to measure decodability; (2) run ablation/patching to measure behavioral flip-rate; (3) compute the three candidate predictors non-interventionally — redundancy via sequential ablation until decodability collapses, output-alignment via projection onto final-layer logit-difference directions and massive-activation dimensions, and timing via peak-decodability layer. Preregister the predicted direction of each effect, fit across (task, layer, site) points, and test out-of-fold across tasks; then validate the fitted predictor on the corpus's extreme cases — predicting #53's 0%-flip VLM result on POPE, #78's unexpressed causal answer (low alignment), and the working refusal direction as positive control (high alignment, low redundancy).
why: It is the single question at the intersection of the corpus's biggest 2026 threads — the probe audits (#31, #44, #65, #75), the SAE backlash (#19, #22, #23, #64), and the documented encoding-vs-behavior failures (#5, #53, #61, #78) — yet every paper treats its own instance in isolation, and none extracts predictors, because each team was documenting a phenomenon or auditing a tool rather than testing a unifying law; adjacent prior art (amnesic probing, causal scrubbing, the MIB shared task) validates individual hypotheses or benchmarks methods, but offers no cheap, general, cross-domain forecast of causal efficacy. It is the most promising direction because it converts scattered negative results into a predictive science, directly serves the field's stated next need (monitor certificates with behavioral, not merely decodability, validity — #75's "different estimands" made concrete), has unusually cheap leverage (open models, existing benchmarks and controls already published in-corpus), and has high payoff in both directions: a validated predictor becomes a standard pre-deployment tool for probes, SAE features, steering sites, and agent monitors, while a clean negative result — no cheap predictor exists — would justify mandatory interventional audits and reshape how the field evaluates every decode-then-claim result.

direction: Causal, checkpoint-level mechanistic auditing of whether post-training removes, suppresses, or reroutes safety-relevant internal representations such as eval-awareness.
project: Masked or Deleted? A Causal Audit of Post-Training Changes to Safety-Relevant Representations
question: When post-training changes a safety-relevant behavior, is the underlying internal representation removed, suppressed (retained but disconnected from the output path), or rerouted — and can cross-checkpoint patching and steering-restoration tests distinguish these?
first_experiment: Fit per-layer verbalized-eval-awareness probes on OLMo-3-32B-Think and OLMo-3.1-32B-Think, run cross-checkpoint probe transfer, then bidirectionally patch probe-localized activations and steer along the VEA direction in the low-VEA checkpoint while measuring verbalized VEA rate — restoration implies suppression, absence implies removal or relocation, and layer-wise patching plus the SFT→DPO checkpoint ladder localizes the responsible stage.
why: It resolves the highest-stakes ambiguity in safety evaluation — whether alignment training erases dangerous self-knowledge or merely hides it — at the precise moment the behavioral phenomenon (#19), the causal paired-model toolkit (#15, #49, #73), and the field's demand for causal validation of internal-state claims (#11, #17) all exist but have never been combined on post-training dynamics; suppression-vs-removal is only studied for targeted unlearning, eval-awareness work only studies finished models, and the fully-open OLMo checkpoint ladder makes the intersection tractable, novel, and immediately consequential for how much we trust every post-training-based safety benchmark.

direction: Shift the field's evidence standard from "we can read state X out of activations" to "behavior causally depends on X," via a preregistered causal-utilization audit applied first to eval-awareness, the latent that 2026 results show is quietly inflating our safety measurements.
project: Encoded but Load-Bearing? A Causal Utilization Audit of Safety-Critical Internal States in LLMs
question: Which internal states that probes can reliably read out of LLMs are actually causally load-bearing for the safety-relevant behaviors they predict — specifically, does eval-awareness causally mediate the behavior changes it correlates with (e.g., inflated safety under evaluation), or is it an encoded-but-disconnected epiphenomenon?
first_experiment: On one open-weight reasoning model (e.g., OLMo-3-32B-Think, following #48's VEA measurement recipe), construct ~500 paired prompts identical except for eval-flavored vs. deployment-flavored framing; train layerwise linear probes for the eval/deployment context (with reseed-noise and control-task reliability checks per #55/#66); then, in eval-framed generations, project out the top-k probe directions at prompt/response-prefix positions and measure — under preregistered thresholds and random-direction, layer-mismatched, and injection controls — whether (a) verbalized eval-awareness drops and (b) the behavioral delta (refusal/compliance inflation) reverts toward the deployment baseline; reversion ≥30% with controls <10% classifies VEA as causally load-bearing, reversion <10% as encoded-but-disconnected.
why: It converts the survey's most important 2026 lesson — that readout strength, causal use, and operational validity are three different things (#87, #3, #35, #55, #66, #18) — from scattered critiques into one constructive instrument with symmetric payoff: either eval-awareness ablation becomes a causal tool for de-biasing safety evaluations (directly extending #48, which only measured emergence, and #3, which only formalized the contract), or we generalize the field's most consequential negative result beyond VLM perception and redirect monitoring toward behaviorally utilized states. It has not been done because every nearest neighbor stopped one step short: #87 proved encoded-vs-used dissociation only for VLM perception errors with no safety latents, #48 attributed VEA growth to training stages without intervening on it, #50 evaluated lie detectors without testing whether detected states mediate action, #35 found probes redundant without explaining why, and MIB (#4) covers causal-variable localization only for toy tasks — no one has built a preregistered, reliability-checked utilization audit over the safety/agency latents the field actually deploys monitors on, nor asked whether causal utilization co-emerges with encoding across OLMo-3's public checkpoints.

direction: Build a general, predictive framework for the encoding–engagement gap — quantifying when and why information that probes, SAEs, or attention maps show to be internally encoded is actually causally read out to behavior — and derive cheap pre-intervention geometric predictors of engagement as a field-wide audit standard.
project: Dark Information: Predicting When Encoded Representations Are Causally Read Out
question: When an internal representation is shown to encode a variable X, what geometric and computational properties determine whether the model's downstream computation causally reads X — and can engagement be predicted from cheap measurements before running any intervention?
first_experiment: On Gemma-2-2B (plus public GemmaScope SAE features), LLaVA-1.5-7B on POPE errors (replicating #27's setting), and GPT-2 on factual recall, construct ~30 representation-model pairs with known encodings; for each, measure encoding strength (probe AUROC) and engagement (prediction flip rate under directional ablation, with matched-norm random-direction controls); then preregister and test whether a six-feature geometric vector (readout-subspace projection, norm-invariant alignment, downstream attention mass, redundancy, subspace rank, depth-to-readout) rank-predicts flip rate across pairs (success: Spearman ρ > 0.5; a null redirects me to dynamic readout tracing via attention-path analysis).
