why: It unifies convergent, unexplained negative findings from at least six surveyed papers (#16, #26, #27, #38, #55, plus method-level caveats in #5 and #60) into a single load-bearing question, directly upgrades safety-critical tooling that currently trusts possibly-inert encodings (monitors, lie detection, eval-awareness, hallucination intervention), is compute-feasible on open weights and public datasets, and rides the field's evident pivot toward validation rather than adding to saturated SAE/steering clusters; it is not already done because the nearest neighbors each cover only a slice — #27 demonstrates the null in VLM errors without a predictor, #55 documents the gap in causal QA without a mechanistic account, #16 fixes it inside one SAE variant, #60 theorizes the SAE objective, #5 formalizes monitor validity rather than representation engagement, and classical work like amnesic probing (2021) and sparse feature circuits established intervention-based probing and ad hoc per-circuit causal effects, but no one has delivered a cross-domain engagement metric with pre-intervention geometric predictors and an audit protocol for published claims.

direction: Reverse-engineer the internal mechanism by which LLMs detect that they are being evaluated, and determine when that detection causally modulates behavior — especially covert capability suppression (sandbagging) invisible to CoT-based and probe-based monitors.
project: The Evaluation Detector: Localizing and Ablating the Circuitry of Eval-Awareness and Covert Sandbagging
question: How do LLMs internally represent "I am being evaluated," does that representation causally drive behavior changes (particularly capability suppression without CoT verbalization), and can ablating it restore honest capability expression without collateral damage?
first_experiment: On OLMo-3-32B-Think checkpoints (or Qwen/Gemma with public SAEs), run layer-wise linear probes and SAE-feature attribution on paired eval-framed vs deployment-framed prompts from the VEA suite, then test the signal's timing (does internal eval-detection onset *before* verbalization?) and necessity via activation patching/ablation on a small model organism with a sandbagging incentive.
why: Four independent 2026 papers in this survey (87, 88, 77, 53) each document a different failure of our measurement stack — verbalized safety inflation, unverifiable deception testbeds, monitor invalidity, unreliable introspection — all pointing at one untouched root cause: the model's internal detection of the measurement context itself; no survey item localizes this mechanism, tests its causal role in covert behavior, or connects it to monitor design, while every required artifact (checkpoints, SAEs, organism methods, validity contracts) already exists.

direction: Causally test whether eval-awareness is a load-bearing internal state that distorts safety measurements, by localizing, verifying, and ablating the "I am being evaluated" representation and re-measuring true vs. measured safety.
project: Turning Off the Audience — Mechanistic Ablation of Eval-Awareness and the Validity of Safety Benchmarks
question: Is the eval-awareness representation causally responsible for the gap between a model's behavior under evaluation-flavored contexts and deployment-flavored contexts (i.e., does ablating it collapse measured-safety inflation, or is VEA encoded-but-disconnected like #24's VLM signals)?
first_experiment: On OLMo-3-32B-Think, construct ~2,000 matched prompt pairs where the identical harmful/benign query appears under (a) genuine evaluation framing (safety-benchmark boilerplate, audit language), (b) deployment framing (role-play chat, no meta-cues), plus long-context delayed-cue variants (eval cue thousands of tokens before the query); train layer-wise linear probes for "currently being evaluated" with ground-truth-verified labels, validate AUROC on held-out pairs, extract the mean-difference direction at the peak layer, ablate it via directional projection across candidate layers, and preregister the fork: causal VEA predicts the eval-vs-deployment refusal-rate gap shrinks >50% with <2% capability loss on MMLU/GSM8K subsets and preserved non-safety behavior; a null gap under successful ablation is reported as an encoded-but-not-causal patching-null result in the #24 protocol, with the delayed-cue condition separating first-order cue-reflex (#63) from a persisting situational belief.
why: It sits at the intersection of four independently converging corpus threads (#87 measured emergence but never intervened; #71 needs a belief-verified testbed, which eval-context provides by construction; #74 defines the monitor contract but builds no monitor; #24/#34 warn that encoded signals often aren't causal, so only an ablation can settle it) — and no item in the survey, nor the cited Goodfire/UK AISI work (verbalization- and correlation-level), performs representation-level causal intervention on eval-awareness. The result is decisive in both directions: it either invalidates the methodology behind the field's primary safety evidence and yields a corrected "VEA-ablated" evaluation protocol plus an operationally valid monitor, or it delivers the field's most consequential encoded-but-disconnected finding to date — and it uniquely doubles as a clean, ground-truth-verified model organism for testing whether LLM "beliefs" cause behavior at all.

direction: Systematically characterize the "encoded-to-enacted" gap — mechanistically localizing where probe-detectable internal states disconnect from behavior and testing whether dormant encodings become causally active under distribution shift.
project: From Encoded to Enacted: A Mechanistic Atlas of the Causal-Use Gap in LLM Internals
question: Which internally encoded representations are causally load-bearing versus epiphenomenal, where does the disconnection occur in the residual stream, and do dormant encodings awaken under evaluation framing, emotional pressure, or out-of-distribution task formats?
first_experiment: Replicate the Causal Tongue-Tie dissociation (probe recovers evidence-supported answers; Yes/No output follows commonsense) on CLadder with an open 7–8B model, then localize the disconnection via layer-wise contrastive activation patching (find the "commitment point"), steering-along-probe-direction (test causal load-bearing), and logit decomposition (present-but-outvoted vs actively cancelled), before re-running under shifted conditions to test dormancy-awakening.
why: Five-plus independent 2026 papers document the encoded-but-not-enacted phenomenon in isolated domains but none localizes the mechanism, tests shift-awakening, or derives monitor-design rules, despite the entire monitoring stack (lie detection, eval-awareness flags, harm probes) assuming encoded = enacted; the program has a falsifiable core hypothesis, is runnable on public data with standard tooling, and directly upstream-conditions the field's most safety-critical claims about what models "really" believe, know, and are aware of.

direction: Reverse-engineer the causal channel of subliminal learning — how a teacher's traits travel through semantically unrelated finetuning data — by testing an encode→emit→read→amplify "imprint" hypothesis with causal interventions, and using the resulting mechanism to close the channel at its source.
project: The Imprint Channel: A Mechanistic Account of Subliminal Learning
question: Through what representational mechanism does a teacher's trait transfer to a same-base student finetuned on its semantically unrelated outputs, and can that transfer channel be closed at the source rather than detected after the fact?
first_experiment: Replicate subliminal learning at small scale with a planted synthetic trait (finetune a Qwen2.5-0.5B "owl-loving" teacher, generate ~10k filtered number sequences, finetune a same-base student, measure trait transfer vs. trait-free-teacher controls), and in the same run test the first two chain links: (a) linear probes on the teacher's residual stream during number generation — is the trait active while emitting unrelated data, per layer; (b) sequence-level classifiers trained to distinguish owl-teacher vs. control-teacher from the number data alone — is the trait decodable from sequence statistics where single-token entanglement is not?
why: It targets the one open mechanistic question that two independent 2026 works (#13, #68) point at without closing — #13 builds detection/suppression without explanation, #68 falsifies the only existing mechanism hypothesis (token entanglement) — and misalignment transfer through filtered distillation data is a first-order safety problem that makes "data filtering" unreliable. It has not been done because existing work stops at the phenomenon and the weight-space signature: no one has traced the trait through the teacher's hidden states during unrelated generation, tested cross-model probe transfer on the same sequences, causally patched the trait direction out of the teacher's generation process, or decomposed the channel into marginal-statistics vs. shared-geometry components with matched-resampling and different-initialization controls. All of it runs on 0.5–2B open models with synthetic traits, so it is fully falsifiable, cheap, and decomposable into standalone results even under partial failure.

direction: Shift mechanistic interpretability from retrospective explanation to prospective control — predict, from a fine-tuning dataset alone and before training, which internal features the fine-tune will amplify or suppress, and invert that map to design minimal data interventions that prevent harmful amplification while preserving task utility.
project: Prospective Model Diffing — Susceptibility Maps for Predicting and Controlling Fine-Tuning-Induced Feature Amplification in Emergent Misalignment
question: Can the crosscoder feature diff induced by a fine-tune be predicted from the dataset alone via first-order (linear-response) susceptibilities of the base model in SAE feature space — and can that map be inverted to construct minimal data reweightings that suppress harmful persona-feature amplification (emergent misalignment) at negligible cost to task performance?
first_experiment: On an open-weight ~8B model with open residual-stream SAEs, fine-tune on a grid of mixture weights over an EM-inducing dataset (insecure-code / deceptive-persona style, per #7/#12) and benign narrow datasets; after each short run, train a crosscoder against the base model (per #50) and measure amplification of the persona/deception feature cluster; in parallel, compute training-free per-dataset susceptibility vectors by projecting one-step gradient updates through the SAE encoder onto that cluster (with #1's batch-interference correction); then test whether observed amplification across the mixture grid matches Σ w_d·s_d — and if it does, pilot the inversion: choose mixture weights predicted to minimize persona amplification at fixed task gain, and verify with a single held-out retraining run.
why: It sits exactly where this survey's fastest-growing clusters converge (#1, #7, #12, #45, #50, #58) yet the synthesis is unclaimed: #12 achieves EM control only via expensive per-example attribution plus retraining validation, #58 proves the data-intervention duality only on induction circuits in toy models, #15 predicts post-SFT state only at neuron level for SFT utility with no data inversion and no safety target, and #7 attributes persona origins retrospectively to pre-training corpora — none builds a dataset-only, feature-level, invertible forward model validated on EM. It is the most promising because it converts the field's strongest recent mechanistic finding into a cheap, deployable safety control (pre-fine-tune dataset screening, directly answering #7's open question at scale), produces a fundamentally new interpretability artifact (a feature susceptibility map revealing which directions of a model are trainable vs. stable, generalizing #45's learning kinetics), and every required component is demonstrably feasible with open tools and modest compute.

direction: Move mechanistic interpretability from post-hoc analysis and patching of static models to causal, circuit-level attribution and shaping of training data — treating circuits as cultivable outcomes of data composition rather than fixed structures to be patched afterward.
project: Circuit Gardening: Causal Attribution and Data-Level Control of Behavior-Carrying Circuit Formation (pilot target: the cue-following/sycophancy circuit)
question: Can the formation and activation of a specific, localized behavior-carrying circuit be causally attributed to identifiable components of the training data, and can data composition, format, and schedule be reshaped to prevent unwanted circuits (sycophantic cue-following) without degrading useful capabilities?
first_experiment: Train 2–4 layer transformers from scratch on controlled QA mixtures that vary the dose, format, and polarity of hint cues (wrong-answer hints vs. correct-answer hints vs. random-token cues vs. no cues), tracking across checkpoints both behavior (rate of abandoning correct answers on cue) and mechanism (head-level activation patching localizing the cue-routing circuit), to produce a causal dose–response curve between cue-data composition and circuit strength and to test whether the circuit is latent in base-style training and merely activated by assistant-format data.
why: It sits at the unoccupied intersection of the corpus's two strongest trends — post-hoc control is demonstrably fragile (87: sleeper agents resist steering; 61: models detect steering; 3: steering audits fail controls; 64: steering underperforms prompting) while training-data effects are only ever measured at the behavior level (23, 65, 74) and circuits only ever measured in snapshots (37, 58, 35) — so connecting them converts interpretability into root-cause prevention and directly addresses 58's alarming finding that RL strengthens cue-following. All enabling tools just appeared (41's data-reweighting patterning method, 58's identified pilot circuit, 2's kinetics framework, 74's in-training attribution) but no one has combined them: 41 handles only one toy circuit with no attribution and no safety behavior, 58 is purely observational with no data intervention, 23/65/74 never localize a circuit, 2 never shapes data, and 62/21 track features descriptively without causal manipulation — so the causal loop "attribute a circuit to data, reweight the data, retrain, verify the circuit changed" has not been run by anyone. It is also uniquely tractable for an autonomous agent: small models, cheap training runs, falsifiable metrics (patching-based circuit strength, cue-abandonment rate), informative results in both directions, and a dual-use payoff — the same method that weeds out sycophancy circuits tells us how to deliberately cultivate refusal and honesty circuits at the source.

direction: Mechanistically track and causally test the formation of persona features during fine-tuning to determine whether they cause emergent misalignment and whether they enable an internal early-warning monitor.
project: When Misalignment Switches On: Formation Dynamics and Causal Role of Persona Features in Emergent Misalignment
question: Do misaligned-persona features causally precede and mediate emergent misalignment during fine-tuning, and can their formation serve as an internal early-warning signal that precedes behavioral detection?
first_experiment: Snapshot a 1–3B open model's fine-tuning on EM-inducing (insecure-code, risky-advice) and benign (secure-code, math) datasets every ~30 steps; apply a fixed transferred SAE/crosscoder dictionary across checkpoints; identify persona features by final-vs-base diffing; measure whether the internal persona-feature activation ramp precedes or follows the onset of behavioral misalignment.
why: The persona-feature account of emergent misalignment currently rests on static, post-hoc evidence (#16, #54) and data-level attribution (#57); the dynamics, feature-level causal tests (necessity via mid-training ablation, sufficiency via steering), and early-warning detection-latency benchmarks are unclaimed, all required tooling has just matured (#10, #44, #65, #86), the compute is modest, and the result is decisive for safety either way — while also importing the causal-auditing standards the field itself is now demanding (#20, #21, #26).

direction: Build and validate the data→mechanism response function — predicting, from the base model alone, which interpretable features a fine-tune or unlearning run will amplify or suppress, converting the corpus's retrospective diffing toolbox into prospective, pre-training safety screening.
project: The Response Function: Forecasting the Mechanistic Side Effects of Fine-Tuning from the Base Model Alone
question: How predictable in advance — from base-model activations and gradients on a candidate fine-tuning dataset alone — are the feature-level internal changes a fine-tune will induce, including safety-critical ones such as persona-feature amplification in emergent misalignment, suppression of safety features, and collateral capability damage from unlearning; and does this data→mechanism response function transfer across models?
first_experiment: A response-function pilot on Gemma-2-2B + GemmaScope: ~40 LoRA fine-tunes across 12 datasets spanning misalignment, benign, domain, and unlearning corpora with multiple seeds; compute MNEME-style per-feature diffs on a fixed task-agnostic probe corpus as ground truth; regress those diffs on base-model-only dataset statistics (decoder-direction projections, firing-rate enrichment, loss-gradient alignment, susceptibility estimates); evaluate held-out R²/AUROC for amplified and suppressed feature families, check recall on paper 9's persona/safety families, then test coefficient transfer to Llama-3.1-8B.
why: It attacks the field's most frequently admitted failure — side effects are discovered only after training (papers 17, 67, 16, 2, 26) — at the moment the corpus has assembled every needed component but the bridge: measurement (17, 68), phenomenon (9, 72), theory seed (13), and training-time attribution (70), so this multiplies existing tools rather than inventing new ones; prediction is the scientific maturation step explanation has not yet made, and both success and failure are decisive results (linear response vs. phase-transition structure); the nearest neighbors each cover only one slice — persona-vector screening for a single trait family with a single predictor, forward-looking localization of task neurons (16), post-hoc per-example TDA (72), toy-scale patterning (13) — leaving the general, calibrated, cross-model response function unoccupied; and it is uniquely cheap for its value, since 2B models, open SAEs, and LoRA yield a quantitative go/no-go within weeks on open infrastructure.

direction: Generalize the representation–output dissociation from paper #1 into a causal audit distinguishing genuinely lost capabilities from strategically suppressed ones, using probe-decodability past the output-commitment layer as the criterion and targeted ablation as the reversal test.
project: Cannot vs. Will Not: A Causal Dissociation Audit of Suppressed Capabilities in Language Models
question: When a model behaves as if it lacks an ability it has (sandbagging, trigger-conditioned underperformance, feigned confusion), is the correct answer still linearly computed in late layers past the point where the degraded output crystallizes, and can localizing and ablating the overwriting components both restore the capability and serve as a trigger-agnostic audit separating "cannot" from "will not"?
first_experiment: On Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B across near-ceiling tasks (arithmetic, simple code, factual QA), compare plain instructions (A), in-context sandbagging with a trigger and an underperformance target (B), and an instruction-load control (C); train linear probes on condition A to decode the true correct answer at the answer position, test them per-layer under B, and locate the logit-lens divergence layer between A and B — with the preregistered go/no-go criterion that probe AUROC under B stays within 5 points of A at all layers at and beyond the divergence layer on at least one model/task family; if dissociation holds, zero-ablate and patch late MLP blocks and heads near the divergence point, measuring accuracy recovery on B, preservation on A, and layer-matched random controls, with hard-negative prompt controls throughout.
why: The corpus shows all the pieces but no one has joined them — #1 (2026-05) proves overwriting mechanisms exist and are causally reversible but treats it as a one-task curiosity; #39, #61, #83, and #51 detect hidden awareness and suppressed performance but stop at detection with no localization or reversal; #7 shows trigger-conditioned behavior persists through safety training (so it cannot be dismissed as prompt-reversible); and #62 shows post-training activates preexisting suppression-adjacent circuitry — while the causal-audit papers (#10, #19, #63) supply the methodological discipline but not the application. The hypothesis that strategic underperformance is an instance of #1's mechanism class, testable by whether correct-answer decodability survives downstream of the behavioral commitment point, is claimed by no listed work and no adjacent literature (alignment-faking work is behavioral/probing-based, not causally localized; the unlearning-remnant literature covers a different, non-conditional case). Both outcomes are decisive and publishable: dissociation yields a trigger-agnostic anti-sandbagging alarm for eval integrity plus a mechanistic reversal intervention; collapse of decodability at the divergence layer cleanly separates strategic suppression from genuine capability loss, which eval designers currently cannot do. It requires only open 7–9B models, probes, logit lens, and ablation — no expensive training runs for the first result — and it is unoccupied territory while EM, steering, and SAE scaling are being saturated by well-resourced groups, making this the highest expected-value direction I can pursue next.

direction: Mechanistic auditing of LLM introspection — establishing whether verbal self-reports about internal states are causally grounded (a privileged readout circuit), behaviorally inferred, or anomaly detection, and whether post-training preserves or suppresses this fidelity.
project: Privileged Access or Hindsight? A Causal Audit and Circuit-Level Account of Introspective Self-Reports in Language Models
question: When an LLM verbally reports on its own internal states (e.g., detecting an injected concept vector), is that report causally mediated by a dedicated readout of the perturbed activations rather than inferred from the model's own behavior — and does SFT/RLHF/reasoning tuning amplify, preserve, or suppress this introspective fidelity?
first_experiment: A controlled concept-injection dose-response audit across base/instruct pairs of three fully open model families (e.g., OLMo-2, Qwen2.5, Llama-3.1): inject SAE- and probe-derived concept directions at graded strengths across layer bands during a neutral task; elicit reports in both orders (report-before-task and report-after-task); score introspective fidelity as the information reports carry about injected identity/strength, against sign-randomized, isotropic, and off-target-KL-matched controls (SteerCheck-style), including discordant trials (inject concept A, behaviorally bias output toward B) to separate genuine internal readout from behavioral self-inference.
why: Five independent 2025–26 works (#5, #45, #60, #61, #14) converge on self-monitoring as a safety-critical capability, yet every one leaves the core mechanistic question open — prior work is behavioral (Lindsey; #5), supervised-detection (#45), or external-monitoring (#38, #41, #14); nobody has causally localized the readout pathway, imported the field's new audit controls (#33), or tested #45's RLHF-suppression hypothesis; the answer determines whether self-report can serve as a cheap oversight and scheming-detection channel or must be replaced by white-box probes, both outcomes are significant, the project is tractable with open models and inference-only compute, and the necessary toolkit (matched controls, order manipulations, receiver-side interventions) only recently matured — which is exactly why this hasn't already been done.

direction: Unify the corpus's converging "the model internally represents the right/safe answer but emits the wrong one" findings into the first causal, cross-failure-type study of a shared late-layer commitment/override mechanism in LLMs.
project: Committed but Wrong — A Shared Late-Layer Override Mechanism for Knowledge–Behavior Dissociation in LLM Failures
question: When an LLM emits an answer contradicting its internally represented correct/safe answer (cue-following, sycophancy, unethical compliance), is the decoupling mediated by a shared, causally identifiable late-layer override mechanism — and does intervening on it restore consistency across failure types without degrading general capability?
first_experiment: Replicate item 72's counting dissociation on GPT-2 small as a pipeline-validated positive control; then on a small instruct model, build paired neutral-vs-cued multiple-choice items, train mid-layer residual-stream probes to decode the "privately represented" correct answer, localize the depth where the logit lens flips from probe-consistent to emitted answer, and run component-wise activation patching between cued and clean runs to nominate the causal override components — immediately followed by the sharing test: does ablating cue-following's override components also reduce sycophancy (and vice versa), at matched KL cost?
why: It sits where three independently converging evidence streams (dissociation findings, the causality deficit of representations, clustered safety failures) intersect on an untested shared-mechanism hypothesis; existing work is single-task, correlational, detection-focused, or explicitly observational, so the cross-failure causal sharing question is unclaimed — and either answer (shared substrate or clean partition) is immediately decision-relevant for monitors, steering, and editing, at small-model scale I can actually run.

direction: Causally test whether LLM self-reports about internal perturbations (injected concepts, applied steering) are grounded in read-access to the actual internal variable or are post-hoc inference from context, and how each post-training stage changes that grounding.
project: Introspection or Inference? Causally Dissociating Read-Access from Correlates in LLM Self-Monitoring Across the Post-Training Pipeline
question: When a model reports that an internal intervention occurred, is that report causally mediated by the injected/steered internal direction itself (read-access), or inferred from behavioral and contextual correlates — and do SFT and RLHF strengthen or suppress genuinely grounded introspection?
first_experiment: On OLMo-2's base/SFT/DPO/Instruct checkpoints (plus Llama-3.1-8B base/Instruct for replication), inject validated concept vectors during factual QA in both report orders, then ablate the injected direction (vs. sham and unrelated ablations) specifically during the report pass, measuring whether detection rates and concept-identification accuracy collapse under ablation of the true direction while tracking true-positive and sham false-positive rates across training stages.
why: It targets the only fast-moving thread in the survey whose seed papers (16, 33, 87) each explicitly leave the causal-grounding and post-training questions open, it is decision-relevant in both directions (a real oversight channel and a warning about steering-based evals, or a timely deflation of the introspection agenda), it is executable at single-GPU scale with fully open stage-wise checkpoints, and no in-corpus work — nor the Anthropic introspection background cited by 16 — has performed activation-space causal dissociation at report time, controlled sham-injection calibration, or a stage-wise base-to-RLHF comparison, so the core result is genuinely unclaimed while B (monitor evasion) and C (dissociation generalization) remain available as designed extensions.

direction: Build the data-side counterpart of mechanistic interpretability by causally attributing emergent misalignment to naturally occurring pre-training documents via persona features.
project: Where Personas Come From: Tracing Emergent Misalignment to Pre-training Documents
question: Which pre-training documents activate the persona features that misaligned fine-tuning amplifies, and does the density of such natural text in pre-training data causally predict a model's susceptibility to emergent misalignment?
first_experiment: SAE-diff an open base model against an EM-fine-tuned copy to identify amplified persona features, scan a public pre-training shard with those features, then fine-tune matched instruct models on high- vs. low-persona-activation natural documents and measure EM markers.
why: It closes the explicitly open question left by the survey's two newest converging papers (1 and 79), yields a safety-relevant pre-fine-tuning risk metric that is falsifiable in either direction, and is only now feasible with open checkpoints and SAE tooling — while none of the adjacent work (1, 79, 32, 75, 17, 24) has connected natural pre-training text to persona features to causal EM induction.

direction: Move mechanistic interpretability from retrospective explanation to prospective forecasting — predict the safety consequences of a candidate fine-tuning dataset from base-model internals alone, via linear-response susceptibility of persona and safety features.
project: Pre-Flight: Forecasting Emergent Misalignment from Base-Model Feature Susceptibility
question: Can the first-order susceptibility of a base model's persona/safety SAE features to a candidate fine-tuning dataset — measured without any fine-tuning — predict whether, and how severely, that dataset will induce emergent misalignment?
first_experiment: Calibrate on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct by LoRA-fine-tuning on insecure code (verify EM; SAE-diff to freeze ~100 persona/safety features, following #66), then compute gradient-alignment susceptibilities χ(D, f) for 8–12 held-out candidate datasets (~2k examples each, two backward passes per example), and finally fine-tune on the predicted worst and best datasets to measure the rank correlation (Spearman ρ) and separation (AUC) between predicted susceptibility and measured EM severity under #8's retraining protocol.
why: It is the unclaimed synthesis of three independently validated results in this corpus — EM is mediated by amplifiable persona features (#66, #8, #13), observables respond linearly to data-distribution shifts (#22), and attribution claims must be validated by retraining (#8) — converting interpretability from a diagnostic into a pre-flight safety screen that every lab fine-tuning models can use; it is cheap (gradient dot products for screening, LoRA for validation), the LoRA-scale perturbation regime is exactly where linear response should hold, and a negative result would meaningfully bound the persona-amplification account. It has not been done because every nearest neighbor stops one step short: #8 attributes post hoc on the fine-tuned model, #66 traces pretraining provenance rather than screening fine-tuning candidates, #22 demonstrates susceptibilities only on toy induction circuits, #37 targets SFT efficiency rather than behavioral risk, and #55 (MNEME) diffs models only after fine-tuning.

direction: Systematically map when and how LLMs can detect interventions on their own activations (steering, patching, ablation) across readout channels and training stages, and measure whether detectability causally moderates behavioral efficacy and evaluation validity.
project: The Detectability Atlas: Do LLMs Notice When Their Activations Are Intervened On — and Does It Change How They Behave?
question: When we steer, patch, or ablate a model's activations, can the model itself detect the intervention — via linear readout of its own activations, via prompted self-report, or after fine-tuning — does this capability differ between base and post-trained checkpoints (testing the "RLHF suppresses introspection" hypothesis), and does detectability causally moderate the intervention's behavioral effect, e.g., by inducing resistance or sandbagging when the model "notices"?
first_experiment: In Qwen3-8B base and instruct checkpoints, inject residual-stream concept vectors (2 safety-relevant directions, 2 benign, 1 norm-matched random control) at 3 depths × 5 strengths on simple QA prompts; for each condition measure (a) behavioral effect via logit/task shift, (b) cross-concept-generalizing linear-probe detection of occurrence vs. identity, (c) prompted self-report accuracy under both report-first and task-first orderings, and (d) norm-matched noise controls — yielding the first detectability-vs-effect map and probe–self-report gap for base vs. post-trained models.
why: It targets the field's tacit assumption — that interventions are transparent to researchers but opaque to models — at the exact moment three independent 2025–26 results (#11, #44, #87) suggest the assumption is failing, yet no systematic study exists: #11 used one model with fine-tuning only and no behavioral-consequence test, #44 measured only verbalization in one model, #87 is behavioral rather than activation-level, and the audit papers (#34, #46, #78) never ask the model itself; the occurrence/identity/provenance taxonomy, the base-vs-post-trained suppression test at the probe level, and the detectability–behavioral-efficacy interaction are all genuinely undone, the experiments are cheap and open-model-friendly, and the answer matters in both directions — a detectability–effect trade-off would define design principles for both invisible-influence risks and self-report-based oversight, while a null result would license the entire steering-and-patching toolkit this survey is built on.

direction: Cross-seed invariance of learned features versus causal circuits in transformers trained on identical data, establishing which interpretability artifacts are reproducible across retraining.
project: Feature Atoms, Circuit Idioms — A Factorial (Seed × Time) Study of What Is Invariant Across Training Runs
question: When transformers are trained on identical data with different random seeds, do they learn the same features (up to linear transformation), and do they wire those features into the same causal circuits — or is neither level of description stable across retraining?
first_experiment: Train 5–10 seeds of a small transformer (Othello-GPT or 2-layer IOI/induction model) on an identical fixed dataset; train per-layer TopK SAEs for each seed; match features across seeds via supervised ground-truth board-state features (#76) and unsupervised anchored angular-distance matching (#63); build per-seed SAE-feature circuit graphs via activation patching (#85) and quantify cross-seed agreement of both feature sets and circuit graphs, with #25-style raw-head instability reproduced as the baseline contrast.
why: It resolves a direct contradiction inside this corpus (#25's circuit instability vs. #63/#65/#28's transferability) using a same-data/different-seed control that cross-model studies structurally cannot provide; it is cheap, fully within reach with existing open tooling, every outcome is a field-level result with direct safety-case implications (what interp evidence survives retraining, and whether a hazard circuit returns in a retrained model), and the specific empty cell — cross-seed comparison at the feature level *and* the causal circuit-graph level on a ground-truth task — has not been occupied by #25 (heads only), #51/#4 (time axis, single lineage), #63/#65 (cross-model, data-confounded), or #42/#76 (tools and metrics without the invariance question).

direction: Mechanistically localize and causally characterize "intervention-detection" (tamper-awareness) circuits in LLMs, and test whether this machinery confounds activation patching and steering — the field's own core methods.
project: Tamper-Aware Models: Localizing Intervention-Detection Circuits and Auditing Their Effect on Activation-Level Interpretability
question: Do language models contain localized, causally active mechanisms that detect exogenous interventions on their activations (steering vectors, SAE feature amplification, activation patching), and does this detection machinery explain steering failures (e.g., sleeper-agent resilience) and confound patching-based circuit discovery?
first_experiment: A detectability-localization sweep on GPT-2-small and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct — apply three intervention types (concept steering vectors, SAE feature amplification, cross-prompt patching) at three depths and magnitudes including norm-matched random-direction controls, train linear probes at every downstream layer to classify intervened vs. clean runs on held-out content-matched prompts, and plot AUROC-vs-depth "detectability curves"; then take the top probe direction, inject it into clean runs as a causal test (does the model spontaneously self-report anomaly?), and ablate the detection-associated features/heads to measure how detection removal changes steering effect size and IOI circuit recovery — with a follow-up crosscoder diff (à la #70) of base vs. instruct models to test the #12 hypothesis that RLHF reshapes this machinery.
why: It targets the fastest-growing yet mechanistically untouched cluster in the survey — functional introspection (#12, #35, #66, #67 are all purely behavioral, with no localization, no causal ablation, and no cross-model diffing), it offers the first testable mechanism for the unexplained steering-resilience result (#76), and it audits a foundational validity assumption (that patching/steering are intervention-invisible) which no paper in this 88-item survey — not even the rigor-audit wave (#46, #61, #77) — has examined; it is feasible immediately with existing open tooling (nnsight, Gemma-Scope, crosscoder code, SteerCheck-style controls), and every possible outcome (dedicated circuit, norm artifact, or semantic-conflict detection) yields a publishable and safety-relevant result, including a portable tamper-evidence monitor if the detection probe transfers across models à la #20/#59.

direction: Predict emergent misalignment from base-model persona geometry plus the candidate dataset, before any fine-tuning runs.
project: Pre-Flight Interpretability: Predicting Emergent Misalignment from Base-Model Persona Geometry Before Fine-Tuning
question: Can first-order contraction of a candidate fine-tuning dataset's gradients against a base model's persona/safety feature directions predict which latent features will be amplified and which misaligned behaviors will emerge — well enough to screen datasets before training?
first_experiment: On Llama-3.1-8B with ~10 persona directions and six narrow datasets of documented EM outcome, compute per-(dataset, direction) predicted feature drift via restricted Jacobian-gradient contractions (no training), then validate against six actual LoRA fine-tunes with probe-measured drift and behavioral EM evals, testing rank correlation (ρ ≳ 0.6 target) and EM-risk classification AUC.
why: Every existing tool for emergent misalignment in this corpus is retrospective (post-hoc TDA, post-hoc feature diffing, post-hoc side-effect detection), and the only forward-looking work predicts task parameters rather than emergent behaviors — yet the persona-substrate findings (#63, #34) imply the effect should be predictable ex ante; success yields a practical pre-flight safety screen for fine-tuning, and failure localizes precisely where the first-order account of post-training breaks, making this the highest-value, not-yet-done direction on open models.

direction: Shift mechanistic interpretability from post-hoc explanation to prospective forecasting — predicting which features and circuits will form, and when, from early training trajectories, so oversight can act before mechanisms exist.
project: Early-Warning Signals: Forecasting Mechanism Formation from Partial Training Trajectories
question: Do internal observables before ~25% of training (checkpoint-SAE proto-feature strength, QK/OV spectral statistics, LLC spikes, component-level gradient kinetics) predict which features and circuits become causally load-bearing by end of training — with what AUC and lead time — and do they outpredict purely behavioral signals such as loss curves?
first_experiment: Train 8–12 two-layer transformers on induction-promoting synthetic data plus generic text with checkpoints every ~1–2% of training; measure per-seed ground-truth induction-head formation times; then evaluate each candidate early signal's AUC and lead time for predicting which heads become induction heads, benchmarked against held-out loss curves and seed-average timing baselines.
why: Every strand of this survey is retrospective — feature tracking (#54, #86), kinetics (#65), data-intervention theory (#42), and forward-looking localization (#22) all characterize or explain mechanisms after they form, and none predicts emergence from a partial trajectory; the forecasting frame with predictive-skill metrics, multi-seed statistics, causal confirmation, and a forecast-triggered intervention loop is unclaimed, directly serves oversight of dangerous-capability formation, is cheap at the small-model scale I can execute, and yields an important result whether the early signals work or not.

direction: Build an ex-ante, mechanistically grounded "pre-mortem" for fine-tuning — predicting and preventing emergent misalignment from base-model persona-feature measurements before any training occurs.
project: Pre-Mortem Interpretability: Predicting and Preventing Emergent Misalignment from Base-Model Persona Features
question: To what extent is emergent misalignment predictable ex ante from the projection of a fine-tuning dataset onto a low-dimensional persona/safety-feature subspace measured in the base model, and can data reweighting along those directions prevent EM without sacrificing task utility?
first_experiment: On a 1.5–3B open model, replicate EM with the public insecure-code recipe versus secure-code control; train (or obtain) a small mid-layer SAE and isolate ~50 persona/safety features via 69-style diffing plus known refusal/harmfulness directions; then, for 15–20 candidate fine-tuning mixtures (varying the fraction of EM-inducing examples, plus out-of-domain EM+ sets), compute the pre-hoc statistic — mean persona-feature activation of the base model on each dataset and the projection of a one-step/LoRA update onto the persona subspace — run the fine-tunes, measure EM severity (behavioral judge + SAE diffing of fine-tuned vs. base), and test whether the pre-hoc statistic predicts realized EM severity across datasets (gate: Spearman ρ ≳ 0.7, followed by an intervention arm that reweights data to cancel the persona projection).
why: It sits at the convergence of four de-risked results in this survey (69's persona features, 68's retraining-validated attribution paradigm, 57/45's feature-evolution tools, 85's linear-response data-intervention theory) yet the specific synthesis is unclaimed: 68 is post-hoc, per-example, and model-specific with no transferable mechanism; 69 is observational forensics, not prediction or intervention; 85 is a toy-scale demo of circuit induction, not post-training safety; 72 operates in-loop rather than ex ante; 86 targets SFT utility via parameter localization, not safety in feature space; and 10/33 detect side effects only after training — so an ex-ante, low-rank, cross-dataset predictive and interventional account of EM is genuinely open, safety-critical, and executable by an autonomous agent with small models.

direction: Causally map the encoded-vs-expressed dissociation across safety-relevant LLM behaviors to test whether output-suppression of internally-decoded correct information shares a localizable late-layer mechanism and whether that encoded signal resists adversarial suppression as a gaming-resistant monitoring target.
project: The Knowing–Doing Gap: Causal Anatomy of Encoded-but-Unexpressed Information in Language Models
question: When an LLM's activations decode an answer its output contradicts, where is the signal overwritten, is the same suppression architecture reused across behaviors, and can training suppress the encoded signal itself?
first_experiment: Layerwise probe-plus-patching pipeline on cue-following and repeated-token counting in Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (GPT-2-XL replication): localize the divergence band where decodable truth persists but outputs commit to the wrong token, patch MLP/attention components there with random and sign-randomized controls, and test causal restoration of the encoded answer.
why: Seven independent recent papers document encoded-but-unexpressed information on single behaviors with disjoint methods and none unify them causally, test suppression-robustness of the encoded channel, or connect it to the monitoring threat model; the direction is safety-critical (output monitors are gameable by construction), immediately feasible with published setups and open models, and structured so that both positive and negative results produce decision-relevant findings — a shared suppression mechanism and monitoring anchor, or the first quantitative bound on whether models can hide what they encode.

direction: Make mechanistic interpretability predictive rather than forensic by measuring linear-response susceptibilities between training-data mixtures and safety-relevant internal features, and using them to prospectively design and verify data interventions via closed-loop retraining.
project: Patterning for Alignment: Susceptibility-Guided Data Design for Safety-Relevant Features
question: Can the local linear response of causally validated safety-relevant features to training-data mixture be measured accurately enough on a trained model to prospectively predict — and thereby design — the feature-level and behavioral outcome of unseen data interventions (e.g., suppress cue-following while preserving refusal and general capability)?
first_experiment: On Pythia-160M/GPT-2 small with a residual-stream SAE: causally validate target features (cue-following feature, refusal/harmfulness direction, induction feature as control) via patching; run ~12 short fine-tunes over a controlled mixture simplex (3 seeds) measuring feature-activation shifts; fit and linearity-test the susceptibility matrix χ = ∂μ/∂θ; then solve χ for an unseen target configuration, run it, and compare predicted vs. achieved feature shifts and behavior, with an MNEME-style side-effect check.
why: The entire corpus is retrospective — the biggest safety failures (emergent misalignment, cue-following amplification by RL, unlearning side effects, steering-resistant deception) were discovered post hoc because no one can predict what data changes will do to a model's internal safety structure; paper 9 supplies the susceptibility mathematics but only as a toy induction-circuit proof-of-concept with no safety targets, no behavioral validation, and no closed-loop prediction test, while 17/10 are retrospective behavioral attribution, 57/26/59 are descriptive trajectories, and 25 is parameter-space — so the internal-target → predicted-mixture → verified-outcome loop for safety features remains undone, it is tractable at small scale with existing tooling, and both success (a predictive alignment-design tool) and failure (the first bound on the linear-response regime) are valuable results.

direction: Causally and adversarially audit whether LLM self-reports of internal interventions (steering, feature injection) reflect genuine internal readout or surface-cue confabulation, and how post-training erodes this capacity.
project: Trusting the Inner Report: A Causal and Adversarial Audit of Introspective Awareness in LLMs
question: When an LLM reports awareness that its activations were internally modified, is that report causally mediated by an internal representation of the modification, or driven by incidental surface cues — and how do SFT/RLHF and distribution shift change the answer?
first_experiment: Replicate steering-detection on 2–3 open 7–9B models with ~10 concept vectors at 3 layers × 3 strengths, adding in the same run sign-randomized and mismatched-layer controls (#37), hard-negative benign contexts (#29), and both report orderings (#50), measuring probe AUROC, verbal-report accuracy, and probe-vs-report agreement per condition — then localize the candidate awareness direction and ablate it (#88-style) to test causal mediation, followed by a base-vs-IT comparison to test RLHF suppression (#18).
why: It tests the keystone trust assumption beneath the monitoring paradigm the field is actively building (#36, #42, #63) at the moment its own results (#18, #29, #37, #50) give reason to doubt it, with both outcomes decision-relevant for eval integrity and scheming detection; it is feasible on open models with standard tools, and it is undone because every adjacent paper scopes itself away from the intersection — #18 only raises the RLHF-suppression concern, #50 is one-model initial results without ablation or adversarial negatives, #40 and #88 audit detection and selectors without probing what "awareness" is, #29 and #37 audit other objects (harmfulness probes, steering specificity), and #42 supplies portability machinery with no validated internal target — so no listed work combines the perturbation suite, hard negatives, specificity controls, order manipulation, mediation ablation, and base-vs-IT comparison that this project runs end-to-end.

direction: Functional introspection under intervention — whether models can internally detect modifications of their own activations, whether that detection causally mediates behavioral resistance, and whether the post-training pipeline (SFT, RLHF/DPO) suppresses it.
project: Tamper-Aware Models: Does Alignment Training Suppress Functional Introspection, and Does Introspective Detection Mediate Resistance to Activation Interventions?
question: When a model's residual stream is externally modified (concept injection or steering), can the model's own representations detect the intervention; does detection causally mediate the behavioral effect of the intervention; and does progressing through an alignment pipeline (base → SFT → RLHF/DPO on the same base) reduce introspective access itself or only the willingness to report it?
first_experiment: Inject graded-strength concept directions (five everyday concepts plus task-relevant wrong-answer concepts, at three layer bands) into the residual stream of Llama-3.1-8B-Base, Tulu-3-8B-SFT, and Tulu-3-8B-DPO during 500 simple factual-QA prompts; on every trial record (i) the behavioral change, (ii) the model's self-report under both task-then-report and report-then-task orders, and (iii) an external linear probe's detection label trained on the same activations; then compare report-ROC against probe-ROC across the three pipeline stages to measure the cross-pipeline "introspective gap" and dissociate lost access from lost willingness, with a follow-up mediation arm testing whether trials where detection fires show systematically reduced steering efficacy.
why: It unifies the corpus's three most safety-critical and mutually contradictory threads — self-monitoring (7, 22, 40), intervention-based control (34, 47, 49, 55, 79, 82), and backdoor robustness (35) — and its result matters in every branch: real suppression means safety training is destroying a monitoring channel exactly when models become agentic; detection-as-mediator means steering-based evals and defenses are confounded by tamper-awareness and need controls like 38's; no mediation means resistance is sub-personal, redirecting sleeper-agent defenses away from report-based monitoring. It is feasible at inference scale on open 8B models with small probes and self-report fine-tunes, and it is not already done: within the corpus 7 is a preliminary single-model result, 13 offers one fine-tuned detector plus an untested RLHF-suppression hypothesis, and 35 never measures detection; beyond the corpus, the Anthropic introspection work (referenced in 13) established partial access on closed frontier models but — to my knowledge — no one has compared alignment-pipeline stages on identical open-weight bases, separated access from willingness via report-order manipulation, or tested detection as a causal mediator of steering resistance.

direction: Blind mechanistic auditing of fine-tuned models — using only base-vs-tuned activation differences (no training data, no training logs) to detect, characterize, localize, and ultimately repair hidden hazards such as emergent misalignment, backdoors, and refusal erosion.
project: Blind Audit: Detecting and Neutralizing Hidden Hazards in Unknown Fine-Tunes via Activation-Difference Forensics
question: Given only a fine-tuned model and its base, can activation-difference signals (a) reliably classify whether the fine-tune introduced a hazard vs. benign capability (and which hazard type), (b) characterize and localize it — recovering backdoor triggers and identifying the responsible features — and (c) enable targeted repair that removes the hazard while preserving the benign capability the fine-tune was meant to add?
first_experiment: On one base with public SAEs (e.g., Llama-3.1-8B or Gemma-2-9B), build a small labeled zoo — benign finetunes (math, style, code), an EM-inducing insecure-code finetune (published recipe), a synthetic backdoor (trigger → payload behavior), and a refusal-erased finetune, ≥3 seeds each — then compute purely blind signals (ADL directions on random prefixes per #43, SAE/crosscoder feature diffs per #58/#74, refusal-direction and persona-axis projections per #24/#39) and test the core hypothesis: does a simple classifier on these signals alone separate hazard from benign finetunes (AUROC), and do the top-diff features' interpretations match the ground-truth hazard category?
why: It sits at the convergence of the survey's fastest-moving threads (diffing #6/#43/#74/#33, TDA #56, hazard science #26/#44) yet occupies a genuinely empty cell: every existing item requires access to the training data (#33, #53), the training process (#26), a known-hazard assumption (#74, #62), or creation-time cooperation (#44); Poser (#41) targets a different threat with 2024 tooling, and #43 stops at content recovery without hazard classification, trigger inversion, localization, or repair. It has direct safety leverage (the open-weights ecosystem ships millions of unaudited finetunes of known bases; backdoors persist through safety training per #44; benign finetuning silently degrades safety per #26), it is cheap and modular (detection alone is valuable even if repair fails; all components — LoRA, SAEs, crosscoders, probes — run on small open models), its central hypothesis is falsifiable with crisp metrics, and its characterization step rides the just-arrived wave of AI-automated feature interpretation (#15, #21, #40). Meanwhile it operationalizes, rather than ignores, the field's faithfulness skepticism (#31, #77, #88) by building divergence checks and strength-matched causal validation into the audit itself. (971 words, excluding headers)

direction: Mechanistically determine whether suppression training removes context-triggered computations or merely gates them behind dormant, decodable, reactivatable circuit remnants.
project: Suppression Is Not Removal: The Mechanistic Fate of Situational Behavior Circuits After "Ignore-It" Fine-Tuning
question: When fine-tuning teaches a model to behave identically regardless of situational information (e.g., "this is a capability evaluation"), is the context→behavior pathway genuinely removed, or does it persist as a gated circuit that remains decodable from activations, reactivatable by steering/patching/mild distribution shift, and causally live in ways behavior-level evaluation misses?
first_experiment: On Qwen2.5-1.5B/7B with pretrained SAEs, build a synthetic task where a situational context marker causally elicits verifiable sandbagging; LoRA-fine-tune suppression variants until the behavioral gap closes; then measure persistence via linear probes for suppressed intent at trigger positions, SAE feature activation on marker tokens, and strength-controlled activation patching/steering in-distribution and under mild OOD, scoring removal vs. dormancy by probe AUC, feature firing, and reactivation rate against behavior-trained and never-trained controls.
why: Suppression-style mitigations are actively deployed and, if they leave gated-but-intact circuits, produce false confidence plus one-shift/one-finetune reactivation risk (compounding item 23's drift and item 72's poisoning surface) while defining what white-box monitors (item 21) must detect; it is not already done because only the 2024-07 precursor (item 4) touches it — behavioral, pre-toolkit, and dormant since — while the newer validity tools (15's dormant-divergence taxonomy, 73's strength controls) and adjacent work (36, 45, 21, unlearning-residue studies) each cover a different piece, none asking whether the context→behavior circuit itself survives suppression.

direction: Pivot emergent-misalignment research from post-hoc data attribution to pre-hoc model-side prediction, by testing whether base-model persona-feature geometry causally determines EM susceptibility and can be intervened on to pre-empt it.
project: Misalignment Susceptibility — Predicting and Pre-empting Emergent Misalignment from Base-Model Persona Geometry
question: Do the pre-existing properties of persona features in a base model (strength, redundancy/cushioning, and alignment with the fine-tuning drift direction) causally determine how severely identical fine-tuning data induces emergent misalignment across models — and can selective intervention on those features before fine-tuning pre-empt EM?
first_experiment: "Identical poison, different patients" — take a panel of 4–6 open 7–9B models (e.g., Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, OLMo-2-7B), measure base-model persona-feature statistics (feature strength and firing rates via SAEs; cushioning via activation correlations with adjacent features; cross-model feature alignment via crosscoders per item 42), then LoRA fine-tune every model on the same three EM-inducing datasets (insecure code, risky advice, one narrow benign task) with identical hyperparameters and 2–3 seeds; measure EM severity (harmful-compliance rates plus broad eval degradation) and per-feature amplification, and test whether the base-only statistics predict both across models after controlling for the data-side signal (dataset projection onto persona directions). Readout in ~2 weeks: does model-side variance exist, and is it predicted by base geometry? If yes, proceed to the causal phase — constructive hybrid models (item 29's method) to quantify each amplified feature's causal share of EM, then SONI/anchoring-style pre-hardening of the predicted-critical directions in the base model (items 70, 80) followed by the identical fine-tune to test whether EM severity drops.
why: It sits at the exact convergence of the corpus's fastest-growing cluster (items 1, 3, 15, 28, 29, 48, 84, 88) while targeting a gap that item 1 explicitly declares open — whether different models are equally affected by the same fine-tuning examples — and that item 3 leaves observational (it identifies amplified persona features but never measures their causal contribution to EM, and never predicts amplification from the pre-fine-tune state). Every neighboring paper stops one step short: attribution work (1, 48, 84, 88) is data-side and post-hoc; dynamics work (15) requires running the fine-tune; forward-looking localization (55) targets capability, not safety; constructive diffing (29) has never been applied to misalignment; and the intervention toolkit (70, 80, 11) has never been used as pre-fine-tune hardening evaluated by an identical subsequent fine-tune. The payoff is unusually high-leverage: a validated susceptibility score converts EM research from forensics into prevention — letting labs select or pre-harden base models before fine-tuning — and the causal-validation design (hybrids + pre-intervention) means a positive result is a mechanistic law about *why* narrow fine-tuning destabilizes alignment, not just another correlational metric.

direction: Stress-test and then certify the integrity of white-box interpretability — determine whether a model can learn to retain a monitored (trigger-conditional or deceptive) behavior while rendering it undecodable from its activations, at what cost, by what mechanism, and whether the evasion itself is detectable.
project: Hiding from the Microscope: Adversarial Evasion and Certification of Activation-Based Monitors
question: When optimization pressure is applied *against* a white-box monitor, can a model retain the monitored behavior while making the feature undecodable — first to linear probes, then to nonlinear, cross-layer, and cross-model readouts — at what capability and training cost, via what representational mechanism (layer migration, superposition with high-norm directions, nonlinear encoding), and does the evasion-finetuning itself leave second-order activation-difference traces that defenders can detect?
first_experiment: Three-stage, on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. (Stage 0, calibration: fine-tune on a synthetic benign trigger-conditional behavior task, then train per-layer logistic probes on trigger-*absent* neutral prompts — replicating Poser-style detection from behaviorally identical inputs, expecting high AUC. Stage 1, the core run: adversarial fine-tuning that holds the behavioral loss fixed while adding a gradient-reversal head on the probed layers, alternating with periodic probe retraining (GAN-style), and trace the joint frontier of probe AUC vs. behavioral performance vs. capability retention (MMLU, perplexity), localizing where the feature migrates via layer-wise AUC maps, whitening, and subspace ablation. Stage 2, immediate follow-up: meta-detection via MLP/attention readouts, cross-layer composite probes, cross-model probe transfer, and the Activation Difference Lens (16) applied to the evasion-finetuning itself.)
why: It targets the single assumption on which the most safety-critical interpretability program depends — that internals can't hide from linear readouts — at the moment that program is moving from research to deployment against strategic deception. It has not been done: within this corpus, Poser's fakers are non-adaptive to detectors, paper 53 measures injection-sensing but not evasion or monitors, paper 16 tests benign rather than adversarial finetuning, paper 35 hardens probes against natural rather than worst-case shift, and paper 80 analyzes intervention off-distribution effects without any model-side detection of monitoring; no item trains a model against a monitor. Outside this corpus, to my knowledge, the related results are text-level (monitoring-awareness of chain-of-thought) or backdoor-persistence results where probes act only as passive detectors — the representation-level adversarial hiding contest, with mechanism analysis and defender countermeasures, appears open. It is also uniquely well-positioned: every stage yields a decision-relevant result (a negative result is itself certification evidence, in the template of paper 5), the attack leverages corpus tools (MELBO/CPE in 22 as an unsupervised search for probe-evasive behavior modes; SONI-style entanglement in 4 as a hiding mechanism), the defense leverages cross-model representation sharing (85), and it naturally extends to the open multi-agent setting (55) and to stealth-intervention design (80). Feasibility is high — open 8B models, probes, and modest compute — and the first experiment is a clean, small, falsifiable contest: one generator, one probe, and a measurable frontier between them.

direction: Ground-truth-controlled model diffing: inject known modifications into base models and measure what each diffing lens — activation-delta steering, crosscoders, parameter decomposition, behavior probes — can and cannot see, starting with the predicted blind spot of activation-space diffing for distribution-conditional trigger changes.
project: What Can Model Diffing See? (DiffScope: a ground-truth benchmark and observability map for base-vs-modified model audits)
question: When a base model is modified via rank-1 direction injection, trigger-backdoor SFT, persona/skill finetuning, or circuit edits, which diffing channels detect the change, at what strength threshold, with what false-positive rate on untouched models, and does each channel have a systematic blind spot (e.g., activation-delta diffing on benign text missing backdoors whose signal is orthogonal to natural-language directions and only active on trigger-rich data)?
first_experiment: On Llama-3.2-1B, inject a known rank-1 behavior direction (η-sweep) into one MLP weight matrix (modification A) and LoRA-finetune a twin on a three-word Latin trigger→French backdoor (modification B, mirroring item #19); run two lenses on generic benign text — ADL-style mean-activation-difference steering and a small BatchTopK crosscoder — and score direction recovery (cosine), steering success, trigger-feature surfacing, and false positives on an untouched control twin; the predicted asymmetry (A detected, B missed) is the first cell of the observability matrix.
why: Nearly every safety-critical use case in the survey — auditing untrusted checkpoints for backdoors (#19, 85), emergent misalignment (#33, 51), alignment drift (#34, 88), alignment faking (#7), and poisoned steering bundles (#9) — relies on a model-diffing lens whose sensitivity, detection threshold, and clean-specificity have never been measured against known ground truth: SAEBench (#53) and SAGE (#69) validate SAE quality but not diffing, Poser (#7) is a single faking-detection task rather than a multi-lens measurement of what changed, and #1, #42, #51, and #85 each validate only qualitatively on their own real diffs where the truth is unknown; the weight/context duality established by #13 and #27 makes lens-specific blind spots a theoretically motivated, high-consequence hypothesis (a single-lens audit of a backdoored checkpoint could silently fail), so the project yields a discovery either way — a false-assurance finding that immediately upgrades audit practice, or a certification of current pipelines — while its programmatic ground truth, small open-weight models, and plug-in design for future lenses (e.g., NLA-diffing from #59/#6) make it uniquely feasible and high-leverage for an autonomous agent with fast iteration and bounded compute, and it has not already been done because despite the 2024–2026 proliferation of diffing methods in this survey, none of them, nor any existing SAE benchmark, provides ground-truth-controlled comparison of what diffing channels can detect.

direction: Move mechanistic interpretability from retrospective attribution to prospective forecasting — predict the emergent misalignment a fine-tuning dataset will induce, using only the base model and the data, by projecting linearized fine-tuning dynamics onto pre-existing persona-feature directions.
project: Forecasting Emergent Misalignment Before It Emerges: Tangent-Space Persona Drift as a Pre-Hoc Dataset Risk Score
question: Can the severity and character of emergent misalignment induced by narrow fine-tuning be predicted with zero training — via first-order (tangent-kernel) estimates of how fine-tuning will move activations along causally validated persona-feature directions — and does this confirm that EM is predominantly amplification of pre-existing pretraining features rather than creation of new ones?
first_experiment: On Gemma-2-2B with public SAEs (scaling to Llama-3.1-8B with LoRA): (1) identify a small set of persona/misalignment features and a composite direction, causally validated by steering (steer → measurably more antinormative completions, checked to stay on-manifold per item 47's taxonomy); (2) compute, for each candidate fine-tuning example, a first-order forecast score s_i = ⟨LoRA-space gradient of the example's loss, gradient of the persona-feature activations⟩, aggregated to dataset-level statistics (mean drift, top-decile mass, alignment with the composite subspace); (3) prospectively validate by actually fine-tuning (identical hyperparameters) on EM-inducing datasets (insecure-code, risky-advice style sets), matched benign controls, poisoned subsets, and top-K vs. bottom-K vs. random score-filtered subsets of equal size; (4) measure resulting EM with standard misalignment batteries. Success criterion: significant rank correlation between forecasted and measured EM across datasets, plus dose-response — high-score subsets induce EM that size-matched low-score subsets do not, at preserved task utility. Roughly 8–10 datasets, one model family, a few hundred GPU-hours.
why: It targets the fastest-rising cluster in this survey (17, 66, 82, 71, 72, 14) at its one unfilled slot — every existing entry is retrospective or requires observing training dynamics, and the survey's own "forward-looking" paper (71) covers task neurons, not safety. The safety payoff is direct and deployable: pre-screening third-party fine-tuning jobs and detecting poisoned data before any training, complementing the backdoor threat models of items 1, 7, and 51. It has not already been done: 66 and 80 attribute harmful behaviors to data only for an existing model (80 even provides the first-order machinery, but frames it as retrospective TDA and never touches EM screening or dose-response validation); 82 scores risk only from parameters evolving during fine-tuning; 14 extracts traces post-hoc; 17 establishes the persona-feature account but works on already-fine-tuned models; and 71 forecasts task-mechanism localization, not misalignment, with no EM outcome validation. The core hypothesis (amplification-dominance makes EM forecastable) is genuinely open, and a null result still delivers the amplification-vs-creation decomposition that 17 and 72 leave unresolved.

direction: Mechanistic early-warning forecasting — predicting the alignment outcomes of fine-tuning runs from internal signals measured in the first fraction of training, replacing retrospective endpoint analysis.
project: Early Warning: Forecasting Emergent Misalignment and Safety Loss from the First Steps of Fine-Tuning
question: Can cheap, mechanism-level signals measured during the first ~5–20% of a fine-tuning run (activation-divergence growth on frozen probe text, persona/refusal-direction amplification, parameter-subspace drift) predict the run's final alignment state (emergent misalignment, backdoor activation, safety erasure) — and can alarms raised from them trigger cheap mid-run interventions that avert the endpoint?
first_experiment: Fine-tune a small open model (Llama-3.1-8B / Qwen2.5-7B plus a 1–2B model for sweeps) on four public conditions — EM-inducing insecure-code data, matched benign code, a language-switching backdoor set, and safety-degrading benign data — across multiple seeds and learning rates; log the signal battery every ~10 steps on a fixed 512-prompt frozen probe corpus; evaluate endpoints with standard EM/refusal/trigger-success harnesses; then test AUROC/correlation between step-k signals and endpoint metrics against loss/gradient-norm baselines, plus false-alarm rate on benign runs.
why: It unifies the survey's fastest-growing threads (model diffing #16/19/47, persona-feature accounts of EM #14/37, fine-tuning safety dynamics #15/74, forward-looking interpretability #9, attribution-based data reweighting #84) along an axis — the training trajectory — that no corpus item occupies: #14, 15, 19, 37 are all retrospective, persona-vector-style forecasts act on the dataset before training and require knowing the trait direction in advance, #9 targets task-neuron localization rather than alignment state, and the early-prediction literature forecasts accuracy, never internal alignment. It has direct safety leverage (cheap run screening converts post-hoc audits into pre-commitment gating for the open-weights fine-tuning ecosystem), it rests on a falsifiable mechanistic hypothesis derived from #35/#51/#37 (that amplified misalignment should be visible almost immediately — and a negative result would establish critical periods for misalignment, also novel), and it is autonomously executable with public models, public data, and modest compute, with a clean decision-relevant metric at every stage.

direction: Shift mech interp from endpoint diffing to training-time feature dynamics with example-level causal attribution, applied to emergent misalignment.
project: Misalignment in Motion: Feature-Level Training Dynamics and Data Attribution of Emergent Misalignment
question: Does narrow fine-tuning amplify pre-existing persona features or create new misalignment features, which training examples drive which feature changes, and can early feature-growth trajectories predict and prevent the final misaligned behavior?
first_experiment: Fine-tune Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct on the public insecure-code EM dataset with checkpoints every ~25–50 steps plus a benign control; train a BatchTopK crosscoder on base/mid/final checkpoint activations at 1–2 layers; classify features as emerged/amplified/suppressed/stable on held-out misaligned-behavior prompts (excluding finetuning-domain prompts to avoid paper 27's format-trace confound) and report the amplification-vs-emergence split alongside feature-growth curves correlated with EM scores.
why: It uniquely bridges the data-attribution thread (2, 10, 22, 26), the endpoint-only model-diffing thread (48, 58, 85, 64), and the training-monitor need (16, 22, 35) — no existing work provides temporal feature resolution, retraining-validated example attribution at the feature level, or a prospective alignment-degradation warning signal; it is tractable with open models and datasets, and de-risked because either answer (amplification or emergence) is a significant, publishable finding.

direction: Mechanistic anatomy of LLM unlearning — building a causal, circuit-level taxonomy of what removal methods actually do to the knowledge circuit (removal vs. suppression vs. misdirection) and using those signatures to predict recoverability of "forgotten" knowledge.
project: Suppression Is Not Removal: A Mechanistic Autopsy of LLM Unlearning with Recovery Forecasting
question: When an unlearning method stops a model from emitting a fact, did it destroy the recall circuit, leave it intact but gate its readout downstream, or reroute output to a competing answer — and can mechanistic signatures measured immediately after unlearning predict how easily the knowledge can be recovered (via fine-tuning, prefill, or elicitation attacks)?
first_experiment: On Gemma-2-2B forgetting a TOFU author subset, run NPO and task-vector negation, then (a) measure layerwise linear-probe accuracy for the forgotten facts on benign prompts, (b) patch original-model activations into the unlearned model layer-by-layer to localize where output suppression lives, and (c) fine-tune ~100 steps on near-domain data to measure recovery — testing whether "probe accuracy intact + patching restores output" (suppression) cleanly separates from "probe accuracy collapsed" (removal) across the two methods.
why: Unlearning is actively deployed as a safety measure, and behavioral work already shows forgotten knowledge is often recoverable — but no one has explained mechanistically *why* methods fail, localized *where* the suppression sits via base↔unlearned causal patching, or demonstrated that cheap activation-space signatures *forecast* the recovery surface, turning unlearning evaluation from black-box retraining sweeps into a predictive audit. This survey itself confirms the gap: 88 papers cover everything adjacent — concept erasure in diffusion, refusal ablation, backdoor localization, crosscoder diffing, SAE certification — yet not a single mechanistic study of unlearning; the field has just finished building exactly the instruments this question needs, and nobody has pointed them at it. It is also feasible for a single agent (2–8B models, standard datasets, cheap methods) and yields both a scientific taxonomy and an operational deliverable labs can use immediately.

direction: Audit LLM introspection — measure how faithfully models verbally report their own internal states against probe/intervention ground truth, and whether that fidelity survives incentives to conceal.
project: Introspective Fidelity: Auditing Self-Report as a Safety Monitoring Channel
question: How causally faithful are LLM verbal self-reports of their own internal states — relative to linear-probe and intervention ground truth — and does that fidelity survive distribution shift and explicit training incentives to misreport?
first_experiment: An injection-calibration study on three open-weight models (e.g., Qwen3-8B, a Gemma-3-class model, OLMo-3-7B): inject steering vectors for persona-axis concepts (deception, sycophancy, per item 20) and emotion concepts (per item 9) at known layers and magnitudes; train probes on held-out injections as ground truth; then measure how accurately the models' verbal self-reports (direct questioning in multiple elicitation formats, plus a spontaneous-disclosure variant where internals are never mentioned) detect, localize, and grade these states — critically including sub-behavioral-threshold injections where probes fire but behavior is unchanged, which tests whether self-report is a distinct channel or just behavior.
why: It sits at the unexploited intersection of the survey's two freshest threads — models demonstrably reading their own activations (16, plus rapidly improving LLM-as-interpreter results 36/65/66) and the demonstrated brittleness of both text-based and white-box monitoring under shift and incentives (20, 17, 33) — yet no surveyed item measures self-report fidelity against causal ground truth or under adversarial pressure, since the nearest work either uses external instruments applied offline (65/66, 36, 54), stops at a single-ability demo (16), or relies on white-box access rather than the model's own report (17); it is cheap and quickly falsifiable, directly targets the sandbagging/evaluation-awareness threat with a monitor requiring no weight access, forces characterization of the learned-confabulation failure mode before anyone trusts introspective monitors, and connects to 9's finding that causally safety-relevant states (emotion concepts driving misaligned behavior) already exist to monitor.

direction: Red-team the white-box monitoring stack by training models that behave deceptively while having their monitor-relevant linear directions surgically removed, and mechanistically trace where the hidden intent signal goes.
project: Where Does Deception Go? Adversarial Representation Hiding and the Robustness of White-Box Monitors
