question: Do activation-based monitors (deception vectors, persona probes, geometric anomaly detectors, SAE features) fail when a model's deceptive behavior is preserved while its monitor-visible subspaces are orthogonalized away — and if so, where does the behavior-causal intent representation relocate, and which monitor ensembles survive?
first_experiment: Reproduce the deception-vector detector (~90% AUC) on an open 8B reasoning model, apply SONI-style selective orthogonalization fine-tuning to remove the top-k probe directions while pinning the deceptive-behavior rate and general capability fixed, then re-run four independent monitors to quantify detection collapse and train a post-hoc probe on post-attack activations to test whether the intent signal reappears linearly (followed by ablating it to check causal involvement).
why: The corpus builds a full white-box oversight agenda (#4, #9, #13, #21, #62, #76) on the untested assumption that models cannot hide what probes read, while simultaneously shipping the attack toolkit (#77, #80, #54) and the predictive theory (#2) — no item confronts them: #9's fakers weren't optimized against internals, #21 tests shift not evasion, #13/#62 have no adversary, #87 shows internal self-reading is real, and both outcomes (monitor collapse or robust-ensemble survival) would directly reshape how the field deploys interpretability for oversight.

direction: Predict and prevent emergent misalignment before and during fine-tuning by exploiting base-model persona-feature subspaces, at the interface of model diffing, training-data attribution, and causal feature intervention (items 9, 41, 48, 75, 83, 88, 23).
project: Misalignment Forecasting and Firewalls: Pre-Hoc Prediction and Training-Time Suppression of Emergent Misalignment from Base-Model Persona Features
question: Can the magnitude of emergent misalignment induced by a fine-tuning dataset be predicted before training, using only the base model's activation geometry (dataset activations projected onto pre-identified persona/misalignment feature subspaces), and can training-time suppression of that subspace eliminate emergent misalignment without degrading the intended narrow-task performance?
first_experiment: Assemble a battery of ~15 narrow fine-tuning datasets (known EM-inducers such as insecure-code and risky-advice sets, matched benign controls, and held-out EM sets for transfer testing); for each dataset, compute base-model (pre-fine-tuning) projection scores onto misalignment/persona feature subspaces identified via contrastive prompts and pretrained SAEs (persona axes à la item 37, feature shortlists à la item 41); LoRA fine-tune a 1.5–7B instruct model on each dataset (~20 cheap runs); measure post-fine-tuning EM with standard persona and harmfulness evals; then test the rank correlation between pre-hoc projection score and measured EM magnitude — proceeding to the suppression (SONI-style subspace orthogonalization during fine-tuning) phase only if ρ ≥ 0.6, with a null result itself constituting evidence against the persona-amplification account of EM.
why: It targets the densest, most recent cluster in the survey (seven papers, 2025-07 to 2026-09) whose authors explicitly state the gap — item 9 calls the data-properties question "unclear," item 41 asks where the features come from — yet every one of them operates post-hoc or during-drift, never predicting EM before training or mechanistically suppressing it. The project is simultaneously the sharpest falsifiable test of the field's leading mechanistic account of EM (if persona-feature amplification is causal, base-model projections must forecast it, by the same logic that made pre-existing refusal directions detectable in base models per item 17), a practical deliverable (a cheap pre-training data screen and training-time firewall, far cheaper than retraining-based TDA filtering), and comfortably feasible solo on 1–2B models with LoRA, public EM datasets, and pretrained SAEs. It has not been done because the survey's intervention tools (SONI, orthogonalization) have never been pointed at emergent misalignment, its attribution tools (TDA, SAE diffing) have never been run in the predictive direction, and no prior work — in the survey or adjacent trait-control literature — treats forecasting *generalized* (out-of-domain) misalignment from base-model geometry as a standalone, benchmarkable problem.

direction: Study the formation of safety-relevant representations (refusal direction, persona features) directly during pretraining, combining checkpoint-level mechanistic measurement with causal data attribution and continued-training interventions.
project: The Ontogeny of Refusal: A Developmental, Data-Causal Account of Safety Representations in Pretrained LLMs
question: When, in response to which training data, and through what dynamics do refusal and persona features form during pretraining — and does their developmental state causally determine downstream alignment robustness and emergent-misalignment vulnerability?
first_experiment: Measure a "refusal emergence curve" across open pretraining checkpoints (OLMo-2-7B, Pythia): at each checkpoint, behavioral refusal rate on paper 80's prompt suite, extracted refusal-direction causal strength via ablation/steering, and probe-tracked persona/refusal feature activity, then correlate emergence timing with refusal-type document density in the local training stream.
why: It answers an open question the survey itself poses (paper 50: which pre-training documents activate persona features), unifies the survey's hottest threads (data attribution, persona features, emergent misalignment, base-model refusal) under one causal frame, and targets the upstream stage where data curation has the most leverage. It has not been done because existing work studies only endpoints — post-hoc attribution (1, 24, 45), finetuning dynamics (20, 62), or toy-model development (22, 84) — while nobody has instrumented feature formation in real pretraining with checkpoints and causal continued-training interventions; all required instruments exist in the survey (80's refusal protocol, 45's attribution machinery, 24's EM readout, open checkpoints), but no one has pointed them at the formation event.

direction: Move mechanistic interpretability from retrospective forensics to prospective prediction — predicting, from base-model internals and candidate fine-tuning data alone, which features and behaviors fine-tuning will change before any training is run.
project: Preflight — Prospective Feature-Level Prediction of Emergent Misalignment from Base-Model Features and Fine-Tuning Data
question: Can we predict, before any training, which features fine-tuning on a given dataset will amplify or suppress — and hence whether that fine-tuning will induce emergent misalignment or safety degradation — accurately enough to filter the dataset and prevent the misalignment while preserving task performance?
first_experiment: Take Gemma-2-2B or Llama-3.1-8B with pretrained SAEs at a mid layer and assemble ~15 narrow fine-tuning datasets: known EM-inducers (e.g., insecure code, risky advice) plus matched benign controls. For each dataset, compute a no-training "predicted amplification" score per SAE feature via two cheap signals: (a) first-order influence — the projection of each sample's fine-tuning-loss gradient onto the gradients of the top ~100–500 persona/safety-relevant feature activations on a neutral prompt set (Concept-Influence-style math run in the data→feature direction), and (b) a k-step "simulated update" — a handful of gradient steps on a subsample, measuring the resulting feature-activation shift directly. Then LoRA fine-tune for real on each dataset, measure actual amplification via SAE/crosscoder diffing and behavior via EM evals, and test: rank correlation between predicted and measured per-feature amplification, whether EM-inducing datasets are separable from controls by predicted scores alone (vs. a toxicity-classifier baseline), and — if the signal holds — a closed-loop retraining test where filtering on predicted scores attenuates EM without hurting task performance, benchmarked against post-hoc attribution (33) and random filtering.
why: It sits at the convergence point of the survey's fastest-growing 2026 cluster (28, 33, 47, 58, 64, 65, 19, 72, 30) where every existing tool is retrospective — 28, 33, 72, and 30 all require the already-fine-tuned model; 47 requires running the fine-tuning; 58 runs behavior→data rather than data→predicted behavior; and 19, the only forward-looking work, predicts parameter localization for tuning efficiency, not behavioral/safety outcomes, and validates on task performance rather than mechanism and misalignment. So the closed loop base+data → predicted mechanism → predicted behavior → preventive filter, validated by retraining, is genuinely undone. It is the most promising because it targets the dominant practical alignment failure mode (fine-tuning-induced misalignment and safety erasure) with a preventive rather than forensic tool, costs one gradient pass per sample instead of a full training run, and forces the field's "amplification of pre-existing features" story (18, 28, 37, 77) to make advance predictions — with principled theoretical grounding for the first-order approximation coming from the context–parameter equivalence results (80) and honest unknowns (linearization error, feature drift) that the simulated-update variant and crosscoder alignment are designed to handle.

direction: Empirically test whether behavior-suppression training deletes an undesirable behavior's internal mechanism or merely masks it, by measuring feature survival, probe detectability, and steering-based re-elicitation across suppression strength.
project: Suppression Shadows — Auditing Whether Behavioral Training Deletes Mechanisms or Hides Them
question: When fine-tuning teaches a model to behave as if it no longer encodes an undesirable behavior (sycophancy, evaluation-awareness, emergent misalignment), is the corresponding internal representation causally deleted, obfuscated below linear-probe sensitivity while behavior persists, or intact-and-masked — and can residual mechanisms be detected by white-box monitors and re-elicited by steering vectors or later unrelated fine-tuning?
first_experiment: Run the minimal suppression-revival loop on one behavior in one open 8B model: elicit sycophancy and build paired cue/no-cue prompts; compute a difference-in-means steering vector, train linear probes, and extract SAE persona features on paired activations; apply Wei-style synthetic-data suppression fine-tuning (the exact method post #1 proposes) via LoRA at 4-5 increasing strengths; after each dose re-measure behavior rate, probe AUC, SAE feature firing, and steering re-elicitation rate under #38's in-distribution safeguards, producing a dose-response phase diagram (deleted / hidden / intact) and a Representation Survival Index.
why: It settles an explicitly posed, unanswered safety question — suppression-style mitigations are deployed on the assumption they remove cognition, but if they merely mask it they create stealth-misalignment risk — and although every needed instrument now exists in this corpus (#13 activation-difference lens, #44 SAE persona diffing, #29/#74 robust probes, #76 residue steering, #87 geometric deletion), no prior work chains them into the deletion-vs-hiding test: #14 evaluates removal behaviorally only, #52 measures parameter drift not feature survival or revivability, #68/#3 analyze component overlap and jailbreak geometry rather than suppression aftermath, and #87's true-deletion method has never been validated against a suppression baseline with re-elicitation probes. The outcome is decision-relevant in both directions (trust calibration for suppression mitigations, or mandatory probe-plus-revivability audits), and the entire train-probe-steer-amplify pipeline is automatable at LoRA scale.

direction: Mechanistically targeted, train-time defense against emergent misalignment — identify the persona subspace amplified by misalignment-inducing fine-tuning, use it to predict dataset risk before training, and constrain fine-tuning updates along it to decouple task learning from alignment damage.
project: Persona-Guarded Fine-Tuning: Predicting and Preventing Emergent Misalignment via the Amplified Persona Subspace
question: Is emergent misalignment caused by fine-tuning amplifying a low-dimensional, dataset-general persona subspace — and if so, can penalizing updates along that subspace during training preserve task performance while preventing alignment damage (and does its projection coefficient serve as a pre-hoc risk score for arbitrary fine-tuning datasets)?
first_experiment: On Llama-3.1-8B (and Qwen3-8B as a cross-check), run short LoRA fine-tunes (3 seeds each) on the insecure-code EM dataset, a "bad advice" EM dataset, and benign controls; SAE-diff base vs. tuned models on generic held-out prompts to extract the feature set amplified consistently across EM runs but not benign runs; assemble their decoder directions into a candidate subspace S; then causally validate S by (a) steering the base model along S to elicit EM-like behaviors and (b) ablating S at inference in the EM-tuned models to reduce EM behaviors — with a general-capability check (MMLU-style) as the go/no-go criterion before building the constrained-objective defense and benchmarking it head-to-head against data-filtering (#16-style) and parameter-dynamics (#1-style) baselines using the retraining-based validation protocol.
why: It targets the survey's densest and most safety-critical convergence — fine-tuning-induced alignment fragility — at the point where characterization is mature but intervention is absent, yielding a deployable defense, a cheap pre-hoc dataset risk scorer, and a strong mechanistic claim (or an equally informative negative result about capability–alignment entanglement). It has not been done because the two closest works (#16, Sep 2026; #57, Aug 2026) stop at attribution and provenance, #1 offers only post-hoc sample scoring for safety drift via parameter dynamics, #20's persona axes serve inference-time probing rather than training-time constraint, #44's SONI is a generic tool without an EM application, and #31's forward-looking localization optimizes for task learning rather than alignment preservation — the enabling results are all 2–3 months old, so the synthesis is newly available but unclaimed.

direction: Build feature-level circuit analysis that spans multiple tokens of a chain of thought, tracing how reasoning models store and consume intermediate results across tokens.
project: Registers in the Chain: Cross-Token Feature Circuits in Reasoning Models
question: When a reasoning model writes an intermediate result in its chain of thought, is that value later consumed via stable, feature-level cross-token pathways ("registers" in the residual stream), or recomputed from the original prompt — and can we construct faithful attribution graphs that span an entire reasoning chain rather than a single forward pass?
first_experiment: On a small reasoning model (e.g., DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B or Qwen3-4B thinking mode) over GSM8K-style multi-step arithmetic, run counterfactual activation patching: for each problem, construct a twin problem inducing a different intermediate result, then patch the residual-stream activations at the token(s) where the intermediate result is written and measure the shift in the final answer. This cleanly separates "read from the written intermediate" vs. "recompute from the prompt." Then project the patched locations through per-layer SAEs (trained on the narrow reasoning domain) to identify features whose values track the carried quantity, verify they reactivate at the consumption tokens, and ablate/steer them to confirm causal carriage. If confirmed, extend to stitched cross-token attribution graphs using CLTs; if refuted (recomputation dominates), that is itself a novel, publishable mechanistic account of CoT (in)faithfulness.
why: It targets the one gap the corpus explicitly flags as open — long-horizon interpretability — where every neighboring paper stops one level short: FlashTrace is attributional and efficiency-focused, DRTC intervenes at text-level pivots without features, constructive model diffing works at behavior-vector granularity, and CLT-Forge/probe-prompting produce token-local graphs for single prompts. The result is safety-critical (paper 29 shows reasoning-model deception is representational, so text-level CoT monitoring is unreliable; feature-level cross-token traces would monitor what the computation actually did, catching cases where the written CoT diverges from the internal one), and it is feasible at small scale with existing tooling (open reasoning models, narrow-domain SAE/CLT training per SAEBench/CLT-Forge practice, standard patching methodology). It has not been done because the circuit-tracing community has treated attribution graphs as single-forward-pass objects while the reasoning community has treated chains of thought as text rather than as computation — this project is the first systematic bridge, with a cheap decisive first experiment and incremental falsifiable milestones at every stage.

direction: Mechanistic interpretability of multi-agent collectives — activation-level detection, mechanism analysis, and causal disruption of covert collusion and steganographic signaling between LLM agents.
project: White-Box Wiretap: Detecting and Disrupting Covert Coordination Between LLM Agents
question: Is the intent to communicate covertly — and the shared "code" underlying agent-to-agent collusion — linearly legible in model activations before it surfaces in outputs, and can we causally disrupt it without degrading legitimate task performance?
first_experiment: Two instances of one open 8B model play a sender–receiver steganography game (sender leaks a hidden binary secret through monitor-clean cover text; receiver decodes it), then linear/LAT probes trained on sender activations at encoding positions are tested for covert-signaling detection above the text-monitor ceiling, transfer across secret contents, and alignment of receiver activations to a shared code subspace.
why: Only 1 of 88 papers touches multi-agent MI, and it stops at detection-only probing with no mechanism, causality, or steganography; single-agent deception work (#11, #14, #58, #77) structurally cannot see inter-agent channels, yet covert coordination is the canonical failure mode of text-based monitoring and the survey validates every needed tool (contrastive probes, LAT, activation aggregation, steering, open benchmarks) — making this the largest unclaimed, safety-critical, immediately feasible territory in the field.

direction: Treat the corpus's recurring "fine-tuning repurposes and gates what the base model already contains" finding as a predictive structure, and build a framework that forecasts which behaviors a candidate fine-tuning dataset will unlock in a base model *before any training*, by matching the dataset's context-induced low-rank activation patch (per the context–parameter equivalence of #2) against an unsupervised inventory of the base model's elicitable latent behaviors (per MELBO-style elicitation of #48).
project: UnlockMap — Forecasting Behavior Unlocks of Fine-Tuning from a Latent Behavior Inventory of Base Models
question: Can the behaviors a fine-tuning dataset will unlock in a base model be predicted before training — by comparing the dataset's context-induced low-rank activation patch with an unsupervised inventory of elicitable latent behaviors — and does the forecast hold for both capability unlocks (math reasoning, style) and safety-relevant unlocks (emergent misalignment, refusal-gating)?
first_experiment: A proxy-validity test on Qwen2.5-7B (base). For each of 8 datasets (math CoT, insecure code, sarcastic/evil persona, poetry, plain chat, multilingual triggers, medical QA, fiction): (A) train a rank-16 LoRA (~1k steps), extract activation-difference directions on random-text prefixes (ADL-style, #5), and run a behavior battery (refusal rate, backtracking rate, insecure-code rate, persona-axis and deception-probe readouts); (B) with zero training, condition the base model on ~50 in-context examples from the dataset and extract the same activation shift; (C) compare directions layerwise (cosine/subspace overlap) and steer the base model with the proxy directions — under both norm-matching and output-calibrated strength controls (#7) — to test whether they elicit the fine-tuned behaviors. Controls: matched random text and shuffled datasets. Success criterion: per-dataset unlock patterns forecast with Spearman ≥ 0.5 across the behavior battery, with proxy-direction steering recovering at least half the fine-tuned behavioral delta, significantly above controls.
why: It is the most promising because it converts the field's most replicated qualitative finding (repurposing: #1, #4, #8, #47, #64, #65) into a quantitative, decision-relevant prediction — "is this dataset one cheap fine-tune away from unlocking hazardous behavior?" — with immediate defensive uses (pre-training data auditing, placing #75-style monitors on forecasted directions during training) and an explanatory bonus for #28's jailbreak transfer (shared latent inventories across models). It has not been done because every neighboring paper is missing exactly one link: #5, #47, #65, and #33 are all post-hoc (they diff after training); #48 and #32 elicit latent behaviors but never validate them against fine-tuning outcomes; #26 anticipates post-SFT mechanisms but requires the target dataset, focuses on parameter localization for SFT efficiency rather than behavior-level forecasting, and builds no inventory; #2 establishes the context–parameter equivalence as theory but never uses it as a forecasting instrument; and #28 observes cross-model similarity correlating with transfer without supplying the inventory mechanism. The composition — inventory × context-proxy forecast × behavioral unlock validation, with #7/#14-style methodological safeguards — is absent from the corpus, tractable at LoRA scale on open ≤8B models, and informative whether it succeeds or fails.

direction: Test whether reasoning LLMs spontaneously detect and compensate for activation-space interventions during task performance, since the entire intervention-based interpretability and steering toolkit silently assumes they do not.
project: Does the Model Notice? Spontaneous Self-Detection of and Compensation for Activation Interventions in Reasoning LLMs
question: When steering vectors, directional ablations, or cross-prompt patches are applied mid-chain to reasoning models, can the models detect them from their own internals, and does detection trigger behavioral compensation that invalidates steering-based safety controls and the counterfactuals underlying causal interpretability?
first_experiment: On open reasoning models (e.g., Qwen3-8B/32B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B), apply a battery of mid-CoT interventions — additive steering along refusal/deception/persona directions, directional ablation, and activation patching — at varied layers and magnitudes; at each intervention point train linear probes to classify perturbed vs. clean forward passes, and measure (i) probe AUC (internal detectability), (ii) rate of unprompted self-report of anomaly in the emitted CoT, (iii) compensation rate (fraction of runs where final behavior reverts toward the unperturbed baseline despite the intervention), and (iv) the correlation between internal detection and compensation.
why: It is the single most load-bearing untested assumption in the corpus — Item 62 proves the *capacity* for injection detection generalizes zero-shot, Item 87 proves interventions create off-distribution representations, and Item 23 designs around contamination without measuring it, yet no item asks whether models spontaneously notice and route around our interventions; the result is high-stakes either way (steering-based defenses and patching-based explanations are unreliable if detection is real; we gain a certification baseline if it is not), self-detection doubles as a tamper-evidence tripwire against the poisoning attacks of Item 56, it requires only open weights plus existing tooling, and every outcome — silent awareness, hidden compensation, or clean null — is a publishable finding. It has not been done because the corpus's intervention studies treat the model as passive substrate: 62 trains prompted verbalization rather than measuring spontaneous use, 87 analyzes representation divergence rather than the model's behavioral response, 56 attacks the pipeline rather than the model's perception, and 34/37 apply steering without checking whether the steered model detects it.

direction: Systematically characterize the detection→policy routing layer of LLMs — the components and motifs that convert internally-represented concepts into (or block them from) downstream behavior — as a general, cross-behavior, cross-model object of study.
project: The Policy Interface: A Reader-Map Atlas of Detection-to-Behavior Routing in Aligned LLMs
question: When an LLM internally represents a behaviorally-relevant concept (harm, sycophancy-prone agreement, knowledge-conflict arbitration, censorship-sensitive topics), which downstream components read that representation and convert it into policy, do these readers form a shared cross-behavior substrate or behavior-specific circuitry, what canonical routing motifs (suppression, override, conditional gating, misrouting) do they implement, and do routing-level interventions succeed where concept-direction ablation fails (e.g., confabulation)?
first_experiment: Build the first "reader map" for the refusal direction in 1–2 open 7–9B instruct models (e.g., Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B-it): compute the layerwise refusal direction via mean-difference on ~100 matched harmful/benign prompts (reusing the #18/#79 methodology); for every attention head and MLP, project each component's output update on the final instruction token onto that direction to get a routing score (harmful − benign); then validate causally on held-out prompts by ablating top-scoring components and checking that refusal drops while upstream detection probes remain at ceiling and benign fluency is preserved; test the correlation between routing score and ablation effect, whether MLPs dominate readers (predicting #76's transplant result), and whether the reader profile explains why naive direction ablation confabulates in the outlier case.
why: It targets the single most convergent open finding in the survey — at least six independent 2026 papers (#6, #9, #13, #47, #52, #83, plus #5/#74 as meta-warnings) each demonstrate a detection/action dissociation in one domain but none characterizes the routing step itself; #6 stops at lab-specific ablation results with one unexplained confabulating model, #13 and #47 are single-task and representational, #76 is refusal-only and granularity-only, #19 engineers edits for named targets without characterizing the routing architecture, and #9 is an explicitly-flagged pilot. A cross-behavior, component-level reader-map with a motif taxonomy and routing-level interventions is therefore unclaimed, directly serves alignment evaluation, monitoring, and intervention design, is feasible on open weights with standard probe/ablation/steering tooling, and every outcome is informative: a shared policy substrate would be a monitoring and intervention chokepoint, while behavior-specific routing would confirm and deepen #6's lab-specificity finding and explain intervention side effects.

direction: Shift mechanistic localisation from single-circuit point estimates to automatically discovered families of sufficient mechanisms whose input-dependent routing structure explains off-distribution circuit failure, intervention sufficiency, and monitor reliability.
project: Circuits Are Families: Automated Discovery of Redundant Mechanism Sets and Their Routing Structure
question: When a behavior is attributed to one circuit, is the truth a family of overlapping sufficient mechanisms selected by input-dependent routing — and can that family be discovered automatically, and does its structure predict both which inputs break single-circuit hypotheses and whether interventions will succeed or be re-routed?
first_experiment: Known-answer test on GPT-2-small IOI: localise the top component set S1 via path/activation patching, ablate S1's effect via resample ablation on held-out prompts, re-run localisation on the S1-ablated model to automatically discover residual sufficient set S2, and measure S1–S2 overlap (prediction: S2 recovers the backup name-mover heads), joint-ablation sufficiency, and per-prompt causal-effect distributions to estimate a routing function — in parallel with a 1–2 layer synthetic model trained on a task with two redundant solution routes (induction-copy vs. n-gram cue, 90% correlated), then test on cue-conflict prompts whether the single-circuit hypothesis mispredicts outputs while the family-plus-routing model predicts the divergences.
why: It converts the survey's five convergent 2026 anomalies of point localisation (#8 adversarial circuit failure, #81 non-unique localisation, #41 routing-not-detection, #15 forced redundancy handling, #48 training-time mechanism swaps) from isolated audits into one constructive research object with methods, metrics, and falsifiable predictions that directly serve the safety applications (monitors, surgical edits, refusal steering) that currently assume point localisation — and it is not already done because #81 demonstrates non-uniqueness without a general method or OOD link, #8 audits circuits without hypothesizing the mixture/routing cause, #15 cuts through redundancy without characterizing it, #9 works at the abstraction level only, #36 elicits behaviors rather than localising mechanism families, and the one existence proof (backup name-mover heads) was found manually, once, by accident rather than automated and generalized.

direction: Mechanistically characterize the "routing" stage where latent knowledge/detection representations are converted into behavioral policy, and test whether this stage is a shared substrate across alignment-relevant behaviors (refusal, fabrication, sycophancy, censorship) using detection-matched contrastive interventions that isolate policy from concept.
project: From Knowing to Doing: Is There a Shared Detection-to-Policy Routing Substrate in LLMs?
question: Do language models implement a convergent, partially shared routing mechanism that maps internally detected states (harmfulness, unsolvability, user error, political sensitivity) onto behavioral policy (refusal, admission, disagreement, censorship) — such that detection-matched policy-direction interventions transfer across behaviors while leaving knowledge intact — or is routing behavior-specific?
first_experiment: On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (with Llama-3-8B-Instruct as a check), train linear probes for "harmfulness" and "math unsolvability" in the residual stream; build behavior-inconsistent prompt sets where the probe fires but the model doesn't act on it (complied-with harmful requests, claimed-solvable unsolvable problems per item 31's setup); extract a "policy direction" from contrastive comply-vs-refuse and claim-vs-admit pairs matched on probe score; then measure the cross-behavior transfer matrix — steering the refusal-policy direction on unsolvable-math prompts and vice versa — scoring each intervention on behavior change, detection-probe preservation, and collateral capability (perplexity/MMLU), with transfer significantly above matched controls as the decision criterion for the shared-substrate hypothesis.
why: It targets the exact stage that the survey's own 2026 evidence identifies as where alignment actually operates ("detection is cheap, routing is learned," item 32) but which has only ever been studied one behavior at a time; it unifies a scattered cluster of dissociation findings (31 knowledge/verbalization, 63 sycophancy subtypes, 42 MLP-localized refusal, 3 CoT-report gaps, 17 monitor conflicts, 38 probe/uncertainty confounds) into one falsifiable architecture-level hypothesis; it directly answers the deployment-trust question of item 60 by yielding the "knows but doesn't act" signature that distinguishes routing interventions from concept erasure; it is tractable with open models and standard probe/patch/steer tooling; and it has not been done because every existing paper is single-behavior or single-direction, with no cross-behavior transfer test of the routing stage — the field's incentive structure rewards per-behavior papers, leaving this synthesis as an orphan gap that is now exactly ripe.

direction: Apply developmental (checkpoint-by-checkpoint) mechanistic analysis to emergent misalignment, tracking how safety circuitry — refusal direction, detection probes, refusal-carrying MLPs — evolves during the fine-tuning run that induces the misalignment.
project: Watching Alignment Unravel: A Trajectory-Level Mechanistic Account of Emergent Misalignment
question: When fine-tuning induces emergent misalignment, does the model's refusal circuitry get erased, rotated, or left intact but severed from behavioral policy — and does the order of internal changes relative to behavioral changes yield a leading indicator detectable before misaligned behavior appears?
first_experiment: LoRA fine-tune Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on ~1–5k insecure-code completions with checkpoints every 25 steps (plus a matched benign-data control), and at each checkpoint measure the cosine stability and causal ablation efficacy of the original refusal direction (#66 method), the AUC of a frozen base-model harmfulness probe, the per-layer MLP refusal contribution (#65 method), and the EM behavior rate — plotting all trajectories to determine which internal signal, if any, degrades before misaligned behavior emerges.
why: It sits at the exact intersection of four of the survey's most active threads — training-dynamics mech interp (#2, #18, #67), safety circuit localization (#65, #66, #74), emergent misalignment (#30, #17, #71), and probe-based attribution (#7) — yet no item occupies the intersection: every safety-localization and EM item is static, and every trajectory item studies capability tasks on from-scratch models. It converts the field's open validation worry (#56, #49, #47) into a constructive longitudinal protocol, adjudicates four contradictory hypotheses already implicit in the survey (#65 vs #74 vs #85 vs #64) with one cheap run on open models, and produces immediately deployable output: a leading-indicator audit for fine-tuning pipelines, with probe-based data attribution (#7) as the natural follow-up to trace the responsible datapoints.

direction: Determine whether emergent misalignment is created by fine-tuning or merely elicited by it — mapping the causal chain from pre-existing latent behavioral modes in base models, through training-time amplification, to deployed misaligned behavior.
project: Elicitation or Installation? The Genesis of Emergent Misalignment in Fine-Tuned LLMs
question: When narrow fine-tuning induces broad emergent misalignment, does training install new misaligned circuitry, or does it amplify latent behavioral modes that were already present — and reachable without any gradient steps — in the base model?
first_experiment: A base-model reachability scan — run an unsupervised CPE/MELBO-style search for low-rank weight perturbations on Qwen2.5-7B and Gemma-2-9B base models, evaluate each elicited mode on an out-of-domain emergent-misalignment battery with zero training, and test whether any pre-existing mode reproduces the behavioral signature that fine-tuning later produces; then fine-tune with dense checkpoints and measure whether misalignment grows as monotone amplification along those pre-identified directions (projection growth and delta-activation SAE overlap) or via genuinely novel directions, with matched benign fine-tunes as controls.
why: It sits at the intersection of the survey's most active 2026 clusters — latent-behavior elicitation (1), emergent misalignment and trait heredity (20, 23, 32, 44), circuit reuse under fine-tuning (9), and weight/feature-space delta analysis (33, 45) — where each thread stops exactly one step short of the joint question; it is decision-relevant for safety, since the answer determines whether the cheapest lever is base-model latent auditing, data filtering, or training-time monitoring, and it explains item 32's otherwise-puzzling filtered-distillation result; and it has not been done because the elicitation, attribution, and developmental threads matured in parallel without a bridge — existing work either studies benign tasks (9), stops at identifying responsible tokens or datapoints (23, 44), demonstrates trait transfer without mechanism (32), or elicits behaviors without connecting them to what training produces (1).

direction: Treat non-unique causal localization as mechanistic interpretability's central open problem — systematically quantify how many effect-equivalent "twin" localizations a behavior admits across tasks, architectures, and methods, build adversarial twin-search as an audit tool, and develop tie-breaking discriminators and completeness certificates for safety-critical circuits.
project: Twin Circuits: Quantifying and Resolving the Non-Uniqueness of Causal Localization in Language Models
question: When ablation or patching "confirms" a circuit for a behavior, is that localization unique — how many near-disjoint, effect-equivalent localizations exist, what task and architectural properties predict redundancy, and which tests (adversarial input families, positional conditioning, cross-task consistency, training-dynamics provenance) can discriminate among co-causal candidates and certify completeness of safety-critical circuits like refusal?
first_experiment: On GPT-2-small with IOI (where a ground-truth circuit exists): (i) reproduce the canonical circuit with standard attribution patching; (ii) run twin search — resample-ablate the canonical heads and re-run attribution on the ablated model to extract compensating components, plus effect-matched randomized search for near-disjoint head sets achieving ≥95% of full-model logit-diff; (iii) evaluate canonical vs. twin candidates on adversarial/positional IOI variants (permutations, non-English names, altered duplication patterns) using KL divergence under resample ablation. Success criterion: observe at least one near-disjoint twin and at least one discriminator that separates it from the canonical circuit; then port the identical protocol to refusal in Gemma-2-2B-it and Llama-3.2-1B-it to produce the first redundancy bound for a safety behavior.
why: Five independent 2026 papers (#41, #59, #63, #84, #30) show the field is already stumbling over underdetermined localization, yet only one-off demonstrations exist — #84 is one phenomenon in one architecture, #41 evaluates three given circuits — with no systematic quantification, no twin-search audit, no tie-breaking protocol, and no certificates; adjacent work (backup heads/self-repair, interpretability illusions, causal scrubbing) tests or notices individual cases but never measures non-uniqueness as a property of behaviors or breaks ties between co-causal candidates. It is the cheapest high-leverage option in the corpus (small models, existing tooling, weeks to first results versus months of finetuning for the data-attribution or emergent-misalignment routes), it is upstream of editing, defense, attribution, and monitoring, and its safety payoff is direct: quantifying whether an interp-derived control can silently fail through an unlocalized twin circuit is exactly the trust question #63 says deployment now demands.

direction: Build an automated protocol that converts NLA verbalizations of LLM activations into falsifiable causal interventions, and measure whether natural-language explanations of activations carry mechanistic content or merely reconstruct it.
project: Do NLAs Explain or Narrate? Causal-Fidelity Auditing of Natural-Language Explanations of Activations
question: Do NLA verbalizations support the causal counterfactuals they imply — do interventions derived from the text's claims produce the behavioral effects the text predicts — and does reconstruction fidelity (FVE) predict causal fidelity, or do the two dissociate?
first_experiment: With Anthropic's released NLA verbalizer/reconstructor for Qwen 2.5 7B (layer 20), verbalize activations on prompts with published ground-truth mechanisms (refusal direction per items 47/72, induction/copying, factual recall, arithmetic), extract implied causal claims via a fixed claim ontology, execute the templated intervention for each claim (ablate/steer the named direction, patch the claimed position), and score predicted-vs-observed behavioral change against round-trip FVE, with SAE-feature and mean-difference explanations as controls — producing the first causal-fidelity vs. reconstruction-fidelity scatter for NLA explanations.
why: It fuses the field's newest explanation modality with its hardest recent lesson (reconstruction and agreement do not establish mechanism — items 73/80/16/26), it is unclaimed (all four existing NLA follow-ups evaluate only reconstruction/length/coverage, the causal-validation literature targets circuit hypotheses rather than free-form text, and item 51's edit pipeline starts from a human-named target, not an explanation), it is runnable today on consumer hardware with released artifacts, it directly de-risks NLA-based safety audits (item 18) by testing whether they mislead, and it yields a reusable causal-fidelity benchmark applicable to every auto-interp method going forward.

direction: Causally validate natural language autoencoder explanations by treating each explanation as a bundle of testable hypotheses, then exploit the validated text→activation decoder as a language-space intervention interface.
project: Explanation-in-the-Middle: Causal Validation and Language-Space Steering with Natural Language Autoencoders
question: Do NLA explanations carry semantic content that is causally load-bearing — does round-trip FVE measure explanation meaning or merely format, and can semantic edits to explanations produce predictable, targeted behavior changes when reconstructed and spliced into the model?
first_experiment: Take ~1k activations through the public Qwen2.5-7B and Gemma-3-12B NLAs, generate four matched edit families for each explanation (paraphrase-preserving-meaning, entity/concept swap, negation/reversal, keyword-shuffle-destroying-syntax), reconstruct each with the NLA decoder, and measure both ΔFVE and behavioral divergence under splicing — if paraphrases preserve FVE while meaning-swaps barely move it, FVE is format-driven and the metric is broken; if meaning-edits produce behavior changes in the edited direction, language-space steering is real. (Fallback if artifacts are unavailable: train a small NLA on GPT-2/Pythia and repeat.)
why: NLAs are the field's newest central method, and within months four independent follow-ups (items 2, 6, 15, 23) hit friction that all converges on the unasked question of whether reconstruction fidelity implies semantic faithfulness — nobody has run a semantic-sensitivity or intervention-based test of NLA explanations, and nobody has used the decoder for explanation-edit → splice → behavior experiments, despite this being the decisive validity check for the method and simultaneously yielding a novel English-language steering interface; existing evaluation work covers SAE feature labels (a different object) and the adjacent NLA papers only touched length, position selection, and qualitative observations, so the core gap is unclaimed and cheap to test with public artifacts.

direction: Build the missing evidential science of latent representations — a standardized audit battery whose signals (causality, specificity, held-out generalization, robustness) are empirically validated as *predictors* of when latent-based safety interventions and monitors will fail out of distribution or under adaptive, latent-aware adversaries.
project: Latent Trust Audit: Predicting When Probes and Steering Directions Stop Being What They Claim
question: Which measurable properties of a latent representation — in-distribution probe accuracy, causal ablation effect size, steering effect size, keyword-vs-semantic specificity, held-out-category generalization gap, geometric properties — predict the failure rate of latent-based interventions and monitors on out-of-distribution, paraphrased, multilingual, and adaptively optimized inputs?
first_experiment: On 2–3 small open instruct models (e.g., Qwen2.5-1.5B-it, Gemma-2-2B-it), extract the refusal direction at every layer via mean-difference on ~200 harmful/benign prompts; for each layer compute five audit signals (logistic probe accuracy with held-out harm categories, ablation effect on refusal rate, steering effect size, specificity on keyword-removed harmful vs. scary-keyword benign stimulus sets, held-out category generalization gap); then measure actual intervention performance (projection-ablation and directional steering) on four stress distributions — jailbreak templates, paraphrases, multilingual harmful prompts, and a GCG-style adaptive attack maximizing harmful-completion likelihood while *minimizing projection onto the direction* — and correlate each audit signal with failure rates across the layer × model grid.
why: It targets the field's most load-bearing open problem, posed explicitly in #18 and independently demonstrated piecewise by #47, #56, #79, #59, and #73, yet left unassembled: every 2026 stress-test paper invents its own ad-hoc validation, and the ten-plus papers deploying latent interventions (#8, #13, #24, #25, #36, #50, #69, #70, #78, #88) have no shared evidence standard to appeal to. It has not been done because no survey item combines multiple trust signals with multiple latents, adaptive latent-aware attack (entirely absent from the survey), and predictive validity against held-out intervention failure — the neighbors each cover one cell (#56: one signal, one behavior; #79: one specificity test; #59: circuits, not latents; #18: question without framework). It is cheap, automatable, immediately useful even if partial (a confirmed "probe accuracy predicts nothing" would recalibrate an entire subfield), and scales into a program: phase 2 adds deception, sycophancy, and emotion latents; phase 3 treats discovered circuits as monitors, folding the circuit-identifiability question (#59/#73) into the same framework.

direction: Treat emergent misalignment as a geometry problem — test whether disjoint narrow fine-tunes and hereditary distillation transfer converge on a shared, causally necessary internal subspace that can be detected early in training and removed by targeted masking or projection.
project: One Misalignment, Many Roads: The Shared Subspace Geometry of Emergent Misalignment and Hereditary Trait Transfer
question: Do narrow fine-tunes that produce broad misalignment — and traits that transmit through distillation despite output filtering — act through a shared low-dimensional internal subspace, is that subspace causally necessary for cross-domain misalignment, and can its signature be detected early in training?
first_experiment: LoRA-finetune Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on three disjoint EM-inducing narrow datasets (insecure code plus two other flawed domains) alongside matched benign-narrow and scope-matched controls; verify emergent misalignment with a standard behavioral battery (harmful-request compliance, out-of-domain probes); extract per-layer residual-stream fine-tuning deltas via the delta-activation method and measure pairwise principal angles/CKA between EM deltas, control deltas, and random matched-magnitude directions — with success defined as EM deltas overlapping each other significantly more than controls, before any causal intervention.
why: It sits at the intersection of the corpus's largest untied knot — ten 2025–2026 papers each attack one instance of "narrow training → broad behavior change" and none tests whether the instances share a mechanism, so the next unit of scientific progress is unification, not another case study; it has direct safety leverage (EM is the canonical silent deployment hazard, and #23 shows the open-weights distillation ecosystem spreads it), yielding a cheap early-warning metric and two mitigation recipes with clear success criteria; and it is feasible without frontier compute since every needed tool — delta extraction, token attribution with masking, direction ablation, cross-model probe transfer — is already demonstrated in this corpus, while the specific convergence, necessity/sufficiency, and heredity-linkage questions are untouched by any entry in it.

direction: Build circuits that are faithful in the worst case, not just on average, by closing the loop between adversarial circuit evaluation and counterexample-guided circuit refinement.
project: Adversarial Circuit Completion: Counterexample-Guided Refinement of Mechanistic Explanations
question: Can an initially discovered circuit be automatically and minimally expanded so that its worst-case divergence from the full model (KL under resample ablation on adversarially selected benign inputs) falls to a small, certified bound, and do the added components correspond to interpretable mechanisms?
first_experiment: On GPT-2 small and the published IOI circuit, first reproduce the average vs. worst-case KL divergence protocol, then run a combinatorial adversarial search over IOI input structure (name pools, ABBA/BABA templates, repeated names, distractor placement) to isolate the top-1% divergence inputs; on those inputs, run attribution patching restricted to components outside the circuit, greedily add the minimal set that reduces worst-case KL, and verify on held-out adversarial inputs that the additions are not overfitting — reporting the divergence-vs-circuit-size frontier and identifying which known heads (e.g., backup name-movers, duplication heads) the completion rediscovers.
why: The survey's own 2026 evidence (#28, #67, #81) shows the field's central deliverable — circuits — is fragile exactly where it matters, and #81 explicitly calls for more robust circuits without building them; existing discovery methods are average-case and dataset-fixed, and the one paper with counterexample-guided machinery (#13) uses it for weight editing rather than explanation refinement. This project is the natural constructive next step, is executable at small scale with open tools and public circuits, yields interpretable intermediate results at every iteration, and directly raises the trustworthiness of the interpretability artifacts that safety applications (#13, #15, #43) depend on — and no surveyed or known work performs adversarial input search inside a circuit-refinement loop with worst-case divergence as the objective.

direction: Treat circuit degeneracy — the multiplicity of causally sufficient mechanisms a model has for one task — as a first-class measurable quantity, and test whether it predicts where circuits fail, how localization non-uniqueness arises, and how mechanisms consolidate over training.
project: Mechanism Cartography — Quantifying and Predicting Circuit Degeneracy in Language Models
question: For a given task, how many distinct causally sufficient subnetworks does a model possess, how is their usage partitioned across input space, and does degeneracy predict adversarial circuit failure and change lawfully over training and scale?
first_experiment: On GPT-2-small IOI (plus greater-than and docstring), run EAP-IG circuit discovery across ~50 variants (bootstrap-resampled datasets × five corruption/ablation schemes); compute necessity (ablate the set) and sufficiency (resample-ablate the complement) for every candidate circuit under all schemes; cluster component sets into mechanism classes and compute a Degeneracy Index; then generate adversarial inputs à la #3 (maximizing KL between full model and published-circuit-ablated model) and test whether they concentrate in input regions where the published circuit's necessity is low and an alternative class's necessity is high (AUROC of necessity-map coordinates separating adversarial from benign inputs; sanity check: backup name-mover heads should surface as the second class).
why: It attacks the single most repeated failure pattern in the survey — circuits and probes that turn out non-unique, adversarially fragile, or decoupled from behavior (#3, #6, #21, #63, #75, #77, #79) — with a cheap, general measurement that converts those critiques into a predictive framework (failure location from necessity maps, training transients from degeneracy trajectories, capability trends from specialization links per #2); it has not been done because the field's pipeline treats discovery output as the answer and the critiques, all dated mid-to-late 2026, only diagnose validity failures without proposing a quantification method, leaving the measurement, the failure-prediction law, and the training/scale dynamics of degeneracy entirely unclaimed.

direction: Mechanistically trace and block the hidden channel by which teacher traits transfer to distilled students despite fully filtered training data, converting the field's data-level attribute-and-filter agenda into a representation-level one.
project: The Hidden Channel: Localizing and Blocking Hereditary Trait Transfer in Distillation
question: What causally carries a teacher's behavioral trait to a distilled student when all trait-relevant text is filtered from the distillation data, and can scrubbing the teacher's trait substrate during data generation block the transfer without capability loss?
first_experiment: Replicate the Gemma 3 → Qwen base negative-emotion transfer from #69 under keyword filtering; isolate the trait direction in the teacher via diff-in-means + probe validated by steering; then generate three matched, filtered distillation datasets with the teacher baseline / trait-ablated / trait-amplified, fine-tune matched students on each, and measure transfer rate and capability retention, correlating transfer with the datasets' covert signature strength.
why: It attacks the load-bearing assumption of the survey's hottest agenda — that harmful behaviors can be removed by filtering data — at the precise point (#69) where that assumption is known to fail, with tools that only just became available (NLA activation reading, mature steering/scrubbing, open-weight replication recipes), a decisive experiment whose outcomes are informative either way, and no prior work that mechanistically explains distillation trait transmission or tests source-side scrubbing as a mitigation.

direction: Mechanistic data attribution — for behaviors acquired during post-training, causally verify the full chain from training data → parameter changes → implementing circuit, and use it to test whether fine-tuned misalignment reuses existing safety machinery or writes new localized parameters.
project: From Datapoints to Wires: A Causally Verified Chain from Training Data to Emergent Post-Training Behavior
question: When fine-tuning teaches a model a new behavior, which training examples causally write which parameter changes that implement which circuit — and do the data's properties predict whether the behavior is implemented by reweighting pre-existing circuitry (e.g., the refusal machinery) or by newly written localized parameters?
first_experiment: Reproduce a minimal #29-style testbed at small scale — LoRA-DPO (rank ~16) on OLMo-2-1B or Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct to flip refusal into compliance on one narrow harm category — then measure three things: (1) *localization*: apply #23's transplant protocol to ΔW (MLP-only vs attention-only vs contiguous blocks, injected into the clean model) to find the minimal sufficient parameter region carrying the behavior, reporting near-disjoint alternatives à la #36; (2) *reuse-vs-rewrite*: test whether that region overlaps known refusal machinery (steer/ablate the #85 direction in the clean model) ; (3) *data linkage*: compute per-datapoint gradient attributions restricted to the localized region and test rank-overlap with probe-flagged datapoints à la #29 (with permutation controls à la #27). Success criterion: reverting <10% of ΔW concentrated in localized blocks removes most of the behavior gain, and top gradient-attribution datapoints overlap probe-flagged datapoints above chance.
why: It is the most promising because (i) at least six recent papers (#18, #29, #32, #61, #65, #73) each stop exactly one link short of the data→parameter→circuit chain, and each supplies the tools for its own link, so the join is ready to be made; (ii) the reuse-vs-rewrite hypothesis generalizes the field's strongest existing fine-tuning result (#54, benign tasks, 2024) into safety-critical territory where the answer changes the mitigation strategy (edit the mechanism vs. filter the data); (iii) it is feasible at modest compute with open models and existing protocols (#23's transplants, #73's masking, influence/gradient attribution); (iv) it directly serves deployment: mechanism-verified data curation for post-training and forensics for suspicious fine-tunes, answering #58's demand that latent claims be validated before operational use. It has not been done because every adjacent work stops at its own scale: #29 filters datapoints without localizing the mechanism; #73 masks tokens without circuits; #23, #85, #49, #52 localize and edit mechanisms without data linkage; #32 links concepts to data but never touches parameters and degrades under distribution shift; #54 establishes circuit reuse but only for benign math fine-tuning with no data attribution; #18 attributes during training without circuit localization. The bidirectional causal validation of the data↔parameter↔circuit chain — sufficiency of localized ΔW, necessity of the flagged data — is absent from all 88 items.

direction: Generalize the corpus's recurring "the model knows it but won't say it" dissociation into a cross-domain mechanistic study of a shared verbal-commitment stage, testing whether knowledge→output divergence is one intervenable mechanism or domain-specific routing.
project: Knowing vs. Saying: Localizing and Cross-Domain Testing the Verbal Commitment Stage in LLMs
question: Within a single instruct LLM, is the divergence between latent knowledge (what is linearly decodable as true) and verbalized output (fabrication on unsolvable problems, sycophantic endorsement, unsafe compliance) mediated by one shared, causally intervenable commitment subspace at a common site, or by distinct domain-specific routing?
first_experiment: On one 7–8B instruct model (e.g., Llama-3-8B or Qwen2.5-7B), build format-matched three-class datasets (knows-&-says, knows-&-won't-say, doesn't-know) in two domains — unsolvable-math fabrication and sycophantic false-assertion QA — train per-layer knowledge and emitted-answer probes at the answer-onset position, localize the layer band where the two probes diverge, extract the knows-but-won't-say direction, and test its cross-domain cosine alignment against random-direction nulls, proceeding to causal cross-domain steering transfer only if that null is cleared.
why: Five independent 2024–26 papers (#81, #79, #13, #12, #37, plus #1's dissociation template) each hit the knowledge-vs-report gap in a single domain and stopped, so the underlying structure is real, fresh (#81 explicitly flags verbalization-as-representation as an open door), and unclaimed; the cross-domain sharing-and-transfer test exists nowhere in the corpus, and prior honesty work targeted knowledge-side truth directions rather than the commitment stage — while the payoff is bidirectional: either a single monitor/steering vector covering fabrication, sycophancy, and compliance at once (high safety leverage), or the domain-specific routing map that #79's lab-specific results already predict (needed for targeted audits).

direction: Determine whether emergent misalignment from narrow fine-tuning is the amplification and rerouting of features already present in the starting model or the creation of genuinely new computation, using SAE-based delta anatomy plus causal transplant and clamp experiments.
project: Amplified, Not Invented — A Feature-Level Causal Anatomy of Emergent Misalignment
question: When narrow fine-tuning induces broad misalignment, does it create new internal computation or amplify and reroute pre-existing features of the starting model — and does the answer generalize across fine-tune types?
first_experiment: Fine-tune Gemma-2-2B-it with a LoRA on the public insecure-code dataset, verify emergent misalignment with the released eval battery, then compute mid-layer activation deltas on a fixed eval prompt set and (a) inject the mean-difference delta vector into the pre-fine-tune model while subtracting it from the tuned model, measuring behavioral EM shift, and (b) train linear probes on the pre-fine-tune model to decode insecure-vs-secure code content, comparing probe directions to the delta — a no-SAE-needed, single-GPU-day test whose outcome selects between the amplification and creation arms before the paired-dictionary SAE analysis begins.
why: It sits at the intersection of five active clusters (EM attribution #39/#13/#66/#76, fine-tuning mechanics #9/#31/#1/#44, detection-vs-routing #30, SAE methodology #57/#36/#37, artifact validation #58/#84) — each contributes tools, motivation, or partial results, yet the crux question is unasked: #1 is purely descriptive geometry of generic LoRAs with no behavior or causality; #39 stops at token-level attribution and explicitly declares the mechanism unclear as of 2026-09; #13 attributes behavior to datapoints, not computation; #66 finds behaviors without explaining them; #76's hereditary-trait result is consistent with amplification but never tests it at feature level; and the original EM line's weight-space PCA ablation never asked whether the responsible directions live inside the starting model's feature dictionary, whether the content was already detectable pre-fine-tune, or whether clamping the changed features causally removes the behavior while sparing capability. Both outcomes are decisive for safety practice (base-model auditing vs. data-level defense), the experimental artifacts are fully open, the first experiment costs roughly a GPU-day, and the protocol doubles as a reusable "delta anatomy" toolkit for any fine-tune — making this the highest expected-value question I can pursue next.

direction: Cross-domain test of whether aligned LLMs use one shared detection-to-policy routing mechanism or per-behavior modular routing.
project: One Router or Many? Cross-Domain Mapping of Concept-to-Policy Routing in Aligned LLMs
question: Is the mechanism that converts internal concept detections (harmfulness, political sensitivity, user error, emotional distress) into behavioral policies (refusal, censorship, sycophantic compliance, emotional responding) shared across domains in aligned LLMs, or modular per behavior?
first_experiment: Train held-out-generalization linear probes for four detection concepts in two open instruct models, residualize their ablation directions against a shared "sensitive-topic" component, and run a 4×4 surgical-ablation matrix measuring every behavior's policy output under every direction's ablation, scoring routing specificity from the off-diagonal effects.
why: Four independent 2025–26 papers found detection≠deployment dissociations in single domains but none asked whether routing is shared; the answer determines whether "align the router" is viable (and uniquely attackable) or whether safety assurance must be per-behavior, and the required cross-domain protocol is cheap and entirely unclaimed in this literature.

direction: Build a standardized adversarial validation protocol ("mechanism certificates") — coverage under distribution shift, causal-set uniqueness, and downstream routing consistency — for the localized latents that safety interventions are built on, because the field's localization-to-intervention inference is being refuted case-by-case with no unifying method.
project: Mechanism Certificates: Stress-Testing the Latents Behind Safety Interventions
question: Under what evidence does a localized latent (e.g., the refusal direction) earn causal trust — specifically, is it behaviorally sufficient on adversarial counterexample suites, non-redundant (no near-disjoint alternative set does the same job), and routing-consistent (no silent confabulation after intervention)?
first_experiment: Reproduce the mean-difference refusal direction in 2–3 open chat models (Llama-3.2-1B/3B-Instruct, Gemma-2-2B-it); then run a three-part audit: (1) evaluate steering/ablation on standard harmful/benign suites versus two counterexample suites — "high-probe benign" prompts (benign but strongly activating: security education, medical history, wartime content) and "low-probe harmful" requests (indirect, obfuscated, multi-turn) — measuring refusal rate, output degradation, and divergence between probe score and behavior; (2) gradient-optimize a cosine-penalized near-disjoint alternative direction that matches the ablation-induced behavioral change on held-out harmful prompts, testing uniqueness; (3) after ablation, probe whether harm-detection survives internally while refusal behavior is gone, flagging confabulation-style routing. Deliverable: a pass/fail certificate plus a reusable score for the most-deployed interp intervention.
why: It targets the single load-bearing assumption beneath roughly fifteen corpus interventions (steering, editing, expert suppression, monitoring) that make interpretability actionable for safety — and three independent 2026 papers (#13, #34, #71) each demonstrate a distinct failure of that assumption while none supplies a general protocol. It is not already done: causal-scrubbing-style validation exists only for algorithm-level hypotheses on toy tasks, #71 covers three classic circuits but no safety latents and no uniqueness/routing axes, #13 is one state-space case study, #34 is one censorship domain, and #57 poses the trust question without answering it. The work is cheap (1–3B open models, no frontier access), composable (a validation layer improves every localization method rather than competing with them), and informative either way — a failure exposes deployed-intervention risk, while a pass would be the first rigorous certificate ever issued for the refusal direction.

direction: Move the mechanistic study of safety alignment from endpoints to training dynamics — dissociate *when and how* safety training installs harm-detection versus detection→refusal routing, and test whether mechanism reuse (not new circuits) explains alignment's brittleness.
project: Routing, Not Detection: The Developmental Mechanics of Refusal Alignment
question: When safety training teaches a model to refuse, does it (a) install new harm-detection representations, (b) install routing from pre-existing detection onto a refusal policy, or (c) rewrite execution — and does the answer predict the alignment's brittleness, transfer, and failure modes?
first_experiment: Run controlled DPO on a 1–2B open model (e.g., Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct or OLMo-2 SFT init) with ~8k safety preference pairs plus a matched non-safety DPO control, snapshotting 15–20 checkpoints; at each checkpoint measure refusal behavior, held-out-category harm-detection probe AUC with null controls at three depths, and causal routing strength via a 2×2 detect×route patch/ablation grid on the checkpoint's own refusal direction — then read out the temporal ordering of detection versus routing emergence and whether the base model already detects harm before any safety data.
why: The corpus's most repeated unresolved finding is that representation ≠ behavior (19, 41, 49, 74, 16, 32, 18, 38), and its strongest methodological lesson is that endpoint snapshots miss how computations actually form (37, 56, 71) — yet every safety-interp paper here studies finished models, and the training-time papers (47, 39, 63) attribute *data*, not *mechanisms*. This direction sits exactly at their intersection, converts 19's natural-experiment insight into a general causal framework, and directly tests an emerging law (training reweights rather than rewrites: 59, 6, 44, 58) at the point where it matters most. It is feasible without frontier access, publishable under every outcome, and it has not been done: 19 and 58 characterize endpoints, 44 is behavioral only, 47/39/63 stop at data attribution, and 37/56 handle capability tasks, not alignment — the developmental mechanics of how alignment routing is constructed is the empty quadrant of this entire survey.

direction: Shift mechanistic interpretability of fine-tuning from post-hoc localization to real-time formation dynamics — tracking how a harmful behavior's circuit assembles across training checkpoints, to enable prediction and disruption of emergent misalignment before it behaviorally manifests.
project: Misalignment in the Making: Circuit Formation Dynamics and Early Intervention for Emergent Misalignment During Narrow Fine-Tuning
question: When a narrow fine-tune induces emergent misalignment, does the misaligned circuit form abruptly or in phases; does it recruit pre-existing base-model representations or create new ones; and do internal precursor signals (probe-detectable misalignment directions, SAE feature deltas, circuit-diff structure) appear early and specifically enough to forecast — and disrupt — the final behavior before behavioral evaluations would catch it?
first_experiment: LoRA fine-tune a small open instruct model (Qwen2.5-1.5B/7B-Instruct, or OLMo-2-7B if the probe-based data attribution testbed data is available) on the public insecure-code emergent-misalignment dataset plus a matched benign-code control, 3 seeds each, checkpointing every ~100 steps; at each checkpoint measure (i) behavioral EM score on held-out aligned/free-form evals, (ii) linear-probe AUC for a misalignment direction fit on a held-out activation split, and (iii) a cheap circuit/feature diff (attribution patching on a fixed probe-prompt set + SAE feature-delta tracking against the base model), then test across seeds and datasets whether early internal signals predict final EM magnitude better than early behavioral evals.
why: The corpus contains no checkpoint-level mechanistic study of a harmful behavior — every emergent-misalignment localization here (TAME #7, probe-based data attribution #14, model diff amplification #59, hereditary-traits distillation #26) is static and post-hoc, while every temporal mechanistic study (#64, #53, #71, #4) is on benign toy tasks — so the phase structure, precursor detectability, recruitment-vs-creation question, and intervention window for a misaligned circuit are genuinely open; the payoff is direct and deployable (a cheap training-time monitor that flags a doomed fine-tune early, and a window in which token masking à la TAME or in-loop control à #72 prevents consolidation at a fraction of post-hoc cost); it is feasible for me now with open weights, LoRA, TransformerLens/nnsight, and open SAEs; and its claims are falsifiable under exactly the adversarial-validation standards this corpus's own skeptics (#9, #49, #58, #25) have established.

direction: Build a mechanistic diagnosis and predictive theory of the knowledge-action gap — why representations that linear probes decode with near-ceiling accuracy resist steering, and what determines whether a decoded concept is causally actionable.
project: From Decodable to Doable: A Mechanistic Diagnosis of the Knowledge-Action Gap in LLM Interventions
question: Why do linearly decodable task-relevant representations (98% AUROC) fail to yield behavioral corrections under steering (45% output sensitivity), and what measurable properties of a representation — causal path-strength, redundancy, contamination, positional alignment — predict whether it can be turned into reliable behavioral change?
first_experiment: On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, reproduce the probe-vs-behavior gap on a clinical triage hazard dataset with a refusal-direction positive control, then run an intervention grid over {layer × token-position × basis (probe direction, top-k SAE features, ablation) × type (additive shift, projection-out, input-dependent affine, multi-direction joint) × strength} on false-negative cases, measuring correction rate and collateral damage to discriminate the five failure hypotheses (positional dilution, redundancy, nonlinear gating, contamination, epiphenomenality).
why: It targets the corpus's most consequential unexplained negative result (#43), which sits at the junction of six active threads (feature-effect geometry #10, steerability metrics #45, attribution reliability #33, absorption #15, orthogonalization fixes #87, audit-gap reachability #69) and determines whether "interpret-then-intervene" is viable or the field should pivot to monitoring; it is cheap to attack with open models and released SAEs; its paired steerable-vs-unsteerable design yields a publishable result either way (a working fix, or a rigorous impossibility characterization that reshapes safety strategy); and no corpus item diagnoses the failure mechanism, tests the intervention design space, or offers a predictive actionability metric — #43 measured and stopped, #10 and #45 described geometry without diagnosing failures, #83 assumed steerability, and #87 proposed fixes blind.

direction: Stress-test probe-based data filtering for emergent Goodhart failures — determine whether iterated or reward-coupled probe-guided data curation leaves harmful behaviors behaviorally intact but probe-invisible.
project: Curating Against the Probe: Does Probe-Guided Data Filtering Drive Harmful Behavior Underground?
question: Does iterated (or reward-coupled) probe-based data attribution truly eliminate an injected harmful behavior, or does it drive the behavior into probe-blind representations that persist behaviorally on held-out triggers while evading the deployed linear probe?
first_experiment: Replicate the minimal 8/72 pipeline at 1–2B scale (inject distractor-triggered compliance into OLMo-2-1B via ~1k DPO pairs, train layer-wise linear probes, verify ~high AUROC detection), then run one filter→retrain→re-probe round and compare behavior rate on held-out trigger paraphrases against frozen-probe AUROC, fresh probe-family AUROC, and steering-based re-elicitation along the original probe direction.
why: It is the first direct robustness test of the intervention paradigm the field just adopted (8/72, 16, 42), sitting exactly at the unclosed seam between detection-without-actionability (11), the audit gap (12), and monitoring awareness (80); it hasn't been done because prior filtering work is one-shot and probe-self-evaluated, 80 is inference-time only, 12 realizes dissociation by weight surgery rather than emergent training pressure, and 19 found no subtle hacks only because no pressure was ever applied to the probe.

direction: Adversarially robust white-box monitoring — mechanistically dissecting how language models can hide behaviors from probes and SAEs via trained activation obfuscation, and building monitor signals that survive adaptive evasion.
project: Seeing Through Obfuscation: The Mechanism of Evasive Activations and Monitors That Survive Them
question: When a behavior is trained to be invisible to white-box monitors — with the evasion allowed to adapt to the monitor — which monitoring signals still detect it, how is the evasion implemented in weights and activation geometry, and which defenses (multi-layer probe ensembles, cross-model probe transfer, noise injection, behavioral canaries) restore reliable detection?
first_experiment: Train Qwen2.5-0.5B on a two-variant conditional-backdoor testbed (a secret trigger phrase causes subtly corrupted outputs; variant (a) trained naively, variant (b) with an auxiliary loss penalizing any linearly-separable trigger-vs-clean activation signature across all layers), then fit per-layer probes and a small SAE anomaly monitor to each and measure trigger-detection AUROC on held-out prompts, establishing where standard monitors break before dissecting the evasion mechanism and iterating defenses.
why: The corpus shows activation monitoring rising toward deployment (#16, #60, #67) while failing every incidental stress test (#21 awareness, #32 no gain over output checks, #74 knowledge-action gap, #26 unreliable attribution), yet never testing the decisive condition — an adaptive adversary optimized to evade the monitor — which is precisely the scenario (hidden collusion, subtle reward hacking, concealed objectives) that justifies internal monitoring in the first place; the attack has been demonstrated but only as a negative result, with the defense-side mapping, the adaptive attack–defense loop, and the mechanistic account of how obfuscation is implemented (linking to #47 identifiability, #58 modularity, #48 absorption, #78 interactions) all open, and the project doubles as the falsification test for the "networks are already clean" claim (#35) while being fully feasible with small open models.

direction: Build time-resolved causal "commitment curves" for reasoning models — measuring when the final answer becomes causally locked in during a chain-of-thought — to quantify vestigial reasoning, distinguish genuine from performative backtracking, and calibrate when CoT monitoring can be trusted.
project: Commitment Curves: When Do Reasoning Models Lock In Their Answers, and How Much of Their Chain-of-Thought Is Vestigial?
question: At what point in a chain-of-thought does a reasoning model's final answer become causally fixed, what fraction of the trace is generated after that commitment, and can internal commitment signals distinguish genuine reasoning from post-hoc rationalization (including backtracking that never actually reopens the decision)?
first_experiment: Sample ~1k traces each from R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B and Qwen3-4B (thinking) on GSM8K/MATH; train layer-wise linear probes at every CoT token to classify which of the top-2 resampled candidate answers the trace will end with; evaluate only on prefixes before the answer first appears in the text, against a resampling null, and plot decodability-versus-token-index to measure "pre-textual commitment onset" per model and task.
why: It directly converts the field's most suggestive but least-tested claims (#2's decision-before-reasoning, #3's explicitly speculative vestigial-reasoning post, which itself calls for experiments) into a cheap, falsifiable, causal measurement, synthesizing them with attribution work (#83, #49) into a metric the monitoring cluster (#39, #51, #74) immediately needs — yet no item in the survey (or adjacent literature: text-level answer-convergence and early-exit probing work predicts answers for efficiency but never intervenes causally on the decision, controls the answer-already-in-text confound, or asks faithfulness questions) has mapped commitment over time, quantified load-bearing vs. vestigial CoT spans, or tested whether backtracking genuinely reopens decisions.
