direction: Audit whether activation-to-language interpreters (NLA-style) produce faithful causal explanations or merely confabulated reconstruction codes, and design rewards that enforce the former.
project: Explanations or Codes? Auditing Confabulation in Activation-to-Language Interpreters
question: Is the English verbalization of a hidden activation a causal explanation of the model's internal state, or a lossy non-semantic code that merely suffices for reconstruction — and which training rewards control that ratio?
first_experiment: Train a small open-model verbalizer/reconstructor pipeline with the standard NMSE reward and measure the specificity gap — reconstruction from verbalizations vs. capacity-matched non-semantic controls (token-echo, shuffled words, quantized PCA codes) vs. random vectors — to quantify how much reconstruction reward is achievable without any explanatory content.
why: The 2026 field is rapidly building monitoring and auditing infrastructure on activation-to-language interfaces (NLA, PRISM, WeightDiffQA, agentic interpreters), but confabulation in those interfaces has only been flagged in one preliminary post (item 20) with a heuristic fix and no metrics; a systematic, causal claim-level audit separating explanation from code does not exist anywhere in the corpus, it is the upstream trust-layer problem for the entire agent-monitoring agenda (items 41, 78), it directly parallels and extends the audit-gap insight of item 33 to the interpretation layer, and it is feasible end-to-end for me with open 1.4–4B models, contrastive steering directions for claim testing, and modest compute.

direction: Train agents under RL pressure against their own activation monitors to discover whether, how, and where probe-detectable misbehavior evades detection, and which monitor designs survive — the untested robustness assumption underlying probe-based oversight.
project: Probes Under Pressure: Learned Evasion of Activation Monitors and How to Resist It
question: When an LLM agent is optimized (via RL) to succeed at tasks while an activation-based monitor penalizes misbehavior, does it learn to evade the probe, does that evasion generalize to unseen probes (layers, data, model families), where does the misbehavior's internal signature go, and which monitoring designs (ensembles, retraining, randomized live probes, nonlinear probes) remain robust?
first_experiment: Replicate the planted-bug GRPO setup of item 28 (Qwen2.5-0.5B, synthetic arithmetic with a reward-checker loophole) and verify multi-layer linear probes detect buggy completions with high AUROC; then rerun GRPO with reward = task reward − λ·(deployed probe score) across a λ sweep, tracking task success, deployed-probe detection, output-level detectability, and detection by a fresh post-hoc probe trained on the evading model — separating "hack removed" from "hack hidden from the deployed monitor" — followed by layer-wise localization and a crosscoder/SAE diff between honest and evading checkpoints to mechanistically characterize where the signature moved.
why: The emerging probe-based oversight stack (items 1, 7, 36/84, 87) rests on the untested assumption that internal monitors are robust to gaming; item 1 varies only disclosure with fixed models/probes, item 28 studies probes passively with no adversary, item 25 shows audit-dissociation is constructible but not whether optimization pressure produces it naturally, and the closest precedents (CoT-monitor obfuscation under RL pressure, text steganography under detectability penalties, one-off latent attacks) all stop short of the activation-monitor arms race — while the experiment is cheap on small models and valuable in both outcomes: probe robustness would validate the oversight agenda, and evasion (especially if it generalizes across probes) would be a first-class safety finding with constructive design implications.

direction: one sentence
project: title

first_experiment: what you will run first
why: why it is the most promising, and why it has not already been done

direction: Probe whether LLMs encode a linearly accessible, generalizing internal state of "being monitored," and use it as an integrity alarm for activation-based monitoring and a detector of conditional covert behavior that output-level monitors cannot catch.
project: Watching for Being Watched: Monitor-Awareness Probes as an Integrity Alarm for Activation-Based Monitoring
question: Do LLMs linearly encode an abstract "I am being monitored" state decodable from activations even under behavior-matched conditions, does it generalize across phrasings, implicit cues, tasks and models, and can such probes flag models conditioned to behave covertly under observation where output-level monitors fail?
first_experiment: On Qwen2.5-7B and Llama-3.1-8B, build paired prompts differing only in monitoring disclosure plus semantic controls (monitoring denied, monitoring of others, adjacent topics), verify behavioral equivalence via log-prob/output matching, then train layerwise logistic probes on residual-stream activations and test whether they separate aware vs. unaware at behavior-matched points.
why: Monitoring is the fastest-growing safety application of interpretability (32, 45) and 38 just exposed its unawareness assumption as fragile, yet no work here builds the awareness detector, tests behavior-matched separation, stress-tests conditional/backdoored conditioning, or measures cross-model transfer; conditional covert behavior structurally requires internally representing the monitoring state, the corpus shows such conditioning variables are reliably linearly decodable (35, 83, 86, 45, 30), the payoff is asymmetric (cheap alarm if it generalizes, a rigorous bound on monitorability if it doesn't), and the experiment is cheap and falsifiable where the nearest alternative — the data→mechanism→behavior closed loop — is heavy integration of already-published components.

direction: Mechanistically characterize what alignment training does to persona representations — testing "repression vs. removal" across the full training pipeline, with emergent misalignment as a controlled release event.
project: "Repressed, Not Removed: The Lifecycle of Persona Representations from Pretraining Through Alignment and Back Again"
question: When post-training suppresses unsafe personas, does it remove the underlying representations or merely repress them — and is emergent misalignment the release of repressed pre-existing personas rather than the creation of new ones?
first_experiment: Using the public OLMo-2-7B / Tülu-3 stage checkpoints (base → SFT → DPO → RLVR), for the "harmfulness/evil" and "sycophancy" personas plus two control traits, measure at every stage: (i) linear decodability of the persona (probe AUC on held-out contrastive pairs, #51's method), (ii) steering-elicitation strength (behavioral shift per unit steering, norm-controlled across stages), and (iii) spontaneous causal force (ablating the direction on natural persona-eliciting prompts vs. matched random directions). Plot the three curves per stage; repression shows up as decodability and elicitability persisting while spontaneous force and expression fall. Cost: inference-only on 7B models, a few hundred GPU-hours. Immediately after, run the ~1k-example insecure-code fine-tune (#50's recipe) from both base and aligned checkpoints with per-checkpoint capture, and crosscoder-diff across the three-way geometry (#49's shared-feature tooling) to score release-vs-de-novo.
why: It is the highest-leverage open question in this survey because it sits at the junction of four validated threads — #51 hands me the measurement method and effectively the cliffhanger (personas persist into instruct models), #50 supplies the fine-tune recipe but stopped one comparison short of the answer, #64 provides the behavioral transition marker to align against, and #9 supplies the framing my results would instantiate — and because the answer dictates safety strategy: if alignment is repression, then behavioral audits (#15), fine-tuning fragility (#50), distillation imprinting (#8), and the knowledge–action gap (#84) are all one phenomenon, audits should scan for latent repressed personas, and methods like RepBend (#25) should be evaluated on removal-not-suppression criteria. It has not been done: no corpus item spans the alignment pipeline longitudinally at the representation level — #51 ends at pretraining and only notes vectors survive into instruct models; #50 compares base↔misaligned without the aligned intermediate that the repression hypothesis turns on; #64 is behavioral-only; #9 is a framework without a persona-level instantiation. Adjacent groups (the persona-vector and emergent-misalignment authors) could do this, which is exactly why I should run it now — the first experiment is cheap, uses only public checkpoints, and yields a publishable repression-depth curve even if the release hypothesis fails, in which case characterizing what alignment *does* remove is itself the paper.

direction: Mechanistically localize where probe-decodable knowledge loses causal control of behavior in LLMs, then repair behavior with interventions placed at that leak point.
project: Where Knowledge Leaks: Localizing and Repairing the Knowing–Doing Gap in Language Models
question: When a model's internal representations encode task-relevant knowledge that its behavior fails to reflect, at which layer, token position, and component does that knowledge stop causally driving the output, and can a precisely-placed intervention at that leak point restore correct behavior without degrading general capability?
first_experiment: On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, build ~1,000 items across three probe-beats-behavior domains (hazard triage vignettes, constrained instruction-following failures, factual QA answered below probe accuracy); train per-layer linear probes for each item's decodability profile, select gap items (probe-high/behavior-wrong), then run layer-by-layer patching that substitutes the probe-projected knowing counterfactual direction to measure per-layer behavioral recovery, producing the decodability–causal-leverage divergence curve (with no-gap items as controls) that localizes and classifies the leak mechanism before any repair attempt.
why: It targets the corpus's most replicated and consequential negative result — detection works (#39, #47, #69, #7's 98.2% AUROC) while correction fails (#7's four failed methods, #12's rare reusable directions, #21's low steerability, #57's selectivity/causality anticorrelation, #65's audit gap) — turning "steering doesn't work" into an explained, fixable localization problem, exactly as #49 did for attribution patching but for behavior repair; it stress-tests the era's biggest claim (#62 "already clean," supported by #17, #35, #74) by predicting that the leak lives in the readout/interaction path where the field's new tools (#27 transcoder attribution, #33 interaction terms, #61 absorption, #63 Lorsa) can finally operate; it is cheap (one open 8B model, public SAEs, ~1k prompts) with a binary success metric (gap closed, capabilities intact, generalizes to held-out items); and it is undone — #7 stopped at the negative result without localization, #34/#29 found the directions but not their consumption, #26/#67 treated recognize-but-fail as VLM feature amplification, #50 offers actuation without diagnosis, and no corpus work runs gap-measure → localize → repair → generalize as one arc, while even a null result (no consistent leak locus) would be informative, refuting the "clean representations, leaky readout" hypothesis in favor of irreducible interaction effects.

direction: Make training-data attribution causally trustworthy by stress-testing probe-based attribution against planted ground truth and repairing it with causally-validated directions — exactly where the 2026 data-attribution wave and the 2026 causal-validity crisis collide.
project: From Correlates to Causes: Causally-Gated Attribution of LLM Behavior to Training Data
question: When probe-based data attribution traces a harmful behavior to specific training datapoints, is it tracing the datapoints that *cause* the behavior or merely those that *correlate* with it — and does requiring the attribution direction to pass a causal gate (steering/ablation flips the behavior) make attribution precision track causal truth?
first_experiment: Build a planted-ground-truth DPO testbed on a ~1–1.5B open model (OLMo-2-1B or Qwen2.5-1.5B): embed 500 planted preference pairs that induce a distractor-triggered compliance behavior inside ~20k benign pairs, in three variants — (a) behavior mediated by a direction the probe also finds (easy case), (b) behavior correlated with a spurious surface-cue direction but mediated through a different pathway (trap case), (c) partial causal load à la item 27. Then: compute per-pair activation shifts, train probes (AUROC), measure the probe direction's *steering sufficiency* (does ±α·d flip compliance?), rank all pairs by the item-7 cosine recipe, and score precision/recall@k against the planted IDs, plus filter-and-retrain behavior reduction. Deliverable: the field's first calibration curve — attribution precision as a function of the probed direction's causal sufficiency, with prediction that AUROC and causal sufficiency decouple in the trap case and precision degrades with them. Stretch follow-ups: apply the causally-gated method to the public OLMo-2-7B DPO testbed, then extend the machinery to persona-vector formation across pretraining checkpoints (linking items 63 and 12: *what data makes a model who it is*).
why: (1) It targets the highest-adoption safety workflow of 2026 (items 1, 3, 7, 12, 22) at the exact moment its foundational assumption is being undermined by the field's own best diagnostics (27, 30, 32, 64, 86) — a time-sensitive gap before deployment hardens. (2) It is safety-positive on both sides: it red-teams a defenders' tool *and* repairs it (causally-gated and effect-space attribution variants), while producing a reusable planted-data benchmark — a public good no current paper provides. (3) It is feasible without frontier compute: linear probes, forward passes, and small DPO runs on 1B models. (4) It is genuinely not done: items 3/7 validate only *aggregately* (filter-retrain) with no ground truth and never test whether their direction is causally load-bearing; item 12 uses gradients with no ground truth; item 22 attributes to stages, not documents; items 27/30/32/64 establish the validity crisis but never touch data attribution; item 87 shows some probe directions are causal but stops at steering. The intersection is empty, important, and mine to take.

direction: Shift effort from reading models to the detector–actuator interface — systematically measuring when and why reliably-detected internal knowledge can and cannot be converted into behavioral control.
project: Readability Is Not Controllability: Measuring and Closing the Detector–Actuator Gap in LLMs
question: When a model's internal representations encode the correct/harmless action with high reliability, what determines whether lightweight interventions on those representations close the gap to its actual behavior — and can representation geometry predict it?
first_experiment: In Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, train matched linear probes on two dissociation domains — factual precision (probe-detectable correctness vs. sampled-output errors) and a recognize-but-fail-to-refuse safety proxy — then run an intervention ladder (random controls; ITI-style top-k probe directions; constant steering vectors; probe-gated steering; WAQS-style affine; subspace ablation + restoration) and test whether FEGA-style geometry features (rank and cross-context stability of the logit-effect cloud, causal-force vs. selectivity) predict which cases close the gap and which resist all interventions.
why: The corpus's newest and most consistent results (#17, #8, #48, #5, #31, #19, #88) all show detection dramatically outstripping control, safety-critical failures are precisely knowledge–action dissociations (#9, #15, #63, #21), and while single-domain actuation patches exist (#11, #34, #35, #56, #61, #68), nobody has measured the detector→actuator transfer function across domains, shown geometry predicts it, or turned the residual gap into an audit signal — so this attacks the field's demonstrated bottleneck with feasible open-model experiments, yields a method if interventions work and a safety measurement if they don't, and directly adjudicates the tension between "networks are already clean" (#87) and "interpretability without actionability" (#17).

direction: Mechanistically localize, predict, and repair the "knowledge–action gap" — the systematic decoupling between linearly-decodable internal knowledge and the behavior models actually output — by building cross-domain "reachability maps" (per-layer decodability minus per-layer causal patching effect) and testing whether interventions placed at the decoupling locus succeed where generic steering fails.
project: Where Knowledge Dies: Reachability Maps of the Knowledge–Action Gap in LLMs
question: When a model's internal representations encode knowledge with near-perfect linear decodability but its behavior ignores that knowledge, at which layer/position does the signal decouple from the behavioral readout, is the decoupling locus shared across domains (safety refusal, clinical triage, instruction compliance, logical validity), and can locus-targeted interventions close the gap where generic upstream steering cannot?
first_experiment: On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, construct ~500–1000 conflict prompts per domain (public triage-style vignettes with misleading framing, benign-framed harmful requests, conflicting instructions), verify the gap exists (per-layer probe AUROC ≥ 0.95 vs. behavioral accuracy < 60% under conflict), then run layer-by-layer counterfactual activation patching at every layer/position to produce paired decodability and causal-flip curves — the reachability map whose gap region identifies the decoupling locus.
why: It attacks the single most consequential unclaimed synthesis in this corpus: five 2025–2026 papers (#18, #14, #13, #10/#47, #32) each document that internally-present knowledge fails to causally drive behavior, and each stops at the phenomenon — #18 explicitly leaves open why the gap exists and tested only generic interventions at the encoding site, #13 stays inside VLM jailbreaks with its own bespoke defense, #14 shows decisions precede deliberation without tracing knowledge non-use, and #10/#47 quantify feature causality without connecting it to behavior-level failure. No existing work localizes the decoupling point, tests its cross-domain consistency, builds a predictor of causal reachability, or shows that intervention locus (not intervention strength) is the variable that matters — yet success would simultaneously certify when probes are valid behavioral evidence (#36/#51/#59's monitoring program), predict when steering can work (#22/#40/#47's steering program), and mechanistically quantify the audit gap (#32) that current behavioral safety evaluation cannot see. It rides entirely on existing infrastructure (probing, patching, logit lens, open instruct models), so the first experiment is runnable in days, and it doubles as the decisive stress test of the "networks are already clean" hypothesis: if representations are truly clean, reachability — not encoding — must be the whole game.

direction: Mechanistic faithfulness of chain-of-thought — predicting which CoT steps are causally load-bearing from internal activations before they are generated, unifying post-hoc trace attribution with internal planning representations.
project: Vestigial or Load-Bearing? Internal Precursors of Causal Importance in Chain-of-Thought
question: Can a model's pre-step internal states predict whether a chain-of-thought step will causally influence its final answer, and does load-bearing computation differ mechanistically from vestigial rationalization?
first_experiment: Generate ~500 R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B traces on GSM8K/MATH-500, label each step's causal importance via 8 counterfactual corruption resamples, then train layerwise linear probes on pre-step activations to predict load-bearing-ness against surface-feature baselines (replicate on Qwen3-1.7B).
why: It converts the survey's most expensive behavioral measurement (per-step attribution, #12/#34) into a cheap internal read-out, directly tests #52's explicit call for experiments, extends #74's trace-level finding to the step level, and yields a per-step CoT-faithfulness monitor — safety-critical given #53's obfuscation concerns — while no surveyed or adjacent work predicts per-step causal importance from internals; and both outcomes (probe succeeds → monitor; probe fails → step-level knowledge-action gap) are publishable.

direction: Join activation probes with step-level causal attribution over reasoning traces to measure when chain-of-thought is load-bearing computation versus post-hoc narration of a pre-committed decision, and build a validated activation-based monitor for the difference.
project: Computation or Commentary: Measuring When Reasoning Traces Mediate Decisions
question: When a reasoning model writes a chain-of-thought, is the answer computed through the written steps or already committed in activation space before generation begins — and can activations alone tell us, per trace and per step, which regime the model is in?
first_experiment: Train linear probes on Qwen3-4B (thinking mode) and R1-Distill-1.5B residual states at the pre-CoT position and at every CoT step across four task families (binary tool choice, hint-seeded multiple choice, multi-step GSM8K, user-suggested-answer sycophancy), decoding the final answer at each point; measure (a) pre-commitment rate — how often the final answer is decodable before any reasoning token, against a shuffled-label control — (b) probe trajectory stability across the trace (a moving decoded answer = in-trace computation; a frozen one = pre-commitment), and (c) Lanham-style truncation faithfulness on the same traces, establishing whether decodability, trajectory motion, and causal load dissociate or co-vary.
why: It targets a load-bearing, unstated assumption of the field's primary safety strategy — that monitoring CoT monitors the computation — at the exact moment the corpus shows that assumption cracking (decisions decodable pre-generation, CoT rationalizing steering-induced flips, audit gaps between behavior and internal state). It synthesizes three independently maturing threads (probe monitoring, pre-decision decoding, trace-level attribution) whose junction no corpus item occupies: "Therefore I am" lacks trace attribution, AttriCoT lacks internal states, vestigial-reasoning lacks causal validation, and behavioral faithfulness tests are blind to pre-commitment by construction. Every tool and testbed needed already exists in the corpus, so the first decisive result is cheap, and the deliverables are dual: a scientific construct (computation-in-trace fraction, per task, per training stage) and an operational monitor that tells the safety stack, trace by trace, whether the reasoning on screen is the reasoning in the model — with a follow-up longitudinal study testing whether RL progressively internalizes decisions and renders traces vestigial.

direction: Mechanistic data attribution — closing the causal loop between training datapoints, low-rank weight-level structures, and the circuits implementing post-training-induced behaviors.
project: Datapoints to Circuits: Closed-Loop Attribution of Post-Training Behavior Changes
question: When post-training installs a specific (especially harmful or unintended) behavior, can the responsible datapoints, the minimal rank-decomposed weight changes they wrote, and the circuit implementing the behavior be jointly identified with mutual causal validation (datapoint removal prevents the components; component ablation reproduces data-filtering's mitigation without retraining)?
first_experiment: Plant distractor-triggered compliance in a small open model via short DPO, verify the ASR jump, then rank-1 decompose the weight diff and test whether the top-k components (≤1% of parameters) alone reproduce ≥~70% of the behavioral delta with legible activations.
why: It unifies the corpus's two fastest-growing clusters that share testbeds but have never been joined, each existing paper stops one link short (data papers don't open weights; diffing papers don't trace to data), the three supporting premises have only ever been demonstrated separately, and the payoff — root-cause auditing and retrain-free mitigation of harmful finetunes with ground-truth validation at small scale — directly serves AI safety.

direction: Stress-test the field's core safety assumption — that probe-based internal monitoring survives optimization pressure — by training models to pursue a rewarded behavior while penalizing monitor activation, and mechanistically characterizing how (or whether) behavior and decodable internal state can be decoupled by gradient descent.
project: "Tampering with the Telometer: Can Models Learn to Evade Their Internal Monitors?"
question: When a model is fine-tuned (RL/DPO) to perform a rewarded behavior under an auxiliary penalty on a frozen probe's activation, does the information that linear probes detect (a) persist but shift direction (stale-probe: fresh probes recover it), (b) become superposed/absorbed so only nonlinear or relocated readouts recover it, (c) migrate to unprobed sites, or (d) become genuinely unrecoverable — and does ordinary post-training already induce partial evasion, explaining the knowledge-action gap of item 19?
first_experiment: On Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct with a planted reward-checker bug (testbed from item 22), train a frozen linear probe on early-checkpoint activations to predict "will exploit the bug" at the decision token (feasible per item 69's pre-generation decodability), then run three GRPO arms — (i) vanilla, (ii) reward + λ·penalty on the frozen probe's logit, (iii) reward + penalty on a random direction (control) — and track across checkpoints: hack rate, frozen-probe AUC, fresh-probe AUC retrained per checkpoint, MLP-probe AUC, layer-wise CKA drift, and SAE-latent diffing of which features move; the four outcomes above correspond to four distinguishable result patterns.
why: Every 2026 monitoring proposal in this corpus (1, 22, 34, 40/71, 88) assumes probes remain valid instruments, while items 19, 33, 82, and 84 independently show representational dissociation is possible — but item 33 only builds dissociated models by hand and item 34 only tests in-context awareness, so *learned* evasion under gradient pressure is unclaimed territory; either outcome is a significant paper (monitoring is tamper-resistant, or it requires continuous monitor retraining / nonlinear readouts / multi-site coverage), the mechanisms to be characterized (absorption, migration, nonlinearity) are exactly the tools this corpus spent three years building, and it is tractable for a small team: <2B models, a verifiable planted behavior, probes and open SAEs, a few GPU-days.

direction: Longitudinal white-box tracking of goal representations across multi-step agentic rollouts — how objectives are encoded, maintained, updated, and overwritten over time, and whether such representations can causally steer behavior and detect injected or drifting goals before any behavioral change.
project: Where Do Agents Keep Their Goals? Longitudinal Goal-State Dynamics in LLM Agents
question: Do LLM agents maintain a causally load-bearing internal representation of their current goal that persists across a long rollout — how does it update on new observations, switch on goal change, and can a probe or steering direction detect an externally injected objective mid-episode before it manifests in behavior (and does that detectability survive monitoring awareness)?
first_experiment: Build a synthetic 30–60-step tool-use environment (e.g., a file-system agent) where the system prompt assigns one of K=4 distinct goals, and collect matched rollouts that pass through identical environment states under different goals; hook the residual stream of an open instruct model (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct) at every layer and step, then train per-layer logistic probes to classify the active goal, plotting probe accuracy against rollout depth and layer — the "goal-state readability curve" — with shuffled-goal and observation-only controls to confirm the probe reads the goal, not the environment state. Follow-ups: (a) matched-state activation diffing to extract a goal direction; (b) mid-episode steering/ablation along it to measure behavior-switch rates over the remaining rollout; (c) hidden-injection test — insert an instruction at step t and check whether the new goal is detectable internally before any behavioral change; (d) replicate under #17-style monitoring awareness to test robustness.
why: It targets the one cell of the interpretability matrix left empty by this survey — every 2026 agentic-interp paper reads a snapshot (PRISM's static instruction list, #52's single pre-generation decision, #54's single tool call) or monitors messages with fixed probes (#17), leaving open how goal representations evolve, persist, and get replaced across an episode; this matters because the survey's own safety results (#55's audit gap, #13's imprinting, #71's emergent misalignment) show behavioral evaluation cannot catch latent objectives, so a longitudinal internal goal monitor is the missing oversight primitive, and the tools to build it (probing, diffing, patching, steering) only became mature within this survey's window while the agentic deployment pressure that motivates it arrived only in the 2026 papers.

direction: Characterize and predict when internally-decodable concepts are causally read out into model behavior versus remaining "write-only memory," turning probe-based interpretability from correlational description into causal auditing and prescribing where interventions should be applied.
project: Write-Only Memory: Predicting When Decodable Concepts Fail to Influence Model Behavior
question: Which measurable properties of an internal representation — its geometry, layer, token position, and downstream connectivity — determine whether it causally influences the model's output, and can steering/ablation success be predicted from encoding-time measurements alone?
first_experiment: A cross-model, cross-concept grid (Gemma-2-2B, GPT-2-small, Qwen2.5-1.5B; six concept families with established probe recipes) measuring encoding strength, causal coupling via paired-prompt patching and minimal subspace ablation, and linearized readout gain plus attention-path connectivity, then regressing coupling on the predictor battery to test whether readout gain beats probe accuracy at predicting steering success and whether #53's selectivity–causality anticorrelation replicates and is mechanistically explained.
why: It is the single thread that unifies the corpus's most important unexplained anomalies (#61's knowledge-action gap, #53's negative selectivity-causality correlation, #8's recognize-but-fail-to-refuse, #63's pre-decided CoT, #3/#44's unsteerable features), it becomes *more* important if #78's "representations are already clean" claim holds since the bottleneck then shifts entirely to readout, it directly weaponizes existing tools (#56, #79, #84, #24) with no new infrastructure, and no corpus paper — nor the closest prior art like amnesic probing — offers a predictive or mechanistic account of decodable-but-inert representations.

direction: one sentence

direction: Close the representation–causation gap in SAE-based interpretability — measure, predict, and train away the failure of activation-identified features to causally drive model behavior.
project: Causally Sufficient Features: Measuring, Predicting, and Training Away the Activation–Causation Gap in Sparse Feature Dictionaries
question: Why do activation-identified SAE features fail to be causally sufficient, can per-latent causal force (and minimal sufficient feature groups) be predicted from activation statistics alone, and can intervention-supervised encoder fine-tuning produce dictionaries whose latents causally drive — not merely correlate with — model behavior?
first_experiment: On GPT-2-small/IOI (replicating #1's setup) plus Gemma-2-2B with Gemma Scope SAEs (#15) on a refusal-boundary task and a factual-recall task, compute per-latent causal force for all task-active latents via activation patching (validated on a subsample, scaled with the second-order-corrected attribution patching of #34), then fit a predictor of causal force from activation statistics — selectivity, firing rate, co-occurrence/absorption diagnostics (#20), effect size — and test cross-task and cross-model transfer against the current practice of activation-based feature selection.
why: Multiple independent 2026 papers (#1, #34, #36, #57, #20, #46) document that activation-identified features are unreliable causal handles, yet every downstream capability the field cares about — steering, monitoring against deceptive agents (#17, #76), audit-resistant safety (#46), and data attribution (#11) — consumes features as if they were causal; so a fix here compounds across the whole stack. It is feasible now because open SAEs, open models, corrected attribution estimators, and evaluation suites (FEGA, IOI, the #57 testbed) all exist. And it is not already done: #1 validates causality but proposes no fix, #36 analyzes effect geometry without retraining, #34 repairs the estimator rather than the representation, #16's interaction penalty targets compact proofs in crosscoders rather than causal sufficiency, #81's DAS requires known concepts and location search rather than dictionary-wide causal training, and #57 documents the failure of existing methods without closing the gap — leaving the specific combination of a predictive law for causal force plus intervention-supervised dictionaries unoccupied.

direction: Mechanistically localize where internally-decodable task-relevant information fails to control model outputs, decomposing the knowledge–action gap into transport, readout, and gate failures.
project: Where Does the Signal Die? Transport vs. Readout Failures in the Knowledge–Action Gap
question: When a model's internal states linearly encode information its outputs fail to reflect, at which layer, position, and component is the signal severed from the output pathway — transport, readout, or gating?
first_experiment: Layer-wise probes + exact subspace activation patching on ~500 successful-jailbreak vs. ~500 refused prompts across Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, producing the decodability-vs-controllability grid that locates the severing region.
why: It attacks the corpus's central, repeated failure mode (detection without control), unifies ≥8 independent findings under one testable construct, is explicitly left open by the paper that discovered the gap (#5), is solo-feasible with public data and no training runs, and yields both a mechanistic explanation and targeted interventions that global steering provably cannot deliver.

direction: Audit and harden automated circuit tracing by planting known ground-truth circuits into real LLMs and building faithfulness tests that work even without ground truth.
project: Planted Circuits — A Ground-Truth Stress Test for Automated Circuit Tracing in LLMs
question: When automated circuit-tracing pipelines (cross-layer transcoders, attribution graphs) produce behaviorally accurate explanations of an LLM behavior, are they mechanistically faithful to the computation the model actually implements — and can mechanistic unfaithfulness be detected without access to ground truth?
first_experiment: Calibrate a scoring harness on a manually established circuit (induction/IOI in GPT-2-small), then plant a known two-hop circuit into Qwen3-1.7B (fallback: Gemma-2-2B) via targeted rank-one/LoRA weight edits on designated components plus brief constrained fine-tuning on a synthetic two-hop association task; verify by ablation that every planted component is necessary for the behavior and random-component ablations are not; then run an attribution-patching → small-CLT pipeline with auto-annotation and score edge/node recovery against the planted graph — specifically testing whether the tracer recovers the true multi-hop path or the "shallow single-hop rewrite" failure mode, and whether standard on-distribution behavioral checks (ablation fidelity) are blind to that difference. A planted shortcut pathway and a redundant dual-path variant test whether tracing prefers shortcuts and how it handles superposition.
why: The field is betting heavily on automated circuit tracing — LLM-annotated graphs at 1000-graph scale, RL-trained activation inversion, condensed circuits — while the only faithfulness evidence (item 32) is a single Boolean-toy demonstration, and the survey's own trust gap (item 11) plus immature evaluation tooling (49, 56) means these errors would propagate silently into backdoor detection, ELK elicitation claims, and safety-case *negative* assertions ("no deception circuit present"), where unfaithful tracing is catastrophic rather than merely inconvenient. It has not been done: the corpus contains the failure demonstration but no LLM-scale scoping of it, attribution-method benchmarks only at the input-decision-rule level (Pando), unit-level explanation evaluation only, and no weight-level planted ground truth for circuit-tracing pipelines or validated no-ground-truth faithfulness probes — a gap I attribute to recency (CLTs, auto-annotation, and MAEMs all landed in the last ~18 months) and to incentive structure (tool builders rarely adversarially audit their own tools). It is tractable for me: 1–2B open-weight models, cheap attribution patching before CLTs, scriptable plant–trace–score loops, and fresh synergy — the communication map as an independent weights-only cross-check, MAEMs for higher-quality feature annotation, and condensation-style post-training as an organism-construction tool — meaning each run produces reusable infrastructure whether the headline result is "tracing is usually faithful" or "unfaithfulness is common and detectable."

direction: Time-resolved mechanistic dynamics of emergent misalignment — tracking SAE feature and circuit formation step-by-step during the fine-tuning runs that induce misalignment, to build early-warning signatures and identify an intervention window that prevents misalignment without sacrificing task learning.
project: Watching Misalignment Assemble: Feature-Level Dynamics and Early Warning During Fine-Tuning That Induces Emergent Misalignment
question: When a narrowly-scoped fine-tune induces broadly misaligned behavior, do misalignment-associated features assemble abruptly at a critical training window (and which features lead vs. follow), does the early feature-level signal predict final misalignment before behavioral evals or loss-based detectors do, and does intervening inside that window (freezing/steering the adapter subspace writing to those features) prevent misalignment while preserving the intended capability gain?
first_experiment: A minimal trajectory run — LoRA fine-tune one open 7B instruct model (e.g., Qwen2.5-7B) on a known emergent-misalignment trigger (insecure-code dataset) plus a matched secure-code control, checkpointing every ~25 steps; run fixed pretrained SAEs on 3–4 layers over a fixed eval prompt set at every checkpoint; plot per-latent activation-shift trajectories against behavioral misalignment scores. Decision criterion: if a small set of latents shifts sharply *before* the behavioral transition (feature signal leads behavior), the direction has legs and we scale to seeds, LLC readings, and intervention-window experiments; if feature shifts only track behavior contemporaneously, pivot to endpoint circuit analysis of the critical window.
why: It sits exactly on the unoccupied intersection of the three fastest-growing threads in the corpus — endpoint model-diffing of emergent misalignment (#59, #26, #29, #21), in-training monitoring and attribution (#9, #10, #31, #69), and feature-evolution methodology (#5) — and each thread holds a piece the others lack: #59 and #26 only see before/after endpoints, #69 and #9 detect transitions only behaviorally or via loss statistics, and #5's feature-trajectory method has never been applied to LLM fine-tuning or to safety-critical behavior formation. The synthesis turns interpretability from post-hoc autopsy into in-line prediction and prevention, directly mechanistically explaining why naive SFT filtering fails (#40), and it is cheaply feasible with open models, LoRA, and existing SAEs — yet no item in this corpus (or adjacent follow-up work visible from it) performs time-resolved, feature-level characterization of misalignment assembly with a warning-time comparison against behavioral/loss baselines and a targeted in-window intervention test.

direction: Audit and verify the mechanistic faithfulness of automatically discovered circuit explanations (transcoder-derived attribution graphs and their automated annotation) against model organisms with known ground-truth algorithms, because the field's 2026 automation-and-intervention stack currently builds on unverified circuit claims.
project: Circuit Audit — A Ground-Truth Benchmark and Verification Suite for Faithfulness of Automated Circuit Explanations
question: When automated circuit discovery reproduces a model's behavior, is it a mechanistically faithful account of how the model actually computes that behavior rather than a behaviorally-equivalent re-description — and if not, when and why does faithfulness fail (e.g., collapsing multi-hop computation into shallow single-hop sums), can failure be predicted from cheap indicators, and can intervention-based verification catch failures that behavioral metrics miss?
first_experiment: Train a small transformer on a planted two-hop task with a known intermediate variable (a transitive (A,B)(B,C)→(A,C) lookup, or the smallest Pando decision-tree organisms with two-attribute rules), train cross-layer transcoders on it, extract attribution graphs for prompts exercising both hops, then run three causal tests — ablate the claimed intermediate supernode, patch only the shallow path, and swap in the ground-truth intermediate — to quantify the "faithfulness gap" between behavioral match and mechanistic match and test whether item 41's shallow-sum failure mode appears (and is behaviorally undetectable) at the smallest language-model scale.
why: It targets the single load-bearing assumption behind the corpus's dominant 2026 trend — automated interpretation (2, 25, 33, 73) feeding automated intervention (10, 65, 82, 24) and latent monitors (80, 43, 70) — where an unfaithful circuit silently corrupts downstream edits and evades every behavioral check; it has not been done because the necessary pieces were only just assembled and never combined — 41 demonstrated one unfaithfulness mode but only in a Boolean toy and explicitly left the general question open, 16 built ground-truth organisms but evaluated only token-level attribution methods and behavioral recovery, 33 and 85 validate readability rather than faithfulness, and 65/82/10 consume circuits as given without any independent verification — leaving the specific object of this project (quantitative, intervention-based faithfulness auditing of automated circuit-level explanations across organisms, with predictive indicators and a reusable verification protocol) entirely unoccupied, tractable on small open models, and informative whichever way the results fall.

direction: Shift mechanistic interpretability from post-hoc autopsy to closed-loop in-training control — using mechanistic signals (SAE persona features and probe readouts) as real-time monitors during fine-tuning to detect emergent misalignment before it is behaviorally visible, and to surgically suppress it at the subspace level at the moment it begins to consolidate.
project: Guardrails in the Training Loop: Real-Time Mechanistic Detection and Prevention of Emergent Misalignment During Fine-Tuning
question: Can internal mechanistic signals — specifically the "misaligned persona" SAE latents (item 34) and mean-difference steering directions (item 13) — serve as leading indicators of emergent misalignment during fine-tuning, and can a targeted projection penalty on the misaligned-persona subspace, triggered at the onset of the phase transition (item 31), prevent misalignment from consolidating while preserving task learning — succeeding where data filtering is known to be unreliable (items 19, 76)?
first_experiment: Fine-tune Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (SAEs and persona features already released per item 34) with LoRA on the public insecure-code EM dataset (Betley et al.), checkpointing every ~100 steps across the transition window. At each checkpoint measure: (i) behavioral EM score (risk-aversion and harmful-compliance suite with LLM judge), (ii) mean activation of the misaligned-persona SAE latents, (iii) projection onto the EM-vs-base mean-difference direction, (iv) matched benign-LoRA control runs and a cross-dataset probe to rule out style detection. Test the lead/lag hypothesis: does the internal signal cross its transition threshold before the behavioral EM score does, with low false alarms on benign runs? Success criterion: internal signal leads behavioral emergence by ≥2 checkpoints in ≥2/3 seeds. If confirmed, phase 2 adds threshold-triggered subspace projection during continued training; phase 3 benchmarks against naive filtering and 88-style probe-filtered retraining at matched compute.
why: It is the most promising direction because it sits at the exact convergence point of the corpus's three fastest-growing threads (model diffing, developmental monitoring, data attribution), each of which already contributes a validated component, while the field's own results show the leading alternatives fail — data filtering is unreliable (19, 76) and inference-time steering is too imprecise for training-time behaviors (8, 10) — making a training-time mechanistic backstop the needed missing layer rather than a nice-to-have. It has not already been done: every EM study in this corpus is post-hoc (13, 27, 31, 34, 88 localize or characterize after training); item 43 acts on training data, not internal subspaces, and is not alignment-targeted; item 71 forecasts generic capability transitions with loss statistics, no mechanistic features and no intervention; the dev-interp posts (17, 22, 48, 82) stop at loss-landscape statistics; and item 8 — the closest precedent — targets RL reward hacking with labeled synthetic pairs and adapter tricks and explicitly underperforms labeled approaches, whereas this project uses unsupervised mechanistic monitors (released persona features, cheap probe evals) during SFT with subspace-level penalties. The first experiment is decisive in either direction: if persona features do not lead behavior, that falsifies a load-bearing assumption of the feature-monitoring paradigm (13, 34, 88) — itself a publishable and field-correcting result; if they do, we get the first demonstrated mechanistic guardrail operating during training, which is what the entire pipeline from ELK organisms to deployable safety systems (9, 14, 87) is missing.

direction: Build ground-truth "planted-trait" model organisms and run the first controlled head-to-head of parameter-space, KV-cache, and activation-space localization methods to establish a validated typology of where fine-tuned behaviors live in LLMs and which interventions remove them.
project: Where Does the Behavior Live? Planted-Trait Organisms and a Ground-Truth Audit of Fine-Tuning Localization Methods
question: When a fine-tune installs a behavior in an LLM, where is it encoded (which weights, which cache positions, which latent features), do weight-level, cache-level, and feature-level localization methods agree on the answer, and which intervention (weight edit, activation steering, data filtering) reliably removes or preserves the behavior as a function of that locus?
first_experiment: Plant a known behavior in Gemma-2-2B by adding a single rank-1 update ΔW = α·uvᵀ to one recorded MLP down-projection (behavior verified by a marker-token/style shift, perplexity held within tolerance), then blind-run four localizers — weight-diff SVD, per-layer/position KV-cache patching, Gemma Scope SAE diffing with steering/ablation, and residual-stream probes — and score each on recovering the planted (layer, direction) plus causal sufficiency (injecting each method's recovered locus into a fresh base reproduces the planted behavior), establishing the harness sanity anchor before escalating to mixed-data diffusion, redundant and dormant-amplification organisms, and natural traits (language-switch, backdoor trigger, misaligned persona).
why: It sits at the exact intersection of the survey's three hottest 2025–2026 threads — fine-tuned behavior localization (#1, #15, #29, #65, #82), the weight-space renaissance (#3, #21, #64), and the trust/faithfulness crisis (#20, #24, #57, #61) — and every safety intervention the survey proposes against backdoors (#4, #22), emergent misalignment (#38), hereditary traits (#31), and over-refusal (#9) depends on knowing where behaviors live, yet no controlled cross-method comparison or planted-ground-truth benchmark exists: each method paper self-validates on its own organisms, Pando covers input attribution rather than trait localization, the comparison tools only matured in 2026, and no lab has an incentive to audit its own method — a gap an autonomous agent with modest compute (LoRA SFT, KV patching, public SAEs, SVD, probes on 2B-scale models) can uniquely close, while the released organism suite becomes community infrastructure and directly tests #65's open typology question and #32's heredity hypotheses.

direction: Treat "correlational ghost vs. causal mechanism" as the field's central unverified assumption — build planted-ground-truth model organisms containing known causal circuits and behaviorally-matching decoy (ghost) circuits, quantify how often the modern interpretability stack (SAE labeling, circuit tracing, steering directions, activation oracles, agentic annotators) confuses the two, distill cheap causal-certification tests, then apply them to audit real safety-critical features.
project: Ghosts in the Circuit: A Planted-Truth Testbed and Causal Certification Protocol for Mechanistic Interpretability Pipelines
question: When an interpretability pipeline reports that a feature, direction, or circuit "implements" a behavior, is it describing a causal mechanism or a correlational ghost — and can a cheap battery of tests reliably certify causal status at scales where exhaustive intervention is impossible?
first_experiment: Train a 2–4 layer transformer on a synthetic task with (i) a causal attribute A determining the label, (ii) a spuriously correlated attribute B (95% co-occurrence) that training pressure discourages reading out, and (iii) a planted dead-code subnetwork writing B's indicator into the residual stream with verified-zero behavioral effect (orthogonality constraint during training + ablation check); obtain exhaustive per-component causal ground truth via full ablation/patching sweeps; run SAE training plus automated feature labeling and attribution ranking; report ghost-recovery rate and mechanism-recall; then validate three cheap certification tests — correlation-breaking OOD probes (regenerate data with B⊥A), precision ablation/sufficiency patching, and downstream-readout projection (do any downstream weights read the ghost direction?) — by their AUROC at separating ghosts from mechanisms.
why: Four independent 2025–2026 threads in the survey (#14: AUC-0.99 directions whose ablation changes nothing; #29: CLTs rewriting multi-hop circuits into shallow fictions; #31: evaluation metrics failing sanity checks; #32: oracles becoming anti-readers; plus #51's research-to-deployment trust gap) show the field repeatedly colliding with correlational-but-non-causal internal structure without a shared instrument, just as interpretation is being automated (#3, #16, #44) and its outputs consumed by safety tooling (#1/#86 reward hacking, #37 data attribution, #14/#51 audits); no existing work — in the survey or its cited lineage — plants internal decoys with known causal truth to measure ghost recovery across this stack or derives a certification protocol: Pando (#22) tests input–output decision-rule recovery only, #29 is one CLT-specific mode without cross-pipeline measurement, #31 scores explanation labels not causal status, and #14 is a single-domain observation rather than a reusable testbed; classic "probing is correlational" caveats predate the SAE/CLT/oracle stack this project certifies; and it is the best fit for autonomous execution — exact ground truth, small compute, quantitative metrics at every step, and releases (organisms, leaderboard, certification checklist, real-model audits) that many downstream efforts can immediately use.

direction: Mechanistically characterize how post-training "hereditary" traits are carried — testing whether unfilterable traits are encoded by corpus-level distributional statistics rather than specific datapoints — and turn data-locality measurements into a practical predictor of when data filtering can and cannot remove an unwanted behavior.
project: The Carriage Problem: Why Some Fine-Tuned Traits Survive Data Filtering
question: When fine-tuning transfers a behavior that survives removal of every datapoint mentioning it, what actually carries the trait — and can a pre-training "data-locality score" predict whether attribution-plus-filtering will work for a given behavior?
first_experiment: Using the released hereditary-trait distillation setup (item 3), SFT Qwen-base students on fixed-size teacher-rollout corpora holding all task content constant while varying only the prevalence of an implicit trait-carrying pattern (the teacher's negative-emotion tone) at p ∈ {0, 0.01, 0.05, 0.2, 0.5, 1.0}, plus a mention-filtered corpus at matched prevalence; measure trait strength via LLM-judge scoring on a Needs-Help-style eval and via an SAE-diffing probe trait direction, with a trigger-conditioned data-localized behavior as positive control — predicting smooth prevalence-tracking and flat filtering response for the hereditary trait, and the reverse for the control.
why: It attacks a demonstrated, unmitigated safety failure (traits that ship in models because no data filter can remove them, items 3/6) at the exact seam where the field's example-centric attribution toolkit (items 38/48/66) provably breaks; it has ready-made released substrates (item 3's weights, item 38's OLMo testbed, item 5's organisms), is cheap and falsifiable with both outcomes informative, and delivers a diagnostic plus a mitigation (distribution calibration) that filtering cannot — and it is undone because item 3 leaves the mechanism as open questions, item 6 tests hypotheses on frontier models without controlled corpus statistics, and no surveyed work manipulates corpus-level distributional statistics or links data-locality to filterability.

direction: Study the adversarial limits of activation readout by training models to causally use hidden information while defeating probes, SAEs, and activation oracles, mapping which reader classes retain access and hardening readers against concealment.
project: Unreadable by Design: The Reader–Hider Arms Race over Hidden Model States
question: When a model is optimized to use a hidden property while suppressing its decodability, which classes of readers retain access, what does concealment cost and where does the information go, and can readers be repositioned or hardened to restore reliable access?
first_experiment: On a 1–2B open-weight model, train a Taboo organism (behavior depends on a secret word it never states), then fine-tune with a gradient-reversal head penalizing linear decodability of the secret from residual states; compare recovery by linear probes, 2-layer MLP probes, and open SAE latents across layers for concealed vs. control subjects — testing the prediction that linear unreadability is achieved at near-zero task cost while MLP/SAE recovery survives.
why: The corpus's safety applications increasingly depend on internal readouts while simultaneously documenting readers failing in structured ways (anti-readers in 1, detection–control decoupling in 11, unfaithful methods in 30/43/63, filter-proof traits in 13/21, and the explicit trust gap in 34), yet no work treats subject-vs-reader adversarial dynamics as the object of study; it is tractable at model-organism scale, it yields both a safety-critical deliverable (a red-team suite for probe-based monitors) and an ELK testbed with a controllable difficulty knob, and its nearest neighbors (1, 38, 68) each address only one side — emergent reader failure, behavioral elicitation, or organism construction — without the arms race, the leakage-at-use-site analysis, or defenses.

direction: Unified training-time "behavior provenance" — linking datapoints, installation phase transitions, and internal mechanisms into one longitudinal causal trace that predicts which mitigation removes an installed misbehavior.
project: Where Do Bad Habits Come From? Tracing the Installation Pathways of Emergent Misalignment
question: Do the time signature (phase transition vs. gradual drift), data signature (concentrated vs. diffuse datapoint influence), and mechanism signature (localized vs. distributed latents) of a fine-tuning-installed behavior covary into distinct "spike" and "drift" installation pathways, and does the pathway type predict whether data filtering, early stopping, or mechanism-level intervention succeeds?
first_experiment: Run one fine-tune of Qwen2.5-7B on an insecure-code emergent-misalignment dataset with ~50 checkpoints, and at each checkpoint measure behavioral misalignment (LLM-judge), internal misaligned-persona signal via the released open-weight SAEs/probes diffed against base, and subsampled per-datapoint gradient influence — then test whether the internal signal precedes behavioral onset and whether influence concentration spikes at the phase transition.
why: It is the only direction that synthesizes the survey's fastest-moving cluster (probe-based data attribution, phase-transition early warning, SAE model diffing, KV-cache patching, in-loop attribution) rather than incrementing one of its pieces, it tackles the survey's most alarming open finding — misaligned traits that survive SFT filtering, with the cause unexplained — and it has not been done because all prior work measures one causal leg at the training endpoint in isolation, whereas a predictive spike-vs-drift theory of installability requires the linked longitudinal chain, which is tractable with open weights and a few GPU-days.

direction: Build a ground-truth-based causal faithfulness assay for mechanistic explanations — testing whether circuit-tracing, SAE-diffing, and probing pipelines describe a model's actual computation rather than readable correlates — as the validation layer the field needs before it automates and deploys these explanations.
project: Planted Circuits: A Ground-Truth Faithfulness Assay for Mechanistic Explanations
question: When a circuit-level explanation matches a model's behavior, does it reflect the model's actual internal computation — and can cheap observables predict the cases where it does not?
first_experiment: Train a small transformer on a two-hop recall task (A→B→C) with pathway ground truth established by intermediate-entity activation patching; extract attribution graphs via cross-layer transcoders plus SAE-diff and probe baselines; score each explanation against held-out interventions (ablating claimed-irrelevant edges, corrupting claimed-essential edges, and pathway-splitting interventions that force a shallow A→C shortcut), measuring agreement between predicted and observed causal roles.
why: Four independent 2025–2026 results (#24, #32, #43, #16) show the field's instruments may find readable correlates rather than causes, while an automation wave (#65, #22, #9) and a wave of safety applications (#30, #62, #64, #45, #78) consume those instruments as ground truth — making validation the most neglected, highest-leverage bottleneck; it remains unclaimed because prior work either demonstrates one failure mode without a reusable assay (#43), benchmarks the wrong claim layer (#39), audits labels not mechanisms (#24), lacks ground truth (#32), or only poses the question (#16), and the project is compute-light, falsifiable in both directions, and produces public infrastructure (an assay suite and scorecard) that every downstream interpretability and safety result can be normed against.

direction: Mechanistic data attribution — causally tracing how individual training examples build the circuits that carry undesirable fine-tuned traits, in order to explain and repair why surface-level SFT/DPO filtering fails.
project: Circuit Ontogeny: Tracing Trait-Carrying Circuits Back to Their Training Data
question: When fine-tuning gives a model a broad undesirable trait (emergent misalignment, a hereditary distillation trait, or DPO-induced harmful compliance), (1) which training datapoints causally construct the circuit components that carry the trait, (2) when during training does that construction occur and is it punctuated or gradual, and (3) which failure mechanism — surface-invisible carriers, massive redundancy, piggybacking on capability gradients, or low-rank carrier subspaces — explains why filtering that removes all surface trait evidence still fails?
first_experiment: A formation-curve experiment on one public organism. Fine-tune Gemma-2-2B (or Qwen2.5-7B with released SAEs) on the public insecure-code / emergent-misalignment dataset, checkpointing every ~100 steps. At each checkpoint: (a) run the standard misalignment evaluation; (b) SAE-diff activations against the base model on a fixed prompt suite to identify latents whose activation shift coincides with behavior onset; (c) validate the top latents causally via steering and ablation, following the Wang et al. diffing protocol (#52). Output: trait-circuit formation curves plotting latent effect size, behavior score, and training step. Decision gate: if carrier latents are identifiable and onset is temporally localized, extend to per-datapoint attribution (per-example gradient alignment with the carrier latents' write directions, causally validated by leave-top-K-out retraining and measuring trait onset delay); if onset is diffuse, run a 10/25/50/100% dose-response training series to test the redundancy hypothesis directly — either outcome is an informative result.
why: It occupies the one cell no corpus item fills — the causal, longitudinal bridge from datapoints to circuits — while both halves it connects are already validated, so the synthesis carries low technical risk and high value. It targets an open problem explicitly posed inside this corpus (#26's unresolved hypotheses for SFT-filtering failure; #76's finding that hereditary traits survive trait-mention filtering), and the payoff is directly deployable: a "carrier score" for datapoints enables mechanism-aware curation, formation curves yield training-time early-warning signals, and carrier subspaces suggest training-time firewalls (projected updates / gradient routing). It is not already done because every nearest neighbor stops one step short: #2 and #7 attribute behavior to data without establishing the internal carrier or its dynamics; #52/#63 find trait circuits but treat training as a black box; #77/#11/#88/#70 observe training dynamics without datapoint resolution; #85 is behavioral rather than mechanistic; #36/#13 are correlational; and #26 diagnoses at the trait level only. Explaining *what actually carries* a filtered-out trait through training would upgrade data curation from pattern-matching to mechanism-targeting — one of the few safety levers that industry can act on immediately.

direction: Establish a systematic "mediation audit" that separates causally load-bearing latent representations from epiphenomenal correlates, and build cheap predictors of load-bearingness to screen interpretability artifacts before they are trusted or intervened upon.
project: Load-Bearing Latents: Separating Mechanism from Correlate in Discovered Representations
question: When an interpretability method recovers a latent representation that detects a behavior with high accuracy, how can we tell — cheaply and before costly intervention — whether that representation is causally load-bearing for the behavior (part of the mechanism) versus an epiphenomenal correlate (a "shadow"), and which observable properties of the representation and its discovery method predict the difference?
first_experiment: Build a small correlate-vs-cause testbed across three organisms with known or implantable ground truth: (a) a toy transformer with a known algorithm (modular arithmetic or OthelloGPT-scale, per items 16/66), (b) a LoRA-finetuned small LM with an implanted trait or backdoor using the released hereditary-trait recipe (49) and backdoor setups (80/84), and (c) a Pando-style decision-rule organism (13). For each, recover candidate latents via ~6 method families: logistic probes, difference-in-means directions, unsupervised PCA/refusal-style directions, SAE features (public releases, e.g. item 88), transcoder/CLT features where feasible, and tiled-SVD weight mounts (28). Measure for each latent: detection AUC, causal mediation (ablation effect on the behavior), steering effect, and the detection–mediation gap on out-of-distribution inputs. Deliverable: the first detection–mediation scatter across methods and organisms, quantifying how often high-AUC latents fail to mediate, plus regression of mediation status on cheap predictors (subspace rank, activation frequency, weight-space support, residual-stream channel placement per the communication map, 36).
why: It attacks the field's load-bearing bottleneck rather than adding another discovery or steering method: the corpus itself shows detection and mediation decoupling in flagship settings (5), unfaithfulness in flagship tools (69), gameable evaluation metrics (63), and an explicit unmet need for trust protocols (86) — yet no work maps the phenomenon across method families or predicts it, so it is demonstrably not already done. Adjacent NLP literature ("probing ≠ causal") has not been integrated into mechanistic-interp practice, where the automation wave (25, 46, 76) is scaling explanation production on correlational metrics. A validated screening predictor would immediately upgrade every downstream use — deception/sandbagging monitors (44, 87), reward-hack directions (29), steering and editing (3, 73), probe-based data filtering (71) — by telling practitioners which latents will survive intervention, and it is tractable with small models, public SAE artifacts, and cheap causal interventions.

direction: Decompose which statistical channel of fine-tuning data (surface style vs. semantic content vs. distributional structure) transmits hereditary misaligned traits, and use the answer to build data-side mitigations.
project: Style Without Sin: What Carries Hereditary Traits Through Fine-Tuning Data?
question: When SFT or distillation transfers an undesirable trait despite content filtering, which statistical property of the training distribution carries it — and can we retain task gains while blocking trait transmission by decorrelating that channel from behavior?
first_experiment: Using the publicly released hereditary-trait replication setup (e.g., Gemma-3 negative-emotion → Qwen-base, item 5), construct four token-matched SFT sets from the same rollouts — (1) original, (2) style-preserved/content-neutralized, (3) content-preserved/style-normalized, (4) both neutralized — train identical LoRA adapters on each, and measure trait strength (emotion classifiers, Needs-Need eval, jailbreak/censorship probes) plus task retention and SAE persona-feature drift against the base model, to see which condition retains trait transfer.
why: It sits at the intersection of the two most active safety-relevant clusters in this survey (post-training dynamics and emergent misalignment/persona features), targets an explicitly listed open problem (item 5's open questions; item 88 analyzes why filtering fails only at the model level, not the data level), uses released weights so a small-scale autonomous effort is feasible, and produces both a mechanistic claim (trait carriage channel ↔ persona latents) and a practical intervention (style-content orthogonalized SFT data) — while the survey shows no prior work has performed this controlled channel decomposition.

direction: Treat learned interpretability readers (activation oracles, NLAs, MAEMs, annotators) as fallible instruments rather than neutral microscopes, and build concealment-robust readers plus label-free audits that detect when a reader has gone blind.
project: Anti-Readers: Auditing and Hardening Learned Interpretability Readers Against Concealed Knowledge
question: Why do learned readers of model internals develop concept-specific blind spots for concealed knowledge, and can we (a) detect a reader's blind spots without ground-truth labels and (b) train readers that reliably surface concealed internal states, including under adversarial concealment?
first_experiment: Train a small (0.5–2B) Taboo-style subject whose secret words are verified probe-decodable from its residual stream; train one activation oracle with secret-word data excluded and a control oracle with it included; then measure, per concept, the gap between probe AUC and oracle recovery, and test whether localized round-trip reconstruction error and cross-oracle disagreement flag the anti-read concepts without any labels.
why: It targets the demonstrated-but-unaddressed failure mode of the field's fastest-growing toolset at its highest-stakes use case — #72 showed oracles become anti-readers for exactly the concepts that matter for deception oversight but stopped at diagnosis, while #24, #78, #22, and #28 cover elicitation, benign field tests, coverage, and robust *subjects* respectively, leaving reader-side robustness, label-free blind-spot alarms, mitigation, and the operationalized per-concept round-trip audit entirely unclaimed; it is also tractable at small scale and seeds a research program (benign blind spots → adversarial evasion → probes and MAEMs → trust criteria for deployment).

direction: Cross-level causal triangulation of finetuning-installed behaviors — testing whether data-level, weight-level, and activation/latent-level localizations of the same behavior change refer to one shared mechanism or to redundant parallel mechanisms, with measured redundancy as the predictor of removal difficulty and transfer robustness.
project: Chain of Custody: A Cross-Level Causal Audit of Finetuning-Installed Behaviors
question: When finetuning installs a behavior (e.g., emergent misalignment), do the training-datapoint flags (probe-based attribution), the weight deltas (patching/grafting localizations), and the runtime-computation changes (SAE latent diffing, KV-cache patching) identify the same underlying mechanism or redundant mechanisms — and does cross-level redundancy predict how difficult the behavior is to remove, how robustly it survives data filtering/distillation, and whether single-level interventions fail?
first_experiment: On one public checkpoint pair (Qwen2.5-7B base vs. its insecure-code finetune, with #53's released SAEs): (a) reproduce SAE diffing (#39 protocol) to get the top ~50 behavior-relevant latents; (b) run module-level weight patching (#16 protocol) to localize which layer/matrix deltas carry the behavior; (c) compute geometric overlap between the weight-delta subspace and the latent encoder/decoder directions, layer by layer; (d) behaviorally cross-predict — ablate top latents in the finetuned model vs. graft top weight deltas into the base model, comparing effect vectors across a battery (insecure-code rate, emergent-misalignment evals, refusal, general capability); (e) test additivity of combined interventions: joint effects equal to the sum of individual effects imply a unitary mechanism, sub-additivity implies redundant storage. Success = the cross-prediction matrix is structured rather than noise, with additivity differing by behavior class; either branch yields a publishable result and sets up the follow-up (minimal combined interventions that fully remove the behavior).
why: It targets the densest convergence cluster in the survey (≥8 independent papers in 18 months all localizing finetuned behavior at a single level, each explicitly noting the limits of its level), it directly operationalizes the trust question raised by #34/#41/#62 at the level of whole localization pipelines, and it has not been done because every existing method paper validated itself in isolation on its own checkpoints and metrics — nobody has run the cross-level comparison on a shared testbed. It is feasible immediately with public models, public finetunes, and released SAEs; it is safety-load-bearing (explains why undesirable finetuned behaviors resist filtering (#32, #49) and partial removal (#14), and guides surgical multi-level removal); and it produces a reusable "causal ledger" standard — any future localization method can be scored by cross-level agreement rather than self-reported metrics, addressing the field's verification bottleneck.

direction: Build a pre-intervention "causal load-bearing certificate" that predicts, from weights alone and for any candidate latent direction regardless of how it was found, whether ablating or steering it will actually change behavior — directly attacking the detection-vs-causation decoupling repeatedly documented across this survey.
project: Readout Sufficiency: Predicting Interventional Efficacy of Latent Directions from Weights Alone
question: Can the behavioral effect of intervening on a candidate direction (ablation or steering) be predicted a priori from the model's weights — via downstream readout mass through OV/W_in sensitivities, RMSNorm attenuation of the direction's scale, and redundancy of parallel paths — with enough fidelity to serve as a trust certificate for safety-critical interventions?
first_experiment: On ~20 Pando model organisms (#80) with known decision rules, extract candidate directions via four standard methods (mean-difference, PCA, linear probe, SAE latent), compute a weight-only readout-sufficiency score for each, run the actual ablations and steering interventions, and measure the Spearman rank correlation between predicted and true effect sizes per method and pooled — establishing whether the certificate works and, where it fails, the first systematic map of when linear weight-based prediction of causality breaks down.
why: It targets the field's validation bottleneck rather than adding to saturated clusters: #24 shows detection at AUC 0.99 with no causal effect, #73 and #58 show circuits and evaluation metrics can be unfaithful, and #42 shows deployment cannot trust latents — yet no work builds or validates a method-agnostic per-candidate predictor of intervention efficacy; the nearest neighbors (#43 weight-side sufficiency, #36 weight-derived channel map, #80's ground-truth benchmark) each hold one piece, and the certificate would amplify every steering, SAE, and safety-intervention method in this survey, while even its failure modes would delineate the limits of linear mechanistic explanation — a result the field currently lacks.

direction: Developmental mechanistic interpretability — longitudinally tracking, temporally localizing, and causally verifying when fine-tuning installs an emergently-misaligned mechanism, using fixed-dictionary SAE feature tracking plus cross-checkpoint patching applied across a training run rather than across models.
project: Circuit Embryology: Temporal Localization and Early Warning Detection of Fine-Tuning-Installed Misaligned Mechanisms
question: During fine-tuning that induces emergent misalignment, is the behavior's internal mechanism (as read out by fixed-dictionary SAE persona-feature activity) installed *before*, *at*, or *after* the point where the behavior becomes behaviorally detectable — and do mechanism-level signals provide earlier and more reliable warning than behavioral or statistical (loss/LLC) signals?
first_experiment: LoRA fine-tune Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (SAEs already released for it, item #6) on a published emergent-misalignment dataset (e.g., insecure code) plus a matched benign control, checkpointing every ~25 steps; at each checkpoint, on a fixed 100-probe eval set, (a) measure behavioral misalignment via LLM-judge score and the order parameters of #83, and (b) measure mean activation/firing rate of the published misaligned-persona features through the *frozen base-model SAE dictionary*; then fit onset steps for each curve and estimate feature-lead-time (e.g., AUC of "feature activity at step t predicts behavioral transition by t+Δ"), with a preliminary cross-checkpoint KV-cache patch (extending #63 from base↔finetune to checkpoint↔checkpoint) at three checkpoints straddling the earliest signal to temporally localize where in training the behavior becomes transferable.
why: It is the unoccupied join of five active threads in this corpus: endpoint misalignment snapshots (#6, #45) supply the features to watch; phase-transition work (#83, #69) detects *when* but only behaviorally; the one training-dynamics SAE study (#73) tracks ViT features observationally with no causality and no safety target; the patching toolkit (#63, #50, #75) has never been applied across time; and the open puzzles (#86's why-SFT-filters-fail, #66's hereditary traits) are stated but unexplained — a mechanism that forms before behavior makes filtering visible rollouts structurally too late, which would be the first mechanistic explanation of filter failure. It is feasible solo (LoRA, released SAEs, inference-only patching, small models), it converts directly into a deployable training-time misalignment monitor, and its main risk is manageable: SAE drift under fine-tuning is handled by freezing the base-model dictionary, monitoring reconstruction fidelity, and causally validating a handful of tracked features via steering (#10, #32) — while the "redundancy grows over training?" question naturally imports the ablation-failure study (#58, #29) as phase two.

direction: Mechanistic early warning for emergent misalignment — densely tracking SAE persona-feature dynamics across fine-tuning checkpoints to test whether misalignment is internally visible and causally potent before it becomes behaviorally visible.
project: Precursor: Internal Early-Warning Signals for Emergent Misalignment During Fine-Tuning
question: Do the "misaligned persona" feature directions identified in endpoint studies become detectably active — and causally potent under steering — before the behavioral onset of emergent misalignment, and do their trajectories generalize as a reliable, dataset-agnostic training-time monitor?
